en: With his own commentary composed by Harivṛṣabha, and [further] by the commentary composed by Śrī Raghunāthaśarman.
This work is accompanied by the commentary of Ambākartrī:
"The beginningless and endless Brahman is the Word-principle (śabdatattva), which is imperishable; it manifests in the form of objects, from which proceeds the evolution of the world. (1)

The reality that transcends all conceptual constructions, which is entered by all powers through the transcendence of both difference and conjunction, and which is non-differentiated despite having the form of the distinction between knowledge and ignorance—this Brahman, which is without beginning or end and is not dependent upon any state, is asserted [as such] by those who follow conventional discourse through the practice of perceiving temporal distinctions and the contemplation of the differentiation of forms, [and yet remains untouched] by merit and demerit.

For in all philosophical systems, no prior or subsequent limits of activity or cessation can be enumerated for the single Brahman, which consists of cause and effect and is both differentiated and non-differentiated. Nor is any limitation admitted anywhere for its parts, whether they be transformations of form above, below, or across. Yet, because even those modifications regarded as having distinct forms are continuous with their primordial source (*prakṛti*), and because it is grasped by words and causes words to be grasped, it is designated as the "Reality of Sound" (*śabdatattva*).

For it is by means of sound (*śabda*) that the distinctions of persistence, activity, and cessation are produced. And because it is the cause of the syllable (*akṣara*), it is called the "syllable. It is for the purpose of awakening another that the manifestation of that which is inwardly situated within immediate consciousness (*pratyak-caitanya*) flows forth. Thus it is said:

"Some know this single Speech—which is subtle, whose essence is undifferentiated from its object, and which does not flow forth—as if it were something other, appearing in manifold forms while established within the self. (RV 8.100.11)

It evolves into the form of objects. Vivarta is the assumption by that which is single and undeviating from its true nature of unreal, distinct, and other forms, through the imitation of difference—like the appearance of objects in a dream.

And it has been said: "The evolution of form and action is merely the operation of the power of ignorance (avidyā); these two are indescribable in relation to the conscious self (vidyātman) as being either identical to or different from it. For this indeed is the 'ignorance-ness' of ignorance."

From that very Brahman, known as Śabda (the Word), from which the evolution of the universe proceeds—once all modifications have subsided, at the time of reabsorption (*saṃvarta*), being formless, prior to its manifestation as the knot of modifications, and thus indefinable—the modifications called the "universe" are evolved.
For it has been said:
"He who does not abide even in the appearance of any conceptual constructions..."
It has been conceptualized in many ways through reasoning, scripture, and inference.
Having transcended difference and union, existence and non-existence, succession and simultaneity,
as well as truth and falsehood, the Self of the universe shines forth through discernment.
He is the inner controller of all beings, perceived both near and far;
utterly liberated, he is worshipped by those seeking liberation for the sake of final release.
He brings about even those transformations that have reached the state of primordial nature (prakṛti),
just as the summer sun [dissolves] the vast masses of clouds at the end of the rainy season.
Even that single consciousness is divided in many ways,
like water from the ocean appearing as sparks in a forest fire.
Therefore, from that which abides in the genus and the form, the changing collections of individuals arise,
just as rain-bearing clouds are produced from the wind.
That supreme light manifests in the form of the triple Veda,
appearing as the basis for diverse perspectives within the various traditions of different schools.
That portion which consists of the nature of tranquil knowledge is, indeed, as if perpetually seized by that ignorance,
which cannot be described.
There is no measure for its revolutions in every direction;
that which has acquired its formative impressions does not abide within itself.
Just as a person afflicted by cataracts perceives the pure sky as if it were filled with various diverse forms, so too does one falsely imagine [the mind].
In the same way, this immortal Brahman, though changeless, appears to undergo transformation into the form of duality, as if it had attained impurity through ignorance.
This Brahman is the emanation of sound, bound by the power of sound;
having unfolded from the subtle measures of sound (*mātrā*), it dissolves back into those very same measures.
That which is traditionally taught as one alone appears divided by virtue of its dependence on powers;
though not distinct from its powers, it exists as if it were distinct from them.

It is taught that everything—whether in the form of unity or diversity, and encompassing both the modifications and the modified—is never beyond the unity of its primordial nature (*prakṛti*). For example: "In the beginning, there was only the Seer, one without a second, alone"; likewise: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second. Again it says: "The *praṇava* alone divided itself threefold. And similarly: "In the beginning, this was indeed non-being (*asat*). What was that non-being? Those *ṛṣis* were indeed that non-being in the beginning; those *ṛṣis* are the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*)."

The differentiation [of powers] arises from their dependence upon [the one] power. Within the Brahman that is the essence of speech (*śabdatattva*), there exist powers that are non-contradictory, unified, and constitutive of its very self, despite the fact of its unity. For example, within a single perception which consists merely in the manifestation of distinct objects, there appear the forms of objects such as "earth" and "world. Indeed, the apprehension of forms such as trees, which reside in the object of knowledge, is not contradicted by the unity of cognition. There is no essential difference between that [cognition] and its forms, because they do not transcend the single reality of cognition.
Thus, there is non-separateness among all powers, even though they appear to one another as distinct.

Regarding "even in their non-separateness from the powers": indeed, there are no powers whatsoever belonging to Brahman that exist as separate entities, like the conventional distinction between a genus (*jāti*) and an individual (*vyakti*). Rather, although they are identical with it—just as light is identical with its objects of illumination—they are nevertheless perceived as if they were separate realities, appearing external to the grasp of the objects of illumination, as if they were mere attributes of the Self.
[Those] who have resorted to His power of Time, upon which various parts have been superposed...
The six transformations, beginning with birth, are the sources of the differentiation of existence.

For all powers that possess birth and are dependent on others are pervaded by the sovereignty known as Time (kāla); thus they follow the operation of the power of Time. Consequently, in every entity, the appearance of the manifoldness of form is observed to assume a sequential character through the limitation of its powers by means of obstruction and permission. Indeed, for all transformations—even those that depend on other causes—Time is the auxiliary cause by virtue of its permission regarding obstruction and birth.

The power of agency belonging to that [Being], being divided by means of its sequentially occurring forms as *mātrās*, superimposes upon it a form of differentiation residing in the *mātrās* of modification—just as a line on a scale-beam marks the point where the weight of another substance joined to it is counteracted. When there arises the conceptual construction of the temporal sequence of priority and posteriority for an entity that is itself neither prior nor posterior, the six modifications such as birth (*janman*) emerge as the sources of the transformations of existence (*sattā*). However, in the section on the enumeration of universals (*jāti*), these modifications of being will be explained in detail within the classification of existence. 3.1.26.
Of that single seed of all, there is this manifold existence in the form of the enjoyer, the object of enjoyment, and the act of enjoyment itself. || 4 ||

For from the one Brahman—which cannot be defined as either identical to or different from [itself], nor as existent or non-existent, and which is embraced by non-contradictory powers and possesses unreal divisions—there evolve, like the objects of a dream-consciousness person, various external realities consisting of the knots of the enjoyer, the enjoyed, and the enjoyment, which are mutually distinct. And for that [Brahman], once it has transcended the state of being other than those knots and has severed the knots of its own manifestation, this manifold worldly order of linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) is established.
4. The Veda is the means of attaining that [Brahman] and its imitation, [revealed] by the great seers (*maharṣi*).
Though it is one, it is traditionally taught as if having many paths, each distinct from the other.

(5) The attainment of Brahman is, according to some, merely the complete transcendence of the knot of egoism (*ahaṅkāra*) in the form of "I" and "mine. Others say it is the return of the modifications (*vikāra*) to their primal state (*prakṛti*). Other alternative views of attainment include: the state of being devoid of constituent elements (*vaikaraṇya*); contentment without means; the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*), which is the desire for nothing but the Self and the absence of adventitious objects; the possession of perfect powers; and the non-involvement of the functions of time within the measures of the Self alone, which is the absolute selflessness (*nairātmya*) of all things through the universal Self. These are the various conceptions of attainment.

The means of attainment is the mass of Brahman (*brahmarāśi*). For example, the means for worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) consists of charity, austerity, celibacy, and so forth. Thus it is said: "From the study of the Vedas, there arises a supreme, internal, white, and undecaying light; when this shoreless darkness has vanished, that light manifests. Regarding "imitation" (*anukāra*): that subtle, eternal, and supersensuous speech which the seers (*ṛṣis*)—who have directly realized *dharma* and are seers of mantras—behold, they hand down as *bilma* (instruction) to others who have not directly realized *dharma*, intending to communicate it just as one recounts a dream-event, desiring to relate what has been seen, heard, or experienced. This is the ancient tradition (*purākalpa*).

It is indeed said: "The seers were those who had directly realized the Dharma; they transmitted the mantras by oral instruction to others who had not directly realized the Dharma. Others, weary of oral instruction, committed this book—the Veda and the Vedāṅgas—to memory for the purpose of grasping the *bilma*. *Bilma* means either *bhilma* or *bhāsana* (illumination). Thus, the Veda, though one, was [divided] by the great seers into many paths.

This single object of perception, which is the Veda, abides within the nature of vision; yet, because it is impossible for the great seers to demonstrate non-difference through differentiation, they brought it into the form of speech—which possesses a sequential order based on its manifestation—and divided its path into the sections of *saṃhitā*, *pada*, and *krama* without overstepping its unity. Thus, for the purpose of study, they chanted it while establishing the designations of the various *caraṇas* (schools) among students.

Another says: Just as speech, though divided by difference of region despite having no difference in its own nature, does not transcend its dependence on a single denotable object, and that very speech is the cause for the determination of the conceptualization of differences such as region; likewise, even when there is a difference in *caraṇas* (Vedic schools), the Vedic sentences do not transcend their dependence on a single meaning. It is precisely the difference in their own form (*svarūpa*) that is the cause for the determination of the conceptualization of the difference between *caraṇas*.

Others think as follows: "Just as the eight-limbed Ayurveda existed as a single whole in a former age, yet in the Kali age it is seen with its limbs divided due to the deficiency of men's capacity; so too this Veda, which is a mass of Brahman, possesses an infinite variety of paths and powers. (5)

The multiplicity of paths among the divisions, the fact that ritual actions are subordinate to a single [central] purpose, and the fact that words possess their respective capacities— all this is observed within its branches.

In that regard, when divided fourfold, there are one hundred branches of the *Adhvaryu* (Yajurveda); the *Sāmaveda* has a thousand paths; the *Bāhvṛcya* (Ṛgveda) is twenty-onefold, though some say fifteenfold; and the *Atharvaṇa* Veda is ninefold—thus, within each division, there are many paths. Yet, the ritual action (*karman*) is unified as a single whole, with all branches serving as its constituent parts (*aṅga*). The ritual act is one, being recognized through all the branches.

For example: medical treatment is one, yet it is based upon all the branches [of medicine]. Likewise, words possess their respective potencies; this is because they have the capacity to convey meaning and because they are the cause of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*). This [potency] is observed within the various branches [of the Veda], as in the rules: "The word *deva* and *sumna* [take the acute accent on the final syllable] in the *Yajus* of the *Kāṭhaka*" and "In the *Atharvaṇa*, the final syllable of *sima* is acute.

However, for those who hold the tradition that this division of branches occurs repeatedly through interruption, their view is that prior to such division, there was no deviation from the rule, as speech existed with its sequence unified. (6)
The Smṛtis are of many forms and serve both visible and invisible purposes; they were formulated by those learned in the Vedas based on that very [Veda] through its various indicative marks.

Among these, some traditions (*smṛtis*) are based on verbal authority, while others are not based on verbal authority but are established as customary practices among the learned (*śiṣṭas*). Some have visible purposes, such as those concerning medical treatment and the like. Others have invisible purposes, concerning what may or may not be eaten, who may or may not be approached sexually, and what may or may not be spoken. When there is a conflict regarding an equal subject matter and no visible purpose is present, they are to be treated as optional alternatives (*vikalpa*). However, in the case of a disagreement among the learned, those [traditions] for which a visible purpose exists possess authority.
But when there is no transgression, even if a visible purpose is possible, there is indeed an option; for example, regarding the expiation for killing a frog.

"Relying on that very [scripture], from the indicative marks (*liṅga*)," it is said. Indicative marks are based upon scripture; they reveal the commonality of the agent for those actions prescribed by scripture as well as those prescribed by tradition (*smṛti*). For those who possess the qualification (*adhikāra*) for actions prescribed by scripture whose purposes are perceived, they are designated by scripture itself as the agents of actions prescribed by tradition as well. For example: "The sacrificer (*yajamāna*) should cook a large goat or a large ox for a guest who has arrived."

And since in some instances signs [of Vedic origin] regarding the subject matter have been observed, this is sufficient for establishing the authority of Smṛti, provided it does not contradict the meaning of Śruti, according to the principle of "the grain from the cooking-pot" (sthālīpulāka). || 7 ||

The various doctrines of those who maintain monism and dualism are considered to be manyfold; they are of the nature of explanatory fictions (arthavāda), certain only within the scope of one's own conceptual constructions.
Vedic sentences consisting of various types of explanatory passages (arthavāda) and non-explanatory passages (anarthavāda) are generally seen to follow the patterns of human compositions.

Furthermore, various conflicting doctrines arise from the conceptual constructions of human intellect. For example, the statement, "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent," is an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise) intended for the glorification of the site for the piling of the sacrificial fire-altar (*agni-cayana*). Based on such a mental construction of its form, there arises this extremist doctrine: "From the non-existent, from the non-being, from the inactive, from the trackless, from the trackless, from the ineffable, from the ineffable, from the substanceless, from the substanceless, the existent is born. However, a single Self is differentiated by means of the prior and posterior states of existence and non-existence.

In that non-dual state, how indeed could there be the distinction between the named and the nameless? Likewise: "Neither non-existence nor existence existed; in the beginning, this was indeed only darkness.
This is neither foam nor any bubble, nor anything at all;
alas, this is Māyā, difficult to cross—thus the wise man perceives it.
A blind man found a jewel; one without fingers strung it;
one without a neck fastened it; and one without a tongue praised it.
Likewise, the statement "In the beginning, this was indeed water" is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) concerning the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice.

From that arises this traditional teaching: "The essence (*rasa*) of the waters is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which consists of both the ripening of the form of consciousness and the ripening of the form of non-manifestation; it is indeed both the whirlpool and the non-whirlpool. Thus, that single form, which is the form of all awakening, abides in the state of being the form of all differentiation.
Even the dualists say: "The sources of the measures (*mātrāyonayaḥ*) are both eternal and non-eternal; within them, this world—both formed and formless, subtle and gross—is suspended. And likewise:
Two companions, inseparable and fair-winged, embrace the same tree;
of these two, one eats the sweet fruit, while the other looks on without eating.
"The collection of senses, the inner controller, the intellect, and the knower of the field.
Now others say: "Consciousness is both manifest and unmanifest, manifold and singular.
"It moves; it does not move. It is far, and it is near."
It is within all this, and it is also outside of all this. Thus [ends the verse]. 8.
Therein, purity is said to be truth, which is knowledge alone as the single path of scripture;
it is joined with the form of the *praṇava* and is non-contradictory to all doctrines.

And because these various conceptualizations of the perceivers arise with respect to a single reality that transcends all conceptualization due to its possession of all powers, for this very reason—indeed, in this very case—the conceptualization regarding Brahman, who possesses all forms, does not differ from other conceptualizations that are held to be of contradictory forms.
Furthermore, the knowers of Brahman say: "Even a single portion of Brahman does not transcend his possession of all forms, and it is free from conceptualization."

Likewise: "In this regard, this internal Person (puruṣa) conceives of every vision as being non-deficient and free from conceptual construction (avikalpa), even though it appears as if possessed of conceptual construction. Here, the Praṇava is the object of universal permission; it is the form of all the Vedas, the common noun for all primordial nature (prakṛti), the source of the arising and setting of all visions, and the receiver of all contradictory meanings. In every way, it grants permission regarding this Brahman, and in every way, it prohibits it. Yet, its essential mode of operation does not fluctuate between prohibition and permission.
As they have said: "It is both one and not one; likewise both, and yet neither both nor neither."
"Those established in their duties may speak with partiality, but those established in virtue are impartial. || 9 ||
The various branches of knowledge, which serve as the causes for the refinement of wisdom, spread forth from that Creator as the primary and secondary constituents of the worlds. (10)

The Veda, indeed, as the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and as the form of the instructor, is the ordainer of both the manifestations (*vivarta*) and the established orders (*vyavasthā*) of the worlds.

Some maintain that the *praṇava* alone is the Veda, for it is the primordial nature of all words and their meanings. And according to this view, the various branches of knowledge (*vidyābheda*), by virtue of having the *praṇava* as their essence, do not transcend the true nature of the Veda. Thus they say: "All speech has entered into the Veda," and "One who does not know the Veda understands nothing of Brahman."

Likewise, it is said: "The Veda consists of injunctions (*vidhi*), that which is to be enjoined (*vidheya*), and reasoning (*tarka*). From the primary and secondary limbs of the *praṇava*, as well as from the Vedas, the Smṛtis, the Upaniṣads (*trayyantādi*), and so forth, various branches of knowledge (*vidyābheda*) arise; these are the causes of right knowledge and the causes of the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the person. Alternatively, because the person is essentially knowledge, they are the causes of the person's own refinement. Among the well-known limbs of the Brahman known as the Veda—such as astronomy (*jyotiṣa*) and the rest—branches of knowledge such as the science of omens (*śakunajñāna*) arise; and from its secondary limbs, branches of knowledge such as the knowledge of dream-interpretation and the science of origins (*yonijñāna*) are well-established in the world. (10)
The wise say that grammar is the nearest approach to that Brahman, the highest of all ascetic practices, and the first limb among the Vedic meters.

For the refinement of the nature of that Śabdabrahman is for the purpose of attaining correctness; therefore, that which is proximate (*āsanna*) is directly beneficial. Indeed, proximity is defined by the production of a specific benefit. Furthermore, another Vedic recension (*āmnāyāntara*) is subject to inference. Once it is established by the principle that "this is to be inferred" and "this is not to be inferred," grammar serves as the basis for the correct modification of gender, number, and so forth. Because it is the cause for the comprehension of other Vedic recensions, it is designated as "proximate."

This is the highest austerity among all austerities. Among those things known in the world as austerity—such as celibacy, sleeping on the ground, living in water, the Cāndrāyaṇa fast, and so forth—as well as the most purifying Vedic studies, this [study] is the most renowned austerity because it is the cause of both visible and invisible specific fruits.

That collection of phonemes (*akṣarasamāmnāya*) through the mere knowledge of which the attainment of the merit of all the Vedas is remembered by tradition—that is the first auxiliary limb (*aṅga*) of the Vedic hymns, because of its preeminence. For thus it is said: "Among the six auxiliary limbs, grammar is the preeminent one; and effort applied to what is preeminent becomes fruitful. || 11 ||
This is the direct path to that most meritorious light, which is the supreme essence of speech once it has attained its full manifestation.

From the undivided *śabdatattva* (the reality of speech), which exists within as a withdrawn sequence, there arises the division of forms characterized by phonemes (*varṇa*), words (*pada*), and sentences (*vākya*)—this being the speech that has acquired its distinctions through differences in place of articulation (*sthāna*) and so forth; or it is the speech that has acquired the apprehension of divisions such as "cow" and so on as objects of denotation (*abhidheya*) through an eternal connection with meaning. Alternatively, the divisions of speech itself persist in the form of "cow" and so on. And these divisions, such as "cow" and so on, which appear as if they were external objects, again transform into the nature of audible sound (*śruti*).
Likewise, some consider the relationship between word and meaning to be precisely that of cause and effect. For thus it is said:
"This very name has manifested as form, and this form has subsisted in the state of being a name;
some have divided that which was originally one and undivided, while others speak of it as having a differentiated form from the very beginning."

Regarding the phrase "the supreme essence": the collection of words whose status as correct (sādhu) is established is designated as such because it possesses denotative power and is a cause for spiritual elevation. For thus it has been said: "That word which is devoid of refinement is but the dregs of speech."

That which is the most meritorious light: here, there are three lights, three illuminations, which manifest both one's own nature and the nature of others. They are as follows: "This Jātavedas (the fire), that internal illumination within persons, and that illumination called 'Sound' which illuminates both the illuminated and the unilluminated—in these, everything is contained, as much as exists, whether stationary or moving. This is the direct path to that [light].

For the definition, characterized by both general and specific features, serves as the means for the swift comprehension of the entire *Śabdabrahman* through its definitions and detailed expansions. Furthermore, in the absence of direct instruction, there is inference from the usage of the *śiṣṭas* (the refined), who have attained a firm footing in the *Śabdabrahman*—which is free from corruption and possesses the necessary linguistic refinement. And based on the knowledge of those *śiṣṭas*, grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) serves as the means for establishing the correctness of words such as *pṛṣodara* and others, because they are employed by the *śiṣṭas*. Thus it has been said:
"The true nature of the causes of the relationship between word and meaning, as well as the distinction between correct and incorrect forms even when the expressed sense is identical."
And he who does not know grammar does not know the refined speakers (śiṣṭas), whose existence is inferred from the correct usage [of words]. 12.
Words alone are the foundation for the reality of the application of meanings;
the comprehension of the true nature of words does not exist apart from grammar. (13)

The reality of the operation of an object consists in the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*), and not in its existence or non-existence as an objective entity. For intention is that which brings about the employment of a suitable word. Indeed, a speaker employs a suitable word for each respective object among those meanings brought into proximity by the intention. Just as one desiring to perceive applies only a suitable sense-organ toward each respective object for the sake of perception.

Another says: In the engagement with an object, that which is the cause of its reality in conventional usage is the basis; for when a cognition arises in the form of the cause itself toward objects by means of that cause—possessing the nature of the cause—it is then possible to engage with the object through that [cognition]. However, no conventional usage exists whose object is isolation (*kaivalya*) through the discrimination of other associated forms. Thus, since names attain their own form within universals (*jāti*), it is maintained that the universal is the basis for verbal expression.

Alternatively, in the context of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), the reality (*tattva*) is relation (*saṃsarga*). When objects appear as if they were entirely interconnected, even though their forms are distinct, linguistic usage is based upon sentences. Indeed, when the perception of relation ceases, no linguistic usage regarding any object whatsoever can be established. Another meaning is this: a mere thing (*vastu*) is simply the objective domain of words such as *tat* (that) and so forth, which have things as their defining characteristic. The reality of its engagement [in language] is relation. For only when related is a thing employed in actions as a subordinate factor (*guṇabhāva*).

Alternatively, activity (*pravṛtti*)—consisting of actions such as birth and so forth—is based on verbal forms (*ākhyātapada*). Of this [activity] which is designated as "activity," its essence consists in being something to be accomplished (*sādhyatva*), the requirement for means of accomplishment, the assumption of a sequential form, and being the cause for the manifestation of time.
The other meaning, however, is mere existence (*sattvamātra*); established by its own nature across all three times, it has its sequential form dissolved and is based on nominal forms (*nāmapada*).

Alternatively, what is the essence of the activity of an object? It is the form of the object itself, consisting of a cognition that is projected onto external things, and that [form] is based on words.

The realization of the reality of words consists in the reality of the word itself, which is its integrity; it is the correct form (*sādhu-svarūpa*) whose grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) has not departed. For that is its complete form. Others, however, being employed with the desire to use that [correct form], may be deficient and thus become corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*). || 13 ||
That [Veda] shines forth as the gateway to liberation, the remedy for the impurities of speech, the purifier of all sciences, and the science that transcends all others. 14.

For one who knows the reality of the non-difference of the nature of sound preceded by [the knowledge of] sound, through the withdrawal of the sequence, one attains yoga. And by the correct usage [of words], having manifested specific qualities and merging with the Great Self of Sound (*śabdātman*), one attains oneness (*vaikaraṇya*). Having reached that undisturbed state of speech, one returns to the creative intuition (*pratibhā*), which is the source of the transformations of speech. And from that supreme source called *pratibhā*, which consists merely of the excellence of existence and which projects the practice of the cultivation of yoga preceded by sound, one attains the supreme primordial nature (*prakṛti*), in which all traces of transformation have subsided.

This is the medical treatment for the impurities of speech, just as Āyurveda is for the physical humors (*doṣas*). For one who knows grammar does not employ corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśas*) which are causes of transgression; "knowledge indeed is his refuge," so it has been said. And it is further stated:
"That which is studied without being understood is merely recited like a chant;
like dry fuel in a place without fire, it never blazes forth."
Likewise, this verse sung by the vigilant [Patañjali]: "Water is the supreme purifier on earth, and the mantras are the supreme purifier of water;
and of those [mantras] consisting of the Sāma, Ṛg, and Yajur Vedas, the great seers have declared grammar to be the purifier."
He speaks with courtesy; for almost everyone follows the rules of grammar in their own field of knowledge and is inevitably ashamed when employing corrupt speech. || 14 ||
Just as all classes of real entities are based upon words and forms, so too in the world this science is the ultimate resort of all sciences. (15)
This is the first station for those ascending the steps of spiritual attainment;
this is that straight royal road for those seeking liberation.
Here, one who has transcended all error perceives the Self alone—
the source of the meters, consisting of the meters, as the body of the meters.
That which is the supreme form of speech, in which all distinctions have subsided, and which as a pure light unfolds even within this very darkness; || 18 ||
They have transcended the perception of forms and activities;
having passed beyond light and darkness, they worship that which is pure illumination.
In that state, the causes of speech appear like signs for the recollection of syllables,
manifesting through a process preceded by sound like reflections.
In which [Veda] the various syllables of the Atharvans, the Aṅgirases, the Sāmans, and the Ṛk and Yajus are established separately, each maintaining its own distinct position. || 21 ||
When that which is one is divided manifoldly through various methods of analysis, it is by resorting to grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) that the supreme Brahman is realized. (22)
In that regard, the eternal relationship between word and meaning has been proclaimed by the great seers who were the authors of the Sūtras, along with their Anutantras, and the Bhāṣyas. (23)

"The word is eternal, the meaning is eternal, and the relationship is eternal"—this is the established doctrine of the treatise (*śāstra*). For in that context, by the term "word" (*śabda*), the word-form (*śabdakṛti*) is denoted. Thus he says: "The word is eternal because its form (*ākṛti*) is eternal. And this treatise is governed by the form; for he says, "It is established through the instruction regarding the form. Furthermore, this form is distinct from the specific universal (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*) of "word-ness" (*śabdatva*).
For "word-ness" possesses a non-contradictory co-inherence in a single object with all the forms (*ākṛti*) which possess contradictory co-inherence in a single object.

For specific word-forms (*śabdākṛtiviśeṣa*), such as "tree-word-ness" (*vṛkṣaśabdatva*) and so on, when there is a confusion regarding the actual object, appear as if they have acquired a form similar to their cause and are designated as "manifested words.

Just as in the case of a jar there is a non-contradictory inherence (*samavāya*) of [universals] such as substance-ness (*dravyatva*), earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*), and jar-ness (*ghaṭatva*), so too in the word "tree" there is a non-contradictory inherence of specific word-forms such as quality-ness (*guṇatva*), word-ness (*śabdatva*), and tree-word-ness (*vṛkṣaśabdatva*).

Now, in the case of objects such as jars whose constituent parts are stable, the whole (avayavin) serves as the cause for the manifestation of universals and particulars. However, the specific manifestations of sound consist of parts that are unstable. Since these parts do not arise simultaneously, are not co-existent, are not perceived as having a fixed form, and lack multiple inherent causes (samavāyikāraṇa), it is impossible for them to produce another distinct sound in which a collection of specific forms could inhere. Rather, the universal "soundness" (śabdatva) is fully present in each individual part.

Likewise, if it is asserted that the specific form (ākṛti) is fully present in each individual part, then upon the utterance of a mere part—such as the letter *va* and so on within the word "tree" (*vṛkṣa*)—there would result the apprehension of the specific form of the word "tree," even when those parts are uttered in isolation. This is not a fault, for it is just as with specific actions such as lifting, rotating, or throwing away, which arise and perish; no other action corresponding to a whole is commenced by those constituent parts.
Nor is it maintained that there is no inherence of specific universals such as "throwing upwards" (*utkṣepaṇatva*) apart from the universal of "action" (*karmatva*).

Furthermore, upon seeing merely the parts of an action, cognitions do not arise that apprehend the forms of specific actions such as "revolving" (*bhramaṇa*). For those constituent parts, though caused by specific efforts and serving as the substrata for "throwing upwards" and so forth in each individual part, do not produce a cognition directed toward a specific universal because the particularity [of the whole action] is difficult to discern.
For even though that cognition is distinguished, it cannot be employed in practical discourse because it does not grasp the specific particulars of its manifesting adjuncts (*upavyañjana*).

However, when a continuous series of actions—whose effects are conjunctions and disjunctions delimited by specific spatial boundaries—is perceived in succession, then linguistic conventions associated with the adjunct of specific universals (*jāti*) become possible.

Likewise, even in the case of words such as "vṛkṣa" (tree), although specific phonemes like the letter *va*—produced by particular efforts and possessing subtle distinctions that are difficult to discern—manifest the specific universals (*jāti*) of the word in each constituent part, nevertheless, it is impossible to engage in linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) by means of those word-forms (*śabdākṛti*) when their numerous specific manifestors (*upavyañjana*) have not been grasped.
However, once the succession of parts has been perceived in its proper order, then linguistic usages, conditioned by the specific universals, become established.

Furthermore, the process of the manifestation of universals (*jāti*) observed in other treatises is not necessarily accepted by grammarians. For it is not the case that the manifestation of things possessing manifestation is invariably effected only when they are supported by manifestors. In that regard, even though there is no inherence of the word's individuality (*śabdavyakti*), the form (*ākṛti*) is determined by the final cognition once the internal organ has been refined; this occurs through cognitions arising in succession, which—having acquired impressions from the apprehension of the phonemes and their parts—either previously failed to grasp or grasped [the form] indistinctly.

The existence of that word-form (śabdakṛti), however, is inferred from the non-difference in cognition—expressed as "this is that very same [word]"—with respect to specific individual instances of words such as "tree" when uttered by parrots, starlings, humans, and so forth.
Even those who do not accept this usage of the word "form" (ākṛti) nevertheless maintain that the eternal individual word (śabdavyakti) itself is manifested by multiple sounds.
Regarding the individual word, some, however, accept a difference in the phonemes (varṇa).
Some, however, maintain that for every letter, every word, and every sentence, there is only one single essence of sound (*śabdātman*) which manifests as an appearance of parts arising in succession.

Others say: "Because their usage is eternal due to an uninterrupted tradition and continuous activity, and because they do not possess a first instance of production when uttered by speakers, words are eternal."

Some maintain that even objects (*artha*) are eternal precisely because their forms (*ākṛti*) are eternal. Thus it is said: "In reference to which category of entity is this analysis (*vigraha*) appropriate? [The answer is: 'In respect to the word, the object, and the relationship, once they are established. He says: 'In respect to the form (*ākṛti*). Within this passage of the *Bhāṣya*, as many positions as are presented, the eternity of the object is explained in various ways; that should be understood according to the *Bhāṣya*.

Regarding the claim that the relationship is eternal: when there is the state of "thisness" (*idambhāva*) between word and object, the relationship expressed as "this is that" (*so 'yam*) is innate (*autpattika*), established by its own nature. Because it is impossible for anyone to designate an object [for the first time], this relationship was not previously unknown to any perceiver and was not created by any agent for the sake of some particular perceiver for the very first time. Therefore, the relationship between word and object is beginningless, eternal, and characterized by an uninterrupted continuity.

Alternatively, the relationship between word and object is a fitness (*yogyatā*) conditioned by convention (*samaya*), existing in the form of a manifestor and the manifested, just like the relationship between a sense organ and its object.

Alternatively, when it is accepted that cognitions which manifest as having the form of an object are projected onto external objects—just as there is a conceptualization of letters based on non-literal signs—and that they share a single objective domain, then the relationship between word and meaning is a connection consisting of a causal sequence that is eternal and uninterrupted. For it has been said: "For those [cognitions] also, from their arising until their destruction, while explaining the cognitions, reveal the existing objects of cognition."

In this regard, it has been declared by the great seers (*maharṣis*), the authors of the *sūtras* and other works. It is precisely those who are the authors of the *sūtras* and so forth who are designated [as such]. In that context, from the very commencement of the *sūtras*, the eternity (*nityatva*) of words is intended. For if words and the like were non-eternal, there would be no purpose whatsoever in the undertaking of the treatise (*śāstra*). Indeed, this [treatise] would be a mere worldly convention and useless; the great refined ones (*śiṣṭas*) ought not to follow what is fruitless.
Therefore, the traditional scripture (*smṛti-śāstra*) has been set forth with respect to words whose correctness (*sādhutva*) has been determined.

Others, however, support the doctrine of non-eternality through such sūtras as "That [suffix] need not be taught, because the conventional usage is the authority. Furthermore, in other systems, there are statements such as: "The relationship between word and meaning is established," "But it is established because words are eternal," "Sphoṭa is the word; sound (dhvani) arises as its manifestation," and "All [sounds] are substitutes for all words," and so forth.

Indeed, it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "In the *Saṃgraha*, this has been primarily examined [under the heading]: 'Sound is eternal. It is also stated in the *Anutantrabhāṣya*: "The letters must be eternal, immutable, and unchanging," and so forth. Likewise, regarding conventional eternity (*vyāvahārika-nityatva*), there are examples such as: "The *khadira* and *barbura* trees have fine leaves and pale trunks; among them, the *khadira* is thorny"; or "To the east of the village are mango trees"; or "The *nyagrodha* trees are milky, possess aerial roots, and have broad leaves."

Alternatively, those very same authoritative persons (śiṣṭa) by whom the Sūtras, Anutantras, and Bhāṣyas were composed regarding the directly perceived Dharma in various parts of the sacred teaching (pravacana), have likewise declared in the field of grammar that the relationship between word and meaning is eternal; and their authority is firmly established in the world. || 23 ||

Those items which are the results of analytical extraction (*apoddhāra*), those meanings which possess established characteristics (*sthitalakṣaṇa*), those words which are to be explained (*anvākhyeya*), and also those which are expressive (*pratipādaka*). || 24 ||
The relations that exist among grammatically correct and incorrect words—whether as cause and effect, as suitability, or as a factor in the cognition of dharma—are the *sambandhas*. (25)
They have been described in this treatise through both their characteristic marks and their own specific terms;
however, only some of them are here followed for the sake of the Smṛti, in accordance with tradition. (26)
In all three of these verses, there is the conclusion of the subject under discussion.

Therein, the meaning of the extracted term (*apoddhārapada-artha*) is one that is absolutely commingled; yet, through its connection with that which is to be inferred, it is conceptually isolated by means of a constructed form once the distinction from the primary context has been made. For the nature of that entity, when thus isolated, transcends conventional linguistic usage.

That [nature], however, is generally established through imaginative intuition (*utprekṣā*), by following one's own cognition in accordance with tradition, and by the power of the repeated practice of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

In the same way, within the undivided essence of the word, for the sake of grammatical operation (*kārya*), one resorts to the denotative status of words extracted from the whole through the method of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) by means of the conceptual construction of a common form. This very "extracted meaning" (*apoddhāra-padārtha*) follows the linguistic usage of the treatise (*śāstra*), as well as worldly usage of differentiation which resembles that of the treatise. And this, being based on a single word, is indescribable in terms of its reality or unreality; for when the verb is not supplied—as in the cases of *vṛkṣaḥ* and *plakṣaḥ*—there is no determination of the meanings of the nominal suffixes (*upagraha*) in their own nature.

As long as specific actions, which serve as the basis for negation, do not remove existence—which is the cause for the application of words—so long is the verb *asti* (is), followed by the present participle suffix (*bhavantī*) and in the third person, understood even when not explicitly employed, being implied by words such as "tree.
And these [utterances], having the form of a single word with an implied verbal action, are explained as sentences.

Likewise, although the meaning of a single word may have an indefinite limit, it is analyzed in various ways by some as being divided into many parts—such as the meaning of the prior member (*pūrvapadārtha*), the meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapadārtha*), the meaning of another member (*anyapadārtha*), the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*), the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), and the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*)—and is extracted in some manner from it.

The nature of the *syat* (potential mood) is as follows: it assumes the form of a sentence, its division into subject and predicate (*uddeśa-vibhāga*) is conceptualized, and it is a single, qualified action-essence (*kriyātman*) to be conveyed by means of the apprehension of word-meanings that are not [actually] severed. Even when there is a perception of separation, it remains undifferentiated at the time of the synthesis of the mental image (*pratibhopasaṃhārakāla*), as seen in such expressions as "he bows," "he fights," "he shaves," "he pounds," or "he chews. As it has been said: "Or rather, because the word is used for the sake of the meaning of the whole. In this context, the word is taken as having its action synthesized; or else, only the continuity of the cognition (*saṃpratyaya-anugama*) is grasped.

For, having accepted the application [of suffixes] to the meaning of a word, he says again: "Indeed, it is that which ends in *kṛt* or *taddhita* suffixes which possesses meaning, not the *kṛt* and *taddhita* suffixes alone."

Furthermore, regarding those words that are to be grammatically explained (*anvākhyeya*), for some the explanation is delimited by the word (*pada*), while for others it is delimited by the sentence (*vākya*). In the case where the explanation is delimited by the word, because there is no distinction in the heard form (*śruti*), once a single word-form is apprehended, the words—having received their grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) based on the universal (*sāmānya*) alone—would proceed by taking up that internal refinement acquired at the level of the universal, even when they encounter specific meanings (*viśeṣa*) that arise upon reaching a connection with other words.

In that case, the word *śukla* (white), being singular in number and neuter in gender, would be heard as connected to substrata (*āśraya*) that possess different genders and numbers. To prevent this, by means of the rule "and [the gender and number] of qualifiers, except for a genus" (*viśeṣaṇānāṃ cājāteḥ*), the gender and number of words denoting qualities (*guṇavacana*) follow those of their substrata, even when the future substratum is external and not yet commenced. However, if the grammatical derivation (*anvākhyāna*) is restricted to the sentence (*vākya*), then because a quality that is eternally associated [with a substance] is absolutely inseparable from its specific substratum, there is no such thing as a general meaning (*sāmānyārthatva*) once all [particulars] have been excluded.

In this regard, it has been stated: "This is inherent. Likewise, when performing the grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) of each individual member as a *dvandva* compound, the rule "there is an elision (*luk*) [of the suffix] when there are not many members in a *dvandva*" is introduced. However, in the context of refining the whole compound, he says: "Or rather, it is not so, because all [members] have a plural meaning in a *dvandva*. Similarly, rules such as "an adjective [is compounded] with a substantive frequently" and "objects of comparison [are compounded] with words expressing the common property" are all accepted only within an explanatory system that takes the word (*pada*) as its unit.

Furthermore, having accepted that a word is something to be explained (anvākhyeya), words such as "bhū," "bhūti," and "bhū-ati" are employed as expressive units (pratipādaka) conceived as causes for the comprehension of other composite word-forms.

When a cognition—which follows the mere appearance of the form of an object through the relation of cause and effect—is determined as being the object itself by having its own form superimposed upon external objects, the word serves as the instrumental cause for that objective nature. Likewise, the observation of the apprehension of the object is the cause for the operation of the word—residing within the internal organ and manifested by sound—due to the well-known relationship between word and object expressed as "this is that."

However, like the relationship between sense organs and their objects, there exists an inherent fitness (*yogyatva*) between specific words—which possess a distinct relationship of illuminator and illuminated—and their specific meanings; this fitness consists in the capacity of expressive words whose correctness is established through an unerring and constant state that is not accomplished by human agency. In the case of those whose connection is not well-known, this fitness is contingent upon convention (*samaya*) when they are first introduced.

In that regard, the relationship which exists for a proficient speaker between the word and its meaning attains the status of an auxiliary factor (*aṅga*) toward the manifestation of merit (*dharma*), whether in cognition or in usage preceded by the sacred scriptures. Furthermore, it establishes a fixed rule through the perspective of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) regarding the production of specific cognitions.

However, from the perspective of inference (*anumāna*), because they are related to that which is related [to the correct word], even corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*) attain the status of auxiliaries toward specific cognitions, just like the winking of an eye.

And [this is known] from the indicative marks (*liṅga*). For when, for the sake of grammatical usage (*śāstravyavahāra*), an extraction (*apoddhāra*) is made from a composite whole to isolate some particular meaning-unit, there arises a variety of options dependent on the speaker regarding which meanings serve as the basis (*nimitta*) relative to each respective limit.

How is this understood: does the suffix *ṇic* occur when the "possessor of a cause" (*hetumat*) is to be expressed, or rather, does it occur after a verbal root that functions in the sense of "having a cause" (*hetumati vartamānāt*)?

Similarly, regarding the rule "in the feminine" (*striyām*): do the suffixes *ṭāp* and so on occur when the feminine meaning itself is to be expressed, or rather, do they occur in their own meaning (*svārthe*) after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that functions in the sense of the feminine?

Likewise, regarding the term "nañ," what is the predominant element of this compound? (Is it predominant in the meaning of the prior member, or predominant in the meaning of the subsequent member? For these alternatives are not merely worldly conventions; since there is no deviation from the conventional meaning of the whole, that alternative which ensures consistency with the established rules of the grammatical treatises—despite the lack of fixed restriction among individual human opinions—is the one accepted.

Likewise, [the views regarding] the meanings of case-endings (*vibhakti*)—such as singularity and so forth—and the meanings of nominal stems (*prātipadika*), such as the fivefold set beginning with the object (*karman*), the fourfold set, or the threefold set, are distinctions of position dependent entirely upon the various theories of persons (*puruṣa*).
Furthermore, even the action (*kriyā*), the means (*sādhana*), time (*kāla*), and so forth, have been categorized by some as being, in some way or another, denotable (*abhidheya*).
"The verbal root (*dhātu*) is called *ākhyāta* (verb) when it denotes the means, the direction, the person (*puruṣa*), or consciousness (*citi*)."
Regarding the question "What is the case-ending (vibhakti) in the term *liṅge*?", this is its name.

Based on the established analytical distinction (*apoddhāraparikalpanā*) that "the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs after [roots expressing] a state (*bhāva*) or an object (*karman*), while the active voice (*parasmaipada*) occurs after [roots expressing] an agent (*kartṛ*"), one merely follows the rule for the sequence of comprehension according to the principle: "Having expressed its own meaning, a word, being independent, expresses the substance (*dravya*) inherent [in it].

For it is not possible for a word to function toward its own meaning and so forth in a sequential manner, pausing again and again, because it is uttered only once and because it is eternally inseparable from its meaning.

Indeed, this sequence of practice is not fixed for either the listener or the speaker. For an object qualified by all its qualifiers—having attained the status of being the object of a single cognition as a simultaneous aggregate of its constituent parts (*mātrā*)—is subsequently divided by other cognitions when one desires it. Yet, even for that which has been divided, no manifestation capable of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) arises without a subsequent synthesis; thus, one again reflects upon it precisely in its form as a unified whole.

Furthermore, even for that speaker or listener who attains comprehension of the *mātrās* (vowels) through their distinction, the sequence of cognition regarding the *mātrās* to be grasped is established without fixed order—either due to proximity, the vastness of the scope, the excellence of the manifesting secondary qualities (*upavyañjana*) which serve as the cause of manifestation, or by virtue of being conducive to the acquisition of the seed-function.
Thus it has been said:
"This single essence of being is divided according to the differentiation of its powers."
By those who maintain that cognition is real, [the object] is described in many ways as conforming to the modifications of the intellect.

But is the meaning of a word (*padārtha*) or the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*) that which possesses the characteristic of being stable (*sthitalakṣaṇa*) according to the treatise? For it has been said: "Or rather, [it is not the word-meaning], because a word is not used in its own isolated meaning; that which is the surplus here is the sentence-meaning. It is also stated in the *Saṃgraha*: "Indeed, no word whatsoever is fixed in name or form anywhere."
The form or the meaning of words arises only from the meaning of the sentence.

Furthermore, even when the specific form of a word to be analyzed has been adopted for the sake of its grammatical description, one observes a lack of fixed rule regarding the adoption of forms in the division into base, suffix, and so forth. This is seen in cases such as *marutta*, *indrāṇī*, *aikāgārika*, *giriśa*, *śrotriya*, and *kṣatriya*, where the analysis is carried out according to the sentence as its limit.
As it has been said:
"The word, together with its denotation, arises from meaning; the determination of the sentence-meaning arises from the word."
"A sentence is born from a collection of words; a word is born from a collection of phonemes.
Thus, in the context of etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*), a word is situated within a sentence, being born from a collection of phonemes.

Furthermore, the relationship [between them] is demonstrated as one of cause and effect. For example: "For they too, explaining their cognitions from the moment of their arising until their destruction, manifest the objects of those cognitions as they truly exist."

The connection [between word and meaning] has been described in various places as being due to fitness (*yogyatā*) as well: "Denotation (*abhidhāna*), moreover, is innate; for instance, when the color is the same, the term 'horse' applies to a bay, a white, or a golden horse, but does not apply to cows and the like. Likewise, this has been stated: "Among those who strive equally and study alike, some are joined with the results [of their efforts], while others are not," and so forth.

Furthermore, the Teacher has indeed taught such classes of roots marked with the *svarita* accent, which possess both [types of application], and for which the fruit of the action belongs both to the agent and to one other than the agent.
The compiler recites:
"In worldly transaction, when there is no distinction between word and meaning, they are treated as separate;
yet, because the reality of word and meaning is one, it remains established as such."
He further stated:
"There is no creator of the relationship between words in common usage and in the Veda;
for how could a relationship of words be established by the words themselves? (26)
Words established by tradition from the learned are correct and are the means for accomplishing dharma;
however, those that are the opposite, despite being indistinguishable in their communication of meaning, are incorrect. (27)

Just as other means of accomplishing dharma—such as those that have come down through an uninterrupted tradition of instruction from the learned (*śiṣṭa*) and are thus established beyond suspicion; and just as prohibited acts like violence, falsehood, and theft are established as such; and just as acts neither enjoined nor prohibited by the learned, such as hiccuping, sighing, and scratching, are established as they are—so too the distinction between the good and the bad is established through the very scripture (*āgama*), being an uninterrupted tradition beyond suspicion. Thus it is proven. || 27 ||
Whether they are eternal or created, their beginning is not found;
and this very arrangement of theirs is called "eternality," just as it is for living beings.

If eternal words undergo manifestation, or incur transformations such as birth and so forth—whether they are already existent or non-existent, whether they possess a nameable character or lack one—in every way, there exists neither the first alternative (that verbal usage has not yet occurred) nor the second (that it has ceased).

As for those who assert that Īśvara, Time, Puruṣa, and Vidya are distinct principles from Kṣetrajña, and those who consider Īśvara, Karma, Time, Puruṣa, and Vidya to be nothing other than Kṣetrajña and mere ignorance (avidyā)—[the same applies to them].

For those who declare that the entire universe, without transcending its unity, consists of a continuous succession of appearances in the form of powers that are non-contradictory and subject to transformation—none of them can point to any first period of time called "the past," which has not yet begun its activity. And this very continuity of activity is beginningless and uninterrupted; for it has been said: "That too is eternal, in which its essential nature is not destroyed. (28)
No one is able to establish this convention as being purposeless;
therefore, the tradition (smṛti) concerning correctness is recorded by the learned. (29)

For what cultured person, even one whose intellect is impaired, who is unattached to the world, would venture to establish the purpose of worldly and Vedic words—words that are difficult to understand, difficult to master, and subject to rules regarding their own inherent phonetic refinements? Nor is such a rule purposeless; for even if established by other cultured persons, it would not be accepted by others, nor would it be an authority for the learned in the world.

Therefore, tradition (smṛti)—which is beginningless, handed down through a succession of teachers, and serves as a cause for the inference of the learned—is established both verbally and non-verbally through synonyms, by means of definitions and elaborations, and by way of the fallibility of logical reasons. || 29 ||
And dharma is not established by reasoning alone, apart from scripture;
even the knowledge of the seers is preceded by scripture. (30)

Even all those who travel far do not transcend their own nature. And regarding the determination of the fruits of actions whose objects are unseen, it is dependent upon nature, consciousness, and scripture. For what trust can there be in human reasoning, which is eternally devoid of certainty because its similarities and differences are unstable? Even in those cases where a certain unsurpassed human quality is heard of—transcending reasoning and consisting of the mastery of various branches of knowledge—it is declared that the knowledge of those objects arises for the sages only through the traditional authority of the seers (*ārṣa*), once their selves have been purified by the dharma of scripture.

For if that [sin] were inherent by its very nature, then human effort would be distinct from the result; and furthermore, it would follow as a consequence that demerit (pratyavāya) would likewise be inherent by its very nature. || 30 ||
Furthermore, regarding the uninterrupted paths of Dharma that have been established, no one can subvert them through mere reasoning, because they are well-known to the world. (31)

Even amidst the manifold practices of the learned, there exist well-known common paths for attaining human welfare, wherein any deviation would be loathsome to the world; nor have these ever been refuted by logic. Granted, some may adopt even censurable conduct that contradicts worldly custom solely based on their certainty regarding the teachings of the scriptures. (31)
Since the potencies of entities differ due to variations in state, place, and time,
their establishment through inference is exceedingly difficult.

In this regard, the establishment of an imperceptible object through the cognition that arises regarding an unperceived related entity—based on the perception of a perceived related entity with which there is an invariable concomitance with the desired [object], or of something similar to it—is difficult to maintain.

For instance, even in those whose strength, vitality, and so forth have been ascertained in one state, their essential natures (*svabhāva*) are seen to deviate when they enter other states accessible or inaccessible to humans. Furthermore, even among external things such as seeds and medicinal herbs, a deviation in potency is observed due to differences in their conditions.

Likewise, there is also [difference] due to difference of location: the touch of the waters of the Himalayas is extremely cold, yet that very same [touch] is perceived as extremely hot in the case of those [waters] in clouds, fires, cauldrons, and so forth. In such cases, one whose intellect is captivated by the similarity of form, being unable to perceive the imperceptible particularity, finds the distinction difficult to know; thus, a person of limited vision, through mere perception, understands it only by means of scripture (*āgama*).

Also because of the difference in time: in summer, winter, and so forth, extremely different touches and other qualities are observed in the water of wells and similar sources. In that regard, what person who is not deluded would strive to establish—merely by inference and without the eye of scripture—that subtle particular state of existence which is natural, yet inaccessible to those not perfected, and thus imperceptible? || 32 ||
When a substance whose power is already known is related to a particular substance for the sake of this or that specific causal efficiency, that power is obstructed. (33)

The capacity of fire and the like to produce transformations such as burning wood is observed; however, that same capacity is obstructed in the case of substances such as clouds. Likewise, by means of mantras, medicinal herbs, juices, and so forth, burning and other effects are obstructed even in substances that would otherwise be suitable [for such effects]. Similarly, the powers of substances whose capacities have been observed in one object are difficult to determine when it comes to other objects. (33)
Even an object that has been inferred with great effort by skilled inferents may be established in an entirely different way by others who are more proficient. (34)

"Substance is distinct from qualities because of its designation. For example: when there is a distinction between the qualifier and the qualified, the kingdom is qualified by the king, not by the wandering mendicant; or, fragrance is qualified by sandalwood, not by color and so forth. Therefore, since substance has been established as distinct from qualities through inference, this [opponent's] designation is not tenable," they say.

This is because words are based on the denotation of either specific or non-specific objects. For instance, when the word "sandalwood" (*candana*) denotes a specific form and so forth, it serves as a meaningful qualifier for its fragrance and other qualities. However, in the case of "form" (*rūpa*) and the like, since they denote only their own essential nature, the qualifier would be redundant, as that much of the object is already fully known. To illustrate: when the question "Whose man is this? is asked, one designates him as "the king's" in order to delimit him from other specific categories; it is not designated as "the man's," because his identity as a man is already known. Others say: even though it is but a single part of a collection of words, a *pada* (word) is designated by means of a *ṛc* (verse), but a *ṛc* is not designated by means of a *pada*.

Another says: "The designation of fragrance and so forth by means of 'sandalwood' occurs precisely because of the admission of their identity; the non-designation by means of color and so forth is unestablished because of the contradiction [between the two]. However, the presentation of the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) is based on the presence or absence of specific scriptural mentions.
Therefore, since the unseen is inferred from the seen, this is established as being without contradiction.

Likewise, for the purpose of inferring cooking and so forth, specific parts [of a word] are employed in various actions according to fixed rules, even if they are used by some in a deceptive manner. || 34 ||
That which cannot be explained to others arises only from practice;
the discernment of gems, silver, and so forth by those who know them is not inferential. (35)

For experts in color, logic, and so forth, are not able to explain to others the means for the comprehension of subtle things—such as kārṣāpaṇas and the like—which possess unestablished technical designations, even after having conceptualized them;

nor do those who are diligent and attentive perceive the distinctions of the musical notes ṣaḍja, ṛṣabha, gāndhāra, dhaivata, and so on, even though they are objects of the means of perception (pratyakṣa), without prior practice. || 35 ||
Transcending both direct perception and inference,
the supernatural powers of the ancestors, Rākṣasas, and Piśācas are produced solely by their past actions.

For in dreams, the perception of sound and other objects by those who are deaf and so forth, as well as the vision of subtle objects within houses and the like—such as walls composed of densely packed parts—without any disintegration of those parts, is established in all philosophical systems; regarding these, what kind of means could possibly exist? Apart from an inconceivable power of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), no other means can be described. 36.
For those whose light has manifested and whose minds are unclouded, knowledge of the past and future does not differ from direct perception. (37)

In that regard, first of all, according to the theory of origination (*utpatti-pakṣa*), how can that which is without locus, without substance, devoid of self-nature, unperceived, and not grasped by the power of any specific cause be apprehended? And in the alternative view (*pakṣāntara*), because the form of a particularized individuality is concealed, that object remains unknowable for practical discourse (*vyavahāra*) and is equivalent to things that are non-existent.

Nevertheless, the learned (*śiṣṭas*), whose defects have been burnt away by austerity and whose cognitions are free from obscuration, perceive everything without error—just as if it were directly before their eyes—through their own cognitions, wherein they grasp the transferred forms in the manner of reflections.
Those who perceive with the vision of a seer (ārṣa-cakṣus) entities that transcend the senses and are not accessible to ordinary consciousness—their word is not sublated by inference. (38)

The internal ruler, the cause of noble birth, the unmanifested Śabdabrahman which is the locus of power, the deities, the continuations and transformations of actions, the deficiencies of power, the subtle transportive body, and other matters well-known in the doctrines of various schools—all of which are as imperceptible to the senses as form and so forth, and as unperceivable by each individual as pleasure and so forth—these the learned perceive without doubt by means of an eye other than the empirical one.

Their statement, which transcends the domain of inference, cannot be refuted by fallacious inferences; for such a state as the perception of form occurring in those born blind has never before been admitted [by them]. How, then, could inference operate with respect to that? || 38 ||
How could anyone else turn back that person who, as the master of his own cognition, does not entertain doubt regarding it, and who stands firmly on the side of direct perception? (39)

There are authoritative persons (āpta) who have practiced [the truth] for each individual; their word, even when unexamined, is like their own perception and is entirely beyond suspicion. Furthermore, even that which is unseen—such as the floating of stones—is capable of being believed through conviction.

For instance, it is well known in the world that the attainment of desired or undesired fruits for actions performed here [in this life] in future bodies and so forth occurs solely by accepting the word of an authority; this is generally followed by humans even without the instruction of a formal treatise. || 39 ||
Regarding these two categories— "this is merit" and "this is sin"—
the utility of the scriptures for human beings is minimal, even down to the outcaste (caṇḍāla).
Because perceptual and prophetic knowledge (ārṣa-jñāna) are sublaters of inference, even when there is a contradiction. 40.
And that scripture which exists as an uninterrupted continuity, like consciousness itself—by relying upon it, one is not subverted by arguments based on logic. (41)

For just as that innate and beginningless consciousness—which is accompanied by notions such as "I am this"—is not severed from worldly usage even for liberated souls, because it is so deeply rooted in the world despite the authoritative instruction that "I am not" and "this is not mine," in the very same way, this scripture characterized by the Śruti and Smṛti is accepted by all the learned.

Regarding matters such as what should and should not be done, what may and may not be eaten, and whom one may or may not approach—concerns that are generally not transgressed even by divergent disputants—one who properly attends to such a [tradition] practiced by the elders is not led away from the path of reason by any sophistical arguments. Established therein, he remains irreproachable in the world. (41)
Just as for a blind man running on a treacherous path by means of his hands,
a downfall is not difficult to encounter for one who relies primarily on inference.

For one who, according to the maxim of the "grains in a cooking pot," understands the remainder of a matter after seeing only a single part, is like a blind man on a treacherous mountain path; without a sighted guide, he rushes forward, discerning a certain portion of the way by the touch of his hand and having passed it, proceeds in the same manner based on that conviction regarding the rest, and thus meets with destruction. In the same way, one who follows logic alone through mere inference, without the eye of scripture, may gain a conviction in some particular instance.
One who proceeds by transgressing the sacred tradition regarding actions that have visible or invisible fruits is inevitably joined with great calamity. 42.
Therefore, relying upon the uncreated scripture and the Smṛti together with its foundational sources, the instruction of words is undertaken by the learned. (43)

Therefore, having accepted as authoritative the Veda—which is not of human origin, is beyond suspicion, and is directed toward the instruction of what is beneficial for man—and having adopted the conduct of the learned (śiṣṭa) regarding the usage of correct words, which is like [the formation of] *pṛṣodara* and other such terms, being an uninterrupted tradition and the practice of one's own school; and having accepted as authoritative the Smṛti-śāstras of the ancient seers (*ṛṣi*), which provide options when there is a conflict, which contain general rules and exceptions, and which at every time reflect the observed variations in the nature of word-powers—this grammatical instruction (*śabdānuśāsana*) undertaken by the Teachers is now followed. 43.
Those who know words recognize two kinds of sounds within the category of "appropriated" (upātta) sounds:
one is the cause of words, and the other is employed for the sake of meaning. (44)

That by which an object is grasped, upon which its own form is superimposed, and which causes it to appear as if it were that very thing, is the term *upādāna*. For it is stated thus in the *Saṃgraha*: "In the view that [words] are not derived from etymological analysis (*avyutpatti-pakṣa*), the expressive word is the *upādāna* because it possesses its own form. However, in the view that they are derived (*vyutpatti-pakṣa*), the cause (*nimitta*)—which is directed toward the object and relied upon—is the efficient factor in the act of deriving the word. Some say that the *upādāna* is the indicator (*dyotaka*), because it is possible for the application of the relationship [between word and meaning] to occur through the designation 'this is that'."

Or rather, the aggregate (*samudāya*) is the material cause (*upādāna*). For instance, in the case of those [phonemes] whose nature is that of individual word-meanings (*svarūpa-padārthaka*), there is no perception of divisions because the parts are not themselves taken up as material causes.

One [type of phoneme] is the efficient cause (*nimitta*) of words. That upon which the auditory perceptions (*śruti*) are based, that which they depend on, and that which they take as their support, so that they convey the object to be signified—that is its status as the efficient cause.

The other [type of phoneme] resides in the object. Having acquired a specific modification through the operation of the causal factors, it follows the sense-organ of hearing; by way of being a manifestor (*prakāśaka*), it is eternally dependent upon the object to be signified and is employed with respect to objects.

(a) Some maintain that the *nimitta* (the cause) is that which has acquired a sequence (*anusaṃhāra*), whereas that which has produced a sequence is the signifier (*pratyāyaka*). They declare that even for this [latter], its status as a signifier belongs to it when it has attained absorption (*samāveśa*) in perceivers precisely through the dissolution of its sequential form.

Another says: that which possesses sequence is the cause of the non-sequential. But in the non-sequential Self of Speech (*vāgātman*), the powers of sound (*śruti*) and meaning (*artha*) are conjoined. For thus it is said:
"The undivided signifier of the object arises from the divided [sounds]."
In that case, the word, whose essence consists of the form of the object, undergoes a state of commingling. || 44 ||
Some who recite the Purāṇas say that there is a distinction between those two;
others declare that the one who is non-different appears distinct due to a difference in intellect. (45)

When the differentiation of the self (*ātmabheda*) is the object of the verb *brū* (to speak), the second case (*dvitīyā*) is used; however, when there is a mere imitation of the form of a sentence, the first case (*prathamā*) is used. In that regard, in the view that cause and effect are distinct, there is "differentiation" (*bheda*). In the alternative view, however, there is a conceptualization of multiplicity due to the mental delimitation (*buddhyavaccheda*) resulting from the assumption of a division between two powers within the single self itself. Alternatively, the difference in the philosophical systems of the earlier teachers may be based on whether they maintain the distinction or non-distinction between the word, its form, and its individual manifestation (*vyakti*). This matter will be elaborated upon later as it pertains to the nature of things. || 45 ||
Just as fire residing in the fire-drill is the cause of other manifestations of light,
so too the word, when present in the intellect, is the distinct cause of various auditory perceptions.

Whether in the case of identity or difference, just as the light existing in the state of a seed—unmanifested at first—is seen to become the cause for the cognition of its own and other forms once it has been ignited by a subsequent manifestation, so too, when the principle of the intellect (*buddhitattva*) is permeated by the cultivation of the distinctions of sounds, this sound which has arrived [therein]...
