When its own seed has reached maturity and become manifest, it evolves, aided by the positions (*sthāna*), articulations (*karaṇa*), and so forth; being differentiated by following the distinctions of the manifesting sounds (*dhvani*), its sequential order is perceived as it becomes the revealer of both its own form and that of others. (46)
That [word-meaning], which was previously reflected upon by the intellect and fixed upon a certain object, is assisted by the sound that has emerged from the vocal organs. (47)

In this context, when the relationship between word and meaning is being pursued through the recognition "this is that," that form of the word which is intended to be superimposed upon the object, and in which the form of the object finds entry through its utility—that [word-form], having previously come into contact with the intellect and being apprehended within the essence of the denotable object, assumes another form by means of a transformation of its own form according to the intention, as if through a reversal of its nature.

Regarding the phrase "distinguished from the instruments": for the reality of the word (*śabdatattva*), whose nature is non-modification, undergoes modification following after *dhvani*, which possesses the property of modification.

And that [Sound], while being accumulated through the operation of the organs within a subtle and pervasive resonance, is perceived as if it were undergoing transformation—though it does not actually transform at all—by means of a gross manifestation in the form of a sound (nāda) that resembles a mass of clouds, appearing as a transformation that conforms to that [subtle] transformation. || 47 ||
Because sound arises sequentially, it is neither prior nor posterior;
though itself without sequence, it appears as if possessed of differentiation through its sequential form. (48)

For the *nāda* (sound-manifestation), which consists of an accumulation being gathered through a sequential operation, illuminates the *sphoṭa* by means of a mode of existence that permits [the manifestation] despite its inherent resistance. At that time, although it is one, it appears as if divided into distinct spatial locations. However, because succession and simultaneity are incompatible with its eternity and unity, these two do not exist [in the *sphoṭa*]; therefore, while not transcending its own unity, it assumes the form of difference belonging to the associated *nāda*. This is precisely the nature of the property of the associated element.

For thus, a whole (avayavin), whose nature is absolutely non-different [from its parts], yet which possesses parts of distinct forms and rests upon a substratum situated in various locations, is perceived with manifold variety. || 48 ||
Just as a reflection, though situated elsewhere, appears to follow the activity of the water due to its own movement,
so too is the relationship between the *sphoṭa* and the sounds.

Whether from the perspective of identity or difference, the reflection of the moon and so forth is perceived as if conjoined with its substrate, yet it is not actually so. Although that [reflection] is devoid of action, by assuming the properties of action—such as the ripples and waves of the water—it indeed follows the distinct movements of the water and other elements. In the same way, the *sphoṭa* remains exactly the same throughout the various modes of the primary and modified sounds (*nāda*)—whether short, long, or protracted, and whether fast, medium, or slow—and conforms to their diverse manifestations.
Just as one's own form and the form of the object of knowledge are both seen within cognition.
In that same way, both the form of the object and its own form appear within the word. (50)

Just as cognition is dependent upon the object of cognition—because it manifests in the form of the object—it reveals its own nature as something distinct from other cognitions, even though its own essence is inexpressible; for indeed, even a past object that is no longer perceived is established as an object of memory by another cognition. In the same way, this word, while entering into a subordinate status toward the meaning, is dependent on the denotable object and assumes its form; thus, it causes its own mere nature to appear as if it were the predominant factor.

In common worldly usage, although that [past tense] appears as something present, it is not accepted because it would contradict its connection with actions such as eating; however, in grammar, since the meaning is not incompatible with grammatical operations (*kārya*), and since that [past tense] is established in the form of a denotable object (*abhidheya*), its connection with grammatical operations is not contradictory. (50)
The sacrifice known as "Word" (Śabda), having entered, as it were, into the state of an egg, possesses a function in the form of action which assumes a sequential order part by part.

Through the withdrawal of the grasping of all distinctions, the external, conventional word—without transcending the mere latent impression (*bhāvanā*) of the prior grasping of its divisions—is dissolved within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), like the fluid within a peacock's egg. And just as there is this dissolution of a single word, so too is there the dissolution of the ten mandalas of hymns (*dāśataya*) and the rest.

But he, thus withdrawn and with his portion extinguished, having grasped the property of the transformations of sentences and words within the internal activity of sound—which has attained the awakening of the desire to speak—seizes the power of sequence by grasping each individual component. And that [power] of his, appearing merely as a process of rising and setting, is determined in the form of action. || 51 ||
Just as a form is produced on a cloth as the object of a single cognition,
so too is a triad observed in the case of sound with respect to another form.

Just as a desired form, such as that of a person, which possesses parts, is produced sequentially in the case of cloth, molasses, and so forth—despite being perceived in succession—it nonetheless becomes the basis for a single cognition; likewise, even though speech is conventionally grasped in a sequence, it becomes the basis for a single cognition when its sequence is withdrawn. Having thus projected its own form—which is partless and of the nature of cognition—as if it were something separate, onto that [single cognition] which consists merely in the manifestation of itself, it brings about the appearance of having attained that very state [of unity].

Furthermore, through the comprehension of the properties of sound—the sequential activity of the instruments—it again enters into worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). Thus, as it revolves without interruption through these three states, it does not transcend the relationship between the grasped and the grasper. || 52 ||
Just as the speaker’s prior cognition operates only upon the words themselves, so too does the determination of the perceivers arise with respect to those very same words. (53)

Just as the speaker, undertaking an effort directed toward a specific word, applies his mind as if touching the individual essences of sound that are delimited on all sides for each respective word, so too the hearer, considering the apprehension of meaning to be dependent upon the delimitation of the form of the word, determines each and every word as being supported by the association with all its related qualifiers.

However, through the repeated practice of cultivating the comprehension of meaning, that state of discerning the form of the word is no longer perceived as diverse. Therefore, having reached the ultimate limit of being the subordinate element (śeṣibhāva), all words, which are the sources of all meanings, attain the status of being subordinate to those meanings. || 53 ||

People do not recognize as [true] words certain things that have fulfilled their purpose because they serve another, when those things are subordinate to a meaning and are not themselves the expressed objects. (54)

Just as when a qualified substratum (*guṇin*) is perceived—such as in the cognition "this is white"—the quality (*guṇa*), though serving as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) regarding a specific action, is nevertheless understood in some cases as being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) because of its distinction [from others]; likewise, when there is a connection such as "this is that very word 'cow' which [denotes] this individual object," ordinary people do not perceive the word—which has fulfilled its purpose as an indicator of the object when there is a desire to express the connection with an action, and which has attained the status of a subordinate element (*śeṣatā*)—as being the means for accomplishing the action, just as they perceive the denoted meaning to be so. || 54 ||
Just as light possesses two powers—namely, the state of being the object of apprehension and the state of being the apprehender—so too these two exist separately in all words. (55)

For objects such as jars are established solely as objects of apprehension; thus, at the time of the apprehension of a jar or similar object, they do not provide even the slightest degree of assistance to the sense organ or the object itself by acting as auxiliary factors for perception.

Likewise, all the sense organs, while themselves not becoming objects of apprehension, serve as the instrumental causes for the apprehension of the object to be grasped. Light, however, being endowed with a specific form that is opposed to the nature of darkness, and having its own essential nature clearly determined, functions as a cause for perception by acting as an auxiliary factor.

A word, too, having its difference determined by its own nature—which is opposed to other entities and opposed to other words—and possessing the specific form of the word itself, reveals the meaning to be communicated; and its two powers, namely those of the signifier and the signified, which are eternally inherent to it, appear as if they were distinct. 55.
An object is not revealed by words that have not attained the status of being objects [of cognition];
nor do those words, merely by their existence, reveal objects when they are not apprehended. (56)

And since this is so, therefore—if words were to attain the status of being subordinate (*śeṣatva*) toward objects without having attained the status of being predominant (*śeṣibhāva*) by way of being apprehended as objects—then, whether they are perceived or unperceived, they would convey their respective meanings merely through a connection with existence (*sattā*), regardless of their status as objects; however, they do not convey them [in that manner]. Therefore, when these words attain a subordinate state toward objects, their contact occurs only in the form of predominance (*prādhānyamātra*), while they themselves have become auxiliary members (*aṅgabhūta*). || 56 ||
Therefore, because its form is not yet known, it is asked, "What does it say?
Just so, the intrinsic nature of the sense organs is not apprehended when their object is being manifested. (57)

Ordinary people, believing that the communication of meaning depends solely upon the cognition of the word’s own form (*svarūpa*), ask "What do you say? even when words are employed whose forms are not [previously] understood, for the purpose of apprehending the specific form of the word. The sense organs, however, while remaining unconnected—without being touched by the state of being subordinate (*śeṣibhāva*) [to the cognition of the word's form]—and possessing their own undifferentiated specific characters (*asparśitāsvalakṣaṇa*), enter into a subordinate role in the perception of the object. || 57 ||
Two properties of words, grasped through differentiation and extracted [from their context], function as causes for the coalescence of distinctions without contradiction. (58)

Just as in the world and in the treatises, with respect to objects that are essentially identical but whose differences are established through the conceptual construction of the intellect based on a distinction of causes—within the domain of what is designated by words—all operations pertaining to actual difference are carried out; so too, in the case of words, where the powers of the grasped (grāhya) and the grasper (grāhaka) are extracted by the intellect, various operations of differentiation—such as the relationship between name and named—are prescribed in the treatise as if they pertained to actual objects. || 58 ||

Just as words such as *vṛddhi* and others, which are based on their own forms, enter into a relationship with the named objects (*saṃjñin*) through the words indicated by the [Aṣṭādhyāyī] rule *ādaic*. (59)

For here, in rules such as "iko yaṇ aci," where the forms and designations are distinct, the uttered word *ik* is not the substituendum (*sthānin*), nor is the word *yaṇ* the substitute (*ādeśa*); rather, it is the relationship of substituendum and substitute that is explained in the treatise between the designations (*saṃjñā*)—which are conveyed by those words and which possess different forms. This is established: even when the bearers of the designations (*saṃjñin*) have identical forms, the comprehension of such a relationship [of substituendum and substitute] occurs.

In this context, words such as *vṛddhi* and others have their own forms as their substrata and possess meaning through their own referents; desiring to grasp the forms of other words by means of their own form, they enter into a relationship with the vowels *ā* and so forth—conveyed by the word *ādi* (and so on)—which are distinguished by accents and nasality. This occurs in the very same manner, even though the distinction [between the individual phonemes] is difficult to discern. 59.
In the same way, this word "fire" is based upon the word "fire";
it enters into a relationship with that which is denoted by the word "fire" through the hearing of the word "fire. (60)

In the rule "the word's own form" (*svaṃ rūpaṃ śabdasya*), the name (*saṃjñā*) and the named (*saṃjñin*) are presented as distinct. In that context, two words are heard as the signifiers; and even though they are both understood, there are precisely two that possess the relationship [of denotation] and are the subjects of the grammatical operation.

Therefore, the word *agni*—by means of its own form, which is non-different from the word *agni* that constitutes its meaning—possesses a meaning; it thereby establishes the status of being a name for another word *agni*, which has an identical sound and is the designatum of that [other] word *agni*. || 60 ||
Whatever word is uttered is necessarily not the bearer of the action;
its capacity to convey another [meaning] is not obstructed. (61)

The author will state the reason for the point asserted in the following verse: For a signifier (*pratyāyaka*), when uttered for the sake of another, enjoins that object for which it was uttered to its functions; it attaches those functions to it. When, moreover, the utterance of that very signifier—which resides within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—is performed for the purpose of demonstrating [the object], then its status as a signifier is not obstructed with respect to another word that conveys a similar form. This is a property of every word being uttered. (61)
Because it is dependent on its utterance, the grammatical quality (guṇa) is not connected with the operations;
therefore, the connection of the operations with that [quality] is postulated through its referents.

Just as the scriptural word in the injunctions "Bring the cow" and "Eat the curd," being dependent on the meaning, does not attain the status of an instrument for the action, so too is it when dependent on another word, since its subservience to another is no different. Therefore, it is understood that every object to be communicated, as well as everything perceptible by the eyes and other senses, possesses the status of an instrument for action. || 62 ||
Whatever common property is relied upon between the object of comparison and the standard of comparison, for each of those standards, another attribute is distinguished. (63)

In this context, three things are established: the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), the object of comparison (*upameya*), and their common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*). Among these, in the expression "the Kṣatriya studies like a Brāhmaṇa," the common attribute, though explicitly heard in relation to the object of comparison, is also understood to apply to the standard of comparison.

But when the two learners are presented as the relation between the standard of comparison and the object of comparison—such as in the expression, "The study of the Kṣatriya is equal to the study of the Brāhmaṇa"—then qualities such as excellence (*sauṣṭhava*) belonging to the two studies, which are distinct in their respective substrates, are perceived as common attributes. Since qualities like excellence, which are related to the study, also possess attributes such as perfection (*pariniṣpatti*), there is no restriction of the distinction [between the two]. || 63 ||
When a quality that is the cause of excellence is taught independently, its state of being superior is understood precisely from that very quality which it inheres in. (64)

That which is primarily apprehended as "this is that" is substance (*dravya*). Since there is no excellence or deficiency inherent in the substance itself, the intended object is brought to excellence by means of causes that are dependent, associated, and instrumental—namely, the various grounds for differentiation that are resorted to and which operate toward the production of excellence.

For example: when one says "the pre-eminent white," although whiteness serves as a qualifier (*upalakṣaṇa*), the substrate that possesses it—being the locus of what is not yet pre-eminent—receives the designation "pre-eminent" by means of that which is actively engaged toward pre-eminence through its form of whiteness. However, in the case of the expression "its color is whiter," since the color is taken here as a substance (*dravya*), the designation "pre-eminent" is established on the basis of a cause residing in the color itself.

Furthermore, since the generality of quality (guṇasāmānya) inherent in white—namely whiteness—cannot be the cause of differentiation because it is a single entity, a further differentiation is postulated even for that one [quality], based on its relation to other related properties.

Alternatively, because there are no other words with a distinct cognition [to denote them], these specific qualities—though not expressible by abstract suffixes (*bhāvapratyaya*) and grasped through identical phonetic forms—are understood as being dependent on color (*rūpa*), like whiteness (*śauklya*), and serve as the causes for the designation of excellence. As long as the designation of excellence is applied primarily to that which is designated as "this" or "that" and upon which it depends, so long does this consequence of postulating a separate causal property (*nimittāntara-parikalpanā-dharma-prasaṅga*) remain severed. || 64 ||
The word that exists as the denotative aspect of that [object], its form is also distinguished from that [object] when it is uttered. (65)

And having done so, after demonstrating the establishment of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) through the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the very nature (*svarūpa*) relevant to the context is again taken up. Whenever the utterance of that which constitutes the denotable object (*abhidheya*) is undertaken for the sake of illustration, then, because everything being uttered possesses such a property (*dharmatva*), another distinct form (*rūpāntara*) which serves as its basis (*nibandhana*) is distinguished.
Some say: "The denotation (*abhidhāna*) recurs, but it does not deviate from being the denotable object (*abhidheya*)."

For thus it is stated in the *Saṃgraha*: "The intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of words does not reside in the instrument [of speech] like the body of a cow or similar objects. Rather, that [nature] is eternally the denotable object itself; and because its form remains identical even when it is situated within the denoting [word], it is determined as being uttered, even though it does not [physically] reside therein. (65)
Prior to its connection with the designator, the name has form as its referent;
it serves as the cause for both the genitive and the nominative case endings. (66)

Even when there is a distinction from other denotable objects (*abhidheya*), he demonstrates that the denotation (*abhidhāna*) itself is not distinguished by its own nature (*svarūpa*). Furthermore, a word whose meaning is subordinate to its own form (*svarūpa-adhiṣṭhāna*) functions with respect to another object. As long as a name (*saṃjñā*) is not connected with the named (*saṃjñin*), it does not have the named as its referent; thus, in the absence of another object, there would be no designation as a nominal stem (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*), and consequently, there would be no connection with case-endings (*vibhakti*).

Moreover, because expressive words are the cause of differentiation (*vyatireka-hetu*), when there is another word related [to the object], a differentiation from the meaning of the nominal stem cannot be established. || 66 ||
In that context, because it possesses meaning, the nominative case is prescribed after a word that is a name;
and the distinction expressed by "of this" (asya) arises precisely from that same meaning. (67)

When there is a desire to superimpose the own-form (*svarūpa*) [of a word] upon external objects that constitute its referents, the nominative case is prescribed because the referents of words possess meaning by virtue of having that own-form as their substratum. Furthermore, the relationship characterized by the delimitation of power (*śakti*) between the name and the named is regulated by the formula "this is that" (*so 'yam*). For example: "The Vāhīka is an ox" (*gaur vāhīkaḥ*), or "The boy is a lion" (*siṃho māṇavakaḥ*). The departure from the mere meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-artha*) is the cause for the application of the genitive case; it arises in the case of named words through their connection with a naming word (*saṃjñā-śabda*) that possesses meaning by denoting its own-form and is thus endowed with that [meaning].
Thus he says:

"That designation which occurs as 'this belongs to that' is based on something meaningful; it does not occur through what is meaningless. Therefore, the relationship between word and meaning is eternal. (67)
However, according to some, "its own form" (svaṃ rūpam) refers to the individual instance (vyakti) as a name;
the grammatical operations apply to the individual instance, while the genus (jāti) is understood through its association with it. (68)
Others, however, maintain that the individual instance (vyakti) accompanied by its name is what is intended to be grasped in the Sūtra;
the individual instance, having been made known through the universal (jāti), presents itself in the specific rules (pradeśa).

In this regard, some commentators read: "The word's own form (*svarūpa*) is the grasper (*grāhaka*), the illuminator (*dyotaka*), and the signifier (*pratyāyaka*). Others, however, read: "The word's own form is the grasped (*grāhya*), the illuminated (*dyotya*), and the signified (*pratyāyya*). This has been set forth by these two verses. Furthermore, regarding the universal (*jāti*) as well, there are two types of views among the teachers.

Some say: individuals (*vyakti*) possess specific, determined essential natures (*svarūpa-bheda*). For the essential nature of individuals is neither unperceivable, nor indefinable, nor merely existent. Indeed, it is the individual that is the "cow," not the form (*ākṛti*). It is the quality (*guṇa*) itself that is "blue," not the universal of blueness (*nīlatva*), which is "blueness. As for the form, it serves as the cause for the persistence of the cognition "this is that very same [thing]" regarding objects that possess distinct differences, even for those things in which no [real] inherence has been produced. This is the inference for its existence.

Others, however, hold this view: words, having acquired their own nature at the level of the genus (*jāti*), cause the individual (*vyakti*)—whose nature is otherwise inexpressible—to be understood precisely through that [genus] form. For in all cases, from a cause, a cognition in the form of that cause arises with respect to the object possessing the cause. In that regard, causes whose designations are observed as distinct and those whose designations are not observed operate by means of a partial similarity and an absolute similarity between the word-cognition and the [causal] factors.

And thus, some maintain that "its own form" (*svarūpa*) refers exclusively to the genus (*jāti*). However, by the phrase "of the word" (*śabdasya*), the individual instance (*vyakti*) is designated by the word "word. For others, however, this designation is the reverse: in their view, the individual instance is the name (*saṃjñā*) of the genus, or the genus is the name of the individual instance. When that [genus] is uttered in the rules (*pradeśa*), it causes the individual instance to be understood through its connection with grammatical operations. Yet, that genus does not occur in utterance without being associated with the individual instance; nor does the individual instance enter the domain of usage without being associated with the genus.

However, the intended meaning (*tātparya*) differs according to what is intended to be expressed; that is, in some cases the genus (*jāti*) is primary, while in others it is an inseparable concomitant (*nāntarīyaka*). This is merely a difference in the proposition (*pratijñābheda*): "the genus is intended to be connected with grammatical operations in this treatise," or "the individual (*vyakti*) is intended to be connected with grammatical operations in this treatise.
Regarding the rule *svaṃ rūpaṃ śabdasya*, there is a great variety of traditional views (*āgama*) among the various sections of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*).

For example: "mere form" (*rūpamātra*) is the name for a single part of a meaningful collection of forms—a word endowed with powers such as universals (*sāmānya*) and particulars (*viśeṣa*), which is based upon its status as a word (*śabdatva*). Alternatively, a meaningful collection, differentiated by its associated powers, is the apprehender of the mere sound (*śrutimātra*). For a word is indeed a collection of phonemes (*mātrā*); the phonemes, such as its own form (*svarūpa*) and so forth, are its parts. And there exists a conventional usage of designating a distinction even between the phonemes and that which possesses them, just as one says "the branch of the tree" (*vārkṣī śākhā*).

Another says: although [the object] is not different from the thing itself, the word-meaning (śabdārtha) is indeed different. For a word functions by grasping the powers (śakti) that have a single object as their domain through delimitation. For example, in the cognition "this is a staff," that very same object is denoted by the pronoun (*sarvanāman*) in its perceptual form, and not by the connection with the universal (*jāti*) "staff-ness" even though it is perceived.

For when there is a designation of a connection with a specific class such as "staff" (*daṇḍa*), the pronoun lacks the capacity [to denote that object]; and although the word "staff," which denotes a specific class of objects, is perceptible, its power to convey that thing in its perceptual form is obstructed.

Likewise, by the rule "its own form" (*svarūpam*), the verbal designations such as "fire" (*agni*) are conveyed precisely as the forms of fire and so on, even though they possess a connection with the class of words; they are not conveyed as possessing a connection with the class of words. However, by the word "word" (*śabda*), only the possession of a connection with the class of words is expressed, not the connection with the verbal designations such as "fire."

In this regard, the meaning of one word becomes the designatum (*saṃjñin*) of the meaning of another word which is being employed as its name (*saṃjñā*), even though that other meaning possesses a well-known distinction [from it]. This is merely an illustration; however, all the various opinions concerning the rule *svaṃ rūpam* (Pāṇini 1.1.68) are cited here in order to terminate the discussion that has arisen from following one line of inquiry into another. 68–69.
Regarding whether [the world] is an effect or eternal, some are proponents of unity;
regarding whether it is an effect or eternal, some are proponents of plurality. (70)

For those who maintain that words are one, this distinction between genus (*jāti*) and individual (*vyakti*) is not possible; therefore, immediately after introducing the [doctrine of] genus, this [objection] is raised. In that regard, if [the word] were eternal, oneness would be absolutely primary. However, if it were a product, then when a phoneme or a word that has been uttered once is uttered again, the non-deviant cognition "this is that very same [thing]" which arises establishes its oneness. And it is with reference to this perception of oneness that it was stated: "The oneness of the *akṣara* is established."

The intervention [of difference] is due to time and sound, not to an intervention of the form of the phonemes (*varṇa*). And the perception of spatial distinctness is like the perception of existence, form, or the reflection of the moon in water.

Even on the view that there is multiplicity, one must necessarily resort to a figurative unity for the sake of linguistic usage when referring to sounds that are products, even upon repeated utterance.

However, those who maintain the doctrine of multiplicity—whether in the case of the eternalist position or the causalist position—accept the absolute distinctness of words with different meanings and of phonemes situated in different words. (70)
Even when there is a division of words, the oneness of the phonemes does not cease;
likewise, a single word is perceived even within sentences that are themselves distinct. (71)

In words such as *arkaḥ*, *aśvaḥ*, and *arthaḥ*—though these words are distinct—the perception [of the phoneme *a*] is mediated by time and other sounds, and its form remains hidden due to the absence of the conditions for its manifestation. Yet, this single phoneme *a* appears in a differentiated form when uttered by different speakers in different locations due to differences in causes; it is employed in the world according to the analogy of reflections appearing differently in a mirror, in water, and so forth.

And within sentences, even when there is a distinction of meaning clearly understood, as long as the form of the word is identical—as in "gaurakṣa"—the whole is considered a single word. Even when there is a difference between a noun and a verb, a word of this kind, such as "akṣyaśva," is indeed one.
Apart from the phonemes (varṇa), no other word (pada) exists;
nor does anything exist apart from both phonemes and words that constitutes a sentence (vākya). (72)

For it is not possible for another word to be originated by phonemes (*varṇa*) that arise sequentially, perish as soon as they are uttered, do not exist simultaneously, and possess parts; thus, the word is merely the phonemes themselves. Since these too possess parts, and because there is no interruption in the continuity of their sequential occurrence, there exists some indescribable form that transcends linguistic usage—a fourth-of-a-fourth (*turīyaturīyaka*)—which lies beyond conventional discourse. Therefore, there is no such thing as "word-knowledge" (*pada-vidyā*). In the absence of phonemes and words, how could there be a distinct entity called a sentence (*vākya*)?

And so it has been said: "In this way, [the word] would result in being non-eternal. Because the aggregate does not exist, there is no such thing as a word that either grasps its own meaning or is grasped by another. || 72 ||
Phonemes do not exist within words, nor do parts exist within phonemes; there is no absolute distinction whatsoever between words and the sentence. (73)
Another says:

Because there is a distinction in the effort directed toward the aggregate [of sounds] arising from the many manifestations of the perception of individual phonemes, even though there is a distinction in the resonance (dhvani) whose object is the manifestation of the word, the cognition of the word arises as a means for the perception of the division of phonemes, due to the persistence of similarity.

The sequence of reality (*tattvakrama*) is indeed one, eternal, indivisible, and without prior or posterior, like the single essence established by the fourth state (*turīya*) of the phonemes (*varṇa*). However, the fourth states of the phonemes—beginning with *a* and so on—which are intended to be distinct, are merely conceptualized as signifiers; they are inexpressible and beyond worldly usage. Therefore, their unity is well-known and easily understood within the conventional practice of the scriptures. Furthermore, since a sentence, consisting of one or many words, is employed for the sake of meaning, the comprehension of words arises as the means for the comprehension of the sentence.
In that very entity which is the self of the sentence, there arise successive cognitions appearing in the form of phonemes and words, though these are not real entities.
Therefore, from such a sentence—which is indivisible and partless as the essence of speech—there is an absolute non-distinction between phonemes and words. || 73 ||
Conventional practice follows by relying on divergent philosophical views;
what is primary for some is the opposite for others. (74)

For the teachers, relying upon various philosophical views (darśana) by adopting different scriptural traditions for each specific topic within the ultimate, internal reality of the Word (śabdatattva), follow the practical application of the treatises.

For instance: "Even when there is multiplicity of meaning due to the non-difference of the Vedic revelation, there is oneness of the word; even when there is oneness of the Vedic revelation due to the difference of meaning, there is multiplicity of words.
In this regard, for some, the difference is figurative and oneness is primary; for others, however, distinctness is primary and oneness is merely conventional.

For thus it has been said: "A single word may have many meanings, as in the case of *akṣāḥ*, *pādāḥ*, and *māṣāḥ*. Having stated, "Likewise, this word *grāma* has many meanings," he provides a specific conclusion by distinguishing them: "That which exists in a forested area (*sāraṇyaka*), together with its boundary (*sasīmakā*) and its common pasture-land (*sasthaṇḍilaka*), of that this is the designation. || 74 ||

They declare that for the *sphoṭa*, which is itself devoid of temporal divisions yet conforms to the duration of the sounds (*dhvani*), there is a distinction in its manifestation due to the differences in the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) of its perception. (75)

In this regard, because the reality of the Self (ātmatattva) is eternal, there is not even the slightest operation of the measurement of time in the persistence of the sphoṭas. However, since the essential nature of the sphoṭa is perceived as conjoined with the manifesting sound (dhvani), the duration of the sphoṭa's perception—which is the duration of the dhvani—comes into play.

And by means of that limiting adjunct (upādhi) consisting of the apprehension whose object is the sphoṭa, which occurs at different times, the modes (vṛtti) of the sphoṭa—namely the quick, the medium, and the slow—are designated as distinct, being associated with an increase in three parts. || 75 ||
Because of the difference in their inherent natures among short, long, and protracted [vowels], the duration of the natural sound (dhvani) is metaphorically attributed to the word (śabda). 76.

If this is so, then even in the case of short (*hrasva*), long (*dīrgha*), and protracted (*pluta*) vowels, sound alone would be the cause of the distinction in duration. Just as in the rule "followed by *t* (tapara) [indicates] its own duration," which applies to long and protracted vowels, the same designation of their respective durations would necessarily follow even when there is a difference in tempo (*vṛtti*). When this objection arises—namely, that "when *t* is used to denote the short vowel in the fast tempo (*drutā*), an addition must be made for the medium (*madhyama*) and slow (*vilambita*) tempos because of the difference in duration"—the following is prescribed:

In this context, sound (*dhvani*) is of two kinds: primary (*prākṛta*) and modified (*vaikṛta*). Of these, the primary is that without which the nature of the *sphoṭa* remains unmanifested and cannot be discerned. The modified, however, is that by which the manifested nature of the *sphoṭa* is perceived for a further, more prolonged duration. Thus the author of the *Saṃgraha* recites: "The primary sound is held to be the cause for the apprehension of the word; the modified sound serves as the cause for its continued differentiation."

In that regard, due to a particular difference in their arrangement (*saṃniveśaviśeṣāt*), certain utterances such as *gārgya* possess equal divisions and dimensions of parts, yet some are perceivable through an accumulation of repeated articulations (*uccāraṇāvṛttipracayagrāhyāḥ*), while others are perceivable through a non-accumulated form of repetition (*apacitarūpāvṛttigrāhyāḥ*). Likewise, due to a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabhedāt*), the short vowel (*hrasva*) is manifested by a diminished sound (*apacitadhvani*). An awareness arises there that grasps the essential form (*svarūpa*) by means of that much manifestation. However, the long vowel (*dīrgha*) is manifested by an accumulated sound (*pracitadhvani*), while the protracted vowel (*pluta*) is conveyed by a more highly accumulated sound (*pracitatara-dhvani*).

And that duration of the ordinary sound, being superimposed due to the non-perception of its distinction [from the sphoṭa], is metaphorically designated as "the duration of the sphoṭa" in the treatise.
After the manifestation of the sound, however, the modified sounds (dhvanis) bring about a differentiation of its functions;
yet the essence of the sphoṭa is not divided by them.

Just as light is the cause for the perception of jars and other objects immediately upon their birth, while its continued presence is the cause for the continuity of that perception; so too, when a word has been manifested, the articulatory sound (*dhvani*), persisting at subsequent moments, brings about the persistence of the cognition whose object is the word, by providing reinforcement to the power of that manifestation.

Therefore, although the essence of the *sphoṭa* is conjoined with the modified articulatory sounds which are perceived as distinct from it, because there is no superimposition of their nature [upon it], it does not undergo the conventional distinction of temporal duration—such as shortness and so forth—as taught in the grammatical treatises. || 77 ||

The embellishment (saṃskāra) is produced by the articulated sounds (dhvani) either of the sense organ alone, or of the sound (śabda) alone, or of both; these are the three positions of those who maintain the theory of manifestation (abhivyaktivādin).
But how does the sound (dhvani) achieve the state of being the cause for the perception of the word (śabda)?

In this verse, only the process of the manifestation of the word is proposed; the following two [verses], however, concern the presentation of examples. Regarding this, some hold the view that the sound, as it arises, conditions the auditory organ, and that organ, being thus conditioned, serves as the medium for the perception of the word.

Others, however, who maintain the theory of manifestation (*abhivyaktivādinaḥ*), hold that it is the word-sound itself which, having acquired refinement (*saṃskāra*) through contact with the articulated sound (*dhvani*), becomes an object of the sense of hearing. For some, the articulated sound functions to benefit both the word-sound and the sense of hearing. By means of these two—the sense organ and its object—being assisted by another auxiliary cause, the cognition whose object is the word-sound is produced. Just as in the case of visible objects, where the powers of causes do not exceed their completeness when they depend on other auxiliary causes such as the illumination of a lamp, so too is it here. (78)
The refinement of the sense organ itself is achieved through concentration, collyrium, and so forth;
however, the refinement of the poison is for the purpose of perceiving its scent. (79)

For concentration—whether ordinary or extraordinary—does not impart any specific quality to the object of perception itself. Just as a substance such as collyrium refines only the eye and not the external object, so too extraordinary concentration favors only the eye for the perception of subtle, concealed, or distant things. For if it were to favor the object, it would follow that the object could be perceived by others as well, since there would be no distinction [between one person's perception and another's].

The refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the object, however, is observed in the case of oils and the like through exposure to sunlight and so forth, and in the case of the earth through water, at the time of the perception of fragrance; it is not observed in the case of the olfactory faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*). If, on the other hand, there were refinement of the olfactory faculty, there would be no difference in the perception of objects whether they are refined or unrefined, because [the faculty] lacks any distinction [in its own state]. (79)
If the eye functions by reaching its object, then an embellishment (saṃskāra) of both the sense-organ and the object is desired through light; that same sequence applies to sound.

In this world, one situated in deep darkness perceives objects such as a jar when they are assisted by light. In that regard, for those who hold that the eye functions without reaching its object (*aprāpyakārin*), the object is generally assisted by the light. However, if the eye functions by reaching its object (*prāpyakārin*), then the rays of the eye are assisted by light of a similar nature.
The apprehension of the sound (dhvani) is held by some to be inseparable from the form of the sphoṭa;
by others, it is postulated that the sound is imperceptible and exists independently. (81)

Now, there are three other divergent views among those who maintain that sound is manifested (*abhivyaktivādin*). According to some, the sound (*dhvani*), being conjoined with the word (*śabda*), is perceived as inseparable from it, like the coloring of a crystal or similar objects by their substrate.

However, according to others, just as the sense organs and the qualities of the senses have unperceivable natures yet serve as the causes for the perception of objects, so too this sound exists as the cause for the apprehension of the word while its own form remains ungrasped.

Others, however, say: "The perception [of sound] from a distance is observed when the *sphoṭa*-form of the pure sound (*dhvani*) is not determined. Others maintain that this is merely an illusion of perceiving the word-sound (*śabda*). For example: in deserts, the increase in the perceived size of objects whose actual dimensions have diminished is observed; likewise, the decrease in the perceived size of the moon and other such objects; and the non-perception of color in things like clouds. Furthermore, there is the non-apprehension of the specific particulars (*viśeṣa*) of fragments, hollows, and so forth, as well as of the generalities (*sāmānya*) and particulars of trees such as the *dhava* and *khadira*. (81)
Just as an *anuvāka* or a verse reaches mastery through repetition, yet that text is not re-examined with every single repetition; [so it is here]. (82)

Sounds, which have phonemes, words, and sentences as their objects and are produced by specific efforts, repeatedly manifest the *sphoṭas* known as phonemes, words, and sentences, and superimpose them upon the intellects. However, since there is no such thing as a collective whole when phonemes are perceived one by one, it follows that the final cognition would lack an object; this has been examined in many ways in the commentary on the *Saṃhitā-sūtra*.

Even though the entire form of the word has been manifested, as long as it has not yet assumed its own nature—that is, as long as it has not taken on its specific qualities and is not established in the intellect—no linguistic usage whatsoever can be accomplished by means of that which remains unperceived.
When a word is manifested by sounds through conditions that are themselves inexpressible and imperceptible, its true nature is then apprehended. (83)

Many cognitions, which serve as means and possess an indefinable form, arise when a word is being manifested by sounds; these are conducive to the perception of the manifest form and become the causes for the apprehension of the word's own nature. || 83 ||
When the intellect has had the seed sown by the preceding sounds and its ripening is completed, the word is apprehended along with the final sound. (84)
In this regard, the sequence for grasping the form [of the word] is as follows:

by means of sounds (*nāda*) which illuminate the essence of the word (*śabda*), seeds of the cultivation of latent impressions (*saṃskāra-bhāvanā-bīja*) conducive to the discernment of the manifest [word] are deposited with progressive excellence. Then, the final particular sound (*dhvani-viśeṣa*), through its assistance, causes the form of the word's own nature to be established in the intellect, whose capacity has reached full maturity through the attainment of the functional activity of the seeds of the cultivation of latent impressions for discernment. || 84 ||
And those words which one considers to exist in the interval between [the two extremes] though they do not exist—that is the incapacity of the cognizer; it is merely a means of apprehension. (85)

In this world, when letters, words, and sentences—which are partless, devoid of prior or posterior, and indivisible—are manifested by sound (*dhvani*), there arise in the case of a letter cognitions that resemble the apprehension of parts of a letter and which seem to be intent upon parts; in the case of a word, cognitions resembling the apprehension of letters; and in the case of a sentence, cognitions resembling the apprehension of words. Through these cognitions, perceivers falsely imagine non-existent, part-constituted sounds to exist. This is indeed the incapacity of perceivers to grasp an object not presented by another [source].

For their perception of the word is indeed accomplished through a sequence of means consisting of various phonemes that have come into being; however, even the *dāśataya* [the ten-fold Ṛgveda] they attain and cause others to attain by means of other methods. || 85 ||
The imitation of differentiation is a constant affliction of both cognition and speech;
speech has a form conditioned by succession, while cognition is dependent upon the object of knowledge. (86)

Even though cognition is undivided and formless, it appears as if possessing division because it assumes the forms of all objects of knowledge—such as "five trees" or "twenty cows. This internal essence of speech (*śabdātman*), in which all seeds have been withdrawn, manifests at the time of its appearance by following the sequence of the differences in the manifesting sounds (*dhvani*). Thus, this very reality of speech (*śabdatattva*), known as *vāc* and *manas*, which is itself undivided, is perceived otherwise when it is overwhelmed by the assumption of the forms of other divisions. For it has been said:
"In practical discourse, cognition does not exist without an object of knowledge."
No meaning whatsoever is expressed by speech that has not attained its proper sequence. || 86 ||

Just as the apprehension of the first number is the means for the comprehension of other numbers despite their difference, so too is the hearing of another word [the means for the comprehension of its meaning]. (87)

Just as one who wishes to understand a number such as "one hundred" or "one thousand"—which serves to differentiate a substrate—understands the various constituent parts of those numbers, such as the units and so forth, which are distinct effects and serve as the means for that understanding (just like the individual fingers of a hand), so too is the apprehension of the form of a sentence the means for delimiting the hearing of other words such as "Devadatta"; thus, the employment of those [words] is an inseparable concomitant. 87.
The manifestors of individual phonemes, words, and sentences are distinct;
yet, even though they are absolutely different, their powers appear as if intermingled. (88)

For specific efforts having phonemes, words, and sentences as their objects impel the vital airs, which strike the points of articulation. Although the sounds (*dhvani*) that acquire refinement (*saṃskāra*) through the striking of these points possess natures differentiated from others, nevertheless—just like the secondary indicators (*upavyañjana*) of the universals (*jāti*) "cow" and "gavaya," or like the substrata of the particular universals of actions such as "wandering" and "shaking"—the distinction between those secondary indicators is difficult to discern.

The self-nature of potencies, even when their effects are distinct, is followed by some degree of generality; it remains established through a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) arising from some particular effect. Consequently, there occurs this determination of the division of measures (*mātrā*) within phonemes (*varṇa*), which are partless; the determination of the division of phonemes within words (*pada*); and the determination of the division of words within sentences (*vākya*). (88) Just as people with impaired vision, or even in deep darkness, determine an object in one way after having first perceived it otherwise from a distance. (89)

Just as this is the very nature of objects and sense organs that those with ordinary vision perceive trees and the like from a distance merely by their general form, yet—while remaining in that same place—gradually perceive them according to their specific parts through the practice of focused attention (*praṇidhāna*); and just as one who has suddenly entered a chamber or similar space from a well-lit area might perceive a rope or such thing as a snake due to the dimly situated light, but then perceives it correctly once the eye has returned to its natural state through the practice of focused attention; so too [is the case here]. || 89 ||
Likewise, when a sentence is being manifested by the causes of sentence-manifestation, the cognition first proceeds in the form of grasping its constituent parts. (90)

For in the case of a sentence, which is indeed partless, the sounds produced by specific articulatory efforts directed toward its manifestation give rise to a cognition that takes the form of grasping the portions appearing as phonemes and words; this occurs because, despite their difference, those sounds are endowed with a common capacity. || 90 ||
Just as there is a fixed sequence of transformation in the case of milk and seeds,
so too is the order of cognition determined for those who perceive.

Just as milk—whether from the perspective of its production or its manifestation—is connected with various specific states such as cream and curd, which are designated by fixed forms through particular terms whether they are conventional or non-conventional; and as it follows the proximity of the properties of its own nature according to each case, it displays the causal power of transformation through a specific sequence without overstepping the established order.

Just as the seed of rice and other grains, impelled by its primary transformation into rice and so forth, appears—while being joined with its inseparable specific stages such as the stalk and sprout—by means of the property of its primary transformation which acts as the efficient cause; likewise, for these perceivers of limited vision, whose cognitions regarding the meaning of a sentence are preceded by the apprehension of the sentence's own form and are impelled by that primary [apprehension], their cognitions proceed toward the *sphoṭas* in that object to be accomplished through fixed means, appearing merely as forms possessing parts characterized by a fixed sequence of transformations. || 91 ||

Even among those very parts of the word-sound, there is a differentiation of form according to the sequence; or else, since the sounds are indivisible, one must resort to the conceptualization of a distinction between parts.

Even those proponents of difference who maintain that the word "cow" (*gauh*) consists merely of the phonemes *g*, *au*, and the visarga (*visarjanīya*), and believe that there exists no other partless essence of sound (*śabdātman*) distinct from them which is graspable by means of perceiving the forms of the phonemes, yet nevertheless accept the eternality of words—for them, it follows that when the fourth part of the phoneme, which cannot be designated in sequence, is manifested, its own form remains undetermined; thus, the final cognition that apprehends the manifest form would result in being devoid of an object.

If, however, all the parts were manifested simultaneously, there would follow the undesirable consequence of no distinction in the auditory perception, such as "gave" (he gave), "vegaḥ" (speed), "tena" (by that), and "na te" (not yours).

This fault does not apply in the case of a different word associated with a different meaning. Even in that case, however, the cognition occurs as distinct due to the sequence of the manifesting sounds (*dhvani*). For it is observed that in the case of ropes and the like manifested by a lamp placed near frogs and other creatures, there is a difference in the cognition of them as snakes and so forth.

Alternatively, cognitions attain the status of being means [to knowledge] by assuming specific powers produced through the conceptualization of divisions within that which is indivisible; this has been described in the subsequent verses. || 92 ||
The genus (jāti) manifested by many individuals is known as the sphoṭa;
by some, these very individuals are conceived as being the sounds (dhvani). (93)

Some, asserting that the eternity of the word follows from the eternity of its form (*ākṛti*), explain that in such statements as "only the *sphoṭa* is indicated on both sides; the hearing of *ra* becomes the hearing of *la*," they refer to the word-form (*śabdākṛti*)—which is distinct from the generic property of sound (*śabdatva*) and is denoted by the term *sphoṭa*—as that which is gradually fashioned and perceived through supports that arise in succession and do not exist simultaneously, serving as the cause for the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). However, the individual manifestations of sound (*śabdavyakti*), though subject to production, receive the designation of "articulation" (*dhvani*) because, while their own forms cannot be designated, they illuminate the *sphoṭa*, whose form is capable of being designated. 93.
The sound (dhvani), though modified by causes, serves as the means for the perception of the unchanging word, just like light. || 94 ||

Others, however, maintain that because of the difference in the processes of linguistic usage regarding form (*ākṛti*) and individual manifestation (*vyakti*), there is only one single essence of speech (*śabdatattva*) which is eternal and undergoes no transformation. Though not supported by the sounds (*dhvani*) that undergo change due to their own causes, this essence—by way of the analogy of the light of a lamp—is manifested within those sounds. Even when there is no confusion regarding the actual object, it appears as if its form were perceived, having acquired an affinity for the modifications of the manifesting sounds. Thus they say. (94)
Furthermore, manifestation is not invariably established in things that are impermanent; nor is the manifestation of eternal universals (jāti) admitted to depend upon their substrata. (95)

In this regard, some point to manifestation (*abhivyakti*) itself as the reason for establishing impermanence: "Sound is impermanent because it is manifested, like a jar. Here, the manifestation of impermanent things such as jars by means of lamps and the like is observed; and it is accepted that this sound is manifested by articulations (*dhvani*). Therefore, [sound] is impermanent. Alternatively, if it is not manifested, then it follows that it is produced; for this reason also, it is indeed impermanent. To those who hold that universals (*jāti*) exist and are eternal, it is replied: "Because it is observed in both ways, [manifestation] is not a valid reason (*anapadeśa*)."

However, against those for whom nothing at all is eternal, who oppose [the argument] on the grounds that it is unestablished (*asiddha*), the proponents of the eternity of sound oppose [them] first and foremost by means of its very unestablished nature. How so? For the reason "because it is manifested for another" is not a valid indicator (*anapadeśa*); or else, because of the state of being doubtful, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) of the reasoning due to the involvement of alternative possibilities. || 95 ||
A connection with place and other factors is observed even for those possessing bodies;
yet, despite the conceptualization of different locations, there is no difference between the sound and the word. (96)

Now, another prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is presented here: "Sound is not manifested due to the difference in location (*deśabheda*). For objects such as jars, which occupy the same location, are manifested by lamps and the like. However, through the conjunction and disjunction of the articulatory organs (*karaṇa*), which serve as manifestors, the perception of sound occurs elsewhere. But this [argument] does not apply to the case of *dhvanis* acting as manifestors. Regarding that, they say: "How can a sound situated in one place be manifested by *dhvanis* located in various places and at great distances?"

To this, the following reply is given: "The unity of location and the diversity of locations is a property belonging to those that possess bodies. Even those things possessing bodies, such as the sun and so forth, are perceived here as having limited locations and residing in various substrates. However, in the case of the two formless entities—sound (*dhvani*) and word-sound (*śabda*)—because they transcend the conventional usage of location and located, even though there may be a conceit (*abhimāna*) regarding the conceptualization of a difference in location, no such difference actually exists between them. (96)
Just as the fixed capacity between the grasper and the graspable is established, so too is it between the sphoṭa and sound by way of the relationship of the manifested and the manifestor. (97)

Now, another prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa): Sound is not manifested due to the restriction of its manifestors. In this world, that which is to be manifested depends upon a specific manifestor; for instance, jars and other objects are manifested by all things such as gems, lamps, medicinal herbs, planets, and constellations. However, sounds are accepted as having restricted manifestors, because one sound is not manifested by the noises that serve as the causes for manifesting other sounds; therefore, they are not manifested. To this, the following reply is given: "Of the grasper and the grasped... (grahaṇagrāhyayoḥ).

For example, just as color itself, when inherent in the eye, is the cause for the manifestation of external color—and not other qualities, nor other sense organs, nor the qualities of other sense organs—so too do [the senses] become the causes for the manifestation of external objects. || 97 ||
Furthermore, that which illuminates similar perceptions of odors and so forth is a specific cause established for each individual substance in the world. (98)
In response to the objection that "this restriction does not exist among things perceptible by the same sense organ," it is replied:

even among things perceptible by the same sense organ, this property is observed. For example, among substances such as river-fragrance (*nadīśaileya*) and others, only a certain other substance in conjunction with them is capable of manifesting the specific fragrance of a particular substance. (98)
The object to be illuminated follows the differences among the illuminators;
this is evident in the case of reflections in oil, water, and so forth. || 99 ||

Now, another prima facie argument: sound is not manifested, because when there are differences in the increase, decrease, and number of the manifestors, the manifested [sound] does not possess those attributes. For, when the manifestors undergo increase or decrease, no increase or decrease is perceived in the objects that are manifested. This is just as, for example, the increase or decrease of a lamp does not entail an increase or decrease in jars and other such objects.

Furthermore, when there is a difference in the number of lamps, it is not observed that jars and other objects—which possess their own distinct numbers—acquire a different number on account of the difference in the number of lamps. However, in the case of sound, a difference in number and magnitude is observed when there is a difference in the striking (impact). Therefore, [sound] is not manifested. To this, the following reply is given:

It is observed that manifested objects conform to the differences of their manifestors. For example: the reflection of a face appears elevated in depressions such as the surface of a mirror; it appears depressed in elevations; it appears long in a sword; it appears dark in *priyaṅgu* oil; and in Chinese mirrors, steel blades, glass, and so forth, it follows the various dimensions of the mirror—thus there is an infinite variety of such distinctions. Furthermore, a difference in number is seen in the reflections of the sun and other objects when there is a difference in mirrors or a difference in water-waves. (99)
In objects of contradictory dimensions, such as the surface of a diamond or a mirror, there is no possibility for entities possessing the same form as mountains and the like to exist. (100)

In this regard, it might be argued that in mirrors and the like, a reflection is perceived as a distinct entity (*bhāvāntara*) situated within, separate from the moon and other objects. To this, the following reply is given:
for it is not possible for entities resembling mountains and the like—which possess dimensions incompatible with their substrates such as diamonds—to be produced by being situated inside them. (100)

Therefore, in the case of phonemes, sentences, words, and so forth, which exist at non-distinct times, the time of their manifestation and their own [inherent] time are distinguished by the difference in the sounds (nāda). || 101 ||

For in the persistence of eternal things, there is no operation of the auxiliary power of time. However, according to worldly convention, all *sphoṭas*—whether in the form of accumulated or non-accumulated phonemes, words, and sentences—do not differ with respect to their persistence, as their essential nature is apprehended by the intellect through both the prior and subsequent limits. When they attain the status of being objects of perception, there arises the conceit that these [phonemes], which are non-distinct in time, persist during the act of perception; this is what is meant by "the time of occurrence" and "one's own time."

The primordial *nāda*, which exists as a reflection within the nature of sound (*śabdātman*), is the cause for establishing the conventional usage of the distinctions between short, long, and protracted durations, in order to prevent the perception of difference. The modified *nāda*, however, brings about the determination of the temporal duration of external activities such as rapid speech and so forth. || 101 ||
That which is produced by conjunctions and disjunctions through the organs is the *sphoṭa*; others have declared that the sounds born from speech are the *dhvanis*. (102)

In the view that [sound] is non-eternal, the sound which first comes into being, caused by the contact and separation of the place and the articulatory organ (*sthāna-karaṇa*), is called *sphoṭa*. However, regarding that which is born from it, because all substances—which grasp the reflection of its form across all directions and times—are themselves partless, and because even space possesses a primary inherent locus (*samavāyi-deśa*), there occurs a metaphorical designation of a spatial division based on another substance with which it is conjoined; thus, through the proximity of spatial contiguity and the uninterrupted succession of cause and effect, [the sound persists].

Those sounds which divide the perception of phonemes—sounds that, like forms illuminated by the light of a dim lamp, possess a progressively diminishing capacity to grasp preceding reflections and perish in succession—are called *dhvanis*. In the theory of the eternal [phoneme], however, the *sphoṭa* is manifested by *dhvanis* produced through conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and disjunction (*vibhāga*). According to some, it is manifested by resonance (*nāda*) arising from *dhvanis* produced through conjunction and disjunction. Furthermore, the *dhvanis* that consist of a process of diminution and serve as the cause for establishing the distinctions between tempos such as fast (*druta*) and so forth, are those whose power of manifestation diminishes progressively while supporting the form of the *sphoṭa*. (102)
Whether the sound is small or great, the duration of the *sphoṭa* does not differ;
however, the subsequent series of sounds consists of accumulation and diminution.

The designations "small" and "large" are applied to sound figuratively due to the commonality of its spatial pervasion, or because of conventional usage; for in all cases, it is conventional usage alone that determines the meaning of a term. Indeed, when philosophical systems and scriptural traditions diverge, the objective status of things remains unsettled. In this regard, since there is no distinction between words denoting effects and words denoting causes—given that all things produced perish as soon as they arise—there is not even the slightest temporal difference between a large and a small sound, just as there is none between the cognition of an elephant and that of a gnat.

However, due to the difference in the cause (*nimitta*), the capacity of sound (*śabda*) varies when initiating its effect. For in some cases, a succession of effects proceeds to a great distance, as if produced by the striking of a drum with a stick; in other cases, like the striking of iron or bell-metal, it initiates a continuous stream that is perceivable in a nearby location for a long duration without interruption. || 103 ||
From a distance, only the sound of a lamp is perceived;
however, in the case of sounds such as those of a bell, that distinct difference is clearly seen. (104)

In this regard, some teachers maintain that the manifest *sphoṭa* is, at the very moment of its manifestation, connected with the innate sound (*dhvani*), which is all-pervasive and far-reaching, and which stands in the place of illumination—just as a particular substance is joined with its fragrance. Just as in the case of a lamp, there is a fiery substance whose constituent parts are densely packed in each substrate, and the illumination dependent upon it follows the modifications of that substance; so too, through the striking of a bell, when all the phonemes (*varṇas*) are produced, the *sphoṭa* and the sound become more clearly manifest. This is their doctrine.
And this distinction between the natural (*prākṛta*) and modified (*vaikṛta*) sounds has been explained by the two preceding verses:

"Due to the impact of a substance, the accumulated [sounds] are distinct, as are the long (*dīrgha*) and protracted (*pluta*); when the vibration has ceased, the sounds produced are the differentiators of the mode (*vṛtti*). (104–105)

Even on the view that sounds are eternal, it is not the case that long (*dīrgha*) and protracted (*pluta*) durations are accumulated through an accumulation of sounds. Rather, they are produced solely from the accumulation of impacts with material substances (*dravya*). For their very nature can be brought about by only so many impacts. Therefore, until their own nature is fully attained, the specific impacts of the articulatory organs (*karaṇa*) result in mutual contact between the constituent parts [of the sound], and a vibration follows, accompanied by the manifest pulsation of air.
Once the vibration has ceased, those sounds born of the resonance (*nāda*) become the cause for the determination of the distinctions between the modes of speed (*druta*) and so forth. || 105 ||
Even when the articulatory organ is unstable, other sounds arise from the *sphoṭa* itself, just as flames arise from another flame. (106)

Even when tremors continue without interruption, whatever sound is produced by the impact does not cease until its effect has been fully initiated. In that process, those sounds born of the tremors—concurrent resonances (*dhvani*) that refine the essence of the *sphoṭa*—are called "tactile," "subsequently manifesting," "intervening between the primary notes," and "continuous.
They further maintain that for each such continuity, a succession of effects persists through the mere assistance of the *sphoṭa* as long as the tremor is not severed.

And this very origination is described by way of the nature of a continuous process of the activity of fuel and flame. Just as flames supported by fuel arise as a continuous succession of effects that are flames, and they benefit objects by illuminating them, so too is this the activity of sound. || 106 ||
Some maintain that air, atoms, and cognition attain the status of sound;
for indeed, differences in philosophical views are not fixed among various doctrines. (107)
The air, having acquired its activity through effort that conforms to the speaker’s intention, attains the state of sound when impelled against the [articulatory] locations. (108)
In this regard, they explain the attainment of the state of sound by air as follows:
"By the power of its cause, the forms of even solid objects are divided through the impact of that [air], which possesses the property of accumulated velocity. (109)
In this manner, all such [cases] are to be understood. || 109 ||
The atoms, due to their possession of all powers, function through both differentiation and conjunction;
they undergo transformation into the states of shadow, heat, darkness, and sound. (110)
When one's own capacity is being manifested, the atoms known as sounds, impelled by effort, accumulate like clouds. (111)
Others maintain that atoms attain the state of being sound; they speak thus, and all such [arguments] are to be understood accordingly. (110–111)
Then this internal knower, abiding in the subtle self of speech, undergoes a transformation into the form of sound for the manifestation of its own nature. (112)
Having attained the state of mind and reached maturation through its own radiance,
it enters the vital breath (prāṇa), and then it is fully aroused.
The wind has become the substratum of the principle of the internal organ;
permeated by its property, it evolves through fire alone.
Dividing the knots of its own self through various forms of sacred revelation (śruti), the vital breath (prāṇa) manifests the phonemes and then merges back into those very phonemes. 115.
Furthermore, others describe how knowledge itself attains the state of being sound (*śabda*);

all such [arguments] are to be understood accordingly. This is merely an illustration; for the views of the authors of the *Śikṣās*, the *Sūtras*, and the *Bhāṣyas* are seen to be manifold. For example: "The internal vital air (*prāṇa*), impelled upward by internal effort and supported by fire, issues forth from the sound-conducting channels and forms a subtle mass, like a column of smoke."

"In the various locations (*sthāna*), the density of sound (*śabdaghana*), being condensed, grasps the undivided image of the word residing within by means of some degree of manifestation"—all such [statements] are to be understood. For example, the detailed exposition of the differing views of the authors of the *Śikṣās* is to be understood as follows: "The wind, impelled by effort from the region of the navel, moving upward, strikes one or another of the locations such as the chest (*uras*), and from that, the production of sound occurs," and so forth.
Indeed, the Teacher also says:
The self, having empowered the objects through the intellect, joins the mind with the desire to speak;
the mind strikes the bodily fire, which impels the vital air.

And so forth. Likewise, another reads: "The wind reaches the location of the *koṣṭha* (the chest cavity) as the *anupradāna* (the source of emission); having reached the throat, it attains the state of breath (*śvāsa*) or the state of sound (*nāda*)," and so on. Then another says: "The bodily fire, impelled by the mind, impels the *prāṇa*. Rising from the navel, struck at the head by another [wind], and being further struck by the rising wind, it becomes sound—either 'ka' or 'kha'," and so forth. All such differing scriptural views seen in the various branches (*śākhā*) and phonetic treatises (*śikṣā*) must be explained through detailed elaboration (*prapañca*). 112–115.
That sound which has a continuous existence but is not perceived due to its subtlety is understood from its manifestation, just as wind is [perceived] from its own cause.

Now, another scriptural authority is followed: Sound exists both internally and externally within all material objects, like a subtle accumulation of air. For some, this is understood as "space" (ākāśa).

Just as when atoms are present everywhere, the air—being compressed—is divided from its locus by the striking of a fan and is set in motion by various actions, in the very same way, sound—having its modifications manifested and accumulated through its own causes—is perceived upon reaching the region of the ear, and it effects an impression there. 116.
That power which resides in his vital breath and that which is established in the intellect, as it evolves through various stations, attains differentiation. (117)

These are merely different positions. This immediate path of accumulation (*pracaya-dharma-adhvani*) is not what is being indicated here in this verse; rather, it is *śabda* (the word/sound), which was the subject under discussion previously, that is being explained through these various theories. Indeed, *śabda* has both the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the intellect (*buddhi*) as its substrata.
Having attained manifestation through the two powers of the mere measures (*mātrā*) of the vital breath and the intellect, it causes the meaning to be understood.

In this regard, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), permeated internally by the principle of the intellect (*buddhitattva*), moves upward like a flame; conforming to the effort that projects it toward the locations of the phonemes (*varṇasthāna*), it undergoes transformation (*vivartate*) through a process of counter-recoil (*prativighātavivartena*) that grasps eternal sound.

Having attained a transformation of power through its conjunction [with the intellect], it assumes differentiation—just as the earth, the embryo, or the seed of a *nyagrodha* tree—and it establishes within the supreme non-dual essence of sound a mere coloring (*anurāga*) by differentiation. (117)

The power residing in words alone is the foundation of this entire universe, since this world, though appearing as differentiated form, is perceived through that which has intuition (*pratibhā*) as its essence. (118)

In that regard, for some, the forms [of speech] are based upon the substratum of subtle sound. These, indeed, come to be established in the relationship of signifier and signified by attaining the manifestation of the Self through the transformation of their substratum. Just as for others, the powers consisting merely of objects dissolve into the sense organs, so too do the powers consisting merely of the sense organs dissolve into the intellects (*buddhi*), and the powers consisting merely of the intellect dissolve into the Self of Speech (*vāgātman*) through the process of reabsorption.
And this activity of dreaming and waking, which imitates distinct persons, remains eternally established even within the Great Cause, the essence of speech (*vāktattva*).
Thus others also say:
"Speech alone perceives the object; Speech speaks; Speech alone extends the object that is deposited [within it]."
The manifold universe is bound within speech alone; that very same one, having divided itself, experiences it. || 118 ||

Since the distinctions of the notes, such as ṣaḍja and the rest, are explained by means of sound and are thus manifested, therefore all varieties of objects are dependent upon the subtle elements of sound. || 119 ||

For every object, being bound to a conventional designation (*saṃvijñānapada*), enters into linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) when it is defined through recollection, verbal expression, and the determination of its form.

Furthermore, the distinction between the notes ṣaḍja, ṛṣabha, gāndhāra, dhaivata, niṣāda, pañcama, madhyama, and so forth—whose conventional designations are not fixed or well-known—is not determined without a cognition based on words that serve as the basis for such determination. Indeed, cowherds, shepherds, and others, having devised conventional designations, initiate linguistic usage regarding specific objects such as cows and the like.

Therefore, in both denotable and non-denotable general and particular words, the object possessing differentiation—which is superimposed [upon the word]—is manifested, grasped, and accepted by a cognition that is permeated by the word, whose nature is the word, and which is conjoined with the power of the word. || 119 ||
Those who know the sacred tradition understand that this is a transformation of sound;
from the meters alone did this entire universe first evolve.
