Just as others, explaining the relationship between cause and effect, observe the presence of the qualities of the cause within the effects and establish a transformation (*vivarta*)—which is subtle, imperceptible, distinct from its differences, permeated by all powers of modification, a collection of atoms whose manifest form has subsided, a mass of the powers of *pradhāna*, having ignorance as its cause, characterized by birth and transformation yet devoid of contact—as such is the causality of the Self (*ātman*), who is speech, taught in the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) as being manifoldly the cause of the withdrawn powers of the enjoyer and the enjoyed: "He indeed is this... [and so forth].

"The Puruṣa consists of the Ṛgveda, consists of the Yajurveda, and consists of the Sāmaveda; he is the Vairāja Puruṣa. The Puruṣa is indeed the world; the Puruṣa is the sacrifice. These three *lokampṛṇā* oblations of his are the three lines of the triple-lined brick (*tryālikhitā*). Indeed, the three worlds are the three lines."

Likewise: "This very first person, consisting of meters and composed of the Sāman, is the Vairāja; he created food, and from him animals were born. From animals, the trees; from the trees, fire. Therefore they say: 'One should not milk [the cow] with a wooden vessel, for this wooden vessel is indeed fire. Therefore, one does not milk with a wooden vessel.
And also the wording of the Ṛgveda: "From Indra, the meter first cast forth food; therefore these two, name and form, are spread out in all directions."
From the vital breath, the form called *nāma* (name) has arisen; this single *chandas* (meter) shines forth in manifold ways.
Furthermore, it says:
"Speech alone gave birth to the children and the worlds; speech is indeed all that is immortal and mortal.
Now speech has enjoyed [all things]; speech spoke in many places; yet there is no track of speech, nor that which it has not spoken."
The Purākalpa also says: "That Prajāpati, the Lord of Chandas, having divided himself manifoldly,
entered him through various measures consisting of the meters."
O Prajāpati, in those men in whom virtuous speech is firmly established, merit and beauty exist in greater measure.
The great splendor belonging to Prajāpati, as if enclosed within vessels,
returns to its own source upon the dissolution of the body of the wise.
This radiant mandala, the abode of manifold prosperity,
having attained its true being, dissolves into primordial wisdom.
In this world, every course of action depends upon words;
even a child understands it through the impressions implanted from before.

Even that which exists, if its form as an object is not grasped through verbal usage, is equivalent to the non-existent. That which is universally recognized in the world as absolutely non-existent—such as a hare’s horn—and that which has attained manifestation and disappearance—such as a city of Gandharvas—appear, when brought forth by speech, as if endowed with primary existence during their respective functions.

Furthermore, for children whose speech is fully internalized within their own species, there arises an understanding of various purposeful actions based on inexpressible words, due to the instillation of impressions from the habitual cultivation of prior linguistic immersion. || 121 ||
The initial arrangement of the instruments, the upward movement of the vital breath,
and the striking of the locations do not occur without the cultivation of sound.

And this linguistic predisposition (*śabdabhāvanā*) is beginningless; it consists in the grasping of the seeds of cognition that reside in each individual. For its being of human origin is in no way possible.

Thus, the arrangement of the vocal organs and so forth are to be accomplished without instruction and are accessible only through intuition (*pratibhā*). For who else but the nature of the word itself is capable of performing or explaining these human faculties? (122)
There is no cognition in the world that is devoid of the accompaniment of words;
all knowledge appears as if permeated by speech. (123)
Just as his verbal cultivation (*śabdabhāvanā*) has been withdrawn, so too no activity is performed by even the non-conceptual [cognition] that has arisen with respect to objects of knowledge.

For example, for one moving quickly, although there is sensory cognition due to contact with grass, clods of earth, and so forth, there is a certain specific state of cognition in which—when the seed of the cultivation of sound has become manifest—the nature of the object is perceived as accompanied by cognition. This appearance in a manifest form, following upon cognition, is known as the essence of the thing being grasped and processed by a cognition that is permeated by sound and conforms to its capacities; [this occurs] regarding the capacities of words—which grasp the objects—which are fixed to each respective object, whether those words are of an expressible form or of an inexpressible form, and in which the cultivation of sound has become present.
Thus it is described. And that [latent impression], arising from other causes when the seeds of the scriptures have manifested, becomes the cause of memory.

Likewise, according to some teachers, even for one who is asleep, there is a continuous stream of cognitive modifications similar to those of the waking state; however, at that time, the seeds of verbal mental impressions (*śabdabhāvanā*) merely attain a subtle modification. Therefore, they call that state "tāmasī" (pertaining to darkness). This very consciousness experiences the manifestation and disappearance of the nature and transformations of sound. || 123 ||
If the eternal nature of speech were to depart from consciousness, then manifestation itself would not shine forth; for it is that [nature of speech] which performs reflective awareness.

Just as luminosity is the very nature of fire, or consciousness that of the Inner Controller, so too all knowledge is permeated by the mere form of speech (*vāk*). Even in that state which is unperceived, a subtle persistence of the attribute of speech recurs. Furthermore, the initial manifestation of external objects, occurring without the grasping of specific causes, presents the object as its bare essential nature through a mode of cognition that cannot yet be designated as "this" or "that."

Furthermore, even at the time of recollection, when such seeds of perception are present before one, there occurs in the intellect a mere following of illumination regarding the verses or other objects to be remembered, in the form of the thought: "This is some particular section (*anuvāka*) or verse (*śloka*) which was previously introduced by me through mere hearing."

And if the nature of speech (*vāgrūpatā*) were absent, even though manifestation has arisen, it would not remain established in its form as the instrument for the act of manifesting, because it would not admit the other's form. Furthermore, when distinct forms—which do not assist one another—appear to each other merely as objects, the subsequent synthesis (*anusandhāna*), which is reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*), consisting in the apprehension of the connection between powers through the differentiation of their performance of a single purpose—that is bound to the nature of speech.

For that [cognition], while connecting and reflecting upon [its objects], does not abandon the mere distinction and connection [of elements] within a cognition that performs a causal function—even though it is qualified by all its qualifiers—by means of the conceptual abstraction of their potencies. || 124 ||
She is the binder together of all sciences, crafts, and arts;
by her power, every object that has come into being is differentiated.
The practical activity of human beings regarding worldly and Vedic matters is for the most part bound up with knowledge, arts, skills, and so forth.

The activities of the rest of the aggregate of beings, both stationary and moving, are dependent upon humans. Furthermore, knowledge and the like are grounded in the intellect, which has speech as its form.

And in the production of objects such as jars, everything—including the instruction, effort, and so on, of those who employ others and those who are employed—is fashioned in accordance with the nature of speech. (125)
This very consciousness of transmigrating beings exists both externally and internally;
it is the pure sentience that transcends even those subtle elements in all classes of beings.

Because this conformity with the nature of speech exists within consciousness, it is by means of that that the designations "conscious" and "unconscious" are applied in the world. For thus it is said:
"Speech impels all embodied beings toward purposeful actions;
upon its departure, this person is seen to be unconscious, like a piece of wood or a wall."

Even among internal cognitions, that which consists merely of the sensation of pleasure and pain lasts only as long as the persistence of the nature of speech (*vāgrūpatā*). This is also the case with external objects. Worldly transaction (*lokavyavahāra*) is based upon that [speech]; in the absence of it, such transaction would necessarily perish.

Indeed, there is no such thing as a genus (*jāti*) permeated by consciousness (*caitanya*) in which the awareness of self and other exists, if it is not followed by speech. Therefore, that which has not acquired the grasp of the power of speech (*vākśakti*) does not exist in the form of the activity of consciousness (*citikriyā*).
Others maintain that the very nature of the principle of speech (*vāktattva*) is the nature of the activity of consciousness. Thus he says:
Through the transformation of the apprehension of difference,
speech itself— having assumed a formalized structure— is declared in all branches of knowledge to be the supreme primordial nature (prakṛti).
Words and eyes do not transcend oneness;
yet, based upon words, cows and other things appear as distinct entities through the differentiation of speech.
Those who indeed worship speech— which has six gates, six foundations, six awakenings, and is sixfold and imperishable— truly transcend death.
Just as the agent proceeds toward an effect through differentiation, so too does that very same [agent] abide as the effect itself through non-differentiation. || 127 ||

For the manifestation (*vivarta*) of the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*) consists of the differentiated forms of the means and the ends [of action]. Having undergone transformations such as birth and so forth, the knots of vocal differentiation follow the nature of speech during the state of waking; through the attainment of cessation and transformation, they exert themselves toward their effects. But in the non-differentiation of dream and so forth, that very same speech, being beyond its own domain and possessing the nature of external objects, assumes the state of an object of action (*karmabhāva*) during the attainments of cessation and transformation. And it has been said: "Having divided itself by itself, it creates various kinds of entities."
The Lord of All, who consists of all things, manifests as the enjoyer in a dream.
Just as a word is introduced by its own etymological derivation (*śruti*) or by the context of another, so too does it attain conventional usage (*rūḍhi*);
for by that [conventional sense], the meaning is enjoined.

For some, the view is that every modification is merely the Self (*ātman*); yet that [Self], though residing within each individual, appears as if external. Because this usage of "internal" and "external" has become conventionalized, it is a mere linguistic convention; for such a distinction is not possible if there is oneness or immateriality. For others, the view is that this transformation of the single reality of conscious activity (*citikriyātattva*) takes the form of all awakenings and the form of all distinctions, and so forth—this is the view of those who maintain that everything is merely the Self. Some hold that consciousness, which is the source of all beings, is divided like the oil within sesame seeds.

But others say: for example, sparks from a great fire; dense clouds from subtle wind; streams of water from a moonstone; *sāla* trees and so forth from the earth; or *nyagrodha* trees with their descending roots and shoots from *nyagrodha* seeds—such is the view of those who maintain that [the world] arises from a single atom (*paramātra-vādin*). The view of those who maintain that [the world] arises from its own constituent parts (*sva-paramātra-vādin*) is to be understood from the *Vidyābhāṣya*.

The *śruti* (the revealed word) initiates [the process]. Through the internalized sound (*śabda*), it proceeds in manifold ways among various living beings by way of states such as pleasure and pain; and through the conventional usage established by worldly consensus (*lokabhāvanāsamaya*) regarding actions such as throwing or falling a clod of earth, it becomes fixed. For it is by that [sound] that the object is enjoined. Indeed, that very *śruti* conceives and refines the meaning. 128.

Even when the causal sign (*nimitta*) is absolutely non-existent, the determination of the form of an object is perceived in things such as a whirling firebrand due to reliance on verbal testimony. (129)

For revelation (*śruti*) alone shows that every word-meaning is established within the essence of its own form; it, as it were, brings that meaning into being, for that meaning is eternally situated within it as its object of cognition. Revelation does not depend upon the existence or non-existence of external objects, nor upon their correctness or error.

For instance, even in the case of a circle of fire (alātacakra), the auditory perception—which pervades all points and is accompanied by the mental impression (*bhāvanā*) of words such as "action" and so forth—establishes the meaningfulness of conventional terms like "circle of fire. When there is an orientation toward that seed of auditory perception, the form constructed by that auditory perception through its corresponding cause becomes established as a conventional reality, despite the superior force of inference.

Even in the case of things that are absolutely non-existent and well-known to be so, such as a hare’s horn and the like, it is *śruti* (the Vedic word) alone that generates the object, conceptualizes it, and establishes it within itself; and it does the same for other objects perceived through direct perception. For the essence of an object—whether it has a basis or lacks a basis—is eternally present within words as their denotable content. However, with respect to each individual person, the comprehension arising from words occurs in diverse forms according to their own mental impressions (*bhāvanā*), whether the object exists or not, following the pattern of their respective cognitions. || 129 ||
They say that the speaker’s own self, the word abiding within, is the Great Bull (Mahān Ṛṣabha), with whom union is sought. (130)

In this context, there are two natures of sound: the eternal and the produced. Among these, the produced is conventional, serving as a recipient for the reflection of the person whose nature is speech.

It is eternal, the source of all worldly transactions, with its sequential order withdrawn; it resides within all things, the origin of transformations, and the substratum of actions; it is the locus of pleasure and pain, possessing an unimpeded power of action everywhere, like a jar or other object whose light is thus constrained, yet bounded by the field of experience it has assumed; it is the measureless primordial nature (*prakṛti*) of all embodied beings, and, through its nature as universal awakening and its nature as universal differentiation, it imitates the dream and waking states of ever-occurring manifestation.

By means of the two terms "active engagement" (*pravṛtti*) and "cessation" (*nivṛtti*), the Great Lord of all, who possesses the power of both production and destruction like a rain-cloud and a forest fire, is the Great Bull of Sound, endowed with all powers. Indeed, those who know the yoga of speech, having severed the knots of the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), become fully integrated within Him through absolute distinction.
And it is said:
"He has four horns, three feet, two heads, and seven hands."
Bound in three ways, the bull bellows loudly; the great god has entered into mortals. || 130 ||
Therefore, that which is the refinement of sound is the perfection of the Supreme Self;
he who knows the reality of its manifestation partakes of that immortal Brahman. 131.

For when the essence of speech (*śabdatattva*) is refined through its established state of correctness (*sādhubhāva*), and once the excellence of its qualities (*dharmaviśeṣa*) has become manifest due to the removal of the corruption of corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*), there is certain spiritual prosperity (*abhyudaya*). Furthermore, by practicing that [correct speech] and attaining yoga preceded by speech, one thoroughly understands existence (*sattā*)—which is the source of intuitive insight (*pratibhā*), the nature of the modifications of being (*bhāvavikāra*), and endowed with the powers of means and ends—and thereby the attainment of ultimate security (*kṣema*) is certain.
And it is said:
"Established in the essence of speech, which transcends the functions of the vital breath (*prāṇavṛtti*)."
Having withdrawn oneself into the Self by means of the yoga of sequential withdrawal.
Having applied refinement to speech and having established speech within knowledge,
one should disentangle its bonds and render it free from bondage.
Having reached another light and severed the collection of knots,
he attains oneness with the supreme light after cutting through those knots.
No one ever accepts a scripture that lacks an author;
therefore, since all other scriptures have perished, the Triple Veda alone remains established as the seed.

In all philosophical systems, the human origin of the scriptural statements is accepted through the acceptance of their authors; however, the Vedic statements are, like consciousness itself, without a human author. Even when the authors of other scriptures have disappeared, these [Vedic statements] remain as the seeds for the investigation of those other scriptures. || 132 ||
When all other disputants have vanished and no others remain,
the world does not transgress the Dharma proclaimed in the Śruti and Smṛti.

In this world, it is not admitted that there has been an interruption even in the traditions of the scriptures, just as there has been none for their authors. Even when those [scriptures] have disappeared, until other authors arise and other scriptures are propagated, during that interval the learned do not transgress the rituals prescribed by the Vedas nor the rules concerning what is fit and unfit to be eaten, which are based on the Smṛtis. || 133 ||
If knowledge were innate, there would be no purpose whatsoever for the scriptures.
If dharma is the cause of knowledge, then the sacred tradition (āmnāya) is its foundation. (134)

For by those who accept that knowledge belongs to no one through instruction, it follows as a logical consequence that the treatises of instruction—which serve to prohibit what is harmful and to establish what is beneficial—would be rendered useless.

For if knowledge were to arise in certain individuals without instruction due to a specific quality (*dharma*), while other individuals must be instructed by means of a treatise (*śāstra*), then that specific quality which causes such distinction among persons would have to possess a fixed basis. Yet, other bases are seen to be severed. Therefore, those who propound various doctrines, while cultivating a quality that lacks a final basis, attain their respective goals through manifold conceptual constructions.
And logic that does not contradict the Vedic scriptures is the eye for those who lack vision;
for the meaning of a sentence is not established by the mere form of the words alone. (135)

For it is by means of reasoning (*tarka*) that the systematic determination of the distinctions between words and their meanings is established for the very statements of the scriptures (*āgama*). And since this [reasoning] serves to assist those of limited vision (*arvāgdarśana*), such reasoning was relied upon by the ancients in the sciences of logic (*nyāyavidyā*). In that regard, as much reasoning as follows [the truth] without contradicting one's own scripture should be followed. Furthermore, much that transcends reasoning is seen in all scriptures to be followed through faith (*śraddhā*).

Now, what is the purpose for one who, without following reasoning (*tarka*), takes scripture (*āgama*) alone as the means of valid cognition? The purpose is the correct comprehension of the scriptural statements. For even though sentences may be identical in form, their potency differs due to other determining factors.

In that regard, he who understands the meaning of a sentence from its form alone, without depending on context (*prakaraṇa*), capacity (*sāmarthya*), and so forth, falls into confusion regarding what is intended and what is not intended. (135)
"The non-intention of one who is conscious, the subservience to another's purpose, and the inferential manifestation of an object"—thus is the manifold principle analyzed by means of reasoning. (136)

"The object most desired by the agent is the *karman* (object); its offspring; he wipes the cup; that which one intends to reach through the action is the *saṃpradāna* (recipient). The establishment of grammatical definitions—such as whether gender, number, and tense are intended to be expressed (*vivakṣā*) or not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣā*), as in the statement, "Those who live off women have reached the mark of death"—is dependent upon logic (*tarka*).

And so it is said: "Having seen the star, one should release speech. Here, the sight of the star serves to indicate the time; since that [sight] is established as secondary when the primary purpose is otherwise accomplished, and because it is for the sake of another, it is performed once the specific time has been determined among the visible luminaries. Just as in the command, "Let the curd be protected from crows," because the intended purpose is the prohibition of spoilage, the curd is protected from dogs and others even when crows are absent. Similarly, in the command, "Let the vessels be cleansed," because the intent is the preparation of the accessories for the act of eating, other accessories are prepared even in the absence of the vessels.

There is also inference based on indicative mark (*laiṅgikī vyakti*). In the case of the injunction, "He places the smeared pebbles," when there is a possibility of any substance serving as the ointment, the specific understanding [that it is clarified butter] arises from the indicative mark, "Clarified butter is indeed splendor. It is by means of reasoning that such a principle is analyzed and its definition is established. || 136 ||
That power belongs to words alone; reasoning (tarka) is that which relies upon persons.
Logic (nyāya) does not follow from words and has no basis in those who lack sacred tradition (āgama). || 137 ||
The word itself is the instructor; following its very power, speakers proceed with an intention based precisely upon the appropriate word.

When a person follows the restricted power of a word through means such as the meaning, context, indicative mark (*liṅga*), or sentence, they consider that this reasoning (*tarka*) which relies on the person is actually a capacity residing in the word. However, that which is not embraced by the form of the word’s power, but merely follows similarity and dissimilarity, is called "dry reasoning" (*śuṣkatarka*); because it is the cause of the subversion of all scriptures, it is said to be "unfounded.
For example:
If a great circle of jars with the color of udumbara fruit,
when drunk, cannot lead one to heaven, how could that which is contained within a sacrifice do so?
When it is said by the word that "it is to be spoken," it must be stated by Drāmilaka. || 137 ||
Just as visible forms and other objects are observed to possess specific powers according to their respective capacities,
so too are words seen to have such powers in cases such as the removal of poison.

It is said that for those who have understood from scripture that there is prosperity resulting from knowledge preceded by the study of the treatises or from their practical application, mere logical reasoning serves only as a corroborative support for that very scripture. Here, the capacities of these [qualities]—form, taste, smell, and touch—are grasped both individually and collectively, having powers directed toward specific objects with both seen and unseen fruits. First, examples of those with seen fruits include poisons, medicinal herbs, magnets, plants, and so forth.

The drinking of water from certain sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and the like has an unseen fruit (*adṛṣṭaphala*). Furthermore, upon the utterance of certain sounds, a visible fruit such as the removal of poison is observed. Likewise, through the repeated practice of hymns (*sūkta*) and the like, a distinguished unseen fruit is accepted.
(138) Just as these [sounds] possess efficacy in those cases, let it be understood that they do so in the case of *dharma* as well.
Therefore, the correct words (*sādhūni*) should be spoken by the virtuous to those seeking prosperity. (139)

Furthermore, there are certain powers in this world whose results are perceived directly, such as those pertaining to an echo; this is understood from scripture alone. Since scripture exists, let it be understood in the same way that the use of correct words is a means of accomplishing *dharma*. Therefore, those who seek prosperity should employ only correct words in their speech, adopting the Smṛti—which is not to be doubted—and the uninterrupted practice of the learned. 139.
One understands all purposes whose fruits are not yet seen through scripture;
moreover, it is possible to state the opposite of everything regarding scripture. (140)

Regarding this, some say: "Just as these [mantras] possess efficacy in removing poison and so forth, why is such efficacy not likewise perceived in the case of unrighteousness (*adharma*)? Let there be an understanding of a reversal of power based on this very same example. To this objection, the following reply is given: In all scriptures, regarding practices that yield both seen and unseen results, it is possible for contrary results to be obtained. Therefore, once a particular scripture has been established as authoritative, whatever logical justification (*upapatti*) is stated in its support gains the status of a corroborative factor for that practice. (140)
This very tradition of grammar is the object of the knowledge of correctness;
it is the foundation of this tradition for the learned, handed down without interruption. (141)

Just as there are established *smṛtis* concerning matters such as what is fit or unfit to be eaten, who may or may not be approached, and what may or may not be spoken—customs which the learned (*śiṣṭas*) do not transgress—so too is this *smṛti* called grammar concerned with the specific distinction between what is to be spoken and what is not. For a matter remembered is recorded again and again through an unbroken tradition; and while a well-known custom is recorded in a *smṛti* that does not explicitly mention words, it is nevertheless preserved by the uninterrupted practice of the learned. (141)
This is the wondrous supreme state of the threefold speech—consisting of Vaikharī, Madhyamā, and Paśyantī—which possesses a manifold division of sacred sites (tīrthas). 142.

That speech which is perceivable by others, restricted as an object of the ear, and consisting of audible form (*śruti*), is *vaikharī*. It is articulated with distinct phonemes, well-known for its correctness, and may also be that whose grammatical refinement has been lost. Furthermore, it possesses immeasurable varieties, such as that which exists in the lute, the drum, the flute, or the violin. *Madhyamā*, however, resides within; it possesses a sequential order and is based solely upon the intellect. It follows the subtle activity of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and although it exists in a state where sequence is withdrawn, according to some, it still maintains a manifest sequential order.

Paśyantī is that in which the sequential order has been withdrawn, yet even while there is non-differentiation, the power of sequence remains inherent. She is both moving and unmoving; she is both attained through meditative absorption (samādhi) and veiled, as well as pure. She possesses the forms of the objects of knowledge, yet her forms are dissolved and she is formless. She is the manifestation of distinct objects, the manifestation of blended objects, and the manifestation of all objects in a state of perfect tranquility; thus, she possesses immeasurable varieties of differentiation.

In this regard, some maintain that the distinction between correct (*sādhu*) and incorrect (*asādhu*) speech, established across all conventional linguistic states, serves as the cause for the refinement of the person. However, they hold that the form of *paśyantī*—which is uncorrupted, unmixed, and transcendent of worldly usage—is attained only through grammar, or through yoga preceded by the Word (*śabda*), which is acquired via the knowledge of correctness; such is the tradition (*āgama*) of these [others].
Accordingly, illustrative examples are found in the *Itihāsas*:
"One [cow], abounding in the finest essence, flows like a cow."
Bhāratī, the cow of speech with her pure smile, [appears] in both divine and non-divine forms.
Behold the difference between these two subtle, vibrating [winds]:
within the interval of the prāṇa and apāna, one [the supreme consciousness] eternally abides as the source of all.
But another [vitality] exists being impelled even without the breath;
for from that, the breath is born again, nourishing what is to be spoken.

Sustained by the vital breath (prāṇa), this speech— which is the basis of all worldly transaction— never speaks at any time without having obtained the out-breath (ucchvāsa). It proceeds as both voiced (ghoṣiṇī) and voiceless (aghoṣā), whether producing sound or being devoid of sound.
And between those two, the silent one is indeed superior to the vocal one.
And it is further said:

"When the vital air is restrained in its locations, speech in its manifest form (*vaikharī*)— which assumes the apprehension of phonemes— is produced by speakers, being bound to the activity of the breath."
Taking up only the intellect as its substrate and following the sequence of forms,
the intermediate speech (madhyamā-vāk) proceeds by transcending the activity of the vital breath (prāṇa).
But Paśyantī is undivided, with all sequential order withdrawn;
it is the internal light of its own nature, the subtle, imperishable speech.
Although this [nature] is constantly being overspread by adventitious impurities,
it is not utterly overwhelmed, just as the final digit of the moon is never completely obscured.
When her true nature has been seen, one’s qualification [for bondage] ceases;
they call that sixteen-fold person the immortal digit.
Having attained a form colored by adventitious disturbances,
that *vaikharī* speech is not intermingled with them, just as the quality of *sattva* is not intermingled with the other *guṇas*.

This very threefold speech, whose measure is inexpressible like the unfolding of the knot of consciousness, manifests among humans through its fourth aspect. Even therein, only a small portion of it is practical for worldly transaction; the rest, however, transcends common usage.
And it has been said:
"Speech is measured in four quarters; those Brahmins who are wise know them."

"Three [parts] are hidden in the cave and do not stir; humans speak only the fourth of speech. Thus it is said. And the unmixed form of that speech is entirely established in this science called grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), which possesses both general and particular characteristics. However, for men of limited vision, their powers are generally characterized by excess, obstruction, and error. But this faultless method for the comprehension of words, consisting of many paths and detailed through its systematic exposition (*lakṣaṇaprapañca*), has been revealed. (142)
The potencies of words are seen by those who know the true nature of things to be established as being manifested through the division or non-division of those [meanings]. (143)

"Division" (*vibhāga*) refers to the distinction between base, suffix, and so forth, which is conceptually constructed for the purpose of instruction to others. For example: "the suffixes *tavyat* and others [are applied] to the verbal root.

And thus it has been said: "He teaches first that much which he is able to teach in a general manner. "Non-division" (*avibhāga*), however, occurs where there is utterance according to its own form (*svarūpa*). For example: "dādharti, dardharti, dāśvān, sāhvān."

Some grammatical treatises, being largely undifferentiated, establish many words through the method of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Others, however, by means of differentiation and the method of inference (*anumāna*), provide an exposition of many composite groups. This very tradition (*smṛti*) is established in various ways according to the time and in consideration of human capacity. Indeed, the learned (*śiṣṭas*) are to be inferred solely from their correct linguistic usage (*sādhu-prayoga*).

With an internal luminosity unobstructed regarding all objects of knowledge, they perceive, at the appropriate time, the power of sound—which possesses a specific division culminating in the *akalā* state—as being invariably endowed with the nature of both dharma and the means to dharma. || 143 ||
They say that the Śruti is beginningless, uninterrupted, and authorless;
however, the Smṛti, being composed by the learned, is not interrupted [in its continuity].

Those who hold that verbal testimony alone is the sole means of valid cognition, and who consider everything based on scriptural authority to be unreliable regarding matters whose fruits are unseen—since human perception is suspect in such cases—and who believe that a person’s vision is not a valid authority for them: for these people, since there is no difference in the uninterrupted continuity of the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, and since the eternity of the meaning of both is equal, the *Śruti*—with its unerring sequence of accents, phonemes, and word-order, and its fixed rules of place and time—is not something previously established by any author through some other means, but exists at all times and in all places, distributed according to the divisions of each lineage (*carana*).

It has been established that memory, however, has as its object something that is eternally uninterrupted; it is merely composed in various ways at different times by the learned, through the distinctions of prose, verses, sentences, and so forth.

Regarding this, some teachers hold the view that no action—whether seen or unseen (or having a visible or invisible purpose)—is [inherently] determined by its nature (*prakṛti*). Rather, through the mere performance of what is prescribed in the scriptures, there is the manifestation of merit (*dharma*); and from the transgression of the scriptures, one becomes joined with demerit (*pratyavāya*). For it is precisely those acts, such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa and so forth, which are sinful in one context, that are ordained by the scripture as causes for excellent prosperity in another context.

Others, however, think as follows: the scripture merely restates that the very power of an entity has its objects restricted [by nature]. For what purpose would the scripture serve for a cause that acts like a mere player, other than through the favor or injury of persons? Since one must accept the inherent nature of the scripture, it appears more logical to accept the inherent nature of substances themselves.

For instance, in the case of Smṛtis concerning perceptible matters such as medical treatment, efficacy is observed in the performance of purposeful actions—just as it is with poisons, medicines, and the like—but not in the case of the Smṛti scriptures themselves. Therefore, just as the nature of the scripture is [established], so too this nature of substances and so forth is restated by the scripture according to another perspective.
Just as the causes of injury and the causes of benefit are established in the world, even so there exists an uninterrupted establishment of the means for attaining those [results]. 144.
The manifestation of evolved things occurs without division, as is known from scripture, like a dream;
however, having discerned the true nature of existence through its signs, the Smṛti has been prescribed.

For those who hold the view that this activity of the world proceeds eternally through its various divisions, such that there is no arrangement of *yugas* or *manvantaras*, nor does any specific division of day and night belonging to Brahmā exist—the practice of dharma according to the *Śruti* and *Smṛti* has already been explained by them in the immediately preceding verse.

But for those for whom the cause proceeds by imitating the eternally distinct Puruṣas through the functions of dreaming and waking, certain sages evolve within the intellect (*pratibhā*); perceiving the Great Self, whose characteristic is pure existence, as the source of ignorance, they attain [the truth] through awakening.

Some, however, turn toward knowledge (*vidyā*). They perceive the knot of the mind—the self—as being within each of the elements, such as space, or within them collectively, as something pure, unbound by conceptual construction; they thus come to be in that very state. For them, the entire conventional usage of ignorance (*avidyā*) is merely adventitious and secondary, whereas their essential nature as knowledge is eternal, non-adventitious, and primary.

And like those in a dream, they perceive through wisdom alone the entirety of the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*)—which is beyond the reach of the ear—as possessing all powers of differentiation and yet endowed with undifferentiated power.

However, some, having perceived the nature of those objects as being within the scope of favoring or harming persons, and having observed indicative marks (liṅgas) concerning them in certain traditional scriptures (āmnāyas), compose Smṛtis that deal with both seen and unseen matters. As for the Śruti, they transmit it first exactly as it was perceived—unalterable in its words and undivided—and then again, having collected it, they recite it with the divisions of its sections (caraṇas) established; such is the tradition (āgama). || 145 ||
The impurities that reside within the objects of body, speech, and mind are purified by the medical sciences and the treatises on inner spirituality (*adhyātma-śāstra*). (146)

For just as the science of medicine was composed after observing the power of the bodily humors (*doṣa*) in the body and the capacity of gems, medicinal herbs, and so forth to counteract those humors; and just as the treatises on the inner self (*adhyātma-śāstra*) were compiled after understanding that passion and the like are afflictions of the intellect, serving as means for the knowledge of the causes that destroy them—so too has this grammatical definition (*lakṣaṇa*) been undertaken for the purpose of making known the refinements of the speech of the virtuous and for the abandonment of corruptions (*apabhraṃśa*), which are its afflictions. 146.
That word which is devoid of grammatical refinement when one intends to employ it as "gauh" (cow), they call an apabhraṃśa (corrupt form), even though it conveys a specific meaning. (147)
Furthermore, what kind of things are corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*)?

The author of the *Saṃgraha* states that "corrupt form is the nature (*prakṛti*) of the word. There exists no independent corrupt form that is not [itself] a nature. For indeed, the correct form (*sādhu*) alone is the nature of every corrupt form. However, certain corrupt forms, by attaining the status of conventional usage through common renown, acquire a sense of independence.

In that regard, when the word *gauḥ* ought to be employed, words such as *gāvī* and others—which are its variants (*tatprakṛti*) and non-corruptions (*abhraṃśa*)—may be used due to incapacity or through negligence and the like. These [variants], having acquired their own forms in reference to that which possesses a dewlap and so forth, abandon their grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*). However, when they are employed in a different sense, they are understood to be indeed correct. For their lack of correctness is not tied solely to their phonetic form. || 147 ||
Words such as *aśvagoṇī* and others are correct in a different sense;
and correctness is established everywhere according to the difference in the underlying cause (*nimitta*). (148)

In the case of *āvapana* (a container for pouring), the word *goṇī* (a sack) and the word *asva* (one who has no horse) possess established correctness (*sādhutva*) when they denote their respective specific applications. Likewise, when these two words—having acquired their grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) in other domains—are applied to something else due to another cause, such as the presence of a dewlap or the sign of neighing, their correctness is indeed recognized. Thus, "this cow is like a *goṇī*" or "this cow is a *goṇī*" is said because of the commonality of being a vessel for holding much milk and so forth. Similarly, one who lacks his own property (*sva*) is called *asva*.
Therefore, there is no fixed entity whatsoever that is not grasped by a cause, wherein correctness or incorrectness could be established. || 148 ||
In the case of virtuous persons, they become the causes for the arising of conviction through inference;
as if having attained identity with them, they reveal the meaning of the words. (149)

For corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*) employed in place of correct words (*sādhūnāṃ śabdānām*) convey their meaning through the medium of the correct word, just as winks of the eyes and the like, once their nature has been grasped through familiarity, become well-known signs; however, they do not possess direct denotative power (*sākṣād-abhidhāna*). This is established by the introduction of the following verse. || 149 ||

The learned do not follow them, just as they do not follow synonymous words; because they are governed by the treatises of traditional law (smṛti), they are therefore not directly expressive [of dharma]. (150)

Now, why are these forms such as *gāvī* and so on not recognized as synonyms for the word *go*? For in matters concerning the composition of traditional law (*smṛti*), no basis other than the established practice of the learned (*śiṣṭa*) is stated for such types of cases. If *gāvī* and the others were indeed synonyms, they too would be followed by the learned through grammatical rules and would be employed [correctly]. That which functions among expressive words according to the standard of direct perception is "correct" (*sādhu*). By means of correct words, the directly expressive form of the meaning is conveyed. This is the meaning expressed in the verse. (150)
Just as a child practicing speech utters "amma-amma" indistinctly, yet by that very sound those who know it reach a certain conclusion regarding the distinct word. (151)

For a child, due to a deficiency in the power of the articulatory organs, even when exerting effort with the desire to employ correct words, may produce an indistinct sound; at that time, the listeners perceive the distinct word which is its source (the original form). They consider that very [distinct word] to be the one connected with the meaning. Therefore, he says: "Not the corrupt form uttered by a child. (151)

Thus, when a correct word (*sādhū*) ought to be employed, if an incorrect form (*apabhraṃśa*) is used instead, some meaning is expressed by that [incorrect form] only through the mediation of the correct word. (152)

When speech is confused, incorrect words (*apaśabda*) are employed even in relation to correct ones (*sādhu*). Through these, the learned who know the grammatical rules (*lakṣaṇavid*) understand the correct words; they perceive that very meaning being expressed by those correct words alone. Just as smoke is the means of inferring fire, so too is the incorrect word [the means] for others. (152)
When corrupt forms have attained common usage through tradition among speakers who lack proficiency, the corresponding correct form is no longer expressive [of that meaning]. (153)

In this world, due to habitual usage, corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*) employed by women, *śūdras*, *caṇḍālas*, and others have become established even among speakers who are prone to error; consequently, linguistic practice is more commonly conducted by means of those very forms. And when doubt arises regarding the use of correct words (*sādhu*), a determination is now made on the basis of that which is the corruption (*apabhraṃśa*). Furthermore, they regard that very incorrect form as the expressive word (*vācaka*) in the position of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), while they establish the correct word in the position of inference (*anumāna*). || 153 ||
This divine speech has been thrown into confusion by incompetent expounders; however, for those who perceive only the impermanent, there is a perversion of intellect regarding this doctrine. (154)

It is heard that in a former age, humans possessed bodies of light, and just as their speech was uncorrupted by falsehoods and the like, so too was it uncorrupted by any corrupt forms (apabhraṃśas). However, as that speech became corrupted through the persistence of the habitual tendencies of previous faults, it gradually attained the status of a naturalized habit for those speakers over time.

However, those proponents of impermanence who do not recognize that [the usage of] the correct words (*sādhūnām*) is the cause of *dharma*, and who consider the established order of correct words to be like the conventions of wrestlers and the like, describe the collection of correct words as *prākṛta*—that which exists in its original nature (*prakṛtau bhavam*). But the *vikāra* (modification) is that which is subsequently established by persons of distinct intellects, and is determined through accent, grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*), and so forth. || 154 ||
Because there is no interruption between the two, when another word is employed with the intention of expressing something else, that other word is not the designator of the [intended] meaning. (155)

Furthermore, even for those who have no ancient tradition (purākalpa) and for whom there was never any unconfused divine speech (*daivī vāk*), this distinction between correct and incorrect words is remembered by the learned (*śiṣṭa*) as an eternal, uninterrupted convention—just like the rules regarding what women may or may not be approached. In that regard, both a word that is conventionalized (*rūḍha*) when used for certain meanings with the intention of expressing another word—like the prattle of a child—and one that is not so conventionalized, are neither denoters (*vācaka*) of that meaning.

In that case, however, the comprehension of the meaning may be mediated by a virtuous person, or else, due to habituation—as in the case of the winking of an eye—it produces merely a conventional understanding among those who are negligent. || 155 ||
Thus ends the Brahmakāṇḍa, titled Āgamasamuccaya, in the Vākyapadīya composed by the illustrious Harivṛṣabha, the great grammarian.
Now begins the second book (*kāṇḍa*).

Thus, the nature and other characteristics of the word (*śabda*), along with its purpose, have been briefly determined; and its status as a general signifier (*vācakatva*) has been established. Now, according to the difference of opinions—some holding that the word (*pada*) is the signifier and others that the sentence (*vākya*) is—the second book is commenced in order to present at length the nature of the sentence, which is the essence of the signifier.
In this regard, relying on the differences among the teachers' views, he first states the definition of the sentence:

The verbal form (ākhyāta), the aggregate (saṅghāta), the genus (jāti) residing in the aggregate, the single partless word (śabda), and the sequence as a mental synthesis—[these are the views regarding the nature of the sentence]. (1)

Regarding the definition of a sentence, the views of the proponents of logic (nyāyavādins) are manifold: some hold that every word is distinct [from others], while others maintain that every word must be semantically expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*). (2)

These are the eight alternative views of sentences held by the teachers. Among them, in the view that the sentence is indivisible (*akhaṇḍapakṣa*), there are three definitions: the universal (*jāti*) residing in the aggregate, the single partless word (*ekonavayavaḥ śabdaḥ*), and the synthesis by the intellect (*buddhyanusaṃhṛti*). In the view that the sentence is divisible (*khaṇḍapakṣa*), however, there are five definitions: the verbal form (*ākhyātaśabda*), the sequence (*krama*), the aggregate (*saṅghāta*), the first word (*padamādyam*), and every word individually as possessing expectancy (*pṛthaksarvaṃ padaṃ sākāṅkṣam*). Here too, "aggregate" and "sequence" constitute two definitions according to the view of *abhihitānvaya* (the connection of expressed meanings).

The division [of definitions] under the theory of *anvitābhidhāna* (expression of the related) consists of three characteristics: "the verbal form (*ākhyātaśabdaḥ*)," "the first word (*padamādyam*)," and "each word is distinct yet expectant (*pṛthagarthaṃ padaṃ sākāṅkṣam*).

In this context, the *Prātiśākhya* states: "The *saṃhitā* is the source of the words (*padaprakṛtiḥ*). Therein, the view that the *saṃhitā* is the cause or origin of the words arises as the "undivided" (*akhaṇḍa*) position; the view that the words are its source arises as the "divided" (*khaṇḍa*) position. Among these, it will be demonstrated later in the section on the determination of word-meaning (*śabdārthanirṇaya*) that the verbal form is the sentence (*vākya*). For example:
"Where a specific means [of accomplishment] is understood from a verb (ākhyāta-śabda),
that too is called a single sentence whose meaning is complete," as stated in the passage beginning with "the meaning [is conveyed] by the word alone."

By means of eight verses, he will demonstrate that the sentence (*vākya*) is a composite whole (*saṅghāta*), through the passage beginning with "Just as a single [entity] has all meanings" and ending with "In the same way, Devadatta and others would be meaningless within a sentence. Likewise, by means of the passage beginning with "The unmanifest, possessing sequence" and ending with "by which the meaning is distinguished from differences," it is shown that the sentence is indeed the indivisible word characterized as *sphoṭa*.

And it has been said: "That which, when uttered, causes one to comprehend the object-form characterized by the dewlap, tail, hooves, hump, and horns—that is *śabda*"; likewise: "*Sphoṭa* is *śabda*; *dhvani* is a quality of *śabda*."

And *sphoṭa* is of two kinds: external and internal. The external is also twofold, distinguished by genus (*jāti*) and individual (*vyakti*). Among these, the definition of that characterized as genus is "genus residing in a collection," while the definition of that characterized as individual is "the single, partless word. As for the internal, its designation is given by the phrase "the synthesis by the intellect" (*buddhyanusaṃhṛti*). Therein, the nature of the external [sphoṭa] characterized as genus and individual is stated again by the passage beginning with "just as one alone... and continuing with "unmanifest and sequential... and so forth.

By the four verses beginning with "That which is the inner essence of sound," the nature of the internal [sentence] is stated; by the four verses beginning with "In the comprehension [of meaning]," he will demonstrate that the sequence is the sentence. And by the two verses beginning with "The goal is fixed upon the means," he will explain the two definitions: that the first word [is the sentence] and that every word is individually expectant of others. Furthermore, there is another technical definition of a sentence in the treatise provided by the author of the Vārttika: "A sentence is a finite verb (ākhyāta) together with its indeclinables, kārakas, and qualifiers, containing a single finite verbal suffix (ekatiṅ)."

There is also a worldly definition stated by the Jaran-Mīmāṃsakas: "A sentence is one because of the unity of its purpose, provided that if it were divided, there would be mutual expectancy. These two [definitions] are included within the category of the *saṅghāta* (composite).

These too will be examined first under the section beginning with "for the sake of establishing the rules for *nighāta* (elision) and so forth. Thus, it should be understood that there are exactly eight varieties of sentences according to different philosophical views.

Furthermore, as for what was stated by him [the author] regarding the *vṛtti*: "This is merely an illustration; he will show other definitions of sentences (*vākyalakṣaṇa*) as well"—this should be understood as being said without regard for the inclusion of the definitions of sentences provided by the author of the *Vārttika* and others. And since he will reveal the nature of the defined sentence-definitions in their proper order later on through the *kārikās* themselves, there is no purpose in demonstrating them here.

In connection with the definition of the sentence (*vākya*), he will likewise demonstrate the various opinions regarding the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*) and its relation. Among these, according to the theory of the indivisible sentence (*akhaṇḍapakṣa*), intuition (*pratibhā*) is the meaning of the sentence in all three definitions. As he will show:
"When the [individual] meanings are perceived as distinct, a unique intuition arises;
they call that the meaning of the sentence."

Among the remaining five characteristics, according to the position that "a sentence is a word containing a verb," the meaning of the sentence is action (*kriyā*). As he will state: "Action is distinct from other actions," and so forth; and as:
"That intuition which possesses abundant meaning, in which practice is based..."

"Since that action which brings forth the fruit is the domain of the sentence. Furthermore, according to the view that [the sentence] is a composite, the meaning of the sentence is a conjunction (*saṃsarga*). And this—when a relation exists, whatever further surplus arises—is [the sentence-meaning].
They have declared this to be the meaning of a sentence, which rests upon many words.

This will be demonstrated by the passage beginning with "ityādi. Likewise, while the position of *abhihitānvaya*—namely that "conformity with all distinctions" (*sarvabhedānuguṇyam*) and so forth—is being expounded under the view of the aggregate (*saṅghātapakṣa*), the verse "The relation is to be inferred from its effect; its form does not exist" indicates that the meaning of the words themselves, as resting upon their specific particulars, constitutes the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). However, in these two positions—that the first word [is the sentence] and that every word is individually expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*)—the sentence-meaning is understood primarily as something already integrated. As he will explain:
"But for them, the entire meaning of the sentence is completed with each individual division," and likewise:
"Just as each subsequent essential nature is followed by preceding meanings..."
"Thus, in the case of primary objects of meaning, it is indeed their association that is under discussion.
By the statement, "The referent of a word is the denotable object, while the purpose is the referent of a sentence," the purpose is shown to be the referent of the sentence.
According to the view of some, that [purpose] is common to all definitions; therefore, the meaning of the statement regarding purpose is not separately divided among the definitions of sentences.

Thus, six types of sentence-meanings have been presented here: intuition (*pratibhā*), syntactic connection (*saṃsarga*), the word-meaning itself as established in its specific state and rendered free of expectancy through the force of that connection, the connected meaning (*saṃsṛṣṭa-artha*), action (*kriyā*), and purpose (*prayojana*).

In the case of *saṃsarga* (relation), and in the case of the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*) which is a specific state of an object established through the force of that relation, there is *abhihitānvaya* (the connection of what has been expressed). In the case of the action (*kriyā*) as related [to its factors], there is *anvitābhidhāna* (the expression of what is already connected). However, since in the case of *pratibhā* (intuitive flash) the comprehension is of a single flavor, there is no discussion whatsoever regarding *abhihitānvaya* or *anvitābhidhāna* therein. As for the *prayojana* (purpose), it is indeed *abhihitānvaya*.

The designations *vidhi* (injunction), *niyoga* (commission), and *bhāvanā* (productive activity) as the meanings of a sentence have not been definitively established, because *bhāvanā* and *kriyā* (action) are for the most part observed to be synonyms. There is merely a dispute here between the Grammarians and the Mīmāṃsakas regarding whether these constitute the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*) or the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*).

Some [scholars] maintain that *bhāvanā* is both "with an object" (*sakarmika*) and "without an object" (*akarmika*), and thus, despite the difference [in terminology], there is no actual distinction between these two because they are equally things to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Just as the action (*kriyā*) which constitutes the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is exclusively of the nature of something to be accomplished, so too is *bhāvanā*; how then could there be a distinction between these two based on a mere internal difference? As for "injunction" (*vidhi*) and "mandate" (*niyoga*), since these are meanings that apply only to sentences ending in the optative (*liṅ*), imperative (*loṭ*), or gerundive (*kṛtya*) suffixes, they are not accepted here because their scope is not universal; therefore, they have not been demonstrated in this context.

The meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*) for the Śākyas is essentially this: it is a specific conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that arises from the awakening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) deposited by various beginningless conceptualizations of sentence-meanings; it is delineated as a form superimposed (*adhyasta*) as having an external nature—though it is actually partless—and which, though non-sequential, appears as if variegated by word-meanings (*padārtha*) that are themselves superimposed as having an external nature and appear to be sequential. Therefore, it should be understood as residing primarily within the interior of the manifestation itself (*pratibhāsa*).

A sentence, too, arises from the awakening of latent impressions (vāsanā) deposited by various beginningless verbal conceptualizations; though its constituent words are sequential, it appears as if variegated by non-sequential words. This specific form, which is superimposed as an external reality and delineated by a distinct conceptualization, is itself superimposed as an external form. Thus, this [sentence] is essentially identical to the "synthesis of cognitions" (buddhyanusaṃhati). Therefore, one should understand that there is no failure to include the sentence and the sentence-meaning here according to that [Buddhist] view.

For the Naiyāyikas and others, however, just as the final phoneme—assisted by the memory of each preceding phoneme—is the word when it is made the object of an experience in its state of perishing, so too the very last word—assisted by the memory of each preceding word—is the sentence when it is made the object of an experience in its state of perishing; thus, this view generally falls within the category of the *saṃsarga* (synthetic) theory.

Likewise, since the cognition produced by the final word—assisted by the recollection of each preceding word—is the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), its inclusion is generally within the "relation" (*saṃsarga*) view itself; therefore, one need not allege an "under-extension" (*avyāpti*) here due to its non-inclusion therein. Alternatively, in this case, the relation between the sentence and the sentence-meaning is one of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), wherein the sentence is a single, partless entity consisting of *sphoṭa*, and the sentence-meaning is characterized as intuitive flash (*pratibhā*). As he will state: "The function of that which resides in the sentence [occurs] with respect to the sentence-meaning," and so forth.

Regarding the remaining positions, from the perspective of the Mīmāṃsakas, the relationship between word and meaning is solely that characterized as "fitness" (*yogyatā*), defined by the relation of signifier and signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*). However, according to the Buddhist view, following the system of the Vijñānavādins, in all cases where the word and its object are mental constructs, the relationship is strictly one of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). But in the theory of sentence-meaning (*vākyārthavāda*), that relationship should be understood there as being characterized by convention (*saṃketa*).

Furthermore, according to the Naiyāyikas and others, this [relation] is merely conventional (*saṃketa-lakṣaṇa*); thus, the essential nature of words, sentence-meanings, and their relations should be understood here in brief. Among these relations, he will demonstrate only superimposition (*adhyāsa*) here; however, in the section on words (*padakāṇḍa*), he will explain all of them.

In this regard, the commentator, intent upon refuting the position of those who maintain that words consist of discrete parts (*padavādin*), establishes the following as the summary of this section: for the grammarian (*vaiyākaraṇa*), the sentence is the indivisible, unitary, partless word characterized as *sphoṭa*; the meaning of the sentence is intuition (*pratibhā*) alone; and the relationship between them is superimposition (*adhyāsa*). (1–2)
Now, in order to investigate whether the two definitions of a sentence stated by the author of the *Vārttika* and the Mīmāṃsaka overlap or have distinct scopes, he says:

"That which is prescribed in the treatise for the sake of establishing rules such as accentuation (*nighāta*), and whose parts are mutually expectant (*sākāṅkṣāvayava*), is not entirely identical in its defining characteristics [to the other definition]. (3)

In this system, the rule regarding word-formation (*padavidhi*) is defined as occurring when there is semantic expectancy (*sāmarthya*). Even though such expectancy exists between words in the following cases, the application of rules such as *nighāta* (accentual suppression) is not desired: "This stick, take it with this" (*ayaṃ daṇḍo harānena*); "Cook the rice; it will be mine" (*odanaṃ paca mama bhaviṣyati*); and "Cook the rice; it will be yours" (*odanaṃ paca tava bhaviṣyati*). Here, because the pronoun "this" (*anena*) refers back to the stick, it possesses expectancy with the verb "take" (*harati*). Likewise, because the referent of the second-person pronoun (*yuṣmadartha*) is connected with the rice, the meaning of the verb "cook" (*pacatyartha*) possesses expectancy with that [pronoun].

And this being the case, if there were semantic connection (*sāmarthya*), the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* would require the suppression of accent (*nighāta*), and the substitutes *temayau* would apply to the singular ending according to the rule *temayāvekavacanasya*. However, these are not desired because they would result in a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*). Yet, even in the absence of semantic connection, these are desired, as in the examples: "He stands on the bank of the river" (*nadyāstiṣṭhati kūle*) and "I shall give you rice of the *śāli* variety" (*śālīnāṃ te odanaṃ dāsyāmi*).

In this case, because the connection between "the river" (*nadyāḥ*) and "stands" (*tiṣṭhati*) is untenable, there is no semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*); yet, the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) is desired. Similarly, there is an absence of semantic capacity between "of the rice-grains" (*śālīnām*) and "you" (*yuṣmad*), yet the substitution of *tema* and *ya* for the singular ending as prescribed by the rule *temayāvekavacanasya* is desired. Having considered this, and specifically the application of the substitutes for *yuṣmad*, the author of the Vārttika initiated [the following rule] for the sake of establishing the proper application of *nighāta* and other accents: "The *nighāta*, the substitutes for *yuṣmad*, and *asmad* must be stated to occur within a single sentence (*samānavākya*)."

And thus, in the case of *evaṃ cāyaṃ daṇḍaḥ*, even though there is semantic connection (*sāmarthya*), there is no occasion for the suppression of accent (*nighāta*), because the two words stand as distinct sentences due to the relationship between the limit (*avadhi*) and that which possesses the limit (*adhimat*). For with the ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) of "is," *ayaṃ daṇḍaḥ* constitutes one sentence, and *harānena* constitutes a second sentence. However, in cases such as *nadyāstiṣṭhati*, although there is an absence of semantic connection between the two words—the limit and that which possesses the limit—they nevertheless undergo suppression and other operations because they are situated within a single sentence; therefore, there is no lack of systematic rule (*avyavasthā*) regarding these.

It has been stated that "depression" (*nighāta*) and other such phenomena are to be explained within a single sentence (*samānavākya*). Since the state of being a single sentence is understood only when the sentence itself is known, the author of the *Vārttika*, in this context, first provides the definition of a sentence: "A sentence consists of a verb together with its indeclinables, kārakas, and qualifiers, and contains only one finite verbal suffix (*ekatiṅ*)."

Thus, it is investigated whether or not there is a complete overlap between this [definition] and that stated by the Mīmāṃsakas in all cases. Regarding the definition of a sentence formulated by the author of the *Vākyapadīya* in the *Śāstra* for the sake of establishing rules such as the *nighāta* accent, the entire definition of a sentence stated by the Mīmāṃsakas is not identical in its characteristics. By the phrase "having parts that are expectant" (*sākāṅkṣāvayavam*), the definition of a sentence stated by the Mīmāṃsakas is indicated. In some instances, these two coincide; for example: *nadī tiṣṭhati kūle* ("The river stands on the bank") and *śālīnāṃ te odanaṃ dāsyāmi* ("I shall give you rice of the *śāli* variety").

In cases such as "Bring this staff," "Take this rice," or "Cook [this] for you," there is no inclusion [of these sentences within the definition of a single sentence]. By adopting the Mīmāṃsaka definition of a sentence, [the rules regarding] *nighāta* (elision of accent) and so forth would apply here because they serve a single purpose; yet these are not desired. Therefore, the definition of a sentence provided by the author of the Vārttika alone is superior. || 3 ||

Now, in this context, he states [the following] in order to demonstrate the definition of a sentence according to the Mīmāṃsakas by way of its meaning: "A sentence is held to be that which has parts requiring mutual expectancy, whose constituent words do not require further external words, which has action as its primary element, possesses qualifiers, and conveys a single unified meaning. (Verse 4)

When there is a division or a distinction and a desire for further specification arises, that whose constituent parts possess such expectancy is [a sentence]. However, in the absence of such division, those words which have no further expectancy are "words" (*pada*). That which consists of such words having no further expectancy is [the definition of a sentence]. The meaning is that it has action as its primary element—that is, the verb (*kriyāpada*) is predominant. The intention is that this is because it is employed by the primary object of expression. It is "possessed of qualities," meaning it is joined with qualifying words (*viśeṣaṇapada*). It has "a single purpose," meaning it has one objective. || 4 ||

Now, having raised the objection that the definition of a sentence provided by the author of the *Vārttika* is under-extended (*avyāpti*), he says: "And that which is a vocative word is a qualifier of the verb;
thus, in the case of 'vrajāni devadatta' (O Devadatta, let me go), there would be a *nighāta* accent [on the verb]. (5)

Regarding the objection that in the sentence *vrajāni devadatta*, the word *devadatta* is neither an indeclinable (*avyaya*), nor a case-factor (*kāraka*), nor a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) [of the verb]; thus, because it is not subsumed by the definition of a "sentence" (*vākya*), the eighth-case rule *āmantritasya ca* (Pāṇini 8.1.19) prescribing the low-pitched accent (*nighāta*) would not apply—the answer is as follows: Since it is stated in general terms that "a sentence consists of a verb along with its indeclinables, its case-factors, and its qualifiers," a verb accompanied by a qualifier of the action (*kriyā-viśeṣaṇa*) is also a sentence; therefore, there is no fault.

For instance: here, the action of "going" (*vrajatikriyā*) has as its object Devadatta who is being addressed; it is entirely distinct from the action of "going" that has as its object Devadatta who is not being addressed, or that which has as its object Yajñadatta who is being addressed. Thus, the action of going here is indeed qualified (*viśiṣṭā*). Furthermore, a qualifier of an action sometimes occurs through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), as in "he does well" (*suṣṭhu karoti*) or "he does beautifully" (*śobhanaṃ karoti*). In these cases, because the meaning of the verb "to do" is perceived precisely as qualified by qualifiers such as "well," words like "well" stand in coreferentiality with the action expressed by "to do."

And thus, since this is an adjective qualifying an action that is not a substance (*asattvabhūtā*), it is connected with the neuter gender—the universal term for gender—because its primary nature is non-substantial. Furthermore, since an action is something to be accomplished (*nirvartya*), it possesses the status of an object (*karman*); this is established by logic itself. Therefore, the statement "the status of being an object and the neuter gender belong to adverbs of action" (*kriyāviśeṣaṇānāṃ karmatvaṃ napuṃsakaliṅgatā ca*) need not have been formulated as a rule. Moreover, an adjective can function even when there is a difference in grammatical coreference (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), as in the example: *vrajāni devadatta* ("I am going, O Devadatta").

For in this case, "O Devadatta, go" (*devadatta vrajāni*), there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between Devadatta and the act of going. Rather, having addressed Devadatta, [the sentence] means "he goes"; thus, the verbal form (*ākhyāta*)—which is the distinct act of going qualified solely by the address to Devadatta—is indeed accompanied by a qualifier. Since the definition of a sentence is fulfilled, the *nighāta* (the low-pitched accent for the vocative) certainly occurs. An example such as "O Devadatta, go" (*devadatta vrajāni*) was not shown [in the rule] because, according to the principle "a preceding vocative is treated as non-existent," the *nighāta* would not otherwise apply. || 5 ||
Furthermore, having raised the doubt that the definition provided by the author of the *Vārttika* suffers from the fault of being under-extended (*avyāpti*), he says [the following] to resolve it:

"Just as even a single word ending in the suffix *-ktvā* can be a qualifier for a word ending in a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*), so too in that case, a word ending in a verbal suffix can be a qualifier for another word ending in a verbal suffix. (Verse 6)

In this case, regarding the sequence "he bathes first, then he cooks, then he goes," the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) does not apply to the word *vrajati* following the word *tataḥ*, because there is a division of sentences (*vākya-bheda*). And yet, such an accent is desired. Here, since the prohibition *atiṅ* prevents the *nighāta* of a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) following another finite verb, the cessation of the *nighāta* is established; therefore, one should not raise the objection that the *nighāta* does not apply to the word *pacati* following the word *snāti*. Rather, what should be raised here is precisely the non-attainment of the desired *nighāta*.

To this it is replied: there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) here. The word *vrajati* ("he goes") stands as the single principal verb; the other verbs are merely its qualifiers. Just as the action of going is qualified by the verbal nouns *snāna*, *bhojana*, and *pāna*, so too here the principal action of going itself is qualified by the finite verbs *snāti* and so forth. Thus, there is only one action of going here, accompanied by its qualifiers.

However, since this [particle] alone forms a single sentence with its qualifier as "pṛthag eva," there is no fault of failing to achieve *nighāta* (the low-pitched accent) due to the absence of sentence division (*vākya-bheda*). Furthermore, in the case of a single sentence, because of the prohibition "after a finite verb (*tiṅanta*), another finite verb is not [accented]"—specifically by the rule *atiṅ*—there is an absence of *nighāta*. As he will state: "Even when there are many finite verbs, if they are mutually expectant, they constitute a single sentence;
thus, the exclusion of *nighāta* for finite verbs after other finite verbs is purposeful."

Since the purpose for including the term *atiṅ* (not being a finite verb) has thus been established, one must state the intention behind what the author of the Vārttika said: "The inclusion of *atiṅ* is useless because of the governing rule [restricting the definition] to a single sentence (*samānavākya*). The intention of that proponent is that a division of sentences (*vākyabheda*) is intended here; this is because, in the rule *ākhyātaṃ savyayakārakaviśeṣaṇam*, the singular number (*ekavacana*) is intended to be significant. Accordingly, the commentator will demonstrate:
"But for one for whom the definition of 'a single finite verb' (*ekatiṅ*) is fixed by the treatise, there is no need for the inclusion of *atiṅ*, as there is no [need for] a division of sentences."

However, from the author of the *Sūtra*’s inclusion of the term "not being a finite verb" (*atiṅ*), it is understood that he intends a single, indivisible sentence even when there is a difference in finite verbs, because of the unity of meaning. Following precisely that intention, he will explain: "Even when there is a connection with multiple finite verbs, those who follow the path of logic maintain that the sentence is indeed one, though it stands as if it were divided in form."
Thus [ends section] 6.

The commentator, considering this very position to be logically sound as it accords with the intention of the author of the Sūtras, and desiring to set forth the view that "the sentence is indeed the *sphoṭa*—which is of the nature of consciousness, consisting of word and meaning, whether external or internal, and devoid of divisions"—proceeds by first presenting the analogies of variegated cognition and variegated form. In that regard, for the purpose of presenting the analogy of variegated cognition, he says: "Just as a single cognition of all objects is divided according to the appearance of diverse visible forms, so too is the comprehension of the meaning of a sentence. (7)

Cognitive awareness (*citrajñāna*), though possessing all forms, is indeed one. Its differentiation is established by relying upon the distinctions within the perceived objects; thus, it is said that consciousness arises with many forms such as blue, yellow, and so forth. In reality, however, there is no differentiation of forms within that cognition. The same essential nature should be understood to apply to both the sentence and its meaning.

By the phrase "so too is the following of the sentence-meaning" (*vākyārthānugama*), it is stated that the indivisibility (*akhaṇḍatva*) of both the sentence and its meaning is exactly the same—as in the case of the taste of a beverage (*pānakarasa*), the yolk of a peacock's egg, a variegated form, Narasiṃha, a gavaya, or a variegated cognition. Just as the sentence, characterized as *sphoṭa*, is an indivisible signifier (*vācaka*), so too the sentence-meaning is of that very same nature; thus, their shared fate (*ekayogakṣematva*) is asserted. || 7 ||
Having thus demonstrated an internal example, he speaks in order to demonstrate an external one as well:
"Just as a painting, though having a single nature, is designated by means of distinctions such as blue and so forth, which possess different characteristics. (8)

For the variegated form belonging to the whole is indeed partless and one; yet, by means of those [colors] such as blue and so forth which possess differentiation through their belonging to the parts, its manifestation—that is, its demonstration—is performed through distinct forms. (8)
Thus, he asks what applies to the present case: "In the same way, the designation of a single sentence that is entirely free from expectancy is followed by other words that possess expectancy. (9)
In this manner, the explanation of a single, indivisible, and entirely complete sentence is carried out by means of other words contained within subsequent sentences. || 9 ||

Or rather, according to the view that "there is no [real division] because of the application [of words] to the meaning," just as a word—which is in fact an indivisible unit—is analyzed into base, suffix, and so forth, which are themselves conceptual constructs, so too in a sentence, the division into words must be seen as occurring among elements that are unreal, for the purpose of instructing the ignorant. To demonstrate this, he says:
"Just as in a word the base, suffix, and so forth are divided, so too in a sentence the extraction (*apoddhāra*) of words is described. (10)

For it should be understood that just as the division between stem and suffix within a word is unreal and is merely constructed for the sake of teaching beginners, so too, the extraction of individual words from a sentence is presented for the purpose of conveying the meaning of the sentence. || 10 ||

To demonstrate that, in the case of words extracted from a sentence, only a mere similarity to other words is observed, he says: "And a similarity to other phonemes is seen within the portions of phonemes; likewise, portions of words remain as similar to other words. (11)
