Just as in the case of the diphthongs (*saṃdhyakṣara*), parts resembling other phonemes (*varṇa*) are perceived, yet in ultimate reality they are indeed partless because they are indivisible; so too, within a sentence, there are parts in the form of words that resemble other internal elements—namely, word-parts (*padabhāga*). Or, within a partless word, those parts consisting of stems (*prakṛti*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*) are likewise established. || 11 ||
Clarifying this very point, he says:
"The bull, water, and barley-gruel are joined with useless parts;
rather, positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) are the basis for linguistic convention. (12)

In the case of "na hi vṛṣabhe" (not indeed in a bull), there is no semantic correspondence whatsoever between the word *ṛṣabha* and the words *udaka* (water) or *yāvaka* (barley-gruel). However, how could an ignorant person be taught [the meaning of] a word in the science [of grammar] without recourse to the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of stems and suffixes? And thus, it is logical that the indivisible sentence alone is the expressive unit. || 12 ||
There is no division in sound; how then could there be one in the object? It is only the ignorant who perceive a difference in grammatical derivation through divisions that do not exist.

(The Commentary in the form of an auto-commentary)—For that word which is thus perceived as being composed of parts that occur non-simultaneously and possess an unestablished sequence of distinctions based on differences in cause, form, and result; for such a word, under the view of its eternity, this division—which is postulated as the object of linguistic usage, which conforms to the causes of the substance’s capacity, and which is superimposed upon words—does not exist. Why? Because when cognitions do not attain simultaneity, there can be no [succession] of one cognition within another cognition.

Alternatively, in order to demonstrate that the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*) is likewise indivisible, he says: "Of the word," and so forth. There is no division in the word characterized as *sphoṭa*; how then could there be one in its expressed object, which consists of intuitive flash (*pratibhā*)? As he will illustrate: "When the objects [of a sentence] are grasped as distinct, an entirely different intuition arises;
they call that the 'meaning of the sentence'."

When [the Self] bestows grace through constant proximity upon objects that are perceived by the intellect of the Pratyekabuddhas—objects which consist of a succession of distinct forms, which are essentially void, and which, though appearing as differentiated, are brought to a state of non-differentiation because they are not separate from the Self; and when, despite the difference in their own nature, all objects appear as mere manifestations of the intellect through its own conjoined cognition, wherein the notion of difference is not accepted as having parts; then, even though there is a difference in their own nature, there will be no differentiation among all objects.
Therefore, the essence of an object, whose prior and posterior states are intended, does not deviate from its own nature, and thus everything remains a reality that transcends all differentiation.

The mention of "division" (*vibhāga*) refers to the distinction between processes; for this division is the means of apprehending that which is non-different, both in its objective nature (*arthātman*) and its verbal nature (*śabdātman*). Indeed, the apprehension of the undivided occurs through division by means of a swift process, preceded by the apprehension of individual words, and employing the grasping of generalities and particulars—just like the apprehension of stems, suffixes, and so forth. However, in this case, the apprehension of the integrated form occurs through a slow process without division, like the recitation of each word as a whole.

But the proficient practitioner perceives all differentiation as not transcending non-differentiation. However, the various methods of analysis (*prakriyā-bheda*) serve as the basis for classification in the treatises. For instance, in the case of *haridru*, *mitadru*, *durdaśa*, and *dustara*: here, *mitadru* is subject to elision (*avagraha*), whereas *haridru* is not. Thus, the method of derivation differs according to the classification: [one may derive] *haridru* from *hari-dru* (yellow wood), or *haridrava* [from *hari-drava*]. Similarly, *dustara* is derived either from the root *tṛ* (to cross) or *tṛṇ* (to spread). Consequently, when the method of derivation differs according to the classification, there is no elision. Likewise: *indrāṇī*, *varuṇānī*, *pūtakratāyī*.

When there is an explanatory analysis based on the distinction between general and specific characteristics—such as *indrādīnām ānuk* and *pūtakrator ai ca*—the unlearned understand [the matter] through the various formal procedures of the grammatical treatise. || 13 ||

In accordance with that word, there is also the conceptualization of its constituent parts within the word-meaning, following the division of stem and suffix. However, the dull-witted person perceives a difference in grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*) through this division, and consequently perceives a difference in meaning—even though it is unreal. What can we do? Furthermore, we shall investigate how it is that words such as "Devadatta," which are perceived as having an audible form, could be devoid of meaning while their referents are being cognized. Moreover:
"Just as there is no such thing as a 'Brāhmaṇa' in a *brāhmaṇākambala* (a blanket belonging to a Brāhmaṇa), so too would words like 'Devadatta' be devoid of meaning within a sentence. (14)

For just as when [the words] "brāhmaṇa-kambala" are uttered with an interruption, the word "brāhmaṇa"—even though its own form is perceived—is well known to be meaningless to those perceivers who grasp the interruption and do not expect the completion [of the sentence], even while its meaning is being cognized; so too, although there is the perception of the division of forms and the cognition [of them], the word-forms such as "Nāda," "Devadatta," and so forth—which are parts considered to be distinct—are actually meaningless, utterly non-existent, and merely imagined natures. 14.

And this is logical: that there is no difference in meaning between the individual words within a sentence. He states this, preceded by the presentation of an example: "the meaning of *brāhmaṇa*. Just as in the word *brāhmaṇakambala* (a Brahmin’s blanket) there is no separate meaning for the word *brāhmaṇa*, so too in a sentence such as "Devadatta, bring the cow," there is no separate meaning for Devadatta and the other words; thus the words themselves are indeed meaningless.
And therefore, it is established that a sentence is an indivisible, self-sufficient unity distinct from the words, and likewise the sentence-meaning is distinct from the word-meanings. || 14 ||

Furthermore, if one accepts that words such as "Devadatta" and others, which are intended to denote parts [of a whole], are connected with their respective objects, then—given the premise that words established in a general sense must come to rest in a particular—the following would necessarily follow:

the general meaning would vanish and not abide in the particular. For how could there be the abandonment of what has already been grasped? And where could that which has ceased [its general function] abide? (15)

In this context, the word *devadatta*, when uttered as having a general application, disappears while still connected only with its general meaning. In that situation, a word by which a specific meaning has not been apprehended at the very moment of its manifestation is not capable of remaining fixed upon a particular [meaning]. Furthermore, the intention (*vivakṣā*) to express both the general and the particular simultaneously is not possible; for when there is an intention to express a particular, the delimitation from the general is understood through every [word] without restriction.

In that regard, since the relationship between word and meaning is eternal for the accepted [view], how could there be any abandonment of it? Furthermore, when the nature of the object is investigated through reasoning and the connection with the act of denotation is absent, the word—its essence being unascertainable because the object commenced by the word no longer exists—becomes a non-object; where, then, could it be established?

Furthermore, in order to refute what is asserted by the Mīmāṃsakas—that the collection of words itself, through the force of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), compatibility (*yogyatā*), and proximity (*sannidhāna*), constitutes a sentence when mutually connected, and that the meaning of the sentence is the relation (*saṃsarga*) [between the word-meanings]—he says: "The general meaning... Here, in the sentence "Devadatta, drive the white cow with a stick," the words "Devadatta" and so forth alone constitute the sentence.

In this regard, if the word "Devadatta" first denotes only the universal (sāmānya), then because speech functions sequentially, that word would have ceased [tirodhāna] at the time of the word "cow" and so forth; thus, being non-existent, how could there be a cognition of its meaning at the time of hearing a subsequent word? Furthermore, precisely because it is non-existent, it cannot abide in a particular (viśeṣa) upon the proximity of another word.

Even granting that a word exists in proximity to other words by virtue of being remembered, its restriction to a specific [meaning] is not tenable; thus he says: "of what has been taken up" (*upāttasya*). Why is the abandonment now—upon the proximity of other words—justified for that general meaning which was previously accepted as the denoted object (*vācya*), even though that general meaning is obscured by the definition common to all word-meanings? For this would entail the non-eternality of the relationship between word and meaning.

Furthermore, this is not the position accepted by the Mīmāṃsaka. Even granting that for the sake of argument, it is said: "It has ceased. Since this word has ceased from its own primary meaning upon the proximity of another word, where could it possibly abide now? How can its persistence be justified, given that it lacks the status of being expressive toward an object understood through another word? (15)

In that case, then, the sentence-meaning is non-verbal (*aśabda*). When the words—being causes for the mere apprehension of their own forms—have receded and a cognition has arisen characterized by a specific, unindicatable mental impression (*saṃskāra*), the words, having conveyed the mere meaning of the individual words, cease to function. At that point, the relationship—which is not denotable by words, which is non-substantial (*asattvabhūta*), and which serves as the cause of differentiation for the general forms of the objects of names—manifests itself and is subsequently integrated into further cognitions, just like grief, joy, and so forth. Regarding this view, it is said: "If the sentence-meaning is non-verbal, then the word-meaning would likewise be so."
And this being the case, the relationship between the word and its meaning is lost. (16)

How is it that, even when the phonemes (varṇas) themselves are devoid of meaning, one establishes their mere form in the intellect; and once they have ceased [to appear as such], through the force of habit, the form of the object—which has been designated by a specific cause—is connected to other cognitions as the means of cognition? In this way, the relationship between word and meaning is lost. Yet, in the same manner, substances, qualities, and actions—whose forms consist of established causes—are explained as being connected with manifesting causes. And cognition consists of the form of the object of knowledge as it has been established therein.

By another mode of relation, it is called a "relation" with respect to the objects to be known (*jñeya*). Furthermore, the cognition that has grasped the form of the object through the act of knowing is called a "relation" with the intellect (*buddhi*). Likewise, by another mode of relation called "fitness" (*yogyatā*), the word—which has grasped the form of the object and has its denotative essence established—is said to have a "relation" with each respective object despite the difference between word and object. However, according to the view that the object is a transformation of the state of consciousness (*arthabhāvapariṇati*), the relation is the closest of all. (16)

Now it is argued: "The comprehension of meaning is observed from a collection [of sounds] such as 'Devadatta'; how can that be denied? To this, he replies: "It is not a word" (*aśabda*). According to the principle already stated, words are not suitable as denoters. If, therefore, it is accepted that the sentence-meaning is "not a word" because of the absence of such [denotative words], then this is another fault for you. Furthermore, there is no such thing as a "word-meaning" (*padārtha*) to be conveyed by a word, because speech resides in many phonemes (*varṇa*) and because phonemes perish as soon as they are uttered; thus, even a single "word" does not exist. In its absence, what could a "word-meaning" be?

In this way, the Mīmāṃsaka would have to abandon the relationship characterized by the signifier-signified relation (*vācyavācakabhāva*) between word and meaning, on the grounds that the sentence-meaning is something not denoted by the individual words. To this he says: "And if this were so... (verse 16).
Certain particular words, which possess the appearance of general terms, are manifested to cognizers through their connection with other words. (17)

According to some proponents of a different grammatical system, words such as *devadatta*—which possess specific distinctions in their connection with actions like "eating" (as in *aśnāti*) similar to [the distinction between] "akṣa" and so on—are always the objects of sentences whose referents function as entirely delimited particulars. Because these are not delimited by perceivers who lack direct knowledge of the particulars due to their intellects being carried away by the universal, they resemble words for universals; yet, through their connection with other words, they are never joined with any adventitious meaning whatsoever.

The intention is this: because they are eternally established and fixed, they transcend any restrictive rule consisting of the superimposition of further qualifications; rather, they are manifested by speakers for listeners through mere restatement (*anuvāda*) so that other words may successfully denote their respective meanings, with their specific distinctions determined [by convention]. || 17 ||

Thus, the proponent of the theory that meaning is conveyed by the syntactical connection of words (*abhihitānvaya*) has been refuted. Now, wishing to demonstrate the definition of a sentence as it was previously stated—namely, that "the first word is distinct and every word is expectant" (*sākāṅkṣa*)—by resorting to the theory that meaning is conveyed by words already connected (*anvitābhidhāna*), he says: "The specific words... In this case, in the sentence "Devadatta, bring the cow," the word *devadatta* is uttered by the speaker as something specifically distinguished from "bring the cow"; however, due to error, it appears to be common to all [words].

Since a specific cognition is manifested at a later time through the connection with words such as "cow" and so forth, that very [initial cognition] is the sentence. And because the meaning, already commenced as something integrated and inlaid with all its qualifiers from the very beginning, is indeed a unified whole, it is the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). As he will state: "Just as each subsequent essential nature is followed by preceding meanings, so too is the integration itself commenced within those initial objective entities. (17)
However, those who maintain that the sentence-meaning is a single, indivisible entity denoted by a single word, while supporting their own view, provide this illustration:
"For them, however, the entire sentence-meaning is completed in each individual part; the manifestation of the meaning, along with its specific features, occurs among the cognizers. (18)

For those who accept that many words refer to a single object whose various specificities have been thus grasped, the entire meaning of the sentence is understood without conceptual differentiation, being completed either word by word or syllable by syllable. This view will be examined along with other alternative positions. For in this way, when the manifesting factors (*upavyañjana*) are clearly expressed, the meaning attains its established status among the cognizers; it does not arise from mere proximity when the manifesting factors are unexpressed. || 18 ||

To clarify this very point, he says: "But of these... At the very outset, for the purpose of communicating the intended meaning, one begins by uttering specific words; thus, it should be understood that the completion of the entire sentence-meaning occurs within the first word itself, whether individually or as a whole. Anticipating the objection that if the entire sentence-meaning were perceived from a single word alone, then subsequent words would be redundant, he says: "manifested... The establishment, that is, the comprehension, of the sentence-meaning among the listeners is "manifested through its indicators" (*vyaktopavyañjanā*).

That [cognition] is so described because it possesses specific words (*padaviśeṣa*) that are manifest, uttered, accompanied by secondary indicators (*upavyañjana*), and expressive (*abhivyañjaka*). Or rather, it is "the comprehension of the sentence-meaning through the manifestation of what is manifested. Thus, there is no redundancy whatsoever for other words within a sentence; this demonstrates the theory of *anvitābhidhāna* (the expression of the related). He will state the refutation of this later in various places, such as: "The Vedic revelation would be for the sake of restriction," and so forth.

For instance: if the entire meaning of a sentence—including all its specific qualifiers—were understood from a single word, then the utterance of subsequent words would serve only for restriction or for restatement. And this is not tenable, as we shall explain later. If the comprehension of the sentence-meaning, complete with all its qualifiers, arose from a single word alone, the subsequent words would certainly be redundant. Yet, the comprehension of the sentence-meaning is never observed to arise from that [single word] alone.

The claim that [words] possess both the primary meaning (*vyakta*) and the secondary indication (*upavyañjana*) is simply untenable. For is the determination of the sentence-meaning derived from a single word, with the others serving as its indicators (*upavyañjaka*), or is it derived from all of them together? In either case, since subsequent words are indeed employed for the cognition of the sentence-meaning, the theory of *abhihitānvaya* (the connection of what has been expressed) is inconsistent; likewise, the theory of *anvitābhidhāna* (the expression of what is already connected) is also untenable, because at the time of the utterance of a subsequent word, the preceding one has already vanished. Thus, there is a flaw regarding the objective portion (*arthabhāga*).

By relying on the division of the word (*śabdabhāga*), he will state the refutation of both positions with two verses beginning with "The words in the sentence are those very same [as those in the isolated state]," and so forth. || 18 ||
This sound, when unmanifest, is recited with sequence as a whisper;
but when it is without sequence, it is expanded out so that the intellect may rest therein.

For a single word possessing limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) exists as if divided across its various states: in the *saṃhitā* and non-*saṃhitā* modes, in the fast, medium, and slow tempos, as well as in the whispered (*śanaiḥ*), loud (*uccaiḥ*), low-voiced (*upāṃśu*), ultra-low-voiced (*paramopāṃśu*), and the state where the sequence is withdrawn (*saṃhṛtakrama*). Among these, that form of the word which, while being assisted by the activity of the vital breath (*prāṇavṛtti*), becomes imperceptible to others is called *upāṃśu*.

However, that which, without the assistance of the vital breath's activity, exists solely within the intellect (*buddhi*)—the very essence of the word consisting of the intellect itself—is the *paramopāṃśu*.

However, when by means of an intellect that has withdrawn its connection with sequential power, the sequential form of words—which was previously superimposed upon the unmanifest sound upon the arrival of other causes—is directly perceived as having its sequence withdrawn, then linguistic usage transcending the [individual] sounds begins; for this occurs when the intellect, whose object is the withdrawal of the sequential form of words, perceives that which is as if its true nature were no longer manifest.

And when their powers are merged, through the process of sequential withdrawal, they enter into the speakers who have mastered speech; having experienced a sequential operation within the vital breath and the organs of articulation by means of effort, they likewise attain immersion in the perceivers through the very dissolution of sequence.

In that state, the differentiation characterized by sequential operation—which follows the means of perception—does not even touch the empirical reality of the essence of sound (*śabdatattva*). For if one does not resort to the withdrawal of sequence, empirical transaction itself would be severed.

Therefore, just like [the perception of] space and so forth, that single cognition which occurs precisely where there is a division of the locations reached is itself the single word called "sentence" at the beginning and the end. || 19 ||

Now, with the desire to explain the distinctions in the manifestation [of speech], the author, adhering to the very position of the indivisible (akhaṇḍa), says: "The unmanifest," etc. Here, it is established that only the indivisible and undifferentiated sphoṭa—whether it be the individual sphoṭa (vyakti-sphoṭa) or the generic sphoṭa (jāti-sphoṭa)—whether external, internal, consisting of both word and meaning, or the mental synthesis (buddhyanusaṃhāra), is the sentence; and that alone is logically the signifier (vācaka). As for the appearance of differentiation, its meaning is that it is produced solely by limiting adjuncts (upādhi).

In the same way, it should be understood that appearances such as "inaudible," "extremely inaudible," "manifest," "more manifest," "slow," "slower," "rapid," and "more rapid" are produced by the manifesting sounds (*abhivyañjaka-dhvani*) and are not themselves real. Therefore, when a word is studied in an inaudible manner while being manifested, it is perceived as possessing a sequence due to the sequence of the manifesting sounds, and as being endowed with various states.

In ultimate reality, however, this manifestation whose nature is *sphoṭa* is indeed without succession; rather, it should be understood that, due to the influence of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), the intellect perceives it there as if it were extended. By this, the essential nature of the individual *sphoṭa* (*vyaktisphoṭa*)—which was previously introduced as "the single, partless word"—has been stated; so it should be understood. || 19 ||

And on this view of unity, there would be only one indivisible individual sound (*śabdavyakti*). Or else, that which is perceived as the individual sound or the form of the word (*śabdākṛti*) would have to be the sentence itself. In that case, how could there be difference or similarity for a single, partless entity? For difference and similarity consist in the distinction of different natures (*ātmāntara*); it is not the non-difference of nature, nor is it similarity. Rather, they are established even without [the categories of] universal and particular, just like other universals and particulars. This is just as, for example, [the action of] upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇatva*) and so forth is established even though its form is not previously known and it is partless. (To this, he replies:)

Just as the distinction between different actions is not perceived despite differences in their projection, so too is the genus manifested through the repetition of actions such as revolving and the like. (20)

In this way, the auditory perception of phonemes, words, and sentences—though possessing identical secondary characteristics—is perceived as if identical in form despite the absolute difference in their essential nature. (21)

For, due to a specific projection (*ākṣepa*), when an action such as whirling—which is distinct in its nature and resides in a particular variety of its own genus (*svajāti*)—is performed, the difference between it and actions such as shaking, throwing, or lifting is not perceived. However, when repetition is observed, conditioned by conjunctions and disjunctions with respect to specific spatial directions, a genus known as "whirling" or "throwing"—which was previously unperceived or only indistinctly perceived—becomes the cause of its own characteristic cognition for the perceivers.

In the same way, as long as there are similar generic characteristics (*jāti*) and secondary marks (*upavyañjana*), every object, even if entirely distinct, is apprehended by means of its similarity (*sārūpya*).

Another interpretation: it is precisely the universal of sound (*śabdajāti*) that constitutes the sentence, and [the examples] such as "wandering" (*bhramaṇa*) are presented as illustrations. For the universals of phoneme (*varṇatva*), word (*padatva*), and sentence (*vākyatva*) are manifested by similar and dissimilar [articulations]; they produce a distinct cognition for as long as there is a conjunction of similar manifestors. How so? First, a single phoneme is manifested by a diminished sound; then, by other similar causes of its manifestation, which are distinct in audition, a single partless word is manifested.
In the same way, a sentence is manifested by similar and dissimilar [articulations], or by those most highly diminished. (20–21)

Now, in order to clarify the *jāti-sphoṭa* (the universal-phoneme) which was previously mentioned as residing in a collection (*saṅghāta*), the author says "just as the projection" (*yathākṣepa*) by way of providing an illustration.

Here, the action-universal (*karma-jāti*) characterized by rotation is manifested by a specific projection produced by a particular effort; because it is fully present in each individual instance, it is not perceived by a bystander. However, upon the repetition of rotations, that [universal] is grasped by the perceiver with respect to each rotation.

Thus, regarding letters (*varṇa*), words (*pada*), and sentences (*vākya*), the audible sound (*śruti*)—which is the manifesting *dhvani*—is perceived as if it were identical in form to the reality characterized by the *sphoṭa* of letters, words, and sentences, even though it is ultimately distinct from it. What is its nature? It is said to have "similar manifestors" (*tulyopavyañjanā*). That is to say, it is that whose manifestors—the points of articulation (*sthāna*), the organs of pronunciation (*karaṇa*), and the impact (*abhighāta*)—are similar.
Therefore, it should be understood that this *jātisphoṭa*, manifested by *dhvanis* produced by different efforts, is indeed distinct [from the individual sounds]. And this is logical. (20–21)
But regarding the position that the sentence is a single unit, it is said in response to the determination of its priority and posteriority:
"In the case of eternal [words], how could there be 'prior' or 'subsequent' in the ultimate sense?
It is simply the power of that very one which appears in such a manner. (22)

For the power called Time (kāla), which is the agent, ordains priority and posteriority among effects through its acts of obstruction and permission; for there is no priority or posteriority among atoms when they exist in conjunction without distinction.

But surely, if it were grasped as eternal, it could not possess priority and posteriority (*paurvāparya*). For in that which is called a sentence—being partless and the object of a single act of perception—priority and posteriority, which concern phonemes and words, are impossible. To this, it is said: "That power belongs to the one alone. As for the phrase "it being thus": for the proponent of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavādin*), the appearance of succession within the non-successive intellect—which does not transcend unity—is like something contradictory, yet it remains non-contradictory.

But for those who know the three Vedas (Trayī), there is a sequential manifestation without overstepping the unity within the Universal Self. The same would apply to the Word as well; thus, there is no contradiction. For, due to the connection with its own power, there is only a difference in manifestation, and consequently, neither the acquisition (upāya) nor the loss (apāya) of that [Word] exists in any respect whatsoever. || 22 ||

Just as for this partless *sphoṭa*, the distinction between prior and posterior parts is produced by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and not inherent, because it is eternal—thus, in order to establish its eternity in detail, he says: "In the case of eternal [sounds]," and so forth.

For in eternal things, although a temporal sequence of prior and posterior is impossible from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), it is nevertheless observed as being produced by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). One might ask: "Why does it not appear as always having a single form? For a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-bheda*) is not possible there. Anticipating this doubt, it is said: "Of the one," and so forth. Even that which has a single nature is endowed with such powers precisely due to the inherent nature of the thing (*vastu-svābhāvya*). Thus, it appears through its extension as the nature of prior and posterior, following after the distinctions of limiting adjuncts. || 22 ||

But how, when words, syllables, and phonemes—whether short, long, protracted, or consonants—are eternal and indistinguishable, can a difference in time be established, such that they appear as "slow" or "quick"? [The answer is: Just as two objects appear at different times due to a difference in the cognition of time, so too is that property [of duration] present in the short and the long. (23)

For example, the nature of the cognition "long" is the same as that of the cognition "quick"; there is no difference whatsoever in the duration of the existence of these two natures. For every cognition that has attained its own being is indistinguishable from other cognitions in terms of time.

Moreover, the single cognition "long" (*cira*)—through another cognition whose nature is the perception of what has passed, and by virtue of the focused attention on that specific cultivation—manifests as if it were a prolongation of time and space, even through the nature of a future perception. In the case of "quickly" (*kṣipra*), however, because its nature is rapid occurrence, time and space appear as if they were shortened.

Furthermore, he states—preceded by the presentation of an example—that the appearance of difference in the word is due solely to the difference in limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and not inherently, because [the word] is eternal: "long," etc.

Just as the cognition of "long" and the cognition of "quick" appear as if they belong to different times—even though they are simultaneous—due to their lack of distinction as cognitions, by virtue of depending upon different objects of knowledge; and just as the cognition of "long" appears as if it has an extended manifestation, while the cognition of "quick" is the opposite; in the same way, the nature (dharma) or intrinsic character of "short" and "long" should be understood. There is no such thing as a "sphoṭa" that possesses a form such as shortness and so on; thus, there is no inherent difference in the sphoṭa itself. [Objection: How is it not contradictory to perceive a difference in the measurement of time and space in cases such as long and protracted vowels?
Time, being eternal, cannot admit of differentiation here by means of moments (mātrās). In the absence of distinct moments, what kind of succession could there be? (24)

Whether one relies upon time (*kāla*) or its constituent measures (*mātrā*), whether in the view that it is eternal or non-eternal, no real increase or decrease exists for the nature of time itself. If time were eternal, its own magnitude would not be increased by many movements of the sun, nor would it be decreased by few; this is just as the measure of a *krośa* or a *yojana* is not altered by the varying actions of a traveler. Furthermore, since time itself—when qualified by limiting conditions (*upādhi*)—is what constitutes measure, how could it have another measure? This will be explained in the section on the exposition of time (*kālasamuddeśa*).

Now, if it is asserted that even movement (*gati*) is eternal and that everything is non-transient, then these constituent elements (*mātrā*) of the universe would indeed be subject to change; in that case, the preceding is not connected with the succeeding, and everything intended [to be connected] falls apart as something entirely unconnected. Furthermore, between two indefinable limits—the prior and the posterior—the middle remains unbound, being without support before or after, and thus itself indefinable.

Pervaded by the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), which reflects upon its own prior and subsequent parts, [the object] reaches the limit of diminution; though it is indivisible, it appears as if long to the ignorant through the apprehension of an unreal external form, even while not at all grasping it, despite the non-difference of its measure.

In this view, regarding all worldly transactions—which are bound to a single property, established in a single property, and occurring at a non-distinct time—what kind of sequence could there be between entities that are real and those that are absolutely unreal?
Indeed, no sequence whatsoever exists between a hare’s horn and a camel’s horn, or between a hare’s horn and the Himalayas.

Although, when a single object is present, a sequence with respect to its simultaneous or non-simultaneous activities cannot logically occur for the wise, nevertheless, in this philosophical system, no other kind of sequence is possible; thus, such an arrangement of sequence is established. It is true that such an arrangement of sequence exists, yet there is no imagined distinction of magnitude for anything whatsoever that transcends the actual distinction of the dimensions of its physical form.

For all entities arise simultaneously; they do not transcend their own essential nature when associated with a temporal path—whether designated as an eon (*manvantara*) or a moment (*kṣaṇa*)—which is imagined as a duration of time, through a distinction that is both adventitious and non-adventitious, and which is non-exclusive.

Indeed, there exists no other temporal path called a "moment" or an "eon" distinct from those entities themselves, which could serve as a substratum such that entities possessing specific states, persisting over a duration of time, would fall within the scope of the proposition that they are either eternal or momentary. || 24 ||

Now it is said: "It is not proper to say that [time] is differentiated due to the influence of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), for that would entail the consequence of a difference in its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-bheda*). Anticipating this objection, he says: "Not eternal" (*na nitya*). Here, time is indeed accepted as being eternal, because of the description of its characteristics such as "eternal," "one," and so forth. How, then, is its practical usage (*vyavahāra*) in terms of moments (*kṣaṇa*), lava, nimeṣa, and so on, now justified? If it is argued that its differentiation is metaphorically attributed (*upacaryate*) through the measures of the Supreme (*paramātra*).

Just as a "moment" (*kṣaṇa*) is defined as the time characterized by an atom's relinquishing the space occupied by itself, and two moments constitute a "lava," and so forth; likewise, what aversion can there be toward the conceptualization of adventitious distinctions within a partless sentence?

Now, if you say: "We do not recognize time as a distinct entity characterized by such definitions as being eternal and unitary; rather, it is merely the entities themselves, existing in a temporal sequence and differing in their intrinsic natures, that constitute time. And the conventional usage of 'succession' and 'simultaneity' is based upon those [entities], and is not produced by a time that is distinct from them and possesses an eternal nature. To this, he replies: "Of the [entities] that are excluded... and so forth.

Since those mere constituents (*mātrā*) existing in a temporal sequence are necessarily subject to arising and passing away, what kind of sequence could there be among them which are so fragile? And how, by relying upon them, can there be the conventional usage of "time"? This is merely a trifle. If that is the case, then the cognition (*buddhi*) produced from those sequential constituents—whether it consists of accumulated constituents or unaccumulated constituents—will suffice for the conventional usage of different measurements; in every respect, it is simply a cognition that has not grasped the form of the constituents themselves. That single cognition which arises from them exists only as a part [of the whole].
For that [cognition], by its own power, appears as if divided while reflecting upon the sequence [of objects].

Indeed, because it is a single unity within the intellect (*buddhi*), distinct principles (*tattva*) of the constituent elements (*mātrā*)—whether they be associated or contradictory—cannot exist [as separate entities]. Rather, that single cognition, being devoid of parts and consisting of the nature of light (*prakāśa*), reflects upon those elements—which possess a sequential order of intermingled priority and posteriority—precisely by withdrawing them, even though they are inherently inseparable, without abandoning their true nature. Such indeed is the reflective awareness of the intellect. (25)
Now, anticipating the objection that "cognition arising by relying upon such objects will bring about the conventional usage of time," he says: "from those [objects]."

The cognition that arises from those mere objective entities (*padārtha*) is likewise unable to effect the linguistic usage of time (*kālavyavahāra*). For since that single cognition is partless (*nirvibhāga*), how could it effect the usage of "prior" and "posterior"? To this he says: "For that... Cognition, as it were, becomes differentiated through its own power as a reflector of succession (*krama-pratyavamarśinī*). Since it arises by virtue of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of experience, accompanied precisely by the delineation of succession, it is indeed capable of effecting the linguistic usage of time.

25–26. Due to the connection with the sequential enumeration, that seed which has been deposited within her does not allow for a definitive definition of either the unity or the plurality of the principles (tattvas).

In this context, that which belongs to the subtle elements (*mātrā*)—which are separated [from gross objects], indefinable, and whose capacities were employed in preceding cognitions—is not characterized by the grasping of form (*rūpopagraha*) nor by delineation; it is a reality beyond designation, like that of seeds.

How then can one describe either worldly unity or worldly plurality within a single cognition regarding those seeds of the power of the self that are endowed with their respective measures and possess contradictory results? For how could a single, partless entity be of a contradictory nature; or how could multiple, contradictory natures constitute a single thing? (26)

To refute this, he says: "In that [cognition]" (*tasyām iti*). Regarding that cognition, the seed—which is deposited by means of the mere objects through the force of experience, which consists of a latent impression (*vāsanā*) and has the nature of a mental trace (*saṃskāra*)—is it distinct from that [cognition] or non-distinct? There are these two possible courses.

If it [the cognition] were distinct from that [object], then it would have nothing to do with it; how, then, could conventional usage such as sequence and so forth proceed by its power? On the other hand, if it were not distinct, then it too would be that same single, partless entity, and like the mere essence of the object itself, how could it sustain the conventional usage of time? Thus, since it is impossible to provide a definitive definition of cognition through either its identity with or its difference from reality, this [position] is trivial. But at the time of contemplative realization (*bhāvanā*), this capacity for sequence is non-sequential;
for by means of it, an object whose distinctions have been excluded is perceived as possessing distinction.

For those whose intellects follow the cultivation of distinctions and who employ them as a unity, due to beginningless false habitual practice, a capacity called "succession" is falsely attributed to all the constituent parts—though they are non-different from and inseparable from a single cognition—in order to establish the appearance of succession.

Thus, even though all objects denoted by words (in the form of sentences) are devoid of internal difference, they are perceived as being employed with a distinction that does not exist, by means of the assumption of a sequence of contradictory properties.

For instance—just as all living beings, despite the oneness of space, possess specific dispositions established according to their respective directions as "above," "below," or "across"; and even clods of earth and the like, though possessed of weight, do not follow the timing of the mental dispositions of living beings as they themselves do; so too, for one who understands a single sentence, although there is no absolute multiplicity due to its eternity, such multiplicity appears through conventional usage. || 27 ||

Furthermore, in order to demonstrate that [the word] is properly understood as being entirely undivided, like the embryo (*kalala*) of a *cātaka* chick, he says: "by means of mental cultivation" (*bhāvanā*). In the *Brahmakāṇḍa*, the nature of the *sphoṭa* was indeed already established after refuting all doubts. Therefore, this sentence is a single denoter (*vācaka*) whose nature is *sphoṭa* and which is devoid of sequence. However, at the time of the mental cultivation of its own word-meanings, by virtue of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), it is understood as having "sequential efficacy"—that is, that which possesses the capacity for sequence.

By which [means] the object, whose nature is denotable, is perceived as being indeed partless (*akhaṇḍa*) yet appearing as if possessing distinctions due to the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) of the word-meanings, though not in an ultimate sense.

(27) If those very phonemes (*varṇa*) that constitute words exist in a sentence, and those same phonemes exist in a word, then within the phonemes there would have to be a division of phonemic parts, like atoms. (28)

Furthermore, for one who maintains that only those very words—which are perceived as real entities—are intended within a sentence, and that there exists no single, partless sentence distinct from them, nor any sentence of an indivisible nature; for such a person, even words do not exist apart from their phonemes (*varṇa*). Since phonemes too possess parts, it follows that differentiation would prevail everywhere to the highest degree. Thus, in order to refute the proponent of words (*padavādin*), he says: "words" (*padāni*).

Just as a single whole (*avayavin*) is not admitted apart from its parts (*avayava*), so too, since the parts themselves possess further sub-divisions, the conceptualization of parts leads to an infinite regress (*atiprasaṅga*), leaving only atoms (*paramāṇu*) remaining. Even regarding these, according to some views, because they are simultaneously joined with six [other atoms], there is no possibility of even the most minute part existing within a mass. Consequently, the world would result in being utterly devoid of any definable objects and entirely motionless. Due to the lack of contact between parts, neither a phoneme (*varṇa*) nor a word (*pada*) could exist.
Since those [parts] are indefinable, what else could possibly be defined? (29)

If it is maintained that those very same words which were perceived separately, and those very same phonemes which were perceived separately, are the ones combined when they are relied upon in words and sentences—and if it is asserted that the essence of sentences and words is not distinct from the phonemes—then, in that case, just as one reaches the ultimate limit of analysis regarding phonemes, it would follow that there is a division of phonemic parts into something like atoms (*paramāṇu*).

And thus, because the successive parts—which have not been attained simultaneously—do not touch one another, there exists no such thing as a single phoneme (*varṇa*) or a word (*pada*). For, being indefinable, there is an absence of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) with respect to each individual part; what then is that single form of sound (*śabdarūpa*) which could be designated as "this is it"? Therefore, there is no linguistic usage based on the reality of speech (*śabdatattva*) that is external, non-composite, and devoid of distinctions between indefinable parts. || 29 ||

In the same way, because there is no conjunction of the constituent parts (bhāga) of phonemes (varṇa), no single phoneme whatsoever would exist. To demonstrate that in the absence of those [parts], even a word (pada) would not exist, he says: "of the parts" (bhāgānām).

Therefore, since the parts do not exist according to the reasoning already stated, and because there is an absence of any designation [for them], let another thing distinct from these be designated as the denoter here. Since an indivisible [unit] is not admitted, and since words are untenable by the logic previously mentioned, there would be no denoter at all. Yet, there is the cognition of the sentence-meaning, and it must have a cause; thus, the established conclusion is that one alone—the indivisible *sphoṭa* manifested by words, whether as an individual (*vyakti-sphoṭa*) or as a genus (*jāti-sphoṭa*)—must be accepted as the denoter. "That single essence of speech which is manifested within by the sounds..."

Regarding this, others say that the word (*śabda*) and its unity reside in the sentence. They maintain that the primary nature of the word is that reality of speech which is the basis for its arising and cessation—though it is designated merely as "word" like external letters and marks—and which, being itself non-sequential, is manifested through sequential parts, just as [an object] is [manifested] by letters and marks despite not being of such a nature. This is what others consider to be the essential form of the word.

And this internal essence of speech, characterized by the synthesis of cognition, is recorded there [in the Veda]. Regarding its nature, when one perceives the division into distinct word-forms, it is well known that this single entity called a "sentence" is just like those called "phonemes" and "words"—this is the established path in the sacred tradition. 30.

Thus far, the sentence has been explained by relying on the external form of the sphoṭa—whether as the individual sphoṭa (vyaktisphoṭa) or the generic sphoṭa (jātisphoṭa). Now, the teachers say that the sentence is that very reality of sound (śabdatattva), which is internal, partless, of the nature of consciousness, consisting of both word and meaning, and undivided; this same [reality] is manifested externally through articulated sounds (nāda). To explain what was designated as "the internal synthesis of the intellect" (buddhyanusaṃhṛti), he says: "That which is within... and so forth.

When the investigation of sentences is undertaken, it is established that their inner essence is one and indivisible; therefore, let that alone be the sentence because it is real—what is the use of a separate sentence that is unreal? This is the meaning. (30) In the same way, the inner meaning of those [words] is revealed through their respective parts of meaning.
Word and meaning are two aspects of the single Self, existing inseparably. (31)

Just as the reality of speech (*vāk-tattva*), which is essentially non-different from the primary nature of sound and which enters into the means of expression consisting of the undesignatable portions of sound, is well known as the principal essence of word; so too, the reality of cognition (*buddhi-tattva*)—which arises sequentially, restricted to each respective object, and in which specificities are accumulated through the undesignatable [sounds] within external objects that are distinct and conventional—is experienced precisely as the reality of the external thing itself.

Or, in the case of the position that [the object] is eternal, it ceases by means of the mere manifestation of the form of its sequential capacity. For an external object is not capable of performing practical causal functions without a cognition that has acquired a form contrary to the actual nature of the object. Therefore, all worldly transaction is carried out by means of an object whose form is internalized.

Others, however, maintain that the accomplishment of the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*) occurs in the conscious self (*puruṣa*), which is essentially awareness, through the entry of the form of the cognition; for, due to the inherence (*samavāya*) of the cognition—which has transferred the form of the object—into the self, the self appears as if it has assumed that very form.

When the intellect (*buddhi*), whose nature is luminosity, apprehends both the form of consciousness (*citirūpa*) and the form of objects through the conjunction of reflections, and when it has assumed the form of the Puruṣa—having undergone a transformation into the form of the perceived object—the distinction between the two powers, the power of the object of enjoyment (*bhogya-śakti*) and the power of the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ-śakti*), which are absolutely distinct yet utterly confounded as if they had attained non-differentiation, becomes possible.
For the power of the enjoyer is indeed unchanging and non-transmigrating, yet, as if transmigrated into the changing object, it follows the modifications of that [object].

And by means of a mental modification (*buddhi-vṛtti*) that merely imitates that mental modification of the intellect (*buddhi*)—which has taken on the form of the apprehension of consciousness—the occurrence of qualified cognition is described.

And in all these stages, as if they were included within it, because the synthesis has been attained from the word—when the objects have been withdrawn as if their forms were already internalized, and are being apprehended undivided without overstepping their divided forms—this very intellect-nature (*buddhyātmā*), which has reached its complete synthesis, remains established through the non-differentiation of the powers of the signifier and the signified; that is, by merely not abandoning the form of the power of distinction between those two selves which are otherwise separate.
For those who maintain the doctrine of eternality, however, this [intellect] is not adventitious, does not transcend [its nature], and is devoid of increase or decrease. (31)

Not only is the sentence thus [indivisible], but even the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*)—which is itself indivisible and consists of intuitive flash (*pratibhā*)—is manifested by means of the constituent parts of word-meanings (*padārthabhāga*). He states this as a corollary with the words "by means of the parts of meaning" (*arthabhāgaiḥ*). In the view of those teachers who maintain that the sentence is internal (*āntaravākyavādin*), it should be understood that here too the sentence-meaning is strictly internal. Furthermore, it should be understood that these two—the word and its meaning—are non-different from a single internal reality; they appear as if they were distinct entities existing externally, though in fact they are not. Thus he says: "of the one alone" (*ekasyaiva*). [Verse 31:
"The state of being the illuminator and the illuminated, and the nature of cause and effect..."

Of that *śabdatattva* (the reality of sound), which is always the inner measure (*antarmātra*), this term "inner measure" (*antarmātrā*) is accompanied by two powers of sound: the non-perishing (*anapāyinī*) and the perishing (*apāyinī*). Within this self (*ātman*) of his, although the state of being the illuminator and the state of being illuminated are undivided, they appear as if divided. Furthermore, due to their mutual conformity of form, they possess the nature of cause and effect—this being the case at all times for that essence of sound (*śabdātman*) which is designated as the "inner measure" (*antarmātra*) of that locus (*adeśa*).

"Always" (*sarvadā*) means that for this [Reality], no other time or path exists. However, the term "always" is employed to demonstrate conventional usage for the purpose of realizing the absence of any distinction between existence and non-existence. Because there is no distinction between existence and non-existence, the word and its referent reside solely within the internal dimension (*antarmātra*). Furthermore, even the occurrence of its manifestation—which is never departing—is established in that very same way, without deviation from or transcendence of it; for since it does not transcend the transcendence of all things, what could possibly act as a cause for cognition therein at any particular time?

The conceptualization of a relationship between locus and located—such as "always" or "at some time"—is not distinct from [the reality of] the object that persists; for, due to the influence of the cultivation of false habitual tendencies, the very nature of the self, though devoid of differentiation, produces delusion by appearing as if it possessed imagined distinctions. || 32 ||

Now, an objection is raised: "Is it not well known that word and meaning are the signifier and the signified? Therefore, how can there be non-difference between them? Anticipating this, he says: "The illuminator," and so forth. For this appearance of difference is not contradictory in the case of that inner essence of the Word (*śabdatattva*), which is of the nature of light, due to the differentiation of its powers. This was stated at the very beginning in the *Āgama-kāṇḍa* with the verse beginning, "Of the one, the seed of all," and so on. "While the capacities for existence and non-existence of that very [Word] are established, there occurs an appearance of succession within the non-successive, which serves as the basis for worldly transaction. (33)

For within a single Self, which is the reality of the word-meaning residing in the internal dimension (*antarmātrā*), there exist two powers known as existence (*bhāva*) and non-existence (*abhāva*). These two powers—which constitute its very essence, are eternal, devoid of coming and going, and do not transcend oneness—are perceived in a sequential form even though they are non-sequential, as if they were contained within a single cognition; thus, existence and non-existence appear as one. Here, the text is missing;
therefore, he says "of that very [Self]" by way of a digression, stating that this too appears due to a differentiation of its powers.

Relying upon that very one, the supreme reality which is undivided, this entire worldly transaction is perceived through the differentiation of powers; how much more so when it consists merely of the distinction between the signified and the signifier? Thus, the position of the partless [indivisible whole] alone is logical. (33) If one postulates the existence of word-meanings based on the authority of common consensus, then by the subsequent accumulation of these word-meanings, the consequence of meaninglessness follows due to their abandonment [of the original unity]. (34)
Now, having raised the objection of the proponent of the word (padavādī), he speaks again in order to refute it:

"If the cognition of the meaning of a word is said to be the means of valid knowledge regarding the existence of the word and its meaning, then in the sentence 'Devadatta, drive the white cow with a stick,' since each preceding word-meaning is subsumed by each succeeding word-meaning, the abandonment of their own specific meanings would result in the futility of employing those respective words."

Furthermore, since the utterance of what is meaningless is futile, and since the cognition of a word-meaning cannot arise from that mere sound once uttered, upon what basis could there be a comprehension of the sentence-meaning? Thus, this [position] is nonsensical. (34) To state that the meaning of "king" is understood through the word "rāja" as something distinct in form, and that because words are not established [as having fixed meanings], the theory of the word (*padavāda*) appears entirely untenable, he says:

The cognition of the meaning "king" is observed through the word *rāja* in its various forms—such as *rājā*, *rājñā*, *rājñe*, *rājñaḥ*, *rājñi*, and *rājani*—which do not possess a fixed nature. If the word were real, it would necessarily be perceived in a single, fixed form. Since it is not so perceived everywhere, we consider words to be merely false. Furthermore, he states that there is no such thing as a word: "In a compound (*vṛtti*), a word resembling a verb is joined elsewhere [in a sentence].
From this also, it follows that the word does not exist.

In the compound *rājapuruṣa*, the word *rājan* is similar to a verb (*ākhyāta*). Consequently, in the phrase *he rājapuruṣa*, there would arise the understanding of the meaning "O King, shine forth, O man! This is not desired. Therefore, ultimate words do not exist at all. Furthermore, if the word *rājan* alone were not observed in usage elsewhere, it would be different in compounds such as *rājapuruṣa*; [one might ask] what causes the comprehension of a specific meaning in cases like *rājapuruṣa* and *brāhmaṇapuruṣa*? To this, it is said: Just as when "horse-ear" (*aśvakarṇa*) is mentioned, it is understood even without [the separate mention of] a horse.
A certain specific meaning is likewise understood in all [compounds].

For example, when "Ajakarṇa" (Goat-ear) or "Aśvakarṇa" (Horse-ear) is uttered, there exists not even the slightest connection with the meaning of "horse" or the meaning of "ear. Rather, by means of a sentence whose scope is differentiation and which is entirely devoid of that [literal] meaning, the intended sense is demonstrated; through designations such as *bahuvrīhi* and *tatpuruṣa*, grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) occurs within other composite wholes.

Even though there is no absolute connection between the referents of words such as "horse" and so forth [with the word "ear"], a certain restricted object characterized by both exclusion (*vyāvṛtta*) and inclusion (*anuvṛtta*) is nevertheless understood. In the same way, even when there is no connection with other meanings in all derivative formations (*vṛtti*), a specific meaning will certainly be understood. He says, "just as in the case of 'aśvakarṇa'," to show that it is not only the case that those [words] lack a restricted form when used alone, but also when they are situated within a derivative formation.

In the case of the word *aśvakarṇa*, even without the referent of the word *aśva* (horse), a certain object qualified by a different genus is understood. Therefore, since all words—even when their individual divisions have been grasped—act as manifesters of the sentence, it is only logical that the cognition of the sentence-meaning is preceded by the comprehension of an indivisible sentence (*akhaṇḍavākya*). || 36 ||

If, then, the semantic connection between the prior and posterior members in compounds such as *rājapuruṣa* is equivalent to that in terms like *aśvakarṇa*, how is the distinction between conventional (*rūḍhi*) and non-conventional (*arūḍhi*) usage established? [To this, he says:

"Similarity is postulated because, in sentences, [the compound] is understood to have a different meaning [from its constituent parts]. For some, the status of being a conventional word is followed [and recognized] in the treatise itself. (37)

In this context, since there is an absolute non-difference of meaning between the *vṛtti* (compound) and the sentence (*vākya*) when established by their own nature, when a subject is introduced by both the *vṛtti* and the sentence, wherever that principal [subject] has an identical connection with the action and so forth, there a similarity is postulated for the sentence as if it were differentiated merely by the function of separation (*vicchedavṛtti*), even though differences such as subordinate qualifiers (*upasarjana-viśeṣaṇa*) and the like exist. And therefore, through this postulation of similarity, it is understood that those are "non-conventional" (*arūḍhi*) words.

However, for those words where the syntactic sequence (*vākya-prakrama*) has one meaning related to verbal action, while the semantic sequence (*vṛtti-prakrama*) has another entirely, they possess the status of conventional (*rūḍhi*) words. Regarding these, grammatical operations such as "in the sense of an artisan, after a root other than *kṛ*" (*śilpini cākṛñaḥ*), "in the sense of a name, except for *ācita* and others" (*saṃjñāyāmanācitādīnām*), "frequently in the sense of a name or in Vedic literature, after the feminine suffixes *ṅī* and *āp*" (*ṅyāpoḥ saṃjñāchandasorbahulam*), and "frequently in the sense of the suffix *taṇ*" (*bahulaṃ taṇi*)—are explained specifically within the grammatical treatise itself. Now, anticipating the objection that if this were the case, the distinction between conventional and non-conventional words being stated would be useless, he says: "In the sentence" (*vākya*).

When a similarity between a derivative formation (*vṛtti*) and its analytical sentence (*vākya*) is postulated, certain words are said to possess the status of a conventional term (*rūḍhi-śabda*) because they convey a different meaning in their sentential analysis (*vigraha*). For example: *tailapāyikā* ("oil-drinker"). At the stage of the sentence—namely, "one who drinks oil" (*tailaṃ pibati*)—the meaning [of the parts] manifests. However, at the stage of the derivative formation, there arises the cognition of some object endowed with a distinct genus (*jātyantara*), such as a specific kind of bird; and since the act of drinking oil is not indicated for that object, it is said to have the nature of a conventional term.

For some, however, there is a derivative nature (*yaugikatvam*) due to the similarity of meaning between the constituent parts (*vṛtti*) and the sentence (*vākya*). For example: *rājapuruṣa* ("king's man"). By the phrase "through conceptual construction" (*parikalpana*), it is demonstrated that all this—such as the division of parts and so forth—is merely a conceptual construct (*kalpanāmātra*) within the conventions of the treatises; in ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), however, it is perceived as entirely undivided at the time of linguistic usage. This very point has been made explicit by the statement that "it is followed precisely in the treatise.
38. Those things which are to be abandoned even after they have been adopted are called "means" (*upāya*). Furthermore, no fixed rule regarding these means necessarily persists.

In this process of word-formation (*śabda-saṃskāra*), words are employed for the benefit of the sentence whenever there is a cognition consisting merely of the comprehension of meaning. Thus, words such as *carca* and others are employed in *saṃhitā*; words belonging to sentences are employed in compounds (*samāsa*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), primary nominal stems (*sub*), verbal roots (*dhātu*), and the operations of *ekaśeṣa*. And when those [meanings] for whose sake they were employed are present, these [words] are necessarily abandoned, because they have served their purpose as means.

For in the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*), there are phonological refinements (*śabda-saṃskāra*) such as the elision (*nighāta*) of a finite verb (*tiṅ*) following a vocative (*āmantrita*), according to the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ*; likewise, "a single substitute [for a vowel] is acute when the preceding is acute" (*ekādeśa udāttenodāttaḥ*); "or it is circumflex if at the beginning of a word that is unaccented" (*svarito vānudātte padādau*); and "the *yaṇ*-substitute for an acute or circumflex vowel is circumflex" (*udāttasvaritayoryaṇ*). Similarly, there are seen even those [rules] intended solely for the comprehension of meaning (*artha-pratipatti-mātra*), such as "in a *tatpuruṣa*, [the first member retains its accent] after words having the sense of 'equal to' or after an instrumental," and "after a locative, or after *hārin*. For example: *yathā me mātā, tathā me pitā*; *susnātaṃ bhoḥ*; *namo bharanta emasi*; and *saubhāgyam asyai dattvāyāthāstaṃ viparetana*.

That which is beyond this is "tapara" (followed by *t*); likewise, that which is beyond even that is "tapara. The state of being devoid of modesty (*viyāta*) is "vaiyātyam. These are the means for addressing a person. However, if persons can be made to understand in other ways as well, then other means for that purpose are also undertaken. How is this stated? He says: "even having employed... The treatise (*śāstra*) is the means for the thorough knowledge of words. Once those [words] are known, because the purpose has been accomplished, there is no further utility [for the treatise], and thus it is abandoned. Furthermore, he states that the means are not fixed: "and of the means... (38).
A certain person may somehow arrive at the meaning [of a sentence], whether the distinctions based on the sentence are combined or separated.

For the understanding of listeners is indeed manifold and varied. Regarding the meaning of the sentence "he has studied the *chandas* (Veda)," there is the expression of the word [itself]: either that the state of being *śrotriya* arises from *chandas*, with the suffix *ghaṅ*; or that it means "an action performed by means of the ears" (*śrotra*). Likewise, one says *ākhanikaḥ* [meaning "one who digs"] when it is stated that "the suffix *ika* should be prescribed," and *ākhanikavakaḥ* when it is stated that "the suffixes *ika* and *vaka* should be prescribed. Alternatively, *ākhanikavaka* is recited among the group beginning with *pātresamita*.

Likewise—regarding [compounds] such as *uṣṭra-goyuga-aśva-ṣaḍgava*, grammatical analysis (*anvākhyāna*) is performed in various ways according to their status as individual words (*pratyayatvena*). If these are ever found in a sentence either as separate elements (*vibhaktāḥ*) or uncombined (*anibaddhāḥ*), they appear as *saṃsṛṣṭāḥ* (e.g., *rājapuruṣaḥ*, *plakṣanyagrodhau*); whereas when they are separated, they appear as *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* and *plakṣaś ca nyagrodhaś ca*.

Another says: "In the case of a compound, as in 'Bring Devadatta’s white cow,' [the words are joined]; whereas in the case of separated words, there is no employment of a word together with other words. In every respect, those words which are taken up for illustration—possessing an uninterrupted form of apprehension and existing in a general form—even they are ultimately bound within *sattā* (being) and are not capable of serving as an illustration in any state whatsoever."

Therefore, whether they are combined or separate, no distinct entities exist unbound within the sentence; rather, the combination of distinctions occurs solely as means for a person’s comprehension through superimposition, restrictive rules, and restatements. || 39 ||

It is not a fixed rule that one teacher acquires words through the grammatical treatise composed by Pāṇini, while another does so through some other means. This very point has been clarified by the passage beginning with "the meaning in some way" (*arthaṃ kathañcit*). Therefore, since it is the sentence alone—whether its meanings are combined or separated—that is the basis for cognition as a single, partless unit, the conceptualization of a division between words and word-meanings is indeed untenable; to demonstrate this, he says: "Or, [the meanings] are combined... (verse 39).
When the connection [expressed as] "this is that" (*so 'yam*) is undertaken by the intellect...

In some cases, even a single phoneme conveys the meaning of the sentence. It is not necessarily the case that a word, whose form consists of distinct parts, conveys a meaning that follows a sequence and possesses a discernible internal division. For when the cognition "samprasāraṇa" arises with respect to the rule "iy and uṇ take the place of iK," or when the connection "this is that" is made regarding "bha-bhi," then—just as through the expression "iy-uṇ" there is a comprehension following a sequence of prior and posterior elements—likewise, through "bha-bhi," there is a comprehension that does not follow such a sequence.

Thus, by means of that single-syllable designation for the object, that very essence of the object is perceived with its temporal sequence (paurvāparya) dissolved. Furthermore, comprehension in this case does not necessarily involve an intervention by the word; for those who have mastered their practice, the comprehension of the meaning is not mediated by another word.

If, moreover, a treatise that is an easy means and endowed with both general and specific characteristics were not pursued by those in the world who perceive it—due to a false obsession (*mithyābhyāsa*) arising from laziness regarding its conventional usage—then practitioners would adopt that very sequence. Furthermore, unity is conflated with the form of difference; thus, the function of speech, which aims at excellence, is indeed at fault when it results in the subversion of the intended sequential order.

For she manifests herself in a completely different way toward men who have committed offenses; therefore, even while seeing her, some do not see her, and even while hearing her, they do not hear her. But the grammarians, who know the application of speech and have realized the essence of sound, perceive her by means of her own true nature, having transcended the perception of duality.

And she reveals herself to them alone. This has been stated: "A certain person understands the meaning in some way or another. Therefore, a mere illustration is provided for the various distinctions in the dimensions of the differences in human comprehension.

Consequently, he says "so 'yam" (this is that) in order to declare that this sentence-meaning—which is partless, devoid of objective referents, and containing within it a connection based solely on superimposition—is indeed perceived even from a single phoneme.

When the speaker intends the sentence-meaning through a connection of the form of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) with the sentence—expressing it as "this is that"—then even a single phoneme indeed becomes the designator of the sentence-meaning; how much more so a word uttered with the intention of expressing a specific meaning characterized by its various parts? Thus, because the sentence and the sentence-meaning are non-different in nature due to the force of superimposition, it is stated that the sentence itself is manifested as having the nature of *sphoṭa* during the manifestation of the sentence-meaning: "then even a single [phoneme]," and so forth.
Whatever meaning is expressed by a word alone, they say that [the word] standing in a sentence is the denoter of that much meaning. (41)

In this context, to whatever extent the word "tree" (*vṛkṣa*) alone expresses a distinct object consisting of the mere universal (*jāti*), to that same extent it conveys its connection [to other properties] even in sentences such as "the tree exists," "the tree does not exist," or "the tree is cut. This connection with existence, non-existence, cutting, and so forth does not demonstrate a nature characterized by being joined with a different universal; nor is the relationship with existence, non-existence, cutting, and so forth itself a property of the universal. For a word whose basis is one universal lacks the capacity to convey another measure [or property] based on a different universal.

Now, in order to demonstrate the position of the "composite" (saṃghāta) by resorting to the theory of "expressed connection" (abhihitānvaya), he says: "by the word alone," and so forth. A word that is [considered] alone is the designator of a certain meaning; even when situated within a sentence, it denotes that very same [meaning].
However, when there is a relation [between words], whatever additional [meaning] arises is [due to the sentence].
They declare that very sentence-meaning (vākyārtha) to be that which rests upon multiple words.

As for the case where there is a relation with another word—such as in "vīraḥ puruṣaḥ" (a brave man)—where there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) due to the relationship of qualifier and qualified, and where an excess [of meaning] is observed among objects based on the prior comprehension of the co-inherence (*samavāya*) of a genus and a quality within a single object, that too is indeed the sentence-meaning. For its internal operation is not relied upon as a cause for the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the individual word.

However, that exclusion (*vyatireka*) which pertains to a single word—such as "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), where [the relation] is produced by an external cause like the object (*karman*) and so forth—restricts the nominal stems themselves within the word when they are joined with specific case-endings. Furthermore, this distinction between the two types of *ādhikya* (augmentation) pertaining to the sentence and the word has been explained in detail in the Bhāṣya itself.

And for this reason, His Honor has said: "Just as within a single word, the meaning residing in the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) becomes the cause of the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the word with respect to its grammatical number, so too, that which resides within a single word is indeed the cause of the refinement of the word, yet it is not the cause with respect to the application of case-endings (*vibhakti*). For example: *grāmo grāmo ramaṇīyaḥ* (‘Every village is beautiful’). However, the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), which relies upon multiple words, is declared to be the cause for the determination of rules such as the prohibition of the particle *ni*. || 42 ||

Therefore, when there is a mutual connection (*parasparānvaya*) among the words in a collection, that which is the "excess" (*ādhikya*) resulting from the meanings of the words—their relation (*saṃsarga*)—is the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). And it has been said: "That which is the excess here is the sentence-meaning. By the phrase "residing in many words," it is shown that a sentence is a collection (*saṃghāta*). (41–42) Furthermore, even though it resides in many words, there is another distinction in view:
"But that [sentence-meaning], although residing in many words, is completed for each individual part."

Others postulate that, like a genus (*jāti*), it [the sentence-meaning] exists in the aggregate as well, just like a number (*saṃkhyā*). Just as a genus such as "existence" (*sattā*), even when connected to multiple substrates, does not fail to produce its full effect in each individual substrate, so too this sentence-meaning for some [grammarians], by transcending any deficiency in repetition, is completed in its entirety upon every single word. Alternatively, there is another view: just as a single number such as "twenty" serves as the cause for the cognition of its respective objects in each substrate, so too the sentence-meaning resides in each word as that which is to be conveyed (*pratyāyya*). || 43 ||

Regarding this meaning of the sentence, there are two positions to be shown: according to some, it is fully present in each individual like a universal (*jāti*), while according to others, it is fully present in the collection like a number (*saṃkhyā*). To show this, he says: "But that [sentence-meaning] is manifold... (43).
Others, however, know the universal (*sāmānya*) as being in accordance with all its particular instances (*bheda*);
through its connection with other objects, it assumes the form of those particulars. (44)
The relation, by establishing itself within a particular [object], cuts off that state of wavering which belongs to it when it does not yet require a specific distinction.

(45) Others, however, think as follows: That which is merely the capacity toward all distinctions while grasping only its own object—that alone is "mere suitability" (*anuguṇyamātra*) and "mere co-referentiality" (*sāmānādhikaraṇyamātra*). For there is no such thing as a state of generality consisting of "neither thus nor otherwise" or "in every way"; all these are indeed only particulars.

In that state of generality (*sāmānyāvasthā*), because no particular differentiation can be determined and due to its inherent suitability, there exists a capacity to encompass all particularities within the object of a fluctuating conceptual construction. Relation (*sambandha*) restricts this [capacity] to a specific object by delimiting it from other objects. And when this mere delimitation of the object's capacity is effected, there is neither a restriction of superimposition (*adhyāropa*), nor is there an incapacity for apprehension; nor is this [delimitation] anything other than the form of the object itself. (44–45)

Now, in this context, by demonstrating *anvitābhidhāna* (the denotation of the related) through a different method within the very framework of the *saṃghāta* (the aggregate), he begins to establish that the meaning of the sentence is indeed the meaning of the word, stating: "sarvabheda... [and so on]. That which possesses the conformity of all particularities (*bheda*) is such a universal (*sāmānya*) characterized by relation; by virtue of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), compatibility (*yogyatā*), and proximity (*sannidhāna*), it assumes a restricted nature through its connection with other words, and this is the meaning of the sentence. 44.

And regarding that point, he says "the distinctions" (*bhedān*), meaning that at the moment when there is a desire [to know], this indistinctness of the sentence-meaning is removed by the proximity of the meanings of the other words. In the previous case, the meaning of the words in a sentence is exactly the same as it is when they are alone; however, their mutual relation (*saṃsarga*) is what is expressed by the aggregate.
