Furthermore, since the injunction (*vidhi*) and the prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) possess equal force, he states a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) due to their opposition: "In the case of the option (*vibhāṣā*) regarding words beginning with *nāsika*, there is a prohibition by way of conflict for those preceded by *sa-* or *nañ*. This is the injunction; that is the prohibition. And this conflict between injunction and prohibition is improper. Moreover, this injunction is not initiated like soft cotton wool upon the very object of the prohibition.

Just as it subverts that which possesses many characteristics and that which is characterized by the condition of conjunction, so too does it subvert that which possesses the characteristic of being previously existent. In this regard, since the principle that "exceptions [apply] before [the general rule]" has been negated in terms of subversion, the determination of subversion is established through conflict (*vipratiṣedha*).
(77) In this context, modification (*ūha*) is logical; its connection is not subverted.
This is an extension (*atideśa*) of the general; here, the particular is extended. (78)

Furthermore, *ūha* (modification) occurs because those words that are capable in the original form (*prakṛti*) lack capability in the modified form (*vikāra*); thus, it is performed by adopting different forms, genders, and numbers from the original. For example: in the original, the word "Agnayaḥ" (O fires! is seen to be capable of serving the purpose of the oblation-offering; in the modified form, there is the modification "Sūryāya" (To Sūrya), and so forth. Thus, due to various causes, *ūha* becomes manifold; this is the Vedic illustration.

In common worldly usage as well—for instance, in the expressions "the high houses of Devadatta" (*devadattasyoccāni gṛhāṇi*) and "the wealthy son of Vidhavā" (*āḍhyo vaidhaveyaḥ*)—one discards the word ending in the genitive case and, by virtue of the underlying cause, infers a word ending in the nominative case. In grammar too, all modifications of case-endings fall within the scope of such *ūha* (adaptation). For in these cases, when a word is perceived as connected with a particular case-ending in one grammatical rule (*yoga*), it undergoes a connection with another case-ending precisely by relinquishing its previous connection.

For example: "In the Upadeśa, a vowel followed by an anusvāra is termed *it*; there is elision of what follows an *it*; 'bhū', 'vā', and so forth are verbal roots; after a root ending in an anudātta vowel that has an *it*, the ātmanepada [terminations] are used."

Now, the non-sublation of the relationship, which serves as the counter-argument to this [objection], is also demonstrated. For example: "Devadatta’s houses are high; it is fitting that they belong to one of noble birth. In this case, since there is the direct hearing (*śruti*) of the word ending in a specific case-ending, so too is there a connection in another sentence. Likewise, they say that in cases such as "the jujube tree has fine thorns and sweet fruit" or "Pañcāla is a country," there is a non-sublation of the relationship.

In the Veda as well, for example: "He initiates the sacrificer with a staff," "he initiates him with water," "he initiates him with a girdle"—here, the word "sacrificer" (*yajamānam*) is connected [to each verb] without any contradiction. In the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*) as well—regarding the rule *bahu-gaṇa-vatu-ḍati-saṃkhyā* (Pāṇini 1.1.23), which prescribes a specific relationship—the term *saṃkhyā* ("number"), which is heard in its own form as the referent of the rule, is understood to function as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) for the technical name (*saṃjñin*) in another rule: "A number ending in *ṣ* or *n* receives the technical name *ṣaṭ*."

Now, the exposition of extension (*atideśa*) is undertaken. Extension is the application of the properties of one thing to another. It has two varieties: general extension (*sāmānyātideśa*) and specific extension (*viśeṣātideśa*). General extension is as follows: properties whose connection is well-established elsewhere are designated by their correlates—which have established renown in objects where the distinction is already known—wherever a distinction yet to be inferred is possible.

For example: "One should behave toward this Kṣatriya as one would toward a Brāhmaṇa. In this case, whatever functions are connected with the meaning that the word "Brāhmaṇa" does not deviate from—those functions are extended (*atidiśyante*) to the Kṣatriya, who has not yet actually received the designation "Brāhmaṇa. Similarly: "One should behave toward the teacher's son as one would toward the teacher. In the Veda, for instance: "One should proceed with other sacrifices as one does with the Darśapūrṇamāsa. And in the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*): "A substitute (*ādeśa*) is like the original (*sthānin*), except in the case of rules concerning letters (*al-vidhi*)."

Now follows the extension of specific [rules] (*viśeṣātideśa*). When persons such as Brāhmaṇas already possess well-known general duties, there occurs, by the power of further extension (*atideśa*), an extension of the duties pertaining to their specific original class (*prakṛti*). For example: "One should behave toward this Brāhmaṇa as one would toward a [typical] Brāhmaṇa. In this case, such an extension is understood to apply to those who behave toward a Brāhmaṇa exactly as they would toward a [typical] Brāhmaṇa. However, for those whose conduct is confused due to intermixture or negligence, a restrictive rule (*niyama*) is established. And it has been said: "The meaning of a word is the universal alone (*sāmānyamātra*); particulars (*viśeṣa*) are subject to deviation (*vyabhicārin*)."
"Therefore, no distinction is extended [to other cases] without [the presence of] functional capacity (*sāmarthya*).

In this regard, as in the Veda: "As in the case of the *Āgneya*, so in the case of the *Saurya*"; here, the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) belonging to that which has a single deity is indeed connected to that which has a single deity. By "ritual procedure" (*vidhyanta*), the sequence of actions (*itikartavyatā*) is meant.

In the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*), the transfer of specific properties (*viśeṣātideśa*) is observed through six modes, beginning with the transfer of form (*rūpātideśa*). Among these, the transfer of form is as follows: in the rule *dvirvacane'ci* ("when a vowel follows, there is reduplication"), the very form of the verbal root (*dhātu*) is transferred to the substitute. Consequently, reduplication occurs only for forms such as *yā* and *kṛ*, as in *yayatuḥ* and *cakratuḥ*. The transfer of cause (*nimittātideśa*) is as follows: in the rule *pūrvavatsanaḥ* ("the suffix *san* is like what precedes it"), whatever caused the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) for the preceding element—such as the marker *ṅ*—is transferred to the root ending in *san*, as in *atiśayati*.

An extension based on identity (*tādātmyātideśa*) is as follows: "A *sub*-ending [word] in vocative address is like a member of the subsequent word with respect to accent. This means that a *sub*-ending word, having attained identity with the vocative—as water merges with clay in a vessel—obtains its accent.

Whether it be an extension of the rule (*śāstrātideśa*) or an extension of the operation (*kāryātideśa*), as in the case of *karmavat karmaṇā tulyakriyaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.87): if this were an extension of the rule, then the suffix *śap* would subvert the suffix *yak*, and thus the addition of the term "agent-as-object" (*karmakartṛ*) must be undertaken in the rule prescribing *yak*. This is because, according to the principle of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), *śap* possesses greater force. However, if it is an extension of the operation, then *yak* is prescribed by the very rule *karmavat karmaṇā*; since *yak* itself is subsequent [in the order of rules], there is no subversion of it by *śap*, and therefore there is no need to undertake the additional statement (*upasaṃkhyāna*).

But the extension of designation (*vyapadeśātideśa*) is not possible at all in grammar, because it would be no different from the view that [the suffix] is a name (*saṃjñā*), and because it would result in the futility of employing the term *vat*.
(78) In this context, "desire" (*arthitva*) is the capacity; the meaning here does not differ.
This person has obtained the entitlement through the treatise (*śāstra*); his exclusion applies to other actions. (79)

Now follows the illustration of qualification (*adhikāra*). Qualification consists of [three factors]: desire (*arthitva*), capability (*sāmarthya*), and being subject to the non-exclusion by the scripture (*śāstrāparyudāsayogitva*). One who possesses these is a qualified person (*adhikārī*). Desire is the cause of qualification; for they declare that the supreme human goal here is liberation (*apavarga*). Even so, since some might neglect this goal despite having desire, capability is also a cause of qualification. For even when there has arisen a desire to see a performance, a blind person is not qualified for the act of seeing.

Furthermore, even for those who are seekers [of results], there is an incapacity regarding certain actions due to their exclusion by the scripture (*śāstra*). For example, Śūdras do not have the qualification (*adhikāra*) for the three Vedas (*trayī*). Indeed, with respect to specific unseen results (*adṛṣṭārtha*), capacity and incapacity are understood solely from the scripture. Therefore, they declare that the primary cause of qualification is the instruction of the scripture. In this regard, it is like how in the world a king appoints someone, saying: "From this day forward, you are authorized (*adhikṛta*) in this village or city."

As it is stated in the Veda: "A Brāhmaṇa desiring heaven should perform the Agnihotra sacrifice. In this case, the Brāhmaṇa’s eligibility [for the rite] is established by his desire for the result and other such factors. However, the eligibility of the scripture (śāstra) pertains to the properties of words, meanings, and persons.

In this regard, sound (*śabda*) is sixfold: correct (*sādhu*) and incorrect (*asādhu*). The correct is further divided into the scriptural (*śāstrīya*) and the practical (*prayogika*). The scriptural is also threefold: that which is to be explained (*pratipādya*), that which explains (*pratipādaka*), and that which possesses both forms. Among these, an example of that which is to be explained is a word such as *dādharti*, which is derived through grammatical derivation (*nipātana*). An example of that which explains is a base (*prakṛti*) or an affix (*pratyaya*), for by means of these, a word existing in actual usage—such as *kumbhakāra* (potter)—is explained. An example of that which possesses both forms is the word *itavya*. For it is explained by the word *tavya*, and it also explains the word *itavya* as it exists in usage.

And the *prāyogika* (applied) is of two kinds, distinguished as worldly (*laukika*) and Vedic (*vaidika*). Thus, together with the *sādhūn* (correct forms), there are six types of words. Among these which are to be explained, the domain of the science of grammar (*vyākaraṇa-śāstra*) is restricted; it does not extend to the *prakṛti* (bases), suffixes, and so forth. For these are not derived through grammar.

The object (*artha*) is eighteenfold. Among these, there is the mere thing (*vastumātra*) and the denotable (*abhidheya*). The denotable is also twofold: technical (*śāstrīya*) and worldly (*laukika*). Furthermore, it is that which causes a specific apprehension and comprehension, as well as its opposite; the primary (*mukhya*) and the one whose form is a conceptualized inversion (*parikalpita-rūpa-viparyāsa*); the expressible (*vyapadeśya*) and the inexpressible (*avyapadeśya*); that which has attained the state of a sentient being (*sattva-bhāva*) and that which is non-sentient (*asattva-bhūta*); that which possesses stable characteristics (*sthira-lakṣaṇa*) and that which is brought into proximity by the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā-prāpita-saṃnidhāna*); that which is being denoted (*abhidhīyamāna*) and that which is being explained (*pratipādyamāna*); and the intended (*abhisaṃhita*).

And [it is] "inseparable" (nāntarīyaka). In that context, the mere thing (*vastumātra*) is the external object which is not intended to be spoken or demonstrated; whereas that which is intended is the denotable object (*abhidheya*). And it is precisely with respect to that [intended object] that the word has its jurisdiction (*adhikāra*). That [jurisdiction] is twofold, by way of the distinction between technical (*śāstrīya*) and worldly (*laukika*). Among these, the technical is characterized by insertion and deletion (*āvāpoddhārika*); the worldly, however, is indivisible (*akhaṇḍa*). And the jurisdiction of the word pertains to the worldly object, not to the technical one; for the technical is artificial (*pauruṣeya*) and merely imagined.

Thus, even though it is not so [eternally] existent, it is understood as the indicator of the correctness of words by virtue of being their cause; and therefore, despite its variability, there is no deviation on the part of the traditionalists (smartṛs). And that [correctness], having an indefinite limit, is divided in many ways by the commentators.

An example of a cause for a cognition involving a specific apprehension (*viśiṣṭāvagraha*) is: "He causes Kaṃsa to be killed," or "He causes Bali to be bound. For here, the object is not [the external thing] as it actually exists, but rather, having been made the object of a cognition through a specific form, it enters the domain of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*). That which is the opposite of this is that which exists externally exactly as it is established; for example, "The cow is white," and so forth. A primary [denotation] (*mukhya*) is, for example, "A cow is that which possesses a dewlap and so on."

The "imagined" (parikalpita) is the perversion regarding form (*rūpa-viparyāsa*) by virtue of a sign (*nimitta*); that which possesses this is called the "imagined-sign-form-perversion," which is stated to be a secondary (*gauṇa*) meaning. For example, as in the case of "the Vāhīka is an ox. It is said that what is expressible (*vyapadeśya*) is merely that which is subject to addition and subtraction (*āvāpoddhārika*), whether it be a genus (*jāti*) or a substance (*dravya*). However, the inexpressible (*avyapadeśya*) is precisely the indivisible (*akhaṇḍa*) nature characterized as the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*).

That which has attained the status of a substance (*sattvabhāva*) is indeed denotable and is termed "subject to insertion and extraction" (*āvāpoddhārika*); that which has not attained the status of a substance (*asattvabhūta*) is characterized solely as the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*). In this context, the distinction [between these two] is generally stated merely on account of the difference in expression. An example of that which is characterized by stability (*sthiralakṣaṇa*) is the case of *rājapuruṣa* ("the king's man"): the state of being related to the king belongs to the man, and that indeed does not deviate [from him].

[The proximity] attained through the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*) is, for example, as in "the king's" or "of the man. For here, the state of being related (*saṃbandhitva*) is variable, since the qualifier and the qualified may be intended according to the speaker's wish. [Proximity] expressed by the word itself (*abhidhīyamāna*) is, for example, in the case of *rājasakha* ("king's friend"), where the meaning "this is the friend of the king" is expressed; when that is expressed, the meaning "the king is his friend" is indeed understood. [Proximity] intended (*abhisaṃhita*) is, for example, in the word "cow," whether one intends the universal (*jāti*) or the substance (*dravya*). [Proximity] inseparable from the object (*nāntarīyaka*) is, for example, in that very same case, the color, shape, and so forth. In this manner, the various types of the denoted object (*abhidheya*) should be demonstrated.

The properties of a person (*puruṣadharma*) include being a speaker, being a comprehender, and so forth. Among these, the properties of a speaker consist of affliction, envy, lack of respect, anger, reviling, threatening, and the like; whereas the properties of a comprehender consist precisely of being reviled and so forth. In this context, the scope of the treatise (*śāstra*) lies in its prescription of [phonetic] protraction (*pluta*), doubling (*dvirvacana*), and other such rules. And here, with reference to those very properties of words or the treatise that have been stated to fall outside its scope, it is said: "its exclusion is a different operation" (P. 1.4.56).
This [sequence] is obtained through direct audition (*śruti*), while this [other sequence] is obtained through pronunciation and the like.

This sequence is powerful here, yet it is not intended [to be the primary factor] in this case. (80) Now, the illustration of sequence: "This is a sequence obtained through direct statement (*śruti*); this is by means of pronunciation (*uccāraṇa*) and so forth. Thus, due to the distinctions between direct statement and the other factors, this sequence is of many kinds. Namely: sequence of direct statement (*śrutikrama*), sequence of meaning (*arthakrama*), sequence of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*), sequence of sections (*kāṇḍakrama*), sequence of commencement (*pravṛttikrama*), sequence of performance (*prayogakrama*), and sequence of cognition (*buddhikrama*). Among these, an example of sequence of direct statement is: "Having bathed, he goes" (*snātvā vrajati*). Here, the sequence is expressed by the direct statement of the suffix *-ktvā* itself.

As it is stated in the Veda: "He cuts from the heart first, then from the tongue"—here the sequence is expressed by the very words *agre* (first) and *atha* (then). In the grammatical treatise as well, in rules such as "for the parasmaipada [terminations], *ṇal*, *atus*, etc.," the sequence is established by the very words according to the principle that "the designation of an equal number [of elements] follows their respective order."

*Artha* means capacity; *arthakrama* is the sequence based on that [capacity]. For example, in the expression "having eaten, having bathed, he goes," although the bathing and so forth are presented by the words in a different order, the sequence of bathing and so forth is indicated by a consideration of the nature of the things themselves. In the Veda, for example: "He offers the *agnihotra*; he cooks the barley-gruel. Here, although the cooking is mentioned later, it is performed first, and then the *agnihotra* offering; this is *arthakrama*.

In the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*) as well, it is stated: "The rule for *lādi* suffixes applies when there is a secondary object (*guṇakarma*). For instance, in the sentence *gāṃ dogdhi payaḥ* ("He milks the cow for milk"), the cow is first connected with the verb *duh* (to milk), and subsequently the milk is connected. Indeed, no one is able to take the milk without having taken hold of the cow. Therefore, the sequential relationship between the cow and the milk in this case arises through the force of the meaning (*arthasāmarthya*).

Therefore, even though milk (*payas*) is the primary object, the cow (*go*) is first connected with the verb *duh* (to milk); consequently, due to its internal status (*antaraṅgatva*), the *l*-suffixes arise only there, as in *gaur dugdhā* (the cow was milked) or *sudohā gauḥ* (an easy-to-milk cow). The order of pronunciation is indeed the order of recitation, as in:
"The moon, gold, the antelope, the elephant, the male cuckoo, and the peacock were conquered by you through [respectively] the beauty of your face, your eyes, your gait, your voice, and your hair."

In this regard, there is a connection between things exactly as they are recited, using those very same recitations. For example, in the Veda: in the *prayāja* offerings, which consist of "He offers to the *samidhs*, he offers to *tanūnapāt*, he offers to the *iḍas*, he offers to the *barhis*, he offers with the *svāhā*-utterance," the performance follows the sequence exactly according to the order of the recitation. In the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*), for example: "In case of conflict, the subsequent [rule] prevails" and "That which precedes is not established [for what follows]. For here, the determination of "this is prior" and "this is subsequent" is established solely by depending on the order of the recitation of the rules.
Regarding the sequence: by whatever order the chapters establishing the social customs of the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas were indicated, they are explained in that very same order.

In the Veda, however, in certain sacrificial rites, the rituals proceed according to the very same sequence in which they are enjoined by the arrangement of the *kaṇḍikās* (sections). This is as in the case of the *yājyā-anuvākyā* verses and the [deities] such as Agni. Here, because the arrangement of the *yājyā-anuvākyā* verses follows the same sequence as the arrangement of the [deities] such as Agni, there is a connection based on the order of the *kāṇḍas* (sections). As it is stated in the grammatical treatise: "From the section on doubling (*dvirvacana*) comes the section on vowel-protraction (*samprasāraṇa*)," and likewise, "when there is a conflict, the former takes effect."

The order of engagement (*pravṛttikrama*) is as follows: by whichever sequence the Brāhmaṇas enter together, by that very same sequence they each receive the task assigned to them according to their respective position. As in the Veda: "One should sacrifice seventeen animals dedicated to Prajāpati"; here, for the seventeen goats, the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), the immolation (*viśasana*), and the carrying of fire around them (*paryagnikaraṇa*) are enjoined in a specific sequence.

Furthermore, for the performer who proceeds toward those [acts] by virtue of his own desire, starting from whichever point the first performance among them was commenced by that performer, he performs the other two in that very same order of commencement; thus, this sequence initiated by the will of the performer is called the "order of performance" (*pravṛttikrama*).

As it is stated in the Śāstra—the Bhāṣya says: "In whatever sequence the manifestation of meanings occurs, in that very same sequence the manifestation of words also occurs. Just as in the case of *apaṭvī* and *mṛdvī*, first the feminine suffix arises due to its connection with gender, and subsequently the singular number arises due to its connection with the object (*karman*) and so forth; in exactly the same way, grammatical operations such as the substitution of *yaṇ* proceed according to that same order."

The sequence of practice is as follows: regarding the rule *luṅlaṅlṛṅkṣvaḍudāttaḥ*, although the augment *aṭ* is pronounced first in actual usage, nevertheless, when we comprehend the meaning of the prescriptive statement (*vidhivākya*), we first comprehend the *luṅ* and other suffixes, and only afterwards the augment *aṭ*; this is a technical illustration from the grammatical system.

In common worldly usage, for example, when it is said "the man of the king," even though the order of utterance is transgressed, the understanding of the man occurs precisely through the determination of the object [of the genitive], namely the king. In the Veda, for example—though the principal sacrifices are mentioned first, they are understood only in accordance with the performance of the intermediate sacrifices. For instance, in the case of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites, and that of the Soma sacrifice. For here, although the principal Soma sacrifice first ascends to the intellect, the understanding of the Soma sacrifice occurs only after the performance of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other preliminary rites.

As for the order of application: a scriptural example is that in the case of *ḍukṛñ* and so forth, the indicatory letters (*anubandha*) receive their technical designations (*itsaṃjñā*) according to the very sequence in which they are applied.

As in the Veda: in the rule "having performed the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, one should sacrifice with another [rite]," the performance of the other rite is to be understood as being preceded by the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices. As for the sequence of the intellect (*buddhikrama*): in the grammatical treatise, regarding the vowels and semivowels in rules such as *iko yaṇ aci*, a temporal succession is mentally constructed. Furthermore, having raised the objection that "if *saṃhitā* (euphonic combination) were a sequence of sounds separated by time, it would not exist because of the absence of 'prior' and 'subsequent' [sounds], or because speech resides in a single phoneme, and because phonemes perish as soon as they are uttered," the Commentator stated: *Vedāntasūtra-bhāṣya* 1.3.28: "Even though the phonemes perish as soon as they are uttered, there is a mental construction (*buddhinirmita*) of them; and because this mental construction is not separated by time, there is indeed *saṃhitā*. Thus, although the phonemes themselves do not endure, a mental representation of them is formed, and through this non-temporal mental sequence, the relationship of prior and subsequent is established, thereby accounting for *saṃhitā*.

"Having performed all activities within the intellect, the wise agent, extending his policy, should perceive the meanings to be expressed through words and establish their sequence within the intellect.

Thus, the sequence of the intellect (*buddhi-krama*) is taught in the treatises. In the world as well, one mentally synthesizes things that exist and proceed in a sequence. In the Veda, the synthesis of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth—which arise and perish—is achieved by the intellect alone; thus it is a mental sequence. Indeed, every sequence is mental and does not originate from the actual object itself. As they say: "The sequence of apprehension does not originate from the object."

Then, one considers the relative strength and weakness of these sequences—thinking, "this sequence is stronger in this context. For example, as stated in the Veda: "First he should be fed, and after that, he should be anointed."

Now, in order to demonstrate the counter-example to sequence (*krama*), he says: "But in this case, it is not intended. The word "sequence" is the subject under discussion. The non-intention of sequence is its opposite. For example, in the Veda, the intention regarding sequence is observed among performers due to specific causes; it is also observed among listeners in common worldly usage. As stated in the *Vārttika* by the author: "There would be over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* before *kṅit* suffixes," and so forth. (80) Now, the instigating (*prayojaka*) and non-instigating (*aprayojaka*) [factors] are illustrated: "This [element], being connected with external members, is a non-instigator of the [internal] members."
"In this context, this is the motivator (*prayojaka*) for those [other factors], and this is its necessary concomitant (*nāntarīyaka*).

Therein, the king is the motivator of the shade of the royal parasol; although the elephants and other [attendants] are not the direct motivators, they are called 'motivators' because they are connected with the shade of the parasol. Thus, there is the status of being a motivator due to having a single result. Even when the results differ, examples should be inferred as they occur in the world. This should also be inferred in the case of the Veda and the Śāstras. This is the primary factor, this is the subordinate (*śeṣa*), and this is the sequence of application (*viniyoga-krama*). || 81 ||
"This is a direct benefactor, this is a remote specific [benefactor].

(82) Now, in order to demonstrate the primary and the subordinate, he says: "This is the primary; this is the subordinate. As in the Veda: "One threshes the rice-grains" (*vrīhīnavahanti*). Here, the rice-grains are the primary (*śeṣin*), and the threshing is the subordinate (*śeṣa*), because it exists for their sake. Examples for worldly usage and the sciences (*śāstra*) are to be inferred accordingly.

In order to demonstrate the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance) of this very relationship between the subordinate (*śeṣa*) and the principal (*śeṣin*), he says: "But this is the sequence of application. Thus, having presented the relationship of subordinate and principal along with its preparatory context, he states the internal subdivisions therein: "This is a direct benefactor; this is a specific [benefactor] at a distance. In that regard, in common worldly experience, a direct benefactor is, for example, ornaments and the like upon one's own self; a [benefactor] at a distance is the same [set of things] in relation to one's wife, children, and so forth. In the technical treatise (*śāstra*) as well, the direct benefactor of a suffix (*pratyaya*) is its stem (*prakṛti*) and so on.

That which is a qualifier of the root (*prakṛti*) and so forth is an indirect auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*). For example, in rules such as *erac*, the fact that the verbal root ends in the vowel *i* is a qualifier of the root; likewise, [the word] "animal" (*paśu*) and so forth is a qualifier of the agent (*kartṛ*). Even in the Veda, threshing (*avaghāta*) and the like are direct auxiliaries of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), whereas the fore-sacrifices (*prayāja*) and so forth are indirect auxiliaries. (82) In this case, there is a distinction between potentiality (*śakti*) and operation (*vyāpāra*), but the result (*phala*) is what differs here.
This distinction, arising from a connection [with the result], is not intended to be significant in that context. (83)

Having thus demonstrated the relationship between the subordinate and the principal (śeṣa-śeṣibhāva), along with its subdivisions and the associated constraints, he now speaks in order to demonstrate the distinction [between them]: "In this [relationship], there is a distinction of power and operation" (śakti-vyāpāra-bhedaḥ asmin). By resorting to the distinction between power and operation, a manifold variety of distinctions is observed. In that regard, in common usage one says, "It flashes from the cloud," "It flashes in the cloud," or "The cloud flashes"; here, there is a distinction among the powers of the cloud as the point of departure (apādāna), the locus (adhikaraṇa), and the agent (kartṛ). Furthermore, according to the intention of the speaker, there is likewise a distinction of operation within this very context as taught in the grammatical treatise; such is the distinction of power and operation.

In some cases, however, there is merely a difference in capacities (*śakti*), but not a difference in operations (*vyāpāra*). For example: *dhanuṣā vidhyati* ("he pierces with a bow"). Here, the capacity of the instrument (*karaṇa-śakti*), which has internally subsumed the capacity of the source (*apādāna-śakti*), operates without distinction from the meaning of the verb "pierces. Otherwise, it would not be possible for the bow to function as an instrument if its status as a source were not subsumed. For this very reason, a conflict between the two technical designations (*saṃjñā*) is described here. However, a pure difference in operation is not possible, because a difference in operation cannot exist without a difference in capacity.

Now, he states the distinction based on the difference in results: "But here, the result is differentiated. For example, from a single act of giving, there are distinct results such as longevity, health, and sovereignty. Others, however, maintain that when longevity and so forth are present, the sole result is simply a particular kind of joy (*prīti-viśeṣa*). Likewise, many actions may have a single result, just as in the administration of justice, there is a single decision for the subjects. As he will say: "In the observation of legal proceedings and the like, although the forms of the activities of the judges are diverse, their collective observation of the case brings about the accomplishment of the objective."* *This refers to the *Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā*, 2.4.13.*

To demonstrate the distinction by yet another method, he says: "This [distinction] arises from a relation. Just as in the case of verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta*), when there is a difference in the agent expressed by the suffix, a difference in the action itself is perceived due to that relation—as in *pacataḥ* (two cook) and *pacanti* (they cook). As it has been said: "Due to the difference in the means (*sādhana*), there is a difference in the results in the case of finite verbs (*tiṅ*); if there is no difference in the result, then cognition indeed arises from the means, for that [cognition] is well-established through the means."

Now, in order to demonstrate the distinction that serves as its counter-position, he says: "But here, distinction is not intended. Here, the non-distinction of capacity (*śaktyabheda*) is as follows: in the rule *samānakartṛkayoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.21), in the example *paktvaudanaṃ bhuṅkte* ("having cooked rice, he eats"), the distinction of capacity—which would otherwise arise due to the difference between the actions of the agent and the object—is not intended by the speaker. And this being the case, the state of having a common agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) is established here.

The non-difference of the operation (*vyāpāra*) has already been shown in the example "he pierces with a bow" (*dhanuṣā vidhyati*); likewise, the non-difference of the result (*phala*) was also stated previously, as for instance when some say that the single result of giving (*dāna*) is joy (*prīti*). This is the opposite of that case where difference arises from a difference in relation; here, there is no difference arising from a difference in relation. For example, in the expression "it is sat by Devadatta" (*āsyate devadattena*), the *lakāra* suffix is produced in the sense of the action itself (*bhāva*); since no difference in the means (*sādhana*) is introduced, it is not able to convey even a difference in the action (*kriyā*).

If it is argued that the cognition of that [object] arises from the word "Devadatta," we reply that this was stated by us with reference to a single word; thus there is no fault. Therefore, since this difference is manifold due to distinctions such as capacity (*śakti*) and so forth, it is for the students themselves to discern through their own creative insight (*utprekṣya*). Likewise, its opposite—non-difference (*abheda*)—should also be understood as being manifold in the same way. Furthermore, regarding these two, difference and non-difference, in some cases they possess reality (*vāstavatva*), while in other cases they rely solely upon intention (*vivakṣāmātra*).
It should also be followed here that intention itself is sometimes worldly (*laukikī*) and sometimes that of the speaker (*prayoktrī*).

Even in the Veda, the conventional usage of distinction (*bhedavyavahāra*) is observed. In such cases as "he sacrifices," "he gives," and "he offers oblations," there is a distinction in the unseen potency (*apūrva*) due to the difference in the constituent elements (*anubandha*) consisting of sacrifice, giving, and offering. There is also non-distinction (*abheda*), as for example when it is held that the six sacrifices beginning with the Āgneya have unity because they aim at a single *apūrva*. Thus, six, twelve, and twenty-four characteristics—both archetypal (*prākṛta*) and modified (*vaikṛta*), along with their respective counter-examples—have been demonstrated. (83)

Now, the commentator, speaking with boldness, demonstrates that there are also these many other types of logical principles (*nyāya*)—distinct from the six, twelve, or twenty-four—that serve as causes for the determination of categories (*padārtha*):
"This is a non-presuppositional negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), this is an exclusionary negation (*paryudāsa*) here;
this is secondary (*gauṇa*), this is primary (*mukhya*); this is pervasive (*vyāpin*), this is heavy (*guru*), and this is light (*laghu*). (84)

In this context, "prasajya-pratiṣedha" (absolute negation) refers to that case where the negative particle (*nañ*) is connected with a verbal action and involves a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*). An example from the technical treatises (*śāstra*) is: "And [the suffix *kṛt* is used] when the agent (*kartṛ*) is not the factor [of the action]" (*akartari ca kārake*).
An example from the Veda is: "A Brahmin must not be killed," "One should not speak untruth," and so forth.

As it is said in common usage: "The king’s wives are *asūryampaśyāḥ*" (those who do not look upon the sun). Regarding this, it is said: "But here, this is a *paryudāsa* (exclusion). Indeed, a *paryudāsa* is the opposite of a *prasajyapratiṣedha* (absolute negation); for in that case, the negative particle (*nañ*) is connected with the verb itself, and there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*).
And it has been stated: "But when [the negative] is connected with a noun or the meaning of a verbal root, it is not a negator at all."

In this regard, as in the technical treatise (śāstra): "The suffix *ka* occurs after a root ending in *ā*, provided no preposition (*anupasarga*) precedes. As in the Veda: "One who sells Soma is a non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇaḥ somavikrayī*); here, by following the mere [etymological] derivation, there is the understanding of someone who merely resembles a Brahmin. And as in the Smṛti rule: "One should not look at the rising sun," and so forth; because such examples are too remote from the present context, only the Vedic example is cited here.

In common usage, for example: "Bring a non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇam ānaya*), where this is considered figurative (*gauṇa*). In the technical treatises (*śāstra*), for example: "A *tatpuruṣa* compound whose members have a common substratum" (*samānādhikaraṇa*). Here, because the members [of the compound] share a common substratum, the *tatpuruṣa* itself is also said to have a common substratum.

In the Veda, for example: "The sacrificial post is the sun; the grass-bundle is the sacrificer. Here, due to shared qualities such as brilliance or similarity, the sacrificial post and so forth are called the sun and so forth.
And in common usage: "The boy is a lion; a hamlet on the Ganges," and so on.

"This is primary (*mukhya*). For example, in this treatise (*śāstra*), in such rules as *dhātoḥ* ("after a verbal root") and *prātipadikāt* ("after a nominal stem"), that which is denoted (*abhidheya*) is primary.
In the Veda, for example: "The sacrificer (*yajamāna*) touches the Adhvaryu priest," where both the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer are indeed primary.
In common usage (*loka*), for example: "The boy is a hero."

Regarding the term "all-pervasive" (*vyāpin*): as it says in the treatise, "The single accent (*ekaśruti*) is used for addressing from a distance. For in that case, the worldly (*laukikī*) form of address is included because of its pervasiveness. Indeed, when that [worldly form] is included, the technical (*śāstrīyā*) form of address is also thereby encompassed. And he will say: "A worldly [term], when uttered in certain contexts, pervades even a technical object;
thus, in the case of addressing from a distance, there is the inclusion of both."
In all cases where there is a mutual benefit, everything therein should be understood as being pervasive.
In the Veda as well, there are prescriptive injunctions regarding entitlement (*adhikāra-vidhi*), such as: "All [rites] pertaining to the primary sacrifice are [performed] by means of the Jyotiṣṭoma.
In common worldly practice as well, for example, one may perform a bath in the celestial river (the Gaṅgā) at Sannihatī by means of a certain procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
As it is said: "Having fasted for one night at Sannihatya, O best of men, one is liberated even from the darkness of the sun, the Gaṅgā, and the moon."

In this context, as an incidental illustration of pervasion (*vyāpti*), it has been stated that by bathing here just once, one obtains the merit of bathing in all the sacred fords (*tīrtha*) situated within the three worlds.

Regarding the distinction between "this is heavy" and "this is light": in that regard, according to the grammatical treatise, the rule "words such as *pṛṣodara* are as they are taught" is a light means for conveying the multitude of correct words established by the usage of the learned (*śiṣṭa*). However, the method beginning with "the case-endings (*svādi*) are applied after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) to express [factors] such as the singular number of the object when not already expressed" is a heavy means.

In common worldly usage as well—in expressions such as "this village possesses red rice"—when a *karmadhāraya* and a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) are applied to the same object, a cumbersome construction (*guruprakrama*) arises; however, lightness of construction (*laghutva*) belongs to the *bahuvrīhi* in that context. In the Veda, however, this pertains to the application of the principles of heaviness and lightness within the rules for *tantra*, *prasaṅga*, and *āvṛtti*. Among these, a cumbersome construction occurs in the case of *āvṛtti*, as in: "He recites the first [verse] three times, and the last three times. But in the cases of *tantra* and *prasaṅga*, the practice of lightness of construction is as was demonstrated previously. || 84 ||
Through differentiation, the relationship of part and whole (aṅga-aṅgin) of this [suggestion] is conceptualized in many ways;
here, this [element] is restricted, and its fitness arises in that [context]. (85)

This refers to the relationship of part and whole (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) through differentiation. As in the *Śāstra*: "In rules concerning compounds, [the term] 'his offspring,' [the suffixes] after the agent, *kṛt* [suffixes]," and so forth. As in the *Veda*: a single constituent part, even when connected with other sentences separated by intervals, enters into a relationship [with them]. For example: "with a flawless [sieve]" and so forth, [connected] with "Citpati" and the others. Previously, the relationship of part and whole was shown for each individual; now, it is shown that a single constituent part serves many wholes. This is why it is mentioned again. Also in common worldly usage:
A gem polished on a whetstone; rivers with their sandy banks dried up in autumn; the moon reduced to its final digit; young women exhausted by lovemaking;
an elephant emaciated by rut; and a victor in battle slain by a weapon.
Men whose wealth has vanished shine with dignity when they are among those who seek their help.
Thus, in the *dīpaka* (illuminator) figures of speech and the like, a single action is connected with many sentences;

this is what is meant by "being conceptualized through many varieties. Regarding this, in the technical treatises (*śāstra*), there is sometimes an option concerning what is already established (*prāpti-vikalpa*), sometimes an option concerning what is not yet established (*aprāpta-vikalpa*), and sometimes an option concerning both (*ubhaya-vikalpa*).

As in the Veda: "Whatever [is performed] prior to the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice, all that must be done in a low tone (*upāṃśu*). Here, since the low tone is already established, the rule prescribing "as one wishes" for the loud tone (*uccaiḥ-svara*) in the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice and so forth constitutes an example.

In common worldly usage, as for example, the imaginative constructions (*vikalpa*) conceived by great poets such as in the verse beginning, "Is this [the moon] the sprout of the tree of youth? Here, [the object] is restricted. In the technical treatises (*śāstra*), as for example: "The word *pati* [is compounded] only when it is in a compound," and "Those [suffixes] come before the verbal root.

In the Veda, as for example: "Having seen the stars, one should release speech. In this case, the release of speech is restricted to that specific time alone. Also in common worldly usage, as for example: "Arjuna (*Pārtha*) alone is the archer"—here, the quality of being an archer is restricted to Arjuna.

"In this case, fitness (*yogyatvam*) arises for it. As stated in the *Śāstra*: "In the place of *u*, fitness arises for *aṇ* when it is about to be applied, with respect to its having *r* as a subsequent element (*raparatva*). Or, for example: "When an acute (*udātta*) or circumflex (*svarita*) accent is applied to a single word, fitness arises for the remainder of what is being excluded (*varjyamānaśeṣa*) with respect to its being prohibited (*nidhyāte*). In the Veda, for example: in the injunction "One should sacrifice with the *Jyotiṣṭoma*," fitness belongs only to one of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*).
As it is said in the world: "The beast of burden is yoked to the yoke. Whatever object is capable and not excluded by the treatise is called "fit" (yogya). || 85 ||
From the mark (liṅga) observed in another sentence, a distinction [from that sentence] is inferred;
this word-meaning is extracted from the word and analyzed. (86)

From a mark (*liṅga*) observed in another sentence, a distinction is understood. As in the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*): by the rule "oḥ puyaṇjyapare," that which is performed in the causative suffix (*ṇi*) is treated as if it were the original element (*sthānivat*).

As in the Veda: regarding the statement "He places down the smeared pebbles," when there is the expectancy "Smeared with what?", the specific detail that they are smeared with ghee is understood from the mark of the praise of ghee in another sentence, namely, "Ghee is indeed brilliance."

In common worldly usage, for example, when there is doubt as to whether "this Rāma" in such phrases as "in the worlds... refers to the son of Daśaratha or to Paraśurāma, the understanding that it is indeed the son of Daśaratha arises from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) found in another sentence: "with the seven notes emitted through the openings of a row of broad palm trees struck by a single arrow. This is what is meant by saying that the word-meaning is extracted and analyzed from the word.
In technical treatises (*śāstra*), for example, from the rule *dhṛṣi-śasī vaiyātye*, the term *vaiyātya* is extracted and analyzed as: "the state of being *viyāta* (shameless) is *vaiyātya*."

As it is seen in the Veda—for instance, from the sentence "One should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu," having extracted [the meaning] from the referent of the word *vāyavya*, one analyzes it by stating, "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity. In common worldly usage as well, when "the king’s man" is said, there arises a question and answer such as "Whose king? and "Śūdraka’s," whereby the referent of the word *rāja* (king) is analyzed. || 86 ||

Now, in order to conclude the objection regarding the subject at hand, he says: "If the word were non-expressive, then all those properties which, in sentences, are based upon the meanings of words would not be possible. (87)

If it is admitted that the sentence is partless (*anaṃśa*), then all those properties which assist in the comprehension of the sentence-meaning—being dependent upon the cognition of specific word-meanings within sentences that consist of a collection of words and are based on real word-meanings—would find no footing here, since there would be no division of referents that actually exist; thus the proponent of the reality of words (*padavādin*) objects, [arguing] that if the word were not truly expressive, this would be the case. (87)

When the host of refutations by the proponent of the word-theory (*padavādin*) against the proponent of the indivisible sentence-theory (*akhaṇḍavākyavādin*) has been concluded, the latter now says this to resolve it:

"Even though the meaning of the sentence is indivisible, because its capacities (*śakti*) are differentiated when abstracted [from the whole], there is no contradiction with what was stated regarding the division of other sentences. (88)

All this as stated is not contradicted in our position. Thus, in our view, even though the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is one—being indivisible and partless—when it is apprehended like the taste of a beverage (*pānakarasa*), and when its constituent parts are extracted by resorting to a distinction of powers (*śaktibheda*), the intermediate sentence-meanings (*avāntaravākyārtha*) arise once that extraction has been performed; such is the intended meaning.

Just as in the Śākya view, a single, partless entity—a *svalakṣaṇa* (particular) distinct from the entire three worlds—is accepted, and some conventional usage of universals (*jāti*) and so forth is maintained by relying on the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of this and other entities; likewise, for one who maintains that the sentence is indivisible (*akhaṇḍavākyavādin*), once the differentiation of the sentence-meaning is made through a distinction of powers (*śaktibheda*), everything is consistent, and thus there is no fault whatsoever. [This is stated] "by means of the division of other sentences."

And the statement, "even when the sentence-meaning is not yet divided," was said because the sentence and the sentence-meaning share the same fate (ekayogakṣema). If it is argued that, regarding an objection preceded by the impossibility of word-meanings, the reply "by means of the division of other sentences" appears as if incorrect, [we reply that] the logic of the relationship between the sublated and the sublator is observed even in the case of sentences.

Thus, it has been shown that even that [objection] is not contradicted by the sublation of subordinate sentences in view of the great sentence (*mahāvākya*); and by demonstrating that, it has already been shown that these logical principles—which are based on the extraction of word-meanings—apply even to sentences of limited extent. (88) To strengthen this very point by means of an illustration well-known in experience, he says:
"Just as there is a conceptual differentiation of a single fragrance in flowers and so forth, so too is a distinction of meaning prescribed within a sentence. (89)

In the case of a garland, sandalwood, and so forth, the fragrance is present as a single entity; however, by resorting to the abstraction (*apoddhāra*) of its components, a distinction is conceived, such as "this is the scent of the flower" or "this is the scent of the sandalwood. Likewise, within the sentence itself, by resorting to the abstraction of meanings, the distinction between word-meanings is established—such as "this is the meaning of the word *devadatta*" or "this is the meaning of the word *go*," and so on. || 89 ||
Just as in the case of a gavaya or a man-lion (narasiṃha), when they are covered by a single cognition, one perceives a portion that is similar to another species. (90)
He states another illustration:

when a gavaya or the like is apprehended, made an object of cognition, and delimited by a single, non-distinct act of knowledge, one perceives therein a portion of that very [animal] which possesses a well-known different genus. Thus, when the justification of all logical principles has been established by resorting to this method of abstraction (apoddhāra), then, by virtue of sharing the same status of proof and refutation (samānayogakṣematā), both the substitute (pratinidhi) and the contradiction with the laudatory statements (stutivākyavirodha) are indeed established. However, the meaningfulness of the intermediate sentences will be established further on. || 90 ||
But when a fool perceives a portion that is unestablished, unseen, and [previously] unperceived, he assumes a lack of awareness regarding that very extent in all cases. (91)
Now, relying on that very same analytical abstraction (*apoddhāra*), he provides an introduction in order to resolve the objection regarding the doubt concerning the cuckoo and other such things:

"In that regard, the deluded person perceives in the *gavaya* and so forth a part that is unestablished, unseen, and uncertain; yet, in reality, no such [distinct] cognition has arisen with respect to that which is everywhere undivided, due to some cause. Everywhere, this person, while not actually cognizing it, nevertheless proceeds as if he were cognizing it. (91)

Likewise, due to the association with words such as "pika" (cuckoo) and others, people consider that even in a sentence which is entirely distinct [from its parts], there is a cognition of a non-existent object as if it were something real. (92)

To apply this to the present case, he says: "Let the cuckoo be brought from the forest" is entirely distinct from the other sentence, "Let the bear be brought from the forest. However, one might think that the meaning of "let [something] be brought from the forest" here is similar to that of "let the bear be brought from the forest" due to its proximity and sequence. But in reality, because of the connection with the cuckoo and so forth, the entire sentence is entirely distinct. When there is doubt regarding even a single word's meaning, the entire sentence is said to be unknown. (92)
Similarity is perceived in one part and difference in another part, by means of a partless consciousness directed toward a partless light. (93)
He provides an illustration:

just as a single cognition of blue, yellow, and so forth, though arising as partless due to its nature of luminosity (*prakāśa*), is considered to have similarity by virtue of being a cognition, yet possesses difference by virtue of being blue, yellow, and so forth; in reality, however, the cognition of blue is indeed distinct from the cognition of yellow, and thus there is no underlying continuity (*anugama*) therein.

Alternatively, one may recognize similarity in one part and difference in another part between two variegated cognitions (*citrajñāna*). For one variegated cognition manifests blue and yellow, while another manifests blue and red; thus, one recognizes similarity therein by way of the blue and so forth, and difference by way of the yellow and so forth. || 93 ||

In the very same way, similarity is determined in one part and difference in another, even in the case of sentences whose properties are entirely distinct, despite the absence of any shared parts. (94)
In order to apply this to the case under discussion, he says:
"The meaning of the verse is clear. (94)
If there were destruction of the forms of words, how could there be the conceptualization of a limit? And if the word has no grasped limit, how can its meaning be expressed? (95)

Now, the proponent of the indivisible [sentence] (akhaṇḍavādī) speaks in order to refute the proponent of words (padavādī): "If only words were real, then since the form [of a word] would be destroyed in a *saṃhitā* such as 'ādadhyāna' (place the firewood), and thus the fixed word would be absent, with what limit could its meaning be analyzed? Therefore, one must admit that only the sentence, devoid of division, is the single reality. (95)

Just as in the case of colors in a mixture, that form, though established elsewhere in the word, is not perceived distinctly among its various forms due to the principle of simultaneous operation (tantra). || 96 ||

Now, regarding the position that [the word] is indivisible (*akhaṇḍapakṣa*), [an objection is raised]: how can "The white one runs" (*śveto dhāvati*) be a single sentence, given that it must resolve two questions? For here, the form *śvā* has been altered due to the rules of euphonic combination (*saṃhitā*); since the meaning of this [original] word-part is impossible [in its altered state], how can there be comprehension of it? To this, he replies: In a case such as "white" (*śveta*), within the indivisible position, the forms are established as if in a state of conjunction; therefore, another form, established by way of a common substratum (*tantra*) among those various forms, is intended to be the conveyor of meaning—thus there is no fault. (96)
In that non-difference, there exists a semblance of difference among distinctions;
therefore, one form is differentiated from another as being non-different from it. (97)
Desiring to explain that very point, he says:

In that single non-duality, which consists of the form "white" (*śveta*), there exists—as if it were a conjunction—of various distinctions such as "dog" (*śvā*) and "gone" (*itaḥ*) and "white" (*śveta*). Therefore, although that form is not different from its constituent parts, by resorting to the logic of the *tantra* (the system of interdependence), it is divided for the purpose of conveying both meanings; thus, in this view, the word "white" (*śveta*) conveys the undivided whole. 97.
In the treatise, the identity of the signifier with the signified is sometimes assumed;
at other times, a distinction between the grasper and the grasped is maintained. (98)

Now, in this very context, as an incidental discussion, he states that the distinction and non-distinction between the signified (*pratyāyya*) and the signifier (*pratyāyaka*) are based on the difference in their objects:
"The letter *ū* is conceived as non-different, according to the respective order.
Therein, he demonstrates the non-difference between the signified and the signifier:

This was stated under the rule *ūkālo’jjhrasvadīrghaplutaḥ*: since there is no established equality of number among the short (*hrasva*) vowels and the others due to a discrepancy between the enumeration [of the vowels] and the description [of the durations], it is established that there is indeed an equality of number because there is a description of the three as modifications (*vikāra*). Consequently, in the rule *ūkālaḥ*, because the one-mora, two-mora, and three-mora durations are described in combination, and because there is equality of number—and thus equality of description—due to the non-difference between the signifier (*pratyāyaka*) and the signified (*pratyāyya*), the application of number (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*) is established; thus the technical names *hrasva*, *dīrgha*, and *pluta* remain distinct, and there is no fault whatsoever.
In the apprehension of the *lṛṅ* and *lṛṭ* [suffixes], the distinction is imagined together with the objects to be grasped. || 99 ||
In order to demonstrate the distinction between the signifier (*pratyāyaka*) and the signified (*pratyāyya*), he says:

in the rule *syatāsī lṛluṭoḥ*, the term *lṛ* would signify both *lṛṅ* and *lṛṭ*; thus, due to the disparity between the cause (*nimitta*) and the effect (*nimittin*), the correspondence according to numerical order (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*) would fail to apply. This was stated under the rule *yathāsaṃkhyamanudeśaḥ samānām*: "If there were equality of number based on the words [themselves], then in cases such as *ṇalādayaḥ parasmaipadānām*, *ḍāraurasaḥ prathamasya*, and *eco'yavāyāvaḥ*, there would be no [correspondence]."

"If it is on the basis of meaning (*arthataḥ*), then there would be a fault in the case of *lṛ* and *luṭ* [affixes], as well as in [the formation of] *nandin*, *arīhaṇa*, *sindhu*, *takṣaśilā*, and so forth"—this objection thus presents two alternative positions.

To this it is replied: in the rule concerning *lṛ* and *luṭ*, the form *lṛ* is the signifier (*pratyāyaka*) merely as a general category stripped of its specific markers (*anubandha*), and it is accepted here as being non-different; it is not, however, admitted to be different based on the difference between the things signified (*pratyāyya*). Consequently, because the cause (*nimitta*) and the thing caused (*nimittin*) are identical, the correspondence of number (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*) is consistent, and thus nothing undesirable follows. || 99 ||

The form *yasya* is the designator of those who possess the technical name (*saṃjñin*), as it is the word *aṇ*. For there is no possibility of a reference being made to that which is merely implied. (100)
Now, in order to demonstrate that there is likewise no difference between the signified and the signifier even in other cases, he says:

The *i* and the *a*: that which is the form of the combined *i*-sound and *a*-sound conveys [the meaning] of those respective sounds; because there is no difference between the phonemes *ivarṇa* and *avarṇa* as they convey their designata (*saṃjñin*), it conveys them. Therefore, even in the case of the *ī*-sound and the *ā*-sound, elision (*lopa*) takes place in words such as *sauparṇeya* and *vainateya*. If, however, the non-difference between the signifier (*pratyāyaka*) and the signified (*pratyāyya*) were not accepted here, then it would be impossible for other [sounds] to be grasped or conveyed by what is being perceived or signified; thus, the desired result would not be established here.

Therefore, because it is uttered as a single compound (tantra) and possesses a combined form, it conveys both meanings; thus, from the expression "the white one runs," there is indeed the cognition of both objects. || 100 ||
This sound "ū" is indeed non-different [from its constituent parts], yet it is based upon distinct words;
and because it is perceived as distinct, it appears like the external form of two [sounds]. (101)
He states this by means of an illustration to show that, through the sublation of intermediate sentences (*avāntaravākya*), this [single rule] will convey both meanings:

"The term *ūkāla* is employed here; its undifferentiated form should be understood as common to the three—short, long, and protracted (*pluta*). Therefore, this single [term] stands in the place of a *grahaṇaka-vākya* (a rule for inclusion), yet it functions as the basis for intermediate sentences. He says: "It is the basis for distinct sentences": "A vowel (*ac*) having the duration of *u* is designated as short (*hrasva*); having the duration of *ū* is designated as long (*dīrgha*); and having the duration of *u3* is to be understood as protracted (*pluta*)."

And therefore, when its apprehension occurs as non-different from [the other element] due to their being combined (*saṃsṛṣṭatva*), then this form *ū* is based precisely on a distinct sentence. Just as the "subsequent form" (*pararūpa*) is seen to be expressive of both even though it is one because of their combination, so too should this be understood. Consequently, in cases such as *śveto dhāvati*, it should be construed that there will be a dual meaning through the superimposition of a subordinate sentence (*avāntaravākya*). || 101 ||

Furthermore, by rejecting the expansion of phonemic components (*aṅga*) in a protracted vowel as well as the combination of vowels (*samāhāra*), he has resorted to an absolute distinction between words (*śabda*). || 102 ||

To demonstrate that the Vārttikakāra favors only the view that words are distinct, he says: regarding the rule *plutāvaica idutau*, it was stated, "An enlargement of the *aṅga* is not possible; for neither the vowel *a*, nor *i*, nor *u* is a constituent part (*avayava*) of the *ai* or *au*. By thus rejecting the enlargement of the *aṅga*, the previously shown non-difference—the idea that those two very sounds are merged into one—is refuted. Likewise, by rejecting the collective aggregate (*samāhāra*) of the vowels, difference alone is intended. As he said: "If it is argued that there is a collective aggregate of the two vowels, no; because of their absence [as separate entities]."

Therefore, in cases such as "The white horse runs," the resolution [of the syntactic connection] through the immediate blending of two similar [words]—whether by the intrusion of an intermediate sentence or by resorting to the principle of *tantra*—is not superior [to the alternative]. || 102 ||

Just as there is a difference in form among words such as *ardharca* and others according to their sequence, so too, within a single word according to the system (*tantra*), there is a different perception for those that are distinct. (103)
Now he begins to conclude the *tantra*:

"Just as by virtue of sequence, one half of a *ṛc* is called an *ardharca*, so too is there a difference in form for a single word; likewise, by resorting to the principle of *tantra*, when there is a single word, the various forms should be understood such that what is heard otherwise is actually a non-differentiated hearing (*abhinnā śrutiḥ*). Thus the *tantra* is concluded. || 103 ||
In the context of phonetic combination (*saṃhitā*), the phonemes remain unchanged in their essential form;
yet, as it were, they undergo the status of being different words by assuming other powers. (104)
To clarify this very point, he says:

"That same word appears in the context of *saṃhitā* as possessing multiple powers and phonemes. Thus, because the single word *śveta* is uttered with *saṃhitā*, it is held to convey both meanings by assuming another power. (104)
When an object among the things to be grasped is perceived through a modification of the sense organs and so forth,
that sequential process of apprehension— occurring apart from the abandonment of its own nature— is what is described in the Śruti.
He states, by means of an illustration, that even for a single entity, a distinction arises due to a difference in its causal conditions (*nimitta*):

"Just as an object of a single form appears in various forms to those whose eyes are impaired by glass or other such defects, so too, by virtue of *saṃhitā*, even a single word appears in another form. (105)
Due to its connection with the act of denotation, even though the words themselves remain unchanged, that very same single form appears as if it were absolutely distinct. (106)
To conclude this very point, he says:

"The act of denotation is indeed the utterance by means of a *saṃhitā* (a continuous phonetic combination). Because of its connection—that is, its relation—to that [utterance], even words that remain unmodified appear as a single entity through the assumption of another power, yet they manifest with absolute distinction. (106)
The *sāman* is either the *ṛc* itself or merely its melody; it is not a separate substance.
It is those very same *ṛcs*, modified by differences in melody, that are distinguished [as different *sāmans*]. (107)
Now, this very point is observed regarding the domain of scripture; therefore, he speaks in order to provide corroboration:

"In such a way that the *ṛc*s themselves receive the designation of *sāman* through their specific utterance, or rather, *sāman* is merely the specific mode of utterance, as it is said: 'The name *sāman* applies to the melodies (*gīti*)'. Or, in order to make known that the *ṛc* is indeed the *sāman*, he says: "Due to the difference in melody," and so forth.

Thus, whether by means of a relationship between the signified and the signifier that is differentiated by the speaker's intention regarding difference or non-difference, or by way of absolute difference—as described in the passage "In the case of *saṃhitā*, the phonemes [are distinct]"—or by means of a simultaneous application (*tantra*) or its opposite, in the form of the superimposition of subordinate sentences, there will be a difference in meaning despite the unity of the sentence "The white horse runs. Therefore, even in our position where words are not admitted as discrete entities, there is no deficiency whatsoever. || 107 ||

In the compendium of the Vedas, when words that have been split apart and are now to be treated as a single remainder are pronounced by way of abbreviation (*tantra*), their grammatical correctness is accepted in the treatise. (108)
Then, in order to further justify this by means of the principle of *tantra*, he says:

"The convergence (*saṃhāra*), that is, the conjunction (*saṃśleṣa*) or being swallowed (*gīrṇatva*), of words that are distinct from the characteristic of *tantra* within a single utterance (*śruti*). To the question "Of what kind of distinct [words]? he replies: "Of those that are subject to *ekaśeṣa*. They are called "subject to *ekaśeṣa*" because they are uttered by way of *tantra*, due to their similarity to *ekaśeṣa*. (108)
Having accepted a single Vedic revelation, even for those [words] that possess different forms, their utterance should be performed by way of a common tantra; otherwise, they would not be correct.

Therefore, in such a case, even for words that are distinct, one should provide an exposition by means of *tantra* (simultaneous application) based on some degree of similarity; thus he says: "Even though in this treatise (*śāstra*) a simultaneous exposition of sentences with identical forms has not been explicitly performed, nor has the exposition of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) been performed, nevertheless, because they follow the same principle, everything useful for the instruction of words (*śabdānuśāsana*) has already been explained and stated. To demonstrate this, he says:

As stated by the author of the Vārttika: "Or [the final *h* is included] because of the mention as a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*). By this, [it refers to] those which are the subjects of the single remainder—that is to say, those that follow the principle of the *tantra* (simultaneous application). This was stated, beginning with "by means of an expedient," etc., in order to clarify the preceding verse, starting with "by simultaneous utterance" (*tantreṇoccāraṇe*), and so forth. || 109 ||

And for sentences that have identical forms, a single form is correctly obtained through the application of the *tantra* principle by virtue of being uttered once, as established by the grammatical treatise. (110)
Just as a single [person] assumes multiple forms by taking on various bodies such as those of a crane and so forth, in the same way, through the Tantra, many may attain a single form. 111.
To conclude this very point by means of an illustration, he says:

"Just as even a single sound, by virtue of being produced through different media such as flutes and the like, arises with various distinctions of form such as Ṣaḍja, Ṛṣabha, and so forth; likewise, by resorting to the Tantras, there is a single uniform nature—namely, the form 'white' (śveta)—even for distinct words such as 'śvā' and 'śveta'. Thus, there is no fault whatsoever in this regard. (111)
Just as there is the possibility of sentences that have the form of words [within them], so too, even in the absence of other distinct sentences, these [words] would possess distinct meanings. (112)

Now, in order to refute the objection that the intermediate sentences would lack meaning, he says: Just as in the view of the indivisible [sentence], even though intermediate sentences—which are of the same nature as words—have no actual existence, their meaning is established for the sake of the great sentence by imagining their possibility through the intellect's process of abstraction (*apoddhāra*). If this were not imagined, there would be no comprehension of the meaning of the great sentence. Likewise, in the absence of other [separate] sentences, these [intermediate ones] would possess distinct meanings of their own.

Since one may assume a separate meaning for these [sentences] even though it is unreal, by postulating other sentences through the recourse to extraction (*apoddhāra*), there is no objection regarding the impossibility of the intermediate sentences. || 112 ||
The meaning of a word is that which is denoted, and the meaning of a sentence is its purpose;
for one who holds this [view], a connection between sentences is not logically possible. (113)
Now, in order to refute the position that the purpose (*prayojana*) is the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*), he says:

"The purpose of a sentence is said to be the function of the sentence, but not its denoted object (*abhidheya*). To the question, "Of what would this be the meaning?", he replies: "The meaning of a word (*pada*) is its denoted object. Thus, the meaning of words is called their denoted object. He refutes this with the words "of whatever it may be," and so forth. For one who speaks thus, there would be no mutual connection between sentences. What would constitute the connection between sentences that are like mere pegs or iron rods? The mutual connection would have to be mediated by the denoted objects.
Furthermore, the claim that sentences have no denotable object results in those sentences being entirely disconnected; therefore, this argument is trivial. 113.
In that case, it is the verbal roots alone that require one another;
therefore, the relationship is understood as being connected to those verbal roots. (114)
Then, in order to establish this by resorting to the theory of *anvitābhidhāna* (the expression of meanings as already related), he says:

"The verb, having projected the entire collection of means [of accomplishment], becomes free from expectancy; the mutual relationship connected to that verb also becomes free from expectancy. Therefore, it is logically established, and there is no defect whatsoever. (114)
Whether it be a repetition or a restatement, when the individual meanings of the words are conceived, the sense is complete in each one, yet it subsists in those things that exist together. (115)

Now, it may seem that the theory of the expression of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*) is not tenable. For instance: if the meaning of the sentence, endowed with all its particulars, were already understood at the very outset, we see no purpose whatsoever in the subsequent denotation of the words "cow" and so forth. Since words whose meanings have already been understood would result in redundancy if spoken again—anticipating this objection, he speaks in order to provide a justification:

Even for those who have already understood the meaning, repetition will serve to establish a restrictive rule (*niyama*); or, it is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the stated meaning for the sake of clarification. Thus, there is no pointlessness in these [repetitions]. Furthermore, even if there were only one [instance], because each preceding one has been obscured, and because simultaneity is impossible, a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) would be impossible, resulting in a failure to understand the meaning.

Furthermore, because the meaning of a sentence—endowed with all its qualifiers—is not understood from a single word alone, and because it is impossible to conceive of subsequent words as being either restrictive or reiterative when their own meanings have not yet been apprehended, the theory of *anvitābhidhāna* (the denotation of the related) is indeed inconsistent. However, when it is asserted that this meaning is complete within each word even while they coexist—as it has been said: "The accomplishment of the object’s meaning among the perceivers is accompanied by manifestation and secondary indicators"—then there is no futility in employing the coexisting words, and thus there is no fault whatsoever. || 115 ||
Even though the meaning of a sentence is non-conceptual, conceptualizations based on mental cultivation arise;
regarding this point, the arguments of former masters have proceeded in many ways. (116)

Thus, the definitions of sentences beginning with *saṅghāta*, along with incidental investigations, have been explained. It will be shown that a sentence is a verbal form (*ākhyāta*). In the course of explaining the sentence, the four types of sentence-meanings—characterized as conjunction (*saṃsarga*), the conjoined (*saṃsṛṣṭin*), the independent word-meaning (*nirākāṅkṣapadārtha*), and purpose (*prayojana*)—have also been presented. He will further demonstrate intuition (*pratibhā*) and action (*kriyā*). Now, having raised the doubt—"How can there be such a proliferation of alternatives regarding a single sentence-meaning?"—he speaks in order to investigate this:

It is logical to accept that the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*) is indeed free from conceptual construction (*avikalpa*) and undivided (*nirvibhāga*). And regarding such a [sentence-meaning], those various conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) that appear must be understood as resting upon the mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) derived from many different treatises belonging to various persons; they do not follow the actual reality (*vastu*) itself. Therefore, it is logical that the sentence-meaning is one alone. To demonstrate this very point, he says: "In this context" (*atrādhikaraṇe*). In this context—that is, in this place of inquiry—the various doctrines of former teachers have proceeded in many ways; since these belong to those whose minds are perfumed by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of their respective scriptures, who can be held accountable for them? (116)

All words are traditionally held by others to be the cause of intuitive insight (*pratibhā*) through repeated practice, as is seen in the communication of objects according to their true nature among children and even animals. (117)

In the ultimate sense, however, the meaning of a sentence is precisely this: every word whatsoever is a cause for *pratibhā* (intuitive flash). To introduce its nature now, [the author] says—according to other teachers—that every word whatsoever is a cause for *pratibhā*. He states that it is a cause for *pratibhā* even for the dull-witted by saying "of children," and so forth. Let alone for one who knows the linguistic convention (*samaya*), will this not be a cause for *pratibhā*? Even for those children, or those who are nearly dull-witted, or animals, who do not know the conventions, it is observed that the meaning of a word is understood through the power of beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

And so, even for insentient beings, a word with a fixed meaning is uttered for the purpose of addressing them. By means of that, a certain specific intuition (*pratibhā*) is awakened, restricted precisely according to their respective species; it is rooted in that very [intuition] that all their various activities occur. By this it is said: if this intuition—which is experienced by all living beings, caused by words, the root of all worldly activity, and undeniable—is denied, then one’s own self is deceived. Therefore, the acceptance of that intuition must necessarily be resorted to. || 117 ||

Some maintain that this practice (*abhyāsa*) is a convention (*samaya*) lacking a prior source; it has been stated that practice is the cause of intuitive insight (*pratibhā*). Regarding this, one might wonder whether this practice belongs to the present life or to another birth, and what its essential nature is. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Immediately after [the perception of the object], there is the demonstration: 'This effect arises from this [cause]. (118)

And that practice is not something recent or lacking in traditional transmission; for it was not taught to the infant by anyone at that very moment. Rather, that convention is held to have existed in previous births. To clarify its essential nature—that it is of the nature of a linguistic convention—he says:

And that [pratibhā] has the nature of indicating that "this is the effect immediately following that. Just as horses gallop forth immediately after the mere stroke of a whip, and elephants upon the strike of a goad, so too other living beings, according to their own kind, carry out worldly affairs by performing appropriate activities as they arise through the power of beginningless habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
