This is established. Thus, it must be accepted that the sentence is indeed indivisible, and *pratibhā* is the meaning of the sentence.

It has been established that, by relying on the extraction of words and word-meanings, the postulation of substitutes and so forth, as well as the maintenance of principles such as incidental application (*prasaṅga*), will be possible. || 118 ||

"The definition of that which is to be signified is that all words have an existent referent (astyartha); they say this is the same for words such as 'cow' as it is for 'the unprecedented' (apūrva), 'deity,' and 'heaven. (119)

Now, if the classification of word-meanings is being relied upon, let that which is the meaning of a word be stated; thus, in connection with this classification, he speaks in order to analyze the meaning of words according to different philosophical views:

Some say that for all words, the denotable object (*vācya*) is the mere referent (*arthamātra*), whose specific form (*ākāraviśeṣa*) has not been apprehended. This should be understood as the definition of the denotable object—that is, the definition of what is to be conveyed—of all words. To the question "To what is this comparable?", he says: "Like the word *apūrvadevatā*," and so forth. For in words such as *apūrva* (the unprecedented) and *devatā* (deity), there is no manifestation of a [specific] form. As for the manifestation of a form in words such as *go* (cow), that should be understood as being inseparable [from the denotation].

Otherwise, from the words *apūrva*, *devatā*, and *svarga*, there would be the manifestation of forms (*ākāra*) and so forth, just as there is from words such as "horse" or "cow. Since no manifestation of form and so forth occurs from them, it is logical that they signify only the bare object (*arthamātra*). || 119 ||
However, that apprehension of form which arises from the practice of observing the application [of words] is not the object of the word; for it depends upon a different effort. || 120 ||

Now, one might raise the objection: "Since the manifestation of a form (*ākāra*) is observed from words such as 'cow' (*go*), it is possible to say that the cognition of a qualified object is appropriate. Anticipating this, he says: "When one observes the use of the word 'cow' only with respect to those things possessing a dewlap and so forth, and the apprehension of a form (*ākāra-parigraha*) that occurs therein due to the habituation to that observation, that is not the cognition produced by the word. Why? He says: 'For that... and so on.

Therefore, through the repeated practice of application (*prayoga*), or rather, through the repeated observation of application, that [object] manifests by means of another effort distinct from the comprehension of the word; consequently, this is not the operation of the word. Thus, it is logical that the denotable object (*vācya*) of the word is the mere thing itself (*arthamātra*), whose specific forms have not yet been apprehended. This is one position. || 120 ||
Some distinctions are manifested by words that denote them; others they consider to be "word-meanings" that arise concomitantly [with the primary meaning]. (121)

Now he states another position: that some things are denotable by words, while others are merely co-emergent forms therein—some distinctions, such as universals (*jāti*) and so forth, are denotable by words, while others, which serve as the actualizing factors of the meaning, are merely co-emergent; likewise, others consider those [co-emergents] to be the word-meaning. (121)

In a word that conveys a universal (jāti), the individual (vyakti) is merely an accompanying factor; the word denoting the universal does not depend upon the specific differences residing in that individual.
To refute this very point, he says:

"Class-words (jātiśabda) convey the class alone; the individual (vyakti), however, is merely an adjunct there, because a class cannot exist without a substratum. Therefore, in the view that the class is the word-meaning, the class-word does not depend upon the specific forms residing in those individuals. (122)
A word does not convey the forms of jars and the like, because it is applied to the mere thing; therefore, the cognition of those [forms] follows as an inseparable consequence.
To clarify this very point, he says:

A denotative word such as "jar" does not convey the well-known forms of jars and the like, because it is restricted solely to the form consisting of a broad base and a belly. For a word is not capable of conveying an object accompanied by all its specific particulars; therefore, it should be understood that the comprehension of the specific form occurs there as an inseparable, co-emergent result. 123.
An action prompted by a word is never observed to occur without its application;
therefore, it is understood that the meaning of a word is the application which follows as a consequence.
In order to demonstrate this very state of invariable concomitance (*nāntarīyakatva*), he says:

"That action which is impelled by the word 'yat' (when) is not seen without the totality of means consisting of agent, object, and instrument; therefore, just as that connection with the means is necessarily produced therein, so too must the meaning of the word be understood. Thus it is concluded. || 124 ||
However, those applications which are fixed and that means which is fixed are understood by others to be denotable by words. (125)
Now, in order to demonstrate the third position—that all aspects (*ākāra*) constitute the meaning of a word through a relationship of primary and secondary importance—he says:

It is proper to state that everything which cannot be established as the denotation of a word without [the presence of] something else is denotable by that word, consisting as it does of both the goal (*sādhya*) and the means (*sādhana*). It is not correct to say that "something is directly conveyed while another is understood therein by way of invariable concomitance" (*nāntarīyakatayā*); rather, this position is superior: that the entire form (*sarvākāra*) is indeed the denotation, and it is perceived from that [word] through a relationship of primary and secondary importance. || 125 ||

To demonstrate the fourth position—that the referent of a word is the aggregate itself, as an indivisible and collective whole where the components are of equal status—he says: "Or else, the denotable object is the aggregate, which is an undifferentiated collection; it is the aggregate alone that constitutes the meaning of the word, due to its equal status [with its parts]."

Now, one might object: "If [the word] conveys only a collection of forms that are combined (*samuccita*), then there would necessarily be a plural number (*bahuvacana*) in that case. Alternatively, if it conveys them as being optionally chosen (*vikalpita*), then there would be an option regarding the number. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "without optional choice or combination" (*avikalpasamuccaya*). This means that from such a [word], which is characterized by the absence of both optional choice and combination, [the meaning] is understood; this is what is being proposed. He will demonstrate this in detail during the discussion of the meaning in the section on Simile (*upamā-samuddeśa*).
Furthermore: "Some maintain that the meaning of a word is even an unreal relation (*saṃsarga*). (126)
Now, in order to demonstrate the fifth position—that the meaning of a word is merely the unreal relation (*saṃsarga*) consisting of genus, quality, and action—he says:

"By words such as 'jar' (*ghaṭa*), the relation of the jar and so forth with its genus and so forth is expressed. And since that [relation] is not perceived here apart from those [entities], it is said to be unreal. Therefore, only the related object (*saṃsṛṣṭa-padārtha*) is real. (126)

Alternatively, that which is real despite having an unreal adjunct (upādhi) is the basis for words; or else, reality itself, variegated by unreal adjuncts, is what is denoted by words. Thus he states the sixth position:
"Or else, the word, having attained the state of being identified with its object (abhijalpatva), becomes the denotable. (127)
To demonstrate the seventh position—that the very nature of the word itself is the denotable object—he says:
"The word itself, having attained a state that is neither [the state of] non-speech nor intermediate, is the denotable of the word, characterized by its own form. (127)
When the form [of the word] is unified with the object through the connection "this is that," they call that word *abhijalpa*. (128)

He states the nature of *abhijalpa*: "The relation expressed as 'this is that' is called superimposition (*adhyāsa*). By means of this, the true nature of the object is concealed, and it is presented as if unified. At that time, the word is called *abhijalpa*. Although word and meaning possess a single identity due to the force of superimposition, the objective aspect alone holds primacy by virtue of its utility. (128)
Since these two do not have separate referents and their conventional usage is unerring, in certain instances one particular form alone remains predominant. (129)

In response to the objection that both [the word and the meaning] are sometimes seen to differ according to the distinction of their respective objects, he states [this] as a corollary: "Because of the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of those two—the word and the meaning—there is, by virtue of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), a restriction such that they are non-deviant, possess no separate referents, and are of a single form; yet, due to etymological derivation (*yoga*), some specific form prevails primarily in certain instances, whether in common worldly usage or in technical treatises. (129)
In the world, a word functions having attained the form of its object. To show that in this context the objective aspect alone is predominant, he says:

"Having attained the form of the object—that is, having reached a state of virtual identity with the object—the word functions," as in "This is a cow" and so forth. In that case, it is the object itself that is determined to be primary by virtue of its externality.
In the treatise, however, the dual nature [of the object] is distinguished according to the speaker's intention. (130)
However, he states that in the treatise (śāstra), the dual nature of the word is also observed through its classification:
"For in the treatise, the designation is sometimes predominant in its own form (svarūpa) and sometimes predominant in its meaning (artha); thus, the dual nature of the word is seen. (130)
Whether due to incapacity or omnipotence, the fixed conceptualization of action and so forth regarding a single object is constructed solely by means of words. (131)

Now, [the author] states the eighth position, showing that the capacity of things does not exist separately [from words], but rather is dependent upon words; that they are understood exactly as they are enjoined by words, and thus the meaning of a word is presented solely through its own majesty: "... [He says: "..."

Alternatively, the object exists as possessing all powers (*sarvaśakti*). To show that it is by means of a word that there is a designation of its specific power (*pratiniyataśakti*), it is stated right here: "or [the view] that it possesses all powers. Sometimes the object is denoted in the form of an action (*kriyā*), and sometimes in the form of an established entity (*siddha*); thus, its restricted nature as action and so forth is presented as the meaning of the word. 131.
Alternatively, some maintain that the meaning of a word is an object of cognition based upon an external thing, which is known as that external thing itself. (132)
Alternatively, in order to present the tenth position—that the object of a word is precisely that which has ascended into the intellect and is not external—he says:

Regarding the word (*śabda*), which is conceptual and not yet mounted upon the intellect, that which is mounted upon the intellect and based on an external object—meaning that for which the external object is the basis by way of generating a conceptual construction—is of such a nature. And that conceptualized object, through the power of error, although it is not external in form, is superimposed as having an external form by way of a single form consisting of the perceived and the conceptualized. Thinking "I understand the very thing thus superimposed from the word," it is accepted that the meaning of the word is the "cause" (*nimitta*) [of the cognition], because the word is the cause. (Thus ends the commentary on verse 132.)
Those things which appear as possessing forms, being objects of cognition, and serving as the basis for distinct memory, are [external]; pure consciousness, however, is otherwise than that.

Now, he states the eleventh position: that for words such as "cow" and the like, the object possesses a specific form (*ākāraviśeṣavat*), whereas for words such as "the unprecedented" (*apūrva*) and so on, the object is mere consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*) with no specific form attended to.

He says: "By certain words, objects possessing specific forms appear as cognizable and denotable, serving as the basis for clear recollection; by others, objects devoid of form, consisting of the nature of consciousness itself, are denoted. Their objects are established accordingly. (133)
Just as a sense organ, when it comes into contact [with its object], manifests a variety [of perceptions], in the very same way, the comprehension of an object from a word occurs in many ways. (134)

Now, he states the twelfth position: that by the power of specific latent impressions (*vāsanā*) alone, an object appears in a specific form; however, in reality, no single fixed [meaning] can be designated.

Just as the sense organ, though not erroneous, manifests an object in various forms due to the influence of defects, so too is the cognition of word-meanings for those permeated by fixed latent impressions; thus, there is no single, fixed meaning for a word. (134)
Furthermore, when there are diverse understanders, the speaker proceeds in one way;
yet the meaning of a word is differentiated according to each person's own internal conviction. (135)
To explain this very point, he says:

"For instance—the Sāṃkhyas, Jains, Buddhists, and others—understand the meaning of a word in entirely different ways according to their respective philosophical tenets; yet the speaker, such as a Vaiśeṣika, begins to speak according to his own conviction.

Thus, for example, when a Vaiśeṣika employs the word 'jar' (ghaṭa) to convey the concept of a whole (avayavin), it is regarded by the Sāṃkhyas as a mere aggregate of qualities (guṇasamāhāra), and by the Jains and Buddhists as a mere collection of atoms (paramāṇusaṃcaya); and in that very manner, the comprehension of the object occurs for each of them. (135)
Even regarding a single visible object, perceptions differ individually;
and even a single person perceives that same object differently at another time. (136)
To demonstrate this very point, he says:

"In reality, regarding an object that is single and of one form when perceived, the perception—that is, the cognition—differs in this case due to the differences in the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) produced by various scriptures. Furthermore, even a single person whose mind has been refined by the Buddhist (*sugata*) view determines an object in one way, yet at another time, through hearing the Vaiśeṣika scriptures, determines it otherwise. (136)
And even for a single word, its meaning is conceptualized in many ways by one person or by many, based on their respective fixed reasons. (137)
To the question "What follows from this?", he says:

By means of the causes [of the word] established through a single uniformity of scriptural refinement (*saṃskāra*), a single person—due to the influence of impressions (*vāsanā*) from various scriptures—gradually conceives of many meanings for a single word such as "jar. Furthermore, by many people whose intellects are refined by various scriptures, it is simultaneously conceived in many ways according to their own respective cognitions. What can we do in this matter? (137)
Therefore, for those who have not perceived the true reality, their vision and speech are always flawed, full of many deceptions, and perpetually unstable. (138)
To the question "What follows from this?", he says:

Since this is so, therefore the vision of persons who have not perceived reality is unstable. And because they have not perceived reality, their speech is faulty; for that very reason, it is full of fallacies and beset by many kinds of contradictions. This being the case, even their words are likewise [unreliable], and thus the statement of truth remains far removed. (138)
That which is seen by the seers (ṛṣis) and which is established in reality does not have any practical application, nor is it the basis for verbal designation. (139)
[An objection: "But surely there exist sages who know both the higher and the lower; we shall establish everything in accordance with them. To address this point, he says:

The vision of the Blessed Supreme Sages is ontological (*tāttvika*); however, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthena*), worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is impossible, as it does not serve as a basis for the means of worldly transaction; thus, no formal determination (*vyavasthā*) can be made on that basis. Furthermore, at the time of worldly transaction, even they appear like those who have not perceived reality; thus, there is again a lack of formal determination. As it is said: "Abiding on the worldly path through both perception and verbal designation, the ignorant child and the wise scholar are alike in their cognition and in their expression. (Verse 139)
The surface of the sky appears like a firefly or like a flame;
yet there is no such surface in the sky, nor is the firefly actually a fire.

One might object: "Let the cognitions of persons indeed be diverse; however, we shall certainly act in accordance with reality exactly as it is perceived by direct perception. Anticipating this doubt, he states the instability of direct perception:
"Even among those whose vision is unimpaired, the statement 'the expanse of the sky is exceedingly pure' is observed; what can we do about that? (140)
Therefore, even regarding an object that is directly perceived, a wise person should examine it through reasoning;
one should not postulate the existence of a visible object merely on the basis of the validity of perception. (141)
Furthermore, concluding that whatever is ascertained through reasoning should be accepted exactly as it is seen, he says:
"Just as worldly people provide designations for things whose true nature is inexpressible in conventional discourse, a wise person should not conceptualize those designations. (142)

He says: "Since for each person, a word-meaning appears exactly according to their own philosophical view, that alone must be accepted as its meaning; therefore, enough with demonstrating these many futile conceptual constructions."

Therefore, at the time of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), one should carry out practical discourse by relying on word-meanings exactly as they are conventionally expressed by worldly people regarding objects whose true nature (*tattva*) cannot be definitively designated; one should not engage in "grinding what is already ground. Thus, having shown the twelvefold categories of meaning according to different philosophical views, the author will determine their essential nature (*svarūpa*) by analyzing them through the elaborations of universals (*jāti*) and so forth in the section on words (*padakāṇḍa*).

In this regard, the conclusion is that for the grammarian, the meaning of the sentence—which is the *sphoṭa* characterized as an indivisible whole—is the superimposition (*adhyāsa*), while the relationship and the word-meanings are merely unreal. || 142 ||
When the meanings of words are perceived as distinct, another kind of intuition arises;
they call that "sentence-meaning" (vākyārtha), which is brought about by the word-meanings. (143)
Now, following up on that very nature of *pratibhā* (intuition) previously introduced, he says:

"When words such as 'Devadatta' are perceived as distinct, their respective objects are grasped as being likewise distinct; yet at the moment of cognition, a single *pratibhā* arises which is entirely non-different from the meaning of the sentence, and the Grammarians call this the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*). What is the means (*upāya*) for its realization? He says: 'Bringing it about by means of word-meanings (*padārthaiḥ*). That is to say, it is brought about—that is, manifested—by word-meanings which, though unreal, serve as limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). (Verse 143)
"This is that"—it cannot be described to others in any way whatsoever;
established as an internal experience, it is not even defined by its agent. (144)
He asks, "Of what nature is it? and replies:

"And that [cognition], as it arises, cannot be described to another; it is established solely through self-awareness (svasaṃvedana). Even by the cognizer, at the very moment of self-awareness, it is impossible to define it in any determinate form. (144)
Unexamined, that [cognition] brings about, as it were, a close contact with objects;
it exists as the object, as if possessing all forms. (145)
Asking what its nature is, he says:

it brings about the conjunction or meeting of word-meanings that were previously unconnected; or rather, it exists as the very object of all word-meanings in every sentence, for it is by being grounded in it that they attain their fulfillment. ||145||
No one can overstep that [authority] which is produced by direct verbal testimony or followed through meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), regarding what is to be done. (146)
And there is no mere living being whatsoever that transcends it; rather, it remains as something to be surpassed. He says this:

"That [consciousness] is sometimes produced directly by words during the time of linguistic usage, or by the force of impressions from other births—as in the case of elephants, horses, and so forth. Thus, the entire worldly activity of everyone, consisting of the form of "what is to be done" (*itikartavyatā*), has its root in that very [consciousness]. || 146 ||
The entire world regards that [speech] as a means of valid cognition;
even the undertakings of animals proceed under its influence. (147)
He clarifies this very point:

everyone perceives that very same divine self-manifestation (*svapratibhā*) as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). And so it is said: "For the wise, when objects are in a state of doubt, the movements of the inner organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) are the authority. Furthermore, even for animals immediately after birth, their worldly activity is rooted in that [self-manifestation]; therefore, one should not deceive oneself by denying it. (147)
Just as the powers of intoxication and so forth are seen to arise without effort from the ripening of specific substances, so too are the intuitive flashes (pratibhā) of those who possess them.
To demonstrate that this intuition (*pratibhā*) is indeed established for everyone, he says:

"Just as the powers of intoxication and so forth are observed in specific substances without depending on any other effort apart from their own maturation, in exactly the same way, this intuition—which is produced by specific latent impressions (*saṃskāra*)—is clearly perceived in those who possess it. (148)
Who transforms the vocal function of the male cuckoo in spring?
By whom have living beings been taught how to build nests and so forth? (149)
To establish with an illustration that this [instinct] has its cause in practice from previous births, he says:

"That the male cuckoo cries out in the fifth note during the month of Madhu is proven to be entirely innate; and the construction of nests by spiders is seen to occur solely through the power of intuition. (149)
In the acts of eating, pleasure, aversion, and the movement of wind and so forth—well-established by birth and lineage—who is the instigator for beasts and birds? (150)
To clarify this very point, he says:
"It is well known that specific activities, such as the recitation of each sacred syllable (*praṇava*), are determined solely by the power of beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*). (150)
This arises from scripture itself when it is accompanied by meditative cultivation;
however, scripture is distinguished [as more authoritative] by its proximity or remoteness [from the object]. (151)

And since sound alone is the root of intuition (*pratibhā*), he says: "That [sound] is scripture (*āgama*); sometimes it is understood in this very life as being proximate, and sometimes in another birth as being remote; thus, by way of proximity and remoteness, sound alone is the cause of intuition. (151)

They know intuition (pratibhā) to be of six kinds: that which arises from the practice of the natural state, that which is produced by unseen merit (adṛṣṭa), and that which is endowed with excellence. || 152 ||

Some teachers maintain that there is a certain innate intuition (*pratibhā*). For example: the first manifestation of the Supreme Nature (*prakṛti*), characterized by existence, which conforms to the Great Self (*mahat*); or like the state of deep sleep conforming to awakening, it is the mere presence of the fruit of sleep. There is also a certain intuition caused by conduct (*caraṇa*), as in the case of [Vasiṣṭha and others], whose specific modes of illumination were determined by their very conduct; and there is a certain [intuition] caused by practice (*abhyāsa*).

For example: [the power] of those who dig wells, tanks, and so forth. A certain [power] has yoga as its cause; for example, among yogins, in the knowledge of others' intentions and so on, which occurs without fail. Likewise, a certain [power] has the unseen (adṛṣṭa) as its cause; for example, among *rakṣas*, *piśācas*, and so forth, in the possession of others, invisibility, and so on. A certain [power] is conferred by distinguished [beings]; for example, that of Sañjaya and others by Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana and others.

Thus, although intuition (*pratibhā*) is of many kinds, it is entirely based upon and conveyed by the sentences of traditional scripture (*āgama*). Even when grammar has ceased and all specific powers have vanished, it remains contained within the causal seed of the latent power of words that has subsided. At the time of its manifestation (*vṛtti*), having first experienced a mere unfolding (*vivarta*) even by way of a subtle path, it gradually coalesces through various unstable forms fixed as phonemes and sentences. Having reached the state of the ripening of its seed, it manifests again and again in a clearly manifest form. || 152 ||
And in order to show that this [meaning] is sixfold according to the distinction of its causes (*nimitta*), he says:

"By nature" (*svabhāvena*), as in the case of a monkey. Examples for the feet and so forth are to be inferred. Thus, even though an indivisible sentence (*akhaṇḍa-vākya*) is accepted, linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) cannot be sustained without the division of words and word-meanings; therefore, the meaning of a word (*padārtha*) has been determined by first presenting the various opinions in a general way. || 152 ||
Just as the word "cow" is employed to denote an object characterized by substances that possess conjunction, yet it does not reveal those specific qualities themselves. (153)
Even though a word is applied to cows and other such things which are conjoined with shapes, colors, and parts, it does not accept those as its own referents. (154)

This is the position: at the time of the application of a word, whether for one who holds that the substance (*dravya*) is the meaning of a word or for one who holds that the universal (*jāti*) is the meaning of a word, the object—which is distinct from the word's own form—is grasped by the word as it is being perceived even at the very first moment. For example, when cows and the like, which have specific owners fixed to them, are designated by qualifiers such as "the giving of milk" for the purpose of identification, these qualifiers are not revealed by the words as their primary denotable meanings.

Likewise, when [objects] are associated with defining characteristics such as "one-ness," "manifestation," and so forth (or "the form [ākāra]," etc.), these [characteristics], even though they are grasped by a primary or intermediate cognition as the cause for the apprehension of the [object's] form and so on, do not themselves attain the status of being denotable by words. || 153–154 ||

Now he begins the investigation of word-meanings by distinguishing between the primary and the necessary concomitants, saying "as follows" (*yathā*). Here, according to the view of Vājapyāyana, the meaning of a word is the universal (*sāmānya*); according to the view of Vyāḍi, it is the individual (*vyakti*). In this context, either the universal alone or the individual alone is understood as the word's efficient meaning; however, the particulars are understood from it as necessary concomitants. Therefore, the meaning of a word is the universal alone, since it is never observed to deviate [from the word].

Just as specific substances conjoined with [an object], such as subtle gems and the like, exist merely as indicators for objects such as cows and do not become denotable by words like "cow," so too are internal features such as shape, color, and configuration; therefore, the word is not said to be the illuminator of those. (153) To clarify this very point, he says: "shape" (ākāra), etc. The meaning is that shape and the other features are not denotable by the word because they are subject to deviation. (154)
When a word is employed for that which is distinguished by its configuration and color, its application to a mere part [of it] is not observed. (155)

A term characterized by a specific configuration, such as "circular," "long," or "quadrangular," does not denote its own constituent parts. Likewise, words such as *muṣṭi* (fist), *granthi* (knot), *sandhi* (joint), *sakta* (stuck), *kuṇḍala* (ring), and so forth, are not applied to those constituent parts. Similarly, color-words such as *citra* (variegated), *kalmāṣa* (spotted), and *sāraṅga* (dappled) do not apply to their constituent parts. By the word "constituent part" (*avayava*), terms such as *śata* (hundred), *sahasra* (thousand), *prastha*, *droṇa*, *māsa*, and *saṃvatsara* are included.

When a particular part is perceived, the universal (jāti) is superimposed upon it; therefore, the word prompted by that universal functions within that limited scope. For indeed, when only a certain part is seen—such as the teeth, horns, or hooves—one certainly uses the expression "this is a cow," or likewise, "a wolf" or "a domestic pig," because some part is indicated by it. Others, however, consider this view to be devoid of logical reasoning. Why? If a word denoted the universal alone, it would convey only the existence of the universal; what then would be the use of qualifiers (upavyañjana)? || 155 ||

One might object: "Should it not be admitted that words such as *sthūla* (large), *hrasva* (short), *karbura* (variegated), and *śabala* (spotted)—which denote shapes—do not have shape and so forth as their denotable objects? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Configuration," etc. We do not claim that there is no cognition of [shape] at all in every case, for shapes and the like are indeed expressed by their own specific words (*svaśabda*). Rather, we maintain that whatever is the primary cause (*prayojaka*) of a word is its denotable object (*vācya*), while anything else is merely an inseparable concomitant (*nāntarīyaka*).

Therefore, it should not be accepted that words denoting [phonemes] such as *ā* and so forth apply to a mere constituent part or a mere portion; hence, by means of words, sometimes a specific feature of an object is expressed, and sometimes only its general nature. || 155 ||
Independent of number, measure, and configuration, it functions as the denoter of "water" and so forth, whether in a single drop or in a collection. (156)

Where the determination of the nature of a universal occurs independently of its form, there only that much is expressed by the word as actually exists. And so it has been said: "The term 'merely ghee' applies whether it refers to a single drop or even to a *khārī* measure. (156)

Therefore, he says "number" (*saṃkhyā*) to show that a word functions with respect to the mere thing (*vastumātra*) alone, without touching upon its specific qualities. Even a single drop of water is called "water," and even a vast river current is likewise called so; even a single stone is "white," and even the Himalayas are "white. Thus, words function by taking as their own object merely the causal factor—the universal (*jāti*) and so forth—while the manifestation of specific features such as shape is an inseparable consequence (*nāntarīyaka*). This is the established conclusion. || 156 ||

That which resides in oil and the like, which are delimited by their constituent factors (saṃskāra) and so forth, asserts itself as a single part in its true nature; thus it exists within the parts [of the whole]. (157)

In this context, whether it be the view that [the word] denotes a modification (*saṃskāra*) or the view that it denotes an impairment (*upaghāta*), when a word is established as applying to a certain known object, this [example] is presented with regard to the requirement for the utility of its constituent parts: "That which was impaired by a crow was eaten by him," or "That which was prepared for the sake of Yajñadatta was drunk by Devadatta. Thus, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the initial mention and the subsequent reference. || 157 ||

But surely, words that function with respect to wholes also function with respect to their parts—as in the expressions "oil has been eaten," "ghee has been eaten," or "it is white, blue, or brown. How is this so? It has been stated:
"In the case of genus-words and quality-words, a distinction of individual form (*mūrti*) is not intended to be expressed.
Those [words] are based solely on the distinction of the relation between the genus and the quality."
Likewise:

"It has not been observed that words denoting universals (jātiśabda) are subordinate to a collection [of individuals]; for they denote either the universal itself or the individuals conjoined with the universal. And here:
"It functions independently of number, measure, and configuration; it denotes both the individual drop and the collection in words such as 'water' and the like.

Anticipating this objection, he says: "due to the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) and so forth. A word such as 'oil' or 'ghee' is established in reference to oil or ghee that is delimited by the destruction of its latent impressions and so on; it expresses a single part by means of superimposing the whole upon it.

This is what is meant: those are not generic terms (*jātiśabda*), but rather they are merely similar to them; by superimposing [the generic property] upon them, they are said to denote a part of that [whole] while expressing a fixed measure.
Therefore, there is no fault in the fact that their application to the parts is stated in the *Bhāṣya*. And it has been said:
"Whether due to refinement (*saṃskāra*) or due to injury (*upaghāta*), [the word] applies to that which possesses a measured size."
"In this context, the word for a genus (jāti-śabda) is understood to apply to the oil and so forth because of their equality. || 157 ||
When a designation is employed because it is connected with a particular object, its employment ceases once that object has disappeared. (158)
Others say that a word is employed [for a purpose]; they declare that this is the fixed definition of the purpose and the subject matter. || 158 ||
To show that this must be understood from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha), he says: "by which object," meaning by which motivating factor such as genus (jāti) and so forth. (158)
However, regarding those properties that are possible [to be expressed] but are not included within [the word], the word does not necessarily require their presence. (159)

Those factors which do not cause the word to function, but are auxiliary to the causes that do, and which are related to it—being perceived at the time of the word's application as if they were constituent parts of the object denoted by the word—their presence or absence is not a cause for the operation of the word. (159)
However, even when a word is employed by including other properties through the speaker’s intention, it does not necessarily convey all of them; thus he says: "Those which... (verse 159).
Just as the word "cow" is seen to apply even when there is deviation regarding such things as hairy hooves, it does not function in the absence of the universal (jāti). 160.

Even in the absence of the specific causes such as horns, hair, and hooves, the primary application (*mukhyā pravṛtti*) of the word "cow" remains. However, when there is a cognition [of the object] by way of "cowness" (*gotva*), the word functions with respect to a substance (*dravya*) that is either qualified by the genus (*jāti*) or is the substratum (*āśraya*) of that genus. In that context, regarding the application of a term to a whole (*avayavin*), it applies to its parts; for instance, in the expression "the village pig is not to be eaten," the act of eating requires a substance-part that serves as the instrument (*sādhana*) in exactly that manner. Furthermore, we observe the application of a term denoting a material cause (*prakṛti*) to both the modification (*vikāra*) and the cause itself;
likewise, we observe the application of a term denoting a collection (*samudāya*) to both the individual parts and the collection as a whole. || 160 ||
Clarifying this very point through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), he says: "Just as a hair... (verse 160).
It is rare for anyone in this world to perceive all the parts [of an object];
however, when certain parts are seen, the whole object is inferred. (161)

Indeed, no person of ordinary vision perceives a collection [of parts] as complete in all its components; for in that case, when some parts are grasped, the whole (*avayavin*) is determined as belonging to a certain class (*vyaktijātīya*). This is as, for example, when one sees the front half or the back half of cows and other such animals. However, in some instances, doubt does not cease at all; this is as, for example, when one sees only curd.

However, in the case of seeing a cloth, a covering, or the like, the visible parts serve as the causes for certain and necessary inference. Regarding this too, some maintain that words belong to the category of direct audition (śruti) for the purpose of excluding other classes [of objects]; others declare that words function within their own respective domains through inference from those parts which are included within the object. || 161 ||

And thus, it is said that even perception—which brings about the direct intuition of an object—does not appear to determine the nature of an object in this manner [as a word does]; he says, "difficult to obtain. Since it is impossible to perceive all parts simultaneously, the determination of an entire object through the perception of only some parts is purely inferential; therefore, even perception does not determine the complete nature of an object. || 161 ||
Likewise, the determination of qualities that coexist with the fragrance of the *jāti* flower and others—qualities that are seen to be in a constant relationship [with it]—is observed. (162)

For when a word is applied to a natural blue lotus (*jātyutpala*) and the like—based on an inference from the cognition of its fragrance as being that of a natural blue lotus—that word does not denote merely the fragrance, nor the inherence of fragrance, nor the substance alone; rather, other concomitant qualities are also inferred therein. Furthermore, it is not accepted that words denoting such [entities] function through inference based on a reason (*hetu*) when the concomitants are perceived.

In some cases, words such as "lotus" denote a collection; however, in the case of the word "cow" applied to cows and the like, its application toward a specific object is observed to be prompted by the proximity of horns and other features, rather than by its being the producer of number, measure, shape, or genus. || 162 ||

In the same way, from a word, through the determination of one part, there arises the cognition of another property that is eternally concomitant; thus he says, "so too" (*tathā*). From words such as *jātigandha* (generic fragrance) or *utpalagandha* (lotus fragrance), there is the apprehension of fragrance in general as qualified [by those terms]; however, it should be understood that the ascertainment of its concomitants—such as color, touch, and so forth—is not inherent (*nāntarīyaka*) [to the word's primary meaning], nor is it primary. || 162 ||

Therefore, when there is a comprehension of a possible object from a word, that object is understood as being connected [to another], even though its dissociation from the unseen has not been perceived. (163)

Therefore, it is understood that even though they are perceived together, the possible concomitants (*sahacārin*) are not the meaning of the word; for a relationship of the word with such an objective nature is not tenable. || 163 ||

He now states [the conclusion] in order to summarize: "Therefore," it should be understood that, due to the absence of any fixed [correspondence] with the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), it is only the genus (*jāti*) and so forth that are perceived as the related object, namely as the denotable meaning (*vācya*) of the word. || 163 ||
The case-endings for duality and so forth may either be expressive of number or indicative of it;
alternatively, the entire complex [of stem and suffix] may be the denoter of the object possessing number. (164)

Alternatively, some say that words such as "cow" and the like denote certain objects—endowed with numerical distinctions—even without explicitly stating a number, by means of the distinction inherent in their own forms. (165)

Just as linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) is carried out by means of the analysis of word-meanings from a sentence, so too in the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*) much usage is observed even from a word through the extraction (*apoddhāra*) of stem (*prakṛti*) and suffix (*pratyaya*).

Regarding this, some maintain: "Only that much meaning is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) as is actually apprehended by those two methods; there is no other 'meaning of the aggregate' (*samudāyārtha*) whatsoever. That aggregate-meaning, like a sentence, is not denoted by the word itself."

The experts in logic, however, hold this view: the bases (*prakṛti*), suffixes (*pratyaya*), and so forth, have been established and rendered functional by the learned solely through the conceptual constructions of their own intellects. Their meanings are accepted precisely as they are divided within the treatises themselves—based on the reasons for the teacher’s purpose—by means of worldly positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). How so? This [division] is merely a means for the intellect to communicate meaning. In every respect, there is no difference in the actual worldly object being understood.

For instance, according to some, the base word (*prātipadika*) expresses its own meaning, substance, gender, number, object (*karman*), and so forth, while the case-endings (*vibhakti*) merely indicate (*dyotika*) the object and the rest. According to others, the base word expresses only its own meaning, substance, and gender, while the case-endings express number, the object, and so forth. It is understood that within the meaning of the base word, number, the object, and so forth are expressed optionally (*vikalpena*) as far as possible.

The gender (*liṅga*) of certain words is indicated (*dyotya*), while for others it is expressed (*abhidheya*). Indication (*dyotana*) is also of two kinds: the manifestation of what was previously unmanifest, or the determination of something by excluding other alternatives when there is a possibility of doubt. For example: *pratiṣṭhate*, *utpucchayate*, *abhimanāyate*. These also apply to those whose usage is well-known or not well-known, whether used separately or combined, such as: *upāste*, *prapacati*, *adhīte*, *adhyeti*; or where they are mentioned together, such as: *yāvakaḥ*, *gopāyitā*, *brāhmaṇādhīnam*, *jugupsate*. (164)

Alternatively, a collection (*samudāya*) is an undivided reference to a numerable object, expressing multiple powers that are conjoined. At the time of the word's application, those objects possessing such [powers]—which would otherwise be delimited by various specific numbers being denoted [as if they were] accidental attributes like a crow’s neck or a woolen blanket—are expressed by collections endowed with distinctions of their own essential nature, even in the absence of the explicit mention of number. || 165 ||

Having thus conducted an investigation into the meaning of the nominal stem (*nāmapada*), he now introduces an investigation into the meaning of its constituent parts. Therein, he first states the investigation into the meaning of the suffix portion (*pratyayabhāga*): "expressed" (*vācika*). By this, it should be understood that for the suffix portion, meanings such as number, object, and so forth, function either as the expressed (*vācya*) or the indicated (*dyotya*).

Now, in order to state the meaning of the base portion—and indeed to state the meaninglessness of both the base and the affix portions—it is said, "Or rather" (*syād vā*), to show that the very aggregate of the base and the affix is the designator of an object qualified by number and so forth. Alternatively, in order to state that the aggregate of the base and the affix expresses an object merely indicated by number and so forth, it is said, "without" (*vinā*). The meaning is: "by means of a difference in essential form," that is, by means of the distinction of duality and so on. (Verses 164–165)

Those words whose relationship is eternal, whose expressive power is known through distinction, and whose meanings are differentiated by means of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka)—[their meaning is thus determined]. (166)

In the case of composite wholes—such as a well or a sacrificial post—which are divided into their respective constituent parts by means of words that possess eternal relations, a distinction is made through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) regarding those parts. These parts are imagined to have an inseparable relation with their correlates; they are mentally extracted and isolated, and they serve as the objects of the cognition of specific forms and the cognition of conceptual construction (*parikalpa*). For the sake of conveying them figuratively, this distinction is made, whether by way of denotation (*abhidhāyaka*) or indication (*dyotaka*), to account for the apparent deviation [of the word from its actual referent]. || 166 ||

Now, one might object: "When words possess eternal relations and their potencies are known through analysis for the purpose of cognizing their own meanings, how then is it understood that 'this is the meaning of the base' and 'this is the meaning of the suffix'? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] says "yaḥ" (that which... in order to demonstrate that the method of analytical extraction (*apoddhāra*) is based upon positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

When there is discrimination, and once the distinction between word and meaning has been made, and when both the nominal stem (prakṛti) and the suffix (pratyaya) are absent, only "treeness" (vṛkṣatva), devoid of [qualities] such as singularity and so forth, is apprehended; thus, through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), the division of the meanings of the base and the suffix is established. || 166 ||

And where it is possible to conceive of those two [the suffix and the base] through an invariable concomitance, there a restriction applies; however, such a restriction does not exist in the case of suffixes such as *nuṭ* and *śa*.

Positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), which have the nature of the object as their domain, are followed only so far as they can be followed without deviation; beyond that, they are not followed. However, in the case of the words *kūpa*, *yūpa*, and *sūpa*, although there is a formal connection with the word *yūpa*, because there is no connection with the actual meaning, [the suffix] is not accepted [as being meaningful]. Likewise, even though the status of being a suffix (*pratyayatva*) for words such as *tathā* is established by their having names whose meanings correspond to their forms (*anvartha-saṃjñā*), since this is not observed in the case of the optative (*liṅ*) and other such suffixes, the meaning is not determined through positive and negative concomitance.

Even in that regard, some maintain that *tiṅ* suffixes are based solely on identity (*ekatva*) and so forth. Likewise, by some, the single form of the suffix—*syati*, *syataḥ*, *syanti*—is established through grammatical analysis (*anvākhyāna*). In the *Bhāṣya* as well, it is stated that the word *bhū* is the base (*prakṛti*) and the word *ati* is the suffix (*pratyaya*). Furthermore, no meaning has been assigned to forms such as *adhuna* (and others whose forms are exhausted). Rather, it is said: "For an augment (*āgama*) belonging to something meaningful is subordinate to it and is included by the mention of that [base]. (167)

In that regard as well, he says—"And where..."—to show that its demonstration must be made by relying on positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) based on possibility and impossibility.

He says—"The restriction (*niyama*)," meaning that the restriction applies only where positive and negative concomitance are observed, and not in the case of an impossible object. [He argues that] in examples such as *bhavatām atti*, since the meaning is seen even in the absence of suffixes like *śatṛ* and *ṅa*, it is established that in cases such as *vṛkṣāṇāṃ pacati*, the suffix merely provides assistance and does not possess a separate meaning.

And it has been said: "If it is argued that the meanings of the *sārvadhātuka* suffixes are the object (*karman*), the action (*bhāva*), and the agent (*kartṛ*), then the restriction [of number] to the singular, dual, and plural would be untenable because those are not their meanings. If it is argued that they are for the sake of the *vikaraṇa* (verbal infix), then there would be an absence of *vikaraṇas* in cases where [the meaning] is already expressed by a *kṛt* suffix. || 167 ||
Or, even if the expression [of the meaning] is possible, a definition [of it] is not postulated;
for the powers of words are relative and restricted to their specific associations. (168)

When the possibility of verbal designation exists, for anyone who accepts that an object is denotable by a word, it is not logical to accept the existence of a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) for it; for in such a case, the expressive power of the word would be subverted, and everything would be accepted as a defining characteristic merely by virtue of one's own desire. Therefore, in the tradition (*āgama*), whatever is the object of conviction is established as its denotation.

Although these powers exist as if divided into categories such as *saṃsarga* (conjunction) and so forth—despite the fact that they are not observed in the usage of isolated [words]—nevertheless, their manifestation is admitted to be independent of one another. It is asserted that the powers of words are established with their divisions fixed according to specific rules. || 168 ||

However, where the meaningfulness of both the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) is observed as distinct, there the denotation of separate meanings must indeed be accepted; one should not, in such cases, assume that their meaning is merely indicative (*upalakṣaṇa*). Thus he says: "In the case of possibility" (*saṃbhave*). When it is possible for the base and the suffix to denote separate meanings, it is not logical to assume that the meaning of the base alone is what is expressed by the word while the meaning of the suffix is merely indicated, or that the meaning of the suffix alone is what is expressed by the word while the meaning of the base is merely indicated.

Now, if the base (prakṛti) and the suffix (pratyaya) each possess the capacity to express their own meanings separately, why do they express their respective meanings only through mutual dependence? To this he says: "They are dependent," and so forth. Because, in the context of the combination of the meanings of the base and the suffix, the word-powers (śabdaśakti), which depend upon positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), are perceived as being necessarily restricted and specific to each individual element. || 168 ||
No etymological derivation of the meaning is observed for the words *kūpa* (well), *sūpa* (soup), and *yūpa* (sacrificial post);
therefore, it is understood that the composite [word] itself denotes a distinct object.

If, then, unity is admitted for whatever possesses a similar form, and it is asserted that every distinct object is based on a distinct form even when there is no difference in other related factors, then the distinction between objects in the case of a well (*kūpa*), a water-channel (*sūpa*), and a sacrificial post (*yūpa*) would be applied as being based on the phonemes alone. This might be so if difference and non-difference were present in this matter.

However, there exists no undifferentiated [entity] such that the word "form" (*rūpa*) could establish a distinction between form and its absence; for since such a thing lacks positive concomitance (*anvaya*), the word would not be established through non-exclusion (*vyatireka*) due to the lack of differentiation among objects. Therefore, it is accepted that for aggregates whose constituent parts have no distinct meanings, their status is based upon a different referent (*arthāntara*). || 169 ||

But where, even when there is dependence [on other factors], no separate meaning is perceived, there the analytical extraction (*apoddhāra*) should not be resorted to; thus he says: "Not in a well," etc. For when one [element] is removed, no particular cognition of meanings whatsoever arises in any case. (169)
Explanations differ regarding the processes of word derivation;
when many meanings are possible, some specific cause is required [for selection]. (170)

In the grammatical derivations (*śabdavyutpatti*) performed through *nipātana* (irregular formation) or *labhana* (acquisition), various distinct explanations are observed for words that denote worldly objects; these are formulated by repeatedly adopting causes (*nimitta*)—whether characterized by activity or serving as indicators—that do not differ from the worldly referent itself. Among the many powers inherent in a single meaning, whichever power is relied upon as a cause in the grammatical description of correctness (*sādhutvānvākhyāna*) attains the status of a subordinate factor (*aṅga*). For example: "The suffix *ulac* and the augment *taṇḍa* [are applied] after the roots *vṛñ*, *luṭi*, and *nitāḍi*."
For it is possible to prescribe the suffix *ulac* and the substitution of *taṇḍ* even from other verbal roots (*dhātu*) in the process of deriving words. || 170 ||

Thus, it has been stated that the grammatical analysis (*anvākhyāna*) of the constituent parts of a word must be performed by means of abstraction (*apoddhāra*), based upon positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) regarding what is possible and what is impossible. Consequently, having raised the doubt as to whether this analysis of the word-parts and of the word itself is motivated (*sanimitta*) or indeed unmotivated (*nirnimitta*), he now says—"The analyses..."—in order to demonstrate that it is indeed motivated. For where many causes (*nimitta*) are possible, it is said that the analysis is carried out by resorting to only some of them without necessity. (170)
The Vairas, Vāsiṣṭhas, Giriśas, as well as the Ekāgārikas and others, have been described by some through various accounts involving a confusion of causes and limits. (171)

*Vīrakarma* means enmity; *vairam* is enmity existing among heroes (*vīreṣu*). *Vāsiṣṭham* is that which was seen or proclaimed by Vasiṣṭha, or it is called *vāsiṣṭham* because the word "Vasiṣṭha" occurs within it. *Giriśaḥ* [is derived] with the suffix *ḍa* in the Vedic language (*chandasi*) from *girau* [meaning "on the mountain"]; or [it means] he who sleeps (*śete*) on the mountain, or he whose head (*śiraḥ*) is on the mountain. *Aikāgārikaḥ* refers to a thief; [the suffix *ṭhan* is applied] after *aikāsa*, *soḍha*, *ahiṃsu*, and *aikāgārin*. [The analysis is: one who endures (*soḍhā*) a single house (*ekāgāram*), or one whose purpose (*prayojanam*) is this solitary house (*ekam asāyam agāram*)—namely, one who desires to kill (*jighāṃsuḥ*)—is called *aikāgārikaḥ*; [this applies to] one who wishes to steal (*mumuṣiṣoḥ*). Thus, *aikāgārikaḥ* [means a thief].

Or likewise, [the forms] *tapparva* and *marudbhyām*, as well as *dadāti* and *vṛttam*—thus the grammarians have proceeded by explaining, without fixed rule, those meanings that serve as the causes [of word formation], whether they consist of base and suffix or their limits. || 171 ||

To demonstrate this very point, he says: "vaira... and so forth. This is *vaira* because it belongs to a hero (*vīra*) or belongs to a heroine (*vīrā*). Likewise, *vāsiṣṭha* refers to that which belongs to Vasiṣṭha, or was composed or spoken by Vasiṣṭha. [The word] *giriśa* is derived as follows: from *he who lies on a mountain*, with the suffix *ḍa* according to the rule "the suffix *ḍa* occurs after 'mountain' in the Vedic language"; or alternatively, from *he who dwells on a mountain*, with the suffix *ka* according to the rule "the suffix *ka* occurs after a root ending in long *ā* when no upasarga is present. Thus, the grammatical derivation has been performed by mixing the various causes and limits [of formation]. || 171 ||
Just as the description of a path by means of trees, anthills, and mountains is not contradictory, even when [the path] is accompanied by distinct associates such as cattle and the like. (172)

For regarding a single object to be understood, such as a path, one person provides an explanation by means of a tree, another by means of an anthill, and yet another by means of a mountain and so forth. Since all of these are present, their status as indicators is not precluded. Furthermore, objects such as cows and the like are explained in every possible way through their relations with genus, quality, body parts, conjunctions, and so on. (172)

One might object: "Surely some fixed cause (nimitta) must be stated here. Anticipating this, he says "yathā" in order to demonstrate that [the cause] is not fixed because the means (upāya) are not fixed. Just as it is not contradictory for the path of someone to be designated by various distinct means such as trees and so forth, so too it should be understood that the grammatical derivation (anvākhyāna) of words such as *go* is accomplished through various distinct co-occurring [factors]. || 172 ||
Furthermore, those who perceive differences in states provide alternative designations for things such as the *kiṃśuka* tree based on the observation of its various parts. (173)

For someone perceives a certain power (śakti) [in a word]; he explains it according to that perception. Whether in the meaning of a word or the meaning of a sentence, even a word of identical form exercises its favor through a particular power only in certain instances. Consequently, when the word is extracted from the sentence, that power is relied upon as the cause [of its specific function]. Alternatively, specific powers with fixed temporal limits, being employed by certain specific words at each respective time, remain as the causes for grammatical correctness (sādhutva).

And these [words] are likewise adopted at the appropriate times by cultured grammarians as their exponents. Alternately combined, infinite contradictory powers manifest a diversity of forms; and therein, when there is a regulation of a certain word’s power through various contradictory causes—just as in the case of *kiṃśuka* flowers at different times—it is not contradictory. || 173 ||
Since there are many different states of an object, and one designates it by the very state that is perceived, he says "otherwise" (*anyathā ca*). [The example is:
"It is not a *kiṃśuka* tree," which shows that the word *kiṃśuka* is applied based on a distinct cause. || 173 ||

By some, various etymologies for the word "gauḥ" have been presented here: from the roots *gṛ* (to swallow), *garj* (to roar), *gam* (to go), *gav* (to move), or even *gatadi* (that which has gone). 174.

For just as the act of going (*gamikriyā*) in the case of a cow is absolutely distinct from acts of going that inhere in other classes of objects, yet—when its identical form is being established—is designated by means of the verb "to go" itself and adopted as the basis for the etymological derivation of the word "cow," in exactly the same way, various specific actions such as "swallowing" (*girati*), "roaring" (*garjati*), and "speaking" (*gadati*), which are common to many things and based on general terms, have been adopted by various teachers in the process of deriving the word "cow."

By taking up phonemes of similar form from the explained words situated within the etymological sentences (*vyutpattivākya*), a word is analyzed (*anvākhyāyate*) as if it were a composite of them, whether it extends merely to the meaning of a verbal root, or includes suffixes such as the primary (*san*) and secondary (*kṛt*) affixes, or even those *ṛc* verses (such as the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā*) in which the meaning of the sentence is obtained. For instance, in a single Vedic sentence such as "Āditya," a connection with the meaning of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*)—namely, the offspring—is observed.

However, when that word *āditya* is connected with another sentence, other etymological derivations (*nirvacana*) are provided for it. If, in these etymologies, one were to perform a mere grammatical derivation (*vyutpatti*) independent of the actual subject matter, then every conventional (*rūḍhi*) word could be derived from any verbal root by merely following the process of derivation, just as in the case of words like *taṇḍula* and others, after applying modifications to the base and so forth; for in every case, any possible cause [for a derivation] can be found for a conventional meaning. (174)
In order to clarify this very point, he says: "By some...
The various states of the object characterized as a cow have been observed; it is by following those [states] that the teachers explain the meaning. || 174 ||
Either the word "cow" applies to cows by virtue of its own essential nature as "cow," or it is derived [from that nature]; or else some maintain that both cases apply to everything. (175)

Other teachers, such as the Aukthikas and others, state that the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) of "cow" (*go*) is simply "cow" (*gauḥ*); [they hold] that the object denoted by the word "cow" is eternally connected with the word "cow. Therefore, regarding the meaning of the sentence, the linguistic analysis (*vyutpatti*) is undertaken with the intention: "I shall express a specific [meaning] for the purpose of establishing a particular capacity within the mere word-meaning. This applies in cases such as "a goat," "a horse," "a broad [thing]," "water," "foot," or "to be maintained as a servant," and so forth. In the *Bhāṣya*, however, both positions are adopted within each case for the sake of a specific purpose.

For some, having ascertained the ultimate reality alone, remain established in the linguistic conventions of the treatise; others rely solely upon the conventional agreements of the treatise as a means for correctly conveying [the truth]. In that context, the linguistic usage found in the treatise—including the perception of distinctions such as verbal roots and suffixes—is not the ultimate reality. However, regarding the distinction between functions such as oneness and so forth, one accepts them exactly as the forms of the verbal roots are accepted.

In the view of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), however, some even derive verbal roots (*dhātu*) and phonemes (*varṇa*) from other roots and other phonemes, following the rules of stems (*prakṛti*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*). (175) Thus, it has been shown that the basis for the application of a word is precisely its stem-meaning (*prakṛtivācya*), and consequently, various types of bases have been demonstrated. Now, in order to present the position that the very form (*svarūpa*) of words is the basis for their application (*pravṛttinimitta*), he says: "The word 'cow' (*gauriti*)."

Now, why is it called "cow" (*gauḥ*)? For the followers of the *Aukthika* school say that "cow" is indeed the cow itself. And for this reason, all words are employed solely based on their own form; thus he states that there is only the position of non-derivation (*avyutpatti-pakṣa*), saying: "Everything is either derived or not. Some say that the word's own form, the denoted object, and the cause [of its application] are expressed; thus he says: "by some. In this way, it has been shown that grammatical explanation (*anvākhyāna*) is accompanied by a cause, and that the cause—the denoted object—is stated in many ways by various people in some manner, whether as the form alone, the cause alone, both, or neither. (175)
And in the treatise, instruction is generally given for the sake of brevity;
its specific details, however, are established just like those of other distinct categories. (176)

In this context, as much as can be taught through the pursuit of form or the pursuit of meaning—even in terms of generality—that much is taught. However, a specific [meaning], whether pertaining to the object or the form, conveys an object or a word that appears as if endowed with a different genus and as if consisting of another word. In that regard, the conventional meaning which is the object of common usage does not reside merely in the primary sense of "going."

Just as the words *sravati* ("flows"), *syandate* ("glides"), *plavate* ("floats"), and *patati* ("falls")—though listed under the general category of "motion" (*gati*)—rely upon their own specific natures while being followed by that general category of motion, so too should it be understood in the case of the word *gaur* ("cow"). Furthermore, the root *gam-* is not necessarily restricted here to the act of moving the feet. Thus, in every instance where a specific action characterized by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) is possible, the application of the root *gam-* is unrestricted, because verbal roots possess multiple meanings.

And this is observed in cases such as *gurutalpagā* (one who violates the teacher’s bed), where the root *gam-* has as its object an action other than [the literal sense of] going. Just as there is a difference in the nature of the result (*phala*) among conventional expressions (*rūḍhi*), so too is there a difference in the grammatical factors (*kāraka*). Therefore, in conventional expressions, even when a general term is denoted, there is the comprehension of a distinct meaning, just as in the case of different classes (*jātyantara*). || 176 ||

Now, it is investigated whether the form of a word is indeed distinct [in each instance], or rather non-distinct. If it were indeed distinct, then in cases such as *gamana*, *garala*, and *gaja*, because the sounds *ga* and so forth are distinct, they would necessarily be treated as separate entities; consequently, due to their infinity, it would be impossible to provide a grammatical derivation (*anvākhyāna*). To this, he says: "In the view that there is a difference between words, for the sake of brevity, the teaching is carried out in the treatise by relying on a commonality among those [sounds] which are distinct; those specific instances are said to be its expressers, just like other universals (*jāti*). (176)

And they know that which occurs in a different sense to be a different primary form (*prakṛti*); it does not, while retaining its identical form, become attached to another conventional meaning. (177)

Those [words] such as *gamyā* and others which belong to the domain of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) are indeed distinct verbal roots (*prakṛti*). Even though they share the same formal character regarding the object (the patient), because there is an absolute difference—just as in the case of the domains of the object and the agent—there exists no connection whatsoever between those belonging to the domain of conventional usage and those not so belonging, nor between those not belonging to the domain of conventional usage and those that do. || 177 ||
He says this very thing:

"And when there is conventional usage (rūḍhi), that which has an identical form is not attached to another by its own nature; in reality, it is indeed distinct, yet on account of similarity, unity is imagined therein. But in the ultimate sense, words such as 'cow' and so forth are distinct. (177)
The two roots *bhī* and *jī* are restricted to different objects by some;
they have been taught in various ways, for indeed, the presentation [of grammatical rules] is diverse. (178)

For just as there is a conventional distinction of meaning established by its own nature even though the general property of "form" (rūpa-sāmānya) is present, so too, even though there is a general conformity of meaning and the instruction in the grammatical treatise involves the inclusion of a common form, the root *ij* in the domain of the suffix *kit* is one thing entirely different from *yaj*, and the simple stem *as-* in forms such as *staḥ* and *santi* is likewise something else entirely, having a specific domain. And all of this is merely a conventional perspective, a semblance of ultimate reality.

In the ultimate sense, no form of a verbal root exists at all; however, conventional usage is maintained by some. Some maintain that there is only the root *sak*, and they prescribe the addition of the vowel *a* to it in specific contexts. For example, in the *Nirukta*, among the roots meaning "to go," another root-form *niga...* is recited. Similarly, others recite the root *āhi* as having five syllables in the sense of "speaking. As it is said:
"O lady of beautiful smiles, for my delight, you alone are my refuge, like the five syllables of the serpent (*āheḥ*) belonging to the dark fortnight, just like the moon (*glauḥ*)."
Some make the word *ya* from the root *svad* (in the form *rakitsvāde*). For indeed, the means of exposition are diverse. 178.
He states that the root *yaj* is indeed distinct from itself by saying "the two are distinct.

One must understand that they are fixed as "one *yaj* is different from another *yaj*": namely, that *ij* occurs only when followed by a *kit* suffix, while *yaj* occurs in other instances. Furthermore, the Teacher says "by some," etc., in order to demonstrate that these two are sometimes indicated based on their distinction and sometimes without such distinction. A certain [grammarian] teaches the vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of *yaj* before a *kit* suffix—as in *iṣṭaḥ* and *iṣṭvā*—but he does not desire that for it before suffixes such as *tṛc*, etc.—as in *yaṣṭā*, *yaṣṭum*, and *yaṣṭavyam*.
Someone else teaches the very same [rule] by stating that one should apply the substitution of *y* for the suffixes beginning with *tṛ*; such is the variety of methods of exposition. || 178 ||
And thus one should treat it like the *jitvarī* plant [used for] curing wind-diseases;
there is no contradiction whatsoever in accepting both difference and non-difference. (179)

For grammarians, when dealing with established linguistic conventions, might either posit a conceptual constituent part, or they might explain the word *vidūra*—which is not common in worldly usage but is the domain of technical treatises—as being a distinct verbal root (*prakṛti*), just as they do with the word *jitvarī*. Alternatively, they might prescribe the word *vidūra* as a substitute (*ādeśa*) for the word *vālavāya*, since they have the same meaning. Indeed, whether one accepts a substitution without distinction, or asserts a distinct verbal root with a restricted scope, there is no difference whatsoever from the perspective of the worldly referent or the word denoting the composite whole. || 179 ||
He says "And thus" because an exposition is also seen to be based upon a distinction of states (*avasthābheda*).

Here, they derive the word *vaidūrya* [as follows]: "The *vaidūrya* gem originates from *vidūra*. Yet, it does not originate from *vidūra*. It is produced in *Bālavāya* and is merely refined in *vidūra*. Regarding this, it is said:
"Either *Bālavāya*, or *vidūra*, or indeed another material cause (*prakṛti*)."

"If one should say, 'That is not so,' then one should treat it like the word *jitvarī*. In the domain of linguistic usage (*vṛtti*), the word *vidūra* undergoes a modification; consequently, it is established that the *vaidūrya* gem originates from *bālavāya*. Thus, the non-difference between *bālavāya* and *vidūra* is accepted. Alternatively, another word *vidūra* is used in the domain of usage, just as merchants refer to Vārāṇasī as *jitvarī*. From the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the words *viśravaṇa* and *ravaṇa* are understood, and thus the difference [between the two usages] should be recognized. Therefore, whether one accepts their non-difference or relies upon their difference, there is no fault whatsoever.

Moreover, when resorting to the position of difference (*bhedapakṣa*), the instruction is given by relying upon the universal (*sāmānya*) for the sake of brevity; however, in the case of non-difference (*abhedapakṣa*), it is done precisely by relying on the undifferentiated form—thus there is nothing faulty. || 179 ||

In the grammatical treatise, the separate conceptualization of roots and prefixes is for the purpose of establishing the rules for *aṭ* and other such elements; however, in reality, it is the root alone that possesses such [a nature]. (180)
For it is thus that the grammatical rule is recorded for the root *saṃgrāmayati* when preceded by a prefix;
likewise, such specific actions are initiated by combinations [of words]. (181)

For verbal roots (*dhātu*) are taught with distinctions for the sake of specific grammatical operations, having as their domain particular types of action. It is only when such distinctions exist that forms such as the *lyap* suffix, reduplication, and so forth—found in examples like *nivāsayati*, *āsphoṭayati*, *jugupsate*, and *mūtrayati*—obtain their desired systematic application. Regarding the root *saṃgrām* meaning "to fight," the prefix *sam-* is introduced specifically to denote a particular type of action; indeed, it is stated that the formation [of the noun] must necessarily be derived from the root *saṃgrām* when accompanied by a prefix. (180–181)
Therefore, if one holds the position that there is a difference between the word (the verbal root) and its prefix, then the separate conceptualization of the root and the prefix is as follows:

he says that roots are taught separately solely for the sake of establishing rules regarding the augment *aṭ* and reduplication; in reality, however, they denote only qualified actions, and thus only those accompanied by prefixes possess the status of being a root. || 180 ||

In order to demonstrate this very point, he says: "tathāhi" (for instance). Because we observe reduplication (*dvirvacana*) only for a root accompanied by a prefix—as in *asaṅgrāmayata* and *sisaṅgrāmayiṣate*—this [root] possesses the status of a verbal root (*dhātu*) only when accompanied by its prefix. Therefore, at the very outset, in the case of a verb (*ākhyāta*), it is a specific action expressed by the root that is undertaken to be accomplished; thus, for the purpose of showing the essential nature of verbs, he says: "particular actions," and so forth. The meaning is: "by means of complexes," that is, by means of the combinations of roots and prefixes. Such [actions] may be either undifferentiated or differentiated. (181)
In this way, the internal relationship between the verbal root and the prefix is such that the action,
being of that very nature, enters into connection with the factors of accomplishment (sādhana).

The determination of the specific meaning of verbal roots depends upon their connection with prefixes (*upasarga*). Once the root's own meaning is established, there must be the presence of another related element. In that case, when the form of the base (*prakṛti*)—which possesses a qualified meaning like the word *gaurakhara* (a white donkey)—is obtained, external relations arise. Therefore, a qualified action, expressed by the qualified form of the base, being itself something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), enters into a relationship with the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). || 182 ||

Therefore, he asks "What happens from this? and answers with the words "of the grammatical operations" (*kāryāṇām*). Thus, those operations which depend on verbal roots and prefixes and are called *antaranga* (internal) first take effect, such as the *suṭ* augment and others. And it is precisely in that state that the action enters into a relationship with its means (*sādhana*); thus he says "with the means. In that very state—that is, specifically as qualified by the prefix—it undergoes connection with the factors of action (*kāraka*). In this way, the *lakāra* suffix in the sense of the object (*karman*) is established in the case of the word *anubhūyate*; likewise, the rule "the [substitution] for *ṣatva* and *tuka* is not established" must be formulated.

It is established that the rule *aḍabhyāsavyavāye 'pi* need not even be commenced. And it has been said: "The engagement of the factors of action (*kāraka*s) toward a specific action is of one kind when it concerns meat-rice, and of another kind when it concerns dry rice. Since the specificity of that action arises from its connection with a prefix (*upasarga*), the connection with the prefix must first occur by resorting to the sequential order [of linguistic elements]. || 182 ||
When it is established that [the action] is fit for application, the object to be divided is specified;
moreover, prior to its connection with the means of accomplishment, the action does not arise at all. (183)
