In this context, when a well-known substantive (*viśe�ya*) is capable of being understood in multiple ways, it enters into a relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*) when expressed by a word whose usage has been observed [in that specific sense]. Furthermore, because an action (*kriyā*) is something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), its completion depends upon its connection with the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). Therefore, prior to the connection with the means, an action that has not yet arisen is devoid of its own nature and is unable to enter into a relationship of qualifier and qualified with a prefix (*upasarga*) which merely indicates it. According to the view of some, the verbal root (*dhātu*) is first joined with the means of accomplishment. (183)

Now, in order to demonstrate the nature of the verb by resorting to the sequence [of its formation]—namely, that first the verbal root (*dhātu*) is joined with its means of accomplishment—he says: "among those fit for usage" (*prayogārheṣu*). Since it has acquired its own essence, it is logically possible for it to function as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*); thus, among the verbal roots fit for usage, the established meaning is to be differentiated—that is, it becomes the qualificand—by means of prefixes (*upasarga*) and so forth. However, in the case of the finite verb (*ākhyāta*), there is no connection with qualifiers prior to that time.

If it is argued that [the action] is a specific action prior to its connection with the means (*sādhana*), even so, since that [action] has not yet arisen and thus lacks an intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), how could there be any connection with the auxiliary elements (*śeṣa*)? To this he says: "prior... and so forth. And it has been stated: "The means brings about the action; the prefix (*upasarga*) qualifies it. Thus, the connection with the means occurs first, and subsequently its qualification by the prefixes is logically established.

And on this view, the rule *aḍabhyāsavyavāye’pi* (P. 6.4.129) need not be commenced; furthermore, regarding the rule *ṣatvatukorasiddhaḥ* (P. 6.1.86), it need not be stated that the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is non-existent when *tuK* is to be applied, because the *guṇa*—which depends on the *ārdhadhātuka* suffix denoting the means—is established by its being *antaranga* (internal) due to the suffix being present. || 183 ||

Just as the nature of a verbal root and its status as an object or a state [of being] are seen through the application of a future accomplishment based on its initial context, so too should other cases be understood.
Now, in order to establish the position that the verbal root is joined with the prefix first, he says:

It has been stated that "a verbal root (dhātu) is that which expresses action. Since action cannot exist prior to its connection with a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), the designation of "verbal root" is applied at the very outset by relying on a future connection with a means of accomplishment. Just as it is said, "from a verbal root [denoting] an object" (*dhātoḥ karmaṇaḥ*), where the status of being an object of the root is mentioned at the outset because the status of being an object of the root is yet to come; so too let another example be seen: let the state of expressing a specific action be seen at the very outset by relying on a future connection. Who...?

This is a fault. And thus, by resorting to a different position, it is said that the production of such specific qualities is not fitting, according to the principle: "Such specific actions are initiated by aggregates. || 184 ||
Just as lac-dye and other substances applied at the time of sowing assist the fruits through the transformation of their color and other qualities, [so too does the impression]. (185)
And since it is logical to accept that this very action is indeed distinguished by its preparatory effort (*upakrama*), he says, preceded by the presentation of an example:

"Just as at the very time of sowing the seed, lac-dye and other substances, through their connection with the seed, later bring about assistance to the fruit by means of the transformation of color, taste, and so forth. (185)
Through the connection with the root, as well as with prefixes and suffixes, a distinction that has been internalized becomes manifest at the time of the word. (186)

Thus, in order to apply this to the case under discussion (*adārṣṭāntika*), he says: "That which is internally implied by the cognition of the relationship between the root and the prefix—when, at the time of the word (*pada-kāla*), upon the formation of the word from that very relationship of the root and the prefix, this distinction becomes manifest, it does so not of its own accord; therefore, it is logical that the application of the grammatical means (*sādhana*) belongs only to that [word] which is already connected with the prefix. (Verse 186)
In some cases, distinctions that are possible but not indicated by the verbal roots alone are manifested through the connection with prefixes such as *pra*, *parā*, and so forth. (187)

Thus, in the context of grammatical analysis (*apoddhāra*), it has been explained in various ways—based on the possible and impossible application of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—how the derivation of a word, its parts, and its stem (*prakṛti*) and suffix (*pratyaya*) can be performed with their respective causes; furthermore, it has been stated that sometimes the meaning is the cause [of the form] and sometimes the form itself is the cause. Consequently, whether a word is single or multiple, the nominal word (*nāmapada*) has been determined at least in part.

The verb (*ākhyāta*) has also been largely demonstrated through the investigation of its distinctions and non-distinctions in such passages as, "Specific actions are commenced by means of combinations [of sounds] of that kind. Now, since the author of the *Nirukta* states, "There are four classes of words: nouns (*nāman*), verbs (*ākhyāta*), prefixes (*upasarga*), and particles (*nipāta*)," and having already shown the nature of the noun and the verb, he says the following in order to demonstrate the nature of the prefixes, which remain to be shown:

In cases such as *kvacit pacati* ("he cooks in a certain way"), since excellence (*prakarṣa*) and so forth are possible, yet these qualities are not perceived by the verbal roots alone, they are understood through their connection with prefixes (*upasarga*). Therefore, it is said that prefixes possess the function of indicating specific distinctions (*viśeṣadyotakatva*) in those instances. For this very reason it has been stated: "The other [the prefix] qualifies that very [root]. (187)
It is either the denoter of specific qualities because they are possible [therein], or it is an illuminator;
or else, it is employed as an auxiliary to the verbal root (dhātu) for the purpose of imparting its power. (188)

In that case, are they merely indicators (*dyotaka*), or is there another alternative as well? To this he says: "They are not only indicators; they are also seen to be denoters (*vācaka*). For example, in expressions such as *pratiṣṭhate*, the verbal root (*dhātu*) has the sense of cessation of motion, whereas by the prefix *pra*, the sense of motion is established. And so it has been said: "One [prefix] subverts the meaning of the root," and "Or it may be an indicator due to possibility"—this was already explained at the beginning of the verse. Now, in order to show the third alternative as well, it is said: "For the purpose of imparting power," and so forth.

Since a root and a prefix together express a meaning, the prefix possesses only a capacity; thus, in the expression of the meaning, the prefixes act as auxiliaries. On this point also it has been said: "Someone follows that [capacity]. (188)
Furthermore, when movement and so forth are understood from "standing" and other such terms used alone, that [action] is said to be their property (dharmā) based on two kinds of inference. (189)

In examples such as *pratiṣṭhate*, the fact that the verbal root (*dhātu*) expresses the cessation of motion while the prefix (*upasarga*) expresses motion has been established by common usage (*prasiddhi*). Now, in order to establish through inference (*anumāna*) that this [prefix] is merely indicative (*dyotaka*) in all cases, he says:

"The verb *tiṣṭhati* denotes the cessation of motion by virtue of common usage; therefore, motion is not conveyed by it alone. Thus, on the grounds that roots have multiple meanings, its status as expressing motion is also established by inference, whereas the prefix is merely its indicator.

However, since the cessation of motion is well-established by the root *sthā* ("to stand"), it is stated that the prefix *pra-* denotes motion; yet, according to the actual state of things, it is established through inference—both by way of general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*) and specific observation (*viśeṣato dṛṣṭa*)—that prefixes such as *pra-* are merely indicators (*dyotaka*). Thus he says, "In that regard," and so forth. By means of inference, it is determined that while the verbal root (*dhātu*) possesses multiple meanings, the prefix (*upasarga*) is an indicator. Inference is of two kinds: specific observation and general observation.

In this regard, the expressiveness (*dyotakatva*) of prefixes (*upasarga*) is established without distinction; thus, it is to be proven that the prefix *pra-* expresses the initial action (*ādikarma*), because it is the word *pra-*, like the previously mentioned *pra-* seen in verbs such as *pac* and others. By means of inference based on specific observation (*viśeṣato dṛṣṭa-anumāna*), every prefix beginning with *pra-* is stated to possess the property of expressiveness, as it shares the same characteristic as that [specific] *pra-*. Furthermore, by means of inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa-anumāna*), the verbal root (*dhātu*) is shown to have multiple meanings.

Just as the root *sthā* has multiple meanings is to be proven—the property to be established—because it is a verbal root (*dhātu*), like roots such as *yaj*, which are accepted by both disputants as having multiple meanings; thus, by means of an inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*), the application is that other roots as well are said to have multiple meanings because they possess that same property. ||189||
In the absence of a distinct action, as far as the prefixes *adhi* and *pari* are concerned, the verbal root that expresses it is meaningless when used together with them. (190)
Now, in order to demonstrate that [prefixes] can also denote a combined meaning, he says:

in the cases of *adhyāgacchati* and *paryāgacchati*, the prefixes *adhi* and *pari* are meaningless; for since the arrival characterized by "superiority" (*uparibhāva*) or "all-around-ness" (*sarvatobhāva*) is already understood from the root *ā-gam* itself through context and so forth, there is no regard for brevity in common linguistic usage. Thus, the employment of *adhi* and *pari* is for the sake of clarity alone.

The meaning is that only the aggregate [of root and prefix] expresses a specific meaning; therefore, since the prefixes *adhi* and *pari* alone, as well as the verbal root alone, are here devoid of meaning (*anarthaka*), they do not express a distinct meaning. Consequently, the root and the prefix together express a particular meaning; thus, the prefixes are auxiliaries (*sahakārin*) in the expression of the root’s meaning. As for the fact that *adhi* and *pari* are said to be "meaningless" (*anarthaka*) due to their conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), this refers to their being meaningless when isolated. For there is no meaning in those two prefixes when they are used alone; hence it has been said: "In some cases, it follows that [the prefix]. (190)

In the same way, certain suffixes added for their own sake (svārthika), when occurring within a compound and conjoined with a meaningless element, merely restate the meaning of the base form (prakṛti). || 191 ||

In this context, he states the nature of self-referential suffixes (*svārthika-pratyaya*): in examples such as *yāvaka*, suffixes like *kan* and others should be understood as conveying meaning only when combined. Since the word *yāva* alone is not the base for the suffix *kan*—rather, the word *yāva* is determined [as the base] only within the aggregate—it must be understood that these suffixes function within a different composite whole. For this very reason, he says: "combined with the meaningless. The word *yāva* is indeed meaningless as the base for *kan*; however, the aggregate, possessing a specific quality produced by the mutual powers of its components, is meaningful therein. Thus, he says: "they reiterate the meaning of the base," meaning that they do not express their own meaning independently, but rather through combination.

[Objection: Has it not just been stated that the constituent part (*prakṛti*) is meaningless? Therefore, how can it be said that [the suffixes] "reiterate the meaning of the base" (*prakṛtyarthānuvādinaḥ*)? [Response: The intention is that this is based on mere similarity. Since the suffix *kan* considers its own base alone to be similar to the word [formed with the suffix], it was said with that intention that they "reiterate the meaning of the base. However, in reality, it should be understood that they "function within a different aggregate" (*saṅghātāntaravṛttayaḥ*). || 191 ||
Some particles are indicators (*dyotaka*), while others express distinct meanings; some may be like suffixes (*āgama*), expressing a meaning only when combined [with other words]. (192)
Now, in order to demonstrate the nature of particles (*nipāta*) as being non-constant, he says:

"In some cases, like prepositions (*upasarga*), they are indicative (*dyotaka*)," as for example in *vṛkṣaśca plakṣaśca* ("the tree and the fig tree"). He states that for some particles, such as the *ca*-group, there is the capacity to denote meaning independently, which establishes their status as signifiers (*vācaka*), by saying "some," and so forth. Some particles are signifiers when combined, like verbal suffixes (*āgama*), according to the reading: "for those whose separate meanings are postulated. In their view, particles are of two kinds: some possess meaning, while others are meaningless.

In this regard, some particles (nipātas), when conceived as having distinct meanings, are denoters of meaning; therefore, they are "significant" (arthavat). This is the description of the essential nature of those that possess meaning. As for those that are meaningless (anarthaka), he states their essential nature with the words beginning "āgamāḥ" (192).
Whether placed above or before [a word], their illuminating function does not differ, even when they are employed in those various ways with distinct meanings. (193)
And thus, stating that there is no fixed rule regarding their usage in worldly practice, he says:

"Whether employed before or after, they bring about the illumination of that meaning"; therefore, when they are employed for such purposes as expressing option (*vikalpa*) or conjunction (*samuccaya*), it is established that their function is solely that of indicators (*dyotaka*). || 193 ||
Particles such as *ca* and so forth are not used alone, even when they possess the status of a word (*pada*);
likewise, a suffix, despite its capacity to denote meaning, is not used in isolation. (194)

Alternatively, one might ask: why are these not called "denoters" (*vācaka*)? Why [are they defined] by way of being "illuminators" (*dyotaka*)? In order to strengthen this point that they are illuminators of meaning, he says: "For these particles, beginning with *ca*, are never used in isolation; therefore, it should be understood that they are not denoters. The thesis (*sādhya*) is that particles such as *ca* are not denoters of the substratum (*dharmin*), because they are not used in isolation. For if they were denoters, then, like words such as "cow," they would be used even in isolation; such is the inference.

Is it not the case that there is a counter-inference here: "The particles *ca* and so forth do not indicate a substantive (*dharmin*)," which is the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), because they are never used in isolation. To this he replies: "provided they possess the status of a word" (*padatve sati*).

This is what is meant: this reason is not without qualification; rather, because unaccompanied [particles] are never employed, they are "indicators" (*dyotaka*). By the phrase "provided that they are words" (*padatve sati*), the suffixes (*pratyaya*) are excluded. To demonstrate this very point, he says: "Even though a suffix may be expressive," and so forth. For even if a certain suffix were expressive, it is not employed alone because it lacks the status of being a word (*pada*). (194)
Even when there is a collective expression, no distinction [between the parts] exists; furthermore, a state that has not yet become an entity is denoted by another term as "action" (kriyā). (195)

Now, if it is argued that the status of being a denoter is established for the particle *ca* because it denotes a non-substantial (asattvabhūta) distinct meaning due to the inherent nature of the power of words, that is untenable. For, just as the genitive case is heard when words denoting those meanings—such as "conjunction" (*samuccaya*) and so on—are employed, as in "the conjunction of the tree" (*vṛkṣasya samuccayaḥ*) or "the conjunction of the fig tree" (*plakṣasya samuccayaḥ*), likewise the genitive case would have to be heard upon the employment of a particle, as in "of the tree and of the fig tree" (*vṛkṣasya ca plakṣasya ca*).

This would indeed be the case if these [words] were denoters of a collection (*samuccaya*), but they are not so; rather, it is said that these are denoters of what is collected (*samuccita*). Furthermore, since there is no exclusion (*vyatireka*) in the denotation of that [collected thing], he says: "If this is so, then in the denotation of the collected thing which has become a substance (*sattvabhūta*), because of the prohibition 'it is not a substance' (*asattve*), the designation of 'particle' (*nipāta*) does not occur; and in the absence of that [designation], the designation of 'indeclinable' (*avyaya*), which is preceded by the former, also does not occur. Consequently, even for words beginning with *ca*, the hearing of case-endings (*vibhakti*) would result. To this, he says: "In the case of non-substance" (*asattve*).

This is what is meant: it is established here that the denotation of meanings by words is innate (*svābhāvika*). In this regard, it is stated with an illustration that particles (*nipātas*) are understood as denoters of non-substantial entities (*asattvabhūta-artha*) precisely due to the very nature of the power of words: "it is done. Here, the word "just as" (*yathā*) is to be supplied.

Just as "cooking" (*pāka*) alone is the denotation of both the nominal stem and the verbal suffix due to the inherent nature of the power of words, so too, by the verbal suffix in *pacati*, that [action] is expressed as something not yet existing as a substance (*asattvabhūta*), whereas in *pāka*, by the nominal stem, it is expressed as having a completed nature, established as a substance (*siddha*). Similarly, by particles (*nipāta*), there is the expression of things such as conjunction (*samuccaya*) as something not yet existing as a substance; therefore, no case-ending (*vibhakti*) arises.

And it has been said: "This is not something based on explicit scriptural statement (*vācanika*); rather, gender, number, and so forth are inherent (*svābhāvika*). For example, among those studying the same [text], some are connected with the meanings [of the words] while others are not. Thus, because they are denotative (*vācaka*), even when there is a collective expression (*samuccitābhidhāna*), there is an absence of case-endings (*vibhakti*) because, like a finite verb (*ākhyātapada*), they denote an entity that is not a substance (*asattvabhūta-artha*). || 195 ||

Even when there is a collective expression, words that denote a qualified meaning are connected with their respective qualities; however, particles such as *ca* and others are dependent on others. (196)

Even if this were so, just as independent denoters [of qualities] are connected with a qualifier because they express a collection [of qualities], the same would apply to particles (*nipāta*) as well. Furthermore, since it is said that "the gender and number of words expressing qualities (*guṇavacana*) follow from their substratum," and since particles do not denote a substance (*asattvavācaka*), they lack case-endings; consequently, one would arrive at the form *śobhanaś ca vṛkṣaḥ* (a beautiful tree). Thus, it has been stated elsewhere: "In every usage, the qualifier enters into a relationship with the constituent part of the genus (*jāti*); thereafter, the genus acquires the properties residing therein."

And thus, it occurs that "the country of Pañcāla is wealthy and beautiful," because [the term] qualifies the individual (*lubanta*) and not the genus (*jāti*). Then, it occurs that "the Pañcālas are a beautiful country," because [the term] qualifies the genus. Anticipating this objection, he says the following to provide a justification:

A relationship with qualifiers (guṇas) is possible for words that denote qualified objects; however, in the case of particles (nipātas), although they denote non-substantial entities (asattva) due to the very nature of their expressive power (śakti), they lack connection with qualifiers because they are invariably dependent [on other words]. Thus, there is no fault whatsoever. What is meant is this: it is precisely due to the nature of their expressive power that they possess this constant dependence on others. Therefore, it is established that even when expressing a collective meaning, there is neither independent usage nor connection with qualifiers. || 196 ||
Having produced some action, the connection ceases;
in other cases, when an action-word is heard, the connection arises. (197)

Thus, the fourfold division of words—consisting of nouns (*nāman*), verbs (*ākhyāta*), prefixes (*upasarga*), and particles (*nipāta*)—has been explained. Now, the *karmapravacanīyas* (governing particles) are accepted as the fifth category of word; therefore, he speaks in order to examine them: "The *karmapravacanīyas* are intended to be the causes for the delimitation of relations. As he will state later: "They are the differentiators of relations. Furthermore, every relation is preceded by an action (*kriyā*) and its factors (*kāraka*). In some cases, the action ceases after having produced the relation, as in the case of *rājapuruṣa* ("the king's man").

For here, in the case of "this is the king's man," because that king supports the man, the action characterized by supporting ceases after having produced a relationship characterized by the relation of locus and located (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*). Sometimes a verbal root produces a relationship while it is being heard; for example, in "he remembers his mother. Here, "of the mother" is an accusative word; therefore, the action of remembering, even while being heard, produces a relationship characterized by the relation of cause and effect (*nimittanimittabhāva*), such that the remembrance is related to the mother.

This very point has been stated elsewhere: "Relation is distinct from the factors of action (kārakas); it is preceded by action and its factors. It is expressed whether the action is explicitly mentioned or not. (Vākyapadīya, Sādhanasamuddeśa, 156). || 197 ||

In that context, the genitive case (ṣaṣṭhī) is prescribed at every step to prevent compounding; however, it is cited as an example with respect to the grammatical factor (kāraka) for the purpose of illustration.

In order to investigate, by way of a digression, why the section beginning with "the genitive [is used] for the object of roots meaning 'to remember' (adhī), 'to love' (day), and 'to rule' (īś)" is commenced—given that the genitive is already prescribed for relations in general—he says:

In examples such as *mātuḥ smaraṇam* ("the remembering of the mother"), since the object (*karman*) is intended to be expressed as a residual relation (*śeṣatva*), the genitive case is already established; therefore, the genitive that is further prescribed by the rule *adhīgarthetyādi* is for the purpose of restriction (*niyama*). When the object and so forth are intended to be expressed as a residual relation, only the genitive occurs. Whatever else [such as the accusative] would otherwise apply is prohibited. Furthermore, since it is impossible to effect the cessation of elision (*luk*) and other operations without cutting off the very source of the problem, only the prohibition of the compound (*samāsa*) is carried out.

Consequently, it is indeed the genitive case [that applies]. When something arrives having been asked about from another source, such as the elision of the *samāsa* suffix (*samāsalaṅ*), that would result; therefore, it should be understood that the genitive is prescribed again for each specific rule (*pratipadam*) in order to prevent such a compound. For this reason, the statement in the *Bhāṣya*, "And the genitive prescribed by a specific rule (*pratipadavidhānā*) is not compounded," need not even be undertaken. If this is so, how is the counter-example "What is the remembrance of the mother's virtues? (*māturguṇaiḥ smaraṇam*) explained?

Just as it is impossible for the qualities (*guṇa*) to be the object of remembrance (*smartavyatva*), so too is it impossible for them to be the subordinate element (*śeṣatva*). If they were intended here as the subordinate element, then the genitive case would have been used for them rather than the instrumental. Consequently, fearing that this [expression] would suffer from a deficiency of two factors (*dvyaṅgavaikalya*), he says: "But for the sake of clarity," and so forth. When it is said, "the remembrance of the mother's qualities," one might doubt whether the qualities are the object (*karman*) or the instrument (*karaṇa*); therefore, it is stated: "remembrance by means of the qualities."

When the instrument (*karaṇa*) is intended to be expressed as a residual relation (*śeṣatvena*), the word "object" (*karmani*) was stated so that the genitive case prescribed by the *pratipadavidhi* (Pāṇini 2.3.65) would not apply; thus, there is no deficiency of two factors [of the rule]. Furthermore, it is established that the restatement of the genitive case is solely for the purpose of precluding compound formation (*samāsa*) and the like. And it has been said: "When the residual relation is designated by means of the instruments [of action] and the verb is actually heard, the genitive prescribed by the *pratipadavidhi* is stated to prevent compounding. The meaning is: "when the residual relation is designated by means of the instruments [of action]."

The authors of the *Vṛtti* maintain that when the object (*karman*) alone is intended to be expressed as a residual relation (*śeṣatva*), the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is employed, whereas for any other *kāraka*, only the instrumental is used. According to their view, there is no genitive at all in the expression "remembrance by means of qualities" (*guṇaiḥ smaraṇam*), because it is "remembrance through qualities" rather than "the remembrance of qualities. However, according to the author of the *Ṭīkā*, if one intends to express the instrument (*karaṇa*) as a residual relation, the form "remembrance of qualities" (*guṇānāṃ smaraṇam*) is also possible; such is the difference between the two opinions. || 198 ||
And that relation which has arisen when the verbal action-word has ceased is regulated in each respective case by a *karmapravacanīya* particle. (199)
It is established that this [relation] is produced by means of an action (*kriyā*). To the question "What follows from that?", he says:

That relation produced by the action, once it has arisen, is restricted to that specific action by means of a *karmapravacanīya*—even when the word for the action is not heard in some instances. Thus, in a state of doubt as to whether "this [relation] might be produced by an action," the specific nature of the relation is made known by the *karmapravacanīyas*. For this very reason, they are called *karmapravacanīyas* because they indicate a specific relation brought about by an action, having themselves been designated as "expressing the object" (*karman*). || 199 ||
That which implies a verbal action is joined with case endings of the *kāraka* relations; for example, in the word *likha*, its status as being without a prefix (*anupasarga*) [is established]. 200.

Now, one might ask: why are *karmapravacanīyas* not accepted as the attractors (*ākṣepaka*) of an unexpressed action? To this he says: here, by that word, the attraction of a verbal root (*kriyāpada*) is effected; it is observed that such [an attractor] is joined with a case-ending belonging to a *kāraka*. For example: *prādeśaṃ viparilikhati* ("he draws a line around the span"). Here, the prefix *vi-* is the attractor of the act of measuring, because the meaning "having measured out a span (*prādeśaṃ vimāya*), he draws a line around" is understood. Therefore, since the object characterized as a *prādeśa* is attracted here by the act of measuring, its connection is indeed with the second case-ending, which belongs to a *kāraka*.

And when the word *vi* implies another action (*kriyāntara*), then, because it has no connection with the action of "writing" (*likhati*), it is not a preposition (*upasarga*) with respect to that [action]. Consequently, by the rule "a motion [is unaccented] after a motion," there is an absence of the *nighāta* (elision of accent). Similarly, if a verbal root were implied by karmapravacanīyas, then in connection with them, only the case-ending denoting a *kāraka* would occur. In that case, the rule "the second case is used when joined with a karmapravacanīya" would not need to be formulated at all.
However, since the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would apply to express a general relation (*sambandhasāmānya*), the second case is commenced to set that aside; thus, its formulation is appropriate. ||200||
The application of the root *sthā* (to stand) is observed in the sense of "not admitting" [a claim], as in *apratyajayan*.
The suffix *sun* occurs in the sense of "facing toward"; furthermore, the prefix *abhi* is employed even when used alone. (201)
Observing that the implication of a verbal action is seen elsewhere as well, he says this very thing for the sake of confirmation:

"In the expression *apratyajayan*, the word *prati* is observed to imply the action of staying (*sthitikriyā*)—as in 'the gods conquered the Asuras who were not standing firm,' where the application of the root *sthā* (to stand) is observed to be implied. Likewise, even when connected with a verbal root, the function of the word *abhi* alone in the sense of 'facing toward' is observed in the case of *sunvanti*; therefore, he mentions this incidentally by saying *sunvanti*."
Thus, the fact that karmapravacanīyas function as determiners of relations has been established solely by relying on their etymological designation. || 201 ||

The status of being a *karmapravacanīya* is prescribed when there is a connection with an action, for the purpose of preventing [undesirable] changes such as the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*, in the case of words like *svati* which possess different grammatical properties. (202)
Now, one might ask: since it is impossible for *svati* and the others to possess that [specific] nature, how can they receive the designation *karmapravacanīya*?

To this he says: here, the status of *karmapravacanīya* is prescribed for *svati* and the others solely for the purpose of excluding other designations; and because of the governing rule of "one designation" (*ekasaṃjñādhikāra*), in the absence of the designations *gati* and *upasarga*, the resulting phenomena such as the substitution of *ṣ* (by the rule *upasargād*) do not occur. || 202 ||
When the connection between cause and effect has been determined by the preceding [section], the third section, characterized by the cause, begins from here and is commenced. (203)

He states something else by way of a further application (*prasaṅga*) with the words "in the sense of a mark" (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth: the designation *karmapravacanīya* for the particle *anu* is established [by Pāṇini 1.4.84]. For a "mark" (*lakṣaṇa*) is that which makes known; likewise, a "cause" (*hetu*) is also so called. Consequently, just as the designation *karmapravacanīya* applies to *anu* in the case of the relationship between the signified and the signifier—as in "the lightning flashes after the tree" (*vṛkṣamanu vidyotate vidyut*)—so too does it apply in the case of "it rained after Śākalya’s recitation of the *saṃhitā*" (*śākalyasya saṃhitāmanu prāvarṣat*).

In that case, when the exclusion of the relationship characterized by the indicator and the indicated (*lakṣaṇa-lakṣyabhāva*) has been effected by the particle *anu*, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) alone would apply because it is intended for the sense of cause (*hetu*), as in "the family [is known] by means of wealth" (*dhanena kulam*). Thus, there would be no scope for the rule *lakṣaṇetthaṃbhūtākhyāna-* (Pāṇini 1.4.90), which governs the relationship of indicator and indicated (*jñāpya-jñāpakabhāva*), as in "lightning flashes near the tree" (*vṛkṣamanu vidyotate vidyut*). However, in the instance "it rained following Śākalya’s *saṃhitā*" (*śākalyasya saṃhitāmanu prāvarṣat*), both rules would apply simultaneously.

In this case, since the relationship of cause and effect (hetu-hetumadbhāva) is possible, the third case ending would apply; however, it does not occur because of the subsequent rule "anurlakṣaṇe" which provides a new prescription. || 203 ||
This [particle] does not indicate an action, nor is it an expresser of a relation; nor does it imply a verbal root for action, but rather it is a differentiator of the relation. (204)

Having thus conducted this incidental investigation into the *karmapravacanīyas*, and having refuted the three possible modes such as denotativeness (*vācakatva*) and so forth, he establishes that they function solely as qualifiers of a relation (*sambandhaviśeṣaka*), stating:

In examples such as *prapacati*, this [karmapravacanīya] does not indicate an action, unlike a prefix (*upasarga*). Furthermore, since the connection is already expressed by the accusative case itself—which serves as an exception to the genitive—it is not the denoter of that connection. Nor, in cases such as *prādeśaṃ viparilikhati*, does it suggest a verbal action, like the word *vi* [in *vilikhati*]. Rather, because this connection is produced by a specific action, the karmapravacanīya is the "distinguisher" (*viśeṣaka*) of the connection. || 204 ||
A collection of meaningless [phonemes] becomes meaningful, and likewise, it may be meaningless; among phonemes, a word is endowed with meaning, but the constituent parts within a word are not.

Thus, in the context of grammatical abstraction (*apoddhāra*), the fivefold division of words has been demonstrated. Having thus shown the analysis of words, the author will subsequently restate it and establish the various types of word-meanings in detail. As it is said: "By some, the word is divided in two ways, in four ways, and even in five ways, having been abstracted from sentences just like bases, suffixes, and so forth."
"Upon the abstraction of word-meanings, there is either the genus (*jāti*) or the substance (*dravya*) alone," and so forth.

Thus, having established the justification for incidental effects (*prāsaṅgika-kārya*) and the like by means of the analysis of word-components (*apoddhāra*) according to the proponents of the indivisible sentence (*akhaṇḍa-vākyavādin*), an investigation into words, word-meanings, whole-word meanings, and the meanings of word-parts was conducted as a consequence thereof. Furthermore, following the system of the author of the *Nirukta*, the definitions of nouns (*nāman*), verbs (*ākhyāta*), prefixes (*upasarga*), and particles (*nipāta*) were presented; and it was also demonstrated that some maintain that "karmapravacanīyas constitute a fifth class of words. In this manner, the opposing views having been refuted and one's own position [established]...

Having established [the position] after first refuting the objections, and desiring once again to support that very same unimpeachable thesis, he speaks [as follows], anticipating an objection regarding a contradiction with the *Vārttika*: ||205||
Furthermore, the combination of words endowed with meaning is divided again, both by the inclusion of another meaning and by the dissolution of their connection. 206.

Furthermore, by the inclusion—that is, the acceptance—of another meaning characterized by a connection (saṃsarga), a certain collection of words such as "Devadatta, bring the cow" is meaningful; whereas another, such as "ten pomegranates," is meaningless because it lacks mutual connection, being thus excluded from [the category of] relationship. 206.
The meaningful and the meaningless do not attain a relationship when distinguished;
some, however, maintain that they do attain it, citing examples such as *kṛt* suffixes and so forth. (207)
To demonstrate this very point, he says:

"When a distinction is made, there are two collections of phonemes (varṇa-samudāya), one meaningful and the other meaningless—such as the word *kuṭī* and the word *uraś*. Some say that these two do not attain a relationship because of [the latter's] meaninglessness. Others say that they do attain a relationship because they possess meaning through the sense to be expressed (*dyotya-artha*). (207)
From meaningful [elements], a composite arises with a distinct meaning; some, however, maintain that it does not arise in the case of compounds, taddhitas, and the like. (208)
In order to demonstrate that because the meaning of a composite whole exists, the meanings of its constituent parts must also exist, he says:

"In cases such as *rājapuruṣa* (king’s man), a meaningful composite arises from meaningful [parts]. However, in the case of words with suffixes having their own inherent meaning (*svārthika*) and so forth, no distinct further meaning has appeared based on the meanings of the constituent parts; therefore, there is no possibility for the meaning of the composite to exist apart from the meanings of the parts. (208)
Some words have meanings that are established through association and whose capacities are known through differentiation;
some have capacities that are merely conceptualized through positive and negative concomitance. (209)
He says that they exist in a twofold form:

those for whom the meaning is established as combined (*yutasiddha*) are of such a nature, such as the *śamī* tree, the *dāḍima* tree, and so forth. Why is this so? He says: "In the case of difference," and so on. When there is a sentence involving difference, because the form (*rūpa*) is not destroyed, certain words such as *saṃjñā* and *upajña* have their powers known separately; thus, their powers are postulated through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

For here, the meaning must be inferred by following the grammatical rule "prasaṃbhyāṃ jānunorjñuḥ" [Pāṇini 5.4.129], as in "one whose knees are extended" (*pragata-jānu*) or "one whose knees are joined" (*saṅgata-jānu*); it cannot be understood separately, because the word *jānu*, which was seen in the original sentence, has been lost. Therefore, it should be understood that the reason "because the composite possesses meaning" (*saṃghātārthavattvāt*) is both partially unestablished (*bhāgāsiddha*) and inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). || 209 ||
It has been demonstrated that the meaning of the phonemes is indeed found only within the meaning of the treatises;
for pure roots and the like, no worldly meaning exists. (210)
The meaning of primary derivatives (kṛt) and secondary derivatives (taddhita), when standing alone, is non-linguistic (alaukika);
likewise, the meaning of that which ends in such a suffix does not exist prior to the addition of an inflectional ending (vibhakti).
That meaning which is perceived as more clearly manifest at the end of suffixes, and which is based on the context of meaningfulness, is of such a nature [as that which is expressed]. (212)
Although it has been stated, "The phonemes possess meaning because meaning is observed in the case of monophonic roots, nominal stems, suffixes, and particles," to that he replies: || 210 – 121 ||

If there is no difference whatsoever between the phonemes of a word and those of a sentence, then the phonemes themselves would be the denoters through their mutual dependence upon one another's capacity. (213)
He states that if one were to admit that phonemes possess meaning, the capacity of words and sentences to denote meaning would be undermined—this is easily understood. || 213 ||
A collection [of phonemes] that expresses [a meaning] is not deficient in its color (varṇa) by any [part];
and since it is not a different word, it is understood as being non-deficient because of that. || 214 ||

Now, in order to demonstrate a difference of opinion, he says: "If a word-group (*saṅghāta*) lacking one syllable—such as *iṣkartāram* and so forth—is held to be expressive, then there are two possibilities: it must be either a different word altogether or the same word. If it is not a different word from *iṣkartāram*, then even with a missing syllable, the very word *niṣkartāram* (which has the full number of syllables) is understood; therefore, it should be understood that the cognition of its own meaning occurs. (214)
Establishing a memory of the object through that expressive word as its cause, he brings forth the object—which is actually mediated—by means of the word as if it were directly present. (215)
To demonstrate this very point, he says:

"If [the word] is deficient by some phoneme (*varṇa*), that deficient phoneme—by means of a cause, namely the study of the treatise (*śāstra*)—produces a memory of the form of the complete expressive word; thus, as if directly, it conveys or presents the object, even though it is mediated, by means of the word established through memory. Now, if it were a different word altogether, then just as the complete phonemic form is expressive, so too would the deficient phonemic form be expressive due to its connection with that [complete form]; therefore, there would be no distinction whatsoever. (215)
Just as in the case of "white donkey" and similar compounds, there is no object denoted by the word that is understood in the aggregate, even though the cognition [of the parts] exists. (216)
When the essence of an object is perceived as if endowed with its constituent parts, the perception of those parts therein is likewise of no assistance [to the cognition of the whole]. (217)
Therefore, in order to demonstrate that it is indeed untenable for the members [of the syllogism] to convey that meaning, he says:

Just as in cases such as "gaurakharaḥ" (wild ass) or "kṛṣṇasarpaḥ" (black snake), there is no other meaning whatsoever for the individual words; or even if there were a cognition of those meanings at the time of hearing them, this specific meaning is not understood at all in the aggregate "gaurakharaḥ," for what is understood from that aggregate is indeed a distinct genus (*jātyantara*) entirely devoid of any contact with the meanings of the constituent parts. In exactly the same way, the meaning characterized by *pratibhā* (intuitive flash), which appears as if connected with the word-meanings in expressions such as "Devadatta, bring the cow," [is likewise distinct].

In ultimate reality, however, it is perceived as undivided, like the taste of a beverage; therefore, the perception of individual objects—the appearance of constituent parts—should be considered entirely unhelpful in that regard. (216–217)

And when the whole and its parts have different meanings within the various linguistic functions (vṛtti), difference and relation—two contradictory properties—would simultaneously follow as consequences. (218)

If this is not accepted, then since the composite whole (*samudāya*) and its parts (*avayava*) would have different meanings, it would follow that at the same time there is a conjunction of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmasaṃsarga*) during the occurrence of the compound. To refute the view of those who maintain that [the meaning of] words is [independent], he says: "In compounds and the like" (*vṛttiṣu samāsādikāsu*). Because in these occurrences, a single meaning—which has attained a state of non-distinction from the composite whole, like dust and water—is conveyed simultaneously, there would be a conjunction; thus, the meaning of the compound and the meaning distinct from the individual words would result in the simultaneous presence of two contradictions: difference and conjunction. And this is not tenable, because such a cognition does not occur. || 218 ||
And who would postulate fuel and so forth as having the mere purpose of being a means?
Furthermore, how could there be a meaning for an unused word within a *bahuvrīhi* compound? (219)

If words and their referents were real, then [words] such as *adhi* and others would necessarily function as denoters of grammatical relations (*sādhana*) within a sentence. Yet this is not observed, because they are never seen to be used independently as denoters of grammatical relations; thus he says:

"In cases such as *adhistrī*, it is observed that the whole (*samudāya*) functions as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), but never a single part. Furthermore, when words possess real meanings, the sense of a *bahuvrīhi* compound could not be accounted for; thus he says: "Not being employed," and so forth.

In cases such as *citragu* ("one who has brindled cows"), if the constituent parts possess real referents—where the word *citra* has some quality as its denotation and the word *go* has certain individuals of the bovine genus as its denotation—then that which has an unapplied expressive term (*aprayuktapada*) would be the referent of Devadatta; for whom, then, would that [referent] be the denotation? (219)
There is no determination of an object by means of constituent parts such as "cognition" (prajñā) or "notion" (saṃjñā);
therefore, the aggregate alone is the basis for a specific object.

Furthermore, if the constituent parts were to possess meaning, then in the word *prajñuḥ* (wise man), the meaning of the element *jñu-* would also be perceived separately; yet it is not so perceived. To demonstrate this, he says:

To provide a summary, he says: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). For this reason—due to the presentation of contradictory meanings in compounds; due to the impossibility of words such as *adhi* functioning merely as instruments of proof; due to the lack of coherence in the meaning of the individual parts [in cases like *bahu-vrīhi*]; and due to the non-perception of the meaning of the constituent parts in expressions such as *prajñā-sañjña*—by these four arguments, since words with literal meanings are untenable, one must accept that the compound itself is a single, indivisible, and partless entity, whose nature is *sphoṭa*, and which is the basis for a specific meaning consisting of intuitive flash (*pratibhā*).

Thus it is established that [the word] is "joined" (*yukta*). Furthermore, because of its similarity to a composite (*saṅghāta*), it is the *sphoṭa* itself that is denoted here by the term "composite. For a composite is permeated by its constituent parts (*avayava*), and the *sphoṭa* is likewise permeated by the sounds (*dhvani*); such is the similarity to a composite. || 220 ||
The word "Gargas" is a single term that functions with respect to many individuals; likewise, a collective compound (dvandva) is a designation for a group that denotes many things. (221)

Now, having raised seven objections from the perspective of others against his own position of the indivisible sentence (*akhaṇḍavākya*), he begins to refute them one by one. Thus, [the opponent] raises this doubt: "If no word-meaning exists at all, then in the case of the sentence *devadattayajñadattaviṣṇumitrā bhojyantām* (‘Let Devadatta, Yajñadatta, and Viṣṇumitra be fed’), a single indivisible aggregate as a whole would be enjoined by means of the copulative compound (*dvandva*). Consequently, since the distinction between word-meanings is not admitted and there is only oneness, the use of the plural number would be untenable. Anticipating this, he says the following to provide a rebuttal:

Just as in the case of "the many descendants of Garga" (*gargāḥ*), where after the formation of a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one), the word *garga* itself—having its internal divisions set aside—denotes a plurality because it functions toward multiple referents and thus ends in the plural; in exactly the same way, a collective known as a *dvandva*, although its internal distinctions are set aside, expresses plurality through the majesty of the word's own power. Therefore, even though the plural number is present, there is no existence of a separate word-meaning apart from the meaning of the sentence. 221.
Just as eating and other such actions reside individually in each part [of a body],
so too an action is distributed individually when it is expressed by a copulative compound (dvandva).

Now, regarding the verse beginning with "atha dhavakhadirapalāśāḥ sicyantām" (Then let the Dhava, Khadira, and Palāśa trees be watered), one might raise the objection that the meaning of the sentence is untenable because the word-meanings cannot exist apart from the sentence-meaning; because it is impossible for the sentence to remain incomplete with respect to each individual tree; and because the act of watering cannot occur simultaneously for the entire collection. Anticipating this doubt, the author speaks as follows to provide a justification:

Just as in the case of the expression "Let them be fed by Brahmā," where the act of eating resides in each individual word-meaning even without the complete sentence-meaning, so too in a *dvandva* compound, although the meaning is characterized as a collective whole, it is distributed to each member; thus, there is no fault whatsoever.

This is what is meant: just as in the case of the expression "the Brahmins should be fed," although the understanding refers to the group as a whole, the act of eating is completed for each individual by mentally postulating its constituent parts through the process of analytical abstraction (*apoddhāra*); in exactly the same way, it should be understood that when a whole is understood from a *dvandva* compound, the completion of the sentence occurs for each individual member by resorting to a division mentally constructed by the intellect. || 222 ||
And as for the dependence of the referent of a dvandva compound upon the word *tat*, that too is merely the application of a pronoun to an object whose form has been excluded [from others]. (223)
Anticipating further objections and seeking to resolve them, he says:

"Since a word-meaning situated between two *dvandva* members cannot exist apart from the sentence-meaning, its reference by means of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) is not tenable—just as in the rule ‘*janapadatadavadhyośca*’. For here, it is desired that the suffix follows from the word ‘*jana-pada*’ and from that very same word which is referred to by the pronoun ‘*tat*’ and serves as the limit (*avadhi*). But if the word-meaning does not exist apart from the sentence-meaning, how can there be a requirement for a non-existent thing by means of a pronoun? Having thus restated the opponent’s position, he provides the resolution with the words beginning “*sāpi*” and so forth.

No pronoun whatsoever exists here. Therefore, how could there be a reference to the referent of a compound (*dvandva*) therein? Since the sentence-meaning here consists solely of a qualified [object] whose nature is merely exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), and since it is connected through mere intuition (*pratibhā*), only the formal similarity of the pronoun appears; however, no actual cognition of that referent is apprehended here. As he will say: "But the cognition that arises within the interval regarding the word-referents is merely a means for comprehension, because its sequence cannot be determined. (223)
Just as in the cutting of a khadira tree there is a sequential process of cutting through its parts,
so too is the perception of sequence observed in the parts of a dual object.

Now, one might object: if, in the absence of individual objects, the sentence-meaning in "The dhava, khadira, and palāśa trees are to be cut" is intended to be simultaneous and undifferentiated, then—since the performance must correspond exactly to the meaning understood from the words—it would follow that the act of cutting occurs all at once; yet it is not possible to perform it in this manner. To this, he says:

Even in cases where you maintain a distinction between the meaning of a word (*padārtha*) and the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*), such as in the example "Let the *khadira* tree be cut," even there it is not possible to perform [the action] simultaneously. For one first cuts the bark of the *khadira*, then its woody part, and after that its pith; thus, the act of cutting results in a process that occurs only in a sequence.

In the same way, regarding a copulative compound (*dvandva*), the perception, determination, and—what amounts to—the performance of that word-meaning which is conceptually constructed through the process of analytical abstraction (*apoddhāra-buddhi*) occurs only in a sequential manner. || 224 ||
Just as those who have departed from one part of the Saṅgha are considered followers of the Saṅgha,
so too is this the sequence regarding the individual members of a compound when specific actions are intended.

Now, regarding the sentence "Let the *dhava*, *khadira*, and *palāśa* trees on this mountain be cut down," the meaning of the sentence is determined to be the cutting of the *dhava*, *khadira*, and *palāśa* trees; yet, when even a single part has been cut, people say, "What was commanded has been done. Anticipating the objection as to how this is tenable if the sentence-meaning is partless (*anaṃśa*), he says:

Just as in the expression "let the Brahmins be fed," the act of eating—though it applies to the entire group—is initiated and proceeds with respect to its individual members, such that one says "the Brahmins have eaten"; so too, it should be understood that even when an operation is initiated with respect to a member contained within a collective denoted by a *dvandva* compound, it does not result in the abandonment of the word's meaning. || 225 ||
While explaining the function [of words] for the unwise by means of sentences, the author has demonstrated in his commentary that primacy belongs to the distinction between word-meanings. (226)

If words and word-meanings were [independently] existent, then the designation of meanings for compounds—such as "the *avyayībhāva* is predominant in the meaning of the first member" and "the *tatpuruṣa* is predominant in the meaning of the final member"—would be untenable. Anticipating this objection, he speaks in order to resolve it: "By teaching the formation (*vṛtti*) characterized by compounds as being preceded by the sentence to those who are ignorant, the Teacher has demonstrated the predominance of the word-meanings within compounds according to their specific types. Regarding the phrase "preceded by the sentence": the meaning is that, on the view that words are merely explained (*anvākhyāna*) for the sake of grammatical operation, the word actually exists only as a sentence within the formation; thus it is so stated.

This is what is meant: for the sake of awakening the ignorant, the scripture has merely demonstrated the ritual action; however, by that much, the existence of words and word-meanings is not admitted. || 226 ||

In a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*), because the referent is non-different [from its absence], the predominance [of the negative particle] is variously postulated in the Bhāṣya; however, the faults reside in the process of derivation. (227)

Regarding the compound *abrāhmaṇa* and others, even though the predominance of the meaning of the first member (*pūrvapada*) has been variously debated in the Bhāṣya, one should understand that this too is merely a demonstration of the grammatical system (*śāstraprakriyā*) for the sake of instructing the unlearned. He says:

"But in ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), there is only one [meaning]. In that case, since the form of the denotable object (*abhidheya*) exists as something well-known to all people, no application of the distinction between the meanings of the prior and subsequent members is tenable. And this will be demonstrated:
"The worldly meaning does not differ according to the different functions of the technical treatises (*śāstra-vṛtti*)."
"In a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*), three positions have been examined therein. (227)
And for one who desires the abandonment of all meanings in the alternative view of *jahatsvārtha*, the abandonment of the entire referent of the *bahuvrīhi* compound is demonstrated. (228)

Now, [the author] says this in order to provide a justification, having raised the objection: "If word-meanings do not exist, then the alternative of 'abandoning one's own meaning' (*jahatsvārtha*) in the case of compound functions is indeed untenable; but if word-meanings do exist, where is this [alternative] being asserted? atha padārthāsambhave vṛttiṣu jahatsvārthavikalpo nopapadyate kila padārthasambhave kutraitaducyata ityāśaṅ‌kya samarthayitumāha— Now, [the author] says this in order to provide a justification, having raised the objection: "If word-meanings do not exist, then the alternative of 'abandoning one's own meaning' (*jahatsvārtha*) in the case of compound functions is indeed untenable; but if word-meanings do exist, where is this [alternative] being asserted?"

Precisely because this is so, for the purpose of demonstrating that very point, the Teacher—desiring the abandonment of all meanings under the view that a word abandons its own meaning (*jahatsvārthapakṣa*)—demonstrated the abandonment of the referent of every constituent member within a *bahuvrīhi* compound. For in that case, a distinct collective meaning alone appears, apart from the individual word-meanings; therefore, one must by no means accept any conventional usage of word-meanings as being ultimately real.

Thus, the five objections—the use of the dual number for a copulative compound (*dvandva*), the completion of the sentence with each individual member, the reference by means of a pronoun (*sarvanāma*), the sequential performance [of the acts], and the misconception that the performance of a single part constitutes the performance of the whole—have been refuted by the proponent of the indivisible (*akhaṇḍavādin*) through recourse to the method of analytical extraction (*apoddhāra*). Furthermore, in the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound under the view that it abandons its own meaning (*jahatsvārthapakṣa*), it is observed that the intended meaning is indeed the indivisible sentence itself, by virtue of the abandonment of all [individual] meanings. || 228 ||
In certain instances in the treatise, the meaning of the root is expressed by the suffix, and when the root has ceased [to function], the meaning of the suffix is expressed by verbal roots. 229.

Now, in order to demonstrate that this entire conventional usage of words and their meanings is purely conceptual and unreal, relying merely upon the various grammatical systems of the treatises, he says:

"Thus, the denotation of a word may depend on its stem-portion, yet even when the stem is non-existent, the suffix alone expresses it—as in *iyān* and similar forms. Likewise, the meaning of the suffix may be expressed by the stem alone even when the suffix has ceased to exist—as in *ahan*. (229)

The single meaning that two distinct suffixes express together is sometimes expressed by the verbal root alone, as in "pacanti" (they cook), and sometimes without those two, as in certain cases. (230)
Furthermore, in order to demonstrate the lack of fixed rule, he says:

"In such cases as *pacanti* ('they cook'), two distinct suffixes—the *śap* and the *tiṅ*—express the meaning of the agent (*kartṛ*) which is characterized by capacity; yet even a single one expresses that very same [meaning] in cases such as *atti* ('he eats') and *juhoti* ('he offers'). In some instances, the verbal root alone expresses that meaning even without those two, as in *ahan vṛtram indraḥ* ('Indra slew Vṛtra'), and so forth. Does this [argument] truly ascend to the heights of valid proof regarding the reality of word-meanings? This is merely something trivial. (230)

And those meanings of suffixes which serve as the basis in the traditional grammatical treatises (*anvākhyāna-smṛti*), have been cited in other traditions (*smṛty-antara*) as the meanings of the stems (*prakṛty-artha*). (231)
To demonstrate that even the grammatical procedures (*prakriyā*) of the treatises are unreal, he says:

"In one traditional grammar (*śabdānuśāsana-smṛti*), those meanings assigned to suffixes (*pratyaya-artha*) which serve as the basis for the application of suffixes are cited in another tradition as the meanings of the base (*prakṛti-artha*) serving as the basis; thus, there is no fixed certainty whatsoever regarding words and their meanings. (231)

It is taught in the treatise as being that which causes vomiting [of doubt] through well-known [conventional usage], because they consider the systematic presentation of the meaning of the treatise to be for the sake of practical discourse. (232)

Furthermore, because it is well known that those whose minds have been refined by the study of the scriptures employ even the division of words within scriptural discourse; for instance, although "udvamati" should be used, they use "udvami" for the sake of brevity. Similarly, although "karoṣi" or "karomi" should be used, they use only a single part of it, such as "karī," and so forth. To state this, he says:

[Objection: "Why are the systematic arrangements (*prakriyā*) of the treatises (*śāstra*), which are real entities, not relied upon? To this he says: "The meaning of the treatise... etc. The systematic arrangements of the meaning of the treatises are solely for the purpose of instructing the ignorant. Therefore, the treatises are not capable of expressing ultimate reality (*tattva*). || 232 ||
In the scriptures, it is described in various ways through different systems of analysis;
yet, free from traditional dogma and conceptual construction, the Vidyā manifests by itself.

Now, [the author] says that ignorance itself is described through various systematic arrangements (*prakriyā*) as being unreal: "If this is so, why do those who act with foresight rely on the systematic arrangements of the scriptures which demonstrate ignorance? To this he replies: "Without scripture" (*anāgama*). For, by means of the destruction of ignorance, at a later time, the systematic arrangement of the scriptures—which is free from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) regarding scripture and devoid of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*)—arises, that is, becomes manifest as knowledge (*vidyā*). What is meant is this: ignorance itself is the means to knowledge. (233)
Just as a fruit that is unattached to its causes is beyond description, so too is knowledge indescribable; it is perceived only through the scriptures. (234)
Now, one might ask: how can ignorance (*avidyā*), which is of a nature entirely distinct from knowledge (*vidyā*), serve as the means (*upāya*) to that very knowledge? To this he says:

indeed, it is not possible for an effect to be described by any definable form as being connected to its causes. For in this case, the fruit characterized as the effect arises in a wondrous manner—devoid of any designation and even lacking the conjunction of causes—from those causal factors that serve as the instruments.

In the same way, when ignorance dissolves, it cannot be said that knowledge arises from itself as something produced by the scriptures; rather, because it is cultivated through the study of the scriptures at no great distance [of time], the scriptures appear to be the means for knowledge. However, one must understand that in reality, this [knowledge] shines forth through internal discernment alone. || 234 ||
For speech strives to convey its meaning according to habitual practice;
and like an innate nature, this false [convention] has been established from beginningless time. (235)

It has been stated that "in the treatises, it is precisely ignorance (avidyā) that is described through various systematic elaborations (prakriyābheda). Consequently, one seeks the comprehension of meaning from words and sounds in the world by not overstepping the study of the treatises; thus he says:
"And that beginningless practice, though false, appears as if it were innate. He says: "It is innate" (svābhāva). || 235 ||
The unwise person imagines the atom to have parts, and likewise imagines the whole to be joined with further parts. (236)
To demonstrate that this is indeed false, he says:

Having inferred the attainment of a minimum limit through the application of degrees of diminution, the atom (paramāṇu) is established; yet one imagines that even that [atom] possesses further parts. Thus, there is no reality whatsoever in the cognitions of men. One also imagines the possessor of parts (the whole) as being joined with further constituent parts. (236)
Because of the perception of jars and other such things, the world is determined to be finite;
and because of the production of entities, the eternal Brahman must possess a beginning. (237)

Likewise, having observed that objects such as jars possess a limited measure, this world—which consists of the manifold expansion of the universe—is determined to exist in a state of limitation; thus he says: || 237 ||
The skillful means of those in training are for the purpose of leading the ignorant away from falsehood; by abiding in the path of untruth, one subsequently strives for the truth. (238)

Because of the undertaking and the arising of entities, this world is designated as "eternal" and as "having Brahmā as its beginning. Therefore, the means—the scriptures—should be understood as mere deceptions and delusions for the ignorant who desire to know; for by abiding in that which is merely the unreal process of the scriptures, one casts off ignorance and strives for, that is to say, attains, the truth, which is Brahman whose nature is knowledge. || 238 ||
Having understood a meaning in one way by first grasping the words, one then understands that very same meaning in another way within the sentence. (239)

Now, in order to demonstrate once again the refutation of words and word-meanings, he says: "If word-meanings were real entities, then at the time of the comprehension of word-meanings, everything would be understood in one way; however, at the time of the comprehension of the sentence-meaning, the fact that understanding is observed to be entirely different through the abandonment of those [word-meanings] would be inexplicable. This he will clarify later with the verse beginning "praise and blame" (stutinindā). 239.
Even many objects that have been apprehended cease when a negation is made regarding them; therefore, one should not rely upon them in that context. (240)

And in order to demonstrate that just as the meaning of a word is first understood preceded by the apprehension of the word, later, at the occasion of understanding the meaning of the sentence, another entirely different meaning arises through the abandonment of that [word] meaning, he says:

In this case, regarding the statement "Today, *dhava*, *khadira*, and *palāśa* trees are not to be cut," at the time of the manifestation of the word-meanings (*padārtha*), a different object characterized by the cutting of the *dhava* and other trees is first apprehended, and subsequently, that is set aside by means of the negation. However, this is not tenable; for if what has been apprehended were abandoned, it would follow that the relationship between the word and its meaning is non-eternal (*anityatva*). Therefore, it is more appropriate not to rely upon them in that context, as he says: "Therefore, one should not rely upon them there. (240)

And the statement "there is no tree" is characterized by the absence of a qualified entity; the connection with the object does not persist in the cognition because of the exclusion [of the tree]. (241)
Therefore, it is logical to accept that here only the sentence and its meaning possess reality; thus he says:

"This very sentence, being indivisible, is characterized as the absence of a qualifier"—it is intended to be the indicator (*pratyāyaka*) of the sentence-meaning, which consists in the cognition of the absence of a tree. If, however, a distinct word-meaning were accepted here, then once the word-meaning characterized as a "tree" is established, its connection with the negative particle (*nañ*) would not be possible; for once that [meaning] has acquired its own existence from its own causes, the cessation of what has already arisen cannot be effected.

Furthermore, if the connection with the negative particle (*nañ*) were only with that which is non-existent, then since it would have already ceased due to its very non-existence, the negative particle would be redundant. As it is said:
"A negation does not apply to existing things, nor does it exist for non-existing things;
by this logic, the meaning of the negative particle has perished in the world."
Therefore, since the object ceases by its own nature, there exists no relationship between that [object] and the expressive word for its cessation. || 241 ||
Furthermore, if it is determined that [the object] exists during the cognition of its cessation, how could that cognition—which is not denotable by words—remain present? (242)

Now, it might be argued that the cognition of "existence" directed toward an object as a distinct entity is determined, and that this is what is negated by the negative particle (*nañ*). To this he says: "And thus, even in the case of cognition, a connection with the negative particle is not tenable. He explains: "It is not denotable by words. The meaning denoted by a word is negated by the negative particle, but cognition is not denotable by words. For it is the external object that is expressed by a word; cognition, however, has the object as its support and does not deserve to be denotable by words. Therefore, how could it be negated by the negative particle? (242)

Now, if that cognition which has arisen is rendered false by the negative particle, how can there be an understanding of non-existence when the operation of the negative particle is directed toward this [cognition]? (243)

Now, if it is argued that the cognition does not cease, but rather its falsity is communicated by the negative particle (*nañ*), he says—[in order to refute this as well]—"By the negative particle" (*naña*). If one accepts that the operation of the negative particle consists in the negation of the cognition of such a nature [as "tree"], then indeed there would be no comprehension of the absence of the tree; for this is possible only when the meaning expressed by *nañ* in a *paryudāsa* (exclusion) is the prescription of a similar apprehension. But in the case of a *prasajyapratiṣedha* (absolute negation), this is not possible, because in that case the sentence-meaning is simply the absence of the tree. || 243 ||
And if it were to function without a substratum, the negative particle would have to function prior [to its connection with the noun];
or else, that very [noun] must be its substratum, and the scriptural mention [of the noun] would serve the purpose of restriction. (244)

Now, if it is argued that even while being negated, its substratum (*ādhāra*) is to be understood as the expressed object, to this he replies: "If it were said that the negative particle (*nañ*) functions entirely without regard for a substratum, then its application would have to occur prior [to the mention of the object]; for in every case where something is intended to be prohibited, people would simply say 'no' (*na*). Then, if it is argued that the mention of a substratum is for the sake of restricting the scope (*viṣayaniyamārtha*), so as to demonstrate that the negation applies to the tree—meaning "it is not a tree"—and not to a jar or other things, to this he says: "Now, the substratum... Here too, he states a refutation: "For the sake of restriction..."

Since the negation of that object has already been accomplished by the negative particle itself, this [subsequent mention] must serve either to restrict the application of that specific scriptural injunction.
Or [the words] may serve to indicate a restriction, or they may be a restatement (anuvāda);
in that case, only some word would be meaningful, while the remaining ones would be meaningless. (245)
With the intention that some particles (*nipāta*) are merely indicative (*dyotaka*), he says:

"Alternatively," meaning that repetition for the sake of clarity would be a restatement (*anuvāda*). He says "restatement" because, in every respect, there would otherwise be total meaninglessness of the word-meanings. He says "some" because, in cases such as "not a Brāhmaṇa" (*na brāhmaṇaḥ*), others maintain that only the negative particle (*nañ*) possesses meaning, which would render the other words meaningless; and this is not tenable.

Therefore, from the [sentence] "there is no tree," the sentence-meaning is itself an indivisible entity in the form of a qualified absence; it is not, however, established in reality as some distinct, truly existent word-meaning. || 245 ||

Furthermore, when a contradiction has been established by means of examples such as "bringing forth" (udāhārya) and so on, one understands the meaning of the sentence differently once the sentence is completed. (246)
Now, in order to explain the phrase "having understood the meaning otherwise," he says:

"By means of words such as *udahāri* (water-carrier), at the moment when there is the appearance of mutually contradictory word-meanings, one perceives a connection. For example, in the case of *udahāri*: 'Sister! You who carry an ox on your head, did you see an eastern water-jar running toward you?'—here, at the subsequent time of understanding the sentence-meaning, the comprehension of the meaning is entirely different [from the individual word-meanings]; thus, no [consistent] word-meaning is established. (246)
In sentences where praise or censure predominates, the meaning is not such as it is imagined to be through the separate division of the words. (247)
To demonstrate this very point in another way, he says:
there is a certain sentence where praise is predominant, yet the meaning of the words involves censure—“The mark on the moon, the base of the neck of Murāri, the conqueror of Smara... [and so forth].
O ornament of the earth’s circle! Even today, the temples of the proud Nāgas, which bear the soot-like ink of their rutting pride, appear as if smeared with blackness;
tell me, what has been whitened by your glories?

In this case, at the moment of the manifestation of the literal meaning (*padārtha*), censure is understood: "O King, you carry a truly vain and haughty neck; for indeed, your fame does not pervade everything. If it were so, why would objects such as the moon, which are already well-known, still appear dark? For if its fame were pervasive due to its whiteness, those objects pervaded by it would surely become white. Here, the literal meaning is censure, while the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is praise.

And so, O King, the entire world has been whitened by your fame; yet, solely because of the difficulty of abandoning one's innate nature, there remain only four things in the three worlds that possess the quality of blackness—beyond these, everything else is pervaded by your glory. This is the meaning of the sentence: you are one whose majesty is celebrated everywhere throughout the three realms. An example of praise as the underlying purpose within a context dominated by censure (*nindā-pradhāne stutiḥ pādarthaḥ*) is as follows: "O you who have effortlessly surpassed the Bodhisattvas, what is the use of elaborate words?
There is no other like you, who has taken a vow to bestow benefit upon others."

"O Ocean! You kindly provide assistance to the desert, which has incurred a heavy burden of infamy due to its failure in providing aid to thirsty travelers. Here, from these words, praise is understood through the excellence of your ocean's accomplishment of the welfare of others—which even surpasses the conduct of a Bodhisattva—whereas the sentence-meaning (vākyārtha) regards the ocean as a fit object for unsurpassed censure. Therefore, if the words and their literal meanings are taken as real, how can this [contradiction] be reconciled?
Now, the meaning that remains uncombined is established within the individual words; it serves as the means for the comprehension of the single sentence-meaning. (248)
Now, he speaks in order to raise the objection of the proponents of the word (padavādin):

"The meaning residing in individual words remains entirely unconnected [with one another], yet it stands as the means for conveying the single sentence-meaning characterized by their synthesis; for the determination of the sentence-meaning is established as being preceded by the meanings of the words. (248)

That which was previously unconnected in its constituent parts and is subsequently accumulated step by step, they do not consider to be particularly superior, because it is like a string of pearls that has been broken and re-knotted.
To refute this, he says:

"That sentence-meaning which, initially, exists as entirely unconnected within the words, and is subsequently built up through connection, is more distinguished; it is indeed firmly distinguished. Why? Because it is like something that was first severed and then strung together. Thus, a comprehension of the sentence-meaning preceded by unconnected word-meanings is not tenable. Therefore, since the meaning is understood from both the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) even when one or the other is removed, and since the meaning is cognized from both sides...

Because a comprehension of meaning sometimes arises from a single cause alone; because in the grammatical treatises the meanings of roots and suffixes are stated as being intermingled; because the meaning of a sentence is distinct from the comprehension of word-meanings; because the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) would be untenable; and because it would follow that everything previously mentioned must be abandoned—by these six arguments, as well as by the four previously stated arguments such as the demonstration of contradictory meanings in compound formations (*vṛtti*), the existence of real word-meanings is untenable.
