And this is likewise the case in the theory of the indivisible sentence (*akhaṇḍapakṣa*).

Because the five objections beginning with "substitution" (*pratinidhi*) and likewise the seven objections based on "duality" (*dvandva*) have been refuted, it is established that the sentence is indeed faultless and indivisible, consisting of *sphoṭa*, and that the meaning of the sentence is nothing other than *pratibhā*. || 249 ||

Some investigators say that a single word has multiple meanings; others maintain that for a single word, its capacity to signify all things is differentiated by the difference in the causes [of usage]. (250)
Now, since the meaning of the word has also been accepted by means of its extraction (apoddhāra), he says [the following] in order to introduce an investigation into the primary and secondary senses:

In this context, there are two positions regarding consciousness (*citi*): the view that there is a single word (*eka-śabda-darśana*) and the view that there are multiple words (*aneka-śabda-darśana*). Within those, there are four positions: the reality of both the word and its referent (*padārtha*) according to the view of the *Padavādins*, and their unreality according to the view of the Grammarians (*Vaiyākaraṇas*). Although he has already refuted these positions, the author of the commentary (*ṭīkākāra*) indeed accepts them for the sake of conventional discourse (*vyavahāra*). For this system of grammar is intended for all audiences, and since he remains within it, he once again accepts the word and its referent here.

In that regard, within the view of the single word (*ekaśabdadarśana*), there is the metaphorical application of the word (*śabdopacāra*) based on the causes of its being well-known or not well-known. In that very same context, there is also the metaphorical application of the meaning (*arthopacāra*) in two ways: as having the word itself as its meaning and as having an external object as its meaning. Thus, there are three positions. The same applies elsewhere. It should be understood that by means of these three positions, all four positions are expressed, resulting in twelve [sub-positions].

In this regard, by relying on the observation that the word "one" (eka) is used [in various senses], he undertakes an investigation into the primary and secondary meanings with the words "They say it is one," and so forth: the single word *go* is the denoter for all these meanings. If this is so, why does it not manifest all meanings simultaneously? He says: "Because of the difference in causes" (*nimittabheda*), and so forth. The difference in causes will be explained later; therefore, its capacity to denote all meanings is differentiated. || 250 ||
Having transcended simultaneity, it abides in succession, either through meaning and context, or through connection, or by means of another word. (251)
And then, he asks "What follows from this? and says:

the meaning is that it does not simultaneously manifest all objects due to the influence of causal conditions (*nimitta*). He states the distinction between these conditions: "by means of the object and the context" (verse 251).
Just as a physical body possessing a dewlap and other such features is denoted by the word "cow," so too that very same word "cow" is established as applying even to a Bāhīka. (252)
He provides an example of the statement that "having transcended simultaneity, [the word] settles upon successive [meanings]"—namely:
"But for that very word, which possesses all powers and manifold properties, its secondary (gauṇa) and primary (mukhya) status are described according to the difference in conventional usage. (253)

If this is so, from where does the distinction between the primary (mukhya) and the secondary (gauṇa) arise? He says: it is explained by the statement, "And the state of being Śakti is present in everything, which possesses manifold attributes. Due to a difference in common usage—that is, a specific difference in usage—the word "cow" (go-śabda) has an intensified common usage with respect to the bovine species, whereas its usage is only slight with respect to a Bāhīka (a person from the Punjab). Therefore, the status of being primary or secondary is caused by common usage and lack of common usage. || 253 ||
A single mantra, likewise, exists with its powers differentiated according to the internal self, the divine, and the sacrificial ritual; it is established for all purposes without confusion.

In the same way, Ekadarśana himself demonstrates the process: "And thus, a single mantra alone is employed for oneself at the time of recitation (japa), as well as for the gods at the time of sacrifice (kratu) during the performance of worship; because its powers are distinct, it attains a fixed status through non-confusion by virtue of having specific, determined purposes. (254)
Some maintain that the connection with "cowness" (gotva) is attributed to the Bāhīka person due to a [perceptual] cause;
however, it is merely the object that is inverted, while the word remains established in its own primary meaning. (255)

Thus, the metaphorical application of words has been demonstrated as being based on both established and non-established conventions. Fearing that this metaphorical application of words might imply the non-eternality of the relationship between word and meaning, he speaks by resorting to the metaphorical application of meanings:

The meaning of a word is twofold: its own form (*svarūpa*) and the external object (*bāhya*). In that regard, due to a cause such as dullness (*jāḍya*), the property of being a cow (*gotva*) is superimposed upon a Bāhīka; however, since the word denotes only the property of being a cow, there is a metaphorical application (*upacāra*) of the external object. But this is the distinction: in the case of "cow," the property of being a cow is primary (*mukhya*); whereas in the case of "the Bāhīka is a cow," that very same property is the denoted object only in a metaphorical sense. || 255 ||
In the same way, the intrinsic nature of words is attached to all objects;
while the mere object may be inverted, the stability of the intrinsic nature remains firm. (256)

Now he explains the metaphorical application of the word’s own form (*svarūpopacāra*): The very form of words is the denotable meaning (*vācya*) in all cases; that [form] is sometimes applied to one belonging to the class of cows (*gojātīya*), and sometimes to a *vāhīka*. Thus, there is no non-eternality (*anityatva*) in the relationship between word and meaning. However, the distinction between the primary (*mukhya*) and the secondary (*gauṇa*) should be understood as being caused by conventional renown (*prasiddhi*) and lack thereof. || 256 ||

Those who follow the path of discerning distinctions declare that there is identity between the primary and secondary meanings of words because they share the same essential nature, even though there is absolute difference between them. (257)
Now, relying on the view that there are multiple words, he says:

those who follow the path of differentiation and maintain the doctrine of the distinction between words assert that there is indeed a difference between two instances of the word *go* (cow) when they denote a secondary (*gauṇa*) and a primary (*mukhya*) meaning. For they consider that a distinction in words follows from a distinction in meanings; since the relationship between a word and its meaning here is established as one characterized by superimposition (*adhyāsa*). The sense is this: if [the word] is superimposed upon one [meaning], having attained non-difference with that very [meaning], how could it undergo superimposition upon another? Thus, in this way, the distinction between words alone is logically established.

And this twofold view, characterized by difference and non-difference, was demonstrated by the author of the Bhāṣya during the course of his commentary on the Vārttika. For it is stated therein: "In that regard, when there is a reference to recurrence (anuvṛtti), there is no inclusion of homogeneous sounds (savarṇa) because [the vowel] is not *aṇ*."

The answer to this is: "It is established because the sound *a* is one. If that is so, then objections such as the confusion of grammatical markers (*anubandha-saṅkara*) and the impossibility [of distinguishing] between monophthongs (*ekāc*) and polyphthongs (*anekāc*) would arise; however, these have already been refuted in that very context. Furthermore, it is established by the fact that various genders are employed for its scope (*viṣaya*), and by the enumeration of repetitions (*āvṛtti-saṃkhyāna*) in the cases of the mention of monophthongs and polyphthongs. In this way, the view that the word "one" (*eka*) [expresses a universal] is established.

Now, relying on the view of multiple [entities], it is stated in that very same work: "But there is a change of state (ānyabhāvya) because of the intervention of the word 'time' and because of the simultaneous perception of spatial distinctness. In this way, difference and non-difference are established regarding words. It should be understood that the commentator provides a presentation of two independent positions precisely for the purpose of explaining that. || 257 ||
And in this manner, it is attached to the repetition between the *sāmidhenī* verses;
and the mantras, through their application (*viniyoga*), attain distinction, just like the *ūha*.
Now, in order to apply this very demonstration of the distinction between words (*śabdabheda*) even to Vedic expressions, he says:

"There are thirteen or eleven *ṛc*-verses for the purpose of kindling the fire, called *sāmidhenīs*. Among them, one recites the first three times and the last three times; thus, by repetition, it is established that there are seventeen or fifteen *sāmidhenīs*. In this regard, it should be understood that each repeated *sāmidhenī* is a distinct entity with a different nature (*vibhinnasvarūpa*), and not that the same single verse is merely repeated—so say the proponents of the distinction between words."

And so, in order to demonstrate that they also speak of a distinction among mantras, he says: "And the mantras. Even though mantras are characterized by their application (*viniyoga*), their utility, and so forth, they must be understood as being indeed distinct. As it has been said: from the mantra "O divine waters, you are pure," a different explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) for the purpose of glorification is inferred, such as "O god, the clarified butter (*ājya*) is pure," and so on. Thus, there is a difference between the mantras used in *ūha* (modification), and likewise, there is precisely a difference between those mantras that have been specifically applied (*viniyukta*). || 258 ||

Those very same [mantras] are recited in other traditional scriptures (āmnāya), yet some are indeed read there as being meaningless; or rather, another [explanation], namely that they are supplementary (śeṣa), is understood. || 259 ||
Raising the doubt as to whether those [other mantras] possess the status of being Veda if they are distinct from the Vedic corpus, he states that their very nature as Veda must be understood:

"All mantras indeed possess the status of being Veda; however, only certain mantras are recited within the Veda. He says, "of those that are purposeless," meaning that not all of them have the status of Veda merely by virtue of this fact; otherwise, everything recited in the Veda would be entirely useless. Mantras are recited in the Veda as mere indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*) for those who lack the qualification [to perform specific rites]; therefore, at the time of application (*viniyoga*), it should be understood that the status of Veda belongs to other [mantras] which are actually perceived through them. (259)
Others describe the meaning as being the nature of the word itself, while the recitation is the text;
there is an absolute difference between all of them, yet those things which possess that [recitation] appear as such because of their connection with it. (260)

Thus, since there is a difference in meaning, there is indeed a difference in the words; it has been demonstrated that the recitation of the mantras is for the purpose of indication (*upalakṣaṇa*). Now, some [opponents] among the Vaidikas claim that the recitation of all [mantras] is for the sake of their own form (*svarūpa*) alone; to this he says:

And therefore, he says "absolutely" (*atyanta*) to show that for all [words], there is indeed a distinction from those possessing their own essential nature (*svarūpa*). Now, one might object: "It is appropriate that only those words being recited possess their own essential nature, since they have that as their meaning; but how can those others, which are employed in sacrifices and so forth, possess an essential nature at all? To this he replies: "Because of the connection with that" (*tatsambandhāt*). Even in those cases, because the essential nature itself exists as the ground for the application of the word (*pravṛttinimitta*), one should understand that they indeed possess it. (260)
One *sāvitrī* of conditioned formations is employed in ritual actions, another in the continuous recitation of prayers; yet it is perceived as being one and the same.

Therefore, because of the distinction in the application of mantras for purposes such as consecration (*saṃskāra*) and so forth, there is the cognition of them as non-different—either because they are indicated by their recitation or because their purpose is their own essential form (*svarūpa*). Alternatively, one must consider that these [mantras] are indeed different. To conclude this, he says:

However, one must understand that the conventional usage of identity (*ekatvavyavahāra*) in that case arises from similarity (*sārūpyāt*). Thus, when multiple words are observed, since there is a difference in meaning, there is a difference in the words: the secondary meaning (*gauṇa*) is one thing, and the primary meaning (*mukhya*) is quite another. Nevertheless, because they are not different due to their similarity, and because the primary meaning is well-established, the word denoting it is merely used figuratively (*upacaryate*). In that instance, only a figurative application of the word can be postulated; however, as in the case of observing a single word, a figurative application of the meaning is not resorted to, because the relationship between the word and its meaning would otherwise be non-eternal.
For this very reason, the commentator, possessing [this] intention, explained there both the metaphorical application of the word and the metaphorical application of the object. || 261 ||
The operation of words upon the nature of their referents is held to proceed from their own form;
the operation of the sentence-form upon the sentence-meaning proceeds independently of anything else. (262)

In the statement "But [the application of words] to those things possessing that [universal] is due to their connection with it," the relationship with the essential nature as the ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) has been established. To clarify that this alone is to be understood as the ground for application for all words, he says:

"In the nature of the object" means, in short, in the objective entity itself. In that regard, it should be understood that the application [of words] for all [of them] arises solely from their own nature as the cause. Not only is the own-nature alone the cause of application for words everywhere, but even for a word in the form of a sentence when it functions toward the meaning of a sentence, its operation should be understood as being by its own nature alone, independent of anything else; thus, in order to establish this as a corollary, he says: "of the sentence-form. (262)

For those by whom the multiplicity of meanings in a single word is understood, the distinction between the primary and the secondary is established based on whether that meaning results in success or failure. (263)

Now, concluding that the distinction between the primary (mukhya) and the secondary (gauṇa) exists within the perspective of the single word (ekaśabdadarśana), he says: "In that regard, the distinction between the primary and the secondary is to be understood by way of success and failure, or by way of being well-known and not being well-known. By this, it is stated that even within the perspective of the single word, although there is non-difference due to similarity, the distinction between the primary and the secondary nevertheless occurs precisely through being well-known and not being well-known. || 263 ||
Others know that [word] which conveys a meaning by depending on context and purpose, or which is joined with other words, to be secondary (gauṇa). (264)
Then, in order to show another cause for the distinction between the secondary (gauṇa) and the primary (mukhya) in both cases, he says:
"It is stated that meaning, context, and proximity to other words bring about the state of being secondary or primary in both instances. (264)
When a word is uttered in its pure form, that meaning which is understood as its well-known sense should be known as the primary one; it is based solely on the [phonetic] form itself. (265)
In order to corroborate this very point by showing the verse stated by the author of the *Saṃgraha*, he says:
"This is the definition of the word whose primary meaning is [the object] itself. (265)
But that which is employed as if through effort by means of another's application, they consider that to be unestablished, being intent upon a figurative meaning. (266)
He also states the nature of words with secondary meanings:
"as by effort, etc. This means: by virtue of the meaning, context, and so forth. || 266 ||

When one who is engaged in his own primary purpose relies upon another for that purpose, the latter is considered the primary cause (nimitta) and the former is regarded as the secondary (gauṇa). || 267 ||
Now, he explains the distinction between the primary and the secondary by another method:

when [a word] is applied to a derivative sense (*bāhika*), it relies upon the meaning connected with the word "cow" (*go-śabda*)—which is currently applied to its own primary sense characterized by a dewlap and so forth—as the cause (*nimitta*). In that context, the primary meaning is the cause (*nimitta*), while the secondary meaning is called the "possessor of the cause" (*nimittin*).

This is what is meant: it should be understood that where a word has an unimpeded application (*askhalad-gati*), its meaning is primary (*mukhya*); however, when its application is impeded (*skhalad-gati*), the meaning is secondary (*gauṇa*). Now, one might object: "By this, a metaphorical application of meaning (*arthopacāra*) has been stated, and that rests upon the observation of a single word. In that case, since it would be said that 'one [word] relies upon another's meaning,' a distinction between words (*śabdabheda*) would have to be asserted. This is incorrect; for even here, since a distinction based on the assumed difference in powers (*śakti*) is logically established, this is consistent, and there is no fault whatsoever. || 267 ||
When two words with mutually contradictory meanings, such as *pura* and *arāti*, occur [in a single expression], their specific determination depends upon the context and the intended meaning. (268)

Now, he points out the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) that would result if context (*artha*), topic (*prakaraṇa*), and so forth were the sole causes for distinguishing between the primary (*mukhya*) and secondary (*gauṇa*) meanings: the words *pura* ("before") and *arāt* ("from afar") function, as the case may be, with respect to mutually contradictory meanings characterized by the future and the past, or by distance and proximity. In such cases, the determination of the meaning would depend on context and other factors; consequently, there would also be a distinction between primary and secondary meanings here [in those instances], which is not desired. Since it is accepted that both of these [words] have their primary meaning in both [contexts], one must understand that context, topic, and the like, taken alone, do not determine the status of being primary or secondary. || 268 ||
When the meanings of individual words are conceptually extracted from the meaning of the sentence, how can a connection with another word be possible for that single [extracted] meaning? (269)
Now, relying on the position that [the sentence] is indivisible (*akhaṇḍapakṣa*), he explains the secondary and primary status:

previously, it was stated while accepting the reality of both word and word-meaning, whether in the view of a single word or multiple words; however, in this [view], the word and the word-meaning must be understood as unreal. Therefore, since the sentence alone—being indivisible—is the conveyor of the sentence-meaning, what kind of secondary or primary status could possibly exist in the absence of word and word-meaning? In the case of "The *vāhīka* is a cow" (*gaur vāhīkaḥ*), if one were to accept the existence of word and word-meaning, the figurative nature of the word "cow" would be asserted because the co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is otherwise inexplicable due to its contradiction.

But when, by the indivisible expression "the Bāhīka is a cow" (*gaur bāhīkaḥ*), an indivisible object characterized as a Bāhīka—delimited by properties residing in a cow—is conveyed, then, since words and word-meanings are unreal, how could there be that division into the secondary (*gauṇa*) based on the relation of one such non-existent [meaning] with another such [meaning]?
If this were the case, how could the distinction between the primary (*mukhya*) and the secondary in this view be established?

It is said: the intention is that, by resorting to the method of analytical abstraction (*apoddhāra*), one should postulate a distinction between words and word-meanings, and thereby accept a division into primary and secondary [meanings] based on whether they are well-known or not. || 269 ||

Furthermore, when a single word is observed anywhere as having the function of expressing an action (astikriyā), they say that it is indeed part of a sentence and is not joined with anything else. (270)

One might object: "Is it not the case that an independent word is indeed employed even without another word? Therefore, in such instances, the distinction between word and word-meaning is real. To this he replies:

He will demonstrate that a single word, because its action has been completed, is itself an indivisible sentence. Consequently, it must be understood that it is never joined with anything else. || 270 ||

And when, in response to the question "What is this?", it is said "It is a cow" or "It is a horse," the very act of questioning there involves the previously initiated activity of perception and so forth. (271)
To clarify and establish this very point, he says:

In the question "Who is this?", some action such as "you are seen" is implied (*garbhīkṛta*); that same [action] is also implied in the answer. Therefore, it should be understood that even that [answer] is a single sentence consisting of an accomplished action (*caritakriya*). || 271 ||
Neither the superiority nor the deficiency of phenomena is a determining factor;
for in some cases, people consider even superiority to be a deficiency on account of common usage. (272)

Now, anticipating the objection that some have accepted the very state of deficiency or excess as the cause for the distinction between the secondary (*gauṇa*) and the primary (*mukhya*), he speaks in order to refute it—beginning with "Why? and answering with "Excess also... Since this [state of excess] is relative, it is indeed unstable; therefore, the conventional usage of "secondary" and "primary" cannot be established by means of it. || 272 ||
Others know that as secondary (gauṇa) where a genus-word is employed even in the absence of the genus itself, due to a quality resembling a related thing. (273)
Now he states that similarity is the cause [of secondary usage]:

"The word 'cow' is applied to a *bāhīka*, even without the universal 'cowness,' due to the similarity of qualities residing in its own individual instance; thus, similarity is the cause for the relationship between the primary and the secondary. (273)

In some cases, that which is called "secondary" (gauṇa), such as the word "cow" and so forth, is where people, due to error and the like, perceive the object as if it were something other than its actual nature. (274)
Now, he explains that error (*viparyāsa*) itself serves as the cause:

"In some [views], it is held that the word 'cow' is applied figuratively (*gauṇa*) when it is employed for a *bāhīka*—who is considered to be an 'other than the object' (*arthāntaratā*)—precisely because they perceive him as having the nature of a cow due to error. Error occurs both through misapprehension (*adhyavasāya*) and through superimposition (*adhyāropa*). In the case of 'this is silver,' there is merely a misapprehension resulting from error. But here, one superimposes the qualities belonging to a cow upon the *bāhīka* and apprehends them; thus, this error consists in the superimposed state of being that [cow]."

For this very reason, it was stated "due to error and so forth"; therefore, there is no distinction between the metaphorical and the primary [usage] that is not prompted by the cause of the conceptualization of that [object] as having such a nature. || 274 ||

Just as ploughs, swords, maces, and so forth, being endowed with specific forms and powers, are understood to be restricted as the means for accomplishing various tasks, [so too are the elements]. (275)
Now, in order to demonstrate the alternative position—that the distinction between primary and secondary usage is based on the power of form (*rūpaśakti*)—he says, preceded by an illustration:

"When it is said, 'Bring the sword-bearer' (*khaḍgagam ānaya*), the conversation concerns those who are fully equipped for battle; this is expressed through the majesty of the power of form. The same applies to [the word] *sīra* (plow) and so forth. (275)
Furthermore, the capacities of these [words] do not arise through another function;
rather, their subservience to that purpose is invariably understood from their very form alone. (276)

It cannot be said that these [words] possess their potencies in other actions, such as the cutting of creepers; therefore, their capacity is determined only for a specific action corresponding to their form. Thus he says:
"In the very same way, a word established through its production by means of both form and potency has a fixed purpose; yet, by virtue of its potency, it may be employed elsewhere. (277)
In order to apply this to the present context, he says:

"By birth, that is, by its very nature. As it is said: "The relationship of a word with its meaning is innate (*autpattika*). This is understood to mean that it is indeed co-natal (*sahaja*). Furthermore, because of the existence of multiple powers, it is also employed in other senses. (277)

When its purpose is determined by the mere hearing [of the word], they consider that to be the primary meaning; whereas that which is established through further derivation is considered secondary. (278)

And then, he asks how the relationship between the secondary (*gauṇa*) and the primary (*mukhya*) is to be known here, and says: "The secondary is established here. This means that even though the capacity for denoting that [secondary meaning] exists, because it is not well-known, its status as secondary is determined through effort by means of context and so forth. Thus, there are two positions: first, the mere presence of the object, context, and proximity of other words, accompanied by what is well-known and what is not; and second, the relationship of subordinate and principal (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) through the beginningless accumulation of those factors such as object and context. Furthermore, there are seven positions regarding that which possesses formal power (*rūpaśaktimat*): deficiency, excess, similarity, reversal, and so on.

In this context, the mere topical section (*prakaraṇa*) is not at all a cause [for secondary usage], because it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), as seen in cases such as "the sun" and so forth. Since the relationship of deficiency or excess is not fixed, it is likewise not a cause. Furthermore, even similarity (*sādṛśya*) is not a cause, because secondary usage (*gauṇatva*) exists even when there is a connection to a primary cause, as in "an image of Kāśyapa is Kāśyapa" and the like.

By process of elimination, context (*prakaraṇa*) and the rest, together with what is well-known (*prasiddhi*) and what is not well-known (*aprasiddhi*), or else well-known and not well-known together with context and the rest—these four modes, namely reversal (*viparyāsa*), superimposition (*adhyāropa*), definition (*lakṣaṇā*), and capacity of form (*rūpaśakti*), are accepted as the causes for both the secondary (*gauṇa*) and primary (*mukhya*) [uses of words]. By these causes, there occurs either the metaphorical application of a word (*śabdopacāra*) or the metaphorical application of a meaning (*arthopacāra*). And that is of two kinds: metaphorical application of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārthopacāra*) or metaphorical application of the essential nature (*svarūpopacāra*); in this way, the distinction between the secondary and primary is to be understood. (278)

O Venerable One, when the suffix *cvī* is used in the sense of "becoming" (*svārtha*) to denote the state of another thing, the primary meaning of that other thing is also observed to be present therein. (279)

Now, in order to apply this very principle to the actual examples, he says: when words such as *go* (cow) are applied to another object characterized as *ago* (non-cow)—that is, when they function while abiding in a state that consists of a superimposed subsequent condition upon a previously established [primary] condition—then the "state of being that" (*tadbhāva*), characterized by the assumption of the form of the cow and so forth, belongs to the other object such as the Bāhīka; at that time, it should be understood that a secondary (*gauṇa*) meaning of those words is observed. It should be understood that not only is the secondary meaning observed in this way, but the primary (*mukhya*) meaning is also observed.

In such cases as "The non-cow became a cow" (*agaur gauḥ samapadyata*) or "the cow became," and "The non-thou becomes thou" (*atvaṃ tvaṃ sampadyate*), the state of being a cow or the state of being the second person (*yuṣmad-rūpatā*) in the non-cow or the non-thou is not actually present in the subsequent state; thus, these are figurative (*gauṇa*) in meaning. However, in cases such as "The small becomes great" (*amahān mahān*), "The non-white becomes white" (*aśuklaḥ śuklaḥ*), or "The moon has become great" (*mahad-bhūtaś candramāḥ*) and "The cloth becomes white" (*śuklībhavati paṭaḥ*), the subsequent state is indeed real in fact; therefore, the words *mahat* and *śukla* remain in their primary sense (*mukhya-artha*), and there is no figurativeness.

Consequently, in the case of *gaurabhavat*, although the word *au* (the dual ending) is a particle (*nipāta*) because it has a secondary meaning (*gauṇārthatva*), there is no application of the designation *pragṛhya* for *au*. Likewise, in *tvadbhavati*, because the referent of *yuṣmad* is understood in a metaphorical sense, the second person (*madhyamapuruṣa*) also does not occur precisely due to that secondary meaning. For this reason, it is established in the Bhāṣya that "between the secondary (*gauṇa*) and the primary (*mukhya*), the understanding applies to the primary."

The author of the Vārttika, however, perceiving that in the example *go'bhavat* the word *go-*—functioning in the sense of the suffix *cvi*—possesses its primary meaning as defined by the sense of *cvi*, and considering that the distinction between the primary and the secondary (*gauṇa-mukhya*) is impossible here, undertook the effort [stated in the rule] "the prohibition of *o* applies when *cvi* follows," in order to prevent the application of the *pragṛhya* designation. The author of the Bhāṣya, on the other hand, being unaware of this intention, held that because the primary is stronger than the secondary (*antaraṅgatvāt*), the *pragṛhya* designation does not apply in such cases according to the principle "between the primary and the secondary, the primary is understood."

Thus, it is established that there is no application of an internal operation [in such cases]. Now, if words do not apply their operations when they have a secondary (gauṇa) meaning, then in the instances "The Bāhīka is a cow stands" (*gaur bāhīkas tiṣṭhati*) and "Bring the Bāhīka, the cow" (*gām bāhīkam ānaya*), the rules for *vṛddhi* and *ātva* would not apply; for here the word *go* has a transferred (metaphorical) sense. To this it is replied: indeed, the operations of words are of two kinds—those pertaining to the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) and those pertaining to the word (*pada*). Among these, the principle of primary versus secondary meaning applies to word-operations, but not to stem-operations.

The figurative meaning (*gauṇārthatā*) of a word is established through the impossibility of its co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a contradictory word; however, the figurative meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) cannot be determined at all, because it is impossible for a stem that is unfit for usage to have co-referentiality with another word. Furthermore, since the grammatical operation of the nominal stem consists in [the application of] *vṛddhi* and *ātva*, that operation indeed takes place. As it has been said: "This is so when based on meaning (*arthāśraya*), but in the case of *vṛddhi* and *ātva*, it is based on the word-form itself (*śabdāśraya*). (279)

The primordial nature (prakṛti) attains both greatness and the state of purity; however, when it is considered as distinct [from the Self], it serves as the cause for its being designated as secondary (gauṇa). || 280 ||

Thus, in cases such as *go'bhavat* ("he became a cow") and *tvadbhavatī* ("he becomes you"), the desired meaning is established through a figurative sense (*gauṇārthatva*). However, regarding the expression *mahad-bhūtaś-candramāḥ* ("the moon has become great"), one might object that since the moon possesses greatness on the full-moon day, there is no figurative usage; consequently, by the rule *ānmahataḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.46), the substitution of *ā* for the final vowel of *mahat* would necessarily apply. Anticipating this objection, the author states the following to demonstrate that even here there is a figurative sense: "In the case of *mahad-bhūtaś-candramāḥ* and *śuklībhavati paṭaḥ* ('the cloth becomes white'), the original state (*prakṛti*) consists of both greatness and the process of becoming white."

It is understood precisely as having a prior state that has been resorted to, which is metaphorically designated as a subsequent state through differentiation; and thus, although this very meaning exists according to the actual nature of things, nevertheless, being resorted to by the speaker's intention, it brings about its figurative character.

This is what is meant: although both magnitude (*mahattva*) and the state of being white (*śuklabhāva*) exist here [in the cloth], nevertheless, it is the very state of primordial nature (*prakṛtyavasthā*) that is expressed here as the emerging form through the function of the word. Since "magnitude" is applied to this [cloth] only by way of metaphorical attribution (*upacarita*) based upon that [primordial nature], the word *mahat* does not undergo the substitution of *āt* (i.e., *mahān*) here. As for the expression "the cloth becomes white" (*śuklībhavati paṭaḥ*), there is no actual transformation of the effect; it is merely presented here for the sake of illustrating the meaning. || 280 ||

Words such as "Agni" and "Soma," which are based on their own intrinsic forms, are applied to the bearers of those names; when they are used for something other than what is well-known, they possess a figurative sense. (281)

Now, regarding the expression *agnisomau māṇavakau* ("the two boys Agni and Soma"), since these are technical names (*saṃjñāśabda*), they possess their primary meaning; why then is the substitution of *ṣ* not applied according to the rule "the word *agni* [takes ṣ before] *stut*, *soma*, and *soma*" (*agneḥ stutsomasomāḥ*)? To this he says: In this context, words such as *agni* and *soma* are possible in three ways: they may denote deities, they may be based on their own phonetic form (*svarūpa*), or they may function as technical names (*saṃjñā*). Among these, when referring to a deity or when based on their own form, these words have only their primary meaning (*mukhyārtha*). In the case of a technical name, however, they are secondary (*gauṇa*). Thus, in the present instance, because they are technical names, they do not take the primary meaning required for the application of the rule.

It should be understood that because Agni, Soma, and others have attained full development in the deity but are not well-known in the boy (māṇavaka), their status as having a secondary (gauṇa) meaning is asserted on account of this lack of common renown, and not through superimposition (adhyāropa). Consequently, the rule for the substitution of *ṣ* does not apply at all. || 281 ||

But as for the fire that is "given by Agni," there the word [Agni], having its own primary meaning as subordinate, attains a secondary (gauṇa) status because it functions with the meaning of "given. || 282 ||

However, where Agni, Soma, and so forth are employed through the superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of that [divinity] upon what is not that, there their figurative meaning (*gauṇārthatā*) is quite evident. Thus he says: "One should understand that those words clearly attain a figurative sense when they denote another object—having subordinated their own primary meaning characterized as a deity—by means of superimposing that [deity] upon it. (282)

Since the derivation of words proceeds based on a distinction in their etymological causes (nimitta), the presence and absence of the augment *suṭ* are established as fixed in the case of Hariścandra and others. (283)

Now, in order to provide a justification for the presence of the *suṭ* augment in the case of *hariścandramāṇavaka*, [the author] begins by stating: "In the case of *hariścandra* and others, the presence and absence of *suṭ* are indeed fixed, because in the process of deriving those words, a difference in the underlying cause (*nimitta*) is relied upon. While *hariścandra* is established as correct when referring to the ancient seer (*ṛṣi*), its absence is clearly evident in the act of derivation when it means 'one whose moon is Hari' (*hariścandro yasya*); thus, there is no confusion. (283)

When a word that has already undergone grammatical refinement in relation to a seer (ṛṣi) or similar entity is joined with another [word], the internal refinement therein does not cease with respect to the external referent. || 284 ||

Now, when it is said that this boy is "directly Hariścandra" because of his observation of the qualities residing in the ancient Hariścandra, one might ask: since this is a figurative meaning (*gauṇārtha*), should the *suṭ* augment not necessarily apply? To demonstrate that there is no such confusion, he says: the word "Hariścandra" was first grammatically formed (*saṃskṛta*) as referring specifically to the Ṛṣi; having subsequently acquired that grammatical formation, when it is applied elsewhere to someone else who possesses qualities similar to those of Hariścandra, then the internal grammatical formation [remains].

The established doctrine of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇasamaya*) is that at the time of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), when there is an occasion for connection with another meaning, [the grammatical operation] does not cease. For example, in the cases "he will do tomorrow" (*kariṣyati śvaḥ*) and "he will go to Varanasi" (*vārāṇasīṃ gamiṣyati*), because of the proximity of the word *śvaḥ* (tomorrow), when the specific time characterized as "future-not-today" manifests, there can be no reversal of the suffix *lṛṭ* which was prescribed by relying on the general category of "future. In the same way here, even though the sense is secondary (*gauṇārthatva*)—as in "Hariścandra is a boy"—the formation of the *suṭ* augment is indeed established. || 284 ||
Even when an object is apprehended as being utterly contrary [to its actual state], the word functions in its primary sense according to that very cognition. (285)

Now, anticipating the objection that according to the perspective of the Nyāya school there is no such thing as a meaning of words [corresponding to reality], and thus no distinction between primary (*mukhya*) and secondary (*gauṇa*) usage among words, he says: "In this world, regarding an object made the focus by the speaker's intention, for as long as a certain word is employed, whenever and however the determination of the object is made—even if contrary [to reality]—then the word, proceeding everywhere solely according to the cognition (i.e., following the understanding), functions only in a primary sense. Thus, within a sentence, there is no distinction whatsoever between primary and secondary usage among words. (285)

Although the determination of the true nature of an object depends upon cognition, not every cognition arises as if it were unestablished with respect to that object. (286) The perception [of water] in a body of water is equal to perceptions such as those of a mirage; yet, despite the equality of the perceptions and so forth, water is not the mirage. (287) Because the specific effect of a rope and a snake is well-known, their difference is to be determined even though the perception of them is the same. (288)

Now, in order to establish here as well the distinction between the secondary and the primary, he first begins the discussion on the distinction between the real and the unreal: "That which is perceived as having its well-known meaning inverted, and the difference that is observed therein—that they declare to be the unreal. (289)

Now, in order to demonstrate that perception is also unreal by virtue of its objects being unreal, he says: "And that which is occasional perception has as its cause the subversion of well-known objects. This means that for a well-known object which exists in the form of reality, the cause (*nimitta*) or reason for its opposite—that is, for that which is characterized by falsity—is a defect residing in the sense organ or the object. Furthermore, whatever distinction or particularity, such as a double moon, is perceived from that [reality], they declare such an object of perception to be of that nature. (289)
And just as in a painting of mountains and the like, there is no appearance of depth and height, yet no action such as obstruction occurs therein; so it is in that case.

Again, he speaks of the difference in perception: "On a variegated wall, depressions and elevations are seen as having the same form as mountains and so forth; yet, by that much alone, there is no difference in effects such as resistance (pratighāta) therein, for the meaning is that the cognition of difference occurs only through another cognition. (290)

Just as the continuous contact of a wheel with the hand exists for those who are present, such is not the case for a firebrand-circle (*alātacakra*), for that is touched only in its interrupted [successive] parts. (291) Just as there is an obstruction to touch by means of ramparts, walls, and towers in cities, it is not so in the case of *gandharvanagara* (phantom cities). (292) To whatever extent a primary purpose is accomplished by means of real goats, cattle, and so forth, that same purpose does not exist even in their clay-made counterparts; therefore, they are not objects [of sensory perception]. (293)

A vast region is encompassed by well-known mountains and other features, yet its reflection is seen as situated within a much smaller space. Furthermore, just as primary causes such as poison and the like—which trigger death and so forth—are effective for oneself in the waking state, they do not establish the same object in dreams and similar states. (294–295)

To establish this very point through further examples, he says: "In such cases as 'he sells elephant-copies' (*hastikān*) or 'he sells horse-copies' (*aśvakān*), having determined the distinction based solely on the difference in function, he has declared that words ending in the suffix *kan* denote a representation (*pratikṛti*). This is the meaning of the verse beginning with "by means of deer, cattle, and so forth. The rest is clear. (291–295)
Whatever is perceived differently due to variations in place, time, and sense faculties, that is determined in accordance with the common consensus of the world. (296)

Now, in order to provide a summary, he says: When there is no spatial separation due to a difference of place, or temporal separation as when, in summer, shimmering rays of heat from the earth produce the cognition of water for one standing at a distance, or when, due to a difference of sense organ, they produce the cognition of two moons for one suffering from ophthalmia—then an object, though appearing otherwise due to such differences of place, time, and sense organ, is determined correctly and without error through the distinction between cognitions of firmness or lack thereof based on worldly consensus, and through the distinction in its causal efficiency (arthakriyā). || 296 ||
There is no linguistic usage based on either cognition born of sensory impairment or cognition that is non-worldly; for words are grounded in the world. (297)

Therefore, he says that the true nature of the matter here must be understood as follows: knowledge arising from impairment—such as the visual distortion of one suffering from summer cataracts (*timira*)—is the opposite of truth; and furthermore, even that knowledge pertaining to the supreme sages (*paramarṣi*), which is non-worldly (*alaukika*), cannot by either of these two fulfill worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). Consequently, just as it is, that knowledge which is non-contradictory, well-known in the world, and capable of fulfilling all transactions is relied upon for the determination of the reality of objects as they truly are.

As it has been said: "Just as worldly people provide designations for objects whose true nature is inexpressible during their practical discourse, a wise person should not conceptualize them [as having ultimate reality]. In this very way, words—bound to the world and serving as the cause for worldly transaction—functioning to convey the essential nature of objects, bring about the distinction between the primary (mukhya) and the secondary (gauṇa) precisely through being well-established or not well-established, and thus through having an unerring or an erring application. Therefore, it is established that the distinction between the primary and the secondary remains firmly fixed even when the word-referent is of a mental (conceptual) nature. || 297 ||
Just as a lamp, when employed for a purpose such as [illuminating] a jar or the like, performs the act of illumination for other things as well by virtue of its assistance. (298)

Having thus explained the distinction between the primary and the secondary, and having established the distinction between the real and the unreal as a consequence thereof, [the author] speaks again in order to conduct an extensive investigation into the primary and the non-primary meanings of words: "In this world, that which is intended to be conveyed for which words are employed is its *prayojaka* (the motivator) and its primary meaning; and at the time of conveying that [primary meaning], whatever else it causes to be understood due to proximity and so forth is called its *nāntarīyaka* (the non-separable)."

He demonstrates this by means of two examples, beginning with the words "In the case of jars and so forth. Therein, the phrase "just as a lamp" presents an example of a signifier (*jñāpaka*). Just as, when objects such as jars have been known, a lamp—which is the signifier—produces an illumination that is inseparable from its causal purpose, namely the act of making known those jars and other things; [so it is here]. (298)
In the same way, when a word is employed for objects that are associated [with one another], it causes those other things as well to be understood, distinct from the primary motivating factor.

To apply this to the case at hand (dārṣṭāntika), he says: "Just as [in the phrase] *bhāva* etc., among many related meanings, that word *bhāva* is employed because it is established by a meaning such as 'existence' (*sattva*) and so forth; therefore, it should be understood that it necessarily conveys other factors such as gender and number which exist through inseparable connection (*nāntarīyakatayā*) due to their proximity. (299)
Just as the fire produced for the purpose of obtaining fire from two pieces of wood by friction generates smoke—which is not the intended object—by means of the same single instrument; || 300 ||

He speaks for the purpose of demonstrating the agent, the cause, and the example: "The friction pertaining to the two fire-sticks (*araṇī*) is for the sake of fire, that is, for the production of fire; the meaning is that fire is its instigator (*prayojaka*). For, by way of being an inseparable concomitant (*nāntarīyakatayā*), it indeed produces even smoke, though that is useless [for the primary goal]. Of what kind? It means having a single means and a single cause. By the phrase 'of the two fire-sticks,' it is shown that both the upper and the lower fire-sticks are referred to therein. (300)
Just as a word, when a certain intended meaning is to be conveyed, reveals even an unintended meaning due to its mere proximity. (301)

Furthermore, in order to apply this to the case under discussion (*dārṣṭāntika*), he says: "In some object to be made known (*pratyāyya*), regarding the property called 'establishedness' (*siddhatā*), it reveals—that is, makes known—even a meaning not intended to be expressed, namely the characteristics of masculinity and singularity, by virtue of its proximity. (301)
Just as an object that is utterly intermingled cannot be abandoned, so too a word that is related [to its meaning] cannot be separated. (302)

"Let it be granted that the nature of things (*vastugati*) is indeed such: just as by means of a lamp or the like, which illuminates the primary object (*prayojaka*) through necessary implication (*nāntarīyakapratyāyana*), other things such as a jar or a wall are also perceived due to their proximity and the necessity of that [illumination]—in that case, this is logical. But as for the word, let it perform its communication exactly as it was intended by the speaker to be communicated; what is the use of its communicating what is necessarily implied? Anticipating this objection, he says: "Just as by one seeking fish or meat..."

Just as fish-meat mixed with a small amount of bark, thorns, and the like cannot be discarded even though it is unfit for consumption, so too the word—possessing an absolute connection that expresses gender and number—cannot be separated or avoided, because one cannot distinguish or exclude the base (prakṛti) alone, nor the suffix (pratyaya) alone. || 302 ||
Even when useless things are present, it is the purposeful object that is manifested by the word; this is held to be so even though there is no difference in the form of the word itself. (303)

Therefore, since many objects are present there, he asks: "Which among these objects would be the meaning expressed by the word? He replies: Among the many associated objects present there, even though they are all manifested without distinction by the word—just as by a lamp—the one that is the *prayojaka* (the motivator or primary cause) of [the cognition] is alone the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*); any other is *anantarīyaka* (invariably concomitant), for even in that case, there is no status of being a motivator, since the form (*rūpa*) is non-different, that is, identical. || 303 ||

In some cases, the predominance or subordination of meanings is not intended to be expressed; in other cases, even their mere proximity is not a cause for comprehension. That which is not directly denoted by a word may nevertheless be understood in certain instances; sometimes a meaning that is primary itself becomes the indicated (lakṣya) of another. (304–305)

He explains this very point in detail, preceded by a demonstration of the different varieties: "In this context, there is a reversal of the status of primary and secondary; the non-intention of expressing a portion of a word-meaning; the non-intention of expressing the entire word-meaning; and the indication of another meaning without abandoning the word-meaning already employed. Thus, by these two verses, a presentation of four varieties has been made. (304–305)
Whatever has been stated as an illustration of the meaning of a secondary derivative (taddhita) shows a reversal of the relationship between the subordinate and the principal qualities therein. (306)

Now, in order to demonstrate the first type [of derivation], he says: "He plays with that" (*tena dīvyati*)—this is stated as the basis for the meaning of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*). Consequently, since the verb (*ākhyāta*) is predominant in action (*kriyā*) therein, the understanding of the meaning of that [derivative] would arise solely from the meaning of the verb. And because, although the verb is predominant in action there, the secondary derivative is by its very nature predominant in the means (*sādhana*), the understanding arises primarily of the meaning of the means.

In the initial instruction regarding [the rule] *tena dīvyati* and so forth, the relationship of subordinate and principal (*guṇapradhānabhāva*) is not intended; rather, the sole motivating factor there is simply the agent of the action of gambling whose instrument is the dice. That is the primary meaning. And he will say: "The distinction between subordinate and principal, or the reversal of [the status of] the person (*puruṣa*) and so forth, as taught otherwise in the treatise, is not contradictory because it is eternal. The meanings of those for whom the treatise is prescriptive should be according to the instruction; however, the exposition stands by relying upon some general commonality."

"Just as in the [Vedic] passage 'yo'śve yaḥ pīṭhe,' the two entities—the horse and the seat—serve as mere indicators (upalakṣaṇa), so too is the grammatical instruction (anuśāsana) regarding meanings. || 306 ||

In an explanatory statement, the proximity of gender and number is not a cause [for restriction]; rather, it is the authoritative means itself that is understood as being applied even in the case of short vowels and the like, though they are not explicitly mentioned. // 307 //

Now, in order to demonstrate that [gender and number] are sometimes present (*sānnidhya*), he says: "A state (*bhāva*) characterized by completion (*siddha-lakṣaṇa*) is intended as the cause for the suffixes *ghañ* and so forth. To establish this, even though gender and number are understood as being inseparable (*nāntarīyakatayā*) from the designation "state," their presence (*sannidhāna*) is not the cause; that is to say, they do not function as the motivators (*prayojaka*) in that context. [Objection: But if they are understood as being inseparable, how can it be said that even their occasional presence is not a cause for their comprehension?

The intention is that [the term *svarita*] is not the cause for the usage of that [term] when the comprehension extends as far as the purpose of the prompter (*prayojaka*). Now, in order to demonstrate the point that "it has been stated [to be] nothing other than a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*), he says: "It is indeed a means of valid cognition. Here, it was stated that the *svarita* is a combination (*samāhāra*) of the acute (*udātta*) and grave (*anudātta*) accents; and the short (*hrasva*), long (*dīrgha*), and protracted (*pluta*) vowels—characterized by one, two, and three morae (*mātrā*) respectively—are of the nature of a combination of acute and grave accents.

In that regard, regarding the short svarita and other vowels, how much is udātta and how much is anudātta? To dispel the doubt as to whether the udātta occurs at the beginning, or whether the anudātta occurs in the middle or at the end, it is stated: "Of that [svarita], the first half-short [portion] is udātta. Here, the mention of "half-short" (ardhahrasva) is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an indicative mark) for the measure characterized by half a *mātrā*; thus, it is precisely that [measure] which is understood from it. Therefore, it is stated that there is no intention (*avivakṣā*) to speak of the secondary element indicated by the term "half-short. || 307 ||

And that which is seen as half of the short vowel, even in the absence of that [long vowel], is designated in the same way, because it serves as the defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa) of the short vowel. || 308 ||

To demonstrate this very point, he says: "And therefore, half of a short vowel is seen to consist of half a mora (*mātrā*); even in the absence of that short vowel, it is said that for the long and protracted vowels as well, the first half-mora is acute (*udātta*). He asks, "Why? and replies: "Because the mention of the 'short' is for the purpose of indicating [the mora]. In the expression "half of a short vowel" (*ardha-hrasvam*), the mention of "short" is intended as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the mora. Therefore, it should be understood that for the long and protracted vowels as well, the first half-mora is acute.

This very point has been stated by others: by the term *ardhahrasvam* (half-a-short-vowel), an *ardhamātrā* (half-mora) is indicated; the mention of "short" (*hrasva*) is not restrictive. Therefore, since "short" here serves as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇārtha*), it is declared that even for long (*dīrgha*) and protracted (*pluta*) vowels, the acute accent (*udātta*) consists of half a mora. To the question "In what way?", he says: "just like that" (*tadvadeva*). The meaning is: just as half a mora is said for that short vowel, so too [is it] in its absence for the long and protracted vowels. || 308 ||
Its distinction would be by means of "long" and "protracted," or else by its measure; or rather, it is a definition of the genus, because in every respect it is like the *saptaparṇa* tree.

Alternatively, three possibilities are presented here; of these, he states the first possibility: by the mention of the term *hrasva* (short), both the long (*dīrgha*) and protracted (*pluta*) vowels are also indicated, because they are taught in a single grammatical rule (*ekayoganirdiṣṭa*) in the sūtra "ū3kālo'j jhrasvadīrghaplutaḥ. Consequently, that [initial] half-measure would be delimited by the long and protracted vowels as well. Even in the sense of an unequal division, the word *ardha* is seen used, as in *grāmārddha* (half of a village) and *nāgarārddha* (half of a city). Thus, in this case, even for the long and protracted vowels, there occurs an acute accent (*udātta*) of one and a half measures (*ardhamātrā*).

He states the second alternative: "by a measure" (mātrayā), or rather, it is a delimitation of half [a mora], because the designation "short" (hrasva) is not intended to be emphasized here. This is illustrated by the expression "half of a short [vowel]. Alternatively, the word *arddhahr̥sva* ("half-short")—which has its internal division of parts discarded—is an indivisible term that serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaka*) for the class (*jāti*) of half-mora sounds, just like the word *saptaparṇa* ("seven-leaved"). He states the third alternative here: "or by the class" (*jāter vā*). || 309 ||
"One must go; let the sun be seen"—such are the signs of time. "Let time be known"—this is stated along with its means. (310)

Now, in order to explain how sometimes the primary meaning itself becomes the indicator (lakṣaṇa) of another meaning, he says: "In some places, travelers speak thus: 'Hurry! Another stage remains to be traversed today; look at the sun! Here, the word 'look at the sun'—though heard primarily for the purpose of seeing the sun—becomes an indicator of the meaning 'know that only a small portion of the day remains,' which includes both the means and the certainty. Thus, there is the indication of another meaning by means of the primary meaning.
The primary meaning, characterized by the sense of another, is not abandoned even when the etymological (śakti) meaning is present. ||310||
In the expression "he pierces without a bow," a specific instance is pointed out; it serves as the locus for a general capacity, being whatever may be presented as such. (311)

To demonstrate this very point at length through examples from both the scriptures and the world by means of three verses, he says: "By the qualification 'without a bow,' the general nature of an instrument (*karaṇa*) is indicated. To the question 'Of what kind is that?', he replies: 'It is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of the power of the instrument. Consequently, whatever substrate (*pratipādaka*) of that [power] is employed..."

This is what is meant: when an injunction is intended to prohibit the use of instruments [in general], the scriptural example is that the status of being the primary object (or the target) belongs to the instrument as such, without abandoning the specific characteristic of being a bow. And it has been said: "One pierces with the non-instrument; otherwise, there would be an over-extension. || 311 ||
Even a child, when instructed, "Let the ghee be protected from crows," does not protect it from dogs and other animals, since the statement is intent only on [preventing] damage. (312)

He says that even in a sentence expressing a specific [action], it is observed in common worldly usage that only the general [meaning] is the operative factor. For instance, in the case of "protecting the ghee from crows," although a specific act is enjoined, it culminates in the result of merely preventing its destruction; therefore, that [general purpose] alone should be understood as the operative factor there. (312) "The washing of the bowls and likewise the scrubbing of the cooking pots, though not explicitly stated in their specific form, is understood because it is an auxiliary to the act of eating. (313)

To show that even when something is not explicitly stated, it is nevertheless understood as being inseparable from the primary meaning, he says: "In the case of the expression 'Let food be prepared for him,' the word conveying the preparation of food necessarily conveys the preparation of its constituent parts, such as the offering of a seat, the washing of the vessel, and so forth. Alternatively, there is a reading "prakṣālane" (in the washing).

When the washing of the bowls (*śarāva*) is mentioned by means of the sound [of the word], even though the wiping of the cooking pots (*sthālī*) and so forth are not explicitly stated, they are nevertheless understood because they are possible and are subordinate members of the act of eating. Thus, this very principle—"this is the motivator (*prayojaka*) for them, while this is its necessary concomitant (*nāntarīyaka*)"—has been demonstrated at length through various incidental diversifications. In this manner, the verse beginning with "the authority [resides] in the half-short vowel, etc. and ending with "the washing of the bowls" has been explained.

By this verse, indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is shown in two ways. Sometimes, by the very abandonment of the primary meaning, there is the indication of something else; this alone is called "the expressed meaning unintended" (*avivakṣitavācya*). Sometimes, preceded by the means of not ceasing from the primary meaning, there is the indication of another meaning; this is to be understood as what was called "the expressed meaning intended but subordinate" (*vivakṣitānyaparavācya*). In this manner, the distinction between the primary and the inseparable has been demonstrated. || 313 ||
Words and their meanings are distinguished through context, the subject matter, propriety, and place and time; they are not determined by form alone. (314)

Now, in this context, desiring to demonstrate the various means for determining specific meanings—such as "this is secondary," "this is primary," or "this is necessary"—in the course of defining word-meanings, he says: "In that regard, the determination of word-meaning from a sentence is as follows: in the case of 'He makes a mat, formidable, magnificent, and beautiful,' although the hearing [of these words] is equal, when the connection with the act of making belongs to the mat alone, then, because a substance without qualities is impossible and qualities cannot exist without a substratum, [the meaning is determined] through expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth."

That coreferentiality [of the case endings] arises from their syntactic coordination (*samanvaya*); thus, the sentence-meaning is precisely the act of weaving performed by the weaver who possesses the black qualities. And the author will state: "The determination regarding the locus and the located is established through the sentence. Accordingly, in the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*), separate sections have been composed for rules such as "the second case ending is used for the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*).

In that regard, since the meaning is connected—namely, that when action (*karman*) and so forth are not already expressed by a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the second and subsequent case endings (*vibhakti*) occur for the singular number and so forth—it follows that, through the force of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and other factors, even though the contexts (*prakaraṇa*) are distinct, the syntactic relationship (*vākyīya-sambandha*) culminates in the determination of meaning for a listener who reflects upon the intended purport (*tātparya*). Thus, the determination of the word-meaning arises from the sentence.

Likewise, in this context, even the absence of a word serves as a cause for determining the meaning of a word; just as in the context of a battle, the mention of "Saindhavas" results in the understanding of horses being brought forward, whereas in the context of a meal, that same word produces the cognition of salt. In the technical treatise (śāstra), for example, when it says "root," it is stated as such because of the context of roots.

And likewise, when both [agent and instrument] are understood, because the *kārakas* have been introduced in the rule "The third case ending is used for the agent and the instrument" (*kartṛkaraṇayos tṛtīyā*), it is not understood that the word "instrument" (*karaṇa*) refers to the action (*kriyā*). Furthermore, in the rule beginning with "śabdavairakalahābhrakaṇvameghartuśubham" and others, since the context concerns verbal roots (*dhātu*), the action is understood from the word "cause" (*kāraṇa*).

The meaning, however, determines the specific word-meaning because it is based on verbal expression; for example, in the cases "he offers with joined palms" (*añjalinā juhoti*), "he worships the sun with joined palms" (*añjalinā sūryamupatiṣṭhate*), and "he brings a full vessel with joined palms" (*añjalinā pūrṇapātramāharati*), the word *añjali* denotes different meanings according to the context of "offers" and so forth. Furthermore, in the grammatical rule *pūraṇaguṇasuhitārtha...* (Pāṇini 2.2.11), where it is stated that a genitive case ending is not compounded with a word expressing a quality (*guṇa*), the understanding that the vowels *a* and *e* (as substitutes for *at* and *et*) are not included is derived from the force of the meaning.

Likewise, in the rule "na śasadadavādiguṇānām," the inclusion of those [roots] that do not possess a vowel as their base occurs by implication (*arthāt*). Furthermore, the determination of word-meaning is seen to arise from propriety (*aucitya*); for example, even when the plough (*sīra*), sword (*asi*), and pestle (*musala*) are mentioned alone without a specified action, the determination of the word-meaning culminates in the suggestion of the appropriate verbal actions—namely, plowing, fighting, and threshing—by virtue of propriety.

Or, for example, words such as *praṣṭha* and so forth, which function by relying on causes such as "being one who goes at the head," are called masculine words because that cause is possible only in a male due to its suitability; yet, through connection with that [cause], they apply to a female, not directly. Thus, the very relationship with a male (*praṣṭha*) is presented as the cause for words like *praṣṭhī* by the rule "A name [is formed] from connection with a male" (*puṃyogād ākhyāyām*). And as in the verse: "He who [cuts] the neem tree with an axe, and he who [anoints] it with honey and ghee..."

In the verse, "And he who [offers] this with perfumes and garlands—he is pungent to everyone," the case-words (sādhana) associated with the verb *anurakta* (attached/devoted), by virtue of propriety (*aucitya*), bring about the cognition of their own appropriate verbs; through the prior suggestion of subordinate sentences (*avāntaravākya-upaplāvana*), they produce the comprehension of the sentence-meaning characterized as *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise).

And so, the intended meaning here is to demonstrate the wickedness of a certain person by means of the maxim: "For one who cuts down a neem tree with an axe and another who anoints it with perfume, the nature of both is difficult to abandon; thus, [the tree] remains bitter and indeed skilled at causing dejection. As it is stated in the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*)—specifically in the rule *puṃyogād ākhyāyām*—"these are words for males (*puṃśabda*), because the grounds for the application of the word 'male' (*puṃśabda*) are present therein."

The determination of word-meaning occurs by means of place; for instance, when it is said, "I am coming from a city to the east or north of Mathurā," it is understood that one is coming from the specific city of Pāṭaliputra. This determination is made on account of the location, because there exists a proximity between Pāṭaliputra and the eastern and northern regions associated with Mathurā.

Indeed, a restriction [of meaning] is observed based on time; for example, when "the door" is said during the cold season, it is understood as "close it," whereas when such a statement is made during the summer season, it is understood as "open it. This should be understood as merely a demonstration of the direction of the means for determining word-meanings. Other methods should also be investigated for the sake of certain determination. It should be considered that only a mere illustration has been shown here due to the constraints of the verse.
To demonstrate that, in every respect, it is impossible to determine the distinction between word and meaning based on form alone, it was stated: "not from form alone. (314)

Association, dissociation, co-occurrence, opposition, purpose, context, gender, proximity to another word, capability, propriety, place, time, individuality, accent, and so forth, serve as causes for the recollection of specific meanings when the meaning of a word is otherwise undetermined. (315–316)

Likewise, he states that others have demonstrated that association (*saṃsarga*) and so forth are the causes for delimiting the meaning of a word: "In this regard, some accept a difference in words based on a difference in meanings, while others accept them as a single word; thus there are two positions. Among these, in the position of plurality, where words are distinct by nature yet identical in sound and not delimited by a difference in form, delimitation is effected through other causes such as association."

In the view that there is identity [between word and meaning], when the meanings are denoted by distinct powers (*śakti*) that have not yet attained distinction due to the mere similarity of their phonetic form (*śruti-sārūpya*), the determination of the meaning is made through association and so forth; thus, since context (*prakaraṇa*) and other factors are skillful in determining the word-meaning in both cases, their presentation is mentioned. In this regard, some maintain that capacity (*sāmarthya*) alone is the sole cause for determining the word-meaning.

They say that even that distinction which is understood there through context, purpose, and so forth, is also perceived here by means of *sāmarthya* (semantic competency) alone; for it is precisely *sāmarthya* that is manifested through association (*saṃsarga*) and other factors. Among these, as for association: in the example "Let the cow with a calf be brought," the understanding arises specifically of a mare because the associated calf serves as the cause for determining the particular [animal]; and likewise, in the case of "the cow with a calf," the understanding arises specifically of a female cow due to the association with the calf. Thus, the determination of meaning results from association.

However, for those who hold the view that by convention only a cow is called a *dhenu*, it should be understood that in this case, the association (*saṃsarga*) is not useful for the cognition of the specific [meaning]. Just as in the grammatical rule *āvād graḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.16), only that which can possibly have a connection with the prefix *ā*—namely, the root *gṛ* in the sense of swallowing (*girati*)—is taken; whereas for *gṛ* in the sense of reciting (*gṛṇoti*), a connection is simply not possible due to its inherent nature and the contradiction in meaning. Likewise, dissociation (*viprayoga*) is also a cause of delimitation, just like association.

Just as it is said of one who has already ascertained the relationship [between words and their meanings]: "Let a cow that is not a *kiśora*, not a calf, and not a *karabha* be brought,"—through the exclusion of the *kiśora* and others, there arises the understanding of a cow specifically belonging to a particular class; so too in the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*), in the rule "the root *bhuji* [is used] except in the sense of protecting" (*bhujo 'navane*), the inclusion is understood to refer to that *bhuji* whose meanings are both protecting and non-protecting, but not to that which has the meaning of crookedness (*kauṭilya*). As in the example: "he bends his hand" (*nirbhujati pāṇim*).

By way of association (*sāhacarya*), for example, when "Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa" are mentioned, there is the cognition of the son of Daśaratha specifically because of his association with Lakṣmaṇa. In this regard, although one [member] may be observed to deviate [from the rule], it should be understood that through association, the other member is known to possess that very property. In the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*), for instance, in the rule "after *vi* and *parā*, the root *ji* [takes *ātmanepada*]," the word *parā* is understood as a preverb (*upasarga*) alone due to its association with [the preverb] *vi*, even though deviation is not observed. Although in examples such as *bahuvivana* ("many forests") the word *vi* is not a preverb, nevertheless, the aggregate [of the two words] possesses meaning.

In the view that a compound functions by abandoning its own meaning (*jahatsvārthāvṛtti*), the constituent parts are indeed meaningless. In the view that it functions without abandoning its own meaning (*ajahatsvārthāvṛtti*), how could that which has attained the status of a prefix (*upasarga*) be grasped as such, since its predominance [in that context] has ceased? Thus, there is no prefix *vi*. However, in the case of *vījayate*, the word is *vī* and not *vi*. This has also been stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "When it is said, 'this cow is for the sake of a second,' only a cow is understood, not a horse or a donkey."

Furthermore, as in the rule "antarāntareṇa yukte," both [the words *antarā* and *antareṇa*] are observed to have irregular applications because they can end in either the second (*ṭāp*) or third (*tṛtīyā*) case endings; therefore, due to their mutual association (*sāhacarya*), only the two particles (*nipāta*) are understood. Thus, association is a means for determining the meaning of words. Meaning is also determined by opposition (*virodha*); for example, in the expression "Rāma and Arjuna," in the presence of Arjuna, only Paraśurāma (the son of Jamadagni), who is a natural enemy, is perceived.

The determination of a specific meaning through the context of purpose, subject matter, place, time, and propriety has been demonstrated by the sentence itself. Furthermore, a distinction from what is observed in other sentences is recognized as well-established on the basis of an indicative mark (*liṅga*). For example, in the case of the injunction "one places the smeared pebbles" (*aktāḥ śarkarā upadadhāti*), although many substances for smearing might be possible, the praise of clarified butter (*ghṛta*) as light is stated. From this indicative mark, it is determined that the action of smearing, which has the pebbles as its object, is accomplished by means of clarified butter.

Likewise, in the injunction "one should sacrifice an animal" (*paśumālabheta*), although there are living beings connected with the category of "animal-ness," it is understood through the indicative mark (*liṅga*)—namely, the phrase "of the goat, the sacrificial oblation, the omentum, and the fat"—that "animal-ness" is inherent in the same referent as the "goat. This is also to be inferred in the case of scriptural texts (*śāstra*). Furthermore, a specific meaning is understood from the proximity of another word, as in "Arjuna Kārtavīrya" or "Rāma Jāmadagnya. A specific understanding arises from capacity (*sāmarthya*), as in "the girl has no belly" (*anudarā kanyā*); by virtue of this capacity, there is the cognition of a negation regarding a particular kind of belly.

Likewise, in the expression "a maiden is to be given to one who is *abhirūpa*," it is understood by implication that she is to be given to one who is *abhirūpatara* (more handsome). In the technical treatise as well, the term "compound" (*samāsa*) applies to the meaning of the compound itself, according to the rule: "That which is designated first in a compound is the subordinate member (*upasarjana*). Furthermore, the term "compound" (*samāsa*) which is inferred in the rule "and that which has a single case-ending, provided it does not occur in the prior position," belongs exclusively to the primary sense. Thus, the function (*vṛtti*), the manifestation (*vyakti*), and the gender (*liṅga*) [are established].

Therefore, the determination is as follows: in order that one may obtain the meaning of "half of the village" (*grāmasyārdham*), the word *ardha-* is used in the neuter when referring to an equal division, as is understood from the fact that it is the neuter form that is perceived [in such cases]. This is also to be inferred in the technical treatises (*śāstra*).
