For example, regarding accentuation: in the injunction *sthūlapṛṣatīm ālabheta* ("one should sacrifice a speckled cow"), because an udātta accent on the final syllable is heard, there is the understanding of the meaning "she who is both large and speckled. However, when the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*) is observed, there is the understanding of a different compound meaning: "she in whom there are large specks."

Similarly, in the case of *vaipāśaḥ kūpaḥ* ("a well without a rope"), because an initial accent (*ādyudātta*) is not heard, there is the cognition of the specific term *vipāśa* (the name of a river) as the latter member of the compound; whereas if an final accent (*antodātta*) were heard, there would be the cognition of its opposite. For instance, in cases such as *susiktam* ("well-sprinkled") and *atistutam* ("excessively praised"), when the terms *su* and *ati* are designated as *karmapravacanīya*, they lack the status of *upasarga*, and thus only those two meanings [of "well" and "excessive"] are understood. However, when the designation *upasarga* applies—as in *suṣiktam* ("sprinkled with excellence") and *suṣṭutam* ("well-praised")—the occurrence of the rule for *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) leads to the understanding of a different meaning.

For example, in the case of the word *praṇāyaka*, when the presence of the prefix (*upasarga*) dependent on the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* exists—as in *praṇāyaka*—there is the cognition of the agent of the action of leading (*praṇayana*). However, in the absence of that substitution of *ṇ* for *n*, there is the cognition of the meaning of the compound as "that place from which leaders have departed," namely, *pranāyako deśaḥ*. Thus, it should be understood that these factors, such as *saṃsarga* (association) and so forth, are causes for the recollection of specific [meanings] and causes for definitive determination (*nirṇaya*), because they serve as the means for resolving ambiguity regarding the meaning of a word and thereby lead to the ascertainment of a fixed meaning. || 315-316 ||

Even on the view that [words] are distinct, words—though having different referents due to their similarity—are manifested as restricted to specific cognitions by means of context and other such factors. (317)

However, it is not tenable to say that "when there is a doubt regarding the meaning of words due to the absence of distinction in the view of identity, the context and other factors are stated for its determination"; for in the case of the theory of difference, one might suspect that the word will convey its own meaning precisely because of its distinctness. Anticipating this, he says—in order to demonstrate that even in that case, for speakers who have doubts produced by the similarity of forms, the determination of the word's meaning occurs through context and other factors alone: "Even in the theory of difference, words, though having different meanings in their respective cognitions..."

Because they appear as if non-different due to their similarity [to the object], it should be understood that—being restricted and delimited by context (*prakaraṇa*) and other such factors whose nature has been described—they serve as the means for the manifestation of meaning; thus, the determination of word-meaning never occurs in the absence of context and the like. || 317 ||
Those words which have the same form as nouns or verbs and are based on other grammatical operations—in the case of such words, the meaning is not understood from their form alone. (318)

And this is logical; why? He says: in this sentence, verbal forms (*ākhyāta-śabda*) are also possible as names (*nāma-rūpa*). For example, from the root *ośvi* (meaning "motion" and "increase") in the sense of "horse" (*aśva*), in the *luṅ* tense, second person singular (*sip*), after the elision of the *ikāra* by the rules "nityaṃ ṅitaḥ" and "itaśca," and after the substitution of *caṅ* for the *cli* suffix by the rule "jṝstambhumrucu... etc., when the final *a* of the root *śvi* undergoes *guṇa*, and after the application of *rutva* and *visarjanīya* to the *s*, and finally the addition of *aṭ* by the rule "luṅlṛṅkṣu... etc., [the form] "aśva" is obtained.

Thus, the verbal form *śvayati* is expressive of the action of swelling delimited by its agent in the past tense, while the nominal form *aśvaḥ* denotes the entity belonging to the class of horses; since there is a similarity [in sound] between them, when doubt arises, the determination of the meaning is achieved through context and other such factors.

For example, regarding the form *ajāpayat*: from the root *ji* (to conquer), when one intends to express the meaning that "someone conquered the unconquerable (*ajeya*) and another caused him to do so," the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied in the sense of a motive (*hetu*). By the rule *krīṅjīnāṃ ṇau*, the vowel *ā* is substituted; then, by the rule *artihrīvlī* etc., the augment *puK* is added, resulting in *jāpī*. When this stands thus, the imperfect (*laṅ*) suffix is applied, followed by the *śap* suffix. After the *guṇa* substitution and the change to *ay* have been made, and after the *s* has been changed to *s* and then to a *visarjanīya*, and finally the *aṬ* augment is added by the rule *luṅlaṅlṛṅkṣvaḍudāttaḥ*, the verbal form *ajāpayat* is produced.

Alternatively, the word *ajāpayaḥ* (goat’s milk) is established as being similar to the nominal form *ajapayaḥ* through its meaning and other factors. Furthermore, verbal forms that resemble nouns include such expressions as *yasya tasya* (of whomsoever). Likewise, from the root *tanu* (to expand), when the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*) is formed in the second person plural, after reduplication has occurred and the substitution of *e* for *a* and the elision of the reduplicated syllable have been applied by the rule "ata ekahalmadhye," the form *tene* arises; this is similar to the third-case singular of the pronoun *tat*.

In the case of the words *tasu* (from the root *tasi*, meaning "to destroy") and *yasu* (from the root *yas*, meaning "to strive"), when the imperative (*loṭ*) suffix is applied to form a command and so forth, and the *sip* ending is substituted for that [imperative], the *sip* is replaced by *hi* according to the rule "serhyapicca. Then, because the roots belong to the *divādi* class, the *śyan* suffix is added, followed by the elision of its indicatory letter (*anubandha*). Subsequently, the *hi* is elided by the rule "ato heḥ. Thus, the verbal forms *tasya* and *yasya* arise. Because these two are identical in form (*sārūpya*), a doubt arises as to which is intended; this is resolved through context and other such factors. Of what kind are they? They are based on different functions.

Those [words] whose basis is a different function characterized by a specific cognition, which is determined by context and so forth, are of such a nature. In their case, the meaning is not understood from the mere form [of the word]. Therefore, the determination of the meaning occurs only through a thorough consideration of the sentence-meaning, as in the cases of "tvaṃ aśvaḥ," "ajāpayaḥ," and "śatrubhavanāni. And it has been said: "No word whatsoever is restricted to a fixed form anywhere; the form of the meaning of words arises only from the sentence-meaning. (318)
A skillful practitioner understands that the fabrication of praise and blame intended for the purpose of inciting activity or cessation is not in accordance with reality. (319)

Now, in the context of determining the meaning of words, [the author] says the following to demonstrate that one must accept the unreality of individual words and word-meanings, and the reality of the sentence-meaning alone as an indivisible whole: "The discerning person considers as unreal that fabrication of praise intended for engagement and that fabrication of censure intended for withdrawal."

From the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārthataḥ*), however, regarding such speech—whether it be "engage" or "desist"—one perceives there a sentence-meaning that is truly real; thus, the cognition of words and word-meanings is entirely unreal in every case. It has been established by some that this very [cognition] is their *tātparya-śakti* (the power of intended meaning). || 319 ||
Whatever action being enjoined has a visible or invisible purpose, it is that which is praised; such praise serves as the motivator for the agent alone. (320)

To make this very point clear, he says: "A certain action whose purpose is visible is praised, as for example: 'He who serves the king enjoys the essence. Likewise, there is also that whose purpose is invisible: 'He who sacrifices with the Agniṣṭoma goes to heaven. Thus it is established that the sentence-meaning must be accepted as something entirely distinct—either characterized by engagement or withdrawal—and based solely upon such sentences. (320)
Just as a child is deterred by the mention of a tiger or similar creature, even though it is unreal, so too is a certain transgression prescribed [as a deterrent], even if it is unreal. (321)

Now, one might object: "Why are engagement and withdrawal not simply enjoined there in a direct manner? What is the use of this accumulation of useless matters such as the description of censure? Anticipating this doubt, he says: Just as it is told to a child, "The tiger eats one who cries," where the eating by the tiger is not possible according to the actual state of things, but rather a prohibition of crying is made for him so that "you might never cry," likewise, [the scripture] indicates the fall into hell resulting from the performance of prohibited acts.
Since only this much—that "it exists"—is accepted, it is not logical to accept words and word-meanings as having a real nature by resorting to their respective objects. || 321 ||
Even after making preparations, no learned person would engage in an act that is prohibited by scripture and results in such a transgression.

Likewise, by teaching of transgression (*pratyavāya*), he states that it is not appropriate for a discerning person to act out of mere self-aggrandizement toward that which is prohibited by scripture, having devised a means to avoid transgression; [he says]: "Even after employing remedies against snakes through mantras, herbs, and so forth, accomplished by the *siddhas*, one should not proceed otherwise; one should not cause [the snake] to go from the tooth. (323)

In order to explain this very point by first demonstrating the avoidance of a visible purpose or transgression, he says: "One should not cause [the cake] to go through the teeth; for if one were to cause it to go through the teeth, serpents would seek to kill him. By this, the eating of the *puroḍāśa* preceded by biting with the teeth is forbidden. In this regard, if someone, having performed a counter-measure against serpents by means of mantras, medicinal herbs, and so forth, nevertheless proceeds in that manner, then his practice of the scripture has been abandoned, and thus he has not acted rightly.
In some cases, the true nature of reality is explained through praise and censure; even there, engagement and withdrawal are taught.

One might object: "Let it be that in those cases focused on injunctions and prohibitions, the meanings of praise and so forth are unreal; however, where praise and censure themselves are the motivating factors, it is appropriate that their referents be real. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Even in some instances where a statement of reality regarding the subject matter of praise or censure, or something related to them, is made, one must understand that in such cases as well, we do not perceive any purpose whatsoever in mere praise or censure alone; rather, it is activity and cessation [from activity] that are being taught. (324)
The form of all word-meanings is that which is bound to the sentence-meaning; however, those sentence-meanings which are dependent are equivalent to the word-meanings themselves. (325)

Thus, having established that while words and word-meanings exist as such, it is the sentence and the sentence-meaning alone that possess absolute reality, [the author] says the following to demonstrate that the very nature of word-meanings is dependent upon the sentence-meaning: "In this sentence-meaning, those [word-meanings], being bound to its form, attain fulfillment; otherwise, they would be utterly fragile. Thus, the sentence-meaning alone is the basis for their mutual coordination. And he will say later: "Of distinct entities possessing distinct natures, which follow their own separate meanings..."

"Just as the functions of the sense organs do not arise without the body, so too for all words that are divided off from sentences and assigned separate meanings, there is no possession of meaning [found] apart from them. As it is said: "For nothing whatsoever... and so forth. Now, one might object: if even a certain sentence-meaning were incomplete, would it not have to be admitted that it too is dependent upon another sentence-meaning? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "dependent" (sāpekṣa).

This is what is meant: since intermediate sentence-meanings possess expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*), they are essentially equivalent to word-meanings; therefore, the designation "sentence-meaning" should not be applied to them. || 325 ||

They also consider that to be a sentence which consists of a word whose action is completed, where a specific means (sādhana) is understood in relation to a verbal noun (ākhyāta-śabda); such a single unit, having a compound meaning, is called a sentence. || 326 ||

Now, raising the objection that even in a case where a complete meaning is understood from a single word, how could it be appropriate to say that its meaning is unreal, he says: "This is what is meant—there are parts of sentences within sentences which convey the meaning of the sentence through well-known usage and so forth. Therefore, even that single word is indeed a sentence."

Because that is "that which has its action performed" (*caritakriyam*): since they employ a sentence consisting of a noun-word (*nāmapada*) whose verbal action (*ākhyātakriyā*) is contained within it—that is, a word in which the action is internalized—it is observed that from such a word whose action is performed, a comprehension of meaning arises that is free of expectancy; thus, here, the status of being a "sentence" belongs to the word alone.

Just as even a single word consisting solely of a noun, when it contains an implied verb, is indeed a sentence because it conveys a meaning that leaves no further expectancy, and since the successful accomplishment of worldly activity up to the point of action arises from the object conveyed by that [sentence], the reality of that object's meaning is established; in the same way, even a single verb is called a "sentence" when it expresses a specific [meaning] by virtue of the suitability of the context and so forth. Thus he says: "the verb."

Just as when it is said "it rains," the sense is complete through the implication of the agent and object—namely, "the god [is] water"—so too, even a single word that has a completed meaning or a full sense is designated as a "sentence" (*vākya*). As in the example "the god rains water," so too that single word is called a sentence because its meaning is finished and its sense is complete. This was stated right at the beginning: "a verbal form (*ākhyāta-śabda*) is a sentence"; this is the meaning. || 326 ||
Cognition mediated by words, which relies on unuttered terms, is said to be the cause for the comprehension of their meaning through inference. (327)

On this point, the Mīmāṃsaka says: That cognition of productive activity (*bhāvanā*) which arises from a word alone—just as it does from a correct word—is said to be the cause of the meaning of that unuttered word, which is the meaning of another word [that is actually used]. Of what nature is it? It is "separated by the word" (*śabdavyavahitā*). Just as in the inference of an object through smoke, there is no implication of fire without the word, so it is not here either; rather, it is separated by that word such as *tiṣṭhati* which is postulated through the presumption based on what is heard (*śrutārthāpatti*).

Now, raising the objection as to how that [cognition] can be immediate (*avyavahita*) if its [verbal] expression is not heard, he says: "having as its basis an unuttered word" (*aprayuktapadāśrayā*). That [cognition] is such because its basis—meaning its door or its means for the comprehension of the meaning of words like "exists" (*tiṣṭhati*) and so forth—is an expressive word that is unuttered (*aprayukta*), i.e., not articulated, but implied through presumptive testimony (*śrutārthāpatti*). He states the reason why it is the cause for the comprehension of that meaning: "through inference" (*anumānāt*).

The meaning is that, having inferred through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) based on what has been heard the word "stands" (*tiṣṭhati*) and so forth, and having projected it [into the cognition], this mental state (*buddhi*) generates the comprehension of that object. Therefore, how can it be said that only the nominal word (*nāmapada*) expresses an object accompanied by action, and the verbal word (*ākhyāta*) expresses [an object] accompanied by its means? For there are parts of sentences within sentences that convey the meaning of the sentence as a whole. || 327 ||
When a particular meaning is understood upon the utterance of a word, that alone they call its meaning; there is no other definition of meaning.

Having raised the objection of another school—asking what purpose is served by the connection with a word through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) from what is heard, since it has been stated that the cognition of a complete meaning arises from a single word alone, as in "the tree stands" and so forth; and how, without a portion of a sentence conveying the entire sentence-meaning, is it logical to postulate another word?—he says: "In this context, they say that the object of which a cognition is observed upon the utterance of something is the meaning of that [word]; and indeed, from the word 'tree' alone, [the meaning is understood] through the context of the matter and so forth."
For the meaning "the tree stands" is understood; it is precisely for this reason that it has been stated that a sentence is that which expresses a meaning. || 328 ||

In this way, when words denoting action are used as subordinate elements, the action of the substituends is understood; likewise, in a compound, the meaning of "having traversed" and so forth is understood through words such as *nir* and others.

Having established this, he says that the fourth [sūtra], *kriyārthopapadasya*, need not even be commenced, because its purpose is already accomplished by the former rule. Regarding the application of the genitive in the phrase *kriyārthopapadānām ca* within the scope of *kriyārthopapadeṣu*, there is the use of the locative. This refers to the action characterized by "bringing" (*āharaṇa*) belonging to those verbal roots (*sthānin*) which are not explicitly employed. In the example *edhebhyo vrajati* ("he goes for fuel"), the word *edha* itself denotes the act of bringing; thus, the understanding arises: "he goes for the purpose of bringing fuel."

Therefore, since the sense of being for that purpose (*tādarthya*) is clearly established, the fourth case is proven. And having done so, the author states in the commentary—“in the compound”—that particles such as *nis* and others convey meanings such as “having crossed” (*krānta*). In examples such as *niṣkauśāmbi*, the particles like *nis* themselves convey the meaning of “having crossed” by virtue of their semantic power; thus, because the meaning has already been expressed, words such as *krānta* are not used at all in the compound.

And it has been said: “For prepositions (*upasarga*) are of this nature: where a word expressing an action is heard, they qualify that action; elsewhere, they express a means (*sādhana*) qualified by an action. (329)
These are indeed other words, like synonyms used in common parlance; however, their specific meaning is restricted by the context and the purpose.

If that is so, then in cases such as "the tree stands" (*vṛkṣastiṣṭhati*) or "he has departed from Kauśāmbī," what is the purpose of employing verbs like *tiṣṭhati*? One might argue that one should employ only the nominal word "tree" (*vṛkṣaḥ*) and so forth everywhere, since the meaning of a sentence can be conveyed by nominal words alone. To this he says: the word "tree" (*vṛkṣa*) that conveys the sentence-meaning is one thing entirely different from the sentence "the tree stands" (*vṛkṣastiṣṭhati*). Due to their similarity, the word "tree" in the phrase "the tree stands" is treated as if it were the single word "tree" (*vṛkṣaḥ*).

[The opponent] thinks: "Let it be so; why is the word *vṛkṣa* alone not used at all times? For from that alone, by means of implication (*sāmarthya*) and so forth, the meaning 'the tree stands' is understood. What is the use of this prolixity of using such expressions as 'the tree stands'? To this he replies with the words "synonym" (*paryāya*). This is what is meant: in common linguistic usage (*laukika-śabda-vyavahāra*), because there is no regard for brevity (*lāghava*), sometimes the word *vṛkṣa* is used and sometimes *vṛkṣastiṣṭhati*.

Just as there is no fault in worldly people employing the word *pādapa* when the meaning of "tree" is already understood through the word *taru* alone for the sake of brevity; so too, one might ask: how could the mere nominal word *vṛkṣa* ("tree")—as in "let some tree be seen" or "there is some tree"—convey a specific, determined meaning? To this he says: "By the meaning... (verse 330). The specific meaning of these single-word sentences is established by means of both the context of the meaning (*artha*) and the context of the discourse (*prakaraṇa*).
However, those means of awakening which are directed toward this or that particular person are not necessarily connected with the object to be known through the words [used]. (331)

Thus, since the sentence-meaning exists as a true reality within the indivisible sentence, he asks: what is the use of imagining word-meanings, divisions of sentences, and subdivisions of words? He says: "This is what is meant"—those means for awakening one to the sentence-meaning depend upon specific individuals, and those word-meanings are indeed unreal. He says: "Not necessarily. This means that they are not necessarily connected with the knowable, denotable, and real worldly object; therefore, they are said to be unreal. (331)
Even when there is no actual comprehension, or when there is a false presentation, those respective words remain established as eternally connected with their own meanings. (332)

Now, if the definition of the relationship between word and meaning is based on the passage beginning with "atha yasminnuccarite" (when [the word] is uttered), then—given that after a word has been uttered, either because the listener’s mind is distracted by something else or because no convention (*saṅketa*) has been established—the meaning might not be understood; or, due to some error, it might be understood otherwise. In such cases, since the meaning is not apprehended, the relationship between word and meaning would necessarily be non-eternal (*anitya*). But this is not tenable. Therefore, the proponent of *śrutārthāpatti* (presumption from what is heard) states in order to demonstrate [his point]: "Those various words, because the relationship of the word is eternal, are established as being exclusively expressive of fixed meanings. (332)
In this scriptural injunction regarding the action "open the door," whether one should "fasten it" or "give it" is understood through the context.

If the meaning were not understood due to some cause, it would follow that the relationship between word and meaning is lost; therefore, he says the following in order to demonstrate that the comprehension of the sentence-meaning in the case of single words is justified through the mental supply (*adhyāhāra*) of other words: "Without overstepping the context, the means [of action] implies the action because of its invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvitā*); thus, in the expression 'door, door,' the heard mention of the object implies the sense 'fasten' or 'give' by way of the word expressing it, through such means as the context. This alone is logical. || 333 ||
A word whose function [in a syllogism] consists in the means of proof and which is based on a substantive entity (sattva) does not denote the primary object that is to be proven (sādhya). (334)

Having thus stated the impermanence of the relationship between word and meaning in the definition of word and meaning beginning with "When [the word] is uttered," he says the following to state another objection: "Having manifested its own object alone, that [word], being expectant, ceases; but its related object manifests its presence. (335)

Since a word that expresses the function of a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*)—being primarily concerned with the substance (*sattva*)—cannot logically be the designator of that very object which is the primary thing to be conveyed if that object were non-existent, because of the contradiction; therefore, this is what is rightly said here: "Whether it be a verbal form (*ākhyāta-śabda*) or a nominal form (*nāma-śabda*), having conveyed its own meaning alone, it ceases while still being dependent and expectant. But the meaning belongs to that [word] once it has ceased."

It brings about the proximity of another meaning by means of the conceptualization of a word that denotes it; and thus, it is only logical that the cognition of the sentence-meaning arises in its complete form. || 335 ||

Since the status of being for the sake of another is not distinct [in this case], there is no proximity of word to word from the word; nor is there proximity of word to meaning from the meaning, nor proximity of meaning to word from the word. (336)

Now, the proponent of the indivisible [unitary] word (*akhaṇḍavādī*) speaks in order to refute the proponent of presumptive implication based on what is heard (*śrutārthāpattivādī*): "In this case, regarding the statement 'Fat Devadatta does not eat during the day,' it is said that Devadatta’s fatness—which is otherwise inexplicable without eating—implies his eating at night by means of the postulation of a word expressive of that [eating]. Now, in this matter, is a word implied by a word, or is a word [implied] by a meaning, or is a meaning [implied] by a word, or is a meaning [implied] by a meaning? These are the four possible alternatives."

In this regard, the implication of one word by another word is not tenable, because a word implies itself only when conveying its own meaning. To this, he says: "The proximity of a word does not [arise] from a word. Now, if it is argued that the word is implied by the meaning, to this he says: "The proximity of a word does not [arise] from the meaning. Nor is the implication of a word tenable; rather, it is logical that the expressed object (vācya) implies the expressive word (vācaka). Therefore, since there is no relationship of expressed and expresser between the meaning of one word and another word, how could a word be implied by a meaning?

Now, if it is argued that when a word is uttered, the object denoted by the word—conceived through presumptive testimony based on what has been heard—is implied, that too is untenable; thus he says: "There is no presence of the object [merely] from the word."

The proximity of a meaning denoted by another word to a [given] word is not possible, precisely because the relationship of signifier and signified does not exist; how then could there be an implication (*ākṣepa*) of a meaning by a word? If it is argued that "a meaning is understood through a meaning," this clearly becomes nothing other than inference (*anumāna*), and it would follow that this is not the meaning of the word—thus the very unity of the word would be abandoned. For this reason alone, the presentation of the fourth alternative here does not violate propriety, and thus its refutation has simply not been made.

Therefore, the claim that the comprehension of the sentence-meaning occurs through the implication of other words by means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) based on a single word is trivial. One must simply maintain that a single word itself, even without a connection to other words, is capable of conveying its respective meaning by virtue of context and other such factors. || 336 ||
It is declared that the nature [of the action] has vanished when it is cast aside by the proponent of the action, if primacy were simultaneously attained by both the state and the entity. (337)

Again, the proponent of *śrutārthāpatti* (presumption based on what is heard) says: If it is argued that in the expression "door, door, action" (*dvāraṃ dvāraṃ karma*), the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is implied by the word "action" (*karma*) itself as something virtually non-existent, then it would follow that two mutually contradictory meanings—one established and one unestablished—would simultaneously be denoted as the primary sense within a single word; and this is not observed. Previously, it was stated by the phrase "wherein the operation of the means [of proof occurs]" (*yatra sādhanavṛttiḥ*) that that which has existence as its primary sense cannot logically be a denoter of the meaning of a verbal suffix.
Now, however, it is stated that the particle *prati* expresses a contrary meaning; this is the distinction. || 337 ||
By means of those [words], the verbal form of the noun is described; through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), linguistic usage is distinguished. (338)

The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*) says: "Door, door"—this is indeed already explained; however, that which is similar in form to a noun (*nāmapada*) is now being described. Therefore, like other nouns, this too, primarily expressing action, is simply a signifier similar in form to a noun. If this is so, why is the accusative case heard after it? To this he replies: "Because of the connection" (*anvaya*).

In expressions such as "close each vessel" (*bhāṇḍaṃ bhāṇḍaṃ pidhehi*) and "close each door" (*dvāraṃ dvāraṃ pidhehi*), it is observed that the verb denotes the action (*kriyā*), while the noun denotes the substance (*dravya*). Through the methods of agreement and difference (*anvaya-vyatireka*), even in other cases where there is a single word such as "door" (*dvāram*), because of its similarity [to the aforementioned nouns], it indeed denotes the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*); thus, the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) is correctly applied. || 338 ||

Nor does the capacity to denote cease even when there is doubt regarding its form; just as, for example, one half of an animal [is determined] through contextual implication (*samarthya*), so too is that [denotative power] conceptualized. (339)

Now, since the word *dvāram* (door) signifies multiple meanings, a doubt arises as to how its denotative function (*vācakatva*) can be established. He says: "Even when there is a similarity of form, the determination of the meaning is settled through context (*sāmarthya*) and so forth. He states this by saying "half" (*ardham*). Here, a doubt arises as to whether the "half" refers to a part of an animal or a part of Devadatta belonging to the owner of the animal. In that case, is the sentence non-denotative (*avācaka*) despite the doubt? No; rather, the meaning is indeed determined therein by means of the sense (*artha*), context (*prakaraṇa*), and other factors. || 339 ||

If every word denoting a substance (*sattvapada*) were dependent upon a conceptual construction (*bhāvanibandhana*), then its meaning would not be distinct from its association [with other words], provided it is not differentiated from them. (340) In that case, the statement that "the verb (*ākhyāta*) has action as its primary meaning, while nouns (*nāman*) have substance as their primary meaning," and that "there are four classes of words"—all of this would be contradicted. (341)
He urges: "The meaning is clear. (340–341)
Having observed that a sentence is eternal in the intellect and possesses worldly connection with meaning, Vārtika and Audumbarāyaṇa maintain that there is no fourth [category].

To refute this objection, the Teacher says: Having observed the eternity of the indivisible sentence within the intellect—that is, within the intellect of the perceiver—and likewise having observed its connection (saṃbandha), characterized as a sudden flash of intuition (pratibhā), with its meaning, the conceptualization of "words" and the conceptualization of "word-meanings" therein simply does not arise; thus the Teacher has stated. Therefore, our fear that the fourfold nature of words is untenable is groundless. || 342 ||
Pervasive and concise, linguistic usage based on words is conceived through distinct divisions for practical purposes in both worldly convention and the treatises.

If this is so, one might ask: "What is the use of a treatise? To this he says: The linguistic usage of sentences, which is based on words, has been taught by the treatise as being pervasive and the cause for the thorough knowledge of all correct words; since it is thus established through systematic analysis, what here is inconsistent? || 343 ||
In the world, established conventions do not arise from the mere connection with objects for those who employ them; therefore, nothing other than the sentence exists that is non-worldly.

Now, raising the objection: "If the distinction between words and their referents is entirely unreal, how can worldly people have functions and so forth based upon them? he says: "In the world, for those who perceive, conventional success—the accomplishment of linguistic usage—does not arise solely from a connection with real objects; for even by means of what is unreal, such as the perception of water in mirages, that [usage] is seen among them."

Alternatively, just as in the case of the line-drawn gavaya (*rekhāgavaya*), even though it is unreal, through this means there indeed occurs a thorough comprehension of the real sentence. In every respect, one must not say that for people there are no activities and so forth without a purpose; rather, it should be understood that sometimes the cognition of the object "gavaya" is produced in him by a real gavaya, and sometimes by a line-drawn gavaya.

Since this is so, the cognition of the sentence-meaning is produced from that real sentence as an indivisible whole; therefore, there exists neither any extraordinary real entity nor any real word, because such a thing lacks logical justification. || 344 ||

And those [meanings] indicated in sentences by means of signs heard elsewhere are understood as being their own primary meanings; they remain unperceived [as secondary] because there is no difference in their form. (345)

He states that a meaning which is to be understood through an indicator (*jñāpaka*) is everywhere understood from the sentence itself: regarding the doubt in the passage "one places the smeared pebbles" (*aktāḥ śarkarā upadadhāti*) as to whether they are smeared with oil or with ghee, elsewhere [in the Veda] there is a praise of ghee beginning with "Ghee is indeed splendor" (*tejo vai ghṛtam*). By this, it is indicated that what is prescribed here is anointing with ghee. Therefore, it should be understood that in the sentence "the smeared [pebbles]," etc., the meaning of the sentence is known to be "one places them smeared with ghee."

If the meaning "he places them smeared with ghee" is understood from the very word *yadyaktāḥ* (if they are smeared), why does he say "according to an indicative mark (*jñāpaka*)"? He replies: "Because there is no difference in form, they are not distinguished. Seeing that the form is identical in the sentence "he places the pebbles smeared," and being unable to perceive a distinction, the determination of the meaning here is established by following the indicative mark; thus, the claim that parts of sentences exist within sentences is indeed without authority. || 345 ||

That which is abandoned in the statement of general rule (*utsarga-vākya*)—though appearing as if wordless—is heard as if possessed of words within the subverting statements (*bādhaka-vākyas*); it is understood elsewhere. (346)

Now, in order to determine the relationship between the sublated and the sublator, he says: "In the general definition, which is the primary statement, that which was initially set aside because it is overtaken by an exception—was that actually abandoned by the word? No; he says: 'as if it were not expressed by the word.'"

"How was it abandoned as if due to the absence of an indicator (*bodhaka*)? It was abandoned just like the word [itself], like the indicator; for it is understood that the rule prescribing the suffix *aṇ* after a verbal root when a direct object is present applies specifically to those roots not overridden by exceptions. Otherwise, if it were to apply without distinction, how could it later be excluded from those roots ending in long *ā*? Therefore, by virtue of reflecting upon the intended meaning (*tātparya*), the sentence-meaning is indeed understood to be that [the suffix] occurs in the domain of roots not overridden by exceptions—so says the author of that [work].

This was not determined at that very time; however, it is understood that when one later encounters subverting statements, what was heard there is excluded elsewhere by means of the general definition. || 346 ||
The Vedic revelation of the Brahmins has proceeded with curd, excluding Māṭhara; because of his connection with whey, Māṭhara explains the matter there according to its true meaning.

To explain this very point by means of a worldly illustration, he says: In the case of the statement, "Let curd be given to the Brahmins," it should be understood that the giving of curd to the Brahmins has commenced there, excluding Māṭhara. Subsequently, the statement, "Buttermilk for Māṭhara," attains its meaningfulness only by setting aside its own object as a sublater of the actual [prior] sense. Thus, one should understand that "sublation" (bādha) is the inference of non-attainment based on the assumption of a distinct sentence. || 347 ||
Even when there is a connection with multiple verbs, some maintain that the sentence is indeed one, though it appears as if it were divided, consisting of a general rule and its exception. (348)

Now, relying precisely on the status of being a single sentence (*ekavākyatā*), he says the following in order to demonstrate the relationship between the sublated and the sublator (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) regarding general rules (*utsarga*) and exceptions (*apavāda*): "Some maintain that even when there is a difference in verbal forms (*ākhyātabheda*) between a general rule and its exception, or between two exceptions, they must be understood as a single sentence; though at that moment it may appear to be distinct sentences, in reality, one should understand that a sentence has attained the status of a single sentence by virtue of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), semantic competency (*yogyatā*), and proximity (*saṃnidhi*). (348)
In that case, restriction and prohibition are supplementary to the injunction; they know that which is called elision (*luk*) in the second [type] to have *aluk* as its supplement. (349)

This being the case, he says that this must be understood therein: the rule beginning with *iko guṇavṛddhī* is a supplement (*śeṣa*) to the prescription of *guṇa* in *sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ*. When these two are unified into a single syntactical statement (*ekavākyatā*), the meaning of the sentence is understood as: "when *sārvadhātuka* or *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes follow, a *guṇa* occurs in place of the *ik* (i, u, ṛ) of the *aṅga*. Otherwise, if *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* were to operate first in place of the *ik* of the *aṅga*, what would be the purpose of the subsequent restrictive rule?

And it has been said: "For if one were to say to someone who has already finished eating, 'Do not eat,' what would have been accomplished by that? Likewise, even a prohibition attains its fruitfulness only by entering into syntactic unity with a positive injunction; thus he says, "And the prohibition... The meaning is that the prohibition must be understood as being merely a supplement to the injunction.

It should be understood that by the rule *aluguttarapade*, the prohibition of elision (*luk-pratiṣedha*) being stated with respect to a following final member (*uttarapada*), functions as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to the rule for elision of case-endings (*supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ*), thereby conveying the intended meaning through syntactic unity (*vākyaikavākyatā*). To demonstrate this very point, he says: "In the second [chapter]. Commentators know that the prohibition of elision found in the sixth [chapter] is a supplementary subordinate element (*śeṣa-aṅga*) to the rule for elision taught in the second chapter. || 349 ||
Being independent regarding their own cessation and being primary in relation to one another, since they do not assist each other, how could there be a single unified statement among them? (350)

Alternatively, the proponent of the doctrine of syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) says: "Sentences are indeed devoid of expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣa*) when there is completion through specific qualifications. Therefore, these [sentences] are designated as being mutually independent; there is no relationship of principal and subordinate (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) among them. Consequently, since there is an absence of the relationship of beneficiary and benefactor (*upakāryopakārakabhāva*) between them, how can a purposeless mutual dependence be postulated? Thus, there is no single sentence (*ekavākyatā*). This is the prima facie position (*pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ*). ||350||

Because there is a desire for a specific injunction, a supplementary statement (vākyaśeṣa) is inferred; therefore, the requirement [for such a supplement] is equal when the object to be accomplished possesses specific qualities. || 351 ||

Now, the proponent of the theory of a single sentence (ekavākyavādin) says: "In every case, the remainder of a general statement (utsargavākya) is inferred; why? He says: 'By means of a specific injunction,' and so forth. Otherwise, its application would be non-specific, just like any other separate sentence. But this is not proper; therefore, there is indeed a requirement for the object to be excluded—that is, the object to be prohibited.

Thus, since the mutual dependence between those two is equal, it is stated that unity of sentence (ekavākyatā) alone is superior, because they attain the relationship of principal and subordinate through their mutual connection, such as expectancy (ākāṅkṣā), by virtue of the consideration of their meaning. || 351 ||
That which is a portion of a name or a word does not undergo elision; that name, being a specific form, does not cease to exist anywhere. (352)

It has been established through four modes that parts of sentences exist within sentences by way of ellipsis (*uddhāra*): by means of context and meaning, as in the case of "the chest" (*vakṣaḥ*) and so forth; by means of conventional usage (*prasiddhi*), as in "it rains" (*varṣati*) and so forth; by means of indicative mark (*liṅga*), as in "the sugar-cubes are smeared" (*aktāḥ śarkarāḥ*) and so forth; and by means of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and the proximity of another sentence, as in "Let curd be given to the Brahmins, but buttermilk to Kauṇḍinya," and likewise in grammatical rules such as "the suffix *aṇ* after a verbal root ending in an object" (*karmaṇyaṇ*) and "the suffix *ka* after a root ending in long *ā*, provided no preposition precedes" (*ātonupasarge kaḥ*).

Now, by way of an incidental discussion based on the method of exclusion (*apoddhāra*), he begins to investigate how parts of words exist within whole words: "In this world, names such as *Devadatta* and others are established; therein, we observe people sometimes using the form *devaḥ* and sometimes *dattaḥ*. How is this justified? For among those name-words, neither their parts nor their elision are taught anywhere in the grammatical treatise."

He states that even instruction cannot be performed by him, beginning with the words "viśiṣṭarūpa" and so forth. For in the world, when a collection of words consisting of a fixed sequence of phonemes is employed as a name, then the constituent parts contained within it are necessarily employed as well; just as a tree moving moves along with its parts, according to common usage, does this [name] become expressive while lacking some phonemes? Indeed, that which possesses a fixed sequence is made complete and does not cease to be so. (352)
Furthermore, no name other than "Datta" and the like is perceived; how then could the word "Datta" denote the bearer of that name, known as Devadatta? (353)

Now, it might be argued that this word "Datta," being fully understood, causes its own bearer (the person) to be cognized; anticipating this, he says: "The word 'Datta' is independent and is simply another name for someone else. Therefore, how could another name, 'Devadatta,' be cognized [as referring to that same person]? For it is a different word and the convention has not been established [between them]. This is the intended meaning. Furthermore, he says "the bearer of the name" (*saṃjñinam*) to show that the word "Datta" alone is not capable of making known the person who is its referent.

If the word *datta* has a completely different designatum (*saṃjñin*) as its object of cognition, how could it cause that [designatum] to be cognized which is denoted by another word? Thus, in this way, the elision of even a single part of that [word] consisting of a fixed sequence of phonemes is not possible; nor is the cognition of the word *devadatta*, which constitutes a part of it, possible from either the word *datta* or the word *deva*; and as for the cognition of its designatum in that case, this is merely a trifle. (353) Some maintain that the individual forms of words have a relationship equal to that of the whole with all their constituent parts, just as a collection [is related to its members]. (354)

To present another view on this matter, he says: "How can the relationship between the designator and the designated be equal in all its parts and simultaneous, just as it is for a whole? Just as the whole is appointed as its designator, so too at that very same time its parts [are appointed]; therefore, what fault is there in saying that a single part of it effects the cognition of it? (354)

The meaningfulness of phonemes, however, arises through their relationship with the things they name; a related constituent part cannot be conceived when there is no distinction from the name itself. (355)

To demonstrate two objections here, he says: "The phonemes that constitute names would then possess meaning by virtue of their relationship to the named object (*saṃjñin*). Consequently, like a single part of one's own intended [word], even a single phoneme would become expressive. But this is not observed. Furthermore, it is not tenable that its individual parts are separately expressive. Thus he says: "Connected" (*sambaddha*).

That constituent part which is conceived by you as the expressive unit is indeed employed as expressive only when it is connected [to others]; its status as an expressive unit cannot be postulated when it is extracted from the aggregate and exists in isolation, because it is of a different nature [than when combined]. || 355 ||

When there is a simultaneous connection with all the individual forms of the named object, it is impossible for that object to be conveyed by means of [words] that resemble only a single part [of those forms]. (356)

To demonstrate this very point with another verse, he says: "In a connection with the forms of all parts simultaneously, those [sounds] denoting a single part are not tenable; or rather, to demonstrate that they are not parts of that [whole], he says: 'Not from those similar to a single part,' and so forth. It was stated, "from those similar to a single part. Those [sounds], such as *dat* and so on, are similar to a single part, but they are not actually parts of that [whole]. (356)
However, from a single part, the memory of the whole arises for some; and from the word, which is the object of that memory, the meaning of the whole is understood. (357)
He states another opinion—the meaning is clear. || 357 ||
How can memory arise from a single part regarding a composite whole that is distinct [from it]? And how could a word, being perceived [as such], be the designator of an object? (358)

To refute this, he says: It is well known that memory arises from the perception of a similar object. In that case, how can memory arise from that aggregate which possesses a distinct nature? And how could that [aggregate], being perceived, be logically established as the designator of the named person Devadatta? If that which is merely perceived were the expressive word, there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga). It is well known that words which have entered the path of hearing are the expressors. || 358 ||

However, those words which are partially similar and endowed with various respective indicative marks are established as technical terms (saṃjñā) by virtue of being produced in accordance [with them]. (359)

He states the established conclusion (siddhānta): "But when a composite whole is employed as a technical name (saṃjñā), at that very time the constituent parts within it, which possess a form similar [to the whole], are also employed as technical names; thus, they should be understood as established as technical names by way of being produced as a consequence (anuniṣpādin). || 359 ||

Because they are common [to all], they are ambiguous; by virtue of their functional capacity, they have fixed bases. Among those, for the correct forms, elision and other operations are taught in the grammatical treatise.

Although the constituent parts contained within [the compound] are employed according to the principle of "simultaneous production" (*anuniṣpādinyāya*), they are nonetheless unable to denote the named object (*saṃjñin*) because they are common [to many]. For instance, the word *deva* denotes the gods as well as some particular named object; likewise, the word *datta* is both a verb (denoting an action) and a proper name. In that case, how could there be a cognition of a specific named object from these [words]? Anticipating this doubt, he says—[in order to establish their restricted meaning]—"restricted to a specific substratum by virtue of semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) and so forth."

Proper names (*saṃjñā*) are established as denoters; it is stated that for these very [names], which arise as secondary products (*anuniṣpādin*), grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) is declared through the mechanism of rules regarding elision (*lopa*) and so forth in the treatise (*śāstra*). Thus he says: "Of those," and so on. Therefore, in the case of Devadatta, the name-word *datta*—which is common to the independent word *datta* expressing the action—is a proper name; one should understand that the word *deva* is also a proper name, and because it arises as a secondary product, it is included within that [compound]. This very fact is explained in the treatise by means of elision and other operations, as it has been said: "In the case of a suffix beginning with a non-consonant (*an*), starting from the fourth [letter], there is elision of the preceding member," and so forth. (360)

When the simultaneous production [of suffixes] is equal, forms such as *jye* and *drāghā* are incorrect; for there is no traditional rule (*smṛti*) regarding them in the explanatory treatise, as there is for *datta* and other such names.

To clarify this, he says: Just as in a composite word (*samudāya*), the constituent *pada*s are employed there according to the principle of "consequent production" (*anuniṣpādinyāya*), it is not the case here that the phonemes (*varṇa*) are employed among themselves even though they are produced in succession. Furthermore, in the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*), phonemes such as *jy* and so on—found in words like *jyeṣṭha*—are not accepted as being correct (*sādhavaḥ*) in their own right; thus, it should be understood that in the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*) as well, the descriptive grammarian (*anvākhyāyaka*) follows up only those [forms] that have already become established in such a way.
Therefore, these phonemes such as *gh* and so on are not denoters (*vācaka*) of the meanings expressed by words such as *magha*. || 361 ||
And those words which have the suffix -ṇatva, such as *kharaṇasa* and others, are declared by the wise to be correct because they are taught as denoting a single substance.

Now, in the context of investigating whether parts of words exist within words, he speaks in order to resolve the doubt that the relationship between a word and its meaning is non-eternal regarding technical (saṃjñā) terms: "In this case, do technical terms possess their defining characteristics prior to the connection with the thing designated (saṃjñin), or subsequent to it? If [they possess them] prior, then since it would not be the designation of anything, how could there be an operation based upon it? To this it is replied: "In this regard, wherever the status of being a designation arises from the connection between the designation and the thing designated, there the defining characteristic applies."

Now, one might raise the objection that if the status of being a technical name (*saṃjñātva*) occurs at a later time—that is, if the application of the definition occurs later—then this word, having previously not possessed the change of *ṇatva*, would now acquire *ṇatva*, and thus words would be subject to impermanence. Anticipating this, he says: "Those which have undergone the change of *ṇatva," and so forth. Here there are two groups: one group consists of those that have undergone the change of *ṇatva* and is eternal; the other consists of those that have not undergone the change of *ṇatva*. Among these, those which have undergone the change of *ṇatva* are the correct [words] and are indeed eternal, because they are taught as denoting a single substance; the meaning is that by their very nature, they are technical names (*saṃjñāśabda*).

In the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*), by the rule "pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām agaḥ," the correctness of those very [words] with the *ṇatva* applied is prescribed; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever in saying that these are stated as having the *ṇatva* applied by resorting to the formal derivation (*prakriyā*) within the treatise. || 362 ||

But they say that these are indeed *gotras* (lineages/species), because of their association with the capacity for designation; the requirement of a causal basis (*nimitta*) in relation to their own referents is not necessarily intended in their case. (363)

To demonstrate this very point, he says: "The classes of words consisting of names are established; in them, no search for a further cause is required regarding their own referent, the named object, because the relationship between word and meaning is eternal. Since those [words] are fixed upon their own expressed objects as denoters, the search for another cause beyond their own nature is simply non-comprehensive. (363)

A restriction of names to a named object exists in some cases for the sake of conventional usage; however, the relationship is indeed eternal, as in the case of "Dittha" and so forth, just like [the relationship between] a cow and its name.

But is it not the case that the eternality of technical terms (*saṃjñā-śabda*) is untenable, because they are created at present? For technical terms are established by being assigned arbitrarily according to human will. And it has been said: "Because it is produced, the relationship [between a term and its object] is non-eternal; for that [relationship] of a technical term is assigned by persons according to their desire."

For instance, just as names such as "Madhura" and so forth are assigned by children to lines drawn in the dust, one might suspect that this same conceptualization applies to all names; anticipating this, he says the following to provide support: "In the case of words that are names, if at some point a mere convention is established by persons for the sake of practical usage with respect to a named object..."

Just as in this house, from today onwards, it should be understood that "this one is the referent of the word *ḍittha*," the relationship between word and meaning in the case of names such as *ḍittha* is indeed eternal, characterized by innate fitness (*yogyatā*). As he will state: "Just as the sense organs possess an innate fitness toward their respective objects, so too the relationship of words with their meanings is an innate fitness. Thus, just as the word *go* (cow) and others possess denotative power through an eternal relationship of fitness toward cows and so forth, the same should be understood to apply to names such as *ḍittha*.

And in this treatise, the relationship between the augment (vṛddhi) and the other [grammatical elements] is an uncreated one, characterized by the delimitation of their respective powers, just like that between a qualifier and a qualificand. (365)

He states that even in the technical treatise (*śāstra*), the rule of linguistic usage regarding technical terms (*saṃjñā-śabda*) is to be understood in exactly the same way: "In the treatise, there is the possession of the capacity to illuminate all meanings for technical terms such as *vṛddhi* and so on, and there is the fitness for being denoted by specific words for the things named (*saṃjñin*), such as *āT*, *aiC*, and so on. Therefore, in the treatise alone, the capacity of terms like *vṛddhi* is restricted solely to the designation of *āT*, *aiC*, etc., by distinguishing them from other technical terms; likewise, for *āT*, *aiC*, etc., their status as being denotable by words such as *vṛddhi* is established."

It is precisely the innate restriction (*pratiniyama*) between the signified and the signifier that is being stated here, and not the imposition of an artificial relationship; just as the relationship between a qualifier and a qualified consists solely of their beginningless status as denotable by words, and it is not the case that the connection with "blue" and so forth is produced there by a person. || 365 ||

Depending on the intrinsic nature of a conceptualization, some worldly [conceptualization] proceeds when a causal sign (nimitta) is present, while another proceeds even in the absence of a causal sign. (366)

Then, in order to investigate the cause for the application of designations (*saṃjñā*), he says: "The very nature (*svarūpa*) of all words that are designations should be understood as the cause for their application. When that [nature] exists, in some cases there is a cause that conforms to an external object, while in others—such as in the case of *ḍittha* and so on—there is simply its absence; this is stated by some. (366)
In the treatise, however, the great designation is based on its own essential nature; it is recognized as inference when the cause is present. (367)

It is not only the very form of single-syllable words that exists as the ground for their application (*pravṛttinimitta*) there; rather, one must understand that even for long [compounds], the very form itself, as it is bound together, is the ground for their application. Thus he says: "In that case, when the meaning of the individual parts (*avayavārtha*) of the ground is present, an inference is perceived regarding its existence; the meaning is that by means of inference, the meaning of the individual parts is also perceived as being a ground for application there. (367)
In that case, either an inference from recurrence is understood through similarity, or there is an inference from the difference in words, or a comprehension of the difference in capacities.

"How is that [word] inferred? he says: "That very same [word] repeats itself twice; by one [repetition], the cognition of the name is established as having its own nature defined, and by the other, its dependence on the meaning of its constituent parts is determined. [Objection: "But is the repetition not itself inferred? What if it were your intention there that [the word is repeated] because of being uttered twice? He says: "Because of similarity" (*sārūpyāt*). Because of similarity, it is understood that the word is uttered as one and the same.

Alternatively, he says "or there is an inference from the difference in words," meaning that it is inferred that two distinct words have been uttered by way of ellipsis (*tantra*). Thus, by one [word] there is the comprehension of the named object whose identity was concealed by its own form, and by the other, there is the connection with the meaning of the constituent parts. To demonstrate the third position as well, he says "or it is the apprehension of a difference in power. That same single word, possessing two powers, is uttered; therefore, by one [power] there is the comprehension of the named object, and by the other, there is the connection with the meaning of the constituent parts. || 368 ||
In some cases, artificial [distinctions] are established through a difference in objects; however, regarding number, the establishment of a single object applies to both as well. (369)

Now, since in this treatise there occurs the adoption of the non-artificial (laukika) sense in some places, the artificial (kṛtrima) technical (pāribhāṣika) sense in others, and sometimes both possibilities, and because in certain cases the non-artificial sense alone is adopted due to its pervasiveness while the other [the artificial] also extends over its own domain, he speaks in order to demonstrate the fourfold nature of technical terms: "The artificial is said to be technical (pāribhāṣika), pertaining to the science."

That [term] is established through a distinction of scope, but it does not apply in the same way everywhere. For example, in the rule *kateri karmavyatihāre*, the non-artificial (*akṛtrima*) is taken, because an artificial designation for "mutual exchange" (*vyatihāra*) is untenable here due to its being based on a technical name (*saṃjñā*). In the rule *karmaṇyaṇ*, the artificial is taken, while in *śabdavaira* etc., the non-artificial is taken; for the artificial [meaning] is untenable here because of the governing context of verbal roots (*dhātu-adhikāra*).

In the rule "The third case-affix is used for the agent and the instrument" (*kartṛkaraṇayos tṛtīyā*), he says "in the case of number" (*saṃkhyāyām*) in order to demonstrate that sometimes both types—artificial (*kṛtrima*) and non-artificial (*akṛtrima*)—are accepted in a single instance. Regarding the subject of number, there is recourse to both artificial and non-artificial [terms] in the grammatical system; for there is an acceptance of the artificial [term] such as *bahuguṇa*, *vatu*, and *ḍati* according to the rule "after *bahu*, *guṇa*, *vat*, and *uḍat*" etc., and also of the non-artificial [terms] such as *viṃśati* and so forth, provided they do not end in *atiśad*. This is understood from the prohibition [found elsewhere], which serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) here. || 369 ||
Even in the case of an artificial [word], a worldly person sometimes employs it as its object when addressing someone from afar; for such is the apprehension of those two.

To demonstrate that in some cases a non-artificial (akṛtrima) conventional term (*saṃjñāśabda*), even when employed, brings about the communication of an artificial one, he says: "A worldly, non-artificial conventional term, while being uttered, pervades the domain of an artificial, technical (*śāstrīya*) term. For example, in the rule *ekaśruti dūrāt sambuddhau*, the word *sambuddhi* [is understood] as 'addressing' (*sambodhana*) according to worldly usage; thus, even the technical sense of 'singular number' (*ekavacana*) is indeed grasped as *sambuddhi*, because addressing is present there as well. This is the meaning.
Regarding the cases of collective, residual, and dual [grammatical operations], some maintain that actions reside in each individual substratum by virtue of their inherent capacity.

Now, in the context of the investigation into sentences (*vākya*), in order to demonstrate that in some cases the completion of a sentence occurs in each individual [word] while in others it occurs in the aggregate, he says: "Like the sentence, the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*) also has its completion in each individual or in the aggregate. Thus, as an incidental discussion, he defines the completion of the sentence-meaning according to different views. Among these, he first demonstrates the completion of the sentence-meaning in each individual [word] with the words beginning: "In the case of *gaṇa*, *saṃgha*, *ekaśeṣa*, and *dvandva*," and so forth.

Sometimes the expression of meaning is carried out by means of a collective singular (*ekaśeṣa*), a dual, or a plural, as in: "The Brāhmaṇas should be fed," "A Brāhmaṇa should be fed," or "Devadatta, Yajñadatta, and Viṣṇumitra should be fed. In these cases, they maintain and accept that the act of eating, which constitutes the sentence-meaning and has the Brāhmaṇas as its agents, resides in each individual substratum (*pratyāśrayam*).

Of what nature is it? It is "characterized by capacity" (*sāmarthyalakṣaṇa*). This means that its nature (*svarūpa*)—whose definition (*lakṣaṇa*) consisting of capacity, which is of the nature of a functional state, will be explained further on—is such [a nature]; the meaning is that it is so because it is characterized by capacity. || 371 ||
The meal is completed in each [instance] by means of both the fruit and the form; for otherwise, if they were established separately, that purpose would not be achieved. (372)

Now, one might ask: why is the act of eating not completed by the mere collection of its constituent factors (*kāraka*), just as the act of drama is? To this he says: "In this world, the washing of the feet is done by one [person], the sitting upon the seat by another, the serving of food by another, and the swallowing of the food by yet another; thus, the act of eating cannot be accomplished in such a manner. For this act of eating is accomplished through its fruit—characterized by satisfaction—in a form where the serving of food and so forth, as well as the eating of the food, share a single substratum (*ekādhikaraṇa*); likewise, it is not accomplished when there is no such reliance [upon a single substratum]."

Because the action of eating is not completed until its cessation, it is directly perceived that this [action], having different substrates, does not divide the essential nature [of the agent]. || 372 ||

And all individuals partake individually of the act of eating—consisting of the taking of food and so forth—which results in the fruit of satisfaction; but they do not [partake] like a theatrical performance.

To clarify this very point, he says: "For the natures of things are seen to be fixed; an action that is accomplished by multiple means does not arise as fruitful [if it lacks a fixed nature], whereas the action of eating is something whose accomplishment depends on each individual factor—such is the nature of things. (373)

Like water for the feet, it remains distinct according to its capacity; the verb *bhuj* performs the action for the sake of the object of enjoyment, not by a single simultaneous application (*tantra*), as in the case of a lamp. (374)

He explains this very point by means of another illustration: Just as in the rite of ancestral offerings (*śrāddha*), the performer prepares water for washing the feet (*pādya*) with many separate vessels for the purpose of honoring the Brahmins, so too this act of eating, by virtue of its inherent capacity and the nature of things, remains distinct for each individual. It does not, however, function through a single common substratum (*tantra*) like a lamp, producing the result of eating—namely, satisfaction—for all simultaneously. || 374 ||
But even a single action such as "seeing" may, when applied to such objects of action, pertain to a collection [of instances] even without repetition. (375)

Now, in order to demonstrate that other actions, like the act of eating, may reach completion as a collective whole by relying on several distinct actions, he says: In the case of the sentence "Devadatta, Yajñadatta, and Viṣṇumitra, let them be seen," the act of seeing (*dṛśi-kriyā*)—unlike the act of eating—is not possible without reaching completion with respect to each individual object situated in a suitable place; therefore, it is not so [treated]. Rather, in this instance, the act of seeing, which has the attainment of perception as its fruit, reaches its collective whole all at once; thus, it would be based upon the collective whole. || 375 ||
When one observes worldly transactions and the like, the agents whose modes of activity are distinct are seen individually as those who accomplish the purpose through their combined effort. (376)

Now, raising the doubt as to whether an action such as "cooking" (pacy-ādi-kriyā) is completed in its entirety by the whole collection [of factors] or whether it is completed in each individual factor, he says: "Devadatta cooks rice in a pot with firewood; he causes the grains of rice, which are softening, to soften. In this context, there is the observation of causal factors (*kāraka*) whose forms of activity are distinct; the activity is distinct, such as the act of requesting and so forth. These, when combined, are seen to be the accomplishers of the collective object characterized by the action of cooking, as observed in common usage and the like.

In this context, "usage" (vyavahāra) is intended to mean utility that pertains specifically to a fixed object. By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi), other such cases are encompassed. "The perception of those" means their undertaking or commencement; the meaning is: "when that exists. What is being said is this: some maintain that whether an action resides in the agent or in the object, the action of cooking (pacikriyā) inheres in the object and not in the aggregate [of the process].

Others, however, say: although [the action] inheres in the object (*karman*), nevertheless even the softening (*viklitti*) subordinate to the placing on the fire (*adhiśrayaṇa*) is the meaning of the root *pac*. Thus, in the absence of other intermediate actions, because there is no distinction in the operation of that which relies upon the principal action, it is brought about by all [factors] acting together; therefore, it is completed as a whole. || 376 ||

Because the object to be characterized is established by common worldly usage, because the indicative mark is seen in the treatise, and because of the desire [to know], the designation "vṛddhi" is completed through the distinction of the specific objects. (377)

Now, in order to demonstrate that in this treatise each individual word is complete in its own meaning, he says: "In the rule *vṛddhir ādaic*, the term *vṛddhi* is applied as a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) to each of the sounds *ā*, *ai*, and *au* individually; for in common usage, it is thus that a single referent is established—namely, *Āmraguptāyaniḥ*, *Aitikāyaniḥ*, and *Aupagavaḥ*."

Likewise, in the Śāstra, the designation *vṛddhi* is seen to apply to each of the vowels *ā*, *ai*, and *au* individually on the basis of indicative marks (*liṅga*). For example, in the rule *prasthe 'vṛddham akarkyādīnām* (P. 6.2.87) and *mālādīnām ca* (P. 6.2.88), it is stated that when *prastha* is the second member (*uttarapada*), the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) is acute (*udātta*) if it is not *vṛddha*; subsequently, it is stated that for *mālā* and so forth, the first vowel is acute. If the designation *vṛddhi* applied to each one [of the three vowels] individually, then by the rule *vṛddhir yasyācām ādis tad vṛddham* (P. 1.1.73), *mālā* and the others would be *vṛddha*. || 377 ||

In the act of taking a hundred, because it is the primary factor, and in the act of punishing for the offense of taking a hundred, even though there is a difference in the qualities of the claimants, the object to be counted does not differ. (378)

Now, in order to demonstrate that the completion of a sentence occurs in some cases within a collective whole (*samudāya*), he says: "In the case of 'Let the Gargas be fined one hundred,' the act of fining, which has the Gargas as its object, is completed with respect to the collective whole. Kings are seekers of gold, yet they do not fine each individual; for kings who understand the meaning of sentences discriminate between them, just as in this instance there are two types of actions: primary and secondary. Among these, in the fining that has 'one hundred' as its object, the taking of the hundred itself is the primary action."

If the gift of a hundred [cows] were completed for each individual, then the Gargas would have to be fined by the hundreds; consequently, there would be a destruction of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the primary rite (*pradhānakarman*). Furthermore, the abandonment of the purpose of the primary rite is not tenable. Therefore, if one were to resort to another number, there would be a contradiction of the sentence (*vākya*), because the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) would result in sublation.

In this case, even though there is a difference in the attributes (*guṇa*) and no difference in the object of punishment (*daṇḍya*), because they are subordinate, it should be understood that here the punishment does not apply to each individual king, but rather the punishment of one hundred kings remains as a collective whole for the sake of the purpose. What is meant is this: whether the completion of a sentence occurs with respect to each individual or with respect to the collective is not determined by the force of a royal command, but rather by the nature of the matter itself; thus, this should be known as established by logic (*nyāya*). || 378 ||

Because it is subject to the Saṃgha alone in the accomplishment of its business, the connection there [in the case] of the technical terms *samāsa* and *abhyasta* is by way of a single underlying principle (*tantra*). (379)

Now, in order to demonstrate this in the treatise (*śāstra*), he says: both the designation *samāsa* ("compound") and the designation *abhyasta* ("reduplicated") are completed only with respect to the aggregate (*samudāya*)—namely, by the rules "with a *sup*-ending word" (*saha supā*) and "both [halves] are *abhyasta*" (*ubhe abhyastam*). Here, the connection of both the designation *samāsa* and the designation *abhyasta* belongs to the aggregate alone, by virtue of their common application (*tantra*). Why? He says: "because it is the aggregate itself that is to be enjoined. For in this context, it is the aggregate alone that is prescribed; indeed, the designation *samāsa* is prescribed for that which consists of the form of the prior member (*pūrvapada*) and the subsequent member (*uttarapada*).

Regarding the phrase "tathā'bhyastam" (likewise, that which is practiced), the designation of *abhyasta* is prescribed for two [sounds] simultaneously in order to ordain a certain grammatical operation (*kārya*). Now, one might object: "In the case of the designation of a compound (*samāsa*), how can the entire aggregate [such as] *rājapuruṣa* and so forth be ordained? For, since the relations between words and their meanings are eternal, it is untenable for them to be subject to such an ordinance. Anticipating this doubt, the author states: "because it is presented as possessing an operation" (*kāryavatpratipādana*). This means that this was said when the position is being maintained that the linguistic analysis (*vyākhyāna*) proceeds by treating the aggregate as if it were something possessing a grammatical operation. || 379 ||
For those for whom praise has the purpose of defining characteristics with respect to some particular action, that dharma is indicated by them, both individually and collectively. (380)

Now, in order to demonstrate that in some cases the completion of a sentence is observed in both ways—either individually or collectively—he says: "Just as in the case of the statement, 'Vṛṣalas must not enter this house,' the entry of both individuals and those acting together is prohibited. (381)

He states an example: "In this case, the prohibition of entry for one belonging to the *vṛṣala* caste is being enacted. And since even a single *vṛṣala* exists therein, by implication, the purpose of the prohibition of entry is accomplished both individually and collectively. (380–381)

When the prohibition against acting together for the sake of desiring wealth and so forth is established, activity is not contradicted, because such activity is not prohibited when undertaken separately. || 382 ||

To demonstrate this by another method, he says: "From this day forward, none of you shall serve the king, nor shall you go to sea, nor shall you engage in agricultural work. In this case, whether the prohibition applies to the group as a whole or to each individual, there is no logical inconsistency in the operation of the sentence. || 382 ||

Because it has the sense of indicating a separation [of sounds], the rule beginning with "aṭ-ku-pu-āṅ" is likewise [applied]; thus, the status of being an *aṇ* is not prohibited either individually or collectively. (383)

To show a scriptural example here as well, he says: "The term *vyavāya* (separation) implies *vyavadhāna* (intervention); because it serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), since these [intervening elements]—namely *aṭ*, *ku*, *pu*, *āṅ*, and so forth—are present both individually and in combination, the occurrence of *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) is established by that very fact, and thus there is no fault whatsoever. (383)
When the act of eating is undertaken for the sake of favoring those who eat, yet that [act] does not favor them due to differences in place, time, and so forth; 384.

Now follows the investigation into the unity or multiplicity of the act of eating. In this regard, one must consider whether the act attains its essential nature when performed in a single place, time, and vessel, or whether it does so when performed with differences of place and so forth. To investigate this, he says: "Without distinction of place, time, and so on. Here, there is no difference whatsoever in the act of eating for the sake of bestowing grace; for in both cases, that grace is fully accomplished. || 384 ||
When multiplicity is taught of that which is single due to differences such as [different] vessels and so forth, or conversely, when unity is attributed to that which is divided. (385)
