Then, in order to investigate its unity and multiplicity, he says: In the view of one [teacher], the act of eating (*bhukti*) is indeed one, because it has a common fruit characterized by satisfaction; for him, there is multiplicity due to differences of place and time, but in itself it is simply one. However, in the view of another, since there is a difference in the fruit due to the difference in the eaters (*bhoktṛ*), there is indeed a difference in the act of eating. In the opposite case, because of the non-difference of the vessel and so forth, its unity is to be understood; yet by its very nature, it is indeed distinct. Such is the difference between the views. (385)
Even though they act together, they are presented as distinct; having each obtained their own respective food, they enjoy it collectively by sharing it out.

Furthermore: in the case of the sentence "Let Devadatta, Yajñadatta, and Viṣṇumitra be fed," although the meaning of the sentence is understood through distinction by virtue of the capacity [of the words], they nevertheless come together and consume their respective food portions collectively, due to the force of the intention [to feed them all]. (386)

Because there is no scope for distributive repetition (vīpsā), because it would contradict another number, and because completion in two ways is impossible, the hundred remains as a collective whole. (387)

Now, in order to establish the validity of the point to be demonstrated—that [the rule] is primarily concerned with the taking of a hundred—he says: "If one were to be fined a hundred for each [offense], then the scope of the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) would be lost; thus, in this case, a punishment consisting of a hundred acts is enjoined as the primary meaning. However, if a fine of a hundred were enjoined as the primary meaning for each individual [offender], then because a different number would arise for each individual fine, the number 'hundred' would be contradicted."

Nor, in this case, does the sentence terminate in two parts; for those who understand the meaning of sentences have reflected that one part is connected with the primary action and the other with the subsidiary actions, and thus it is said that the taking of a hundred is established as a single aggregate. || 387 ||
Where [the two arms] remain as the sole remainder by the rule of *ekaśeṣa* among many, there too the sentence is completed in two ways for the sake of indicating the characteristics. (388)

Now, even though the act of eating is completed for each individual, when it is said, "One must eat together with Devadatta, Yajñadatta, and Viṣṇumitra," the meaning of the sentence is completed in both ways—both individually and collectively. Thus he says: "Because it serves as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇārthatvāt*)," since in this case it is merely defined (*lakṣyate*) that there is either eating together or, conversely, the prohibition of that [eating] together.

In this regard, it is now stated whether one should eat together with many, or with two or three, or not at all. Thus, whether one should eat together or not, the injunction or prohibition is prescribed for the group as a whole; it should be understood that here the meaning of the sentence is completed both in the individual case and in the collective case, depending on whether the intended rule is merely the injunction to eat together or its prohibition. || 388 ||
Some maintain that each sentence is complete in itself; by this [view], there is a collection of sentences joined together in different forms. (389)

Thus, by relying on the meaning of the individual sentences, it has been demonstrated that there is a completion of the sentence in each [part] as well as a non-completion of the sentence in the aggregate. Now, in order to demonstrate this by relying on the sentence as a whole, he says: "In this context, whatever single sentence is heard, by means of that, the inclusion, definition, and communication of other sentences in the form of sentences is intended. Those [other sentences] are expressive. Therefore, the great sentence (mahāvākya) is completed in each [part], and from that, the comprehension of the meaning occurs in exactly that way. (389)
There are no distinct sentences that constitute the denotata of a sentence; rather, when that [sentence] is uttered, one likewise apprehends various distinctions within it. (390)

Alternatively, having raised the objection that perhaps a single one among those various sentences is said to be the expressive great sentence (*mahāvākya*), he says: "Therefore, when the meaning is understood from what has been uttered, it is said that the comprehension of the subordinate sentences (*avāntaravākya*) occurs by virtue of the reflection upon that meaning; however, it is not the case that they are denoted by it. (390)
For those for whom the entire meaning of a sentence is completed at each individual word, what purpose would there be at that time for the existence of a distinct word-meaning? (391)

Here, the proponent of the indivisible sentence (*akhaṇḍavākyavādin*), speaking with boldness, states the following in order to refute the position of the proponents of words (*padavādin*): "Since the indivisible sentence-meaning alone is fully established in each [word], word-meanings are of no use; therefore, the postulation of word-meanings is entirely futile. (391)
Now, if that very purpose produced by those [words] exists in a different form, there would either be a contradiction with the previous meaning or a coexistence with it. (392)

The proponent of the sentence (vākyavādī) speaks in order to raise an alternative: "Now, it might be said that the meaning of the sentence is produced by the word-meanings themselves and resides in distinct [entities]. In that case, there are two possible courses: either there would be a contradiction between the former [the word-meaning] and that [sentence-meaning], characterized by non-coexistence, or else there would be coexistence. (392)
If the qualified and the unqualified were co-existent, there would be contradiction; however, if the relationship is abandoned, it follows that the object is subject to deviation. (393)

Regarding their coexistence therein, he raises an objection—the meaning being that difference (*bheda*) and connection (*saṃsarga*) would here result in a contradiction. Now, if one argues that there is no simultaneous existence of the word-meaning (*padārtha*) and the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) here, such that the former—whether it be the word-meaning or the sentence-meaning—subsides once the sentence-meaning has been completed, then he states the fault: "it would be inconstant" (*vyabhicārī*). For if words, which have the sentence-meaning as their fruit, were to abandon the meanings they have already conveyed, it would follow that the relationship between word and meaning is inconstant and non-eternal.
Therefore, under the view that the sentence is completed with each individual word, there is simply no possibility of words or word-meanings existing as real entities. || 393 ||
One [meaning] is common and must be expressed as residing in every word; it is the essence of the meaning that manifests its presence both in the aggregate and in the individual members. || 394 ||

Now, regarding the view that the sentence is a single collective whole (*samudāya*) whose meaning is completed as a whole, he speaks in order to investigate whether only the collective entity (*saṅgha*) possesses meaning while its parts do not, or whether its parts also possess meaning: "That essence of meaning, which is the denotable, real, and characterized as the sentence-meaning—unitary and indivisible—is to be understood as residing in each word; for it exists as the common denotable object for all [the words]. Then, he says "and in the constituents" (*saṅghiṣu ca*) to show that it does not reside in those [words] alone.

Because it is common [to all], it is said to reside in the aggregate as well as in its individual parts. If it were situated within each individual word, then why would it not be perceived at the time of apprehending a single word? To this he says: "it is indicated by proximity. That is to say, it is one for which the proximity of other words is the indicator. As was stated previously: "The meaning, though complete in each [word] individually, resides in those that occur together.
Therefore, it is cognized at the time of apprehending the entire set of words; thus there is no fault whatsoever. || 394 ||

Just as ownership of wealth is common [to all] and the fruit of its relinquishment is the same, and there is likewise unimpeded joy [in that act], so too is the relationship with the object; it is not [exclusive] to the one who possesses it. (395)

To clarify this by means of an illustration, he says: When wealth is common to many, the sense of ownership—the relationship of owner and owned, or the state of being one's own—belongs to all; and so too does the fruit of renunciation, characterized as giving. Furthermore, the joy and satisfaction of the mind, which is likewise complete, arises for all precisely because of that commonality. In the same way, having made that object equal [to all], the relationship between those who possess it—the members of the community and the community itself—should be understood. || 395 ||
When the phonemes possess meaning, through that very meaning, the unity of the collection is established as distinct [from its parts] in that which possesses it. || 396 ||

Now, in this context, in order to explain the rule *varṇād* [Pāṇini 1.2.45]—which states that the absence of case-endings (*sub*) occurs because a composite (*saṅghāta*) has a single meaning—he says: "When even individual phonemes (*varṇa*) possess meaning, and the composite also possesses meaning, then, since the possession of meaning there is common to both, the singular number arises from the composite itself to express its oneness, and not from each individual phoneme. (396)
Just as all see common property by means of a single lamp, in the same way, number is designated by means of a single unit. (397)

To demonstrate this very point by means of an illustration, he says: "Just as in total darkness the knowledge of the nature of a common object of wealth is accomplished by a single lamp alone, so too here, for the sake of manifesting the meaningfulness of the common [substratum], the number characterized as unity—which has departed from the aggregate—is expressed by a single case-ending (sup) produced from that aggregate; thus, there is no separate production of case-endings for each individual. (397)
Thus, there is no difference in the meaningfulness of a word, a phoneme, or a sentence; however, a different sequence resulting from repetition appears as if it were contradictory. (398)

Therefore, this meaningfulness is common [to all], being expressed by the single case-ending (*sup*) alone; consequently, since it occurs in phonemes, words, and sentences alike, it is not distinguished [as unique to any one], nor is it necessary to state it separately—this is how it should be understood. To express this, he says: "But surely, the meaningfulness of the sentence alone has been established at great length previously, while words were declared to be entirely devoid of meaning."

What need is there even to speak of the meaningfulness of individual phonemes? Now, one might raise the objection: "Since it is proclaimed that meaningfulness applies equally to phonemes, words, and sentences, why is this being said? Anticipating this, he says: "Because of repetition" (abhyāsāt).

In this world, various scriptural systems have diverged; and among worldly people who hold limited vision and are attached to those systems, the distinct methods and arrangements of the treatises appear as if they were contradictory. However, in the ultimate sense, reality—which is of the nature of truth—is one and entirely non-contradictory, abiding everywhere. Therefore, because this [system] is intended for all audiences, it has been adopted in some way through its connection with them; yet one should understand that by this much, there is no abandonment of the accepted, indivisible position. || 398 ||
Apart from its application (viniyoga), a word does not reveal its own meaning; they declare that the means for expressing the meaning is the connection with the act of denotation. (399)

Now, wishing to examine the word's own function in the denotation of meaning, he says: "In this world, a single word has many meanings. When it is employed by a speaker for a specific, restricted meaning, it is observed that it conveys that very meaning. Therefore, they say that a word's capacity to communicate a meaning occurs solely through the medium of utterance. (399)
Just as the eye is prepared for the act of seeing according to its specific intention, so too a word, being intended [by a speaker], becomes the designator of a meaning. (400)

Now, is the relationship between word and meaning innate, or has it reached such a state that these words have their connection dependent upon looking toward the speaker’s application [of them]? Alas! By speaking thus, you have merely adorned the position of the Grammarians. Anticipating this objection, he says the following in order to support his own view: Just as the visual organ, by its very innate capacity, brings about the perception of objects while depending on the attention belonging to the seer, for otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of perception arising at all times.

In the same way, although a word conveys its meaning through an inherent relationship, it nonetheless depends upon the intention (*abhisandhāna*) associated with the speaker. This is what is meant: one should understand that sentences, in their own operation, possess specific meanings determined by themselves; they manifest the denoted object by prioritizing their own operation called "denotation" (*abhidhā*), thereby effecting the revelation of the object. And this operation called "denotation" is caused by the intention associated with the user.

It is designated as such by way of intention (*abhisandhāna*). As it has been said: "A word becomes the designator of an object when it is so intended. For here, it is precisely the intention that is extended [to the word] as its function characterized by utterance. But when the position of non-difference (*abheda*) is held, then the intuition (*pratibhā*) itself, which has arisen within the speaker and takes the form of intention, becomes identical with the word. Thus, the indication of non-difference between the intention and the utterance is quite clear.

Therefore, even the operation of the eye, which is its outward movement, consists essentially of mental application (*praṇidhāna*); for it is said: "Speech and the arrangement of instruments do not exist without the *bhāvanā* of sound. Thus, the own-operation of sound is caused by such mental application; or rather, *abhidhā* (denotation) is itself the mental application of sound, and it should be understood that *abhidhā* is the very essence of sound. || 400 ||
A relationship between an instrument and its object is observed to be mediated by an action; therefore, there is a restriction regarding the expression and the expressed. (401)

One might object: "Is it not already well-established that there is merely the denotation, the denoted, and the relationship between the two? As for what is here set forth—the utility of this tetrad consisting of application (*viniyoga*), expression (*ukti*), intention (*abhisandhāna*), and denotation (*abhidhā*)—that is indeed unknown. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In this world, the factors of action (*kārakas*) are like iron rods, entirely unconnected to one another; yet, as is observed, they come to be related through the mediation of an action, by taking recourse to that action."

In the same way, the relationship between the signifier and the signified, characterized by the nature of the denoter and the denoted, is regulated by the verbal operation called *abhidhā* (denotation); thus, nothing new has been stated here. || 401 ||
When many words have a single denotation and all produce the same effect, the word remains fixed upon that which the speaker intends.

To clarify this very point, he says: "And likewise, when many objects such as cows and so forth—entities denoted by a single name, that is, conveyed by a single word—and the words themselves are present there among those objects, being of the same class and performing a single function, the speaker intends that specific form of the object; through that intention and its application, he makes it the object of expression. It is clearly observed that the word abides as the designator only for that particular object, and not for any other. (402)

Some say that when the words of the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) are not repeated, they are meaningless; others hold that they function merely as their own forms for the purpose of conveying other things. Those who perceive the non-duality [of the Self] consider those very words to be distinct injunctions (*niyoga*), because of the difference in the act of denotation and because they convey a specific meaning. (403–404)

To clarify this very point by means of another context, he says: "Likewise, Vedic words belonging to the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) do not express any meaning whatsoever at the time of recitation; then they call them indeed meaningless. But when those same words are taught to disciples for the purpose of grasping their own forms, then they are considered to have the form as their primary object, and thus they are said to have that [form] as their meaning."

Furthermore, when those very [words] are employed in some sacrificial rite through a distinction of application (*niyoga*) and a distinction of intention (*abhisandhāna*), they then, by means of their own operation called *abhidhā*, become signifiers of that object and established in that object; thus, it is quite clear that *abhidhā* appears as something emerging distinct from the denoted meaning itself, and therefore its denial is not tenable. (403–404)

Those who employ conventional designations for diversity declare that there is absolute non-difference among them, because they are connected with a single universal, just as in the case of the sense organs and so forth. (405)

Thus, by relying on the operation characterized by intention, denotation, and indication (*abhidhā-lakṣaṇa-vyāpāra*), the expression of various meanings by a single word has been established. Now, however, by relying on the distinction (*bheda*) within words themselves, he speaks in order to establish that the manifestation of these respective meanings occurs through context (*prakaraṇa*) and other factors: "The proponents of the distinction of those words declare their manifoldness (*nānātva*); they possess only a similarity consisting in the connection with a single genus (*jāti*). He provides an example: "Just as in the case of *akṣa* and so forth."
Just as words such as "akṣa" and others remain distinct, yet they are perceived as non-different due to their similarity. || 405 ||
In my words, there is no intentional design resulting from deliberate application; for, regarding the subject matter, I abide therein according to my capacity. (406)

And what follows from this? He says: *prayoga* is utterance (*uccāraṇa*). Therefore, other than that, there exists no intention (*abhisandhāna*), expression (*ukti*), or denotation (*abhidhā*) within those [phonemes]. How then does a word denote a specific object? He says: "In its respective domain" (*viṣaye*). Because it possesses a fixed power (*niyata-śakti*) with respect to each respective domain, and precisely because its powers are differentiated, that word is established in each respective case. || 406 ||
The cognition of diversity itself [arises] from the context of the meaning and other factors; never, in any way, do words with one meaning function toward a different meaning. (407)

Likewise, even when there is similarity, the distinctness [of the meaning] is understood because the denotation of the object is restricted by context and other factors; thus he says: "And this is logical. Otherwise, since the occurrence of a word in one sense has been observed in one place, how could that same word subsequently be established as having another meaning? To state this, he says: "Never," and so forth. (407)

However, regarding that word which is a sentence whose nature consists of a thing and which is bound up with existence, let this inquiry be directed toward it; it does not apply to the word as a constituent part of the sentence. (408)

Now, in order to grasp what was previously stated, he speaks again—beginning with an uninterrupted sentence—to provide a concise determination of the sentence and its meaning: "This reflection (vimarśa), which is the deliberation (vicāra) here, may well apply to a word; for in that case, the sentence is established as being of the nature of that single word alone as the signifier. What is the nature of that sentence consisting of a word? He says: 'the basis of existence' (astitvopanibandhana). That is, it is that whose basis for being a sentence and for being a signifier is the act of existence (astitva)."

As he will say: "Or [the word] is connected with existence," and so forth. Alternatively, this phrase "the connection with existence through context and the like" should be understood as an illustration that includes the case where [the word] functions as a non-existent entity. In this regard, the investigation is as follows: expressiveness (*vācakatva*) is mediated by the operation of denotation and is produced by specific powers; it does not belong to a "word" (*pada*) postulated through grammatical abstraction (*apoddhāra*) as a constituent part of a sentence, because such an abstraction lacks a referent (*arthavattā*). This is the intended meaning. || 408 ||
Just as a specific meaning is expressed by means of phonemes that are themselves devoid of meaning, so too is a specific meaning expressed by means of words that are themselves devoid of meaning.

Therefore, one must accept that the sentence is an indivisible entity in the form of *sphoṭa*, which is independent and expressive; in order to state this by means of an analogy, he says: "Just as in your own view, the *sphoṭa*—the essence of a word (*pada*)—which is the expressive agent denoting a specific meaning, is said to be manifested by meaningless phonemes (*varṇa*); in the same way, the *sphoṭa*—the essence [of a sentence]—which is the expressive agent denoting a specific meaning, is said to be manifested by meaningless words (*pada*). (409)

The cognition that arises with respect to objects in the interval [between the initial perception and the final ascertainment] is a means for comprehension, because the [final] determination has not yet been reached through the process. (410)

[Objection: Surely the comprehension of word-meanings does indeed arise there; but if words themselves are devoid of meaning, how can that [comprehension] exist? To this he says: This knowledge of words and word-meanings, which takes the form of an error (*vibhrama*), must be understood as being merely an intermediate means for the apprehension of the sentence and the sentence-meaning. Therefore, even though the sentence and the sentence-meaning are partless (*niraṃśa*), their form is not determined at the very outset—that is, at the first moment. || 410 ||
Just as the supreme Self follows previous meanings according to its true nature, so too does it proceed through mere association with other objective entities.

Having thus explained the three modes based on the expressive words (*vācaka*), he now speaks in order to demonstrate the same [three modes] by relying on the expressed meanings (*vācya*): "By this verse, through reliance on the theory of the expression of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*), the presentation of the sentence-meaning as a composite whole (*saṃsṛṣṭa*) is effected. For instance, according to the proponent of the theory of the connection of the expressed (*abhihitānvaya-vādin*), the sentence-meaning is a relation (*saṃsarga*) following upon each preceding meaning; whereas for the proponent of the theory of the expression of the related (*anvitābhidhāna-vādin*), it is understood as already related from the very beginning, in accordance with each successive word-meaning."

It should be understood that, at most, the presence [of a statement] here serves as an indicator; that is, they require it only for the sake of understanding the nature of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). || 411 ||

But when some means of proof have already been accepted as having the intended object as their probandum, the restatement of those means of proof is solely for the purpose of restricting their substratum. (412)

When, according to the view of some, the means (*sādhana*)—characterized as assistance—is accepted, embraced through its inseparable connection (*avinābhāvitā*), and itself determined by way of a relation with the object to be established (*sādhya*), namely the object residing in that which is to be established; then, the repeated mention (*punaḥśruti*) of those means within that sentence must be understood as being for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*) regarding the factors of action (*kāraka*). It should be understood that a restriction is made there concerning the ultimate substratum (*paramādhāra*).

The fuel possesses the power of being the agent (*karaṇa-śakti*), and the pot possesses the power of being the locus (*adhikaraṇa-śakti*); so it is in other cases as well. Because there is no restriction regarding the locus, there is no implication (*ākṣepa*) of it; its occurrence follows from the inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*), while the explicit mention (*śruti*) serves to exclude anything else.

In this regard, he states that since an action cannot exist without a means (*sādhana*), only the means itself is implied as having an unspecified substratum (*ādhāra*), but not necessarily accompanied by a specific substratum. He says: "There is no fixed restriction of substrata for the means. For while the powers of the instruments (*karaṇa*) and so forth are seen to have fixed substrata, there is an implication of a substratum here; however, in that [case of the action], no such means exists.

If, by implication, one merely infers the possibility of that means [of action] existing therein, then it must be understood that these powers of the means are the substrata of the action; thus, the scriptural expression "the staff [is used] for the cow" and so forth results in the exclusion of any other substratum for those powers. || 413 ||
An action is distinct from other actions and possesses a fixed substratum and means; it is undertaken by cognizers, and its various distinctions are the causes for full comprehension. (414)

Now, relying on action (*kriyā*) as the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), he says: "Action itself, being qualified, is everywhere presented as the sentence-meaning from the very outset; it is distinguished from other actions"—this is the statement of its specific nature. To clarify this very point, he says: "having a fixed substratum and means" (*niyatādhārasādhanā*). It should be understood that in that sentence, the employment of various distinctions (*bheda*) or qualifications (*viśeṣa*) is merely a means for addressing [the listener]. (414)
But for others, the sentence and its meaning manifest as indivisible from the sequential sounds, even though they appear without the sequence of words. (415)

Now, in order to demonstrate the meaning of the sentence according to his own school of thought, he says: "The sentence-meaning is indeed non-sequential and undivided, consisting of intuitive flash (pratibhā) like the taste of a beverage; and the sentence is of the nature of *sphoṭa*. Because they share the same status of existence and function (*ekayogakṣema*), it is said that 'the sentence is indeed the sentence-meaning itself. (415)
The self of that which possesses an intrinsic nature cannot be defined; however, the self of that which lacks an intrinsic nature is indeed defined.

Now, in order to demonstrate with reasoned analysis that the meaning of a word is a real form despite having unreal adjuncts (*upādhi*), he says: "In the case of an object whose nature is determined by means of valid cognition such as perception—as for instance, 'blue' or 'yellow'—its true self is not fully defined by that alone, nor is it brought within the scope of practical usage."

This is what is meant: although the word-meaning (*padārtha*) exists as a distinct entity, it is like a cripple and is prevented from being brought into the sphere of linguistic usage; since the relation (*samsarga*), which is of the nature of a connection (*anvaya*), is primary and is established through that [word-meaning] as its subordinate means or gateway, the determination of that [relation] alone attains fulfillment. Therefore, it is logical that the reality belongs to that [relation] alone. || 416 ||
Others understand the determination of the form of an object to be wordless; for memory, which has the appearance of the object, arises from words. (417)

Now, having first established the unreality of the individual word-meanings (*padārtha*), he begins to demonstrate that the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) consists precisely in the relation (*saṃsarga*) permeated by them: "The determination of the nature of an object—that is, the delimitation of its own form—is non-verbal; in that regard, the word does not function as a means. The meaning is that this [nature] is to be apprehended solely through indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*). If so, one might ask: what is the utility of the word therein? To this he replies: "In the manifestation of the object," and so forth.

The utility of words lies solely in a memory that resembles the appearance of the object; the word is extremely remote from the object itself. Consequently, since how could a word denote an object? It follows that the relationship between word and object is ultimately unreal. || 417 ||
Through contact with fire, one who is burned perceives the burning in one way; however, by means of the word "burning," the object of burning and so forth is understood in another way. (418)

Therefore, one must understand this very point, as he says: "If an external object were conveyed by a word exactly as it is, then why would that object, brought near by the word, not perform its specific causal function? Since, however, through contact with fire one experiences burning in one way, whereas through the word 'burning' one understands the burning in another way, it must be understood that there is no real, ontological correspondence between word and object. (418)
Just as the functioning of the sense organs—which are established separately and pursue separate objects—is not possible without a body, so it is with [the self]. (419)

Thus, having stated that the nature of the word-meaning (*padārtha*) is unreal—whether it be of the nature of "misapprehension" (*viparītakhyāti*) or "apprehension of the non-existent" (*asatkhyāti*)—he speaks in order to establish the reality of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), which is permeated by that [word-meaning]: "Of those whose essence or true nature (*tattva-svarūpa*) is established separately"—that is, whose essence is manifested as distinct through attributes such as "earthiness" (*pārthivatva*) and so forth, or whose essence is established and made manifest by resorting to their respective individual locations; "of those" refers to such things. Thus, [the compound means] "those whose objects are separate and separate."

Those who follow and take as their objects that which is characterized by sound and so forth are "those [who act] in such a manner"; for them, just as no individual effect is possible apart from the body even though it possesses a distinct nature, in the same way, words existing in isolation, apart from a sentence, are observed to lack meaningfulness. || 419 ||
Likewise, for all words that are established as having separate meanings, once they are extracted from sentences, no possessiveness of meaning is found. (420)

In order to apply this to the subject at hand, he says: "The nature of conjunction is perceived in objects that have been conjoined; however, the true reality (tattva) is not described here, because it is seen to be beyond the scope of [conventional] categories. (421)

In order to demonstrate the true nature of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), he says: "Furthermore, at the time when the individual word-meanings appear separately, its reality is not explained—that is, it does not manifest—because the nature of the sentence-meaning is seen to be entirely distinct from the form of the word-meanings. (421)
Even that which is the truth of perception does not exist as perception; in the form of contact with an object, it is characterized as being without that [perceptual] form. (422)

Now, one might object: "How can you say that everything exists when it is as unconvincing as saying 'there is no hare, yet there is a horn'? Even the appearance of words and word-meanings, though being experienced, is not admitted [as real], while the sentence-meaning, conditioned by the word-meanings, is instead established as the truth. Anticipating this doubt, he says the following to demonstrate that it is only that which has been established as the highest of all that enters the sphere of worldly transaction, and not anything in its own right: "In this system, consciousness alone is the ultimate reality; apart from that, nothing else [exists]."

Because it cannot be established when subjected to critical examination. And just as that [consciousness] exists by way of its own clarity and so forth as if it were real, the manifestation of its own nature as cognition does not exist at the moment of the appearance of an object. At that time, although it is devoid of such [intrinsic] forms, it is determined as "cognition of blue" or "cognition of yellow," being associated with blue, yellow, and so forth, in the form of a relation with external objects.

Thus, this [notion] of association and so forth—whether it takes the form of a connection between entities, or is presented as qualified by a word-meaning, or appears in such a manner even while devoid of that specific form—is nonetheless described. What fault, then, has been committed here? Therefore, in every respect, a purely isolated word-meaning or word is simply non-functional; and for this reason, it is said to be unreal. || 422 ||
Since an object is expressed as being either connected with existence or situated within its own nature, a sentence is employed for that purpose. (423)

However, since both the sentence and the sentence-meaning are real insofar as they are subject to linguistic usage, he says that it is the sentence alone that is employed for the sake of communicating meaning: "Without connection to an action, a word-meaning is not perceived; whether it be real or otherwise, such [an isolated meaning] does not exist in linguistic practice. (424)
To clarify this very point, he says: "Therefore, it should be understood that in conventional discourse, an isolated object does not exist at all. (424)
However, a sentence such as "It is indeed existent" or "It is not," is not considered [to convey meaning] without a connection to an action or a designation of an action. (425)

Even where there is a single word such as "existent" (*sat*), which conveys a state of being that is self-sufficient, even there the meaning is not complete without a connection to a verbal action—such as "it was," "it will be," "it is not," or "it does not exist. Thus, to demonstrate that a solitary word alone has no meaningful content whatsoever, he says: "And in that sentence, the goal (*sādhya*) and the means (*sādhana*) are mutually inseparable, dependent upon one another, and established only through their interaction."

For instance: just as a means (*sādhana*) is said to require an action (*kriyā*) due to the force of the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) that it cannot be without action; so too, with respect to the characteristic of action conveyed by a verb (*ākhyātapada*), the expectancy does not cease without the expression of existence (*sattva*). || 425 ||

When the meaning expressed by a verbal form is connected with its means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), the expectancy [of the sentence] is not removed without the expression of existence (*sattva*). (426)

To demonstrate that in this context action necessarily requires a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), he says: "However, because of its predominance, action is first distinguished from the object; its members are employed for the sake of what is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), and its fruit is the motivator (*prayojaka*) thereof. (427)

The means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is that which serves as the basis for the meaning expressed by the words of the narrative; in such a case, the expectation regarding that [meaning] is not removed without the mention of a substance (*sattva*). For the means of accomplishment denotes a substance; therefore, it remains fixed upon that.

What is the basis for the relationship of primary and secondary between those two, such that it is said that the analysis of the *sādhya* (the goal) comes first? Anticipating this doubt, he says: Because the meaning characterized as the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), which is conveyed by the verb (*ākhyāta*), has action as its primary element, action alone is analyzed first due to its primacy, not the means (*sādhana*). Since the means are employed for the sake of the goal—that is, for the accomplishment of the *sādhya*—they are subordinate members (*aṅga*) to that which is primary; therefore, there is no analysis of them therein.

In this way, those things impelled by action are to be understood. Incidentally, he also states the prompter of action: "Its fruit is the prompter. Since action is also prompted by the fruit, it should be understood that action possesses the status of a subordinate member (*aṅga*) in relation to the fruit. || 427 ||
The speaker alone intends the nature of the goal and the means, or he seeks to construct the conceptual connection between objects. (428)

Now, demonstrating that this entire conventional practice of the probandum (*sādhya*) and the means of proof (*sādhana*) is conceptual, and that the mutual relationship between these two is merely relative and not real, he speaks again in order to establish the unreality of all things: "This is the probandum, this is the means of proof, and the connection between them—all of this is conceptual. Therefore, reality is indeed emptiness alone; that is to say, it has its life solely in the mere activity of the agent. (428)

"I perform the act of cooking" is expressed as the object (*karman*); however, "cooking" (*pakti*) is perceived as the instrument (*karaṇa*) in its aspect of being that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*). (429)

For if this were real, then because it would be impossible for Brahman to alter the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of an entity, this state of affairs would remain fixed; yet it is not observed to be so. To demonstrate this, he says: In the expression "Devadatta cooks," the act of cooking (*pākakriyā*) is perceived as the primary element; however, in the expression "Devadatta performs the act of cooking," that very same act of cooking is established solely as the object (*karman*). But the performance of the act of cooking [in the latter case] has its form submerged in the primary element [of the agent].

It has been established that this is not the actual nature of things; furthermore, in the *Sādhanasamuddeśa*, he will demonstrate in detail that all of this is merely conceptual (*vaivakṣika*). Likewise, he will state that the relationship itself is purely imaginary; therefore, it is not elaborated upon here. || 429 ||
Whatever assistance that [word] is intended to provide for the agents by means of which [assistance], it remains established in exactly that way, because the object possesses all powers. (430)

Alternatively, an object, though possessing multiple powers, manifests its very self in whatever way it is intended by the speakers according to the influence of its various services; thus he says: "The connection [of a word] with distant functions is sometimes expressed; that which is embraced [by one function] is sometimes perceived as unattached. (431)

Likewise, in order to demonstrate that objects also endure because they are inlaid with manifold powers (*śakti*), he says: "Sometimes, even in the case of objects that are remote and extremely distant, a mutual relation or conjunction (*saṃśleṣa*) is spoken of; however, sometimes that which is embraced or connected is understood—by virtue of the speaker’s intention—as unjoined, unconnected, or far away. (431)
The discernment of things that are mixed together, and the mixing of things that are discerned; the unity of things that are diverse in nature, and the diversity of things in the opposite case. (432)

He states another form [of linguistic usage]: "Even when there is identity, diversity among things is perceived due to the power of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), as in the case of 'the head of Rāhu'; and even for things that are diverse in nature, such as the *dhava*, *khadira*, and *palāśa* trees, unity is perceived in the form of a synthesis within a single cognition, as in the case of 'the forest'; and for discerning people, the connection of mutually distinct objects—which are like iron rods—is perceived in the form of a sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), as in the expression 'Devadatta [is cooking] with wood,' and so forth."

And there is the state of being divided among those who were previously combined, as in "The people of Mathurā are wealthier than those of Pāṭaliputra," and so forth; for these, having been mentally aggregated, are subsequently established through division. || 432 ||
Whether because an object consists of all things or because it is devoid of self-nature, it is established that sound alone is the basis, owing to its being possessed of absolute power.

He explains how this is logically possible: "Since everything possesses all powers (*sarvaśakti*), it is determined by this or that form; thus, it becomes the recipient of various designations. Therefore, it is established that it is designated in such and such ways by words whose powers are restricted [to those specific forms]. Alternatively, since this [object] is indeed soulless (*nirātmaka*) and unreal (*asatyabhūta*), it displays its state in whatever way it is determined according to the speaker’s intention; thus, it should be understood that it is designated by words in exactly that manner. (433)
A word is a designation of an object; it does not express an absence of benefit. Therefore, it is not possible for it to touch upon the inherent power of things. (434)

Now, in order to state that words do not touch the actual nature of an object at all, but rather reach their utility in worldly transaction by standing as mere indicators of the object through a remote connection, he says: "Conjunction (*saṃyoga*), which is a property of the related things, is denoted by its own word; likewise, inherence (*samavāya*) is understood as a relation by virtue of being a related thing. (435)

The relationship of denoted and denoter (*vācyavācakabhāva*) between word and meaning is not tenable; for if that were so, words would have to assume the very nature of the object they signify, yet this is not observed. Thus he says: from the word "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*), a conjunction of two substances is understood as having its own well-established form; therein, the nature of a relation (*sambandhasvabhāva*) is perceived, yet that [relation] does not possess the nature of those [two substances]. Likewise, from the word "inherence" (*samavāya*), inherence is understood; thus he says: "Inherence is a relation," and so forth.

Intrinsic inherence (*samavāya*) is understood from the term "inherence" as being a relation by virtue of its being a related thing, despite the absence of an intrinsic nature of relation. Alternatively, when this relation is denoted by the word "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) as something independent, then inherence is understood therein as a relation; thus, when the reading is "when it is understood as a relation," it should be construed in this manner. || 435 ||
Objects are established by way of their characteristics, but not in reality; that very object is somehow understood through its functional efficacy. (436)

He says that the intrinsic nature of entities does not remain fixed at all; rather, however they are analyzed, they assume that very form. Thus, because a single object is designated differently by someone for some purpose or another, it is established in summary that an entity, through its manifold elaborations, is composed entirely of the unreal. (436)

The connection that exists between the meanings of words within the meaning of a sentence does not reside anywhere as its own essence; yet, in linguistic usage, they designate that very [connection] as the essence of word-meanings. (437)

Now, in order to demonstrate that the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*) is indeed real, he says: "The meaning of a sentence, whose nature consists in a mutual interconnection—like the taste of a beverage (*pānakarasa*) and so forth—is indivisible and partless; it cannot be apprehended as having its self established in some separate form. This is the sense.

Furthermore, when it comes to the occasion of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), people regard this [exclusion] as the very soul or life of word-meanings—which are otherwise like iron rods [lacking inherent connection]—because, under its influence, every activity or cessation of activity directed toward the objects denoted by words becomes fruitful. And that [exclusion] should be understood as being fully present in a single object or in a collection of them. (437)
Whether it be completed in a single word-meaning or in a collection, its essence is never divided anywhere by means of a distinction in the form of the word-meanings. (438)

Alternatively, this [sentence-meaning] is not at all completed anywhere as a distinct entity such that one could observe it by saying "this is that," because it is not perceived as having a separate form; rather, one apprehends the nature of the indivisible sentence-meaning solely through its own nature as it relates to the word-meanings. To demonstrate this, he says: "This is what is meant—it is not possible to discern its nature separately by pointing to it like a horn; rather, its definition must always be understood as being mediated by extrinsic adjuncts. (438)
The distinction that serves as the basis for comprehension for the sake of grammatical exposition is described as something distinct, consisting of parts that possess mutual expectancy. (439)

To clarify this very point, he says: "The distinction among word-meanings (*padārtha*) which is extracted for the purpose of explaining that [sentence] should be understood as the basis for the comprehension of that very [sentence]. Therefore, when a distinction among word-meanings is made, by means of that extracted distinction of word-meanings, the nature of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), which is something entirely different from the word-meanings, is described—that is, it is revealed. Of what kind? 'Having parts that possess expectancy' (*sākāṅkṣāvayavam*)."
When there is a division, the members—which are the essential natures of word-meanings—are expectant; that [sentence] for which they are the means of comprehension is "of such a nature. || 439 ||
The differentiation of that which possesses manifold powers is observed; for the unity of meaning of a sentence is indeed perceived even by a slight degree. (440)

And for such a sentence-meaning (vākyārtha), which is inlaid with various powers and is indivisible, a division produced by limiting adjuncts (upādhi) through the medium of word-meanings is followed as having manifold forms. However, in ultimate reality, it is cognized as being only one; thus he says: "The sentence, whose nature is *sphoṭa* and whose form is expressive, has a single meaning. That is to say, it is that whose denotable object is a single, indivisible essential nature (*svarūpa*). Its state—that is, its essence—is cognized. How? He says: "even by a fraction" (*mātrayāpi*).

When its connection—that is, its relation—is observed with a word of limited measure and fixed number, it is as has been stated: in the rule *igyaṇaḥ*, the sentence-meaning characterized by the relationship between the original element (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*) is designated as "vocalization" (*saṃprasāraṇa*).

Therefore, because it is lighter by virtue of having a single number, it is designated by the measure [of that number] as "samprasāraṇa. When its connection is not perceived, it is understood that this sentence-meaning is partless, singular, and of an indivisible nature; otherwise, how could it be expressed by means of this term "samprasāraṇa," which possesses a single number? || 440 ||

An external object, whether existent or non-existent, is distinguished for the sake of cognition; however, this distinction made by treating it as external is characterized by the abstraction of its powers.

Thus it has been determined that while the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*) is of the nature of reality, the meaning of the individual words (*padārtha*) is indeed unreal. To demonstrate that this sentence-meaning is purely mental (*bauddha*) and lacks external form, he says: "Cognition (*sampratyaya*), intellect (*buddhi*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are synonymous."

That which has for its object a conviction (*sampratyaya*) consisting of a denotable form is "of such a kind. From that mental verbal meaning (*bauddhavākyārtha*), whether it be an external object existing as something external in form, or rather one that is non-existent, being unreal as something external—it is "divided," that is, followed through its distinctions and established. How so? He says: "having made external" (*bāhyīkṛtya*).

This [sentence-meaning] is indeed not external; it manifests as if it were external because of the failure to discern its distinction [from the parts], or rather, because of the unification of the perceived object and the conceptual construction. Having first understood the sentence-meaning through this unification, it is subsequently followed by way of analysis. To the question, "What kind of analysis is there in that case?", he says: "characterized by the extraction of the powers" (*śaktyapoddhāralakṣaṇa*). That whose characteristic is the extraction—that is, the separation—of the powers belonging to the word-meanings is such [an analysis]. The meaning is that the powers of the word-meanings are extracted from that [sentence-meaning].

But here, since the meaning of the sentence is based on the Buddhist [view], and because capacities (*śakti*) do not exist therein, what kind of extraction (*apoddhāra*) of them could there be? Those individual word-meanings are not established there. For if they were present there, then indeed the attainment of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) would occur even when the object has passed away and is already known.

Therefore, those capacities are established in external objects themselves, rather than in mental objects; consequently, even though their form exists in the external object apart from the mental object, it is perceived by a cognition that is itself devoid of form (*nirākāra*). Thus, since linguistic and practical activity (*vyavahāra*) cannot be accounted for unless the form of the cognition and the external object are identical through these capacities, it is said [in the verse] "having made it external."

And thus, because they share a common destiny (ekayogakṣema), it is logical that there should be a distinction—characterized by the exclusion of expressive power (śaktyapoddhāra)—even regarding the mental object (bauddhārtha). In this regard, if the form of cognition, which has been identified with the external due to the power of the latent impressions of conceptualization (vikalpavāsanā), truly exists as an external object by which [the cognition] is produced, then the word-meaning is indeed the external; if not, then the non-existent external is merely a mental construct, and the word-meaning is purely mental (bauddha)—this is the conclusion. || 441 ||

Even when there are many finite verbs, they constitute a single sentence if they are mutually expectant; thus, the exclusion of the *nighāta* (tonal suppression) from finite verbs becomes meaningful. (442)

Now, in the context of an inquiry into sentences (*vākya*), he speaks in order to demonstrate—according to differing views—whether the unity of sentences constitutes "sentenceness" (*vākyatva*) or whether it is rather the multiplicity of sentences that does so: "In this regard, because the author of the *Vārttika* intends the singular number in his definition 'A sentence is a finite verb (*ākhyāta*) together with its indeclinables, case-roles (*kāraka*), and qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*)', and because he provides another definition of a sentence as 'that which contains a single finite verb' (*ekatiṅ*), it is accepted that when multiple finite verbs exist, there is indeed a division of sentences. However, for the author of the *Sūtra*, by the force of employing the prohibition 'not [ending] in a finite verb' (*atiṅ*), even when many [finite verbs] are present..."

Because the meaning [of the injunction] is expectant of further specification within those [passages] ending in verbal suffixes (tiṅanta), it has been demonstrated by the phrase "even in many" that they are intended to constitute a single syntactical unit (ekavākyatā). || 442 ||

In the treatise, a sentence is defined by the rule that it must contain exactly one finite verb (*tiṅ*); for such a person, there is no need to mention the absence of a finite verb (*atiṅ*), because the distinction between sentences is already established. (443)

To demonstrate that, according to the opinion of the Vārttikakāra, there is a syntactical split (vākyabheda) in that case, he says: "The definition of what is restricted" means "that whose unity is intended. || 443 ||

Furthermore, when joined with other verbs ending in verbal suffixes (tiṅanta), or even when joined with [other] joined words—as in "Look, the deer is going"—neither difference nor non-difference remains.

Furthermore, [the author] states that even when there is the presence of multiple finite verbs (*tiṅanta*), the distinction or non-distinction of the sentence-meaning remains firmly established: "In this case, in the phrase *mṛgaḥ paśyata yāti* ('Look, the deer is going'), because of the presence of another finite verb, there is indeed a division of sentences; yet, due to the connection between the word *mṛga* and the word *yāti*, it is one sentence. Subsequently, by changing the case-ending and referring back with the object-word (*karmapada*), *etaṃ mṛgaṃ paśyata* ('Look at this deer') constitutes a second sentence."

But another says: because it is joined with what is already joined, there is indeed non-difference even among many finite verbs (*tiṅanta*). For in this case, the word *mṛga* is joined with the word *yāti*; by that word *yāti*, which is itself so joined, there is a connection with another finite verb; thus, through that word, there is a connection with another finite verb.

Therefore, in this case, the instruction "see the fleeing performed by the deer" (*mṛgakartṛkaṃ saraṇaṃ paśyata*)—even with respect to the action of seeing (*dṛśi-kriyā*)—possesses the status of having a single finite verb (*ekatiṅ*) when understood in relation to the principal finite verb; thus, it indeed conforms to the opinion of the author of the Sūtras. Consequently, there is no difference of opinion between these two [views]. Any difference of opinion should be understood as belonging only to others. || 444 ||

When the manner of performance (itikartavyatā) of an object is required by its own inherent capacity, that which lacks a verbal indicator for such a requirement and whose purpose is complete is said to be [independent]. (445)

Alternatively, one might object that the unity of various sentences (*ekavākyatā*) cannot be understood prior to knowing the completion of a sentence (*vākya-parisamāpti*), nor otherwise; anticipating this doubt, it is stated that the completion of a sentence must be understood as characterized by words (*śabda-lakṣaṇā*), not as characterized by meaning (*artha-lakṣaṇā*). To this effect, he discusses the investigation into expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and its absence: "When expectancy, which is based on words, is no longer present, that sentence is said to have a completed meaning."

It should be understood that when, upon the comprehension of a meaning, an expectancy arises regarding its specific procedure (*itikartavyatā*)—characterized by the requirement for the actual state of things as determined by the capacity [of the words]—the sentence is not thereby said to be incomplete. For example, in the case of "The rice grains are to be threshed in abundance," there is no linguistic expectancy at all; however, since the threshing of the rice cannot be accomplished without the proximity of the mortar, pestle, the action, the agent, and so forth, the sentence is not [incomplete] here due to that [practical] expectancy.
It is not proper to say that [the treatise] is completed, because it is impossible for it to depend upon the definition of words. ||445||
But in the mere restatement of a fact, whatever purpose follows—even without the employment of that [injunctive suffix]—the sentence of the Śruti reaches its completion. (446)

In this context, only the threshing of rice is being explained; and since that [act] exists, it should be understood that the proximity of the mortar and other implements which is here attached [to it] is already complete in that sentence through direct audition (śruti)—that is, by the operation of the word—even without the employment or explicit expression of those [implements]. "Wander about and study here; while muttering, perform the wandering. Although the purpose [of the two acts] is not different, a distinction is perceived from the words themselves.

Now, although there is no difference in the communication of the meaning, it is possible for words to denote things through their function as either subordinate (*guṇa*) or primary (*pradhāna*). In this context, he states the following to explain the properties of words: "While walking here, perform the recitation (*japa*)," or "Performing the recitation, walk. In both cases, the injunction regarding the recitation is understood. However, in the phrase "while walking, perform the recitation," the recitation is denoted as the primary element, whereas the walking is denoted as subordinate.

In the injunction "Perform recitation and walking," however, recitation is subordinate while walking is primary. Alternatively, since walking is joined with recitation in both cases, there is no difference in meaning whatsoever; one concludes that there is merely a distinction in the manner of verbal expression. || 447 ||
The various actions that bear fruit are dependent upon other actions; though they are innumerable and designated by their sequential order, they are all illustrated by a single verbal root.

Thus, although the meaning is not different, the variety in the presentation of words has been demonstrated. Now, in order to show that a variety in the comprehension of meaning arises from the difference in words through their inherent power—even where there is no verbal operation—he says: "He performs the *agnihotra* as long as he lives," and likewise, "Devadatta sacrifices. In such cases, various distinctions of action (*kriyābheda*) are perceived, even though they are characterized by a single verbal form—that is, those for which a single verbal word serves as the illustration or the expressive indicator.

He states that differentiation occurs both by way of essential nature (*svarūpa*) and by way of the fruit (*phala*) with the words "possessing fruits" (*phalavantaḥ*), meaning they possess a distinction of fruits. For instance, one desiring heaven sacrifices at one time, at another time one desiring an elephant, and at yet another time one desiring a son or wealth. He describes the nature of the distinction of fruits with the words "based on other actions" (*kriyāntaranibandhanāḥ*); those for whom other actions serve as the basis (*nibandhana*) regarding the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) are such [actions].

Moreover, what need is there for much? It should be understood that those varieties of action are indeed impossible to enumerate—whether by way of their sequence, their individual procedures (*itikartavyatā*), their specific purposes, or the nature of their results—and yet they are indicated by the verb (*ākhyāta*) as a single, undifferentiated form. || 448 ||

Every action, in its entirety, with all distinctions set aside, is denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*); for it is impossible to conceive of a differentiation of distinctions based on the [mere] hearing of the word. (449)

Having clarified this very point, he says in order to establish it: "In a verbal form (ākhyātapada), every action, with its distinctions set aside, is denoted in a general sense; for from the mere hearing of the word—that is, from the word heard in a general way—it is impossible to discern the specific nature of the various distinctions. (449)
"Kings will sacrifice with the horse-sacrifice; Brahmins are sitting for a sacrificial session"—from this form of expression, no distinction [between the two] is perceived. (450)

He states an example: "In this case, although there is a difference in the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) due to the difference between the means and the result, there is no cognition of that difference from the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*); rather, its difference is understood through the force of the meaning (*arthasāmarthya*). Thus, the properties of words are manifold. (450)
A ritual action that is heard only once and is not repeated among the *prājāpatya* offerings undergoes differentiation by virtue of its inherent capacity. (451)

He also cites a Vedic example: "One should sacrifice seventeen goats of various colors to Prajāpati, hornless and with erect ears. Here, it should be understood that although the act of sacrificing is not repeated and is understood from the single, non-repeated word as being performed once, it subsequently remains distinct due to the plurality of the objects to be sacrificed. || 451 ||
In cases such as "Devadatta and others," the verb *bhuji* (to eat) resides with each [individual]; or rather, each is an independent sentence, for no distinction is made between them. (452)

And because the verbal root contained within a finite verb (*ākhyāta*) expresses an action whose distinctions have been set aside, therefore, since distinctions are impossible, a connection according to their respective order (*yathāsaṃkhya*) is untenable; thus, the act of eating resides individually in Devadatta and the others. He says this—namely, that "the eating characterized by Devadatta and the others as its agents, which constitutes the meaning of the sentence, resides here in each one"—in order to demonstrate the completion of the word's function by showing the completion of the sense (*arthasamāpti*), he states: "each independent," and so forth.
It should be understood that in this context, the sentence itself exists separately with respect to each [individual], such as Devadatta and the others. || 452 ||
In the utterance of sentences, one form is suppressed; but in their comprehension, another form is perceived for those very same distinct words. (453)

One might object: "In the sentence 'Let Devadatta, Yajñadatta, and Viṣṇumitra be fed,' a single sentence in the form of non-differentiation has been employed; therefore, how can there be a determination of them as distinct from this? To this he says: At the time of utterance, words function according to their own individual forms (*svarūpa*), but at the time of comprehension, the determination of their forms occurs quite otherwise. Thus, even though there is no difference in the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), through a consideration of the meaning, it is said that here the completion of both the sentence and the sentence-meaning occurs individually for each. || 453 ||
A single sentence of general application is stated once—for example, "by the agent"—and that [rule] is then divided among the various cases such as animals and so forth. (454)

To demonstrate that this very principle applies to the subject matter of the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*) as well, he says: "In the treatise too, the rule *kartari kṛt* is employed as a general introductory statement (*grahaṇakavākya*) conveying the meaning of the suffix; and that [rule], having been brought into a specific relationship with each distinct object—such as the 'animal' (*paśu*) and so forth—which serves as a limiting condition (*upādhi*) for the meaning of the suffix, is then applied to bring about the intended formation of the linguistic item (*lakṣya*), and thus it is completed in each individual case. (454)
If the expectancy were to cease upon the single hearing of that which has come into being, it could never in any way enter into a connection with anything else. (455)

If, however, it were taken up according to the rule of conjunction (*saṃyuktavidhi*), then the desired result would not be achieved; thus he says: if that [suffix] were taken up by the very rule prescribing the suffix (*pratyayavidhāyaka*) alone, and the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) were thereby satisfied because the purpose was fully accomplished, then—since its power would be exhausted right there due to that connection and it would lack the status of being a governing sentence (*grahaṇakavākyatā*)—it could never enter into a relationship with another rule prescribing a suffix. Consequently, the intended target form (*lakṣya*) would simply not be produced. || 455 ||
It is of a single form yet possesses manifold meanings; therefore, it is the basis and the source of the analytical statements, existing as if non-different from them. (456)

Therefore, one should understand that this single sentence (*sakṛdgrahaṇavākya*), which serves as the basis for the connection [of the parts], is not itself joined with the generalities, but is taken up by the injunction alone; it is the source (*yoni*)—that is, the cause—of the various intermediate sentences (*avāntaravākya*) that constitute the divisions. Thus he says: "That which has many meanings to be conveyed is such [a sentence]; it is the 'basis' (*upanibandhana*) because intermediate sentences are composed within it. Furthermore, it stands as if non-different or inseparable from them; yet, having entered into a distinct relationship with each [part] individually, it is capable of accomplishing the intended object (*lakṣya*) in its proper manner. || 456 ||
In some cases, an action proceeds toward assistance through its individualized parts; in other cases, it is the universal aspect alone that accomplishes the purpose.

Now, regarding what has been stated: concerning that action (*kriyā*) denoted by a verbal root—which is non-substantial (*asattvabhūtā*), consists of successive parts (*pūrvāparībhūtāvayavā*), exists in a state of being accomplished (*sādhyamānāvasthā*), and is composed of a succession of moments (*kṣaṇapracayātmikā*)—what kind of treatment as a genus (*jāti*) or an individual (*vyakti*) is adopted? To this he says: "In some cases. In objects such as negation (*bādha*), option (*vikalpa*), conjunction (*samuccaya*), excellence (*atiśaya*), and praise (*praśaṃsā*), action proceeds by means of its individual parts (*vyaktibhāgaiḥ*) for the sake of accomplishing the intended purpose; for option, conjunction, and so forth are not possible if one relies upon the genus (*jātisamāśrayeṇa*).

For in cases such as "Devadatta cooks" or "Yajñadatta cooks," a collection (*samuccaya*) or other such relations of universals (*jāti*) is not possible. However, in instances such as "he sacrifices" or "he cooks," where there is no mention of place, time, or means, the treatment of a single individual (*vyakti*) would be unreal; therefore, for the sake of establishing worldly convention through conventional truth (*saṃvṛtti*), the general aspect alone constitutes the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) in some cases by virtue of referring to the action. || 457 ||

Furthermore, the distinctions that differ in time, as well as those found in cases such as "camel" (*uṣṭra*) and "sitting" (*āsika*), do not differentiate the essence of the word from the aspect of the universal (*jāti*) within its initial application.

Here too, [the author] states that words convey only the generic aspect (*jātibhāga*) as related to action: "Those various actions (*kriyābheda*), i.e., specific actions (*kriyāviśeṣa*), differentiated by time—such as *pacati* (he cooks), *apākṣīt* (he cooked), *pakṣyati* (he will cook)—and those which are differentiated by their means (*sādhana*) in cases such as *uṣṭrāsikā* (camel-sitting) and so on, as in *uṣṭrāsikā āsyante* (camel-sittings are being performed) or *hataśāyikāḥ śayyante* (dead-man’s-beds are being made), in all these, because the generic aspect is introduced through its connection with action, it proceeds by way of generality alone, without regard for place, time, or means; and in this introduction, the essence of the word (*śabdātmā*), i.e., the verbal form itself..."
It is not divided; that is to say, the distinction produced by its connection with a means of accomplishment does not manifest therein. || 458 ||
When a single word is heard once, the various actions distinguished by genus and other factors among the individual instances are applied separately according to their respective distinctions. (459)

Thus, by means of the passage beginning with "In the case of Devadatta and others, the verb 'to eat' resides in each [individual]," it has been demonstrated that, based on the distinction of the grammatical definition of words, a single action enters into a syntactic connection with multiple instruments through the individual fulfillment of its purpose.

Now, raising the objection as to how, in a case where there are actions of different types denoted by distinct words, yet the factors of action (*sādhana*) are denoted by a single word, those factors could be connected with these diverse actions, [the author] says the following in order to demonstrate that even there, by relying on the time of comprehension, the factors of action are understood as indeed being distinct; thus, these actions likewise attain a connection with the sentence through each individual completion of the meaning with those very distinct factors of action.

Regarding those specific means of accomplishment (*sādhanaviśeṣa*) which correspond in number to the various divisions [of the sacrifice], it is said: "by means of genus (*jāti*) and so forth. It should be understood that those actions which are distinct and unrelated—whether by way of genus (the word "and so forth" including the procedure *itikartavyatā* and other factors)—are employed and enter into a relationship with the words denoting the means of accomplishment through differentiation alone; this occurs by relying on a distinction in comprehension, even though the words are heard only once without differentiation. || 459 ||

Just as in the case of dice and other such objects, distinct actions such as breaking, eating, and gambling remain separate for each individual instance, even though there is no difference in the time of their performance. (460)

He provides an illustration: "Let the dice be cast, let them be enjoyed, let them be played! These actions, belonging to different classes and denoted by different words, remain distinct from one another despite being devoid of any explicit mention of syntactic separation, because each reaches its own completion individually. Since other means [of accomplishment] are connected there as distinct entities, at the time of comprehension, the action relates to its respective correlate only through that distinction. || 460 ||

The stringing together of the strings of the senses is the means; their uniformity is the sequence of these [senses] when differentiated, and the simultaneous hearing is that which is bound to them. (461)

He says this in order to state [the meaning] preceded by an exposition of the principle of *tantra* (abbreviation): "By the phrase 'having a common form,' he explains *tantra*. And this is appropriate, because words are sometimes employed in succession with distinct divisions, and sometimes, by resorting to the principle of *tantra*, they are used simultaneously. Thus, at the time of the employment of words, sequence and simultaneity are the means; here, by means of *tantra*, the distinct [words] are employed simultaneously as 'dice' (*akṣāḥ*), and through the difference in action, they enter into a relationship with them. || 461 ||
Two methods are established for the employment of words: either succession or simultaneity, which the world does not transcend. (462)

Now, having introduced the nature of succession and simultaneity here, he says [the following] to explain them: "In succession, the form is differentiated; in simultaneity, it is not differentiated. But even in simultaneity, the action follows the form of succession. The two powers of differentiation and synthesis remain as if distinct from the word. Even in simultaneity, when there is usage by many, the audition is differentiated. (463–464)

In this regard—by means of the very division of form, there is sequence; by way of generality, there is simultaneity. Therein, when words are employed with distinct actions, even though there is simultaneity, the nature of sequence alone follows. Because the state of the object is such, it must be understood as following the nature of sequence; to demonstrate this, he says: "action."

And thus, just as it is the breaking of the cart-axle itself that occurs, and not the breaking of the *vibhītaka* or the gambling-die; and just as it is the eating of the *vibhītaka*-die itself that occurs, and not the other two; and just as it is the gambling with the gambling-die itself that occurs, and not the previous two—because of the factual state of things being so, even when there is simultaneity, this [cognition] follows a sequence. Consequently, those two—sequence and simultaneity—which consist in the capacity for the connection of words and which are the very operation of the word, appear as if they were distinct from, or separate from, the words themselves. ||463||

But from the perspective of ultimate reality, sequence and simultaneity are indeed nothing other than the powers of the word; thus he says: "What then? These two are simply the two powers of the word: that by which it appears sequentially through its power of differentiation (*bheda-śakti*), and by which it appears simultaneously through its power of synthesis (*saṃsarga-śakti*)."

[Objection: But surely, in this way, when there is a distinct application [of the word], because it is connected with multiple verbal roots (*kriyāpada*), the common [verbal root] is indeed differentiated, since there is a difference between its simultaneous and sequential natures. How then can it be said that the sequential nature of the action is stated by the scripture (*śruti*) even in the case of simultaneous application? To this he says: "In simultaneity" (*yaugapadye*). Even in the case of simultaneous application of the means (*sādhana*), the common scriptural form is indeed differentiated due to its connection with distinct verbal roots; for in the case of *tantra* (simultaneous application), that [common form] is taken as being distinct. This is the meaning. || 464 ||
When a single entity, which is non-differentiated, is intended to be expressed through its differentiated forms, the whole is then understood by means of the properties of its parts. (465)

Alternatively, in the word *akṣāḥ*, the collection itself, whose constituent parts have manifested as distinct, is what is being referred to; there, the collection is designated by means of the property of its constituents. Having thus established this distinction, he states that the application (*viniyoga*) of distinct actions is made either individually, according to their respective requirements, or through the completion of the meaning for each: "In this context, where the intended meaning is the undivided nature of the collection which has manifested as distinct through the differentiation of its parts, [the action is performed] by means of the distinction that is the property of the parts, sequentially."

As long as the aggregate is assisted—that is, reinforced—there is a connection of the actions with the distinction itself during the comprehension of that distinction. Therefore, when this aggregate is presented through its distinctions, the meaning of the sentence is completed in each individual part. || 465 ||

Regarding the definition of difference, however, the scriptural statement (śruti) either concludes with each individual [word] or, being distinct in its expression, remains fixed upon the difference between the sentences.

Alternatively, let the word *akṣa* itself, though singular in form, be understood as distinct according to the difference in the verbal expression—such that in sentences like "let the die be eaten" (*akṣo bhujyatām*) or "let the die be played with" (*akṣo dīvyatām*), the hearing of the means (*sādhanaśruti*) remains established through differentiation due to the interference of these subordinate clauses. Thus he says: "In that case, either that word *akṣa* is employed in the singular, or there is a division into plurality for each [die] according to the literal hearing. (Verse 467)

He explains the manner of division based on the completion of the words: when a single sentence is being treated as having multiple sentences through a division of its constituent parts, there may sometimes be the use of the singular word *akṣaḥ* (die), as in "let the die be eaten" (*akṣo bhakṣyatām*). Alternatively, he says "each" (*pratyekam*) to indicate that there is no division of the sentence according to the literal hearing [of the words], but rather each [part] ends in the plural, such as "the dice are to be eaten" (*akṣā bhakṣyantām*). This differentiation must be made among the single sentences without overstepping the literal hearing of the text. || 467 ||
Even in those statements which appear to reside in two [places], for those who perceive their unity, the inherent power of a single entity possessing manifold powers is divided.
