Now, in order to state that even in the view of those who maintain non-difference (*abheda-vādin*), the division of sentences residing in two [meanings] occurs precisely through a difference in power (*śakti-bheda*), he says: "Those which reside in two meanings" refers to those sentences—whether scriptural or worldly—which abide in two senses; even among those, according to the view of those who perceive the oneness of the word, this very power of that single expressive word is itself divided into multiple powers.

Just as there are scriptural rules such as "igyaṇaḥ saṃprasāraṇam," "dvirvacane'ci," "taddharati vahatyāvahati bhārādvaśādibhyaḥ," and "tadasya brahmacaryam," as well as worldly sentences such as "the white [horse] runs" and "the fall of the Alambusās," in these too the capacity [of words] is divided in order to convey two meanings; thus is the exposition of the system of capacity (śaktitantra). 468.

Or rather, the application characterized by a "tantra" (commonality) would pertain to two things that are absolutely distinct; in that case, the means is their conjunction, which varies according to the cognizers. (469)

However, in the view of those who perceive a distinction, the two words are indeed distinct but are employed by means of *tantra* (coalescence). To explain this *śabdatantra*, he says: "In that case, when there is such a usage with two meanings through *tantra*, since it is impossible to convey [both meanings simultaneously], that connection—which is characterized as the denotation of the sentence—becomes differentiated according to the mode of comprehension, possessing a dual nature."

Just as one person asked, "What should be the designation for the phoneme that takes the place of a *yaṇ* and is characterized by *i*? and another replied, "In the case of *yaṇ*, what is the meaning? It is the relationship characterized by the status of original (*sthānin*) and substitute (*ādeśa*); what is its designation?"—the Teacher, for the sake of brevity, resorts to the principle of *tantra* (economy of expression) and gives the answer with a single word: "it is *samprasāraṇa*. Similarly, when one asks, "What kind of creature is running? and another asks, "Of what color is it running? the latter answers with brevity: "A white [dog] is running."

In that regard, this sentence-meaning differs among the listeners; for one who asks, "What kind of dog is running from here?", it is established in the form [of the answer], while for one who asks, "What color is it?", it arises as having the meaning "it is running endowed with the quality of whiteness. Thus, due to the constraints of the context (*tantra*), the manifestation of the meaning occurs in two ways. This is to be explained similarly in other cases. (469)
Previously, two words of identical sound were understood as distinct; now, however, they have been presented by the speaker to the listener through the method of abbreviation (tantra).

To explain this very point, he says: "Those two words previously understood as distinct—'dog' and 'white'—on account of their difference in form, are themselves perceived by the cognizers through a single [tantric] method (*tantra*) as having identical sounds yet being distinct, because they have been presented and made known here by the speaker by resorting to the principle of *tantra*. (470)

Even when there is an intention to express only one [meaning], the other follows as a consequence; the word, being of the nature of power, manifests itself even without a deliberate intention [to convey it]. (471)

Now, in this context, when a single speaker intends to convey a single word, another [word] follows as a consequence once that intention has arisen; thus, in order to establish the principle of *tantra* (simultaneous application) by way of a different method according to the theory of the distinction between words (*śabdabheda*), he says: "Even in the absence of the speaker's intention, because the other is common [to both], it arises, and from that, the comprehension of two meanings. He then states another method for *tantra* even in the view of those who maintain non-distinction (*abhedavādin*): "without... [the following].

In the absence of the speaker’s intention, that word, due to its commonality, manifests as possessing two powers. This is what is meant: the word *śveta* uttered there possesses either the power to convey the genus "white" or the power to convey a specific living being; while conveying one meaning therein, it necessarily brings about the manifestation of the other meaning through its inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*) by way of *tantra*. 471.
The simultaneous possession of multiple powers by a single entity is observed in some cases; for instance, fire is employed for both illumination and burning even when situated in one place. (472)

Alternatively, based on the principle of the dependence upon powers (*śakti*), it is said that because the two powers are of equal status, they manifest two meanings simultaneously. Thus, in certain cases—such as the expression "the white [dog] runs"—two powers capable of conveying two meanings are simultaneously resorted to for a single word. The meaning is that, just as fire, which is endowed with both burning and illuminating, may at a certain occasion be employed for either illumination or burning, and is thus utilized for both properties according to the requirement, so too is this the case here.
In the same way, because it possesses multiple powers, a word is resorted to for the simultaneous manifestation of two meanings. || 472 ||

Even when a sentence whose meanings are differentiated by the power of repetition is heard only once, it remains distinct [in application] either through indicative mark (liṅga) or through the principle of common application (tantra). || 473 ||

Now, in order to demonstrate that this [principle] also applies to the subject matter of the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*), he says: "In the sentence *igyaṇaḥ saṃprasāraṇam*, even when heard but once, what is the case according to the view of those who maintain the difference of words (*śabdabheda*)—where the meaning is differentiated by repetition—and according to the view of those who maintain unity (*ekatva*)—where the meaning is differentiated by two powers?

For in that case, the difference in meaning arises from the difference in power; subsequently, that sentence stands divided by means of a mark (*liṅga*) or indicator, according to the doctrine of the difference of cognitions (*pratipatti-śabdabheda*); the meaning is that it stands as the communicator of both the phoneme and the sentence-meaning."

Since one perceives in the rule *yasmāt pratyayavidhistadādi pratyaye* (Pāṇini 1.4.13) a reference to an already existing case-ending (*bhūtavibhakti-nirdeśa*), one concludes that the phoneme (*varṇa*) is the named entity (*saṃjñī*). Alternatively, because of the reference to a future case-ending (*bhāvivibhakti-nirdeśa*) in rules such as *vasoḥ saṃprasāraṇam* (Pāṇini 6.4.131), one concludes that even the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is the named entity. Thus, the proponent of the theory of distinct words (*śabdabheda-vādī*) infers nothing other than repetition (*āvṛtti*). The proponent of non-difference (*abheda-vādī*), however, infers a difference in power (*śaktibheda*) based on the principle of "economy" (*tantra*), which is characterized by the unification of powers. In this view, the word *saṃprasāraṇa*—by virtue of its two powers—simultaneously effects the communication of both meanings: the phoneme and the sentence-meaning. 473.
Regarding the technical designation *samprasāraṇa*, the distinction between a phoneme and a sentence is established within that single sūtra by means of two indicators. (474)

By means of the two indicative marks (*liṅga*) shown—characterized by the indication of future and past case-endings—the application of both the phoneme (*varṇa*) and the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) as the named entities (*saṃjñin*) is obtained within that very same sūtra. (474) Likewise, regarding the rule *dvirvacane 'ci* ("before a vowel in reduplication"), the indication by way of *ekaśeṣa* (retaining only one of two identical items), which serves as a method for the application of the term [to both vowels and consonants], has been explained in the Bhāṣya itself. (475)

And it has been said: "The specific mention of case-endings (*vibhakti-viśeṣa-nirdeśa*) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the dual designation [of both *sthānin* and *ādeśa*]. This principle (*tantra*), which yields the same result as *ekaśeṣa*, has been presented in various sections of the *Bhāṣya*. To demonstrate the establishment of this principle through the acceptance of the *Bhāṣyakāra*, he says: "In the rule *iha dvirvacane 'ci* (P. 1.1.59), the meaning of the sūtra is explained as follows: when an *ac* vowel is the cause of reduplication (*dvirvacana-nimitta*), any substitute (*ādeśa*) for that *ac* is treated as the original (*sthānivat*) only while the reduplication itself is being performed. Regarding this, it was stated: "Furthermore, the second..."

He states that the mention of "doubling" (dvirvacana) need not be made—it need not be made—by saying: "It is established by means of the mention of *ekaśeṣa*. If it were a case of *ekaśeṣa*, then doubling would follow; therefore, what is expressed here by the word *ekaśeṣa* is actually the *tantra* method, which shares the same result as *ekaśeṣa*. Thus, for the reason that *tantra* serves as the means, the mention of *ekaśeṣa* is shown to be merely an illustration of the rule (*lakṣaṇa*).

Therefore, it is established that even in the absence of *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one from among identicals), because the principle of *tantra* (simultaneous application) is resorted to, the *tantra*—which serves as a means for the operation of a grammatical rule yielding results equivalent to *ekaśeṣa* and ensures semantic coherence in the rule *dvirvacane'ci*—"is accepted in the Bhāṣya. || 475 ||
For the most part, when the *Saṃgraha* had disappeared, grammarians were encountered who took pleasure in brevity and possessed only a meager grasp of knowledge. (476)

Now, the commentator, having first introduced the *Mahābhāṣya* and explained its purpose, describes its greatness and states the lineage of his own teacher in order to declare the succession of gurus for the work he has composed: "In this ancient grammar of Pāṇini, there once existed a treatise called the *Saṃgraha*, composed by Vyāḍi and measuring one hundred thousand verses (*grantha-lakṣa*). However, due to the passage of time, it came to an end upon reaching grammarians of feeble intellect; for those people, being afraid of hardship, were inclined toward brevity."

For this very reason, those whose grasp and acceptance of the sciences was slight were such [as they remained]; consequently, when the study of compendia was neglected by them, that compendium fell into ruin. ||476||
Then, when the Mahābhāṣya—the compendium of all the seeds of logic—had been composed by the venerable Patañjali, the seer of the sacred sites, [the following occurred].

In order to state that the venerable Patañjali, impelled by compassion, composed the *Mahābhāṣya*—preceded by an exposition of the *Vārttikas*—so that the tradition of grammar (*vyākaraṇa-smṛti*) would not be interrupted and so as to provide utility for those who have found it necessary through its being a means of accomplishing *dharma* by way of being instrumental for the knowledge of correctness (*sādhutva*), he says: "By the Guru," which is a term of honor for the author of the *Bhāṣya*. "Tīrthas" are specific scriptures; one who sees (*paśyati*) them, that is, understands them, is a "tīrthadarśa."

By this, the excellence of the Blessed One’s power, rooted in his gravity, has been stated. Furthermore, it should be understood that this *Bhāṣya* is not merely a compendium of grammar, but rather the source of all seeds of logic (*nyāyabīja*). For this very reason—precisely because it is the cause of all seeds of logic—it is distinguished by the word "great" and is called the *Mahābhāṣya* in the world. || 477 ||
Because its depth was unfathomable due to its profundity, yet it seemed shallow due to its elegance, those of unrefined intellect could not establish any firm conviction regarding it.

Now, in order to establish its very greatness by means of a qualification, he says: "Gādha" means a limit, a determination, that is to say, a measure; "this" [Bhāṣya] is that which has not been obtained [as such]. Why? He says: "Because of its profundity. Profundity is depth, the state of being difficult to fathom due to the vastness of the subject matter (*prameya*). For the Bhāṣya composed by the venerable Patañjali is exceedingly profound; thus, no one is able to delimit its subject matter.

"Why is this commentary (*bhāṣya*) so extremely profound? He says, "No; it is as if shallow," and so forth. It is "shallow" (*uttāna*) because its clarity (*sauṣṭhava*) and systematic arrangement (*paripāṭī*) are evident; that is to say, due to this clarity characterized by its systematic order, it appears for the most part as something shallow. Therefore, the meaning is: this is not to be shunned like the mind of a virtuous person, yet it is naturally very deep; for this very reason, it is called the *Mahābhāṣya*.

By this, it should be understood that it has been stated that the venerable Patañjali composed his commentary (*bhāṣya*) almost entirely as a compendium of the *Saṃgraha*. Thus, in the section on Brahman (*brahmakāṇḍa*), the praise of the author of the commentary is expressed through the verse beginning with: "Those impurities which have the body, speech, and intellect as their objects," and so forth. And by means of such praise of the commentary, the greatness of both the treatise and its author is described by the commentator.

For this very reason, he says "in that [work]" (*tasmin*), meaning that those of unrefined intellect are not at all capable of understanding this *Mahābhāṣya*. Those whose great intellect (*mahatī buddhiḥ*) has reached excellence through cultivation are so described; conversely, those who are "of unrefined intellect" (*akṛtabuddhayaḥ*) due to such a deficiency are said to possess meager wisdom. For them, "certainty"—that is, an understanding culminating in a definitive conclusion—was not established here, nor did it find a firm footing.
By this, it is implied that there is no one other than our venerable teacher Vasurāta who is able to plunge into this ocean of the *Bhāṣya*. || 478 ||
When the scriptural texts, which serve as a protective covering for the compendium, were corrupted by the Yakṣas known as Baiji, Saubhavya, and others who followed dry logic, [the Lord acted].

And so, he says that this [system] has been flooded over and rendered fallacious by teachers who are merely knowers of the science of logic (*tarkavidyā*) and who act as opponents to the means of summary comprehension (*saṃgraha*), due to their lack of intellectual acuity: "Dry logic" (*śuṣkatarka*) is said to be purely [speculative], devoid of the fragrance of other scriptures; those who follow only that for the sake of determining the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) are called "followers of that" (*tadanusārin*).

For the *Mahābhāṣya* is established as the authoritative word of the sages (*ārṣa*), possessing the strength of various types of scholarly discourse; therefore, how could one who is merely skilled in oral recitation determine its meaning? Thus, it has been corrupted by those who follow mere logic (*tarka*). And logic is simply a form constructed from the mere intellect of men, and is therefore inherently unstable. As it has been said: "Even a matter that has been inferred with great effort by skillful inferents may be demonstrated in an entirely different way by others who are more proficient. (479)
That tradition of grammar which had been lost among the disciples of Patañjali remained, in the course of time, among the Southerners merely as a written text. (480)

And thus, due to mutual disagreements and the loss of the traditional designation (*āgama-saṃjñā*), the grammatical tradition (*vyākaraṇāgama*) as it truly existed fell away from the disciples of Patañjali over the passage of time; having become lost, it remained in the South as mere books and mere recitation. Thus he says: "In this way, the grammatical tradition has become almost extinct. (480)
Having received the tradition from Parvata, Candrācārya and others, following the seeds of the Bhāṣya, further expanded it into many branches.

Then, after some time, Candrācārya and others obtained the tradition (*āgama*); by means of that as a method, they followed those seeds of logic (*nyāyabīja*) contained within the commentaries (*bhāṣya*) and brought the tradition of grammar back to its former flourishing state. To express this, he says: "From the mountain, from a portion of the three-linga situated on a part of Trikūṭa."

For on that stone slab lies the original grammatical scripture composed by Rāvaṇa; it was brought there by a certain *brahmarākṣasa* and given to Candrācārya, Vasurāta, Guru, and others. It is traditionally reported that they, having correctly understood the true nature of grammar from that source and constantly explaining it to their disciples, brought it to a state of manifold branching and extensive expansion. || 481 ||
Having studied those paths of the systems of logic as well as our own philosophical view, this compendium of our scriptures has been composed by our teacher. (482)

Then, at one time, having reflected through yoga, the Blessed One Vasurātaguru perceived that "this scripture is mine" and, out of affection, composed it. To state the lineage of his own teacher for this work he himself composed, he says: "The foundations of logic (*nyāya-pratiṣṭhā*) are its starting points; the paths of those [foundations] are the 'paths of the starting points of logic' (*nyāya-prasthāna-mārgān*), meaning by way of many paths established upon logic."

Having studied various systems of logic (*nyāyaprasthāna*) and his own philosophical system characterized by the established tenets of grammar (*vyākaraṇasiddhānta*), this [work] was composed. By this teacher, Saṃjñāyana, this compendium of our tradition (*āgamasamgraha*) was likewise composed; it is said that one should not have doubt regarding it, but rather apply oneself with careful attention. By the use of the plural "our" (*asmākam*), other fellow students are also included.
Alternatively, by stating "I have made this compilation so that it would not be lost," he has manifested his own high regard for it. (482)
In this [chapter], only the mere substance of certain paths has been illustrated; a detailed investigation will be conducted in the third section. (483)

One might wonder: "Is this entire collection of the two sections (*kāṇḍa*) the extent of the grammatical tradition (*vyākaraṇāgama*? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In this *Vākyakāṇḍa*, or in both sections, only the mere substance—the mere seed—of certain paths of reasoning has been shown as it were. However, in the remaining third part of this work, which is the natural outflow of the two preceding sections on words (*padakāṇḍa*), there will be an investigation concerning those who abide by our own tenets and those who follow the tenets of others; that is, a determination preceded by the deliberation on what is logical and what is illogical, characterized by a special degree of reverence.
Therefore, this [work] is not merely a summary of the grammatical tradition. (483)
One attains discernment through wisdom by means of various scriptural perspectives; for how much can be inferred by one who merely follows his own reasoning? (484)

One might object: "What is the purpose of practicing the paths established by those various logical systems? Why not simply investigate one's own philosophical system with certainty? To this he replies: Indeed, through various scriptural perspectives and the established tenets of the scriptures, wisdom attains discernment and achieves proficiency. Consequently, for one who refines their own established doctrine, power arises through the various scriptural perspectives, such that the doctrine becomes free from doubt.

Otherwise, for a cognizer who has not perceived the nature of another's scripture and who merely follows his own imagination regarding various positions, it would be impossible to either infer or refute [the opponent]. It is only fitting that the supreme seers, perceiving objects as they truly are through the power born of yoga-generated merit, should establish the final doctrine.

However, for those beginners who desire to ascend [the path] and whose mental dispositions are still impure—who determine the nature of objects that are past, future, or concealed solely through the scriptures—it is logical that the divine intuition (pratibhā) becomes gracious toward them only through the service of various traditional authorities (āgama). || 484 ||
Knowledge does not become fully manifest for those who speculate on this and that without the aid of the Purāṇas and Āgamas, and who have failed to serve their elders.

To explain this very point, he says: For those practitioners who, lacking the wisdom derived from the scriptures, imagine and conceptualize various things all on their own—without the support of the many diverse traditional teachings that have been established since ancient times; for those who are self-styled scholars, devoid of intelligence, whose grasp is struck down by the obsession of pride—the venerable Vidyā, characterized as pure discernment and intuitive flash (*pratibhā*), does not manifest at all. Rather, it belongs to those who attend upon the elders and are devoted to the scriptures.
It is established that this blessed wisdom attains clarity only for those whose pride has dissolved. || 485 ||

Thus, here is the summary of the objects of knowledge: First, the eightfold division of sentences has been proclaimed; thereafter follows the mention of two types of sentences according to the Śāstra and the Mīmāṃsaka.

Even the consideration of strength and weakness is scriptural, because it results from the determination of pervasion (vyāpti); therefore, here follows a concise determination of the definition of a [valid] statement. (2)

Doubt has also been shown regarding even the traditional scripture (āgama) due to the resulting split in the sentence; however, in the final doctrine (siddhānta), it has been established that the sentence among sentences is indeed the *sphoṭa*. (3)
However, it is established in grammar that the theory of the word-meaning alone (padavāda) is not accepted; therefore, [the theories] of abhihitānvaya and anvitābhidhāna [are considered]. (4)

A multitude of refutations has been proclaimed by means of the two components—the word-part and the meaning-part; furthermore, six other types of sentence-meanings have been demonstrated here incidentally. (5)

And regarding the position that the sentence is an indivisible unit (akhaṇḍa-vākya), there is the presentation of the five-fold objection; first, as follows: "There is no justification for a substitute. (Verse 6)

Furthermore, the doubt as to whether [the term] refers to the *pika* bird or something else is untenable; for when there is a conflict between a Vedic statement and a sentence [of ordinary usage], the Vedic statement alone is more authoritative. (7)
In this way, even an established principle would entail abandonment; furthermore, the logical consistency of intermediate statements would be contradicted. (8)
Likewise, there is an impossibility regarding the characteristics in the case of incidental [meanings] and so forth; thus, these faults have been illustrated in this indivisible sentence. (9)
By relying upon the process of analytical extraction (apoddhāra), these faults are refuted; for when the division of the *saṃhitā* occurs and the two words subsequently merge back together. (10)

"Let the meaning of those two [words] be conceived in order to establish a limit for the substratum (upādāna). Thus did the master of sentences (vākyavid) offer this objection here regarding both the word and the sentence. (11)

In this regard, by the force of logic, the concealment of faults in our own position [is established]; furthermore, the distinction between the meanings of the sentences here has been conceived through conceptual construction. (12)

Furthermore, in the established doctrine (siddhānta), the meaning of a sentence is demonstrated through its various divisions; here, by relying on those divisions, the meaning of individual words also becomes possible. || 13 ||

And that [intuition] is divided into twelve kinds, as has been established here; it has been composed in a continuous sequence in order to correctly define the characteristic of intuition (pratibhā). || 14 ||
The meanings of the word-parts and the sentence-parts have been set forth in detail; their distinctness has been established through positive and negative concomitance.
And that [speech] here is also accompanied by signs (sanimittā), based upon nouns and verbs, as well as prefixes, particles, and prepositional adverbs (karmapravacanīya). (16)

The various divisions of words have been characterized incidentally by their defining marks; now that the investigation of phonemes has been concluded by way of their meaningfulness and meaninglessness. (17)
Even when [the theory of] indivisible parts has been established here, the presentation of the four faults regarding the theory of word-meanings (padavāda) is now proclaimed. (18)

In compound words, the attainment of contradictory meanings was illustrated at the outset; likewise, in sentences beginning with "adhi" and so forth, there is the expression of the means of accomplishment (sādhana). (19)

In this context, the lack of semantic connection for the *bahuvrīhi* compound has also been illustrated; likewise, in words such as *prajña* and *saṃjña*, there is no meaning [corresponding to the compound] even in its constituent parts. (20)

Thus, by means of this tetrad of objections, the theory of words (*padavāda*) has been refuted; yet, even when the position of the indivisible [sentence] (*akhaṇḍapakṣa*) has been established, a heptad of objections has been presented. (21)
In a *dvandva* compound, the case-ending itself would have to express the plural meaning; this is the fault first proclaimed here. (22)
The completion of the meaning of the sentence cannot occur with each [individual member] separately; furthermore, there would be no reference by means of pronouns at all. (23)
Furthermore, the performance of the meaning of the sentence can never occur sequentially; if it were non-sequential, its performance would be impossible in any way whatsoever. (24)
The notion that a whole performs its function through the performance of a single part is not tenable in the case of an indivisible [entity]. (25)
These five objections have been properly resolved by one who maintains that the sentence is indeed indivisible, through recourse to the method of analytical extraction (*apoddhāra*). (26)
Now, when the sentence is indivisible, the description of the meaning within compounds occurs separately; that [description] is proclaimed as such in the treatise. (27)

Furthermore, in the Bhāṣya, after postulating the predominance of the meaning of the word in a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) through various alternatives, several positions have been examined. (28)
If this sentence were an indivisible whole, such an assumption would never occur; moreover, even these two defects are merely a matter of linguistic convention.
And this refutation of these two [positions] occurs in the context of the engagement with the treatise; thus, that sublation of the position of the indivisible [whole] has been demonstrated. (30)

On the contrary, it is proclaimed that in the theory of the word (padavāda), there is rather the fault of [improper] cognition when one resorts to compounds such as the *bahuvrīhi* through the alternative view that [the compound] abandons its own meaning (*jahatsvārtha*). (31)
The meaning of the base and the meaning of the suffix are distinct from one another; as long as both persist, how can there be comprehension through the removal of only one of them? (32)

And how could that [non-existence] be perceived as real in the sense of "it does not exist here"? Furthermore, the fault regarding the referent has been raised against the theory of word-referents (padavāda). (33)

If an object is understood through two conditions, then according to that view, how could there be truth in a series of words such as "attī" (he eats) and so forth, when [the action] arises from only one [condition]? (34)
Furthermore, if words were real, how could there be a systematic arrangement in the grammatical treatises through the intermingling of the meanings of stems and suffixes? (35)
First understanding the meaning of the word-constituents in one way, and then again in another way, while still perceiving the meaning of the sentence—this is not consistent. (36)

Those who know the nature of sentences have declared that [negation applies] when the word-meanings are real; for since the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is untenable [otherwise], there can be no discourse based on words [that refers to non-existence]. (37)
The refutation that [the self] would attain both the appropriated and the abandoned [bodies] applies everywhere; thus, eleven faults have been proclaimed along with those previously mentioned. (38)

Furthermore, regarding the theory that words [denote] individuals (padavāda), the wise have extensively examined the faults in two separate positions, according to whether they consist of the word-part or the meaning-part. (39)

Therefore, since [the objection] has been refuted, it is proper to adopt the discourse on the sentence; that fault which was raised regarding the nominal stem (*saṃjñin*) has been transcended, as intended by the author of the Sūtras. (40)

Based on the process of analytical extraction (apoddhāra), the investigation into what is primary and what is secondary has been conducted here with great care and diligence by the author of the commentary. (41)
The distinction between true and false cognitions has also been established; for in the case of both the primary object and the invariably concomitant object, there is no sublation. (42)
Thereafter, the contemplation of the fourfold purpose is prescribed in due order; the means for determining the meaning of words are proclaimed with reverence. (43)
Thus, both the purport of the sequence and the purport of the meaning residing in the sentence have been briefly examined separately. (44)
The distinction between the general rule and its exception has been fully proclaimed; furthermore, a definitive resolution regarding technical terms has been established over many years. (45)

The determination of the sentence occurs through completion either in each individual word or in the collection as a whole; the logic considered here is both characterized and now explicitly stated. (46)
Now, by means of the previously mentioned summary, the determination established in relation to both the sentence and its meaning, as well as the individual word, has been set forth. (47)

The investigation into syntactic unity (*vākyaikavākyatā*) has also been established; it is proclaimed that sentences are characterized by either expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*) or lack of expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatva*). (48)

Alternatively, even in the case of a compound with *cintā*, [the suffix] is applied to another word that denotes the object; thus, here the establishment of the principle of *tantra* is considered to be in accordance with the Bhāṣya. (49)
The introduction to the commentary was also set forth by the author of the sub-commentary when the summary, which is the cause for composing a treatise, had come to an end. (50)

It has been established that [the teaching] possesses a nature conducive to the means of attraction (*saṃgraha*) and so forth; now, its subversion is explained as being the opposite of those means of attraction. (51)

Therefore, this was composed by the teachers and astrologers who were overwhelmed by [divine] possession, for one who has fallen from the essence of the tradition and has become a follower of grammar. (52)
Then, having personally obtained from the mountain the fundamental scripture (āgama), he, the teacher Vasurāta, reflected upon the paths of logic (nyāya).

This traditional scripture of my own exposition has been composed by me in an excellent manner according to the prescribed rules, based on the commentaries taught by my teachers, for the purpose of preventing the loss of logical reasoning. (54)
This treatise has been proclaimed by the author in this work according to the sequence of three sections; herein, his own lineage of gurus is clearly manifest. 55.
Thus, the concise, clear, and orderly connection of the *Vākyakāṇḍa* with its objects of knowledge has been succinctly proclaimed. (56)
Having approached that one who is indeed celebrated everywhere in the world among learned men, this [work] was composed by the one named Rājānaka Śūravarma. 57.
Having heard this concise section of discourse from the disciple of Śaśāṅka, Puṇyarāja has stated its connection based upon the *kārikās*. (58)
Salutation to the preceptor Bhartṛhari, the knower of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman), who consists of the nectar of the essence that dispels the confusion of all philosophical systems.

Thus ends the commentary on the second book (*kāṇḍa*) of the *Vākyapadīya* composed by the illustrious Puṇyarāja. Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. Om. Salutations to the venerable Pāṇini, Kātyāyana, and Patañjali. We praise that intuitive wisdom (*pratibhā*), whose form is strengthened by the nectar of the bliss of the Light, which—when it comes face-to-face with a person—some wondrous, ever-new, and most proximate majesty unfolds within the mind of that person whose nature is light; and which, without the tasting of sense-objects, bestows supreme and eternal satisfaction. (Verse 1)
In these two sections, we—who follow the meaning of the scriptures—have composed this treatise according to the actual mode of occurrence and the true nature of the established doctrine.

In this section, which constitutes a supplement to that [work] and is extensive in its exposition of the essential nature [of the subject], this *Prakāśa* is composed for the purpose of illuminating the meaning of the verses. (3)

Since the *Vākyapadīya* has ceased its investigation of the eight categories (*padārtha*) with the first book (*kāṇḍa*), and since the purpose and other such categories have been determined therein, the investigation of the word (*pada*)—which consists of the analytical extraction (*apoddhāra*) necessary for that [investigation]—is now commenced. This is because, through the arguments established in the subsequent books, the two categories of the sentence and its meaning, which exist as the objects to be explained (*anvākhyeya*) by their defining characteristics, have already been determined.

In this regard, the indeterminate analysis consists of an extraction according to one's intention; thus, he points out the various divisions of words as they occur: "Some divide a word into two parts, others into four or even five, having extracted them from sentences just like bases, suffixes, and so forth. (1)

Anticipating the objection that since only the indivisible sentence (*vākya*) is expressive and the intermediate apprehension of words is an illusion, what is the use of teaching unreal words? [The author] replies: "Having extracted [words] from sentences. This means having separately isolated the word by means of a conceptualizing intellect (*kalpanābuddhi*). For those who maintain that the sentence is the primary unit (*vākyavādin*), the analysis of words is merely a means for the analysis of the indivisible sentence; just as for those who maintain that the word is the primary unit (*padavādin*), there is an analysis of supposedly real roots, suffixes, augments, and substitutes.

The meaning is that because sentences are infinite, it is impossible to achieve mastery of them through their specific individual characteristics (*svālakṣaṇya*); therefore, such mastery is achieved by means of similar words. Furthermore, for both [theories], the unreality of the extracted elements is equal. To explain: for those who maintain the reality of the sentence (*vākyavādins*), the extraction of words is based on an imagined positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) according to the purpose, with no fixed order. Likewise, for those who maintain the reality of the word (*padavādins*), the extraction of stems, suffixes, and so forth, occurs by virtue of the extraction of meanings based on scriptural positive and negative concomitance.

As the author of the *Vākya* states: "It is established, however, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). In this context, "distinctness" (*bhinnatva*) is the universal (*sāmānya*), while "twofold" (*dvidhā*) and so forth are the particulars (*viśeṣa*). Thus, the suffix *-dhā* is justified in the sense of "mode" (*vidhā*). For "mode" indeed signifies a way of being; and that [mode] is a particular which differentiates the universal. According to the view of some—indicated by the phrase "by some"—similarity alone is held to be the mode everywhere. However, it is stated that even in the case of difference, some accept what is called a "mode."

Alternatively, in this context, the intended meaning is simply similarity as conceptualized by the form of cognition (*buddhirūpa*). For similarity—consisting in the external object's conformity to its reflection in cognition—is everywhere the sense of the suffix *prakāra*. Alternatively, because an external object possessing imagined similarity is produced, it is logical that the extraction of a word from a sentence occurs precisely when it is meaningful through the conceptualization of a portion of the sentence-meaning. Indeed, the extraction of the word is caused solely by the extraction of the meaning.

For if that [sentence-meaning] were devoid of parts (*animitta*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of extracting even the phonemes (*varṇa*); consequently, those [phonemes] too would have to be subject to grammatical derivation (*vyutpādyatā*). Furthermore, the sentence-meaning is established as being partless (*niraṃśa*), its nature consisting of an action whose body is constituted by the various factors of action (*kāraka*). In that case, if one were to perform an extraction (*apoddhāra*) through the conceptualization of parts and sub-parts, the components consisting of the *kārakas* and the component consisting of the action would be subject to division; thus, it would concern two parts characterized as "accomplished" (*siddha*) and "to-be-accomplished" (*sādhya*). Consequently, the primary extraction of words (*pada-apoddhāra*) is of two kinds, in the form of nouns (*nāman*) and verbs (*ākhyāta*). Due to the non-difference between power (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimān*), the part consisting of the *kārakas* is of an accomplished nature.

And although, in the case of nouns and words, number and so forth—which constitute the meaning of the suffix—possess verbal predominance (*śābdam prādhānyam*), nevertheless, from the perspective of actual meaning (*arthataḥ*), predominance belongs solely to the substance (*dravya*) as manifested by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), which is characterized by a genus (*jāti*) and exists in a completed form (*siddharūpa*). This is because the powers of number and grammatical relation (*kāraka-śakti*) have that [substance] as their substratum. Furthermore, the various categories of words characterized as particles (*nipāta*), prefixes (*upasarga*), and prepositions (*karmapravacanīya*) are included within these very two classes: noun and verb, insofar as they function as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*).

For instance, since a noun-word denotes an established meaning (*siddhārtha*), a particle (*nipāta*) that illuminates a specific quality residing in that meaning is included within the noun itself. Whether it directly denotes the established meaning or reveals a specific quality inherent in it, there is no difference [in its status] by this much. As for certain particles such as *svar* and others, they primarily denote existence (*sattā*) and are therefore also merely noun-words. However, those such as *hiruk* and others, which primarily denote action, are included within the verb (*ākhyāta*).

For it is not only that which ends in a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*) that is called a verb (*ākhyāta*), since this definition applies to everything whose primary element is action (*kriyā*). For this very reason, even words consisting of prefixes (*upasarga*) or prepositional particles (*karmapravacanīya*) are indeed verbal words, because they illuminate specific qualities pertaining to the object to be accomplished (*sādhya-artha*). The same applies to indeclinables (*nipāta*) as well. However, when there is a desire to express further internal distinctions within them, some treat even prefixes and indeclinables separately. Thus, in the process of analytical abstraction (*apoddhāra*), there certainly exists a distinction in their respective meanings alone.

For these two do not express the object directly, but rather illuminate the specific qualities inherent in it; thus they are distinguished from the denoters, namely nouns (*nāman*) and verbs (*ākhyāta*). Because particles (*nipāta*) illuminate specific qualities pertaining to objects that are either established or to be accomplished, and because prefixes (*upasarga*) are restricted solely to what is to be accomplished, there is a mutual distinction between them.

However, since *karmapravacanīyas* are the causes for delimiting a relationship produced by a specific action, they are included within the *upasargas* themselves because they reveal a specific action by way of illuminating a specific relationship; thus, some maintain that the word is divided into only four types. Others, however, maintain that this is a fifth category of word, because it lacks the direct revelation of a specific action.

For it has been stated that "karmapravacanīyas" are those [words] which express an action (*karman*); thus, while an operation characterized by the expression of a past action is possible here, a present one is not—this constitutes their distinction from *upasargas*. For in this case, the delimitation of a relationship occurs preceded by the manifestation of a specific quality inherent in the action. Indeed, every relationship is produced by action, because it is brought about by assistance (*upakāra*), and because such assistance cannot exist without action.

In this regard, an action-word (*kriyāśabda*) is heard in some instances and not in others. Where it is heard, the determination of the specific relation is based solely on that verbal expression (*śrauta*). For example: "he remembers his mother" (*mātuḥ smarati*), "his mother is remembered" (*mātuḥ smṛtam*), "he knows ghee" (*sarpiṣo jānīte*), and so forth. For an action, by its very nature, connects with substances without the intervention of another action.

Others, however, explain that because this recollection proceeds toward or rests upon the mother, it is related to the mother; thus, they maintain that even this relationship is preceded by a relationship of action and agent (*kriyā-kāraka-bhāva*). But when an action-word (*kriyāpada*) is not heard, there are two possible ways of understanding it. In some cases, since the specific action is established by the very power of the nature of the related entities themselves, the fact that the residual relationship (*śeṣa-sambandha*) is preceded by a specific relationship of action and agent is understood even without the use of a *karmapravacanīya* particle.

For example, in expressions such as "the offspring of Upagu" (*upagoḥ apatyam*) or "the branch of the tree" (*vṛkṣasya śākhā*), the relationship between the offspring and its progenitor is caused by the act of generating (*janikriyā*), while the relationship between the part and the whole is caused by the act of abiding (*sthitikriyā*), and so forth. However, in some cases, there is no capacity to determine that relationships are preceded by specific actions. For instance, in the expression "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), one understands only that the relationship of owner and owned (*svasvāmibhāva*) is caused by various actions such as maintenance (*bharaṇa*); the specific action that serves as its cause is not determined.

And so says the Bhāṣya: "That which is called 'one's own' (sva) occurs in four ways: through supporting, taking away, buying, or begging. Since [actions such as] giving and the like are invariably concomitant with one or another of these, the action is indeed inferred. However, in some cases, even the invariably concomitant action is not perceived. Thus, in such instances, the *karmapravacanīya* makes known the specific nature of the relationship—that it is produced by a particular, restricted action.

As it has been said: "Having produced some relation, a certain action ceases; when an action-word (*kriyā-śabda*) is heard, a relation is generated in some cases. And that relation, once produced, even after the word for the action has ceased, is regulated in each instance by a *karmapravacanīya*. The restriction (*niyama*) of that [relation] consists in its being produced by a specific, restricted action.

For instance, in the expression "it rained following Śākalya’s *saṃhitā*," the relationship characterized as that between cause and effect—which exists between the *saṃhitā* and the rain—is understood by means of the prefix *anu* as being produced by a restricted action. In the case of *anuniśamya*, since the prefix *anu* is observed to co-occur with the action of "listening" (*niśamayati*), and since here the *saṃhitā* consists of recitation, it is appropriate to infer that [action] there; therefore, its status as denoting an action in this context should not be assumed based on its usage elsewhere.

Furthermore, expressiveness (*dyotakatva*) consists in being based on a meaning that is to be expressed; thus, that too is absent here because no verbal root (*kriyāpada*) is employed. Nor is there an implication (*ākṣepaka*) of a verbal root, as in the case of "he draws around [the altar] for a span" (*prādeśaṃ viparilikhati*). In that instance, because the connection of the act of drawing (*lekhana*) with the prefix *vi-* is otherwise untenable, it implies the act of constructing (*nirmāti*). For here, since the word "span" (*prādeśam*) is in the accusative case—a kāraka-case—an implication of a verb appropriate to it is justified. But in this case, since the word "Saṃhitā" (*saṃhitām*) possesses a secondary derivative suffix (*śaiṣikī*), how could there be an implication of a verb?

For it is logical that the relationship of mutual implication between the action (*kriyā*) and the factor of action (*kāraka*) alone is established through invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), as in examples such as "Enter, [eat] a cake" (*praviśa piṇḍīm*). Nor does the prefix *anu* here denote a relation, since that is already expressed by the case-ending (*vibhakti*) itself. Since no other means for conveying the delimitation of the relation is possible, it is determined by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) that the capacity of *anu* lies here in its power of indication. As it has been said: "This [prefix] is neither an indicator (*dyotaka*) of the relation through the action, nor is it a denoter (*vācaka*) of it."

"Nor does it imply a verbal action, but rather it is a differentiator of the relationship. The meaning of "differentiator" (*bhedaka*) is "that which indicates a distinction. This is the underlying point here: where something is not otherwise established (*ananyathāsiddha*), it is appropriate to postulate an operation for the prefix (*anu*).

Furthermore, since that which is established by other causes such as the capacity of the meaning (*arthasāmarthya*) cannot have its power attributed to that [karmapravacanīya], it is established that because other words are directed toward different meanings, the status of being a *karmapravacanīya* belongs to that whose specific relation is not understood from them. Now, one might object: why is it not stated that the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is the delimitation of the relation—characterized by being produced by a specific action—in accordance with the principle that "whatever is additional here is the sentence-meaning"?

"Let it be that [the relation] consists merely in its occurring after [the word-meanings]. To this it is replied: Here, the "excess" (ādhikya) being presented as the sentence-meaning must be understood as following immediately upon the word-meanings (*padārtha*), and not by transcending them. For the "excess" in that context is the connection of the *sādhya* (the thing to be accomplished) or the *viśeṣya* (the qualificand)—as presented in each respective sentence—with the very *sādhana*s (means of accomplishment) and *viśeṣaṇa*s (qualifiers) that have been presented. For example: "Bring a white cow," and "A blue lotus."

For this very reason it is said: "The restriction [of the relation] between the locus and the located is established by the sentence. Thus, since there is no cognition of a word-meaning that has not been directly expressed through the sentence, one cannot postulate here that the delimitation of the relation—which is not itself a word-meaning—is the sentence-meaning; therefore, this concerns only the domain of *karmapravacanīyas*. As he will say: "The restriction of the cause for the relation is not grasped from the word [itself]; rather, it is restricted to a specific [instance] by means of the *karmapravacanīyas*."

In this regard, there are two views: either the relationship, which by its very nature is distinct from other types of relationships, is delimited by the *karmapravacanīya* [particle], or it is so delimited because it is produced by a specific action. Among these, when delimitation occurs by way of the essential nature [of the relationship], the cognition that it is produced by a specific action is obtained through a consideration of the specific relata. For instance, in the expression "The Pañcālas are under Brahmadatta" (*adhi brahmadatte pañcālāḥ*), the fact that this relationship is one of owner and owned (*svasvāmibhāva*) is made known by the particle *adhi*.

Brahmadatta is the master (*svāmī*) and lord (*īśvara*), and the Pañcāla country is his own (*svam*); thus, it is understood that this relationship between these two related entities is justified precisely by the activities of protection and the collection of taxes. Similarly, in the case of "Abhimanyu from Arjuna" (*arjunataḥ pratī*), the particle *prati* indicates that this relationship is characterized by similarity. Furthermore, upon examining the nature of the related entities, it is understood that in this instance the relationship is produced by actions such as combat.

And thus, even in the case of the expression "it rained following Śākalya’s *saṃhitā*," this particle *anu* rests upon the mere fact that this relationship is one of cause and effect. Because the *saṃhitā* is a specific kind of recitation (*pāṭhaviśeṣa*), there is an understanding of the act of hearing it. For, through the power of the relationship—namely, that "the god rained upon hearing the sound"—one concludes that the event is brought about by that specific action. Some, however, say that the function of *anu* extends only this far.

Even when the action delimits its own nature, the meaning "they have spoken" (*proktavantaḥ*) is indeed consistent, because the action is past in relation to the connection that has become its effect; for in reality, it is the connection itself, which is the fruit of the action, that is manifested. However, as the intention of the venerable Bhartṛhari is observed in various places, the established conclusion (*rāddhāntaḥ*) is that the status of being a *karmapravacanīya* is established solely by the delimitation of a specific causal condition (*nimitta-viśeṣa*).

In the expression *adhibrahmadatte pāñcālāḥ* ("the Pañcālas [are subordinate] to Brahmadatta"), the fact that the relationship of owner and owned (*svasvāmibhāva*) is established through the act of protection is manifested by the prefix *adhi*. In the expression *abhimanyur arjunataḥ prati* ("Abhimanyu is a match for Arjuna"), the relationship of imitation between the model and the imitator—arising from such things as the defeat of enemies—is revealed by the prefix *prati*. This principle should be applied everywhere in similar cases.

In cases such as *sustuta* ("well-praised") and *atistuta* ("excessively praised"), the designation *karmapravacanīya*—established by rules such as "the prefix *su-* [is used] in the sense of praise" and "*ati-* [is used] in the sense of exceeding"—applies independently of its own primary meaning (*svārtha*) specifically for the purpose of subverting the designation *upasarga*. As it has been said: "The status of being a *karmapravacanīya* is prescribed when there is a connection with an action; it serves to prevent [the occurrence of] the substitution of *ṣ* and other such changes for words like *su-*, which possess different properties."

However, when the classification [of words] is undertaken according to their functional form (*ārtha-rūpa*), since terms such as *svati* are included within the category of prefixes (*upasarga*) because they illuminate specific actions, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*). Thus, the differentiation of the word (*pada*)—which is extracted from the sentence (*vākya*)—based on its specific meaning as derived through extraction, has been demonstrated as far as possible as a means for the analysis of sentences that are devoid of parts (*niraṃśa-vākya*).

For this very reason, the category beginning with *svādi* (the nominal suffixes), because it is not a constituent of the derivation of sentences (*vākya-vyutpatti*), has been conventionally designated in the *Śāstra* as a means for the derivation of words ending in *sup* (*subanta-pada*). It is not to be included here in the enumeration [of the primary objects of analysis], just like *prakṛti* and *pratyaya*; thus, it is relegated to the side of the examples, and there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*). Indeed, this extraction (*apoddhāra*) is from the word (*pada*), not from the sentence. || 1 ||

Thus, having demonstrated the extraction of words (*padāpoddhāra*), he speaks in order to show the essential nature—according to different philosophical views—of their extracted meaning, which possesses two forms: that which is already established (*siddha*) and that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*). "In the extraction of word-meanings, either the universal (*jāti*) or the substance (*dravya*) alone is described as the eternal word-meaning of all words. (Verse 2)

A word is examined by way of its meaning; thus, first, there is an investigation into the meanings of words as extracted [from sentences] according to different philosophical views. For instance, in the view that maintains the existence of universals (*jāti*), for all words in the form of *pada*s—whether their nature be nouns (*nāman*), verbs (*ākhyāta*), or otherwise—it is the universal alone that is the meaning, not the substance (*dravya*). In the view that maintains the existence of substances, however, it is the substance alone that is the meaning, not the universal. Or, by a second [interpretation], another category of word-meaning is indicated: the denotation of a substance qualified by a universal.

For this very reason, it has been made clear that those two very things, in the form of a synthesis, constitute the word-meanings (*padārtha*). Otherwise, if the meaning were [treated] separately, this conclusion regarding the meaning would not be tenable. However, if they are expressed as such, the verbal expression (*abhidhāna*) is indeed common to both, because a word lacks further operation once it has ceased [its initial function]. But the relationship of subordinate and principal (*guṇapradhānabhāva*) between the universal (*jāti*) and the substance (*dravya*) is a matter of the sense (*ārtha*).

Alternatively, this position—that in the system of Pāṇini, the universal (*jāti*) and the substance (*dravya*) are denoted by the word as distinct objects of reference according to their predominance—is stated here as "the two word-meanings" (*padārthau*). In that regard, for a nominal word such as *gaur* ("cow"), the denotable object is the universal of cowness (*gotva-jāti*), which has attained the state of being a specific number and a universal inherent in a single object that serves as the means for a restricted action. This is because a universal cannot exist without a substratum. The substance is understood through the force of implication (*sāmarthyāt*).

Likewise, the denotative power (*vācaka-śakti*) of a verbal form (*ākhyāta-pada*) has as its object the action-genus (*kriyā-jāti*), which is the cause of a single designation and cognition associated with distinct moments of action. Here, however, the genus of the *kāraka* (participant) is subordinate; the action-genus belonging to the verbal form attains connection with the *kāraka*-genus belonging to the nominal form (*nāman-pada*) by means of the individual instances (*vyakti*). The substance-genus (*dravya-jāti*), on the other hand, experiences connection with the action through the power of the instrument (*sādhana-śakti*) due to inherence in a single object (*ekārtha-samavāya*).

Even a universal such as "number" (saṃkhyājāti), through its inherent connection with a single substance, becomes associated with action by means of its own manifestations (vyakti) via its power (śakti). Thus, when the coordination of all word-meanings is established, the sentence-meaning (vākyārtha) is conceptualized. Just as the universal "throwing upwards-ness" (utkṣepaṇatva) is manifested through the repeated occurrence of moments of throwing upwards and so forth, even though they exist at different times, so too will it be examined how the universal of the action "cooks" (pacati) is manifested through the successive moments of the action such as placing [the pot] on the fire (adhiśrayaṇa) and so forth.

Furthermore, its status as something to be accomplished (*sādhyatva*), even though it is eternal, is established by way of individual instances (*vyakti*). In this view, even prepositions (*upasarga*) and the like, when occurring alongside nouns (*nāman*) or verbs (*ākhyāta*), function solely as class-entities (*jāti-padārtha*), because they illuminate specific distinctions within that meaning. Since a distinction is apprehended only as resting upon a qualified entity, even a "karmapravacanīya" (governing particle) is grounded in the genus of the relation itself. Likewise, for quality-words such as "white" (*śukla*) and so forth, the denotation is the genus of the quality.

It will also be demonstrated that even for words of proper names, such as "Ḍittha" and the like, the denotation is a genus (*jāti*). Thus, according to the view of the teacher Vājapyāyana, the universal rule that the word-meaning is a genus is established. However, according to Vyāḍi, the meaning of all words is the individual substance (*dravya*), because it alone can be directly connected with action, and because it is the object of injunction by virtue of being a constituent of the sentence-meaning. As he said: "And because it is the starting point in injunctions. Furthermore, in this view, the application of linguistic convention is possible through the connection with a single genus.

Even when not explicitly expressed, a genus (*jāti*) is employed as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the meaning of a word, just as a crow is [indicated] in the case of a house and so forth. Furthermore, according to the view of Vyāḍi, in the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), the primary significance belongs to the substance that serves as the substratum of the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). This is because, in an expression such as "Devadatta cooks," grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is possible only with the substance. Action (*kriyā*), however, is subordinate here; for the meaning of the verbal suffix is a substance permeated by activity (*vyāpāra*), and it is this substance that is fit to be referred to by pronouns such as "this" or "that. This is the universal rule.

And so he will say: "But in the case of a category (*padārtha*), the property of substance (*dravyadharma*) is stated; in the case of a substance (*dravya*), every object is expressed. For this very reason, it is established that even qualities such as "white" and the like have the status of being the referent of the word "substance" (*dravyapadārthatā*). Alternatively, Brahman itself, as delimited by various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), is denoted by the word "substance" and is the object of all words—this indeed will be stated later. Or, the word "substance" is a synonym for the individual (*vyakti*); thus, through the alternative of either the universal (*jāti*) or the individual, it is the object of all words.

And thus, because it is stated that "this applies to all words," even when a word is extracted [from a sentence], the referent of the extraction—whether it be action, grammatical relation (*kāraka*), number, and so forth—is assigned accordingly to the word in the form of a stem (*prakṛti*) or an affix (*pratyaya*), being handed down as either a genus (*jāti*) or an individual (*vyakti*). Alternatively, since both are cognized from the word, both together constitute the word-meaning (*padārtha*); the various alternative views, however, are based on the distinction between the subordinate and the primary status [of these two].

And the description of its permanence is found in the Bhāṣya on the passage "the relationship between word and meaning being established" (*siddhe śabdārthasaṃbandhe*): "that in which the true nature is not destroyed. Thus, even the substance is permanent, because it is always perceived from the word through the permanence of its stream (*pravāha*). || 2 ||

Thus, since it has been stated that the referent of a word (*padārtha*) is either a universal (*jāti*) or a substance (*dravya*) according to different philosophical views, the present section undertakes an investigation relevant to the treatise concerning the universal as the word-referent. For this book is intended for the examination of the word (*pada*); the examination of the word occurs by way of its referent, and that investigation is conducted because it is useful for understanding the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*). In the theory that the universal is the word-referent, how can there be a syntactic connection (*samanvaya*) with the action (*kriyā*) denoted by the verb (*ākhyāta-pada*), which constitutes the sentence-meaning? For it is the means (*sādhana*, i.e., the substance) that connects with the action, and a universal is not a means.

If it is argued that the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is that which has the universal (*jāti*) as its substrate, even so, since the universal is directly enjoined by the word, the substrate is understood through implication (*sāmarthya*); thus, there is adherence to what was enjoined. Anticipating the objection—"In the absence [of the primary], let there be no substitute for a compulsory (*nitya*) rite, nor for a desired (*kāmya*) rite already commenced; otherwise, there would be an omission"—and fearing the resulting impossibility of a substitute, he states the following justification: "For some, the universal is indicated by the power [of the substance] through association; when the *khadira* and other such trees are incapable, a capable one is substituted. (Verse 3)

In this regard, some proponents of universals (*jāti*) hold the view that when a capacity is communicated through inherence in a single object, the universal (*jāti*) serves as a mere indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), that is, a means (*upāya*). Others, however, maintain that the universal itself is primarily expressed by the word, while its connection with an action occurs sometimes directly and sometimes through the medium of an individual (*vyakti*). Alternatively, the phrase "of some" refers to certain words.

Regarding those who maintain that [the word] expresses the capacity (*śakti*), there the genus (*jāti*) is mentioned as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) with reference to the capacity; its mention is therefore inseparable [from the capacity], because a case-ending (*vibhakti*) expressing capacity cannot be employed in isolation. Consequently, since the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) must necessarily be employed, the capacity is delimited by the genus denoted by it, provided such a genus is possible. In its absence, however, the capacity is grasped even as associated with another genus similar to it, because of the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the injunction.

For when the mere means (*sādhana*) is already implied by the action (*kriyā*) which constitutes the sentence-meaning, even though the term for the means is employed for the purpose of conveying a specific kind (*jāti*), if that specific kind is impossible, the genus (*jāti*) is used with the intent of making known the capacity to accomplish the action. Thus, lest there be a failure of the action due to the abandonment of even the primary capacity, the capacity residing in a substance of another genus is also accepted, according to the practice of the learned.

And there is no such over-extension [of the principle], because this rule is intended to apply only to the case of a substitute for what has been enjoined. Thus, in injunctions regarding the milking of cows and the like, if that [cow] is incapable, there is no contingency of implying a buffalo or similar animal. Furthermore, because it is capable of being understood, the genus does not impose a restriction. For example, when a sentence is intended to ward off a nuisance, the mention of a "crow" or the like as a representative instance does not constitute an abandonment of the literal meaning. And where the literal meaning that was enjoined is possible, there the direct Vedic statement (śruti) is fruitful.

Therefore, in cases such as "one binds [the sacrificial animal] to a *khadira* tree" or "one binds it to a *palāśa* tree," when a *khadira* or similar tree capable of binding is unavailable, it is appropriate to adopt a substitute such as a *kadara* tree that possesses the same capacity. Since a capacity cannot exist without a substratum, the genus (*jāti*) is mentioned as an inseparable concomitant; however, because no restrictive rule (*niyama*) is prescribed, the genus serves merely as an indicator of the capacity and is not itself connected to the function. Thus, if the substratum of that genus lacks the capacity, the capacity is accepted even if it resides in another substance, independent of that [specific] genus.

If, however, only that which belongs to that same class were capable [of performing the function], then, because there would be no reason to abandon what is present, only that which belongs to that class would be employed. But if those of that class are incapable, then since the purpose of the secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*) has been fulfilled by characterizing [the class], the capacity characterized by it is enjoined by the scripture even when it resides in another thing provided it is capable of that effect; thus, because it is not excluded, it is employed, and there is no restrictive rule [against this]. And since the capacity residing in another similar object is grasped, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). || 3 ||

Now, raising the objection: "How can a substitute be possible for those proponents of the theory of universals (*jāti*) who maintain that the universal is the primary denotation and not a secondary indicator of capacity (*śakti*"?—he says in response: "Binding results in a lack of independence; thus, even when a universal is denoted, that which is devoid of capacity is not apprehended, just as [the means of knowledge] such as *pramāṇa* are taught. (4)

Regarding the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*): because bondage—which has lack of independence as its fruit—is enjoined by the injunction (*codanā*), even though the genus (*jāti*) is what is to be conveyed, and even though it lacks the status of a defining characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*), the *kadara* wood and the like, which are capable, are substituted for the *khadira* wood and the like, which are devoid of capacity, by virtue of the power of the injunction for the bondage that serves the purpose of [ensuring] non-independence. For since the act of binding, which constitutes the meaning of the sentence, is the primary element, it is logical to adopt a material substance that possesses the capacity to accomplish that act.

Now, one might object: "What necessity is there for insisting on the tethering post (*bandhi*) when its result is visible? Anticipating this doubt, it is said: "Just as the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and so forth remain [as necessary]. Just as the means of knowledge and other factors, though their results are visible, are enjoined [as necessary], so too is the tethering post, which is a constituent part of them; therefore, it must be insisted upon in every respect. For instance, if the animal were not tethered to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), the means of knowledge and other factors would be rendered untenable; consequently, since the portions to be offered (*avadāna*) and the cups (*graha*) would be absent, the sacrifice itself—which has heaven as its fruit—would fail to be accomplished. Therefore, out of regard for that [sacrifice], and for the sake of fulfilling its constituent parts, one must employ the appropriate implements suitable for it.

In this context, the *pramāṇa* (the means of measurement) is the commencement of injury (*hiṃsā*). For the word *mī* has the meaning of injury; its form *māna* arises when the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied in place of *ey*, and once the vowel change (*ātva*) has been made, the prefix *pra-* signifies the "commencement" (*ārambha*) of that act. By the inclusion of the term "beginning" (*ādi*), there is an adherence to the entire set of subsidiary elements (*aṅgakalāpa*) relevant to the context, starting from the immolation (*ālambhana*) and ending with the taking of the portions (*avadāna*). This is the intended meaning here in both views.

Even if it be granted that the genus (*jāti*), which constitutes the primary meaning and is employed as the delimiting factor of capacity (*śakti*), is impossible—because that which is delimited by such a genus lacks capacity—nevertheless, it is not proper to abandon the capacity of the suffixal meaning, even though it is the delimited [object]. Rather, that capacity is grasped even when residing in another [entity]. This is so that the word expressing it does not become meaningless, and the action of the sentence-meaning is not frustrated. Furthermore, in all cases such as "one should sacrifice a cow" (*gām ālabheta*), the operation of the action resides only in a capable individual. Therefore, why this agitation regarding a substitute (*pratinidhi*)? 4.

Now, he establishes the substitute by means of gender (*liṅga*) as well: "If what is intended [by the author] were merely the act of binding [the word] through phonetic conjunction, then gender would be the instruction regarding the number of powers (*śakti*) based on the authoritative means of knowledge. (5)

The root *badh* (to bind) is said to signify "purpose" (*artha*) through figurative usage (*upacāra*). "Binding" (*saṃśleṣaḥ*) refers to the tethering of the animal to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*); that alone, without regard for the result characterized by the lack of independence [of the animal], constitutes the mere act itself.

If this is intended as the meaning of *badh*, then since it could be accomplished even by a *khadira* tree, there would be no capacity [in the injunction] to employ *kadara* wood. Therefore, the subsequent instruction provided by the authoritative means of knowledge—such as the statements, "One should sacrifice the animal," "He cuts off the heart," and "Then the chest"—which prescribes the use of a suitable substance, serves here as the inferential mark (*liṅga*) for the inference [that *kadara* is not to be used].

Alternatively, previously the root *bandh* itself was the indicative mark (*liṅga*); now, if the root *badh* signifies mere connection, then the meaning is that the "indicative mark" refers to the instruction regarding the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth. For it is appropriate here to employ the root *bandh*, whose meaning is "to bind," as a subordinate part of the immolation of the sacrificial animal (*paśuviśasana*). Since the meaning of *badh* is incapable of [denoting] immolation, it is not a subordinate part of that; thus, the substitute (*pratinidhi*) is obtained through a consideration of the meanings of the means of valid cognition and so forth, which are presented within a single context.

Previously, the substitute was stated on the basis of the capacity of the word-meaning (*padārtha-sāmarthya*) and subsequently on the basis of the capacity of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha-sāmarthya*); now, however, it is stated on the basis of the capacity of the context (*prakaraṇa-sāmarthya*). This is the distinction among the three positions. The connection is as follows: *śakteḥ āśrayaḥ* refers to the *kadara* substance; when that is employed there, it serves as the indicative mark (*liṅga*). Alternatively, *śaktiḥ* is the excellence of the substance (*dravya-ātmātiśaya*) which brings about the accomplishment of the task; the meaning is "when that [excellence] is accepted as its substratum" (*tad-āśraye*).

Thus, that which was stated in the *Vākyakāṇḍa*—"And there is another difference of opinion regarding the substitute (*pratinidhi*) in the *Jātisamuddeśa*"—has been explained here. Furthermore, another difference of opinion was set forth therein: "the abandonment of the rule of impossibility" and "the sublation of the mere rule."

For instance: in the injunction "one should sacrifice with rice" (*vrīhibhiryajeta*), since the meaning of the root *yaji* (to sacrifice) consists in the relinquishment of a substance for the sake of a deity, it follows by implication that "one should sacrifice" refers merely to the substance which has become a constituent part of the act of sacrificing. Indeed, this much alone is the meaning of *yaji*; thus, the substance alone is brought into proximity by the direct statement (*śruti*) itself. Since a mere relinquishment devoid of both substance and deity cannot constitute the meaning of *yaji*, once that [act] is understood, it is impossible for the substance to be implied subsequently through the force of the sense (*arthasāmarthya*).

And thus, although the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) has action as its primary meaning, the general substance (*dravyasāmānya*)—which serves as the substratum for the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) and constitutes a part of that [action]—is indeed verbal (*śābda*), as its proximity is established by direct audition (*śruti*). In this regard, the term "with rice" (*vrīhibhiḥ*) provides a specific nourishment through its non-contradictory co-inherence with the nature of rice; for there is no universal devoid of particulars. Indeed, the scriptural mention of "rice" is for the purpose of specification (*adhyāvāpa*); it does not sublate the mere state of being a substance (*dravyatvamātra*) obtained through the power of the word itself, because there is no contradiction between them.

For that [substance-ness] is obtained through the power of the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), whereas the specific quality of being rice (*vrīhitva*) is arrived at through the power of the contextual meaning (*arthasāmarthya*), because there can be no universal devoid of particulars. Thus, while the status of being a subordinate element (*aṅgabhāva*) for substance-ness alone is enjoined by the *śruti*, it is not so for the particularity of being rice. Consequently, even when that [rice] is unavailable, there is no sublation of what is enjoined regarding the substitute, since the mere universal is fulfilled through another particular.

But surely, in the case of insertion (*adhyāvāpa*), since the generic property of being a substance (*dravyatva*) is not restricted by the mention of rice (*vrīhi*), an option (*vikalpa*) would result everywhere—such as "with rice or with barley," and so forth. For the generic property of being a substance is obtained through the force of the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*); if that [generic property] is not delimited from other specific instances by the mention of "rice," then those other specific instances are also accepted by it as if they were already present. Thus, there would be the contingency of an option, and consequently, the mention of "rice" would be rendered purposeless.

To this it is replied: Here, when substance-ness (*dravyatva*) is qualified by rice-ness (*vrīhitva*), the impossibility of barley-ness (*yavatva*) and so forth follows from the very nature of things. For it is not possible for that which inheres in the same substrate as rice-ness—in this case, substance-ness—to also inhere in the same substrate as barley-ness. Therefore, this is what is called a "rule of impossibility" (*asaṃbhavaniyama*). Indeed, there are two kinds of rules: one arises from the power of words, occurring where a scriptural statement (*śruti*) applies even though [the meaning] has already been reached through logical possibility (*pakṣaprāpti*).

Just as in the case of a specific individual (*vyakti*) as the referent of a word, according to the rule "in the event of a conflict, the latter prevails" (*vipratiṣedhe param*), some maintain that even in the absence of a direct verbal operation, because there is no mutual confusion of the forms of word-referents (*padārtha*), the injunction of one thing results in the exclusion of its opposite; thus, upon examining the nature of the word-referent, this is called a "restriction resulting from impossibility. Accordingly, in the present case, since "substantiality" (*dravyatva*) is arrived at through the capacity of the word, the phrase "with rice-grains" (*vrīhibhiḥ*) functions there as a verbal operation of inclusion (*adhyāvāpa*).

For even within the theory that the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is indivisible, there arises a conceptualization of distinction (*bheda*), relation (*saṃsarga*), and so forth, during the stage of analytical extraction. In that regard, according to the view of Vyāḍi, distinction is the sentence-meaning, because the substances denoted by the words are expressed with the intention of excluding other substances. However, in the view of Vājapyāyana, who maintains the doctrine of universals (*jāti*), relation is the sentence-meaning, because the sentence-meaning consists merely in the conjunction of the word-meanings, which are universals.
