When the word *vrīhi* has fulfilled its purpose in this way, since the inherence (*samavāya*) of *vrīhi*-ness in a single object is incompatible with *yava*-ness and so forth, those [other grains] are excluded from it. Consequently, although the restriction—which arises from the inherent capacity of the substance—is set aside in the case of a substitute (*pratinidhi*), there is no abandonment of the enjoined object because the verbal [meaning], namely mere "substance-ness" (*dravyatva-mātra*), remains uncontradicted.

But surely, since a universal devoid of particulars is impossible, the nature of substance (*dravyatva*) must be implied by the root *yaj* as residing specifically in the particulars; and because all particulars would thus be obtained through the force of the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), the repeated mention of "with rice-grains" (*vrīhibhiḥ*) would merely serve the purpose of restriction (*niyama*). Since this [restriction] is already established even by the form of the direct scriptural statement, how can there be no abandonment of the literal meaning? This is not tenable in the case of a substitute (*pratinidhi*). For a word does not follow the investigation of the actual entity, since only a certain portion of the entity falls within the scope of the word's operation.

And thus, the capacity of the word *ṭajati* extends only so far as to imply substance in general (*dravyamātra*), and not its specific qualities. Otherwise, since a substance devoid of qualities is impossible, why would this word not be described as implying quality (*guṇa*) as well? Therefore, the verbal implication (*śābdākṣepa*) is only of the universal property of substantiality (*dravyatvamātra*). Consequently, the introduction of other specific qualities for the sake of its fulfillment does not result from a restrictive rule; rather, it establishes those other specific qualities that have not been excluded by the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*) as substitutes.

Thus, the abandonment of the rule of impossibility has been described. Now, the sublation of the mere rule is also stated. Here, in every case, the meaning of a sentence is primarily action (*kriyā*). Accordingly, a suitable substance is implied as a means (*sādhana*) for the sake of accomplishing that [action]. And that very [means] is expressed by another word as being qualified. This being the case, where the mentioned means is impossible, another means is substituted for the sake of the accomplishment of the primary action.

For an action (*kriyā*) is not substituted because of its primacy. Furthermore, by resorting to another action, there would be a transgression of the scriptural injunction due to the performance of a different rite that was not prescribed. Therefore, the learned have practiced substitution only for the means (*sādhana*), which is subordinate. In that case, there is no abandonment of the mere means prescribed by scripture and implied by the primary verbal element denoting the action; rather, there is only the sublation of the restriction regarding the substance, such as rice (*vrīhi*), which is expressed by the specific word.

And that [implication] does not constitute a fault, because the mere capacity—which is of the nature of a means and is implied by the efficacy of the action—is primary, and thus there is no transgression of the meaning enjoined by the scripture. || 5 ||

Thus, these two views have been established in the immediately preceding section, and the concept of a substitute (*pratinidhi*) has been considered as far as possible. Now, fearing that if the universal (*jāti*) were denoted by the word, the application of the word would result in being without a basis—since no other universal exists therein—the author speaks in order to demonstrate [the correct view]: "By all words whatsoever, their own universal is denoted first; thereafter, there is the conceptual superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of that [universal] upon the forms of the universals of objects. (Verse 6)

"Own" (svā) means unique to itself and belonging to its own [word], such as "cowness" (*gośabdatva*) and so forth, but not "wordness" (*śabdatva*) and so forth, which is common to all words. And thus, by qualifying it as "unique," it is shown that there is no deviation in the relationship of the word with that [unique universal], even though there may be a deviation in its relationship with the universal of the object. Therefore, it is stated that the primary denotable meaning is the word's own universal (*jāti*) alone. And so says the author of the *Vākya-kāra*: "Or rather, the cognition of an object is preceded by the word."

For this very reason, he says "first" because the denotation of the word for the universal of the object (*arthajāti*) necessarily involves the denotation of its own form (*svarūpa*), which is invariably concomitant with it. This "priority" here consists merely in the fact that when one thing is perceived as non-different from another, the latter must necessarily be perceived there; it does not, however, consist in a sequential order of denotation. Alternatively, priority is relative to the time of the acquisition of the linguistic convention (*saṃbandhavyutpatti*). For indeed, at the time of acquiring the convention, there is no connection [of the word] with the universal of the object.

If that were the case, its application there as a denoter would be purposeless, since the meaning would already have been understood; thus, that meaning has not yet been understood by that word. Furthermore, if it were the denotation of its own universal (*jāti*) at that time, then—because of being meaningless—there would be no connection with case-endings. Thus it was said: "Prior to its connection with the named object (*saṃjñin*), the name (*saṃjñā*) has its own form as its referent (*padārtha*). For "form" (*rūpa*) is described according to different philosophical views as either the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) or its own universal (*svā jāti*). [This applies] to all [names].

[The universal is expressed] by words that denote both their own form and their objects, because it is precisely as the form of that [universal] itself that it is conventionally designated. Even by words for which [this relationship] has not been mastered, the universal is apprehended through its presence within the very form of the word due to an inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*).

Although the object is immediately understood as non-different from the form of the word, nevertheless—by relying on the aforementioned sequence and following from the subsequent cognition of its own universal—the conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) of superimposing that class of words onto the natures of the universals of objects, such as "cowness" (*gotva*), is not the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*); for since the object is a transformation (*vivarta*) of the word, there is no real difference between the object and the word.

Alternatively, at the time of learning the relationship [between word and object], because the universal of the word (*śabdajāti*) is absolutely distinct from the universal of the object (*arthajāti*)—as in the cognition "this is the meaning of this word"—the superimposition of identity is postulated due to the otherwise inexplicable nature of their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). This is just as in the case of "the Vāhīka is an ox. For otherwise, it would be impossible to establish the convention itself. And just as this relationship between the signified and the signifier (*vācyavācakabhāva*) is beginningless and not of human origin, so too is this superimposition.

Otherwise, the very relationship between the signifier and the signified would not be possible—just as for the Buddhist, the unification of the perceived object and the conceptualized object is characterized by the non-determination of their difference, rather than being a superimposition based on human whim, as in the case of "the Vāhīka is a cow. Since in linguistic usage there is always a determination of non-difference between word and meaning, one might ask: how can this unique universal (*jāti*), which is manifested through each individual letter, be manifested by letters that do not exist simultaneously? We reply: it is just like the universal of "upward-throwing-ness" (*utkṣepaṇatva*) and so forth.

For instance—even though each individual moment of action serves as a manifestor [of the universal], the first moment of upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*), because it consists merely in the occupation of a space the size of a single atom, has its distinction from the moment of whirling (*bhramaṇa*) unperceived due to their similarity; thus, being individually incapable of manifesting the restricted genus, it requires another moment. Nor is there no difference between that [first moment] and the moment of whirling, since at the very beginning it is produced by an effort such as "I shall throw upward."

Although this effort, "I am uttering the word *go*," is indeed distinct from the effort that produces the sounds *gā*, *na*, and *ga*, and because of the difference in their causes, there is likewise a distinction between the two instances of the letter *ga*, nevertheless, due to their similarity, this [distinction] is difficult to discern. Thus, even while being the manifestor, the first sound (*dhvani*) manifests [the phoneme] indistinctly; and although it recurs, it is not the cause for the manifestation of the more clearly defined universal and particular characteristics.

But when the succession of its constituent parts is perceived in sequence, then linguistic usages—conditioned by the specific universals (*jāti*) of sounds—become established. At that time, due to their constant association and through mutual delimitation, they appear as distinct. Just as a verse is not grasped when recited only once, but becomes clearly manifest through repetition, so too does the reality of the *sphoṭa* shine forth in the final moment of consciousness, like the true nature of a gem.

For by the first syllable, merely a semblance (*ābhāsa*) of the universal (*jāti*) is produced; however, by the subsequent series of phonemes, there is the establishment of a clearer and most distinct determination. This is because, as seen in the case of the true nature of a gem and so forth, a specific manifestation occurs through the production of a specific mental impression (*saṃskāra*).

Therefore, because of the linguistic convention that "we understand the meaning from the word," it is untenable for individual phonemes to be the generators of the determination of meaning; and since the refutation of such a [phonemic] process was already established in the first book (*Pūrvakāṇḍa*), one must accept the reality of the Word (*śabdatattva*) as a partless signifier whose very nature is *sphoṭa*, though it appears divided by the distinction between genus and individual. Furthermore, because the object of expression is perceived as non-different from the expressive word—as in the thought "this object is a cow"—the object of linguistic usage has a form inlaid with the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of that [word].

And in that regard, the denotability of the essential nature (svarūpa) has already been determined in the first book (kāṇḍa), but it will also be determined here in this "Exposition on Relation" (saṃbandhasamuddeśa). || 6 ||

In this regard, it might be argued: "How can a universal inherent in a word designate the class of objects through non-difference, given that they belong to different substrata? Anticipating this objection, he explains this by means of an illustration: "Just as the property of being red is designated in the dye, yet it is perceived in clothes and other items as well due to the contact with the thing possessing that quality. (7)

Likewise, through the relationship between word and meaning, the universal (jāti) resides in the word; it serves as the basis for the function of the universal when denoting the universals of meanings.

In the case of the quality "red," the reality [is as follows]: the state of that red quality is called "redness" (*raktatva*), which is the universal of redness (*lauhityasāmānya*) inherent in the individual instances of the quality. Due to its inherence in that [universal], it is designated—i.e., it serves for designation—with respect to the substance *kaṣāya*, which is the substratum of the red quality. For that substance *kaṣāya* is denoted by means of that [quality] as its qualifier, as in the expression "the red lac."

Therefore, there are garments and so forth that are conjoined; the contact or mingling of those two conjoined things—the dye and the garment—is the cause, and from that cause, that redness is perceived even there [in the garment]. Due to the relation of inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavetasamavāya*), there is also a designation based on the redness in the garments and so forth, meaning "the red garment. Likewise, it is said: "from the relationship between word and object."

Just as there is a designation by means of the word-generality (*śabda-jāti*) arising from the very relationship—which stands in the same grammatical relation (*samānādhikaraṇa*) as the connection with a substance possessing redness and astringency, and which is innate and known solely at the time of linguistic derivation—it is through that relationship alone, and because it could not otherwise be accounted for, that the superimposition (*adhyāropa*) is postulated. Here, "object" (*artha*) refers to the object-generality (*artha-jāti*), since it is precisely that which is established as being denotable.

It is capable [of functioning] in designation by way of non-difference from its own form; it is capable for the sake of the function of a genus—that is, the genus existing as the denoter among genera when applied to words such as "genus" (jāti) is capable not only for designation, but also for the function of a genus. Alternatively, the meaning is that, once there is designation, it is capable for the sake of the function of a genus.

Since universals are themselves devoid of further universals—meaning that the classes of objects (*arthajāti*) are inherently lacking a genus—the effect thereof, characterized by the recurrence of words and cognitions, is achieved as follows: because of the relation between word and object as non-different in the form "this is that," the universal inherent in the word is superimposed upon the object as non-different from it, and thus it is figuratively said to become identical with the nature of that object. Furthermore, since the inherence of the universal resides in the word in its manifested form (*vyakti-rūpa*) and not in the phonemes (*varṇa*), it is logically established that [the universals] are stable.

Since phonemes (varṇas) lack simultaneity, they are not expressive; how, then, could the genus (jāti) of sound inhere in them? There are merely two views regarding the sphoṭa, distinguished by the categories of genus and individual: in the view of the individual-sphoṭa, the genus inheres [in it]. Indeed, a genus must necessarily be admitted as the cause of the non-differentiated designation and cognition of an eternal word that appears differentiated due to differences in meaning. For this very reason, it is the individual itself, as permeated by the genus, that possesses expressiveness.

However, it is the genus (*jāti*), which serves as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), that is relied upon; therefore, one should not raise the objection: "How can there be denotative power for an individual (*vyakti*) that is non-pervasive? Furthermore, the relationship between word and meaning intended here is characterized by fitness (*yogyatā*). For every word, when being assigned as a name (*saṃjñā*), is already connected to every possible object through a relationship characterized by fitness. The function of the namer consists merely in delimiting this capacity, and not in creating a new convention, because the connection with the object is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*).

Thus, it has been stated that the word "growth" (*vṛddhi*) was not merely coined as an arbitrary convention for this specific instance; rather, since all words have multiple meanings—whether due to the multiplicity of objects or the difference between speakers—one must seek a universal (*jāti*) as the basis for the cognition of a uniform form. For example, although space is conceptually differentiated according to its various conjuncts, the single nature of "spatiality" (*ākāśatva*) is indicated despite this apparent multiplicity. Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence of cognizing every object from every word, because the cognition of an object occurs through established usage (*prasiddhi*), and such usage is restricted to particular objects in particular instances.

The causes for the differentiation of well-known meanings—such as context and so forth—have been stated. For example, although nine meanings are present when the word "cow" (*go*) is uttered, a specific meaning is determined through context and other factors. Thus, the actual sequence is this: first, the individual instance of the word is denoted by the word-generality (*śabda-jāti*) without distinction; then the generality of the object (*artha-jāti*); and finally its individual instance. However, in the process of communication itself, there is indeed no sequence.

Even when the object is suffused by the word, there is no disappearance of its own nature (*svarūpa*). For just as a jar, though suffused by light, does not vanish from its own form, so too is the object colored by the nature of the word; for it is observed that both sound and light reveal an object precisely by superimposing their own forms upon it.

Just as in the expression "the Vāhīka is an ox," it is not merely the nature of an ox (*gotva*) that is perceived, but rather the Vāhīka who has the form of an ox superimposed upon him; so too here, what is intended is not the co-inherence of the collection of words within the object—as if in a crystal gem—but rather that the object itself is what is to be communicated, just like the Vāhīka. Furthermore, this natural relationship arising from non-difference between words and their meanings is the means for communication; thus, the person to be instructed understands the object in exactly that same way. For this is not dependent upon human agency.

Since the understanding of this relationship has occurred in this very manner throughout beginningless saṃsāra, who here can be postulated as a fixed superimposer? Furthermore, it cannot be argued that because a non-different cognition arises even for one who has not mastered the convention, there must exist a real "universal of objects" (arthajāti) and thus the "universal of words" (śabdajāti) alone need not be considered superimposed. This kind of verbal cognition has been explained by means of the visual cognition of redness and so forth, which serves as an illustrative example.

Furthermore, even though the word-universal (*śabda-jāti*) lacks any actual objective basis (*vastu-sanniveśitva*), this beginningless superimposition (*adhyāropa*) is firmly established. Because in everyday linguistic usage there is always a determination of non-difference between the word and its object, and because even when there is a difference—as in the case of "the *vāhīka* is a cow"—there is still a semblance of identity, this is not a false cognition (*mithyājñāna*). Moreover, prior to the time of perceiving the relationship [between word and meaning], the various classes of objects (*artha-jātayaḥ*) indeed appear as distinct.

When a cognition arises as distinct with respect to individual objects possessing dewlaps and other such features before a child who has not yet mastered linguistic conventions, then—due to the absence of the presence of a denotative word—the universal (artha-jāti) which is the cause of that non-distinct cognition is determined. For this very reason, one should not raise such objections as: "How can the class of words (śabda-jāti) be superimposed upon the class of objects when the latter has not been determined through distinction? [Verses 7–8]

He clarifies the very point already stated—that [the word] serves for the purpose of denoting a genus (jāti)—in the following verse: "In the case of a single-remainder compound (*ekaśeṣa*) of genus-words, that [genus] is held to be the genus of the genera; in the expression 'classes of words' (*śabdajātayaḥ*), that genus [resides] within the classes of words. (9)

Regarding the statement, “Vājapyāyana [holds that] in the case of a single inflection, it is because the form (*ākṛti*) is denoted,” since the *ekaśeṣa* (single-remainder) rule was rejected under the view that the genus (*jāti*) is denoted, the result of that [rejection]—the employment of a single word—is here called *ekaśeṣa*. Furthermore, co-intention (*sahavivakṣā*) is indicated by means of *ekaśeṣa*. Or, it should be construed as follows: when the application of *ekaśeṣa* to words denoting a genus has been proposed, [it is said that] this [genus]—namely, the class of words (*śabdajāti*)—which is perceived as non-different from the classes of objects (*arthajāti*), brings about the effect of a genus (*jātikārya*), namely, the status of being a single word, for the genus residing in the word.

For example, in expressions such as "the cows" or "the trees," the application of a single word (*ekaśabda*) based on a non-differentiated universal (*abhinnasāmānya*) occurs because of its inherence in a single object (*tadekārthasamavāya*), and thus it is associated with a specific number. Similarly, the expression "these universals" (*jātaya imāḥ*) is also justified by the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of a verbal universal (*vāgarajāti*) upon the universals that serve as the substrata for other universals, since there is no further universal residing within those substrata. Furthermore, it is said that a universal residing in words metaphorically performs the function of a universal; however, no one imposes a restriction that this applies only to universals belonging to actual objects.

When even word-genera (*śabdajātayaḥ*) are to be conveyed, then within these as well, that which resides in the denotative word (*abhidhāna*) is indeed capable of performing the function of a genus; thus he says, "in the phrase 'these word-genera'. The "genus of that" (*tajjātiḥ*) is the "genus of words" (*śabdajātiḥ*), meaning the universal residing in words. The meaning is this: when the single word *śabdajātayaḥ* is employed in the phrase "these word-genera," the genus belonging to that uttered word *śabdajātiśabdaḥ* serves as the basis for the non-different application of the word with respect to those word-genera—such as "word-ness" (*śabdatva*) and so on—which are to be conveyed as if they were individual instances (*vyakti*). || 9 ||

Anticipating the objection that "if this is so, then there would be an infinite regress—since the genus of 'word' (śabdajāti) would itself be distinct from the genera residing within words, and there would be yet another genus for those [latter] as well," he says: "That genus which exists in words and is characterized as distinct from words—that genus exists even by transcending the state of being the genus of words. (10)

The intention is as follows: although there are many words for word-universals (*śabdajāti*) due to differences among their users, that universal which serves as the basis for the cognition of non-difference exists within the very same words that constitute its own substratum; it possesses a nature distinct from them and is included within the category of universals such as "the word-ness of the word *go*," rather than being fit for a separate designation. Furthermore, since even the word "word-universal" is itself understood by the single expression "word-universals"—just like "the word-ness of the word *go*" and so on—there is no resulting infinite regress of usage.

Thus, by relying on the doctrine of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) established within our own school, the universal determination of the category of the universal (*jāti*) has been demonstrated. For the universal, being the very essence (*svarūpa*) of all words, is to be understood first because it is internal, unique, and non-removable. Now, even without relying on superimposition, he speaks out of a desire for bold argumentation (*prauḍhavāditā*) in order to establish the pervasion of the category of the universal: "Even when the meaning [of a word] is the universal, all [words] denote the universal;
for all word-meanings are established as being characterized by their activity (*vyāpāra*). (11)

Otherwise, the connection here would be as follows: Granted that the universal of words may have the function of a universal with respect to the universals of objects, the acquisition of the relationship [between word and object] is not possible. For the universal of the word is superimposed only upon that where there is a convention; however, since the universals of objects are manifold, such a convention is not possible without another commonality (sāmānyāntara). Thus he says: "Even when denoting the universal of objects," and so forth.

When it is maintained that these pure classes (*jāti*) are denoted by words, then all words denoting a class—even those such as "class" (*jāti*) and so forth—are at that time expressive of the class itself. One might object: "Since it is an established tenet that 'universals are devoid of further universals,' how can even words like 'class' denote a class that serves as the substratum for a universal? To this, he says: "They are characterized by their function (*vyāpāra-lakṣaṇāḥ*)."

Activity (*vyāpāra*), effect (*kārya*), and purpose (*prayojana*)—that very thing by which something is characterized (*lakṣyate*) is the "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*), which serves as the cause (*hetu*) for those meanings signified by words that possess such [defining] natures. This is the intended meaning: let the Vaiśeṣikas and others maintain that universals (*sāmānya*) are devoid of further universals. For these [universals] are determined by the cognition of concomitance (*anvaya-pratyaya*) among individuals; they consist of extrinsic adjuncts (*paropādhi-rūpa*) because, like independent individuals, they lack the manifestation of "this-ness" (*idantā*) and thus are not themselves limited by another universal.

For grammarians, it is accepted that the meaning of a word is the object [it denotes]; since a verbal cognition arises through the delimitation of a form that persists [through individuals], the admission of a universal (*jāti*) even in the case of universals themselves is not contradictory. Indeed, this very reason applies to the admission of a universal even in the case of individuals; so what aversion can there be to admitting it here as well?

Even perceptible objects are designated as "existing" when they perform their own functions, such as producing cognition; how much more so, then, are those objects denoted by words? By this general statement, substances and the rest are also characterized precisely as being denotable by words. For those for whom the word is the authority, whatever the word expresses is its ultimate reality (*paramārtha-rūpa*). Thus, even a quality (*guṇa*), when expressed in its inclusive form (*anvayi-rūpa*), is nothing other than a universal (*jāti*), just as in the case of "dark-complexioned" (*śyāma*) and so forth in a simile-compound (*upamā-samāsa*).

And so it is said: "Comparisons [are formed] with words denoting common properties. In this way, even an action, when expressed non-differently, is a genus (*jāti*). Likewise, genus, quality, and action, when expressed independently as the qualificand through the form "this is that," are indeed substance (*dravya*); this will be determined in due course further on. Furthermore, this is expounded in this treatise in accordance with worldly usage; for a system established in other sciences is contrary to the world.

For in common worldly usage, one says, "the horn is in the cow" (*gavi śṛṅgam*) or "the branch is in the tree" (*vṛkṣe śākhā*); and likewise, in grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), the locative case is used for the substratum (*ādhāra*). However, according to another treatise, since the whole resides in its parts, one would say, "the cow is in the horn" (*śṛṅge gauḥ*) or "the tree is in the branch" (*śākhāyāṃ vṛkṣaḥ*). And thus, because the object denoted by the word is the meaning intended here, all words denote the universal (*jāti*), since things (*padārtha*) are indicated through the operation of the word.

Although external objects do not exist, they are nevertheless conveyed by words in that manner; therefore, because they are conveyed in a connected form through the power of the denotative function (*abhidhā-vyāpāra*), it is established that pervasion resides in the universal (*jāti*) as the word-meaning—this is the meaning [of the verse]. || 11 ||

He clarifies precisely the function of denotation and indication: "Since, when the universal is the word-meaning, either the universal itself or the individual is expected by words as if it were a universal, therefore those [words] are denoters of universals. (12)

He establishes the delimitation of the thesis (*pakṣāvaccheda*) as "in the case of a thing that is a universal" (*jātau padārthe*). For on this view, it must be admitted that every word denotes a universal. Whether or not there exists a universal within universals, words nevertheless require a single nature consisting of a universal, distinct from [particular] universals, as the object to be conveyed; this is accepted as the denotatum. For the difference between things in their specific individuality (*svālakṣaṇya*) cannot be touched by words, since a word's capacity to denote arises through the acquisition of a relationship [with its object] by way of entering into a recurring form (*anvayirūpa*).

And likewise, the mutual difference between universals (*jāti*) is not denoted as a real entity; rather, they are denoted through the conceptualization of non-difference. Since this non-difference is the universal (*sāmānya*), it is established that universals possess a single word-denotation. Similarly, even that specific [particular] which is the referent of proper nouns (*saṃjñāśabda*) and is restricted by cognition, is like a well-known universal in that it too is required by words in the same manner as a universal.

Even there, the distinctions between stages such as infancy and childhood are not touched by the word; rather, it is only the underlying persisting form that is apprehended, for that must necessarily be admitted as the cause of the cognition of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). Therefore, since everything is required by words just like a universal (*jāti*), he concludes the pervasion of the denotation of universals by stating that all words, whether they convey a universal or a particular, are denoters of a universal.
And thus, even for proper names (*saṃjñāśabda*) under the theory that words denote universals, they possess the nature of universal-words; hence, there is only one mode of operation for words. (12)

Thus, even in other philosophical systems, the establishment of pervasion (*vyāpti*) occurs only by relying upon the operation of words; so he says: "But in the case of a category (*padārtha*), every object is said to reside in a substance (*dravya*), because it possesses the attributes of a substance (*dravyadharma*). Therefore, by virtue of being the locus of the attributes of a substance, every object is accepted as being a substance. (13)

It is not only by me, as a proponent of the category of genus (*jāti*), that it is accepted that every object is a genus; rather, even when the category of substance (*dravya*) is the referent, under the view that the category is substance, every object is said to possess the properties of substance. Why? Because one relies upon the properties of substance. Therefore, every object is intended to be a substance. The meaning is that pervasion (*vyāpti*) is thus established. This must also be admitted by the proponent of substance in order to establish pervasion.

The intention is that every object expressed by a word is necessarily endowed with the properties of a substance (*dravya*). Just as for you, the proponent of substance (*dravyavādin*), some words denote primary substances while others denote metaphorical substances, so too for me, the proponent of the universal (*jātivādin*), some words denote a primary universal while others denote a metaphorical one; thus, there is equality between the two views.

In this context, the properties of substance (*dravyadharma*) include such qualities as the capacity for reflective determination (*pratyavamarśayogyatva*)—that is, the state of being able to be identified as "this is that"—as well as perfection (*pariniṣpannatā*), independence (*svātantrya*), and connection with gender and number. These are called "properties of substance" because they are superimposed even upon qualities such as whiteness; thus, these are the properties which belong to them just as they do to a substance. For instance: "white," "blue," "feminine," "masculine," "neuter," and "qualities of existence" (*sattvaguṇa*).

Likewise, qualities and so forth, which are conveyed by words such as "oneness" and the like, appear in the form of independence and other such attributes despite being properties of substances; thus, every object is denoted in the form of a substance. || 13 ||

Thus, pervasion has been established by relying on the operation of words. Now, even from the perspective of the Vaiśeṣikas, he states the pervasion of the category (jāti) as a real entity by relying on common properties residing in the objects themselves: "Or, in all [lower] universals (jāti), the universal (jāti) may be a property of recurrence; in a particular (viśeṣa), the universal is held to be a commonality of properties of exclusion. (14)

This is the "genus-ness" (*jātitva*) of genera: namely, that which is the conformity of all genera to their own substrata, a property common to every genus. And although this [conformity] is non-different from those [genera], it is perceived as non-distinct due to its similarity; thus, it is the "genus" (*jāti*) of them all. For every genus indeed conforms to its own individual instances (*vyakti*). Furthermore, this property is merely an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*); by means of it, there is the production of a cognition corresponding to itself, through the power of which a substance appears in that form.

It is the cause for denotation according to its own form; by virtue of which a substance becomes expressible through a name corresponding to that [universal]. Furthermore, the common characteristic of a genus (*jāti*) is that it is fully present in its entirety within each individual substratum. If the genus were to exist only partially, then the cognition of "cowness" and so forth would likewise occur only partially. However, even when one perceives only partial parts such as the horns, a complete cognition in the form of "cow" is immediately produced.

Furthermore, the qualities, though fully established in their respective substrates, are distinct in each individual substance, whereas the universal (*jāti*) is one and the same; such uncommon properties (*asādhāraṇa-dharma*) are to be stated. And just as the universal "cowness" (*gotva*) pervades all individual cows, so too these properties pervade all universals; thus, by virtue of having a form similar to that of a universal, they are capable of performing the function of a universal. In this way, all particularities (*viśeṣa*) are excluded.

Because they follow otherwise, they would be universals and not particulars; thus, the exclusion (vyāvṛtti) common to all particulars is a property similar to a universal (sāmānyasama), and being present in them, it is called the "genus" (jāti). [Objection: In that case, since the connection with parts such as the dewlap, tail, hooves, hump, and horns is also common to individual cows, let that very thing be the genus. [Reply: Not so. Through the possession of a dewlap and so forth, there arises the cognition "one possessing a dewlap," and so on, but not the cognition "cow, cow."

For an effect postulates a cause that is appropriate to it; for example, in the cognition "one with a staff," the causal factor is the connection with a staff, not the desire to obtain a staff. If this were so, then even in the case of a continuous application [of a term], it would not be logical to have the cognition "universal" (*jāti*) regarding a universal, nor "particular" (*viśeṣa*) regarding a particular based on exclusion. This is not the case. Because there is no other possible recourse, here the similar properties themselves are postulated as the "universal," while the primary possession of a universal has already been established.

Regarding the *viśeṣas* (ultimate particulars), which reside in eternal substances and produce the cognition of differentiation: if one were to postulate a *sāmānya* (universal) in them to dispel doubt, then by postulating yet another *viśeṣa* for those [universals] as well—since they too would be objects of doubt regarding their inherence in a universal—an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would result. Alternatively, if some *viśeṣa* were to exist without a universal, then, due to the lack of distinction, all [other particulars] would likewise be so; this has been explained at length elsewhere.

Since there is no subverting argument against the acceptance of a universal (*sāmānya*) in the case of lumps of cow dung, one need not postulate some kind of cause for it there. Thus, wherever there is a subversion by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the acceptance of a genus (*jāti*), the genus consists of similar properties (*sadṛśadharma*). Likewise, even in the case of non-existence (*abhāva*), if a universal were accepted, it would result in its being an entity; therefore, because it has as its object a conceptual cognition of continuity (*anvayipratyaya*) based on a universal property consisting of the nature of non-becoming, that very [non-becoming] is the genus there as well. || 14 ||

Since time, space, and the directions are unitary and, being eternal, lack any distinction of states, how can there be a genus (jāti) by which pervasion (vyāpti) could be established? To this, he says: "When a location is conceptually constructed through the differentiation of properties associated with conjunction, the universal (sāmānya) of space also exists within those locations. (15)

Just as for universals and particulars, non-difference consists in the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of a common property (*anvayidharma*), so too for space (*ākāśa*), difference consists in the limiting adjunct of conjunction (*saṃyoga*). This is a cumulative statement (*samuccaya*) with reference to the subject at hand. Those substrata of space, such as jars and the like, which possess conjunction with space, are "conjoined" (*saṃyogin*). For space is the substratum of all corporeal things; it is called "space" precisely because it provides room (*avakāśa*). Corporeal entities, however, are mutually obstructive; therefore, they do not provide room.

The distinction in properties among conjoined things consists in their limitedness, which is established by means of valid cognition such as perception, or in their occurrence in limited space, which is well-known in the world on that account. For that portion of space in which a conjunction is fully contained becomes a "limited space" (*pradeśa*) of ether; this is because of the etymological definition that a "space" (*deśa*) with respect to an effect is a "limited space. Furthermore, some qualities, such as color and so forth, are all-pervading (*vyāpyavṛtti*), whereas conjunction, since it resides in objects delimited by material form, always resides only in a limited space.

Therefore, because conjunction is restricted to specific locations, the conjoined entities also exist in restricted locations; thus, through the differentiation of the attributes of the conjoined, a differentiation of space occurs that is produced by limiting conditions (*upādhi*), not inherently. As it has been said: "And when a location is conceptually constructed... Due to the difference in location, a universal (*sāmānya*) also exists for space. Consequently, for every location, there exists a universal of space—characterized by the persistence of identical designations and cognitions such as "this is space, this is space"—which is the objective referent of the word "space."

In this same manner, because the principle is identical, the universal (*sāmānya*) of time and the other categories should also be described by means of the postulation of spatial locations (*pradeśa*). For instance, although time is divided by virtue of its conjunction with Yudhiṣṭhira and others, there exists an undivided universal of time which is denoted by the word "time."

In this way, as the sun revolves clockwise around Mount Meru, there arise conjunctions with specific regions held by the world-protectors (*lokapāla*). Due to these limiting conditions (*upādhi*), when the sun is in conjunction with the directions, one must postulate a non-differentiated "direction-universal" (*dik-sāmānya*) denoted by the word "direction," despite the apparent difference. Just as the self (*ātman*) is indeed distinct in each body, so too does the universal "selfhood" (*ātmatva-sāmānya*) exist therein. Similarly, although inherence (*samavāya*) appears to be manifold due to the diversity of its relata, a genus (*jāti*) must be postulated because the notion of "here" (*ihabuddhi*) persists everywhere.

But surely, the spatial determination of space occurs by means of the location of that which is conjoined with it; thus, there would be mutual dependence between space and those things conjoined with it. This is not so. It is precisely the nature of the mutual exclusion of chariots and other objects—due to their corporeality and their having limited dimensions—that makes them known. However, the spatial divisions of space, which are conceptually constructed and well-known in common worldly usage, indicate the state of having limited spatial extent belonging to the substances with which they are conjoined.

For if the all-pervasiveness (*vyāpitva*) of chariots and other objects—which contradicts their forms established by perception and other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—were superimposed upon them on the grounds of their having space as their locus in a general sense, that [superimposition] could be refuted by their own inherent limitedness through the conceptualization of parts (*pradeśakalpanā*) of space. If this were so, how could these imagined locations produce in space—which is inherently partless—the effects based on spatial differentiation, namely the establishment of universals (*jāti*) or the application of universal-words (*jātiśabda*), by virtue of which a universal would be denoted as residing in them? It is replied: [The answer follows:]... [text continues] ...it is said: "Just as the parts of a tree, though themselves devoid of parts, are designated as 'branches' when they are perceived as distinct from the trunk, so too, even though space is partless, its parts are designated as such when they are perceived as distinct from one another. Just as the parts of a tree, though themselves devoid of parts, are designated as "branches" when they are perceived as distinct from the trunk, so too, even though space is partless, its parts are designated as such when they are perceived as distinct from one another. This is because, in common usage, the term "part" is applied to whatever is perceived as distinct from something else. Furthermore, just as the term "branch" is applied to the parts of a tree, so too the term "space" is applied to those very things that are perceived as distinct from one another. Therefore, it is not the case that space is without parts; rather, it is the same as the parts of a tree. Thus, the universal "space" is established by the application of the word to those very things that are perceived as distinct from one another. Consequently, there is no contradiction with perception and other means of valid cognition. Just as in the Advaita philosophy the reality of the regions that occupy the place of individual manifestations will be stated in the verse, "Individuals are remembered as unreal," so too here, there is no contradiction whatsoever in the reality of space [while individual manifestations remain unreal]. || 15 ||

Alternatively, he states that the regions of space are indeed primary, just like those of jars and the like: "Just as there are regions belonging to jars and so forth which are themselves devoid of regions, so too there are regions belonging to space, which is itself devoid of regions. (16)

In this context, "place" (deśa) is said to mean a part (avayava). Pots and the like, as wholes (avayavin), are themselves partless in their own nature. Those things which constitute their parts—such as potsherds and so forth—are indeed distinct from them; they are the originating causes (ārambhaka-kāraṇa) that stand in a relation of inherence (samavāya-sambandha).

In this way, space (*ākāśa*) as well—because it is not produced by anything, is formless, all-pervading, and partless—lacks any spatial location that constitutes its own self; therefore, substances and the like are its locations only by virtue of being in conjunction with it. Thus, although there is a distinction of space due to those [conjoined] distinctions, the conceptualization of it as a "universal" (*jāti*) arises because of the persistence of a non-differentiated cognition everywhere. For objects that delimit space become its "locations."

And space (*ākāśa*), too, when delimited by those [material objects], becomes their locus (*ādhāra*) due to its state of being the substratum; thus, there is a mutual relationship of "locus" between the material and the immaterial. However, since material objects are non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*), they do not act as delimiters for one another; therefore, for these [material things], the locus is simply their own substratum. (16)

How, then, is there the conventional usage of "secondary" (gauṇa) with respect to a location? For if certain primary parts were the very self of something, then this [usage] would be appropriate; otherwise, it would not. To this he says: "The cognition based on distinct objects persists among things that are conjoined (saṃyogin); among things that are inherent (samavāyin), the apprehension of distinction ceases. (17)

Therefore, the status of being secondary is attributed to the locations of the conjoined, while the status of being primary belongs to the inherent substrates, due to the lack of distinction from those locations. (18)

When an object is divided and established as separate, that cognition which has [such] a basis is the cognition of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), defined as "the attainment of two things not previously attained. Thus, the cognition of conjunction has as its object entities that are separately established. The apprehension of difference ceases; for inherence (*samavāya*) is the cause of the cognition of "here" with respect to things that are inseparably established (*apṛthaksiddha*), such as "the jar is here in these potsherds. Therefore—meaning, because it is apprehended as distinct—and due to the lack of discrimination (*aviveka*), meaning the impossibility of discriminating [them].

Since the cognition of those things joined by conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is distinct, the spatial points (*pradeśa*) therein are secondary (*gauṇa*). Since the cognition of those things inhering (*samavāyin*) is non-distinct, they possess primacy (*mukhyatva*) there. For, due to the power of inherence (*samavāya*), the inherent things cannot be distinguished from their spatial points; thus, the composite substance (*avayavidravya*) produced from them is perceived only in those very locations, namely the shards (*kapāla*) and so forth. Therefore, the inherent things are established as being primary in the sense of being spatial points (*pradeśatva*) therein.

By the statement "but for those that are conjoined, it is not so," the metaphorical nature—that is, the figurative status—of the spatial points of space (*ākāśadeśa*) is established. Now, an objection may be raised: even when conjoined objects such as jars are mutually conjoined with one another, they do not become each other's spatial points; likewise, this should not occur with respect to space either. This is not the case. Since chariots and the like are always connected with space, the superimposition [of their spatial points] upon it is appropriate, whereas it is not so for jars and the like, whose conjunctions are not constant.

For this very reason, the cognition of space as inherent in jars and other objects is indeed observed, such as "the space of the jar" or "the space of the cloth"; and it has been stated that upon superimposition (adhyāropa), there is no dissolution of difference. || 17, 18 ||

Thus, the pervasion of the category of *jāti* (universal) has been established by relying on the Vaiśeṣika system. Now, he states the determination of categories even according to the Vijñānavāda school: "Some recognize that which is known as *ākṛti* (form/structure) as having the nature of continuous recurrence (*anupravṛtti-rūpa*), while others declare it to be substance (*dravya*) in the form of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti-rūpa*). (Verse 19)

"This treatise is for the entire assembly"—this is the established definition of the meaning of words or the meaning of a term. They call that which appears in a cognition of a uniform (anugata) form, its very nature being determined as an objective entity (*artharūpatayā*), a "universal" (*sāmānya*), because of the conceptual identification (*abhedādhyavasāya*) between the perceived object and the mental construction. Furthermore, in this philosophical system, it is stated incidentally that the form situated within a cognition of an excluded (*vyāvṛtta*) form is the "substance" (*dravya*).

And thus, since there is no external universal (*sāmānya*), one need not even attempt to establish it in the case of space and so forth. For the arising of a cognition with an undifferentiated form—which cannot be denied—is established everywhere; and in the system of Vijñānavāda, everything is indeed admitted to be of the nature of cognition. When a word is uttered, a cognition possessing a form arises; therefore, it is that form alone which constitutes the meaning of the word, not the cognition itself. Whether that form be external or not, there is no impairment whatsoever to its status as the denotation of a word.

Now, one might object: "Since the difference between entities is caused by factors such as place and time, they are established as being non-different when those factors are disregarded; so why exert oneself in postulating a separate universal (sāmānya)? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Whether [entities] are 'different' or 'non-different,' this manifold world (prapañca) arises only among things that are mutually related through external adjuncts (upādhi). (20)

Since a thing devoid of adjuncts (nirupādhin) cannot be the object of linguistic convention, all convention is dependent upon something else; thus, the intended meaning here is that the conceptualization of a distinct universal was formulated precisely with respect to universals and the like. || 20 ||
He elaborates on this very point by way of negation as well: "Neither unity nor plurality, neither existence nor non-existence is found in the realities of the self when they are unconditioned. (21)

The linguistic usage of "oneness" is dependent on the cognition of the number one; that of "manifoldness" is based on distinctness (*pṛthaktva*); that of "existence" is based on being (*sattā*). However, for universals (*sāmānya*) and the rest, there is no adjunct of non-existence based on their own essential existence (*svarūpasattva*); thus, in the view of relation (*saṃsarga*), this entire manifold world is a diversity consisting of dependence on another. 21.

Having thus presented the view that limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are distinct [from the Self], he now speaks from the standpoint of the non-dualistic (*advaita*) doctrine, asserting that the limiting adjuncts are indeed its own powers: "The determination is that the nature of all powers belongs to the One alone; therefore, the conceptualization of a difference in the self-nature of existing things would be purposeless. (22)

Since this fact—that Brahman alone possesses all powers—is established by authoritative means (*pramāṇa*), and since the differentiation of entities imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*) lacks ultimate reality, it is logical that for the One there is only a differentiation of powers inferred from the diversity of effects, and not a differentiation of essential nature (*svarūpa*). || 22 ||
And thus, from that [substance], all powers such as substance and so forth possess distinct characteristics; when combined, they accomplish the purpose of the person, but not when isolated. (23)

The categories (padārthas) characterized as substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, and inherence are not distinct entities. They are merely the powers of a single reality, inferred from their diverse functions; these powers, when properly integrated, perform purposeful actions such as providing clothing and so forth. In this view, the distinction between genus and individual is everywhere conceptualized, as will be explained in the passage beginning with "the two parts, the real and the unreal. Thus, the meaning is that there is no difference even in the case of space and other such entities.

For just as the Vaiśeṣikas [assert] a universal (sāmānya) that is distinct [from its particulars], it is not so here; rather, there is merely the power (śakti) of the single entity whose form is the universe. It was mentioned incidentally that it is not only the universal, but also substance (dravya) and the other categories. Even if one were to admit the distinction between substance and the rest, the meaning is that it is better for there to be only a single possessor of power when these are in conjunction, since they are what produce effects. || 23 ||

In this regard, one might object: "If the means [of cognition] consist of things in conjunction, then those individual things lack the capacity [to produce cognition], because it is the conjunction itself that possesses such efficacy; and if that conjunction is distinct [from its constituents], it would result in the fallacy of duality. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Just as the totality (samagrata) which constitutes the very essence of the sense organs and so forth is perceived, so too is the conjunction of the relationship between related entities perceived. (24)

The eye, visible form, light, and mental attention—or the self, the mind, the sense-faculty, and the object—are observed through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) to be the causes of consciousness when they are combined and have acquired their mutual specific qualities. Therefore, this so-called "assemblage" (*sāmagrī*) is not a distinct entity that produces [consciousness] apart from these [factors]. For this very reason, it is the factors that produce the assemblage which are designated by the word "assemblage," since no other real entity is perceived. Likewise, because a single related factor serves as the substratum for all powers (*śakti*), the relation [of inherence] is established among the powers of substance and the rest.

Therefore, since there is no separation from a single substrate, the conjunction—which is the blending of forms—is understood as a state of completeness inherent in that very conjunction when it serves the purpose of the Person (*puruṣārtha*). For even in that case, this completeness is indeed identical with the substrate itself, as established by logic; for there is no linguistic usage of "substance" (*dravya*) by means of the substance alone, devoid of its connection with qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth. Likewise, because one cannot determine a distinction between the substance and the others, such as the qualities, from the necessary conjunction [of them], that [conjunction] is simply their own inherent nature.

In some readings, it is stated: "Likewise, even the mutual connection (*saṃsarga*) of the relations (*saṃbandha*) with their relata (*saṃbandhin*) is perceived. Regarding that as well, the explanation is as follows: by the "relatum," which is the substratum of all powers (*sarvaśakti*), there are "relations" (*saṃbandhāḥ*), namely the powers (*śakti*) such as substance (*dravya*) and so forth; the mutual connection of those relations, which are the powers, is also essentially identical (*ātmabhūta*) [to that substratum].

Alternatively, even when there is a conjunction of the powers belonging to an entity that possesses all powers—even in the state of such conjunction—that relation remains exactly as it was; the meaning is that this conjunction is indeed identical with its own nature (*ātmabhūta*). Furthermore, because the universal consciousness (*citsāmānya*) permeates everything, the non-difference of the universe is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), as was determined in the first book (*kāṇḍa*). || 24 ||

Thus, it has been established that the universal (*jāti*) is conveyed by the word according to its manifestation. And since that [universal] is eternal, the meaning of the word is eternal. Accordingly, it was stated: "The two [word and meaning] have indeed been described as eternal. Regarding the eternality of the universal therein, he states its utility for causal action: Nothing whatsoever is produced for which a universal does not exist; the universal is the motivator of causes for the sake of the manifestation of the self (the individual). (25)

The manifestation of a genus (jāti) is dependent upon the individual (vyakti); thus, the genus assumes the role of an instigating agent (prayojaka-kartṛtva) with respect to the causes of its own substratum. The meaning is that, being eternally present, it acts as a cooperative factor (sahakārin) for the causes in the production of the effect. Since genera are efficient causes (nimitta-kāraṇa) according to the Vaiśeṣika system, this meaning is expressed by the term "instigating agent" through a figurative turn of phrase. || 25 ||

[Objection: But since they are not present among the causes, how can they be the instigators? To this he says: "Having taken their place among causes—both eternal and non-eternal—the universals (jātis) repeatedly attain manifestation in certain effects. (26)

Because universals (*jāti*) are omnipresent, they are present even in their causes; thus, there is a connection with the word [denoting the universal]. Likewise, since effects reside within their causes by way of the nature of the universal, and because they are determined as such through the coloring of the form of the universal, when the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) operate toward the production of the effect, there occurs the manifestation of the universal inherent in that [effect] once its substratum has been repeatedly perceived. The eternal atoms are the causes, or in another system, the *pradhāna*, the *puruṣa*, and so forth; or the non-eternal *vīraṇa* grass and so on. "In some cases" refers to this.

Among visible things, there is indeed some effect that, though produced based on a genus, remains invisible, such as the substance air; for in that case, there is no manifestation of its genus. || 26 ||

And by establishing this, since the universal (*jāti*) exists even prior to its manifestation, its permanence is supported. Thus, he demonstrates the utility of the category of the universal (*jāti*) here: "The action that is being produced—the universal is also a means (*sādhana*) therein; in the accomplishment of its own substratum, it is the instigator of actions. (27)

Regarding the objection, "How can there be the status of a means (*sādhanabhāva*) for an action when the object (*karman*) being produced is non-existent—as in 'he makes a jar'?"—this does not apply here. Because the universal (*jāti*) exists, it serves as the motivator (*prayojaka*) toward the action for the sake of producing its own substratum, according to the principle of the causal connection of words. Thus, the status of being a means is based on the form of the universal, while the status of being the object is based on the form of the individual (*vyakti*). Consequently, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the expression "the factor of action (*kāraka*) which is the object (*karman*) being produced" is logically established.

For the universal (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*) are not absolutely distinct like a cow and a horse; rather, because their natures are intermingled (*saṃmūrcchita-svabhāvatva*), the designation based on both forms is not contradictory. However, since the objects of action (*karman*) that are to be reached (*prāpya*) or modified (*vikārya*) already exist, their status as means (*sādhana*) is established by themselves alone; thus, he specifies them as "that which is being produced" (*nirvartyamāna*). Furthermore, having determined an object through its universal nature, those seeking it proceed toward suitable causes; therefore, [the cause] is called "the instigator" (*prayojikā*).

And this is possible under the view that the universal (*jāti*) is the denotation [of a word], because the universal is denoted by the word "jar. However, under the view that the individual (*vyakti*) is the referent, he will state that the status of being a means (*sādhanatva*) is based on metaphorical existence (*upacārasattā*): "When the individual is the referent, the status of being a means for the action produced by the word is thus established as being conceptually constructed (*buddhirūpaprakalpita*). Therefore, it is logical that the universal is the motivator (*prayojikā*) of causes.

And thus, in the view that the universal (*jāti*) is the primary meaning of a word, it is not the substance (*dravya*) that serves as the means for action, but rather the universal itself is the means for both injunctions and prohibitions; so he says: "In an injunction or in a prohibition, [the universal] such as 'Brahmin-ness' (*brāhmaṇatva*) is the means. The universal of number, which resides in that which resides in the individual, is the qualifier of the universal. (28)

If the universal (*jāti*) is the meaning of the word, then when an injunction regarding it is promulgated—such as "One should sacrifice a Brāhmaṇa"—the purpose of the scripture is fulfilled by performing it even once, because that universal is fully present in each individual instance. Likewise, a prohibition such as "One should not kill a Brāhmaṇa" also refers to the universal itself. Furthermore, even though the act has been performed only once, if one transgresses again, there is a fault for having violated what was enjoined. For instance: non-killing was enjoined, yet killing was performed at some point; thus, due to the performance of a contrary action, there is indeed demerit (*pratyavāya*).

However, there is no contradiction when an injunction is performed in one instance and its absence occurs elsewhere; as they have said: "Injunctions do not obstruct what is causeless, but a prohibition brings an action to a halt. Therefore, whenever the thought of killing arises, the prohibition operates everywhere within the class of Brahmins. And in this case, the object to be performed is the volition (*saṅkalpa*) which manifests as the prohibition of an obligatory duty delimited by the [Brahmin] caste.

Thus, the utility of the genus (*jāti*) has been demonstrated everywhere within human goals consisting of engagement and withdrawal. Because the performance (*anuṣṭhāna*) is primary, its subordinate member—the universal (*sāmānya*)—is connected with the number of substances, according to the principle to be stated later: "The universal, being a subordinate factor, is joined with the number of substances. Here, he states that the number is intended to be significant (*vivakṣā*) by saying, "it rests upon the individual (*vyakti*)."

The universal (*jāti*) which has as its substratum the number one—this number one being inherent in the individual substance (*dravya*)—is that which, as the cause for the recurrence of the same cognition among the qualities of unity (which are themselves differentiated by their distinct substrates), delimits the meaning of the nominal stem through its inherence-in-inherence (*samavetasamavāya*) within the substance and the universal denoted by that stem. Since the universal is the referent of the word (*padārtha*), the case-ending (*vibhakti*) also denotes the universal of number; thus, in its real form (*vāstavena rūpeṇa*), the universal of number is the qualifier (*viśeṣikā*). However, from the perspective of verbal expression (*śābdena*), because the meaning of the suffix is predominant, this [universal] is the qualified (*viśeṣyā*).

And thus, since singularity is intended here as the number, the performance is not enjoined as having multiple individuals as its object simultaneously. Even though the word denotes a genus (*jāti*), there is no deficiency whatsoever, because the genus is fully present in its entirety within even a single individual. Furthermore, since an injunction is caused by desire, when that desire exists, there is no contradiction in performing the rite with respect to other individuals as well. Likewise, in the case of a prohibition, the cognition of killing is the efficient cause; therefore, once that cognition arises, the application of the prohibition occurs everywhere.

Thus, when the universal (*jāti*) is the meaning of a word, its compatibility with the injunctions (*codanā*) is established. As the author of the *Vākya* says: "And the treatise on Dharma is likewise. But is it not the case that the restriction—that the universal alone is the meaning of a word—is untenable, because a universal is inseparable from its inherence in its own substratum?

For this very reason, since these [universals] exist in the substrata of their causes because of the accomplishment of their effects, one might suspect that the universal (*jāti*), being impossible to distinguish from its substratum, cannot be denoted by a word in isolation. Anticipating this objection, he says the following to establish this point through an illustration: "Just as the face itself is denoted when it is manifested by water and so forth, so too the universal itself is denoted when it is manifested by substances. (29)

The production of a distinct entity within a reflection was previously refuted by the passage beginning with "in those of contradictory dimensions" (*viruddhaparimāṇeṣu*). Therefore, the reflection of a face or the like, though perceived in a mirror and so forth through illusion, is designated by the word "face" as something pure, devoid of the manifesting medium such as the mirror. In this same way, a word also denotes a universal (*jāti*) as being devoid of individuals (*vyakti*). This is the intended meaning: since there is no difference [between the universal and its instances] everywhere, even in the absence of inherence in a substratum, the application of convention (*saṅketa*) is possible; thus, the universal is the pure denotation of a word, because it is perceived as such in verbal cognition.

In the case of sensory cognition, however, because there is no determination of the distinction [between them], let there be a blended appearance of the universal and the individual. But in the case of the word, there is no harm whatsoever in its being the cause of cognition according to how it is intended. (29)

If this is so, one might object: "How can individuals (*vyakti*), which are not perceived from the word, qualify the universal (*jāti*) as being the object of the cognition produced by that word? To this, he says: "Just as a distinction residing in a sense organ, though unperceived in the objects of the senses in the absence of the operation of that organ, is capable of producing a distinction in the cognition [of those objects]. (30)
Thus, for some, even without the perception of individual instances, things become the cause of the various cognitions of universals through the apprehension of their own form. (31)

The sense organs, whose existence is inferred because the perception of sound and other objects would otherwise be inexplicable, are themselves unperceived due to their eternal transcendence; thus, their specific internal qualities—such as being the eye or the ear—are not perceived. Nevertheless, they are invariably established as the causes of the specific cognitions, such as visual perception, regarding the objects of the senses: sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. For indeed, visual cognition is not the effect of the auditory organ. In the same way, these individual manifestations have ungraspable intrinsic natures.

At the time of denotation by means of a word, certain individuals become causes for only some specific varieties of generic cognition, just as they are for perceptual cognitions. Since, in verbal cognition, the individuals communicate their particularity through the necessary inherence (*samavāya*) of the universals (*sāmānya*) which constitute the word's referent in reality, there is no confusion regarding the word's meaning; this is the sense.

Even though the individual form (*vyaktirūpa*) is not being grasped at that time, because it was grasped at another time—namely, at the moment of perception—the absence of contradiction in determining that object remains even for one who has mastered the relationship [between word and meaning]. Thus, it is observed that even what is not currently being grasped can be a cause for a specific cognition. By this much similarity, the sense organs (*indriya*) serve as the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) here. From the phrase "of certain particular cognitions of universals" (*sāmānyajñānabhedānām*), it follows by implication that only certain individuals are meant. In this way, the position that the universal alone is denoted has been established.

But when that [substance] is what is denoted, the genus, though not itself being denoted, serves as a qualifier for the substance by way of non-difference for the sake of the convention; thus, since the connection with action is perceived in that very [substance], it is the substance that possesses the status of being the word's denotation. As it has been said: "And because its commencement occurs in the injunctions" (JS 1.1.31).

Now, regarding what was stated previously: "He describes the division of that which consists of all powers: 'The two states, real and unreal, are established in every individual entity; that which is real therein is the universal (jāti), while the individuals (vyakti) are considered unreal. (Verse 32)

Because all things, which consist of the activity of ignorance and are subject to appearance and disappearance, are unreal, they are conventionally designated as "manifestations" (*vyakti*). On the other hand, the non-dualists (Advaitins) employ the term "universal" (*jāti*) for that which is real, stating: "That alone is real in which the true nature (*tattva*) is not sublated"; thus, the persisting form (*anvayirūpa*), which remains unsublated amidst cognitions of difference, is conventionally called "truth" and "universal."

For example, transformations such as bracelets, svastikas, and earrings, which arise through the mutual displacement of one another, are objects of unstable cognitions; however, "gold" alone is the truth, its reality being determined by a persistent cognition (*anvayi-vijñāna*). Likewise, when there is a desire to express a further non-difference, "fire" alone is the truth. Even there, the non-difference is its cause; thus, the knowers of the scriptures (*āgama-vidaḥ*) maintain that the ultimate, supreme primordial nature (*prakṛti*)—which follows all transformations, is devoid of waves, and is a single mass of consciousness—is the true Brahman.

As it has been said: "What is real in the earth-element? Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). What is real in conceptual construction? Consciousness (*vijñāna*). What is real in consciousness? *Oṃ*, or rather, that Brahman. [This is stated] "with respect to every entity. According to the view of others, because there is a difference between objects, there is a distributive repetition (*vīpsā*); yet, because the universal consciousness (*cit-sāmānya*) pervades everything, that which is the nature of Great Being (*mahāsattā*), the counter-correlative of non-existence, and the true form of the entire universe, has been pointed out by those of pure vision after having realized it directly. For us, the Blessed Ones are the authority. (32)

Thus, in this non-dual system, there is in the ultimate sense only one single genus called "Great Being" (*mahāsattā*), whose nature is the Supreme Brahman; it is through the illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) of that very [genus] in the form of distinct genera such as "cowness" and so forth that linguistic usage occurs. Thus he says: "Being itself, appearing as if divided among cows and other things due to the difference of its correlates, is called a 'genus' (*jāti*); all words are established in that [Being]. (33)

Existence (*sattā*) itself—the Great Universal (*mahāsāmānya*)—is the genus (*jāti*), such as "cowness" (*gotva*) or "horseness" (*aśvatva*), which constitutes the lower universal (*aparasāmānya*). This [lower universal] is differentiated by its own related correlates, such as the substrata (*āśraya*) and so forth to be mentioned hereafter; thus, it is merely a case of figurative differentiation (*upacaritabheda*) among cows, horses, and the like. No other [universal] exists that is ultimately distinct [from existence]. For instance, the existence of a cow is "cowness," and no further recurring entity appears [apart from it]; likewise, the existence of a horse is "horseness," and so on, should be stated.

And within that very genus called "existence" (sattā), which is differentiated by distinctions such as "cow" and so forth, all words such as "cow" and "Dittha" are established as denoters; thus, by virtue of restricted limiting conditions (upādhi), they are proven to be denoters of the genus without any confusion. || 33 ||

It reveals that [the Supreme] alone is the object of all words: "They declare her to be the meaning of the nominal stem (prātipadika) and the meaning of the verbal root (dhātu); she is eternal, she is the Great Self (mahān ātmā), and they call her the suffixes beginning with 'tva' and 'tal'. (34)

In all entities, there is a nature of existence (*sadrūpa*) that is a pervasive universal (*sāmānya*). Since even non-existence (*abhāva*) is determined by way of a mental form (*buddhyākāra*), and because it is never dissociated from this Great Existence (*mahāsattā*), existence is what is expressed by the mere nominal stem (*prātipadika*). As it has been said: "Existence is the meaning of the nominal stem. Furthermore, even by means of verbal roots (*dhātu*), it is this very existence—which, though manifold as apprehended through limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), inheres in individual actions that have come into being dependent upon their instruments (*sādhana*)—that is brought to the state of being the denotation.

Because its occurrence consists in that very [Being] in the form of two aspects—the accomplished (*siddha*) and the to-be-accomplished (*sādhya*)—and because there is no other state besides these, Being (*sattā*) is the object of all words. Furthermore, even by means of the suffixal portion (*pratyaya-bhāga*), it is Being itself that is denoted here, as qualified by various limiting conditions (*upādhi*) such as number and grammatical relation (*kāraka*), according to the case. And since it is devoid of arising and passing away, it is eternal, because the cognition of "being" (*sat-pratyaya*) persists at all times.

These are the six specific transformations of the Great Self, which is mere existence; for that Great Principle, the Great Reality which is a mere sign beyond the specific objects, having remained within that very Great Self which is mere existence, experiences the culmination of its growth.

And when they are being reabsorbed, having remained in that very Great Self which is pure existence (*sattāmātra*), they return to that which is neither non-existence nor existence, which is unmanifest (*avyakta*), without marks (*aliṅga*), and beyond both being and non-being. Thus, in the Sāṅkhya system, the first cause of the world, designated by the term "the Great" (*mahat*), is identified as the principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*). Consequently, because the entire subsequent aggregate of transformations conforms to the nature of its cause, it is not contradictory for it to possess the nature of existence; thus, the entire world is declared to have the nature of existence, which constitutes the doctrine of the non-duality of existence (*sattādvaitavāda*).

It is also reinforced by the Sāṅkhya system. Thus, existence (*sattā*), which is denoted by the word "flow" (*srava*), is the ground for the application of words; it is that very same [existence] which is expressed through various conceptual cognitions of distinct limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) as appropriate. [Objection: But if this is so, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) in the word *gotvam* (cowness) have the same meaning. [Reply: This is not so. Because existence is differentiated by the difference of its limiting adjuncts. The nominal stem (*prātipadika*) denotes that [existence] as residing in a cow, whereas the suffix denotes the universal (*sāmānya*) abstracted from its substratum; thus, there is no fault.
And since the distinction between abstract suffixes (bhāvapratyaya) is based on the meaning of the base (prakṛti), there is no risk of confusion. || 34 ||

As it has been said: "They declare that to be both the meaning of the nominal stem (prātipadika) and the meaning of the verbal root (dhātu). To demonstrate this very point, he says: "That same action, when its sequence [of moments] has reached specific [individual instances], is designated as such; when the form of that sequence is withdrawn, its pure existence (sattva) is called 'being' (bhāva). (35)

A verbal root (*dhātu*), which denotes action, attains the state of denoting a being (*sattva*). And it is taught that both action and being are indeed being (*sattaiva*). For instance: due to the influence of the non-vibrating means (*sādhana*), the generic nature (*jāti*)—which corresponds to the manifestation of actions expressed by specific words and is subordinate to them—appears as such in its temporal sequence (*paurvāparya*). Thus, that very [nature] is action with succession, and it is the domain of all verbal roots. It will be explained immediately hereafter that the internal distinctions within that [action] constitute the various meanings of verbal roots.
