When there is no apprehension of a distinct form that extends [through various objects] due to contact with their respective means of proof (*sādhana*), "existence" (*sattā*) itself is called "being" (*sattva*) or "substance" (*dravya*). Thus, the two-fold manifestation (*vivarta*) of the supreme Brahman, which consists of pure existence (*sanmātra*), has been established as being both the already-accomplished (*siddha*) and the yet-to-be-accomplished (*sādhya*). For that alone is the underlying continuum (*anugata*) everywhere. And in this system, existence is not ontologically distinct from existing things; therefore, everything is composed of that. Consequently, since all words denote existence, the category of the universal (*jāti*) pervades all word-meanings.

And although he will state that even in the view where substance (*dravya*) is the category, the substance "Brahman" is denoted as differentiated by various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), nevertheless, there is a distinction of states due to a difference in intended meaning (*tātparya*). In the view where the universal (*jāti*) is the category, Brahman is intended in its nature as the universal, which is the persisting form in all things. In the system where substance is the category, however, it is intended as the ultimate reality in its perfectly established form; such is the alternative of philosophical perspectives. And from the standpoint of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-dṛṣṭi*), this very [view] is the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) in the form of the unification of both positions.

In this regard, because it is intended for a universal audience, other philosophical systems are introduced here once again. This is the intention of the author throughout this entire work; for in matters concerning the investigation of categories, the determination of relations and so forth is made solely according to the method of the Brahman-view. || 35 ||

Now, in accordance with the opinion of the author of the *Nirukta*, he states a corroboration that the entire complex of activity is merely a transformation of existence (*sattā*): "That very [existence] undergoes six states among the modifications of being; through its own powers, it thus appears as various cognitions in succession. (36)

"The Blessed Vārṣyāyaṇi said that there are six modifications of being," so says the author of the *Nirukta*. In this context, the meaning is that birth and the other [five] are modifications of "being" (*bhāva*), which is of the nature of ultimate reality and consists of existence (*sattā*). For existence, whose very essence is pure being (*sanmātra*), attains the designations "is born," "exists," "transforms," "grows," "declines," and "perishes" as it undergoes successive modifications.

Furthermore, the mere existence (*sanmātra*) as such is not denoted by the word "exists" (*asti*); rather, it is a specific state occurring subsequent to birth. For that form which arises immediately after birth is what is conventionally designated as "existent" (*sat*) in the world. However, the states occurring prior to and subsequent to that [moment of birth] are conventionally designated by means of birth, transformation, and so forth. Thus, by the power of its own potentiality, it is determined that it "is born" first and "exists" afterwards.

The transformation of that which is established is what is meant by "it undergoes modification. And that modification does not persist even for a moment; thus it increases as long as there is anything to be increased by it, and thereafter it diminishes precisely because it does not remain even for a moment. For this very reason it has been said: "thereafter it is joined with decay. From that, too, comes destruction; such is the established sequence. Such are certain powers belonging to her, by virtue of which, though she is one, she manifests in various ways through diverse forms.

Furthermore, this term "modification" (*vikāra*) is not intended in the sense of a real transformation (*pariṇati*), for that would entail the consequence of [Brahman] being impermanent; rather, it is a synonym for "apparent manifestation" (*vivarta*). For thus say those who know the scriptures: because Brahman is the self of all powers, there exists a power called ignorance (*avidyā*), characterized by the capacity to display manifold modifications, which possesses a diversity that is merely figurative due to the differentiation of its effects. And in this way, through its own powers—which are non-different from itself—it appears within ignorance in the form of birth and so forth.
That very Brahman, whose nature is pure existence, is uniform in all things because there is nothing else apart from it; this is the meaning here. || 36 ||

If, then, existence itself manifests in the form of birth and so forth due to the majesty of its own power (*svaśakti*), why does it not manifest simultaneously? Why [does it appear] sequentially? For one might object that "sequence" is nothing other than a specific type of action. Anticipating this doubt, he states that the power called "time" (*kāla*) also belongs to Brahman alone: "Sequence is also inherent in this [Brahman], wherein this perception of time exists, appearing as if divided into forms such as priority and posteriority. (37)

This sequence of actions is also inherent to this very existence; it is not merely those actions themselves, for a sequence distinct from the successive actions cannot be conceived. Regarding this sequence, there is this perception of time (*kāla*); the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) perceive time as a separate entity (*padārthāntara*) divided into forms such as priority and posteriority. It is said that because time is divided, its perception is also divided.

In its essential meaning, however, time is as if divided into forms such as priority and posteriority through the influence of the limiting adjuncts of action. For the power of time, known as sequence (*krama*), belonging to Brahman, brings about the appearance of priority and posteriority among objects that possess birth solely by means of actions such as birth; there is no other time that exists as a substantial entity. As it is said: "Depending upon whose power of time, which has superimposed parts, the six transformations—birth and the rest—are the sources of the differentiation of existence."
This point has been determined here in the *Śabdaprabhā*. || 37 ||

Now, one might object: "Since birth and destruction are non-entities (avastu), how can they consist of existence (sattā)? Anticipating this doubt, he first establishes that destruction indeed consists of existence: "In the case of the acceptance of the concealment (tirobhāva) of entities, that very [concealment] is their non-existence. When concealment has attained its sequence, it is perceived as 'it perishes'. (38)

Because it is not subject to arising, perishing, or modification, the existence whose nature is Brahman is eternal and cannot undergo destruction without residue; thus, what is called "non-existence" is not distinct from existence itself. What we accept as non-existence is merely the concealment of the manifestation of an entity before its appearance or after its disappearance. Existence itself, when concealed, remains in its own causes in the form of potentiality (*śakti*); this is the destruction of things, and not some indefinable state.

When all entities have become latent and their sequential process has been withdrawn, the perfected state is denoted by nominal terms such as "latency" (*tirobhāva*) or "destruction" (*nāśa*). However, when that very non-existence, in the form of the state of latency, is intended to be expressed as having its nature extended through contact with causal factors, it is denoted by verbal forms. The preceding state is said to be "diminishing" (*apakṣīyate*), while the subsequent state is "perishing" (*vinaśyati*); these two are modifications of being characterized by a reverse transformation.
And in that regard, since the existence of an entity characterized by the nature of coming into being is opposed to its non-existence, destruction is merely its disappearance. || 38 ||

In this way, having first established that even the counter-correlate of existence (sattā) is a modification of that [Being], he explains how birth is a modification of it: "Having fallen away from the preceding state and not yet having reached the subsequent state, that which serves as the locus for the various distinctions in the interval between them is called 'birth'. (39)

Existence (*sattā*), having fallen away from its prior state known as abiding in the cause in the form of potentiality, and having not yet reached the final stage characterized by the manifestation of other properties, is designated as "being born" when it assumes successive specific states directed toward the effect, having taken up a temporal sequence; however, birth is not the production of that which was previously non-existent. Just as there is no absolute destruction of that which exists, so too birth is not the manifestation of something that never existed before.

And this will be made manifest by such statements as: "Non-existence is not born; existence does not pass into the state of the indefinable. Precisely for this reason—since cause and effect are non-different because they are merely different states—the agency of the act of being born is established according to one's intention, as in expressions such as "the sprout is born. This will be explained more thoroughly in the *Kārakasamuddeśa*. Furthermore, when there is an intention to express the sequence of a series of moments occurring between prior and posterior states, the connection with the act of being born applies to that process, and not to the final, completed state.

And so he will say: "Not abandoning its prior state, while touching upon a subsequent property, the essence of the object is said to be 'being born,' as if it were in a state of coagulation. Furthermore, agency arises from the superimposition of the subsequent state onto the prior states; for when people observe an active causal factor, they employ the conventional expression "it is being born. Once the action is completed, however, one says "it exists," whereby existence at a time subsequent to birth is designated. Even after that, when there is a tendency toward the manifestation of another property, it undergoes transformation.

In that case as well, since it "increases" when there is growth, these very specific births are what are separately grasped by this [term]. Thus, this is a transformation in the direction of natural order (*ānulomya*). And in that very state of being accomplished (*siddha*), there is substantiality (*dravyatā*); for accomplishment is indeed completion, and thus the action, which precedes it, is not an entirely distinct entity. || 39 ||

Now, regarding what was stated—that "existence itself appears differentiated due to the difference in its correlates"—the author now says the following in order to demonstrate those correlates: "The substratum, or its own nature alone, or entities that are distinct from it, or its own powers—these are the causes for the perception of differentiation within existence. (40)

Since it has been established that action and substance consist of existence (*sattā*), and since there is no other entity apart from them, everything is indeed composed of the Supreme Brahman, which is of the nature of existence; nevertheless, in the context of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), which consists of the operation of ignorance (*avidyā*), this differentiation based on the existence of substances and so forth is not contradictory, because the unreal distinction, just as it appears, cannot be denied.

In this context, the substratum (*āśraya*) is the locus of existence (*sattā*), because it acts as its manifestor; it is the cause for the perception of difference—that is, the appearance of difference—and not for difference itself, since [existence] is inherently non-different. For example, even a single face appears in various forms in oil, water, a mirror, a gem, a sword, and so forth. Likewise, due to the difference among the manifestors such as cows and other things, existence appears in the form of "cowness," "horseness," and so on; this is the meaning.

Or rather, the measures (*mātrā*), portions (*kalā*), conceived parts (*parikalpita-bhāga*), or fragments (*aṃśa*)—namely, the specific universals such as "cowness" (*gotva*) and so on, which have delimited objects—demonstrate a state of fragmented appearance for Being (*sattā*), which otherwise has all things as its object; by means of these very [parts], that [Being], though undivided, appears as if divided. And those [parts] possess their distinction only because of the difference in their substrata; thus, they are distinctions conceptually constructed (*parikalpita*). Accordingly, it will be stated [later] that "either universals are denoted, or Being as qualified by them," thereby expressing the differentiation of Being through "cowness" and the like.

Furthermore, the appearance of difference is observed through its own parts that are merely imagined, as in the case of a whole (*avayavin*). Since another self (*para-ātman*) can also exist through a difference constructed by conceptualization (*kalpanā*), it is qualified by the term "own" (*sva*); that is, it is both "own" (*sva*) and "self" (*ātman*). And a conceptual difference is indeed observed, as in the expression: "the self kills itself by means of the self. For no killer appears as something distinct from the self.

Alternatively, things such as space, direction, time, and the sense organs appear as distinct entities and are the causes for the perception of difference in *sattā* (Being). Herein, the differentiation of objects based on place and other factors is expressed as: "this is here now, and that is elsewhere at another time. Likewise, there is a different appearance of objects caused by proximity or distance from space. As they say: "Just as in deserts, even a very small thing appears large when far away. Similarly, there is a different appearance of blue lotuses at night compared to during the day; thus, there is a distinction caused by time.

Similarly, for those whose eyes are impaired by conditions such as *kāca* (cataract) or *kāmalā* (jaundice), there is the appearance of yellowness in a white conch; thus, this difference is caused by the sense organ (*indriya*). Furthermore, regarding existence (*sattā*), there are other differentiators (*bhedaka*) such as place and so forth; therefore, because the differences reside in the objects (*viṣaya*), there is no circular reasoning (*itaretarāśrayatā*). Such is the ultimate truth here: there exist within existence itself certain inherent powers called "capacity" (*yogyatā*), by which it constructs the manifold universe (*viśvaprapañca*).

Just as a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) manifests various forms according to the inclinations of those who desire them, so too does Brahman—which possesses infinite power and consists of pure existence—appear in manifold forms within the sphere of transmigratory subjects, who are products of the play of ignorance; thus, in the end, the true nature of reality has been revealed. 40.

Thus, having first presented the views of other schools and established the formal arrangement of the category of "universal" (jāti) within his own system, he now examines the internal property of the distinct universals such as "cowness" (gotva) as they apply to worldly usage: "In the case of manifestation in earth and the other elements, the universal does not depend upon configuration (saṃsthāna). Because its substratum is never severed, the universal persists even when the substratum is non-eternal. (41)

Specific universals such as earthness (*pṛthivītva*), waterness (*aptva*), and so forth, attain manifestation in both large and limited substrates independently of any fixed arrangement of constituent parts. For instance, even a clod of earth is perceived as "earth," and likewise a mass of clay, a jar, or even a mountain [is perceived as such]. In the same way, it should be stated that even the ocean and even a single drop are perceived as "water," and so on.

In some cases, however, it is stated by implication that the universal (*jāti*), such as "cowness" (*gotva*) or "sāl-ness" and "tāla-ness," necessarily depends upon a specific configuration (*saṃsthāna*) for its manifestation. Likewise, even though it is inherent (*samaveta*), a universal does not perish through the destruction of its substratum (*āśraya*), unlike a quality (*guṇa*). For qualities in things like a jar arise dependent upon their substratum; thus, it is logical that they should perish following the destruction of that substratum. But for universals, the acquisition of their own nature (*ātmalābha*) is not dependent upon the substratum; they merely require the substratum for their cognition.

Furthermore, even when a single individual instance perishes, because the existence of an inferential cognition—namely, the cognition that persists in other instances—is otherwise inexplicable, the universal (*jāti*) remains firmly established. Thus, its destruction does not follow from the destruction of its substratum; the meaning is that the substratum is not the cause of its destruction. Moreover, since a perishing substratum might be suspected of being the cause of its destruction, the meaning is that there is no destruction of this [universal] due to the destruction of its substratum. Alternatively, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used in the sense of the instrumental (*tṛtīyā*); the meaning is that it does not perish along with its substratum. || 41 ||

An objection is raised: "Since all eternal things are destroyed during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), how could universals (*jāti*) persist in the absence of a substratum? To this, he says: "Some declare that every universal has an indestructible substratum; they maintain that there is no simultaneous destruction of everything at the time of dissolution. (42)

Regarding the phrase "some" (*eke*): those who do not accept that these [universals] can exist without a substratum at the end [of time] assert that there is no such thing as the destruction of their locus (*āśraya*). For they say this: asserting the non-existence of a great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), they maintain that just like the universal of atom-ness (*paramāṇutva*) and so forth, universals such as pot-ness (*ghaṭatva*) have locuses that are indestructible—that is, impossible to destroy in any way. Thus, since universals are eternally established, even when the locus of one is lost, they persist by residing in another locus; in this way, their permanence is proven.

Alternatively, even when the earth and other elements have perished, the properties of earthness (*pṛthivītva*) and so forth reside in the atoms of earth and the rest, and the properties of color-ness (*rūpatva*) and so forth reside in the colors and other qualities contained therein. According to this view—that there is no simultaneous dissolution of all things as occurred at the beginning of creation—the term "one" is established as a consistent application (*samanvaya*). Thus, it has been stated based on the perspective that even within a single cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), there is no simultaneous dissolution of all entities.

Alternatively, even when one cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) is destroyed, because another cosmic egg comes into existence, there is no simultaneous dissolution. Thus they say: "There is no such thing as a total enumeration of such cosmic eggs. (42)

Regarding those who maintain that there is a great dissolution (mahāpralaya), he explains how it occurs in their view: "When the particularities have dissolved into primordial nature (prakṛti), the universals (jātayaḥ) revert to the existence of the substance itself, remaining inherent in their own substrata. (43)

Those who perceive the world as being one—that is, non-different—from the root-prakṛti (pradhāna) or from the Supreme Brahman, maintain that because there is no absolute destruction (niranvayavidhvaṃsa) of the phenomenal manifold of existence, the Great Dissolution (*mahāpralaya*) is merely a merging into that supreme root-cause which is the form of the Great Universal (*mahāsāmānya*). Thus, it is not contradictory that at that time the various categories, existing in the form of potentialities (*śakti*), remain in association with their respective classes (*jāti*); for the classes continue to exist at that time in the nature of substance (*dravya*), since they do not exist as entities distinct from substance.

For this very reason, although it would have been sufficient to say simply "existence" (*sattva*), the inclusion of the term "substance" (*dravya*) is intended to indicate non-difference from substance. Alternatively, "substance" refers to the fundamental cause; the meaning is that existence belongs to that [cause], or rather, it depends upon the existence of the cause. For the Advaitins, the cause itself is the pervasive universal (*sāmānya*). Or, the word "substance" (*dravya*) is a synonym for "entity" (*vastu*).

Therefore, "substantial existence" (*dravyasattva*) is the primary existence (*mukhyaṃ sattvam*) of the object itself, which is its actual presence, and not a figurative or common [existence], because it exists in the form of potentiality (*śakti*); this is the meaning. In the Vaiśeṣika system, however, universals such as "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth remain without any support during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*). For there is no need for a support so that they do not fall downward due to gravity, since a support is useful only for their manifestation. And at that time, let them remain unmanifest; what contradiction is there? The author of the treatise, however, has concluded according to his own established doctrine. || 43 ||

Thus, the omnipresence of universals has been stated by relying on their presence in individual instances. Now, he speaks also according to the principle of being omnipresent in all [things]: "The entities such as Brahminhood and so forth reside in all living beings; they are manifest and effect their own functions—such also is the traditional teaching (smṛti). (44)

The term "existents" (*bhāvāḥ*) refers here to all general and particular properties (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*), such as Brahminhood, Kṣatriyahood, and so forth. Because they reside in living beings—that is, in physical bodies such as those of Kṣatriyas and others—they are omnipresent (*sarvagata*).

Nevertheless, there is no risk of confusion in cases such as "one should sacrifice a Brāhmaṇa," because even though [the universal] is omnipresent, it is manifested by specific manifestors; thus, since it is perceived as a constituent of the ritual action, it brings about its own effect only where it attains manifestation through a manifestor such as instruction, and this is remembered through an unbroken lineage of tradition. The meaning is that just as omnipresence has been handed down through tradition, so too has the state of being manifested by specific manifestors.

And thus, by the force of the context, it is stated that at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), universals such as "jar-ness" reside in atoms and so forth. By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the all-pervasiveness of even non-conscious universals is intended here; for he states the full extent of all-pervasiveness: "Even conscious universals reside in non-conscious things. Some maintain that universals are manifested even in paintings and the like. However, when those [universals] residing in living beings are reached, they become the cause of merit and demerit. (Verse 45)

Even in the case of a Brāhmaṇa created through painting, book-work, or wood and other materials, because of the similarity [to the real thing], there arises a cognition that conforms to that form; thus, even there, the manifestation of that genus occurs. However, since demerit (*adharma*) results from the injury of a living being, such [demerit] is absent when the injury is directed at one depicted in a painting. Likewise, merit (*dharma*) also does not arise from the worship of a Brāhmaṇa depicted in a painting. By the phrase "by some" (*kaiścit*), he indicates his own lack of approval regarding this view.

It is logical that the persistence of cognition regarding images occurs due to their primary similarity [to the original], but not because of the inherence of the universal (*jāti*) therein. Thus, by the earlier statement, "That action which is being produced," etc., the eternity of the universal was established on the grounds of its existence even prior to its manifestation; now, however, its establishment as a complete eternity is achieved through its persistence even upon the destruction of its substratum, since it extends across both the prior and subsequent limits and is thus incompatible with non-existence either before or after its manifestation. || 45 ||

Indeed, for one who has not yet learned the relationship between words and their referents, the form that is excluded from others and common to cows—namely, "cow, cow"—does not appear [to them]. And if that universal is manifested by those individual instances, why would there not be a cognition of it? If, on the other hand, one were to understand it without having been taught by others, then from where would they have understood it? Thus, in the absence of an all-knowing seer who perceives directly, an infinite regress of the blind would result.

Furthermore, regarding the relationship between all words and their meanings, the term "tradition of the blind" (*andhaparamparā*) would have been applied to the usage of elders because it lacks a foundation. [The author], considering that for [categories] such as Brahminhood there is no appearance of positive and negative concomitance—as there is for "cowness" and the like—due to the similarity of physical form and characteristics, and that this [knowledge] is like the cognition of children or the mute, he says: "But they know that those superior to us possess knowledge of all [objects] through all the senses, due to practice, just as experts [know] the specific qualities of gems, silver, and so forth. (46)

*Asmāt* is the ablative plural. When the substitute *at* is applied according to the rule *pañcamyā at*, there exist the primordial teachers (*ādiguravaḥ*), the all-seeing ones who are distinguished from those who perceive only specific objects. And so says Patañjali: "He is the teacher even of the ancients, because he is not limited by time. The Lord is the teacher and instructor of all the omniscient ones; and his eternity follows from the fact that his intellect, senses, and body are not limited by time.

Otherwise, once the dissolution has occurred and Brahmā and the other deities have been born again, who would be their instructor? Consequently, the world would be devoid of scripture, lacking in practice, and for the most part blind and mute regarding injunctions and prohibitions. Now, the followers of Jaimini (the Mīmāṃsakas) maintain that there is no such thing as dissolution, but rather that "this world was never otherwise than it is now. This is incorrect, because the dissolution is recorded in all the scriptures. Furthermore, if it is argued that since the Veda is intended for action (*kriyārthatva*), any sentence consisting of a nominal stem denoting an already existing fact (*bhūtārtha*) is not authoritative; [we reply:]...

For instance: since the understanding of the relationship between word and meaning arises from the linguistic usage of elders solely through the mediation of purposeful action (*kāryaparatva*), according to the principle that "the meaning of a word is that toward which it is directed," there is no purpose in the mere description of a narrative or the expression of an established fact (*siddhārtha*). Because such statements lack injunctions or prohibitions, they do not enjoin anything at all; therefore, as a treatise on words (*vākyaśāstra*) whose subject matter is merely an existing state of affairs (*bhūtārtha*), they do not deserve the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). They attain coherence, however, by functioning as subordinate members of sentences that impel one to action.

In the Śāstra, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) possess syntactic connection because they function as praises, thereby becoming subordinate members of injunctive sentences (*vidhi*). For in this way, the injunction is strengthened. Here we respond: there are two possible positions. Are explanatory passages—like mere phonemes—useless and yet enter into a subordinate relationship within the great sentence (*mahāvākya*) which is injunctive and conveys a purposeful action; or rather, do they possess some specific meaning of their own, in which they produce comprehension and thus become directed toward that purposeful action? These are the two alternatives.

The first position is not tenable. Since words whose meanings are already established are seen to convey their own referents accordingly, it is impossible for that which is ineffective and purposeless to function as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) in relation to another; rather, one must investigate whether that cognition regarding its own object is valid (*pramāṇa*) or otherwise. Where there is sublation (*bādha*), it is non-valid; but where there is no sublation, it is indeed valid. For the system of Jaimini holds that an uncontradicted cognition is intrinsically valid (*svataḥ-pramāṇa*).

We perceive no contradiction whatsoever in the words of the omniscient Lord and the deities as they are understood through the scriptures. But surely, one hears in the scriptures meaningful statements regarding cats and the like, yet there is no correspondence with reality; thus, everything concerning unperceived objects (*adṛṣṭārtha*) is invalid. Do not speak thus. For the words of those who have become omniscient are indeed uncontradicted, since their meaningfulness is observed even through other scriptures (*āgama*). Those with only physical eyes do not recognize anything beyond this.

For thus the Blessed Patañjali taught: "From the restraint [of the mind] upon word and meaning, there arises knowledge of the cries of all beings. Therefore, where there is no corroboration—where an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) results merely in sublation—it may serve its purpose by conveying an unreal matter; but where there is no sublation and there is corroboration by another scripture, that is indeed authoritative, and in such cases it does not have the status of being subordinate to an injunction (*kāryaparatā*).

For it is observed that the sentences of the Purāṇas and Itihāsas reach their conclusion in the question and answer regarding the demonstration of the goal (*siddhārtha*); furthermore, since it is accepted that *dharma* arises from the mere knowledge of that [goal], there is no lack of purpose for the sentences that demonstrate the Lord and so forth. Moreover, once the object of meditation (*dhyeya*) is fully known, meditation and the like can be practiced. Thus, the scripture states: "The Self is to be known, to be reflected upon, and to be meditated upon."

The *Pātañjala* [Yoga Sūtra] also states: "The *praṇava* is its designator; its repetition and meditation upon its meaning lead to the realization of the inward-turned consciousness and the absence of obstacles. Furthermore, the acceptance by the authors of the *Smṛtis*, such as Manu and others, while rejecting Mahendra, Rudra, and so forth, constitutes partiality. For how could the words of Manu and other great sages (*maharṣis*)—who were not omniscient or free from passion—be authoritative if they possessed passion and the like, or were ignorant?

"Therefore, there were seers (*ṛṣi*) who had directly realized the Dharma; they transmitted the mantras by oral instruction to later generations who had not directly realized the Dharma. Later generations, weary of oral instruction, committed this book—the Veda and the Vedāṅgas—to memory for the purpose of preservation. From such scriptural authority (*āgama-pramāṇa*), omniscient beings exist; it is precisely these sages who are designated as the "First Teacher," the Lord who expounded all the scriptures, in order to eliminate the notion of a blind succession (*andhaparamparā*). It is by these very sages that [the existence of omniscience] is established.

For even though the scripture (*śāstra*) consists of eternal words, because it possesses a specific composition, it is indeed authored by God (*īśvara*). Thus, God is understood through the scripture; therefore, since the scripture has come into operation, the scripture is its instrumental cause (*nimitta*). But what is the instrumental cause of the scripture? It is God as its instrumental cause. It has thus been stated that the relationship between these two—the scripture and its excellence—subsisting in the existence of God, is beginningless (*anādi*).

And likewise, it was stated by the Blessed One in his incarnation as Kṛṣṇa—who, through being possessed by the nature of Maheśvara, spoke in the Gītā: "I am the author of the Vedānta and the knower of the Veda. Even so, there is no impairment to the eternity of the scripture, because it consists of the very intellect of the Lord. The eternity of the Lord has already been explained as being due to his not being delimited by time.

Since the Veda, possessing its specific arrangement, is seen to exist eternally within the cognitive self of God (Īśvara), it is stated in the Brahmakāṇḍa that, like Smṛti, there is no creator of its arrangement at any particular time, as in the case of Manu and others: "They say that the Śruti is beginningless, uninterrupted, and authorless; however, Smṛti, being composed by the learned, is not [eternally] uninterrupted."

Thus, on the authority of scripture, there exist among the learned (*śiṣṭas*) those who perceive the reality of existence and who see objects beyond the reach of the senses; they directly perceive, according to their respective capacities, universals such as "cowness" and "brahminhood" through the discrimination of their substrata. And that knowledge of these learned ones is operative through all the senses, because it does not depend on specific restrictions [of sense-faculties]. For the omniscient perform the functions of one sense-organ even by means of another sense-organ.

And thus says the scripture: "They see the river even with their [other] senses; they hear sound by means of the sense of smell; they see forms from behind; and they perceive the objects of all the senses even with the tip of a finger. Alternatively, their cognition regarding the castes such as Brahmin and so forth is not exclusively visual, but is also connected with other senses; the meaning is that it is capable of discerning subtle distinctions of caste within sound and the rest.

Thus, by relying on the authority of scripture (*āgama-prāmāṇya*), the proof of the Omniscient One (*sarvajña*) has been indicated here by the first half [of the verse]. The detailed determination of the authority of scripture has been established by us in the first book (*kāṇḍa*) of the *Vākyapadīya*, in the *Śabdaprabhā*; therefore, it should be understood from that very source. By the second half [of the verse], he states an inference that corroborates the Omniscient One already established through scripture, beginning with the words "from practice" (*abhyāsāt*). Here, an excellence of knowledge, power, and so forth, is observed in certain individuals due to the force of practice.

Just as among jewelers there is a gradation of excellence according to their practice in the examination of the true nature of gems, and among those skilled in silver in the discernment of the superior qualities inherent in silver; and whatever possesses such excellence must necessarily reach its ultimate limit somewhere—just as brilliance reaches its limit in the sun, burning power in fire, and coolness in water.

Likewise, qualities such as knowledge, sovereignty, power, and strength, which are seen to possess degrees of excellence among persons, indicate that their excellence reaches a limit that pervades all objects of knowledge; they thus necessarily lead one to infer a substratum appropriate for them—one who possesses the fullness of all perfections. For it is the very excellence of knowledge and the other qualities, observed through their gradations, that constitutes the seed of omniscience. Nor should it be argued that wherever excellence is observed, it does not transcend its own specific object.

Because it is impossible to establish one's own object [of cognition] in accordance with its own substratum, and because in the case of the sun and so forth, the quality of being an illuminator is observed to transcend its own object; therefore, the proof of an omniscient being is appropriate even by means of presumptive inference (*saṃbhāvanānumāna*). As it has been said: "In that regard, the seed of omniscience is unsurpassed. The meaning is this: that which is characterized as the excellence of knowledge and other qualities—the seed of omniscience—is "unsurpassed" in that [state]; he in whom it is unsurpassed is the omniscient one.

Furthermore, the mention of "omniscience" here is an indication of sovereignty (*aiśvarya*); by this, it is established that he in whom there is unsurpassed sovereignty is the Lord of All (*sarveśvara*), the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), since we observe a gradation in the sovereignty of kings and others. And thus, because of the existence of the fundamental Lord, it has been stated: "Even the knowledge of the sages is preceded by scripture. The Supreme Lord, however, is unconditioned by time and is endowed with innate qualities such as knowledge and sovereignty.

If this conscious [Lord] intends the insentient world to obey His will—just as the body obeys the inner self—then, due to the specific configuration of the relationship between the beneficiary and the benefactor, He, as the Knower, creates it; thus it is established that this entire universe here has an intelligent creator. Therefore, there exist beings superior to us who are established by scripture.

Furthermore, their knowledge—which consists of direct perception and is independent of the specific determination of the sense organs—perceives the true nature of objects that are past, future, subtle, concealed, or remote. Thus, yogins who perceive all universals such as "cowness" and "Brahminhood" directly, provide instruction regarding them without confusion. There exists, within Brahminhood and the like, a certain secondary mark (*upavyañjana*) comparable to a dewlap, which is beyond our sensory reach; having discerned this, the learned have established these designations.

As it has been said: "The application of a name is preceded by perception. From the instruction of our venerable teachers, we both determine the universals such as "cowness" (gotva) and so forth, according to their respective fitness, through the succession of tradition.

And this formulation of names by those superior to us is merely a manifestation of the relationship between word and meaning as it actually exists; it is not the creation of a new convention, because the relationship between word and meaning is innate. Thus, on the authority of the learned (śiṣṭa), there exist distinct universals such as "Brahminhood" (brāhmaṇatva) and others, which are appropriately denoted by abstract suffixes (bhāvapratyaya). || 46 ||

In this regard, the following is considered: It has been stated that "the suffixes *tva*, *tal*, and so forth, express that [abstract property]. Now, in cases such as *jātigandhatvam* (the nature of generic fragrance), *utpalagandhatvam* (the nature of lotus fragrance), and *mallikāgandhatvam* (the nature of jasmine fragrance), one might wonder: does the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) refer to the higher genus, namely fragrance in general, or rather to a lower genus, a specific commonality residing in a particular substrate of fragrance? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "When the reality of differentiation (*bhedatattva*) which resides in the fragrance of a species, a lotus, and so forth, is not expressed by abstract suffixes in common usage due to its impermanence," (verse 47).

In this worldly linguistic usage, which depends upon the speaker’s intention, when a suffix denoting an abstract state (*bhāvapratyaya*) is applied to a compound such as *jātigandha* (the smell of a genus), then—since the formation of a compound is prescribed only where there is semantic capacity—that very [capacity] is the ground for the application of the word; thus, the abstract suffix is applied to that alone. This is because of the rule stating, "In compounds, primary derivatives (*kṛt*), and secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), there is the expression of a relation. Therefore, in a locative compound (*saptamīsamāsa*), the relation between the locus and the located is expressed, while in a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), it is either that preceded by it, namely, the residual relation (*śeṣasambandha*). That [relation] is what is signified by the compound.

But when the intention is that the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) occurs first from the word "fragrance" (*gandha*) alone, and the compound follows later, then the ultimate reality (*tattva*) of the specific fragrance—which resides in the lotus and so forth and serves as the object (*karman*)—is not denotable by an abstract suffix; for that which serves as the substratum (*āśraya*) and functions as the agent (*kartṛ*) is another universal (*aparasāmānya*), and because it is impermanent, it is not present in all instances [of fragrance].

Alternatively, the "distinct universal" (*viśiṣṭaṃ sāmānyam*) is the reality (*tattvam*) of a particular fragrance; these are co-referential terms meaning that which is "resorted to" (*āśritam*) or "inherently connected" (*samavetam*). The meaning here is as follows: the distinct universal that is inherently connected to the fragrance of a blue lotus is not present in the individual instance of the fragrance of sandalwood and so forth. Therefore, because it deviates [from its locus], it is impermanent; however, it is not the case that the universal itself is impermanent.

Since the word *gandha* (fragrance) applies without distinction to fragrance in general, its basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) must be that which pervades fragrance in general and is denoted by an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*). Now, a specific universal inhering in the fragrance of a blue lotus cannot pervade all fragrances; therefore, this [specific universal] is not the non-distinct basis for the application of the word *gandha*. However, through the particularity of its substratum, the genus [fragrance-ness] is designated as "fragrance-ness" or "blue-lotus-fragrance-ness"; thus, by means of inherence-in-what-is-inherent (*samavetasamavāya*), the determination of the qualified [particular] is established.

Nor is it the case that there is no such thing as a specific universal (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*), for since individual instances of odor differ according to the difference of their substrata, it is possible for them to possess a subordinate genus (*uparajāti*), just like "being a *śābaleya* cow" and so forth. And thus he states what the reality of difference depends upon: he will indeed say later that "the difference of qualities arises from the difference of their substrata. Furthermore, since there certainly exists a recurring cognition (*anvayī pratyaya*) regarding the odors of blue lotuses that is excluded from other things, who can deny the possibility of a universal (*sāmānya*) as its cause? For this very reason, the word "worldly" (*loka*) is employed [in the verse].

In common worldly usage, it is not designated as "other. However, those experts who are skilled in the science of perfumes do indeed perceive a specific universal (*viśiṣṭasāmānya*). Furthermore, even when a suffix denoting an abstract state (*bhāvapratyaya*) is applied to a compound, because the relationship between the universal and the particular is expressed by the compound itself and is not conveyed by the [individual] word, it is not designated as "non-eternal" (*anitya*). || 47 ||

However, there are certain classes of beings for which no conventional designation exists; thus he says: "But classes such as the Man-lion (Narasiṃha) are not denoted by their own [component] words; in them, the auditory perception resides in the parts that possess similar forms. (48)

The universals such as "man-lion" (*narasiṃha*) and "donkey" (*gaurakhara*) lack specific designators [of their own]. That word—such as the scriptural term *narasiṃha*—whose two constituent parts possess an identical form when uttered is the designator therein. For this scriptural term, appearing through its similarity to the two words "man" and "lion" which have the universals of "man-ness" (*naratva*) and "lion-ness" (*siṃhatva*) as their objects, produces an appearance of those very universals of man-ness and lion-ness.

Nor is a man-lion produced from two [individuals] who are themselves man-lions; rather, in this object which possesses a variegated form, a distinct genus (*jātyantara*) inheres therein, just as "variegatedness" inheres in a variegated color. Therefore, this [word] is unable to convey its specific [referent]. Furthermore, since this word is in reality partless, even the similarity of parts is not real; thus, the word "as if" (*iva*) indicates that there is here merely a subjective conceit of similarity.

Just as in the case of words situated within an indivisible sentence, because a mental reflection (*pratibhā*) is produced regarding universals such as "human-ness" through delusion, this scriptural expression (*śruti*) for the *narasiṃha* (man-lion) type is not unique; nor does any other [such expression] exist. Regarding the term *asvaśabdābhidhāna*: there is no word of its own (*svaśabda*); it is that whose designation (*abhidhāna*)—meaning that by which it is expressed—is thus characterized. || 48 ||

Thus, when the word is examined by way of its meaning, having established that the base portion (*prakṛti*) possesses pervasion (*vyāpti*) because its referent is the universal (*jāti*), he says the following in order to establish the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of the base and the suffix by demonstrating that the suffix portion also possesses the capacity to denote the universal: "In the delimitation of the state of the universal, number—or even the nature of number itself—contributes to the assistance [of the denotation] through its association, despite the distance [between them]. (49)

The "state" (*avasthā*) of a substance-class (*dravyajāti*) or an action-class (*kriyājāti*)—which are denoted by the stems of words ending in nominal or verbal suffixes—is their subsistence (*avasthāna*) or inherence (*samavāya*) in their own substratum, which constitutes their determination (*pariccheda*). This determination takes the form of an inquiry: "Is the inherence of that [class] intended to reside in a single substance, or in many? When this is being ascertained, the number-class (*saṅkhyājāti*), denoted by the nominal or verbal suffixes, becomes functional through its inherence in that which is inherent in a single object (*ekārthasamavetasamavāya*), even though there is no direct relationship [between the number and the substance].

Even for the genus of number (*saṅkhyājāti*) expressed by a verb-ending word (*tiṅanta*), there exists indeed a relation of inherence-in-what-is-inherent-in-the-same-substratum (*ekārthasamavetasamavāya*) with the genus of action (*kriyājāti*) through its own substratum. Alternatively, the state (*avasthā*) of the genus—which is a difference in form characterized by connection with its own specific substratum—is [the relation]. Or rather, the individual instance of number (*saṅkhyāvyakti*), which is implied by the force of the genus of number as perceived through the word, qualifies the genus denoted by the base (*prakṛti*) due to inherence in the same object; for that which is already perceived serves as a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*).

Furthermore, comprehension arising from a word—whether through its direct denotation (*śabda*) or through its inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*)—is not distinguished [in its mode]. Alternatively, in the view that the substance (*dravya*) is the referent of a word, number (*saṅkhyā*) and individual (*vyakti*) are the denotations of the word and function as qualifiers; however, in the view that the universal (*jāti*) is the referent, number and the universal [are the denotations]—this is the alternative. In cases such as *gauḥ* (cow), *pacati* (he cooks), and *pacataḥ* (they two cook), an object characterized by a specific universal and delimited by a specific number is primarily comprehended; thus, the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) functions as the qualifier, while the meaning of the stem (*prakṛti*) functions as the qualificand.

And thus, the statement "a verb has action as its primary meaning" is justified. In cases such as *pacati* ("he cooks"), because the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*) is that which is yet to be accomplished (*sādhya*), it is primary; and since it is qualified by the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), such as the *kāraka* (participant), that [action] is predominant. However, in cases such as *aupagavaḥ* ("the descendant of Upagu"), there is a denotation of the meaning of the suffix—characterized as offspring—which is colored by the meaning of the root, and this is stated as being primary. This very point is the subject of the rule: "The root and the suffix express the meaning of the suffix together. This is, however, a general rule (*prāyika*).
For instance—number is mentioned here for the sake of qualifying the meaning of the base; thus, in examples such as "bring the cow," that which is qualified by it is the primary element. || 49 ||

Thus far, it has been stated that the meaning of the base (prakṛti) qualified by the meaning of the suffix (pratyaya) is expressed by the word in a general sense; and that, through the connection mediated by the substance (dravya), the co-occurrence (samabhivyāhāra) of the base and the suffix—both of which denote universals (jāti)—is logically established. Now, however, because in certain cases a meaning, even if explicitly heard, is not intended due to a difference in the speaker's intent (tātparya), he says the following in order to examine how the word-meaning serves as a means toward the sentence-meaning: "Metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā) is an operation within the grammatical refinement (saṃskāra) of the word for the sake of accomplishing the task [of communication];
it is observed [to occur] even when the powers (śakti) such as number, object, and so forth are identical in their explicit mention (śruti). (Verse 50)

Just as number, so too the powers such as the object (karman) and others, which are expressed by case-endings, are [powers]; thus, even though there is equality between those powers—the object and so forth—and the *śruti* (the word), namely the root-initial *am* and so on that expresses them, there are two kinds of operation regarding the sentence-meaning: one is indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and that occurs in the domain of verbal refinement (*śabda-saṃskāra*).

Since the mere meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) devoid of number, object, and so forth is impossible, the rule "a base should not be used alone" necessitates that an inflection (*vibhakti*) is sometimes employed for the sake of grammatical refinement (*śabda-saṃskāra*), even when it does not determine its own meaning [number] for the meaning of the base. For example, in the case of "he cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ sammārṣṭi*). To the objection—"How is it that singularity is not intended here? Is it not the case that the singular number has as its sole fruit merely the grammatical refinement?"—the author will state the logical principle (*nyāya*) later. Here, however, there is merely the introduction of the thing itself (*vastu-mātra*).

Likewise, when the powers of the object and other factors are employed for the sake of verbal refinement (*śabda-saṃskāra*), there is no intention to express [their status as objects]. For example, in the case of "He offers the groats" (*saktūn juhoti*). Here, indeed, only this much is intended to be expressed: that the oblation has the groats as its means (*saktusādhana*). Since the act of offering possesses a result by virtue of having an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) as its purpose, it is primary; thus, although the groats are the most desired (*īpsitatama*) merely by being the objective of the action, they have fulfilled their function simply through their connection with the action.

For one does not perform a *homa* sacrifice with the thought, "How indeed might the groats become ashes? Rather, [one acts] so that an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) may be produced by means of those groats as the instrument. If this is the case, since the action has an unseen purpose, the groats are certainly not the most desired object; thus, there is no objective case-power (*karma-śakti*) here at all. How, then, can there be a non-intentionality (*avivakṣā*) regarding that which does not exist? For it is logical that there be a non-intentionality only toward something that exists and is expressed by the word, such as the singularity in the word "cup" (*graham*), but not toward something that does not exist.

For when one says, "The wood cooks," it is not said that the wood's capacity as an object (*karma-śakti*) is unintended; rather, its capacity as an instrument (*karaṇa-śakti*) is intended. This is true. However, the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) itself would simply not be accomplished if the groats (*saktu*) were not accepted as the most desired end (*īpsitatama*), because [the result] cannot be achieved by any other means. Therefore, by the very force of the fact that the action has the unseen merit as its purpose, the fact that the action is for the sake of the groats must be admitted—just as the act of propitiation is for the sake of the deity.

For a deity is worshipped solely for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*); thus, if the *saktu* (groats) were not for the sake of a deity, their status as having an unseen purpose would be lost. In this case, although the *saktu* are the subordinate factor (*aṅga*) and the primary factor (*pradhāna*) is for the sake of the unseen, they nonetheless remain the most desired object (*īpsitatama*). However, that status of being the most desired is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*), because the action is not undertaken with that alone as its fruit, and because the *saktu* are prompted by another result. Their status as the fruit of the action is not intended to be significant because it is not apprehended through a distinct form, as is the case with the cups (*graha*).

Therefore, it is established that the state of being the most desired (*īpsitatamatva*) is non-existent with respect to other *kārakas* and is not intended [as such] because of its dependence on something else. However, in certain cases, for the sake of accomplishing the effect, there is the operation of capacities such as number, objecthood (*karman*), and so forth; this is the utility of delimiting the substance, which serves as the cause for the accomplishment of the action that constitutes the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). This is because the action is presented as being accomplished by a substance possessing specific qualities such as number, as in the injunction: "One should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*).

For in this case, it will be stated according to the established principle that the number is indeed intended to be significant, since the sacrifice is accomplished without deficiency even with a single animal. Furthermore, the intention regarding the potency of the action is seen in the injunction "one threshes the rice-grains" (*vrīhīnavahanti*). For the rice-grains, being the objects to be refined by the act of threshing, are what is most desired to be attained; no one engages in the act of threshing for its own sake, but rather for the sake of the rice-grains.

Because those [rice grains], having been refined by that act of threshing, attain a specific excellence of nature suitable for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), their status as a constituent part of the sacrifice is established; thus, the action of threshing is subordinate here, while the rice grains themselves, which are to be refined, are the primary object, since they, once turned into rice, are utilized later. As for the husks, however, having been reduced to ashes, they lack existence and thus have no further utility. As they say: "A substance that has already served its purpose or will serve it in the future is held to be the object of refinement."

"The groats shall not be consumed, nor have they ever been consumed anywhere. Here, the act of threshing is described as secondary in its real (vāstava) form; however, in its verbal (śābda) form, it is everywhere enjoined as something to be accomplished, and thus that alone is primary. Consequently, the status of the object as a *kāraka* (participant in action) is here relative to that [action]; we have explained this in detail in the *Kriyāviveka*, where it is stated that the action constitutes the primary meaning of the sentence, so it should be understood from that very source.

Thus, the statement that "those [words] are of two kinds, being either subordinate (guṇa) or predominant (pradhāna)" regarding bhāva-words should be understood as intending their actual nature. However, those who read "lakṣaṇā is the refinement of the word (śabda-saṃskāra), the operation for the accomplishment of the effect" explain the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) by asserting that *lakṣaṇā* is a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the substance (*dravya*), and that the mention of number therein is for the purpose of the word's refinement alone; thus, because it has that [substance] as its object, the refinement of the word is said to be *lakṣaṇā*. || 50 ||

Now, the operation known as *lakṣaṇā* (secondary indication) within the refinement of words (*śabda-saṃskāra*) is analyzed: No entity (*sattvabhūta-artha*) is ever expressed without a number. Therefore, in the designation of everything, the number would be unintended (*avivakṣita*). (51)

A substance (*dravya*) is that which is capable of being referred to by pronouns such as "this" or "that," and which is compatible with the application of number. In an expression such as "the offspring of that" (*tasyāpatyam*), that [substance] is what is intended to be directly designated; thus, because it is invariably present in any designation whatsoever, the rule "a base alone should not be employed" finds its fulfillment. Consequently, number is not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣita*); this is the general principle (*utsarga*). As it has been said: "In the designation of the meaning of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), gender and number are not authoritative, because they are not intended to be expressed."

Since a genus (*jāti*) is employed in order to distinguish a substance from other substances, it is not logical to disregard it. For if there were no intention to express it in any way whatsoever, there would be no use of the word at all, as the meanings of both the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) [would remain unexpressed]. And thus, he will state that the number expressed by the base is indeed intended to be conveyed. (51)

Regarding this general rule (utsarga), some state a specific exception: "For certain [words], neither singularity nor plurality is intended to be expressed; for that [number] serves to denote the genus (jāti). However, duality would indeed be intended to be expressed. (52)

That which is not possible in the genus (*jāti*) is determined as being resident in the individual (*vyakti*), serving as its indirect delimiter. Therefore, it is logical that number residing in the substance (*dravya*) serves as the delimiter of the genus, rather than the unity or plurality inherent to the genus itself. For unity is never absent from the genus, while plurality is merely extended to it by metaphorical transfer (*atideśika*). [Objection: But surely there is no number at all in the genus, since number is a property of substances. [Reply: Here, the methodology established in other systems is not the authority; rather, some internal tenet of our own system must be maintained.

And there is proof for its unity, because a universal (jāti) is established by means of valid cognition as being specifically qualified by unity. Likewise, there is the extended rule (*atideśika*): "The plural is used for a single entity when denoting a universal. When an injunction refers to a universal, neither singularity nor plurality is intended to be expressed, as in: "A Brāhmaṇa must not be killed," "Liquor must not be drunk," and "One must not enter with Śūdras. However, where such intention does exist, the injunction refers to a substance (*dravya*). But since duality is not prescribed in the case of a universal being denoted, it is always intended to be based solely on a substance in every instance. || 52 ||

He states that even this [meaning] is not intended in certain cases: "If these two were diseased, this medicine should be given"—in such a case, the duality of the object's meaning would be unintended. (53)

In this context, the duality expressed by the word *etāvat* (of such extent), which is employed as a secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the purpose of identifying the sick person who is the object of the gift of medicine—having proceeded in this manner by taking the disease as the occasion—is not intended to be significant here. Furthermore, this locative case (*saptamī*) is used in the sense of "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇe*), meaning "in the making known," or "in the characterizing of the object that is the scope of the gift of medicine. For the status of the disease as the object is established here solely through the inherent power of the nature of the medicine itself.

The phrase "of that gift there are these two" is employed to exclude other diseases; yet, since the occurrence of a disease from either one of those two might be anticipated, the intended meaning here does not restrict the giving of medicine to the duality [of the two]. Furthermore, because the possibility of disease is the object of such anticipation, when the possibility exists for both, then the combined pair alone becomes the object of the medicine's administration. Thus, the injunction is meaningful through the intention to express them together.

Furthermore, the giving of medicine is intended as a remedy for disease; thus, it is possible even when only one person is afflicted. Moreover, since there is no possibility of referring to "these two" when many people are the subject, even if duality were not intended [by the dual ending], there would still be no occasion for the giving of that medicine to many. Furthermore, in this context, the number is not intended to be significant with respect to the primary object, namely that "two persons are to be benefited by the giving of medicine."

In a case where the understanding of the meaning of the injunction for both [breasts] occurs even through a sequence—as in "the two breasts are to be cut"—there is indeed an intention [to express both]. But here, the injunction is made by anticipating the state of being ill as a possible object; thus its validity is established whether the illness occurs sequentially or simultaneously. For the coexistence of a future event is not determined with absolute necessity. || 53 ||

Thus, having established that the number acquired through a suffix may be intended or unintended according to the analysis of the sentence-meaning and the distinction of its objects, he now states that the number acquired by the base (*prakṛti*) is invariably intended: "The status of being a subordinate factor (*aṅgatva*) in respect to the object is desired for the number expressed by words such as 'one' and so forth; for it is understood from the form [of the word] 'he digs with two' (*dvābhyāṃ khanati*) that it is dependent [on the base]. (54)

In the cases of "he digs the earth with two mantras," "he takes [it] with four," and "he carries [it] away with six," it is accepted that the numbers two and so forth—which serve as the basis for the application [of the terms], which are denoted by the nominal stems (*prātipadika*), and which delimit the action—are indeed intended to be expressed (*vivakṣita*). Otherwise, the very meaning of the word would be abandoned. Thus, because the employment of the nominal stem would otherwise be inexplicable, and by virtue of its inherent nature (*svabhāva*) as expressing a specific number, there is an intention to express that number here due to its semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*).

The word *rūpa* is a synonym for *prātipadika* (nominal stem); thus, the meaning is "not [the deletion] of the case-ending (*vibhakti*) from the nominal stem (*rūpa*)," as in examples such as *dviputra*. For here, the distinction expressed by the case-ending ceases to exist within the compound due to *ekārthībhāva* (the unification of meaning), whereas that which is expressed by the base (*prakṛti*) certainly remains. For in its absence, the employment of the word would indeed be fruitless. However, in cases such as *graham*, the suffix assists in conveying the meaning of the nominal stem and is therefore meaningful; hence, in this context, it is appropriate not to intend [the deletion of the case-ending].

Regarding the injunction, "If both of one's two oblations should meet with ruin, one should offer five *śarāva*-measures of cooked rice to Indra," the word "both" (*ubhaya*) here denotes a collection composed of two parts, rather than denoting the number two. Therefore, even if only one part is destroyed, because the whole collection is not destroyed, the offering (*nirvāpa*) is indeed performed. || 54 ||

Now, that which was stated—“the operation [is for] the accomplishment of the effect”—is being analyzed. It was previously stated that in that context, only duality is intended to be expressed, and not singularity or plurality. However, he now says that even singularity is sometimes intended to be expressed: “In the case of ‘one should sacrifice with an animal,’ since the refinement [of the animal] is also possible, singularity is understood as a means of accomplishment, just like the genus. (55)

Although it may be possible here that the case-ending (*vibhakti*) has the purpose of grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*), nevertheless, just as the genus of the animal (*paśujāti*), which is denoted by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), functions as an auxiliary to the ritual action, so too "oneness" (*ekatva*), though denoted by the case-ending, is not abandoned because it is presented within the same word. The meaning is that, like the genus, oneness is also an auxiliary to the ritual action. For how could a referent presented within a single word—which revolves in the intellect as a unity—be connected through a distinction such as "one should sacrifice with an animal" and "with one [animal]"?

For the meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is touched by that specific word-meaning which is expressed through both the stem (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) by means of a single, non-distinct operation; this is because, when there is a single word, the internal relationship within the word is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*). Therefore, both [the substance and the deity] can be enjoined together. However, if they were touched separately, it would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), and thus they could not be enjoined. But when they are presented as distinct words, they might indeed be connected separately, since such a separate injunction is possible.

Just as in the case of the command "bring a red horse," where there is a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*)—namely, the syntactic connection (*samanvaya*) being "bring the red" and "bring the horse"—but when expressed by a single word, as in "bring a crimson [horse] (*śoṇam*)," the application (*viniyoga*) is based on the inclusion within that single term. However, in the case of "he cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ sammārṣṭi*), how it cannot be enjoined as such will be demonstrated later. By this, he indicates that the previously unknown nature and the non-primary status of the meaning of the word *paśu* (animal) are dependent upon the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*).

The meaning is that from this very statement, [the number] is understood as being a means (*sādhana*). However, he will demonstrate this clearly later on. Now, an objection is raised: by the enjoining *śruti*, the status of the substance as a means to the action is enjoined, but not that of the quality, namely the number; for since the enjoining authority is exhausted with respect to the substance alone, there is a lack of evidence for the enjoining of the quality. True. This [evidence] called "appropriation" (*upādāna*) is distinct from the sixfold set of authorities beginning with *śruti*.

For a mere substance devoid of number is not grasped by a positive injunction, because it is impossible to abandon a quality that is conveyed by the same word. Indeed, a substance accompanied by its qualities is perceived through a single, unified verbal cognition; thus, there is a syntactic connection between the quality and the substance as appropriate. || 55 ||

Thus, this proponent does not accept non-intentionality [of number] in the absence of a subverting argument (*bādhaka*). To the question, "How then do those who maintain that number exists solely for the sake of grammatical refinement (*śabda-saṃskāra*) intend singularity here?", he says: "But from an indicative mark (*liṅga*), there may be a second [number] and so forth; therefore, that singularity is intended. And when [the word] has a single object as its referent, that indicative mark belongs to both the genus (*jāti*) and the number. (Verse 56)

The singular number in the word *paśunā* ("with an animal") is solely for the purpose of grammatical refinement (*śabdasaṃskāra*). However, the intended plurality is understood from an indicative mark (*liṅga*) found in another sentence. For instance, after stating, "One should sacrifice a goat (*aja*) dedicated to Agni at the *agniṣṭoma*," it continues, "A second [goat] dedicated to Indra-Agni at the *ukthya*, and a third, a speckled one (*pṛśni*) dedicated to Indra, at the *ṣoḍaśin*. Thus, by virtue of being designated as "second" and so forth, the goat is qualified as plural.

Furthermore, if the singularity in the word *ajam* were not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*), then since the status of being "second" and so forth would be unestablished, there would be no need for the further injunctions "the second," etc. Therefore, by the force of this very expression, it is determined that singularity is indeed intended. [Objection: Even if singularity were not intended, the designations "the second" and "the third" would still be appropriate here, because they serve as qualifiers [specifying] "being the second and so forth" in a context where an indefinite number might otherwise result. [Reply: This is not so. For if it were thus, there would be the fault of restating what is already established (*anuvāda-doṣa*) in certain cases.

But if [the number] is a gender-indicator (*liṅga*), then the second case-ending and so forth, which are prescribed as something previously unknown, are heard in the scripture as being constant and non-optional; thus, they are not contradicted. For if it were a restatement (*anuvāda*) in one alternative (*pakṣe*), the scriptural statement would become optional, and consequently, the hearing of the word as non-optional would be abandoned—such is the undesirable consequence (*doṣaprasaṅga*). Furthermore, he states this incidentally: that the completion [of the action] rests upon a single substratum is precisely the indicator (*liṅga*) for both the number one and the genus (*jāti*).

For just as oneness is fully realized in its substratum, so too is the universal (*jāti*), even when there is a co-inherence in multiple objects; from this it is determined. Likewise, regarding the statement that "the number one has a single common object, domain, or substratum for this universal," the very same secondness and so forth serve as the logical mark (*liṅga*). Otherwise, if the universal were to function only partially within its substrata, then that which completes a pair would not belong to that genus, but would instead be merely a portion of the universal. And a portion of a universal does not constitute a universal.

Furthermore, since the substratum is the same for both the universal (*jāti*) and the oneness (*ekatva*), the universal is taken up as a constituent of the action in its entirety as the meaning of the base. Otherwise, if the universal were not fully present in that substratum in its entire essence—just as oneness is—it would be impossible to take up oneness there; for the universal is not fully present in its entirety in a single [individual]. Consequently, the existence of a second [individual] and so forth would be undermined. Therefore, this indicator (*liṅga*), while implying oneness, also implies the full presence of the universal in its substratum in its entire essence.

For this is an indicator (*liṅga*) of only that much of a meaning which cannot otherwise be established. Just as singularity is not possible without the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*), so too is the genus’ having the same object [as the individual] not possible without it. Otherwise, if the genus were not fully contained therein, the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) would not be taken up in its entirety as a constituent of the action (*kriyāṅga*), resulting in the undesirable consequence of obstructing the meaning of the base.

Because duality and the like reside in multiple substrata, they do not exist in their entirety within each individual substratum; therefore, this [residence in multiple substrata] is not a mark for the universal (jāti) having the same object as that [duality]. For in that case, it would merely indicate that [the universal] resides in multiple [substrata], and that is already established by its very nature as a universal. Thus, it should be understood that this [residence in multiple substrata] is a mark for the universal's inherence in the same object only with respect to unity. || 56 ||

Now, regarding what was stated—that in the injunction "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*yajeta paśunā*), the singularity is intended to be expressed just like the genus—he clarifies the basis for that intention, which was previously indicated, by contrasting it with the case of the cups (*graha*): "That injunction first applies to the animal as something not already prescribed elsewhere; and its status as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) in the ritual action follows from that very fact. Therefore, [the singularity] is intended to be expressed. (57)

Since the necessity of performing the sacrifice (*yajati*) is established by another sentence, the statement "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*) is, in its intended sense, an injunction regarding a quality (*guṇavidhi*). Thus, because this [sentence] is the first to make known the previously unknown quality of the animal through a means of valid cognition, it is an originative injunction (*utpattividhi*) for the animal; for the animal is as if produced for the first time from this sentence, since it is made known by this alone. Indeed, making known (*jñapti*) itself is called "first production" (*prathamotpatti*).

And that productive injunction (*utpattividhi*) pertains here as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) within the scope of the sacrificial action (*yajikriyā*), not as a principal element (*aṅgin*); for these two reasons, that singularity is intended to be expressed here. For we take scripture (*śabda*) as our authority, and since the object is enjoined by the word as qualified by singularity, how can that singularity be abandoned? As it has been said: "Just as the genus (*jāti*), so too is singularity understood as a means of accomplishment. The principle indicated here is that just as the genus is enjoined by the word, so too is singularity.

Furthermore, the word first expresses this [the animal] and not another word associated with a different number, as is the case with the *graha* and other [vessels]; thus, the initial instruction is the cause for the intended meaning (*vivakṣā*). Moreover, there is an instruction regarding its status as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) because the sacrifice is the primary element (*pradhāna*). For if the instruction were of the animal as the principal element, then—as in the case of "he cleanses the *graha*"—there would be no intention to express that specific number. This is the meaning.

Therefore, since there is no reason for abandoning the number heard [in the text], the primary element is understood to have a fixed form by virtue of being accomplished through a means qualified by singularity; thus, the employment of an indefinite or multiple number lacks authority. On this point, some read "of the state of being a subordinate member in the action" (*kriyāyāmaṅgabhāvasya*) and have construed it as: first, there is an injunction regarding the state of being a subordinate member in the action. (57)

By way of contrast with this principle, he describes the operation known as *lakṣaṇā* (indication) in the case of the injunction "he cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ sammārṣṭi*): "But the cups (*grahāḥ*) are prescribed elsewhere as having different numbers, being distinct from one another, and endowed with such distinctions as 'nine for Prajāpati' (*prājāpatyā nava*). (58)
When those things understood as subsidiaries (the *aṅgas*) are again specified in relation to the primary act (*aṅgin*), how could that number be intended [as significant]? (59)

In originative injunctions such as, "There are nine *grahas* belonging to Prajāpati," "The Adhvaryu draws these ten *grahas* at the morning pressing," "He draws the *aindravāyava* *graha*," and "He draws the *maitrāvaruṇa* *graha*," the *grahas*—which are vessels for the Soma—are presented separately in their respective contexts with distinct numbers and are experienced as such; they are then brought to mind through recollection (*smṛti*) in the subsequent statement, "He cleanses the *graha*."

In this context, it is logical that the presentation [of the number] in the cognition based on recollection (smṛti-buddhi) should correspond precisely to the experience of the original injunctive statement (utpatti-vākya). Therefore, the numbers are indeed perceived as distinct. For in the original injunction, the cups (grahas) are taught as subordinate elements for the purpose of holding the Soma; thus, because they lack primacy there, the number is not intended to be significant.
