Furthermore, because it is a novel teaching (apūrva-upadeśa), just as in the case of the word "with an animal" (paśunā), the number is necessarily intended to be significant since it constitutes the meaning of the nominal stem (prātipadika-artha), such as "nine" or "ten."

However, in its real nature (*vāstavena rūpeṇa*), the cleansing (*sammārge*) has the cups (*graha*) as its primary objects (*aṅgin*) because it serves the purpose of producing purification for the cups; thus, even though the action is primary in its verbal form (*śābdena rūpeṇa*), the cups themselves are the principal elements to be refined (*saṃskārya*). Consequently, regarding the reference "the cup" (*graham*) found in the cleansing injunction—which is distinct from the original injunction of origin (*utpattivākya*)—those very same cups previously heard are taken up by way of intent (*tātparyataḥ*) as the objects of the act of cleansing; therefore, they are connected with the number [of the previous injunction].

For the meaning of a sentence is established through a thorough consideration of the context (*prakaraṇa*), and one should not rest with the mere literal meaning of the individual words. This is according to the maxim: "In sentences where praise or censure is predominant, the meaning is not such as is imagined by the separate division of the words. Thus, the extraction of word-meanings occurs by following the meaning of the great sentence (*mahāvākya*) through the connection of subordinate sentences; herein, there is the grasping of planets whose number was perceived differently through the context.

Thus, by this, two reasons for the lack of intention [to express plurality] have been stated: its prescription elsewhere and its predominance. Although oneness is experienced as non-contradictory even among many things, nevertheless, the oneness experienced here is that which falls within a plurality and not one that is solitary; therefore, the recollection here is of that which is accompanied by plurality. For this very reason, he says "separately, separately" (*pṛthak pṛthak*)—using the frequent observation of the number "many"—in order to establish the stability of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) arising from that [observation], and thereby to ensure the non-deviation of the recollection.

The meaning is that because distinct numbers have been experienced individually, there is a corresponding recollection (*smṛti*) in this restatement (*anuvāda*) regarding the cleansing (*sammārjana*). Since the cups (*graha*) are employed in the oblation according to the injunction "He offers with the cups," they are objects to be consecrated (*saṃskārya*); for subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) are fit for consecration in order to assist the primary rite (*pradhāna*). Furthermore, it is not logical that the injunction for cleansing should be qualified by the singularity of the cup.

Because a quality (*guṇa*) lacks the status of being a subordinate factor (*aṅga*) in an action due to its parity with the substance (*dravya*), it becomes subordinate only by means of the substance; thus, when it follows the substance, it relies upon the distinction of the substance as previously experienced. However, in cases such as "He binds the brindled cows" (*citragavīr badhnāti*) and "Yoke the red one" (*śoṇaṃ yojaya*), the intention to express the quality is inherent, because otherwise the direct mention (*śruti*) of "brindled" (*citra*) and "red" (*śoṇa*) would be inexplicable. (Verses 58–59)

Now, since the non-intentionality [of number] is general everywhere, and because the case-endings are employed for the sake of grammatical refinement (*śabda-saṃskāra*), he states the intention with effort: "There is no injunction elsewhere; there is neither refinement nor the status of being a primary factor (*aṅgitā*). Number is the cause for the intention [to express it], for that [intention] is indeed expressed through effort. (60)

Since there is an injunction for cups (*graha*) of different numbers in other sentences, for this reason it is not correct to say that the singular number in the phrase "he cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ sammārṣṭi*) is merely for the sake of grammatical refinement (*śabda-saṃskāra*). Nor is the singularity here a cause or motive for the non-intentionality (*avivakṣā*) of the cup's status as the primary object (*aṅgin*) or its predominance (*prādhānya*) in the act of cleansing; rather, according to the principle stated—that "nothing exists without a number"—the mention of the number everywhere serves only as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-artha*), and is thus unintended.

But where there exists some principle in the form of a logical justification, then, because of that effort, the number is intended to be expressed; this is an exception to the general rule of non-intentionality regarding number. || 60 ||

And there is no effort based on the speaker’s intention in cases such as "the cup" (*graham*); thus he says: "And the specific act of wiping is not in any way dependent upon the cup; they (the cups) are prescribed as things to be consecrated, and therefore they are the substratum for all [the mantras]. (61)

In the injunction "he cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ sammārṣṭi*), a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) is prescribed for the cup whose specific identity has not been mentioned but which was previously determined. Previously, however, multiple cups were observed; thus he says, "they have been enjoined. For indeed, no single cup is enjoined in its own originative statement (*utpattivākya*); rather, many are enjoined, such as "nine" or "ten. Nor is only one among them fit for the rite, but rather all of them are so; thus he says, "and they are to be purified."

The consecration (*saṃskāra*) applies to all [the cups], because subsequently, at the time of holding the Soma, all those that have been consecrated are employed. Therefore, if only one among the many prescribed [cups] had been intended, some specific characteristic serving as its mark would have been pointed out, such as "he cleanses the Ārka, the Āśvina, or the Maitrāvaruṇa cup. But no such [specificity] has been pointed out. Furthermore, the singular number is not a distinguishing feature.

Because that [universal] lacks a fixed single object, if one were to adopt a single [object] without restriction, there would be no determination of the specific [object] as to whose [it might be], resulting in the undesirable consequence of teaching an object that is impossible to practice. Therefore, this singular number (*ekavacana*) should be understood as referring to the genus (*jāti*), and not to the individual (*vyakti*); thus, the intended meaning is not established by this effort. Furthermore, it has already been established that the singular number is used everywhere merely for the sake of grammatical refinement (*śabda-saṃskāra*); and so, the singular number is not an intentional effort [to denote a specific individual].

Therefore, because of the general instruction and because the state of being an object of refinement is common [to all], it is established that the refinement is to be applied to all cups (grahas) whose number has been determined by the originative injunctions. || 61 ||

Regarding the statement "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*), he asks: what effort is there in the intention to express the number? He says: "If the genus were completed in each individual substrate, and the action were performed with only one [animal], then the sacrifice could not be accomplished by means of 'an animal' (*paśunā*); therefore, that [intention to express the number] must indeed exist. (62)

It has already been established by means of an indicative mark (*liṅga*) that a universal (*jāti*) is fully present in each individual substratum; therefore, since the universal of "cowness" (*paśutva*) is not incomplete even in a single instance, its status as a constituent of the ritual action (*kriyāṅgatā*) is possible. Why, then, would the accusative case ending (*dvitīyā*) be employed [in the plural]? For if a universal were to reside in its substratum only partially, then when it is employed in a single individual, the universal as the word-meaning (*padārtha*) would be sublated, because a mere portion of a universal is not itself a universal. Thus, the accusative case ending and so forth would be employed on the strength of the capacity of the base meaning (*prakṛtyartha*). But this is not the case, because a universal is fully established even in a single instance. This might be argued:

Granted that the meaning of the primary term (*prakṛtyartha*) may be established even with a single [animal], one might raise the objection: "Since the action that constitutes the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) cannot be accomplished by a single instrument, another auxiliary (*aṅga*) must be employed in accordance with the principal. Anticipating this, he says: "If the action could not be accomplished by a single animal. For a sacrifice whose fruit is transcendental (*adṛṣṭa*) is fully accomplished through the assistance rendered by even a single animal via the offering of portions (*avadāna*); therefore, there is no lack of fulfillment that would necessitate the postulation of multiple animals here.

By implication, the word "that" (tat) points to the conceptualization of multiple numbers present in the mind. From this very authoritative sentence, "One should sacrifice with an animal" (paśunā yajeta), it is understood that a single [animal] serves as the means for the action. Otherwise, if—as in the case of the [word] "vessel" (graha)—another number were not determined from another sentence, and there were an indefinite choice of one, then an impossible matter would have been taught. || 62 ||

Anticipating the objection that "since the abundance of fruit results from a hymn that is a subordinate member [of a rite], other sacrificial animals may be employed as appropriate," he says: "If, when a ritual action is already established by one [animal], another animal were to be employed because it is possible [to do so], then such employment would be purposeless. (63)

Now, this is the meaning: here, does a single individual soul possess the causal agency for the accomplishment of an action, or not? If the second alternative were true, it would constitute a transgression of the scripture; therefore, the first alternative must be accepted. Furthermore, since the action is accomplished by means of a single [cause] due to parsimony (*lāghava*), for what purpose would the qualified practitioners (*adhikāriṇaḥ*) undergo the exertion of searching for other means when their desired goal is already within reach? For the injunction of the scripture does not say "according to what is possible."

Furthermore, if one were to perform what has not been enjoined, it would constitute a transgression of the Teacher’s [Vedic] injunction and thus result in futility; consequently, there would be no increase in the fruit [of the sacrifice]. For when a sacrifice is to be accomplished by one or more [animals], there is no excellence in the essential nature of the cause of the fruit [that arises from adding more animals]. Therefore, because of the simplicity of the means, since the set of portions to be cut (avadānagaṇa) is accomplished by the very first animal, the immolation of another animal after one has already been immolated is purposeless. || 63 ||

To the question of why no further effort is required for the accomplishment of that which has already been accomplished, he provides an illustration: "Just as the rite of impregnation (garbhādhāna) is useless for a woman who is already pregnant, so too is another sacrificial animal useless when [the goal] has already been achieved by one. (64)

That in which an embryo has been "implanted"—meaning deposited in the form of a seed—therein, a further *garbhādhāna* (conception) would be fruitless, because there is no distinction in the act of depositing what has already been deposited. Likewise, in a sacrifice to be accomplished by a single animal, another animal would be fruitless, because the means for what is already established is redundant. If, however, another animal were employed, that act of means would constitute a different ritual action altogether; yet, in that case, there would be no understanding of an injunction (*vidhi*) for it. Thus, in accordance with the illustrative example (*dārṣṭāntika*), it has been stated that *garbhādhāna* is purposeless, and not that it is impossible.

If the demonstration were undertaken with the aim of proving futility, then even if the impossibility [of the rite] were possible, it would not be accompanied by the probandum [futility]. Alternatively, if the *saṃskāras* performed during the latter half of pregnancy—those enjoined by the scriptures—are intended here by the term "conception" (*garbhādhāna*), then their futility in the case of a woman who has already conceived is well-established; thus, the similarity between the example and the subject of the illustration is perfectly consistent. || 64 ||

Thus, according to one school of thought, unity is resorted to in the animal sacrifice because it has been enjoined for that purpose with brevity. However, others state a different reasoning here, which he demonstrates: "Because the purpose is accomplished by that much alone, some desire the non-transgression of unity; yet in this case, it is not taken as a subordinate element of the number. (65)

In this context regarding the animal, the number one is not intended to be expressed; rather, it serves merely as an indicator of the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). The meaning of the nominal stem, when conjoined with number in general, constitutes the means (*sādhana*). As for that [means], its prior lightness (*lāghava*) was stated to be the reason for the employment of singularity.

Now, since multiplicity is preceded by unity, and because there is no purpose in deviating from the sequence, the employment of that which possesses the number one alone is stated; for the accomplishment of the action occurs through that measure itself, and thus, by implication (*sāmarthyāt*), there is no deviation—that is, no abandonment—of unity. Thus, when the previously mentioned lightness (*lāghava*) or the aforementioned capacity (*sāmarthya*) has been taken up here, this [number] is merely a residual element (*śeṣabhūta*); it is not grasped here as a constituent part of the number itself.

The earlier commentators, out of a desire for fault-finding, offered an interpretation based on a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), even though the matter is satisfactorily explained through a single unified statement (*ekavākyatā*). However, since unity is not transgressed by virtue of its inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*), it is not grasped as a subordinate element of the number itself. It would not be the case that the status of number as a subordinate element of the action is established by direct scriptural injunction (*vacana*); rather, there is merely a non-transgression due to capacity. Thus, the earlier commentators, having separated this from the components of the verse, formulated the following objection: "If unity were enjoined by the word [directly], it would entail the performance of a meaning not originally intended."
However, the author of the treatise will provide a refutation of this view in another verse beginning with "By means of positive and negative concomitance" (*anvayavyatirekābhyām*). || 65 ||

How then is it that the second case-ending and so forth have been mentioned elsewhere when there is no intention to express singularity? To this he says: "The case-ending and so forth which are stated for the second [case] and others follow the logical rule; they are not understood as expressing number, because they function as instruments [of action], like a genus. (66)

This indicative mark (*liṅga*) is not for the purpose of establishing the intention to express singularity; rather, it is a restatement of the two principles already mentioned: first, that because an action is accomplished by a single agent, there is no purpose in employing multiple agents, and second, that since there is no purpose for deviating from the sequence [of the *ṛc*], singularity is adopted. Thus, the indicative mark such as "in the *uktha*, the second" does not convey a new meaning, because by those two immediately preceding principles, singularity is not abandoned, and therefore the number is not [intended] in its literal form.

It is understood as a means [of accomplishment], because the singular number has the purpose of merely refining the word. Or rather, for that reason, the number is not intended here, since even when it is not intended, the desired result is established by logic (*nyāya*). Alternatively, the meaning is that by that indicative mark (*liṅga*), the number is not made known as a means, because the desired result is established through logic alone; thus, it is a mere restatement (*anuvāda*). "Like a genus" (*jātivat*) is an example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*):

just as a genus enjoined by the word is understood to be a constituent factor (*aṅga*), so it is not with "oneness," because even though it is not a constituent factor due to the very logic already stated, the desired goal is nonetheless accomplished. || 66 ||

The phrase "some say" indicates the opinion of others; he refutes this as follows: "If number is accepted on the basis of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), then it is logical that it should function as a means of accomplishment (sādhana), but not as a mere indicator of another object. (67)

Number follows and conforms to the case-suffix; when that [suffix] exists, it is perceived, and in its absence, it is excluded—that is, it ceases to be perceived. If it is admitted that number is perceived in such expressions as "one should sacrifice a beast" (*paśum ālabheta*) because it is expressed by the word [the suffix], then how can there not also be an injunction? It is not proper to abandon what is conveyed by the word; rather, it is more reasonable that [number] constitutes the status of being a means (*sādhanatva*) or a constituent part of the action (*kriyāṅgatva*), and not merely an incidental indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of another thing or an incidental indicator of the meaning of the verbal root.

The meaning is that this is logical. When an entity (*sattvabhūta*) is denoted by a word, the mention [of number] is for the sake of understanding its refinement (*saṃskāra*); thus, it serves merely as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the base-meaning (*prakṛtyartha*). And this is not tenable. For just as the genus (*jāti*), which is expressed by the base and denoted by the word, is not abandoned through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), so too is number; this is the logical conclusion. The sense is that it is not proper to have partial application or non-application of an object denoted by a single word—which shares a single destiny (*ekayogakṣema*)—by treating one part as a subordinate member (*aṅga*) and another as the principal (*aṅgin*).

However, when oneness is not enjoined by the word, but is understood through implication (*sāmarthya*), then if—due to some divine or human deficiency—one of the eleven portions (*avadāna*) taken from a single animal should be lost, other animals would have to be procured for the sake of those portions. For in that case, there is no contradiction of the meaning of the word, since oneness was not enjoined by the word. Consequently, that ritual act could not be accomplished with clarified butter (*ājya*), and thus there is an absence of a substitute (*pratinidhi*). Indeed, a substitute is procured only in the absence of the primary substance.

Furthermore, when no specific number is mentioned by the word, the primary [unit] indeed exists. For one, however, for whom singularity is enjoined by the scriptural word, a substitute is appropriate here; thus, in the event of the loss of the *avadāna* (cutting-off), that rite is accomplished with clarified butter (*ājya*), and another animal is not procured, because that would entail the abandonment of the enjoined singularity. If this were so, then even upon the destruction of the omentum (*vapā*), another animal should not be procured. This is not the case, because the animal is not procured merely for the sake of accomplishing the act of seizing (*ālambhana*), but rather for the sake of the sacrifice (*yāga*).

And in that very context, that singularity (ekatva) is intended to be expressed. Furthermore, the sacrifice cannot be accomplished without the omentum (vapā). Therefore, even when another animal is taken up, the singularity is not transgressed. Since the sacrifice is completed by means of that one [animal] alone, when another animal is enjoined for the purpose of further portions (avadāna), singularity is no longer obtainable; thus, the logical conclusion (nyāya) is that the function of the further portions is fulfilled by clarified butter (ghṛta). || 67 ||

And since it is logical that [the number] functions as a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), therefore: "The capacity of the word-meaning to function as a means of accomplishment is not bestowed [by the number]; rather, number is a property of the operation (*vyāpāra*). Therefore, it is understood through that indicative mark (*liṅga*). (68)

When there is an equality between the genus (*jāti*) and the number (*saṅkhyā*) because both are expressed by the word, then the capacity of the word-meaning (*padārtha*) to serve as the means (*sādhana*) is not lost. "Of the word" (*padasya*) is the ellipsis to be supplied. For if the entire word-meaning were the means, the capacity of the word—characterized by its denotation of that [meaning]—would not be deprived. And thus, since the complete word-meaning is the means, the property called "activity" (*vyāpāra*), characterized by the number one, is understood through that indicative mark (*liṅga*).

Since the capacity of that word is not to be discarded, therefore, by that indication of capacity—which is a logical mark (*liṅga*)—the number, which is the property of the operation, is understood. Since that [capacity] is not to be discarded, it becomes the reason for the comprehension of the operation of number. Just as, since smoke is invariably concomitant [with fire], it becomes the cause for the comprehension of fire.

Alternatively, by that indicative mark (*liṅga*)—namely, the second [case-ending] and so forth—it is understood that this [is the case], and not merely the non-apprehension of what was previously stated by virtue of its capacity; nor is the indicative mark a restatement (*anuvāda*) of that, as they have claimed, but rather it is consistent with my own reasoning. The sense is that where there is no indicative mark indicating the operation of number (*saṅkhyā*), there is no intention to express it (*avivakṣā*), as for example in the case of "he cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ sammārṣṭi*).

For this very reason, some explain that in certain cases there is a property characterized by non-operation (*avyāpāra*) belonging to number; they say that it is understood through that indicative mark (*liṅga*), thus applying an elision of the vowel *a* (*akārapraśleṣa*). In the absence of such an indicative mark—as in the case of "he cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ sammārṣṭi*)—the lack of intention to express [number] follows from logical principle (*nyāya*); in that context, the absence of an indicative mark is the most effective means of proof (*sādhakatama*). This is just as the absence of a means of accomplishment is understood in expressions such as "released from a little" (*stokānmuktaḥ*). Thus, by these two verses, the same point has been established which was determined in the passage beginning with "of that very thing not prescribed elsewhere."

But surely, by one who acknowledges the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*), the status of number as a means (*sādhanabhāva*) is admitted. And while number is a qualifier of the substance (*dravya*), power (*śakti*) is the means; how then could that which is not its qualifier be so [a means]? This is not a fault. Since power cannot exist without a substratum, it follows that, in effect, the substance itself—having attained non-difference from that [power]—is rightly the means. Thus, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is observed, as in: "The mat is the object (*karman*)," and "Devadatta is the agent (*kartṛ*)."

Now, if it is argued that [the word] "action" (*karman*) and so forth denotes that which functions as a substance (*dravya*), then in the formulation of case-endings such as "the second case ending is used for the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*), it is precisely the substance delimited by the power (*śakti*) that possesses number and other qualifiers. And this is logical; for number does not inhere in powers. Therefore, since the substratum is the means (*sādhana*), the number is likewise so. Indeed, this alone constitutes the status of number as a constituent of action (*kriyāṅgatva*): namely, its delimitation of the means. Thus, everything is well-established. || 68 ||

Previously, because the planets were the objects to be consecrated (*saṃskārya*), their primary status was established by the force of the meaning (*ārthena rūpeṇa*); thus, it was stated that they were not intended to be expressed [as the primary object]. Now, however, he speaks in order to establish the distinction between what is intended and what is not intended by means of another method: "Because that which is new (*apūrva*) is to be enjoined (*vidheya*), its primacy is determined; because that which has been enjoined serves another purpose, its subordinate status (*śeṣabhāva*) is perceived. (Verse 69)

Previously, the relationship of subordinate and principal was discussed in terms of their actual nature; however, this [discussion] relies upon the function of the sentence—this is the distinction. For instance, since the *apūrva* (unseen potency) is the object to be enjoined by the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*) regarding the animal, it possesses primacy; thus, the singular number as heard in the text is not abandoned. Since the *apūrva* is already implied by the very fact of its being the object to be enjoined, the explicit mention [of the singular number] serves the purpose of ensuring pervasion (*vyāpti*).

The meaning is this: although action (*kriyā*) is primary as the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) is primary in all cases, because it is that which is enjoined by being made known through what was previously unknown. However, since that which has been enjoined already exists as something known, it is secondary when restated for the sake of another purpose; therefore, in such cases, it is proper to follow the form found within the injunctive sentence (*vidhivākya*).

He applies this very point to the subject at hand: "Because the cleansing (saṃmārga) is what is to be enjoined, when it is performed upon a cup (graha) already enjoined elsewhere, the number heard in the injunctive sentence is not sublated by the indicative power (lakṣaṇā). (70)

In the statement "He cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ sammārṣṭi*), because the previously unestablished cleansing is what is being enjoined, it holds primacy. In other cases, such as the injunctive sentence "Nine cups for Prajāpati" (*prājāpatyā nava grahāḥ*), where the injunction has first been made known, the term "cup" (*graha*) refers to the class of cups in general.

Furthermore, the number—such as nine or ten—that is expressed by a numerical word in that injunctive sentence is not sublated or discarded in the subsequent restatement (*anuvāda*) "He cleanses the cup," which is intended to point back to the cup previously mentioned; this is because the number possesses primacy within the original injunction.

In this case, however, within the restating sentence (*anuvādavākya*), the number is incidental, intended merely for the grammatical refinement of the word, and serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the substance; for the scriptural mention of the "cup" (*graha*) would otherwise be purposeless. Thus, it is for the sake of indicating the genus (*jāti*) of the cup so that there may be no taking up of cups with a different number than prescribed, lest the primary element be obstructed by a subordinate quality. For subordinate elements function for the benefit of the primary; therefore, here the number of the subordinate is set aside by the number of the primary.

But surely, the originative injunction, "The Adhvaryu takes these ten cups at the morning pressing," has as its object the act of taking; whereas the restating injunction, "He cleanses the cup," has as its object the act of cleansing. Thus, because their objects differ, there is no contradiction; so let many cups be taken, but only one be cleansed—there is no sublation [of the number]. To this it is replied: although there is no contradiction because the two have different objects due to the difference in external operations, nevertheless, in the case of the disposal (*pratipatti*), there is indeed a contradiction between those two numbers.

For instance—previously nine or ten [grahas] were established in the intellect; now, by uprooting those, one must be brought into the intellect. Thus, once the principal [element] has been understood in one way, it is not logical for there to be a different understanding at the time of the subordinate [elements]. Rather, since this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of what is already established, it is proper to determine the number of *grahas* only as they were understood at the time of the principal [element] during the *saṃmārga* (cleansing). For the essential nature of a *graha* must be followed from that very state in which it was restated.

And thus, through the accumulation of means (sādhana), because the cleansing (saṃmārga) also assists the primary act, the favoring of both is accomplished. Since it is situated in the midst of many [cups] and is subordinate (anūbhūta), a restatement (anuvāda) by way of recollection (smṛti) is appropriate exactly in that manner. And so, it is precisely the conformity to the assistance of the primary act that has been stated here otherwise. Previously, because the cleansing was for the sake of the cups (graha), the primacy of the cups was stated in the very sentence concerning the cleansing; here, however, the primacy residing in the injunctive sentence (vidhivākya) is expressed—this much is the distinction. || 70 ||

Raising the objection that "in the case of 'one should sacrifice with an animal' (*paśunā yajeta*) as well, since the sacrifice is what is enjoined, the animal would be secondary, and thus its singularity should be disregarded," he says: "In another injunctive sentence, there is no number [of the animal] that is contradictory [to singularity]. Therefore, this [animal], possessing its quality, is understood precisely through its singularity. (71)

The sacrifice qualified by the quality of the animal is enjoined; thus, because the animal itself was previously unknown, it too is enjoined. Furthermore, it is a general rule that the number mentioned in the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*) is not abandoned. This is as in the case of the animal. However, in the case of the cup (*graha*), with respect to the originative injunction, the number contradictory to it in the injunction of the cleansing (*saṃmārga*) is abandoned. But in the case of the animal, since there is no other injunctive statement, the primary number characterized as singularity is not abandoned; therefore, together with that [number], it partakes in the status of being a subsidiary to the ritual action.

"Saguṇa" (with qualities) means that it exists together with a quality characterized by gender, namely masculinity. Alternatively, "guṇa" refers to qualities such as whiteness and so forth. Where there is no explicit mention of a quality—as in "one should sacrifice with an animal"—the meaning is that it possesses an implied general quality. Even where there is no explicit mention of a quality—as in "drive the white cow hither" or "one should immolate a white goat"—there too, "tadguṇaḥ" (possessing that quality) is understood to mean being endowed with the quality mentioned within that same sentence.

And this has been stated as an introduction to the meaning that is about to be explained. However, some say: "The phrase 'with qualities' (*saguṇa*) itself has been clarified by the words 'as being one with existence' (*sadaikatvena*). But in this case, there is the fault of tautology; for it is not proper to explain a portion of a *kārikā* by means of another portion [of the same verse]. Alternatively, "quality" (*guṇa*) means a qualifier, namely the genus (*jāti*) characterized as "cowness" (*paśutva*); [the animal] is understood together with that.

This statement contains an illustration: just as in the case of a genus (*jāti*), because there is no reason to abandon its unity, that unity is also understood; thus, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) has been established here in accordance with the view of the Logicians (*nyāyavādin*). To explain: the Logicians have formulated the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) here as follows—"It is connected with unity, because of its association with the singular [grammatical] hearing (*śruti*). In the Soma sacrifice, following the injunction "One who, knowing thus, should sacrifice with Soma," it is heard in the text: "He cleanses the cup (*graha*) with the *daśāpavitra*."

In that context, the cleansing (*saṃmārga*) of one [cup] is obtained, for this ritual act is heard in connection with the singular number. Having thus established the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is stated: "Or rather, it applies to all, because it is a defining characteristic; for a defining characteristic is non-distinct. Since the cleansing is enjoined in relation to the second and subsequent cups, it follows that because the animal (*paśu*) serves the purpose of the sacrifice, its singularity is intended to be expressed as a means of delimiting it so that it may assist the sacrifice. This is the settled doctrine (*rāddhānta*) of those who know the nature of sentences: "But when something is enjoined for the sake of another, it should be understood according to the scriptural statement. (Jaimini Sūtra 4.1.17).

Now, as an incidental discussion following upon the treatment of number, it must be considered whether other qualities (guṇas) are also employed as auxiliaries to the action by way of delimiting their substratum, or not. To this end, he says in the introduction that such a quality is indeed possessed [by the substance]: "When a quality is taught in relation to an action whose connection with a substance is already known, its requirement for that [action] is understood to be through that substance, just as [the requirement of the substance itself is understood]. (72)

In that action (kriyā) whose first connection with a substance has been ascertained, whatever quality such as "white" is prescribed, by that [quality] also there is a requirement for that action—which is characterized by the act—just as there is for the substance. And thus, there is a connection; this is the introduction of the seed of the inquiry. Furthermore, the phrase "connection with a substance" is stated assuming the category of substance (dravyapadārtha); however, regarding the category of genus (jātipadārtha), he will say: "But when it is the genus or the power," and so forth.

Now, it may be argued that while an action must depend upon a means because it produces an effect, what dependence could an action have on a quality? Or, if it is said that since an action produced by a substance possessing qualities is impossible for a substance devoid of qualities, there is a dependence on both, then why this particular sequence? Once the relationship with the substance is fully known, there is subsequently a dependence on the quality just as there was on the substance; thus, because the nature of the dependence is not identical, the comparison is not tenable. To this, it is replied:

Action, being by its very nature something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), requires a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), and that [means] is substance (*dravya*). Therefore, even the requirement for a quality (*guṇa*) taught with reference to that [substance] exists for action, because that quality is useful for delimiting the means of accomplishment. In this regard, that which is immediate and internal must be required first; and such is the case with substance. Quality, however, is the substratum of that [substance]; since it can only be connected through the medium of the latter, it is external and is to be required later. For this very reason, the term "known" (*nirjñāta*) expresses a state already accomplished (*bhūta*).

The meaning is that because a substance (*dravya*) is the substratum of power (*śakti*), its connection with action (*kriyā*) occurs first. And thus, because there is no direct syntactic coordination (*asamanvaya*), there is a comparison (*upamā*). This is stated with reference to the sequence of meanings (*arthakrama*), but not with reference to the operation of words (*śabdavyāpāra*). For the sentence "Bring the white cow" expresses, all at once and by way of the relationship between the subordinate and the principal, a meaning qualified by that connection; therefore, there is no intervening operation of pausing (*viramya-vyāpāra*) therein. || 72 ||

Thus, the direct scriptural connection between quality (*guṇa*) and substance (*dravya*) through action has been stated. Now, in order to demonstrate their mutual syntactic coordination (*vākyīya-samanvaya*), he says: "A certain quality in a substance, such as that characterized by capacity (*sāmarthya-lakṣaṇa*), likewise [implies] a substratum for the quality itself, which is also characterized by capacity. (73)

The impossibility of a substance devoid of qualities constitutes its functional capacity (*sāmarthya*), by which [the substance] is indicated as being therein. Furthermore, the substratum, which is the substance itself, is indicated by the capacity of the quality—namely, by the inherent nature that a quality cannot exist without a substratum. Since a mere quality requires a substance and a mere substance requires a quality, he says "only some [substance]" on account of this functional capacity. Substance and quality, when their specific generic differences are not yet grasped, are mutually required. "Obtained" means acquired through cognition.
Because there is no deviation in the cognition of the mere universal, whereas there is deviation regarding particulars. || 73 ||

Thus, when the relationship between the locus and the located (ādhārādheya) has been established as a general connection, [the author] states their mutual relation through syntactic coherence (*vākyīya-samanvaya*), because those two very words form a single sentence: "But when those two have distinct meanings, whatever relation is perceived between them, there is no sublation (*upaghāta*) therein; nor is anything else to be imagined that is not heard in the text. (74)

By the capacity previously described, when there is a mutual expectancy between a quality (*guṇa*) and a substance (*dravya*), the syntactic connection (*samanvaya*) that is perceived occurs only between those two items presented within a single sentence; in that case, there is no sublation (*bādha*), because there is no abandonment of the directly heard meaning (*śrauta-artha*). When the cause for abandoning it is absent, it is not logical to postulate what is not heard in the text. For this very reason, he states by saying "it is perceived" that the cognition is established as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) being free from sublation. And this is stated with reference to the employment of the analytical method (*apoddhāra-buddhi*).

For in a sentence that is partless (*niraṃśa*), the intention to express a specific meaning exists from the very beginning. To explain: by means of a sentence that is without parts, a qualified meaning alone is conveyed. In order to facilitate comprehension, the referent of the extracted word (*apoddhārapadārtha*)—which consists of a universal—is conceptually constructed as having parts. That very [universal] becomes a particular when there is a connection with a particular; such is the sequence of the method of exposition.

And thus, even when there is a connection with a particular, the word-meaning, which is universal in nature, does not deviate from its own essential form; rather, it remains established as being grounded in that very particular. However, it is not logically tenable for words that are actually established in the universal to be established in the particular. Since those words whose function is the universal, having been uttered, simply vanish while remaining in that same state, what [word] could possibly remain in the particular at a later time? Furthermore, the simultaneous intention to express both the universal and the particular is not possible.

For when there is a desire to express a particularity, the exclusion from the universal is invariably understood; thus, there would be the undesirable consequence of abandoning the universal that has already been introduced. And this is not tenable if the relationship between word and meaning is eternal. Furthermore, once the word has become obscured, ceased, and its nature is no longer apprehended, since every other word is likewise grounded in the universal, and since no particularity has been expressed by anything else, where could that word abide, being devoid of an object? As it has been said: "The universal meaning, having become obscured, does not abide in the particular."

"Whence could there be the abandonment of what has been grasped, and where could that which has ceased abide? Therefore, only a specific meaning is to be understood from a sentence; thus, there is no room for the postulation of what is unmentioned or imagined, nor is the abandonment of a mentioned meaning possible. This inquiry, however, was introduced by relying on the meanings of words as extracted [from the sentence]. Accordingly, having raised the objection that the means of proof such as direct statement (*śruti*) and the rest are not tenable under the view of the indivisible sentence (*akhaṇḍavākyapakṣa*), they were established in the *Vākyakāṇḍa* precisely through the postulation of the meanings of extracted words.

It is not logical to abandon what is suitable as taught by the scripture and instead assume what is not heard; thus, being contained within a single sentence is here the cause for their connection. For indeed, mutual connection is desired in the state of a single sentence. Since subordinate elements are implied by the principal meaning of the sentence, if one were to accept what is not heard [as a separate element], there would be the consequence of a syntactical split (vākyabheda) everywhere, and thus no single-sentence unity would ever exist. || 74 ||

But surely, if both the relation between action and its factors (*kriyākāraka-sambandha*) and the relation between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣya-bhāva*) were to be expressed, there would be the contingency of sentence-splitting (*vākyabheda*), and that is not logical. This is not a fault. For here, two relations are possible by way of the subordinate and the principal (*guṇapradhāna-bhāva*), and this is not contradictory within a single sentence. To illustrate: he states that there are two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) here, namely direct audition (*śruti*) and syntactical connection (*vākya*): "The relation between those two—the substratum (*āśraya*) and the dependent (*āśrayin*)—which is brought about by the action is established by direct audition (*śruti*); however, the restriction [of the specific substratum] is established through syntactical connection (*vākya*)."

Through direct audition (*śruti*), that is, by means of the case-ending (*kāraka-vibhakti*), the relationship between the substance and the quality with respect to the action is presented as being of equal status. When an undivided intuition arises from the sentence, through the process of analytical abstraction (*apoddhāra*)—such as the division of word-meanings into "drive the cow" and "drive the white one"—the application of the quality and the qualified entity as "the cow itself" and "the white one itself," both being conveyed within a single sentence, is established by the authority of the sentence itself.

For if one were to postulate a substance (*dravya*) and a quality (*guṇa*) that have not been previously heard [in the context], there would be a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) because the action differs for each individual object—as in the case of "Bring the cow, and [bring] the white one. Therefore, when a substance qualified by a quality is connected with an action through a single, uniform application, its status as a single sentence (*ekavākyatva*) is sustained. Restriction (*niyama*) consists in the exclusion of the substance and the quality from other possible substrates and other possible superstrates, provided that there exists a mutual relationship between them.

Furthermore, since there is no other word that serves as a denoter through the mere exclusion of others, the employment of the word termed "single sentence" (*ekavākya*) does not constitute a direct (*śrautī*) indication; rather, it remains a syntactic (*vākyīyā*) one. This has been stated by the proponents of Nyāya: "When there is unity of purpose, there is a restriction [of relation] between substance and quality because they share a single function. Where unity of purpose is heard in a sentence, there a restriction consisting of mutual connection occurs between substance and quality. Why? Because of their sharing a single function. For there is indeed a single function, characterized as an action, which constitutes the meaning of the sentence.

The meaning of the Sūtra is that, with the primary element (pradhāna) as the objective, the substance (dravya) and the quality (guṇa) are prescribed as subordinate elements; thus, because these two have a mutual expectancy, they are determined to be in grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) within a single syntactical unit (ekavākyatā), which is consistent with our own system. || 75 ||

This being the case, he says that the following conclusion follows here: "In that situation, in the absence of substance and quality, there would be an option for each; for a connection established by direct audition (śruti) is stronger than one characterized by syntactical connection (vākya). (76)

The relationship between action and its factors (kriyākāraka-sambandha) obtained through direct audition (śruti)—that is, presented by direct audition—is stronger than the sentence (vākya), which is defined as that by which a nominal stem (prātipadika) is characterized; therefore, there is no abandonment of it under any circumstances. Direct audition of the accusative case-ending and the verbal suffix (tiṅ-vibhakti) are indicators of a relationship based on direct audition, because there is a cognition of the action and the factor as mutually interpenetrated in their own forms.

However, in the case of syntactical connection (*vākya*), there is no direct expresser; rather, the mutual relationship is established solely through the inclusion of both elements in a single sentence, the association of other words with compatible meanings, and their proximity. Thus, it is weaker than direct statement (*śruti*). Furthermore, because it depends on other words and because there is no necessary proximity of those specific words, the syntactical connection characterized by the relation of qualifier and qualified is not necessarily fixed. Therefore, even when that external factor (*bahir-aṅga*) ceases to apply, there is no cessation of the internal factor (*antaraṅga*) consisting of direct statement. || 76 ||

And thus, regarding the sentence "one should sacrifice a white goat," the objection here in this view is that in the absence of the white [quality], one might perform the sacrifice with a black [goat], and in the absence of the goat, one might be satisfied by sacrificing a ball of flour. However, in the theory where the universal (*jāti*) is the word-meaning, the desired distinction is established; as he says: "But when the universal or the power (*śakti*) is taught in relation to the action, then the substance and the quality are brought into proximity there by virtue of their inherent capacity. (77)

"In some cases, the universal (jāti) indicates the capacity (śakti) by way of concomitance"; thus, it is the capacity indicated by the universal that is enjoined as the means for accomplishing the action, for the sake of substituting a proxy when the substance is unavailable. Therefore, he says "either the universal or the capacity. In this view, there is no direct scriptural connection between the substance or the quality and the action; rather, the connection—conveyed by the case-ending—is between the universal and the action, or between the capacity and the action.

Since a genus and a power cannot exist without a substratum, by implication (sāmarthya) their own substratum—the substance—is brought into proximity; and by that [substance], its own dependent quality is also brought into proximity. Thus, both the substance and the quality are obtained through implication. || 77 ||

And therefore, regarding the subject of substitution: "When the generic class (*jāti*) and the qualities (*guṇa*) are equally auxiliary to the ritual action, the qualities of the goat and other animals may be substituted, but not their generic classes. (78)

Because both the genus (*jāti*) and the quality (*guṇa*) are mediated by the substance (*dravya*), they both participate as auxiliary factors (*aṅgabhāva*) to the ritual action; thus, they are equal in this regard. Nevertheless, among those [auxiliaries], the genera belonging to goats and the like are not substituted; in the absence of a goat, a ram is not sacrificed. Rather, it is well known that only qualities may be substituted—for instance, in the absence of a white goat, even a black goat may be sacrificed. || 78 ||

"What is the reasoning here? he says: "Genera are closer to the power of manifestation than qualities are; substance is directly connected with action, whereas quality is therefore subject to variation. (79)

The term "of the individual power" (vyakti-śakteḥ) means "of the substance-power" (dravya-śakteḥ), that is to say, of the potent substance. The mention of "power" (śakti) is because the application of a substance to action depends upon its power. Since it persists from production until destruction, and since its inherence and its connection with its substratum exist at the same time, the universal (jāti) is proximate to the substance. Qualities (guṇas), however, arise subsequent to that [inherence] and, due to their maturation over different times, undergo mutual transformations of their own natures; thus, they are remote from the substance.

If indeed the qualities (*guṇa*) are not proximate, how can there be such a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)? To this he says: "Substance (*dravya*) is directly connected with action. This is what is meant: if a quality were directly connected with action without depending on substance, it would not be subject to conceptual construction. But when substance is directly connected with action, while genus (*jāti*) and quality are so only through that [substance], then the consideration of proximity (*pratyāsatti*) and remoteness (*viprakarṣa*) arises.

For instance: a substance (*dravya*) is directly capable and fit for connection with an action; therefore, by means of it, it is suitable for integration (*samanvaya*). In that regard, the generic form (*jāti-rūpa*), being proximate, is not subject to substitution; thus, there is no substitute for something belonging to another genus, but rather for another quality (*guṇa*). Even when a black goat is used, the cognition of "goat" still persists. However, if one were to take up something of a different genus, since the generic form—which is as dear as one's own self—would be abandoned, the action would become entirely different due to the difference in the means (*sādhana*).

In some cases, however, when there is a total abandonment of the genus (*jāti*)—which is considered its own self—the action would indeed become a different action altogether due to the difference in the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). In other cases, however, because of similarity, the cognition of *khadira* does not depart. And this is logical in the view that the genus is the primary meaning, since the form of the genus, which is directly expressed by the word (*śrauta*), is not abandoned. But in the view that the individual substance (*dravya*) is the referent of the word, since the genus—which is not directly denoted—is merely an incidental indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), even if that [genus] is abandoned, there is no abandonment of the directly expressed meaning; thus, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of using a substitute belonging to a different genus.

Regarding the Vedic connection and the position that the word-meaning is the substance (*dravya*), the equality between quality (*guṇa*) and substance was previously stated; however, here, since the genus (*jāti*) is not abandoned because it is proximate when [the substance] is implied by implication (*ākṣepa*), this has been deliberated precisely in order to exalt the genus as the word-meaning. For this very reason, the word "but" (*tu*) in the phrase "when, however, the genus" (*yadā tu jātiḥ*) is intended to distinguish it from the previous case.

This has been stated in the Bhāṣya: "For where the substance is internal, that is the primary factor; one does not fulfill the injunction 'one should sacrifice a white [animal]' by sacrificing a lump of flour. Because it is more proximate, the word *dravya* (substance) is intended here as denoting the genus (*jāti*), not as denoting a substance qualified by a quality. For a substance whose form is undetermined, the genus—which serves to determine its own nature—attains a form colored by its own essence through the surrender of its own self;
otherwise, since there would be a different entity in the case of a substitute for that [genus], there would follow the abandonment of what was enjoined. || 79 ||

He summarizes the previously mentioned position as the view of others: "Some maintain that when there is an absence of either due to equality, there is an option; therefore, the goat would lack those qualities, or the ram would possess them. (80)

Just as a genus (*jāti*) is a defining characteristic of a substance (*dravya*), because an object devoid of attributes cannot be designated in linguistic usage, so too is a quality (*guṇa*). Likewise, like a genus, a quality such as "blue" is restricted to a substratum, since it does not exist in things like wind or space. Given this similarity, those who follow the system of Vyāḍi—the proponents of the category of substance (*dravyapadārthika*)—who maintain that a quality, like a substance, is to be denoted because it possesses the characteristics of being divisible and so forth, hold that a quality, like a genus, requires a substance as its medium in order to enter into a relationship with action.

In order to nourish the connection based on direct Vedic statement (*śrauta-sambandha*), he points out—using the phrase "by some"—a position that is not his own, namely that the substitution of both qualities and substances is possible by abandoning the syntactic connection (*vākyīya-samanvaya*). For the substitution of a substance has not been accepted by the learned, beginning with the author of the Bhāṣya. || 80 ||

Having thus concluded the incidental discussion, he says in order to follow up on the main subject: "The occurrence of a number residing in a genus is observed; sometimes, setting aside that specific number, the genus itself functions [as the referent]. (81)

Because the original subject was interrupted by this incidental discussion, this matter, though already stated, is recalled once more in order to state further details regarding the general [topic]. || 81 ||

For instance: A universal that has become a subordinate member [of a compound] is joined with the number of the substance; however, when it functions for its own sake, it does not depend upon number. (82)

Previously, it was established that even in the case of a subordinate element (*guṇa*), such as the *graha* (cup), the number is intended to be significant, by relying on the relationship of primary and subordinate based on whether something is being enjoined or merely restated through the verbal operation (*śābda-vyāpāra*). Now, however, the principle is introduced that the number is intended to be significant in the subordinate element by relying on the actual, ontological relationship of primary and subordinate (*vāstava-guṇapradhāna-bhāva*). || 82 ||

In the injunction "one should sacrifice with an animal," when the word "animal" is heard as being for the sake of the meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice), the primary action is accomplished by means of a single animal that has fulfilled its purpose. (83)

Since the sacrifice is primary, the animal is merely its means; thus, when the sacrifice is accomplished by a single [animal], the primary meaning of the sentence—characterized as the action—is fulfilled. Consequently, there is no regard for a difference in the number of subordinate factors (*guṇa*), and here the animal-generality (*paśu-sāmānya*), being a subordinate element, is conjoined with the number of the substance. Thus, the number inherent in the genus (*jāti*) operates here. For instance, if the primary [action] were to repeat itself due to a difference in the number of subordinate factors, this would result in a different action altogether.

Consequently, it would follow—which is undesirable—that the qualities (guṇas) do not follow the primary substance (pradhāna), but rather that the primary substance follows the qualities; thus he says: || 83 ||
If one should perform the touching with as many qualities as are possible for it, then by that means the primary [substance] would be rendered effective. (84)

Regarding the phrase "of whom" (yasya): it refers to the qualified performer (adhikārin). The intention is that if the primary rite were prompted by its subsidiaries, then it would no longer possess the status of being primary; consequently, the status of being subsidiary would also not belong to the subsidiaries in relation to it. Therefore, this principle must be preserved. || 84 ||

Regarding the statement, "But that which functions for its own sake does not depend upon number," he provides an illustration: "But where there is an explicit mention of an action with respect to a vessel (graha) within a ritual context (tantra) that is being prepared, we do not take any account of the grasping of a specific number. (85)

Where the object of cleansing is the *tantra* (the ritual procedure) within the context of a cup (*graha*)—that is, where there is the word "cup"—or where this is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*), meaning "the *tantra* which is being cleansed" in that cup; since the cup is the primary object to be refined, the word for the act of cleansing is not primary. In such a case, as in the scriptural statement "He cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ saṃmārṣṭi*), there is no intention to express the specific number, namely singularity, even though it is denoted by its own word.

Because, according to the original injunction (*utpattivākya*), it is precisely that which possesses a manifold number (*anekasaṃkhya*) which is intended here. For conjunction (*saṃsarga*) is not the governing factor (*tantra*) here; if it were, then once that [conjunction] were accomplished by even a single means characterized as a *graha*, the employment of multiple [vessels] would be as fruitless as in the case of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*). Rather, the *graha* itself is the governing factor; thus, the refinement (*saṃskāra*) applies to it according to its possibility. Therefore, setting aside the specific number, the genus (*jāti*) prevails here. || 85 ||

Thus, regarding the statement that "number is intended to be expressed with respect to a quality (guṇa), but not when it is the primary element (pradhāna)," he states the authoritative indicator from the Śāstra: "In the sūtra *śiṣyamāṇapara* [Pāṇini 1.2.53], the mention of the word 'eka' (one) is clearly a sign [indicating] that even when the remainder (*śeṣa*) possesses a specific number, [the singular is used]. (Verse 86)

In the rule *sarūpāṇām ekaśeṣaḥ*, the word *śeṣa* is derived as a passive noun (*karman-sādhana*), meaning "that which remains" (*śiṣyamāṇaḥ*) or "that which persists. Since the remaining element is the primary one (*paraḥ pradhānam*) because it is the object to be refined by the grammatical operation characterized as *ekaśeṣa*, it follows that even though the word *śeṣa*—being singular—is understood to possess the number one, the further employment of the word *eka* ("one") serves to indicate that the primary universal (*sāmānyam pradhānabhūtam*) which functions according to its own inherent sense does not operate by depending on the number residing in its substratum.

This clearly indicates the aforementioned meaning. However, if the word *śeṣa* were formed by means of the abstract action (*bhāva-sādhana*), then the act of remaining (*śeṣaṇa-kriyā*) would be primary, not that which remains (*śiṣyamāṇa*). Consequently, even when two or many [elements] remain, there would be only one act of remaining; thus, even if singularity were intended to be expressed, the word "one" (*eka*) would still be meaningful for the purpose of excluding two or many, and therefore it would not serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). || 86 ||

Having thus established the maxim "number is intended to be expressed when it qualifies a quality" by means of Vedic examples, he now provides an example from grammar to demonstrate its application to the present subject: "Just as the Vedic revelation (śruti) occurs in the formulation of rules for compounds and suffixes, so too does it accord with the very same logic regarding qualities that are dependent on others. (87)

In the rule *sup-supā*, since it is a prescription for a compound (*samāsa*), that [compound] alone possesses primacy. For this is not an instruction regarding the individual members; because they are included within the whole, they lack independence. Furthermore, no individual members exist here as real entities, because the compound word functions as a single, undivided unit with respect to its specific meaning. As it has been stated in the *Vākyakāṇḍa*: "Just as there is no such thing as 'Brahmin-wealth' in the case of a 'Brahmin-cloth' (*brāhmaṇakambala*)."

It is precisely the undivided compound word itself—though its division into prior and posterior members is merely imagined—that is intended to undergo grammatical refinement (*sañcikīrṣitatva*). For the determination of a specific meaning and word occurs through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), and these two are present here in compound words such as *rājapuruṣa*. This is because the relation of a qualified [object] is conveyed by the whole (*samudāya*), whereas it is not conveyed by the individual members. Furthermore, the grammatical refinements of the members—such as the elision of case endings, shortening of vowels, and masculine substitution (*puṃvadbhāva*)—are indeed prompted by the refinement of the whole.

Because the refinement of the whole is inseparable from the refinement of its parts, therefore, in this rule for compound formation (*samāsa-vidhi*), the scriptural statement (*śruti*)—namely "sup supā"—which, by adopting a singular number, conveys singularity and has entered the range of the auditory faculty as it occurs in the words, is established and justified by that very same method and principle. The meaning is that the singularity heard in the text is intended to be significant (*vivakṣita*). He asks, "What is that principle? and replies, "Of qualities (*guṇas*) that are dependent on others... [and so forth].

Because the *guṇas* (subsidiary elements) are subject to the control of the *pradhāna* (principal element), the rule "sup-supā" (*Pāṇini 2.1.4*), having operated upon a certain number of case-endings (*sup*) to apply to a meaning, conveys only that meaning which is connected with that specific number. Consequently, a compound such as *kaṣṭaśritaḥ* occurs between each individual *subanta* (inflected word), and not among many [simultaneously].

The meaning is as follows: because [the rule] "mahatkaṣṭaṃ śritaḥ" involves a second-case ending (*dvitīyānta*), and since the application of the *jāti* (genus) suffix is not fixed when multiple members are compounded—due to its instability—the compound, which is the primary element, would be perceived without restriction. Consequently, due to this confusion, the favoring of that [compound] would be rejected; for, by virtue of the division of the compound at every constituent part, the primary would become dependent upon the subordinate, rather than the subordinates following the primary.

In the case of *dvandva* and *bahuvrīhi* compounds, however, by the force of the rule stating "many [words]," it is indeed accepted that these compounds consist of multiple constituent members. And for this very reason, based on this indicative mark (*liṅga*), the non-intentionality (*avivakṣā*) regarding number is established elsewhere.

Even in the rule for the introduction of suffixes (*pratyayavidhi*), in the statement "after a nominal stem ending in *ṅī*, *āp*, or a *prātipadika*" (*ṅyāpprātipadikāt*), there is a reference to the established form of the base characterized as a *prātipadika*—which was previously indicated by a collective compound (*samāhāradvandva*). Since the suffixes beginning with *su* (the case endings) are introduced by virtue of their status as a governing topic (*adhikāra*) within the rule-formulating sentence, the suffix is enjoined as part of a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*). Consequently, because the suffix is primary, the *prātipadika*—as its subordinate element (*aṅga*)—is understood to retain its literal number.

But surely, since the number one is expressed by the case-ending in the rule *sup-supā*, let there be a desire to express that number; however, in the rule *ṅy-āt-prātipadikāt*, what number one is heard so that its expression could be desired? If it is the oneness of the aggregate (*samāhāra*), that is incorrect, because that belongs to the whole (*samudāya*) and the suffix is produced from the whole; therefore, its oneness is not to be expressed here as something intended, but rather the oneness of each individual member.

And since they are included within the operation (*vṛtti*) here, their oneness as correlates (*pratiyogin*)—such as that of the feminine suffix *ṅī* and so forth—is not perceived; rather, they are nominal stems (*prātipadika*) ending in *ṅī*, *āp*, etc., in their mere essential form (*svarūpamātra*), with their specific number remaining unspecified. You have indeed shown us the direction; we shall now explain even the dissolution (*laya*) in this very way. Just as the revealed text (*śruti*) has fallen [into its place], in whatever manner it has fallen, it presents both the meaningful verbal form and its essential form in their mere essential state as they have fallen.

And thus, since the intention (tātparya) extends only that far, it does not require a second [element]; for there is no compound of words ending in dual or plural suffixes, and because no specific number is understood in a complex formation (vṛtti), and because duality and so forth do not arise without a dependence on a counter-correlative (pratiyogi). Therefore, by implication, singularity is intended for each individual element, as stated in the rule "from a nominal stem ending in ṅī, āp, or a prātipadika."

Others, however, explain that from this *grahaṇaka-vākya* (the introductory rule), whatever nominal stem (*prātipadika*) arises—whether ending in a *ṅī* suffix or an *āp* suffix—it is the singular number explicitly heard therein that is intended to be significant; but in this case, the statement "the scriptural word (*śruti*) occurs as it happens" is incorrect. For a sentence in which a nominal stem appears is not the object of the scriptural word (*śruti*).

In this case, if the number were intended to be expressed, since it would be impossible for a suffix such as *svādi* to follow from many *ṅyāp*-ending nominal stems (*prātipadika*), the suffix would have to recur according to each individual stem. Consequently, the principal element (*pradhāna*) would have to conform to the subordinate elements (*guṇa*), rather than the subordinate elements conforming to the principal. But surely, since the connection of the *svādi* suffixes with their respective stems is what is being enjoined, how can they be considered the principal?

Thus, it is established that the *prakṛti* (base) possesses the quality of being a *guṇa* (quality/secondary element); therefore, our position—that "number is intended to be expressed with respect to the *guṇa*"—is proven. Furthermore, it is not the *prakṛti* alone that is intended to be modified by virtue of its being followed by a suffix (*pratyaya*), because it is the word (*pada*) as a whole, through the conceptualization of *prakṛti* and *pratyaya*, that is to be grammatically explained (*anvākhyeya*), since it is that very word which is employed in common usage.

Although the base (*prakṛti*) alone, when refined by its subsequent suffix (*pratyaya*), constitutes the word (*pada*), nevertheless, from the perspective of the intended meaning (*tātparya*), the grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*) of the base is unreal; thus, the application of refinement proceeds with the aim of the word itself as the sole reality, which is free from conceptual construction (*avikalpa*). However, since the primary meaning of a sentence consists in the unprecedented suffix (*apūrva-pratyaya*) being enjoined, that suffix possesses primacy. For this very reason, he says: "In the rules for compound formation and suffixation... (*samāsa-pratyaya-vidhau*).

And thus, there is no prescription of a relationship here through syntactical split (*bhinnavākyatā*), because in the *prakriyā* (derivational process), the suffixes (*svādi*) are prescribed in syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) by way of restating the base (*prakṛti*). As for the statement "because *sup* and *tiṅ* are prescribed without distinction," this refers to the difference between the sentences concerning number (*saṃkhyā*), but one should not think that syntactic unity with the sentence regarding the base is not intended here either. Furthermore, if the prescription is made through syntactic unity, the connection with the technical designation "suffix" (*pratyaya-saṃjñā*) cannot be established without a distinct mode of operation (*pravṛttibheda*).

For first there is the connection with the rule (*vidhi*), and then, once their existence has been established through that prescription, the suffixes (*svādi*) are connected with the technical designation "affix" (*pratyaya*). It must be stated that an existing entity (*kāryin*) must be present for an operation (*kārya*) to apply; however, because even future entities are brought within the scope of cognition, the application of designations such as "affix" occurs precisely while they are in a state of being brought about (*bhāvyamāna*). Thus, the author’s intention here is that the rule for affixes is intended as a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*). 87.

Is this the general rule—that number is intended to be expressed when it qualifies a quality? No, he says: "Number is not accepted even as qualifying a quality for the sake of establishing another primary [referent]. Likewise, the agent and the object are perceived without distinction. (88)

"Likewise, the agent (kartā)"—the connection is as follows: this being the case, the agent is understood as non-distinct [from the action]. For that [agent] is a subordinate factor (guṇa). But the object (karman) is the primary factor (pradhāna), which receives a refinement (saṃskāra) imparted through its designation as the "most desired" (īpsitatama). This refers to the rule "in the case of the object" (karmaṇi).

In the rule *kartur īpsitatamaṃ karma* ("the object most desired by the agent is the *karman*"), when the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of *karman* is being prescribed, because that very [designation] or the object being refined by it possesses primacy, the agent—referred to as "that which is most desired by the agent through his action"—is mentioned as a subordinate factor (*guṇa*). This subordinate factor is undifferentiated, meaning it is not delimited by the gender and number expressed by the words of the sūtra. This is for the purpose of establishing the designation of *karman* even for that which is most desired by two agents or many agents, thereby further favoring the primary element [the action].

It is understood, that is, it is comprehended. However, in the case of rules for compound formation (*samāsa*) and suffix application (*pratyaya*), if many *subanta* (inflected nominal) words were to form a compound, there would be a lack of restriction, because plurality is not fixed. But in the case of the technical designation "object" (*karman*), there is no fault, as it applies to many objects and thus experiences an accumulation [of instances]. Furthermore, a rule for suffix application does not occur from many bases (*prakṛti*), because priority (*paratva*) could not be established. Thus it is stated in the *Sarūpa-vārttika*: "If it is argued that [the rule] 'in a single case-ending' [is unnecessary], we say no; because of the absence of a case-ending."

Thus, since a greater favor is rendered by the accumulation of primary elements (*pradhāna*), it is established that the number of the primary element is not intended to be expressed; consequently, the number residing in the subordinate element (*guṇa*) is not resorted to. Otherwise, there would be an obstruction [to the rule] due to the restriction of the primary element, and thus another primary element would be established. This purpose, which contains a logical core, should be understood as follows: because of the very principle of the dependence of subordinate elements, the reason stated in the rule "the object most desired by the agent is the *karman*" is that the number is not intended to be expressed. || 88 ||

To reinforce this point here, he says: "When there is another [element] that has become applicable, and a repetition of the scriptural statement is for the purpose of restriction, then the number is not intended to be significant, because its purpose is fulfilled by the exclusion [of the others]. (89)

Furthermore, the connection is with the word "repetition" (*punar-śruti*). Since it was previously stated that there is only one scriptural injunction (*śruti*) due to a general objection, that very same injunction is here called "repetition. Alternatively, the word *punar* has the sense of the particle *tu* ("but"). It was previously stated that number is intended to refer to the subordinate element; in contrast to that, the word *punar* here serves to highlight a distinction. He asks: for what purpose is this repetition? He replies: it is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārthā*), meaning for the sake of exclusion (*nivṛttyarthā*) of another [action] such as [an alternative] ritual act (*karman*) which might otherwise be applicable or obtained.

For it is thus: since [the term] *kartṛ* is a relative term (*saṃbandhiśabda*) denoting that which is most desired (*īpsitatama*), there is an implication (*ākṣepa*) of that by which the object (*karman*) is most desired; thus, even though the status of being most desired might apply to the instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth as well, the statement "of the agent" (*kartuḥ*) is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*), because its intent is the exclusion of other factors (*kāraka*). Although two or many agents are not thereby excluded, nevertheless, the intended exclusion of other factors is indeed accomplished; therefore, the number [singular] here serves merely for the sake of formal designation (*nirdeśārtha*).

[Objection: But surely, by this very logic, since the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) implies its auxiliaries (*aṅga*) without restriction, it would follow that when it is stated with the instrumental case *paśunā* ("with an animal") for the purpose of excluding other instruments, the number [of the animal] would be unintended (*avivakṣita*). [Reply: This is not a fault. Just as, because the term "most desired" (*īpsitatama*) is a relative term (*saṃbandhiśabda*), the mere implication of some means (*sādhana*) is already established, and thus the further mention of the word *kartuḥ* ("of the agent") occurs; it is not so with the root *yaj*, for the implication of an instrument is not necessarily inherent.

Since the mere act of casting the oblation (*havis*) toward a deity constitutes the meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice), there is no implication of the instrument (*karaṇa*) [of the sacrifice] for that which is being renounced; thus, because there is no necessary implication of the instrument, the repeated mention of "with the animal" (*paśunā*) is not redundant. Rather, this is an entirely new injunction regarding a subsidiary (*aṅga*) element. If it is argued that "the animal itself is what is being renounced here," then the verb *yaj* is indeed seen to be used even for mere renunciation—as in the expression, "he sacrifices well into the fire."

If it is argued that here too there is an implication of the oblation (*havis*), then indeed, in the case of worldly actions with visible purposes, there may well be an implication of the means by virtue of their functional capacity. However, in the case of those actions with invisible purposes (*adṛṣṭārtha*), since they are based solely on verbal authority (*śabda-pramāṇaka*), from the word "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), the cognition arises simply that "the sacrifice must be performed. Therefore, this injunction regarding the animal is entirely new (*apūrva*); thus, it is logical that the number exactly as heard in the text is intended to be significant. Furthermore, in that sacrifice, the accomplishment of another primary act does not occur through two [animals].

Nor does it apply to another sacrifice, because the accomplishment of every sacrifice is achieved by that one alone. But [one might object]: if the intention is the exclusion of other factors (*kāraka*), then in the case of *sārthāddhīyate pathikaḥ* ("the traveler departs from the caravan"), since the traveler—the most desired object (*īpsitatama*)—is designated as the ablative (*apādāna*), how can there be the production of a verbal suffix (*lakāra*) in the sense of the object (*karman*) for the verb *dhīyate*?
