Therefore, upon the dissolution of ignorance through inquiry, all philosophical systems find their ultimate rest in Brahman alone. As it has been said: "In that [state], purity is real; it is indeed knowledge," and so forth. (7)

Thus, Brahman alone is conceptualized in various forms; therefore, it is established that the object of all words is that very [Brahman] through the medium of their respective limiting adjuncts (upādhi). He says: "The unconceptualized Reality itself assumes a conceptualized form; yet there is no temporal distinction here, even though a temporal distinction is perceived. (8)

From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), that very reality which is non-conceptualized and beyond the scope of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) appears, in conventional discourse, as mere conceptualization alone—since nothing else exists—manifesting as various diverse distinctions in the form of conceptual constructs. Due to the power of beginningless ignorance (*avidyā*), it assumes [this state] by abiding as the individual soul (*jīvātman*). Thus, through its location within those [souls], it possesses a multiplicity of spatial divisions based on the substrates of formal manifestations (*mūrti-vivarta*). It is capable of supporting the temporal sequence of causes and effects.

The meaning is this: although reality is thus beyond time (*akālakalita*) and without beginning or end, it appears as if possessing a temporal sequence—designated by the modifications of existence such as birth and so forth—due to the power of the obstructions and permissions bestowed by the independent energy known as Time (*kāla*). || 8 ||

Now, having raised the objection that it is illogical for that which does not exist to appear as reality, he establishes this by means of an illustration: "Just as the properties of an object are absolutely impossible in cognition, yet that [cognition] is established as being like the nature of that [object], while in fact it is absolutely not of that nature. (9)

In the Vijñānavāda (Idealist) doctrine, because the form of the object is unreal in its substantial existence, the blue and so forth—which are properties belonging to that [object]—are insentient; and since such [insentience] is utterly impossible in non-insentient cognition, there is no similarity whatsoever between the insentient and the non-insentient. Thus it is said: "If there were similarity in one part, everything would be the knower of everything. But if there were similarity in every respect, cognition would become non-cognition. (Verse 9)

Alternatively, it is accepted that consciousness—which, though its intrinsic nature is pure awakening—is permeated by the phenomena of possibility, appears within the sphere of worldly convention amidst ignorance. To illustrate this further, he states another example: "Likewise, modifications and forms are absolutely impossible in reality; yet that very reality, while being essentially that [reality], is absolutely not of the nature of those [modifications]. (10)

The *pradhāna* (primordial matter) accepted by the Sāṃkhyas is unmodified; it exists as the state of the seed for the entire web of modifications, undivided and indeed unmixed with the forms of modifications such as the *mahat* and so forth from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*). For that [pradhāna], though endowed with the potencies for modifications such as the *mahat*, consists of a state of equilibrium among the *guṇas*; yet, due to the diversity of modifications arising through the power of the imbalance and suppression of the *guṇas*, it is indeed distinct [from those modifications].

Moreover, in empirical practice, since the perception of that [subtle cause] is impossible without the determination of its modifications such as the Great Principle (mahat) and so forth, ignorance is present in all philosophical systems. Thus, the concomitance with the probandum is established: the appearance of reality is proven to occur through the imposition of unreal forms. || 10 ||

But how is it understood that the forms (ākāras) are unreal, while that which is other than them is real? To this he says: "That which remains at the end when the collection of forms has been withdrawn is the eternal; it is what is denoted by words, and that reality of the word (śabdatattva) does not differ. (11)

This is stated in accordance with the Bhāṣya: "For that alone is eternal in which the reality (*tattva*) is not destroyed. Indeed, it is said there: "Gold alone is real; yet, when joined with another form, it becomes two golden earrings having the color of khadira-wood embers. By this very example, the reality of Brahman—which is distinct from its modifications—is asserted.

For just as in that case, by the sublation of forms such as the *rucaka* (necklace), "gold" alone remains true, so too, upon the disappearance of the entire multitude of infinite modifications, the form of Brahman—which abides at the ultimate limit and is imperishable—is the truth; and that alone is real and eternal in its essential nature (*bhāvataḥ*). However, the eternity of genus (*jāti*) and so forth is spoken of only in a relative sense within conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). For instance, when an individual is gone, the genus such as "cowness" (*gotva*) that remains is eternal. Even there, upon the abandonment of distinctions such as "horseness," "earth" alone remains true.

Even there, when distinctions such as "newness" (apūrva) and so forth have ceased, that which remains as mere being (*sattvamātra*) is the truth conveyed by all pronouns. Furthermore, because the nature of consciousness (*saṃvidrūpa*), which never departs, persists even there, that alone is the ultimate truth once the forms of objects are excluded; thus, one is enjoined to meditate with the thought, "One should worship [it] as 'not this, not this' (*neti neti*). And since consciousness in the form of *paśyantī*, the supreme speech (*parā vāk*), consists of the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahma*), the reality of Brahman does not differ from the ultimate Word. However, in the state of phenomenal manifestation (*vivarta*), there is a distinction in the form of *vaikharī*.

And in that regard, it is precisely that eternal [reality] which is denoted by words in the form of genus (*jāti*) and so forth. Furthermore, because the status of being a signifier is established through its resting upon an internal material cause (*upādāna*), and because the object inherent within its own nature is what is denoted, the non-differentiation of the signified and the signifier is proven; this was determined in the First Book (*Prathama-kāṇḍa*). For this very reason, he will state immediately thereafter here: "Of that [eternal word], the form of the relationship between word and meaning is seen as one. (11)

Regarding what was stated—"That reality is like its own self, yet it is absolutely not of that nature"—he first explains its absolute non-identity with that [duality]: It is neither existent nor non-existent; it is neither one nor diverse; it is neither conjoined nor divided; it is neither modified nor otherwise. (12)

Because it transcends all empirical transactions (*vyavahāra*) involving modification (*vaikārika*), the reality (*tattva*) is not, in its ultimate form (*pāramārthika-rūpa*), of the nature of modification. To explain: it cannot be designated as "it exists," because the essential nature (*svarūpa*) conditioned by existence (*sattva-upādhi*) is incompatible with the true nature of reality (*tattva-svarūpa*), and thus no transaction can occur through that identity. Nor can it be designated as "it does not exist," because even that which is conditioned by non-existence (*abhāva-upādhi*) is not such [the ultimate], and because reality, being of the nature of existence, is not indicated by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as being non-existent.

Reality does not possess a specific nature conditioned by the attribute of oneness (*eka-saṃkhyā*), because reality, being devoid of attributes, is in fact non-different [from itself], and thus "one" would not even be perceived. Nor does it possess a specific nature produced by separateness (*pṛthaktva*), because that which is different from it is unreal. Nor is it conditioned by conjunction (*saṃsarga*) or separation (*vibhāga*), because a second entity is not established by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); for how could it be non-different and yet divided, or with what could it be conjoined?

Because transformation (*pariṇāma*) is negated and illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) is accepted, it is not "modified" (*vikṛta*); yet, because it manifests through a wondrous mode of being as the form of the totality of manifold non-existents, it cannot even be designated as "unmodified" (*avikṛta*). Thus, the supreme reality, the Brahman, transcends all designations. || 12 ||

And yet, that very Self is perceived within ignorance; thus he says: "It does not exist, and yet it exists; it is one, and yet it is manifold; it is conjoined and it is divided; it is transformed, and yet it is otherwise. (13)

That very [Brahman] possesses the power to produce the appearance of modifications such as existence and non-existence; thus, it is capable of being designated by the conventional terms "is" and "is not," conditioned by the attributes of existence and non-existence. In reality, however, the Supreme Brahman is devoid of both existence and non-existence, and is beyond both being and non-being. Conventionally, that same [Brahman] exists as the basis for the linguistic usage of unity and plurality through the nature of universals (*jāti*) and individuals (*vyakti*); thus, it is also characterized by the attribute of number. Likewise, it is characterized by the attribute of conjunction, because it appears as if associated with something else. Such is the determination of its distinction [from the world].

Likewise, although it appears as if being produced in the form of all modifications such as space and so forth, it shines forth as that very same immutable reality; thus it has been said that its true nature is that [immutable] self alone. || 13 ||

And having established this, he says that because everything is composed of that [ultimate reality], even contradictory worldly transactions are subsumed within it alone: "Of that [reality], one perceives the form consisting of word, object, and their relation; that which is perceived, the perception, the perceiver, and the purpose of perception. (14)

The relationship between the signified and the signifier is, in reality, non-dual. For within that internal reality, the powers of the Word (*śruti*) and its meaning (*artha*) are merged; thus, during the state of phenomenal manifestation (*vivarta*), because that very reality expands itself through the branches of word and meaning, there appears the duality of the signified and the signifier. This [duality] is indeed nescience (*avidyā*) in the form of knowledge and the knowable. This point has been determined by us in detail in the *Brahmakāṇḍa* itself, and should therefore be understood from that source. Furthermore, it is the manifestation (*vivarta*) of that very same reality in the form of the seer and the seen.

For indeed, the entire range of perceivable objects, having ascended into the nature of consciousness, possesses consciousness alone as their ultimate reality because they are experienced as one with it; for that which is not luminous cannot possibly be manifest. This has been investigated at length in the *Pūrvakāṇḍa* and in the *Advayasiddhi*. Furthermore, the perceiver—the individual soul (*jīvātman*)—is also essentially Brahman alone; though limited by ignorance, it is bound, a transmigrator, and an enjoyer, yet there is no possibility of actual difference [between them] due to their shared nature as consciousness. This too has been explained in that very same work.

By this indication of the primary grammatical factors (*kāraka*)—namely the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*)—other factors are also implied; thus, the manifestation (*vivarta*) as an established entity (*siddharūpa*) is demonstrated. Furthermore, by the word "vision" (*darśana*), which denotes the primary action, other actions are implied; thus, the manifestation as an action whose nature is yet to be accomplished (*sādhyasvabhāva*) is also stated. For the manifestation of action is delimited by the power of time (*kāla-śakti*), while the manifestation of form (*mūrti*) is delimited by the power of space (*dik-śakti*); in this way, the universe, consisting of the manifestations of both form and action, is demonstrated.

By the word *prayojana* (purpose), there is an indication of the fruit of all activity; thus, through its nature as the goal (*sādhya*), the means (*sādhana*), and the result (*phala*), the conformity of Brahman to all manifestations (*vivarta*) within the synthesis of the universe has been established. And this was set forth in the *Brahmakāṇḍa*: "Of that one seed of all, whose existence is manifoldly as the enjoyer, the object of enjoyment, and the act of enjoyment. Furthermore, the determination of its true nature (*satattva-nirṇaya*) was stated by us in that very same place.

Furthermore, because linguistic usage consists of both cognition (*prakhyā*) and verbal expression (*upākhyā*), when there is duality, this is designated here as a distinction between the "object of vision" (*dṛśya*) and the "act of seeing" (*darśana*), which takes the form of the relationship between word and meaning. This is said to be a form consisting of ignorance (*avidyamaya*). However, he will later describe the ultimate reality (*pāramārthika*) as being a nature in which the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) has subsided: "The knowers of the Vedanta rely on the truth of that very reality wherein the seer, the seen, and the act of seeing are non-conceptualized. (14)

This has been stated: "That which remains at the end of the dissolution of forms is the Truth. In this regard, one might think: "Nothing remains at the end; this entire universe appears from that which is non-existent. Anticipating this doubt, [the author] speaks in order to establish, by means of a positive example, that there is no origination from what is non-existent (*apūrvakatva*), showing that the cause is of a non-different nature: "Just as gold is the truth when its modifications (such as earrings) have disappeared, so they say the Supreme Nature is the truth when its modifications have disappeared. (15)

Just as when the modification consisting of the state of being an earring ceases, the single gold remains as the truth within the earring, so too, upon the disappearance of modifications such as earth and the rest, the underlying primordial nature (prakṛti) remains as the non-different truth; this is what must be accepted. By the phrase "they say," [the author] indicates that this is established by the authority of scripture (āgama) regarding Brahman. And thus it has been said: "That which is taught as one alone," and "The Self alone is this truth. For such is the Śruti. Furthermore, inference serves merely as a corroborative illustration (upodbalana). To explain:

The manifestation of a modification from that which is non-existent and indefinable—that is, from nothing—is not logical, because non-existence is contradictory to the nature of existence. Indeed, the emergence of anything from a rabbit’s horn is never observed. Furthermore, since there is a pervasive continuity (*anvaya*) throughout the world in the form of consciousness, this world must be preceded by that [consciousness]. And so it will be said: "Non-existence does not become existence, nor does existence pass into indefinability."

The power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) belonging to that whose nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*) is non-transforming; thus, because there is an absence of modification, this is not a doctrine of transformation (*pariṇāma*) like that of the Sāṃkhya system, but rather the position of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*). The distinction between these two has been explained by us in the *Vākyapadīya*, and should therefore be ascertained from that very source. It will also be stated here in the *Saṃbandhasamuddeśa*. Furthermore, the exclusion of other causes has been set forth in the *Advayasiddhi*; hence, if there is a desire to know it, it should be understood from that very place. || 15 ||

That [ultimate reality] must be the denotable object of all words, and words are not distinct from it; yet, if they are not distinct, there can be no relationship between them, just as there is none between two different entities.

The meaning stated is this: because of the abundance of distinctions imagined through various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), and due to the prevalence of ignorance (*avidyā*) in worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), Brahman alone—possessing a variety of forms imposed by these specific limiting adjuncts—is the referent of all words. For even such words as "Self" (*ātman*), "Brahman," and "Reality" (*tattva*), though they depend upon limiting adjuncts, revolve around the substantial essence (*dravyātman*), since that which is devoid of adjuncts transcends the sphere of speech. Indeed, the knowers of Brahman teach that Reality is beyond both speech and mind.

In comparison with words such as "jar" (ghaṭa), however, words such as "self" (ātman) are more proximate [to reality]. Since everything consists of that [Brahman], words also have that as their essence, as was previously explained according to their distribution. And although ultimate non-duality exists, there is a conventional, unreal distinction in worldly affairs; this is why the word "as it were" (iva) is used. For this very reason, the occurrence of a relation residing in two things is established. || 16 ||

Now, one might object: "Is this not a mere magical illusion—that there be a teaching regarding the ultimate reality of non-difference, while disregarding the established distinctions between entities? Anticipating this doubt, he says the following to prove it by means of an illustration: "The self, the other, the beloved, the hateful, the speaker, the spoken, and the purpose—just as these contradictory forms belong to a single mind in a dream. (17)
In that which is unborn, likewise eternal, and devoid of priority and posteriority, the nature of birth and so forth is perceived as contradictory to reality. (18)

It is the consensus of all disputants that the manifold world (*prapañca*) existing in the state of dream is unreal because it is sublated by the waking state. By that very example, the diversity of entities even in the waking state is established as unreal, since it does not persist in the fourth state (*turya*). For that alone is real which persists through all states; and that is the uncontradicted nature of pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*). However, the distinction between states, being subject to appearance and disappearance, is sublated and thus unreal, like pleasure, pain, and so forth.

For indeed, since passion and the like, as well as pleasure and the like, lack intrinsic nature (*asvabhāvatva*), they do not distort the form of pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*). Likewise, even the differentiation of states is brought about by the impurity of manifold forms. In that regard, the perception of contradictory forms in a dream is a conceptual vision (*vaikalpikī dṛṣṭi*) determined for each individual subject (*pratipramātṛniyatā*). For the conceptual [subject] follows the activity of the mind; he is the transmigrating enjoyer (*bhoktā*), and yet, because he is essentially emergent (*utthana*), he is like Brahman itself.

And thus, by virtue of that much autonomy, the Lord, having created [the world] without any other material cause (*ananyopādāna*), experiences entities as pleasant or unpleasant through the delusion of *saṃsāra*—which consists of passion, hatred, and so forth—following the distinction between self and other amidst the discourses of others and the like. As those skilled in the true principles of Vedānta have said: "Having divided himself by means of himself and created various kinds of entities, the Lord, who is identical with all, proceeds as the enjoyer within a dream."

By the word "enjoyer" (*bhoktṛ*), this creation of the inner self (*pratyagātman*) is stated. And because he is the Lord of all, his capacity for creation is declared when he exists in the form of Brahman. Furthermore, because he consists of everything, they say that his own self is the material cause (*upādāna*) for the arrangement of the manifold phenomena, which have no other material cause. For this very reason, by the phrase "having divided himself by himself," the non-distinction between agent and object establishes that the nature of this creation is purely optional (*vaikalpika*). However, the divine creation pertaining to the waking state, which has external material causes, is denoted by the term *viśva* and is common to all subjects (*pramātṛ*).

The distinction [between the two states] is caused by the obsession with grasping at stability or instability; however, their falsity is exactly the same, because both consist in the activity of ignorance (*avidyā*). Only when ignorance is present is there another delusion called "sleep" (*nidrā*) which veils the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*). Under its influence, those of limited vision (*arvāgdṛś*) harbor the conceit of being deluded in this very state.

But for those who perceive the ultimate reality, it is established that the entire world—including all states such as waking and dreaming—is unreal, consisting of the transformations of form and action within the supreme Brahman, which is of the nature of consciousness and bliss, undivided, immutable, and free from birth and death. Only the universal essence of the underlying consciousness (*anvayicit-sāmānyamātram*) is the ultimate reality. One who says that "a contradiction is perceived" merely accepts a contradiction within ignorance (*avidyā*).

For this indeed is the very nature of ignorance (*avidyā*): that it brings about the appearance of even what is logically untenable; for if it were tenable, it would simply be knowledge (*vidyā*). Therefore, those who perceive reality dispel this notion—which is charming only so long as it is not investigated—that there exists in Brahman a beginningless power to manifest an unreal proliferation (*asat-prapañca*), which, having fashioned a pair consisting of the grasped and the grasper in accordance with itself, spreads out the drama of the world. (17–18)

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Determination of Substance" (*dravyasamuddeśa*), in the *Prakīrṇaprakāśa* composed by Helārāja, son of Bhūtirāja. **Chapter 3.3: The Determination of Relation** (*sambandhasamuddeśa*) Having established the word-meaning (*śabdārtha*) through the two preceding chapters as being either a universal (*jāti*) or a substance (*dravya*) according to different philosophical perspectives, [the author] now states that a relation (*saṃbandha*) is the cause for the denotation of an object by a word; otherwise, everything would be signified by every word. To explain this relation, he says: "The cognition of the speaker, the external object, and its own form (*svarūpa*)."
It is understood that when those words are uttered, their relationship is already established.

By means of sounds ignited by their application (*prayoga*), a triad is understood: its own form (*svarūpa*), the object which is the means to an end (*phalasādhana*), and the intention of the speaker (*prayoktr-abhiprāya*). And this [understanding] does not occur with necessity unless there is a connection; therefore, the determination of a real connection between word and meaning is not conventional (*sāmayika*), because the restriction of denotation (*abhidhā-niyamana*) is beginningless (*anādi*). For this very reason, he says "well-established" (*samavasthita*); the meaning is that it is established by its very nature (*svabhāvataḥ*), and not introduced by a person (*puruṣa*).

In this context, the essential nature (*svarūpa*) is the internal subject matter; therefore, the primary relationship is the restriction of denotation (*abhidhāna-niyama*). For this very reason, even though it appears otherwise in the order of recitation, by virtue of functional capacity (*sāmarthya*), the understanding of the essential nature must first be distinguished, followed by that of the superimposed nature which performs purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). Through these two aspects of the object—the essential and the superimposed—there exists for the word the relationship of signifier and signified (*vācya-vācaka-sambandha*). However, with respect to the intention of the speaker, there is a relationship of cause and effect (*kārya-kāraṇa-bhāva*). Now, one might object: "But the relationship under discussion is characterized as the relation between the signified and the signifier."

In that regard, what connection could there be between the two natures of cognition? True, this treatise is intended for all audiences; however, in order to include the view of those who do not accept that an external object is the denotation of a word—namely, that the meaning of a word consists solely in its being mounted upon the intention of the speaker—he states the relationship of cause and effect therein. As they say: "The object which appears in the intellect as the domain of the speaker's activity—that is where the word possesses authority; it does not depend on the actual state of the external object."* *Ślokavārttika, 5.1.2-3.10.*

For this very reason, the category of relation is established as being of two kinds: compatibility (yogyatā) and the causal relationship (kāryakāraṇabhāva). Superimposition (adhyāsa), however, is in reality nothing other than these two; it does not exist as a separate form. || 1 ||

Just as he will later state that here a thing permeated by metaphorical existence (upacārasattā) is the meaning of a word, so too the relation of cause and effect [is metaphorical]; however, the intrinsic nature (svarūpa) alone possesses the primary status of being denotable. Thus he says: "Regarding an object or a cognition, there may sometimes be doubt; but when the intrinsic natures are perceived, no deviation exists. (2)

Because of the appearance of non-difference between word and object in the form "this is the cow" or "this is the meaning," it is determined that a word denotes an object only by denoting its own form (*svarūpa*). For the apprehension of an object is called "denotation" precisely through the non-distinction from [the word's] own form; this is because the relationship [between word and object] is learned in that very way from the linguistic usage of elders.

For instance, the convention "this is a cow" is established; however, the notion that "the meaning of this word 'cow' is distinct [from the object]" belongs to the level of the commentator and not to the state of linguistic usage. Here too, there is indeed non-difference (*abheda*) between the word and the object. When "cow" is uttered, the convention proceeds through a reference as non-different—namely, "this object possessing a dewlap and so forth is to be understood"—for a convention has practical application as its fruit. And just as cognition occurs in worldly usage, so is that [convention] logical.

And in that case, there is a cognition [of the object] as non-different [from the word]. For in the process of cognition, some things are seen to be merely instrumental (*upāya*) while remaining external to it and not entering into it, such as the sense organ; others, however, enter into that very cognition while producing it, and thus become distinct from it, like a staff or an inferential mark (*liṅga*) such as smoke. But a word does not experience a relationship with the object in the mere capacity of being its producer; rather, when the object is expressed by the word, it appears as consisting of the word itself.

For that very nature of cognition is indeed such [as you describe]. And because it is firmly established, it is not an error. [Objection: But a sequence of phonemes (*varṇamālā*) is not perceived in the object. [Reply: Your Majesty, you are ignorant of perception! Here, "word" (*śabda*) is said to be the denoter; it is that activity of the power of consciousness whose essence is speech, which has "articulation" (*śabdana*) as its synonym, and which is designated as "sound" (*śabda*) even when not being uttered aloud, as in the case of whispered recitation (*upāṃśuprayoga*). This is why [it is so called].

And that [power], in its initial state of emerging—whose nature consists of sound and meaning in an undifferentiated condition—subsists in its own form as the supreme Speech (*paravāc*). Subsequently, however, it subsists with its own nature supported by the ground of the mind (*manas*) vitalized by the function of breath (*prāṇavṛtti*), resting upon the two non-dual branches distinguished as the signified and the signifier.

And in this intermediate state, the denotative word, whose nature is reflective awareness (*parāmarśana*), without abandoning its status as the supreme speech (*paravāk*)—which consists in the overflow of non-differentiated consciousness—reflects upon the object as merged with itself through the medium of its own form as the signified, by way of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), such that "this object is a cow. And thus, that signified object is said to possess the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the denotator.

Thereafter, that very same word, which is reflective in nature, ascends to the state of being produced by the striking of the articulatory places and instruments while still supported by its prior condition; attaining manifestation and becoming clearly manifest through a form in which the signifier and the signified appear distinct, yet by means of a self capable of becoming an object of hearing—this much constitutes the pervasion of the word.

Consequently, because this word—which consists of the vibration (*niṣpanda*) of another's speech—follows that very form, its denotation of an object, which is characterized by a specific nature through a single function (*vṛtti*), exists as non-different from the verbalization of the object-form itself, due to its co-referentiality with its own [verbal] activity. For example, in the case of "this cloth is white," there is a simultaneous recollection of the qualified cloth through the permeation of the quality of whiteness; for here, there is no separate recollection of the quality of whiteness.

Thus, in the cognition "this is a jar," the reflection upon the nature of the jar occurs precisely through its entry into the primary qualificand (*viśeṣya*). Therefore, this single cognition, consisting of verbal expression, pertains to both the word and the object. However, in some cases, there is a resting solely in the [verbal] form itself, as for example in "Study the word *agni* with an acute accent on the final syllable" or "The suffix *ḍhak* [is applied] after *agni*. For here, the form of the imitation (*anukārya*) alone remains predominant.

However, when there is a desire to communicate an external object, the appearance occurs through the very fusion of the [cognition's] own nature and the object; thus, there is no separate reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the own nature, but rather that [awareness] belongs to this object as well, since it partakes in non-difference from it. For instance, by the word "jar," the object is made the content of cognition precisely through the expression of its own nature, just like the object itself. Indeed, the three illuminators—cognition, the word, and the lamp—illuminate themselves by the very same illumination by which they illuminate another.

And so, just as cognition illuminates and manifests an object, it likewise illuminates itself as well. In this way, a lamp, while revealing form, also reveals itself by becoming the very object of that manifestation. Similarly, it is logical that a word, as a signifier, while illuminating its referent through the act of denotation, also illuminates itself through that very same denotation.

However, it is not the case that the nature of the word—having attained co-referentiality with the object by entering into the state of being an object for the sense of hearing, and being reflected upon as if it were the object itself—is the denotatum, the objective domain of the word's denotation. For in the capacity of being a signifier (*vācakatā*), there is no state of being denoted (*abhidhīyamānatā*); this is because the act of reflection (*parāmarśa*), which consists of the supreme self (*paravagātman*) and is mounted upon the locus of the agent, is the signifier. Furthermore, in that state, there is a contradiction with its status as the denotatum (*vācyatā*), since its essence is that which is being reflected upon. Thus he says: "And for that which functions in the form of a signifier, there is no state of being denoted."

Thus, having established this, its denotable form (vācya-svarūpa) must be that which is common to all words such as "jar," which takes the form of a universal (sāmānya-rūpa), which is included within the category of the object (artha-pakṣa-nikṣipta), and which is in grammatical apposition with the object (artha-samānādhikaraṇa).

It possesses meaning because it stands in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that [object], because it is perceived as such even there, because the convention (*saṅketa*) is logically possible only for that which has a universal form, because the object stands in coreferentiality with that very [form], and because the listener perceives it in that very way during linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*). Furthermore, it is precisely in accordance with that [perception] that the convention is established for the purpose of the relationship between the communicator and the communicated, once they abide in a single unifying cognition (*ekaparāmarśa*). For this very reason, the listener infers the speaker’s cognition according to his own intention, and having understood the object as superimposed upon the nature of the word itself, [the communication proceeds].

In the same way, inference regarding the speaker is appropriate; thus, by means of non-difference alone, the speaker’s cognition is determined as superimposed upon the word "jar. And so, the word also conveys the cognition—even that which has been understood by the speaker—only through superimposition. Therefore, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), superimposition alone is the relationship even in that case. Word, object, and cognition, having become fused (*lolībhūta*), are apprehended as "jar. As it has been said: "There is no cognition... and so forth.

For this very reason, there arises the question: "In the word 'cow' (gauh), what is the word? Even for one born on that very day, this commingling with the word certainly exists, because it is capable of receiving convention (*saṅketa*). And having established this, from the perspective of the intended meaning (*tātparya*), superimposition (*adhyāsa*) alone remains as the primary [relation], whether in terms of semantic fitness (*yogyatā*) or the relation of cause and effect; thus, it is that alone which is primary.

Since linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) is indeed the mutual transfer of cognition, and since cognition superimposed upon its own form is also communicated by means of a word elsewhere, it follows that even that [superimposed form] is to be communicated through the denotation (*abhidhā*) of that very word. When commanded, "Bring the jar," one understands, "I have been sent by this person for the purpose of bringing the jar," precisely preceded by the word. Thus says the author of the *Vārttika*: "Or rather, the comprehension of an object is not independent of the word."

Thus, when linguistic activity—consisting of the operation of sound—is engaged in the discourse of another person's speech, it is established that the relationship known as "superimposition of non-difference" (abheda-adhyāsa) exists between the word and its object. This is because manifestation is the very life of that [discourse], because a single word enters into both, and because of the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) of the word and the object.

However, in the state of non-differentiation, which is designated as the Visionary (paśyantī), there is no consideration whatsoever regarding superimposition (*adhyāsa*), because the distinctions between the signified and the signifier have not yet emerged. And this being the case, since meaning has sound as its sole life-force, and because in worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) meaning is never separated from that [sound], the universe is established as having the nature of a manifestation (*vivarta*) of that [sound]. Let this suffice, for the full elaboration of this point has already been investigated previously. In that context, the essential nature (*svarūpa*) is the primary signified, because it is internal, because it is not to be discarded, and because it is unique.

For in that case, the operation of the word is independent of convention (*saṅketa*). And that has been established in the *Brahmakāṇḍa* according to the various positions regarding universals (*jāti*) and so forth. Furthermore, because of the distinctions between the designator, the designated, and the cause [of the designation], it possesses different forms; thus he says, "in their own natures" (*svarūpeṣu*).

For instance: the expressive [word] consists in the arrangement of the phonemes; the expressed [meaning] consists in the word’s own form as projected onto the side of the object and perceived as non-different from the external thing; and the cause for activity toward the object consists in that which was experienced at the time of perceiving the relationship, because it determines the scope of the identical hearing. This triad is invariably present in all cases. However, due to the habituation of linguistic usage and the identity of the sounds, this triad is not discerned through analytical distinction.

Furthermore, because there is no distinction in the scriptural testimony (*śruti*), it is conventionally designated as "its own nature" (*svarūpa*), yet not because of an absolute lack of differentiation. For one who has not yet established a linguistic convention (*saṅketa*) regarding an object, the doubt "is this also the object of the speaker’s cognition? certainly arises. Moreover, it is established that even for one who has not established a convention, doubt arises regarding the sense-organ (*akṣa*) and so forth from the very word "sense-organ" (*akṣa*) which denotes a universal (*sāmānya*), but not regarding its own nature (*svarūpa*). || 2 ||

It has been stated that the relationship is established by its very nature and is firmly rooted, rather than being conventional. He states the mark for its existence: "This is the designator of this [object], and this is the designated"—it is perceived through the genitive case. Therefore, the connection between word and object is designated as their *tattva* (essential reality). || 3 ||

It is determined that there exists indeed an innate connection between word and meaning, because the use of the genitive case—expressing "this word is the designator of this meaning" or "this meaning is the designated object of this word"—would otherwise be inexplicable. For unrelated things such as a jar and a cloth could not function in this way through mutual dependence for the sake of linguistic usage. And for this very reason, since there would otherwise be no possibility of such usage based on an innate [connection], [the connection must exist].

And for this very reason, due to the innate relationship between word and meaning, they are treated as non-different in the conventional usage "this meaning is a cow"; such is the sense. Alternatively, from this genitive case [in *śabdasyārthasya ca*], the "reality" (*tattvam*)—that is, the essential nature (*svarūpam*)—of the relationship is being expressed. || 3 ||

Now, one might object: "The genitive case expresses the relation (*saṃbandha*), whereas a definition (*lakṣaṇa*) should be stated as that which establishes its own essential nature. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The relation has no denoter by means of its own property; because it is absolutely dependent, its form is not designated. (Verse 4)

In this context, having determined the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of things, a definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is formulated by applying a word that conforms to it. Among these, there exists no denotative expression—other than the genitive case—that signifies that which is characterized by its own unique property (*asādhāraṇa-dharma*), its very essence (*svabhāva*); for its nature cannot be determined as "this" [independently]. Although qualities (*guṇa*), though dependent on substance (*dravya*), are sometimes expressed primarily by words such as "white," the same does not apply to the relation (*saṃbandha*); hence the inclusion of the term "absolute" (*atyanta*).

For a relation is eternally dependent; its nature consists of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of others, and its essence is the mutual orientation of the related entities, characterized as a mere property (*dharma*). Therefore, when extracted from those [entities] and denoted by the word "relation" as if it were an independent primary entity, it cannot be directly perceived; thus, it is an "unknown term" (*asaṃvijñānapada*), to be understood only through its effects. 4.
Thus it is said: "Wherever that assistance exists, there the property (dharma) is inferred; it is the power even of powers, and the quality even of qualities. (5)

The relationship between the benefactor and the beneficiary is produced by the act of benefiting, because there can be no relationship among things that are unrelated due to the absence of such benefit. By the term "dharma," he expresses a state of eternal dependence; for if it were the substratum (*dharmin*), it would possess independence, which would necessitate another relationship, leading to the fallacy of infinite regress.

Nor is power (*śakti*) itself the relation, because even for powers, it is precisely the relation that acts as the regulator in their dependence upon a substratum and in the production of specific effects; and since it is also the relation that establishes the dependence of qualities (*guṇa*) upon substance (*dravya*), it is—by virtue of being an auxiliary to those things that are themselves dependent—an entity whose nature is everywhere inferred and which is eternally dependent. 5.

Anticipating the objection—"But has not the relationship characterized as conjunction (saṃyoga) and inherence (samavāya) already been stated by others? What is the point of propounding this [new] distinction?"—he says: "But the designation of those two [terms] belongs to their respective substrata; conjunction and inherence themselves are merely fixed limiting adjuncts (upādhi) for the sake of serving those [substrata]. (6)

Dependence (*pāratantrya*) is the defining characteristic of a relation (*saṃbandha*); thus, the term "relation" applies to conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*) because they possess this quality in relation to substances (*dravya*), qualities (*guṇa*), and so forth. Those two [conjunction and inherence] have that as their property—that is, they possess the property of dependence characterized by being dependent upon others. For in their own essential nature alone, they imitate a relation. Consequently, the word "relation" applied to those two is secondary (*gauṇa*); it refers to conjunction and inherence figuratively, but they are not relation in a primary sense.

For instance, when there is a desire to express internal attributes (*upādhi*) for those two [the related entities] just as there is for independent (*svatantra*) distinct objects, then—because they are being assisted by those attributes and thus possess independence—their status as a relation (*saṃbandha-rūpatā*) is lost, since independence entails the absence of dependence (*pāratantrya*). "Aimed at assistance" means having assistance as their purpose. "Fixed" means uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*). "Their attributes" means those things which have the relation as their attribute; for that which is not a relation cannot be a regulator.

And thus, how could those two—conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*)—which possess limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), are independent, and whose relation is useful for the delimitation of those adjuncts, attain identity with a relation that is dependent and consists of the nature of an adjunct? For they share the same characteristics as a relation, because they are the causes for the cognition of the related entities within their own substrata. 6.

In that regard, first, the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) of conjunction are as follows: For there is indeed a certain state, indicated by the production of an effect, in which a conjunction arises between a certain [entity] and something else. (7)

Through the mutual conjunction of parts, aided by the causal factor of their coming together, a composite substance (*avayavidravya*) is produced; thus, conjunction is determined to be the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) by the fact that the composite would otherwise be impossible. Furthermore, since being restricted to a single substance is a quality (*guṇa*), its connection with existence (*sattā*) is a conjunction; therefore, conjunction serves as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). In that case, its [the universal's] delimitation is effected through that relation.

That which is dependent (*paratantra*) is delimited by that relation (*saṃyoga*), which is assisted by its adjunct (*upādhi*); thus, what is called "dependence" (*pāratantrya*) is the general form of relation itself, which is inherent in it (*anvayi*), but dependence is not its sole lifeblood, because dependence exists even in qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*karman*), and universals (*sāmānya*), whereas this [delimitation] is restricted solely to substances (*dravya*).

Furthermore, since conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is a quality (*guṇa*), the relation and the relation between the quality-ness and conjunction-ness are not the same as the relation of categories (*padārtha*). This is because that [conjunction] is distinct from substance, quality, and action, yet it assists all categories. Moreover, conjunction possesses the capacity to produce a real effect (*vastubhūta-kāryakāritva*), whereas a relation is merely the cause of a formal connection (*yojanāmātra-hetu*); this is the distinction between them.

He states the distinction of the relation [of inherence] even from the perspective of inherence itself, by restating the nature of inherence as restricted by specific limiting conditions (*upādhi*): "The restriction that occurs only in certain cases regarding the production of those things devoid of self-nature (insentient matter), and the non-cessation [of that restriction] which is brought about by that very [restriction] when there is no difference in their attainment—[this is the nature of inherence]. (Verse 8)
That by which the self of another is determined as being like one's own self, and because of which the multiplicity of a single entity is not apprehended as its true nature; || 9 ||
That power called "inherence" (samavāya), which assists other powers, transcends both difference and non-difference, and is established in a manner entirely distinct [from them].
The Dharma transcends all categories of objects and possesses all characteristics; it favors [all things] through its relationship—such is the tradition from the predecessors. (11)

In the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), the cause itself becomes the effect; thus, since it is produced by specific sounds, its perception is logically restricted to that very [cause]. In the theory of the non-existence of the effect (*asatkāryavāda*), however, the inherent relation (*samavāya*) is accepted as the basis for such cognitions as "the cloth is in the threads" and "the jar is in the potsherds," whereby the effect resides only in its determined causes.

And even though there is a difference between cause and effect, it is precisely by that same cause—which is the object of the restriction—that the non-separation of the effect [from the cause] is established; for, despite the difference in place and time, this constitutes a form of relation, being no different from conjunction (*saṃyoga*) in this respect, yet it is produced by inherence (*samavāya*). Thus, there is a distinction between conjunction and inherence. For this very reason, although cause and effect, part and whole, attribute and substrate, and genus and its possessor, as well as quality and the qualified, are not separate categories of existence, they appear as identical through the relation of identity (*tādātmya*).

However, because there exists a specific distinction inherent within each [entity] according to its own nature, their identity is not real; this is the meaning of the word "iva" (as if). This is a statement of the result of what was previously said regarding "non-cessation" (*avyapavarga*) by that very same [reasoning], and thus there is no tautology. For it is precisely due to non-cessation that one thing appears as another's self. For this very reason, there is disagreement among proponents: some desire oneness between the part and the whole, or between the attribute and the substratum, while others desire their difference. Thus, even due to delusion regarding *samavāya* (inherence), [the truth] does not become established from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).

By this, inseparable existence (*ayutasiddhi*) is stated to be the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of inherence (*samavāya*). Thus, the rule that "inherence is the cause of the cognition of 'here' (*ihapratyaya*) for things that are inseparably existent, and not for others" is made known through the relation of inherence. For wherever there is dependence (*pāratantrya*), there it produces the cognition of "here" as well as the notion of non-difference, as in the case of substances, qualities, actions, and universals; even potencies (*śakti*) are restricted by that [inherence] through their dependence on a substratum.

Furthermore, just as in the case of the inherent causes (*samavāyin*), the difference of inherence (*samavāya*) from them is not perceived, because it appears as having its form merged with them. However, on the basis of the cognition "here" (*iha*) and its functional effect, it is inferred to exist in reality as something distinct from the related entities; this is how it is established according to the views of others. By using the word "by which" (*yena*) to refer back to inherence, the text assigns to it the nature of a power (*śaktitva*). The meaning is that since inherence functions as a facilitator (*anugrāhaka*) for words, it is improper to mention it as being on the same level as those [words].

Precisely because they are powers (*śakti*), they transcend both difference and non-difference. For powers are indeed indefinable in terms of being either identical to or different from the reality (*tattva*). Thus it has been said: "If powers were of the nature of the real entity, the investigation into their identity or difference would be appropriate; however, for those that are conceptualized, it is logical that they are devoid of duality. For instance, because they appear as merged with the inherent substrate (*samavāyin*), they are neither different from it nor non-different.

Because it produces an effect characterized by the cognition "here" (ihapratyaya) which cannot exist without its substratum, it is inexpressible as being either identical to or different from [its substratum]. Consequently, it exists in a manner distinct from other categories of entities. Alternatively, since the effect—the cognition "here"—is non-different [from it], it is non-different in itself; yet, because that very effect possesses a difference constructed through inherence (*samavāya*), it is also different. Thus, although it is one, it is established in a different way as having a constructed difference due to the multiplicity of its relata.

And it is by means of its abiding as a substratum that it assists the powers of the *sādhana* (means) and so forth. Thus, although this power called *samavāya* (inherence) exists, [the relation in question] transcends the property characterized by independence residing in all categories; rather, it is characterized by eternal dependence. Therefore, every entity, being dependent upon assistance, serves as its indicator (*jñāpaka*)—unlike *samavāya*, which is restricted to a specific related form alone. Such a relation favors and regulates [the entities], establishing them as eternally dependent and inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*).

Those who know the traditional scriptures (āgama) state that because dependence (pāratantrya) is common [to both], one applies its own designation; they say that the characteristic of relation is dependence. Thus, he confirms through scripture that what is called "relation" is a category distinct from the categories of substance and so forth, and functions as such an effect. 9–11.

And having established this, he says that conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*) alone are not the relations here, as is the view of others: "The relation, which has been made into a category by others, is accepted everywhere; therefore, the meaning of a word cannot be distinguished [from it]. (12)

By the Vaiśeṣikas, who maintain that there are six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*), conjunction (*saṃyoga*) was included within the category of quality (*guṇa*). However, according to the principle stated that inherence (*samavāya*) is an independent category, the relation—though not a formal category—is treated as if it were one; for, being dependent, it takes the form of a power (*śakti*), and through the superimposition of that nature upon it, it is made into a category.

Furthermore, since the specific distinction that "this is the meaning of this word" cannot be established through a fixed rule regarding word and meaning, the Vaiśeṣikas' compendium of categories suffers from the fallacy of non-pervasion (avyāpti), because they maintain that there exists a relation between the two distinct from them. For instance: "Through inherence (samavāya), its own substrate and its own genus are perceived; but through inherence in the same object, the quality [is perceived] only in its own substrate. (Verse 13)

Words such as *khā*, *ākāśa*, and *gagana* convey their own referent, that which is called "space" (*ākāśa*), because of its inherence (*samavāya*) therein. All words cause the genus (*jāti*) inherent in themselves—which is characterized by their own form—to be understood through the relation of inherence, since that genus inheres in the individual word-entities (*śabdavyakti*). Furthermore, the word "sound" (*śabda*) conveys the universal "soundness" (*śabdatva*) because of its inherence therein.

However, those qualities of space such as magnitude (*mahattva*) and so forth, words convey through inherence in a single object; for the specific qualities such as magnitude, which are the uncommon [referents] of words like "magnitude," inhere together in one place within space. Likewise, specific manifestations of sound characterized as thundering, warbling, speaking, neighing, and so on, are the uncommon qualities of the sky; and the words "thundering" and so forth, which denote them, function precisely because of inherence in that same single object. (13)
Likewise: substance-ness, existence, and conjunction are bound to their own substrates; so too are the disjunctions from those parts and those qualities such as duality and the rest. (14)

Substantiality (*dravyatva*) is a lower generality (*aparasāmānya*), while existence (*sattā*) is the highest generality (*mahāsāmānya*); these are conveyed by words such as "substance" (*dravyatva*) due to their inherence in the same object. For existence and substantiality are restricted by their own and other substrata; that is, the word "substance" would apply to its own substrate, space (*ākāśa*), as well as to others, such as earth (*pṛthivī*), and thus it is delimited by both its own and other substrates, being restricted within its own sphere.

And likewise, [the term "ether"] functions with respect to both itself and other substrates, because it is fully established in its own locus; for although universals may inhere in other substrates, there is no contradiction in their inhering in each individual one. Thus, those conjunctions, disjunctions, duality, separateness, and so forth—which reside in specific locations of other categories along with ether—are also denoted by the words "conjunction" and so on precisely because of their inherence in the same object, since conjunctions and the like reside in two places, and thus inhere in ether as well. || 14 ||
Likewise: some [qualities] are conjoined with their own substratum; some are inherent in that [substratum]; and others are inherent in things that are themselves conjoined and inherent. (15)

Space is the substratum of words denoting itself; therefore, chariots, jars, and so forth, which are conjoined with it, are made known by the words "chariot," "jar," and so on, through the relation of inherence-in-what-is-conjoined (*samaveta-saṃyoga*). Furthermore, qualities such as color and so forth, as well as specific actions such as upward throwing and so forth, which inhere in jars and the like, are made known by the words "color" and so on, through the relation of inherence-in-what-is-conjoined-with-the-substratum-of-itself (*svāśraya-saṃyukta-samavāya*). Moreover, universals such as "colorness" and so forth, which inhere in the colors and so forth that inhere in jars and the like, are denoted by the words "colorness" and so on, through the relation of inherence-in-what-inheres-in-what-is-conjoined-with-the-substratum-of-itself (*svāśraya-saṃyukta-samaveta-samavāya*). || 15 ||
Likewise: "But the all-pervading [entity] is understood as being conjoined with those things conjoined with its own substratum; no other relation for inherence is observed there. (16)

Since it is impossible for there to be an attainment preceded by non-attainment between the all-pervading entities of space, time, and the self and space itself—and thus no direct connection exists—space, time, and the self are perceived through the words "space," "time," and so forth, by means of conjunction with that which is conjoined with their own substratum. For earth and the other elements are conjoined with space, and space, time, and the self are indeed conjoined with them.

Thus, following the previous reasoning, it is determined that qualities inherent in substances, as well as the generalities and particularities inherent in them, are denoted by their own respective words through the relations of inherence in what is conjoined with their own substratum (*svāśraya-saṃyukta-samavāya*) and inherence in what is inherent in what is conjoined with their own substratum (*svāśraya-saṃyukta-samaveta-samavāya*); therefore, this has not been stated separately. In this way, the cause for the cognition of substances, qualities, actions, and generalities has been explained. As for the particularity (*viśeṣa*) inherent in atoms and the internal organ (*manas*), its denotation by its own word occurs through the relation of inherence in what is conjoined with its own substratum (*svāśraya-saṃyukta-samavāya*).

However, it has been stated that the cognition of that which inheres in space—such as that which inheres in direction, time, or the self—occurs through inherence in a single object (*ekārthasamavāya*), while the cognition of that which inheres in its own substratum depends upon inherence in what is conjoined with its own substratum (*svāśrayasaṃyuktasamavāya*). Thus, even when analyzed here according to the specific application, there would be no relation whatsoever for the word "inherence" (*samavāya*) in conveying its own meaning, because inherence is not a substance and thus lacks conjunction with anything, because it exists in itself (*svarūpavṛtti*), and because there is no further inherence (*samavāyāntara*).

It might be argued: "The word 'inherence' (samavāya) inheres in space, and jars and other objects are conjoined with space; since inherence resides in those [objects], it will denote that [space] through the relation of being connected to what is conjoined to its own substratum. This is not correct, because there is no further inherence [of inherence]; thus, the aforementioned conceptualization regarding inherence in jars and other objects is untenable. || 16 ||

For instance: "Since the relationship [between word and object] would be indistinguishable, there could be no restriction here; therefore, no relationship at all is postulated between word and object. (17)

If this meaning is that [the word] lacks a specific relation, then the word "inherence" (*samavāya*) would not convey its own meaning without a relation; thus it would be meaningless. Alternatively, even if it did convey it, it would not necessarily convey every possible meaning—this is the explanation. Or, the lack of restriction is with respect to the subject at hand: if the word "inherence" were to denote its own meaning without a cause, then because the characteristic of a relation—which consists in being non-restricted—would be indistinguishable [for all words], every word would convey every meaning.

But when the meaning is that the relation is "undifferentiated," "equal," or "common" to others, then this is the explanation: if the word *ākāśa* (ether) were to denote its own substratum through inherence (*samavāya*), then words such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*) and so forth would also be denoters of the sky, because the inherence in ether is undifferentiated. And in that case, if the word "sound" (*śabda*) were to denote the genus inherent in itself, it would follow that it must also denote "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*) and "existence" (*sattā*).

Furthermore, because there is no distinction in the conjunction with their own substrates, words such as "pot" would also cause cloth and other objects to be conveyed; thus, this attempt to establish a fixed relationship between word and meaning through either under-extension (*avyāpti*) or over-extension (*ativyāpti*) falls apart. Therefore, it is not logical to conceive of the category of "relation" here as being of the nature of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*). 17.

In order to support the Vaiśeṣika system through the use of bold assertion (prauḍhivāda), he says this: "Just as the conjunction of the self [with the body] occurs in a particular instance through the attainment of the operation of the unseen force (adṛṣṭa)—known as the union of owner and owned—so too is that same sequence applicable elsewhere, despite the absence of difference. (18)

Just as, although the conjunction of the all-pervading self with all substances is indistinguishable, the relationship characterized by the status of owner and owned occurs only in relation to the body and so forth due to the influence of *dharma* and *adharma*; likewise, here too, even though the inherence in its own substratum or the conjunction with its own substratum is indistinguishable, the specific restriction of word and meaning will be established solely through the influence of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). Thus, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*).

The "activity" (*vṛtti*) of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), which is a quality of the self characterized as merit and demerit, is its operation toward the granting of results; the "attainment" (*lābha*) of that activity is its acquisition through the influence of auxiliary factors such as place and time. This rebuttal has been stated as trivial because this position is itself to be rejected. It is logical that experience—consisting of one's own pleasure and pain and their means—is projected by karma, but it is not logical that everything is of such a nature.

Now, if it is argued that when there is a fixed rule for the communication of meaning by means of a word, its status as an object of experience is also necessarily implied by karma (past action), then, since the entire world exists in such a state, the rejection of unseen causes (adṛṣṭa) would follow everywhere.

Now, the intention here is as follows: just as even though conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is common [to all], not everything belongs to one's own self, nor does it belong to all selves—due to the restriction imposed by the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) residing in each individual self—so too, despite the non-difference of the relation, not everything is denotable by every word. This is because [the denotation] is dependent upon the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced in people through the repeated observation of usage. Therefore, let the relation be simply this: a mental impression in the form of a capacity (*yogyatā*), whose nature is determined by convention (*saṅketa*) arising from the repeated observation of usage, which has a specifically restricted object. What is the use of any other groundless relation?
There is no need for that which is invariably concomitant, characterized by conjunction or inherence. || 18 ||

But he accepts that inherence itself is indeed inexpressible; for neither the speaker nor the listener apprehends through words that "attainment" called inherence, which transcends the properties of expressible things. (19)

The property of the objects denoted by words—such as cows and the like—is their being colored by a form that involves relation (*saṃsargirūpa*), because those things devoid of adjuncts (*nirupādhi*) cannot be the objects of words. Inherence (*samavāya*), however, is devoid of adjuncts; for no adjunct such as a quality (*guṇa*) or a universal (*sāmānya*) is accepted by others [the Vaiśeṣikas] in its case. Thus, it transcends the property of the denotable. Furthermore, its fitness to be the object of a reflective cognition in the form "this is that" transcends the property of the denotable.

Furthermore, this inherence (*samavāya*), being eternally dependent in nature, cannot be determined even from the word "inherence" by either the speaker or the listener; thus, there is no descriptive term that captures its essential form. Consequently, it is inexpressible in reality. However, inherence is understood from the word as something independent insofar as it possesses the nature of a relation between related entities.

And thus, because it is perceived as a substratum (*dharmin*) and because it can accommodate connection with other attributes (*dharmāntara*), there certainly exists a conjunction with its own locus. When that [conjunction] is denoted by the word "inherence" (*samavāya*), the term "relation" (*saṃbandha*) applies; therefore, there is no fault whatsoever. Since the word "inherence" is seen to be used in other senses, such as for a gathering or assembly, it is not a unique conventional term (*saṃvijñānapada*) for this [entity] in common worldly usage. What then? It is established (*rūḍha*) specifically within the Vaiśeṣika system. A speaker, desiring to express a particular meaning, employs a word that is appropriate for that purpose.

However, since inherence (*samavāya*), being of the nature of dependence, lacks the status of being denotable, the speaker has no activity in uttering a word capable [of expressing it]; and because of that absence, there is no one who understands it either. Thus, both [the speaker and the hearer] are mentioned. || 19 ||

Regarding this statement that inherence (samavāya) is inexpressible, the Naiyāyika raises a verbal quibble (vākchala): "When that which is expressible as 'inexpressible' is determined to be expressible by virtue of its being inexpressible, then it would indeed be expressible. (20)

By the word "inexpressible" (*avācya*), that which is intended to be expressed is meant; at the very moment it is understood as being expressible by means of the word "inexpressible"—that is, as something to be designated—it becomes expressible. The meaning is that it attains the status of being expressible precisely at the time of its communication. And thus, when it is said "it is expressible," the inexpressibility of the word "inexpressible" itself is contradicted. || 20 ||

Moreover, even if one thinks "this is inexpressible," that which is intended to be expressed is not understood as such; for the very state of the object that one wishes to convey is not determined. (21)

If even the word "ineffable" were itself ineffable, then the intended meaning—that inherence (samavāya) is not denotable by words—could not be understood; therefore, that [word] must indeed be denotable. And thus, there is a contradiction. This is the meaning. || 21 ||

Now, suspecting that [the self] might be inexpressible as having a dependent nature but not in every respect, he says: "Even in that case where its inexpressibility is asserted 'thus,' 'otherwise,' or 'in every respect,' even there that state is not negated by those words. (22)

Even when one negates a particular mode by saying "it cannot be expressed as having dependence as its nature," it is the possessor of that mode itself that is negated. For it is not the case that it is inexpressible by that specific mode, by another mode, or by all modes; rather, these words negate the mere mode characterized as the state [of being]. This is because, if the substratum (dharmin) were not negated, the negation of the attributes (dharmas) dependent upon it would be impossible.

Therefore, even when there is a negation of a specific [quality], expressibility (*vācyatva*) itself is what is negated regarding inherence (*samavāya*); thus, the objection—“How can this [inherence] be the denotable object of the word ‘inexpressible’?”—is indeed a valid one. Alternatively, by the statement beginning with “whether in that way or otherwise,” even if there is a negation, that very state cannot be negated as long as the substratum of the state has not been negated; thus, its negation is necessarily concomitant.

The earlier commentators explain that since a specific form cannot be negated without a reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) of its being an object of words, it is established as expressible (*vācya*) by virtue of being an object of words; thus, there is no contradiction in its being inexpressible [in another sense]. || 22 ||

To provide an illustrative example similar to this for the purpose of stating a reply to verbal quibble (*vākchala*) by superimposing a different meaning upon the speaker's intended sense, he says: "For when an object in the form of doubt is established as a subordinate element, another doubt regarding its own nature does not arise so long as that [initial] nature has not been excluded. (23)

When a doubt arises regarding an object—such as a post or the like—due to the perception of common characteristics, the failure to determine specific differences, and the recollection of those specific differences, such that one thinks, "It might be a post or it might be a person," then, within that knowledge consisting of doubt, which stands as a subordinate factor (*śeṣatvena*) and as a constituent part for establishing its own object, no further subsequent doubt can arise regarding that same object. This is because this [doubt], being dependent on the object and having not abandoned its state of dependence, possesses a cognition of its own object.

Because this would contradict the very nature of becoming an object. For if this [consciousness] were to become the object of its own cognition—which is itself of the nature of doubt—then, being doubtful by its very essence, it would remain unestablished and could not abide within its own nature, which consists of the reflective awareness of the external and is itself of the nature of doubt. Consequently, the oscillating state of the external object would not be determined, since the simultaneous relationship of object and subject is untenable.

By that very doubt which is directed toward an object, there arises a state of being doubted with respect to its own nature as well, because the operation [of the doubt] is one; for the object and its own form are both subject to doubt. Thus, just as doubt, excluding its own nature, casts doubt upon its object, so too the word "inexpressible" (avācya), excluding itself, expresses that which has been made its object; this is the point of similarity (*sādharmya*). The meaning is: when the object in the form of doubt is designated by the term "doubt," it refers to the entity that is the content of cognition. Here, the determination established as a remainder is, by implication, an entity whose object is a real thing (*vastu*). || 23 ||
He states another example as well: "And when a determination is undertaken as a determination within the cognition of determination, then that cognition abides by its own characteristic. (24)

When a cognition in the form of a definitive determination (*nirṇaya*) regarding an object being determined is occupied at that very moment with the delimitation of that object, no other internal determination can arise. For dependence upon the object is indeed the inherent property (*svadharma*) of cognition. If one were to abstract it from that and examine its own nature, it would be separated from its inherent property, because it would then fall into the state of being an object in its own right. For this very reason, it was previously established that [cognition] cannot be grasped by another cognition; for if it were an object of another cognition, it would lose its status as a subject (*viṣayitva*), resulting in the loss of its inherent property.

Thus, just as a cognition cannot be an object of cognition within a single act of consciousness because that which is occupied with one object at that very time lacks operation upon its own object, so too a signifier cannot be the signified within a single act of consciousness. Consequently, the word "inexpressible" (*avācya*), while standing in the state of being a signifier, does not negate the expressibility of the object *per se*, for that would involve a contradiction of an action operating upon itself. Furthermore, since there is no other word at that time to negate its expressibility, the meaning of the word "inexpressible" necessarily arrives at the status of being a subject of denotation.

For indeed, it is clearly understood from the speaker’s intention that the other word, namely the word "inherence" (samavāya), is not to be denoted by the essential nature of inherence itself. || 24 ||
For example: "I speak everything falsely"—this sentence is not intended [to be true]. For if it were stated falsely, the matter under discussion would not be understood. (25)

In order to demonstrate the falsity of one's own statements, if one says, "I am saying everything falsely," this statement itself must not be subject to the consequence of being false, because it too is a statement. For if that were so, the intended subject under discussion—the falsity of one's other statements—would not be understood. Alternatively, another meaning here is this: even if this statement were false, its capacity to convey meaning would remain the same as that of the other statements; thus, the attempt to demonstrate the falsity of those [other] statements would be rendered fruitless.

Right here he states the reasoning: "And for that which functions in the form of a signifier, there is no state of being a signified; for that [signifier] cannot be what is signified therein by means of which another thing is signified. (26)

It is contradictory for that which is situated as an instrument (*karaṇa*) to be the object (*abhidheya*) at that very same time, because that which is engaged in conveying another [object] cannot simultaneously turn back toward itself and function upon itself. This is the nature of things: that which is endowed with the power of an agent (*kartṛ-śakti*) cannot at that same time be the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of the power of an object (*karman-śakti*), because independence (*svātantrya*) and dependence (*pāratantrya*) are mutually exclusive in a single entity at one and the same time—this is the meaning. He concluded by summarizing this point through all the illustrations, beginning with the words "that which is to be conveyed is not there."

That which is the means of communication is not itself that which is communicated, just as, for example, a doubtful cognition or a certain cognition [is not what is communicated by them]. And since verbal expression is the means of communication, it follows that this [expression] is not itself that which is communicated; such is the formal argument (*prayoga*). || 26 ||

Now, one might object: let there be no denoter or denoted, for they are contradictory. However, since this [self] enters into the commonality of sentences whose agent is the self, by what false self could it be maintained? Anticipating this doubt, he establishes this very point through another illustration: "The proposition is not established"—this is not merely stated; likewise, no property whatsoever of this [self] is perceived. (27)

When it is stated that "the statement of the probandum (sādhyanirdeśa) is not a member of the proof (sādhanāṅga)," this does not apply only to the Buddhist [proposition], because there is no difference in its being a proposition (*pratijñā*). For if it were meaningless, the intended object would not be established. Rather, this applies to all other propositions except for this one. Thus, even when the untruthfulness of the sentence "I say everything is false" is being demonstrated, falsity (*anṛtatva*) as a property (*dharma*) is not understood; for if that were the case, since the intended meaning would not be conveyed, the employment of the argument would be futile.

The same should be asked regarding the term "inexpressible" (avācya). He concludes: "Since there is no other operation whatsoever for an operation, one should therefore never resort to contradiction or infinite regress in any case. (28)

The operation of the word *avācya* (inexpressible) that conveys its own meaning is of the nature of *abhidhā* (denotation); at that very moment, it does not possess another operation directed toward itself by which it could, through one operation, negate being denotable by other words, while through another operation, [negate] its own denotability. Thus, if this were the case, even the meaning of the word *avācya* would not be expressible, and consequently, the intended inexpressibility of all other words would not be perceived—this would constitute a contradiction. Furthermore, if one were to admit an additional operation without a basis, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

For instance, if another operation were possible even for the word "inexpressible" (avācya) in order to negate its status as an object, then yet another operation would be required for that second operation to negate its own engagement with its object, and so on; thus, due to infinite regress (anavasthā), there would be no comprehension.
