However, because there is no further operation, this undesirable consequence does not arise.

"In all cases" means not only in the case of being denotable (*vācyatā*), but also in the case of a relation (*saṃbandha*). For if there were no further relation between the relation and its two relata, then the relation between those two relata—the word and the meaning—would also not exist. Alternatively, if one were to postulate another relation for that relation, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*); this infinite regress must not be accepted. The meaning is that since a relation is itself of the nature of a relation, it is impossible for it to require something else to connect it.

Alternatively, "in all cases" means "I speak everything falsely; the proposition is unestablished," and so forth. Thus, by relying on relations characterized as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*) as established by the opponent, the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) regarding the distinction between word and meaning has been avoided through the power of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*).

There is also no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*); for even if inherence (*samavāya*) is not directly denotable, it is denotable as being related by way of a conceptualized form. Thus, there is no contradiction in establishing the non-denotability of inherence when it is presented by the word "inherence" from a detached standpoint. Therefore, out of a bold assertion (*prauḍhivāda*), the restriction of word-meaning has been established even by resorting to relations proven in other systems of thought. || 28 ||

Now, in order to establish the relationship as established within his own school, he says: "Just as the capacity of the sense organs for their respective objects is beginningless, so too is the relationship of words with their meanings, which is their capacity, beginningless. (29)

Since the cognition of the meaning of a word arises from the mere utterance of it, without depending on causes such as inherence (*samavāya*) and so forth, an uncreated power (*akṛtrimā śakti*) is inferred. For even those who have not yet learned the linguistic convention understand the inseparability of the mere word from the mere object. Thus, fitness (*yogyatā*) is established as inherent; the convention merely manifests that [fitness]. This is just as the eyes and other sense organs possess a capacity for apprehending objects such as form, independent of human effort.

For indeed, even with effort, it is impossible to place the sense of taste within form; likewise, applying the word "jar" to the meaning of "cow" is incorrect. Thus says the Bhāṣya: "If one were to say 'cow' when referring to a horse, there would never be any comprehension [of the intended object]. For when a convention is established according to one's whim, well-known words do not function toward a different object by being preceded by their own expressive power (*vācaka-śakti*); rather, that is merely a matter of arbitrary agreement (*samaya*).

Although names and words possess the capacity to convey all possible named objects (*saṃjñin*), their power is conventionally restricted to a specific named object. Furthermore, this fitness of words must be established solely by following the actual cognition of the meaning; since the cognition of word and meaning occurs as non-different, it exists as the result of superimposition (*adhyāsa*). Therefore, that alone is the primary relationship.

For this very reason, because the object is also required as a constituent factor (*viṣaya*) in the act of cognition, it is designated as a "relation" (*saṃbandha*) due to the commonality of its dependence on another. Furthermore, even though the sense organs produce cognition while remaining themselves unknown—since they are *kārakas* (instrumental factors)—whereas a word, being a *jñāpaka* (indicator), causes the cognition of another thing through its own cognition; nevertheless, there is parity between them in that their capacity does not depend upon human effort. || 29 ||

The employment of words here is for the purpose of conveying meaning; and since the comprehension of meaning is more effectively achieved through correct words than through corrupt ones (apaśabda), one might suspect that even the latter possess a connection with meaning. Anticipating this, he says: "Some maintain that the incorrect word is expressive by means of inference; or, given that there is no difference in their capacity to express, there is a restriction regarding merit and demerit. (30)

Divine speech, when corrupted by the incompetent, has its original nature inferred from those who are like children, the blind, and so forth; it is thus expressed by the learned. For the learned do not directly determine the meaning from a corrupt word (*apaśabda*); therefore, there is no connection whatsoever between corrupt words and meaning. It is for this very reason that it is stated in the *Brahmakāṇḍa* that in the ancient age (*purākalpa*), speech was free even from corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*), just as it was free from falsehood and the like. Corrupt forms are indeed non-expressive; however, they lead one to infer the correct word (*sādhuśabda*) through similarity. From these [corrupt forms], the comprehension of the meaning arises.

And thus says the author of the *Saṃgraha*: "Apabhraṃśa has sound as its material cause. However, in the present day, due to the abundance of unrighteousness (*adharma*), there is a conventional usage of verbal expressions such as falsehoods and the like. Consequently, since the meaning is understood from corrupt words (*apaśabda*) without any mediation, the scripture states, "One should not speak barbarously, one should not speak corruptly; one should speak with correct words (*sādhu*). By virtue of the authority of this scripture, correct words alone constitute a constituent of dharma; therefore, their employment is enjoined by the scripture.

And likewise, since differentiation is preceded by non-differentiation, and since there is no fixed rule for the mental constructs of persons and thus [the number of] corrupt words is infinite, it is certain that they must be preceded by a single, non-differentiated correct word; thus, the corrupt word is established as having the correct word as its source, and the word itself is knowledge (*vidyā*). Therefore, just as the state of knowledge has as its essence the non-differentiated Brahman, so too the state of the correct word is knowledge.

Just as there is a distinction regarding the object within knowledge (*vidyā*), so too, the state of corruption (*apabhraṃśa*) is a form of verbal impurity; thus, the conceptual distinction (*vikalpa*) depends on the perspective of the ultimate state versus its opposite. It is precisely with reference to the state of ignorance (*avidyā*) that the Bhāṣya states: "When the comprehension of meaning is the same, whether by means of a word or a corrupt word (*apaśabda*). By the expression "in the comprehension of meaning," they acknowledge that corrupt words do indeed convey meaning. The sense is that because one generally employs corrupt words during ignorance, there may simply be the cognition of the meaning.

However, because linguistic usage is firmly established, the author of the treatise states that there is no distinction [between correct and incorrect forms] in common practice. In this regard, the scripture serves as the regulator: "The meaning must be expressed using only correct words (*sādhu-śabda*) and not through corrupt words (*apaśabda*); when done in this way, it brings about spiritual prosperity (*abhyudaya*). A restriction is made regarding merit and demerit based on their causes: from the knowledge of correct words, or from their usage preceded by scriptural authority, spiritual prosperity arises. In the case of using incorrect words, however, the mere absence of merit is figuratively treated as demerit. Some maintain that demerit indeed results from the transgression of the prohibition, "One should not speak like a barbarian" (*na mlecchitavai*). || 30 ||

It was previously stated that there is no further relation within inherence (samavāya); however, he says that under this view, such a [regressus] does not apply: "In the word 'relation,' the relation is with respect to fitness; [inherence is] fitness. (31)

The word "relation" (*saṃbandha*) conveys the relation characterized by fitness (*yogyatā*) through that very fitness. Likewise, the word "inherence" (*samavāya*) also conveys its own meaning through fitness established from time immemorial. The same applies to the word "fitness" itself; thus, this relation pervades all cases. To the question, "In that case, what is the utility of linguistic convention (*saṅketa*? he says: "Convention [is useful] for the cognition of fitness, like the relationship between mother and son. (31)

In the case of words whose function concerns objects established from beginningless time—such as *ga* and *gha*—it is their inherent capacity (*svābhāvikī yogyatā*) that is determined through convention (*samaya*), which is synonymous with the lineage of usage among the elders; it is not appropriate for such a status to arise through mere convention even regarding that which is not so constituted. For this relationship between mother and son, expressed as "this is Mākeki's son," is not conventional; rather, it is presented as something established by the nature of things (*vastusiddha*).

Now, as for the claim that the act of naming is preceded by direct perception—that is, the application of a word to an object by those superior to us is merely conventional—this is not so. For even they apply [words] according to suitability, based on prior practice. As it has been said: "And that practice, which is not derived from scripture, is held by some to be convention (*samaya*). What do you mean? Having understood the invariable concomitance with the mere object, one determines it through a specific inquiry.

The word possesses the capacity to convey meaning even toward those for whom the convention has not been learned; for even when a person establishes a convention elsewhere, there is an immediate comprehension of the established meaning from words such as "cow" (gavādi). Furthermore, he will state that it is impossible for a person to effect a restrictive injunction (niyoga). || 31 ||

Now he states the causal relationship as the connection between word and meaning: "The word is the cause of the meaning, for it is produced by that [meaning]; and likewise, the word is cognized from the meaning which is the object of the intellect. (32)

The word is the cause of the object that has ascended into the intellect of the hearer, because it is its producer. For the object of the word is indeed the object as it is determined through an external form. Furthermore, since the word reaches the domain of hearing from the object residing in the intellect of the speaker—which serves as its cause—the object is also the cause of the word.

Thus, by describing the relationship between cause and effect in both ways, the connection between word and object—which is characterized as superimposition—is established through their non-difference, unlike the case of smoke and fire. For instance, in the intellect, word and object first exist in a state of non-difference; indeed, the intended object is not devoid of the commingling of the word, since it appears in the form of internal verbalization (*antaḥsañjalpa*). For even the cognition of animals is permeated by the beginningless mental impression (*bhāvanā*) of words.

Therefore, the word—manifested through the operation of the places of articulation (*sthāna*) and the articulators (*karaṇa*), variegated with the nature of its own form and its meaning—is apprehended by the hearers and, through the permeation of its own form, causes the meaning to be understood. For linguistic usage consists in the mutual transfer of intention between the speaker and the listener; thus, the word transmits to the listener the meaning residing within [the speaker], which has reached its fundamental state yet remains inseparable from it, and which is fully present in the intellect of the speaker.

Furthermore, the listener is likewise established [in the meaning] according to the expansion of his own latent impressions (*vāsanā*), being permeated by the mental cultivation of the word (*śabdabhāvanā*). It has been determined in the *Vākyapadīya* that, through this, the listener proceeds with the mental cultivation of the word awakened within him. Thus, it is precisely this state of becoming one-sided (*ekapakṣībhāva*) that constitutes the relationship of syntactic unity; this is established as being in accordance with the final doctrine (*siddhānta*).

A word conveys its meaning according to the speaker's intention, being characterized by a fixed sequence of accents and phonemes; thus, when there is a reversal of accent—as in the case of the word *indraśatru*—another intention must be understood, because the word becomes something else through the difference in accent. A word causes only its own cause [the speaker's intention] to be known; therefore, an intermediate intention, though indistinctly manifested due to parsimony [of postulation], is inferred just as the utterance of a second phoneme follows immediately after the utterance of the first phoneme. || 32 ||

Anticipating the objection—"If the referent of a word is mounted upon the intellect (buddhi), how can there be such worldly usage as 'he eats rice'?"—the author says: Even [acts] such as eating are considered to exist within the realm of the intellect when they are impossible [in reality]. Since everything exists only within the realm of the intellect, even that [eating and so forth] is seen to occur within the realm of the intellect. (33)

In the system of consciousness (*vijñānavāda*), the relationship of means and end (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) between action and its factors (*kriyākāraka*), which revolve within the intellect, is established as consisting essentially of appearance (*pratibhāsasāra*). For instance, the object of cognition, the cognition itself, the meaning of a word, the act of eating, the eater, and their mutual relation—even that which is considered impossible [in the external world] is indeed possible. When? He says: precisely at the time of the appearance of the object of cognition, such as rice and so forth, other than the [object] being consumed.

When the cognition of the factors of action (*kāraka*) has arisen, for the proponent of the sentence (*vākyavādin*), comprehension is not completed by a mere word alone. This is a statement made on the basis of a formal admission (*abhyupagamavāda*). For even in the externalist system (*bāhyadarśana*), since the meaning of a word is cognized as revolving within the intellect, the establishment of linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) indeed occurs through the determination of non-difference between the perceived and the conceptualized when there is the relation of action and its factors. For instance, perception occurs only when an external object exists.

In perception, there is the appearance of an object; when that exists, there is the desire to speak; from that, through effort and so forth, there is the utterance of sound. Thus, it might be argued that by this sequence, the external object itself is what is denoted, and activity occurs toward it. However, even without an external object, it is possible—even in the view of consciousness-only—to coordinate the relationship between action and its factors (kriyākāraka-sambandha) by virtue of that [conscious] appearance; this is precisely what has been set forth. || 33 ||

And since the meaning of a word resides within the intellect, he states that for this reason the relationship between word and meaning is established as eternal: "Even though [the word] is non-eternal, its eternity exists by way of its denoted object; or else, its own power is what constitutes its non-eternality, and that power does not differ from the eternal. (34)

Since a cognition that grasps the form of an object always arises from the utterance of words such as "jar" (ghaṭa), even though the word perishes in its external form, the relationship between the signifier and the signified is eternal because the meaning of the word is eternal; thus, it was stated in the *Paspaśā* [section of the Mahābhāṣya] that "the connection of meaningful words with their meanings is eternal," by relying on the eternity of the stream [of usage].

Relying also upon the immutability of the eternally established, he says: because existence is incompatible with the non-existence of existing entities, that which produces the cognition "it does not exist" regarding the two paths of the past and the future is simply the power of one's own non-dual reality—the Self, Brahman, characterized as a substance. Therefore, since there is no difference from that eternal, non-dual form, the term "non-eternal" merely refers to that very same reality as it appears divided by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), according to the logic already stated. Thus, there is no such thing as "non-existence," for in its absence [there is nothing else].

The meaning is that [it is] "something" among existing things (*bhāva*). Consequently, by words such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*), it is established that the eternal substance of Brahman itself, qualified by [attributes] such as "clay-ness" (*upādhi*) in all its states, is what is expressed; thus, the eternal relationship between word and meaning is proven. As it has been said: "Even when the referent is a substance (*dravya*), this analysis (*vigraha*) is logical, provided that the word, the meaning, and the relationship are established. (Verse 34)

Having thus established the inherent nature of the relationship, he states there an argument for its strengthening according to the view of another: "The refinement of the meaning residing in the word, which serves both seen and unseen purposes, how could it be produced without a relationship? (35)

The capacity of spells such as those of Śabara and others to pacify poison and so forth is observed even though they do not express any [conventional] meaning here. Furthermore, the fact that seed-syllables (bījākṣara), which are well-known in their respective systems, serve as causes for the unseen (adṛṣṭa) when recited is inferred from this very [capacity]. Therefore, some maintain that even in the case of words that are non-expressive, a relation exists with the meaning because the mental impression (saṃskāra) would otherwise be inexplicable; thus, a determination of the relation occurs everywhere. 35.
He refutes this: "Such a latent impression (saṃskāra) is not necessarily [required] regarding the objects denoted; nor is such a relationship as you intend observed. (36)

Since no refinement (*saṃskāra*)—whether for a visible or invisible purpose—is observed in the case of objects such as a jar when derived from words like "jar," there would be no connection [of the word] to such an object here; therefore, this [word] is not intended to have such a refinement as its cause. || 36 ||
Moreover, a relationship is only possible when there is the state of being a condition and a cause; for it is understood that a relationship exists between a word and its object. (37)

The meaning is that our own position is superior: that the relationship between word and object is characterized by fitness (*yogyatā*), just as [the relationship] between the eye and visible form, because otherwise the communication of a specific object would be impossible. Since the causality of a fixed cognition regarding a fixed object is only logical when a relationship exists and not otherwise, it is therefore determined from the effect called the communication of the object that there is a relationship of the word to its object.

In this context, a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) that takes the form of a specific object or wealth is not the indicator of the relationship [between word and meaning], because such a cognition could arise even from something composed by a powerful person possessing only a particular sequence [of sounds], without depending on a [real] signifier. Therefore, the relationship between word and meaning—which is the cause for the restriction of the cognition of meaning—is produced by cognition and does not consist in physical contact; its establishment is due to the assistance characterized by cognition.

As for what the Mīmāṃsakas have stated—that the relationship is that by which the object is understood when the word is known—this too must be explained according to this very same view. For the reason that the cognition of the object arises immediately after hearing the word, that is the relationship; thus, what is being said is simply that [the relationship] consists in being the cause of the cognition [of the object]. Otherwise, if one were to describe a causal relation between the word and the object, the specific basis [for that relation] would necessarily have to be stated. || 37 ||

He states that a conventional (sāmayika) relationship, however, is not tenable: "Whether the object to be expressed be eternal or non-eternal, it is in no way possible for a person to establish a relationship between words whose [own] relationships have not already been established. (38)

First, regarding an eternal object—such as a universal (*jāti*) and so forth, or in the view that the meaning of an eternal word [is eternal]—it is impossible for a person to establish the convention (*saṅketa*) of a word for the first time with respect to anything whatsoever. This is precisely because of its eternality; for a person who has only now come into existence cannot have any prior activity (*avyāpāra*) toward it. Furthermore, whether one considers the view of eternal words or the fact that Brahman is the denotation of all words, since the connection between all words and their meanings was established by the Primordial Person (*ādipuruṣa*), it has been demonstrated that the capacity [of words] follows from that. And since the usage [of words] has proceeded from the beginning of creation, what else could there be besides eternality?

Even regarding impermanent objects such as jars or the perception of words as effects, it is impossible to grasp them in their entirety through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, even if they were grasped by way of universals (*jāti*), since many universals can coexist in a single object, their differentiation would be untenable. Moreover, since an object is understood through inference (*anumāna*) by means of the identity of the word, it is impossible for a convention (*saṅketa*) to be established for the sake of proving the word-meaning relationship [if that identity were not primary]. Therefore, by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), the convention must be made after the object has been determined by the words themselves.

And likewise, for words that define [an object], the same situation applies regarding their convention; thus, if those too are defined by other words, there would be an infinite regress, because definition is impossible for those for whom no convention has been established. Therefore, even after going very far, one must seek some word whose capacity is innate. And since this applies without distinction to all words, it follows that the relationship between word and meaning is innate, its nature being manifested through the force of convention. (38)

Now, regarding what was stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the *Matup-vārttika*: "So that [the suffix] may apply when there is existence at the present time, but not when there is non-existence in the past or future," he says the following in order to establish the eternality of the relationship under discussion, under the guise of explaining the existence of the past and the future: "In the designation of things, there is another, figurative existence which manifests the essential nature of all things in all their states. (39)

In designation, the cause of designation—the existence of external objects, which are the referents of words and are conveyed by speech, yet which is distinct from their external nature—is a mentally superimposed existence that differs from the existence of external objects; for it is of the nature of the form of objects as they have ascended into the intellect. Therefore, this [existence] is merely figurative (*aupacārikī*).

Metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) is superimposition (*adhyāropa*); since this is its purpose in all states, it manifests the form of the object even in past and future states, because the mental image (*buddhyākāra*) appears in that very form. Thus, because the objects of words such as "past" and "future" do exist [in this manner], the permanence of the relationship [between word and object] is indeed established. This same mode of existence applies to objects even in the state of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) or a qualified (*viśeṣya*).

Otherwise, how could there be a distinction for all [cognitions] regarding a reality that is eternally undifferentiated and partless? Thus, even words such as "hare's horn," which have non-existence as their object, involve the delineation of a mental image (*ākāra*). For words have as their object a thing determined by the intellect (*buddhi*); and the conceptualizing intellect arises in the form of grasping an image through the maturation of its own seeds and latent impressions (*vāsanā*), even when no external object exists.

And since an object is understood from a word in exactly that same way, words—having disregarded external existence—adhere to the object as it appears in the intellect. Thus, because even words such as "fire-brand circle" (*alātacakra*) or "hare's horn" (*śaśaviṣāṇa*) are eternally inseparable from their objects, the eternity of the relationship is established. For since linguistic practice occurs within the ascent of consciousness, it is logical that the existence of an object consists solely in being composed of that [consciousness]. Prior to consciousness, however, because it lacks any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), that existence is accessible only through faith.

And since the conceit of substantial existence (*sattābhimāna*) has been struck down therein, the linguistic usage of "figurative existence" (*upacārasattā*) is employed in accordance with that [conceit]. For this very reason, just as objects acquire their own nature, these [objects] lack any contact with form in the absence of the reflective awareness of words (*śabdaparāmarśa*). || 39 ||

And thus, when conventional discourse is already filled by this very existence (*sattā*), if some other existence is postulated based on a foundation such as the performance of causal efficiency—which is, for all intents and purposes, like wood-chaff—then let that [other existence] flourish; we have no concern with it. For it has no entry into our conventional discourse; at most, it is merely this very [primary] existence that is treated conventionally as being reflected therein. To demonstrate this, he begins with an illustration: "Just as a substance such as crystal, through its own inherent power, enters into a relationship of identity with various supporting objects of different forms. (40)
In the same way, the word also, having previously been established in this Being (sattā), enters into relation with properties that are both non-contradictory and contradictory. (41)

Since an external object possesses a fixed nature, it is impossible for it to be common to both existence and non-existence; therefore, when one says "jar," there would be a contradiction with the association of other forms imposed by subsequent words such as "exists" or "does not exist. Thus, the meaning of a word is permeated by a figurative (upacāra) existence. For instance—just like glass, clouds, or crystal—that object is capable of accommodating the specific forms imposed by other words which are common to all [entities]; thus, depending on the circumstances, it is perceived as fixed through its connection with existence and non-existence, according to whether one says "it exists" or "it does not exist."

For instance: because of its transparency, a substance such as crystal, while not abandoning its own nature when in contact with blue or other colors, appears as if it were that very color. Likewise, Being (sattā) itself—standing in the place of the crystal gem—without abandoning its own form, comes to assume their likeness when connected with limiting adjuncts (upadhāna) such as negations; it appears as if it were of the nature of those negations and so forth. Transparency is the inherent power of the crystal and the like to be capable of assuming various forms, and for Being as well, it is the capacity to take on all particularities.

Because its nature is universal (*sāmānyātmakatvāt*). "The word also" means the referent of the word, since it is that which is expressed by the word; or rather, the word, established as its signifier, is connected through its object with properties expressible by other words. The mention of "contradictory" is for the purpose of demonstrating totality. "In this existence" (*sattāyām asyām*) means in that which consists of the form of the cognitive image (*jñānākāra*). "Previously" refers to the stage of appearance, where there is the exclusion of glass and so forth from the word. Non-contradictory properties are those whose essence is positive existence (*bhāvātmaka*).

Furthermore, these [external objects], such as jasmine flowers and the like in relation to a crystal, are conducive to the existence of the metaphorical entity (*upacārasattā*); thus, they are not causes for the concealment of its true form. For this very reason, in their proximity, the existence of the metaphorical entity finds its rest in that very nature [of the substrate]. Indeed, the external existence is not contradictory to it, as it is proximate by virtue of its full form. And so it is said: "Where another verb is not heard, there the verb *asti* (is) is understood, with the present tense suffix," and so forth.

And because the present state is that which renders [the essence] complete, it is said to be "beyond becoming" (*bhavanti-para*). Alternatively, existence (*sattā*) is the commonality of contradictory attributes; its fulfillment occurs through its respective particularities (*viśeṣa*). As for the contradictory attributes, they consist of non-existence, for they are of the nature of negation. They effect the concealment of form, just as the *japā* flower and the like [conceal the color] of a crystal, in the case of the metaphorical existence (*upacāra-sattā*).

Although there is no contradiction regarding the application of both [the substance and the quality] within the context of metaphorical existence (*upacārasattā*), this is nevertheless stated here with reference to external objects. Because an external object such as a blue lotus is non-different from its specific qualities, it is distinguished as "the blue lotus" precisely within metaphorical existence; thus, the essence of the substance is apprehended as distinct due to the difference in its association with qualities. Furthermore, the process to be described later is applicable to the relationship between qualifier and qualified in expressions such as "separately. Just as a pure crystal appears variously according to the different substances with which it is joined.
"It is perceived as having colors such as blue, red, yellow, and so forth"—this is another scriptural reading here. (40–41)

He explains that very relationship between contradictory and non-contradictory properties in sequence: "And thus, when [properties] are resorted to by way of metaphorical attribution (upacāra) among those things to be negated, in order to establish the negation, the negation proceeds. (42)

The application of the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) in cases such as "non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇa*) is possible because the mental form (*buddhyākāra*) is capable of being associated with various properties (*dharma*). To explain: since it is impossible to negate that which exists due to its contradiction with non-existence, a Brahmin does not exist here [in the sense of the negation]. But if he were non-existent, how could there be the application of a word to him for those who maintain that the external object is the word-meaning? Furthermore, in that case, the negation itself would be untenable. As it has been said: "There is no negation of things that exist, nor is there any among things that do not exist. By this logic, the meaning of the negative particle has come to an end in the world."

Thus, when the meaning of a word is permeated by metaphorical existence (*upacārasattā*), then—by way of generality and through its commonality with both existence and non-existence—the referent "brāhmaṇa" is projected onto kṣatriyas and others due to similarity, and this superimposed meaning of "brāhmaṇa" is brought to mind. Once the object of negation has been shown, the negation "not" (*na*) proceeds; for a negation cannot function without an object.

Furthermore, since the form of a cognition is not necessarily restricted to existence alone—because it exists only through the very existence of the cognition itself—it cannot be negated as something common [to both]. Therefore, the negation results only with respect to that external form which is superimposed by those engaged in worldly transaction (*vyavahārin*) through the unification of the perceived and the conceptualized. For instance, when it is said, "This object which is a Brāhmaṇa is not outside [the Kṣatriya]," the negative particle (*nañ*) illuminates here the cessation of the natural status of being a Brāhmaṇa, insofar as it has been merely superimposed upon a Kṣatriya due to delusion while not existing externally.

This has been stated in the Bhāṣya: "If, however, this word *brāhmaṇa* has its referent (*padārtha*) ceased, for what purpose is it employed? It is so that it may be understood thus; for if one were simply to say 'not,' there would be doubt as to whose referent is being negated. Here, since usage would be impossible if the referent were ceased in every respect, the state of having a ceased referent is only with respect to external objects. It is clearly stated, therefore, that usage occurs with respect to figurative existence (*upacārasattā*).
And the employment [of a term] is for the purpose of conceptualizing the object of negation; thus, that alone is the fruit of metaphorical usage (upacāra). || 42 ||

In order to demonstrate that [the relationship with] non-contradictory properties belongs only to that which is permeated by figurative existence (*upacārasattā*), he first states its impossibility in the case of primary existence (*mukhyasattā*): "The acquisition of self-nature is called 'birth'; existence is that which is acquired, and that which is to be acquired is acquired. If that which exists is born, from what could it be born? Or if that which does not exist is born, how can it be born? (43)

The attainment of its own nature (*ātmalābha*), that is, the acquisition of a thing's essential form, is called "birth. In this regard, a triad is invariably present: the attainer (*labdhṛ*, the agent), the object to be attained (*labhya*, the object), and the act of attaining (*lābha*, the action). This triad has existence as its domain; thus, there is a contradiction between birth and existence, because that which exists cannot undergo the attainment of its own nature. For it is only that which has already attained its own self (*labdhātmā*) that is said to be "existent."

Even if the cause exists in the form of a potentiality (*śakti*), since the birth of that which is entirely non-existent is impossible, one must necessarily admit the acquisition of some previously non-existent factor. Consequently, that form in which [the cause] exists cannot be the form in which there is birth, and that form in which there is birth cannot be the form in which it exists; thus, the linguistic usage "the sprout is born" (*aṅkuro jāyate*) is untenable. If one admits non-existence in order to conform to the fact of birth, then because agency (*kartṛtva*) is impossible for the substratum of the verbal root's meaning (*dhātvartha*), there is a contradiction with the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*). Conversely, if one admits existence in order to conform to that [suffix], there is a contradiction with the meaning of the verbal root characterized as birth. This is the sense. || 43 ||

Regarding this very point, he states a corresponding illustration: "For the movement of an existing mover proceeds toward an existing object of motion; if [the mover] were like the mover [in the case of non-existence], the purpose of birth would not exist, and likewise, it is not born. (44)

The action of going, characterized by the extension of one's own nature, is similar to the action of being born. In that case, movement is observed to belong only to an existing goer, having as its object an external, existent form distinct [from the goer]. Likewise here too, for that which is about to manifest, birth is untenable—just as it is for the goer. If, on the other hand, birth is admitted, then since it arises from what already exists, how can there be an agent? Thus, the status of being an agent is impossible. Furthermore, just like the "object to be gone to" (*gamyam*), there is no separate "thing to be obtained" (*labdhavya*) here either; thus, if one accepts the existence of external word-meanings, this [theory] is untenable. (44)

However, he says that birth occurs by means of the substratum of the sentient being who has taken possession [of a body]: "But for the sake of the operation of verbal designation, one metaphorically designates an agent; and again, [one designates] that action as an object and its substratum. (45)

Therefore, in that case, the suffixes such as *la* and others must be understood as denoting a figurative existence; for a primary existence does not exist there, because it is contradictory to [the notion of] birth. (46)

The word "tu" (but) highlights the distinction of metaphorical existence (*upacārasattā*) from external existence (*bāhyasattā*) by virtue of its capacity to encompass everything. Here, that which is established in its entirety is not designated as "being born"; nor is it something whose nature is entirely non-existent. Rather, the object of the term "is born" is a thing that possesses a nature both existent and non-existent, which assumes prior and subsequent states and is oriented toward the attainment of existence.

And thus, by figuratively attributing there [to the seed] a subsequent state of non-existence—characterized by the causes' orientation toward the effect during their prior state—the application of the designation "sprout" occurs, whereby the status of being an agent in the sense of "it is born" (*jāyate*) is established. Furthermore, because it has relied upon its prior state, the meaning of "birth" is also established. And this being the case, the object of the designation "is born" is the essential nature of the thing which, having relied upon its prior state and figuratively assumed its subsequent state, becomes coagulated (*saṃmūrchita*).

And because the agent alone is metaphorically designated as the "object" (karman) by virtue of being obtainable through recourse to his prior state, this analysis is undertaken based on the understanding that no other [factor] is so designated. Thus, the "basis" (āśraya)—meaning the locus—of those two means (sādhana), namely the agent and the object, is the cause of their status as means, since that status depends upon the action; or else, the reading may be interpreted both ways: that the agent and the object are the basis of [the action], because its birth is dependent upon those means.

By superimposing upon that act of arising—which consists of a collection of parts occurring in a temporal sequence—the expression "the sprout is born" (*jāyate 'ṅkuraḥ*) is justified. The word *atha* serves to indicate this acceptance. And this being the case, it is only a metaphorical existence (*upacārasattā*) that is thus resorted to. Consequently, in that very context, there occurs the verb ending *-ti* in "this is born" (*ayaṃ jāyate*), the past passive participle suffix *-kta* in "it has been born" (*jātaḥ*), the agentive suffix *-ktavat* in "it has become born" (*jātavān*), and the genitive case in "the birth of the sprout" (*janma aṅkurasya*).

Alternatively, by the conceptualization of an agent, the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) is a suffix denoting the agent (*kartari pratyaya*); by the conceptualization of an action, the verbal root (*dhātu*) is the base (*prakṛti*); and by the conceptualization of an object, in the sentence explaining the "object-agent" (*karmakartṛ*), the sprout obtains its own self; thus, the accusative case is used for the object (*karmaṇi*). The same should be stated for such expressions as "existing while sustaining itself by itself" (*ātmānam ātmanā bibhrad asti*). Or rather, this entire apparatus is "figurative existence" (*upacārasattā*); because it is based on that [figurative existence], there is such a designation through non-difference. However, primary existence (*mukhyā sattā*) is not tenable, due to the contradiction previously mentioned.

Therefore, this prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that birth is the acquisition of self-nature (*ātmalābha*). The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that birth is the state of being oriented toward the acquisition of self-nature. And so he will say: "Falling away from the previous state and not yet having reached the subsequent state, that which serves as the locus for the various distinctions in the interval between them is called 'birth'. Likewise: "Not abandoning the prior state while touching upon the subsequent state, the essence of an object, as if in a state of coagulation (*saṃmūrchita*), is designated as 'being born' (*jāyamāna*)."
Furthermore, there is a reading in some places as "tam" (him) in the sense of an object (*karmabhāvena*). In that case, the construction is: "he again treats that very agent as an object. 45, 46.

Now, regarding existence occurring at a time subsequent to birth—a modification of the entity—the word "this exists" (*asti*) expresses that very thing as being permeated by a metaphorical reality (*upacārasattā*), for otherwise it would be untenable; thus he says: "Bearing itself by itself, it is designated as 'it exists. And because [the action] is included within it, it is not transitive with respect to that object. (47)

The meaning of the root *as* (to be) is "to sustain oneself by oneself. Thus says the author of the *Nirukta*: "The term 'is' refers to the sustaining of one's own self by that which has arisen. The expression "by oneself" (*ātmanā*) is intended to negate a separate agent. Accordingly, the meaning is that there is no real distinction between agent, object, and action, because a thing possesses a distinct nature [in these respects]. To the objection that since the root *as* is transitive when used with "by oneself," its well-known intransitivity would be lost, he replies: "Because it is included within," and so forth.

The word *asau* refers either to the verbal root *as-* or to its meaning. He explains this incidentally by showing that because the object (*karman*) is subsumed within the meaning of the root, this root-meaning is intransitive (*akarmaka*). Just as in the case of the root *jīv-*, since the object characterized as the self (*ātman*)—namely, the vital breaths (*prāṇa*)—is denoted by the root, this [root *dhṛ-*] is explained as a distinct action: "the self sustains itself by means of the self. The meaning is that here there is no connection with an object in the sense of a substantial entity (*bhāva*). As he will state: "In that case, there is neither a root *dhṛ-* nor the vital breaths; rather, *jīvati* is a distinct action."

Likewise, in the case of the expression "is born" (*jāyate*), when the meaning is defined as "obtains a self," one should understand that the status of being an object (*karmatva*) is inherently included. For that which is external to the primary meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*)—namely, the sense of succession—is the cause for the designation of a verb as "transitive" (*sakarmaka*). When the completion of the root's own meaning has been achieved, if there is a connection with something external to it based on a distinction [from that original meaning], then the status of being an object—whether expressed directly by words as in "bring the cow" (*gām ānaya*), or obtained through contextual implication as in "enter [and eat] the cake" (*piṇḍīm praviśa*)—is the basis for the designation of a verb as transitive.

In this case, however, since the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha) extends as far as the connection between the action and its factors (kriyākārakasaṃsarga), there is an absence of distinction [between the root-meaning and the sentence-meaning]. || 47 ||

Having thus demonstrated that this conventional usage is not logically tenable from the standpoint of ultimate reality due to the absence of any differentiation, [the author] now demonstrates its logical possibility only within the context of metaphorical existence (*upacārasattā*), because [an entity] cannot possess agency—as in the expression "it is born"—and because it lacks an essential nature (*svarūpa*). "And prior to its connection with existence, how could there be primary existence? Being non-existent, it could not be the agent of the verb 'to exist' (√as); however, the metaphorical usage is as explained before. (48)

The notion that "it exists" (*asti*) refers to an existence (*sattā*) consisting of a temporal sequence of prior and posterior stages, which is understood as being in a state of being accomplished (*sādhyamānāvasthā*). In this state, there is no agent (*kartṛ*) possessing a completed form (*niṣpannarūpa*), nor does there exist a presence [of the agent] even prior to its connection with the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). Furthermore, no object distinct from these two is perceived here as the means of accomplishment. Thus, in a primary sense, it is impossible for that very same existence to be both the object to be accomplished and the means of accomplishment. For indeed, the means of accomplishment must exist in a completed form (*siddharūpa*).

Nor is existence itself perceived as something already established; and since existence, once its relation to the experienced object has been established, is no longer the probandum, the existence characterized by the maintenance of self for that which has attained its own being is expressed by the intellect precisely as a process consisting of a prior and subsequent sequence.

In that regard, for that which has ascended to the level of figurative existence (*upacāra-sattā*), the prior portion is the agent (*kartṛ*) and the subsequent portion is the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*, *karman*); since both are included within the nature of the action (*kriyā*) which rests upon them, the usage "it exists" (*asti*) is justified by relying on agency through figurative existence, just as one says "it is born" (*jāyate*). Thus, the usages "it exists," "it does not exist," and "it is born" are established by resorting to figurative existence. These alone are the three modifications of being (*bhāva-vikāra*), and the other three [modifications] are included within these very ones.

For instance, since growth (*vṛddhi*) consists of the accumulation of parts and is thus included within "birth" (*janman*), this usage of "grows" (*vardhate*) must be justified in the same manner as "is born" (*jāyate*). Likewise, transformation (*pariṇāma*), characterized by the manifestation of a different property, is included within this very [category]; this is to be understood through the same principle applied to the term "transforms" (*pariṇamate*).

Since "complete exhaustion" (parikṣaya) does not exist [as a separate category], it is included within "destruction" (vināśa); even there, the usage "it is completely exhausted" is to be justified by resorting to metaphorical existence (upacārasattā). Thus, because the entire manifold of activity (kriyāprapañca) originates from the six modes of being, linguistic usage is based upon conceptual existence (bauddhasattā). || 48 ||

Since actions imply their means, the words denoting those means are likewise employed; thus, he states the following to conclude the universal pervasion (*vyāpti*) that the existence of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) constitutes the meaning of words: "Therefore, among distinct and contradictory properties, there exists a non-contradictory [quality] which is resorted to by those very words solely for the purpose of manifesting the contradiction. (49)
[The speaker conceives] that which exists at a single time across objects situated at different times, as the figurative cause of application for all words. (50)
For no entity whatsoever transcends this being (sattā); and it has been demonstrated in the Bhāṣya that this [being] is distinct from present being (sampratisattā).

For those external properties such as existence (*bhāva*) and so forth that are mutually contradictory, there is no contradiction with their metaphorical existence (*upacārasattā*), according to the reasoning already stated. For this very reason, he says: "Precisely for the purpose of manifesting the contradictions. This means [existence] is grasped by various words such as "Brahmin" and so on, for the sake of revealing those contradictories. By these words, the object of the properties is indicated; and those properties are distinct from the external thing, because the distinction is merely conceptualized (*parikalpita*) by the word itself.

He states that even by words such as "blue lotus," which refer to objects like blue lotuses through the relation of qualifier and qualified—whether by way of a contradictory or a distinct existing entity, or by means of repetition (vīpsā)—these [conceptual constructs] are resorted to. Even in that case, the process of differentiation and integration is appropriate within the context of figurative existence (upacārasattā). Otherwise, as has been stated, this conceptual construction would not be possible regarding an object that is a mere conglomeration. Furthermore, because it pervades both past and future times, this [conceptual construct], though restricted to specific moments, is universal and applies to external objects across all times.

For this very reason, this [mental apprehension] is the cause for the application of all words. This is because words are applied to an object only after it has been determined by the intellect as "Caitra existed" or "he will exist," since such application is impossible regarding an object not so determined. Thus, even an existing object belonging to the present time remains outside the scope of words as long as it is not grasped by the intellect; therefore, it is stated that in all cases, the meaning of a word is established solely upon its existence as a mental construct (*upacāra*). Furthermore, the determination of objects through the relationship of action and agent is likewise purely mental.

For indeed, because it is currently being cultivated (bhāvyamāna), the action does not exist at present; and since that [action] is absent, how can there be the status of a means (sādhanatva) dependent upon it? Thus, for every verbal form denoting action and for every nominal stem (subanta) denoting a factor of action (kāraka), the expressed meaning remains as one grasped by the intellect and permeated by metaphorical existence (upacārasattā); therefore, the universal pervasion (vyāpti) of all [words] is established.

Since non-existence (*abhāva*) exists by virtue of being cognizable, no category of entity whatsoever transcends this metaphorical existence (*upacārasattā*). Therefore, because all [entities] are objects of that [cognition], even words such as "non-existence" are eternally inseparable from their referents; this is established. Furthermore, this metaphorical existence is not without foundation, but is indeed accepted by the author of the Bhāṣya himself.

In the *Matup-vārttika*, it is stated that "the category of existence (*sattā*) does not deviate from the referent of a word. Since this implies the meaning of the word "exists" (*asti*), in order to justify that [usage], it is said: "So that it may apply to present existence, but not to past or future existence—as in 'cows were his' (*gāvo'syāsan*) or 'cows will be his' (*gāvo'sya bhavitāraḥ*). From this statement in the *Bhāṣya*, it is understood that figurative existence (*upacārasattā*) exists, for this statement is authoritative (*pramāṇabhūta*). Indeed, there is no such thing as a past or future existence that could be deliberated upon by the word "exists" (*asti*).

Since the past and the future lack any describable nature, they possess no primary existence whatsoever. However, because the past has been experienced and the future will be encountered through its causal efficiency, when these are apprehended by the intellect, linguistic usage is applied to objects that exist within the flux of cognition; thus, a figurative existence (*upacāra-sattā*) is possible for the past and the future. Consequently, in order to exclude those [two] and to embrace external existence, the qualification "exists" (*asti*) is appropriate.

For external existence is one thing, which occurs at the present time; distinct from that is this existence which consists of the cognition of the past and the future. Although even the existence of an external object in its present state is to be designated as existent only by virtue of being grasped through cognition, nevertheless, that very same [existence] is intended by the qualification "exists externally" as referring to the present time. Any other [existence], however, which relies solely on mere cognition, is excluded.

Thus, since external objects themselves—whose intrinsic natures have been projected onto the existence of the metaphorical—are conveyed through states such as the past and so forth, verbal usage is indeed in accordance with reality; in this way, the eternity of the relationship [between word and meaning] has been established. (Verses 49, 50, 51)

Now, since all verbal usage proceeds according to reality and is thus not subject to confusion, one must admit that words such as "cow" possess a meaning established even without investigation. And so, he begins to demonstrate the equality of words—even those whose objects are non-existent things like the past and so forth—with words such as "jar," which are considered to have positive entities as their objects: "Verbal usage proceeds by way of [denoting] a part of a location, or by way of a characterization through another [object], or by way of error, or by way of non-existence. (52)

In this world, verbal discourse proceeds for those of limited vision in a manner that does not correspond to reality. For, since it is impossible for words to directly touch the fullness of reality (*tattva*), verbal discourse pertains only to specific delimited objects such as jars, which are mentally constructed by ignorance (*avidyā*). By the term "delimited object" (*pradeśa*), it is indicated that a jar or similar thing is but a single part of Brahman; this is intended to demonstrate the incapacity of words to encompass the entire reality.

Furthermore, it is not the entire spatial locus consisting of a collection of parts that is denoted by a word, but rather a single part of it. For instance, by the word "jar" (*ghaṭa*), the universal "jarness" (*ghaṭatva-jāti*) is expressed; in that very same [locus], the quality "redness" is expressed by the word "red" (*rakta*). In this manner, one should provide examples of the denotation of specific entities by other words as well, as well as their determination by other factors such as universals.

In the view that [the universal] arises from association, a cow is not a cow by itself; rather, it is a cow through its connection with "cowness. Thus, a substance that is essentially like Brahman—directly beyond all empirical usage—enters into empirical discourse only when its specific form is imparted by another. In that regard, error consists in the differentiation of the non-differentiated Brahman due to the influence of various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Alternatively, according to the Vijñānavāda school, erroneous cognition (*viparītakhyāti*) is the appearance of an external form as having an external nature.

In the view of the proponents of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*), non-existence is conventional, because external objects are denied in every respect and because consciousness alone cannot possess a plurality of forms; thus, this entire variety of distinctions has words as its object. Therefore, in these four philosophical systems, the relationship between words and their meanings is not real. For instance, in the first system, there is an object for words such as "cow" and the like; however, a relationship would only be possible there if that objective portion were to become the range of cognition. But it does not so become, because it is not determined through discernment.

Furthermore, other properties (*dharma*) are admitted that are beyond the reach of the senses; therefore, even in this case, the connection with the object is not complete. In the other alternative positions, the connection is unestablished precisely because of the absence of an object. For instance, in the case of determination by another, that which is being imparted a form is itself formless, yet it is determined and expressed as having form; thus, the connection does not have a real entity as its object. The same should be stated regarding the two positions concerning the absence of error (*viparyaya*). || 52 ||

He establishes this very point by means of an illustration: "Just as, due to a defect in the sense organ, a cognition arises from objects as if it were superimposing existence, so too does the cognition born of mere enumeration. (53)

One whose vision is impaired by cataracts (*timira*) sees even a single moon as many; one suffering from jaundice (*kāmalin*) perceives even a white conch shell as yellow. Due to a defect in the sense organ (*indriya-doṣa*), a cognition arises from objects that appears as an object colored by another form. Because [the cognition] is dependent on those objects and because its objects are fixed, the superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of the properties of the cognition does not affect the real thing (*vastu*). This is the meaning of the word "as it were" (*iva*). Thus, that by which something is pointed out or explained is the "designation" (*uddeśa*), namely, the word.
The cognition produced from that [word] becomes possessed of a superimposition of an unreal form. (53)

He asks: "What defect is there in the word, as compared to the sense organ? He replies: "Depending upon a cognition in which the object does not appear in its entirety, the word expresses the object through another form, [an object] that is not determined in its own true nature. (54)

In this world, the effect conforms to its cause. Since sound has as its object an entity that has been conceptually determined (*nirūpita*), the cognition of determination (*nirūpaṇā-pratyaya*) is its cause. As it has been said: "And thus, from an object that is the domain of the intellect, the word is cognized. Furthermore, the cognition of determination is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). And because it is restricted to the exclusion of each [other] individual, conceptual construction presents an appearance of an incomplete object. For it has been stated that an object is not touched by conceptual construction according to its true nature, because it touches it only through a partial location or a single part, and so forth.

Therefore, a word conveys only an incomplete object, one whose distinct forms are superimposed [upon it]. For a cognition consisting of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arises from a word by virtue of the relationship between cause and effect. As it has been said: "Words have conceptual constructions as their source; conceptual constructions have words as their source. Likewise: "The meaning of a word is that which is grasped by a conceptual construction based on its effect and its material cause."

Thus, because of the dullness of ignorance, conceptual constructions lack the proficiency to determine things according to their true nature; since all disputants admit that determination occurs through a superimposed form, it is established that all words—having as their objects the referents presented by those [constructions]—have as their domain external objects that do not exist [ultimately], and they denote forms mounted upon cognition. Therefore, one should not dispute the connection between words such as "past" and so forth with their referents. || 54 ||

In this regard, one might think: "For those whose cognition is free from obscuration and who perceive the true nature of reality, verbal discourse is indeed consistent with reality; and since they are our teachers, that discourse is not unreal. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Abiding on the worldly path through both conceptualization and verbal designation, knowledge and expression are similar to the perceptions of infants and the masses. (55)

Because worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) consists in the convergence of mutual intentions, those who possess pure vision and perceive the reality of existence (*bhāvatattva*), even while engaging in worldly transactions, are similar to other ordinary people of limited vision (*arvāgdarśana*), as they likewise abide on the path of the world. "Forming" (*rūpaṇa*) means perceiving (*ālocana*). Having perceived, the conveying [of that object] by means of a word is "designation" (*vyapadeśa*). Those who engage in transactions by means of these two are equal [to others] on the mundane path. To the question "In what respect? he says: "With regard to knowledge," and so forth.

The cognition of a child whose mind is perverted, which consists of the conceptualization of objects and verbal expression in the form of designation—these [cognitions] pertain to that object. Just as a child conceptualizes an object and expresses it, so too do the wise who perceive ultimate reality. For they too, having examined and intended to speak of an object, designate it exactly according to their intention, thereby beginning to synthesize with the perspective of others.

Just as they first determine the very intention of another, so too their knowledge of that determination is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and the verbal expression preceded by it is like ordinary worldly speech. However, in that state of theirs which transcends conventional usage, there is pure knowledge, ultimate and non-conceptualizing. || 55 ||

If cognition always grasps only its own specifically determined object, what then is its purity? To this he says: "The purity of cognition is its state of being the form of all objects, which is independent of any external support. Beyond even that, some declare its supreme purity to be formless. (56)

The two "decades" consist of the commencement and the completion of purification. At the commencement, the omniscient knowledge—which is inlaid with the manifestation of all objects due to its independence from external supports such as the contact of the senses—is said to be pure. This is because no impurity, consisting of dependence on the senses and so forth, is perceived in its apprehension of its own objects. And at the conclusion, due to the disappearance of the turbidity of forms, it is the Supreme Brahman: pure, consisting of a single mass of consciousness, luminous, with its waves stilled, devoid of the manifold expansion of subject and object.

For he says that the apprehension of a fixed form is indeed impurity: "The falling away from knowledge is its following after external forms; it is like a turbidity produced by the intermingling [of elements] during contact. (57)

When there is contact with an object, that very object causes a differentiation within pure consciousness; through the power of reflection, this results in non-differentiation, a state of intermingling. From this arises this affliction—the outward orientation toward external objects—just as water becomes turbid through contact with dust. Upon the removal of that [affliction], there is a gradual abiding in one's own clear nature; this supreme purity is accepted by all philosophical systems. Thus it is said: "Then the seer abides in his own nature. By the word *iva* (as if), he indicates that although there is a commingling with the form of the object, the self-luminous nature of consciousness remains unperceived. || 57 ||

He states that even the object is impure in conventional usage: "And just as cognition, due to its representation, remains impure, so too the object, by virtue of its dependence [on cognition], is removed from its own true nature. (58)

"Ālekhya" (representation) is the coloring by the form of the object. Therefore, having established that knowledge is impure, [the author] provides an illustration for the point to be proven, namely, the impurity of the object. "Upāśraya" (substratum) refers to the genus and so forth, which act as an "upadhāna" (adjunct); through that medium, the object enters the path of linguistic usage according to how it is perceived. Since that [object] devoid of adjuncts is not amenable to linguistic usage, the contact with adjuncts—which is unreal—is this impurity of the object.

An objective entity is perceived and designated as variegated by means of its inherent limiting adjuncts (upādhi), such as genus (jāti) and so forth; it is thus that it enters into linguistic usage. However, the substance is not in every respect indefinable, for its very nature is that which is conjoined with limiting adjuncts, since it is always cognized as being conjoined with them. || 58 ||

He applies the stated meaning to the present context: "Thus, when there is a reversal of the object, the word, and the cognition, they follow worldly convention through the distinction between existence and non-existence. (59)

The impurity of an object consists in its being colored by association with universals (*jāti*) and so forth. The word, too, is impure because it denotes an incomplete object and because it denotes [the object] through the form of that [external] adjunct (*upādhi*). Knowledge is impure due to the coloring by an external form. Thus, all three are distorted. Consequently, even a positive entity (*bhāva*), when denoted by a word or when arising, stands on an equal footing with a non-entity (*abhāva*) because it exists only as a form dependent on another.

For even non-existence—such as the non-existence of a jar or the non-existence of a cloth—is subject to verbal designation and cognition only through extrinsic adjuncts (*paropādhi*); thus, there is a parity between the two. Indeed, when non-existence is examined by the intellect, it is delimited precisely by the form of existence. That which is its ultimate nature is the very basis for linguistic usage. Now, an objection may be raised: "Error is a property of the cognizer; therefore, let it be said that the cognizer alone is mistaken. But how can the object itself be mistaken? It is replied: [The text continues: ...For even non-existence—such as the non-existence of a jar or the non-existence of a cloth—is subject to verbal designation and cognition only through extrinsic adjuncts; thus, there is a parity between the two. Indeed, when non-existence is examined by the intellect, it is delimited precisely by the form of existence. That which is its ultimate nature is the very basis for linguistic usage. Now, an objection may be raised: "Error is a property of the cognizer; therefore, let it be said that the cognizer alone is mistaken. But how can the object itself be mistaken? It is replied: [the error belongs to the object as well].
Because it is the object of error and does not appear in its own true nature, the object is likewise [erroneous]; and the word is also said to be so because it is the cause of error. (59)

To the question, "How does [the distinction] enter into conventional discourse without being differentiated? he says: "Just as the non-existence of a thing is understood by relying upon its existence, so too the existence of that thing is understood by relying upon its non-existence. (60)

Since non-existence devoid of any limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is indistinguishable [from mere nothingness], it is through the limiting adjunct of existence that practical discourse (*vyavahāra*) enters into it. Even for existence, since its reality is established only at the stage of its manifestation, in practical discourse its essence is precisely that which is delimited by prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*). Furthermore, even in the case of eternal entities, because they do not manifest prior to the time of their manifestation, their practical discourse as non-existent does not differ [from the case of other things]. || 60 ||

Thus, having accepted the distinction between existence and non-existence, it has been demonstrated that they are equal in conventional usage due to their mutual dependence. Now, in order to refute non-existence as something distinct from existence, he says: "Non-existence is not born, nor does existence pass into the state of the indefinable (*anupākhyatā*); existence and non-existence are conceptualized as non-different from the one Self. (61)

In the dualist system (*dvaitanaya*), the production of an entity occurs through the destruction of its prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*); the occurrence of a subsequent non-existence (*pradhvaṃsa*) occurs through the destruction of the entity. Both of these are untenable, because it is impossible for existence and non-existence to assume each other’s essential nature (*svabhāva*), since an essential nature cannot be lost. Consequently, if there were absolute distinction between them, there could be no cognition of non-existence as having existence as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), nor of existence as having non-existence as its limiting adjunct.

Therefore, the single, non-dual reality, denoted by the word *ātman*, appears in the state of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) and during the condition of conceptualization (*vikalpa*) as divided into the forms of the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) of existence and non-existence. For when the supreme reality—which is of the nature of light, whose essence is entirely undifferentiated, which is the Great Being (*mahāsattā*), and which is the counter-correlative of non-existence—manifests externally as "this" due to the power of ignorance (*avidyā*), it assumes the form of existence; this manifestation is capable of effecting the worldly course of conventional reality (*saṃvṛta-lokayātrā*) and functions as an agent of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākārin*) through the limiting condition of the present time.

Because they persist internally in the form of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), conditioned by the times of the past and the future, and because they do not attain the status of objects for the external senses, they are treated as non-existent (*abhāva*) despite performing causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) common to all cognizers. Nor is it the case that they are entirely non-existent at those times, since they are both remembered and mentally constructed (*utprekṣyamāṇa*). Thus, for one for whom these entities exist in the form of latent impressions, those [entities] present in memory or mental construction certainly perform some kind of causal efficiency.

For this very reason, the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the very nature of an entity in its intermediate state is designated as "non-existence" when it is in a condition not clearly discernible by the senses; likewise, the subsequent non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) is so designated after that time. However, when the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of an entity have ceased in every respect, no such thing as "non-existence" characterized by a total absence of all causal capacity appears in the mind. Therefore, since entities are proclaimed to belong to the three times, there is no such thing as non-existence. 61.

In this regard, one might ask: "How are existence and non-existence conceptualized? Anticipating the objection that they must be real because their causes differ, and that they ought to exist according to how they are perceived, [the author] proceeds to establish his own position on the doctrine of non-duality by refuting dualistic views through a demonstration of the impossibility of the relation between cause and effect based on the distinction between the positions of existence and non-existence: "Since non-existence is indefinable, a cause cannot establish it.
But what can a cause do for an existent thing that already possesses definition? (62)

In this world, a cause operates with the aim of bringing about the acquisition of its own nature by the effect. In that regard, since that which lacks intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva) cannot serve as an aim, depending upon what could the causal process be established? If it exists by way of its universal nature (jātyātmanā), then because that [universal] is eternal, its being an effect would be impossible; thus, where again would the cause operate? If it is argued that there is some kind of non-difference between the universal and the individual, then the effect would exist by way of the individual's nature, and the aforementioned fault remains. Furthermore, there would be no apprehension of a specific, restricted cause.

Since there would be no distinction for that which is non-existent, it would likewise flow even from sand. If it is argued that the cause possesses a restricted power, how is this determined? If it is argued that [the effect] exists when that [cause] is present, this very point is being questioned: "How can there be the existence of that which is absolutely non-existent when that [cause] is present? If it is argued that there is no fault because it is perceived, this very point is being questioned: "How can there be the existence of that which is absolutely non-existent when that [cause] is present?"

If it is argued that there is no fault because [the causal relation] is commonly recognized, then let there be mere recognition; what is the use of describing a cause-and-effect relationship that lacks logical justification? And so he will establish in his final position: "The essential nature of entities, which previously did not exist, becomes manifest. Now, if one holds that the effect exists [prior to its production] and the cause [is merely its manifestation], these faults do not apply. Even in this view, since the cause would be acting upon what is already accomplished, the cause would be ineffective. For it is not tenable that the cause operates here, yet nothing new is attained.

Now, as for manifestation (*abhivyakti*), it is produced by the cause acting upon the effect; is this [manifestation] different from that [effect], or not? If it were different, would it be existent or non-existent? If it were existent, then—just as before—it would be impossible for a cause to produce it. If another manifestation were to be produced, the same difficulty would recur, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If it were non-existent, then the production of what is non-existent (*asataḥ janma*) would follow; and if that were so, why this aversion toward the effect itself? Furthermore, if manifestation were produced by the operation of the cause, the effect could no longer possess the status of being an "effect" (*kāryatā*).

Furthermore, if another entity arises, what is it that causes this [manifestation] to arise without even being suspected? If you say it is due to the cause of the manifestation of its relation [to the manifestor], then what is this relation between the produced and the producer? Even if such a relation exists, if the manifestation were produced by that [relation], then the operation of the cause would not have that [entity] as its object, because the manifestation would be produced by the effect itself. Likewise, if the effect were produced, the operation of the cause would also not have that [entity] as its object. And thus, if that which is non-existent were produced, there would be the undesirable consequence of the theory of *asatkāryavāda* (the non-existence of the effect in the cause).

Even if [the manifestation] exists, this same problem recurs: if it is argued that the relationship between the manifestation and its effect is one of beneficiary and benefactor (*upakāryopakāraka-bhāva*), by what means is the benefit conferred? And is that [benefit] distinct or non-distinct [from the manifestation]? If it is distinct, what is the meaning of the genitive case in "of that" (*tasya*)? If another benefit is postulated, the same objection applies and there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). But if it is non-distinct, it ultimately results in nothing other than the relationship of producer and produced (*janyajanaka-bhāva*).

And in that case, the fault has already been stated: if there is non-difference [of cause and effect], then because manifestation is the effect, the cause itself would be something produced; thus, one would be resorting to the theory of the non-existent effect (*asatkāryavāda*). Furthermore, the impossibility of that position has been demonstrated. Therefore, this path is a difficult strait.

And thus, because the status of being an effect is negated, both antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*)—which have as their objects things produced by action—do not exist either. This concludes the previously mentioned point that existence and non-existence are merely conceptualized through different states: "Therefore, everything is held to be either non-existence or existence; there is no other state whatsoever that exists independently of the one Reality. (63)

Because of the absence of a causal relationship, it is not tenable that a single entity—which is unproduced and unmanifest in its prior and subsequent states, yet produced and manifest in the intermediate state, and which perishes through connection with a cause of destruction—should possess both existence and non-existence. Therefore, existence and non-existence are not real states belonging to a single persisting entity based on the view of transformation; rather, within the context of conventional practice, which consists of the activity of ignorance, they are merely states of the real, undivided pure consciousness. However...

In the state of empirical transaction (*vyavahāra*), which consists of the activity of ignorance (*avidyā*), the reality (*tattva*) that is pure non-dual consciousness does not appear as it truly is; therefore, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārthataḥ*), the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is indeed non-existent and merely non-ultimate. And since that [non-existence] is formless and nothing at all, it cannot tolerate being the negation of an entity (*bhāva-vyatireka*).
