For only something possessing a form can be excluded from something else. Furthermore, because mere difference—which consists in the non-apprehension of the non-dual reality—is itself a void (*śūnya*).

However, in its conventional form (*sāṃvṛta-rūpa*), everything consists of existence (*bhāva-ātmaka*), because that which is manifest is a real entity (*vastu*), and it is impossible for a non-entity to manifest. For entities possess existence precisely by virtue of being known—that is, by being mounted upon cognition—and they also possess existence through external determination (*adhyavasāya*). This distinction, limitation, and grasping is nothing other than ignorance (*avidyā*). Yet, since the differentiated light (*prakāśa*) persists therein, this is actually the state of knowledge (*vidyā*).
Thus it is said in the *Brahmakāṇḍa*: "Brahman is the non-distinction between the distinction of knowledge and ignorance. (63)

And since everything is thus conventionally real, the conceptual constructions of the various proponents regarding it are mere arrogance; thus he says: "Therefore, those in the world who maintain the doctrine of existence do not accept non-existence as the characteristic of reality, nor do those who maintain the doctrine of non-existence accept existence [as such]. (64)

The supreme seers who maintain the doctrine of existence (bhāvavādins) assert that birth and destruction are merely the manifestation and disappearance of that which already exists. For them, so-called "non-existence" is not anything distinct from existence; rather, it is simply the conventional designation for the prior and subsequent states of an existing entity. To illustrate: the clay state is the prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) of the jar, and the sherd state is its posterior non-existence (pradhvaṃsābhāva). This is how it must be understood.

Even for those who maintain that this entire world is empty—that is, proponents of non-existence—there is no such thing as ultimate non-existence; thus, they do not accept existence as the defining characteristic of reality or as having the nature of the ultimate. Even while speaking thus, they do not deny in conventional discourse the distinction between existence and non-existence, which is based on the capacity or incapacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Consequently, everything is established through the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) in a state of equality; therefore, one must abandon attachment to this [view]. (64)

If, then, non-existence is rejected, the distinction between existence and non-existence would be without foundation; therefore, he says: "And even though everything is non-dual, having the single characteristic of intrinsic nature, a manifold variety of boundaries is perceived within conceptual constructions. (65)

In all the various classes of differentiated things that are perceived, which in their essential nature (*svabhāva*)—that is, in their ultimate form (*paramārtharūpa*)—are of a single nature consisting of Brahman due to the presence of the universal (*sāmānya*), this manifold boundary and established order is seen through the diversity of assertions regarding existence and non-existence among various conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*). This is governed by the power of beginningless necessity (*niyati-śakti*) under the influence of ignorance (*avidyā*). The meaning is that although no real difference exists, this difference caused by ignorance is firmly rooted in worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*); thus, it should be understood as established only so long as it is not critically examined. || 65 ||

However, he demonstrates through an illustration that this distinction between existence and non-existence is not real: "For just as four states are imagined in that which is indefinable, so too is this twofold division dependent upon existence and non-existence. (66)

The meaning is as follows: since a formless entity cannot possess a differentiation of forms by virtue of adventitious conditions (*upādhi*) characterized as prior non-existence, destruction, absolute non-existence, or mutual non-existence—just as the fourfold division of non-existence is merely conceptual—in the same way, the distinction characterized as existence and non-existence must also be understood as purely conceptual. The convention is that a portion of Brahman conditioned by external sensory objects and causal efficiency is designated as "existence," while that which is devoid of external causal efficiency is designated as "non-existence. || 66 ||

In reality, however, since [the Self] transcends all worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*), it does not manifest the principle of the Self as being distinct from existence and non-existence; thus he says: "Whether contradictory or non-contradictory, existent or non-existent, according to reason—whether successive or non-successive, non-existence is not tenable. (67)

Because non-existence (abhāva) is devoid of form (nīrūpa), its opposition or non-opposition to existence (bhāva) cannot be logically established. For non-existence neither destroys nor favors existence such that it would be its opposite in the respective order; since what is existent cannot become non-existent, and since that which has acquired a form cannot possess any further excellence, existence is contradictory to the nature of non-existence. Likewise, its non-existence, being of that very same nature, cannot be established as something distinct from it, just as [existence] is not distinct from itself.

For in this way, there would be the consequence of [the non-existent] being an entity; moreover, succession is a property of an entity and is not applicable to a non-entity. This is because an entity cannot be destroyed, and thus succession belongs to an entity in relation to that [destruction]; nor does it depend on another non-entity, since that very thing is unestablished, and because that which is formless lacks differentiation. Likewise, simultaneity is also impossible: since this [non-entity] depends on something else, there is no simultaneity with another, as it does not exist at the same time as anything else; thus, it is not tenable according to reasoning. (67)

Non-existence is indeed such a phenomenon that, whether it be non-contradictory or contradictory, existent or non-existent, and whether it occurs successively or simultaneously, in reality no such entity exists. (68)

Since non-existence (*abhāva*) is thus untenable in this way, existence (*bhāva*) likewise cannot be established from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). For instance, because existence is indestructible and unsurpassable, its opposition to or non-opposition with non-existence is not logical. The same applies to succession and simultaneity (*krama-akrama*).

Now, if it is argued that an entity is contradictory with another entity, even in that case, since that which is not inherently destructible and is without distinction cannot be destroyed by anything, nor can it be assisted by anything, such [contradiction or assistance] is simply impossible. Furthermore, succession and simultaneity are not ultimately real because there is no difference [in the entity itself]. Even existence, which is defined by the capacity for a specific causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), does not truly abide as a reality, since it does not perform other types of causal efficiency.

Furthermore, since no connection with existence is perceived, that [connection] cannot be the cause; and because it appears [as such], its non-existence is also not ultimate. Thus, all worldly transactions are indeed constructed by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); therefore, both existence and non-existence should be understood in the same way. And this conceptual construction is the power of ignorance (*avidyā-śakti*). It has been determined in the *Brahmakāṇḍa* that this [power] is indefinable as being either identical to or different from reality. || 68 ||

He states that even the distinction caused by time is not ultimately real: "In the absence [of difference], there is no possibility of distinction across the three times; when that [distinction] does not exist, even existence does not persist throughout the three times. (69)

Regarding the phrase "in the three times": there is no distinction based on the three times whose object is non-existence (*abhāva*). For instance, because non-existence is devoid of form (*nīrūpa*), it cannot be delimited by the present. Since that [present] is absent, its dependence upon connection with the past and future times is likewise not real. Thus, even for an existent entity (*bhāva*), a threefold temporal status dependent upon non-existence does not exist.

For instance, since "futurity" has prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) as its basis and "pastness" depends upon destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*), it is untenable [to claim these states] because there is no difference between prior non-existence and destruction. Due to the absence of those two, "presentness" also does not exist. Nor can it depend on itself, because there is no distinction between its prior and posterior limits; thus, for an entity (*bhāva*) to be connected with the three times is impossible. Furthermore, according to the Sāṃkhyas, the entity remains a single unity throughout its prior and posterior limits, being of an undifferentiated essence; therefore, once again, the connection with the three times is untenable.

Since the states are not distinct from that [entity], they too lack its existence. Or, even if there were distinction, it would be impossible to characterize the entity as having different times for those [states]. Thus he says: The abandonment of the self-nature by another is not tenable; But the self-nature, whether from another or from itself, is not possible. (70)

The destruction of an existing entity cannot be established through a cause. For if destruction, being formless, were produced by the causal capacity [of a cause], it would necessarily acquire a form; consequently, if it were related to the entity, it would be perceived just as the entity itself was previously. Thus, if that [destruction] were to perish, the same logic would apply to it as well, leading to an infinite regress. Furthermore, because the nature of "being" is inherently opposed to "non-being," there can be no destruction even intrinsically. Therefore, no referent for the word "non-existence" (abhāva) remains established.

Even "coming into being" (bhavana) is not tenable for that which is already established through the existence of its own being (*bhāva*), because it would lack a cause. Furthermore, for that which exists by itself, "coming into being" is impossible; since the nature of non-existence is contradictory to being, there is no referent whatsoever for the word "being" (*bhāva*). // 70 //

And even so, existence and non-existence are not one in reality; thus he says: "In reality, when there is contradiction and multiplicity, there is no mutual assistance whatsoever. When both identity and difference are abandoned, worldly transaction ceases. (71)

The identity of affirmation and negation is contradictory. If they were distinct, however, there would be no conventional usage between existence and non-existence—which, being mutually independent, would offer no assistance to one another—and no possibility of conceptual construction (vikalpa) apart from "that" or "not-that," since there is no third category. Thus, it is established that the world, appearing in the form of existence, non-existence, and so forth, transcends all conventional discourse; it is established as conventionally real (sāṃvṛta), being proven only when left unexamined. || 71 ||

He says that this is the ultimate reality here: "Those who know the Vedānta have taken refuge in the truth of that very object wherein the seer, the seen, and the seeing are no longer conceptualized. (72)

The knowers of Brahman declare that the supreme Brahman—which is without beginning or end, is the truth, and is free from conceptual construction—is the reality that transcends all manifoldness (*prapañca*) because the proliferation of subject and object and so forth, being fashioned by conceptual thought, is unreal; it is beyond speech and mind. The Veda consists of the three collections (*trayī*)—the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma* Vedas—and the portion consisting of the Upaniṣads is its concluding part, which comprises the determination of the essential meaning.

For at the conclusion [of this work], the true essence of the meaning of the treatise is stated in brief. Those who possess that disposition give rise to it; they thus speak of non-duality as the nature of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), not the duality projected by the performance of ritual action (*karmānuṣṭhāna*). For duality is imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*); it is false and conceptual. Furthermore, it has been established in detail in the *Brahmakāṇḍa* that ignorance itself—being indefinable as either identical to or different from the Supreme—is that which causes the appearance of duality residing in the individual soul (*jīvātman*), which is established as beginningless; therefore, this should be understood from that very source.

Thus, since verbal usage is based on objects that do not exist in the manner they appear, it does not find rest in the non-differentiated reality; rather, differentiation arises here as a cognitive distortion (upaplava). To this effect, he says: "Because words express either a universal or a particular as if they possessed specific distinctions, therefore words are established only upon unreal differences. (73)

Even a universal is expressed by words as being excluded from other universals, and likewise a particular is excluded from other particulars; thus, since words are fixed upon these very unreal distinctions, they are incapable of touching the undifferentiated non-dual reality, and so verbal discourse is indeed futile. Even the discourse "it exists" has its counter-correlative in non-existence.

In this same way, words such as "the knowable" (*jñeya*) and "the object of cognition" (*prameya*) are also conceptually constructed; they have as their objects that which is excluded from the "knowable" and so forth. Thus, the entire collection of words falls under the category of differentiation (*bheda*). As it is stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "The universal (*sāmānya*) is also like a particular (*viśeṣa*). The suffix *-vat* in the word *viśeṣavat* is used in the sense of fitness (*arha*). Thus, "that which deserves to be denoted as a particular" is *viśeṣavat*; or, it is a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*), meaning "that in which a particular exists. This qualification is provided to prevent the possibility that a particular qualified by a universal might be denoted; therefore, it is connected with the term "particular" (*viśeṣa*) as well. (73)

Thus, it has first been explained on the basis of formlessness—that is, by relying on non-existence as a non-entity—how there is a contradiction between existence and non-existence. Now, relying on non-existence as the seventh category according to the Vaiśeṣika system, he says: "For when non-existence exists, the essence of existence is not lost; nor is the essence of existence produced when non-existence is absent. (74)

If non-existence is something other than existence, then why should an entity perish when a destruction (pradhvaṃsa) arises? And why should an entity be born when a prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) ceases? (74)

He confirms this very point by means of an illustration: "The existence of the brindled cow does not sublate the existence of the black cow; nor is it on account of the thought 'the brindled cow does not exist' that the black cow is conceptualized. (75)

The meaning is that just as the existence and non-existence of two entities that are separate and unrelated do not serve as causes for one another's existence or non-existence, so it would be for existence and non-existence in such a state as well. || 75 ||

Thus, he concludes that this collection of faults arises if non-existence is accepted as a real entity distinct from existence: "If non-existence were a real entity, then this investigation would apply; and consequently, even in the case of its absence, this [same] investigation would have to be undertaken once again. (76)

If non-existence (abhāva) is accepted as being a real entity (vastu) in the form of the seventh category (padārtha), then this consideration is appropriate: that the presence and absence of an existent thing (bhāva) would not be logically possible through the presence and absence of that [non-existence]. Furthermore, if non-existence were a real entity, then since another distinct non-existence would arise and cease there as well, the [original] non-existence would accordingly lack those two [states]; moreover, one must state that there would be an infinite regress (anavasthā) of yet another non-existence in that case as well. || 76 ||

Furthermore, when—according to the Buddhist view—an absence (*abhāva*) that is the cessation of existence is accepted as being indeed formless (*nīrūpa*), then: "Since it is a non-entity, that which has passed beyond the range of conventional discourse cannot be described in terms of a real distinction regarding its substance. (77)

In the view that "an entity (bhāva) disappears, but no such thing as non-existence (abhāva) is known to exist as something distinct," this [objection] need not be considered—namely, that "there is no real existence of non-existence" and so forth. Since non-existence consists in the departure from being, how could it persist? This objection does not apply to what is called "being. Furthermore, upon the cessation of antecedent non-existence (prāgabhāva), it is not that "being" arises, but rather [it is the manifestation of] that which possesses the nature of becoming; thus, non-existence, being of the nature of a void, cannot possess any real plurality.

And thus, because it transcends all conventional usage, being non-existent and formless, it is either a non-entity or the determination of real difference and so forth; this has been stated and concluded previously. || 77 ||

Now, having recalled the previously mentioned impossibility of the relation between cause and effect, he states [the following] to establish the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) as his own settled conclusion: "The placement of a footstep upon a place where there is no ground—that is, a cause does not exist for an effect that is non-existent. And yet, when the cause exists, the prior non-existence of the effect is observed. (78)

Prior to its production, the object characterized as the effect is "without a locus" (*apada*), meaning it lacks a basis for cognition because it does not exist. Therefore, the "placing of a footstep" (*padanyāsa*)—that is, the operation—of the cause is not possible therein. For the operation of causes, which is the "placing of a footstep," is grounded in an effect that exists as a real entity capable of entering into the activity of being produced. And that [operation] does not exist when the effect is non-existent. Indeed, causes are not able to function directed toward that which has no form whatsoever, because what is non-existent cannot be an objective referent (*uddeśya*). Furthermore, it has already been stated that if the effect were existent [prior to production], the causal process would be untenable.

Now, the "placing of the foot" (padanyāsa) regarding an effect consists in following the intention of an agent who would employ it; that too is impossible for what is unreal. Furthermore, this placing of the foot upon an effect is even more impossible for an insentient cause. And yet, when a certain cause exists, the effect is seen; therefore, the meaning is that it is only that reality which appears in such a way, and there is no real relationship of cause and effect whatsoever. || 78 ||

Now, regarding the claim that "prior to its arising, there is a prior state of the entity," and thus that object does not exist at that time [as an absence], he says in response to that: "What is its prior state? This [notion] moreover depends upon a real thing (vastu); for neither of these two [the 'prior' nor the 'state'] exists in what is non-existent (avastu). (79)

The objection—"What is the prior state of the effect before its production?"—is based on a real entity (*vastu-āśrita*) and has a real entity as its object (*vastu-ālambana*); that is to say, it takes the form of a formal inquiry. For in this inquiry, there are two factors: "prior" (*prāk*) and "state" (*avasthā*). Neither of these two applies to a non-entity (*avastu*). This is because "priority" (whether spatial or temporal) is impossible for that which is formless and lacks connection with space and time. Furthermore, the term "state" (*avasthā*) is necessarily dependent upon a state-possessor (*avasthātr*).

Furthermore, no persisting entity (*avasthātṛ*) that remains constant through the states exists prior [to their manifestation]; thus, in that case, there is simply non-existence. In this way, according to the theory of the non-existent effect (*asatkāryavāda*), because the effect does not exist previously, this [notion of persistence] is not tenable. Even in the theory of the existent effect (*satkāryavāda*), the meaning of "prior" is untenable, because the entity exists even now. For this very reason, since arising is impossible, there is an absence of a persisting form. If it were to arise in some form, then in relation to that, the birth of what was non-existent would follow; and thus, in that case as well, the matter is untenable. (79)

He says that even in destruction, there is simply non-existence, which is formless and beyond the scope of words regarding an entity: "And after [destruction], there is no basis for saying 'it exists' or 'it does not exist'; this state of being without a locus is what they call the limit of speech. (80)

Because it has undergone destruction without leaving a trace (*niranvaya-dhvaṃsa*), a thing that lacks the aspect of existence cannot be designated as "it exists" or "it does not exist. For the Sāṃkhyas maintain that even at that time [of destruction] it still exists; however, that is not tenable. Why? Because there is no basis (*anibandhana*). The basis for such a statement is perceptibility, and since that is absent in what has been destroyed, non-existence is beyond the range of words due to the lack of a basis. Thus, an entity is inexpressible in its prior and subsequent states. (80)

He says that this is seen only in the intermediate state: "But this process is most wonderful, in that the essential reality (ātmatattva) of entities—previously non-existent, partless, and beyond sequence—is made manifest. (81)

Since the real relationship of cause and effect has been refuted by the distinction between the positions of existence and non-existence, the relationship of cause and effect—which is essentially nothing but a mere appearance—is false and conceptual, being constructed in various ways by those whose eyes are blinded by ignorance (*avidyā*). It is seen that an effect, previously unperceived, partless, and sudden—occurring without sequence when a certain fixed condition is met—arises through a process that is devoid of logical justification and is truly marvelous.

The meaning is that the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is a transformation (*vivarta*) of the single reality—which does not deviate from its own nature—into forms that assume unreal, differentiated other-natures by imitating diversity. This mode of operation is most marvelous. To ask what this is, he says: "that which is partless," and so forth. Such is the grammatical construction of the words. Alternatively, the connection is: when this mode of operation exists, the partless, undivided, and therefore non-sequential reality shines forth as all entities.

If [consciousness] were composed of parts, then its arising would occur sequentially; since one could then determine the efficacy of the cause through such delayed operation, this [phenomenon] would not be a marvel. However, because in every philosophical system the effect arises instantaneously and without succession, it is impossible to investigate the operation of a cause; thus, manifestation—which is established as a marvel due to the exhaustion of ignorance—is itself a marvel. (81)
For it is thus: all worldly transaction is carried out by means of an entity produced solely by conceptual construction, just as if it were a primary, real object. (82)

In dependence upon the visible form existing in the middle state, and by means of the conceptual construction of prior and subsequent states, worldly convention—established without critical analysis—is firmly rooted, whether in terms of a causal relationship or as the nature of existence and non-existence, provided that there is a sense of succession.

In this same way, whatever other conventional transaction (*vyavahāra*) there may be, all of it arises solely through the force of the latencies (*vāsanā*) of beginningless false habitual practice; it is merely conventional (*sāṃvṛta*), yet due to the determination of reality (*tattvādhyavasāya*), it is firmly rooted in this world—which is itself of the nature of the activity of ignorance—as if it were non-conventional. In the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), however, this so-called "difference" that is perceived is not real; rather, reality is strictly non-dual (*advaya*). 82.

He says that this [succession] is perceived by those whose vision is blinded by ignorance, through the power of that which is called ignorance: "Those who maintain the doctrine of permanence consider this [succession] to belong to the possessor of the power of existence; they declare that succession is existence itself, for there is no succession other than existence. (83)

Those who assert that the reality of Brahman consists of two eternal principles maintain that such a power—residing within the beginningless individual soul—belongs to the supreme non-dual Brahman itself. It is by virtue of this power that the reality remains concealed and worldly transaction proceeds through non-reality and duality in a sequential manner. Even though Brahman is non-sequential (*akrama*), the appearance of duality therein is produced by ignorance (*avidyā*); likewise, the appearance of sequence within that very [Brahman] is produced by the sovereign power known as Time (*kāla*).

And those two powers are not ultimately different from the existence of Brahman; thus, it is that very [Brahman] which shines forth in this way in reality. For it is impossible for anything else to appear as something distinct from it, since what appears is non-different from light (*prakāśa*), and what is not light cannot be so [manifest]. This has been determined elsewhere. And so, because succession appears through the conditioning of the state consisting of Brahman, there is no repetition in the formulation [of the argument], as it is joined by way of the relation of cause and effect, such that in worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) there is no form of that [succession] apart from its existence.

In this regard, he states that simultaneity, which is the counter-correlative of succession, is likewise a mere appearance: "In reality, there is no difference whatsoever between succession and simultaneity; just as non-existence is not perceived as anything other than existence. (84)

The single reality (*tattva*), which is boundless, uninterrupted, and impossible to be perceived as such by those whose vision is obscured by ignorance (*avidyā*), appears as if it possesses succession through the superimposition of internal spatial and temporal priority and posteriority; and through the assistance of other objects, it appears as non-successive. Thus, in its true nature (*bhāvataḥ*), neither succession nor non-succession exists, just as it was stated regarding existence and non-existence. The absence of succession is simultaneity (*yaugapadya*).

And according to the view already stated, succession is nothing other than existence; for, since the distinction and the substantiality of non-existence have been previously negated by its being prior to existence, even simultaneity—which consists of those two—is nothing at all. This is made clear by the example of non-existence. Furthermore, because it is perceived as conditioned by existence, the association with another entity is the very nature of that existence. This is logical, for what is called "association" is not perceived as something distinct from the associated things when they are distinguished from one another. (84)

Now, one might object: "Are not succession and non-succession perceived as distinct through the notions 'done successively' and 'done simultaneously'? Anticipating this, he says: "Ordinary people indeed point to another time even for time itself; yet, mere designation does not establish a real distinction. (85)

In common usage, there is the designation "present time" (*adyatana*) for that which occurs today and "future time" (*śvastana*) for that which occurs tomorrow; yet, as stated in the *Bhāṣya* regarding the rule for the *laṅ* [imperfect tense], there exists a "non-present" (*anadyatana*) time which is not actually present. Thus, through the conceptualization of a distinction between the whole and its parts, the single reality of Time is seen to be designated by means of the distinction between locus and located. However, the actual substance of Time does not thereby become divided, since such a distinction is merely optional.

Likewise, even when sequence and non-sequence are designated as distinct, the meaning is that there is no real difference between them, nor any mutual exclusion from the ultimate reality of Being (*bhāva*). || 85 ||

This very point is further elaborated: "One who fashions a support through the intellect does not remain fixed even upon the navel; for no one's creative imagination is obstructed, even regarding non-existent things. (86)

In conventional usage such as "in the absence of an enemy there is happiness," "in the absence of a friend there is suffering," or "in the non-arising and absence of the category of suffering—the mass of afflictions such as passion and so forth—there is nirvāṇa, that is, liberation," one might postulate a supporting power (*ādhāra-śakti*) in the absence [of the object] because its existence would otherwise be inexplicable. However, no one remains as the supported (*ādheya*), such as happiness and so forth. The meaning is that, because the verbal root implies a causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*), no one is able to establish [the supported].

Even while imagining a state of being a substratum, nothing whatsoever attains the status of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) or the status of being contained (*ādheya*) within non-existence as its substrate. In reality, there is no fixing of words for this [non-existence] therein; yet, the meaning is that people do so by way of imagination. This is because it is impossible for non-existence—which is formless and characterized by the absence of all causal capacity—to possess the relationship of a locus with respect to that which is contained. However, having imagined such a state of being a substratum, this designation proceeds. Thus, expressions such as "a hundred herds of elephants reside on the tip of a finger" are seen to be stated through imaginative construction (*utprekṣā*); therefore, there is no ground for conceptualization [regarding the actual existence of such things]. 86.

Since this is so: "Therefore, by means of the differentiation of its powers, a single object—eternal and consisting of both being and non-being—manifests in many forms when it is denoted by words. (87)

The summary of the intent of this section is as follows: Reality (*tattva*), which transcends all conceptual constructions (*parikalpa*), is Brahman permeated by all powers (*śakti*). In accordance with worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), words express this [Reality] as having the nature of existence and non-existence, inlaid with various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Thus, even for those words that denote non-existence, their connection with words denoting existence is equal, because there is no distinction among words. Regarding the word "one" (*eka*): it is because difference (*bheda*) has been refuted by the negation of non-existence.

For this very reason, it is eternal, because there is no non-existence and because the relationship of cause and effect has been negated. Regarding the phrase "in being expressible by words": this is stated as a purpose using the locative case of motive (*nimitta-saptamī*) for the sake of linguistic convention. Regarding the phrase "possessing many forms": this is because the very reality of non-duality, as previously described, is manifested through forms such as succession and simultaneity. || 87 ||

And thus, since this conventional application of categories within worldly affairs is firmly established, it is followed exactly as such in this treatise; therefore, the conceptual constructions of logicians are irrelevant. To this effect, he says: "And the worldly transaction proceeds by means of categories that are conceptually constructed. In the treatise, the worldly category is analyzed for the sake of accomplishing a purpose. (88)

Even though the reality of existence has been resolved through conceptual reasoning, it does not enter into worldly transactional usage according to its analytical investigation. For in worldly usage, there is no conformity to the contradictory natures of entities as established by different philosophical systems; nor can a determination be made in accordance with reality without such investigation.

"The fool and the wise man are alike in their susceptibility to form and designation. Observing this through the "closing of the eyes like an elephant," ordinary people are seen to conduct their worldly affairs by determining the true nature of things based on the convergence of mutual intentions. And this treatise is an instruction precisely for those worldly words.

Therefore, in this matter, one must rely on the very analysis of word-meanings as established in common worldly usage; for the sake of establishing the technical operations of the grammatical system, the "extracted" (apoddhāra) word-meanings—characterized as action, substance, quality, and so forth—are divided from the indivisible sentence-meaning, such that it is said: "the verbal root denotes action," "substantives have being as their primary sense," and "an affix is that which causes comprehension. Thus, all words, sharing a single destiny within the course of worldly life, have as their object meanings intended as either existent or non-existent. This is the meaning [of the passage].

Because it is eternal through its continuity and because the cognition [of it] consists merely in the modification of words, it is established that the relationship between word and meaning is eternal. || 88 ||

Thus ends the third chapter, the *Saṃbandhasamuddeśa*, in the *Prakīrṇaprakāśa* composed by Helārāja, son of Bhūtirāja. Now begins the fourth chapter, the *Dravyasamuddeśa*. Having thus explained the relationship between word and meaning, it was previously stated that the worldly categories of meaning (*padārtha*), which are useful for grammatical derivation (*anvākhyāna*), are analyzed in this treatise for the sake of specific operations (*kārya*). For it was previously asserted in the passage "the relationship between word and meaning being established" (*siddhe śabdārthasaṃbandhe*)—for the purpose of supporting the eternity of meaning—that the meaning of all words consists of both genus (*jāti*) and substance (*dravya*).

Now, since the meaning of the words extracted through analysis (*apoddhāra*), such as substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and so forth—which serves as a limb for grammatical exposition (*anvākhyāna*)—must be set forth, it is said that they are "divided. To the question "From what are they divided?", he says: "Arising from the nature of the composite whole (*saṃsarga*), they are extracted from the nature of consciousness (*saṃvit*); they are distinguished in the treatise from the meaning of the sentence, just like the meanings of stems and suffixes [are distinguished from the meaning of the word]. (1)
Certain categories of meaning, which serve as indicators for grammatical correctness and whose nature is inferred from the treatise, will be explained here in brief according to tradition. (2)

Since only the indivisible sentence (*niraṃśa-vākya*) possesses the capacity to denote meaning, word-meanings are established as distinct from that [sentence-meaning]. And that sentence-meaning is "of such a nature" (*tathā*), meaning its form or essence (*ātman*) is precisely the relation (*saṃsarga*). The sentence-meaning is the relation between the action, the factors of action (*kāraka*), and their respective qualifiers. By this, he states the seed for the division [of the sentence-meaning]; for if the sentence-meaning were in every respect indivisible, there would be no form to be divided. However, in the case of a relation, the division of the related meanings is appropriate. For this very reason, he says they are "produced" (*sambhūta*).

The meaning is that they are "existent" (vidyamāna) because they occur in the state of association (*saṃsarga*). Therefore, being associated and existent, they can be extracted (*apoddhartum*). For those things that are non-existent—being like iron rods (*ayaḥśalākākalpa*)—there is no mutual connection, and thus no extraction is possible. "Cognition" (*saṃvit*) means the act of cognizing; however, the nature (*rūpa*) or essence (*ātman*) of this [cognition] is the intellect of extraction (*apoddhārabuddhi*). For that reason, they are "extracted," meaning separated. This is what is being said:

Although the word-meanings are never apprehended through a distinct separation from the sentence-meaning—given that such a relation presupposes a prior distinction as to what kind of relation it might be—nevertheless, because a listener cannot simultaneously comprehend a partless whole, they perceive it through a sequence of parts. Since the linguistic usage of a relation presupposing a distinction occurs in this way, meanings are indeed analyzed by means of that very process of analytical abstraction (*apoddhāra-buddhi*), intended for that purpose.

For example, just as the ingredients of a beverage, such as molasses and so forth, even when devoid of distinctness [from one another], are nevertheless designated separately by those who taste them through the discrimination of gustatory consciousness; likewise, when "form" (*rūpa*) is a synonym for "aspect" (*ākāra*), then this [ablative case] is the fifth case (*pañcamī*) used with the elision of the suffix *-lyap* (i.e., *āśritya*). The meaning is that it is based upon the form, which is the aspect, of cognition—that is, of the conceptualizing intellect (*kalpanābuddhi*).

Because the sentence-meaning, being impartite, cannot be apprehended instantaneously, there arise in the interim delusive cognitions (*vibhrama*) in the form of word-meanings, which are colored by their respective parts. Since the form established in those cognitions is determined (*adhyavasāya*) to be the real entity, it is conceptually constructed as a "word-meaning" in the preceding stage, which serves as a means. However, once the complete sentence-meaning is understood, that distinct mere generality is sublated by that non-distinct, real [sentence-meaning].

He states what the purpose of abstraction (*apoddhāra*) is: "They are divided in the treatise. By proximity, this should be understood as referring to the science of grammar (*vyākaraṇa-śāstra*). For here, categories such as substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and so forth, are presented as the means for the definitional statements (*lakṣaṇa-vākya*) through a division of objects. Thus, the purpose of abstraction from the sentence-meaning is that the definition may remain restricted to its specific object according to that division.

For instance, the status of meanings as auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) is traditionally taught in the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*) by way of indication (*upalakṣaṇa*), not as something to be enjoined (*vidheya*). This is because, following the worldly convention expressed in the rule "due to the non-instruction of meanings" (*arthānādeśanāt*), the instruction is given for the sake of phonological refinement (*saṃskāra*) such as accentuation, etc., by restating meanings already well-known in the world. This is like the meanings of bases (*prakṛti*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*); here, the respective meanings of the base and suffix—which fall within the domain of nouns (*nāman*) and verbs (*ākhyāta*)—are merely conceptual (*kālpnika*).

The meaning is that just as the referents of stems (*prakṛti*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*) are extracted from an impartite word-meaning by those who maintain the theory of words (*padavādin*), through the analytical cognition (*apoddhārabuddhi*) based on positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*), so too are word-meanings extracted from the impartite sentence-meaning by those who maintain the theory of sentences (*vākyavādin*). Thus, the process of extraction is identical in both cases. Regarding the phrase "serving as causes" (*nimittabhūtā*): since their status as causes pertains to the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of words, they are said to be "distinct" (*vibhaktā*). Furthermore, those meanings are of two kinds.

[These categories] are both well-known in the world and defined by treatises such as the Vaiśeṣika. Among these, those well-known in the world—such as "animal," "offspring," and "deity"—are not defined here precisely because they are already well-known. However, regarding those defined in other treatises, he says that they are characterized according to the systematic arrangement of their own respective schools: "some [categories] have their nature inferred from the treatise. This refers to this very treatise called Vyākaraṇa due to its proximity, and not to the Vaiśeṣika or others.

The meaning is that those things whose nature (*svabhāva*) or characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is apprehended through inference [are substances]. For instance, by the commencement of the *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one from among identicals), differentiability (*bhedyatva*) is inferred as the characteristic of substance (*dravya*), since the commencement of that [retention] is purposeful only when there is the consequence of verbal differentiation (*śabdabheda*) due to substance being primarily denotable. Furthermore, from the statement of the author of the *Vārttika*, "For when a word is applied to a substance because of the presence of a certain quality (*guṇa*), the suffixes *tva* and *tal* are used to denote that [quality]," dependence (*āśritatva*) is inferred as the characteristic of quality (*guṇa*).

Since even a genus (*jāti*) is denotable by an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*), this [quality] is established as a quality (*guṇa*) in this manner. Likewise, in the rule "after a word expressing a quality ending in the suffix *u*," one who has spoken of a quality is called a "quality-expresser" (*guṇavacana*); thus, the designation applies when a substance is to be conveyed through the former existence of a quality, provided that it serves as a qualifier. Furthermore, since time is characterized by its nature as action, its states—past, present, and future—are understood as adjuncts (*upādhi*) to the meaning of verbal roots (*dhātvartha*).

Furthermore, the fact that number consists in the counting of distinctions is understood from the rule: "When a single individual is denoted by a word expressing a genus (*jātyākhyāyām ekasmin*). Since number is established as a quality (*guṇa*) in the Vaiśeṣika system and is restricted to a substance (*dravya*), when words are formally analyzed in their general application to feminine, masculine, and neuter, the characteristics of gender (*liṅga*)—namely, contraction (*saṃstyāna*), expansion (*prasava*), and stability (*sthiti*)—are inferred as being subordinate factors (*aṅgabhāva*) to the meaning.

For indeed, it is not possible for a bedstead (*khaṭvā*) and the like to possess worldly femininity, nor for a eunuch (*ṣaṇḍaka*) and the like to possess masculinity, nor for a jar (*kuṇḍa*) and the like to possess neuter gender. It is inferred from the usage of the term "remainder" (*śeṣa*), from the acceptance of [gender] as being both object and agent (*karmakartṛtva*), and from the rule regarding *avyayībhāva* compounds used in the sense of case endings (*vibhaktyartha*). For if substance (*dravya*) were the means (*sādhana*), then because substance possesses a single nature, its status as a "remainder," its state as an object, and its state as an agent would not be logically tenable.

Furthermore, since a substance (*dravya*) alone functions in the sense of a case-ending (*vibhakti-artha*), as in the expression *adhistri* (on a woman), there would be no word "woman" (*strī-śabda*) [to function as a separate term]; thus, with what could there be a compound? Moreover, in the rule *upasargāc chandasi dhātvarthe*, the inclusion of the word *artha* (meaning) is for the purpose of indicating a substance (*dravya*) possessed of gender and number; this makes known its non-status as a mere instrument (*asādhana*). Otherwise, one would simply say *sādhane* (in the presence of an instrument); why then say *dhātvarthe* (in the meaning of a verbal root), which implies that the meaning is produced by the root? As for the person (*puruṣa*) and the voice (*upagraha*), their establishment as technical terms arises solely from the usage of the ancient teachers.

As for direction (*dik*) and action (*kriyā*), they are indeed well-known in common worldly usage; however, since the treatise (*śāstra*) also establishes the arrangement of "east" and so forth, it is inferred from this qualification that their defining characteristic is their status as attributes (*upādhi*) of word-meanings (*padārtha*). Action, too, is characterized in the *Bhāṣya* on the *bhūvādi-vārttika* as being sequential (*pūrvāparībhūta*), having the nature of something to be accomplished (*sādhyasvabhāva*), and cognizable through inference. Regarding the phrase "word-meanings": although the existence of things is always only in a state of mutual association, they are nevertheless extracted [individually]. Furthermore, for each single word, there are many meanings, some of which are subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) and others primary (*pradhānabhūta*).

Namely, for the verb (*ākhyāta*), there are [the categories of] action (*kriyā*), time (*kāla*), means (*sādhana*), number (*saṃkhyā*), person (*puruṣa*), and voice (*upagraha*); and for the noun (*nāman*), there are substance (*dravya*), gender (*liṅga*), number (*saṃkhyā*), means (*sādhana*), action (*kriyā*), and time (*kāla*), and so forth. Alternatively, the status of being a "word-meaning" (*padārthatā*) is established by virtue of being denotable by a word (*padavācyatva*). This is because isolated [categories] such as "cooking" (*pacati*) lack the status of being denotable by a word. Regarding the phrase "according to tradition" (*yathāgamam*): it means without transgressing whatever tradition (*āgama*) belongs to the grammarians;

that is to say, without overstepping the lineage of instruction (*upadeśapāramparya*) of the commentators, whatever category serves as a subordinate factor (*aṅgabhāva*) in whichever explanatory analysis (*anvākhyāna*), that is what is stated. (1.2)

In that regard, since qualities and so forth are dependent upon substance, he first defines that substance which is their locus: "That object which is intended as the thing to be distinguished, wherein a pronoun is employed to indicate the thing itself—that is called 'substance' (dravya). (3)

In this context, there are two ways of functioning for pronouns (*sarvanāman*): some denote the mere thing-in-itself, such as *sarva* and others; while others denote a qualified thing, such as *antara* and others. Among these, by the former, the substance (*dravya*) is indicated. For instance—a substance is that which is capable of being referred to by a pronoun as "this" or "that."

The word *idam* denotes a perceptible object, while *tat* denotes an imperceptible object known through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Thus, by employing these two pronouns (*sarvanāman*)—*idam* and *tat*—which refer to the forms of both perceptible and imperceptible objects, it is stated that they signify "mere entity" (*vastumātra*). Consequently, by disregarding the distinction between the forms of the perceptible and the imperceptible, the "substance" (*dravya*) characterized as mere entity is indicated as their denotation.

For since the nature of individual substances is infinite and impossible to define individually, the common characteristic of all substances is stated in this way, because the state of being a real entity (*vasturūpatā*) exists everywhere. This very point was expressed by the author of the *Nirukta*: "That which is perceived as 'this' is a substance. He also states a second, specific definition: "that which is intended to be expressed as something to be differentiated. The meaning is that it is intended to be spoken of as a qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) by means of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), such as universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth.

By the inclusion of the phrase "intended to be expressed" (*vivakṣita*), he states that this is not a definition of the thing itself (*vastu*), but rather of the word-meaning (*śabdārtha*). Thus, if even a genus (*jāti*) and so forth are intended to be expressed as the substantive (*viśeṣya*), then it is a substance (*dravya*); for, by disregarding the definitions of substance offered by other schools, the universal determination of the category of substance is established according to the system of Vyāḍi. For example, in the system of Vājapyāyana, the meaning of all words is the genus, which is the cause of the cognition of the related [substance].

The existence of the universal (*jāti*) is established because the cognition of things as being connected [to an action] could not otherwise be accounted for. Otherwise, how could there be the identical cognition "he cooks" (*pacati*) in every instance? If the meaning of "cooks" were merely the softening (*vikleda*), then since acts such as placing the pot on the fire would be understood only through implication (*sāmarthya*) and would not constitute the literal meaning of the word, Devadatta’s status as the agent (*kartṛtva*) would not be possible. For those operations such as placing the pot on the fire are not denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*). Furthermore, if the operation of the agent denoted by the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) were understood through implication, there would be no syntactic connection (*samanvaya*) with it.

And thus, since softening alone is what is denoted by the verbal root, in that case *odana* (rice) would be the agent like a reflexive object (*karmakartṛ*), and never the object. Furthermore, that softening—which is imperceptible in form and lacks temporal sequence—is not "cooking" (*pacati*), because only an action characterized by a sequence of prior and posterior stages is a "process. In this way, even the acts of placing [the pot] on the fire and so forth are necessarily included therein, for the cognition "he cooks" arises even with respect to that much alone. Therefore, one must accept a genus of action (*kriyājāti*) that is determined by a single, non-differentiated cognition at every moment.

In this same way, the universal (jāti) such as "whirling-ness" (bhramaṇatva), which is manifested by the momentary actions of whirling and so forth, must also be understood as being perceptible. Even in that case, because of the distinction between the momentary actions produced by specific causes such as particular volitions, the manifestation of the restricted universal is difficult to ascertain due to similarity. For instance, even among moments that possess motion, the manifestation of the universal occurs through their being either clear or obscure.

Furthermore, the connection with the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) occurs by way of the individual (*vyakti*), because it is the individual that is the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), even though the universal (*jāti*) is eternal. This is just as, in the absence of milking for the universal, there is a connection with action by way of the individual in the expression "Let the cow be milked" (*gaur duhyatām*). And although the action of "being" (*asti-kriyā*) differs due to differences in its means and differences in time, another universal that serves as the cause for a non-differentiated cognition is not contradicted.

Furthermore, even though the universal (*sāmānya*) is eternal, it possesses the capacity to yield a result upon the manifestation of the individual (*vyakti*); thus, the injunction "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), which aims at the manifestation of the individual, is purposeful. Let both disappearance and decay be the substrata of the action-universal (*kriyājāti*), precisely because they are determined by the word in that very way, and because here it is the meaning of the word that constitutes the object.

Since the remaining arguments for establishing action (*kriyā*) as a category have already been set forth, the universal determination of the substance-category (*dravyapadārtha*) is likewise established when this definition of substance is accepted. For even in the case of the verb (*ākhyāta*), it is substance itself—possessing the nature of a means (*sādhana*)—that is the expressed meaning. This is because, even though action is predominant, that [substance] is admitted to be expressed as a subordinate factor (*guṇabhūta*). Otherwise, in relation to what would there be predominance? Thus, let that very [substance], as engaged in activity (*vyāpārāviṣṭa*), be the expressed meaning by way of predominance.

For even in other philosophical systems, there is no total disappearance of this [agent] by virtue of its being subordinate, as in the case of a subordinate word within a verbal operation; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in such expressions as "Devadatta cooks. Therefore, let there be absolute primacy [of the agent], since coreferentiality would otherwise be inexplicable. Furthermore, its fitness for reference by pronouns is indeed observed in such cases as "this one who cooks. Moreover, its state of being distinguishable (*bhedya*) certainly exists in relation to its own qualifiers, such as correctness (*sādhutva*) and so forth.

Furthermore, since the characteristics [of a substance] do not depend upon their current operation, "the state of being capable of differentiation" (*bhedayogyatā*) is here what constitutes "differentiability" (*bhedyatva*). Thus, because it is referred to by pronouns such as "this" (*idam*) in expressions like "it is sat" (*āsyate*) or "it stands" (*sthīyate*), and because it is the substantive (*viśeṣya*) in expressions such as "pleasure" (*sukham*), it possesses "substantiality" (*dravyatva*); therefore, even the meaning of a verb is a "substance" (*dravya*) according to the view of Vyāḍi. But surely, since only that which has the form of an action (*kriyārūpa*) is perceived as something to be brought into being (*bhāvyamāna*), and because there is a contradiction between the accomplished and the unaccomplished, the verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) express "productive activity" (*bhāvanā*)?

The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that the cognition of a substance is obtained through implication (*sāmarthya*) from the meaning of the word, and is thus something attained by implication rather than being the direct denotation of the word. This is incorrect. Because, according to the method of agreement and difference (*anvayavyatireka*), the verbal root alone expresses the productive operation (*bhāvanā*), while the suffix denotes the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). Furthermore, there is a syntactic connection between the established (the accomplished) and the unestablished (the to-be-accomplished) by way of the relationship between the goal and the instrument. Thus, there is a co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of both the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*).

Otherwise, the Grammarians’ claim that the designation of a "means" (sādhana) is obtained through implication would be nothing more than a settled dispute; for they maintain that the means is a potent substance (*dravya*) and not mere potency (*śakti*), thus establishing its status as a substance. Furthermore, particles such as *ca* ("and") are denoters of substances or denoters of actions, because they illuminate conjunction (*samuccaya*) and so forth, which are essentially either substances or actions. Consequently, their referent likewise admits of the same alternative between individual instance (*vyakti*) and class-form (*ākṛti*).

Even qualities (*guṇa*), when expressed as qualified by a universal (*sāmānya*), undergo the grammatical operation of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) such that "substance is the meaning of the word" becomes "form and so forth [are the meanings of the word]. Likewise, when it is explained as "by a common substance," a compound with a quality also occurs, as in *sarvagandha* (possessing all fragrances) and *ekarasa* (having a single taste). But if this is so, how is it that in the rule "and that which expresses contradictory things, provided they do not denote a substratum (*anadhikaraṇavāci*)," the example *śītoṣṇaṃ* (cold and hot) and *sukhaduḥkham* (pleasure and pain)—where the substratum is indeed a substance—is cited as an instance of singular treatment (*ekavadbhāva*)?

Because terms such as *śīta* (cold) denote substances by this definition, they would fall under the exclusion [of the rule] "not denoting a substratum" (*anadhikaraṇavācin*). To this it is replied: Since the rule for the substitution of *ai* and *au* for the final vowels of a *dvandva* compound applies specifically to those ending in case-suffixes (*subanta*), and since every such form denotes a substance qualified by a genus (*jāti*), the prohibition "not denoting a substratum" would apply universally, thereby rendering the injunction devoid of scope. Consequently, by the force of that very injunction, the prohibition is understood to refer only to well-known substances, as in the example *śītoṣṇe udake* ("the cold and hot waters").

For it is well known in the world that a substance (*dravya*) is an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) possessing action and qualities; therefore, only that which denotes such [a substance] is excluded [from the application of the rule]. Thus, when words like *śīta* (cold) and *uṣṇa* (hot) denote substances such as water and fire, the formation of a singular compound (*ekavadbhāva*) does not occur. It occurs only when they denote qualities such as coldness and heat. Accordingly, in the *Samarthavārttika*: "For when the word-meaning (*padārtha*) is a quality (*guṇa*), then there is semantic competency (*sāmarthya*)."

"For heroism (*vīratva*) is one quality, while manhood (*puruṣatva*) is another. By this definition, although the word *vīra* denotes a substance (*dravya*), it expresses its own meaning—which is subordinate to the substance and dependent upon it—as the object of its capacity; thus, it denotes [the substance] by means of the qualities characterized by association and so forth. For manhood (*puruṣatva*) is exactly the same. In that regard, he states the quality:

Even though, according to common worldly usage, the form of a genus (*jāti*) is also its "state" (*bhāva*), the phrase "because of the existence of which quality a word is applied to a substance" (*yasya guṇasya hi bhāvād dravye śabdaniveśaḥ*) was stated for the purpose of avoiding over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding that [genus] and so forth. Thinking that substance and quality are non-different, one might fail to understand the distinction between the meanings of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*); therefore, it was stated that "substance is other than sound and the rest. One should not, on account of this Bhāṣya, fall into the error that sound and the rest do not constitute substance according to this definition.

For in this case, since even color and the rest possess substantiality (*dravyatva*) within this [category of] substance, there is an absence of the suffix *ām* when expressing the excellence of a non-substance; for example: *samayataraṃ śītam* (a colder temperature), *upāṃśutaraḥ śabdaḥ* (a quieter sound), and *uccaistaro dhvaniḥ* (a louder noise). Thus ends the fourth chapter, the "Designation of Substances," in the *Prakīrṇakaprakāśa* composed by Helārāja, son of Bhūtirāja.

3.5: Exposition of Qualities (Guṇasamuddeśa) Now, he states the definition of a quality as inferred from its technical indicators in the treatise: "That which is perceived as being in contact [with a substance], as distinguishing it, and as possessing an operation—its status as a quality is declared in the treatise because of its dependence on another. (1)

A conjoined [quality] is that which is mixed with its substratum by means of a fusion of form (*rūpasambheda*), not merely by way of a relation. For this very reason, it effects a delimitation of the substratum from other substrata, as in "this is white" (and not blue). Likewise, in the case of "this is a cow" (and not a horse), even the universal *gotva* (cowness) becomes a quality by means of the delimitation from other substrata and so forth.

Thus, by means of the distributive expression "whatever... whatever," he states the technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) that everything of this kind—even universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth—is a quality (*guṇa*), thereby indicating that this [quality] does not exist as a substantial entity (*vastu*). By this, he expresses the distinction of a quality from the substance (*dravya*) which is to be delimited, insofar as the quality functions as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*). The meaning is that it is designated as a "quality" when it is perceived in its capacity as a delimiting factor, and not in any other form. The syntactical connection is: "that which is of such a nature possesses the status of a quality."

Now, one might ask: "Is this merely a technical convention (*paribhāṣā*) that 'guṇa' [means subordinate], or is there a basis for it here? To this he says, "Because of being dependent" (*paratantratvāt*). The meaning is that since in common worldly usage that which is dependent is called a *guṇa*, this understanding is not a mere technical convention. Thus, it is stated that this is a restatement of a worldly definition itself, intended to set aside the definitions established by the Vaiśeṣikas. In this way, the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) is purposeful. This is what is meant by the phrase, "as illustrated in the treatise."

The meaning is that in grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), only a worldly quality (*guṇa*) is accepted as a constituent of the explanatory sentence (*anvākhyānavākya*). For instance, in the *Samarthavārttika*: "An addition [to the rule] is required for words in apposition because of a lack of semantic capacity (*asāmarthya*); if it is argued that 'the referent of a word is a substance (*dravya*),' then since there is an absolute non-difference between the two substances in a case like *vīrapuruṣaḥ*, there would be no semantic capacity; thus, under the view that the referent of a word is a substance, the absence of compound formation is raised as an objection. However, if the referent of the word is a quality (*guṇa*), then semantic capacity exists."

For heroism (*vīratva*) is one quality (*guṇa*), while manhood (*puruṣatva*) is another. Thus, because birth (*jāti*) is dependent and because it inheres (*samavāya*) in a substance (*dravya*), its status as a quality has been stated. And so, the capacity perceived through the distinction of qualities is based on the unity of the substance; thus the compound is established. Likewise, the definition that "the application of a word to a substance occurs due to the presence of a certain quality" follows precisely this principle: the quality is the differentiator and the substance is the differentiated.

For instance: when there is a suffix denoting an abstract state (*bhāvapratyaya*) upon a word expressing a mere qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), as opposed to a word expressing the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) itself, [it denotes that quality]. When the word "cow" (*go*) denotes a substance delimited by a genus (*jāti*), the term "cowness" (*gotva*) refers to the genus alone. However, when it denotes the mere form of the word (*śabdasvarūpa*)—which serves as the invariable ground for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*)—its status as both the denoted object and as something distinct has already been established previously. For a qualifier colors another entity by means of its own form, just as a quality such as a genus does.

Likewise, for a word that conveys an object by means of its own form (*svarūpa*), that form becomes an attribute (*guṇa*) because it serves as a coloring agent; it is the ground for the word's application (*pravṛttinimitta*) upon the object, and the cognition of the object occurs through the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of that form onto it. It is not the word when invested with the function of denotation (*abhidhāvyāpāra*) alone that is the denotable (*vācya*), but rather that which is common [to both] and present in actual usage. This relationship has been established by such statements as "when the quality is red" (*rakte guṇe tattvam*).

When words such as *śukla* (white) denote a substance delimited by a quality (*guṇa*), the relation [of the abstract suffix] is established in such expressions as *śuklatvam* ("whiteness") and *tattvam* ("that-ness") with respect to the quality. When words such as *śukla* denote a substance delimited by a quality, the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) in *śuklatvam* refers to the quality. If they denote the quality itself, it refers to the genus (*jāti*); if they denote that [genus], it refers to the essential nature (*svarūpa*), as in the previous case. Thus, in the first mode of word-application, even for names such as *ḍittha*, the abstract suffix refers only to the essential nature.

Since a name conveys its bearer through the superimposition of its own form (*svarūpa-adhyāsa*), that [form] alone is the ground for its application (*pravṛtti-nimitta*) therein. As for the expression "this is his *ḍitthatva*," however, when it is applied elsewhere due to the superimposition of an action or a quality (*kriyā-guṇa-adhyāsa*), the abstract suffix (*bhāva-pratyaya*) denotes the action or quality that co-exists with *ḍittha*. Thus, the Bhāṣya statement "this is your *ḍitthatva*" intends the superimposition of non-difference between the action or quality and the person.

Alternatively, from the time of its production until its destruction, even through various states of the individual object (*piṇḍa*), it is the universal (*jāti*) alone that serves as the basis for the cognition of recognition; this is what is expressed by abstract suffixes (*bhāvapratyaya*) when a word is first applied. However, in cases such as *rājapuruṣatvam* (the state of being a king’s man), *pācakatvam* (the state of being a cook), or *aupagavatvam* (the state of being Upagu’s descendant), the relation itself—acting as a qualifier according to the specific case—is the basis of application (*pravṛttinimitta*) denoted by the abstract suffix.

For in this case, a related entity (*saṃbandhī*) is perceived as delimited by a specific relation; thus, because the relation itself serves as the coloring factor (*uparañjaka*), it occupies a subordinate position (*guṇatva*), and the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) expresses it. Indeed, a person (*puruṣa*) or similar entity is not perceived merely as delimited by a relatum such as a king, but rather as delimited by that relation. And since the distinction (*bheda*) is manifested, the relation itself—which is the substratum of that distinction—is expressed as the ground for the application of the word (*pravṛttinimitta*), being thereby included within its denotation.

However, where the cognition is colored by the relation and the distinction [between the property and the substrate] is concealed, there the relation itself—such as the universal (*jāti*) and so forth—is the ground for the application of the word, expressed by an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*), as in "the quality of cowness" (*gotva*) or "the quality of whiteness" (*śuklatva*). For here the cognition is not colored by inherence (*samavāya*), but rather it is the substance that is suffused with the universal or the quality, while inherence remains concealed due to its subtlety. The relation, moreover, serves to delimit the locus for the universal and the quality. In cases such as "elephant-ness" (*hastitva*), which are based on conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), the universal alone is the denotable meaning.

The same applies in cases such as *kumbhakāratvam* (the state of being a potter). For here, the relation that serves as the basis for the derivation of the word is indeed the universal (*jāti*), which is what is expressed by the word. Even in the case of *sattā* (existence), since the relation between existence and the existent is invariable and thus cannot serve as a limiting factor, it is the universal alone that is expressed by the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*). As it has been said: "In compounds, primary derivatives (*kṛt*), and secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), there is the denotation of a relation, except in cases of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), non-differentiated connection (*abhinnayoga*), or invariable relation (*avyabhicaritasaṃbandha*)."

In this context, the qualifier is presented in the sūtra by the word *bhāva* as that which, by its own nature, colors the substance. It is called *bhāva* because from it a substance comes to exist in that particular form. For instance, a substance is perceived in the form of a cow through the universal "cowness" (*gotva*), and in its own specific form through qualities such as whiteness; for without external adjuncts, objects would be incapable of being designated and would thus be as if non-existent.

And therefore, since the word denotes that which has been brought to non-difference with the qualifier, the cause for the operation of the word is also related to the form of the object. Thus, in the view that "it is due to the presence of a certain quality," the base (*prakṛti*) expresses the object; for example, "the state of being a cow is cowness" (*gorbhāvo gotvam*).

Alternatively, regarding the position that "all entities (*bhāva*) exist by means of their own being (*bhāva*); that is their *bhāva*," in this case the base (*prakṛti*) denotes the word itself; thus, the *bhāva* of the word "cow" (*go-śabda*) is "cowness" (*gotva*). For it is so: all entities—that is, all words—exist by means of their own being, according to the etymology "they exist from this"; they exist by means of the object characterized as the ground for the application (*pravṛtti-nimitta*). Since verbal roots have multiple meanings and the root *bhū* signifies "to be employed," they "exist" in the sense that they are employed.

That entity (bhāva), characterized as the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of those words, is what is expressed by the suffix; thus, in this view, the *prakṛti* consisting of the word itself becomes that which is denoted by the word. In this manner, the definition of a quality (*guṇa*) has been illustrated here in the treatise. However, where a quality is not so grasped in the treatise, there a logical justification must be stated. For instance, in the rule *voto guṇavacanāt*, this is not a quality, because of the governing context (*adhikāra*) of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

Furthermore, since femininity (*strītva*) is a property of a substance (*dravyadharma*), only a certain nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that denotes a substance is understood here by virtue of the mention of "quality-expressing" (*guṇavacana*). A "quality-expressing" word is one that has expressed a quality; thus, the suffix is applied to words like *paṭu* (clever), which denote a substance where the quality is subordinate. Moreover, the "quality" (*guṇa*) intended here is not defined as something merely associated with a substance (*saṃsargyādi*), for if it were, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of applying this even to genus-words (*jātiśabda*). Therefore, that [quality] is understood as defined by the rule: "That which enters into a substance and departs from it," and so forth.

[Objection: In that case, only the *guṇa* (quality) as defined by the Vaiśeṣikas would be grasped; consequently, the feminine suffix *īkār* would not occur in words such as *paṭvī* (clever) and *mṛdvī* (soft). [Reply: This is not a fault, because this very definition applies to sharpness (*pāṭava*) and the like as well; indeed, it is for this purpose alone that this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) was commenced. Otherwise, since the quality-status (*guṇatva*) of color (*rūpa*) and so forth would be established simply by the force of common perception, this rule would be useless. Furthermore, in the rule "from words denoting qualities (*guṇavacana*) and from *brāhmaṇa* etc.," it is precisely this technical *guṇa* that is understood.

For instance, the author of the *Vākya* [Patañjali] stated: "A meaningful base (*prātipadika*) is a word expressing a quality (*guṇavacana*)," thereby initiating the designation "expressing a quality" for the nominal stem alone. If this is so, since the desired result is already established by the governing context of "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*), what is the purpose of the term "expressing a quality"? Furthermore, the inclusion of the group beginning with "brāhmaṇa" would be redundant. It is replied: although the designation "expressing a quality" does not apply [to all stems] due to the governing context of "nominal stem," this rule is formulated so that it may apply specifically to those [stems] designated as "expressing a quality."

Indeed, the technical designations of *samāsa*, *kṛt*, *taddhita*, *avyaya*, *sarvanāman*, and *asarvaliṅga-jāti* were introduced precisely as subverters (*bādhikā*) of the designation *guṇavacana*. Consequently, a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that does not denote a *samāsa* produces the suffix *ṣyañ*. For this very reason, the inclusion of the word *brāhmaṇa* and others in the rule is also justified; because the word *brāhmaṇa* ends in a *taddhita* suffix, it lacks the designation *guṇavacana*. The word *māṇava* is likewise a *taddhita* derivative, meaning "the offspring of Manu."

Likewise, the word *vāḍava* [is formed] by the rule "when *vaḍavā* is the base and *vṛṣa* is to be expressed. However, [the form] *arhataḥ* [is derived] from the rule "*arhato num ca*," which bears the technical designation *kṛt*. In this same manner, other instances should also be applied where the designation *guṇavacana* is superseded within the *brāhmaṇādi* group. Furthermore, the mention of the *brāhmaṇādi* group is intended so that the suffix *ṣyañ* may occur there as well. Moreover, the mention of the *brāhmaṇādi* group is also justified so that *ṣyañ* may occur even after superseding those suffixes which would otherwise supersede *ṣyañ*.

For instance, regarding the word *brāhmaṇa*, if one follows the view that it is not a derivative (avyutpatti-pakṣa), the suffix *añ* would apply by the rule *prāṇabhṛjjāti...*. However, since *māṇava* and *vāḍava* are names of lineages (*gotra*), the suffix *vuñ* would apply by the rule *gotracaraṇāt...*; thus, the same should be inferred in other cases as well. But for those words for which neither the designation of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) nor any exception (*apavāda*) applies, their recitation here is for the sake of detailed exposition (*prapañca*). According to the opinion of the author of the Sūtras, however, the term *guṇavacana* means "one who has spoken of a quality" (*guṇam uktavān*); therefore, by virtue of the inclusion of the word *vacana*, what is understood here is that which denotes a substance (*dravya*) where the quality is subordinate (*guṇopasarjana*).

In the rule "The third case [is used] with a quality-word (*guṇavacana*) whose object is produced by that," even here, only a specific substance characterized by a quality subordinate to something produced by the meaning of the third-case ending—such as a "broken" piece—is understood. For it is through connection with the quality of being broken that a substance becomes denotable by the word *khaṇḍa*. In the rule "Of a number, when measuring a quality (*guṇa*)... (*pā. 2.1.50*), the quality to be grasped is one consisting of equal portions; it is not the quality defined as above, nor is it the quality defined by the rule "That which enters into a substance... (*pā. 5.1.119*).

"Two parts of flour and one part of buttermilk" (*dvimayam udaśvit*) means that when buttermilk is being purchased, two equal portions of barley-flour are the measure for that single portion of buttermilk. Although there is a mutual dependence [between the two], the compound formation (*vṛtti*) occurs because the meaning is clearly understood. Furthermore, an adjective (*guṇa-śabda*) is observed to denote a constituent part, as in "a three-strand rope" (*triguṇā rajjuḥ*). In the rule *guṇavacanebhyo matupo luk* ("there is elision of the suffix *matup* after words denoting qualities"), those words are intended which, having identical forms, denote a quality and then apply to the substratum possessing that quality due to the inherent nature of their expressive power—such as "white" (*śukla*) and so forth.

And thus, the rejection [of the objection] with the words "it is established because there is no exclusion" (*avyatirekāt siddham*) is based on the suitability for the metaphorical treatment of non-difference (*abhedopacāra*). By this, color and other qualities—which are unsuitable for such treatment—are excluded; therefore, they are valid only when followed by a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*), as in "the pot is colored" (*rūpavān ghaṭaḥ*) and so forth. In the rule "*prakāre guṇavacanasya*," since the doubling applies to every word, the term *guṇavacana* refers to independent substances like "sharp" (*paṭu*) where the quality is subordinate to the substance.

In the rule *pūraṇaguṇa...* and so forth, because the word "guṇa" (quality) is intended to include [all] meanings [of the term], there is no application of the prohibition to these [words]. Furthermore, if one were to include every property (*dharma*) that is merely dependent, such as those characterized by conjunction (*saṃsarga*) and so on, then the functional capacity of the substance (*dravyasāmarthya*) and other such properties would not be established. Therefore, the "guṇa" to be understood here is defined by the characteristics beginning with "*sattve niviśate...*" (it resides in being...). And this is the "guṇa" well-known in the Vaiśeṣika treatises.
