For instance, in the case of earthy substances, qualities such as color (*rūpa*) undergo production and destruction due to contact with fire.

Since [properties] such as *paramamahattva* (ultimate magnitude) in time (*kāla*), space (*ākāśa*), and the self (*ātman*) are also not produced by action (*akriyājanya*), the category of quality (*guṇapadārtha*) is pervaded by that definition. Consequently, since a prohibition would also apply to color (*rūpa*) and so forth, it is argued that because [the term *guṇa*] cannot possibly refer to those qualities residing in the object of the meaning of the root (*māṇārthagata*), it is logical that [the word *guṇa*] has as its cause qualities whose action is perceived. However, since a compound (*samāsa*) finds its scope in cases such as *īṣatpiṅgala* ("slightly tawny"), how could it apply here?

As for the statement in the Bhāṣya—"If *ākṛti* were what is being expressed... then here [in the case of] *īṣattakaḍāraḥ*, there would be no compound"—how can that be so? For since no relationship between action and factor (*kriyākārakasambandha*) is perceived here, this [compound] is simply unformed (*avyutpanna*). It is merely for the sake of making known the sequence of phonemes (*svarṇānupūrvī*) that an etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) is resorted to—such as "from the root *gaḍi*, with *kaḍa* substituted"—even though such a derivation does not actually exist. Therefore, this Bhāṣya should be explained solely as being intent on demonstrating the meaning of the Sūtra: "Because it is a word denoting a quality (*guṇavacana*), there is a compound here."

In the rule *ajāder guṇavacanādeva*, the term "quality" (*guṇa*) is understood as that characterized by the definition "that which enters into a substance" (*sattve niviśate*), and not as that characterized by being a relation (*saṃsargin*) and so forth. For if it were so, since every nominal stem (*prātipadika*) denotes an object qualified by an attribute (*upādhi*), the mention of "quality-words" (*guṇavacana*) would be redundant when a suffix follows immediately after a nominal stem. However, in the rule *naño guṇapratiṣedhe sampādyarhahitālamarthāstaddhitāḥ*, the "quality" (*guṇa*) is taken precisely in the form of a relation and so forth.

For instance—the meaning of the rule is that secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) ending in *saṃpādya*, *arha*, and so forth, which follow the negative particle *nañ*, are oxytone when they denote the negation of a quality (*guṇa*). Here, there are four things subject to negation: the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*), the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*), its limiting adjunct (*tadupādhi*), and the relational connection (*saṃbandha*) which constitutes the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). Among these, because of the expression "negation of a quality," in the case of the phrase "a face with ear-ornaments" (*akarṇaveṣṭakamukha*), neither something other than the ear-ornament nor the mere absence of it is resorted to. What then?

The phrase "the face is not completed by the two ear-ornaments" (*karṇaveṣṭakābhyām na sampadyate mukham*) negates that which is a subordinate condition—an auxiliary factor—which would otherwise constitute the completion of the face as it is being formed. In that case, because the negative particle (*nañ*) has no syntactic connection with the word *karṇaveṣṭaka* (ear-ornament) in its base form, one must understand from this very indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) that there is an *asamartha-samāsa* (an irregular compound where the members are not semantically connected). Furthermore, even though there is a prohibition, the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) still occurs, because it is based on the meaning conveyed by the term used in the original injunction.

However, at a later stage, the negation by the particle *nañ* through another word is external (*bahiraṅga*) and does not sublate the internal (*antaraṅga*) grammatical refinement (*śabda-saṃskāra*). Thus, in cases such as "he does not go to the village" (*grāmaṃ na gacchati*), even though there is a negation of the action, the accusative and other case endings still occur for the object and so forth. Others maintain that the negation by *nañ* applies to the sentence-meaning (*vākya-artha*) in the form: "the face is produced from two ear-rings."

The meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*) is the relationship that establishes a specific instance for words that otherwise reside in a general sense. And because it delimits the meanings of the individual words (*padārtha*), this [sentence-meaning] is called a subordinate factor (*upasarjana*) or a quality (*guṇa*). Furthermore, when this relationship is brought about, there is also the cognition of the cessation of the two related entities—the meanings of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*). In this view as well, the fact that the negative particle (*nañ*) forms an *asamartha-samāsa* (an irregular compound) with the base when there is no connection [with the suffix-meaning] is to be understood from this very indicative mark (*jñāpaka*). This incapacity (*asāmarthya*) arises because the base is dependent upon the meaning of the suffix.

Because that which is dependent lacks syntactic capacity (*asamarthya*). However, there is no fault when there is a connection with the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*), for in that case the meaning of the suffix is the primary element (*pradhāna*). A compound formation (*vṛtti*) certainly occurs even for a primary element that is dependent. Others, however, say: "In this context, the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) is subordinate (*guṇa*) in relation to the meaning of the suffix because it is secondary; thus the opinion of the author of the *Bhāṣya* is inferred."

For instance, regarding the rule "not from a *tatpuruṣa* preceded by *nañ*," the author of the *Bhāṣya* stated: "The activity of the Teacher makes it known that every secondary derivative (*taddhita*) arises from a [base] that requires a correlative, since he says 'in the negation of a quality, [the suffixes] *sampādya*, *arha*, etc., [are applied after *nañ*]'. To illustrate: in the case of "the state of not being large is *apārthiva*" or "*aprathima*," the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is negated by *nañ*.

And likewise, due to a lack of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*), the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) would not occur at all, because of the rule stating, "from [stems] that are semantically competent, [the suffix is added] optionally after the first word. Therefore, this meaning is stated by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*). In that context, just as the meaning is "the state of being different from what is prohibited" or "the state of something else being different," so too, through the connection of the negative particle (*nañ*) with the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), it is understood that the face is produced by ear-flaps that are themselves prohibited, or produced by something other than those; thus, the meaning of the base functions as a subordinate factor (*guṇatvena*).

"It is the intention of the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*). But this is not correct. When a primary and a non-primary element are in proximity, the application of the grammatical operation occurs only with the primary; thus, the prohibition concerns the object that is being accomplished (*sampadyamāna*), and it is logical that it applies to the accomplishment (*sampatti*) itself, not to the non-primary meaning of the root (*prakṛtyartha*). Furthermore, a meaning conveyed by the same word is "internal" (*antaraṅga*) and becomes the correlate (*saṃsargī*); for this reason as well, it is logical that the accomplishment alone is the subordinate factor (*guṇa*), and not the distant meaning of the root conveyed by another word. Moreover, the indicator (*jñāpaka*) functions by following established logic (*nyāya*), not by acting as a causal agent (*kāraka*).

By the *jñāpaka* (indicative statement) that "when the negative particle (*nañ*) is connected with the meaning of the principal member, there would be no compound with the base form due to a lack of semantic capacity," the author of the *Bhāṣya* has indicated that a suffix is applied to a base form that already presupposes a compound. Thus, the interpretation of the rule (*sūtra*) presented previously is indeed correct. For example, in the word *ābhaidikam*, a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is used here in the sense of "deserving" (*arha*); in *avasīyaḥ*, it is used in the sense of "beneficial" (*hita*); and in *asāmparāyikam*, it is used in the sense of "sufficient for" (*alam*), being a secondary derivative meaning "capable of [withstanding] the next world" (*samparāya*).

Following this direction, the nature of the qualities (*guṇa*) should be explained in other instances of excellence as well, according to the commentaries on the Sūtras and Vārtikas; only a mere indication has been shown here. || 1 ||

In the Bhāṣya on the *atiśāyana* sūtra it is said: "The meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is indeed the substance (*dravya*), and there is no excellence or deficiency in a substance. If that is so, then the quality (*guṇa*) must be the meaning of the nominal stem. [Objection: "But both are the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*). Why then is it said that 'there is excellence of the quality'? [Reply: "To this it has been stated: 'That which possesses excellence, its excellence will occur.'"

The statement "both [the substance and the quality] are indeed the meaning of the nominal stem" (*prātipadikārtha*) is the reason why the quality, characterized by its relation to the substance and so forth, is understood here. For that quality—such as "white" and the like—is conveyed by the nominal stem as being subordinate to the substance. Now, one must state the reason why it is the quality alone that possesses excellence (*prakarpa*), and not the substance. Since the quality, like the substance, is presented by the word as having a completed form, why should the effect-substance (*kāryadravya*), which likewise depends on causes, not also possess excellence?

Likewise, one quality is perceived while another is expressed. In that case, the excellence of a substance must depend solely upon the quality being expressed; here too, the reason must be stated. Since many limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) can possibly apply to even a single object, it is improper to adopt only one as a rule. How is it that in every instance that quality which serves as the locus for the substance's excellence is present? For it is said: "A quality does not have another quality as its primary object; qualities are devoid of qualities."

Furthermore, there is no delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) among universals (*sāmānya*), because of the established tenet that "universals are devoid of further universals" (*niḥsāmānyāni*). Likewise, since there is no quality (*guṇa*) in actions (*karman*) and so forth, on what basis could there be excellence (*prakarpa*) in them? Moreover, it must be explained how it is logical for one thing to possess excellence when another thing is being excelled; for Caitra does not become brave through the bravery of Arjuna. And it is from verbal testimony (*śabda*) that people understand a substance (*dravya*) to be excelled.

In order to refute these alternatives in succession, he says: "The quality that is employed to distinguish an inexpressible substance for the sake of its expression—that excellence [of the quality] is designated [as 'intensity']. (2)

In this context, a substance cannot even be defined by means of a distinction from its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). For it is not possible to perceive [a substance] as "this" without the categories such as *sāmānya* (universals) and the rest. And how could that which cannot even be defined in its own form be endowed with excellence (*prakarpa*) by itself? Therefore, the phrase "of the indefinable" (*avyapadeśasya*) is employed as a reason under the guise of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Thus, in this way, excellence is caused by another related property (*saṃsargi-dharma*).

A substance (*dravya*), being distinguished by its associated qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth, is differentiated from those of its own class. Since many such associated qualities are present there, he asks: "By what is this excellence (*atiśaya*) produced? He replies: "The quality that is employed as a differentiator for designation. That quality which is employed to designate the substance—that is, to distinguish it from others—and which is grasped by means of a word, the excellence produced by that [quality] is what is expressed by the suffix.

But [the quality] is not [the cause of differentiation] when it is unexpressed, because there is no cause for its restriction by another, because the cognition [of it] is unstable, and because it is extrinsic (*bahiranga*). However, a quality that is expressed is intrinsic (*antaraṅga*) and has a restricted cognition. For it is logical that the excellence belongs to the very self of the substance through whose influence the substance is expressed; this is because excellence is an attribute of the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*), and only that which is expressed constitutes the meaning of the base. He says that the nature of "quality" (*guṇa*) as defined in our own treatise—namely, "quality is that which differentiates"—is what is understood here.

"Whatever is associated and differentiating is indeed the definition [of a quality]; and here, differentiating power is primarily the defining characteristic of a quality. Even though a staff is inherent in the person holding it, it is a quality because it serves to differentiate him from those who do not possess a staff. Thus, in the expression 'the whiter cloth,' the excellence of the substance is caused by the quality of whiteness, and not by a quality such as heaviness that is merely perceived [as a consequence]. || 2 ||

Just as there is no excellence (*prakarṣa*) in a substance that is devoid of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), so too, for a quality (*guṇa*) abstracted from its substance and existing independently—such as in the expressions "whiter" (*śuklataram*) or "more beautiful" (*rūpataram*)—there is no excellence inherent in itself. Rather, because at that stage the quality functions as a substance (*dravyāyamāṇatvāt*), its excellence is caused solely by another property (*dharma*) that does not coalesce with it. Thus he says: "For no primary [quality] possesses excellence without a cause of differentiation; nor does [excellence] become the denotation of a word. (3)

Even a quality (*guṇa*), when denoted by a word as the primary meaning, follows a nature capable of being referred to by a pronoun such as "this" or "that," namely, that it possesses the character of a substance (*dravya*). Since that [quality] in its unqualified state is not an object of designation, any designation [of it] is based solely upon a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*); and excellence (*prakarṣa*) is contingent precisely upon that adjunct. In this regard, although the universal (*jāti*) is the cause of designation, it has no operation with respect to excellence. For excellence pertains to that which is of the same genus (*samānajātīya*), and in that case, there is no differentiation within the universal.

For this very reason it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "It is called a *jāti* because it is obtained through birth (*janana*). And for this [kind of] object, there is no excellence (*prakarṣa*) or deficiency (*apakarṣa*). Because a *jāti* is connected with the time of birth, its application does not depend on the presence of other causes once the substance has been produced—unlike qualities such as white, which may be intensified due to differences in their causes.

Therefore, because the universal (*jāti*) is eternal, there is no state devoid of that universal; thus, even at the time of birth, it remains established in that very form, proceeding without separation from the individual (*vyakti*). Consequently, it is capable of effecting a differentiation from only those things belonging to the same class—this is the meaning. And for this reason, since it is impossible for the universal itself to possess excellence, specific qualities such as brilliance, purity, and being unmixed with other colors—which are inherent in the same substrate as that universal—are the basis for the occurrence of excellence.

Although the excellence (*prakarṣa*) of a quality may occur through its own nature due to contact with fire and so forth, nevertheless, since designation depends on external conditions (*paropādhi*), it is logical that excellence is caused by those very [conditions]. For not every internal distinction can be expressed by a word, because words such as "color" (*rūpa*) denote everything belonging to the genus "color-ness" (*rūpatva*) without distinction.

Therefore, when even qualities such as luminosity (*bhāsuratva*) are designated as primary, the excellence [expressed by a term like] "more luminous" (*bhāsuratara*) must be understood as being mediated by another quality dependent upon that [first quality]. In that case as well, if yet another quality is primary, the excellence is caused by a further quality dependent on that one; thus, as long as the operation of words is possible, there is no end to the succession of qualities. Consequently, it is that quality which is taught as the cause of excellence in its own right that is termed a *guṇa*.

"It is precisely from the quality (guṇa) inherent in that [object] that its excellence is perceived"—this has already been stated. For this very reason, the term "of every primary [object]" (*sarvasyaiva pradhānasya*) here includes the word "all" (*sarva*) to indicate pervasion (*vyāpti*). However, when the operation of the word ceases, the search for another property comes to an end. || 3 ||

Now, one might object: "Since qualities such as brilliance (*bhāsuratva*) are not the direct denotations (*vācya*) of the word 'white,' and since excellence here is mediated by these non-denoted, implied properties, an indefiniteness (*aniyama*) would result due to the proximity of multiple limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Anticipating this, he says: "Not all factors that cause differentiation, even when present, are expressed by specific words (*viśeṣaśabda*) which denote distinct objects, unless they are manifested in the primary [qualities]. (4)

In this world, within primary substances, there exist many real properties (*dharma*) that serve as the causes for the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) of those things from others of their own class or of different classes. And all of these cannot be denoted by any single word, because there exists no single word that is directed toward multiple exclusions. Indeed, many words operate upon a single object, each being directed toward a single specific exclusion. Consequently, they are called "particularizing words" (*viśeṣa-śabda*) in that context, because they denote specific, restricted particulars.

If a substance qualified by all its particularities were denoted by a single word, that single word would be common [to all]. But this is not the case. Therefore, because words denoting objects qualified by specific exclusions do not touch upon all particularities, excellence is singular, having as its cause only the particularity that has been grasped.

Furthermore, subtle qualifiers such as "brilliance" (*bhāsura*) and the like, whose meanings are not explicitly recognized by words such as "white," must indeed be denotable by those very terms; for it is impossible for the primary entity "white" itself, when divested of its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), to enter the domain of verbal expression. Since that which is expressed by a word is necessarily conditioned by the form of its correlates (*saṃsargin*), there can be no excellence (*prakarpa*) based on the universal (*jāti*). Moreover, because we observe usage such as "a whiter color" (*śuklataraṃ rūpam*), it is determined here that the excellence is caused by brilliance and the like.

Nor is that [cognition] caused by a property that is not denotable by a word, because that would lead to over-extension; therefore, since luminosity and so forth are also established through the authority of usage, let it be determined that they too are denotable by words here. || 4 ||

Now, let it be granted that for a substance which is inherently inexpressible, the application of expression occurs by means of its associated attributes (*saṃsargidharma*). However, since those associated attributes are exhausted within that very act of expression, how can the operation of excellence (*prakarpa*) be postulated there? To this, he says: "If a particular attribute (*viśeṣa*) were active in the indication of the object (*vastūpalakṣaṇa*) therein, then excellence would be causeless, because there would be no restrictive rule [regarding which attribute should be indicated]. (Verse 5)

If the purpose were fulfilled by the mere indication of the substance, then that which is perceived as white would be understood as "whiter" (śuklatara) when it is superior due to weight (*gariman*) and so forth; in that case, the specific quality (*viśeṣa*) would not be known as the basis for the excellence. However, such is not the established usage, because excellence is understood as being caused solely by the quality of whiteness itself.

Therefore, since both cognition and reasoning conform to that which is most proximate to the denotation of the word, it is logical to postulate that the operation of the cause of designation—the specific quality (*viśeṣa*) itself—is directed toward excellence (*prakarṣa*); this is the meaning. (5) Anticipating the objection as to how there can be a cognition of excellence in cases such as "more inferior" (*nikṛṣṭatara*) or "more excellent" (*prakṛṣṭatara*), he says: "Everything is necessarily and invariably made excellent by a related cause, whether that cause be inferior or superior. (6)

When there is an excellence in the cause of designation, there is a cognition of excellence; thus, when that which is characterized by inferiority (*nikarṣa*) is denoted, excellence must be expressed in relation to that very inferiority, and when that which is the basis for excellence (*prakarpa*) is denoted, it depends on excellence itself. Since excellence is possible for everything when there is a dependence upon its own kind (*sajātīya*), this is logically consistent. For superiority is indeed possible precisely because that which is inferior is inferior, and that which is excellent is excellent.

Thus, even when a quality is predominant, there is an excellence caused by another property; and even when that [other property] is predominant, there is an excellence caused by yet another. He states this infinite regress (anavasthā) according to the method previously shown. || 6 ||

In this world, the usage *gotara* (a better cow) is observed. And it has been stated that in that case, excellence (*prakarṣa*) is not caused by the genus (*jāti*). Nor is any other cause here perceived as being active; thus, the excellence of the substance is without a [perceived] cause. Anticipating the objection—"In the same way, this will apply to *śuklatara* (whiter) and so on; why then is excellence proclaimed to be caused by a quality (*guṇa*)?"—he says: "If a cause were not required to be active for the excellence of a substance, then the mention of the substance with respect to that excellence would be purposeless. (7)

A substance whose form is fully established is, by its very nature, incapable of being connected with decrease or increase; therefore, it does not experience excellence (*prakarṣa*) on its own account. Thus, if one does not admit that the causal factor (*nimitta*) consisting of an adventitious attribute (*upādhi*) is operative toward excellence, then its mention when excellence is to be expressed would be purposeless. The meaning is that the usage "whiter" (*śuklatara*) and so forth would simply not occur.

Therefore, since excellence must conform to what is logically possible according to the authority of linguistic usage (*prayoga-prāmāṇya*), that [excellence] must everywhere be established as being caused by a property inherent in the object of designation (*vyapadeśa-hetu*) that is related to it. And when the genus (*jāti*), which serves as the cause of designation, is absent—as in the case of "whiter color" (*śuklataraṃ rūpam*), where excellence is established through properties such as brilliance (*bhāsura*) inhering in the same substrate—so too in the case of "better cow" (*gotarā*), this [excellence] must be established through a property such as the capacity for carrying or milking that inheres in the same substrate.

Just as in the case of luminosity and so forth, one should understand here that even the capacity for carrying loads, yielding milk, and the like constitute the meaning of the word, based on the authority of its usage. Consequently, it is entirely consistent to say that a cow possessing superior capacity for carrying loads and yielding milk is called "a better cow" (*gautara*). || 7 ||

In order to conclude the meaning of the section, he says: "Therefore, the quality, being active and based upon its own excellence, indeed differentiates the nature of the substance by establishing itself within its own excellence. (8)

Since a substance (*dravya*) is inherently devoid of excellence (*niratiśaya*), a quality (*guṇa*) that is in contact with it and strives to impart its own causal excellence brings about a distinction from other substrates through a particularity caused by its own excellence. Anticipating the objection—"How can the excellence of one thing make another excellent?"—he says: "Just as a formless substance is designated by means of another's form, so too is a quality that lacks excellence distinguished by means of excellence. (Verse 9)

Since a substance that is formless and devoid of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) cannot be admitted into linguistic usage, when such usage is admitted for a substance colored by the form of its adjuncts, the meaning is this: all linguistic activity, which follows upon the objects denoted by words, has its form determined by its own adjuncts. Furthermore, because the distinction between the adjunct and the possessor of the adjunct is difficult to discern, there is a "confusion" (*saṅkara*); thus, in linguistic usage, the excellence of a quality (*guṇaprakarṣa*) finds its rest in the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*), and does not abide solely in the quality itself as an abstracted quality-possessor, nor does the quality itself abide solely in the quality-possessor as an abstracted quality. This is established. || 9 ||

Thus ends the fifth chapter, the *Guṇasamuddeśa*, in the *Prakīrṇakaprakāśa* composed by Helārāja, son of Bhūtirāja. Now, having briefly indicated those categories (*padārtha*) that share a common purpose (*ekayogakṣema*), he speaks in order to examine them sequentially: "Space, means, action, and time—these [terms] denote entities whose forms as capacities (*śakti*) are absolutely unstable. (1)

Words such as "direction" (*dik*) and so forth, while conveying their own referents by virtue of being properties of substances whose natures are already established, are devoid of contact with the objects of direction as they are defined [in common experience]. For indeed, direction and the like are powers (*śakti*) whose form consists of extrinsic conditions (*paropādhi*); and since dependence (*pāratantrya*) is the defining characteristic of power, even action (*kriyā*), being dependent upon a substance, is designated as a power. Furthermore, in the Vaiśeṣika system, it is not tenable for direction to be a substance, because it is more logical for power to be the nature of that which assists other categories, being inferable from its effects.

Such a form of power (*śaktirūpa*) is not directly touched by words that denote established entities (*siddhasvabhāvavastu*); therefore, this uncommon nature of the category (*padārtha*) must be established through its definition (*lakṣaṇa*). For there is indeed usage of these [terms] in this treatise, such as: "From words for directions (*dikśabda*), [the suffix *asi* is applied] to direction, place, and time... and so forth. In that context, while the definitions of the means of proof (*sādhana*) and so on are to be analyzed as already inferred from the treatise, the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of direction, time, and the rest must be explicitly stated.

In that regard, he first defines the essential nature of the directions through inference: "That which is the cause of the distinction between the limit and the object to be reached, and by virtue of which the cognition 'straight' arises even without anything else [to compare it with]. (2)
That power upon which the manifestation of the various distinctions of action depends, being differentiated by its own limiting adjuncts, is called "space" (diś). || 3 ||

The distinction between the object to be designated (*idam*) and its limit (*asmāt*), characterized by the relationship between a limit and that which possesses a limit—expressed as "this is prior to or posterior to that"—is a differentiation of the meaning of the nominal stem that cannot be accounted for by the inherent nature of the thing itself; it therefore indicates another cause. That other cause is called "direction" (*dik*). For this cognition is not caused by genus (*jāti*) and so forth, since no coloring by those factors is perceived. By process of elimination, it is caused by direction. As the Vaiśeṣikas say:

"From which [it is known] that 'this is from here,' that is the mark (liṅga) of the directions. Furthermore, since direction is always perceived as a limiting adjunct (upādhi) of objects—being inferred through its effects—it does not exist as an independent substance. Indeed, direction is not perceived in the manner of earth and the other elements. For this very reason, it will be stated later that time, too, is a power (śakti). And inherence (samavāya) has been described as "that power called inherence... and so forth.

Likewise, the cognition "this bamboo pole is straight" arises without another [object], since it does not depend even on a limit (avadhi), and occurs without the assistance of other causes such as the earth; and that [cognition] is caused by space (dik), because it arises from the extension of parts toward a single direction. Since the term "straight" is merely illustrative, cognitions of "crooked" and so forth should also be explained as being caused by space.

Likewise, for the moments of action (*karmakṣaṇa*) arising transversely, upwards, or downwards, there occurs a manifestation of subordinate universals (*aparajāti*) such as "whirling-ness" (*bhramaṇatva*), "throwing-upwards-ness" (*utkṣepaṇatva*), and so forth, which are caused by direction (*diṅnimitta*). For it is through their connection with and separation from directions such as "upward" that these distinct moments of action become capable of manifesting their specific universals. The term "of action" (*karmaṇaḥ*) refers to the sub-classifications of the universal of action (*karmasāmānya*), such as throwing-upwards-ness and the like; the singular number is used because it refers to the genus (*jāti*).

The meaning is: the various specific types (*jātibheda*) of the moments of action such as wandering and so forth. The followers of Kaṇāda (*Kāṇāda*) maintain that space (*diś*) is one, because there is no distinction in its defining characteristics (*liṅga*) and because there is an absence of any specific characteristic. Furthermore, although space is one, it is conventionally designated as tenfold due to the diversity produced by fixed limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). And thus they say: "The 'east' is [defined] from the past, future, and present conjunction with the sun."

The designation "east" (*prācī*) arises from that conjunction with the sun at the beginning of each day—whether it has occurred, is occurring, or will occur—by virtue of which a particular direction and location is determined; it is so called because one faces toward the east (*prāgañcati*). Likewise, there are the sūtras for "south," "west," and "north. From that very same conjunction with the sun, the designations "opposite" (*pratīpa*) and so forth arise. For instance, that direction where the sun faces back (*pratīpam añcati*) due to its setting is the west (*pratīcī*).

For the conjunction with the solar disc, which is limited by its physical form, pervades only a measured space. A portion delimited by that [disc], whether past, future, or present, establishes a fixed spatial orientation. Thus, even though the movement of the sun is invisible, that direction which one avoids by turning one’s back is the South (*dakṣiṇā*); that which one does not avoid is the North (*uttarā*). At midday, the solar disc moves facing northward; therefore, it is also called the North (*udīcī*).

And by this very method, the intermediate directions such as the southeast and others are also explained; thus it is said in the Sūtra: "By this, the other directions are explained. For instance, the tenfold division [of the directions] based on the conjunction with the regions presided over by the world-protectors (lokapālas) as the sun revolves clockwise around Meru has been determined in detail in another treatise, and should be understood from that source. Here, however, it is merely restated as "the direction beyond" and is not described by being divided.

Nor is this division of direction merely figurative; for since a figurative designation is a property of cognition, it would not apply to the physical direction itself. Rather, the distinction of direction is designated through conceptualization, whereby direction produces various effects by depending on specific conjunctions with the sun as auxiliary causes. For this very reason, even if a real distinction exists, the auxiliary causes must be depended upon as its manifestors. Since those very causes will be required for the diversity of effects, the unity of direction is accepted because the distinction can be explained otherwise.

For what person who accepts valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*) would, while admitting the diversity of effects, deny the multiplicity of causes? Moreover, if the directions were real and manifold, then because they are all-pervasive (*vibhu*), the cognitions of "east," "west," and so forth would be confused, since effects are observed everywhere. Therefore, it has been stated that direction is in reality one; the variety of its effects, however, arises from the difference in auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*). || 2,3 ||

Nor is it logical that the effect arises from the auxiliary causes alone without regard for space (*dik*), because those [auxiliaries] are by nature devoid of prior, posterior, and so forth, whereas that state [of being prior or posterior] is produced by connection with space; nor is there a cause corresponding to that [state]. Thus, space—which is characterized by the cognitions of "prior," "posterior," and so on—and time must be accepted. Regarding their distinctness, he states the specific difference in their indicative marks: "The priority and posteriority of corporeal things are based on differences in location; they are determined from that very source [space]. But when they take the form of a temporal sequence, they are determined from time. (Verse 4)

Form (*mūrti*) is the dimension of a substance that is not all-pervading. Furthermore, because they are apprehended as non-different from it, the substrata (*dharmin*) are indicated here [by the term "form"]. Priority and posteriority do not exist in all-pervading substances such as space (*ākāśa*). The conventional usage of "prior" and "posterior" regarding non-pervading entities occurs due to their connection with prior and posterior locations. Since the priority and posteriority of a location itself is caused by direction (*diś*), it follows by implication that the priority and posteriority of direction are themselves caused by location.

The intention is that since the sequence of actions—such as "it was before" and "it will be later"—is established by virtue of the permission and obstruction effected by the power of time (*kāla-śakti*), there is no confusion of indicators (*liṅga-saṃkara*) regarding space and time. || 4 ||

He states that even for formless entities, there exist conceptual priority and posteriority: "By means of the space-points of ether and by its various other parts, each distinct from the others, that [ether] serves as the limiting adjunct (upādhi) for conjunctions and disjunctions. (5)

The spatial division of space has been described through the distinction of its conjoined attributes (*saṃyogidharmabheda*). Thus, that portion of space which is conceptually constructed by means of conjunction with a corporeal substance (*mūrtadravya*) residing in a specific location, and which—because it does not pervade the parts belonging to that corporeal substance—is characterized by conjunctions and disjunctions occurring respectively according to their respective [locations], serves to delimit direction (*digavaccheda*) as "east," "west," and so forth. Consequently, the conventional usage of "east," "west," and so on, applies to the imagined locations of space; and thus, that which is conjoined with the eastern space [is designated as "east"].

The meaning is that this conventional usage regarding corporeal objects—such as "the former is joined with the distant space" and "the latter"—is established by being preceded by [the same usage regarding] incorporeal things. || 5 ||

In this world, the distinction of directions such as "east" and "west" for locations is established by the directions; but by what are the directions themselves established? If they were caused by some other entity, one would ask, "By what is that [other entity] established? leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If the directions possess their own inherent "east," "west," and so forth, then what fault have the locations committed? Anticipating this objection, he says: "The establishment of locations depends on the directions, but the establishment of directions does not exist [by anything else]. Indeed, the capacities (*śakti*) of entities are brought about by their mutual assistance. (Verse 6)

Since the independent nature of directions—consisting of their essence as supports and so forth—is being determined, and since the state of being "prior," "posterior," and so on is absent from their own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), another cause called "direction" (*dik*) is postulated, [providing] assistance produced by direction itself. In that case, if [direction] were postulated as having a dependent nature (*paratantrasvabhāva*), no further distinct cause would need to be sought for the purpose of the state of being prior, posterior, and so on.

For whatever the nature of that [effect] may be, it is to be conceived as the effect only to that extent; reality is nothing other than that, because in that case, the dependence of powers (*śakti*) alone is logically established. If another power were to be postulated, it would follow that [the entity] becomes a possessor of power (*śaktimat*), which would result in the loss of its status as a power. The intention is that the conjunction with the sun does not bestow a new quality such as "easternness" or "westernness," but rather merely manifests its own inherent nature. || 6 ||

In order to nourish this very power so that it may assume the nature of independent existence, he says: "Direction, whose form is withdrawn from [external] entities, is designated as 'East' because it is the cognition of 'prior'; otherwise, it would be a mere name. (Kārikā 7)

That which has been superimposed upon entities as their limiting adjunct (*upādhi*)—that form of theirs—is what is conventionally designated as "the East" and so forth. From which [direction] there arises the cognition of "East," namely the knowledge that "this object is to the East. "East-ness" is an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*); by it, "West-ness" and the rest are also included. The meaning is that direction is of the nature of a limiting adjunct (*paropādhirūpa*).

Otherwise, if one disregards the nature of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and resorts to independence, then direction does not exist in reality; rather, at that time, "direction" is merely a designation. It is a mere word whose object is an independent substance, failing to touch upon the actual reality. For it has been said: "The means of accomplishing [an action] is the action"—such [terms] denoting a real entity are utterly unstable when applied to the nature of the power (*śakti*) of things.

Thus, because the direction (*diś*)—which is to be inferred solely from its effects—is eternally dependent, there is no room for alternative possibilities regarding an independent category of entity. Whether it possesses an inherently manifold nature (*nānā-svabhāvatva*), in which case what need would there be for the specific movement of the sun as a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*); or whether it possesses a single nature (*eka-svabhāvatva*), in which case it could not produce diverse effects even when the cooperative causes differ. To say this is impossible. For just as the direction must be accepted as having the form of a power (*śakti-rūpā*) whose existence is inferred by its effects characterized by cognitions such as "east" and "west," so too [must its dependence be accepted]. (7)

But surely, the cognition of "prior," "posterior," and so forth, will be caused by factors such as being face-to-face or not face-to-face? As it is stated in the *Bharata*: "O Bharatas, that direction from which people enter facing [them] should be considered the 'eastern' direction. In common worldly usage as well, one who stands facing [another] is called "in front," while one who stands behind is said to be "behind."

Likewise, suspecting that common usage such as "here is the path on the right hand" and "here is the path on the left hand" is based on one's own limbs and thus has no basis in the conceptualization of directions, he says: "In worldly convention, the determination [of direction] based on one's own limbs does not involve fixed directions; for that which is behind a person facing west becomes in front when there is a reversal. (8)

The fixed determination of directions—such as "east" and so forth—is established in relation to one's own body, such as the face; however, these directions do not remain constant. For indeed, that which was behind a person facing west becomes in front of him when he faces east. Consequently, there would be no fixed rule such as "one should eat facing east or north. Therefore, one must accept that the determination of "east," "west," and so on, is based on the beginningless conventional usage of the directions. 8.

However, he says that in some cases the designation of directions such as "east" and "west" for locations is conventional even without regard for [absolute] direction: "The fixed rule for the arrangement of locations does not hold with respect to the directions; even that which is conventionally established as 'west' is designated as 'east'. (9)

The determination of directions based on spatial orientation—such as the designation of "eastern regions," "the southern path" (*dakṣiṇāpatha*), and "the northern path" (*uttarāpatha*)—is not fixed. For instance, in relation to a particular direction, even what is behind is conventionally referred to as the "eastern region. Thus, one traveling from the southern path toward the eastern region says, "I am going to the eastern region," even though by the fixed rule of directions he is actually heading north. Therefore, the mere status of being "east" and so forth is conventional (*rūḍha*) and independent of absolute spatial direction.

However, conventional usage based on direction is appropriate here as well; for instance, after raising the objection in the *Bhāṣya*, "Why does this not occur here: 'He dwells in the eastern region'?", it was resolved with: "This is not a fault, for this [word] is a qualifier of a location. This word "eastern" (*pūrva*) does not function by depending on a limit because it is used conventionally; therefore, the word for direction (*dik-śabda*) does not apply to a specific location. Rather, it qualifies the general notion of "location" (*deśa-sāmānya*) which is understood from the word "region" (*deśa*).

The meaning of the Bhāṣya is that the suffix being prescribed after the word *pūrva*—which functions as a term for direction (*dik*)—does not occur after a conventional (*rūḍha*) word. Some explain: "This word *pūrva* does not denote a location by way of its own form as a location, because that [location] has already been expressed by the word 'location' (*deśa*) itself. Rather, the word *pūrva* denotes a certain specific quality residing in a location, which is not understood from the word 'location' alone, and which is based on the delimitation of a particular direction. This is incorrect.

Because [the term] "place" (deśa) is used in grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with those things that reside in a place, and because the cognition [of "east," etc. is intended to refer to them; for it is necessary to employ the word "place" in order to distinguish [them] from space and time—otherwise, in the absence of such a cognition, what would be the object? Thus, in cases such as "the eastern region" or "the Deccan," although the status of being "east" and so forth is innate and conventional (rūḍha) without depending on anything else, there also exists another form caused by direction (diṅ-nimitta). Just as when a convention based on one's own limbs functions differently, there is a different convention based on direction; therefore, it has been established that the status of being "east" and so forth is primarily caused by direction alone. || 9 ||

And thus, he brings this into agreement with the Bhāṣya: "In the case of the directions, the application of terms such as 'east' and so forth is independent of other limiting conditions (upādhi), whereas in the case of a location, it arises through connection with a direction. Therefore, because [the word *pūrva*] is treated as having been previously mentioned as masculine (*bhāṣitapuṃska*), the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) is not established. Regarding this point, the production [of the feminine form] is never expressed by the word itself. || 10 ||

Regarding the rule *dakṣiṇottarābhyāmatasuc*, the Bhāṣya states: "What is the purpose of the vowel *a*? Let *atasuc* alone be used. In this way, the letter *c* would not be made for the sake of accent, since [the desired result] is established by the accent of the suffix itself. To this, it was replied: "By the *liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā* (the maxim that a grammatical operation applies to a word-form qualified by its gender), this suffix also occurs after the word *dakṣiṇā*. In that case, if the vowel *a* were not present, the elision of the final syllable (*yasyeti lopa*) would not take place."

In this context, having raised the objection that if the suffix *pratyaya* were to elide the vowel *ā*, then by the *liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā* (the maxim regarding forms qualified by gender), the rule would apply to the two forms ending in *ṭā*; and since the vowel *a* would not exist [at that point], the elision of *yasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.148) would not occur, resulting in the forms *dakṣiṇataḥ* and *uttarataḥ* being unestablished; and having stated the purpose that if the vowel *a* were present, the *ākāra* would be elided and thus the vowel *ā* would not be heard; and having further objected that this is established through *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like treatment); it was replied: "It is not established, because *puṃvadbhāva* applies to that which has been previously mentioned as masculine (*bhāṣitapuṃska*), and these two [words] have not been previously mentioned as masculine."

It is further objected: "But aren't these two also words whose masculine forms have been mentioned—namely *dakṣiṇa* and *uttara*—since a masculine is indeed spoken [for them]? To this it was said: "The substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) applies to that which has had its masculine form mentioned within the same general configuration (*ākṛti*). However, these two have their masculine forms mentioned in a different configuration; for *dakṣiṇā* and *uttarā* are directional terms (*dikśabda*), whereas *dakṣiṇa* and *uttara* are terms of relative position (*vyavasthāśabda*). This statement from the Bhāṣya is appropriate if the words *pūrva* and so on are conventional terms (*rūḍhiśabda*) for the directions, and not otherwise. For such is the meaning: [The text continues: "In the case of a word like *pūrva*, when it denotes a direction, there is no application of the masculine form because it is a conventional term. But when it denotes a relative position, the masculine form is applied. This is what is intended. Furthermore, the word *pūrva* is used in the sense of "east" by convention, even though it is derived from the root *pṛ* ("to fill") with the suffix *kan*. Therefore, since it is a conventional term, the masculine form does not apply. But when it means "prior" in terms of time or space, the masculine form is applied. Similarly, the word *dakṣiṇa* is used in the sense of "south" by convention, even though it is derived from the root *damś* ("to bite") with the suffix *ṇa*. Therefore, since it is a conventional term, the masculine form does not apply. But when it means "clever" (*dakṣa*), the masculine form is applied. Likewise, the word *uttara* is used in the sense of "north" by convention, even though it is derived from the root *tṛ* ("to cross") with the suffix *kan*. Therefore, since it is a conventional term, the masculine form does not apply. But when it means "superior," the masculine form is applied. Thus, the Bhāṣya is consistent. It is not the case that the masculine form is applied to *dakṣiṇa* and *uttara* simply because they denote directions; rather, the masculine form is applied to those words when they denote relative position, while the feminine form is applied when they denote directions. This is the established conclusion. As for the objection regarding the word *pūrva*: it is not the case that the masculine form is applied to it when it denotes a direction, because it is a conventional term. But when it denotes relative position, the masculine form is applied. This is the intended meaning. And this is how it should be understood. Thus, the point is established. The objection raised by the opponent—that the masculine form should apply to *dakṣiṇa* and *uttara* when they denote directions—is refuted by the fact that they are conventional terms in that sense. In the case where "bhāṣitapuṃskam" (having a masculine form) is taken as the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) of the compound, its denoted meaning is not logically tenable. Since its "padārtha" is ultimately designated as its "ātman" or "svabhāva" (essential nature), there is no deviation from its having a masculine form; therefore, what would be excluded by this [term]? Consequently, the external referent is the meaning characterized by the ground for the application of the word (*pravṛttinimitta*). Even in that case, wherever the ground for application differs, there is always the status of having a masculine form.

Ultimately, by means of the word "and so forth" (*ādi-śabda*), because of the impossibility [of the operation] in the actual object (*artha*), the state of having been used in the masculine (*bhāṣitapuṃskatā*) is resorted to based on the capacity [of the word] with respect to a single ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*). And since the operation is impossible in the actual object, the word expressing that [object] is called "having been used in the masculine" (*bhāṣitapuṃska*) by virtue of the property of its denoted meaning (*abhidheyadharma*). Thus, when the ground for application is the external referent (*anyapadārtha*), the established meaning is: "In the case of a word that has been used in the masculine, provided the form (*ākṛti*) is the same, there is the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*)."

Regarding the directions "south" and "north," because the designation is inherent, in this sense characterized as direction (*dig-lakṣaṇa*), the term "procreation" (*prasava*)—that is, masculinity—is not denoted by these two words in any context whatsoever; rather, it is caused by the direction. When their application is based on location, then the two words "establishment" (*vyavasthā*) denote procreation. Establishment is a state of existence consisting of mutual dependence. For example, when it is said, "the southern slope of the mountain," there arises a cognition of a limit [asking], "from where? [and thus the direction is implied].

In this regard, since these two [words] are *bhāṣitapuṃska* (having a masculine form), there is no *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine substitution) when the basis for their application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is one and the same, because that [basis] is absent in another form (*ākṛtyantara*). Here, although the result could be established even from the forms ending in *ṭāp* (i.e., *dakṣiṇā* and *uttarā*) by relying on the supplementary rule (*aupasaṃkhyānika*)—namely, that for a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), there is *puṃvadbhāva* in all compound formations (*vṛtti*)—the letter *a* has been established as a qualifier for the suffix *val* (in the rule *ṣaṣṭhyatasarthapratyayena*) so that the form may be derived even without the *akāra* of the suffix *atasuc*.

But here it is objected: "Surely, in the case of 'southern' (dakṣiṇā) and 'northern' (uttarā), a limit must necessarily be expected, because without that, their own meaning cannot be established. And since words such as 'eastern' (pūrva) and so on function in the context of direction (*dik*) by depending on a limit, they too are words of relative determination (*vyavasthā-śabda*). Thus, when a single [limit] establishes the determination, the quality of having been previously mentioned as feminine (*bhāṣitapuṃskatva*) certainly exists. Moreover, because their application to direction depends entirely on something else, words for direction (*dik-śabda*) are distinguished from words for place (*deśa-śabda*)."

Beyond this, it was stated that the functions of words denoting direction (*dik-śabda*) do not apply at all. The intention [of the objection] was that since directions do not function as names (*nāmadheya*), these cannot be considered words denoting direction. To that, the reply is: "When directions will express a fixed determination (*vyavasthā*). [The objection continues: "If that is so, then whatever exists in a direction would be a word denoting direction; thus there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to such things as 'pleasant' (*ramaṇīya*) and the like."

For just as words such as "east" and so forth—though based on relative determination and common to both space and time—are called "direction-words" (*dik-śabda*) when they refer to direction, so too words such as "pleasant" (*ramaṇīya*), which are based on qualities, would also be "direction-words" if they were applied to direction. To this, the following solution is stated: "A 'direction-word' is a word observed in [the context of] direction; it is that which does not deviate from direction. In that regard, words of determination such as "east" and so forth also apply to space and time.

And thus it is said that "from words denoting direction, [the suffixes occur] in the senses of direction, place, and time" without distinction. To justify the Bhāṣya statement, "How is it that [the word *pūrva*] does not deviate from its direction?", he says: "But when the power of direction is expressed, the perception of 'east' and so forth is restricted to the direction, just as the perception of 'sixty' is restricted to the duration of life. (11)

By the mention of "conventional usage" (*śaktigrahaṇa*), he indicates that the application of words such as "east" (*pūrva*) is established there [in space] without dependence on any other object; however, in the case of space and time, their application is based on their status as limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) which serve as the cause for systematic determination. Thus, the usage of words like "east" is fixed and non-deviating with respect to direction. But with respect to space and time, usage is not established by convention (*rūḍha*) as being the cause of systematic determination. When it is said, "the eastern direction," the conventional understanding involves a notion of a relative limit (*avadhibhāva*) inherent within the name itself.

But as for the expression "the eastern jar," why is it so? It requires a limit (avadhi). Furthermore, from the word "jar" (*ghaṭa*), its own primary meaning is understood; the word "eastern" (*pūrva*) indicates its relative position with respect to that [jar], but it is not its name. Thus, there is indeed a difference in essence between these words for direction and these words for place and time; however, due to their similarity, they are determined to be identical. For an identity between conventional (*rūḍhi*) terms and etymological (*naimittika*) ones is not possible.

And likewise, in the rule "From words denoting direction [the suffix occurs] in the sense of direction, place, and time... (*dikśabdebhyo dik-deśa-kāleṣu...*), because words such as *pūrva* (east) are intended to function as the grammatical effect (*kāryabhāk*), the inclusion of the term "word" (*śabda*) implies that those whose "words" are like the word for direction are qualified by their similarity in form, even though they apply to place and time. And it is observed that such words possess, by their very nature, a power to convey a specific meaning with necessity regarding certain objects.

For example, in the expression *ṣaṣṭir bhṛtaḥ* (*ṣaṣṭikaḥ*), when the measure of life is to be expressed, the word *ṣaṣṭi*, although it is a numeral, necessarily denotes time. Thus, it generates the suffix prescribed under the heading of "time" by the rule: *tam adhīṣṭo bhṛto bhūto bhāvī*. In this context of grammatical derivation (*vṛtti*), even though the word *ṣaṣṭi* is a numeral in the sentence (*vākya*), it invariably takes on the sense of time as the object to be numbered, due to the specific restriction of the word's inherent power (*śakti*).

For this reason, from the word *varṣa*, the measure of the birth-time is understood as being precisely the period called "the rains. Furthermore, the word denoting time is not employed in its derivative form (*vṛtti*) such that, through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the numeral-word itself might be understood as functioning in reference to time. Thus, like words such as *māsa* (month) and so on, this word *varṣa* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in reference to time independently of any other word. And accordingly, regarding the rule *tad-asya parimāṇam* (Pāṇini 5.1.57), it has been stated: "The statement 'and in the case of the measure of life' is redundant, because it is already established by the rule [5.1.58] *kālāt*."

For there is no need for the supplementary rule stating that "if one has lived sixty years, his lifespan is indeed measured at sixty," because such an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) does not apply to cases like *ramaṇīya* and so forth, since their duration is not perceived as being fixed. Furthermore, this grammatical explanation must follow common worldly understanding regarding the words employed; thus it has been said: "Due to the absence of denotation, the [suffix] will not arise in the case of *ramaṇīya* and similar words."

Thus, just as the word "sixty" (ṣaṣṭi) is a numeral whose primary object is a number, yet by its very nature it is conventionally established here upon time as the thing to be numbered, so too the word "east" (pūrva) and others—though elsewhere used to denote spatial or temporal arrangement—are necessarily established by their own nature in reference to direction. Therefore, it is rightly said that [the term] "does not deviate from direction," which means it does not stray from its primary sense.

And thus, because the application [of the term] is restricted to a specific direction, and because there is an absence of the masculine form (puṃvadbhāva) due to the absence of having been previously mentioned as masculine (*bhāṣitapuṃskatva*) within the same generic form (*ākṛti*), it is stated: "In all simple formations (*vṛtti*) involving pronouns (*sarvanāman*). However, regarding the rule "in the sense of restriction (*vyavasthā*) when not a technical name (*asaṃjñā*)," since it follows merely the restriction of a limit (*avadhi-niyama*) within the technical designation of pronouns, words such as *pūrva* and others—even when denoting direction, place, or time—are specifically qualified. For instance, there exists a persistence (*anugama*) of that state of being "eastern" (*pūrvatva*) which is a delimitation of form established by means of a limit.

Because it denotes an object established in space just as it does in time and place, the word "east" indeed refers to a direction established relative to a distinct limit (*avadhi*), yet it does not touch upon that limit as its own qualifying attribute (*upādhi*). For example, the word "red" (*śoṇa*) applies only to the object that is red, and yet it does not depend on redness as the ground for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*). Likewise, the word "black" (*kṛṣṇa*) applies to the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, yet it does not adopt the quality of blackness as its ground for application.

Thus, the words for directions such as *pūrva* (east) and so forth are conventional (*rūḍha*) and have their limits (*avadhi*) already internalized. However, the distinction is this: in the cases of space (*deśa*) and time (*kāla*), there is an expectation of a limit expressed by a word; whereas in the case of direction, the restriction of the limit is common [to both]. Therefore, even when [the term] *vyavasthāyām* (in the sense of fixed determination) is used as a qualifier, the grammatical operation pertaining to the designation of pronoun (*sarvanāma-saṃjñā*) certainly applies to the direction-denoting words *pūrva* and so forth. || 11 ||

Now he describes another function of the directions: "Through shadow and light, the differentiation of parts is established for mountains and the like; in those things whose nature lacks these properties, the differentiation of parts is not established. (12) Shadow is the absence of light; light is illumination. One mountain peak may be colored by the mass of the sun’s rays, while another is streaked with much shadow; such a division of components [is possible]. However, this differentiation characterized by shadow and sunlight is not possible in the absence of direction, because, lacking distinctions such as "east" and "west," there can be no multiplicity of parts defined by those limiting conditions (*upādhi*).

For in this way, that property characterized by direction—which consists of "easternness," "westernness," and so forth—exists only in those formless objects; thus, the meaning is that even the distinction of parts caused by the connection with direction serves as an indicator (liṅga) of direction. || 12 ||

For indeed, the initial conceptualization of the division of parts for corporeal things depends upon direction; thus he says: "The division of the partless atom is established by means of direction. They call that [direction] the primary power capable of conceptualizing parts. (13)

Because they are uncreated and eternal, even atoms—which are partless—are conceptually assigned four sides, as well as upper and lower portions, by way of the directions (*diś*). For there can be no real division of parts in a partless atom; rather, such a distinction is derived solely from the directions. Consequently, conjunction with six other atoms situated in those directions occurs. When conjunction exists, the effect arises through the sequence of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth. And thus, even in that case, the conventional usage of "east," "west," and so on, is established.

If direction were non-existent, then even when joined with six [other atoms], the mass would be partless and merely atomic in size; thus, the manifestation of gross parts would not occur. Therefore, from the very moment of production onwards, the superimposition of parts depends primarily on the power of the directions themselves; it is by means of the directions that all material objects are assisted through the conceptualization of the differentiation of their parts. In other cases, such as mountains and the like, which possess parts, the differentiation of parts is brought about by shadow and sunlight.

However, regarding those partless atoms for which that [distinction] caused by shadow and heat does not exist, they explain that it is caused by the directions (*diṅ-nimitta*). For instance, where no other cause exists, the activity of the directions operates upon those partless things that do not possess such properties; whereas in the case of composite things like mountains, where there is another cause—such as shadow, heat, and so forth—which indicates a distinction of parts, that very cause is what initiates the conventional usage of the distinction of parts. This was stated in the first verse.

The operation regarding direction (*dig-vyāpāra*), however, is explained by the second verse. For instance, since shadow and so forth—which establish the differentiation of parts—do not exist because [the atom] is partless, therefore "direction" (*dik*) is here designated as a "part" (*bhāga*) of this atom by means of the category of direction (*dipadārtha*). The meaning is that the conventional usage of "parts," such as "eastern" and "western," proceeds [in this manner].

Others explain that just as the conventional distinction between parts (*bhāgabhedavyavahāra*) in mountains and the like is produced by another cause, so too in the case of atoms—when they are distinguished by the conjunction of shadow and light—an additional cause must be sought; and that [cause] is Space (*dik*). This is the illustrative example provided by the first verse. However, all of this is untenable. For instance, when there is shadow on one side of a jar, it is the conjunction of the potsherds themselves with the shadow; thus, the jar itself has no connection with either the shadow or the sunlight.

Now, because it occupies that same location, the composite substance as a whole would also be connected [with the light], just like its parts; consequently, since it would be fully pervaded in its entirety, it would appear in every respect [as illuminated]. Furthermore, because there is no other side [to the object] apart from the sunlight, there would be a total lack of connection with shadow.

Now, if that location as well is not connected with the sunlight, then there would be non-difference of location between the part and the whole, because the part and the whole would both be [respectively] conjoined and unconjoined with the sunlight. In that case too, by this same reasoning, the connection with shadow and so forth belongs only to the parts; and in their case as well, it belongs to further sub-parts, until one reaches the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*). Consequently, it is solely due to the connection with spatial directions that even a gross object, like an atom, acquires the designation of "eastern," "western," and so forth, as well as qualities such as "high" and "low."
And likewise, he will indeed state later: "The state of being partless is equal for both the atom and the jar," and so forth. (13)

Now, one might object: "Do not entities arise with their specific forms and structures by themselves? What benefit do they derive from space? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Entities are indeed without location, without parts, without movement, and without support; yet, through their form as related to others, a differentiation of powers is conceived. (14)

All-pervading entities such as space and the like possess no location. As for material objects such as earth and the like, which are composed of parts (*avayavin*), there is an absence of a location that constitutes their very self. Furthermore, for both types of entities, locations are merely conceptualized, whether they be those joined by conjunction (*saṃyogin*) or those inherent by inherence (*samavāyin*). Thus, the constituent parts (*avayava*) of things do not exist in themselves; rather, they are conceptualized as distinct entities (*arthāntara*) that are related through association. Moreover, because there is an absence of any differentiation among parts, sequence (*krama*) is also secondary, since sequence is grounded in differentiation.

Likewise, those things for which there exists no supporting condition (*upāśraya*) or limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) that could induce a change in their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-anyathātva*) are "without support" (*nirupāśraya*). Even such entities, although there is no actual alteration of their own-nature (*svarūpa-anyathātva*), are perceived as distinct according to the difference of place and so forth, by means of a differentiation of capacity (*śakti-bheda*) brought about through association with other forms. For instance, even when the relationship is non-distinct due to connection with another direction, a certain thing that has attained the status of a substratum is perceived as "place"; thus, the conventional usage of "place" is caused by direction (*diṅ-nimitta*).

That very same locus, through the force of inherence (*samavāya*), has its distinctions concealed; thus it is designated as a "part" (*bhāga*) or a "constituent" (*avayava*). And because of that [inherence], there is sequential production. The appearance of sequence, as well as the determination of a qualified object (*viśiṣṭāvasāya*) when distinctions are set aside due to inherence with qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth, occurs by means of the relation of conjunction (*saṃsarga*); this is the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding entities. However, their essential nature (*ātman*) therein consists in their capacity for connection (*yogya-svabhāva*).

Thus, just as entities that are themselves devoid of spatial location and so forth come to possess effects such as spatial location through their association with distinct things, so too do entities whose parts are produced by space come to possess the conventional usage of distinctions between parts such as "east" and so forth; this has been established by the presentation of this illustrative example. || 14 ||

An objection might be raised: "Since a composite whole such as a jar is perceived as having parts divided by spatial distinctions and possessing a large magnitude, how can the state of being non-spatial (adeśatā) and so forth be established in its case? Anticipating this, he says: "The nature of being partless is equal for both the atom and the jar. What is called a 'part' there is merely a difference in capacity (*śakti*), as is their respective magnitude. (15)

The emptiness of parts (*avayava-śūnyatā*), which constitutes their very nature, is common to both the jar and the atom. However, those portions designated as "parts"—which are conceptually constructed through a specific power characterized by spatial direction (*dig-lakṣaṇa*) and thus possess a fabricated priority and posteriority—are merely the substrates themselves appearing indistinctly due to inherence (*samavāya*). Because they are caused by that power, they are conventionally designated as "powers" (*śakti*); for if they possessed parts inherently, unity would be impossible. Furthermore, a state of having parts based on a connection with something else is not primary, as this would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even the atom possesses parts.

Nor is there a primary distinction of parts based on size, because even for those two—the jar and the atom—size, characterized as largeness and minuteness, is a distinct entity; for size is a specific power that serves as the cause of the cognition of largeness and minuteness. It is precisely due to this difference in size that there is a distinction between the jar and the atom, and not due to the connection or non-connection with constituent parts. Thus, when there is no dependence on the connection with limiting adjuncts (upādhis), every undesignatable reality, being like Brahman, is entirely equal. || 15 ||

Nor is it the case that a difference imposed by limiting conditions (upādhi) inheres in the essential nature (svarūpa) of things; thus he says: "Since difference is conceptualized [as dependent], difference is also seen therein. Therefore, the wise know that difference which has its cessation in the unseen (adṛṣṭa) to be more logical. (16)

There is a distinction between the parts and the whole; likewise, there is a distinction between the parts and their own parts, and those [parts] with their own parts, until one reaches the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*). Even there, a division of parts is postulated by means of spatial direction (*diś*). But how could spatial direction itself, which is devoid of inherent division, serve to produce division? Even the distinction of spatial directions is brought about by the distinct conjunctions with the sun. Those conjunctions with the sun, moreover, arise from the distinct locations on Mount Meru. There too, the distinction arises from the distinction of parts; and since that too arises from a distinction of parts, one is once again situated within spatial direction itself.

In that case as well, [the opponent] thinks: "It is thus"—meaning this is like a circle—wherein the cessation or finality of a distinction is unperceived; they consider such a distinction to be especially untenable due to the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā-doṣa*). The point is that not only is a distinction among entities (*bhāva*) itself illogical, but since distinctions among limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) also require something else, the distinction remains endless; therefore, it is utterly incapable of establishing a distinction between entities. This is the intended emphasis.

Thus, since distinctions such as place and so forth apply to entities both intrinsically and by virtue of adventitious conditions (upādhi), [the author] will conclude that conventional usage—which has taken root in the form of the relative (sāṃvṛta)—is impossible to deny, by means of the passage beginning with "like consciousness" (caitanyavat). // 16 //

Now he states that space is all-pervasive because it is formless: "Because its effects are observed everywhere, it is held to be omnipresent; this alone is what they call omnipresence; for other things, the rule is to be like their effects. (17)

Because the previously mentioned effects, such as exclusion (*vyatireka*) and so forth, are universal, Space (*dik*) is all-pervading and its nature is omnipresent. For incorporeal things, this alone constitutes omnipresence: the capacity to produce their own effects everywhere. However, for corporeal bodies, omnipresence consists in the pervasion of various locations by means of their constituent parts. (17)

Now he concludes what was stated previously: "The conceptualization of space and time exists in the world like consciousness itself; for who indeed can establish that nature of living beings otherwise? (18)

For even if an object exists, as long as it is not cognized, it is as if its existence has not been attained and is thus not capable of performing a causal function; therefore, consciousness—which is knowledge—is something that cannot be denied by any disputant. Furthermore, this consciousness belongs to the self (*ātman*). As the Sāṃkhyas have said: "Consciousness is the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the person (*puruṣa*). And this [nature] is impossible to deny. Similarly, although the conceptualization of space and time lacks logical justification regarding their distinctness, they are established in accordance with common experience.

For, since entities—according to the previously stated reasoning—are logically untenable in terms of distinctions, non-distinctions, existence, non-existence, and so forth from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the manifold conventional usage has become firmly established through the power of beginningless, deeply ingrained ignorance (*avidyā*). Having become as natural as the very nature (*prakṛti*) of those who engage in worldly discourse, it cannot be otherwise established even by the wise who know reality as it is.

For just as consciousness is indeed their very nature, so too are space and time established through their roles as "prior," "posterior," and so forth, for all worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*), since the accomplishment of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is impossible without them; otherwise, even the state of being a living being would be undermined—this he indicates by the use of the term "living beings" (*prāṇin*). Furthermore, in worldly transaction, it is not tenable to deny the existence of categories of objects exactly as they are perceived. || 18 ||
Because there would be a confusion of worldly transactions if there were a reversal of the primary elements, therefore, even while abandoning these states, one clings to them once again. (19)

Worldly practices whose fruits are both seen and unseen—such as "one should eat food facing the east" or "one should perform the *śrāddha* rite in the forenoon"—would not be possible if direction and time were not established.

When the conceptualization of space and time—which has attained the nature of the very essence of primordial matter (prakṛti)—is reversed or inverted, and if it were admitted to be the cause of notions such as "prior" and "posterior," there would result a confusion and instability of worldly transactions (vyavahāra) such as the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana) that are firmly established in perception and scripture. Therefore, although this universe is indeed without prior or posterior in terms of form and action, nevertheless, the wise man, though fallen into worldly transaction and having abandoned the appearance of the phenomenal world (prapañca), still relies upon that very world. Thus [he says] these...

Even while refuting objects such as space and time by presenting what appear to be subverting arguments, he does not abandon them, because the cognition conditioned by those very factors is unavoidable. By using the plural number, he shows that even objects such as the "whole" (*avayavin*) cannot be relinquished in worldly discourse. By stating "he abandons yet he relies upon," he suggests through hyperbole (*atiśayokti*)—due to the simultaneity of abandoning and relying—that the opponent accepts two contradictory meanings at once, thereby highlighting the contradiction between his own words. (19)

Just as time is the power (*śakti*) of Brahman, which—through the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of its functions of obstruction and permission—has a manifoldness superimposed upon it, so too space (*dik*), divided by its own limiting adjuncts, serves as the basis for the linguistic usage of distinctions among entities such as "east," "west," and so forth.
