Thus he says: "But the distinction of that power into 'east' and so on has other entities as its substratum; therefore, space, being differentiated by that distinction, is made available for the very purpose of [further] differentiation. (20)

Although it was stated in general that "it is divided by its own limiting adjuncts," the distinction is here again taken up in its specific form as being "east" and so forth. Furthermore, the conjunctions with the sun, which are designated as distinct entities, have been explained. The phrase "for the sake of distinction alone" means for the purpose of generating a cognition of the qualified object as colored by its own particularizing adjuncts. By the restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*), he states that direction is inherently non-different; it relies upon adventitious difference only at the very moment of the cognition of the qualified object as divided, and not otherwise. || 20 ||

Now, the treatise states the rule regarding the indicators of direction: "In the context of a relation involving dependence, the rule for direction is characterized by [specifying] a limit; 'this is to the east of that'—only the genitive case is seen when it refers to another property. (21)

The worldly function of dependence in the form of a limit—such as "this is prior to that" or "this is posterior to that"—is a secular matter; in that very context, the fifth case (pañcamī) characterized by connection with direction (*dig-yoga*) applies specifically. If one asks, "How then is the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) seen in this context? he says: "In the expression 'prior to this,' only the sixth case is seen," and so forth. When the relationship between a limit (*avadhi*) and that which possesses the limit (*avadhimat*) is required, the fifth case is used; therefore, in that very instance, the sixth case is set aside by the fifth because the latter serves as an exception (*apavāda*).

However, when there is a requirement for another property—namely, the state of being a part—the sixth case (genitive) indeed occurs for the whole, as in "the front of the body" (*pūrvaṃ kāyasya*). For here, there is no requirement for the whole as a limit; thus, this is not the domain of the fifth case used in connection with direction (*digyoga-pañcamī*). Indeed, the fifth case is not used in the relation between part and whole, but rather in the relation between a limit and that which is limited.

For this very reason, when one part serves as the limit (*avadhi*) for another part, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) indeed occurs, as in "the front part of the body from the navel" (*pūrvaṃ kāyasya nābheḥ*). Here, there is the status of being a part in relation to the whole (the body), while "front-ness" (*pūrvatā*) is in relation to other parts; thus, because the relata differ, there is no contradiction, and the employment of two case endings is justified. However, in the rule prescribing compounds (*samāsa*), by the inclusion of the term "one who possesses a part" (*ekadeśin*), the directional nature (*dig-rūpatā*) is not relied upon. || 21 ||

And in common usage, the status of being "eastern" and so forth for objects is caused by the directions such as East, and not by their own parts; thus, [the definition] is not unstable. He says: "The reversal of 'East' and the others is never observed when there is no confusion regarding the limit (avadhi). Furthermore, the mark that 'this is straight for him' does not get interchanged. (22)

Since no confusion or lack of restriction regarding priority and so forth has been observed in the absence of a reference point—that is, when there is no mixing of perspectives—this conventional usage remains firmly established. For instance, that very thing in relation to which "priority" is conventionally designated cannot, in relation to that same thing, be designated as "posteriority"; thus, priority and posteriority produced by direction (*dikkṛta*) are fixed.

Thus, for this lineage, the fact that the root is straight and clear is also a characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of the directions that does not become confused; for there is no dependence on a limit (*avadhi*). Indeed, confusion might be possible only if there were dependence on a limit, because limits are not fixed. But since there is no dependence on a limit regarding this characteristic mark, the directions remain entirely unmixed. And so, even when established from one's own body, there is no confusion precisely because of the restriction by a limit.

However, worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), which has both seen and unseen purposes, must be sought as being restricted by the determination of directions based on the limit known as the conjunction with the eternally established sun; thus, any arbitrary limit whatsoever should not be resorted to. In this way, direction (*dik*) has first been established according to the system of external objects. Now, he speaks according to the system of internal objects of cognition: "Or else, it is a property of the internal organ that appears externally in this manner. But in this process, the state of being internal or external does not exist. (23)

The term *caitanya* (consciousness) is used thus because its activity (*vyāpāra*) consists in [the manifestation of objects] while remaining within. For, although—due to the power of beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*)—there is an appearance of external forms as "this" through the extraction of its own nature, yet in the ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*), since an external object is impossible, the world manifests only within its own belly; thus, the activity belongs solely to that which remains within. And so he will say: "The sky, the earth, the wind, the sun, the oceans, the rivers, and the directions are portions of the reality of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇatattva*) situated externally."

This property of that internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), independent of external objects, appears as its very nature through the power of ignorance (avidyā). Thus, it is determined as manifold through forms such as "east" and so forth. If it is asked, "In the absence of an external [object], how can it be called 'external'?", he replies: In this conceptual construction (kalpanā) which consists of the determination of externality belonging solely to the manifestation itself through the power of ignorance, neither internality nor externality is primary; rather, they are spoken of in this way merely by force of appearance, out of deference to others. This is the meaning.

For if there were no external object, even internality would not be primary; thus, the distinction between internal and external is merely conceptual. In this way, priority and posteriority—superimposed upon entities by ignorance—appear as properties of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), characterized by the impressions of beginningless false habituation, even though those entities are essentially internal in nature. Therefore, there is no such thing as an external direction. || 23 ||

Therefore, he states that even the inquiry into whether these powers are one or many is entirely fruitless: "Having understood that the conceptualization of these powers as being either one or many falls within the realm of the non-real, one should not contemplate them as such from the perspective of ultimate reality. (24)

The primary unity of the directional powers (*dik-śakti*), which appear as distinct through their limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as "east" and so forth, exists; yet, due to the difference in those adjuncts, they possess multiplicity. This very primary multiplicity, established from beginningless time and inferable from its diverse effects, is thus conceived in two ways, both of which fall within the realm of non-substantiality (*avastu*). Since the directions are ultimately non-substantial according to the Vijñāna school—due to the absence of any external object—the meaning is that once one has understood them to be objects of non-substantiality, they need not be investigated from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). This is because worldly transactional usage (*vyavahāra*) is established in accordance with how things are perceived.

Therefore, intending to express their plurality based on the diversity of their respective cognitions as they are thus experienced, there is the designation "of these" (*āsām*) using the plural number. || 24 ||

Furthermore, there is no purpose whatsoever in investigating the nature of categories (padārtha). For it is said: "In regard to entities whose true nature transcends conceptual construction, linguistic conventions are based upon mental designations; in such matters, one follows worldly usage. (25)

In this world, the categories of things (padārtha), whose bodies are constructed by the fixed conventions imagined by the non-Buddhist outsiders (tīrthika), exist in reality as they are, transcending those conceptual constructions (vikalpa) imagined by the outsiders. For the true nature of entities (bhāva) does not consist in the possession of contradictory forms demonstrated by each respective philosophical system. Therefore, even by the wise, the categories of things established in the world—which are agreeable when left unexamined—should be accepted. Enough with these unstable conceptual constructions of logic! And thus, the ten directions, well-known in the world, are established.

He says that through conceptual constructions based on reasoning, neither difference nor non-difference is established: "There is no unity without plurality, and without unity there is no other; in the ultimate sense, this distinction between the two does not exist at all. (26)

Since their nature is mutually dependent, if one is not established, the other is not established either; thus, there follows the contingency of both being unestablished. Therefore, the unity and plurality of the directions are not definitively established. However, in conventional practice, by closing one's eyes like an elephant (*gajanimīlana*), worldly usage is firmly rooted according to how things appear. But in the investigation of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), even difference and non-difference—which are mutual opposites—are unreal, because the primary non-different Supreme alone is the true essence. Furthermore, it has been stated that "Direction" is a power (*śakti*) existing as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the Supreme. (26)

And he states that power is unfit to be the subject of an inquiry into difference and non-difference: "The distinction among powers is not such as the status of the possessors of power; nor does worldly unity exist within their own selves. (27)

Because independent entities possessing powers are apprehended as distinct, their difference is determined; it is not so for the powers themselves, which appear as dependent upon their substratum. Therefore, the difference [of the powers] from their substratum and from one another is established by perception. Nor is there, for an independent possessor of power, a unity such as that commonly recognized for a jar and the like, because [in the case of the powers] there is no appearance of non-difference.

Likewise, although the powers possess a distinction inferred from the diversity of their effects, they are non-different from themselves and from their substratum; thus, all powers are indeed indefinable in terms of both difference and non-difference. For this very reason, the power of ignorance does not establish a difference from Brahman, which would result in the emergence of duality. || 27 ||

Regarding what was stated—"There is no unity, nor is there plurality... and so forth—he concludes that very point by showing its lack of fixed stability, stating that it is not proper for logicians to adhere to a single-sided position: "Unity would not be established if one did not conceive of plurality; and plurality would be lost if one did not conceive of unity. (28)

If one does not conceptually construct or rely upon plurality as the counter-correlative through the intellect, then unity, acting as its correlate, would not obtain its own fixed nature. Likewise, if plurality were not to rely upon unity as its counter-correlative, it too would not remain established. Thus, because these two are mutually dependent, they cannot both abide in the same place; it is therefore established that the worldly perspective, which is charming only so long as it is not investigated, must be accepted as the basis for the directions [of discourse]. || 28 ||

Thus ends the sixth chapter, the *Dik-samuddeśa* (Exposition on Space), in the *Prakīrṇaprakāśa* composed by Helārāja, son of Bhūtirāja. **The Exposition on the Means of Accomplishment (*Sādhana-samuddeśa*)** Since "the means of accomplishment" (*sādhana*) was mentioned immediately after "space" (*dik*), [the author] speaks in order to define it: "They know the *sādhana* to be the capacity for the production of actions that are inherent in their own substratum as well as in other substrata. (1)

The scholars beginning with the author of the Bhāṣya maintain that the capacity (*śakti*) of a substance for the accomplishment of an action is the means (*sādhana*), because by this [capacity] the action is accomplished. For it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "A quality (*guṇa*) is the means. Here, it is precisely the capacity that is expressed by the word "quality" (*guṇa*), because it is dependent upon its substratum and because it differentiates its own locus from others.

Regarding the objection that there would be a contingency of denoting a distinction between the two *bhāva*s (the action and the state) expressed by a primary derivative (*kṛt*) and a verb (*ākhyāta*), the *Bhāṣya* states: "Substance (*dravya*) attains the status of an instrument (*sādhana*) with respect to the accomplishment of the action. This statement must be understood as being based on the intervention of a capacity (*śakti*), since it explicitly excludes the status of substance as an instrument in other contexts; for it is the substance endowed with capacity that is the instrument, and a capacity cannot exist without a substratum.

Regarding the rule *parokṣe liṭ* ("the perfect tense is used for what is beyond the senses"), the Bhāṣya states: "If the collection of qualities (*guṇasamudāya*) is the means (*sādhana*), then the means is also cognizable through inference. But if the means is something other than the qualities, then the possibility of being perceptible or imperceptible arises. This too must be interpreted in the same way. Since power (*śakti*) is eternally imperceptible, it is improper to use it as a qualifier for an action because of its non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*). Therefore, by the force of the qualifier "imperceptible," it is the substance (*dravya*) permeated by power that is presented as the means.

Thus, regarding the rule *upasargācchandasi dhātvarthe*, the *Bhāṣya* statement—"this [suffix] occurring in the sense of an instrument (*sādhana*) will be connected with gender and number"—is to be explained as referring to a substance (*dravya*) qualified by the power of the instrument. For, if only *dhātvarthe* (in the sense of the verbal root) were stated, since a word's function is possible within a linguistic item (*śabda*), the comprehension of the action (*kriyā*) would already be established; therefore, by the inclusion of the word *artha* (sense), which serves to effect the compound *dhātukṛto'rthaḥ* (the sense produced by the root), a substance is resorted to. Indeed, the word *artha* is a synonym for *vastu* (an objective entity).

Since a substance (*dravya*) is established by its own nature and thus cannot be produced by an action (*kriyā*), its production occurs only through the form of the factors of action (*kāraka*), such as the object (*karman*). For it is action that brings about the *kārakas*, since the conventional usage of those terms depends upon it; therefore, it is said that a substance is "produced" by action insofar as it takes on the character of a means (*sādhana*). As for the interpretation that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*) is the "purpose" (*prayojana*) of this [action], that explanation of the *Bhāṣya* is incorrect.

For in this way, since action is the goal to be accomplished by means of power (*śakti*) alone, the substance (*dravya*) would not be conveyed [as the primary factor]. As for the statement in the Bhāṣya on the explanation of the excellence of non-substances—"The substance is indeed the instrument (*sādhana*), and there is no excellence or deficiency of a substance"—it should be understood that this designation of the substance as the instrument is made without intending to express a distinction between the power and the possessor of power (*śaktimat*).

For instance: since a suffix denoting excellence (*prakṛṣṭa*) follows a verbal form (*tiṅanta*) that expresses the accomplishment of an action, and since this power (*śakti*)—which is inferred from its effect, namely the momentary action—is understood as excellence only through its effect, one might raise the following objection: "If the intended suffix is accepted as expressing the excellence of the action, then since power has substance (*dravya*) as its substratum, why is there not also excellence by way of the substance which serves as the cause, just as there is excellence by way of the effect? Anticipating this, this [verse] was stated in order to declare the absence of such excellence in the substance; thus, the distinction (*vyatireka*) was disregarded. In that regard, the action belongs to the agent and the object.

The term "inheres" (*samavaiti*) means that the two [the agent and the object] possess the status of causal factors (*kāraka*) with respect to the accomplishment of an action that inheres in their own substratum. However, instruments (*karaṇa*) and the other factors possess the status of means (*sādhana*) with respect to an action that inheres in another substratum; for an action does not inhere in the instrument and so forth. The plural number in the phrase "of actions" (*kriyāṇām*) is used with reference to the distinction between individual instances. Alternatively, all [factors] possess the status of being a means with respect to an action inhering in their own substratum when considered in relation to subordinate actions (*guṇakriyā*). For in a subordinate action, all are agents (*kartṛ*), since it is impossible for that which accomplishes nothing to function as a means.

For this very reason, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of terms such as "instrument" (*karaṇa*) and "agent" (*kāraka*) with the word "means" (*sādhana*) is logically established. In this way, the plural number in the expression "of actions" (*kriyāṇām*) becomes fully justified. However, while the primary action resides in the agent or the object, the [subsidiary] actions of the instrument and so forth are inherent in other substrates. || 1 ||

But how is it understood that potency (*śakti*) is the means (*sādhana*) and not the substance (*dravya*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Because the universe, which is a collection of mere potencies and possesses manifold properties, exists at all times and in every way, something or other is intended to be expressed in a particular instance. (2)

Entities such as jars are denoted by the word "universe" (*viśva*). They consist of a collection of powers (*śakti*) capable of accomplishing their respective functions, such as fetching water. For this very reason, those powers are the "measures" (*mātrā*) or "parts" therein; thus, jars and the like are merely an aggregate of powers. Furthermore, these powers are of many kinds. Some arise solely from their own causes and perish even upon the destruction of their substratum, such as the power of illumination belonging to lamps, consciousness, and so forth.

Some human qualities cease while their substratum remains, such as the powers of strength and so forth; for these arise through the practice of exertion and the consumption of aphrodisiac substances. Others are maintained by human effort while the substratum persists, such as the lethal power of poison or the sprout-producing power of a seed. Still others are transformed by one possessing extraordinary power, such as when a yogi effects a transformation of the form of all things.

Some [powers] are manifested through the passage of time, such as the power of dharma, adharma, and so forth, in the yielding of their fruits; thus many such varieties are to be inferred. In this way, since the collection of powers possesses multiple natures, when there is a desire to express a specific distinction according to its respective power within a manifold effect, the occurrence of a restricted causal efficiency is established. However, if the substance itself were the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), then because it is of a single form, there would be no variety of effects—this is the meaning. Thus it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "The means of accomplishment is a collection of qualities (*guṇas*)."

Because the principal action (*pradhānakriyā*) cannot be accomplished by each individual power (*śakti*) alone, there is a reference to the collection [of powers]. However, with respect to the subordinate actions (*guṇakriyā*), each power possesses the status of a means (*sādhanatā*). And because that [status] varies according to the principal action, it takes the form of the object (*karman*) and so forth. Alternatively, even though each [power] is a means individually, the reference to the collection is for the purpose of avoiding an over-extension (*avyāpti*); for if the powers themselves were the means, their distinctness would result in a plurality of effects for a single [agent].

Therefore, although an entity possesses multiple powers and always remains in that state, it is intended that a particular power manifests in a particular instance; thus, the fixed status of [the pot] as an object (*karman*), instrument (*karaṇa*), and so forth—expressed in such cases as "see the pot," "bring water with the pot," or "place water in the pot"—is logically established, and there is no contingency of confusion among the factors of action (*kāraka*). This reasoning, which must be understood regarding the capacity (*śakti*) being the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), is implied here: because a substance (*dravya*) has a single nature, its status as object, instrument, and so on would not otherwise be possible. || 2 ||

But surely, it is appropriate that those capacities which exist should necessarily be intended to be expressed. However, where they are seen not to exist, how can there be an intention to express them? For example: "he bestows a capacity," "he accomplishes by means of a capacity," "he exerts himself toward a capacity," or "he departs from a capacity. Indeed, a capacity cannot possess another capacity, for that would lead to an infinite regress. Likewise, in the case of an entity that is indefinable (*nirupākhya*), such as when one says "he causes the destruction of wealth" or "he is joined with the absence of wealth," what capacity could there be?

Regarding the expressions "he cooks in a pot" (*sthālyāṃ pacati*) and "he cooks with a pot" (*sthālyā pacati*), one might wonder how a single pot can possess the distinct functions of instrument (*karaṇa*) and locus (*adhikaraṇa*)—namely, assisting through the acts of containing and supporting. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The linguistic usage of the means [of action] (*sādhana*) is based on the states of the intellect. Whether existing or non-existing, the distinction among the forms of objects is constructed by the intellect. (Verse 3)

The linguistic usage of factors such as the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth has as its basis those specific states of the intellect—which takes the form of the desire to speak—that are caused by words and are restricted to particular words. For instance, since a word is employed after an object has been determined, the application of the word occurs in accordance with that determination. Furthermore, the determination [of the object] independently constructs various specific objects through its own autonomy, even without depending on an external object.

In that regard, since power (*śakti*), which is functioning as a substance (*dravyāyamāṇā*), is determined by the intellect as independent, it is contradictory for it to possess another power when it is denoted by a word. For at that time, while it is in the state of power, there is no possession of that [other] power such that an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would occur; rather, even non-existence, when its form is determined by the intellect and thus functioning as a substance, is what is expressed by the word.

Thus, because its nature as a potsherd is extremely attenuated, the cooking vessel (*sthālī*) is intended to be expressed independently, without requiring the application of an agent (*kartṛ-viniyoga*), and is therefore called the *kartṛ*. However, when there is an intention to express that very vessel as the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) without regard for the assistance provided by fuel, it is the *karaṇa*; and when there is an intention to express the actual substratum (*ādhāra*), it is the *adhikaraṇa*. Consequently, all such usages as "he kills himself by himself" (*hantyātmānamātmanā*) and "the self's abiding within itself" (*ātmanaḥ svātmanyavasthānam*) are established as being highly valid.

And this will be stated later: "The one is divided by the intellect, and the divided attains unity," and so forth. Since worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is possible through the determination of non-difference between the perceived object and the conceptual construction, the application of the term here must be established as referring to the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*), and not to its own nature nor to another; for it is the own-nature itself that exists, and not the state of another, as in the expression "the body of a stone statue."

And thus, even when a word has been extracted from a sentence, if its grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) occurs while another word intended by the speaker has not yet been employed, it is indeed possible to perform a grammatical analysis (*anvākhyāna*) based on that word alone—provided that a general relation is required—since the specific meaning intended remains undetermined due to the similarity of forms. Otherwise, how could the form of an object determined by the intellect, which depends on its connection with an action or other factors, be ascertained?

Since there is no such thing as a generic meaning (*arthasāmānya*) that exists independently of its relational form, grammatical derivation is accepted as being limited to the word (*pada*). This is because in the *Śāstra*, rules such as "suffixes [are applied] when there is a connection with a verbal root" (*dhātusaṃbandhe pratyayāḥ*) are rejected. Furthermore, where there is an absolute lack of coherence—as in "the pot cooks the rice with wood" (*sthālī modanena kāṣṭhaiḥ pacati*)—that is not even a sentence; therefore, how could there be any occasion here for the grammatical derivation of words extracted from a sentence?

For this very reason, a scriptural statement such as "my eyes are beautiful to behold" is indeed meaningful for the purpose of precluding a state of disjunction. For even a universal (sāmānya), being an entity that is capable of connection with other things, is praised; however, a statement such as "a hundred elephants stand on the tip of a finger" is not so praised, as it is simply incoherent. And having established this, in the Vedic language, a grammatical deviation (vyatyaya) in passages such as "those who carve the wooden ring for the horse-sacrifice post" is indeed meaningful for the purpose of removing the suspicion of incorrectness.

Since metrical sentences possess a fixed sequence, it is logical to extract individual words from them in that very same manner. In common worldly usage, however, there is no such thing as a sentence with an unstable or non-fixed sequence that is incoherent; therefore, there is no occasion for extraction from such cases. Consequently, even when words are extracted from a sentence for the purpose of grammatical instruction, the analysis based on words as its limit remains entirely faultless.

And in that case, because the object qualified by all its attributes is partless, when it is abstracted [from its context], the mere universal has a body that is purely a mental construction (*buddhiparikalpita*). However, since there is a requirement for specific details from the very outset, the grammatical derivation (*anvākhyāna*) is stated with the sentence as its limit; yet, a direct derivation of the sentence is not tenable due to its infinity. For it is only through the conceptualization of the division into base (*prakṛti*), suffix (*pratyaya*), and so forth, that the instruction (*anuśāsana*) of the word itself becomes possible.

And since that [element] cannot exist in isolation, there is this distinction between the two views: when it resides within a sentence and requires a general relation, the grammatical analysis (anvākhyāna) is delimited by the word; but when it requires a specific relatum supplied by that very sentence, the analysis is delimited by the sentence. || 3 ||

In the Buddhist practice of proof, he states what is in agreement with the position accepted by the Commentator: "When a speaker, having unified the Pañcālas with the Kurus by means of the intellect, divides them again, then disappearance (apāya) is perceived. (4)

Regarding the statement "the Pañcālas are more handsome than the Kurus," the sūtra *pañcamī vibhakte* (Pāṇini 2.3.42), which prescribes the ablative case, was rejected in the Bhāṣya. This is because the status of an *apādāna* (ablative point of departure) is established by the very possibility of a conceptual separation (*apāya*). For, by means of the common quality of beauty, the Pañcālas are mentally brought into a state of identity with the Kurus as part of a single collective; then, due to their superior handsomeness, the Pañcālas are distinguished from the Kurus. Thus, there exists a separation preceded by a prior connection, which constitutes the *apāya*.

This has been stated in the Bhāṣya: "He who has attained equality with them employs [the word] in this manner. The meaning is that he is one who first perceived the similarity of the Pañcālas to those Kurus—on account of their shared capacity for deliberation (*sampradhāraṇā*) and their physical beauty. By this, the author of the Bhāṣya expresses the spatial proximity of the Kurus and Pañcālas through their being established within a single cognition. Furthermore, the distinction of the surpassable from the unsurpassable is preceded by that [proximity]. As for the word *pañcamī* (ablative), it was not mentioned by the author of the Bhāṣya because it bears the technical designation of *apādāna* (point of departure).

Even for one who maintains that the *sūtra* is intended as an original formulation (*ārambhavādin*), these [words] must be understood as having a collective state (*samudāyabhāva*) through the intellect alone, on account of their being the substratum for selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) due to their sharing common qualities. Otherwise, since the division would already be obtained from the very context of "selection" (*nirdhāraṇa*), the mention of "divided" (*vibhakta*) would lead to the perception of an absolute separation; in that case, a real collective state would not be tenable. Thus, it is determined from this that the status of being a means (*sādhanabhāva*) is conceptual (*bauddha*). Furthermore, because of the inclusion of the suffix *-tama* in the section on *kārakas*, excellence (*prakarṣa*) is not intended to be expressed; therefore, the technical designation of "ablative" (*apādāna*) applies here even when the departure is figurative (*gauṇa*). || 4 ||

He states another corroborative passage from the Bhāṣya: "And [the agent] regards Kaṃsa and others—who have had their forms presented by words and have thus become objects of cognition—as if they were perceptible, as being the instruments [of the action]. (5)

Regarding the phrase "and [the suffix] when there is a cause," the supplementary rule beginning with "from a verbal derivative (*ākhyāna*), one expresses that which performs the action... has been rejected by the statement: "Or rather, it need not be stated, because it is established by the general rule, for it is not distinct from the cause. For in the case of paintings, sculptures, and the like, since the relationship between the instigator and the instigated is determined within the form of the representation, expressions such as "he causes Kaṃsa to be killed" and "he causes Bali to be bound" are established. Similarly, in drama, which is an imitation of what has been done, the actors attain the status of having that very nature through their resemblance to Kaṃsa and Vāsudeva by means of their imitation of them.

In that regard, it was asked: "How is it so among the *granthikas*? There, the *granthikas*—that is, the storytellers (*kathakas*)—narrate the slaying of Kaṃsa solely by way of the plot-structure (*vṛtta*). And since there is no representation (*pratikṛti*) therein, the objection arises as to how there can be the relationship between the instigator and the instigated. To this, a resolution has been stated.

"For they too, by explaining the supernatural powers [of Kaṃsa and others] from their birth until their destruction, reveal them as existing objects of cognition. Because Kaṃsa and the others have long since passed away and are non-existent externally, [the poets] reveal them as existing—that is, present—as objects of cognition; they manifest them through words. For the meaning of a word is indeed a form appearing in the intellect, not a real external object.

And so, because the narrator generates in the listener a cognition in the form of Kaṃsa and others, he causes the "intellectual" (buddhi-) Kaṃsa to be slain by Vāsudeva; thus, through the superimposition of the status of an instigator (*prayojakatva*), the usage [of the verb] is justified. For the author of the Bhāṣya considers Kaṃsa and others—who have acquired specific forms arising from the power of the words uttered by the narrator, who have entered the range of the listener's intellect, and who possess an active nature—to be the instruments (*kāraka*) such as the object (*karman*). Thus, it is established that the linguistic usage regarding the instruments is based upon their state within the intellect.

Even though the causal agent (*prayojaka*) is secondary (*gauṇa*), since the section on *kārakas* does not rely on [the notion of] excellence (*prākarṣa*), the designation "cause" (*hetu*) applies; thus, the suffix *ṇic* is used here according to the sūtra to denote its operation. The term *pratyakṣam* is an indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva*). It functions as an adverbial modifier of the act of reflecting (*manana*). The meaning is: "one determines with extreme clarity by means of knowledge caused by the senses. This is an explanation of the intended meaning of the Bhāṣya passage: "explaining the supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*)."

For when an object possesses an excellence of power, a cognition with a clear form arises by virtue of one's respect for it; and when the cognition is clear, the aspect appearing within it is determined to be of an external nature. (5)

Thus, since the practical application of means is established through the intellect, he concludes that even for a single entity, the multiplicity of powers is intelligible as a conceptual construct: "By speakers, having superimposed the form of the activity of the intellect, a conceptualization of the various powers is made with respect to objects. (Verse 6)

The activity (*pravṛtti*) of cognition (*buddhi*) is its operation characterized by determination (*pariccheda*). Its form (*rūpa*) is its aspect (*ākāra*), which appears as the object. By superimposing that [aspect] upon external objects, speakers postulate a multiplicity of capacities (*śakti-nānātva*) in those [objects]. This is the meaning: because of the determination of non-difference between the perceived and the conceptualized, and due to the conceit that the distinction of capacities—which is actually mental—is external, people imagine a variety of causal efficiency (*sādhanatva*) therein.

Because the appearance in cognition is not understood as being self-established, one understands it—following the distinctions of action and the dependence upon a cognizer—as a real entity possessing manifold potencies; thus, the word is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding external objects. Since there is no sublation of the connection between action and its factors (*kāraka*), and because there is correspondence, speakers recognize the validity of the sentence. For the Buddhists, however, because they do not admit the differentiation of the reflection in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), there is no engagement with external objects.

The validity (*prāmāṇya*) of words, however, pertains only to the speaker’s intention (*vaktrābhiprāya*), not to the external object, because of the suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). As for their being restricted to the mere exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*), this applies to the external world. For the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*), on the other hand, the object is the excluded entity (*vyāvṛttavastu*); since there is a determination (*adhyavasāya*) in that very way, validity resides in that alone—such is the difference between the philosophical systems. Furthermore, because they are regulated by fixed limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), there is no confusion (*sāṅkarya*). And the powers (*śakti*) that provide assistance are distinct according to each limiting adjunct; because the entity has a "congealed" body, they cannot be defined as either identical to or different from it. Thus, there is no contingency of [the power] being a non-adjunct, or of its being a part of the assistance, and so forth. (Verse 6)

And since the state of being a means of accomplishment depends upon the basis of a mental state, he says that this too is established: "When the word-meaning is an individual (vyakti), the status of being a means of accomplishment for an action such as sound, which is being produced, is likewise established as being conceived in the form of the intellect. (7)

It has been stated that when an object belongs to a genus (*jāti*), one first determines its future state through its non-difference from that genus; then, by the application of suitable means, its status as an auxiliary (*aṅgatā*) in the accomplishment of an action is established by way of the genus, while its status as the object being produced (*nirvartyamānatā*) is appropriate by way of the individual (*vyakti*). Thus it was said: "Even in the case of an object that is being produced, the genus is the means (*sādhana*)."

When an individual (*vyakti*) is to be conveyed by a word, as in "he produces sound" or "he effects a conjunction," the object (*karman*)—such as the sound being produced—which is yet to come (*anāgata*), is nevertheless treated as something being brought into existence (*nirvartya*). Because it resembles the present individual, even though there is no communication of a genus (*jāti*), and because its distinctness is not apprehended, one delineates a mental form (*buddhyākāra*) and employs appropriate means. Since this mental [form] is determined to have an external nature, it is "being brought into existence" by way of an external form; however, its status as a means (*sādhanabhāva*) is properly established through that mental form. This is the meaning.
By the phrase "of that which is being produced" (janyamānasya), there is an exclusion of the modified object (vikārya) and the attained object (prāpya). || 6 ||

For that which is to be transformed (*vikārya*) exists already in the form of its material cause (*prakṛti*). Regarding that which is to be attained (*prāpya*), he says that even to some extent it is not superimposed by the intellect (*buddhi*) of its own accord: "Independence and dependence, as well as the nature of sequence, have been shown to be based on conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) with respect to inactive entities (*bhāva*). (8)

Since the relationship between cause and effect has been refuted through the analysis of the positions of existence and non-existence, all entities are devoid of action and empty of activity. In that regard, "agency"—characterized by independence, dependence, and so forth, and taking the form of the agent, the instrument, and other factors—is [merely] a state of being an actor. Furthermore, this very nature of succession, which constitutes action, is a reality constructed by the conceptualizing intellect through the power of beginningless tendencies from false habitual practice, according to how it appears.

The meaning is that this manifestation of cognition as the relationship between action and its factors (kriyākārakabhāva) regarding objects occurs because the universe—which, in reality, has no prior or posterior—appears here through the Lord’s sovereignty as having a sequence of before and after.

For in the Advaita system, everything is sublated because of its unreality; thus, verbal usage constructed by conceptualization must be accepted as established according to common experience without critical investigation. Therefore, the establishment of the categories of the means of proof (*sādhana*) is like that of the categories of direction (*dig*) and so forth. This has been demonstrated by the commentators and others who follow the Advaita method; the meaning is that the verb is employed for the sake of establishing usages such as "the bank wishes to fall" (*kūlaṃ pipatiṣati*). || 8 ||

Thus, the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) has first been characterized by showing that power (*śakti*) is distinct from the substance. He now speaks also by showing that power is non-distinct: "According to the proponents of relation (*saṃsargavādinaḥ*), all entities—both powers and those possessing power—are [related]. When these are not expressed by their own specific names, their status as a means of accomplishment is determined. (Verse 9) Those who maintain that there is a non-difference between a property (*dharma*) and its locus (*dharmin*), even though they are distinct, on account of inherence (*samavāya*), are the Vaiśeṣikas, the proponents of relation.

And they maintain that the nature (*svarūpa*) of things and their auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) constitute the capacity (*śakti*) for producing their own effects. The auxiliaries are the capacity, and the cause is the possessor of capacity (*śaktimat*). Thus, the cause of the auxiliaries themselves is the capacity, which takes the form of an auxiliary with respect to its own effect. Therefore, all entities whatsoever are characterized by capacity and the possessor of capacity; there exists no other capacity whatsoever that is beyond the senses or distinct from the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*).

Even so, the status of things (bhāvas) as means (sādhanatva) is not conveyed by words such as *apādāna* and the like, but rather by case-endings (*vibhakti*) alone. And thus, while this conveyance occurs through mere fitness (*yogyatāmātreṇa*), the application of terms such as *apādāna* proceeds [on that basis]. In instances such as "he sees the jar" (*ghaṭaṃ paśyati*), the power (*śakti*)—which is the means—is the thing being conveyed as restricted to its substratum (the jar) by the accusative and other endings.

However, magnitude (*mahattva*) and the like, when not delimited by a substratum (*ādhāra*), cannot accomplish anything at all as they are denoted by words such as "action" (*karman*); thus, they are to be understood solely through their case-endings (*vibhakti*). This is because those [case-endings] arise from the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) which denotes the substratum. Since the status of being a means (*sādhanatva*) involves contact with the inherence in a substratum, it is observed through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that there is "potency" (*śaktitva*) in the state of being an auxiliary (*upakāra*) and "possessing potency" (*śaktimattva*) in the state of being the beneficiary (*upakārya*). Therefore, there is no inconsistency whatsoever. For this very reason, since there is no connection with another potency during the state of potency, there is also no infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
In this view, since non-existence (abhāva) is to be brought into being as the nature of the highest category (padārtha), its connection with potency (śakti) is not contradictory. || 9 ||

Regarding that, he provides an illustration as to what the entity is, to which it belongs, and where its capacity lies: "In the case of a jar being the object of the act of seeing, largeness and so forth are the means; in the case of color being the object of the act of seeing, the quality of color and so forth are the means. (10)

In the expression “he sees the jar,” the substance *ghaṭa* (jar), which has become the object (*karman*) of the act of seeing, possesses as its inherent capacities the qualities of magnitude (*mahattva*) and being composed of multiple substances (*anekadravyavattva*), which serve as the means (*sādhana*) for its status as the objective factor (*karmakāraka*). For instance, the Sūtra of Kaṇāda states: “Perception occurs in that which is large and composed of multiple substances, owing to [its] color. The meaning of this is as follows: that which has multiple substances as its inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) is “composed of multiple substances” (*anekadravya*), such as a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth. That which possesses such [a substance] is “composed of multiple substances” (*anekadravyavat*), namely, that which has been produced from it.

The state of being that [cause] is its essence (*tattva*). Therefore, perception occurs in a large substance (*mahad-dravya*) because of that cause. By means of this *bahuvrīhi* compound and the possessive suffix *-matup*, two meanings of possession are expressed. Among these, by one [the suffix], the atom (*paramāṇu*) is excluded; for although it possesses color (*rūpa*), it is not perceived due to the absence of multiple constituent substances (*dravya*). By the other meaning of possession, however, dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth are excluded. For this very reason, another aphorism was stated: "There is no perception in the atom because it does not consist of multiple substances."

The mention of the "atom" (*paramāṇu*) here is for the purpose of indicating that which is not visible. Since the possession of multiple constituent substances (*anekadravyavattva*) is the cause of visibility when something large is perceived, the largeness of the triad (*tryaṇuka*) arises from the plurality, largeness, and accumulation of its causes. Because [the triad] is composed of three dyads (*dvyaṇuka*), although it possesses multiple constituent substances, there is an absence of that [visibility] due to the lack of largeness. For this rule—that the possession of multiple constituent substances is the cause of visibility—is prescribed as a restatement (*anuvāda*) regarding what is already large and visible; therefore, there is no contingency of invisibility in the case of the invisible solar ray.

For even "largeness" (*mahattva*) is not prescribed here as a cause for perception. For, according to the principle that "the usage [of a term] is established by the practice of one instance," the introduction [of the term] would have been made with the ablative case alone to signify distinction. Furthermore, since largeness is never absent from that which possesses multiple substances, the word "large" (*mahati*) is not an indication of a logical reason (*hetu*), but rather merely a characterization of the object. And "from color" (*rūpāt*) is the second cause of perception; for a sound-wave (*vāṇu*), though large and possessing multiple substances, is not perceived if it lacks color.

This has been stated in the Sūtra: "And because of the absence of the formation of color (*rūpa-saṃskāra*), there is no perception of air. Since it is the possession of multiple substances (*anekadravyatva*) and color that is the cause of visibility, and not magnitude (*mahattva*) itself, the exclusion of only these two [conditions] is demonstrated. Furthermore, although magnitude is not a direct cause, it is included in the expression "magnitude and so forth are the means of accomplishment" (*sādhana*) in the plural, because it is useful indirectly, as perception has magnitude as its object.

Alternatively, the plural number is used because the term "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the generalities and particulars (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*), such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) and the like. In this context, the generalities and particulars are indeed the primary basis for perception; for objects are perceived through their adjuncts (*upādhi*), since they are apprehended as having their own nature distinguished from the forms of others. However, if one were to say merely "in a large [object]," there would be a deviation in the case of space (*ākāśa*) and so on; therefore, by using the possessive suffix *-mat* in the phrase "possessing multiple substances" (*anekadravyavattvāt*), the cognition of a composite substance (*avayavidravya*) is manifested.

If, however, one were to state simply "because of having multiple substances" (*anekadravyavattvāt*), then by the possibility of interpreting it as a *tatpuruṣa* compound, it would be understood as merely an accumulation of substances. In the case of "one sees color" (*rūpaṃ paśyati*), the means for the act of seeing color is the universal of "color-ness" (*rūpatva*) inherent in the color itself, as well as its inherence in a substance composed of multiple substances. And thus says the Sūtra: "The perception of color occurs because of its inherence in a substance composed of multiple substances and because of the specific quality of color."

That composite substance which has many constituent parts is called "multisubstantial" (*anekadravya*); [the visual ray is not perceived] because of its inherence in such a substance, that is, because it is inherent therein. The specific quality of color (*rūpa*) is its manifestness (*udbhūtatva*). Therefore, the color of the visual ray is not excluded [from perception], as it is overwhelmed by the color of external luminous substances. Others, however, explain that "color" (*rūpa*) is qualified—that is, distinguished from others such as taste—by means of this [term *rūpa*]; thus, they maintain that "color-ness" (*rūpatva*) itself is taught here as a particular universal (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*).

Furthermore, because the atom lacks the state of being composed of multiple substances, the color residing within it is imperceptible. The mention of the plural number [in the sūtra] indicates that factors such as being in a suitable location are also, by implication, means of proof. || 10 ||

In the world, the tastes and other [qualities], which possess their own specific and general characteristics, have restricted perceptions; likewise, those powers are [restricted] by their respective substrates. (11)

One tastes taste, smells odor, touches touch, and hears sound; thus, the specific universals (sāmānyaviśeṣas) such as taste and the rest, being inherent [in their respective sense organs], serve as the means for the functions of tasting and so forth belonging to the tongue and the other senses. For it is by these [specific universals] that [the objects] are apprehended determinately; they are apprehended determinately solely by the power of their own class, and not indeterminately like substances.

For a substance (*dravya*) is sometimes apprehended by means of its universal (*sāmānya*), as "substance"; sometimes by means of a quality (*guṇa*), as "white"; and sometimes by means of an action (*karman*), as "it moves. However, in the case of capacities such as *rasatva* (tastiness), their own substrates alone are the delimiters when their own nature is apprehended; this is the force [of the argument]. For just as when taste is perceived, tastiness is also perceived—since it is perceived as qualified by that [taste]—there is an implication of the substrate (*āśrita-ākṣepa*); so too, upon the perception of *rasatva*, there is an implication of its own locus (*svāśraya-ākṣepa*).

Likewise, when taste is perceived, its substratum—the substance—should also be understood as a power (*śakti*). And as before, in the case of a substance composed of multiple components, inherence (*samavāya*) is also apprehended, because taste and other qualities residing in atoms are not perceived. The same should be stated for the remaining [qualities] as well. Thus, entities are mutually powers and possessors of power. Consequently, there is no fixed, independent power; rather, entities that are in contact with one another are mutually powers and possessors of power. And thus, there is no fixed, independent power.

Because the associated factors possess their respective natures in relation to one another, and because other auxiliary conditions, such as the suitability of the location, likewise possess their respective natures. || 11 ||

In some cases, the means [of cognition] is the relationship between the sense-faculty, the object, the mind, and the agent; whatever assists in a particular instance at a particular time, that is the means in that instance. (12)

In the case of [the perception of] form and so forth, knowledge is produced from the contact of the self, the sense organ, the mind, and the object; thus, contact alone is the instrument (*sādhana*). But in the case of pleasure and so forth, [knowledge arises] from the contact of the self and the internal organ; thus he says "in some cases. Or rather, what is the use of this enumeration? Whatever assists in a particular instance is the instrument there; accordingly, all entities consist of powers and possessors of power. For instance, number, dimensions, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, and action are said to be visible because of their inherence in substances that possess color.

In the production of a composite whole (*avayavin*) from its parts (*avayava*), conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is the power (*śakti*); however, in the production of qualities (*guṇa*), inherence (*samavāya*) of the composite whole is the power. Thus, everything that assists another and is dependent upon it conforms to the definition of power. 12.

Furthermore, that state of being dependent on its own causal function cannot be denoted by a word that expresses an object whose nature is established through means of proof (*sādhana*) and so forth; rather, it is said that the case-endings (*vibhakti*) and other grammatical elements are capable of conveying this state according to their respective functions: "But when [the word] is denoted by its own primary term (*svaśabda*), that property (*dharma*) is not denoted; this assistance (*upakāra*) is understood precisely through the case-endings and so forth. (13)

That *dharma* is the state of being subordinate (*śeṣabhāva*) with respect to the action. By such terms as "kāraka," "sādhana," "apādāna," and so forth, it is the substance (*dravya*), characterized by its assistance to the action, that is primarily denoted; however, the emergent state of being a means (*sādhanabhāva*), defined as assistance to the action, is not what is perceived from it. For even here, the means is presented in the form of a substance.

The category (*dharma*) characterized by action and assistance is expressed by the accusative case; thus, the object that has received the assistance of an action and is expressed by the second and subsequent case-endings is a *śakti* (capacity), which is what the case-ending denotes. In some instances, it is denoted by a secondary suffix (*taddhita*); for example, in *śatyaḥ* or *śatikaḥ* ("bought for a hundred"), the state of being the most effective instrument (*sādhakatamatva*) in the act of buying is what the suffix denotes. In cases such as *yatra* or *tatra*, the state of being a locus (*ādhārabhāva*) is what the suffix *-tra* denotes.

In expressions such as "milk digests milk," "he looks at honey," and "he eats curd," the capacity (śakti) is understood from the nominal stem (prātipadika) itself. However, in cases such as "between you and me" (*antarā tvāṃ ca māṃ ca*) and "having set aside the water-pot" (*kamaṇḍalu-parityajya*), the indeclinable (*avyaya*) word *antarā* expresses the locus (*adhikaraṇa*); this is what is meant by the phrase "and so forth" (*ādi-grahaṇam*). || 13 ||

What, then, is this factor characterized by assistance that serves as the means of accomplishment? He says: The causal state (*nimittabhāva*) of entities, resorted to for the sake of providing assistance—being understood as "inclination" (*nati*) or "attraction" (*āvarjanā*)—is established as the intended means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). (14)

The causal state (*hetubhāva*)—that is, the state of being a cause (*nimittabhāva*)—of entities whose nature is already established, for the sake of assisting an action whose nature is yet to be accomplished, consists of: *nati* (inclination), which is bowing toward assistance; *āvarjana* (attraction), which is the surrendering of one's own self as a subordinate factor (*aṅgabhāvena*); and the intent to bring about the production of the action. The word "iti" indicates a manner. Even another [factor], though established—that is, perceived as already accomplished—or determined by such a property, is not called a "means of accomplishment" (*sādhana*) merely by its existence as a thing. || 14 ||

Having thus established, according to the Mīmāṃsaka and Vaiśeṣika systems, that power (*śakti*) is the means of accomplishment, he now abandons the apprehension of [power] as being either distinct or non-distinct from [the substance] in his own system: "Whether it is distinct from them or their very self, it is conceived as a means of accomplishment by resorting to its distinction [from them]. (15)

The term ‘that’ (saḥ) refers to the causal state, which is synonymous with potency (*śakti*). While some may hold that potencies—which are beyond the senses and distinct from the objects themselves—are the domain of inference based on the necessity of effects (as stated: “The potencies of all entities are within the scope of the presumption [arthāpatti] of their effects”), [we reply: an entity, assisted by the conjunction of auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*), produces its effect by its very own nature; what is the use of postulating an unseen potency? Thus, the self of the entity itself is its potency. Furthermore, the associated or auxiliary factors are not distinct entities.

For an entity, having arisen through a succession of its own causes, becomes qualified such that it is capable of producing this or that effect upon contact with this or that auxiliary cause; what, then, is the use of a separate, unseen power (*adṛṣṭa-śakti*)? If one were to postulate such a power, one must state that the very nature of the entity itself is the cause for its restriction [to specific effects]; therefore, it is better that the nature alone suffice. Thus, let there be the doctrine of non-distinction (*avyatireka-vāda*), or let there be powers distinct from the entity; we have no preference here regarding the doctrine of distinction or non-distinction.

For we take scripture as our authority; whatever scripture declares is our authority. And scripture conveys the status of being a means (sādhana) as something distinct from the word-meanings themselves, as in such cases as "the pot's status as the object (karman) in the act of seeing. Thus, linguistic usage is based on scripture and relies upon distinction. And so, when a substance is denoted by a nominal stem (prātipadika), the power that has established its bond proceeds toward the capacity (śakti). || 15 ||

Having stated the pervasion (vyāpti) that "whatever assists something at a particular time is the means (sādhana) for it at that time," he says the following to bring this into agreement with the view of the Bhāṣyakāra, who maintains that even action (kriyā) is a means: "Vision [is the means] toward prayer; immediately following that, resolve [is the means]; and likewise, resolve serves as the means toward undertaking. (16)
That very same action which exists in the former [subject] is considered the means in the latter; however, in the act of perception, they know consciousness itself to be the specific means. (17)

Regarding the designation of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), it is stated that "the mention of 'action' (*kriyā*) must also be included. In this context, someone perceives some object; having perceived it, he forms an intention through desire; from intention comes undertaking; and from undertaking comes the attainment of the result. Since [the object] is obtained through these stages beginning with perception, it is stated in the *Bhāṣya* that "action (*kriyā*) is also a grammatical object (*karma*) by convention."

In that context, even though it is of the nature of something to be accomplished (*sādhya-svabhāva*), because it is attained through acts such as showing and so forth, the *Bhāṣya* states: "Action (*kriyā*) is also an artificial object (*kṛtrimaṃ karma*). In this regard, although the act of showing and so forth is of the nature of something to be accomplished, its status as a means (*sādhana*) is relative. "Showing" (*sandarśana*)—meaning seeing thoroughly or completely—is the resolve directed toward the fruit. That [resolve] serves as a means—that is, becomes a means—for the purpose of praying for or desiring the fruit, which is the means to the goal.

For when there is the perception of an object, desire arises. Resolve (*vyavasāya*) is firm grasping; it is the ascertainment that a specific action is the means to a particular end. In this context, "immediate" longing (*prārthanā*) is the means, because once desire exists, one forms a determination. Resolve, moreover, is the means for the undertaking of activity—that is, mental engagement—because by the power of resolve, one begins to perform purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). And since it is attained through that activity, physical action becomes the "object" (*karman*); such is the summary.

When each preceding operation is required, that very action which is to be performed—having ceased from the preceding stage and occurring at an earlier time—becomes the means (*sādhana*) for the subsequent, later-occurring goal (*sādhya*), because it is utilized as something already accomplished (*siddhatvena*) in the attainment of its own nature. This is the meaning: the action such as "requesting" (*prārthanā*) that occurs in the preceding perception is considered the means with respect to the subsequent one.

Now, he asks what the instrument (*sādhana*) of the act of seeing (*sandarśana*) is, and says: "But in seeing, it is consciousness (*caitanya*). The word "but" (*tu*) serves to highlight a distinction. The Self, whose nature is consciousness, is that which experiences objects. Its specific quality (*viśeṣa*) is its fitness for desire, which is the fruit [of the act]. And although an action is by nature something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and is thus unaccomplished, nevertheless, because it is established in its state of completion (*niṣṭhā*), and because the term "instrument" refers to the capacity (*śakti*) even when it does not inhere therein, its status as an instrument is appropriate through its distinctness from the substratum.

And since one action does not reside within another action, that very [action] is the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the agent in the bringing-about of another action. This is the ultimate truth here: whatever is established in relation to something else becomes its means (*sādhana*), its producer, its *kāraka*. For at that time, there is no other instrument for the agent in the accomplishment of the action. Furthermore, a future part (*bhāvī aṃśaḥ*) becomes the object (*karman*) because it is being reached by a past part (*bhūtenāṃśena*). For that which the agent desires to obtain through his action is the object.

And here, it is precisely the factor of action (*kriyāṃśa*) that is desired by another already established factor of action; because it is being attained through an undertaking—a mental operation—it is a physical action that constitutes the *karman*. By this, the status of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) for that which is intended [by the agent] is established, as in "he prepares for battle" (*yuddhāya saṃnahyate*) and "he exerts himself for the sake of the *śrāddha* rite" (*śrāddhāya nigṛhṇate*). Regarding verbs whose meaning is motion (*gatyartha*), there will be a desire to express either difference or non-difference [between the action and its result]; in cases such as *pac* ("to cook"), there is only a desire to express non-difference; and in cases such as "he exerts himself for the sake of the *śrāddha*," there will be only a desire to express difference. This will be explained later.

Thus, it is established that the relationship between action (*kriyā*) as the means (*sādhana*) and the goal (*sādhya*)—which, as stated in the Bhāṣya, consists in a relationship of benefactor and beneficiary based on exclusion (*vyatireka*)—has been illustrated by the statement: "In this way, relying on exclusion, it is conceived as the means. Consequently, it is generally said that action, though distinct from capacity (*śakti*), is resorted to for the sake of assistance and is thus called a "means" (*sādhana*). || 16,17 ||

In the *Vārttika*, the technical term (*saṃjñā*) "kāraka" should have been provided with the designation of its referent (*saṃjñin*) as "sādhana" (the means of accomplishment). Alternatively, one might argue that the meaning of "sādhaka" (the accomplisher) is obtained through the understanding of the term as being etymologically significant (*anvartha*). To this, it was said: "If [the term] is taken as etymologically significant, then the word 'agent' (*kartṛ*) would be inapplicable to non-agents. To justify the application of the term "kāraka"—specifically the word "agent"—to instruments and other factors that are not agents, he says: "In every case, the status of being an agent exists merely in the sense of bringing about production (*niṣpatti*); however, when there is a requirement for specific distinctions in activity (*vyāpāra*), the status of being an instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth arises. (18)

Since actions are accomplished by a collection of factors (*sāmagrī*), all [factors] attain the status of being "kārakas" (grammatical participants) according to the distinction of their respective roles in the production of the action. However, when there is the intention to specify "who cooks" or "how he cooks," then the *kārakas*, possessing diverse operations for the accomplishment of the primary action, receive designations such as "instrument" (*karaṇa*) and so forth, based on the excellence of their own respective operations. For instance, the agent (*kartṛ*) is the factor whose operation consists in the employment of other means of accomplishment.

The object (*karman*) is that which is most desired by the agent through its own activity, having been brought about by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) resulting from production, transformation, or attainment. The instrument (*karaṇa*) is that whose operation is not interrupted by the operations of other factors, as it experiences [the action] such as flaming and so forth. The recipient (*sampradāna*) is that which connects with the object through an operation consisting of impelling, consenting, or not rejecting. The ablative (*apādāna*) is that which accomplishes [the action] by becoming the limit (*avadhi*) for departure. The locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is the support of the action, which is mediated by the agent and the object. The cause (*hetu*) is that which prompts [the agent] while being independent.

Furthermore, because the particular is preceded by the general, even in its intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*), it possesses the status of a *kāraka* (agentive factor) through persistence; thus, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the expressions "the instrument is a *kāraka*" is justified. Moreover, that which is not a *kāraka* lacks specific designations, as in the case: "The leaf of the tree falls. And when the agent's operation is not intended to be expressed, these [factors] possess agency only with respect to the primary action, as in: "The pot cooks," "The fuel pieces cook," or "The sword cuts. There is no intention to express independence (*svātantrya*) regarding their own operations in the case of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) and the point of departure (*apādāna*).

This is because one must take into account both the recipient and the one who departs. For this very reason, it is stated [in the Vārttika]: "But it is established that [the term *kāraka*] applies to each individual factor, because of the difference in actions. Thus, regarding the various operations of the factors (*kārakas*) corresponding to their respective roles for the sake of the principal action, the application of terms such as *pacati* ("he cooks") and so forth has been described. This has been stated in the Bhāṣya: "The action exists as a generality; the factor (*kāraka*) is that which brings about its accomplishment. (18)

Right here he provides an illustration: "Just as, at the birth of a son, the agency of the parents is spoken of—saying 'this [son] is his' and 'she is from him'—the distinction is made according to the speaker's intention. (19)

When the distinction between the two generative operations is not intended to be expressed—as in the statement "the parents produce a son"—it is well known that both possess the status of agent (*kartṛtva*) with respect to the act of birth. However, when the distinction is intended to be expressed as to how each produces—the father, depositing the seed, places the embryo in this mother; whereas this mother, retaining the seed falling from this father, experiences the status of agent of the act of birth—and thus the mother possesses the status of locus (*adhikaraṇatva*).

The father possesses both the status of agent (*kartṛtva*) and the status of source (*apādānatva*), whereas the mother possesses only the status of agent; thus, the activity differs. Furthermore, since the particular is preceded by the general, the term "birth" (*janis*)—which signifies the acquisition of selfhood through the general—denotes, in the context of the particular, the depositing of the seed, the emission of the seed, and the act of impelling. Alternatively, while the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha*) remains undifferentiated, the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*) is the sense of the causative (*ṇijartha*), such as impelling and so forth, wherein this distinction lies. Although this has been included among the positions of the proponent (*sādhayapakṣa*), it serves as an illustration because it is well-known. || 19 ||

Thus, it has been established that the grammatical relation of *karaṇa* (instrument) and so forth is expressed through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the primary action itself, by way of the relationship between the general and the particular. Now, [the author] states the following verse to explain the Bhāṣya statement, "The action exists as a generality," by means of another perspective: namely, that independence with respect to subordinate actions remains unlost even while there is dependence on the primary action: "The agents of subordinate actions have their powers suppressed by the [agent of the] primary action;
yet, even when suppressed, they are endowed with their own complete operations. (20)
Known as instruments and so forth by virtue of following various specific actions, they subsequently attain autonomy and reach the state of agency within the primary agent.

Because subordinate qualities and actions, which consist of intermediate operations such as "flaming" and so forth, possess independence, they are all [theoretically] agents; however, with respect to the primary action, their capacity for independence is suppressed by the independent agent who employs them. Thus, having been brought to a state of subordination and lack of independence according to their respective roles, they do not lose their independence within their own specific operations—even while remaining subordinate—because it is impossible for that which is ineffective to serve as a cause for the accomplishment of an action. Therefore, they proceed to the performance of their own respective operations.

Because they enter into the state of being auxiliary members (*aṅga*) to the primary action (*pradhānakriyā*), even when they are employed by the agent (*kartṛ-viniyoge*), they remain inseparable from all their own respective operations—such as burning and so forth—which are characterized by the designations of "instrument" (*karaṇa*) and so on, directed toward the specific objects of those actions. As if not abandoning that very nature, even after the time of employment, having attained independence (*svādhīnatva*) consisting in the performance of their own operations, they become independent (*svatantra*) regarding the various subordinate actions within themselves, and thus assume the status of a "factor" (*kārakatva*) and the role of an "agent" (*kartṛtā*) specifically with respect to the primary action; such is the instrument (*karaṇa*).

The meaning is that the logical justification begins with the term "kāraka" (the factor of action). For the instrument and other factors, being subordinate to the instigation of the agent, perform their respective operations; thus they become [factors] as they exist. Since they are enjoined by the agent for the sake of their own agency in their respective operations, and since the accomplishment of the primary action occurs when those who have been so enjoined experience independence in their own operations while functioning as instruments and so forth, there is no contradiction between independence and dependence.

For that very independence (*svātantrya*) which exists in respect to its own operation is itself the dependence (*pāratantrya*) in respect to the principal action, and nothing else. And that [dependence] occurs only after the agent has been assigned [to the action]. Prior to that, however, independence is spoken of merely by virtue of the capacity [for action] prior to the assignment of the agent. In this way, there is no difference in scope between [the definitions] "instrument" (*karaṇa*) and "kāraka," because independence in its own operation is precisely what constitutes being an instrument and so forth in respect to the principal action. This is exactly what was stated.

"But it is established that each factor [of action] is distinct because of the difference in their activities; thus, in the case of roots such as *pac* (to cook), there is the status of agent (*kartṛbhāva*) for both the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). In this regard, after stating that the agent, instrument, and locus possess subordinate actions by means of the passage beginning with "placing on the fire, pouring water," etc., and after the objection was raised again that "the status of the ablative (*apādāna*) and so forth is not established," the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) was established once more: "Not so, because of their independence and dependence; they are expressed in alternation, and the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) depends upon the verbal expression."

For they say that in the expression "the cloud flashes" (*valāhako vidyotate*), because there is no intention to express a non-difference from lightning (*vidyut*), the agenthood (*svātantrya*) of the ablative (*apādāna*) indeed exists with respect to its own operation. However, when one says "he comes from the village" (*grāma āgacchati*), because another meaning is understood and the operation of the ablative is not determined, such usage does not occur. Nevertheless, the village as the ablative possesses a certain operation for the accomplishment of the action, characterized by its attainment of the state of being a limit (*avadhi*).

Otherwise, just as in the case of "he comes from near the village," even in the expression "he comes from the village," the village would lack the status of a *kāraka*. Furthermore, since there is no rejection by the agent (*kartṛ*), the status of being a recipient (*saṃpradāna*) exists indeed through the agent's instigation or consent, and thus its own operation is present. However, the usage "the Brāhmaṇa gives" does not occur, because when [the Brāhmaṇa] is a recipient, the intended meaning is not determined from this [expression].

For this very reason, the verbal root does not denote the operation of the *apādāna* (ablative) or *saṃpradāna* (dative) cases; rather, it denotes only the operation of the *karman* (object), *karaṇa* (instrument), and so forth—as in such examples as "the rice cooks by itself," "the sword cuts," and "the pot cooks. Thus, since a distinction in action is possible in all these cases, the term "agent" (*kartṛ*) applies even when something functions as an instrument or other factor, because of its independence (*svātantrya*). If this were so, then even when functioning as an instrument or the like, there would be the designation of "agent" due to independence. This is not the case.

Since independence (*svātantrya*) is already obtained through the governing rule on *kārakas*, the repeated mention of "the independent is the agent" (*svatantraḥ kartā*) is for the purpose of conveying an independence that is not obscured by dependence (*pāratantrya*); thus, the designation of "agent" remains restricted to the primary sense of independence alone. Even so, because it is a subsequent rule, the designation of "agent" would prevail, overriding the designations of "instrument" (*karaṇa*) and so forth. This is not a fault; for since the designations of "instrument" and so on have no other scope, they override the designation of "agent" in this instance.

The designation of a *kāraka* occurs here by virtue of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) [of the term]. Alternatively, since the technical name *kāraka* is based on independence (*svātantrya*), there is no relationship of sublation between the cause and the effect [of these definitions] here. For in this case, while independence is the basis for the [general] designation, dependence (*pāratantrya*) is also inferred in the state of being an instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth; thus, the designation *kāraka* indeed applies even when [specific roles like] *apādāna* and so on are present. Therefore, there is simply a co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of this [designation] with the designations *apādāna* and the rest.

However, where the intention to express independence is inseparable from the intention to express dependence, it is said that the *karaṇa* (instrument) subordinates the others; for example, in "he pierces with a bow" (*dhanuṣā vidhyati*). For in that case, there is an intention to express independence which is invariably concomitant with the bow's being the most effective means (*sādhakatama*).
