Furthermore, in the rule "the independent is the agent" (*svatantraḥ kartā*), it is not understood as meaning that one is independent in all circumstances; rather, it means that one is indeed independent. Thus, even in cases such as "the pot cooks" (*sthālī pacati*), the designation of "agent" (*kartṛ*) is established.

Furthermore, by virtue of its functional authority (*adhikāra-sāmarthya*), it is not contradictory that the application of the term "agent" (*kāraka*)—which is based on inferred independence—occurs even during the state of being an instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth; thus, everything is well-established. In this way, having previously relied upon the non-difference of action (*kriyā*), it was explained that agency consists merely in the accomplishment [of the result], and thus action, as a general category, has the nature of mere accomplishment. Now, however, by relying on the distinction between actions according to their subordinate (*guṇa*) or primary (*pradhāna*) status, the application of the word "agent" even to one who is not the [primary] agent has been justified.

And in that case, the meaning of the Bhāṣya is that there exists a principal action which, being common to all, serves as the object to be accomplished (sādhya) and is thus shared by everyone. || 20,21 ||

He provides an illustration for the fact that while [the factors] are independent in their own respective functions, they are dependent upon the primary function: "Just as the status of being a warrior resides in those warriors appointed by a king, yet it is the king who obtains victory or defeat based on their performance. (22)
Likewise, when all [factors] are directed by an agent and perform a single purpose, their status as agents is not contradicted by their subsequent designations as instruments and so forth. (23)

Just as when warriors are appointed and dispatched by a king, their lord, the quality of being a warrior resides in those soldiers through their deployment in battle arrays and so forth. While they are fighting, whatever activity there is—such as the destruction of the enemy's great divisions and territories—once that has been accomplished, the king obtains victory or defeat in turn. This is what is said: the warriors are the agents in the act of fighting because the operation [of fighting] previously resided in them; yet, due to the king’s command, they are not independent.

Furthermore, they are independent and autonomous when engaged in that [activity]. Thus, the autonomy that arises in the instruments and so forth—similar to servants who, once appointed by an agent, perform cooking and other tasks collectively—is produced after the time of appointment; this does not contradict their status as instruments and so on, which exists at the time of the appointment. This is the meaning. Therefore, if there is a designation of the term "kāraka," there must also be a designation of the thing designated (the *saṃjñin*).

Otherwise, an undesirable consequence would follow; for when it was urged that "one who comes from near the village" (*grāmasya samīpād āgacchati*) would be designated as a *kāraka* despite not being one, and this was refuted by the fact that the specific designatum is established through the understanding of the term as a descriptive name (*anvarthasaṃjñā*); and when it was raised that the designation of *kāraka* would be inapplicable to the instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth because it would not carry over into subsequent rules due to the governing heading (*adhikāra*), this was refuted by resorting to agency (*kartṛtva*) based on the mere requirement of accomplishment (*niṣpatti*), and by resorting to independence (*svātantrya*) with respect to the subordinate action (*guṇakriyā*) through the differentiation of actions for each respective *kāraka*. This is the meaning of the section. (22, 23)

Having established that whatever brings about an action is an instrument (*karaṇa*) by relying on the principle that technical designations correspond to their actual meaning, one might ask: since a cause (*hetu*) also brings about an action, it would already be established as an instrument; why, then, is the rule "in the sense of a cause" (*hetau*) stated again? Anticipating this objection, [the author] shows the distinction between a cause and an instrument: "When its operation (*vyāpāra*) is not dependent [on another], a cause is considered a motive (*nimitta*); but when it assumes the state of a limit (*avadhibhāva*), the wise know it as a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). (24) [This means: When a thing brings about an action through its own independent operation, it is called a cause; however, when it indicates another object by depending on a relation of limit, it is known as a characteristic. Thus, the cause and the instrument are distinct.

A *hetu* (cause) is that which, without depending upon an actual operation (*vyāpāra*), is resorted to as a causal factor merely by virtue of its fitness (*yogyatā*) for the accomplishment of the intended meaning. It is the domain of the "residual" (*śeṣa*) case-ending, which is the third case (*tṛtīyā*) that supersedes the genitive of relation (*saṃbandha-ṣaṣṭhī*). For example: *adhyayanena vasati* ("He dwells because of his study"). Here, study is the cause and dwelling is the possessor of the cause. When the residual genitive would otherwise apply to the relation between these two, the third case is used for the cause. The Naiyāyikas, however, state: "The *hetu* is that which is the cause of [the distinction between] quality and substance."

And that [cause] is the domain of non-agentive case-endings (*akāraka-vibhakti*). However, that which is the cause of an action expressed by a verbal root is indeed an agentive factor (*kāraka*), as in examples such as "he dwells because of his learning" (*vidyayā vasati*). Thus, in the rule *anarthalakṣaṇe*, since even a cause (*hetu*) is designated by the word *lakṣaṇa*, one might suspect there is no distinction between these two; this suspicion is dispelled by the words "having resorted to," etc. In the term *lakṣaṇe*, the word *lakṣaṇa* is derived in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva-sādhana*). But in the phrase "they know the definition" (*lakṣaṇaṃ viduḥ*), it is derived in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa-sādhana*). In the context of "in the definition" (*lakṣaṇe*), it refers to the manifestation of the object being defined (*lakṣyamāṇa-vastu-prakāśane*).

When there is "that which possesses the state of being a dependent limit"—that is, where the state of being a dependent limit (*āśrito'vadhibhāvaḥ*), consisting of a boundary (*maryādārūpa*), is observed—those who know [the matter] understand that to be a *lakṣaṇa*, a signifier (*jñāpaka*). Where the state of being a limit is recognized, even in the case of a cause (*hetu*), that is a *lak�aṇa*. For this very reason, the particle *tu* indicates a distinction. Others, however, say: "The cause is useful for the production of an effect, whereas the *lakṣaṇa* is for the production of a cognition. That is incorrect.

Since an operation is observed even in the case of a cause arising from conditions—for instance, because knowledge (*vidyā*) and so forth operate toward the reliance upon clothing and the like—the definition [of a condition] is that which is resorted to as a limit (*avadhi*), regardless of whether it possesses the capacity for the production of the object being characterized or not. For example, in the expression "the lightning flashes following the tree," the tree is the characteristic mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of the flashing; the meaning is that it flashes having reached the tree.

How then is the example "śākalyasya saṃhitāmanu prāvarṣat" (it rained after Śākalya’s *saṃhitā*) to be understood in the rule *anurlakṣaṇe*? For in this case, the *saṃhitā* is not perceived as defining the rain merely by way of being a limit (*avadhi*), but rather by way of being its cause (*janaka*). And that which is a cause is a *hetu*, not a *lakṣaṇa*. Therefore, there is no contradiction, because here the word *lakṣaṇa* is used for the *hetu* itself on the basis of their commonality in being an indicator (*jñāpakatva*).

Now, it might be argued that smoke, whose concomitance with fire is well-established and determined through repeated observation, serves as an indicator (*lakṣaṇa*) even when seen alone, pointing toward a fire produced by some other cause that is not currently visible. But what of *saṃhitā* (the Vedic collection), which is perceived only at the very first instance? Since there is no repeated observation or recurrence of its perception, how could it be an indicator? To this, it is replied:

Although it is true in the world that "that by which something is repeatedly characterized is its definition" (*lakṣaṇa*), nevertheless, even a cause whose capacity for producing an effect is well-known becomes a definition (*lakṣaṇa*) in such a manner. For when there is the determination of an effect, the cause also serves as a definition by virtue of being its reason (*hetu*), because it determines the effect.

For just as that which has had its invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) grasped through repeated observation makes another thing known, so too a cause—producing [its effect] independently of anything else—becomes a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) by virtue of being a determiner of the effect, due to the non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) of the effect. For example, the rising of clouds, though determined to be the cause of rain, becomes a defining characteristic because it determines [the possibility of] rain even when the rain itself is absent; this is why people, upon seeing the rising of clouds, infer rain. But surely, the status of being a cause is determined by the force of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)?

When B exists whenever A exists, but does not exist even when another thing exists if it lacks A, then A is the cause of B. Positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) arise from repeated observation; for if they are observed only once, there is no certainty regarding positive and negative concomitance. Furthermore, although a conjunction (*saṃhitā*) may be the cause of rain, its causality is not ascertained by a single occurrence, because the production of the effect might possibly occur even from some other object present at that time.

And thus, its nature is not established as being like the appearance of clouds. To this we reply: causal status is understood even from a single observation. For that which does not produce something is never seen to produce it even once, just as a rice sprout is not produced from barley. Nor is there another producer at that same time, because it is not observed to do so at other times. As they have said: "If something occurs only when X is present, yet one imagines it to be caused by something else, then there would be an infinite regress of causes in all cases."

Nor does its production from that occur by way of the "crow-and-palm-fruit" maxim (i.e., by mere coincidence), because that which lacks the nature of a cause cannot produce an effect even if it were present once. Furthermore, the *saṃhitā* is perceived through direct observation as producing rain; thus, even from a single observation, its status as a cause is determined here. Moreover, its causality regarding rainfall is also established by scripture (*āgama*). Therefore, it is said that in this context, the cause itself is the *lakṣaṇa* (indicator) due to the commonality of being a signifier. As it is stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "The cause is also pervaded by the indicator."

Its definition (*lakṣaṇa*) consists in its pervasiveness. For even a cause becomes a definition when it characterizes its effect, just as the rising of clouds [is the definition] of rain. Nor is there any deviation (*vyabhicāra*), because that which is complete and unimpaired is the producer; furthermore, there is no deviation when one analyzes it in this way. And the principle is that the capacity for attainment (*prāpaṇa-śakti*) is the validity (*prāmāṇya*), not the actual attainment itself. If, then, by the word "definition" the state of being the cause for the determination of another object is described, how is it that [the definition] has a dependent limit (*āśritāvadhi-bhāva*)?

Even when the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) possesses the state of being a limit (*avadhi*), its very nature as a cause of delimitation (*paricchedahetutva*) is what constitutes it as a definition; otherwise, how could that which does not delimit be a definition? However, this is the distinction: while a tree is a cause of delimitation by virtue of being a limit, *saṃhitā* and the like possess the status of a definition due to their commonality as indicators (*jñāpakatva*), even though they do not rely on the state of being a limit. For a definition occurs in many ways; in some cases it is by way of being a limit, as for example, a lightning flash, while shining, serves as the basis for determining a forest tree.

In some cases, it is by way of delimiting the cause, as smoke is [the indicator] of fire; in other cases, it is by way of being the cause for determining the effect, as the rising of clouds is [the indicator] of rain. Furthermore, according to the manner already stated, the *saṃhitā* (conjunction) is both a definition (*lakṣaṇa*) and a reason (*hetu*). If this is so, then since the designation of *karmapravacanīya* is already established by the general definition in the rule "lakṣaṇetthaṃbhūtākhyāna... and so forth, the restatement "anurlakṣaṇe" would be purposeless. This has been said:

"Because [the suffix] *an* is used in the sense of a secondary characteristic (*anurlakṣaṇe*), the statement [of the word *hetu*] would be purposeless, since that meaning is already established by the general rule. To this, the reply is given: "But the word is stated for the sake of the cause (*hetvartham*). Here, the word *artha* is not a synonym for "denotable object," but rather a term signifying "cessation" (*nivṛtti*). By metaphorically applying the word for the cause (*kāraṇa*) to the effect (*kārya*), the instrumental case of the cause (*hetutṛtīyā*) is expressed by the word *hetu*. Furthermore, since the sublation (*bādha*) is nothing other than the sublated (*bādhyāt*), the compound is analyzed as: "that whose purpose (*artha*)—namely, the cause—is to be set aside (*nivartya*)."

Therefore, it is said that the re-enactment of the technical name (*saṃjñā*) is for the purpose of setting aside the notion of [the case-ending] "cause" (*hetu*). But, one might object, from this re-enactment of the name, the cognition of the named entity (*saṃjñin*) in the specific rules (*pradeśa*) would become more stable; however, how then could the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) be set aside? For that [third case] is a sublater by virtue of its being subsequent in the order of the rules. This is not so. A technical name that is enjoined more than once presents itself twice in specific rules such as "the second case is used when joined with a *karmapravacanīya*. Of these two presentations, one serves the purpose of the second case.

As for the statement that "the second case-ending (*dvitīyā*) is for the purpose of indicating proximity (*anurlakṣaṇa*)," this is intended so that it may not be meaningless; thus, setting aside the third case-ending used in the sense of a cause (*hetutṛtīyā*), it establishes the second case-ending itself. Now, one might object: "From the repetition of the proximity, the designation (*saṃjñā*) and its application (*pratyaya*) would both be doubled, but the injunction of the second case-ending does not undergo such accumulation. The designation exists for the sake of the grammatical operation (*kārya*) and is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*), whereas the operation known as the second case-ending is primary (*pradhāna*). And there is no change in the primary element due to a difference in the subordinate element. For what purpose, then, is the subordinate element stated twice?

Let it be purposeless; however, the application [of the rule] does not cease on that account. And although the primary element (pradhāna) goes to the location of the subordinate element (guṇadeśa) for the sake of its own refinement—just as technical definitions (saṃjñā) and interpretive rules (paribhāṣā) go to their respective locations—nevertheless, since the primary element, being expectant (sākāṅkṣa), attains satisfaction through a single subordinate element, why would it go to the location of another subordinate element? Thus, there is only one second case ending (dvitīyā). That [second case ending] would be sublated by the third case ending (tṛtīyā) due to its posteriority.

But surely, since there would be the consequence of the loss of their own nature in the absence of a primary principle (*pradhāna*), the qualities (*guṇas*)—having their purpose unfulfilled—would manifest another primary principle; just as ministers, seeking to maintain their own essential character in the absence of a king, establish another king, for by establishing him their own form is realized, since ministers and the like do not exist without a king. This is not the same case, because between a king and his ministers there exists a mutual relationship of benefactor and beneficiary.

Because there is no certainty regarding the rule of the subordinate and the principal status [of the means and the end]. For instance, a king establishes his subjects within the boundaries prescribed by the treatises on dharma and follows them himself; yet those subjects also discipline the king. Thus, due to the very distinction of the principal, there is a distinction of the subordinate therein. If that is so, then the injunction regarding the means would itself become the injunction regarding the end.

For example, when it is said, "Be a member of the army" (*anīkastho bhava*), the state of being a member of the army consists in the accomplishment of guarding the elephants, fodder, and water; thus, by means of prescribing the status of being a member of the army, that very task is enjoined. In the same way, by means of prescribing the technical designation *karmapravacanīya*, that very task known as the accusative case is enjoined. And so, when the accusative case is prescribed once again, it serves the purpose of subverting what would otherwise subvert it, according to the principle of "that which was not already obtained."

For the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would have been required in the context of a relationship; this [use of the accusative] is its sublater. Here, the basis is the force of the specific statement (*vacana-sāmarthya*). Otherwise, how could the prescription of the technical name (*saṃjñā-vidhāna*) itself be justified as being for the purpose of prescribing the accusative? And by adopting this view, another interpretation also becomes tenable, because the general rule is set aside by the statement that "the distinction of the primary follows from the distinction of the quality. Thus says the Bhāṣya: "In the case of an illustration as well, the human effort serves to exclude [the application of the original rule]."

Alternatively, due to the difference in designations (*saṃjñā*), the word denoted by the designation (*saṃjñin*) is differentiated; however, the injunction regarding the accusative case (*dvitīyā-vidhi*), being the primary element, is not differentiated. For it would only be logical for the primary element to be differentiated on account of a difference in its subordinate qualities (*guṇa*). Furthermore, the injunction regarding the accusative—having acquired superior strength through the differentiation of the designated objects—sublates the injunction regarding the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā-vidhi*). Moreover, according to the *yathoddeśa* view, the primary element, while proceeding toward the location of the subordinate quality, does not achieve its purpose through a single subordinate quality alone. This is because it requires everything contained within that context, as there is no distinction in its relationship [to them all].

For this very reason, let a subordinate element whose purpose has not yet been fulfilled postulate another primary, just as subjects [postulate] another king. Nor is there a lack of analogy with the case of subjects; for although they depend on the assistance provided by the king, they remain subordinate in every respect, since their dependence on his assistance is solely for the sake of fulfilling their status as his subordinates, and not for the sake of attaining independence themselves. Even under the view that the application of a term occurs at the time of the function (*kāryakālapakṣa*), the two names in the operational rule present the two named entities as distinct from one another.

Therefore, it is logical that the second rule (*dvitīyā-vidhi*), which has attained excellence by reaching a different scope due to the power of the statement characterized by the prescription of the designation (*saṃjñā-vidhāna-lakṣaṇa*), sets aside even the subsequent third rule (*tṛtīyā-vidhi*). And so he will say: "When the connection between cause and effect has been delimited by the [designation] *anu*, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) prescribed for the cause, though it has been reached, is set aside by the [commencement of the new rule]. Thus.

Thus, in the rule *taditthamanurlakṣaṇe*, the cause (*hetu*) itself is employed as the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) in order to state that the cause pervades the definition, even though there exists an internal distinction between these two. For instance, in the rule *lakṣaṇahetvoḥ kriyāyāḥ*, the cause is presented as distinct from the definition with the intention of expressing its status as a producer (*janakatva*). In this way, the general category of "efficient cause" (*nimitta*) is divided into three types: the *kāraka* (case-role), which brings about an action by means of its specific nature; the *hetu* (cause), which produces [the result] in a general sense; and the *lakṣaṇa* (definition), which makes known [the object]. || 14 ||

Although there is a similarity in their being producers (*janakatva*), he states the distinction between the cause (*hetu*) and the instrument (*sādhana*) due to the difference in their objects: "The cause has substance (*dravya*) and so forth as its object; the instrument is that which performs a specific action. A thing capable of accomplishing a substance, quality, or action is the cause of substances and the like. For example: a sprout [is produced] by a seed, a lineage by wealth, grief by a daughter, fame by knowledge, skill by the practice of an art, and cooking by fire.

Even though they are capable of accomplishing an action, if they do not depend upon an [actual] operation, they are considered merely "causes" (*hetu*). Thus, although cooking and the like are actions, here—because fire and so forth are intended to be expressed as assisting through their mere presence after their operations have ceased—they lack the status of instruments (*karaṇa*) and are therefore connected with the third case of the cause (*hetutṛtīyā*). For example: *dhanena saha kulaṃ sampannam* ("the family has prospered along with wealth"). For the fame of the family is produced by means of the wealth.

And in that case, wealth whose activity has ceased is connected with the word "family" by means of an instrumental of cause—which supersedes the genitive of remainder—on the basis of mere fitness; likewise, a daughter is [the cause] of her father’s grief by way of the act of giving birth. Learning, too, is the cause of fame only when it is being acquired by one who is already famous; thus, here the relationship of remainder is produced by the act of acquisition. In other cases as well, this should be inferred accordingly. Skillfulness through the practice of an art, and dwelling through study—here the cause has for its object both a quality and an action.

An *kāraka* (grammatical participant), however, is defined by its relation to the accomplishment of an action (*kriyā*). For in that case, the action itself is the fixed object, and the state of being engaged in an operation (*vyāpāra*) constitutes a difference in essential nature. Yet, it is stated that for some things, even though they are engaged in an operation and are objects of the action, there is a "causal" status (*hetutva*) prescribed by the technical treatises; thus he says: "The agent (*kartṛ*), when dependent on another agent, is accepted as the cause (*hetu*) with respect to the action. (25)

The instigator (*prayojaka*) is one who, being employed in an action through the mediation of the power of the agent who is the prompted (*prayojyakartṛ*), prompts that prompted agent; thus, according to the grammatical treatise, he is accepted as the "cause" (*hetu*). The meaning is that although he is a specific type of *kāraka* by virtue of this technical statement, he is not a "cause" in its conventional sense. || 25 ||

Now, although the status as the object of an action is the same for both the cause (*hetu*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*), he states the distinction between them: "Just as a substitute for an instrument used for the sake of an action is observed, so it is not the case that a substitute exists for a cause, because the action is for the sake of the cause. (26)

The instrument (*karaṇa*) is subordinate, being that which provides the most excellent assistance for the accomplishment of an action; the action, however, is primary, as its nature is that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Therefore, because subordinate factors must conform to the primary, when no specific instrument is prescribed by scripture, the learned practice the use of a substitute.

For action, being the primary element, is capable of implying suitable means because it is that which is to be accomplished; thus, while the application of means is heard [in the text] for the purpose of filling in the general category of means already implied, even if that specific application is impossible, the general category of means implied by the primary nature of the action itself—being further nourished by another particular—is not capable of abandoning the meaning of what is directly stated in scripture.

Since the generic class (*sāmānya*) is also heard [in the injunction] and since it is capable of encompassing all its particulars, the justification for a substitute has already been discussed at length previously. Even when a subsidiary element (*aṅga*) fails, because the primary act (*pradhāna*) is not destroyed, the cultured (*śiṣṭa*) adopt a similar subsidiary—known through the traditional lineage—as if it were the principal itself, in order to preserve the essential nature of the act of offering. This is the fruit of the primacy of the action.

For this very reason, some explain that the word *karaṇa* here denotes all the factors of action (*kāraka*), and that the singular number is used because it refers to a genus; thus, since all the factors of action are subordinate (*guṇabhūta*), a substitute for a subordinate element is logically possible. As for the expression "he dwells for the sake of Vedic study" (*adhyayanena vasati*), although the act of dwelling is understood from the verb as the primary element, by the force of the actual state of affairs, it is dependent upon the cause called "Vedic study. For it is commonly said by speakers: "My stay here is for the purpose of Vedic study."

Furthermore, the principal factor does not conform to its subordinate qualities; therefore, in the absence of study, it is not proper to substitute anything else here for the purpose of residing. For if something else were employed, the action would be understood as being for that other purpose, and thus that [other thing] alone would become the primary cause at that time. Consequently, in the expression "he resides by means of study" (*adhyayanena vasati*), this is not an instrumental case denoting an instrument (*karaṇa-tṛtīyā*), but rather an instrumental case denoting a cause (*hetu-tṛtīyā*) alone.

For dwelling is not accomplished by study while it is engaged in an activity; rather, study itself is what must be completed as the primary object for the sake of dwelling. Thus, study—being devoid of further activity and being merely fit for the purpose—is the cause of dwelling insofar as it is intended as the goal. If, however, one intends to express that study is conducive to dwelling while it is engaged in its own activity, then, because it performs what is capable of bringing about that result (like begging for alms, for instance), it possesses the status of an "instigating agent" (*prayojaka-kartṛ*), as in the expression "he causes [the boy] to dwell through study. Therefore, in this context of grammatical factors (*kāraka*), the factor is subordinate while the action is primary.
By the phrase "but there is a reversal regarding the cause," the distinction is stated that there is a difference between a causal factor (*kāraka*) and a logical reason (*hetu*). || 26 ||

Now, in order to distinguish the scope of the fourth [case-ending], namely *tādarthya* (the state of being for the sake of that), from the scope of the third [case-ending], namely *hetu* (cause), he says: "The cause (*hetu*) establishes the purpose of an object through both reverse (*pratilomya*) and direct (*ānulomya*) order; however, *tādarthya* follows the direct order and is subsumed under the nature of being a cause. (27)

A cause in a state of diminution is characterized by its contrariety when it produces an effect that is likewise non-increasing; for example, water whose form has become diminished through a specific contact with heat is conducive to a succession of states characterized by progressive degrees of further diminution—diminution, greater diminution, and extreme diminution. Conversely, a cause characterized by its conformity is one that, while its own specific form is increasing due to contact with another entity, produces an effect that is increasingly augmented.

For example, a seed that has acquired a specific transformation through its contact with water and heat, being in a state of swelling and capable of producing a sprout. Thus, the cause is of two kinds. Its "specificity" (*tadviśeṣa*), however, is its "being for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*). That which is invariably conducive and serves as the ground for the accomplishment of the object—that nature of causality or productivity which follows from such conduciveness is the form of the specific cause. The meaning is that "being for the sake of that" is the manifested form of the relationship between cause and effect. In this context, the dative case [ending] expresses that form of the specific cause which follows from it.

The meaning is that "being for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*) is the manifested form of the relationship between cause and effect. In this regard, the example is *kuṇḍalāya hiraṇyam* ("gold for a earring"). In the expression "this is for the sake of that" (*tasmā idaṃ tadartham*), the word "this" (*idam*) refers to the benefactor (*upakāraka*), while the word "that" (*tat*) refers to the beneficiary (*upakārya*). Through the formation of a compound followed by an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*), the relationship is expressed as a manifested form. In that case, because the referent of the second member of the compound—the causal form—is what is to be made known and thus possesses primacy, the relationship attaches itself to the subordinate factor denoted by the word "that."

For in that case, since "this has arisen therein" implies the cause's state of being a benefactor for the sake of that [effect], the fourth case (*caturthī*) prescribed upon the emergence of the causal relationship applies only to the word denoting the effect. This is because the relationship residing in the cause is also understood through that [relationship]. Therefore, it is incorrect to assert that the third case (*tṛtīyā*) does not apply after a word denoting the cause, on the grounds that the effect itself, having transformed into the motivator (*prayojaka*), is called "for the sake of that" (*tadartha*).

Since the word *tādarthya* (being for the sake of that) has the meaning of the final member as its predominant sense, it is logical that it expresses the cause; for this very reason, *tādarthya* is understood as being concomitant with causality. It is a specific kind of cause, not the effect itself. However, in the case of the statement "that for the sake of which his going occurred has been accomplished by him," because the subordinate element denoted by the pronoun *yat* is referred to by the coreferential pronoun *tat*, it is appropriate that the referent of the pronoun (*sarvanāmartha*) be connected with the effect. Nevertheless, even so, there is no predominance here of the referent of the pronoun, because it functions as a subordinate element relative to the meaning of the final member. || 27 ||

Thus, although the agent (*kāraka*), the cause (*hetu*), the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and that which exists for the sake of something else (*tādarthya*) are identical in being instrumental causes (*nimitta*), the categories of meaning (*padārtha*) have distinct individual natures; therefore, there is no risk of confusion regarding their definitions. Having thus concluded this incidental matter, the author now introduces the discussion concerning *kārakas* under consideration, stating: "In every case, an innate power (*śakti*) persists as long as the substance (*dravya*) itself exists. However, at the time of action (*kriyākāla*), it becomes an auxiliary through its manifestation from its substratum. (28)

The power that arises simultaneously [with the entity] is the emergence of impermanent objects from their own causes as already capable; for since entities cannot have an excellence added to them, it is impossible to impart power to what was previously incapable of arising immediately thereafter. However, the power of eternal things is innate. Furthermore, powers are inherent in their substrata; since they cannot remain without a support once that substratum has perished, they exist as long as the substance exists (*yāvaddravyabhāvinyah*).

Even so, when auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) are present, entities (*bhāva*) that are intent upon their own effects rely upon the manifestation of their power (*śakti*); thus, they are called "means" (*sādhana*) precisely at the time of manifestation because they are then serviceable for the effect, and not at other times, even though they exist then as well. For instance: "The wall has the power to obstruct, while iron and such have the power to pierce; yet that property, though always present, is only discerned at the time of action. (29)

A wall is an obstructor, and a weapon is a cutter; since these are known when the objects to be obstructed or cut are present, it follows that existing power (*śakti*) has its manifestation dependent upon its object. Even though it pertains to all three times, it is delimited by those of limited vision. Indeed, due to the necessity of the material cause (*upādāna*), power exists prior to the effect; and furthermore, it exists after the effect and cause as well. Scripture also corroborates this: "Just as the nooses of Varuṇa attached to the limbs of the Daityas are manifested [only when they act], so too are the powers of substances manifested for those who desire victory. (30)

According to the traditional teaching (āgama), the nooses of Varuṇa, which are fashioned by the very actions of the Daityas, reside eternally within the palms of their own hands in the form of latent power (śakti). It is heard that these [nooses] become manifest at the time of conquering the enemy army. Likewise, it is logical that the powers of substances, though always present, are revealed at the time of accomplishing their own specific effects. || 30 ||

That which was stated—that there is a power (*śakti*) in weapons and the like for the purpose of rending—is now further elaborated: "When the sword, by means of its own sharpness, weight, hardness, and configuration, is engaged toward that which is to be cut, it is then apprehended as possessing power (*śaktimān*). (31)

Sharpness (*taikṣṇya*) is the excellence of thinness in parts that are densely compacted and gradually become finer toward the tip; it is the quality that serves as the cause for cutting. Weight (*gaurava*) is the quality that causes falling, resulting from the accumulation of parts whose intervals have been separated through the disruption of the intermingling of heterogeneous parts. Hardness (*kāṭhinya*), a quality consisting of density, belongs to iron parts stimulated by heating, from which a specific stroke is produced.

A specific arrangement (*saṃniveśaviśeṣa*), which is the cause of its internal differentiation and the basis for designations such as "the tip of the circle" (*maṇḍalāgra*) and so forth, is its shape (*saṃsthāna*). From this, a variety of strikes arises. It is by means of these properties that a sword or staff is perceived as possessing the capacity to begin the acts of cutting or splitting. However, when devoid of activity (*vyāpāra*), even though these properties are present, it is not perceived in that way. The same should be stated, as appropriate, for other objects as well, since the sword is used merely as an illustration. (31)

He states that other alternative positions are also possible regarding this proof: "Some maintain that the means of accomplishment arises from another cause prior to the action; some [hold it to be] innate; others maintain that the action exists prior [to the means]. (32)

If the existence of power (*sattva*) were already established, then waiting for its manifestation would be appropriate. However, since the existence of powers is itself inferred from their effects, it is not established prior to the action; therefore, prior to the action, the powers of substances arise precisely from that necessary cause which is required before the action. Even if the power exists, a cause for its manifestation must be required, and thus that [cause] alone is the producer.

For indeed, since entities that depend upon auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) are productive, it is inferred that they possess mutually distinct potencies (*śakti*) which serve as the causes of their own effects; because those same entities alone are not productive, they are not potent at that [earlier] time. Thus, the birth of potency does not arise from the very producer of its own substratum, but rather from another instrumental cause (*nimitta*). Furthermore, some maintain that because there is recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), there is no difference in the entity despite the presence of both potency and lack of potency. For this very reason, the restriction regarding the material cause (*upādāna*) is also established through the determination of fitness (*yogyatā*).

Others, however, maintain that because power (*śakti*) is non-different from the entity itself, the states of being capable and incapable are merely differences in its own nature (*svabhāva*). This is a restatement of the previously established position that "the innate capacity of substances is what is intended by the term 'instrument' (*sādhana*). Some, on the other hand, hold that the instrument is not produced by the same cause as the action; rather, it is produced by another cause entirely. Thus, considering the instrument to have a distinct causal basis relative to the action, they explain even its "innateness" only in relation to the action.

For indeed, entities that are auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) bring about an action by conferring their respective powers upon one another; thus, the birth of actions—which consist of functional operations—is held to occur simultaneously with the powers of the means (*sādhana*). Consequently, since the powers arise from the very same sources from which the action arises, they are co-nascent (*sahaja*). Furthermore, because those [entities] possessing the newly arisen powers bring about the action in the subsequent moment, there is no deficiency in the relationship between the means and the end (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*); for the coexistence of the means and the end is not established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). || 32 ||

Others, however, consider that the action exists prior to the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). To the question of how this is tenable, he says: "Activity itself, first unattached to anything whatsoever, draws [the means] toward a single substratum, like a flowing stream. (33)

Eternal action (*kriyā*) is said to be independent of the operation of causes and not dependent on anything whatsoever; however, it is indeed inherent (*samaveta*) in its own substratum (*svāśraya*). For this very reason, within that substratum, it manifests the potencies of the means of accomplishment (*sādhanaśakti*), which bring about their respective specific effects. Others, however, say that it is entirely non-dependent (*anāśrita*). According to the tradition of certain elder Mīmāṃsakas, action—characterized by activity—is like the current of a river, which, flowing in a continuous stream, draws along and carries away grass, leaves, creepers, and the like; such is the nature of the potency of the means of accomplishment.

The Sāṃkhya system maintains that activity (pravṛtti), characterized by *rajas*, is eternal and follows after all entities; being capable of producing its own effects, it generates those effects. Since everything engaged in operation is a generator of effects, the operation must exist as a prior state. Therefore, it is logical that power (*śakti*) is projected by that [operation]. || 33 ||

He asks: "How can this beginningless activity be eternal? [At this point, a portion of the text has been lost; the following is written by Phullarāja to bridge the gap. Now, in order to describe the nature of the means (*sādhana*) according to other philosophical views, he says: "Some describe that entity (*bhāva*) characterized in such a way as being either the *apūrva* (unseen force), the power of time (*kāla-śakti*), action (*kriyā*), or time itself. (34)

Some say that there is an unprecedented entity called *dharma* and *adharma*, designated as the "unseen" (*adṛṣṭa*), which is of such a nature and characterized by causal capacity (*sāmarthya*). For it is through the power of the unseen that everything either comes to be or does not; thus, the unseen alone should be understood as the cause of all effects. However, some proponents claim that the means [of creation] is the power of Time belonging to the Lord Brahmā. For everything, when animated by the power of Time, becomes capable of action.

Or they say that action (*kriyā*), whose nature has just been described as being of the *rājasa* type, is the means (*sādhana*). However, it is impossible to define any means whatsoever that exists at a subsequent time. Previously, the means was explained as having action as its root; now, the distinction is that action itself is the means. For it is that very [action], proceeding by itself, which becomes the specific factor. Those who maintain the doctrine of substance and time (*dravyakālavādinaḥ*) say that the means is simply time, characterized by such definitions as "eternal," "one," and so forth.
For all things arise by the power of time for the accomplishment of their effects; thus, time alone is the means. As he will say: "If it were not to obstruct... (34).

Now, in order to investigate the number of *śakti* (potency), which was previously defined as having the characteristic of capability (*sāmarthya*) and established as a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), he says: "The six potencies of others are eternal, endowed with both difference and non-difference, and reside in objects for the sake of the successful accomplishment of action, just like a universal (*jāti*). (35)

According to the opinion of others, it is established that six eternal powers—beginning with *karma* (action)—are situated within objects, characterized by distinct definitions. Of what nature are they? They are endowed with both difference and non-difference. For if they were described as being exclusively different from the objects, the object would become formless (*nīrūpatā*) due to its lack of power. On the other hand, if they are said to be non-different [from the object], then the emergence of diverse effects would not be possible.

Therefore, some maintain that powers (śakti) exist in objects like generic categories (arthajāti), endowed with both difference and non-difference—being different in one respect and non-different in another—just as the generic categories of existence (sattva), substantiality (dravyatva), cowness (gotva), and Śābaleya-ness (śābaleyatva) are always present in objects through a constant conjunction of difference and non-difference. 35.

Although these powers are infinite due to the distinctions of substance and so forth, their reality does not transcend the state of being exactly sixfold; thus he says: "Though they appear as if immeasurable through the distinctions of substance, form, and so on, in the investigation of reality, they do not transcend the six powers. (36)

Power (*śakti*) is differentiated by the difference in substance (*dravyabheda*). For example, a sickle cuts in one way, whereas a sword cuts in another. It is also differentiated by the difference in form (*ākārabheda*); for instance, a sword [cuts] in one way, while a sword-vine (*khaṅgalatā*) cuts in another. By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), that same power of burning (*dahanaśakti*) attains a variety of forms in fire due to differences of place and time; yet its sixfold nature (*ṣaṭtva*) does not transcend its own essential character (*svarūpa*). || 36 ||

Now, he states that it is indeed a single power which, having attained a sixfold state through the distinction of its causes, constitutes the means (*sādhana*): "Due to the distinction of causes, a single power is perceived as divided; they call this very sixfold agency the basis for its activity. (37)

One should understand that agency itself—existing in six states through various causal conditions such as being the most desired (*īpsitatama*) or being the act of flaming (*jvalana*)—is the basis and the cause for the differentiation of the technical designations of *kārakas*, which arises from the manifestation of distinct powers within its activity. As it has been said: "The fuel [is so called] until the cooking is completed; it will flame" (referring to the instrument of the act of flaming). According to this principle, agency itself assumes the form of designations such as "instrument" (*karaṇa*) when there is an intention to express its intermediate operations.

Thus, it has been established whether power (*śakti*) is one or many. Now, raising the doubt as to whether this [power] might be distinct or non-distinct [from its substratum], he says: Whether in identity or in difference, that is called "distinct. The world has verbal testimony (*śabda*) as its authority; it is followed by the treatise (*śāstra*). (38)

It has been stated that this [power] is indeed indefinable in terms of either difference or non-difference, being merely endowed with both difference and non-difference. Now, if you subject this to a rigorous refutation (*niṣkoṣāṇikā*), what purpose does that serve for us? In every respect, the reality of the power and the possessor of power is either absolute identity, non-distinction, or simply non-difference. However, we, who follow the system of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*), maintain that capacity (*sāmarthya*) is indeed distinct. For the world takes verbal testimony (*śabda*) as its authority.

He states that this very [power] is followed by the treatise: "That [power] is followed by the treatise. For the meaning of a word is expanded in accordance with worldly convention (*lokapratīti*). And the world follows precisely the non-difference (*avyatireka*) of power from the cause of verbal action; for it has been stated that if there were no non-difference, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the constant production of action. (38)

Now, if you do not find peace without an investigation into the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it is said in response to this: "Something is stated here": "But in the ultimate sense, oneness does not have a characteristic distinct from difference. Reality itself manifests in the form of both difference and oneness. (39)

Because of its distinctness, oneness does not exist apart from the characteristic of distinctness; for reality itself manifests in the form of both distinctness and oneness. It should be understood that in the state of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), it manifests as distinctness, whereas upon the dissolution of ignorance (*avidyā*), it manifests as oneness. || 39 ||
To explain this very point, he says: That which is an indubitable distinctness does not differ from unity; that which is an indubitable unity does not differ from distinctness. (40)

That distinctness which is rendered free from doubt through the realization of the true nature of things is not different from unity; and that unity which is free from doubt and devoid of delusion is not different from distinctness—that is, from manifoldness. || 40 ||

And thus, when unity has reached its ultimate limit, then that very [unity] alone shines everywhere; so he says: "Heaven, earth, wind, the sun, the oceans, the rivers, and the directions—these are portions of the reality of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇatattva) situated externally. (41)

Alternatively, let the investigation into plurality and unity regarding a few specific objects stand aside. Consider these: heaven and space, and earth—these two, "heaven-and-earth," are great entities designated as the gross elements (*mahābhūta*); between them is also the wind as a third; likewise, there is the divine light characterized by the sun, the foremost among all luminous bodies; there are the waters, whether as rivers or oceans, which are modifications (*vikāra*); all these are the gross elements that constitute the life-force of the entire world; or else, there are the directions (*diś*), which serve as the basis for worldly convention.

And time is that which will be described hereafter. All this—expressed by the phrase "of the reality known as the internal organ" (antaḥkaraṇatattvasya)—refers to those parts, reflections, and appearances situated externally, which belong precisely to that reality (tattva) designated as the internal organ, appearing as internal by virtue of being the internal organ. But in the ultimate sense (paramārthe), what kind of internal-external distinction can there be? The meaning of the verse is that there is only one supreme Śabdabrahman, consisting of consciousness (saṃvinmaya), which exists in such and such various ways. || 41 ||

Having described its nature as the great elements and its nature as the directions, he speaks in order to establish that very same [reality] as having the nature of time: "That single reality alone exists in the form of temporal division; for it, which has no prior or posterior parts, is perceived through the form of the other. (42)

For that [time] is indeed without prior or posterior from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Alternatively, it is perceived through the sequence of "slow," "quick," and so forth, by virtue of the power of time. Thus, according to the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*), the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is established through the inherent capacity of things and worldly convention.

Alternatively, it may be understood as having the nature of a mental construction according to the Vijñānavāda school; or as having the nature of a relation (*saṃsarga*) existing as a distinct category (*padārthāntara*) according to the Saṃsargavāda school; or as being designated by the word "prior" (*pūrva*) with the characteristic of the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) according to the Mīmāṃsaka view; or as the power of time (*kāla-śakti*) inherent in Brahman according to the Advaita philosophy; or as action (*kriyā*) in the form of passionate activity (*pravṛtti*) according to the Sāṃkhya system; or as an eternal, singular substance characterized as a substance (*dravya-lakṣaṇa*) according to the opinion of those who maintain that time is a substance (*dravyakālavādin*).

In the context of the discussion on the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), there is an investigation into the terminology of the factors of action (*kāraka*). In connection with that, after first defining the distinctions between cause (*hetu*), characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), agent (*kāraka*), instrument (*karaṇa*), and purpose (*tādarthya*), their essential nature has been briefly stated. Following that, there is an analysis of time, considering whether power (*śakti*) exists simultaneously [with its substrate], prior to it, or subsequent to it. Then there is an analysis of number, considering whether that power is distinct according to the divisions of object (*karman*) and so forth, or whether it is a single entity that is merely conceptualized in various ways.

And whether that [difference] is indeed distinct from the category of the object or non-distinct—this is the inquiry into distinction and non-distinction; and by way of introducing that, the nature of Brahman is defined. This is the collective meaning of the section. || 42 ||

Now, continuing with the very position of the Grammarians (vaiyākaraṇa) under discussion, and establishing the existence of *śakti* by demonstrating its positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) through the method of exclusion (*vyatireka*), he says: "For even when there is no exclusion [of the object], an exclusion [of the word] is observed; and even when there is presence [of the object], [the word] is absent. Therefore, the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhakti*) is held to be something distinct from the meanings of 'tree' and so forth. (43)

Even when there is no exclusion—that is, even in the absence of difference—between the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) as in *vṛkṣaḥ*, *vṛkṣam*, *vṛkṣeṇa*, *vṛkṣāya*, and so forth, there is an exclusion of the meaning of the suffix (*vibhaktyartha*), characterized as the factor of action (*sādhana*). Likewise, in those very instances, even when the meaning of the suffix has no connection, the connection—that is, the following along—is observed for the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*). Therefore, we conclude that there exists a certain distinct meaning, consisting of the suffix-meaning, which cannot be denied, characterized as the factor of action, and denotable by the word "power" (*śakti*); thus is the proof of the factor of action established. || 43 ||

Now, he states a verse for the conclusion of what has been explained and the introduction of what is yet to be explained: "The general category is the *kāraka*; its seven primary sources of division are as follows: six through the distinctions of 'object' (*karman*) and so forth, while the seventh is the remaining distinction. (44)

The statement "the general [category] is the factor" (*sāmānyaṃ kārakam*) is the conclusion of the explained meaning; the statement beginning with "its seven... (*tasya sapta...*) is the introduction to the meaning to be explained. In this context, the first [seven] are the primary ones; in relation to the general means of accomplishment (*sāmānya-sādhana*), they are of the nature of distinctions and are the sources (*yonayaḥ*) of their own respective distinctions, thus they are called "sources of distinction" (*bhedayonayaḥ*). Alternatively, the first seven are the sources—that is, the causes—of their own respective distinctions. To the question "How so?", he says: "Six by way of the distinction of those called 'action' (*karma*) and so forth," and so on.

Thus, the seven powers of the factors (*kāraka-śaktayaḥ*) are now indicated through the different designations such as "object" (*karman*) and so forth; this constitutes the connection to the "Exposition of the Means of Accomplishment" (*Sādhanasamuddeśa*). || 44 ||

The grammatical factor (*kāraka*) has been indicated as being divided into seven types according to the distinctions of *karman* (object) and so forth. Now, following that sequence, he speaks in order to explain *karman* first, preceded by a demonstration of its numerical divisions: "It is considered to be threefold: the produced (*nirvartya*), the modified (*vikārya*), and the reached (*prāpya*). Among these, the object most desired (*īpsitatama*) is fourfold; the other [types of objects] are likewise conceived. (45)

The specific indication of the *kārakas* is presented here according to the sequence of case endings (*vibhakti*). In the grammatical rules (*sūtras*), however, they are stated in the order of *apādāna* and so forth, following the technical rule regarding conflict (*vipratiṣedha-paribhāṣā*). In this context, the case endings are *su*, *au*, *jas*, and so on. A *kāraka* may be either expressed or unexpressed. Among these, the nominative (*prathamā*) is prescribed as the case ending expressing the *kāraka* when it refers solely to the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-artha*).

Since all case-endings beginning with the second (accusative) are case-inflections (*kāraka-vibhakti*) used when [the relation] is not already expressed, and because they share a single commonality, the discussion begins in accordance with the meaning of the second case and the others. The meaning of the second case and the rest is "object" (*karman*) and so forth, as stated in the rule: "The second case is used for the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*), etc. Therefore, the explanation of the "object" itself has first reached its proper occasion. In that regard, the definition of the object—namely, that which is most desired by the agent through his action, being what he most wishes to attain—is precisely what was set forth in the first sūtra.

Karma is threefold; it should be understood as being divided into many internal types through three modes, namely the forms of that which is produced (*nirvartya*), that which is modified (*vikārya*), and that which is reached (*prāpya*). Now, he says "but another [kind] is conceived as fourfold" in order to further differentiate that which is also indicated in other sūtras. || 45 ||

He asks, "How so? and replies: "That which is obtained through indifference, that which is not desired by the agent, that which is not designated by other names, and that which has belonged to another. (46)

That which is to be reached through indifference or neutrality, such as the base of a tree for one going to a village; likewise, that which is not desired by the agent, such as thieves or poison—this is the twofold category indicated by the second sūtra, "and likewise that which is not desired though connected [with the action]. Furthermore, in whatever manner something is most desired by the agent, if in that very same manner it is undesired—meaning other than what is desired, such as poison which is loathed—and the other, namely that which is reached through indifference, such as the base of a tree, has been mentioned.

Likewise, even that which is not designated by other technical terms such as *apādāna* (ablative) and so forth, yet serves as the cause for an action, is to be understood as what is indicated by the third sūtra, "and that which is unspoken" (*akathitaṃ ca*). This applies also to the rule: "whatever has another [kāraka] as its antecedent. That is, that for which another *kāraka* was previously applicable. For example: *devadattam abhikrudhyati* ("he is angry with Devadatta"), *devadattam abhidruhyati* ("he bears malice toward Devadatta").

For here, by the rule *krudhadruhorupasṛṣṭayoḥ karma* (P. 1.4.38), when the roots *kruddh* and *druh* are preceded by a prefix—that is, when they are connected with an *upasarga*—the *kāraka* toward whom the anger is directed receives the designation of *karman* alone, even though it would have received the designation of *saṃpradāna* by the preceding rule. Similarly, in the example *akṣān dīvyati*, by the rule *divaḥ karma ca* (P. 1.4.43), that which is the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*) of the root *div* receives the designation of *karman* alone, even though it would have received the designation of *karaṇa* by the preceding rule. || 46 ||

Now, he speaks in order to explain the threefold [classification] beginning with the "to-be-produced" (*nirvartya*): "That whose material cause (*prakṛti*), whether existing or non-existing, is not admitted to be subject to transformation (*pariṇāminī*), is declared to have the nature of being 'to-be-produced' (*nirvartyatva*). (47)

When the material cause (*prakṛti*) of an object being produced—such as a jar—is not conceived as non-different [from the effect], whether it be existent like clay and so forth, or non-existent like sound [is to the] conjunction and so forth, and is not intended to be expressed in such forms as "he makes a jar out of clay," but rather with a sense of distinction as "he makes a jar by means of clay"; when there is such an intention regarding the material cause, those who know the categories of action call that object which is to be produced the "object" (*karman*).

In order to explain the *vikārya* (the object that undergoes transformation), he says: "But when there is an intention to express the modification of the material cause (*prakṛti*), then it is called a *vikārya* object. When the intention is made to express the material cause as undergoing a transformation, as in "he makes clay into a jar," "he makes grass into a mat," or "he makes charcoal into ash," and so forth, then it is designated as a *vikārya* object. Now, under the guise of presenting another opinion, with the desire to state a different classification, he speaks in order to define the *nirvartya* (the object to be produced) and the *vikārya*: "By some others, the *nirvartya* and the *vikārya* objects have been demonstrated differently in the treatise. (48)

To the question "How so?", he says: That which is non-existent [before] and is brought into being, or that which already exists and is manifested by birth—that object is established as twofold: the *nirvartya* (that which is produced) and the *vikārya* (that which is modified). (49)

Whether, according to the followers of Vaiśeṣika and others, that which is non-existent (*asat*) is produced, or according to the Sāṃkhya doctrine, that which is already existent (*sat*) is produced—both cases are termed "to be accomplished" (*nirvartya*) because they are manifested through the act of birth. This is what is meant: for us, who maintain the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), it can be said that there exists an action that is to be accomplished. Whether its material cause (*prakṛti*) is existent or non-existent, in every respect, there is no impairment whatsoever of its status as something to be accomplished by virtue of being manifested through birth.

That which is manifested through birth, whether existent or non-existent, is "to be produced" (*nirvartya*). The statement "the non-existent is born" reiterates what was previously stated—that there is a state of being produced by an action from a material cause that does not [previously] exist—namely, that "it is manifested through the birth of the non-existent. This is the distinction here: for example, in such cases as "she gives birth to a son" or "he utters a word," there is a manifestation through the acts of procreation and utterance of a son who already exists within the womb, and of a word intended to be spoken.

For here, "birth" (janman) is intended to mean the manifestation of that which already exists; and the manifestation of a word intended [to be used] occurs through its production (prasava) and its employment (prayoga). Indeed, "birth" is intended here as the manifestation of the existent. By the mention of "birth," he indicates that when there is an intention for it to come into being (pravṛtti), it is something to be modified (vikārya). Otherwise, by the mention of "birth," he also indicates the absence of the status of a "consummate object" (nirvartya-karman) for that which is merely manifested.

In such cases as *tena vedam adhīte* ("he studies the Veda by means of that"), since the Veda and so forth—which are being manifested through the act of study—lack the status of a *nirvartya-karman* (an object to be produced), it is said: "If [it is argued] that [the definition applies] to an object that is being produced (*nirvartyamāna*) or modified (*vikriyamāṇa*), then there must be an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for the study of the Veda and similar cases. Thus, some maintain that this was stated as a *nirvartya-karman* only when the meaning of the root itself is intended; others hold a different view, which is inconsistent. Therefore, this should be explained according to the distinction between the doctrines of those who maintain that the effect pre-exists (*satkāryavāda*) and those who maintain that it does not (*asatkāryavāda*). Previously, this was stated in accordance with worldly convention; here, however, the distinction is that it is also stated by resorting to the views of the non-Buddhist schools (*tīrthika*). || 49 ||

"And the object of transformation (*vikārya-karma*) is established as being twofold. Having previously stated the distinction between individual instances (*vyakti-bheda*) in order to describe the definition for each instance, he states the definition: "Some [objects] arise from the destruction of their material cause (*prakṛti*), such as the ashes of wood and the like; some [arise] through the production of a different quality (*guṇāntara*), such as the transformation of gold and the like. (50)

Because of destruction without a trace (*niranvayavināśa*), there is the annihilation of the material cause (*prakṛti*). For example, ashes and so forth [result] from wood and the like; one turns wood into ashes. As before, the connection with the action between the material cause and its modification (*vikāra*) should be applied. However, according to the previous definition, this object is "to be produced" (*nirvartya*) when the material cause is not intended to be expressed. But when it is intended to be expressed, it is "to be modified" (*vikārya*). In the present case, however, even though the material cause is not intended to be expressed, because the effect—such as ashes—is understood to arise precisely through a specific change in form after having destroyed the wood and so forth, it is "to be modified."

In the previous case, however, the material cause (*prakṛti*) is the object (*karman*) to be directly modified, and the modification (*vikāra*) is also [the object] by way of non-difference from it. Here, however, the distinction is that it is the modification itself that is directly [the object]. In the expression "he burns the wood" (*kāṣṭhāni dahati*), the material cause alone is expressed by the word; the modification, namely the ash, is understood through implication (*sāmarthya*). This should be understood similarly in cases such as "he cuts the stalks" (*kāṇḍāni lunāti*) and "he makes a hide" (*carma karoti*).

However, some *prakṛti* (material cause), not abandoning its own nature, is called "modified" (*vikṛta*) due to the attainment of another configuration; thus, the other type of object of action, the "transformable" (*vikārya*), is characterized by the arising of a different quality, such as the property of being arranged [into a new form]. For example: "the gold becomes two earrings. Although in the theory of the non-existent effect (*asatkāryavāda*) there is the production of something previously non-existent here, nevertheless, because of recognition and the worldly determination of identity, it is said to be merely the attainment of a different quality.
And this is also included within the previous definition when the *prakṛti* is intended [to be expressed]. || 50 ||

Now he states the definition of an object that is reached [by the sense organ]: "That in which the accomplishment of the specific qualities residing in the action is not perceived either through perception or through inference is called a 'reached' (prāpya) object. (51)

In the case of a *nirvartya* (produced) object, the very acquisition of its own being (*ātmalābha*), which is the distinction produced by action, is determined through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) itself. In the case of a *vikārya* (modified) object, such as ashes or a bracelet, the modification—the distinction produced by action—is determined by direct perception. However, in some cases, the determination of the distinction occurs through inference (*anumāna*), as for instance, the determination of [the state] produced in another person by means of signs such as a brightened face.

Furthermore, the specific transformation (viśeṣa) produced in plants by actions such as the sprinkling of water is born at every moment; because it is subtle, it is not perceived immediately after its arising, yet it is ascertained in its final stage through the observation of a highly intensified transformation. For this highly intensified transformation cannot arise suddenly and unexpectedly without depending upon a sequence of stages. Thus, it is inferred at every moment in its subtle form, for that subtle form is indeed difficult to discern.

Just as there is no perceived difference between the high and low pitches of specific notes such as *ṣaḍja* and so forth, so too, when no difference produced by action is observed, that which is the object of the agent's action—being the most desired simply by virtue of being the objective domain of the action—is the "attained" (*prāpya*) object. For example: "He sees the sun," "He approaches the city," "He studies the Veda," and so on. Indeed, in the case of the sun and others, no specific quality produced by the action of seeing and so forth can be discerned.

By the two means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), only the connection with action is indicated, but that alone is not the specific distinction (viśeṣa). For when the connection with action has occurred, a distinction inherent in the object is observed in the case of both produced (*nirvartya*) and modified (*vikārya*) objects. However, in the case of a city, although the conjunction produced by the act of going is a distinction residing in both [the city and Devadatta], it remains unperceived because of the city’s immense size, just as the contact between Mount Himavat and a finger is unperceived by Devadatta due to his small stature.

And a single portion of the earth, conceived in relation to its own parts as a specific substratum for that which is supported by it, is well known as denoted by the word "city"; thus, there is no inconsistency whatsoever. || 51 ||

Some maintain that there is no such thing as an action that reaches its object, because in every case one determines a specific result produced by the activity. For instance: "In all cases, a gain of distinction is found through seeing and other means; for some, the manifestation of that [distinction] is established in the case of 'poisonous looks' and the like. (52)

According to the opinion of some, modification (*vikāra*)—defined as the acquisition of a specific quality produced by actions such as seeing—is present everywhere; however, due to its subtlety, it is not perceived by everyone. For those for whom poison is visible, there is the establishment of certainty regarding its manifestation in relation to that object. Indeed, an object gazed upon by snakes whose poison is visible is perceived as if licked by tongues of flaming fire. By analogy with that, in other cases as well, some specific quality produced by seeing and so forth should be inferred in the object.

For the eye is composed of fire (*taijasa*) and functions by reaching its object; therefore, the object it encounters is necessarily transformed, just as by the gaze of a venomous serpent. However, there is this distinction: in the case of a venomous serpent, the fire is intense and burns the object due to contact with the poison, whereas in other cases, its presence is subtler. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), magnets and the like are included. In their proximity, iron revolves; and in the proximity of the *kataka* fruit, water becomes clear—in such instances, there is indeed a transformation produced by action.

And this is not the opinion of the author of the treatise, because it is presented as the view of "some" (*keṣāṃcit*), indicating it is an alternative position. Furthermore, even when a specific characteristic is observed in one instance, it is not logical to assume that such a state exists everywhere, especially where no such specific characteristic is perceived. Moreover, what is intended here by "modification" (*vikāra*) is the result of an action; however, the visible object is the cause of the action, not its result. Even in cases such as a "poisonous glance," the modification in the object occurs due to contact with light (*tejaḥ*), not by the power of the action itself.

In this way, the nature of things such as the magnet is simply this; it is not some modification produced by an action. Therefore, there certainly exists an object to be reached that does not depend on assistance produced by an action. 52.

If there is no connection with modification (*vikāra*) for an object that is reached [by the action], how can it serve as an auxiliary member (*aṅga*) for the accomplishment of the action—that is, for the attainment of its status as a means (*sādhana*)? It is said in reply: "Approaching the appearance (*ābhāsopagama*), manifestation (*vyakti*), and endurance (*soḍhatva*): these are the specific characteristics of the object being reached, established for the accomplishment of the action. (Verse 53)

An object enters the range of vision by abiding in a suitable location; thus, reaching a suitable location (*yogyadeśāpatti*)—that is, the arrival at the field of manifestation (*ābhāsopagama*)—is an auxiliary factor for its perception as an intrinsic nature. Even for an object situated in a suitable location, its manifestation depends on causes such as lamps, which function through the presence or absence of obstructions like mist and the like; this is an auxiliary factor. Furthermore, regarding an object situated in a location capable of being illuminated, the fact that it is not seen when there is no obscuring agent—such as a *piśāca* or similar being whose nature is inherently invisible—is its "endurance" (*soḍhatva*), its capacity to be cognized, and its visible nature (*dṛśyasvabhāvatā*); this too is an auxiliary factor.

Through these excellences (*atiśaya*), the object to be attained (*prāpya-karma*) undergoes the state of being a means (*sādhanabhāva*) in the act of seeing; yet these [excellences] are the causes of the act of seeing and are not produced by it. Even in cases such as "he goes to the village," endurance (*soḍhatva*) and other qualities should be understood as applicable to the village and so forth, as appropriate. For villages and the like, when made the objects of effort (*samīhā*) and thus appearing, accomplish the act of going and so forth by being capable of enduring that going. Likewise, the Veda and so forth being studied are capable of enduring the act of studying.

In the expression "he remembers his mother" (*mātaraṃ smarati*), the mother—having been a benefactor—enters the path of memory even for one of cruel heart and thus establishes that recollection. However, when there is no regard for the status of being the most desired object (*ipsitatamatva*), and one intends to express the general nature of the relationship, the genitive of the residual relation (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*) is used: *mātuḥ smarati* ("he remembers [the mother]"). || 53 ||

Thus, action has been characterized according to its divisions. However, this must now be stated: it was previously said that all specific instruments (*sādhana*) are the agents (*kartṛ*) of qualities and actions. How, then, is the possibility of their being objects (*karman*) established? He provides the introductory lead for the investigation into the object-agent relationship: "Having first experienced independence in the case of those [objects] to be produced (*nirvartya*) and so forth, they subsequently become objects when they function as agents for other agents. (54)

In the actions of production (*nirvṛtti*), transformation (*vikriyā*), and attainment through appearance (*ābhāsāpatti*), there arises—respectively according to their order—an object (*karman*) characterized as that which is produced (*nirvartya*), that which is modified (*vikārya*), and that which is attained (*prāpya*). This occurs by relying upon the agenthood (*kartṛtva*) or independence (*svātantrya*) [of the primary agent]. With respect to that [primary agent], for many other agents who possess the status of objects such as the "produced" and so forth, an object (*karman*) arises in the sense of being a command (*praiṣa*) regarding their activities of producing and so on, because they are being caused to act (*īyamāna*) by him.

For indeed, [the factors] "accomplishes," "transforms," "brings into manifestation," and "illuminates" are agents with respect to their own respective operations due to the distinction of their functions. When the operation of the primary agent is intended to be expressed, they—subordinating themselves like servants in the presence of a master when commanded by that agent—undergo the state of being objects (karma), such that [the agent] causes them to accomplish, causes them to transform, and causes them to attain the status of being objects of manifestation and so forth. || 54 ||

If that is so, then the agent becomes the object; having become the object, how does it become the agent such that the status of being both object and agent is possible? To this, he says: "Even when its [the object's] own operation has ceased, it remains established in its own operation; it receives certain rules prescribed for the object based on the authority of the grammatical treatise. (55)

In cases such as *kusūlaḥ bhidyate* ("the granary splits"), when there is the fulfillment of the agent's instigation because the granary itself experiences the splitting due to its fragile nature; or in cases such as *lūyate kedāraḥ* ("the field is being reaped"), because of its extreme dryness there is no dependence on the effort of an agent; or even in cases such as *pacyate odanaḥ svayam eva* ("the rice cooks by itself"), because of the excellence of its facility there is no dependence on an agent—at that time, since the independence residing in its own operation constitutes "agent-hood" (*kartṛtva*), the rule of "acting like the object" (*karmavadbhāva*) is prescribed by the grammatical treatise with effort, for the purpose of obtaining the operations belonging to the object.

Thus, even though one is the agent (*kartṛ*), one undergoes the operations (*kārya*) prescribed and ordained for the object (*karman*).
