Now, one might object: "Just as there is the usage 'he causes him who is going to go' (*gacchantam saṃprayukte gamayati*), so too [in the case of] 'he causes her who is flowing to flow' (*kṣarantīm kṣārayati*), the meaning is 'he milks' (*dogdhi*). Anticipating this, he says: "But that sentence which contains the causative suffix (*ṇyanta*) and that which exists in the base forms of *nī* and *duh*, because they are different words, have no contact whatsoever with the verbal root. (77)

The statement beginning with "he employs [the goat] as it is going" (*gacchantam prayuṅkte*)—intended to demonstrate the distinction between the meanings of the root and the suffix in causative forms such as *gamayati*—as well as examples like "he employs the goat reaching the village" (*grāmam prāpnuvantīm ajām prayuṅkte*) and "he employs the cow yielding milk" (*kṣaratīm gām prayuṅkte*), show that in usages such as *nayati* ("he leads") and *dogdhi* ("he milks"), these are indeed different words with distinct meanings. For this [meaning of leading or milking] is not, in the ultimate sense, the meaning of the verbal root itself; rather, it is merely a description of the general sense by way of proximity.

Just as in expressions such as *rājapuruṣa* ("the king's man"), where one says *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* ("the man of the king"), so too in sentences such as *gacchantam prayuṅkte* ("he employs one who is going"), there is an indication of the instigator (*prayojyakartṛ*). However, in the causative form (*ṇyanta*) such as *gamayati*, only the action of the instigator is perceived; the object to be instigated (*prayojya*), however, is expressed by its own word, as in "Devadatta. And where this distinction is remote in the causative, it is all the more remote in the case of roots like *nayati* ("to lead"). For in these cases, no part of the sentence-meaning is directly denoted by the verbal root itself.

Therefore, there is no connection between that sentence or its meaning and a verbal root such as *duh* (to milk). Consequently, there is no inclusion of the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) here; thus, the attempt to justify the specific object by relying on two actions is also incorrect. Therefore, this is indeed a single, distinct action directed toward two objects, and all that is called an "unexpressed object" (*akathita-karman*) is understood to be of a different status. "Because of the difference in the aim of the root-meaning, that [object] is indeed considered the most desired" (*tad īpsitatamaṃ kila*). This is the position established.

Even though the "unspoken object" (*akathitakarma*) is not primary, because it is more internal (*antaraṅga*), the rule for *l*-suffixes and so forth is stated first due to its prior connection with the action. However, in verbs such as *nī* ("to lead"), since the agent (*ajādi*) is primary, the *l*-suffixes occur there alone. In the causative (*ṇyanta*), however, because the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇyartha*) is primary and the original agent is made the object by that very suffix, the agent itself becomes the primary object; thus, the *l*-suffixes occur there alone. Consequently, it is said: "For roots with two objects (*dvikarman*), when the [indirect] recipient-object (*pradānakarma*) is to be expressed, they say the *l*-suffixes occur there. For roots such as *duh* ("to milk"), they occur in the non-primary [object]; and in the causative, they occur in the object which was the agent."
Thus, this has been cited as established by logic. || 77 ||

Now he reveals the established conclusion (siddhānta): "Just as a single grammatical ablative case is shown with distinctions in the treatise, so too a single object (karman) is presented with distinctions. (78)

By the very rule *dhruvam apāye* (Pāṇini 1.4.24), the designation of the *apādāna* (ablative) is established everywhere, as demonstrated even in the Bhāṣya; for even in cases involving the meanings of "fear" (*bhī*) and "protection" (*trā*), there exists a conceptual (*bauddha*) separation (*apāya*). Indeed, the separate statement beginning with *bhītrārthānām* (Pāṇini 1.4.25) is intended solely to instruct those who are not yet learned. And so he will say: "The rule concerning that which is separated in a selection (*nirdhāraṇa*), and the rule concerning [the roots] meaning 'fear' and 'protection,'—these involve a separation that is either explicitly mentioned or implied, and they are taught for the comprehension of the unlearned."

In this way, the object (*karman*) is also only one—that which is most desired—since the state of being reached by the agent through his action exists everywhere. The meaning of the verse is that the subsequent elaboration of sūtras is for the sake of favoring those of dull intellect. And although there is the taking up of a cow or the like for the sake of milk and so forth, nevertheless, it too possesses the state of being reached by the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). For example: "He cooks rice-grains into porridge. For the meaning of the root *pac* (to cook) is indeed the act of moistening characterized by the softening of the rice-grains.

In this context, by way of the quality termed "softening" (*viklitti*), the rice grains (*taṇḍula*) are also the object (*karman*) of the act of moistening, while the boiled rice (*odana*) is the direct object. The meaning is that "by softening the rice grains, one brings about the boiled rice. And thus, just as there is a distinction of objects here based on the difference between the actions expressed by a single verbal root, where one action is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) and the other is primary (*pradhānabhūta*), so too in the case of the root *duh* (to milk), when its sense is "causing to flow" (*kṣaraṇa*) subordinated to "causing to flow forth" (*kṣāraṇa*), both the cow (*go*) and the milk (*payas*) equally attain the status of being the object. Consequently, it is also logical that the causative meaning (*ṇyartha*) is included within the root itself.

Even in the case of a causative (*ṇyanta*) form, because the meaning of the suffix is predominant as qualified by the meaning of the base, the independent [agent] is devoid of action. For here the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is not applied such that its usage would pertain to one who possesses action; rather, the meaning of the causative is expressed by the verbal root itself. For example, in "he causes to cook" (*sādhayati*), the meaning of the causative is expressed by the root *pac*. However, a sentence expressing a distinction is not far removed from it, as it refers to a different object in view of an absolute difference.

From the perspective of their general meaning, however, they have the very same referent, just like the sentence "the king's man" (*rājapuruṣa*). And indeed, this sentence-meaning is precisely what is perceived in this usage. Furthermore, it is not logical that cows and the like should be devoid of action (*niṣkriyatva*), because in the absence of inherence in an action (*kriyāsamavāya*), they would lack the status of being a *kāraka* (participant in an action). Even if the construction of the *akathita* rule were initiated, the designation of "object" (*karman*) would not apply. If it is argued that they are devoid of action prior to the actual usage [of the verb], this is equally true in the case of the causative (*ṇyanta*) as well.

Just as in that case [of the *prayojaka*], the application of the agent’s operation is possible because he is the instigator of one whose action is intended, so too here there is nothing faulty. Furthermore, since the inclusion of the suffix *-tamap* has been rejected, there is no reliance on the excellence (*prakarpa*) of desire. As for the example given for the inclusion of *-tamap*, namely "I would eat with curd" (*dadhnā bhuñjīya*), since both the curd and the rice are equally desired (*īpsita*), the inclusion of *-tamap* is of no consequence there.

For if curd were merely a purificatory agent (*saṃskāraka*), then the boiled rice (*odana*) prepared with it would alone be the most desired object (*īpsitatama*); thus, this [example] would not hold. And so says the Bhāṣya: "In that case as well, it is the rice alone that is desired; he has no regard for the subordinate qualities (*guṇa*)."

As for the statement that the inclusion of the suffix *tamap* is intended to demonstrate the distinction between the spheres of the object (*karman*) and the point of departure (*apādāna*), there too there is no fault, because it can be explained thus: since verbs meaning "to ward off" (*vāraṇārtha*) denote the act of warding off those things which are to be warded off, that which is desired among those things capable of being warded off is the *apādāna*. For instance, cows and the like are the things to be warded off—that is, they are to be prohibited; the barley and the like, which are desired by them, are precisely the *apādāna*. Thus, in this way, everything [that is related to the action] is indeed the object (*karman*).

Thus, this is not an exhaustive enumeration for the purpose of illustrating examples such as *duhi* (milk) and others. In cases such as *naṭasya śṛṇoti* ("he listens to the actor"), the actor (*naṭa*) and so forth are merely the cause (*nimitta*) for the act of listening; they are not intended to be expressed as the "desired object" (*īpsita*) by that act, and therefore the technical designation of "object" (*karman*) does not apply. Furthermore, since the actor is an active participant (*savyāpāra*) in the act of listening, he is excluded from the designation of "ablative" (*apādāna*) by the inclusion of the term "utility" (*upayoga*). Since no other designation has been prescribed for him, he falls under the scope of the genitive case as a "remainder" (*śeṣa*).

However, this [case of the root *ni-śri*] is not the domain of the instrumental case used in the sense of cause (*hetu*), because of the following statement: "When the operation (*vyāpāra*) is not dependent [on another], the cause is accepted as the motive (*nimitta*); the cause has substance (*dravya*) and so forth as its object, whereas a kāraka possesses a restricted action. || 78 ||

An objection is raised: "Since it has been stated that there is a distinction among objects (*karman*) such as the 'to-be-produced' (*nirvartya*) and so forth, how can it be said that there is only one kind of object? Anticipating this, he says: "Whether it be the 'to-be-produced,' the 'to-be-modified,' or the 'to-be-reached,' [the object] is the locus of the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). Because actions themselves are what is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), [the object], though existing in a state of being already established (*siddharūpa*), is designated [as such]. (79)

In this context, that which is the substratum of accomplishment, the locus of power, and of perfected form is expressed by nouns (*nāman*). However, by means of verbs (*ākhyāta*), the object whose nature is to be accomplished and which consists of action (*kriyā*) is denoted. Thus, the definition of action and substance as having the natures of the unaccomplished and the accomplished, respectively, is stated through the forms conveyed by words. As the Bhāṣya says: "For it is action alone that is brought into being; substance is established by its own nature."

And thus, in expressions such as "he makes a mat," "he cooks rice into porridge," and "he sees the sun," the object is conveyed by the nominal words as an undifferentiated substratum of capacity, established as an accomplished entity; therefore, there is no internal difference in its own nature. Furthermore, because they exist for the sake of action, things are designated in reality according to the properties of the action.

For actions, characterized by production (*nirvṛtti*), transformation (*vipariṇati*), or attainment (*prāpti*), manifest an assistance toward the object that depends upon their own capacity, thereby attaining the status of being the cause for distinct designations. And this being the case, since the object is established as having a verbal form, its status as a means (*sādhana*) is also logically consistent. However, if one does not rely on the distinction of designations imposed by specific actions, it is established that everything is called an "object" (*karman*) by the general name "that which is desired" (*īpsita*) by virtue of being the cause for the *kāraka* with respect to the action. || 79 ||

[The author], having removed [any] pride, addresses the following doubt: "How can there be the status of being desired (*īpsitatva*) in such cases as 'he eats poison' or 'he looks at thieves'? Anticipating this, he says: "When a desire arises in an agent toward harmful things due to greed, he proceeds toward poison and the like for that very reason, even though [the result] arises from fear and other such motives. (80)

When, due to an imbalance of the bodily elements such as wind (*vāyu*), a patient—unable to endure the restrictions on food—desires that which is beneficial for him, or when one who is tormented by fear of a king or others, or afflicted by the pain of a chronic disease (*kṣetriya-vyādhi*), thinks that "swallowing poison alone is better," then poison becomes an object of desire through the act of swallowing; likewise, there is that which is unintended (*anīpsita*) even though it is connected [to the action]. This too is established by the previous [definition of action]. Thus says the author of the *Bhāṣya*:

"And when this person is afflicted by suffering, having reflected upon other sufferings, he considers the consumption of poison itself to be better. Regarding the phrase "out of rashness": the meaning is that desire is not everywhere constituted by acting with foresight (*prekṣāpūrvakāritā*), but rather it is possible through another manner as well. It is understood from the very inclusion of the term *tathāyukta* (connected in that way) that here "desirability" (*īpsitatva*) consists precisely in the attainment of the status of being the object of the act of eating.

Even at the commencement of the action of eating, poison imparted by another—its poisonous nature being unknown—is indeed desired while it is being eaten. In the same way, by the action of seeing, a thief and the like are indeed desired [as objects]. That which is other than the desired is neither desired nor undesired, such as the root of a tree and so forth; yet even that, though not previously intended, becomes desired at the very moment of approaching it. Otherwise, it would not attain the status of being the object of the action of approaching.

And since that inclusion of the word "tam" (the desired) has been rejected, it is established by the previous rule alone that even when traveling to a village for the sake of dispelling fatigue, the act of approaching the foot of a tree along the way is designated as an *object* (*karman*) simply because it is something desired. Even in cases where another technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is applied first, it is established by the general definition that an object is "that which is desired."

In cases such as *grāmamadhiśete* (he lies down in the village) and *nagaramupatiṣṭhati* (he stands near the city), because the verbal roots possess an object when connected with a prefix (*upasarga*), the designation "object" (*karma*) applies by virtue of its higher priority; thus it is said that the location (*adhikaraṇa*) becomes the object, as in *gehaṃ praviśati* (he enters the house). In the absence of a prefix, however, the designation "location" (*adhikaraṇa*) occurs.

In the expression "he plays with dice" (*akṣān dīvyati*), when the verb *dīvya-* denotes the act of throwing as subordinate to the desire for victory, the dice possess the status of the most desired object (*īpsitatva*). However, when it signifies mere play, as in "he plays with dice" (*akṣair dīvyati*), the dice possess the status of an instrument (*karaṇatā*). Since both [grammatical statuses] are established, the rule "and [the object] of *div*" (*divaḥ karma ca*) is intended to effect their co-occurrence (*samāveśa*). This is stated in the Vārttika: "And there is inclusion of [roots] having a motion [as an upapada], *div*, and those having a cause. In the absence of this rule for co-occurrence, the designation of "object" (*karmasaṃjñā*) would find its scope in cases such as "he plays mentally" (*manasā dīvyati*).

In the word *manasādeva*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule for the object (*karman*). However, regarding the technical designation of the instrument (*karaṇa-saṃjñā*), as in *devanokṣaḥ* (the die used for gambling), the suffix *lyuṭ* would apply; thus, by virtue of its higher status, it would override the second case (*dvitīyā*) and result in the third case (*tṛtīyā*) alone. In the absence of elision (*aluk*) by the rule *manasastṛtīyāyāḥ*, this very example—*manasādeva*—serves as the scope for the designation of the instrument as well. But if the sūtra were formulated with the particle *ca* (i.e., *manasaś ca tṛtīyāyāḥ*), then because the co-occurrence of both designations would otherwise be untenable, the second case is also established.

In this same way, even in the case of the roots *kruḍh* (to be angry) and *druh* (to bear malice), when they are without prefixes (*anupasarga*), the recipient (*sampradāna*) status applies; however, when they are accompanied by prefixes (*upasṛṣṭa*), the object (*karman*) status applies due to its higher priority. An object of this kind has already been explained by us previously, and we have merely reminded [the reader] of it once again. || 80 ||

This has been explained. Now this is considered: here, when there is a conjunction of two actions, the suffix *la* (the verbal ending) is stated to occur with respect to the primary action by relying on its predominance (*prādhānya*). However, since the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) arises even from two nominal stems (*prātipadika*), one might raise the following doubt: "In that case, even though the objective capacity (*karma-śakti*) pertains to two actions—one subordinate and one primary—since one of those capacities has already been expressed by the suffix *la*, why does the accusative not arise to express the other capacity? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "When there are two actions belonging to a single substance, and their capacities are distinct, with the capacity of the subordinate [action] depending [on the primary], then the primary [action] is followed. (81)

In this context, there is a syntactic connection (*samanvaya*) among meanings conveyed within a single sentence. Among these, a mutual relationship of subordinate and principal (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) is not possible between two principals because they are equal; nor is it possible between two subordinates, according to the principle: "And because subordinates exist for the sake of another, there would be no connection [between them] due to their equality. However, when a syntactic connection is established through the relationship of principal and subordinate, there is unity of the sentence (*ekavākyatā*). Thus he says: "Where there is [the relation] of the principal and the other... (81).

In that regard, because the subordinate factors (*guṇa*) follow the primary factor (*pradhāna*), when the objective case-power (*karma-śakti*) directed toward the action of the primary factor is expressed, the substance's power directed toward the action of the subordinate factor is also manifested as if it were expressed. To explain this general principle of conformity to the primary factor, he says: "When the power directed toward the primary factor is expressed by the suffix, then, in the case of a subordinate factor, it is manifested even though it is not expressed, just like that [primary factor]. (82)

When the objective power (*karma-śakti*) directed toward the primary action is expressed by a suffix such as *la* produced from a verbal root that denotes the primary action, then the power directed toward the subordinate action (*guṇa-kriyā*), though not explicitly stated, shines forth in the same manner. Thus has this "governing extension" (*anuvṛtti*) been explained. Here he provides an example: "In the case of *pac*, when the object is not expressed [by the suffix], but is expressed by the suffix *ktvā* which denotes the state (*bhāva*), even though a different power [the instrumental] is expressed in the verb *bhuj*, that very property [of the object] shines forth. (83)

‘*Paktvā odano bhujyate*’ (The rice is eaten after having been cooked) is the example. Here, according to the opinion of the Bhāṣyakāra, the suffix *ktvā* is prescribed in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāve*), following the continued application of the rule for the sense of the infinitive suffix *tum*. For the Vārttikakāra indeed read: ‘*ā ca tumunaḥ samānādhikaraṇe*’. The meaning of the Vārttika is that, as far as possible, suffixes such as *ṇamul*—which denote the same object as the verb used in the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*)—should be stated [as alternatives] to those suffixes beginning with *tumun* that are prescribed by rules such as ‘*śakadhṛṣajñāglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhāstāraksamakhāpavṛṣa...*’.

Therefore, in the expression *svādukāraṃ yavāgūr devadattena bhujyate* ("The gruel is eaten sweetly by Devadatta"), because the object is expressed by the suffix *ṇamul*, the second case does not occur after the word *yavāgū*. Furthermore, the third case occurs after the word *devadatta*; otherwise, since the *ṇamul* suffix would have arisen in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) due to its being already formed, the third case would not occur after the word *devadatta*.

By this very same reasoning, even in the case of *paktvā odanasya bhujyate* ("Having cooked rice, it is eaten"), the suffix *ktvā* arises with reference to the very same object (*karman*) expressed by the verb of subsequent application (*anuprayoga*), namely *bhujyate*. Thus, according to the opinion of the author of the Vārttika, there is no non-expression of any [kāraka] power whatsoever; it is with this intent that he states the following. However, the author of the Bhāṣya rejects the Vārttika on the grounds that, by this same reasoning, the accusative case would not occur in a construction such as *paktvā odanaṃ gamyate grāmaḥ* ("Having cooked rice, one goes to the village").

By the continued application of the rule regarding the suffixes denoting purpose (*tumun*), it is understood that the *ṇamul* suffixes and others are prescribed in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*). For the meaning of *tumun* is indeed the abstract action. Since [the agent] would already be established by the general rule for *kṛt* suffixes, the mention of "the meaning of *tumun*" serves to exclude the agent from [the scope of] *ktvā* and similar suffixes. Furthermore, since no other meaning for *tumun* has been specified, and because suffixes whose meanings are not explicitly stated occur in their own inherent sense, it is established that the "own" meaning of the base is the abstract action (*bhāva*).

Thus, in the form *paktvā* ending in a *ktvā*-suffix, which expresses the action (*bhāva*), the objective capacity (*karma-śakti*) of the rice (*odana*)—which is the object of the act of cooking—is not expressed. When that same objective capacity, pertaining to the act of eating, is expressed by the suffix *-lyap*, the property belonging to that very principal [element], namely the characteristic of being signified, becomes manifest; therefore, the accusative case does not arise after the word *odana*.

In the expression *paktvaudanaṃ bhuṅkte* ("having cooked, he eats rice"), the instrumental case denoting the agent (*kartṛ*) does not arise for Devadatta due to this very principle, precisely because the act of cooking (*pacikriyā*) has already been expressed. However, in the expression *pakvaudanaṃ gamyate grāmaḥ* ("the cooked rice goes to the village"), the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) does arise because the capacity for being the object (*karmaśakti*) residing in the rice has not been expressed by the suffix of the verb *gamyate*.

And although the case-ending *vibhakti* is produced as "is eaten" (*bhujyate*) with reference to a number inherent in the same object as the means (*sādhana*), nevertheless, because the number is not expressed as being qualified by the object of the act of cooking (*paciviṣayakarma*), it follows that the accusative (*dvitīyā*) would arise; this is the principle proclaimed here. For even in the case of singularity and so forth, which are the meanings of the case-endings, the [grammatical] objects (*karman*) and so forth must necessarily be expected as subordinate factors (*aṅga*). || 83 ||

He states another example: "And because of its contact with the root *gam* (to go), the suffix *lo* is prescribed for the root *iṣ* (to desire) when it means 'village'; therein, the enjoyment of the action of going is accomplished by the very act of desiring. (84)

"‘It is desired that the village be gone to’ (iṣyate grāmo gantum) is the example. Here, there are two objects for the root *iṣ* (to desire), whereas for the root *gam* (to go), there is only the village. Thus, when the karmasaṃjñā (object designation) is not expressed for the object of *iṣ* located in the village, the [designation] pertaining to the village likewise manifests. In that case, the desire is for the purpose of going. And so, since the suffix *tumun* occurs when one action is the object of another action, one might suspect that here the act of going, being the result, is the primary element and not the act of desiring; therefore, this is another example [provided to address such a doubt]."

For when an object is expressed by a verbal root (ākhyātapada), its primary status (*pradhānatā*) exists because it is that which is to be brought into being (*nirvartyatva*). However, in the expression *paktvā bhujyate* ("having cooked, he eats"), even the [action of] eating possesses primacy, because the cooking is for the sake of eating. Regarding the phrase "due to contact with the act of going" (*gāmisaṃsparśāt*): the desire for another substance always occurs through the mediation of another action. Thus, here the desire for the village is through the mediation of seeing and so forth, but specifically through the verb *gam* (to go) as presented within the same sentence. *Nirbhoga* means chewing, that is to say, experiencing or describing.

Regarding the phrase "by the *iṣi*-suffix" itself: by the *l*-suffix (*lakāra*) prescribed for the object (*karman*), [the agent is also expressed]. For it has been determined in the *Vākyapadīya* that a suffix denotes both powers simultaneously through a single operation (*tantra*). || 84 ||

He states an argument for this point according to another school of thought: "In the expression 'having cooked, it is eaten,' some maintain that the verb 'to cook' does not require [an expressed object]; that object is understood through inference. (85)

According to some, in this sentence the act of cooking (*pacikriyā*) does not require the rice (*odana*). This is because there is no syntactic connection between the rice, which is in the nominative case, and the word *paktvā* (having cooked). The rice has a connection only with the verb *bhujyate* (is eaten); thus, there is only one objective power (*karmaśakti*), and since that is already expressed (*abhihitā*), how can this [rule] apply? For when the primary power is expressed, the power of the subordinate action appears as if it were also expressed.

If, then, there were no connection between the cooking and the rice, the meaning would be that after cooking something else entirely is eaten as rice; and in that case, the intended fact—that the cooking of the rice is an auxiliary factor for eating—would not be understood. Anticipating this objection, he says: "That [connection] is understood through inference. The word "that" (*sa*) refers back to the rice which has been mentally apprehended, while "this" (*asau*) is a demonstrative reference imitating direct perception.

Although rice (*odana*) is not directly capable of being conjoined with the act of cooking (*paci*), it is understood by implication (*sāmarthya*) as something that must be expected in relation to that act. If one asks what this implication is, we reply: it is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*). For a directly stated connection (*śruta-sambandha*) is simpler than the postulation of a connection not explicitly stated. And this [implication] occurs only when there exists a relationship of subordinate and principal (*guṇa-pradhāna-bhāva*), and not otherwise; thus, the very principle previously mentioned must be relied upon here, and the previously stated view alone is logical. It is precisely for this reason that [the alternative view] was presented merely as the opinion of another, out of dissatisfaction [with the primary position].

Since "cooking" (*pāka*) requires "eating" (*bhuj*), the expectancy must be fulfilled by that which is proximate. Because cooking precedes eating in time, the relationship of subordinate and principal (*guṇapradhānabhāva*) is established, and thus the status of being a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) is achieved. || 85 ||

This rule does not apply only to the agent known as the *karman* (object); rather, it applies to other *kārakas* as well. To demonstrate this universal application (*vyāpti*), he provides another example: "In that case, when the object (*karman*) is expressed by a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*), or even when it is expressed by the suffix *-ktvā*, it is designated as the locus (*adhikaraṇatva*); yet they do not accept the use of the locative case (*saptamī*) there. (86)

In the expression "having eaten, he settles in the city" (*bhuktvā nagaram abhiniviśyate*), by the rule *abhiniviśaśca*, the city—which is the locus (*ādhāra*) of the action of settling—is designated as the object (*karman*). Consequently, in the finite verb form *abhiniviśyate*, the capacity for the object (*karma-śakti*) is already expressed (*abhihita*) with respect to the primary element, the object. Therefore, although there is also the capacity for the locus (*adhikaraṇa-śakti*) with respect to the suffix *-ktvā* in *bhuktvā*, because it is subordinate (*guṇatva*), it does not produce its own effect, namely the seventh (locative) case ending.

For in this case, if the locative case were used, the objective power (*karma-śakti*) directed toward the primary action would not be perceived; thus, the primary action would be obstructed by the subordinate one. And this is not logical. Since subordinate elements follow the primary, they remain indifferent toward their own function when it conflicts with the primary. Furthermore, primacy belongs everywhere to the meaning of the finite verb (*tiṅanta*), which is the resting point of verbal usage and constitutes the sentence-meaning (*vākya-artha*).

By this very principle, in the expression "having entered the city, he eats," the city's status as the object of the act of entering is set aside by its status as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) for the act of eating. || 86 ||

This has been explained. Here, how is there the status of being an object (*karmatva*) in the expression "he eats molasses" (*guḍaṃ bhakṣayati*)? For molasses, being already accomplished, does not require any further distinction pertaining to the action of eating; thus it is "desired" (*īpsita*).

Rather, it is employed for the purpose of indicating the specific substratum of the act of eating; thus, this substance is for the sake of the action, and the action is not for the sake of refining the substance. The grinding against the teeth and so forth is not the fruit of the act of eating, but rather [the means] of eating, which is characterized by the consumption of food in the form of swallowing. Satisfaction, characterized by satiety, is the fruit; therefore, there is no distinction such as "origination" (*utpatti*) and so on produced by the action here. As it has been stated in the *Vārttika*:

"If that which is desired [by the agent] is designated as the *karman*, then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of designating it as the *karman* even when it has already been accomplished (*nirvṛtta*), because it remains something desired by the action. By the term "already accomplished," he rejects its status as a *karman* in the sense of being something yet to be produced (*nirvartya*). This is also an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*); since there is no modification (*vikāra*) or other such change, it cannot be another kind of *karman* either. The phrase "of that which is already accomplished" means "of that which is no longer expectant" (*nirākāṅkṣasya*). The term "in its capacity as a *kāraka*" indicates its status as a causal factor for the accomplishment of the action; for molasses (*guḍa*) is employed for the sake of accomplishing the act of eating.

For this very reason, in the case of "jaggery for eating" (*guḍo bhakṣaṇāya*), the action itself is the desired object (*īpsita-karma*) because it is attained through seeing and other such means, and not the substance. For it is the mere act of eating that is desired with respect to the jaggery, and not any specific quality produced by it that results from the rejection of eating. Regarding this, a solution is stated in the *Vārttika*: "Or rather, because both are desired" (*na vobhayepsitatvāt*). || 86 ||

In that regard, in order to explain how molasses and the like possess the status of being "desired" (*īpsitatva*), he says: "When an action has its locus already accomplished, yet remains unaccumulated until its attainment, and is differentiated by falling into the category of 'food' and so forth—that is what is 'desired'. (87)

"Completed" (*nirvṛtta*) means "accomplished," and for that very reason, it is "free from further expectation. This refers to the substratum—the substance such as molasses—which serves as the basis for the action (*karman*) or the capacity for action; thus, the status of being an "effected object" (*nirvartya-karman*) is excluded. Furthermore, because there is no expectation of a transformation (*vikāra*), the status of being a "transformed object" (*vikārya-karman*) is also set aside. Regarding the phrase "unaccumulated due to attainment" (*prāpterapracitam*): since there is a connection with the act of eating, there might otherwise be a distinction between accumulation and depletion; however, because [the object] is not employed [in such a way], it is "unaccumulated. Thus, even the status of being an "attained object" (*prāpya-karman*) is excluded according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

For by the first half-verse, the meaning of the *pūrvapakṣa* (prima facie) commentary is summarized; by the second half-verse, the explanation of the subsequent commentary (*uttaravārttika*) is given. The meaning is that this object, such as molasses (*guḍa*), which is desired and is to be attained, is the "object" (*karman*) because it is differentiated—that is, distinguished—by its undergoing the state of being the objective domain of actions such as eating (*bhakṣi*) or enjoying (*bhuji*). To explain: it is not the action of eating and so forth alone that is desired here; for if it were, one would achieve one's purpose even by eating a clod of earth.

Nor is molasses desired as the locus of another action; rather, it is desired as the locus of eating. Thus, both together, in the relationship of locus and located, constitute the desired object. For one who desires the eating of molasses, the molasses itself is also desired. And here, the distinction created by the action consists precisely in the connection with the act of eating, since no other distinction is required for the status of an "attained" (prāpya) object. Otherwise, what would be the difference between this and the categories of the "produced" (nirvartya) or the "modified" (vikārya)? In this case, the result of the eating is the excellence of pleasure.

And that [transformation] occurs when there is a connection with the molasses; this is precisely the distinction. For *saṃskāra* (refinement) is indeed the capacity for the production of a fruit corresponding to an action. Now, if molasses is merely an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the pleasure characterized by satisfaction, how can it possess the status of an object (*karman*) in the form of a primary factor (*pradhāna-kāraka*)? It is said in reply: while the molasses is an auxiliary to the satisfaction, this specific procedure (*itikartavyatā-viśeṣa*) is that its primacy with respect to that [satisfaction] consists in its being made the object of the act of eating; otherwise, satisfaction cannot be accomplished.

Thus, this is the primary operation [of the agent] in its status as a subordinate factor (*aṅga*) for the attainment of satisfaction. For example, a teacher, when being served, becomes a subordinate factor for the arising of Dharma; yet that [status] does not occur for him unless he becomes the object of the act of service. Therefore, the expression "he desires to serve the teacher" (*guruṃ śuśrūṣate*) is logically justified as expressing predominance (*prādhānya*). Thus, in this prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), while the desire for the substance itself is set aside, the desire for the mere action is demonstrated. Consequently, in the refutation (*parihāra*) which conforms to that, the desire for the substance is also shown.

If, then, the status of being an object (*karmatā*) were established merely by entering into the state of being the domain of an action, then in that case, every action whatsoever would be transitive (*sakarmaka*). Consequently, the designations of "intransitive" (*akarmaka*) in the grammatical treatise would be contradicted; yet they are not so contradicted. For it is not necessarily the case that an external object exists for every mere action. Indeed, some actions rest solely in the agent and do not depend upon an external entity, such as "he sits" (*āste*), "he lies down" (*śete*), and so forth.

Because of the statement that "the root *pac* has two meanings," even in the domain of all verbal roots, since the activity characterized as *bhāvanā* culminates here in the meaning of the root itself, that alone is the object to be brought about (*bhāvya*). For example: "he performs sitting" (*āsanaṃ karoti*), "he performs lying down" (*śayanaṃ karoti*). Therefore, in this case, the *bhāvanā* is directed toward an external state of being; because it possesses that external object as its *bhāvya*, it is transitive (*sakarmaka*). And in that regard, the question "what? is asked, such as: "What does he cook? Rice," and so forth.

Since the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is never absent from any instance, even though it is that which is to be brought about (*bhāvya*), it is not possible to establish the distinction between transitive and intransitive verbs based upon it alone. Rather, this distinction depends on external objects (*bāhya-karman*), for such objects do vary (as in the case of time and other factors). Consequently, the proponents of the *Nyāya* maintain that when the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is pure, the meaning of the verbal root is its object; but when the efficient force is qualified by the meaning of the verbal root, the external object is its object. For this very reason, they hold that when the efficient force is directed toward an external object, the meaning of the verbal root serves as the instrument (*karaṇa*).

The meaning of the sentence is that "he cooks rice" or "he brings the rice into being through the act of cooking. Although in this view *bhāvanā* (the process of bringing into being) is indeed the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), it nevertheless extends up to the result and consists of the agent's activity; thus, it is capable of being treated as distinct from the mere collection of its constituent actions, which are more limited in duration. This principle should be applied everywhere in the same way. || 87 ||

Furthermore, he states that in some cases, even when an external object exists in reality, there is the designation of "intransitive" (akarmaka): "An action is intransitive due to the occurrence [of the root] in a different sense, due to the inclusion [of the object] within the meaning of the root itself, due to conventional usage, or due to the lack of intention to express the object. (88)

When a verbal root functions with respect to a meaning other than its well-known one, then in that context its action is understood as being expressed without the accompaniment of a common object (*karmasāmānyāvayarahita*). For example, the root *vahati* is well known to express the act of bringing something to another location and is transitive, as in "he carries a load" (*bhāraṃ vahati*).

When, in the expression "the river flows" (*nadī vahati*), [the verb] denotes the action of flowing, then—since that flowing, which consists of the movement of water, is identical with the river itself—there is no possibility of an inquiry as to "what" [it flows], and thus it is intransitive (*akarmaka*). This *bhāvanā* depends solely on the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), such that one understands: "it flows" means "it performs the act of flowing. Even when the object is included within the action denoted by the verbal root, it remains intransitive; for example, "he lives" (*jīvati*).

For here, in the expression "he sustains the vital breaths" (*prāṇān dhārayati*), the meaning of the verbal root includes the action characterized as the vital breaths; likewise in "he dies" (*mriyate*) and "he abandons the vital breaths" (*prāṇān jahāti*). Similarly, in "he exists" (*asti*) and "he maintains himself" (*ātmānaṃ bibharti*). Where there is the cognition of a specific, invariant action, there too the linguistic usage is that the action has no [external] object (*akarmikā kriyā*). For example, "it rains" (*varṣati*).

For here, just as in the act of raining the god is understood to be the agent despite the [seeming] absence of an object, so too, because it is well-known that water is the object, the suffix *kta* is cited in the sense of the agent based on its being intransitive, as in "the god has rained" (*vṛṣṭo devaḥ*). However, when the object is not well-known, this action is indeed transitive, as in "it rains blood" (*rudhiraṃ varṣati*) or "it rains arrows" (*śaraṃ varṣati*). In the case of "dust has been rained down" (*pāṃsavo vṛṣṭāḥ*), the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*).

Alternatively, even where an object exists, if the connection with an object is not intended to be expressed because the purport is merely to convey the action itself, there too the status of being "intransitive" (akarmaka) is possible. For example: *neha pacyate* ("it is not cooked here"), *neha bhujyate* ("it is not eaten here"). Because the purport is the negation of the action, the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) occurs in the impersonal sense (*bhāve*). In [the passage] *dīkṣito na dadāti, na pacati, na juhoti* ("the initiated one does not give, does not cook, does not sacrifice"), there is no intention to express the object. Why is it not expected here? Because the purport is the negation of the action. || 88 ||

Thus, there are four ways in which the designation "intransitive" (akarmaka) occurs in the treatise. He says that other types are also possible: "These four distinctions which have been shown in general are further divided in many ways according to the distinction of causes (nimitta) and so forth. (89)

These four varieties, which have been described as the basis for the intransitivity even of transitive roots, arise in many forms through differences such as cause (*nimitta*), companion (*sahāya*), prefix (*upasarga*), and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), place, time, and others are included. For example, the root *car* becomes intransitive by virtue of its application to a different location, as in "the steam rises" (*bāṣpa uccarati*) or "the smoke rises" (*dhūma uccarati*). By the power of the prefix *ud*, this root is intransitive when it denotes upward movement.

By the inclusion of the word "ādi" (and so forth), the manifestation of intransitivity is seen through the use of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) in certain cases, such as *uttapate* and *vitapate*, which mean "shines. In the phrase *yāvadbhaktamupatiṣṭhate*, the meaning is "he waits until the time for eating. The middle voice is used here according to the rule *akarmakācca*. In the examples *sarpiṣo jānīte* and *madhuno jānīte*, the verbal root refers to an activity preceded by knowledge, in the sense that "he proceeds by means of that [clarified butter or honey]."

With the continuation of the rule *apahnave jñaḥ* ("after the root *jñā*, when there is concealment"), the rule *akarmakācca* ("and after [a root] that is intransitive") prescribes the middle voice (*ātmanepada*). By the force of the sentence, in certain cases, an intransitive character is manifested. For example, in "the river flows" (*nadī vahati*), the root has an intransitive sense because of the specific agent characterized as a river, which implies the act of flowing. Similarly, in "the wind blows" (*vāyurvahati*). Likewise, in the domain of the reflexive object-agent (*karmakartṛ*), where the status of the object as the agent is perceived, the root is intransitive when it expresses only a part of its full meaning, as in "the rice cooks by itself" (*pacyate odanaḥ svayameva*).

And having established this, the grammatical treatise operates in this context on the basis of the designation of a root as "intransitive" (akarmaka), as in the rule: "The vowel of *muc* is optionally substituted by its *guṇa* when it is intransitive. For example: *mokṣyate vatsaḥ svayameva* ("The calf will release itself"). Thus, although the root functions in a different sense [of "releasing"], its status as intransitive is based on that; yet, through the distinction of causes (*nimitta*) and so forth, the difference arises. Even when the meaning of the root is subsumed [within a larger verbal complex], the distinction remains due to the difference in causes and so forth.

For example: in some cases, when an action is included within an object because its distinction is obscured due to a cause characterized by the inherent capacity of its own form—as in the case of *jīvati* ("he lives") and similar verbs—it receives the designation "intransitive" (*akarmaka*). In other cases, there is inclusion even when a distinction of form is determined through the rules of grammatical derivation (*anvākhyāna*), as for instance, the object "son" in the case of *putrīyati* ("he wishes for a son").

From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the characteristic of "son" (*putra*)—which is an action (*karma*) inherent within the body of the action—is resorted to as a cause for grammatical derivation (*anvākhyāna*) through a distinction that lacks real existence within the process of linguistic formation. As he will state: "In the case of *putrīyati*, there is no actual son; rather, such a desire is of that nature, which, even without following an actual son, is established with respect to a son. In the case of the *kyac* suffix [in *ācāryaka*], however, the object of comparison (*upamāna-karman*) is internalized, while the transitivity (*sakarmakatva*) arises from the object of comparison (*upameya-karman*).

In the expression "he treats the student like a son" (*putrīyati chātram*), [the object is not internalized]. However, in "he shaves the boy" (*muṇḍayati māṇavakam*), the general object is internalized, while the specific object remains external, thereby making the verb transitive. The same applies in cases such as "he mixes sesame seeds" (*miśrayati tilān*). In expressions such as "he steams" (*bāṣpāyate*), "he heats" (*ūṣmāyate*), and "he chews the cud" (*romanthāyate*), it is precisely the specific object whose form has been determined that is internalized. For the roots *pac* ("to cook") and *bhid* ("to split"), the objects—earth and a composite thing respectively—are well-known as external; they are not internalized.

Because [the action] is expressed by its own word as well—as in "he cooks what is to be cooked" (*pacati pākyam*) or "he splits what is to be split" (*bhinatti bhedyam*)—there would be no mention by its own word if [the action) were included within [the root]. For one does not say, "he lives his breaths" (*jīvati prāṇān*). However, one does say, "it rains water" (*jalaṃ varṣati*). And because the object is included [within the root], the dative case does not occur in the expression "he pays homage to the gods" (*namasyati devān*) when used in conjunction with the word *namaḥ*.

Accordingly, in the *Vārttika*, having raised the objection that "the use of the accusative case after *namas* is untenable when the suffix *kyac* follows," it is resolved by stating, "It is established because [the word] is a different base (*prakṛtyantara*). With this very intention, the meaning is that the word *namasyati* is indeed a different verbal root (a *dhātu*) whose meaning is "to honor," and that the word *namaḥ* itself cannot possibly exist here; rather, it is derived in this manner through the conceptualization of its constituent parts. However, the Commentator (*Bhāṣyakāra*), considering that such a possibility exists because *namas* is accepted as the base during the process of grammatical derivation (*anvākhyāna*), raises the objection once again.

"Is it not the case that the word *namasyati* contains the word *namaḥ*, and by its connection [with a word denoting the object], the dative case would be required? He refutes this, saying: "The word *namaḥ* is taken [in the rule] as having a meaning, and in the word *namasyati*, the word *namaḥ* does not have a meaning. This is a commentary on verbal roots (*sub-dhātuvṛtti*). Here, the meaning of the subordinate element (*upasarjana*) has become secondary to the meaning of the suffix. Thus, the meaning of the *Bhāṣya* is that because there is scope for the application of the dative in cases like *namo devebhyaḥ* (where it connects with the word *namaḥ* which is the primary element), the dative does not occur here [in *namasyati*].

Even in cases where a verb is established as intransitive (*akarmaka*), a further internal distinction arises depending on place and time. For example, in the Deccan, when it is said in the forenoon, "Let it be cooked," cooking with gruel (*yavāgū*) as the object is understood; at another time, however, it refers to rice (*odana*) as the means; but in a region abounding in meat, cooking with meat as the means is well known. Due to the inherent capacity of the action's own nature, an object is sometimes established as fixed: from the word "it rains" (*varṣati*), water is cognized.

An action is also established through the capacity of the agent; for instance, when it is said, "The wicked man acts," an action characterized by injury is understood, whereas when it is said, "The virtuous man acts," assistance is understood. This well-known usage is to be followed as being limitless according to different social circles and different regions—how much could be cited? Furthermore, in some cases, even the non-intentionality (*avivakṣā*) of an object is observed in a sentence, because the sentence is intent upon conveying mere similarity.

For example, in the expression “Kaṭha repeats the [text] of Kalāpa,” what is intended to be conveyed is the similarity between Kaṭha and Kalāpa in their speaking; thus, the object (*karman*) is not intended to be expressed. Likewise, when conveying a specific capacity for action in response to the question “What does Devadatta do? with the answers “He cooks” or “He speaks,” the connection with an object is not intended to be expressed. Even when conveying the uninterrupted continuity of an action, the object is not intended to be expressed, as in “He cooks indeed” or “He gives indeed. Thus, the various types of usage are accepted according to the requirements of the context. || 89 ||

Thus ends the section on the object (*karma*) in the *Prakīrṇaprakāśa* composed by Helārāja, son of Bhūtirāja. In this context, following the sequence in which the case-terminations (*vibhakti*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*) are prescribed in the rules for the declensional endings (*svādi*), there follows an investigation into their respective meanings, the grammatical factors (*kāraka*). Among these, once the object (*karman*)—the meaning of the second case—has been examined, the instrument (*karaṇa*), the meaning of the third case, is first investigated. As for the agent (*kartṛ*), however, because it is common to the sixth case as well, it will be discussed later due to its subordinate status.

In this regard, one might raise the objection: "Since the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is the means for the successful accomplishment of an action, what excellence does the instrument (*karaṇa*) possess such that it should be considered the 'most effective' (*sādhakatama*)? Anticipating this, he states the definition: "When the completion of an action is intended to be designated as occurring immediately after the operation of a particular factor, then that factor is traditionally recognized as the instrument (*karaṇa*). (90)

Among all the causal factors (*sādhana*) that provide assistance through conjunction (*sannipatyopakārin*), that one whose operation is observed to be immediately followed by the action, having attained excellence, is the most effective instrument (*karaṇa*). For example, in the act of cutting, the sickle, by penetrating the object to be cut and effecting the separation of its parts, attains a state of superior utility compared to other factors such as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) and so forth. In the same way, the eye being directed toward seeing, and so on, should be cited as examples.

And because the linguistic usage of "means" (*sādhana*) is based entirely upon states of the intellect, he says, "it is intended to be expressed. For in grammar, an object is a constituent factor (*aṅga*) only when it has ascended into the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*), not by virtue of the existence of an external thing; this is the meaning. Thus, in cases such as "he cuts with strength" (*balena lunāti*) or "he sees with light" (*ālokena paśyati*), disregarding the sickle and so forth, strength and the like are intended as the "instrument" (*karaṇa*) because they are the most effective means (*sādhakatama*).

In that regard, although other means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) possess a real status as substratum (*ādhāra*) and so forth, they appear otherwise through cognition, as in the case of "he cooks in a pot" (*sthālyā pacyate*). However, since the very nature of the instrument (*karaṇa*) is dependent on the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*), even though it has been stated that "the linguistic usage of a means of accomplishment is based on the state of cognition," the phrase "is intended to be expressed" (*vivakṣyate*) is redundant. || 90 ||
He says this very thing: "In reality, that [agent] is indefinable, for no entity is fixed [in its role]; since we observe the intended meaning (vivakṣā) expressed as 'the rice-pot cooks'. (91)

It is impossible to define this very object as an instrument (*karaṇa*) based on its fixed nature alone; for no object exists as a fixed instrument by its own inherent status. Indeed, even a cooking pot (*sthālī*), though its status as a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is well-known, experiences the state of being an instrument according to the speaker's intention, because it accomplishes the effect of cooking more quickly due to having thinner walls. Thus, the use of the instrumental case ending to express instrumentality—as in the common worldly expression "it is cooked in a pot" (*sthālyā pacyate*)—is well-established. For, compared to wet fuel, a well-constructed pot is more proximate to the accomplishment of the action. || 91 ||

And since the instrument (*karaṇa*) is that which provides the most excellent assistance toward the accomplishment of an action, it is for this reason that agents exert their effort upon it; thus he says: "But regarding the instruments, they repeatedly undertake the burden of refinement (*saṃskāra*) and specific applications (*viniyoga-viśeṣa*) for the sake of the successful accomplishment of the primary [action]. (92)

For the sake of accomplishing the primary object characterized by action, those seeking the fruit undertake the refinement—such as sharpening—and the repeated application of the instrument itself, which provides the most excellent assistance; for activity toward the end (*upeya*) proceeds by way of the means (*upāya*). In that regard, the placing of wood [upon the fire] is the refinement (*saṃskāra*); and its repeated presentation is the application (*viniyoga*). For the sickle, the induction of sharpness is the refinement; and its raising and lowering is the application.

The refinement of the eye consists of collyrium and the like; its application is the act of directing the gaze. This and other such factors should be stated accordingly in other cases as well. || 92 ||

Regarding how excellence in assistance is expressed here—as in the phrase "he goes by horse along the road with a lamp"—where it is intended that many [factors] act at the same time, he says: "There is no excellence among the instruments within their own respective spheres; rather, the definition of excellence in that case is the possession of a superior quality derived from another. (93)

In this context, the excellence (*prakarpa*) relative to its own class (*sajātīya*), which exists in the state of being an instrument (*karaṇabhāva*) within its own category, is not what is expressed by the suffix *tamap*. Rather, it is the excellence of the general means (*sādhanasāmānya*) as it persists [through various functions], which—being relative to other factors of action (*kāraka*)—is expressed by the suffix *tamap* and indicates the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*). For when the suffix *tamap* is produced after the word *sādhaka*, which denotes the general category of a factor of action (*kāraka-sāmānya*), it conveys excellence precisely from that [general category]. The phrase "from another" (*parataḥ*) means from another means of accomplishment (*sādhanāntarāt*).

Thus, since no excellence (*atiśaya*) dependent on the genus of the instrument (*karaṇa-jāti*) is required, it is not contradictory for all things—such as horses and so forth—to function as instruments when they have attained preeminence through dependence on other means. For instance, in reaching another location, a horse is a superior auxiliary compared to the agent (*kartṛ*) and others; likewise, a path is excellent when free from dangers such as thieves; and even a lamp, by dispelling the mass of darkness with its light, attains a superiority over other means. || 93 ||

An objection might be raised: "Since the operation of the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) occurs after the agent has assigned them their tasks, it is logical that the agent alone possesses the status of the accomplisher (*sādhaka*) in relation to that [operation]. Anticipating this, he says: "Even though they possess independence, the users [of the means] assist only from afar; for the activity of all [other factors] is mediated by the instrument (*karaṇa*). (94)

If it is stated that "the instrument (karaṇa) is that whose operation immediately precedes the accomplishment of the action," then it would follow that the agent (kartṛ) is also an instrument. For the accomplishment of the action does not occur immediately after the operation of the agent alone. Rather, the operation of the agent consists in the employment of the means (sādhana); however, the action is accomplished only when the means have been employed and are engaged in their respective operations. In that case, the operation of the agent—just like that of the locus (adhikaraṇa) and other factors—is remote from the accomplishment of the action, because there is no further employment of another agent once the action has begun.

Even when there is dependence on other instruments, those who employ them are the agents; yet, due to the intervention of the operations of the various instruments employed, they accomplish the action only from a distance. The accomplishment of the action, however, occurs immediately after the operation of the instrument. || 94 ||

Alternatively, he states that a consideration of excellence in relation to the agent is simply not possible: "Either excellence [belongs] to the accomplishment of the action, or rather, subservience belongs to the agent; for when the accomplishment is established, the general property of being the instrument (sādhakatva) is what is intensified. (95)

In this context, regarding the accomplishment of an action (*kriyāsiddhi*), the excellence (*atiśaya*) of the instrument (*karaṇa*) over other means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is intended. And when the factors of action (*kāraka*) have been set in motion and have assumed their respective functions, then the accomplishment of the action becomes the objective domain. However, when the agent’s application [of the factors] is required, the means of accomplishment remain subordinate to the agent. Since these means, not yet permeated by their own specific functions, do not even attain the designation of "means of accomplishment" (*sādhana*)—which is based on autonomy and constitutes a general state—how could there be any excellence of the agent in relation to them?

Thus it is said: "When its accomplishment is established, the instrumentality of the general factor attains excellence. That which is the general nature of being a means (sādhana) attains pre-eminence (*prakarṣa*) when its accomplishment (*niṣpatti*)—that is, its completion—is realized. And this completion occurs when, following the agent's application [of the means], the means enters into its own specific operation. Consequently, when an excellence is considered at that stage, it belongs to the instrument (*karaṇa*) alone, as it stands on an equal footing with the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) and other factors, but not to the agent (*kartṛ*).

For that master is independent prior to the activity [of others] and does not compete with those subject to death; for excellence (prakarṣa) depends upon its own kind. But the agent (kartṛ) is indeed of a different kind, because other factors of action (kāraka) consist of both independent and dependent forms. And this being so, it is logical that the superior capacity of the locus (adhikaraṇa), which is dependent on another, to act as an instrument (sādhakatva) is relative to other factors of action, since their spheres of operation are distinct. Therefore, one should not object: "How can an instrument that is not independent possess excellence? || 95 ||

If, then, there is a formal distinction between the agent and the instrument, how can the instrument also possess agency—as in the expression "he cuts with a sword"? Anticipating this objection, he says: "But when the sword and so forth are considered the agents, they know sharpness and the like to be the instruments. When sharpness and the like are independent, the self (ātman) stands as twofold. (96)

In this context, when the sword is intended to be expressed as independent—disregarding its assignment to an agent because of its extremely sharp edge for the act of cutting—it does not function merely as an instrument (*karaṇa*). Rather, the status of being an instrument belongs precisely to that [action] which immediately follows it, such as [the action of] sharpening, weighing, hardening, or shaping. Even in the case of that [action], when there is an intention to express it as an agent, its status as an instrument depends on the differentiation of forms brought about by the speaker's intention.

For instance, sharpness cuts by its own capacity; thus, although sharpness is one, it assumes the distinct roles of agent (*kartṛ*) and instrument (*karaṇa*) due to the differentiation of forms imparted by the distinction of words. The self, when conceived as being independent, is the agent; when conceived as being the most effective means of accomplishment (*sādhakatama*), it is the instrument—thus there is a twofold determination. Because an action is inseparable from an instrument, this injunction is intended to exclude other instruments. Its purpose lies in nourishing that excellence [of the instrument], namely: "Sharpness alone is the most effective means for cutting, and nothing else. Thus, in this way, the agent and the instrument are indeed distinct. (96)

If this is so, one might ask: since two designations do not apply simultaneously to a single thing, how can the rule of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*)—namely, that "the subsequent [rule] prevails"—be introduced here? To this he replies: "Even though there is a distinction between the two selves, the object remains the same; because agency depends upon that [object], agency persists despite the distinction, and thus [the designation] prevails. (97)

The meaning is that even though there is a difference in form due to being designated as agent (*kartṛ*) or instrument (*karaṇa*) by virtue of the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*), that single object remains established as the locus of capacity (*śakti*) and does not deviate from its essential nature. The justification for this is "because it is the substratum of that" (*tadāśrayatvāt*). This means because it is the substratum of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*); for a conceptual distinction does not destroy actual unity. Alternatively, some explain "because it is the substratum of that" (*tadāśrayatvāt*) to mean "because the designations of agent and instrument share a common substratum in that single object."

Even though there is a distinction between the two capacities (*śakti*), because the substance (*dravya*) to which they belong is one, a single object arises as the domain of the conflict between the two technical terms (*saṃjñā*). For a technical term indeed applies to the substance itself as qualified by its capacity. Thus, when the unity existing in the entity is taken up through the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*), then, since there is a single object, in the case of a conflict, the designation of "agent" (*kartṛ-saṃjñā*) prevails due to its posteriority and subverts the designation of "instrument" (*karaṇa-saṃjñā*); this is illustrated by the example: "the sword cuts" (*asiś chinnatti*).

For here, the desire to express independence (*svātantryavivakṣā*) is invariably concomitant with the lack of desire to express the state of being the most effective instrument (*sādhakatamatvāvivakṣā*). Thus, when both apply to the same object, the designation of "agent" (*kartṛsaṃjñā*) prevails due to its higher status in the rules. Indeed, independence is superimposed upon that which is the most effective instrument; for example, in the expression "he pierces with a bow" (*dhanuṣā vidhyati*), the bow possesses the status of the most effective instrument precisely because it is the locus of departure (*apāya*). Therefore, it is established that the instrument (*karaṇa*) is that which is the most excellent contributor toward the action. || 96 ||

He also dispels this doubt: that benefit is produced by you through an object that exists, and not through one that does not exist. Just as instrumentality is understood through proximity, so too is it understood from the accomplishment of the action even in the absence of proximity. || 98 ||

Just as the giver and other factors, being present and attaining a superior degree of assistance to the action, are recognized as instruments (*karaṇa*), so too in expressions such as "he is liberated by the absence of wealth," even though the wealth is not present, the absence of wealth is well-known as the very instrument that accomplishes liberation. 98.

Right here, he states the view of the author of the Sūtras as corroborative: "Because of the production or the non-cessation of that which is small, they declare that the status of being an instrument belongs to 'small' and the rest. (99)

Regarding the rule "and [in the case of] *stoka*, *alpa*, etc., [the third case is used]," the examples given are *stokānmuktaḥ* (released by a little) and *stokena muktaḥ* (released with a little). Here, although words such as *stoka* denote substances (*satvavacana*), they are treated as denoting non-substances (*asatvavacanatā*) because their employment is intended solely to express a mere quality (*dharmamātra*). That mere quality, characterized as "little,"—whether existent or non-existent—is said to be the instrument (*karaṇa*) because it exceptionally assists the action of being released. Since a small amount of the object to be given has been produced and no other [gift] is possible due to his poverty, he is therefore "released."

Alternatively, if only a small portion of the object to be given remains or has been exhausted, then he is released; however, if much were to be given, he would not be released. Thus, by saying "released with a small amount that was not [fully] present," it is meant that because one is absent, there is a negation of twenty—namely, "not nineteen, not twenty. In this way, the absence of one constitutes the means for the negation of twenty. || 99 ||

Thus, since the conventional usage of a "means" (sādhana) depends upon the speaker's intention, whatever is intended as the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*) is that which constitutes the "instrument" (*karaṇa*). And so, because of the difference and non-difference of properties from their possessor, [the means] is distinguished; it is differentiated according to the specific delimitation of the action, just as in the following example: 100. Just as [a single substance] is distinguished by its various functions, such as being a "cow," a "white thing," or a "goer," so too is the instrument distinguished by the specific delimitation of the action.

The word *dharma* denotes merely that which is dependent [upon a substrate], while the term *tadvatā* refers to the substrate itself. For instance, in the expression “Devadatta cooks with firewood,” there is a usage based on the intention to express non-difference between the firewood and the heat residing within it. Thus, this act of cooking has Devadatta as its agent (*kartṛ*) and firewood as its instrument (*karaṇa*). However, when the heat is intended to be expressed as distinct from the firewood, then the expression is “the firewood will cook by means of heat”; in this case, the act of cooking has heat as its instrument and firewood as its agent.

Even though heat (*auṣṇya*) is distinct from fire (*tejas*), an action is differentiated by a specific means of accomplishment; just as an action is differentiated—that is, specified—by a particular delimitation such as a village or the like acting as a limit, as in "he comes from the village" (*grāmād āgacchati*) or "he comes from near the village" (*grāmasya samīpād āgacchati*), so too should it be understood here. For when the word "village" denotes a place with its surrounding forest, its boundaries, and its open spaces, the usage "he comes from the village" (*grāmād āgacchati*) occurs without [internal] differentiation.

However, when that which is enclosed by a boundary is designated by the word ‘village,’ the limit [of the action] is differentiated non-distinctly in such expressions as “he comes from the village. And due to that differentiation, the action is qualified. Likewise, even due to a difference in the instrument based on intention (*vaivakṣika*), that very same primary instrument is expressed according to the speaker's intention by means of a verbal suffix (*dhātupratyaya*) such as *lyuṭ*, *ghañ*, or the third case-ending; for example: *pacanamedhaḥ* (the fire of cooking), *pacanaṃ tejaḥ* (the heat of cooking), *pacanī sthālī* (the cooking pot), *pacanam auṣṇyam* (the heat of cooking), and so forth. Such a collection of usages is accepted as being illustrated according to the speaker's intention.

Thus ends the section on the Instrument (*karaṇādhikāra*) within the *Sādhanasamuddeśa* of the *Prakīrṇaprakāśa* composed by Helārāja, son of Bhūtirāja. The Instrument having been examined in its sense as the third case (*tṛtīyārtha*), the Agent (*kartṛ*), who possesses that same sense [of independence], is now examined. Its definition is: "The independent one is the agent" (*svatantraḥ kartā*). "His own" (*sva*) refers to the self (*ātman*); "whose primary basis" (*tantram pradhānam asya*) is this [self]. For among the instrument and other factors, the agent alone is the primary basis (*tantram pradhānam*), because they are employed by him for the accomplishment of the action.

An agent (*kartṛ*) is defined as one who is independent, not being prompted by another. In this regard, one might raise the objection: "Since instruments (*karaṇa*) and other factors also possess independence with respect to their own respective operations, what is the distinction of the agent? Anticipating this, he establishes [the agent's superiority] as follows: "Because [instruments] have not previously acquired their capacity from another, because they are brought into subordination, because their activity is dependent upon him, and because he causes those already active to desist. (101)

Because no substitute is observed, and because [the action] is seen even in the absence [of the agent], it is said that the agent possesses independence, even when [the action] is assisted from afar. || 102 ||

Prior even to the engagement of the instruments (*karaṇa*) and so forth, [the agent] acquires capacity from another cause, namely desire for the result (*arthitā*) and the like, and not solely from the auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*). For it is the agent who, desiring the fruit, procures the instruments and so on. Thus, he is already previously endowed with power and independent. As for the instruments and so forth, their independence regarding their own respective operations arises only from the agent’s employment of them, and not from anything else. For this very reason, they are brought into a state of subordination and dependence upon him; their operations are contingent upon him.

The agent, however, desiring the fruit, is himself possessed of activity; and the instruments and other factors, which have become excessively active, are withdrawn by the agent. But he himself ceases from activity upon the attainment of the fruit. A substitute for the instruments and so forth has been mentioned when the enjoined [agent] is unavailable; but there is no such substitute for the agent. For another person who performs the action is not called a "substitute," because that person, being a seeker of the result, capable, and not excluded, possesses the entitlement [to perform the rite].

Furthermore, in the absence of other causal factors (*kāraka*), the agent is observed [as the sole performer], as for example in such cases as *asti*, *bhavati*, and *vidyate*. Although locative objects (*adhikaraṇa*) and the like are possible here, they are nonetheless inseparable [from the action] and are not perceived because they do not function through the operation of the word. Consequently, since there can be no action devoid of an agent, the agent is distinguished even from those who act in concert.

By this collection of reasons, it is stated that even though the agent (*kartṛ*) is a remote auxiliary (*viprakṛṣṭopakāraka*) in the accomplishment of an action in dependence upon the instrument (*karaṇa*), his sovereignty (*svātantrya*) is based on his predominance (*prādhānya*); thus, he alone receives the designation of "agent," and not the instrument and so forth, even though they are independent with respect to their own respective operations. By this, the following *Bhāṣya* is explained: "When all the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) are present, the agent is the one who sets them in motion."

This commentary was stated in brief, with its implicit meaning internalized; therefore, it has been explained here by making explicit that internalized meaning. For instance, by the phrase "because its activity is dependent upon that," the status of being the direct instigator (*pravartakatva*) is explained. And the subordination (*nyagbhāvana*) and so forth, which are implied by the force of the context, are indicated. To explain: because activity depends on the agent (*prayoktṛ*), the subordination of the instruments (*karaṇa*) and other factors is expressed there through the sense of the words.

And since that instigation (*pravartanā*) is for the sake of the result, its cessation (*nivartanā*) is also implied when there is excessive engagement in order to attain it. Furthermore, it has been explained that the instigator must necessarily obtain power from something other than the one to be instigated. Moreover, in the case of impossibility, the absence of the instigator itself implies the absence of a substitute; thus the [absence of a] representative mentioned by implication has been clarified. Since one who is directly capable does not depend on others in certain cases, the observation regarding their distinction is explained as being obtained through implication. Thus, the commentary (*bhāṣya*), which was stated in a condensed form, has been expanded and explained. (101, 102)

Anticipating the objection that, since such a collection of properties does not exist in insentient things, they cannot possess agency, he says: "In the case of a word, there is a restriction regarding properties that have been brought forth, but not regarding the actual object. When the speaker intends to express the properties of an agent, the agent is understood from the word. (103)

A rule characterized by the necessity that "the agent is independent and defined by such properties as being the initiator [of action], which are manifested through these aforementioned qualities—such as the acquisition of power—that were previously not present elsewhere," must necessarily be accepted regarding the domain of words.

That by whom these properties (dharmas) are made known through a word should be understood as the agent; however, one should not seek the existence of these properties as having a real entity (vastu) as their object, for if that were so, agency would not occur in the case of insentient objects, such as in "the fire burns," "the fuel cooks," "the pot cooks," and likewise in "the bank falls" or "the river flows."

For when these factors (*dharma*) are intended to possess the characteristic of an agent (*kartṛ-lakṣaṇa*), and are communicated by a word according to that intention, then from the word an agent with well-established characteristics is understood; thus, like an instrument (*karaṇa*), the agent is also presented as being dependent on intention (*vaivakṣika*). And this being the case, agency is not even a metaphorical (*upacarita*) attribution in the case of insentient things, because the usage occurs without failure everywhere and thus primary (*mukhya*) status is possible. For in grammar, the meaning is the word-meaning (*śabdārtha*), not the actual objective reality (*vastvartha*).
