Consequently, it is stated that the two definitions set forth in another grammatical treatise—namely, "the agent who desires [the action]" and "that which is similarly connected"—are not skillful, because they apply to both sentient and insentient objects. || 103 ||

And when independence belongs to the desire to speak and so forth, then this [following] point is also established; thus he says: "When a distinction is conceptually constructed for a single entity through its various mental states, the status of object, instrument, and agent arises. (104)

In the expression "he kills himself by himself," we observe the application of three grammatical factors (*kārakas*) to a single self, which depends on the differentiation of forms brought about by the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*). This [application] does not hold in a real, ontological usage of grammatical factors; for it is impossible to determine that a single entity simultaneously possesses multiple distinct forms. Furthermore, for the formless self, death produced by the operation of weapons and the like is not possible. However, the speaker's intention, which is based on linguistic usage, is not obstructed in this case.

For indeed, the state of cognition consists in the multiplicity of appearances; following that, a conceptualization of difference is made according to one's intention to speak. One who possesses the activity of raising and bringing down a weapon and so forth is the "agent" (*kartṛ*). Here, the self itself, having entered into the state of being an object, is likewise the "object" (*karman*). When there is an intention to express an excellence of ease, the activity of the weapon and so forth is set aside, and the self possesses the status of the "instrument" (*karaṇa*). Since elsewhere the object and the instrument are seen as distinct, in order to exclude that [distinction], it is said here that the agent himself is expressed as such through differentiation.

For this very reason, the treatment as an object-like agent (*karmavadbhāva*) is rejected in the *Vārttika* by this principle: "But it is established because of its being an original object; for in the case of contact with oneself, an intransitive agent is seen to function as an object," as in: "He kills himself" (*hantyātmānam*), or "He is killed by himself" (*ātmanā hanyate*). || 104 ||

He states that even another [point] is established regarding verbal agency: "The non-existence prior to production is based on a state of cognition; being indistinguishable from any other existent, it becomes the agent of birth. (105)

Regarding the statement "the sprout is born," does the status of being the agent of birth belong to something existent or non-existent? On this point, [it is argued] by such means as: "If that which exists is born, from what [could it be born]? Or if that which does not exist is born, how [could it be born]? In that case, even if agency is intended merely figuratively, it is said that there is no [justification for it] whatsoever. For instance, the specific states of the intellect—which consists of the intention to speak and is caused by words and are the basis for particular linguistic expressions—are relied upon here; thus, the status of being the agent of birth is established as being equivalent to the status of being the agent of another action.

For when an object is brought into proximity by the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*), the word "sprout" (*aṅkura*) is employed; and that word indicates an entity that is already existent. Consequently, since its birth is determined through its association with the word "is born," one might wonder from where its existence comes. Thus, for an entity whose existence is ascertained by the intellect and which has acquired its capacity for the accomplishment of an action, the meaning of the sentence is established as "birth" in terms of its external form.

Therefore, the meaning is that since existence does not possess agency in the same form by which it exists, nor does agency possess existence in that same form, this arrangement is not real but merely verbal; and since the meaning of a word is itself the object, because its application is unerring, it is primary in every case and not figurative at all. || 105 ||

He states that even in the case of the activity of real entities, there is the conventional expression "the sprout is born": "Just as a cause exists in the form of its effect, having then acquired the designation 'effect,' it is born as an effect. (106)

It has already been established that agency and birth are not tenable through the distinction between the positions of existence and non-existence when viewed from the perspective of the effect; this was previously demonstrated by relying on the states of the intellect (*buddhi*). Now, it is being demonstrated from the perspective of the cause. For this very reason, the word "or" (*vā*) indicates an alternative position. In that regard, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) stated that the effect arises as something entirely distinct from the cause. However, in the view of transformation (*pariṇāma*), this is said regarding the position of non-difference.

Since cause and effect exist in the form of a material cause and its modification (*prakṛti-vikāra*), there is the conventional usage of non-difference, such as "milk becomes curd" or "the seed becomes the sprout. The reality (*satattva*) consists merely in one persisting substrate (*avasthātṛ*) assuming particular states (*avasthā-viśeṣa*). Thus, in the process of producing a specific modification directed toward an effect, because of the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the denotative word onto a specific subsequent state, it is logical that the cause itself—being of the nature of existence and acting as the agent—undergoes "birth," which is characterized by the accomplishment of the subsequent state. This is the meaning of the expression "the sprout is born. || 106 ||

And this is logical—that the cause itself persists in the form of the effect; thus, in order to establish this according to his own established tenet, he says: "Just as the coiling of a serpent, or the coming together of things that were separate, so too do some declare the nature of birth to belong to existing things. (107)

Having previously established the impossibility of the relation between cause and effect through the distinction between the positions of existence and non-existence, the author has now concluded by means of the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) with the words, "But this process is most wonderful," and so forth. And therein, when the meaning of birth is investigated, it remains only this: that it is merely a particular arrangement [of parts] in such and such a manner.

For example, the crookedness of a snake is not distinct from the snake itself, and the collection of separate parts such as fingers constitutes a "fist" and so forth; thus, the relationship between cause and effect consists merely of a specific state. Since there is no difference between the entity possessing the state and the state itself, and since the entity persists through its various states, the status of being the agent of production is established for that which exists. || 107 ||

Now, even within the doctrine that cause and effect are distinct, he speaks in order to demonstrate that the status of being the agent of production exists in its true nature: Whatever effect proceeds from causes as something possessing a distinct origin, its own genus remains established within it in the form of an individual manifestation. (108)

The "origin" (*yoni*)—which is distinct and separate—is the cause of this non-existent transformation that is being produced. Although such a thing does not exist in its manifested form prior to its emergence from its causes, it does exist in the nature of a genus (*jāti*). Since it is determined as belonging to that genus and the application of the means of production occurs accordingly, it is the genus itself that prompts the causes for the sake of achieving its own manifestation. Thus, because of the conventional usage that "the genus is born in the form of the individual," agency belongs to the genus in its generic form, while being produced belongs to the individual in its manifested form.
The meaning is that because there is no absolute difference between the universal (jāti) and the individual (vyakti), their grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is established. || 108 ||

Now, in order to conclude his own established doctrine that "the meaning of a word is the object," he says: "The application of a word occurs only toward existent things (bhāva), whether it be of cognition or of speech. Even the statement 'it does not exist' does not apply to what is non-existent; therefore, it is not distinct from the existent. (109)

Since the operation of cognition and verbal expression occurs through the apprehension of a form (*ākāra*), it is impossible for them to be without an objective basis (*nirālambanatā*). Therefore, the very form that is being perceived is always the object denoted by the word "existence" (*bhāva-śabda*) and the locus for the application of those two [cognition and word]. For instance, cognitions and words directed toward non-existence (*abhāva*) do not arise by taking as their basis some form imagined by another or conceived by oneself; rather, they arise by taking a form that is already existent as their basis. Thus, there is no distinction between these two—cognition and word—regarding their reliance on an existent form, because they are identical in their apprehension of their own respective forms. Consequently, in conventional usage, the entire range of things, whether existent or non-existent, is treated as equal.

The discussion of external objects, however, is not a necessary part [of the argument], since practical discourse is completed by this much alone; thus, the formulation "the sprout arises when the apprehension of the eternal form has occurred" is easily established—this is the meaning. || 109 ||

He states that, apart from their status as objects of cognition and words, no external existence whatsoever exists for things in practical discourse: "Just as the intellect and words function with respect to existing things, there is no practical discourse regarding them by means of any other reality. (110)

The meaning is this: since linguistic usage consists solely of denotation (*abhidhāna*) and cognition (*pratyaya*), the true nature of an object must be sought in accordance with its cognition and its denotation; one should not take a stand by resorting to some other intrinsic nature of the object that is neither perceived nor denoted. Thus, because a cognition devoid of the reflection of an object is impossible, the agent is defined as being produced by a reality established through that [cognition]; and once defined, it is denoted.

Just as in the cognition "it does not exist," an object that, though non-existent externally, is negated at a specific place and time, appears with a form perceived at another place and time and is expressed by a verbal suffix denoting an agent; likewise, even an object that is future, when oriented toward its effect, becomes present before the intellect through the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of an experience of its own kind and arises by virtue of an efficient cause. Thus, it is expressed as the agent of birth—this is the meaning of the section. 110.

Now, having fixed in his mind the principle stated in the *Saṃbandhasamuddeśa*, he demonstrates the impossibility of birth and destruction according to the doctrine of non-duality: "Just as there is no actual division in space, and just as there is no real movement in a shadow, so too birth and destruction are merely imagined by some, even though there is no [real] differentiation. (111)

It has been stated that even though space is partless and eternal, a conceptualization of differentiation occurs through the superimposition of spatial divisions based on the distinctness of objects with which it comes into contact. Furthermore, although shadow—which consists of the absence of light—is motionless, it is superimposed as being active because it follows the movement of the obstructing substance.

Thus, since non-existence has already been refuted previously, and since the operation of a cause regarding birth has been negated, and since it has been explained that such an operation is likewise untenable regarding destruction, and because causeless destruction has been prohibited, it follows that for the eternal reality—which is undivided and non-dual—birth and destruction are impossible. Therefore, conventional usage proceeds through the forms of imagined existence and non-existence, which are based solely on appearances arising through the power of ignorance and under the influence of [conceived] birth and destruction; this has been determined in detail in the *Saṃbandhasamuddeśa*.

And thus, the meaning that [the world] arises as a mere conventional designation of existence and non-existence is established as something charming only so long as it is not investigated; this is the sense. || 111 ||

In order to establish that destruction is merely conceptualized, he says: "Just as the non-existence of space is described as being formless and unreal, so too the non-existence of form is unreal and dependent upon space. (112)

Since the all-pervading ether exists everywhere as a real entity, it is never absent anywhere. Nevertheless, the non-existence of ether—which is actually non-existent [in that sense]—is conceptually constructed by virtue of its being obstructed by the forms of objects such as jars, which occupy limited spaces. For wherever jars and the like exist, there is the conventional usage: "the ether is non-existent."

In this way, the non-existence of corporeal objects such as jars and the like in certain places is determined by their not being perceived in the intervening space; for it is a logical principle that what exists in reality cannot have its own nature destroyed, and what lacks the nature of existence cannot appear at any time. Indeed, when the presence of corporeal things is concealed in the interval, people perceive the sky itself as being devoid of them and thus conclude [to their absence]; this is to be understood from the context of the passage.

And thus, the fact that both birth and destruction are merely conceptual constructs is established. Furthermore, because worldly transaction proceeds according to conventional determination, things are proven to be without birth or cessation. For space is not a non-entity in reality; and since there is no absence of the existence of entities, nothing whatsoever ever undergoes birth. || 112 ||

Now, in order to justify the usage "it is born" even in the case of actual birth by means of another perspective, he says: "Just as the essence of action (kriyātman) is designated by means of those purposes and activities [of its causes], so too is this sequence of cause and effect [established] due to the apprehension of non-difference. (113)

By the statement beginning with "the instrument [is defined] by way of its being an effect," the real non-difference between cause and effect was established. Now, however, it is stated by resorting to a figurative non-difference: for just as the softening [of rice] is the primary meaning of the root *pac* (to cook), so too the operations of subordinate factors—such as placing [the pot] on the fire, pouring water, and so forth—which belong to the agent and other factors, are superimposed upon the agent and the rest because they serve that purpose; thus, they are described as having the form of the principal action itself, namely the actions of placing on the fire, pouring water, pouring the rice, and adding fuel, which belong to the principal agent.

"Cooking": as in "the pieces of wood cook" or "they burn until they are softened," the sequence of the cause—such as "the cooking"—is designated as such because the cause exists for the sake of the effect; thus, in common usage where there is no distinction [between cause and effect], it is appropriate to designate that the cause itself, being denoted by the word "sprout," arises in the form of the effect. This is the meaning. || 113 ||

Now, one might object: "Even if there is a superimposition of non-difference between cause and effect, agency with respect to birth belongs only to the effect, not to the cause, because the cause is already established. Anticipating this doubt, [the author] begins to establish that agency belongs to both cause and effect alternately, according to different usages, regarding the relationship between the material cause and its modification: "Regarding the doubt as to whether the modification (*vikāra*) or the material cause (*prakṛti*) is the agent of birth, the views of observers differ based on the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*). (114)

In this context of the relationship between the material cause (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikāra*), grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is observed in such instances as "milk becomes curd" (*kṣīraṃ dadhi sampadyate*). Here, however, there is a doubt. For since the relationship of primary and secondary status must necessarily exist in order to account for the consistency [of the usage], one must determine whether here the material cause is primary and the modification is subordinate, or the reverse. In that regard, agency with respect to the act of production belongs to the primary; as for the subordinate, its contact with the act of production occurs through the medium of the primary. Thus, coreferentiality is established.

But when there is a description in terms of difference, such as "the sprout is born from the seed," then the modification (vikāra) is undoubtedly the agent. This is because the material cause (prakṛti) is designated as the ablative (apādāna), according to the rule: "The material cause [is the ablative] of that which is the agent of birth. In this regard, the intention of those who hold that the modification is the agent is as follows: the acquisition of self-existence is what is called "birth," and that which does not exist must acquire its own self. Thus, it is logical that the modification itself is the agent here.

However, others maintain that the *prakṛti* (primordial nature) is the agent; for since it is impossible for a non-existent modification (*vikāra*) to be oriented toward the attainment of its own selfhood, agency is untenable with respect to an origination characterized by that [attainment]. Indeed, origination will be established as being the state of being oriented toward the attainment of one's own self. Since the self is already obtained in the form of *prakṛti*, it remains in a state of orientation toward the attainment of its own self characterized by the subsequent condition; therefore, it is appropriate that agency belongs to *prakṛti* alone. || 114 ||

In order to establish these two views through observations of indicative marks (*liṅga*) characterized by differences in usage and a division of subject matter, he says: "The dative case used when something is being transformed [into another] is based on the state of being a modification (*vikāra*). For example, the expression regarding a gold lump (*suvarṇapiṇḍa*) as the material cause (*prakṛti*) is based on the earring (*kuṇḍala*). (115)

The meaning of the *vārttika*—"the dative case should be prescribed when [something] is being transformed (*klṛpi sampadyamāne*)"—is that the dative is to be enjoined for the agent of the action of transformation. Furthermore, because traditional grammatical memory (*smṛti*) is rooted in actual usage, the dative heard in expressions denoting a modification (*vikāra*) indicates that the modification itself is the agent of the action of transformation. For example, in the expression "the gruel transforms into urine" (*mūtrāya sampadyate yavāgūḥ*), it means "the gruel is produced as urine. Here, the connection of the material cause (*prakṛti*) with the action occurs through the medium of the modification, not directly.

However, when a distinction is intended, the ablative case (pañcamī) as a *kāraka*-case applies here—specifically as the source (*apādāna*) according to the rule "the source of the agent of birth" (*janikartuḥ prakṛtiḥ*)—as in the expression, "urine is produced from barley-gruel" (*yavāgvā mūtraṃ jāyate*). But when non-distinction is intended, the dative case (*caturthī*) finds its scope. It is for this very reason that this definitive decision was made when a doubt existed in that regard.

Furthermore, in the statement, "Likewise, a lump of gold, having returned [to its original state], when joined with another form, becomes two earrings the color of acacia-wood embers," although the lump of gold is the material cause (*prakṛti*), its unity—which would follow from that—is not observed; rather, the dual number in the form of the agentive suffix in the word *bhavataḥ* ("they become") is observed, based on the duality of the earrings which are the modified forms (*vikāra*). From this indicative mark as well, the modification is determined to be the agent. || 115 ||

He states another indicative mark that infers the agency of both the material cause and its modification through a distinction in their respective domains: "In a sentence, the agent is said to be 'becoming' [the object] when the root is used with the suffix *saṃpadya*; in a compound, however, as in 'the Brahmins are becoming united,' the Brahmins possess independence. (116)

The suffix *cv-* is prescribed when there is a desire to express the transformation of something into that which it was not previously, provided that the agent of the transformation is the one who becomes [the result]. To illustrate its meaning, a sentence is constructed wherein the transformation is seen to function as the agent of the transformation. For example: "The Brahmins, who were not a *saṅgha*, become a *saṅgha*. Because we observe the use of a word based on the singularity inherent in the *saṅgha*, the *saṅgha* itself is the agent. However, in the *vṛtti* it is stated: "The Brahmins become a *saṅgha* (*saṃdhībhavanti brāhmaṇāḥ*)."

In this case, because the plural number is observed as residing in the Brahmins who constitute the material cause (*prakṛti*), it is determined that the agency belongs to the material cause. Thus, in this manner, through the distinction of usage, the agency of both the material cause and its modification (*vikāra*) should be inferred as firmly established. || 116 ||

Now, he states the evidence cited by the author of the Bhāṣya regarding the agency of primordial nature (prakṛti): "That which you do not become—though you are [the self]—in that [state], the primordial nature does not have you as its substratum; yet it is designated as 'belonging to the person' (prākṛta). (117)

The *Bhāṣya* cites: "‘atvaṃ’ becomes ‘tvaṃ’; [the form] ‘tvaṃ’ comes into being. Here, there is a modification (*vikāra*) of the referent of the pronoun *yuṣmad*. Yet, the second person (*madhyama-puruṣa*) based upon that [referent] is not observed; rather, because one observes the first person (*prathama-puruṣa*) residing in the base (*prakṛti*) which consists of a non-*yuṣmad* referent—namely, in the word ‘bhavati’—it is concluded that the agency belongs to the base itself. || 117 ||

Regarding how this [process] is logically established through the authority of its application according to the distinction of objects, he states the proof for this: "Not abandoning its prior state, while touching upon a subsequent property, the essence of the object is said to be 'arising' as if it were in a state of coalescence. (118)

In this context, it is not said that non-manifestation arises in an entirely absolute sense; rather, since it does not abandon or relinquish its prior causal state, the possibility of the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) being the agent is established here. Nor is it entirely indifferent; rather, by touching upon or attaining a specific subsequent state, the possibility of the transformation (*vikāra*) being the agent is also established.

And thus, a single entity delimited by the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) of its prior and posterior states arises as something being determined—appearing, as it were, as if its form were extending toward the attainment of a subsequent state in accordance with its prior state; in this way, it achieves consistency between the meaning of the verbal root and the meaning of the suffix. Consequently, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the material cause and the modification is established, as is the agency (*kartṛtva*) of both. || 118 ||

Anticipating the objection that, if this were so, both would be the agent in every case, he says: "In some instances, a certain property is perceived as possessing a more prominent activity; furthermore, the powers of entities, though distinct, are intermingled. (119)

Although both the material cause (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikṛti*)—by the logic already stated—are capable of being conjoined with the act of origination due to their non-difference, it has been said that when an agentive suffix arises, in some cases the modification is active and in others the material cause is. Even so, by way of distinguishing the respective domains, the agency of both has been established in the expression "it is born" (*jāyate*) according to the manner described. The meaning is that the powers (*śakti*) of entities, though distinct elsewhere, sometimes even attain a state of conjunction.

Alternatively, in all cases both possess agency; however, the distinction is that for one [of them], agency is direct (*sākṣāt*), which is described as being more intensely active (*saṃvyāpāratara*). For, since the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the material cause (*prakṛti*) and the modification (*vikṛti*) would otherwise be untenable, it must be understood that when one is the agent of production, the other necessarily possesses that agency as well. Indeed, that which is the object of prescription (*vidheya*) is the primary factor and thus possesses the activity of production preeminently (*prakarṣeṇa*); the other, however, being merely restated (*anūdyamāna*), is subordinate (*guṇa*) and its activity is not preeminent. || 119 ||

And so, if there were a conjunction between the agent and the power [of action], then one might ask: why does the person (*puruṣa*), which is the substratum of the state of modification, not become the object in the expression *tvadbhavati*? Anticipating this objection, he says: "In the case of the opposite [i.e., the absence of conjunction], the person would be understood as having a contrary function; for here, the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is perceived as being endowed with activity. (120)

In such cases as "atvaṃ tvaṃ sampadyate" (you become you) or "tvadbhavasi" (you become from you), when the second person is intended based on the referent of the word *yuṣmad* (you), the intended meaning is not perceived as being that the base (*prakṛti*) is the referent of *yuṣmad* and the modification (*vikṛti*) is the referent of *yuṣmad*. Rather, the referent of *yuṣmad*—being active in the production of the suffix—is itself perceived as the modification of something else.

For the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), expressed by the second person pronoun in the phrase "you become" (*saṃpadyase*), is perceived as possessing activity; consequently, by virtue of its being productive of a result, it would entail a further modification. And thus, the referent of the second person would be understood to undergo a state contrary to itself—that is, to attain the status of a non-second-person referent. Therefore, in order to convey that the primary subject (*prakṛti*) of the non-second-person referent is that which becomes [the effect], the first person alone is appropriate here. || 120 ||

He explains precisely the occurrence of a contrary meaning: "The conceptualization there would be that 'you are someone else'; just as such a transition occurs when a king has fallen into the state of a servant. (121)

Just as when it is said, "O King, you become a non-king," because the meaning of the base word *rājan* (king) is conveyed by the verb (*sampadyase*) as the referent of the second person pronoun, one understands that the king—who is characterized by activity—is the agent of the action of becoming through his transformation into the state of a servant, which is the opposite of his own [original] status; so too, here, when it is said "you become" (*tvadbhavasi*), since the referent of the second person pronoun is determined to be the agent in the attainment of another state, the intended meaning—characterized by the attainment of a status other than that of the second person—would not be perceived. Therefore, for the sake of that comprehension, the third person is used.

The [agent] is the principal. For one who intends to express one thing, another cannot be expressed. However, in the case of "the gold lump becomes two earrings," even though the modification (*vikāra*) is the agent, there is no occurrence of a contradictory meaning—namely, that "the two earrings transform into the nature of the gold lump"—because the agent necessarily lacks a requirement for a modification. Indeed, it is only in the domain of the *cvī* suffix that the agent's necessary entry into another modification is stated.

Since the suffix *cv-* is prescribed when there is a desire to express the original form (*prakṛti*), and because the original form is established by its own nature, it is logical that the agent—which undergoes the state of a modification (*vikāra*) and is thus active—is denoted by the word expressing the modification, for the purpose of conveying the cessation of the specific modification. This is because, in the case of a word ending in *cv-*, the rule prescribes the designation of "gati" (indeclinable prefix) when it is connected with a verb; and since a "gati" functions as an adverbial modifier of an action.

Since agency is impossible for that which is not a sentient being (*asattva*), it is appropriate that Primordial Matter (*prakṛti*) alone is the agent in an action characterized by the suffix *cvi*—which denotes the state of becoming a modification (*vikāra*)—as in the case of [the example] "it becomes you" (*tvadbhavati*). However, in a sentence such as "the Brahmins become a multitude" (*saṅghībhavanti brāhmaṇāḥ*), because both the original form (*prakṛti*) and the modification (*vikṛti*) are expressed by their own respective words following the suffix *cvi*, there is a restriction regarding the agency of both, depending on whether they are intended as subordinate (*guṇa*) or primary (*pradhāna*).

For indeed, the innate reality (*nijam eva tattvam*) of the base (*prakṛti*) is intended to be expressed as predominant when it is engaged in the state of perfection (*sampad*). Occasionally, however, a superimposed form of modification (*vikāra*) is intended. For example, in the expression "the great being, the moon" (*mahadbhūtaś candramāḥ*), because the agent is of the nature of the base which does not possess the meaning of "great," that very [moon] is denoted by the word *mahat*, which expresses a modification; thus, it has been stated that because it is figurative (*gauṇatvāt*), the substitution of *āt* for the meaning of "great" does not occur.

However, in the case of the expression *mahadbhūtā brāhmaṇī*, since it is intended that the modification (*vikāra*) itself, in the sense of "great," functions as the agent (*kartṛ*) by being the subject of the action (*bhavitṛ*), it has been stated that the masculine substitution (*puvadbhāva*) indeed occurs by virtue of the rule concerning coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*). || 121 ||

The incidental discussion is concluded. This must now be addressed: independence (*svātantrya*) has been explained by the passage beginning with "prior to obtaining power from another. However, that [independence] is not applicable to the instigator (*prayojaka-kartṛ*). For he, like an instrument (*karaṇa*) or other factors, becomes subordinate to the activity of the instigator and is thus not independent, even though he possesses independence regarding his own activity.

Consequently, the designation "agent" (*kartṛ*) would not apply to this [instigator] based on independence; thus, in the sentence *pācayaty odanaṃ devadattena yajñadattaḥ* ("Yajñadatta causes Devadatta to cook rice"), the instrumental case expressing agency (*kartṛ-tṛtīyā*) would not occur for Devadatta, the instigated agent. Accordingly, the *Vārttika* states: "When the designation 'agent' applies to that which is independent, an addition must be made for that which possesses an instigator (*hetumat*), because [the instigated] is not independent. Here, "instigator" (*hetu*) means the prompter, and "possessing that" (*tadvat*) refers to the one being prompted.

If the designation *hetu* (cause) were applied to the instigation (*adhyeṣaṇa*), then even when one is being directed toward an object, that person’s status as the *prayojaka* (instigator) would not be contradicted; thus, it is appropriate to take the term *hetumat* (possessing a cause) as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). Regarding this, the *Vārttika* provides the resolution: "Or rather [it is not so], because of independence" (*na vā svātantryāt*). Since the person being directed possesses independence (*svātantrya*) with respect to their own action, the designation of *kartṛ* (agent) is established. [Objection: If this were the case, the same would apply to instruments (*karaṇa*) and other factors as well. [Response: This is not so, because for those [factors], the designations of *karaṇa* and so forth are prescribed according to their respective roles.

However, since no other designation has ever been stated for the *prayojya* (the one being prompted), it retains its designation as the *kartṛ* (agent) alone. This being the case, one might raise the objection: "Since the activity of the *prayojya* depends upon the prompter (*prayojaka*), how can he possess independence (*svātantrya*)? Anticipating this, the author establishes [his position] as follows: "Because of the possibility [of success], one who is relied upon as the agent for the accomplishment of an action is the prompter of the means in an action to be accomplished by himself. (122)
Merely through its application, it relies on its own sovereignty to become subordinate; thus, it becomes indistinguishable from other independent [deities] who are free from doubt. (123)

First, that which is to be employed while its activity has not yet commenced is employed only after its capacity for action has been inferred; otherwise, there would be no employment at all. For no sensible person would ever employ one who is incapable of any action. Therefore, once its power is ascertained and its potential for action is conceived, it is the agent alone—being independent—who is employed.

Even one who is engaged in an action to be accomplished by himself, being active and employing the entire collection of causal factors such as instruments and the like, is indeed an independent agent (*kartṛ*) while performing that action; yet, out of the concern that he might desist, he is "employed" with the thought, "May he not stop. Thus, although he is an independent agent in his own operation, he becomes subordinate and dependent solely upon the instigator’s command for the mere act of employment, because the command exists for the sake of accomplishing the action.

And thus the action is accomplished provided that the person being employed attains independence characterized by the application of other means of accomplishment, and not otherwise; therefore, independence is not contradicted by the act of employment. Furthermore, due to the difference in scope, there is dependence in the employment [of the means], while there is independence in one's own operation; indeed, independence in one's own operation exists precisely as the means for the dependence in the employment.

Thus, by being independent—meaning not being prompted by another—and being determined by his own will, he is established as a self-reliant prompter (*prayojya*) who is equal to others. This has been stated in the *Vārttika*: "Otherwise, it would follow that [the agent] causes [an action] to be performed even when [the other] is not performing it. If you say, 'He is self-reliant because he does not perform it,' [we reply: no, because the employment of one who is indifferent, lazy, or incapable is impossible."

The meaning is that only one who possesses recognized independence (*svātantrya*) is the "instigator" (*prayojya*). If this were so, then since an independent agent is indeed the instigator of a cause (*hetu*), there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even the instruments (*karaṇa*) and other factors—which are independent in their own operations—would receive the designation of "cause" (*hetu*) when they are themselves the instigators of another agent. If you ask, "Let it be so; what is the harm?", [the answer is: regarding the rule "even when there is a cause," there would follow the application of the *ṇic* suffix to express that operation.

If it is argued that this is not a fault because [the agent] has already been expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*), we say no. For the injunction (*praiṣa*) would be included within the meaning of the verbal root only when that root has an object, since the agent's efficient force (*bhāvanā*) exists for the sake of the result and thus the root-meaning comes into contact with it. However, in the case of a verbal root that lacks an object, the application of an instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth, though existing in reality, remains unascertained; therefore, the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is produced in order to convey that. From the word, one understands only the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) consisting of an action qualified by its specific means; but there is no injunction from the agent regarding the instrument and the other factors.

Furthermore, if the object of the action (*prayojya*) were also designated as the *hetu* (cause), then the reference to the "independent" (*svatantra*) as the "instigator" (*prayojaka*) would be redundant; for that term is intended to exclude the instigators of instruments (*karaṇa*) and so forth. Moreover, if the instigator of those very instruments—which themselves rely on independence regarding their own operations—is also designated as the *hetu*, then that specific reference is likewise redundant. Furthermore, the designation of *hetu* itself would be purposeless; since it is merely the agent (*kartṛ*), let it simply be governed by the rule: "The suffix *ṇic* occurs after a verbal root when there is a sense of agency. And thus:

In the rule *bhīsmyorhetumaye*, [the suffix] *ṣuk* is prescribed for *bhi* and *smi* when there is a cause of fear (*hetu-bhaya*). In the rule *bibheterhetubhaye*, if the statement *kartṛbhaye* were applied, an undesirable result would follow. Therefore, one must strive to exclude the designation *hetu* (cause) for an instigator who functions as an instrument (*karaṇa*) or similar factor, such that he is merely the instigator (*prayojaka*) of another independent agent. To this, it is replied:

Regarding the phrase "the instigator of that" (*tasya prayojakaḥ*), because the pronoun *tasya* refers back to the independent agent who possesses the designation of "experiencer" (*anubhava-kartṛ*)—and not to the instruments (*karaṇa*) and so forth which have acquired the designation of "agent" (*kartṛ*) [only] through [their relation to] that [primary agent]—the latter do not receive the designation of "cause" (*hetu*) as the instigator. For although the instrument and so forth are independent with respect to their own specific operations, they lack independence with respect to the primary operation; therefore, they do not receive the designation of "agent. Indeed, by the force of the explicit mention of "independent" (*svatantra*), it is intended to signify preeminent capacity (*sāmarthya*).

However, since instruments (*karaṇa*) and the other factors, when merely following [the agent], cannot possess the status of being a causal factor (*kāraka*), the independence (*svātantrya*) inferred from the impossibility of their otherwise existing—which pertains to their own respective operations—could at most be useful for the designation "instrument" (*kāraka*). It is not, however, useful for the designation "agent" (*kartṛ*); for that [independence] is eclipsed by the application of the primary [agent], as there is an absence of predominant independence. Consequently, they are not directed toward action while remaining agents.

The person to be employed (prayojya), even while being employed, does not at all relinquish his superior independence characterized by being the director of other instruments; therefore, he is rightly considered the agent in every respect. For this very reason it has been said: "resorted to as the agent. Thus, it is established that [he is the agent] by way of agency—whether past, future, or currently conceived by the intellect. || 122, 123 ||

It was stated: "In mere application, [the agent] remains dependent on independence. To the objection that even this is not the case, he says: "All beings indeed act toward their own ends because of external causes; even compliance with another's intention is for the sake of accomplishing one's own purpose. (124)

Everyone who acts out of a desire for their own self-interest does not thereby incur dependence on another in that activity; rather, it is merely because the activity of one person serves as a means for the accomplishment of another's purpose that the state of being "employed" is attributed to a servant or similar subordinate by virtue of following the will of a master or superior. For the activity of servants is indeed motivated by wages; however, even in the case of those free from passion who act out of compassion, the accomplishment of the welfare of others is itself their own interest and the fruit of their action, since that is defined as what is desired.

This has been stated in the Bhāṣya: "All these beings strive for their own welfare; no one here is to be favored by another. To the objection—"When they act for the sake of their own welfare, what is the purpose of the instigator?"—the resolution has also been stated: "They become attached to the intentions [of others]. The intention of the instigator is the accomplishment of the action. And that the instigated person accomplishes, even while acting with the aim of achieving a result for his own sake, is indeed so.

And having established this, [the rule] "and in the case of that which possesses a cause" (*hetumati ca*) is explained as follows: the intention of the instigator (*prayojaka*) is the accomplishment of the action. And even though the person being prompted (*prayojya*) proceeds by aiming for a result for his own sake, he certainly accomplishes that [action]. Having established this, the supplementary rules (*upasaṃkhyāna*) regarding the [rule] "and in the case of that which possesses a cause" have been rejected [by the statement]: "Or rather, it is not necessary, because it is already accomplished by the general rule; for it is not distinguished from the cause."

Because it proceeds spontaneously, the rising of the sun over Māhiṣmatī—which was intended by the traveler—has occurred by chance (*kākatālīyāt*). Since this follows the [traveler's] intention, the sun becomes the "instigator" (*prayojya*), and so on; this is to be applied accordingly. Thus says the author of the Vārttika: "For the activity occurs in both cases without regard [to anything else]. Even in the case of that which is instigated (*prayojya*) when doubt has been removed, the activity does not depend upon the instigated object’s own purpose, but rather upon its own [purpose]; such is the meaning.

In cases such as "he narrates the killing of Kaṃsa," however, this has already been established previously by the statement, "as if [he were seeing] Kaṃsa and others directly. Even in the case of insentient objects, as in "alms cause him to dwell" (*bhikṣā vāsayati*), the status of being an instigator (*prayojakatva*) is to be justified through the superimposition of intention (*abhiprāyādhyāropa*) based on the suitability of the dwelling and so forth. Thus, it is said that "the cause is the instigator merely by virtue of its capacity, [acting] from among the causes" (*nimittabhyaḥ*).

It is also stated in the Vārttika: "The mention of a 'cause' (*hetu*) is merely a 'condition' (*nimitta*), because it is observed in cases such as alms"; thus concludes the investigation into the agent (*kartṛ*). 124.

Thus ends the section on the Agent (*kartṛ-adhikāra*) in the *Prakīrṇaprakāśa* composed by Helārāja, the son of Bhūtirāja. The agent himself, when acting as an instigator, is the "cause" (*hetu*). Consequently, immediately following the investigation of the agent, he now investigates the cause: "By issuing commands or making requests, and by performing actions conducive to those [ends], the agent alone acquires the designation 'cause' (*hetu-saṃjñā*) as prescribed in the grammatical treatise. (125)

The act of employing (*vyāpāraṇā*) preceded by a command is *preṣaṇa* (sending); the meaning is that it is an assignment whose object is inferior. On the other hand, when one employs someone who is more worthy, that is *adhyeṣaṇā* (requesting); the meaning is that its object is a superior person. These [actions] are capable of that; they are activities conducive to the accomplishment of the action of the instigated (*prayojya*). And this alone is the primary activity of the instigator (*prayojaka*), namely, performing what is capable of accomplishing the action of the instigated. This is because it is all-pervasive, as it exists even in cases such as begging for alms.

This very [activity] is divided into the forms of *preṣaṇa* (commanding) and *adhyeṣaṇa* (requesting) according to whether its object is inferior or superior. Thus, by the maxim of the "cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*), what is intended here is that which is distinct from those two—a performance of service conducive to the goal directed toward begging. These are mentioned separately because of the difference in worldly usage. Just as being made to act (*prayojyatva*) was defined as conforming to another's intention, so too is being an instigator (*prayojakatva*) the manifestation of one's own intention; therefore, in all cases, the function of the instigator is precisely this performance of service conducive to the goal.

Regarding the phrase "the agent alone": he explains the inclusion of the word *ca* (and) in the rule *tatprayojako hetuśca* for the purpose of the co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of designations. If the *ca* were absent here, because of the governing rule of "one designation" (*ekasaṃjñādhikāra*), the designation *kartṛ* (agent) would not apply; therefore, it serves the purpose of co-occurrence. This has been stated in the Vārttika: "The mention [of the term] applies also to those [roots] that have motion as their object and to those whose cause is expressed by *div*. Regarding the phrase "prescribed in the Śāstra": the meaning is that this very [term] should be understood in its specific application within the rules (*pradeśa*). For a worldly cause (*laukiko hetuḥ*) is an entity capable of being a means to achieve a result, having substance (*dravya*) and so forth as its domain.

However, this is its distinction: as the object of an action, the *kāraka* (participant) is the cause (*hetu*), consisting of the instigator and the instigated. Therefore, here the agent's own operation—such as commanding (*preṣaṇa*) and so forth—is specified by virtue of its status as a *kāraka*. In that regard, in the rules "when there is a cause" (*hetumati ca*) and "in fear caused by [the root] *bhī*" (*bhiyo hetubhaye*), the term "cause" refers to the technical (*kṛtrima*) cause. But in the rule prescribing the third case ending (*tṛtīyā-vidhi*), in the phrase "when there is a cause" (*hetau*), since the instigator would already be established as the agent (*kartṛ*) and thus [already require] the third case, the term "cause" refers to the worldly (*laukika*) cause.

Even in the formulation of the fifth case (pañcamī), the technical term "non-agent" (*akartari*) is excluded by way of *paryudāsa*. Furthermore, in the rule "when [the cause] is a characteristic or a cause of an action" (*lakṣaṇahetvoḥ kriyāyāḥ*), since the prompted agent (*prayojya*) is a factor of action (*kāraka*), and because its connection with an action is never absent, it is understood that—by virtue of the restrictive capacity [of the word] and because there is both possibility and non-occurrence [of the cause] as an object of substance, quality, or action—it is only the worldly (*laukika*) cause that is grasped. This is likewise because of the governing context of the verbal root (*dhātu*); for a verbal root does not function in the sense of a cause that is a grammatical means (*sādhana*).

Thus, even in the rule *hetuhetumator liṅ* ("the conditional suffix *liṅ* is used for the cause and that which possesses the cause"), since the cause is a qualifier of the verbal root-meaning (*dhātvartha*), and because the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is not the meaning of the verbal root, the "cause" here is purely worldly (*laukika*). Likewise, in the rule *kuño hetutācchīlyānulomyeṣu* ("the suffix *ṇic* follows the root *kṛñ* in the senses of cause, habituality, and compliance"), the "cause" is not the instigator (*prayojaka*). This is because the suffix *ṇic* is prescribed there, and the mention of *kuñaḥ* (the form *kṛñ*) is made excluding the suffix *ti*. Therefore, in this case, the worldly cause is a qualifier of the agent (*kartṛ*) which is obtained through the presence of the *kṛt* suffix; and because there is no contradiction, the agent is not set aside by it.

And since the agent is denoted by the suffixes (*kṛt*) precisely in the form of fitness (*yogyatā*), the cause (*hetu*) being presented merely as a causal factor (*nimitta*) becomes a qualifier; furthermore, the repetition of the word establishes a restriction, namely: "it is only the cause. By this, learning (*vidyā*) and the like are established as non-deviant causes for fame and so forth. And here, these factors such as the cause, though understood through the capacity to convey a specific agent, are ultimately word-meanings (*padārtha*) themselves through a mediated process.

Otherwise, those [suffixes] perceived in the state of the sentence would not serve as the cause for the grammatical derivation (anvākhyāna) which has the word as its limit. Regarding this, it is objected in the Bhāṣya to the sūtra *praiṣātisarga...* and so forth: "Since the suffix *loṭ* is conjoined by the particle *ca*, there arises the contingency of an option (*vikalpa*) because both the causative (*ṇic*) and *loṭ* are prescribed for the sense of command (*praiṣa*). Thus, in examples such as *pṛcchatu mā bhavān* and *anuyāṅktāṃ mā bhavān*, why does the causative suffix (*ṇic*) not occur?"

By using the self-reference "mā bhavān" (do not [you]), he demonstrates that the instigation (*praiṣa*) rests upon the instigator (*prayojaka*), thereby strengthening the application of the *ṇic* affix. A resolution for this is stated in the Bhāṣya: "Because of the absence of agency. The meaning is as follows: since the *ṇic* is prescribed when there is an instigator of an independent agent regarding that agent's activity, and because that person lacks agency in the act of questioning (as they have not yet engaged in it), the one who instigates them lacks the designation of "cause" (*hetu*); consequently, the *ṇic* does not occur in the instigation of that activity.

The opponent, however, argues that because one who is incapable cannot be enjoined by means of a question regarding time and so forth, and because an injunction would be purposeless for one already engaged in action, this must be an instigation (*preṣaṇa*) directed toward a person capable of performing the act. He says: "Furthermore, sir, an agent can only exist for an action in the present tense, not for one in the past or future. To this, the reply is: "In that case, a connection is established. This means that the relationship between action and its factors (*kriyā-kāraka-bhāva*) is established through logical possibility (*sāmarthya*) with respect to actions in the past and future.

And in that context, regarding the domain of the *loṭ* (imperative) suffix, only the action of the instigator (*prayojaka*) is possible; thus, [the meaning is] "be the agent of the action," and not some other operation of the instigator directed toward the operation of the one being instigated (*prayojya*). Immediately following this is the Bhāṣya: "And as for how the agent is expressed by an affix denoting an agent. To this, the answer is: "How does this verb *pṛcchati* (he asks) apply when he is not asking? It is said: 'In that case, a connection is made [with the sense]: "perform this action. "

It was stated immediately before: "In that case, the connection is also made by the agent [of the action], [in the sense]: 'May you become the agent in this action. And thus, just as here the verbal root *pṛcch* (to ask) occurs even when one is not currently asking, because of the intention toward the act of asking, so too the imperative suffix (*loṭ*), which expresses the agent, is employed due to the connection with that agent; therefore it was said, "In that case, the connection is also made by the agent."

By stating this, the author of the Bhāṣya implies that the causative suffix *ṇic* does not apply here because there is currently no agency (*kartṛtva*). For indeed, the agency being enjoined here is something new, not something already existing. One is exhorted, "Become an agent in the action," but not as one who is already an agent. Therefore, the exhortation directed toward one who is already an agent—which constitutes the domain of the causative suffix *ṇic*—is inherent to the instigator (*prayojaka*). However, the imperative suffix (*loṭ*) is prescribed for agents and so forth; its exhortation, moreover, is manifested through the adjunct of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*).

Furthermore, that [impulsion] is not denoted by the verbal root or the suffix; rather, by virtue of its inherent capacity, it remains as the instigator (*prayojaka*) who is the speaker himself. Thus, the impulsion (*praiṣa*), which resides in that [instigator], is not delimited here by the temporal restriction inherent in the verbal root and suffix. Consequently, even when one is currently asking, the usage "let him ask" (*pṛcchatu*) is employed. However, in the case of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), since the impulsion is what is denoted, it—being a property of the expressed meaning due to being directly conveyed by the word—is delimited by a temporal restriction through suffixes such as the present indicative (*laṭ*), which denote specific times.

For when a suffix such as *lakāra* (the verbal ending) or *tṛc* and so forth is produced from a causative (*ṇic*) stem and denotes the agent, that which is perceived as the instigator—the agent—is understood as being related to him [the actual doer]; thus, this is a property of the expressed meaning (*abhidheya-dharma*). Indeed, in the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*), meaning is presented in two ways as a constituent part of the formal derivation (*anvākhyāna*): one is a property of the speaker (*prayoktṛ-dharma*), such as repetition (*vīpsā*), obstruction (*bādha*), envy (*asūyā*), censure (*kutsana*), and so forth; the other is a property of the person being addressed (*pratipādya-dharma*). Among these, the command (*praiṣa*) which is the domain of the imperative (*loṭ*) is a property of the speaker—like obstruction and the rest—and is therefore excluded from being a property of the expressed meaning. || 125 ||

This very point is established with full precision: "In the case of a command regarding a mere substance, the *loṭ* suffix is prescribed for [verbs such as] *pṛccha* and others; however, when there is the employment of that which possesses an action, that is the domain of the causative (*ṇic*). (126)

When the sense of agency (*kartṛtva*) itself is to be expressed through a command (*praiṣa*) directed toward a mere substance whose activity has not yet commenced and which has not yet attained the status of an agent, the suffix *loṭ* (imperative) is taught; it is a suffix following roots such as *pṛccha* and *anuyuñj*, with the agent (*kartṛ*) and other kārakas to be expressed. However, when there is a suspicion that an agent whose activity has already commenced might desist, and with the intention "let him not desist," the suffix *ṇic* is taught as denoting the operation of the instigator (*prayojaka-hetu*) of that very independent agent.

For the position that the suffix (*pratyaya*) is the qualifier of the meaning has been established as the final doctrine (*siddhānta*) in the rule *hetumati ca*. Thus, the *Vārttika* states: "The mention of the 'agent' (*kāraka*) in the term *hetumatī* is for the purpose of including the suffix. Consequently, the domain of both the causative suffix (*ṇic*) and the imperative (*loṭ*) is strictly distinct, because a difference in the nature of the command (*praiṣabheda*) is determined here from the usage of words in common parlance.

Because the *praiṣa* (the act of commanding) pertaining to the *ṇic* suffix is denoted by the suffix itself as a property of the expressed meaning (*abhidheya-dharma*), there is a distinction [from the imperative] due to that difference in properties; whereas the *praiṣa* pertaining to the imperative (*loṭ*) is manifested (*dyotya*) and is a property of the agent (*prayoktṛ-dharma*), thus there is a further distinction. For this very reason, it should be connected with the two occurrences of the word "but" (*tu*). In examples such as "May you ask" (*pṛcchatu mā bhavān*), there exists no expresser (*vācaka*) whatsoever for the agent of the command; rather, only the utterer is understood as the agent through implication (*sāmarthya*). Therefore, the command here is not a property of the expressed meaning.

Nor is it denotable by its own form (*svarūpa*), because that [form] is not denoted by the imperative suffix (*loṭ*); for upon the utterance of a word ending in *loṭ*, the instigation (*praiṣa*) is understood as a property of the speaker, like the prohibition (*abādha*) and so forth, yet there is no specific [word] that denotes it. If, then, there is such a clear distinction between these two types of instigation, why was it questioned in the *Bhāṣya*: "Why does the causative suffix (*ṇic*) not occur here in 'pṛcchatu mā bhavān'? This distinction is to be understood from worldly usage; since the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*) does not establish a formal distinction, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) proceeds by considering the mere act of instigation to be common to both. 126.

This has been explained. Here, one might raise the objection that since everything involved by the instigator—through such acts as commanding or entreating—is attained through the instigator’s operation, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the designation "object" (karman) applying to the person being prompted. Anticipating this, he says: "Because of its independence with respect to the subordinate action (guṇakriyā), [the person] has attained the status of an object in the act of commanding; yet, due to the restrictive rule regarding the designation 'object,' he is expressed according to his own primary characteristic. (127)

Without relinquishing its own independence (*svātantrya*), the prompted agent (*prayojya*) attains a state of dependence upon the activity of the prompter (*prayojaka*). For it has been stated that its independence is not actually destroyed by the prompter; otherwise, one could say "he causes [something] to be done" even when it is not being done. Thus, even in the case of an injunction (*praiṣa*), the designation of "agent" (*kartṛ-saṃjñā*) certainly applies because of its independence with respect to its own activity. However, the designation of "object" (*karma-saṃjñā*)—which would have applied because it is being caused to act by means of the injunction—is restricted by the rule beginning with *gati-buddhi-...* (Pāṇini 1.4.52).

The term *prayojya* (the one caused to act) is to be designated as the *karman* (object) only when it is the object of roots such as *gam* (to go) and others, and not otherwise. Thus, in examples such as *pācayaty odanaṃ devadattena* ("He causes Devadatta to cook the rice"), the *prayojya* is expressed by its own property, namely *kartṛtva* (agency). Now, an objection may be raised: since independence (*svātantrya*) has not ceased even in the case of the *prayojya*, the designation *kartṛ* (agent) alone would apply by virtue of its higher status; so how can a restrictive rule (*niyama*) such as *gatibuddhi-* etc. be stated? For if the designation *kartṛ* were applicable, the designation *karman* would have to be introduced [as an exception], and thus the rule would function merely as an injunction (*vidhi*).

To this it is replied: It has already been established that, regarding the two powers (śakti) whose objects are the two actions—one subordinate and one principal—the principal power alone impels its own effect, not the subordinate power. In that context, the operation of the prompted agent (prayojyavyāpāra), which is denoted by the verbal root (dhātu), is subordinate because it serves as a qualifier of the meaning of the causative suffix (ṇyartha); however, the operation of the prompter (prayojakavyāpāra), which is denoted by the causative suffix (ṇic), is the principal.

For in all cases, the meaning of the suffix is primary because it is delimited by the meaning of the base; as it is said, "the base and the suffix express the meaning of the suffix together. Therefore, since the operation of the instigator (prayojaka) is primary here, it is the objective capacity (*karma-śakti*) alone that brings about its own effect in relation to that [primary operation], and not the agentive capacity (*kartṛ-śakti*) which has the operation of the person being impelled (*prayojya*) as its object.

For example, although there is independence (*svātantrya*) with respect to the softening of the rice, it does not receive the designation of "agent" (*kartṛ*); rather, because it is that which is most desired to be reached through the act of moistening—the activity of Devadatta—it receives the designation of "object" (*karman*), as in the expression *pācayaty odanam* ("he causes the rice to be cooked"). Thus, since there is no possibility here for both designations to apply simultaneously, and therefore no conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the designation of "agent" would already be established; consequently, the rule is formulated for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*) so that the designation of "object" is secured even in cases involving motion (*gati*) and the like.

It is established that when, in the case of [verbs] such as *pacati*, the primary action has been extended by rule, the independence (*svātantrya*) of the subordinate action—being without opposition—indeed brings about its own effect, namely the designation of "agent" (*kartṛ*). || 127 ||

It has been stated that the instigator (*prayojaka*) is the cause (*hetu*). However, one might raise the objection that since even the object (*karman*), which is the result of the action, possesses the quality of being an instigator with respect to the action, it too would follow as a cause. Anticipating this, he demonstrates the distinction between the cause and the object: "The object is the instigator of the action; the cause is the instigator of the agent. And the production of the action is for the sake of the object, through its refinement and attainment. (128)

Because it accomplishes the three types of action—namely, that which is produced (*nirvartya*), that which is modified (*vikārya*), and that which is acquired (*prāpya*)—through the processes of production, modification, and acquisition respectively, the fruit of the activity (*kriyāphala*) employs the activity for the sake of the attainment of the object itself (*karmātmasampatti*). Furthermore, the cause (*hetu*), seeking the activity, employs the agent (*kartṛ*) in the application of the means (*sādhana*), but not the activity directly; for the agent’s engagement is indeed for the sake of fulfilling that [activity].

Because of the statement that "one who prompts the agent [is the prompter]," the distinction in the essential nature of the prompter (*prayojakatva*) is clear, since the cause (*hetu*) and the object (*karman*) have different domains. The word "and" (*ca*) indicates the reason. Since action exists for the sake of the object due to the assistance provided through its production and so forth, the object is the prompter of the action. For that which exists for the sake of something else is designated as the prompter of that thing, because the latter proceeds with that [former] as its aim.

Other factors of action (*kāraka*), however, exist for the sake of the action, but the action does not exist for their sake; therefore, they are not the motivators (*prayojaka*) of that action. For the commencement of an action is not for the sake of the instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth; rather, those are merely means (*upāya*). Thus, this investigation of the cause (*hetu*) is concluded. || 128 ||

Thus ends the section on *hetu* (cause) within the *Sādhanasamuddeśa* of the *Prakīrṇaprakāśa* composed by Helārāja, son of Bhūtirāja. In the investigation of the grammatical factors (*sādhana*) according to the sequence of the prescription of case-endings, once the agent (*kartṛ*)—the referent of the third case—has been determined, he states the following in order to investigate the recipient (*sampradāna*), the referent of the fourth case: "Because the agent does not reject it, that which is desired by the object as a part of its relinquishment, or [that which receives] instigation or consent, attains the status of a recipient (*sampradāna*). (129)

Because the term *sampradāna* (recipient) is etymologically significant, it acquires the definition "an auxiliary to the act of relinquishing. Relinquishment (*tyāga*) is the production of another's ownership through the cessation of one's own ownership over that which is being given. Since even the hand and other such [limbs] serve as an auxiliary (*aṅga*)—that is, a cause (*nimitta*)—in that process, he says: "that which is desired by the object" (*karmaṇepsitam*). The meaning is: that which is the object (*karman*) being relinquished, and by means of which [object], as an instrument (*karaṇa*), the agent desires to reach [the recipient] at the very outset. Thus, the definition "whom one intends through the object" (*karmaṇā yam abhipraiti*) is encompassed.

Anticipating the objection—“How does such an element of renunciation (tyāgāṅga) acquire the status of a *sampradāna* (recipient), which is a specific type of *kāraka*?”—the author points out the operation that grounds its status as a *kāraka* for the accomplishment of the action, beginning with the words “because of non-rejection” (*anirākaraṇāt*). In cases such as “He gives a cow to the teacher” (*upādhyāyāya gāṃ dadāti*), the object being relinquished, such as the cow, is connected with the recipient, such as the teacher; this is precisely because the act of giving is performed with that [recipient] in mind.

And that teacher, being thus approached, does not reject it, nor does he enjoin a rejection by saying "do not abandon it" to one who wishes to give it up; for if he were to reject it, the very act of giving would not be accomplished, since that act extends until the attainment of ownership by another. Furthermore, he consents to what is being given. Likewise, when he does not reject what is being offered—such as an oblation (*bali*) and so forth—to a deity and the like, that too is an auxiliary to the ritual action.

Furthermore, in the case of a gift preceded by a request, the instigation—the urging toward giving through entreaty—is also the operation (*vyāpāra*) of the recipient (*sampradāna*). Thus, because it assists the act of relinquishment (*tyāga*), the recipient is indeed a causal factor (*kāraka*) that constitutes a limb of the relinquishment. Now, one might object: since the gift is for the sake of the recipient, and the dative case is used to express such "being for the sake of" (*tādarthya*), what is the purpose of the technical designation "recipient"? This is not correct.

For the recipient (*sampradāna*) exists for the sake of the act of giving; the act of giving does not exist for the sake of the recipient, because all factors of action (*kāraka*) exist for the sake of the action. Since that which is being given is the object (*karman*), the act of giving—which constitutes the meaning of the sentence—is not for the sake of the recipient. Therefore, since the dative case would not apply by virtue of being "for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*), it is logical that the designation "recipient" (*sampradāna*) applies when there is such a purpose. However, in cases such as "he gives the garment to the washerman" (*rajakasya vastraṃ dadāti*) or "he gives his back to the one who strikes him" (*ghnataḥ pṛṣṭhaṃ dadāti*), the meaning of the root *dā* (to give) is absent; for that [act] is indeed relinquishment (*tyāga*).

And by that very act of relinquishment—which consists in loss—the transfer of ownership to another is also accepted, precisely because it implies the severance of one's own sense of "mine" through the intention to benefit another. In this case, however, since that [intention] is absent, the use of the verb *dadāti* (he gives) is figurative. But in the case of a gift to a deity, the donor’s resolve regarding the deity’s ownership certainly exists. Thus, in expressions such as "he gives food to one who has no appetite," the absence of utility is not a matter of verbal expression (*śābda*).

Even in the case of the injunction, "One should not give instruction (*yati*) to a Śūdra," there is indeed a benefit to another as the continuum of cognition (*mati-saṃtāna*) passes away [to that other]. Thus, in the expression "he causes [the student] to learn from the teacher" (*upādhyāyād āgamayati*), the teacher becomes the recipient (*sampradāna*) because the continuum of study passes away [from him]; since a portion of the continuum of cognition is being relinquished, the primary meaning of the root *dā* (to give) applies here, characterized by the cessation of one's own ownership and the production of ownership in another. Others, however, say that because no connection with a giver of the cognition is perceived, the term is used figuratively.

In the expression "he gives his daughter," even though the relationship of produced and producer is not excluded, the primary meaning of the root *dā* (to give) applies because the relationship of owned and owner has ceased; this is as in "the teacher Khaṇḍika gives him a slap," where, although there is in fact no ownership of the slap, the giver indeed possesses the intention of ownership by virtue of being its benefactor. Even if, due to its adverse nature, the slap serves no immediate purpose at that time, it nevertheless possesses utility for another through its ultimate result.

Because one who can endure a slap is fit for the study of the scriptures and thereby attains the fruit [of that study], the dative case is used in the sense of "for the purpose of" (tādarthye), according to the rule: "The root *mṛj* is taught specifically with this meaning. The meaning is that the root *mṛj*, though listed in the general [list of roots], also possesses the meaning of the word *mārjaka* ("one who cleanses"). || 129 ||

Thus, the first [type of] recipient (*sampradāna*) has been explained. Now, in order to explain the subsequent one, he says: "When it functions as a cause (*hetu*), when it receives the designation of object (*karman*), or even when it is a residual factor (*śeṣa*), that *kāraka* is designated by the technical treatise as a 'recipient' (*sampradāna*) in the case of verbs meaning 'to please' (*rucy-artha*) and others. (130)

Just as action (*karma*) was previously explained as being preceded by a different designation (*saṃjñāntara*), so too this recipient (*sampradāna*) is explained in the treatise as being preceded by another [designation], by means of the rule beginning with *rucyarthānāṃ prīyamāṇaḥ*. For instance, in the sentence "The sweetmeat is pleasing to Devadatta" (*devadattāya rocate modakaḥ*), the meaning of the root *ruc* is a desire whose agent is another; thus, Devadatta employs the sweetmeat—which has become the object of that desire—and, out of greed, acts in accordance with it. Consequently, when the designation of the instigator (*prayojaka*) would have applied to Devadatta under the category of "cause" (*hetu*), the designation of "recipient" (*sampradāna*) is stated instead.

And thus, when the designation "cause" (*hetu*) is set aside, there is an absence of the causative suffix (*ṇic*); consequently, since a second action inherent in the cause is not perceived, the sweetmeat (*modaka*) becomes the agent (*kartṛ*)—not the object (*karman*)—with respect to its own action expressed by the verbal root. The meaning is that it "pleases," i.e., it attains the state of being an object of desire. This is because even the designation "agent" (which would otherwise apply to Devadatta) is superseded by the application of the designation "cause," and [therefore] the sweetmeat lacks the status of being that which is most desired by the agent's action.

Even though the verbal root *kṛ* (in *hīyate*) expresses independence (*svātantrya*), the designation of "object" (*karman*) does not apply to the caravan here in order to justify the use of the *l*-suffix in the sense of the object. For the status of being an object based on that [independence] would only occur where independence is perceived with respect to an action expressed by the word itself. Thus, in the case of *hīyate*, since the act of abandoning (*hāna*) is expressed by the word, the designation of "object" applies to the traveler, who is the substratum of that [abandonment], while the caravan is the object of the act of abandoning.

In this case, however, when the action of eating the sweetmeat (*modaka-kriyā*) is expressed by the word [in *devadattāya rocate modakaḥ*], Devadatta’s independence (*svātantrya*) is not perceived from the verb *rocate*. For if one were to disregard the operation of the word, actual independence would pertain only to the general category of *kārakas*, and thus the explicit mention of the agent (*kartṛ-śruti*) would be redundant. But when the meaning is "the sweetmeat is pleasing to Devadatta," which is to say "the sweetmeat pleases Devadatta," and the qualifier "being pleased" (*prīyamāṇa*) is applied, then since the designation of object (*karman-saṃjñā*) would otherwise apply, the designation of recipient (*sampradāna-saṃjñā*) is initiated. For it is only when the verbal root functions in a different sense that it possesses transitivity (*sakarmakatva*).

Thus, in the expression "he praises Devadatta" (*devadattāya ślāghate*), Devadatta—who is being praised for his excellence of qualities—is designated as the *hetu* (cause) because he possesses qualities and performs actions conducive to them, thereby having the status of an instigator superimposed upon him. Alternatively, he is intended to be made known through the proclamation of his qualities; since he is that which is to be made known (*jñāpyamāna*), he receives the designation of *karman* (object). Consequently, by the rule beginning with "ślāgha-hnuṅ," etc., he is stated to receive the designation of *sampradāna* (recipient). The same should be explained, as appropriate, for the verbs beginning with *hnau* (to be ashamed).

For in this context, verbs such as *hnauti* ("to owe") are transitive because they denote the act of making known [something] while subordinating their own primary object. Accordingly, the term "the one being made to know" (*jñīpsyamāna*) is employed as a qualifier for the designated entity. In the example "He owes a hundred to Devadatta," the creditor Devadatta is the cause of the act of owing by means of the act of giving, while the debtor remains established in the state of owing that hundred. Thus, Devadatta is the cause of the act of owing through the mediation of the act of giving.

Since he gives a hundred, yet the act of giving (*dadāti-kriyā*) is not heard [as a separate verb] there, the genitive case would apply here as a residual relation (*kāraka-śeṣa*) regarding a context where no such action is heard; however, by the rule "the creditor in the case of *dhāri*," the designation of recipient (*sampradāna*) is applied. For what is stated applies to the three [categories] beginning with cause (*hetu*) as they may occur, but not individually. Regarding "he desires flowers" (*puṣpebhyaḥ spṛhayati*), it was stated that because flowers are the most desired object (*īpsitatama*), there is the contingency of them receiving the designation of object (*karman*). In the case of verbs such as *druhi* (to injure), however, there is the contingency of the object designation.

Since *druh* (to injure) signifies harm, its objects are transitive. The same applies to roots meaning envy (*īrṣyā*) and malice (*asūyā*). However, in the case of "he divines for Devadatta" (*devadattāya rādhyati*) or "he looks for Devadatta" (*īkṣate*), since the act involves deliberating upon fate, Devadatta is employed as an astrologer; thus, although the designation of "agent" (*hetu*) would have applied, the status of "recipient" (*sampradāna*) is assigned by the rule "for the roots *rādh* and *īkṣ*" (*rādhīkṣyoḥ*).

In the expressions "he promises a cow to Devadatta" (*devadattāya gāṃ pratiśṛṇoti*) and "he hears [the request] from Devadatta" (*aśṛṇoti*), since Devadatta employs the one who promises the cow through a formal request, the designation *hetu* (cause) would otherwise apply; however, by the rule "after the roots *śru* preceded by *prati* and *āṅ*, [the agent of the former action becomes] the recipient" (*pratyāṅbhyāṃ śruvaḥ*), the status of *sampradāna* (recipient) is established. For Devadatta, being the agent of the preceding verbal sense characterized by requesting, becomes the instigator (*prayojaka*) with respect to the subsequent act of promising, which consists of acceptance.

In the cases of "he responds to the Hotṛ" (*hotre 'nugṛṇāti*) and "he chants in response" (*pratigṛṇāti*), although there is the possibility of the Hotṛ being designated as the *karman* (object) in the sense that "he encourages the Hotṛ by means of recitation," the status of the recipient (*sampradāna*) is established by the rule "and [the roots] *anu-gṛ* and *pra-gṛ*" (*anupratiguṇaśca*).
