Regarding the example "be recited for one who has been hired for a hundred" (*śatāya parikrīto 'nubrūhi*), the status of the recipient is stated as an option for the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*) when there is a fixed-term acceptance in the act of hiring. In that context, since the meaning of the root *ruc* and others is easily understood through the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the rule, the possibility of the designation *karaṇa* (instrument) was not mentioned.

And here, in the absence of an intention to express a specific distinction, since the status of being a *śeṣa* (residual category) would apply everywhere based merely on being the cause of the action, the status of being a *sampradāna* (recipient) must be illustrated [as the intended meaning]. For, due to the enumeration of roots such as *duh* (to milk) and others, the status of being an *akathita-karman* (unexpressed object) does not apply here. But surely, even previously, it was stated by the very rule for *sampradāna*: "whom one intends through the object" (*karmaṇā yam abhipraiti*). So how can there be this specific statement [of the present rule] as "by this rule"? It is said in reply:

Because the term *sampradāna* (recipient) is etymologically descriptive (*anvartha*), the worldly sense of "recipient" was explained previously. However, in this context—concerning the domain of roots meaning "to please" (*rucy-artha*) and so forth—the actual sense of "recipient" is absent; rather, because of the power of the grammatical treatise's commencement, the status of being a recipient is stated merely to establish the formal refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the word. Thus, the recipient has been explained as being of two kinds: based on the distinction between the worldly and the technical (*śāstrīya*). || 130 ||

In this context, regarding the examples "he swallows with faith" (*śraddhayā nigalate*), "he arms himself for battle" (*yuddhāya saṃnahyate*), and "she lies down for her husband" (*patye śete*), since these involve roots that are technically intransitive (*akarmaka-dhātu*) and thus lack an object, the status of the recipient (*sampradānatā*) for that which is intended by the agent would not be established. Consequently, it was stated in the *Vārttika*: "The mention of 'action' (*kriyā*) must also be made [in the definition of *sampradāna*]. According to this, the designation of recipient (*sampradāna-saṃjñā*) should apply here to that which is intended by means of the action. This was refuted in the *Bhāṣya*. Since action (*kriyā*) itself is also something to be accomplished by an action, it is a formal object (*kṛtrimaṃ karma*).

In examples such as *śrāddhāya nigalhati* ("he swallows for the sake of the funeral rite"), it was stated that by which action is [the subsequent action] being made the object; namely, by the action of "beholding" (*saṃdarśana*) and so forth, because that action of beholding and so forth is denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*) without distinction [from the main action]. To justify how the relationship between action and factor (*kāraka*) is possible when based on non-distinction, he says: "When there is an intention to express distinction, each preceding action is the object (*karman*) with respect to the subsequent subordinate member; therefore, the term 'action' (*kriyā*) was not included [in the definition]. (131)

Since it is attained through resolutions such as the desire for sight (*sandarśana*) and so forth, even an action (*kriyā*) is an artificial object (*karma*). In that regard, when one who acts with foresight engages in activity, [actions] such as "seeing" are necessarily perceived as being present; thus, when there is a desire to express the distinction between these and the primary action, it is not contradictory for each subsequent factor—which serves the primary action—to function as an object (*karman*) relative to its preceding action, because it is brought about by that preceding action. Therefore, even an action may possess the status of an object.

Since the status of the recipient (*sampradāna*) for one who is connected by that [action] is established by the sūtra itself, the inclusion of the word "action" (*kriyā*) has been rejected. This [interpretation] that it refers to the object of the root *dā* ("to give") is not accepted. In this context, the primary action alone is expressed by the verbal root; however, actions such as "showing" (*saṃdarśana*), which are obtained through contextual implication, are distinct from that [primary action]. Thus, the relationship between action and its factors (*kāraka*) is logically established. For example:

Regarding the phrase "he is separated from the caravan" (*sārthād dhīyate*), the independence of the caravan that is implied is the cause for its status as the object (*karman*). Alternatively, because [the caravan] exists for the sake of that [action], even though it is denoted by verbal roots as being non-different from the primary action due to having attained identity with it, there is no total suppression of difference. Thus, the status of being an object is established through the cognition of difference inferred from the effect called non-difference. || 131 ||

If this were so, then even in cases such as "he cooks rice" (*odanaṃ pacati*), that which is intended for the action by means of the object would receive the designation *sampradāna*. However, since the designation *karman* (object) has its scope in the objects of the action [itself], he says: "But when unity is intended in the collection of actions, then the object, through its connection with the action, is figuratively designated by its own name. (132)

When a collection of actions such as "showing" (*sandarśana*) and so forth—which have not lost their mutual status as auxiliary members (*aṅga*), but rather exist in a state of equal rank and are combined as a composite—is accepted by the verbal root (*dhātu*) as non-different because they share a single result, then, since the relationship between action and its factors (*kriyākārakabhāva*) based on differentiation is no longer perceived, the object (*karman*) such as boiled rice (*odana*) connected with that action which has not yet attained the status of an object is designated by its own name through the very technical term "object" (*karmasaṃjñā*), which is caused by the action being most desired (*īpsitatama*). It is not, however, [designated otherwise].

The meaning is: by means of the technical designation *sampradāna*. Because they are expressed as being in conjunction (*samuccaya*), there is no relationship of subordinate and principal (*aṅga-aṅgibhāva*); therefore, in this view, the action does not possess the nature of an object (*karman*). || 132 ||

Anticipating the objection that "in that case, if one intends to express a distinction [between the self and the body], there would be the status of recipient (sampradānatā) here," he says: "The intention to express either distinction or non-distinction is established by its own nature. Therefore, no deviation is observed regarding the status of being the object of a verb meaning 'to go'. (133)

The meaning is as follows: since worldly usage is well-established, when providing grammatical analysis (anvākhyāna) with reference to that usage, one may employ various means according to the specific instance, resulting in a desire to express either difference or non-difference as determined by the context. In this way, the rules prescribing the second and fourth case endings for the object of a verb meaning "to go" (gaty-artha-karmaṇi) are also established based on the respective desire to express both [difference and non-difference]; thus, there is no need for a separate rule to initiate them. Furthermore, because there is a restriction toward expressing non-difference elsewhere, there is neither deviation nor over-extension (atiprasaṅga). || 133 ||

He confirms this very point with scripture: "If both designations were applicable everywhere by means of conceptual construction alone, then the rejection of the undertaking of yoga would be equivalent [to its acceptance]. (134)

If one does not rely on a restriction regarding the intention to express either difference or non-difference, then since the designations of *karman* (object) and *saṃpradāna* (recipient) would apply everywhere, the author of the Bhāṣya would not have rejected the rule beginning with *gatyarthakarmaṇi* for the sake of restriction; for if it were rejected, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). However, when the restriction of intention flashes before the mind of the author of the Bhāṣya, then, considering there to be no distinction between its formulation and its rejection, it is appropriate that he should reject it. Thus, in the domain of roots meaning "to go," there are two possibilities of intention.

In examples such as *śrāddhāya nigalhati* ("he swallows for the sake of the ancestral rite"), there is indeed an intention to express distinction (*bheda*). In examples such as *pacaty odanam* ("he cooks rice"), there is indeed an intention to express non-distinction (*abheda*). Furthermore, even in the counter-examples for the rule *ceṣṭāyām anadhvani*, there is an intention to express non-distinction, as in *manasā pāṭaliputraṃ gacchati* ("he goes to Pāṭaliputra mentally") and *adhvānaṃ gacchati* ("he goes along the road"). Regarding the formulation of the sūtra, since the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) would apply to cases such as *striyaṃ gacchati* ("he approaches a woman") and *ajāṃ nayati* ("he leads a goat"), it was stated: "But [the desired result] is established by the mention of 'not having reached' (*asaṃprāpta*)."

Regarding an action that is not reached (*asaṃprāpta*) by going and is not connected [to the agent], the second and fourth case endings should be prescribed. However, because the rule "the second and fourth cases are used for actions that are reached (*saṃprāpta*)" applies specifically to feminine nouns such as *ajā* ("she-goat") and *stri* ("woman"), there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, regarding the formulation of this specific sūtra, it was stated that "it is not an exception to [the rule concerning] the path (*adhvan*). Thus, the prohibition "on the path" need not be stated. For here, the intention is to prohibit [the application of the rule] to the path when it is an action that is reached; however, its exclusion is already established simply by the mention of "not reached."

For this very reason, it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "A prohibition regarding that which has already been established must be formulated. Here, the path that has already been traversed (āsthita-adhvā) is to be understood as the object of the prohibition. || 134 ||

Because of the statement, "The term 'road' (adhvan) includes its synonyms," there is a prohibition [of the designation *gamyamāna*] even for synonyms of a road, as in examples such as *panthānaṃ gacchati* ("he goes along the path"). A road is "occupied" (*āsthita*) when it is traversed by the action of going. An example: indeed, a path on which the act of going has commenced is said to be "occupied. In this case, this action of going is twofold: with respect to that portion of the occupied path which is yet to be crossed, the action takes the form of relinquishment (*tyāga*), that is, the form of departure (*hīna*).

However, regarding the portion that is to be reached and set down, there is a twofold action characterized by the distinction between the parts of relinquishment (*tyāga*) and acquisition (*upādāna*), namely the form of contact and the form of attainment. Thus, the path traversed by an uninterrupted flow of action consisting of the forms of relinquishment and acquisition falls within the scope of the technical term "object" (*karman*) as prescribed merely by its status as the domain of action; it is not, however, connected with the action itself as its object, because there is no differentiation of the action. Consequently, the designation "recipient" (*sampradāna*) does not apply.

The connection with that [suffix] occurs only in the case of villages and the like when they are not reached by the means [of travel] and are of the nature of a non-path (*anadhvan*). However, in the case of a path that is not fixed (*anāsthita*), only two case-endings occur. And how does a path become "not fixed"? When one reaches the path by a wrong way, as in *pathe gacchati* ("he goes on the path") or *panthānaṃ gacchati* ("he goes to the path"), then such a distinction must be stated at the beginning of the Sūtra. But if it is rejected, the desired result is established simply through the restriction of the speaker's intention (*vivakṣāniyama*). || 135 ||

Thus ends the section on the recipient (*sampradāna*) in the *Sādhanasamuddeśa* of the *Prakīrṇaprakāśa* composed by Helārāja, son of Bhūtirāja. Now, following the sequence for the application of case-endings (*vibhakti*), once the meaning of the dative has been determined through an investigation of its referents, the author speaks in order to examine the ablative (*apādāna*), whose occasion has now arrived: "The ablative is said to be threefold: that whose object is explicitly stated (*nirdiṣṭaviṣaya*), that whose object is implied (*upāttaviṣaya*), and likewise that which requires an action (*apekṣitakriya*). (136)

When "separation" (*apāya*) is to be established, that which is constant, uniform, and characterized by an action not yet entered into by separation—even when another [entity] has already entered into separation—is the cause of that [separation] and is called the *apādāna*. Because it depends upon a specific limit (*avadhi*), the object of the *apādāna* is a separation whose agents are both one who has initiated [the action] and one who is indifferent; that [agent] is "indicated" (*nirdiṣṭa*) when it is expressed by its own word, and such is the single *apādāna*. For example: "He comes from the village," "He descends from the mountain," and so forth.

*Upāttaviṣayapādāna* (appropriated-object ablation) is that where the object characterized by departure (*apāya*) is appropriated as either a subordinate or a primary factor for another action. For example: *valāhakād vidyotate* ("it lightens from the cloud"), *kusūlāt pacati* ("he cooks from the granary"), and *brāhmaṇācchaṃsī* ("the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin priest"). In these cases, the verb *vidyuti* ("to lighten") occurs with respect to the departure which is a subordinate part of the act of lightning, or with respect to the departure which is a subordinate part of the act of emerging; thus, the departure characterized as "emerging" is appropriated as a subordinate or primary factor for the act of lightning.

The meaning is that light flashes forth from a cloud, or that what is flashing forth emerges from a cloud. In the expression "having taken [grain] from the granary, he cooks," the root *pac* (to cook) refers to the act of cooking as being subordinate to the act of taking. In "having received [instruction] from a Brāhmaṇa, he recites," the root *śaṃs* (to recite) functions with reference to the recitation as being subordinate to the act of receiving. Regarding the form *brāhmaṇācchaṃsī*, the elision (*luk*) of the suffix is not applied according to the rule "In the section on the fifth case, there is an addition [of the suffix] for *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*. In this context, the author of the Vārttika intends the fifth case to have the sense of the second case; as he says: "And [this applies] when it has another meaning [than that of the ablative]."

He who recites the *brāhmaṇas*, which are specific types of texts, is called the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsī*. In this context of grammatical derivation (*vṛtti*), it should be stated that the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used in the sense of the accusative (*dvitīyārtha*). However, the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*), stating that the root *śaṃs* (to recite) functions here with reference to the act of recitation as a subordinate part of the act of "bringing forth" (*āharaṇa*)—meaning he recites after having taken up or brought forth [the text] from the *brāhmaṇa*—considers this [ablative usage] to concern the object already acquired.

The *apādāna* (ablative) is that which requires an action (*apekṣitakriya*), where, because no verbal expression for the action is found in any way whatsoever, an unexpressed action is inferred; this inferred action serves as the cause for the manifestation of distinct capacities (*śaktibheda*) among the related substances, which serve as the grounds for specific technical designations (*saṃjñāviśeṣa*). For example: "The people of Mathurā are wealthier than those of Pāṭaliputra. Here, by the force of the suffix denoting excellence (*prakarṣa*), an action of "inferiority" (*apakarṣaṇakriyā*) characterized by "departure" (*apāya*)—which is the cause of separation—is inferred; thus, such an action is required here.

However, in the case of an object that has been appropriated (*upāttaviṣaya*), the departure (*apāya*) is accepted by the verbal root itself, because roots have multiple meanings. For instance, in examples such as *valāhako vidyotate* ("the cloud flashes"), *caitraḥ pacati* ("Caitra cooks"), and *dāśatayīḥ śaṃsati* ("he recites the ten-fold hymns"), although the roots denote merely the acts of flashing and so forth, there is no contradiction in their application elsewhere to include components such as "going out" (*niḥsaraṇa*). Indeed, the departure is understood here by the force of the heard fifth case (*pañcamī*). Furthermore, since that [departure] is logically possible only when the meaning of the root includes the component of "going out" and not otherwise, its status as the meaning of the root is determined. (136)

But what is this "departure" (apāya)? Is it merely a motion? No; he says: Just as motion itself, though having a single nature, appears divided due to the difference in its conjoined objects—as in the case of [the perception of] rotation—so too does departure, which has a fixed limit, appear as inherent in that which is not fixed. (137)

By association through concomitance (*sāhacarya*), even disjunction (*vibhāga*) is accepted as a limiting factor (*avadhi*). Therefore, just as the effects of conjunction and disjunction delimited by a specific direction are designated as "going" (*gamana*) itself—such that "revolving" (*bhramaṇa*) is called "going"—and just as the Kaṇādas maintain that by the mention of "going," revolving, receding, vibrating, and so forth are included and not distinct classes (*jātyantara*), likewise, that which has a fixed, immovable, unoccupied, and non-disappearing limit is [the locus] of that which is inherent in the unfixed and moving.

The specific movement known as *apāya* (separation/departure)—which is to be understood as having the characteristic of a division residing in both the agent and the object of that action, and which is to be accomplished by means of an active (*saṃrabdha*) or indifferent (*udāsīna*) instrument—is indeed the result. Although this action inheres in the mover (*gantṛ*), it receives the name *apāya* because it requires a limit (*avadhi*). Thus, the intention is that the status of being a *kāraka* (grammatical participant) is established for the fixed point (*dhruva*) because it serves as the cause for the accomplishment of the action.

Furthermore, that *apāya* (separation), which exists as the objective domain for the designation *apādāna*, is expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*) either explicitly or by implication; since it is established that the *apādāna* is the fixed point (*dhruva*) in the process of separation, the status of being a cause (*nimittatva*) belongs to the *kāraka* designated as "fixed. Thus has *apāya* been explained. For in common worldly usage, "fixed" (*dhruva*) is well known to mean stable and immovable. Consequently, this was raised as an objection in the *Vārttika*: "The designation *apādāna* is not applicable to things connected with motion, because they lack fixity."

The meaning is that in cases such as "he fell from the running horse" (*dhāvato'śvāt patitaḥ*) or "he was left behind by the departing caravan" (*sārthād gacchato hīnaḥ*), since the [moving] entities involved in the action of going lack the quality of being fixed (*dhruvatva*), stationary (*sthiratva*), or immobile (*acalatva*), the designation of *apādāna* (ablative) does not apply. To this, the following solution is stated: "Or rather, it is not so, because the state of being fixed is not intended to be expressed. (137)

To explain this, he says: "In the sūtra, the state of being a substance is understood as non-permanence; however, that which is intended here is permanence with respect to the object of departure. (138)

In the Sūtra, the nature of a substance (*dravyasvabhāva*)—namely, that which is fixed (*dhruva*), immovable (*kūṭastha*), and inactive (*niṣkriya*)—is not what is intended by the term *dhruva*. Rather, here the word *dhruva* refers to that which is unshakable (*asaṃtuṣṭacalana*). For instance, when something is fixed (*dhruva*) in relation to a removal (*apāya*) that is to be accomplished, the meaning is that it remains untouched by that removal. And this being the case, in the example "he fell from the running horse," since the act of falling does not have the horse as its agent, the horse remains unaffected by it; thus, the horse's status as *dhruva* (fixed) is indeed present there. For a removal (*apāya*) is accomplished either by an active agent (*saṃrabdha*) or by a neutral instrument (*udāsīna-sādhana*).

In that context, the horse is indifferent (*udāsīna*), whereas the one who has departed is agitated (*saṃrabdha*). In the example "He comes from the village to the mountain by way of the path," although the path (the instrument) and the mountain (the object) possess the status of being fixed (*dhruva*) because they do not enter into the action of departure, the designation of "ablative" (*apādāna*) does not apply; rather, it is set aside by the designations of "instrument" (*karaṇa*) and so forth due to their higher priority. Thus, the Vārttika states: "The subsequent [designations] supersede the ablative: he pierces with a bow, he eats from a bronze plate, he milks the cow, he draws the bow."

Thus, because the object of destruction (the horse) is resorted to, and because the destruction does not enter into the horse itself, non-eternality—which in reality pertains to that [destruction] as its object—indeed exists, yet it remains unintended; such is the meaning of the Vārttika. || 138 ||

For instance: "Devadatta's permanence [is seen] in his remaining alive, whereas the horse's permanence [is seen] in its falling; that which is entered by passing away is declared to be impermanent. (139)

Just as Devadatta possesses stability (*dhrauvya*) despite his rapid motion consisting of running, because he is not permeated by that running, so too the horse (*vājinaḥ*) possesses stability despite its falling—the action of falling—inhering in Devadatta, because it is not permeated by that [falling]. This is an illustration presented by way of the relationship between the example and the thing exemplified (*dṛṣṭānta-dārṣṭāntika*). In both cases, stability is established through the non-penetration (*anāveśa*) of the departure [of the action], which is stated by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) as the logical reason (*hetu*).

Even though Devadatta remains stationary (*dhrauvya*) while the horse is running away, the designation of "ablative" (*apādāna-saṃjñā*) does not apply; for it will be stated later that "without a limit (*avadhi*), there is no departure (*apāya*)," and thus Devadatta is not presented here as a limit (*avadhi*). However, if he were so presented—as in the example "the horse runs away from Devadatta who is himself running"—then the designation would indeed apply. Anticipating the objection, "In cases where both [parties] possess motion, how can the distinction between the stationary (*dhruva*) and the non-stationary (*adhruva*) be determined? the author says:
Although both rams are unstable when the disjunction is produced by the actions of both, the two actions are nevertheless intended to be distinguished therein. (140)

In the case of "the hawk flies away from the post" (*sthāṇoḥ śyeno'pasarpati*), since the separation arises from the action of only one [of the two], the post is determined to be the fixed point (*dhruva*) because the act of going away (*apāya*) does not inhere in it. Even in the case of "one ram flies away from the other ram" (*apasarpato meṣānmeṣo'pasarpati*), where the separation arises from the actions of both, although both rams are non-fixed points because the act of going away inheres in them, nevertheless, because the act of going away of one does not inhere in the other, the two actions characterized as going away are distinct due to the difference in their agents. || 140 ||

Consequently, the status of being a limit (avadhitva) for each of the two rams is distinct, depending respectively upon the action of the other ram; and their status as agents (kartṛtva) is also distinct, depending respectively upon their own individual actions. (141)

Because there is no mutual penetration of one action by the other, when one performs an action distinct from the other's, both remain stable in their respective actions; thus, both possess the status of agent (*kartṛtva*) with respect to their own actions. However, when the state of being a relative limit (*avadhibhāva*) between them is not intended to be expressed, but rather the two actions—though residing in two [different substrates]—are intended to be expressed as conveyed by a single word, [then the rule for *parasmaipada* applies]. 141.

Regarding this, he says: "If an action is intended to be expressed as one and the same, though accomplished by two [agents] without distinction, then the two rams are the agents at the time of their departure, provided there exists another limit. (142)

In the expression *meṣāvapasarpataḥ* ("the two rams move away from each other"), the verbal suffix conveys a single action accomplished by two agents; thus, both rams possess agency through their involvement in that action. However, because of the act of moving away (*apāya*), one of them cannot simultaneously function as the point of departure (*avadhi*), which would constitute the status of an ablative (*apādāna*). This being the case, the rams possess the agency of the act of moving away when [the construction is] *anyaḥ parvatād apasarpati* ("one moves away from the mountain"), or *parasparam meṣāv apasarpatas* ("the two rams move away from each other"), or *parasparato meṣāv apasarpatas* ("the two rams move away from one another").

Thus, in this formulation, it is stated that for the two [entities], there is the status of being a limit (*avadhitva*) with respect to the action of the other sheep, and the status of being an agent (*kartṛtva*) with respect to their own respective actions. For here, despite the unity of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), an inference regarding the difference in actions is perceived due to the difference in agents.

If another limit (avadhi) exists, then [the agent] is the cause of the departure of the ram, and not otherwise; he says the following to establish this through agreement with the text of the Bhāṣya: "It is understood that there is no departure without a limit; this is illustrated in the Bhāṣya by the example: 'The leaf of the tree falls. (143)

In the *Kāraka-sūtra*, the instruction to specify the technical name (*saṃjñin*) was enjoined as something that must be stated: "It should be said that a *kāraka* is that which effects [an action]. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of even that which is not a cause of action being called a *kāraka*. This was illustrated in the *Vārttika*: "And [the rule for] the *apādāna* [would apply], as in the example: 'The leaf of the tree falls'. Since the *Bhāṣya* includes the *Vārttikas*, he refers to it as the "*Bhāṣya*. Furthermore, this is not an indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the fact that motion (*gati*) has a limit (*sāvadhi*) as its object; rather, it is for the purpose of providing a rebuttal [to that objection] with the words: "Or rather, [it is not so] because the departure (*apāya*) is not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣitatvāt*)."

By the phrase "as it has been stated," the body of the Bhāṣya is indicated here. And this is the meaning: since the intended sense of the sentence is the falling of a leaf belonging to a tree, there is no intention here to treat the tree as a limit (*avadhi*). Consequently, this does not constitute a "separation" (*apāya*).

Because it is not intended to be expressed as an *apādāna* (ablative) in the form of a limit (*avadhi*) with respect to separation (*apāya*), the tree does not possess the status of an *apādāna* here; however, if separation were intended to be expressed here, then because the tree would be the limit, the expression "the leaf falls from the tree" (*vṛkṣāt parṇaṃ patati*) would occur, and consequently, it would not be known whose leaf it is—whether of a heron (*kaṅka*) or of a crow (*kura*), as has been stated.

Therefore, since the tree is intended as a qualifier of the leaf (*parṇa*), this usage occurs even when the leaf has not left the tree but is touching the ground while on a branch; thus, the intention to express "separation" (*apāya*) has been stated. From this it is understood that separation is movement with a limit (*sāvadhika-gati*), not pure [movement]. Otherwise, if the limit were not intended to be expressed, the status of the ablative (*apādānatva*) would certainly apply here because separation is possible; thus, this serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). And so, since the limit is implied by the very act of separation, it is its [the leaf's] own qualifier.

Just as in the case of the word "sound" (*śabda*), the inclusion of the term "constant" (*dhruva*) is for the purpose of conveying the understanding of a named entity; it is explained that this is intended to show that ruin can be brought about by both those who are actively engaged and those who are indifferent. || 143 ||

[The author] has removed pride. Now this must be stated: Kātyāyana has stated that there is a conflict (vipratiṣedha) based on the rule "the subsequent [kāraka-designations] supersede the ablative" (*apādānam uttarāṇi*). Thus, since the ablative is superseded by the kārakas already mentioned, the co-occurrence of designations shown in the Bhāṣya—such as *valāhakād vidyotate*, *valāhake vidyotate*, and *valāhako vidyotate*—is contradictory; having raised this doubt, he says the following in order to justify the Bhāṣya: "Difference and non-difference, separation and persistence—all these mutually exclusive properties are not intended to be expressed simultaneously with respect to the cloud. (144)

A cloud (*valāhaka*) is a conglomeration of smoke, light, water, and wind; therein, there is the flashing of the light-component. And when that light is intended to be expressed as distinct from that cloud which consists of the aggregate, then—under the intention of expressing distinction—it is either intended to be expressed as separate, or as existing within it.

When separation (*pṛthagbhāva*) is intended to be expressed, then the cloud (*valāhaka*) is the limit (*avadhi*) of the departure (*apāya*) characterized by that separation; thus, this *apādāna* is explained as having its object explicitly mentioned (*upāttaviṣaya*). In the expression "the lightning flashes from the cloud" (*kalāhakād vidyotate vidyut*), the lightning flashes in the form of light after becoming separate from and emerging out of the cloud; therefore, the verbal root *vidyotate* has emergence as its constituent part (*niḥsaraṇāṅga*).

However, when—because light cannot exist without a substratum—the cloud (*valāhaka*) is intended to be expressed as its substratum because it serves as the cause for its persistence, then that [cloud] acquires the designation of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), as in the expression "it flashes in the cloud" (*valāhake vidyotate*). The meaning is: "having stayed in the cloud, it shines. Since lightning-fire (*vaidyuta jātavedas*) has water as its fuel, the cloud—even though it is full of water—is a suitable substratum for it.

Thus, because of the distinction of water and because of the obscuration by earthly smoke, there is no difference from the cloud (*valāhaka*) so long as fire lacks the capacity to act as an illuminator; however, when the intention is to express their difference, the manifestation of two powers is shown in the cloud. Furthermore, distinctness and persistence exist only with respect to different objects.

But when, due to the transparency of the substance of the cloud (*valāhaka*), water and so forth do not act as an obstruction to the light of fire even there, and thus the aggregate called "cloud" is intended to be capable of flashing by virtue of its fiery components—without [perceiving] a distinction between them—then the power of the agent alone manifests in the expression, "the cloud flashes" (*valāhako vidyotate*). For designations pertaining to the parts indeed extend to the whole.

For example, in the expression "the grove has put forth new shoots" (*kisalayitam upavanam*), although the word "grove" (*upavana*) denotes a collection of trees, that collection is fit to be designated in such a way when its constituent parts have produced new shoots. Thus, due to a difference in intended meaning (*vivakṣābheda*), the cloud (*valāhaka*) is cited in the Bhāṣya as having distinct capacities in turn; however, this is not in the case of an intention regarding a secondary capacity (*upacchakti*). Therefore, there is no contradiction whatsoever with the statement concerning the prohibition of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). 144.

Regarding the example cited as a contradiction, he states that in that case there is a simultaneous intention to express both capacities: "In the expression 'he pierces with a bow,' since the status of the instrument does not exist without the intention to express the departure [of the arrow], therefore those two are expressed together. (145)

It has been illustrated that because the designation *karaṇa* (instrument) takes precedence, it subverts the designation *apādāna* (ablative) in the expression "he pierces with a bow. In that case, there is a simultaneous application of both designations as they are necessarily required; thus, both the state of being the most effective means (*sādhakatamatva*) and the state of being the point of departure (*apāya*) reside together in a single substance. This is because, in the act of piercing, the status of the bow as the most effective means does not exist without the intention to express the point of departure.

For one does not pierce with a bow as one does with a staff; rather, it is the bow that, by coming into a state of contact with the retreating arrow, becomes the instrumental cause of the piercing. Thus, when there is an intention to express both [functions] simultaneously, even though their capacities have different objects, they exist in a relationship of cause and effect (*nimitta-naimittika-bhāva*). Consequently, because they coexist in a single substance, there arises a conflict regarding the production of two distinct technical designations (*saṃjñā*) based on their respective causes, since it is impossible for two case-endings (*vibhakti*)—which are the effects of those designations—to arise simultaneously from a single nominal stem (*prātipadika*). This conflict occurs within the scope of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning "one designation" (*ekasaṃjñā*).

Because it is predominant, the case-ending occurs on account of the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "instrument" (*karaṇa*). For there is no contradiction here between the two capacities, as they have different objects of application: the bow is the "ablative" (*apādāna*) with respect to the departure of the arrow, but it is the "instrument" (*karaṇa*) with respect to the piercing. Since the substance itself, possessing its manifesting capacity, is the object of the technical designations, there is an application [of both] to one and the same thing when that distinction is disregarded. For, in the formulation of the rules for case-endings, it is the substance itself that is qualified by specific designations such as "ablative" or "instrument."

Furthermore, since there is no contradiction even when multiple designations (*saṃjñā*) apply to a single object, the contradiction here should be explained by way of the differentiation of their functional effects (*saṃjñākāryavibhakti*). This example has been cited as an illustration; therefore, in other instances of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), one should likewise apply the principle that simultaneous expression is not intended. For instance, in the case of "he eats from a bronze vessel" (*kaṃsapātryāṃ bhuṅkte*), the bronze vessel is the substratum for the act of eating—which consists of consuming food—for one who is holding the vessel while eating.

Furthermore, its status as a substratum (ādhāra) is not tenable so long as it does not possess the status of an ablative (apādāna). For when food is taken out from a bronze vessel and eaten, the vessel becomes the ablative; however, for an elephant or similar creature that consumes food together with a leaf-cup, there arises no cognition of that cup as a substratum, such that one would say, "it eats there."

If the bronze vessel (*kaṃsapātrī*) were not the limit for the taking of food, then eating itself could not be accomplished; thus, since there can be no status as a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) without the intention to express the "ablative" (*apādāna*), when both [statuses] are intended simultaneously, there arises the contingency of two technical designations (*saṃjñā*). In such a case, by the rule "the subsequent [designation] prevails over the preceding" (*apādānam uttarāṇi*), the subsequent designation of "locus" (*adhikaraṇa*) sublates the prior designation of "ablative. In the expression "he milks the cow" (*gāṃ dogdhi*), when the verb *duh* expresses the act of causing to flow (*kṣāraṇa*), the separation (*apāya*) is necessarily implied.

For it is not the case that because saltiness does not result when milk is removed from a cow, the cow’s capacity for action—which is invariably concomitant with that removal—does not impel the effect due to its being "other" (para). Likewise, in the expression "the bow pierces," even without the intention to express removal (*apāya*), the bow lacks independence (*svātantrya*) with respect to the act of piercing; thus, when both [conditions] are present, the designation of agent (*kartṛ-saṃjñā*) alone prevails according to the rule: "The subsequent [designation] supersedes the apādāna. || 145 ||

Thus, having accepted two distinct powers (*śakti*) here in this irregular case, it was stated that when they coexist in a single substance due to their inseparable nature, a conflict arises regarding the application of the two designations by way of their respective grammatical operations (*kārya*); therefore, a resolution was given based on the principle of "priority" (*paratva*). Now, relying on the non-difference of the powers, he states the convergence of the two designations upon a single object: "That very same power, being one, exists in two forms. Therein, the cause for the two designations is such that the latter sublates the former. (146)

Even when directed toward different actions, the power (*śakti*) of a substance is one and the same; for by that [single power], the substance accomplishes two actions. Thus, with respect to those two actions, it receives two designations—*apādāna* and *karaṇa*. When two designations apply to a single power, the subsequent designation does not sublate the preceding one because of their mutual contradiction; this means it is due to the governing rule (*adhikāra*) for a single designation.

In the case of the arrow’s departure from the bow, the status of the bow as the limiting factor (*avadhibhāva*) is already included within its very power of being the most effective instrument (*sādhakatamatva*). Therefore, because that [status] is not separate from it, only one single power is postulated for the bow. This is because there is no basis for postulating two distinct powers with separate forms for two effects that are mutually independent. For in the act of piercing, the action of the arrow’s departure is subordinate; thus, it does not imply a separate power within the [bow's] own nature.

It is simply that a single power alone appears as if it were of different forms by virtue of having two actions—one subordinate and one primary—as its objects. [Objection: In that case, let the substance itself be the instrument (*sādhana*) that accomplishes the two actions; what is the use of postulating a "power"? [Reply: This is not tenable. Because this [substance] has an undivided nature, it is impossible for it to be the object of multiple distinct actions. Power, however, is capacity (*sāmarthya*), and it can have many effects. As it has been said: "The distinction among powers is not such as the distinction among the possessors of power."

If this were so, then in the case of the sentence "Having cooked, let the rice be eaten," there too there should be only a single power. This is not tenable; for it is established that when a means is included [within the action], it does not acquire a separate nature and thus does not entail distinct powers based on its own causes. || 146 ||

Previously, however, two powers were described as pertaining solely to two actions, without relying on the relationship of subordinate and principal. Now, this *apādāna* (ablative) is characterized by the rule "that which is fixed (*dhruva*) in separation (*apāya*) is the *apādāna*"; thus, everything within the scope of the ablative case for the *apādāna* is covered by this. But there is another [type], namely the rule concerning selection (*nirdhāraṇa*), separation (*vibhakta*), and those beginning with fear (*bhītrādi*), where the separation is not explicitly mentioned but implied; that is for the sake of the comprehension of the unlearned. (147)

Regarding the rule *pañcamī vibhakte* ("the fifth [case-ending] when there is a distinction"), the prescription characterized by the fifth case that is stated when a distinction (*nirdhāraṇa*) qualified by a case-relation is understood, requires a departure (*apāya*). Since it requires an inferred departure, it is already established by the technical term *apādāna* (ablative). An example of this is: "The people of Mathurā are wealthier than those of Pāṭaliputra."

In this context, since the function of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) has as its object that which is already distinct, the term "distinct" (*vibhakta*) is employed for the purpose of conveying absolute distinction. Thus, its scope consists only of those things presented as being separate, and not such cases as "among cows, the black one has the most milk," because there is no separation from the nature of "cowness. Even when absolute distinction is intended therein, a prior conceptual similarity based on wealth must necessarily be presupposed.

For instance, although the quality of wealth is common to both, the unity of cognition is established; yet, by virtue of a wealth characterized by excellence, there occurs a separation (*pṛthakkriyā*). Thus, there is a dissociation (*viśleṣa*) preceded by a mental connection, which is termed "departure" (*apāya*); consequently, the fifth case ending is established here as *apādāna*. Indeed, this *apādāna* involves an action that is expected [to be supplied]. As stated in the Bhāṣya: "He who has attained equality with them uses the expression in this way."

Since the inclusion of the suffix *-tama* in the section on *kāraka*s indicates that excellence (*atiśaya*) is not intended here, the status of being an *apādāna* is not contradicted even in this case of a figurative, conceptual (*bauddha*) departure. For indeed, the entire linguistic usage of *kāraka*s is based solely upon mental states. As it was stated previously: "When a speaker, having mentally conceived the unity [of the Pañcālas], subsequently divides them from the Kurus, then a departure (*apāya*) is perceived."

Since this is already established by the general rule alone, the commencement of this specific sūtra is for the purpose of restricting the intended meaning (*vivakṣāniyama*) with respect to one who does not understand the Buddhist notion of "falling away" (*apāya*). The meaning is that here, only the intention of "falling away" should be applied.

Likewise, rules such as "the cause of fear for those [roots] meaning fear" (*bhītrārthānāṃ bhayahetuḥ*) and "that which is not endured in the case of *parā-ji*" (*parājerasoḍhaḥ*), which define the technical term *apādāna*, are included here as being subordinate (*guṇabhāvena*). That which possesses such a scope—namely, an action characterized by falling away—is of this nature. Thus, this is in the form of an illustration of the various types of *apādāna* where the scope is explicitly mentioned (*upāttaviṣaya*), intended solely for the instruction of the ignorant, just as before.

For instance, regarding the fear of wolves or the expression "he fears the thief," a person who acts with foresight perceives through his intellect: "If wolves were to reach me, an undesirable event would certainly occur. Having first apprehended the wolves through one cognition, he subsequently effects a separation from them through another cognition. Since the verbal root *bhī* (to fear) functions in this cessation preceded by fear, there is indeed an "undesirable consequence" (*apāya*).

In the expression "he protects from thieves," which denotes the warding off of misfortune, when one says "the protector," having determined through his intellect that association with thieves is a misfortune, he removes his own kinsman from that situation; thus, the possibility of such a misfortune exists. In the case of "he fails at study," one who is exhausted by the practice of study and fears the exertion of attending upon a teacher [desists]; having reached the study, he turns back from it—thus, there is indeed a possibility of failure.

In this context, the verb *parājayati* (to be defeated) refers to turning back preceded by weariness; the meaning is that one turns back from study because one has become weary. However, when there is no engagement from the very beginning, weariness is considered through the intellect [as a reason for non-engagement]: "He constantly serves his gurus with great difficulty and austerity."

Thus, in the case of "he wards off the cow from the barley," this [act] prevents the transgression caused by the destruction of the barley that would result from the cows reaching the barley; therefore, this is a primary *apāya* (separation). In the case of "he wards off the boy from the well" or "he wards off the boy from the fire," one considers the reaching of the well or the fire to be a cause of undesirable results and, out of compassion, causes him to turn away from them; thus, this is an *apāya* preceded by a mental connection (*buddhi-saṃśleṣa*).

"Disappearance from the teacher" (*upādhyāyād antardhatte*) means that, having mentally determined that reaching the teacher's presence involves suffering such as being sent on errands or being reproached, one withdraws from him; thus, there is "separation" (*apāya*). "He studies from the teacher" (*upādhyāyād adhīte*) and "he causes [the text] to come from him" (*āgamayati*) mean that he takes up the text from him; thus, there is separation. For the words uttered from the teacher’s mouth enter the student through a continuous stream (*saṃtāna*); therefore, their departure from the teacher, who stands as the limit (*avadhi*), is perceived. This is stated in the Bhāṣya: "Because of continuity. (*saṃtatatvāt*)

In the case of "he hears from the actor," however, since there is no utility [in the knowledge], the "separation" (*apāya*) is not intended to be expressed. For he does not take up the text from the actor; rather, the true nature of the meaning here is simply that he hears what pertains to the actor. As for the statement "the arrow is born from the horn," since people understand this as "it emerges from it," separation certainly exists. And it has been stated that the categories of meaning in the technical treatises are distinguished based on worldly usage; thus, there is no regard for the systems imagined by outsiders.

For some non-Buddhist (tīrthika) schools, there is a state of distinction based on the transformation of cause and effect; thus, there is a sense of separation. In the statement "the Gaṅgā originates from the Himavat," the Gaṅgā in the form of a stream flows forth from there, which constitutes a primary departure (apāya). And by relying on a figurative departure, the proposal for an "addition" (*upasaṃkhyāna*) regarding the senses of "disgust," "cessation," and "negligence"—namely, *jugupsā-virāma-pramādārthānām upasaṃkhyānam*—has been rejected.

For instance, one who possesses right view (*āstika*) feels aversion toward and desists from unrighteousness (*adharma*); having understood that unrighteousness entails suffering in the hereafter, he withdraws from it preceded by such aversion—thus, there is an "away-from" (*apāya*). On the other hand, an atheist (*nāstika*), having understood that dharma has affliction as its fruit in this very life, turns away from it through negligence; thus he is said to "neglect. In all these cases, since the designation of the ablative (*apādāna*) is already established by the preceding rule, the subsequent injunction is for the purpose of elaboration (*prapañca*). For grammar proceeds by means of definitions and elaborations, as it has been stated: "From that very [source] come the rules," and so forth. Thus it is established. || 147 ||

Thus ends the section on the Ablative (*apādāna*) in the *Sādhanasamuddeśa* of the *Prakīrṇaprakāśa* composed by Helārāja, son of Bhūtirāja. Now, having bypassed the meaning of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*), which follows in the sequence of the rules for case-endings (*vibhakti*) and is characterized as the "residual" (*śeṣa*), he examines the meaning of the locative (*saptamī*), namely *adhikaraṇa* (the locus), which follows in the sequence of the specific grammatical factors (*kāraka*). "That which, though separated from the agent and the object, sustains the action indirectly, and assists in the accomplishment of the action, is recorded in the treatise as the *adhikaraṇa*. (148)

In common worldly usage, [the term *adhikaraṇa*] is expressed with reference to a specific locus (*adhikaraṇa-viśeṣa*) as pertaining to substance, quality, or action. However, in this treatise, because it deals with the section on *kārakas*, when an action is implied, the designation *adhikaraṇa* applies specifically to the action itself by virtue of its specific assistance characterized by "supporting" (*dhāraṇa*). In that context, since the action resides either in the agent (*kartṛ*) or in the object (*karman*), the designation *adhikaraṇa* would apply to those two alternatively (*paryāyeṇa*) by virtue of the explicit statement regarding their supporting the action.

One might suspect that the designation of "agent" (*kartṛ*) would apply to the object of an action residing in the agent, or the designation of "object" (*karman*) would apply to the object of an action residing in the agent; thus, in those cases where the designations of agent or object are precluded as appropriate, the designation of "locus" (*adhikaraṇa*) would follow by default. Anticipating this, it is stated: "intervened by the agent and the object," and so forth. In examples such as "he sits on a mat" (*kaṭe āste*) or "he cooks in a pot" (*sthālyāṃ pacati*), the locus is an indirect auxiliary to the action inherent in [the agent or object], because it supports the agent or the object.

For if there were no substratum (*ādhāra*), the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*) would not be able to receive the assistance (*upakāra*) of the action; thus, by assisting those two, the substratum also assists the action situated within them. Furthermore, since there is no gradation (*taratama-yoga*) in the section concerning *kārakas*, the designation of locus (*adhikaraṇa-saṃjñā*) finds its scope in that which is indirectly the substratum of the action. Consequently, because they are the direct substrata of the action, the designations of agent (*kartṛ*) and object (*karman*) prevail due to their higher status.

Furthermore, since you yourself accept that factors of action (*kāraka*) are causes for the action (*kriyā*), there is no contradiction in their assisting the action through mediation. Even though it was stated "mediated" (*vyavahitām*), the addition of the word "not immediate" (*asākṣāt*) is intended to reinforce the mediation of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) with respect to the support of the action, even when establishing the nature of categories according to worldly convention. For indeed, an object perceived from a word is said to be the cause of linguistic refinement (*saṃskāra*) in accordance with worldly usage.

In expressions such as "he lies on the ground" (*pṛthivyāṃ śete*) or "it is cooked in a pot" (*sthālyāṃ pacyate*), from the verbal form one understands the agent or the object as qualified by the action, not the action alone in its abstracted form; thus, in common usage, the assistance rendered to the action by the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is perceived precisely through its being the substratum of the action, not directly.

Now, he states that even though the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) differs according to distinctions such as "proximity" (*upaśleṣika*) and so forth, this general definition applies to all of them: "In sesame seeds, space, mats, and the like, there is no difference in the proximity; however, the benefits conferred by things that are conjoined or inherent do indeed differ. (149)

Adherence (*upaśleṣa*) is the relation of the locus with that which is located within it; it is by virtue of this that something is a locus. This [relation] is non-different across all three types of loci. However, it is designated as distinct based on the difference in the related entities: in one case, the relation is conjunction (*saṃyoga*) in the case of a locus through contact, while in another case, it is inherence (*samavāya*) in the case of a locus through essential connection.

For instance, in the expression "Devadatta sits on a mat," the contact of Devadatta with the mat—which is a locus through conjunction—is not seen to pervade all its parts; rather, it pervades only a few parts. Because there is no distinction [in this regard from other types of loci], this locus is designated by the general term *aupāśleṣika* (contact-based). However, in the case of "oil in sesame seeds," because the oil-essence, which is a locus through inherence, is connected to the sesame seeds by pervading all their parts according to worldly convention, this is an *vyāpaka* (pervasive) locus.

In the example "birds in the sky" (*khe śakunayaḥ*), since space lacks real parts, this locus is *vaiṣayika* (objective) by virtue of its connection with an imagined region; furthermore, in this case, the meaning of the object (*viṣaya*) is "not existing elsewhere. Similarly, in "fish in the water," this is an *aupśleṣika* (contact-based) locus with respect to the spatial region of the support. In "he dwells with the teacher" (*gurau vasati*), the teacher is the *vaiṣayika* locus regarding the students' conduct which is dependent upon the teacher; here too, the contact (*upaśleṣa*) is conceptual (*bauddha*).

Thus, in the expression "he equips himself for battle," because the activity of donning armor and so forth is undertaken with the intention of fighting, "battle" is the objective (*viṣaya*). In the expression "cows on the Ganges," the word "Ganges" refers to the region by virtue of proximity; this is the locative case based on immediate vicinity (*aupacārika adhikaraṇa*). It has already been determined previously that in cases such as "there is happiness in the absence of the enemy," non-existence functions as a causal factor (*kāraka*) through its conceptual nature. || 149 ||

What, then, are the benefits [of these]? He says: "The non-destruction of gravity, independence when there is an obstruction, delimitation by a specific direction, and so forth—these are the causes of differentiation. (150)

The non-destruction of oil is the benefit conferred by the sesame seed; for if the sesame seed were destroyed, the oil would be dispersed and perish. In the expression "he sleeps on a couch," the substratum (ādhāra) is the independent agent who prevents the gravity of the sleeper from acting; otherwise, there would be a falling due to gravity. In expressions such as "birds in the sky," the utility of that [substratum] consists precisely in the prevention of the connection between the birds and the downward direction by means of the sky. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the attainment of a specific location by means of a substratum such as a cart is included.

The teacher imparts excellence through the refinement of his disciples, and the bedstead and other such items provide stability; thus, these and similar things serve as benefactors. This section, however, serves merely to establish the connection with specific directions: that the sun rises in the east, sets in the west, Agastya is in the south, and the Pole Star is in the north. || 150 ||

Since the existence of all embodied things is dependent on something else, and since even the embodied substratum requires another locus, he asks what the ultimate, primary locus is: "Space alone, because it provides the conceptualization of spatial distinctions for some, is considered the primary supporting power for all things that possess conjunction. (151)

It is well known that the celestial palaces of the planets, stars, and so forth have space as their substratum (*adhikaraṇa*). Even for those things, such as chariots, whose substratum is a portion of the earth, since that portion of the earth itself rests upon space, space alone is the ultimate substratum through a traditional succession; thus he says "all" to include them. However, for things that exist through inherence (*samavāyin*), their own constituent parts are the substratum; even there, ultimately, atoms (*paramāṇu*) are the substratum.

And for those [entities], space alone is the cause of the differentiation of locations and their support; thus, the primary supporting power of entities rests upon space. Nor does there arise a confusion due to their occupying the same location, because space attains the status of a location through its own conceptualization of distinct parts, each facing a limited portion of space occupied by its respective object. As it has been said: "Because of the conceptualization of the distinction of locations."

The meaning is that space (*ākāśa*) is the non-confused substratum for all things because the differentiation of space—which is conventionally treated as a location for those things in conjunction—is postulated by those very things in conjunction, which are themselves non-pervasive. The phrase "of some" refers to the view of those who accept space, namely the proponents of transmigration (*saṃsāravādins*). In this regard, one might ask: what is this so-called space, which lacks direct perception (*anadhyakṣa*) as its means of valid cognition?

If it is argued that the possessor of the quality (the substance) is inferred by means of its quality, sound, [we reply] that this is irrelevant because the fact that sound is a quality of space (*ākāśa*) is itself unestablished. Sound is not a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of a tangible substance (*sparśavat*), because it does not persist as long as the substance exists and because it is perceived elsewhere than its substratum; these arguments and others like them apply equally to color and the other qualities.

Even if a substratum exists, since transformation is observed due to other causes, and since the substantiality of space (*ākāśa*) is unestablished—its being the substratum of sound being a matter of dispute—the quality of "existing as long as the substance exists" (*yāvad-dravyabhāvitva*) is unestablished in sound. Furthermore, because it is perceived only in the region of space delimited by the ear-cavity, its being perceived elsewhere than its substratum is unestablished. Moreover, the possession of multiple momentary specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) perceivable by the same sense organ is restricted by our own established doctrine (*svakṛtānta*) to those things possessing touch; having raised these doubts, [the author] establishes what is well-known in the world regarding the existence of space.
He states the defining characteristic [of space]: "Because of the absence of entities here and there, no designation is possible; they declare that to have space as its cause. (152)

In this context, the foundational power (*ādhāraśakti*) itself, because it cannot otherwise be accounted for, leads one to infer the existence of space (*ākāśa*). For indeed, for those who rely on verbal testimony as a means of valid cognition, the meaning of a word is the referent of that word. And there exists this word: "This constellation stands here. That which is indicated by the term "here" must be some kind of entity; since it is distinct from earth and the other [elements], it takes the name "space. Nor is this a non-entity, for a non-entity—characterized by a total absence of all causal capacity—cannot be designated in such a manner.

For designation (*vyapadeśa*) and definition (*nirūpaṇā*) are based on real entities (*vastu*), because in verbal discourse only that which has been defined possesses the status of a real entity. For this very reason, in cases such as "the absence of a sword is happiness," there exists a basis for the well-known worldly usage [of defining] the absence being defined, namely, space (*ākāśa*), which has become the locus of that absence. However, when one investigates the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of things, everything of the nature of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*) is non-existent, since only the non-dual (*advaya*) is real. Therefore, the intention is that the application of definitions—which relies upon worldly categories that are charming only so long as they are not investigated—is itself contradictory. || 152 ||

Regarding that which was stated—that space is the substratum of all entities—he says that this refers to entities whose nature is already established (*siddhasvabhāva*), whereas time is the substratum of entities whose nature is yet to be established (*sādhyasvabhāva*): "From time actions are differentiated; from space all corporeal forms [are differentiated]. This is the extent of their difference, yet it is based upon non-difference. (153)

"By means of obstruction and permission, the universe is divided by that [Time]"—according to this principle to be stated later, Time, by assisting entities through the differentiation of birth, persistence, and cessation, establishes their distinction by becoming the substratum for their activities. Space, however, by assuming the state of a substratum without confusion for the various distinct objects produced through conjunction with substances that are not all-pervading, divides the individual manifestations of objects according to their specific locations.

This universe, which consists of the manifestation of forms and actions and is characterized by a profusion of diverse appearances, is obtained in worldly transaction according to its respective state; yet, even though it is non-different [from the source] in the primordial state, it is—relative to this—conditioned by the non-duality known as Time and Space (*kāla-ākāśa*). The meaning is that this non-duality called Time and Space is the basis and cause for this manifestation of forms and actions. For even the differentiation of form caused by the power of direction (*dik-śakti*) reaches its final determination through the divisions of the support of space, consisting of "eastern" and "western" locations.

Furthermore, even the distinction between time (*kāla*) and space (*ākāśa*) is caused by the Supreme Brahman, with whom they are absolutely non-different because they are its powers (*śakti*); for it has been established in the First Book (*Pūrvakāṇḍa*) that those two powers are treated as separate. Regarding the rule "The locus of *vasati* preceded by *upa*, *anu*, *adhi*, or *āṅ* is designated as the object (*karman*)," the author of the Vārttika stated: "There is a prohibition [of the designation of object] for *vasati* when it does not mean 'eating' (*aśana*). For example: "He dwells near the village" (*grāme upavasati*).

The author of the Vārttika maintains that just as the verb *tiṣṭhati* denotes a state characterized by the cessation of movement, so too the verb *upavasati* denotes a dwelling characterized by the cessation of eating. Consequently, just as with *tiṣṭhati*, the village has a connection with *upavasati*; thus, the designation of [the village] as an *object* (*karman*) which would otherwise apply is set aside. Furthermore, this Vārttika makes known a restriction of intended meaning (*vivakṣāniyama*): the intention here is not to express the village and so forth as the most desired object (*īpsitatama*), but rather as a locus (*ādhāra*). However, in the Bhāṣya, this Vārttika is rejected.

"In this case, the village is not the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of the root *vas* (to dwell) when preceded by an upasarga. Of what, then? Of [the root] without an upasarga—as in: 'Dwelling in the village, he fasts for three nights. Here is the intention of the author of the Bhāṣya: In this context, the meaning of *upa-vas* is the cessation of eating delimited by a specific period of time. Therein, the specific period of time is an internal factor (*antaraṅga*), while the object (*karman*) is merely the natural one. However, the staying of one who is not eating cannot occur without a locus; thus, a locus is necessarily required. And since that [locus] is not connected with the root *vas* when preceded by *upa*, the designation of 'object' (*karmasaṃjñā*) does not even arise. (153)

Anticipating the objection that—even if this were so—when location (*deśa*) is also required as a restriction just as time is, as in "he fasts at a sacred site" (*tīrthe upavasati*), there would indeed be a connection of the verb *upavasa-* with the location, and thus it would receive the designation of "object" (*karman*); the author states the following to justify the Bhāṣya: "Even though the act of fasting (*upavasi*) depends upon a specific location, it relies solely upon time because of its inherent nature as a verbal activity. (154)

Although there is a connection with a specific location even when the prefix *upa* is used in the sense of abstaining from food by relying on a particular place such as a sacred site (*tīrtha*), nevertheless, that connection with a location is not one established by the inherent power of the word itself; for the meaning of *upavāsa* is simply the cessation of eating.

Furthermore, since that [time] which is indefinite is not possible, a specific time—namely, the moment of death—is implicitly included. The operation of denotation (*abhidhāna*) is simply the activity of a word; its property is its own nature, which is to say, the power of the word (*śabdaśakti*). As for the location, although places such as a riverbank (*tīrtha*) are intended because an existence like Devadatta’s cannot be established without a substratum, they are not included within the meaning of the word, because there is no connection with the location once the eating has ceased.

In this context, the connection with the place is established precisely through that which is an auxiliary (aṅga) [of the vow], namely the act of dwelling. Thus, by means of the act of dwelling as an auxiliary, the place is understood to function as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) for the fast (*upavāsa*). However, its direct connection is indeed with time alone; for since the cessation from eating is restricted to a specific time, and since that [cessation] consists in the nature of not eating, it is mediated by time. But since the dwelling is an auxiliary to that [fast] and is restricted to a specific place, the place functions here as the locus by means of that [dwelling].

For this very reason, the Bhāṣya demonstrates that in the statement "He dwells in the village for three nights fasting" (*grāme vaṃsastrirātramupavasati*), the connection with the village belongs to the act of dwelling (*vāsa*) which is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the fasting, and not directly to the fasting itself. And since that act of dwelling is here merely implied (*ākṣipta*) because it is a constituent part of the fasting, the relationship between the action and its factor (*kriyākāraka-sambandha*) is intended by way of that [dwelling]. For the meaning of the root *upa-vas* is the cessation of eating for a fixed period, which is indeed an auxiliary to the act of dwelling. Therefore, when it is said "he fasts in the village," the village functions as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) in relation to the act of dwelling, which is the subordinate element.

And since the status of time as an object (*karman*) is understood even when it is not explicitly employed, provided there is an expectation of the cessation of the primary act of eating, [the author] says: "Then, even when 'dwelling' (*vasati*) is not employed, the location is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*); and even when the three-night period and so forth are not employed, they are traditionally held to be the object (*karman*) in the context of fasting. (155)

The word "bhāṣye" (in the commentary) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Because a village or similar location is unfit to be connected with the expressed action of fasting (*upavāsa*), it serves as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) for the action of dwelling (*vasati*), which is obtained through implication even though it is not explicitly stated. For a grammatical factor (*sādhana*) implies a suitable action even when that action is not heard. For example, in the command "Enter the cake," the action of eating is implied as the object (*karman*). And in this case, because there is no basis for apprehending a specific [action], existence (*sattā*) is understood in its general form, as its connection [to the locus] is invariable.

In the case where existence has the village as its locus, such that one says "he dwells in the village," the village and other locations stand as the locus with respect to the act of dwelling. However, when the act of fasting (*upavasati*) is being expressed, time alone is the internal locus; thus, even though it is not explicitly stated, this [time] is implied by virtue of its fitness, just as a house is implied by the act of entering.

And in that case, the technical designation *karman* (object), having fulfilled its purpose with respect to the direct substratum (*ādhāra*), does not apply to the location such as a village which is the substratum arrived at by way of the action of "staying" (*vasati*) that serves as a subordinate member (*aṅga*) of the action. This is because, between the primary and the subordinate, the grammatical operation (*kārya*) is understood to apply to the primary; and furthermore, within the section on *kārakas*, the inclusion of the superlative suffix *-tamap* indicates that no emphasis is placed on the degree of excellence among the direct *kāraka* powers themselves. However, this does not imply a disregard for the internal or external relationship (*antaraṅga-bahiraṅga-bhāva*) based on the connection to the action; otherwise, since the object possesses independence (*svātantrya*) in its own operation, it would incur the designation *kartṛ* (agent).

It may be so. Since the designation of "object" (*karmasaṃjñā*) is established by [Pāṇini 1.4.49] through the rule stating that what is most desired (*īpsitatama*) by means of actions such as seeing, etc., the designation of "object" is already fulfilled even in the case of a location, as in *grāmam upavasati* (he dwells near the village), which means he presides over it. Therefore, when the root *upa-vas* has the sense of abstaining from food, time is directly the locus (*ādhāra*) and is designated as the "object"; however, it is settled that the location, even though intended, is a locus only indirectly through its being a constituent part of the action of dwelling (*vas*), and not directly.

As for one who explains that because it consists of cessation (*nivṛtti*), fasting (*upavāsa*) has no connection with a substratum (*ādhāra*), for him there would likewise be no connection here even with time as a substratum. Yet, even for the verb *tiṣṭhati*, which expresses the cessation of motion, there is a connection with a substratum. It is not contradictory for cessation—which is characterized by the suspension of all activity—to possess the nature of an action, as in "he sits in the village" (*grāme āste*), provided it does not exclude other actions. For an action is indeed a specific mode of engagement of the factors of action (*kāraka*), inferable from its result.

And here, this [abstention] consists clearly in the cessation of eating at fixed times. Nor is cessation merely a mental operation consisting of a specific resolve (*saṃkalpa*). For it has been stated that in cases such as "he girds himself for battle," the distinction between the primary action and its components is not intended, since there is no difference between the seeing and so forth and the principal action itself. Thus, in this context, the meaning of the verbal root *upa-vas* is the agent’s activity preceded by a resolve, taking the form of eating and so forth, characterized by the interval of a fixed period of time.

Although the term *kriyātmā* (the nature of action) possesses a connection with its substratum (*ādhāra*), it does not directly connect with that substratum characterized by aversion; rather, such a connection occurs only through the medium of the subordinate action of "staying" (*vasati*). Therefore, it is established that the rule for the designation of the object (*karman*) applies only to the inevitable connection with the substratum known as time (*kāla*). || 155 ||

Thus ends the section on the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) in the *Sādhanasamuddeśa* of the *Prakīrṇaprakāśa* composed by Helārāja, son of Bhūtirāja. Now, the seventh variety of the *kāraka*, the meaning of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyartha*), is investigated. This is the relation characterized as the "residual" (*śeṣa*). To establish how it is both a variety of *kāraka* and yet residual, he says: "The relation is distinct from the [other] *kārakas*; it is preceded by action and *kāraka*.
It is expressed whether the action is explicitly stated or not. (156)

The *śeṣa* (remainder) is that relation which is other than the six specific types of relations characterized as *kārakas*, such as the object (*karman*) and so forth; this is based on the word *śeṣa* meaning "that which is other than what has been employed. Thus, the *Bhāṣya* statement, "The non-intentionality (*avivakṣā*) of the *kārakas* is the *śeṣa*," is explained. By the phrase "preceded by action and *kārakas*," he explains the nature of the *śeṣa* as being a *kāraka*.

For instance, in expressions such as "the king’s man," "the tree’s branch," "the animal’s foot," or "the father’s son," where no action is explicitly heard, there exists a relationship—such as that of owner and owned, part and whole, or producer and produced—in which the status of being a *kāraka* (participant in an action) that existed previously, brought about by actions like giving, abiding, or producing, persists even in the subsequent state. Thus, the *śeṣa* (remainder) is indeed a *kāraka*. For the king gives to the man, and because of that, the relationship of owner and owned subsists as "the king’s man."

In this context, the relationship between action (*kriyā*) and its factors (*kāraka*) is causal in nature, whereas the residual relationship (*śeṣasaṃbandha*) is the result. Indeed, once the relationship between action and its factors has occurred, it ceases after having deposited its result—the residual relationship—within its own substratum. In that process, initially the agent (*kartṛ*) and recipient (*saṃpradāna*) take the forms of "king" and "servant" (*rājapuruṣa*). However, at the time of the residual relationship, since the specific forms such as "agent" and so forth are no longer perceived, there remains only the general status of being a *kāraka* which is subordinate to that [residual relationship], because the causes for designating the distinctions among the instruments (*karaṇa*) and other means have ceased to exist.

The *śeṣa* (remainder) is that which is other than the *kārakas*, [occurring] when the *kārakas* are not intended to be expressed. Furthermore, in the phrase "preceded by a *kāraka*," the word *kāraka* refers to the specific types of instruments (*karaṇa*) and so forth—which are distinct means of accomplishment (*sādhana*)—insofar as they reside in a single substratum with the state of being a *kāraka*; it does not refer to the general category of *kāraka* itself. For substances, whose nature is already established and which are like iron rods [standing independently], there can be no mutual connection; therefore, such a connection is produced solely by action (*kriyā*). Indeed, action, like a ladder, brings substances into contact with one another.

And thus says the Bhāṣya: "Distinctions among the meanings of nominal stems arise through action, such as 'object,' 'instrument,' and so forth. In that context, since no other distinction is observed apart from the forms of object and the rest, the relation called *śeṣa* (residual), which remains in the form of object and so on, establishes its locus upon the word while the specific distinctions of object and the rest have been experienced; it thereby manifests itself in a form where the distinctions of object and the rest are not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣita*).

Consequently, when the states of being the giver (*dātṛtva*) and the recipient (*sampradānatva*) exist between the king and the man, they are fit to be designated as having a "relation" (*sambandha*) in their general form, since in the state of the result their own specific natures are not predominant. Thus, this seventh case (*saptamī*), whose specific forms are not indicated, is reckoned as the source of the *kāraka* [relation], due to the difference in the comprehension of the word's meaning. For the comprehension is different in the case of "the king gives to the man"; for from this [sentence] alone, a gift motivated by the relation of owner and owned is not necessarily understood.

Since a gift can occur even through such instrumental causes as "making" (karaṇa) and so forth, the expression "the king's man" is distinct [from the mere denotation of the stem], because it conveys a relationship of ownership.
