Thus, since their difference is established by this distinction in cognition, the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) is expressed as being differentiated by this factor called "subsidiarity" (*śeṣa*), just as it is by specific factors such as the object (*karman*) and so on. Therefore, this relation—which has for its object a verbal action not explicitly heard—is [determined] because actions such as "giving," which serve as the basis for relationships like that of owner and owned, are not heard [in the sentence].

Furthermore, since acts such as giving are inferred through the otherwise inexplicable nature of the relationship that constitutes the effect, they are indeed present; thus, the coherence [of the sentence] is established by way of them. Moreover, the fact that the relationship between the two related entities and the result is caused by action is certainly based upon their status as *kārakas* (factors of action), just as it is in the case of an object (*karman*); therefore, everything is logically consistent.

Even in cases such as "he comes from near the village" (*grāmasya samīpād āgacchati*) or "the leaf falls from the tree" (*vṛkṣasya parṇaṃ patati*), there is indeed a precedence of action and factor (*kriyākāraka*) in the relationship of proximity and that which is proximate. For the village is the locus (*āśraya*) of the proximity, and likewise the tree is the locus of the leaf. This very principle applies everywhere. However, with respect to the action of coming and so forth, the village and other such entities are said to lack the status of a kāraka.

However, a relation whose object is an action currently being heard is indeed a specific *kāraka*; it is not preceded by that [general relation], because its nature is a general relation (*saṃbandhasāmānya*) in which specific distinctions such as the object (*karman*) are not intended to be expressed, yet it remains precisely a relation between an action and a *kāraka*. An example is "he hears the actor" (*naṭasya śṛṇoti*), and so forth. This is because the technical designations (*saṃjñā*) such as "instrument" (*karaṇa*) do not apply here due to the absence of their respective conditions, and because it lacks the status of an "unspoken object" (*akathitakarman*) despite the inclusion of roots like *duh* in the relevant list. Thus, this "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is distinct from the *kārakas*, yet it is itself a *kāraka*.

Thus, it has been stated that the inclusion of the term *upayoga* (utility/connection) is purposeful. Likewise, in examples such as *mātuḥ smarati* ("he remembers his mother"), *na māṣāṇāmaśnīyāt* ("one should not eat beans"), and *sarpiṣo jānīte* ("he knows [the nature] of ghee," i.e., he uses it), it is stated that the "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is precisely that relationship where the distinctions of object (*karman*), etc., are not intended to be expressed. And in this context, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is prescribed for the remainder. Since a relation resides in two things, it was raised as an objection that the genitive would consequently apply to both related terms: "If it is argued that 'the genitive is used for the remainder,' then there is a prohibition regarding the substantive (*viśeṣya*)."

The meaning is that since the word *puruṣa* (man) in the expression *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* (the king’s man) would also entail the application of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), a prohibition must be made. Furthermore, because the relation [of possession] has already been manifested, the nominative case (*prathamā*) does not apply to the substantive (*viśeṣya*); thus, it too must be prescribed, as stated in the rule: "In that case, there is the prescription of the nominative. To resolve both of these issues, it was stated: "It has been explained by the preceding [rule]. Regarding the objection raised in the *Prātipadikārtha-sūtra*—"An addition must be made for coreferentiality with a cloth, because [the cloth] is additional"—it was replied: "Or rather, no, because it is the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*). That very same point has been restated here by way of extension (*atideśa*).

The meaning of the sentence here is that the relationship of a person [to the king] is understood through the commonality of the constituent parts of this word *rājñaḥ*. Therefore, the sentence-meaning—the relationship—does not serve as the cause for a grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) based solely on the internal word-meanings, because it is external. Consequently, as in the cases of "the brave man" (*vīraḥ puruṣaḥ*) or "the blue lotus" (*nīlam utpalam*), there is an absence of the genitive case here, and the nominative case is established. If this were so, then by this same logic, the genitive case would not occur after the word *rājan* (king), just as it does not occur after words such as *vīra*, and the nominative case would instead apply.

This is not so, because the excellence residing in the qualificand alone constitutes the meaning of the sentence. For that [excellence] is primary; it first attains the state of being assisted by the quality—which requires such assistance—without abandoning its own nature, and thus it is said that the excellence of that [qualificand] alone is the meaning of the sentence. However, for the quality, which functions for the sake of assisting the primary object, since it is impossible for it to be self-sustaining or to provide assistance while remaining in its own form, at the very outset of its operation, it undergoes a transformation into another form that is capable of serving the primary object, in relation to the general category of the related entity.

This has been stated in the Bhāṣya: "An object of this kind is of the very nature of the referent (*artharūpa*) itself. And thus, it is logical that the genitive case of subordination (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*) applies [in cases like *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*]. However, an adjective in grammatical apposition, such as "blue" (*nīla*), attains, as it were, identity with the principal term, such as "lotus" (*utpala*), and does not maintain a state of distinction; therefore, the genitive case does not occur there. || 146 ||

This establishes the true nature of the entity: "Although it resides in both, because it exists for the sake of another, it is distinguished among the qualities; being expressed therein, it is enjoyed even by the primary. (157)

A single relation resides in two loci; therefore, in that case, only a single genitive is logical. If there were two genitives, two relations would be understood. And since that single genitive occurs, it occurs only on account of the subordinate element (guṇa), not from the principal element (pradhāna).

Since this relation resides in both relata—because they form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) through a relationship of subordinate and principal (*guṇapradhānabhāva*), and because it is appropriate for the subordinate elements alone to undergo a transformation of form by conforming to the principal—it bears fruit precisely therein; therefore, it is logical that the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), which expresses the effect of the relation, should arise from the subordinate element alone. For in this way, the relation demonstrates a distinction (*vyatireka*) or an excess (*ādhikya*) in the subordinate elements, whereas the principal element experiences the relation while remaining entirely unmoved from its own essential nature (*svarūpa*).

For its predominance is established only if it does not undergo a change of form in accordance with the subordinate qualities (*guṇa*). And when the relationship is expressed by means of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) based on its being the substratum of the qualities, the form residing in the predominant element is "enjoyed," meaning it is touched upon and indeed expressed. This is what is meant by the statement that the predominance residing in the principal element constitutes the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), because it is perceived through its connection with the subordinate qualities; for a collection of words that are mutually expectant constitutes a sentence.

For when "of the king" (*rājñaḥ*) is understood as denoting lordship (*svāmitva*), it indicates a distinct relation characterized by ownership (*svatva*) in the person (*puruṣa*) as well, since no other [relation] is possible. Thus, because the genitive occurs first with respect to the person, who is the more intimate factor, the external relation is understood solely through the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the syntactic connection (*samanvaya*) with the other word; therefore, the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) alone is involved, and the additional element does not enter into it. However, when the qualifier-qualified relationship is taken at will such that "the king of the person" (*puruṣasya rājā*) is said, then the genitive occurs from the person itself as the subordinate factor (*guṇa*); thus the rule is not violated. || 157 ||

It has been stated that a relation is preceded by an action and its factors (kriyākāraka). In that regard, the relation between the action and its factors is the cause of this [verbal] relation; and since that [causal relation] is inferred from the relation which is its result, it cannot be inferred in its specific form, but only in a general sense, because such is the nature of inference. To the question, "From what, then, is this determination of the specific [relation] derived? he says: "The restriction of the cause of the relation is not grasped from the word itself; however, by means of *karmapravacanīyas*, it is restricted to a specific [instance]. (158)

In expressions such as "the son of the father" or "the foot of the animal," it is precisely through the determination of the specific nature of the related entities that the relation is perceived as being conditioned by specific actions, such as the act of generating [in the case of a son] or the act of standing [in the case of a foot].

In cases such as *rājapuruṣa* ("the king's man"), however, since the relationship of owner and owned can exist even through begging, barter, seizure, and so forth, the specific cause of the restriction (*niyamanimittatva*) cannot be determined at first; nevertheless, because [such a relationship] is invariably concomitant with one of the acts such as giving (*dāna*) and the like, that action is indeed inferred from the very nature of the related entities. Therefore, this is not a domain for *karmapravacanīyas*. In some instances, however, the specific cause is not determined by the power of the word itself; rather, there is a determination of the general cause.

Such is the nature of the objects of *karmapravacanīyas*. By means of those [terms] such as *anu* and others, the meaning of the relation is delimited by a restriction based on a cause (*nimitta*). For instance, in the sentence "It rained after Śākalya’s *saṃhitā*," the causal relationship (*hetu-hetumadbhāva*) between the *saṃhitā* and the rain is communicated by the particle *anu*, as it is produced by the act of perceiving (*niśamati-kriyā*).

Likewise, because [the word *anu*] is observed in association with action in such instances as "having heard elsewhere" (*anyatrānuniśamya*), and because it is accepted that among the *karmapravacanīyas* the expression "they have spoken" (*proktavantaḥ*) serves to manifest an action that has already passed, it does not manifest an action at present. Furthermore, since no verbal form (*kriyāpada*) is heard, and since there can be no manifestation of something residing in that [action] in the absence of an expresser of what is to be manifested, it is not a denoter of that [action] either; for the relation [of the preposition] to its own form is conveyed by the case-ending alone.

However, it lacks the capacity to imply a verbal action because it is devoid of a case-ending that functions as a *kāraka*. Thus, it has been established that *karmapravacanīyas* indicate a specific type of relation. As it is said in the subsequent section: "This [particle] is neither an indicator of an action, nor an expresser of a relation, nor an impeller of a verbal action; rather, it is a differentiator of the relation. Even so, in the expression "The Pañcālas are under Brahmadatta" (*adhi brahmadatte pañcālāḥ*), the relationship of owner and owned is made known by the particle *adhi* through its being caused by such actions as protection and so forth.

In the expression “*abhimanyurarjunataḥ prati*,” the relationship between Arjuna and Abhimanyu—consisting of the roles of the model (*anukārya*) and the imitator (*anukaraṇa*), produced by the action of defeating the enemy and so forth—is revealed by the word *prati*. In other instances as well, this should be understood accordingly. Thus, this is the power of the *karmapravacanīya*s when the relationship concerns an unexpressed action; however, when the action is expressed, the very action being heard is invariably determined to be the cause [of the relationship]. || 158 ||

In this regard, the following is considered: since the genitive case is already established by the rule for the "remainder" (*śeṣa*), what is the purpose of its re-vidhāna by the rule beginning with *adhīgartha*? Furthermore, there is the objection that the qualifier "when the object is the remainder" (*karmaṇi śeṣe*) is untenable due to a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). For if one intends to express the status of being an "object" (*karmatva*), it is not a "remainder" (since it has been stated that the "remainder" consists in the non-intentionality of the *kārakas*). And if one intends to express the "remainder" as the resulting fruit, the status of being an "object" is obscured. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "When [the object] is designated by means of an instrument (*sādhana*) and the action is explicitly heard, the genitive is prescribed word-for-word (*pratipadam*) to prevent compounding. (159)

The factors of action (*kāraka*s), such as the object (*karman*) and so forth, are employed here for the purpose of designating the "residual" (*śeṣa*), and not for their own sake. The sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) occurs in relation to the residual. In what sense is it "residual"? By qualifying the residual through its dependence on the state of being an object and so forth—as in "the object" or "the instrument"—the meaning established is that the residual is that which results [from the action] and is inherent in the same referent as the object and other *kāraka*s. In this way, the application of the qualifier is justified.

The genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*), although already established by the rule "after roots meaning 'to know' (*adhi-i*)," etc., is prescribed here with a restricted scope so that, by means of this re-enactment, the compound might be precluded. For a restatement (*punaḥ-śruti*) serves the purpose of restriction. Thus, the meaning of the sentence is that "only the genitive occurs. In a restrictive rule, the exclusion of others is the primary element, and the other [case] is the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) to be excluded. Here, that which is to be excluded is the absence of the genitive; and since that absence occurs in the case of a compound, by implication (*sāmarthyāt*), this results in a prohibition of the compound.

This has been stated: "The genitive case ending prescribed by each individual rule is not compounded. By this Vārttika, only the operation of the Sūtra is being explained; no new matter is introduced. But where does this prohibition of compounding apply? Wherever the application of a compound is possible. And where is there such possibility? In cases involving words ending in *sup* (case endings), as in *mātuḥ smṛtam* ("remembered from the mother"). || 159 ||

For it is said here: "In the case of a past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*), the genitive case denoting the object of the action is not prohibited; however, a compound with that genitive, when it is characterized as 'residual' (*śeṣa-lakṣaṇā*), is not desired. (160)

It has been stated that the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) connected with a *kṛt* suffix is subject to compounding (*samāsa*). Accordingly, in cases such as "the recollection of Dharma" (*dharmānusmaraṇam*) or "the recollection of Artha" (*arthānusmaraṇam*), where the genitive occurs by the rule "of the agent and the object when a *kṛt* suffix follows" (*kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti*), compounding indeed takes place. For this is not a restriction on the genitive [meaning that the genitive is always compounded]; rather, because the word "object" (*karman*) is repeated in the rule "of the agent and the object when a *kṛt* suffix follows," the reference to the "residual" (*śeṣa*) is excluded. Thus, this is a novel injunction. Therefore, by means of the restriction "only the genitive," it indicates a prohibition of compounding through the gate of the genitive case.

In examples such as *mātuḥ smṛtam* ("remembered by the mother"), when a past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) is used, the genitive case prescribed by the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* is prohibited by the rule *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhā...*. Consequently, since the genitive is established in a general sense by the rule *adhīgarthadayeśāṃ karmaṇi*—which prescribes the genitive for the object when that object is intended to be expressed as a residual relation (*śeṣatvena vivakṣite*)—the fact that this [genitive] is restated here must be understood as being for the purpose of prohibiting compounding (*samāsapratiṣedhārthā*). [Objection: But surely the genitive here is obtained by the rule *ktasya ca vartamāne*, supplemented by the statement *napuṃsake bhāve upasaṃkhyānam* (the addition of the genitive after a neuter past participle used in the sense of an abstract action). [Reply: This is not so.

Because the rule "it is established from the remaining [usage] regarding cognition" (*śeṣavijñānāt siddham*) has been rejected, this [genitive] must be the genitive of the remainder (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*). Furthermore, by its re-statement, it indicates the absence of compounding. Even so, the usage *mātuḥ smṛtam* ("the mother is remembered") would be untenable; since the root *smṛ* is transitive, the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) would have to apply to the object, and due to coreferentiality with "mother," one would have to say *mātā smṛtā* ("the mother is remembered"). However, when there is a requirement for another related entity, the usage *mātuḥ smṛtāyāḥ* ("of the mother who is remembered") is logical. This is true.

It has been stated: "In the case of [verbs] such as *kṛ*, there is an expression as if they were intransitive. Thus, since the object is expressed here by means of a word ending in the suffix *-kta* while the verb is treated as intransitive, when the remaining relation (*śeṣa*) is intended to be expressed, the genitive case is prescribed again; consequently, this results in the prohibition of compounding. This is the established conclusion. Similarly, in rules such as "of the root *jñā* not meaning 'to know,' [the genitive is used] with the instrument," one should cite examples of the prohibition of compounding for specific prescriptions, such as *sarpiṣo jñānam* (the knowing of ghee) and *madhuno jñānam* (the knowing of honey).

But surely, once this compound is formed, only a general relationship is perceived, and not a relationship preceded by an instrument; since there is no capacity to express the meaning of the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*), the compound will not occur here—what is the use of this effort? This is not so. Even in the analytical sentence, there is no verbal determination of a specific relationship, because of similarity. For indeed, such a sentence would be exactly the same even if the genitive were used in the sense of the object (*karma-ṣaṣṭhī*).

In that regard, when the root *jñā* (to know) is understood through context and other factors to have the sense of "knowing thoroughly" (*vid-arthaka*), a compound with the genitive case of the object (*karman-ṣaṣṭhī*) occurs, as in examples such as *tattvajñānam* ("knowledge of reality") and *varṇajñānam* ("knowledge of letters"). Likewise, in the case of *sarpiṣo jānāmi*, if through context and so forth it is understood to have the sense of "knowing thoroughly," a compound with the instrumental genitive (*karaṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*) would also be possible; therefore, it is established that this [objection] is to be resolved by relying on a restatement of the rule here as well, based on the continued application of the mention of the term "remainder" (*śeṣa*).

Even though the rule for the prescription of case-endings forms a single syntactical unit with the rule for [the suffixes] *su* and so on, there is no inconsistency in their being prescribed as *pratipada-vidhāna* (specifically prescribed), because the individual constituent rules have ceased their own respective operations. || 160 ||

It has been stated that a relation residing in two things is distinct [from its relata] when applied to qualities (*guṇa*). Furthermore, because the status of being primary (*pradhāna*) and secondary (*guṇa*) is contradictory in a single entity, it is said in the *Bhāṣya*: "In that case, this expression 'the king’s man' would not be possible. To this, the following resolution was stated: "[The expression] occurs with respect to an external object. He explains this *Bhāṣya* as follows: "When one thing, having been designated by another, acquires a distinction in yet another [context], it obtains two properties in that different domain. (161)

In expressions such as "the king's man's blanket," there arises a relation—characterized by a distinction and an excess—of the man (who is the primary element) with another primary correlate, such as the blanket; this occurs because the man has been designated by the qualifier "king" and thus made known as the substantive. Consequently, he acquires two properties characterized by the relationship of subordinate and primary, which have distinct objects. By using the past participle "designated" (*vyapadiṣṭasya*), the author indicates that the conjunction of the two correlates is not contradictory, even though it is caused by subordinate and primary qualities belonging to different times. || 161 ||

And therefore: Having attained primacy through its own quality, it becomes subordinate to the principal [agent]; thus, in the case of association with a companion (*sahayoga*), its status as the principal is not lost. (162)

Therefore, due to this difference in the objects [of relation], the primary status of the person with respect to the king, his relative, does not cease. For in that case, he has already attained primacy with respect to his own subordinate quality characterized as "kingship. However, in the case of another primary object such as a blanket, he enters into a state of subordination or subsidiarity; thus, when conjoined with his own [object] like the blanket, he no longer perceives the primacy previously understood [with respect to the king], because the objects differ.

The meaning is that there is no contradiction in the relationship of subordinate and principal existing in a single instance. By way of illustration, following the occasion of the rule "in connection with *saha*," he states an example where the security and welfare (*yogakṣema*) are identical: "the instrumental case is prescribed after a subordinate [word] when joined with *saha*," as in "he has come together with his son" (*putreṇa sahāgataḥ*).

In that regard, as in the case of "the son of Devadatta," when [Devadatta] is being qualified, he is the primary element (pradhāna) with respect to that [son]; yet, by virtue of the capacity of the meaning of "together" (saha) in the act of coming, because of the connection to the arrival, the [son], whose connection to the arrival is merely inferred, becomes the secondary element (apradhāna). Consequently, the third case-ending (tṛtīyā), which has the characteristic of the secondary element, is applied. Similarly, although a man is the primary element in relation to the king, he is the secondary element in relation to his own qualifier; thus, in the expression "the king’s man’s wealth" (rājñaḥ puruṣasya dhanam), the sixth case-ending (ṣaṣṭhī) is attained. This is established. || 162 ||

Thus ends the section on the remaining [cases] (*śeṣādhikāra*) within the *Sādhanasamuddeśa* of the *Prakīrṇakaprakāśa* composed by Helārāja, son of Bhūtirāja. In this manner, the meaning of the case-endings (*vibhaktyartha*), consisting of the grammatical factors (*kāraka*), has been examined. As for the nominative (*prathamā*), it has been prescribed by some according to the rule: "The nominative occurs when [the factor] is already expressed (*abhihite prathamā*). That is to say, when a *kāraka* such as the object (*karman*) is already expressed by verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) and the like, the nominative occurs.

The examples "the rice is being cooked" (*pacyate odanaḥ*), "fire is a cooker of meat" (*māṃsapacano vanhiḥ*), "the guest is a slayer of cows" (*godhno'tithiḥ*), "the pillar is a leaper-over" (*praskandanaḥ staṃbhaḥ*), "the night is a destroyer" (*niśā nīśāṇā*), and "Devadatta cooks" (*pacati devadattaḥ*) illustrate, respectively, the designation of the case-factors (*kāraka*s) beginning with the object and ending with the agent by means of verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) and so forth. The designation of the object by a primary derivative suffix (*kṛt*) is shown in "the mat was made" (*kṛtaḥ kaṭaḥ*); the designation of a relationship by a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) is shown in "Aupagava" (*aupagavaḥ*); and [the designation of a relationship] by a compound (*samāsa*) is shown in "Citragu" (*citraguḥ*).

In the expression *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* ("the king’s man"), when the sentence reaches its completion in the mere relation between two mutually dependent terms, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) attached to one of the words denotes a relation that resides in both. Consequently, the nominative (*prathamā*) is applied according to the rule for what is already expressed (*abhihita-lakṣaṇā*). Regarding this rule, it has been stated: "The verb *as-* (to be), in the third person singular, is understood even when not explicitly employed. Thus it is said: "The verb *as-* is present, following the word *bhavantī* (the present tense) and in the first person."

Since a thing (*padārtha*) cannot be the subject of linguistic usage (*avyavahārya*) without being connected to an action (*kriyā*), the action of existence (*asti-kriyā*)—which possesses a relationship that is never absent from its general form—is present everywhere. Thus, in the sentence "the tree exists" (*vṛkṣo 'sti*), this nominative case is used for the agent (*kartṛ*) when it is expressed by a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*). As it is stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "A thing does not deviate from existence."

The meaning is that because the employment of words and the act of determination depend upon a substratum for the objects to be grasped, and because they depend upon existence (*sattā*), every object denoted by a word is permeated by figurative existence (*aupacārika-sattā*). Thus, as was stated previously: "This figurative existence is the cause of application for all words; indeed, no object whatsoever transcends it. Furthermore, even the grammatical connection (*anuṣaṅga*) of such expressions as "it does not exist," "it is bound," or "it is led" occurs only for that which is existent (*sat*); therefore, this existence is universal and fundamental.

Furthermore, it has already been stated—and indeed resolved in that very context—that the word remains established in this state while being connected with both contradictory and non-contradictory properties. Even so, the objection was raised: "In the case of [a case-role] being expressed or unexpressed, there would be an absence of the nominative. In examples such as *prasāde āste* ("he sits on the terrace"), the locative capacity (*adhikaraṇa-śakti*) is not expressed in relation to the action of sitting (*āsikriyā*), but it is expressed (and thus marked) in relation to the action of existence (*sattikriyā*). Consequently, the nominative case, characterized by being expressed, would result [where it is not desired].

Likewise, in cases such as "the trees have borne fruit" (*phalitā vanaspatayaḥ*) and "the cuckoos sing with melodious notes" (*tārasvarāḥ parabhṛtāḥ*), since there is no deviation from the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) in the relation of grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa-sambandha*), nothing would be expressed by anything else; consequently, the nominative case (*prathamā*), which is characterized by being "expressed," would not occur.

Because the indeclinables *uccaiḥ* and *nīcaiḥ*, which primarily express the locative capacity (*adhikaraṇa-śakti*), cannot be connected [to a verb] through the ellipsis of an existential verb (*asti-pada-adhyāhāra*), they are not denoted by anything; thus, how could the nominative alone [be used]? Likewise, the rule "the nominative is used when coreferential with a finite verb" (*tiṅ-samānādhikaraṇe prathamā*) is, by this very same example, shown to be no rule at all. Furthermore, another objection has been stated here: "And because of the presence of the conditions for the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac*, there is an absence of the finite verb (*tiṅ*), since those two [suffixes] are exceptions (*apavāda*) to it."

In this context, according to the view that the analysis [of the sentence] is to be explained by breaking it down into its parts (*vibhājyānvākhyāna*), when the state *devadatta pacati* has been established, as long as the *tiṅ* suffix has not yet arisen, the nominative case does not apply because there is no coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a *tiṅ*. Consequently, all case-endings beginning with the accusative (*svādayaḥ*), which are prescribed without distinction, remain available after the word *devadatta*. Thus, the present participles *śatṛ* and *śānac*, which are prescribed as substitutes for the present tense marker *laṭ* when there is coreferentiality with a word ending in the second case or others, would apply as exceptions (*apavāda*), rather than the *tiṅ* suffixes. For those *tiṅ* suffixes, however, forms such as the optative (*liṅ*) and so forth would constitute their scope of application.

And since that same [number] belongs to the nominative as well, a usage such as *pacati devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta cooks"), which is in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the present indicative suffix (*laṭ*), would not be possible with a word ending in the nominative case. Thus, when this alternative definition has been rejected, the definition of the Master [Pāṇini] himself—beginning with *prātipadikārtha-liṅga-parimāṇa...*—is established as the correct one. Regarding that, an investigation is now undertaken.

Since the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in *ṅī* or *āp* is understood to be the base for the case endings beginning with *su*, and since it is already established that the meaning belongs to the nominal stem itself, the explicit mention of "nominal stem" (*prātipadika-grahaṇa*) as a qualifier of "meaning" (*artha*) is unnecessary. Consequently, that [mention] is indeed disconnected from the word "meaning. To prescribe the nominative case even for meaningless elements, the designation of "nominal stem" (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) has been added [as a supplement] for particles (*nipāta*) such as "he comes near" (*adhyāgacchati*) and "he goes around" (*paryāgacchati*), which are themselves meaningless. If this is so, then the nominative case will occur by virtue of the force of that designation.

Indeed, there is no possibility here for any other prātipadika-activity (i.e., nominal stem function) than the prescription of case-endings (*vibhakti*). Furthermore, regarding the rule *adhiparī anarthakau* ("*adhi* and *pari* are meaningless [when used with certain nouns]"), because the prescription of the technical term *karmapravacanīya* serves the purpose of subverting the technical term *gati*, it is inferred from this indicative mark (*liṅga*) that these [prefixes] possess meaning. Otherwise, in the absence of the indication of a specific action (*kriyāviśeṣa*), the application of the *gati* designation would not even occur. In the view that the rules for the introduction of case-endings (*svādi*) constitute separate sentences, the case-endings produced without distinction are already established.

Even in this view that [the sūtra] forms a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*), since the restriction applies to the suffixes by virtue of its dependence on the context, the second case (*dvitīyā*) would apply only to the object (*karman*) and not to the instrument (*karaṇa*); thus, there would be no exclusion of those [suffixes] used meaninglessly. Alternatively, one must resort to a restriction of meaning (*arthaniyama*), such as "the second case alone is used for the object," and so forth. Having established this, it has not been cited here even in cases like *uccaiḥ* and *nīcaiḥ*, because suffixes beginning with *su-* (the nominative) occur after indeclinables (*avyaya*) which lack number. Furthermore, the rule regarding the elision (*luk*) of case-endings after indeclinables serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for this very point.

And since there is no purpose for deviating from the sequence, the very first [case] arrived at through the order of recitation (pāṭhakrama) applies here. Therefore, the mention of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) serves as a qualifier of the meaning. Although it is established by the force of the context, it prescribes the nominative case (*prathamā*) in the sense of the nominal stem alone for the sake of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), and not from indeclinables (*avyaya*) and so forth. Regarding this, some say that the meaning qualified by the general category of "nominal stem" is "existence" (*sattā*).

For that [denotation], having a relationship that is non-deviating with respect to all meanings, is first perceived and established as the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) alone, independent of its connection with case-endings and the like. Indeed, the determination of technical (*śāstrīya*) meaning proceeds by means of the assumed presence and absence (*anvaya-vyatireka*). In this regard, even when the meaning of the case-ending follows—as in *vṛkṣam*, *vṛkṣeṇa*, and so on—the meaning of the pure nominal stem is determined because it persists as mere existence (*sattāmātra*).

Since existence (*sattā*) cannot occur without a substratum, its referent is necessarily a substance as its substratum; for it is only with respect to that much that the word is independent. Because it requires a suffix for gender and so forth, and because of the inclusion of the particle *mātra*, this specific meaning is established. Consequently, there is no contradiction with the position that [the category of substance] consists of five [qualities].

Even by him who has stated that the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is "accomplished" (*siddha*), it was intended that nouns (*nāmapada*)—by virtue of their distinction from verbs (*ākhyātapada*)—denote objects whose nature is accomplished; however, he did not intend this "accomplishment" to mean being already established as something to be produced (*sādhya*). For if it were so, one might object that because it is understood through the employment of other words, it could not be the meaning of the nominal stem alone.

Furthermore, since a word finds no rest in mere *dharma* (the property), some explicitly state that the base meaning (*prātipadikārtha*) is the possessor of the cause (*nimittin*), which has been brought to the state of its own form by the cause (*nimitta*). The causes are genus, quality, and action; the possessor of the cause is their substratum, whose own form is indeed concealed due to its complete absorption [in them]. For this very reason, it is said that "it has been brought, as it were, to the state of its own form by the cause. However, what is intended here is not an actual transformation into another form in reality, but rather a mere permeation (*ācchuraṇa*) through such a cognitive determination (*adhyavasāya*).

Nor is there an operation here involving a pause [between the cognition of the substance and its qualifiers], because the substance is understood from the word as being already colored by its adjuncts (*upādhi*). It is not the case that the pure substance is first cognized from the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and only afterwards is the specific gender and so forth, which has emerged, perceived. For if it were so, the meaning of the nominal stem would be differentiated by that [gender, etc. even though it is conveyed by the same word, just as it is by the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*) and the like.

But this is not the case; therefore, since it is precisely a qualified meaning that is denoted by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and since gender-tinted meaning is also the meaning of the nominal stem, the inclusion of the word "only" (*mātra*) serves to exclude anything additional. Consequently, examples such as *kumārī* (a young girl), *vṛkṣaḥ* (a tree), and *kuṇḍam* (a bowl) are given as illustrations for the inclusion of gender (*liṅga*). For just as the nominative case does not occur when the meaning of the nominal stem is augmented by an object (*karman*) because of the inclusion of "only," nor when there is an injunction for the nominative in the sense of address (*saṃbodhana*) due to the [specific] gender [of the word], so too it would not occur when the meaning is augmented by gender; thus, the inclusion of gender is made.

The mention of "measure" (*parimāṇa*) is intended so that the usage of terms denoting the means of delimitation—such as *prastha* and the like—in non-difference from that which possesses it may be grammatically correct; for example: "A *prastha* is the measure of these grains," or "the *prastha* [is] the grains," "the *khārī*," or "the *āḍhaka*. However, if there were a figurative application of non-difference based on the thought "this is that," the relationship between the measure and the object measured—which consists of distinct entities—would not be perceived.

Alternatively, it might be understood that there is another relationship, such as that of immediate succession (*ānantarya*) and so forth; therefore, when the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-artha*) exceeds [the categories of gender, number, and case], the nominative case is prescribed for the sake of expressing the distinctness of the capacity [of the word] through the metaphorical application (*upacāra*) of the relationship between the means of measurement and the object measured. However, if this prescription of the nominative did not exist, then by the analysis of the rule "that is its measure" (*tad-asya parimāṇam*), a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) would apply, or else a full sentence would be required in certain instances. But now, by the force of this specific statement, all three [the suffix, the derivative, and the sentence] occur.

This very point he will state: "When a specific relationship between the means of knowledge (*māna*) and the object of knowledge (*meyādi*) is accepted in that manner, the incorrectness of words such as *prastha* would follow in the absence of a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*). That suffix, or alternatively a sentence, may be optionally employed according to a distinction in grammatical connection (*yogabheda*). In that case, when there is a quantity exceeding [the standard], the nominative case (*prathamā*) is again prescribed. Since the word "measure" (*parimāṇa*) is used here in its sense of the cause of action, it includes "height" (*unmāna*) and the other types of measurement as well.

In the case of words such as *śukla* ("white"), because the possessive suffix (*matup*) is elided in the formation of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), the first case ending is established by the very mention of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself, provided there is no intention to express a distinction [between the quality and the qualified]. Similarly, this applies to words such as *viṃśati* ("twenty") when they denote the possessor of the quality. By the word "number" (*vacana*), "count" (*saṅkhyā*) is intended according to the convention of the ancient teachers. Therefore, even though the count is already expressed, the first case is prescribed by this rule. For example: *ekaḥ*, *dvau*, *bahavaḥ*. However, the second case and the others are established after these stems according to their respective functions, such as the object (*karman*) and so forth.

Because these [suffixes] do not convey oneness and so forth as qualified by the object (*karman*) and other factors, the word *mātra* has the sense of restriction; thus, the nominative case does not occur when [the number] is qualified by the object and so forth. Alternatively, the accusative and subsequent cases serve as sublaters (*bādhaka*) in that context. Or rather, because the nominative is prescribed for what is qualified by the vocative, the absence [of the nominative] in cases exceeding the object and so forth is established by this indicative mark (*liṅga*).

Indeed, when the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) possesses an additional attribute (*atirekavat*), the rule for the first case (*prathamā*) in the sense of existence (*bhāva*) or address (*saṃbodhana*) is not applicable, because it is already established by this very [rule]. Thus, the inclusion of the term *mātra* was rejected. "Measure" (*mātrā*) means that by which something is measured; it refers to number (*saṃkhyā*). Its mention is made through a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*). In that context, the purpose of including the term *mātra*—namely, so that [the suffix] may apply after words such as *eka* and others when a number is expressed—is already accomplished by the inclusion of the term *vacana* (gender/number).

"It can be stated as either one or the other," so it is said in the Bhāṣya. However, some maintain that the inclusion of the word *mātra* is for the sake of completeness (*sākalyārtha*), intended to include unmāna and the rest by dispelling the suspicion that the word *parimāṇa* is a conventional term (*rūḍhi*) restricted to a specific measure. Once the word *mātra* is established as having the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇārthatva*), it is stated: "An addition [to the rule] is required when there is coreferentiality with a word [denoting a substance], because [the measure] is greater. To this, the refutation is stated: "Or rather, it is not [necessary], because it is the meaning of the sentence. And here, the resolution is set forth.

The meaning is that the rule for the first case-ending (*prathamā*) applies to the nominal stem-meaning (*prātipadikārtha*) alone, even when it is distinct from the mutual connection of other word-meanings, as in examples such as *vīraḥ puruṣaḥ* ("the hero, the man"). Thus, the rule for the first case is appropriate exactly according to the traditional grammatical system (*yathānyāsam*). The first case is also stated to occur in the sense of address (*saṃbodhana*). Regarding this, he explains the nature of address: "They know address to be merely the bringing of an already established entity into the presence [of the speaker]. For it is an object that has attained presence which is then employed in actions. (Verse 163)

Addressing (*saṃbodhana*) is that act of directing one’s attention toward an entity whose form is already complete, for the purpose of employing it in an action; this alone constitutes its form as something additional to the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*). By the inclusion of the word "mere" (*mātra*), [the author] excludes the status of addressing as being a means (*sādhana*) such as the object (*karman*) and so forth. For indeed, the very same agent who is enjoined to go and so on, when directed [by addressing], becomes additional to the meaning of the stem through addressing. And once directed, after the time of the injunction, that which is addressed experiences its status as a benefactor of the action (*kriyopakāraka*) through the mediation of being a means to the action, but addressing itself is not a direct factor of action (*kāraka*). (163)

Even in the case of action (*kriyā*), he states that in the vocative there is no status as a sentence-meaning (*vākyārthatā*)—as there is in the case of the relation between qualifier and qualified—but rather it has the status of a word-meaning (*padārthatva*) alone, like the instruments of action such as the object (*karman*). "The traditional teaching (*āgama*) of the elders is that the vocative is not a sentence-meaning. Tradition (*āgama*) is the authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that provides certainty. Since the state of being addressed is understood independently of other words, the vocative is indeed a word-meaning, even though it requires an action.

Just as the status of being a means (*sādhana*) is not possible for actions such as *karman* and so forth if they are independent of an action (*kriyā*), and thus an action must be resorted to [as a necessary factor], yet this does not mean that the action itself constitutes the sentence-meaning (*vākyārthatva*); so it is with the case of address (*saṃbodhana*) as well. Furthermore, even a single word like "tree" (*vṛkṣaḥ*) is a sentence when an implied action is understood; therefore, address is indeed a sentence-meaning. Now he concludes the present topic: "By way of indication (*uddeśena*), the meanings of the case-endings (*vibhaktyartha*) are extracted from the sentence-meaning. (164)

A brief statement is an *uddeśa* (enunciation). For that reason, the meanings of the case-endings (*vibhakti*), which consist of the factors of action (*kāraka*) such as the object (*karman*) and so forth, are extracted separately from the ultimate, indivisible sentence-meaning—which is of the nature of an action qualified by multiple specific factors—by means of the analytical cognition (*apoddhārabuddhi*) through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Just as words are extracted from the indivisible sentence, so too are word-meanings extracted from the sentence-meaning. Furthermore, the meaning of a case-ending is indeed a word-meaning (*padārtha*).

Even in that case, however, when there is an extraction [of elements], the extraction of the meaning of the case-ending from the word-meaning must be explained; yet, since the sentence-meaning alone possesses a stable definition while the word-meaning is unreal, he says "from the sentence-meaning. Others, however, say: "From the 'sentence-meaning' as characterized by the 'mention'—that is, from the word-meaning which constitutes a single part of the sentence-meaning—they are distinguished. This is indeed the clear meaning. || 164 ||

Now, since the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*) is distinct from the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*), he states the scriptural authority for this gender: "From the rule regarding *avyayībhāva* compounds, it should be understood that the meaning of the case-ending is something other than substance (*dravya*); that [meaning] is expressed by the indeclinable. (165)

Regarding the rule "an indeclinable [is compounded] with a case-ending"—it has been stated that an indeclinable expressing a case-meaning is compounded with a compatible subsequent word, as in *adhistri*. In that case, if the case-meaning were indeed a substance (*dravya*), then since that meaning would already have been expressed by the word *strī* itself, the indeclinable would be unfit for use; and how could there be a compound of something that is not being used?

Therefore, from the rule governing *avyayībhāva* compounds regarding the meaning of case-endings (*vibhakti*), it is understood that the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) alone does not denote the instruments of action such as the object (*karman*) and so forth. For instance, an indeclinable word denoting the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) forms a compound with a subsequent word by following [the rules]. This point was previously established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) in the passage beginning, "For even when there is no deviation [of the stem], a deviation [of the suffix] is observed when there is concomitance. Now, this same point is further reinforced by the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*).

But surely, under the view that the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) consists of five factors, since the undivided, qualified substance is expressed by the nominal stem itself, even an indeclinable (*avyaya*) ought to be eligible for usage in order to indicate a qualifier, just like case-endings (*vibhakti*); for there is no restriction regarding indicators (*dyotaka*). How, then, is this [restriction regarding] gender (*liṅga*) appropriate? This is true; however, this gender is presented under the "threefold" (*trika*) view. For it is so stated: "An indeclinable [is used where there is] a case-ending... (*avyayaṃ vibhakti...*), whereby the meaning of a case-ending is indicated.

In the view that the word consists of five parts (*pañcakapakṣa*), however, since the particularity (*viśeṣa*) which constitutes the substance itself is manifested by the case-endings (*vibhakti*), the meaning would be apprehended by the *pada* alone, because it denotes the aggregate; it would not be apprehended by the case-ending alone. Alternatively, even in the *pañcakapakṣa*, since a fixed particularity consisting of power (*śakti*) is not perceived from the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) alone, this [particularity] is the domain of the case-endings themselves. Thus, it is rightly said that the meaning of the case-ending is a substance with fixed power, distinct from the substance with unfixed power denoted by the nominal stem.

And having established this, positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) operate, as the case may be, upon both sides [of the argument]—either in the expression of what has not been previously stated or in its indication. || 165 ||

Now, one might object: since it is understood from such indicative marks as "when there are two actions with the same agent" (*samānakartṛkayoḥ*) and "in the case of the animal" (*paśau*) that a substance (*dravya*) functions as the means (*sādhana*), how can the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhakti-artha*) be something other than the substance? Anticipating this doubt, he says the following in order to establish that it is the capacity (*śakti*) which is the means: "But a substance, in whatever state it exists, remains exactly so [even when its properties change]. Even when there is a difference in action, its essence as a substance is not lost. (166)

If a substance were always immovable, possessing a single nature that never departs across all states, then the diversity of grammatical means (sādhana) in expressions such as "tree by the tree" would be impossible. Furthermore, the claim that the distinction of a substance is caused by the multiplicity of actions—as in "see the tree" or "the tree is laden with fruit"—is also false; for even when there is a multiplicity of actions, the substance certainly does not deviate from its own essential nature, since a thing cannot undergo change merely through the difference of its relations. (166)
And if this were the case, then that substance which is the instrument would not be the object; furthermore, there would be a transformation of its entire substantial nature. || 167 ||

A substance that has been designated as an instrument (*karaṇa*) is not manifested as an object (*karman*). This is an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) [of the principle] applicable to other *kārakas* as well. Furthermore, that which is understood as an object would not be recognized as a residual relation (*śeṣa*). Moreover, because a substance, as a means (*sādhana*), is singular, in such expressions as "he sits in the palace" (*prāsāde āste*) or "he lies on the seat" (*āsane śete*), the locative case for the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) would not occur, since it is already denoted by the suffix *-lyuṭ*.

However, since the capacity (*śakti*) is the means of accomplishment, it varies according to the difference in the action; thus, when the capacity as the locus (*adhikaraṇa-śakti*) is expressed in relation to the action of sitting (*sadikriyā*), yet remains unexpressed in relation to the action of sitting (*āsikriyā*), the locative case is established by resorting to the principle of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), which states that "that which is unexpressed [is used] other than where it has been expressed. And so says the Vārttika:

"For [the designation of a case-ending] is prescribed when [the relation] is not already expressed. Now, if there were a transformation of the instrument (*karaṇa*) into the nature of the object (*karman*) upon connection with another action, then the entire substance (*dravya*), by its very nature, would undergo the acquisition of the state of being another entity, and not merely the instrumental portion, because that [portion] is distinct from the substance. However, since capacity (*śakti*) functions as the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), even though it differs according to the difference in actions, the substance which is its substratum persists as a recurring entity; thus, through the process of abandoning one capacity and assuming another, its occurrence in the form of the instrument and so forth is logical.

Since an incapable substance cannot be a factor (*anga*) in the accomplishment of an action, it is logical that capacity alone—having that [substance] as its locus—is the means (*sādhana*). Nor, on this account, is it reasonable to postulate that the substance itself possesses the status of a means simply because it is the locus of the means; for when Devadatta is the means for the act of cooking, one does not likewise postulate that status for the stool which serves as his locus. Thus, capacities alone are the means, and not the substance possessing those capacities.

In the rule "samānakartṛkayoḥ," however, the identity (*samānatva*) between the two agent-powers (*kartṛ-śakti*) is based on the superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of the unity of the substance that serves as the locus of those powers. Thus, in the phrase "when the animal is the agent" (*paśau kartari*), it should be explained as: "when the one who is the agent of the substance [the animal] is the same as the two agents of the substances [the elephant and the hunter]. Alternatively, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) because the animal itself, as the substratum of the agent-power, is the agent.

In rules such as "the second case-ending [is used] for the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*), because numbers are connected to powers (*śakti*s), it is the substance (*dravya*) which serves as their substratum that is actually indicated. Therefore, the meaning is that case-endings [denote] number as inherent in the same object as the action (*karman*). Since a power without a substratum is untenable, the substance itself, permeated by power, is the means (*sādhana*) expressed by the verbal suffixes (*lakāra*). And since that [substance], being of a specific nature, performs the action, it is manifested by another word when not already expressed by its own specific form; thus, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in expressions such as "Devadatta cooks" (*devadattaḥ pacati*) is logically established, and everything is well-ordered. || 167 ||

Thus ends the seventh chapter, the *Sādhanasamuddeśa*, in the *Prakīrṇakaprakāśa* composed by Helārāja, son of Bhūtirāja. Now, since a means (*sādhana*) is dependent upon that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), he states the technical definition of action (*kriyā*) as intended by the treatise: "Whatever, whether already established or not yet established, is designated as being in the state of being accomplished (*sādhya*), is called 'action' because it possesses a nature characterized by sequential succession. (1)

Regarding the definition of a verbal root (*dhātu*) as "that which expresses action" provided by the ancient masters, it was objected: "It must be stated that *as*, *bhū*, and *vid* possess the status of verbal roots. For instance, just as in the case of "What does he do? He cooks," where roots such as *pac* are determined to express specific actions because they stand in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the verb *karoti*, this is not the case for roots such as *bhū*. Indeed, one does not say, "What does he do? He exists" (*bhavati*). Therefore, these [roots] would not be expressive of action.

Furthermore, in common worldly usage, action (*kriyā*) is well known to have the nature of motion (*parispanda*). However, since the meanings of the verbs *asti*, *bhavati*, and *vidyati* do not possess the nature of motion, the definition of action was formulated in the *Bhāṣya* as a characteristic that pervades all verbal roots: "Action is a specific kind of activity (*pravṛtti-viśeṣa*) of the factors of action (*kārakas*). In this regard, it is investigated whether there is one single specific activity belonging to all the factors of action, or whether the activity is distinct for each factor of action.

Regarding the first position, there arises a dilemma: is the activity (*pravṭti*) of the factors (*kārakas*) one that results in the fruit, such as the production of cooked rice and so forth, or is it something else? In this regard, first of all, there cannot be a single specific activity common to all [the factors], because that is impossible. For the activity of the instrument (*karaṇa*) is not the same as that of the agent (*kartṛ*), nor is that of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) the same as that of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), and so on; for a single action residing in multiple substrates is never observed. Therefore, the activity—namely, the action—is distinct for each factor.

In this way, the rule that "a verbal root (*dhātu*) expresses action" would result in the root expressing the operation of all the factors of action (*kāraka*). What follows from this? This follows: the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) would have to express all the *kārakas*. For it is logical that a *la*-suffix, when employed after a root, should be the means for accomplishing the operation denoted by that root. This is not so; because the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) prescribes the *la*-suffixes for the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*), it is precisely their operation that is understood from the suffix ending in *la*.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the meaning should not be caused by the word, but rather the word should be caused by the meaning? Therefore, let *la* be taught merely as denoting the "means" (*sādhana*). [Response: This would be so if the operation of the mere means were understood from the suffix *la*; however, since it is the operation of the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*) that is perceived, it is proper that the grammatical rule follow the expressive power of the word. In that case, the verbal root (*dhātu*) does not denote the operation of the mere means.

This is because that [meaning] is not understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), and because there is no other means for following the root and the suffix. This is true; however, in cases such as "Devadatta cooks rice in a pot with firewood," since the verbal root *pac* is observed to encompass the operations of all the factors of action (*kāraka*) without distinction, it is the view of some that the meaning is understood from the root as it stands at the end of the entire set of factors. Others, however, think that the root does not apply (*na-vṛtti*) to the operation of the recipient (*sampradāna*) and so forth, but its application (*vṛtti*) is only to the operation of the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the rest.

And thus, the intention to express independence (*svātantrya*) applies only to the *karaṇa* (instrument) and other [kārakas], not to the *apādāna* (ablative) and others. In this way, the author of the Vārttika demonstrates through the passage beginning with "placing on the stove, pouring water... that the operation of the agent (*kartṛ*) and the others alone constitutes the action of cooking (*pacikriyā*). Consequently, when it is stated that "action is a specific kind of activity (*pravṛttiviśeṣa*) of the kārakas," only the essential nature of action is being described, not its status as something denoted by a verbal root (*dhātu*). Whatever the activity of a particular kāraka may be, that is the action; therefore, because they have many kārakas as their domain, there are indeed many distinct actions of cooking.

However, a certain [action] is denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*) as residing either in the object or in the agent, as in "it is cooked" (*pacyate*) or "he cooks" (*pacati*). For this very reason, the *L*-suffixes arise only for the agent and the object, because it is precisely their operation that is denoted by the verbal root. Others, however, placing the emphasis on the term "particularity" (*viśeṣa*), explain that "particularity of activity" (*pravṛttiviśeṣa*) refers to the result—such as the softening [of rice]—which is produced by all the factors of action (*kāraka*) and constitutes the "coming-into-being" (*bhūti*); they thus define "action" (*kriyā*) as the activity of the factors of action resulting in such a fruit.

Others, however, maintain that what is intended here as the primary factor is the agent (*kartṛ*) in its active form, and not the instrument (*karaṇa*) or other subordinate factors. The plural number is used because there is a plurality of agents due to the distinction between multiple actions. The term "agent" alone was not employed so that the exclusion [of the agent] might not apply to it, since the *lakāra* suffixes are seen to occur in the sense of the object (*karman*). Therefore, wherever the object is possible, the operation of that object is also an action. If this is so, then the plural number should be explained solely with reference to that [object].

And because activity is for the sake of action (*karman*), that [action] too is the primary factor. This is not so, because action does not have everything as its object. Since the agent (*kartṛ*), however, exists everywhere, it is precisely he who is intended here as the primary *kāraka* due to his pervasiveness. And on this point, the *Bhāṣya* itself provides the evidence, stating: "In one way the *kārakas* operate toward dry rice, and in another way toward rice with meat. For instance, toward rice with meat the agent operates with zeal, whereas toward dry rice he operates with sluggish effort.

Since it demonstrates activity through both impetuosity and sluggishness, it is therefore concluded that the agent alone is intended here by the term "kāraka" (the causal factor). For it is precisely because of its consciousness that the agent itself acts in such a manner. Thus, the author of the Bhāṣya himself has illustrated that action (*kriyā*), which consists of a specific form of activity, is either characterized by impetuosity or the opposite thereof.

On this point, some raise an objection: since such activity is possible only for a conscious being, an unconscious agent would not be accepted [as the agent], and thus it would not have been stated that "activity is action" (*kriyā*). Furthermore, since instruments and other factors are also possible in the case of rice-porridge and the like, how is it that only the agent is specified here? To this it is replied: excitement and dullness are possible only for an agent.

For neither a vessel such as a bronze bowl, nor any other *kāraka*, functions by means of exertion (*saṃrambha*) or sluggishness; and since the agent and the object are grasped in their general sense, the activity of insentient things is indeed included. However, by the passage beginning with "otherwise, in the case of the rice and meat," etc., a specific kind of activity characterized by exertion and sluggishness is indicated. But this does not restrict the previously mentioned activity of the agent alone. Therefore, the meaning is that the specific activity of the agent is what constitutes action (*kriyā*).

And having established this, the summary is that activity (*pravṛtti*) alone is the specific [action]. Since the object (*karman*) is also indicated, it is understood that by the word "kāraka" (participant), its operation (*vyāpāra*) is also denoted as "action" (*kriyā*). Otherwise, it has been stated that he would have used only the word "agent" (*kartṛ*). In this view, how is the *Bhāṣya* to be explained: "Now, what is the primary meaning of the root *pac*? It is that softening (*viklitti*) of the rice grains"? For action is the operation of the agent expressed by the verbal root; and that is the act of softening (*vikledanā*), not the state of being softened (*viklitti*).

There is no contradiction. Here, the meaning of the word (*śabdārtha*) is not being defined; rather, the meaning of the thing (*vastvartha*) is intended. Thus, it is stated in this way because, from the perspective of the actual object, the softening (*viklitti*) is primary. However, from the perspective of the verbal form (*śābdarūpa*), the meaning is the act of softening (*vikledana*), with the softening itself as a subordinate element. Some maintain that when the *lakāra* suffix occurs in the sense of the object (*karman*), the meaning is softening alone. Others hold that the meaning is softening, with the act of softening as a subordinate element. Therefore, according to this view, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) everywhere consists precisely in the operation of the agent and the object.

Others, however, following the Bhāṣya statement “the action exists as a universal,” maintain that action is merely activity (*pravṛtti*)—unspecified and following after all the factors of action (*kāraka*). For instance, they hold that the very production of a result, which is common to all [factors], is called a specific activity (*pravṛtti-viśeṣa*), being both an activity and a particularity. This particularity consists in its nature as the production of a result, and not merely in its form as placing on the stove (*adhiśrayaṇa*) and so forth. Thus, action is the particularity of activities known as production.

For all causal factors (*kārakas*), there is indeed a single activity characterized by the production of a result; for all of them act toward the production of that result. Therefore, that which consists in the production of the result is common to all causal factors. Indeed, while a particular factor produces [the result] in a specific manner, the production of the result itself is a form common to all. However, the designations such as "instrument" (*karaṇa*) and so forth arise from their productivity through intermediate distinctions. Furthermore, in the system of Kaṇāda, a single action cannot reside in multiple [factors].

And the view of other non-Buddhist schools (tīrthika) is not relied upon here. For this very reason, activity (*vyāpāra*) characterized by physical motion (*parispanda*) is not [what is meant by] "action" (*kriyā*). For if only the term "engagement" (*pravṛtti*) were used, then by common worldly consensus, activity characterized by physical motion would be understood. However, some explain that because of the inclusion of the specific term [“activity”], it is understood as mere engagement (*pravṛttimātra*).

For indeed, every activity, being distinguished from other activities, attains a specific form; thus, this definition applies to all actions. And a specific form is [defined] by its distinction from both the homogeneous and the heterogeneous. Among these, the distinction from the homogeneous has been established by the statement: "The causal factors operate in one way toward dry rice, and in another way toward rice with meat. For the act of eating is said to be distinguished here precisely by the difference in the causal factors. The operation of the causal factors toward dry rice occurs with indifference [to the previous state].

However, it is specified [in the definition] as "an effort toward *māsaudana* (rice cooked for a month). For if the action (*kriyā*) of the means were merely the nature of effort itself, then the act of eating (*bhuj*) would not attain the status of an action in the case of dry rice; therefore, "a specific kind of activity" is the general definition of action. Furthermore, the distinction from heterogeneous things is quite clear in cases such as *pacati* ("he cooks") and *paṭhati* ("he recites"). Now, one might ask: how is it established that action is indeed distinct from substance? To this, it has already been stated:

"In this world, when all the means [of cooking] are present, sometimes 'he cooks' occurs and sometimes it does not," and so forth. Through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the action denoted by words such as "cooks" is distinct from the substance (*dravya*) which is endowed with the capacity for causal factors (*kāraka*). For instance, even though the means are present during a state of neutrality (*audāsīnya*), because there is an absence of both the manifestation and description of "he cooks" and the like, those two [words] must have a different object as their referent. This is just as, for example, qualities produced by cooking (*pākaja*), which do not arise even when a jar is present, depend upon contact with fire.

Alternatively, another point stated here is: "Just as Devadatta, having been here, comes to be in Pāṭaliputra—that must surely be an action. By the preceding passage, the cause of action was stated to be a specific manifestation occurring at a particular time, provided that [action] is distinct [from the substance]. However, since such a manifestation could occur even when no object exists—like the perception of water in a mirage—this further mark (*liṅga*) is presented here. For instance, the result characterized by attainment, which does not arise from the mere substance, makes known an operation other than that [substance].

Because if there were only false cognition, the object would be absent, leading to the undesirable consequence that no result could arise. Nor is the production of a result possible from the causal factors alone in their state as mere potencies; for even when potency exists, a result is not observed in the absence of activity. Therefore, there must be some such entity which, depending upon a specific sequence, brings about the effect. And since that activity cannot be pointed out as a solidified mass, it is said to be cognizable through inference.

But surely, since the verbal expression "he cooks" (*pacati*) would be erroneous due to its lack of a real objective basis, it would be improper for it to function as an inferential mark (*anumāpaka*). If, however, it does have an objective basis, then the action itself must be perceptible, because it is the object of that specific verbal expression. Furthermore, even if the action were inferred from its result, it could not be denoted by the word once it has been perceived [by another means], nor could it be denoted if it has already ceased after producing its result, for to speak of it as "present" (*vartamāna*) would be contradictory. To this it is replied: In this science of grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), the object is not the external reality (*vastvartha*), but rather the object is the linguistic meaning (*śabdārtha*).

Furthermore, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*) which is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) cannot be perceived directly. For the nature of the object (*artha-ātmā*), which follows a temporal sequence, is primarily understood from the verb as "action" (*kriyā*) in its linguistic form; indeed, it is action alone that is brought into being (*bhāvyate*). It has been stated, however, that substance (*dravya*) is established by its own inherent nature (*svabhāva-siddha*). How could there be an inherent establishment of a substance—which is impermanent and whose existence depends upon its means of accomplishment (*sādhana*)—in its real form?

Even though an object, when being brought into existence, possesses a nature that is conceptualized through verbal form, it is expressed by nominal stems (*prātipadika*) as having an established form. For instance, substance-words (*dravya-śabda*), when functioning, produce a cognition that relies upon the aspect of pure existence (*sanmātra-ākāra*), even in the case of things in a state of being produced, such as "a jar is being made" or "a cloth is being made. Indeed, the state of being produced for a jar is the gradual manifestation of its various stages, such as the lump of clay (*śivaka*), the elongated lump (*stūka*), and so forth.

Furthermore, this [existence] is not understood from the word "jar" (*ghaṭa*), because it is understood precisely through the employment of the word for action (*kriyā*) as in "it is being made" (*kriyate*). And thus, that meaning which is understood from a word independently of other words through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is the meaning of that word; since from the solitary word "jar" only the meaning in the form of existence (*sattā*) is understood, it is determined that existence is the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). However, due to the employment of the verb, the state of having a sequential nature (*āśrita-krama-rūpatā*) is understood, and thus the meaning of verbal suffixes (*tiṅanta*) is established as something being brought into being (*bhāvyamāna*).

In the expression “the jar is being made” (*ghaṭaḥ kriyate*), the word-meaning that is apprehended by the cognition “jar” is what is brought into existence; such is the syntactical connection of the words. Even in cases such as “the jar was” or “the jar will be,” because there is a cognition of the form of existence (*sadākāra-pratyaya*), objects are eternal by virtue of their nature as denotable entities (*abhidheya-ātmanā*). Thus it has been said: “Even among non-eternal things, eternity exists by way of their nature as denotable entities. Therefore, action (*kriyā*) is that which is being brought into being through its verbal form. It will be explained later that even in cases such as “it sounds” (*dhvanati*), there is the status of being an action.

And thus it will also be stated: "Because an object consisting of a sequence of prior and posterior states is subject to arrival and departure, and because its constituent parts do not exist simultaneously, there is no perception [of it]. Therefore, in this way, action is inferred from substance through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). But even so, would not verbs such as *asti* (is), *bhavati* (becomes), and *vidyate* (exists) lack the status of being action? For these do not occur only when all the factors of accomplishment (*sādhana*) are present; rather, they occur at all times, since their existence is constant.

Just as there is no excellence [expressed] in *astitarām* and so forth—as there is in *pacatitarām* and so forth—and just as there is no absence of questions and answers such as "What is he doing? and "He cooks," or "What is he doing? and "He exists," and because existence (*sattā*) is devoid of distinctions, there is an absence of differentiation [between verbal roots]. To this we reply: here, in the case of "the means of action (*sādhana*)s proceed otherwise toward 'existence' (*asti*), and otherwise toward 'perishing' (*mriyate*)," there is indeed the nature of being a specific mode of activity. For in the case of *asti*, the activity of the means of action consists in the maintenance of the self (*ātmopagraha*).

Thus, while both [existence and being] are present, death consists in the relinquishment of the self; therefore, there is indeed a distinction between them based on their different natures. Furthermore, since existence is to be accomplished by means that do not require strenuous effort, the presence of those means is necessarily constant; thus, there is an absence of occasional occurrence in the manifestation and description [of these states]. Moreover, a superlative suffix is observed [in the term *vidyatetarām*]: "this one exists more intensely here" because of its constant proximity. For the existence of that which is constantly present is distinguished from that which is only occasionally present.

Therefore, although it is not differentiated because its means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) are the same, it is appropriately connected with excellence. Furthermore, when asked "What does he do?"—a question regarding a specific action—the reply is: "He exists; he performs no action such as cooking. For this question is appropriate only when existence (*sattā*) is understood in a general sense; thus, this [question] does not have action as its object at all. Moreover, when destruction is imminent, one asks "What is Devadatta doing? and the very questions and answers you yourself employ are: "He exists," or "He is present."

Furthermore, while it is true that all actions produce their results immediately thereafter, this [state] also possesses that quality. If one asks what the result here is, we reply: it is the Self in its form as liberation (*apavarga*). According to the statement of the author of the *Nirukta*, "There are six modifications of being" (*ṣaḍ bhāvavikārāḥ*), existence (*sattā*)—which is denoted by the word "being"—is the source of all actions; thus, there is no dispute regarding its fundamental nature as action (*kriyātva*). And although the verb "to stand" (*tiṣṭhati*) is not included among the modifications of being, it nevertheless possesses the characteristics of action.

For it has been said: "Action is the negator of action, and substance is the negator of substance. When it is said "he stands," the cessation of growth and decay is understood; thus, this is an action consisting of the engagement of the factors of action (*kārakas*). For when unconnected to growth or decay, the factors of action remain in a state of indifference. Thus, as long as the factors of action are active, they are perceived as a specific mode of activity whose nature is being accomplished (*sādhyamāna*), composed of prior and subsequent parts.

That upon which the accomplishment of a result depends is the meaning of the word "artha" (object/purpose); this is the definition. Thus, although it is established in reality, action (*kriyā*) is expressed as something yet to be accomplished (*sādhyatvena*). For example, [the root] *dhvani* ("to sound") means "it sounds. In this way, since even [verbs like] *as* ("to be") and others are denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) as being in a state of accomplishment, they possess the nature of action; thus, the status of these as verbal roots (*dhātu*) is established. Likewise, for *sthā* ("to stand") as well, because it expresses the cessation of other actions, this very same definition of action applies to it as well.

For instance, when it is said "he stands," it is understood that he neither increases nor decreases; thus, by excluding other actions, it possesses the nature of an action because it is a specific mode of operation of the factors of action (*kāraka*).
