[Regarding the phrase "actions having numerable constituent parts": this means those actions whose constituent parts are numerable. The meaning is this: because it has a single result and a single agent, the action is one; yet, it undergoes repetition characterized by recurring performance. In that case, the entire stream of actions is denoted by the verb (ākhyāta) as a non-differentiated whole.

However, the word for number (*saṃkhyāpada*) undergoes a differentiation based on repetition (*āvṛtti*), which has the constituent parts (*avayava*) as its locus; thus, the suffixes *kṛtvasuc* and others arise. For repetition is not possible in the case of absolute difference or absolute non-difference, but rather through both difference and non-difference. Thus, in the first place, there is no inherent connection of number with the action itself. In cases such as *pacati*, *pacataḥ*, and *pacanti*, there is indeed a cognition of the number residing in the means (*sādhana*). But how, then, is the distinction of number understood here in *pākaḥ*, *pākau*, and *pākāḥ*?

For there is no proof here [that this is a fault], because since the action is presented as already accomplished by means of verbal nouns ending in *kṛt* suffixes, its connection with number is not contradictory. || 41 ||

In this regard, if there is a designation [of the object] as something already accomplished (*siddha*), then how can an accomplished thing, such as cooking and the like, be connected with a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*)? Or, if it is something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), then there would be no difference whatsoever between [the meaning of] a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*) and that of a primary derivative (*kṛt*). (42)

A word-meaning that has already reached its completed form (*pariniṣṭhita-rūpa*) does not undergo a connection with a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). And since this is the case for "cooking" (*pāka*) and the like, there too—due to the absence of a connection with a means—the rule prescribing the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) for the agent and the object when a *kṛt*-suffix is employed would be untenable. If, on the other hand, it is argued that in "cooking" and the like expressed by a *kṛt*-suffix, the state of being something yet to be accomplished (*sādhyatā*) still exists, then that would contradict the distinction between *kṛt*-forms and finite verb forms (*tiṅanta*) intended by the author of the Bhāṣya. For the author of the Bhāṣya does not accept a usage such as *pañcakṛtvaḥ pākaḥ* ("five times cooking"), just as he does not accept *pañcakṛtvaḥ pacati* ("he cooks five times"). 42.

Now, having raised the objection that even though cooking and the like are already accomplished (*siddha*), there are cases where the verb expresses them as being yet to be accomplished (*sādhya*) through the use of the genitive case, he refutes this: "In that case, if the verb were the basis for the connection with a *kāraka*, then the genitive would be excluded from that connection by the [rules for] the agent and the object. (43)

Because of the rule "kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti," the sixth case (genitive) is not the domain of a verb (ākhyāta) at all. Even granting that it might be [its domain], it is said: since the sixth case is prohibited by the rule "na lokāvyaya... when there is the employment of a verbal suffix (lakāra), this is not its proper scope. For this very reason, since the mention of "kṛt" [in the sūtra] would be useless for excluding this [case of verbal suffixes], this was stated while disregarding it. However, the mention of "la" there is for the purpose of excluding [the application of the genitive] to forms such as the present participle in -śatṛ. || 43 ||

Anticipating the objection that "in that case, at the time of connection with the means (sādhana) in the act of cooking and so forth, there will be the state of being an object-to-be-accomplished (sādhyatva), whereas at the moment of the cognition of the distinction of number, there will be the state of being already accomplished (siddhatva)," he says: "When there is a single denotation, there is a single object which simultaneously possesses two properties [of being accomplished and being accomplished]. This is not possible; if it were already accomplished, how could it again be an object-to-be-accomplished? (44)

Since a single object cannot simultaneously possess two contradictory properties, there is no dual nature—both established and being established—for a single term such as "cooking" (*pāka*) and so forth. However, when expressed by different words, that same object certainly possesses those two properties, as in: "he cooks," "the cook," "cooking," and so on. || 44 ||

Now, he begins to establish that it is not merely a case of having a single designation here, but rather a case of having distinct designations; thus, there is no contradiction in the two words—consisting of a verbal root and a suffix—conveying both meanings, namely the accomplished and the to-be-accomplished, in the case of "cooking" (*pāka*) and so forth: "The conceptualization that 'this much is the means' (*sādhana*) and 'this much is the end' (*sādhya*) exists only within the technical treatise (*śāstra*), for in reality (*paramārthataḥ*) there is no such division in the sentence. (45)

For when a single word is employed, it is possible to effect a division of meaning through the analysis of stem and suffix, based on the method of presence and absence (*anvaya-vyatireka*) in the process of extracting [meanings] from the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*). However, in common usage (*loka*), the word is indeed indivisible and denotes an indivisible meaning; thus, in that case, there is neither a real division of meaning nor a real division of the word. Because linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) occurs there by means of the sentence (*vākya*), he says "in the sentence" (*vākye*). || 45 ||

Regarding this, he explains how much is the means (*sādhana*) and how much is the goal (*sādhya*), and how they are conceptualized in the treatise: "Just as in the case of a verbal form (*ākhyātaśabda*), the status of being the goal and the means is conceptualized through its two parts according to the treatise, that same sequence applies even in the case of [nominal stems ending in] *ghañ* and other suffixes. (46)

In expressions such as *pacati* ("he cooks"), it is postulated in the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*) that, by virtue of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the verbal root portion (*dhātu-bhāga*) refers to the action (*kriyā*), while the affix portion (*pratyaya-bhāga*) refers to the factors of action (*kāraka*) and so forth. As the author of the *Vākyapadīya* has said: "Because the meaning of the affix does not vary across different roots, and because the meaning of the root does not differ across different affixes, there is a constant connection [of each part] with its respective category. This is likewise the case for *pāka* ("cooking") and other such nouns. (46)

For instance: "In cases where the action is the object to be accomplished and is based on the form of a verbal root (dhātu), that which constitutes its state of being a substance (satvabhāva) is based on suffixes such as *ghañ*. (47)

Regarding the application of two properties despite having distinct designations, he provides an illustration here: since roots and suffixes are taught repeatedly in the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*), and because their meaningfulness is asserted through the determination of non-difference for the sake of establishing grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*) by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), that very same verbal root which occurs in a finite verb (*ākhyāta*) is the same one found here at the end of a primary derivative (*kṛdanta*). Consequently, the nature of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya-svabhāva*) is also non-distinct based upon that.

Consequently, in this context, the means (sādhana) required for the object to be accomplished—which is expressed as a portion of the verbal root—indeed employ a refinement (saṃskāra) characterized by case-endings for their own sake. However, a suffix such as *ghañ* following the root reveals the state of being a substance (*sattvabhāva*) of that meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), whereby it comes into connection with gender and number. And for this reason, even the distinction [of meaning] produced by a finite verb form (*tiṅanta*) is logically established. || 47 ||

Regarding the case where there is a difference in designation despite the connection with two properties, he provides an illustration here: "Kinship (bandhutā) is established in the word 'bandhu' in its form as a singular entity; however, the collective state of those kinsmen (bandhusamūha) is expressed by means of a suffix. (48)

In the word *bandhu* (kinsman), the state of being a kinsman (*bandhutā*) exists as the denoted meaning in a differentiated form. In the case of the collective suffix [in the word] *bandhutā*, which means "a collection of kinsmen," the state of the kinsmen exists as the denoted meaning in an undifferentiated form; for a so-called "collection" is nothing other than the kinsmen themselves. And thus, just as in this case the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) denote the meaning through both difference and non-difference, so too in the case of cooking and the like, the root and the suffix denote the meaning through the states of being already accomplished (*siddha*) and being to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

He states that there is no contradiction here because the difference in words entails a difference in their objects: "In that regard, that toward which [the property] is unestablished as being the probandum is [regarded as] an action; but that toward which it is established is not again [regarded] as being the probandum. (49)

Because it is yet to be accomplished in dependence upon the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), the action (*kriyā*) denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*) is unmanifest; however, in relation to the *kṛt* suffix, it is already established, and thus it does not possess the state of being "to-be-accomplished" (*sādhyatva*) with respect to that [suffix]. And so, the meaning is that there is no connection with the means of accomplishment. || 49 ||

He provides an illustration for the connection with two natures due to the difference in what is required: "The king's son is the grandson; this does not differ from the king. The status of being the son’s referent [as 'grandson'] does not cease to belong to him. (50)

In the expression "May the grandson of the king’s son be victorious," although there is a distinction (vyatireka) in that the son is subordinate relative to the grandson, there is no such distinction relative to the king. Thus, his status as the primary [referent] relative to him does not cease; likewise, the meanings of the two words—namely, the accomplished (siddha) and the to-be-accomplished (sādhya)—are not contradictory with respect to the act of cooking. This is the meaning. || 50 ||

He provides a more appropriate illustration: "Look, the deer runs"—this constitutes the nature of the probandum and the probans; thus, through the distinction of objects, the act of running is established as being twofold. (51)

In the expression "he runs" (*dhāvati*), the action of running is that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*) with respect to the agent denoted by the verbal suffix. With respect to the action of seeing, however, it assumes the status of an instrument (*sādhana*) and experiences the state of being an object (*karman*). For in this case, the deer is not the object [of the verb "to run"], as that would entail the use of the accusative case; rather, the action of running itself is the object. And because there is a misconception of perceptibility regarding the perceptibility of its instrument, the status of being the object of the action of seeing—as expressed in "see [him]"—is logically established. Furthermore, the status of being an instrument does not exist only in the state of being to be accomplished, for that which is unestablished and incapable of assisting another cannot logically function as an instrument.

However, it is only at a subsequent time that the status of being a means (*sādhanatva*) arises for an action that has already been accomplished with respect to another action. Likewise, even in the case of *ghañ* and other suffixes, while the action is expressed by the verbal root as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the suffix expresses its state of being accomplished (*siddhatā*). Since both the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix express the meaning of the suffix together, and because the state of being accomplished is predominant—thereby precluding the recurrence of the state of being to-be-accomplished—suffixes such as *kṛtvasuc* do not occur.

The *kṛtya* suffixes and others, like the *lakāra* verbal endings, denote by their very nature an action (*bhāva*) in its state of being accomplished (*sādhya*). However, since the accomplishment (*sādhana*) of these [actions] is understood through the employment of other words, they indeed come to be connected with *kṛtvasuc* and similar suffixes expressing frequency. For example: *dviḥ śayitavyaṃ bhavatā* (you must sleep twice); *trirbhuktaṃ devadattena* (Devadatta ate three times); *dvirbhuktvā gataḥ* (having eaten twice, he went away); *dvirdattavān* (he gave twice). || 51 ||

Thus it is: "The verbal root is the denoter of that which is to be accomplished (sādhya), whether it appears as [stems ending in] kṛt suffixes other than those with the sense of the past participle or the gerundive, as well as those formed by indeclinables, or as established forms such as past participles (niṣṭhā) and ghañ-derivatives. (52)

In all cases, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the verbal root (*dhātu*) denotes an object whose nature is that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Even in the case of technical or conventional terms (*saṃjñā-śabda*), there is an application of action (*kriyā*) in the process of their etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*). Among these, in the case of verbal suffixes (*lakāra*), the action is denoted as the primary element. The same applies to the *kṛtya*, *kta*, and *khal* suffixes. The *kta* suffix used in the neuter gender is stated to be distinct from the *niṣṭhā* suffix. Thus, because it denotes the state of being to be accomplished, its connection with the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is not contradictory. In this context, the determination of the state of being to be accomplished arises precisely from the connection with the means of accomplishment.

For it is not the case that the status of being "to be accomplished" (sādhya) and "already accomplished" (siddha) of the meaning of a verbal root are communicated by the root-stem (dhātu) and the nominal stem (prātipadika) respectively. Rather, the cognition of the verbal root's meaning as something to be accomplished depends upon its connection with a means of accomplishment (sādhana). Furthermore, the case-terminations (vibhakti) arising from the nominal stem communicate the state of being already accomplished for that stem's meaning. This point has been established. 52.

Regarding the statement that "the future tense (*śvastanī*) is to be added as an exception for the sense of lamentation," and that "the comparison is due to the distance of time," this was rejected. In that regard, it is stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "[Indeed,] there is no comparison by means of a verbal form (*tiṅanta*). This explains how there is no comparison by means of a verbal form: because the object to be accomplished is not yet fully realized, there is no apprehension of identity such as "this is that. Therefore, since such a comparison cannot exist without [the identification of] verbal forms, there is no comparison by means of them. (Verse 53)

In this context, the meaning of a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*) is of the nature of something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), its form being as yet unestablished; thus, it cannot be grasped by identifying it with the object of comparison (*upameya*) through the conceptualization of non-difference, such as "this is that. This is because words ending in verbal suffixes cannot possibly convey anything that is already established in form. Consequently, in examples such as "When will she go?", an action is not compared with another action. Just as in the case of "The boy is a lion," where there is a relationship involving a transferred sense based on the determination of non-difference as "this is that," such is not the case here.

Precisely because [the action] is unestablished, there is an absence of the very relationship expressed as "this is that. Consequently, without the use of the word *iva*, there is no relationship of comparison based on identity here, as in the case of "The boy is a lion. However, when the word *iva* is employed, a relationship of comparison based on difference is perceived, as in "He sings as if he were crying. And in that case, because it is something yet to be accomplished (*sādhyatva*), it does not pertain to the action itself. Rather, it pertains to the agent: "He who sings does so as if he were crying"; thus, there is no similarity between the two actions.

Rather, by means of a pronoun, the instrument (sādhana), although subordinate to the operation (vyāpāra), is referred to as the primary element and thus connected [with the result]. For example, in "the offspring of him who cooks," the offspring is not connected with the meaning of the verbal suffix (tiṅanta). However, in the verse "Darkness, as it were, smears the limbs; the sky, as it were, rains collyrium," this is a poetic fancy (utprekṣā) and not a simile (upamā), because there is no mention of an object of comparison (upameya). || 53 ||

Now, one might object: "Granted that there can be no relationship of standard of comparison and object of comparison (*upamāna-upameya-bhāva*) between two actions because they are not established as such in their own right; however, it will exist by way of their instruments (*sādhana*). Anticipating this, he says: "Since the status of being an instrument is well-established for those things related to verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*), therefore there can only be a superimposition (*adhyāropa*); a true simile (*upamā*) does not exist. (54)

In a domain expressed by a verbal suffix (tiṅanta), those correlates that are employed possess a determined status as *kārakas* (factors of action) with respect to the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Otherwise, there would be no relation [between them]. Therefore, in such instances as "the mountain moves" (*parvataś calati*) or "the sky moves" (*nabhaś calati*), the status of being a means (*sādhanabhāva*) is conveyed by the direct expression (*śruti*) regarding the mountain and so forth.

Even if it were the case that [the literal sense] is not tenable, and thus words such as "mountain" attain the status of a means (*sādhana*) for movement by virtue of an imputed capacity, nevertheless, from this sentence, a relationship of standard of comparison and object of comparison (*upamānopameyabhāva*)—such as "it moves as it were"—is not perceived. For example, someone might say, "He splits a mountain" or "He crosses the great ocean," in order to manifest an excellence of power; yet from these, there is no cognition of "he splits as it were" and so forth. Rather, a means whose capacity is merely possible is connected with the action.

Thus, in such cases as "The Veda fears one of little learning," the grammatical consistency is achieved solely through superimposition (*adhyāropa*) and not through comparison (*upamā*); therefore, even from the perspective of the factors of action (*kāraka*), there is no relationship of standard of comparison and object of comparison (*upamānopameyabhāva*) within the action itself. In this manner, the justification for instances such as "When indeed will she go? must be explained as being due to superimposition alone; for when the future in general is intended to be expressed as a non-remote future (*anadyatana-bhaviṣyat*) by virtue of its long duration, there occurs a superimposition of the state of being a "goer" (*gantṛtva*) upon that [action]. || 54 ||

For this reason as well, he states that there is no relationship of standard of comparison (upamāna) and object of comparison (upameya) between two actions: "And a standard of comparison is prescribed for things that are deficient so as to complete the sense; yet every action is completed within its own respective substratum. (55)

In such expressions as "Her face is as beautiful as the moon," the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is well-known to possess complete qualities, whereas the object of comparison (*upameya*) possesses fewer qualities. However, action (*kriyā*), being accomplished by its instruments and fully realized within its own substratum, is entirely equal [in both cases] and thus does not fall within the scope of simile. || 55 ||

Regarding this, he states an example: "By the very same reason for which it is said that 'the swan flies,' because that [reason] is fully contained within the root [√pat], there exists no purpose for a simile. (56)

The meaning is as follows: when a *haṃsa* (swan) accomplishes the action of going, it is said that "it flies by means of its two wings"; likewise, an *āti*, which is a specific kind of bird, accomplishes the same action of going by means of its own two wings and is thus designated as "it flies. Since the action is fully realized within each respective substratum (*pratyāśraya*), there is no deficiency or excess in the action; therefore, despite their being of the same genus (*sajātīyatva*), there is no relationship of standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and object of comparison (*upameya*), just as one cannot say "a *gavaya* is like a *gavaya*. However, in the expression "the *āti* flies like a *haṃsa*," the relationship of standard and object of comparison exists between the two instruments (the wings), not between the two actions denoted by the verbal suffixes (*tiṅanta*). || 56 ||

Now, one might object: "Let there be no relationship of standard of comparison and object of comparison between two actions of the same genus; however, it may exist between those of different genera. Anticipating this, the author refutes that case as well: "Similarity is not determined among actions that differ in genus. Furthermore, once [an action] is established as the starting point, it cannot be used as a standard of comparison because it remains something yet to be accomplished. (57)

Actions such as "cooking" and "going," which belong to different classes and are mutually and utterly distinct from one another, do not attain the relationship of standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and object of comparison (*upameya*), which is based on similarity. It is impossible to bring about a connection between a standard of comparison—which must be apprehended as an established entity through the cognition "this is that"—and an action-form that exists elsewhere in the nature of something yet to be accomplished (*sādhya*). This is because an action understood from a verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) cannot logically be regarded as an established entity.

Thus, since there can be no relationship of standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and object of comparison (*upameya*) between the meanings of verbal suffixes (*tiṅanta*), this is the meaning of the Vārttika: "But [the suffix is used] as a standard of comparison because of the distance in time. Since going and studying are objects of indolence, when there is a possibility [of their occurrence], even though the future is general, the suffix is established by the intention to express the non-current day (*anadyatana*) within the comparison due to its long duration; the meaning is that this future time is like the non-current day.

Regarding the rule "lakṣaṇahetvoḥ kriyāyāḥ," the connection of the action (*kriyā*) with that [the characteristic or cause] occurs because the relationship between the characterized (*lakṣya*) and the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is understood through the use of the *śatṛ* and *śānac* suffixes. Similarly, the relationship between cause and effect (*hetu-hetumadbhāva*) is also understood from the optative suffix (*liṅ*). Furthermore, even from the use of the particle *iti*, as in "he flees because he kills" (*hantīti palāyate*) or "he runs because it rains" (*varṣatīti dhāvati*), [the connection is established]. Moreover, the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyabhāva*) does not exist at the stage when the verbal ending (*tiṅanta*) expresses [the action]; rather, it arises for the action when there is a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of it in its independence.

In that very way, however, the relationship of standard of comparison and object of comparison is not possible, due to the absence of a state of deficiency or superiority. They say that there is a state of deficiency or superiority among those things connected to the action, as in *pacatikalpam* (he cooks somewhat) and *pacatitarām* (he cooks exceedingly). This point has been explained. || 57 ||

Now this is considered: here, the meaning expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*) has a nature that is yet to be accomplished (*sādhya*), whereas the meaning expressed by *ghañ* and other such suffixes has an accomplished nature (*siddha*). Thus, the distinction between these two states—the external and the internal—is stated in the Bhāṣya. To explain that very point by means of an illustration, he says: "Just as 'the forest' and 'the trees' [are related] by resorting to both difference and non-difference, so the essence of the object is differentiated within the state of being; such is the sequence of the external and the internal. (58)

A collection of trees is called a "forest" non-differentially (*abhedenā*), whereas "trees" are spoken of differentially (*bhedena*) as a plurality. Thus, the distinction in the nature of the referent (*arthasvabhāva*) is not caused merely by the power of the word; this is why the term "itself" (*ātman*) is employed. Since difference and non-difference are distinct, the collection and its parts are indeed different. In this way, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), which is the "being" (*bhāva*), exists internally within the form of the base (*prakṛti*) as the denoted object; it is "internal" because it belongs to the primary level of meaning.

In its state as something being accomplished (*sādhyamānāvasthā*), it differs from an external, established entity (*siddharūpa*) expressed by suffixes such as *ghañ* and others. For the entity expressed by the verbal root (*prakṛti*) is perceived without differentiation, since that which is in a state of being accomplished lacks connection with established properties such as number. And because differentiation is perceived in the verb (*ākhyāta*) precisely through the perception of a difference in the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), it expresses the action solely through the differentiation of the verbal roots.

However, the *bhāva* (action/state) expressed by suffixes such as *ghañ* is conveyed through gender and number with a sense of distinctness (*bheda*), because it is denoted as an accomplished entity (*siddhatayā*), as in *pākaḥ*, *pākau*, *pākāḥ*. In the verb (*ākhyāta*), however, because the *bhāva* exists in a state of being brought about (*sādhyamānāvastha*) and is primary, it is connected with its own properties—namely, tense (*kāla*)—and with the properties of the means (*sādhana*) such as person (*puruṣa*) indicated by the suffixes. Furthermore, because the action possesses a result, it is connected with the "auxiliary" (*upagraha*)—that is, the property of the result indicated by the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) and so forth, which signifies whether the result is intended for the agent (*kartrabhiprāya*) or not.

In the case of *ghañ* and other such suffixes, however, because the action is already established (*siddha*) and functions as a substance (*dravyāyamāṇa*), there is no such connection with time and so forth; rather, there is only a connection with gender and number, which are properties of a substance. Thus, there is this distinction between these two—the meanings of the base and the suffix—which are respectively internal and external. As for the action denoted by the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) in expressions such as "he lies down" (*śayyate*) or "it is slept" (*syīyate*), that follows the very state of being-to-be-accomplished (*sādhyatā*) expressed by the verbal root itself, and not an established form (*siddharūpa*) as in the case of *ghañ* and the like.

For a state (*bhāva*) that abides in its own nature, being unconnected with the form of a means (*sādhana*) or with the state of being accomplished (*siddhatā*), is what is expressed by the verbal suffix (*lakāra*). However, that which is expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*) is joined with the state of being to-be-accomplished (*sādhyatā*); thus, this suffix is not *svārthika* (expressing its own inherent meaning alone). For example, the nominative case (*prathamā*) prescribed for the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) when it is established in its own nature is not treated as *svārthika*. Furthermore, because this state follows the state of being to-be-accomplished denoted by the verbal root, it is connected with time (*kāla*) and other such factors.

Furthermore, because it is something to be brought about (*bhāvya*), this [action] is never dissociated from its agent; thus, even external entities (*bāhya-bhāva*) are spoken of as being of two kinds: one expressed by a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) and the other expressed by a primary derivative suffix (*kṛt*). Moreover, in rules prescribing the *tumun* suffix and others, the governing word (*upapada*) is employed based on the general nature of action, without regard for whether it possesses the dual characteristics of being already established (*siddha*) or yet to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Consequently, forms such as *bhoktuṃ pākaḥ* ("cooking in order to eat") and *kārakasya vrajyā* ("the going of the agent") are established.

There is no fault [in the grammatical system], for the rule governing suffixes such as *tumun* depends upon the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*)—which is of the nature of an action (*kriyārūpa*)—as it is perceived in its state of being accomplished (*sādhyamānāvastha*). However, since repetition (*abhyāvṛtti*) is a property belonging to that which is being brought into being (*bhāvyamānadharma*), and since that [repetition] is absent in the domain of what is already established (*siddhatā*), suffixes expressing frequency (*kṛtvas-artha*) do not occur in the usage of words such as *pāka*. Thus, in this way, the "being" (*bhāva*) denoted by suffixes such as *ghañ* is distinct [from the action].

In this regard, since the rule *kartari kṛt* prescribes that *ghañ* and other suffixes occur in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), the meaning "in the sense of the action" (*bhāve*) is specified; however, because the injunction for the suffix is primary, this [meaning of the action] is subordinate here. Consequently, if one were to intend to express the number (singular) as a subordinate quality and intend to express the gender exactly as heard [in the sūtra], then those suffixes would not occur when there is another number or another gender. Therefore, the author of the Vārttika enjoined that the instruction "in the sense of the action, [the term] is indicated in all genders" must be formulated.

Since the mention of gender (*liṅga*) is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*), number (*saṃkhyā*) is also included therein. Therefore, the following designations must be formulated: *bhūtaḥ* (masculine singular), *bhūtau* (masculine dual), *bhavane* (neuter singular), *bhāve* (locative singular), *bhāvayoḥ* (locative dual), and so forth. Thus, the derivation of forms such as *paktiḥ*, *pacanam*, *pākaḥ*, and *pākau* is established; this is the meaning. || 58 ||

In this regard, the author of the Bhāṣya has established the universal validity [of the rule] by stating: "In an indicative statement (*nirdeśa*), because [the gender and number] are inseparable [from the meaning], they are non-essential (*atantra*). Therein, he explains how their non-essentiality follows from their being inseparable: "The gender that is perceived in the expression 'existence in the general' (*sāmānye bhāvaḥ*) is not intended to be expressed with respect to the particulars (*bhedāḥ*), because those particulars are to be inferred. (Verse 59)

Since it is stated that *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as* denote action in general (*kriyāsāmānyavacanāḥ*), the definition of their meaning provided by the word *bhavati* is made applicable to the meanings of all verbal roots. Thus, when there is a general injunction regarding "being" (*bhāve*)—that is, regarding the general form which is the referent of the word *bhāva*—it is impossible for suffixes to occur after verbal bases of diverse meanings unless they result in specific [meanings]. Therefore, because the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "being" would otherwise be untenable, one must conclude according to the specific [gender] as follows: "in the feminine in the sense of being" (*striyāṃ bhāve*) and "in the neuter in the sense of being" (*napuṃsake bhāve*).

The meaning is that, because the rule for the suffix is more strongly favored by the requirement of grammatical favor (*anugraha*), the employment of a specific gender and number belonging to a particular individual instance is non-essential (*atantra*) and unintended (*avivakṣita*). For it is the general meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha-sāmānya*), which pervades all individual instances, that is intended to be indicated here. Since that [general meaning] cannot be indicated without a substratum, the employment of a specific individual instance is necessarily implied (*nāntarīyaka*). However, as for other specific individuals, their presence occurs through the force of the context; thus, there is an inclusion of all genders and numbers according to each specific case.

Because when there is an injunction regarding a universal for the sake of including all its particulars, it is impossible for that injunction to be restricted solely to those particulars that are necessarily and invariably included. For example, in the general injunction, "This cow must not be touched with the foot," the restriction does not apply only to that specific individual pointed out by the demonstrative "this" (idantā). || 59 ||

Now, one might object: "Granted that in the case of a general injunction, because it must resolve into a particular instance, there may be a cognition of various forms such as 'cooking' (pāka) and so on; however, since the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is 'being' (*bhāva*), how can its masculine gender be abandoned? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In the case of the [technical] designation, the gender is not intended to be significant with respect to 'being,' because its purpose has already been fulfilled; furthermore, in the case of roots like *pac*, the [action] is other than 'being' because it does not conform to the rule for comparison. (60)

Since the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*), being an existent entity, cannot be devoid of gender, the mention of gender is necessarily implied when that [meaning] is indicated. Consequently, that gender-indicatory element is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*). In an injunction (*vidhi*), the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) alone, stripped of its adjuncts, is the operative factor. And here, that [root-meaning] is similar to the object of comparison (*upamāna*) because of the commonality of the verbal roots in the injunction; just as "becoming" (*bhāva*) is the meaning of the root *bhū*, so too "cooking" (*pāka*) from *pac*, "abandoning" (*tyāga*) from *tyaj*—the meaning of the root is to be understood here as the meaning of the suffix. This is the sense.

Therefore, in the domain of verbal roots such as *pac*, there exists a distinct objective form (*artharūpa*) other than the sense of "being" (*bhāva*), namely the form of "cooking" (*pāka*) which is the meaning of the suffix. Likewise, although in cases such as *pakti* (the act of cooking) there is gender (*liṅga*) distinct from the sense of "being," nevertheless, the relationship of comparison between two things of different genders is not contradictory; this is the meaning. || 60 ||

Regarding the statement, "That which [is denoted] by *bhavati* when *pacati* is pointed out," he explains another solution stated in the Bhāṣya: "In this context, that which belongs to *pac* and the other roots is indeed taught by means of *bhavati*; however, the gender of *pac* and the others does not reside in *bhavati*. (61)

Previously, it was stated that in the case of a general injunction (*sāmānyacodanā*), because the intention pertains to all individual instances (*vyakti*), gender and number are not restrictive in the *tantra* system. Now, as for these [two]—masculinity and singularity—which are employed, they are indeed unintended (*avivakṣita*). This is because the universal (*sāmānya*) is singular; even when persisting through a difference in individuals, it does not abandon its oneness. Otherwise, it would not be a universal at all.

Therefore, even when specific individuals are associated with different genders and numbers, the form of roots such as *pac* that exists in the sense of *bhavati* (becoming) persists in the form of pure being (*sanmātra*)—as in *paktiḥ*, *pacanam*, *pākau*, *pākāḥ*, and so on. Because this form of pure being continues without abandoning its own gender and number, the grammatical operations (*vidhi*) based upon it are applicable everywhere; this is the meaning. || 61 ||

Now, one might object: since a universal has the nature of its particulars, a gender associated with a particular must necessarily belong to the universal as well; therefore, if a specific gender is prescribed [for a particular], how can there be a rule for other cases? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "That single entity called 'Being' (sattā) is expressed in some way by various [words]; yet its genders differ, just as they do in the case of differences such as cooking or form. (62)

That single entity, denotable by the word *bhāva* (action/state), which consists of the universal inherent in the state-of-being (*siddhatā*) common to all verbal roots and expressed by suffixes such as *ghañ*, is called *sattā* (being). By its own power, it is denoted by certain words in a certain manner through general terms such as *bhāva* or *sattā* when it has a universal form; and by specific terms such as *pāka* (cooking) or *tyāga* (giving) when it has a particular form.

And in that regard, just as the meaning called "existence" (sattā) is differentiated in the expressions "the color in cooking" (pace rūpam), "the color in cloth" (paṭhe rūpam), or "color as intrinsic nature" (svabhāvaḥ), by virtue of relying on specific individual instances; so too, through the differentiation of words such as "cooking" (paktiḥ) and "the act of cooking" (pacanam), its genders—femininity and so forth—are distinguished. Even though there is such differentiation, the pervasive form that follows all individuals remains undivided; thus, by relying upon that [undivided form], it accomplishes its own function everywhere.

However, it is not restricted by properties such as gender or number belonging to a specific individual, because the universal, having a vast scope, possesses the capacity to admit particulars, whereas the particular lacks the capacity to assimilate the universal to itself; thus, if it were restricted by its own gender, it would be unable to bring about the application of another gender through a rule. And so says the Bhāṣya: "That which belongs to *pacati* (the verb 'to cook') belongs to *bhavati* (the verb 'to be'), but that which belongs to *bhavati* does not belong to *pacati*. Moreover, what is it that belongs to *pacati*? It is the universal."

Furthermore, [it is asked]: "Does the verb *bhavati* become *pacati*? The meaning is that the capacity for mutual inclusion by way of the relationship between the general and the particular has been stated [and] the incapacity [for such inclusion] has also been stated. For the verb *bhavati*, as a general term, includes *paci* [as a particular], but the particular *paci* does not include *bhavati*. || 62 ||

The Teacher explains the illustration presented in the Bhāṣya regarding how a single entity appears in multiple forms due to a difference in its relations: "Just as one and the same person is designated as 'uncle' and 'maternal uncle,' so too is the essence of an object [designated] by that rule in the states of being cooked and being a cook. (63)

This has been stated in the Bhāṣya: "A student goes to the sister's son of his teacher and says, 'Please pay your respects to my teacher. Having gone there, he pays his respects to the maternal uncle. Likewise, the sister's son of the maternal uncle goes to the student of the teacher and says, 'Please pay your respects to my maternal uncle. Having gone there, he pays his respects to the teacher."

And here, just as a single entity is designated as a "teacher" with respect to one person and an "uncle" with respect to another, so too should that mode be understood in relation to the action (*pakti*) and the state (*bhāva*). With respect to its own internal particulars, the action (*pac*), though possessing a universal nature, is a particular with respect to the state (*bhāva*); the state (*bhāva*), however, remains a universal with respect to the action (*pakti*).

And thus, just as a maternal uncle—even though not designated by the word "teacher" (*upādhyāya*)—nevertheless performs his own function because he is a maternal uncle in reality, so too a particular—even though not directly denoted by the word "being" (*bhāva*), which expresses the universal—is nevertheless understood through implication to be in close proximity [to it], and thus performs the function occasioned by the universal. For instance, being a maternal uncle does not exist apart from the form of a teacher; likewise, the form of "cooking" (*pacati*) does not exist apart from "being."

Because there is no absolute difference between the universal and the particular, it is impossible for the form of the universal to exist while excluding all particulars; thus, [the argument] is established in every case. || 63 ||

Thus ends the eighth chapter, the *Kriyāsamuddeśa*, in the *Prakīrṇakaprakāśa* composed by Helārāja, son of Bhūtirāja. **The *Kālasamuddeśa*** Time (*kāla*) was indicated immediately after action (*kriyā*), for it is the delimiter of action. Regarding this, he first states its essential nature as characterized in other philosophical systems: "Some declare time to be distinct from activity; it is an eternal, single, all-pervading substance that serves as the measure of those things possessing action. (1)

Time (kāla), which is characterized by the notions of "prior," "posterior," and so forth, is all-pervading, unitary, and formless; for this very reason, because it is uncreated, it is eternal. It is distinct from action, yet it delimits entities through the medium of actions such as birth and the like—thus it is taught by the Vaiśeṣikas. This [topic] should be understood in detail from that very source. || 1 ||

He states the distinction of time from other delimiting factors by way of its distinctness as that which is delimited: "Measurements such as *diṣṭi*, *prastha*, and *suvarṇa* serve to differentiate material forms; but time serves to differentiate actions, while number is the differentiator of everything. (2)

Form (*mūrti*) is the dimension of a substance that is not all-pervading. It is delimited by means of a measure such as a *diṣṭi* or a *vitasti*. Thus, this [measure] pertains to things possessing form, such as "a *diṣṭi*" or "a *vitasti*. Furthermore, by means of this [measure], there is a delimitation of the object through its restriction to a single spatial direction; and this is a measure (*pramāṇa*). However, by means of a *prastha* and so forth, there is a delimitation of rice and the like from all sides by way of both height and circumference. *Prastha*, *droṇa*, and *āḍhaka*—these are measures. The prefix *pari-* signifies "on all sides" (*sarvatobhāve*).

Gold and the like, as measures of weight (*unmāna*), determine a substance by means of a specific gravity, as in "a *niṣka* of gold" or "a fruit [weighing] one *niṣka*. Time, which is distinct from these, is the cause for determining formless actions; for the movement of the sun and other celestial bodies is measured by time, such as "a month" or "a year. Number, however, provides the determination of everything, both material and immaterial, as well as of measurement and so forth: "two jars," "many selves," "two actions," "one span (*vitasti*)," or "two cubits (*hasta*)."
There are four *prasthas*. There are five *phalas*. Even number is measured by number: two twenties, five fifties. || 2 ||

He explains how actions are determined by time: "Regarding the arising, the persistence, and likewise the destruction of things, they say that time alone is the cause, existing with its nature divided [into distinct aspects]. (3)

Since birth, duration, and destruction are the causes for including all other clusters of activities within themselves, they call Time the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) of those entities that possess birth and the rest, by means of these [three]. For the arising and so forth of entities depend upon Time, which exists with its body divided [into parts]. To illustrate: some things are produced in spring, others in autumn, and still others in the rainy season, and so on; the same applies to their duration and destruction. And because it is differentiated by various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), Time is capable of producing differentiation among related objects.

Since time is the cause for the arising and other states of entities, they declare it to be the stage-manager of this world-machine; by means of its prohibitions and permissions, the universe is differentiated. (4)

The universe resembles a mechanical man, its activity bound by Time, which acts like a master puppeteer. For it is by Time, through its own power, that the manifestation and concealment of entities—the alternating cycle of birth and destruction—are brought about; just as a puppeteer, by means of moving the strings, causes a mechanical man to perform actions such as opening his eyes, Time effects the activities characterized by differentiation within the universe, which thus acquires a sequential distinction of before and after. (4)
For instance: "If [the cause] were not to obstruct [the effect], nor to relinquish its obstruction, then the states would become intermingled, devoid of any sequence of priority and posteriority. (5)

Since there would be no obstruction caused by time, there would be the simultaneous arising of all things; consequently, due to the absence of a fixed sequence for seeds, sprouts, stalks, stems, and so forth, there would be a total confusion. Therefore, because we observe that even those things which arise from their causes undergo a period of maturation in time, time must necessarily be accepted as a necessary efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*). || 5 ||

Now, having demonstrated the oneness of time, he states that its manifoldness is established through the distinction of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*): "By means of distinctions based on other attributes, its self is divided in many ways; for there exists no entity whatsoever that is either distinct or non-distinct. (6)

The other factors (*dharmāntara*) to be described hereafter are those that are conjoined and consist of action (*kriyā*). Due to the distinctions residing within them, even a single time (*kāla*) is designated as manifold; thus, it is the producer of various kinds of effects. Furthermore, in every case, the difference among entities is purely adventitious (*paropādhika*), because they cannot be defined as either inherently different or non-different. As it has been said: "Whether [entities] are 'different' or 'non-different,' this phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*) regarding the nature of things arises only when they are conjoined with external adjuncts. (Verse 6)

For it does not clarify [the point] by means of an example such as "it is either different or non-different": "It is neither one nor many, neither white nor black; yet the nature of the substance appears in such a form solely through its conjunction. (7)

The nature of a substance, being devoid of limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhi*), does not itself fall into common usage (*vyavahāra*). Rather, through the inherence (*samavāya*) of numbers such as "oneness" and so forth, there arises the linguistic usage of "one" and so on. Furthermore, due to the inherence of qualities such as white or black color, a substance is designated as "white" or "black. In this same manner, one should understand that linguistic usages such as "cow" arise from the inherence of universals (*jāti*) such as "cowness" (*gotva*). Similarly, with respect to time (*kāla*) as well, by virtue of its connection with actions such as origination, there occurs the linguistic usage of "time of origination," "time of duration," "time of destruction," and so forth. This is the meaning. || 7 ||

And for this reason: "The distinctions among those things that are in contact are considered to be its [Time's] own particularities (viśeṣas). Distinguished by them, Time serves as the cause for the differentiation of established states. (8)

The "associating time" (*saṃsargin kāla*) refers to specific actions consisting of the movements of the sun and other celestial bodies with which [time] is connected. Through the differentiation of these [actions], this [time], whose own nature is qualified by that distinction, attains various divisions such as day and night, fortnight, month, season, half-year, year, yuga, and manvantara. For instance, time delimited by the limits of the rising and setting of the sun is designated as "day," while that which is differentiated by the interruption of its rising is "night."

Revolving through day and night, it sequentially acquires the designations of fortnights and so forth as appropriate; yet, through the distinctions imposed by actions such as the closing and opening of the eyes and eyelashes, it establishes the conventional usage of moments (kṣaṇa), instants (lava), and measures of time (kāṣṭhā) and the like. || 8 ||

Thus, time, possessing specific distinctions imparted by the difference of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), is apprehended in entities through its non-confused causal status by means of the delimitation of actions such as origination. For instance: "Through connection with a specific time, the acquisition of activity is established for potencies; it does not remain [as the cause] merely in the sense of being the cause of their conjunction. (Verse 9)

Since the activity of the potencies for accomplishment is observed during seasons such as spring, time is inferred as their instigating cause, that is, the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*). For it is indeed by being impelled by time that the potencies bring about the actions of entities, such as their birth and so forth. (9)
And likewise, the rules governing birth and manifestation are dependent upon application; and because its persistence is reliant on what is eternal, persistence is preceded by a rule. (10)

When applied at the proper time, causal powers, being authorized, produce the effect and manifest it. In the view that the effect pre-exists (satkāryavāda), there is a fixed rule regarding the persistence for a determined period of what has been produced and manifested. For this very reason, he says that stability is preceded by a fixed rule. Furthermore, that [stability] is dependent upon eternal form and time. Destruction as well—due to the efficacy of destructive agents whose powers are exercised by time—is dependent on time for all entities.
Thus, by this [verse], what was previously stated in the passage beginning with "In production and in stability" is elaborated. 10.
He speaks of other [states] as well, produced by time: "From those associated qualities, there then follows for the Self favor, obstruction, concealment, and abandonment. (11)

Therefore, even for an object that remains stable, all transformations—such as the gradual favor consisting of growth and decay by means of other related entities like builders or destroyers; the obstruction of the entity's own nature; its incapacity for its own effects; its concealment; its invisibility; its abandonment; its state of perishing, and so forth—are dependent on time, because they occur at fixed moments. ||11||

And having established this, he says that those sequential specific actions of entities, because they are dependent upon time, do not appear as separate [from it] and are therefore designated as "time" itself: "But here, the operation of time is established in every state; for Time alone, being the self of the universe, is called 'operation'. (12)

Because it is invariably concomitant with the conventional usage of time during the states of persistence, production, and cessation—determined by distinctions such as favoring [certain things] and so forth—and because the entire universe is dependent upon this [time], it is the Self that stands in the place of a thread; and since it is the cause of activity, it is designated by the term "activity" itself without distinction. || 12 ||

In order to demonstrate that he is indeed the self of the universe, he says: "Therefore, the separate accumulations and depletions of all distinct forms are perceived through transformation, which is characterized by differentiation. (13)

Because it effects transformation in entities of both animate and inanimate forms during that time, their gradual increase and decrease are perceived distinctly throughout the stages of youth and old age. "By means of differentiation" (bhedayoginā) means by way of the multiplicity imparted through specific conjunctive actions. By the mention of "taking form" (mūrtigrahaṇa), he indicates the absence of any benefit conferred by time upon eternal things. For it is through obstruction and permission that entities subject to birth and destruction are governed by time. (13)

He states that time itself, by its very name, is the cause of the world's manifold diversity: "By means of activities resembling the whirling of a water-wheel, the all-pervading Lord, fashioning all the *kalās*, receives the designation 'Time' (*kāla*). (14)

For the purpose of drawing up water, there is a machine such as a water-wheel (*araghaṭṭa*); its "revolving" (*bhrama*) is its turning around, and the "impulse" (*āveśa*) resulting from that is its agitation. Similar to this are the revolutions of time as it revolves again and again through the states of spring and so forth. By means of these, this all-pervading and eternal Lord causes the "parts" (*kalāḥ*)—the various manifestations of existence—to waver and be scattered; He emits them and sets them in motion from their own causes. Thus, He receives the name "Time" (*kāla*), which is etymologically significant. By this, he indicates the following:

The sole reality, designated as the Supreme Brahman, is the universal self; it alone is the true being. It is designated as possessing infinite power (*ananta-śakti*) by virtue of its performance of various types of effects. Thus, manifesting entities that revolve in succession like the whirling of a firebrand, it impels all beings; therefore, it is called "Time" (*kāla*). It is all-pervasive and independent. For this very reason, it is established in the *Vākyapadīya* that the power of independence (*svātantrya-śakti*) is Time. [Those] who rely upon its power of Time, which has superimposed time [upon itself]...

Thus [it is stated] here; and he will establish this very point as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) later on: "The view of time is divided according to the positions of power (*śakti*), self (*ātman*), and deity (*devatā*). For just as a turner rotates a water-wheel with his arm, so does the omnipresent Lord rotate all entities by means of the power of time (*kāla-śakti*). || 14 ||

The progression of time, characterized by causal connection, is also implied by that very same permission; thus, he states the total dependence on Time by means of an illustrative example: "And those various activities of the universe which are bound by it, He alone permits them, just as a spider [permits] its little webs. (15)

The causal powers, which were obstructed by time when the distinctions of seasons such as winter occurred, are released by that very same [time] when it attains states such as spring; thus it is said that "it causes time" (*kālayati*). For example, a spider releases its fine insects—which serve as the means for capturing large birds—by extending its binding thread, and it binds them again by contracting that very same thread.

For fishermen indeed cause birds bound by strings to move in order to catch other birds; and thus, those birds bound by strings experience restraint and release through the contraction and expansion of those [strings], yet they are not able to fly away unshackled, because the string is pulled according to their [the fishermen's] will. In the same way, objects bound by the "thread of time" (kālasūtra) incessantly experience arising and destruction, characterized by contraction and expansion—this is the meaning.

And therefore, the universe, contained within the pouch of Time, is brought forth when its time has arrived; once born, it remains; and having remained and accomplished its purpose, it perishes. || 15 ||

To the question "How so?", he states the sequence right here: "When the powers (śakti) have attained their maturation through connection with specific times, the eternal action (kriyā) is manifested by the operation called 'employment' (prayoga). (16)

In this world, for the enjoyment of living beings, there is this manifold expansion of cosmic creation; thus, at the time of dissolution's conclusion, by the power of unseen destiny (*adṛṣṭa*), capacities that produce their respective effects manifest within the atoms.

In another philosophical system, when the primary cause (*pradhāna*) or the eternal root causes are oriented toward their effects and possess their inherent powers, a specific action called "impulsion" (*preraṇā*) arises for the sake of their mutual conjunction; by this, the activity that constitutes the general nature of things—as previously explained—and which is an eternal function inherent in all entities, is manifested. Thus, the causes, being endowed with operation, become conjoined with one another. (16)
And therefore, the manifestation of the fruit in that [action] is perceived as being prompted by the genus; it is regulated by powers through some wondrous mode of operation. (17)

When that eternal activity has become manifest, the manifestation of the effect—the manifestation of the product—arises within the causes. That activity is the motivator for the accomplishment of its own substratum; thus, the motivating nature of the universal (*jāti*) has been stated. Since the operation of causes is established through a directed intention toward a specific, determinate class (*jāti*), the universal is the motivating agent. Having previously rejected the two views based on the distinction between the positions of existence and non-existence, he says: "by means of a mode of being that is not false in any respect."

"This mode of being is truly most wonderful, in that the essential nature (ātmatattva) of entities previously non-existent manifests in a way that is without parts and without sequence. This has been established here. And that manifested effect, once born, is regulated by the potencies of the causes, whereby it remains in those very [causes], and is designated as being related to them.

Furthermore, since the operation of causes is refuted in both the positions of existence and non-existence, the establishment of the effect within its own self is a regulation (niyama) that is likewise a most wonderful and marvelous mode of being. (17)

He states what happens immediately after that: "Then, however, the power called 'inherence' (samavāya), which sublates difference, brings about a state of oneness in those individuals by means of its causes. (18)

In this context, *samavāya* (inherence), which is the cause of the cognition "the cloth is here in these threads" and so forth, was previously established as being a *śakti* (power) due to its similarity in terms of dependence (*pāratantrya*). Following the discussion on restriction (*niyama*), that [inherence] conceals the difference between cause and effect; for in this case, identity (*ekatva*) appears as if it were real. Thus, some do not accept the effect as distinct from the cause. The word "as if" (*iva*) is used because there is no actual identity, since the whole (*avayavin*), which is the object of a cognition of non-difference, is in reality different from its parts, which are the objects of cognitions of difference. || 18 ||

When the individual object has been thus established—then, following this rule, all those universals (jātis) which are the motivators [of linguistic usage] descend into that individual, like reflections in clear water. (19)

The word *atha* (then) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaye*). Since the word *ūrdhvam* (afterwards) expresses immediate succession (*ānantarya*), when the manifestation (*avyakti*) is restricted within itself by the potencies of its causes, immediately thereafter—because the time of completion (*niṣṭhā*) and the connection [with a universal] are simultaneous—the manifested effect is indeed born and becomes connected with its own genus (*jāti*) by means of the productive cause (*prayojikā*). However, at the end of the moment following completion, due to the arising of qualities such as color (*rūpa*) and so forth, and through the contact of the sense organ with the object (*indriyārtha-sannikarṣa*), the universals become manifest via the relation of inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyukta-samavāya*), namely, through their inherence in the colored substance.

Just as the reflected images of trees and other objects appear in clear water as non-different from the water itself, so too are universals (jātis) perceived as if they have attained identity with the individual (vyakti); such is the similarity of the illustration. "All" refers to existence (sattā), substantiality (dravyatva), earthness (pṛthivītva), and so forth. || 19 ||

Immediately following this, he describes the production of the qualities (guṇas): "Because they conform to their cause, the qualities there arise preceded by their cause; they are the causes for the manifestation of their own respective classes. (20)

By stating that the effect arises after the cause has arisen, he indicates that it conforms to its cause. Thus, in a single moment, the individual effect is indeed devoid of qualities; thereafter, from the qualities of the parts—which serve as the non-inherent causes—conjoined with the inherent cause that is the whole (the composite), color and other qualities arise in the whole. Once produced, these colors and other qualities manifest their own respective universals, such as "color-ness" (*rūpatva*) and so forth.

The summarized meaning is as follows: by the power of the unseen (adṛṣṭa), action arises in the atoms; preceded by the destruction of the conjunctions and disjunctions with their former locations, it produces objects that are the means of experience through mutual contact, beginning with dyads (dvyaṇuka) and so forth. In all these cases, it must be admitted that the power of time, known as "sequence" (krama), is active. || 20 ||

The successions of births of entities brought about by time have been explained. Now, duration (sthiti) is being explained: "The permanence of the substrata and the permanence of the things dependent upon them—duration favors those manifestations; therefore, it is so designated. (21)

Insofar as those individual effects have eternal substrates as their causes, they possess stability because there is an absence of destruction preceded by the destruction of their causes. Consequently, the eternity of the causes, such as atoms, assists the individual effects by acting as their agent through establishing them in a state of permanence; otherwise, due to the destruction of their support, they would not endure.

Even though the substrata are impermanent, the persistence of the universals (*jāti*) residing within them—which are the causes of their non-destruction—is sustained by their own respective universals, because it is possible for them to persist for that duration as members of a fixed genus. Otherwise, if the universals inherent in things were to perish, the substances would become virtually non-existent, as they would no longer be fit for linguistic or practical usage.

And thus, just as its arising is dependent on another, so too is its endurance; he says: "Just as there is dependence on another in the production of the impermanent, so there is in its endurance. They know that it was created for the sake of destruction alone, its endurance being not under its own control. (22)

Because there can be no arising without a cause, just as that [effect] is dependent upon it, so too, in the absence of support from a cause, it could not exist by itself; thus, a produced thing would perish immediately after its arising and would have been created solely for the sake of destruction, not for the sake of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Lest its birth be purposeless, the Vaiśeṣikas maintain that its duration is dependent upon a cause. (22)

Now, one might object: "Since causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is impossible for a permanent entity—whether successively or simultaneously—and since destruction is observed at the end, there can be no dependence [on other factors] therein; therefore, being produced, it perishes by its very nature, and thus there is no stability. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Abiding, that [entity] is assisted in its activities by associated entities. The activity of those things that possess birth is not recorded as occurring without depending on their existence. (23)

An entity, when assisted by its associated auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), is capable of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). Indeed, nothing whatsoever is a producer in isolation; rather, the accomplishment of an action arises from a causal complex (*sāmagrī*). Thus, for entities that have already arisen, there is no activity or operation toward an effect without the existence of those associated auxiliary causes. In this way, the capacity to perform multiple effects occurring in succession is logically established as the characteristic of "stability" (*sthiti*) upon the acquisition of their respective auxiliaries. And so, the admission of stability until the final limit [of the series] is justified.

As for the objection raised as to what auxiliary causes do, the meaning of "auxiliary" (sahakāra) is simply "acting together," since [the notions of] "excellence" (*atiśaya*) and so forth have been examined elsewhere; thus, the proponents of that [theory of permanence] have established stability in accordance with common experience. || 23 ||
Now he explains the operation of time characterized by obstruction: "The power of time known as decay, which is opposed to other powers, obstructs that power; and opposing factors arise. (24)

That by which a state (*bhāva*) decays is called "old age" (*jarā*); it is a power of Time (*kāla*) that obstructs other powers such as youth common to both living and non-living beings. It hinders the capacity of manifested effects (*kāryavyakti*) to perform their functional activities (*arthakriyā*), which had been determined [to occur] after a lapse of time. Consequently, specific states (*avasthāviśeṣa*) that oppose that capacity—such as dullness of intellect and emaciation—manifest in both living and non-living beings, whereby destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*) is perceived as being imminent. || 24 ||
Thus, when an entity is presided over by decay, all those factors that serve as causes for its persistence vanish, whereby the self is abandoned. (25)

Those causal factors, acting as conditions for the subsistence-phase, which were set in motion by their associated co-operating causes to perform their respective functions—all of them withdraw from this entity presided over by decay, like ungrateful companions even though they have lived together. Once they have withdrawn, the essential nature of this entity, having completed its task, falls away. || 25 ||

But he says that nothing whatsoever is produced for this [self] by causes of destruction: "Just as everything is born through a wondrous mode of being—without exit, without support, and without a place—so too is its self abandoned. (26)

Regarding origination (*janman*), since the operation of a cause has already been refuted previously through the distinction between the positions of existence and non-existence, the reality [of things] remains unmanifested. Because there is no existing causal basis—and precisely because of the absence of causal operation—the entire universe, being produced without sequence (*akrama*) through the successive completion of parts and sub-parts, is perceived as arising simultaneously; this was already determined earlier in the investigation of *vivarta* (illusory manifestation). The same applies to destruction (*vināśa*).

The meaning is that if [cessation] were occurring [as an active process], it would result in its being a positive entity (*bhāvatā*); thus, the abandonment of entities depends entirely on the passage of time, which serves as the basis for their cessation. Therefore, it has been determined here that the operation of Time—the soul of the universe—consists everywhere in this very process: the occurrence of creation, maintenance, and dissolution through the power of Time’s permission and obstruction. As it has been said: "But in every state, the operation of Time is established here. (26)

Now he states another reason for inferring time: "How could there be a determination of two actions that have a termination and are inherent in different objects, without a single related entity [to connect them]? (27)

In this context, action (*kriyā*), consisting of a collection of multiple moments, is sequential because moments do not exist simultaneously; thus, it is indeed supported by the power of time (*kāla-śakti*). For sequence is a property of time. Furthermore, although two actions are identical in their nature of perishing immediately after arising, a distinct determination such as "done slowly" or "done quickly" is not possible without a single related entity serving as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). By the phrase "inhering in different objects," he states that there is a difference between actions due to the difference in their substrates.

Furthermore, this designation is not caused by a single action, because it persists even when the substrata are different—as in the expressions "the cloth was made long ago" and "the jar was made long ago. This is because it would be impossible for a single action, which inheres in distinct substrata, to remain identical while those substrata differ. For this very reason, the designation is not caused by the effect-substance (*kāryadravya*), since it is impossible for a distinct effect-substance to serve as the cause of a non-distinct designation. Nor is the cause here the instrument (*kāraka*) and so forth, because that too differs according to the variation in the substrata.

Therefore, that which is the cause in this case is time. If that [time] were also distinct [in each instance], then there would not be a recurring cognition; thus it was said by the word "by one" (*ekena*). For time, being single due to its commonality, produces a recurring cognition. || 27 ||

Anticipating the objection, "If this is so, from what source do the designations of 'dissimilar,' 'long,' 'quick,' and so forth arise?", he says: "Just as weight placed upon various substances on a scale or in the hand is measured by time alone, so too is the movement of action. (28)

Just as a single scale-rod, through the distinctions introduced by its connection with lines and strings, determines the weight inherent in substances such as gold and silver in terms of measures like *pala* and so forth, so too Time—experiencing manifoldness through the application of its own powers—measures the continuum of actions, which possesses diversity due to the distinctions of specific actions such as the *nimeṣa*, in terms of durations such as "long" or "short. Furthermore, the hand of merchants who possess great skill and practice determines the specific weight of objects; thus, that too serves as an illustration.
Just as that hand [is one], so too time, being essentially one and unconditioned, delimits the distinctions found within action by its own inherent capacity. || 28 ||
And thus that single time abandons both the co-existent activities and those established in inherence; like a grain of rice [losing its moisture], it thereby attains the designation of a "year. (29)

When a single time remains constant, various actions along with their concomitants pass away; therefore, that time acquires the name *hāyana*, a synonym for *saṃvatsara* (year). It is called *hāyana* because it causes actions to abandon (*jahāti*) it. For example, just as water that remains together with rice seeds is designated as *hāyana* because it causes them to abandon [the seed], for this very reason the author of the Sūtra taught the etymology simultaneously with the simile in the rule *haś ca vrīhikālayoḥ*.

Just as rice is assisted by water with which it coexists, so too time assists entities through its concomitant activities; thus, its differentiation is conditional (aupādhika), whereas its primary nature is non-differentiation. || 29 ||

If, then, time is a single, stable entity, how can it possess a sequential nature? To this he says: "The activity of that [time] is eternal through both obstruction and permission; being divided by that [activity], it assumes a sequential form. (30)

Obstruction (*pratibandha*) is the hindrance of the operation of the causal capacities (*sādhana-śakti*) of some action; its opposite is permission (*abhyanujñā*). Time’s eternal activity with respect to entities is characterized by these two. For among entities that are in a state of constant transformation, it is an established fact that something arises and something perishes. Thus, sequence, which resides in effects, is superimposed upon time, but it is not real (*bhāvika*) there. For sequence is primarily a property of action; elsewhere it is merely metaphorical.

For priority and posteriority are observed as adventitious attributes (upādhi) residing in preceding and succeeding entities, and not as independent [qualities]. Likewise, simultaneity—which is a property incompatible with sequence—is superimposed upon time by way of its presence in effects. (30)

He states that even the state of being even or uneven belongs to time through metaphorical attribution: "Due to the difference in agents, excellence or deficiency occurs in their respective objects; it is that single [time] which attains the state of evenness or unevenness. (31)

In this context, when practitioners perform the conduct (*ācāra*) established by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, that very time reaches its excellence and is designated as the single period beginning with the Kṛta age; the meaning is that it is differentiated by the abundance of those qualified for virtuous conduct. That conduct, which has the agent as its means of accomplishment, is the purpose of that [time]. However, when agents become unrestrained and transgress proper conduct, then, due to the decline of conduct and the resulting diminution, time is called by names such as Kali, which are distinct from the former.
Thus, although this time is one, it attains division through the difference among those who perform the rites. || 31 ||

He states another superimposed division of time: "Just as the designations 'carpenter' and so forth apply to a single person due to the difference in his actions, so too do the designations 'season' and so forth arise for a single [entity] due to the difference in its actions. (32)

Just as the designations of "carpenter," "ironworker," and so forth are applied to a single agent based on specific activities such as carving or forging, so too do distinct names—such as "spring" and the like—arise for time, which is in fact one, due to the differences in specific activities characterized by the production of particular flowers and so forth. By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (ādi), the designations of the bright and dark fortnights, the day and night, and the evening and dawn are likewise understood to be applied according to their respective distinctions in activity. || 32 ||

He states that other distinctions of time are also superimposed: "The beginning, the action itself, and the completion are thus designated due to the distinction in the superimposition of other attributes upon that which is both existent and non-existent. (33)

Before its production, an object is of the nature of non-existence; once produced, it is of the nature of existence. When that [existence] is accepted as a real entity through the unification of cognitions, the times of commencement and so forth are designated as distinct by virtue of the difference between their distinct attributes (*dharma*). For instance, having intended the form of the object through cognition, the acquisition of suitable means is the time of commencement (*ārambha-kāla*). The employment of those acquired means is the time of action (*kriyā-kāla*). The completion of what was to be done is the time of conclusion (*niṣṭhā-kāla*).
Thus, according to the respective times, there is a distinction of the times of commencement and so forth through the conceptualization of different attributes. 33.

And he says that this [space] is equal everywhere: "Whatever extent belongs to dyads (dvyaṇuka) and so forth, that same extent belongs even to that which possesses magnitude (bimavat); for the self (ātman) of anything cannot be divided or measured. (34)

Since composite wholes (*avayavin*) are partless, the time of their commencement and so forth is identical for all of them. However, the parts (*avayava*) are entities distinct from that [whole]. Furthermore, dimension (*parimāṇa*), as a quality (*guṇa*), is something entirely other than the composite whole; therefore, when there is a difference in those [parts], it is impossible to either increase or decrease the form of the [whole] itself.
