Consequently, because the composite substance as a mere effect is uniform, the time of commencement and so forth for things of small dimension and things of large dimension is not differentiated by virtue of that [composite]; rather, the meaning is that it is differentiated by virtue of other properties distinct from the composite whole.
Regarding this, it is said: "By other entities, the accumulation of others is conceptualized; through that, it is perceived as 'this is slow' or 'this is quick. (35)

The accumulation (*pracaya*) of composite wholes (*avayavin*) of small or large dimensions is postulated and superimposed by means of many constituent parts (*avayava*) that are indeed distinct from them, while their diminution (*apacaya*) is likewise attributed to few parts. Thus, a composite with many parts is produced slowly, whereas one with few parts is produced quickly; in this way, a distinct temporal sequence is determined there for the time of commencement and so forth. Because the difference [between the whole and its parts] is concealed by inherence (*samavāya*), the properties of the parts are designated as belonging to the whole, yet in reality, there is no difference in the time of the composites. //35//
For there is no sequence for that which is non-existent, since it cannot be divided; and even regarding that which exists, its essential nature remains exactly as it is. (36)

An entity is non-existent prior to its arising. Because it lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), there is no division into earlier and later parts; therefore, there is no sequence. Furthermore, for that which has arisen and exists, because its own-being (*svarūpa*) persists in that very same manner and cannot be differentiated, sequence is non-existent. Thus, when one reflects through the intellect, the conventional usage of "sequence" does not apply to what is both existent and non-existent; this is what is meant by implication. For sequence is necessarily dependent upon differentiation.

Furthermore, that differentiation—the state of an object as it is being produced—is impossible at every stage for that which, in reality, consists of the two states of existence and non-existence; thus, through the synthesis of these stages, there is a superimposition of prior and posterior forms. In this way, the very first sequence is conceptual; everything of that nature is not primary.

Not only do designations such as "season" and so forth proceed with respect to a single time based on the distinction of actions, but even designations such as "past" and so forth do so; thus he says: "And being conditioned by action, the states of past, future, and present are apprehended as divided into eleven modes. (36)

When actions have arisen and are already destroyed, the time characterized by them is designated as "past. When actions have their means present and their emergence is imminent, the time characterized by them attains the state of "future. However, that which is characterized by an action that has begun but not yet been completed is termed "present. Furthermore, these divisions of time—past and so forth—are subdivided again into eleven types. (37)
To the question "How so?", he says: "Therein, the past is fivefold and the future is fourfold; the present is said to be twofold—thus there are eleven conceptualizations. (38)

The general property of past time (*bhūtasāmānya*) is counted as a single division of the past because it is excluded from the specific [divisions]. As it has been said: "Just as the general is a particular, so too is this. The first is the division of the past pertaining to today (*adyatana*). The second is that pertaining to non-today (*anadyatana*). The third is the aggregate of both today and non-today, which is distinct from those two. The remote past (*parokṣa*) is not counted separately as a division of the past, because it is not a distinct division of the non-today.

That which, although future, obtains the functions of the past through extension (*atideśa*)—that is the fifth division of the past, the secondary (*gauṇa*) one whose state as past is superimposed. There are four divisions of the future: the general future, the present-day, the non-present-day, and the combination of both present-day and non-present-day. That which, by virtue of being prohibited like the non-present-day, acquires the functions of the general future—even though it is non-present-day—is, in the technical usage of the treatise (*śāstra*), simply the general future. The primary (*mukhya*) present is one alone.

That which has become proximate to the present, having its state extended [to the past], is the second [type of] past and future according to the rule "in proximity to the present" (*vartamānasamīpye*). Thus, these divisions of time have been conceptualized for the sake of distinguishing the functions of the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*), but they are not actually as numerous as the sky. In this way, because there are infinite divisions due to the differentiation of actions, the distinction between the past and so forth has been stated. || 38 ||

Anticipating the objection—“How can an action that has passed away and no longer exists confer the designation of ‘become’ upon time?”—he says: “When one’s own form is deposited in time and restrained by wisdom, then all entities turn back from it, their powers having been transferred into that [time]. (39)

Objects brought into being by action are called "past" when they have departed from their own nature (*svarūpa*). In that regard, the nature of those objects which was grasped by the intellect during their state of existence is now projected onto the enduring time (*kāla*) as its own substrate; thus, they come to exist in a state of being remembered after having been experienced. Consequently, with their powers transferred to the past path, they follow along with memory-based worldly activity (*vyavahāra*). This is what is meant: the principle of time (*kālatattva*) manifests itself through the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of objective entities.

When entities are experienced, their state of having already come into being (*bhūta*) is imagined by means of its own limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) as that which is being remembered. Thus arises the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) such as "the jar existed. Therefore, this very fact is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) that makes known the existence of time; for if the object were non-existent, such usage would be untenable. Since the usage "it existed" occurs when the form [of the object] has been transferred to time, time is established. || 39 ||

If that is so, how can there also be an instruction regarding the future? To this he says: "The very form of things yet to come, and its reflection, appears in time itself, as if in a perfectly polished mirror. (40)

At the time when the efficient cause (*samarthahetu*) is present, for those entities whose arising is anticipated, there is a certain external form, as well as a reflected image (*pratibimba*) of that external nature which is determined in the intellect. The "ascent" (*samāroha*) into a stable time occurs through the determination of the identity between these two—the perceived object and the conceptual construction—due to their single form. This means that by the superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of that [external form] onto the time, one determines its future existence and thus arrives at the ascertainment of its fixed nature. The meaning is that objects shine forth only as being included within the service-vessels of time and so on; hence, they possess a similarity to a mirror. (40)

And thus, because things possess the nature of being subject to the transition of time, there is a constant transformation; so he says: "Just as a stream carries away grass, leaves, creepers, and the like, so too does Time set in motion the measures of those who possess measures. (41)

Just as the current of a river pushes certain things like grass and so forth, displacing them from their place, while others it seizes and settles back in that same place; even so, time, in its incessant flow, repeatedly seizes and casts away entities, and sets in motion the transformations of the properties of those things thus cast away. || 41 ||

He confirms that very point by means of another illustration: "Just as the wind, having entered as it were, coordinates the movements of those who possess motion, so too does the self of time (kāla-ātman) ordain the nature of succession. (42)

Just as the vital air called *prāṇa*, residing within the joints of the limbs of embodied beings, effects activities such as coming and going, so too does the self of Time (*kālātman*), having entered into the very nature of entities, brings about sequence—characterized by priority and posteriority—by means of obstruction and permission, causing them to sink and emerge. 42.
Then he says that this is established: "The division of the solstices, the fixed course of the luminaries, and the very origin and cessation of living beings are dependent upon it. (43)

The division into the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*) and the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*) is dependent upon the boundaries established by time. Furthermore, the fixed motion of the constellations, consisting of their rising and so forth, follows time. And at the time of the creation and dissolution of the great elements (*mahābhūta*), birth and destruction, characterized as manifestation and disappearance, are dependent on time. Thus, time, which benefits all, is called the "Soul of the Universe" (*viśvātman*). || 43 ||

He states that the luminaries, synonymous with the constellations (*nakṣatra*), are forms of the divisions of time and nothing else is their true essence: "Those which follow the course of time as the measures of the [temporal] units are called 'constellations' (*nakṣatra*); among them, the stars (*tārakā*) are merely the marks. (44)

Those specific transformations of entities that occur by virtue of their connection with particular times are distinguished and separately designated by the names of constellations such as Kṛttikā and the rest. For instance, whatever state arises in Puṣya and the others when they are in conjunction with the moon receives that designation, such as "Tiṣya" or "Punarvasu" applied to a young boy. It is for this very reason that the non-observation of the notion of "born" (*jāta*) in these cases is explained; for it is the inherent denotation of meanings by words that is being elucidated here.

The specific entity that arises through that [conjunction] is designated as "stationary" (tiṣṭhat) and so forth; thus, in reality, time is merely a modification of the constituent parts (mātrā-pariṇāma) conditioned by the lunar mansions (nakṣatra). Because of its separate mention, the names of the lunar mansions—such as Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, and so on—are understood to apply to time as well. For that portion of time is a condition (upādhi) for entities by way of the action of birth. However, the luminaries are merely indicators of it; the form of the lunar mansion is not limited to that alone, since its manifestation occurs through conjunction with the moon. || 44 ||

And just as the specific fixed time is made known by the signs consisting of luminous bodies which are its effects, so too it is indicated by other means; thus he says: "By the cries of wild animals and birds, by the activities of stationary beings, and by the changes in shadows and the like, the abode of the seasons is determined. (45)

The seasons (*ṛtu*) are its abode (*dhāma*), because it manifests as being of that very nature. For the power called Time (*kāla*), which is the sovereign power (*svātantrya-śakti*) of Brahman, shines forth divided into the distinctions of spring and so forth. Thus, this fixed division of seasons is determined by the warbling of male cuckoos and other birds, by the appearance of ever-new sprouts, by the specific movements of the sun and other celestial bodies as indicated by the variations of shade and sunlight, and by the particular blossoming and spreading of creepers. To illustrate: * *Ṛtavo dhāma sthānam yasya*: "The seasons are the abode—that is, the locus—of that [Brahman]," because it appears as having those [seasons] as its essence. * *Kālākhyā hi svātantryaśaktir brahmaṇo vasantādibhedena pravibhaktā cakāsti*: For the power known as Time, which is the independent power of Brahman, shines forth clearly, differentiated by the divisions of spring and so on. * *Tathā cāsau niyataṛtubhedaḥ... avadhāryate*: And thus, this fixed distinction of seasons is perceived through the warbling of the male cuckoo and others, through the connection with ever-fresh shoots, through the specific variations of shadow and light marked by the particular movements of the sun and so forth, and through the specific blooming and spreading of creepers. * *Tathā hi*: For instance: [The passage continues with examples illustrating these points.]

The summer season is perceived as being filled with bees intoxicated by the fragrance of sweet-smelling flowers; its forest regions resound with the cries of male cuckoos. It possesses a pleasant breeze accompanied by the most sweet humming of bees, and it awakens lovers clinging to the blossom-clusters on the arms of their beloveds. Beautiful with the scent of jasmine, it causes the trembling of elephants distressed by the heat. The wind shakes the mass of flowers upon withered creepers, and the hot season, full of heat, is perceived as seizing the multitude of living beings who suffer from thirst and parched mouths amidst heaps of scorched dust.

With the movement of the sun’s heat stilled, the sky covered by clouds, the regions of the earth flooded with water, and the paths difficult to traverse in some places; filled with the cries of peacocks in every direction, with throngs of lovers staying within bowers of creepers, and causing trembling to those longing for absent ones—the rainy season is being experienced here in its proper order. By the cry of swans, by clusters of lotuses shining with liquid lac-dye, by the purity of the quarters, and by the clouds that mark the sky with their pure whiteness—

The season known as Hemanta is clearly perceived here by the beauty of the ripened rice with its lovely forms, by the heart-stealing gait of the deer, and by the stars shimmering in the stainless sky freed from autumnal clouds; by the spotless flowers blooming in every direction, by the animals whose limbs are numbed with cold, by the crows dwelling in the forest, and by the most beloved expanses of night for those with longing hearts.

Where the snowy wind blows incessantly, its path through the Urva mountains blocked by falling snow, where withered leaves are scattered and even the cold is perceptible; where the flocks of birds shiver, afflicted by the chill, and the surface of the earth is veiled by streams of mist; where the wind is skilled at breaking up masses of frost and carries forth the fragrance of clusters of blossoming *kunda* flowers; and where the excellence of the trees is most abundant on all sides. (45)

Now, he explains the utility of time even within the doctrine of non-duality (advaitavāda): "This appearance of the universe—which, though itself devoid of succession, is perceived as if possessing succession—is the activity of Time. (46)

In accordance with the direction shown in the *Saṃbandhasamuddeśa*, the universe is a sequential manifestation (*vivarta*) of Brahman. That which constitutes its sequential appearance is due to the capacity of the power of Time (*kāla-śakti*) to obstruct and permit. Indeed, it has been determined in the *Brahmakāṇḍa* itself that the power of Brahman called Time is none other than *avidyā*, and it becomes effective for individual souls (*jīvātman*) by causing sequential manifestation. Thus, first, the operation of Time here consists in the manifestation of sequence. (46)

He states that even the temporal distinction immediately following that is merely conditional: "Just as the determination of nearness and distance is based on space, so too the determination of long and short duration is based on time. (47)

The determination that "this path is distant" or "this path is near" is based on the difference in the movement of the traveler, not because there is any actual division in the path itself. For that very same path which is distant for those of slow gait is near for those of clever exertion. Likewise, even though time is stationary, the designation "long" is established through the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of accumulated serial actions, while the designation "quick" is established through the limiting condition of non-accumulated serial actions. (47)

Now, although the previously mentioned divisions of time—such as the past and so forth—are conditioned by action (*kriyā*), they are taken up again here to state a specific distinction: "Of that undivided time, three divisions produced by action are established for the sake of conventional usage, which the world does not overstep. (48)

Since it is impossible to function [linguistically] with undifferentiated time, there are three divisions in common worldly usage, as if they were distinct, although in ultimate reality they are one. These well-known designations—past, future, and present—are conditioned by action (*kriyā*). It is called "past" when the action has ceased; "future" when the action is yet to occur; and "present" when the action is proceeding in the form of a continuous flow of moments. This [distinction] is indeed primary. (48)

To explain how there is no division of this [time], he says: The three powers of the one time are established as inherent; through connection with them, there is the perception or non-perception of existing entities. (49)

The difference in effects does not entail an inference of a difference in causes, because the difference in effects is accounted for solely by a difference in capacities (*śakti*). There is no primary difference in that which is called Time, the cause of the universe. To explain: through connection with the capacity of the present, there is the manifestation—birth—of entities that already exist. Through connection with the capacities of past and future time, however, there is the concealment—invisibility or non-manifestation—of those very same existing entities; this constitutes destruction in the form of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and posterior non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*). Thus, since the difference in effects is established by a difference in capacities, the postulation of a difference in Time is groundless. (49)

He indeed distinguishes between manifestation and non-manifestation through the differentiation of powers. By means of two powers, he is the veiler of entities; however, the power called "the present" is that which illumines the form of the entity. (50)

Time effects the veiling or concealment of existing entities through its past and future powers; through its present power, it brings about the manifestation of the form of entities when they are perceived. (50)

Now, one might raise the objection: "Just as for those things whose obscuration is caused by a future capacity, a re-manifestation is seen to involve a connection with a present capacity, why does the same not occur for those whose obscuration is caused by a past capacity? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The capacity of birth belonging to the future is non-obstructive; however, that capacity which is called 'past' is contradictory to birth. (51)

The future capacity (*anāgata-śakti*) is not incompatible with the present capacity (*vartamāna-śakti*) that accompanies birth; it does not create an obstruction to its arising. For it is by that [future capacity] that it is held back at its own time. However, when the collection of efficient causes (*samartha-hetu*) has come together, the future capacity partakes in the conformity to the arising of the present capacity. Indeed, that which is to become present at another time is precisely what is called "the future. But the power of birth, known as "subsistence" (*vartanā*), is indeed contradicted by the past power; for there is no rebirth for one who is dead. Thus, an entity that has fallen into the past path does not manifest again. || 51 ||

An objection is raised: "Since powers (śakti) reside in the possessor of power (śaktimat), they must always be present just like the possessor of power; therefore, because of their constant conjunction, there would result the simultaneous perception and non-perception of contradictory forms in entities. Anticipating this, he says: "These three paths are established like darkness and light; though they are without succession, a succession of entities is perceived within them. (52)

The three divisions of time—past, future, and present—are like "paths" (adhvan). Just as travelers on paths carry out a continuous process of going and coming, so too do entities, undergoing transformation within these [divisions], construct a continuous sequence of "having gone" and "not yet having gone. That very entity which stands in the future path, having fallen into the present path, falls again into the past path.

And likewise, proponents of transformation (pariṇāmavādins) accept that entities belong to the three time-periods. As it is stated in the *Pātañjala*: "The properties (dharmas) belong to the three times. Although these three are specific powers existing without succession within the nature of Time, nevertheless, by manifesting activity toward the objects to be supported (ādheya-bhāvas) through their nature as darkness and light, they establish priority and posteriority by means of perception and non-perception, through the conceptualization of existence and non-existence.

Just as the qualities characterized by *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, though existing simultaneously due to their eternity, bring about the accumulation of various states through their respective manifestations of their own functions by entering into a relationship of primary and secondary factors (*aṅga-aṅgibhāva*) and through diverse transformations; so too these divisions of time, by virtue of the majesty of their own power, are skilled in arranging the succession among the various states of existence. This is the meaning. 52.

He analyzes the nature of darkness and light as follows: "Of those two, the two forms of darkness remain like a single mass in the absence of light; moreover, for some, even that which has passed away returns again. (53)

The past and future time-periods (*adhvan*) are of the nature of darkness (*tamas*), because they are the cause of the obstruction of existence; for obstruction is indeed the property of darkness, as it is said: "Darkness is heavy and solely obstructive. Rajas, however, is the commonality of activity, the very form of time, and is pervasive everywhere. Through both hindering and permitting, it is the instigator and takes the form of impulsion; thus, rajas is essentially temporal. Furthermore, the fact that the transformation of the three qualities (*traiguṇya*) constitutes the nature of Brahman is also logically consistent with respect to time, even when time exists in the form of a potentiality (*śakti*).

For the powers of knowledge and action, as well as the triad of qualities (*guṇatraya*), reside in the individual soul (*jīvātman*). It has been stated previously that the power of time (*kālaśakti*) resides in that very same place; it is a power transcending those [other] forms and acts as an obstacle to the power of birth (*janmaśakti*). Some, however, believe that even that which has fallen into the past path (*atītādhvan*) may emerge again at another time during the revolutions of the cycles (*parivarta*). For entities (*bhāva*) that have been completed and finalized remain within the service of *pradhāna* and manifest their own nature according to the proper time; they do not, however, vanish into that very same state during the dissolution (*pralaya*).

This is the traditional teaching (*āgama*) of the Sāṃkhyas, who maintain five grounds for their philosophical system. Furthermore, in this view, the existence of the three time-periods (*traiyadhvikatva*) is even more thoroughly established, since everything arises within all three times. In a world that proceeds as a continuous stream (*prabandha*), the past does not possess presentness. Even during a transformation of the world, it is not that very same thing which returns, but rather something similar; thus, the contradiction between past power and present power was stated previously.

But here, in contrast, another philosophical view is stated: "Non-existence does not exist for that which exists," meaning that very same entity returns after its concealment. Thus, having accepted a certain degree of distinction between the attribute (dharma) and the substratum (dharmī), this view is set forth: the substratum is permanent and present, whereas the attributes belong to the three times. || 53 ||

Now, relying on the real non-difference between the property and the possessor of the property (*dharmidharmin*), he states the view of the *Mahābhāṣya*: that even simultaneously, three designations of the possessor of the property proceed by way of its properties. "It attains the state of being present through those properties; and because some [of them] are present, it likewise expresses the state of being past. (54)

Those phenomena (*dharma*) which are past, present, and future belong to that which is the possessor of those phenomena (*dharmī*). Simultaneously, and all at once, it attains the state of being present—the state of being current—because the phenomenon is present. Since the possessor of the phenomenon is not distinct from it, and because it likewise possesses the state of being present, it also enters into the immediately following state of being past; thus, it simultaneously reaches the state of being past as well. The meaning is that because a certain phenomenon is past, the possessor of that phenomenon—which is not distinct from it—is likewise [past].

Thus, because a certain dharma is future, it attains the state of being future. In this way, although the substratum (dharmī) always exists as a reality according to its own nature, it is conventionally designated as belonging to the three times even at a single moment due to the threefold nature of its attributes (dharmas). Furthermore, it has been established elsewhere that attributes are not distinct [from the substratum], like a configuration. 54.

Anticipating the objection that there can be no coexistence in one place due to the contradiction between the past and the present, he says: "Drawn forth by the operation of its cause, it attains the state of being present; once the operation of its cause has ceased, it does not come into view again. (55)

When causes, being fully activated, begin to produce an effect, then the entity arising through their power, entering the path of perception and accomplishing purposeful actions (*arthakriyā*), is designated as "present. However, when the operation of its causes has ceased, it is designated as "past" or "future. Thus, even for a single entity, a distinction in designation based on extrinsic conditions (*paropādhi*) is not contradictory; rather, the distinction in designation is caused by the presence or absence of purposeful action.

[Objection: But surely, only that which performs a causal function (*arthakriyākārin*) is ultimately real (*paramārthasat*). Since such a function is absent in the past time-period (*adhvan*), how can there be existence [there]? [Reply: We do not accept that existence is contingent upon the performance of a causal function; rather, entities exist by virtue of their own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*). And their intrinsic nature consists of the three *guṇas*. Furthermore, there is no destruction of that which is eternal.

Because it follows everywhere and at all times, and because it has been established by the [chapter] on the "Removal of the Fivefold" (vītapañcaka), it has been said: "This very triple world departs from manifestation, but not from existence. || 55 ||

Intending that the non-perception of an entity in the past and future time periods is the same, some who prefer brevity accept that time possesses only two powers, which are synonymous with obstruction and permission; thus he says: "For some, there are only two paths of power belonging to all-pervading Time, by means of which it effects the opening and closing of entities. (56)

Since the non-perception of an entity prior to its arising and after its destruction is indistinguishable, there is but one power of Time—which consists of the nature of grasping all entities—that is characterized by obstruction. The second, however, is characterized by permission; it brings about the manifestation of entities and consists of the nature of giving rise to all entities. Thus, the nature of Time has been explained. 56.

However, on this point some disagree, saying: "Since it is impossible to engage in linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) with a non-differentiated time, that very limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) such as action (*kriyā*) which is postulated as its differentiator is itself the cause of linguistic usage; what is the use of a postulated essence of time (*kāla-ātman*) that is unperceived and logically untenable? Furthermore, if there is a difficulty in linguistic usage without a postulated form of time, then let the reality of time (*kālatattva*) be exactly like that. To refute this view, he says:
Some describe those [cognitions] as being characterized by the synthesis of the intellect, which are distinct in meaning and divided by time according to their own nature. (57)

Diverse actions, when synthesized by the intellect (*buddhi*) and integrated through the process of conceptual unification (*saṃkalana*), become the cause for designations such as "long" or "short," and likewise for designations such as "day and night. Thus, it is established that the nature of time—whether long and so forth—is nothing other than a distinct conceptual synthesis performed by the intellect; it does not possess an independent ontological reality. For instance, even within a "long duration," its constituent parts—the various moments (*kalā*)—are conceptually differentiated as its own internal divisions. The same applies to "short duration" and to periods such as "days" and so on.

However, this distinction of "long duration" (*ciram*) and so forth does not arise from the influence of the limiting adjuncts of action (*kriyopādhi*), because, according to the reasoning previously stated, the intellect (*buddhi*) possesses its own inherent distinctions. Furthermore, that very [distinction] is superimposed upon the continuum of action when it is being conceptualized as its own object. For it is observed that a property of the intellect conforms to the form of its object; thus, the state of "long duration" and so forth belonging to the mental synthesis—which is of the nature of time—is designated in accordance with the production and magnitude found in the characteristics of the objective substrate. Such is the true nature of time. 57.

"Most Buddhists maintain that there is no other external time whatsoever. [The author] says: "Let it be so; we have no disagreement on this point: 'Whether as a power inherent in cognition or as existing externally in reality, it is impossible to engage in worldly discourse without relying upon the nature of time. (58)

Whether time be of the nature of a mere synthesis of cognitions—consisting of potencies that follow upon the intellect and take its forms, appearing in various modes such as slow or rapid occurrence—or whether it be some external, ultimate substance characterized by distinct potencies such as the present and so forth, it matters not; for we have not undertaken an investigation into the distinction between philosophical views, but rather must examine whatever factor is a constituent of linguistic usage (*śābda-vyavahāra*). And there exists such a linguistic usage involving distinct times, as in: "it was," "it is," and "it will be."
In this regard, the meaning is that time should be accepted as being agreeable when not critically examined, according to the circumstances. || 58 ||

For instance, some maintain that time is indeed distinct from entities; thus he says: "According to some, there are three powers of being belonging to every entity. By means of those inherent powers, everything both exists and does not exist at all times. (59)

According to the system of the Great Sage (Kapila), in entities that are in a state of constant transformation, there exists the mere potency of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, which is designated by the distinctions of time such as the past and so forth. Thus, since all entities consist of the three *guṇas*, they are endowed with the three potencies; and according to whether these potencies are respectively manifest or unmanifest, they are conventionally designated as "existent" or "non-existent. (59)
For it is thus: those three are established as non-different from existence; and because they are not distinct from that, neither their sequence nor their being existent and non-existent differs.

Those very powers (*śakti*), which are not distinct from the entity (*bhāva*), are called "sequence" (*krama*). For it is through the manifestation (*āvirbhāva*) and concealment (*tirobhāva*)—occurring by virtue of the conjunction with powers such as the present—that entities, as they come into being, display the form of sequence within themselves. Thus, in the ultimate sense, those powers alone are sequence. Furthermore, although the powers are non-distinct from the entity and always abide together with it, there is no confusion [of their functions] due to the diversity of their activity (*vṛtti*). For it is the perception and non-perception of these [powers] that constitutes their operation, and that [operation] is distinct [in each case].

And since the conventional usage of "existence" and "non-existence" occurs solely by virtue of that [perception], even that [usage] does not differ from the state of being. For, regarding an object in its past or future states, the absence of perception is not [itself] existence; thus, because the conventional usage of non-existence is simply the absence of perception, while existence remains present even at that time, existence and non-existence do not differ. (60)
For that which is seen through seeing and not seen through non-seeing is indeed the same; yet there is no unity of the paths, nor does anything ever cease.

Manifestation—meaning seeing or perception—occurs through the power of the present; however, concealment—meaning non-seeing or non-perception—occurs through the powers of the past and the future. Because these two exist in mutual exclusion, they are not identical. Thus, due to the difference in their effects, there is indeed a distinction between the paths (adhvan), and no confusion of them. Furthermore, that entity which is seen, unseen, and past is one and the same in its nature as the substratum (dharmin); for the substratum does not deviate from its true essence even through the arrival and departure of its attributes (dharma).

Therefore, in this system, although the temporal phases (*adhvan*)—such as the present and so forth—are non-different from the existent entity (*bhāva*), there is no confusion regarding their unity because there is no commingling of their respective effects. Furthermore, since an absolute destruction (*atyanta-niranvaya-vināśa*) of the nature of existence (*sadrūpa*) is not possible, there is only concealment (*tirobhāva*). Consequently, existence and non-existence are not distinct; there is no difference between existence and non-existence, for that which is merely concealed is designated as "non-existent," whereas non-existence is not some definable entity in its own right. This is the meaning.

This has been stated in the *Pātañjala*: "The substratum (dharmī) does not belong to the three times; rather, it is the attributes (dharmas) that belong to the three times. Being characterized by those [attributes], they are designated as being different when they reach various states. Thus, having abandoned the future characteristic, the attribute has entered the present characteristic, yet it is not separated from the future and the past. || 61 ||

Now he summarizes the various philosophical views regarding the reality of time as they occur: "The view of time is divided into those consisting of power (śakti), the self (ātman), and the deity; the first [of these] exists in ignorance (avidyā), whereas it does not exist in knowledge (vidyā). (62)

The intention of the venerable Bhartṛhari is that time is the power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*) of Brahman. However, commentators explain that time is simply the causal power (*kāraṇa-śakti*). For instance, the seed-power, while permitting the production of a sprout and simultaneously obstructing the production of a stalk at that same moment, is "time" because it performs the function of time. In this way, even regarding the powers of the sprout and so forth, the principle of time is to be understood through the production of subsequent effects and the obstruction of remote effects in successive order.

And this is seen to be incorrect. For entities have fixed causes; they arise when their own causes are present and not otherwise, so this is simply the causal capacity itself. In that regard, because time is a fixed factor, it is logical that the auxiliary cause (sahakārī) must be something other than [the material cause] itself. Furthermore, since a sequence is observed among entities as they are produced through a succession of causes, one must accept that the power of time, known as "sequence," is a limiting adjunct (upādhi) of entities.

Therefore, since that very [Lord] is the master in the manifestation of the differentiation of entities, He is likewise the master in the manifestation of the sequence that follows them; thus, it is logical that this power called "Time" belongs to the independent conscious Self (cidātman) as it pertains to the individual soul (jīvātman). For this has been stated by us in the *Vākyapadīya*: "For this very reason, he states another view consistent with this perspective: the Self, the Person (puruṣa), and the individual soul (jīva) are indeed Time itself, because the manifestation of sequence belongs to that [Self] alone."

For he, being unable to perceive objects according to their true nature, determines succession therein by following the sequence of his own manifestations. And thus, from that construction of temporal differentiation, he himself receives the designation "time" through metaphorical usage. Indeed, this very power of time is the ground of the fruit for the power of ignorance as it accompanies [the soul]. Furthermore, it is solely by the force of that unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) and so forth that there is restriction or permission regarding entities. Others, however, have accepted a deity possessing a physical form and great power as being time itself.

In this regard as well, it is precisely in accordance with the fact that the power (*śakti*) of Brahman, whose nature is consciousness, is indeed the Deity herself who devours the entire universe—that this very [view] constitutes the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) here. For this reason, it is called the "Doctrine of Time" (*kāla-darśana*): "In ignorance (*avidyā*), which is the cause of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), there first arises the appearance of duality, for transmigratory existence consists of the manifestation of duality; and duality [is constituted] by space and time, among which the differentiation of time is the primary factor in the creation of the world."

For consciousness, which is by nature non-sequential and of the form of *paśyantī*, appears as if it has assumed a sequence once it has mounted upon the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*); this conclusion was established in the *Vākyapadīya*, and may be understood from that very source by us in the *Śabdaprabhā*.

For the reality of Brahman, which consists of pure knowledge and is untouched by time, undergoes a manifestation (*vivarta*) in various ways by assuming the form of succession due to the power of ignorance (*avidyā*). Thus, because of the penetration of time, the sequential appearance of objects resides within the individual soul (*jīvātman*), which is established as beginningless; this is because the entire range of duality is composed of ignorance. Furthermore, even regarding time, this division that arises from differences in perception is likewise merely the unfolding of ignorance.

However, when knowledge (*vidyā*) has arisen, because the entire manifold of duality (*bhedaprapañca*) has ceased, this [distinction between the appropriate and inappropriate] also vanishes. Therefore, in this context, deliberation as to what is logical or illogical is merely the fruit of futile effort; for in the realm of empirical transaction (*vyavahāra*), since everything is unreal, the establishment of a true nature (*tattvavyavasthā*) is untenable—this is the intended meaning. Thus, it is established that time is useful in the empirical transaction of things subject to birth.

How, then, can there be a distinction such as shortness and so forth among eternal sounds caused by time? We say it is merely imagined (*kalpita*). Just as in the case of two cognitions—"this was done long ago" and "this was done quickly"—wherein, although the cognitions themselves are inherently simultaneous, a temporal distinction appears to be perceived within them due to the increase or decrease in the duration of the objects, so too in the case of short vowels and the like, although the essence of sound (*śabdatattva*) is eternal and thus simultaneous, a temporal distinction is metaphorically attributed to it. || 62 ||
If time were non-different, then the appearance of distinction seen in short, long, and protracted [vowels] would be like the perception of duration and brevity in cognition. (63)

In the case of water in a tube, salt, and so forth, how could there be a conjunction of accumulation through the repetition of short, long, and protracted [vowels], if it were caused by mere conceptualization? (64)

In reality, although there is no difference in time between the short vowel and the others, when a conventional distinction of time is resorted to—just as there is a distinction in the cognition of "slow" and "quick"—then upon the repeated utterance of a short vowel, the flow of water from a water-clock (*nālikā*) is slight; that of a long vowel through its repetition is one-third greater than that; and that of a protracted (*pluta*) vowel is again one-third greater than the latter. How could this progressive relationship of the flow of water arise from a distinction of vowels such as the short and so on, which are inherently devoid of temporal division, based merely on a distinction of time created by conceptual construction?

For the non-difference in time of short vowels and the like is ultimate (pāramārthika), whereas their difference in time is merely conceptual (kalpitā). And an object constructed by conceptualization does not persist through causal efficacy (arthakriyā); thus, upon the pronunciation of short vowels and so forth, the flow of water would be of a single uniform nature. By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (ādi), other instances—such as the observed difference in the production of other entities during the pronunciation of short vowels and so forth—should be cited as examples. Therefore, since short vowels and other sounds are in reality distinct in time, there is no contradiction with their permanence [as asserted] in accordance with the Kātyāyanavṛtti; such is the meaning.

In this regard, the solution is as follows: through the accumulation of the causes of manifestation, [the cognition] increases; yet the essence of the word, though non-different, is not of the nature of accumulation. (65)

Since sound (*śabda*), even though it is divided by distinctions such as shortness and so forth, is eternal, there is no limitation by time; nevertheless, due to the increase and decrease of the collection of manifesting sounds (*dhvani*) which reveal it, and because the distinction between the manifested and the manifestor is not perceived, a distinction of time is also attributed to the sound itself. For the primary sounds (*prākṛtadhvanayaḥ*), being heard in close conjunction with the nature of the sound, cause their own temporal distinction to appear therein. Indeed, the true essence of the sound is not grasped through a separation from the manifesting sounds.

It has been stated that "the word appears in the intellect along with the final sound. Consequently, since the perception of the true nature of the word depends upon its manifesters (*abhivyañjaka*), its properties are superimposed upon its own form according to the manifesting agent; thus, there is no difference in the flow of water from a pipe. For this very reason, the rule *taparaḥ tatkālasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.70) is justified through the superimposition of time belonging to the sound (*dhvani*). Furthermore, it was already established in the first section (*pūrvakāṇḍa*) that the variation in the mode of articulation (*vṛttibheda*) produced by the modified sounds (*vaikṛtadhvani*) does not cause a distinction [in the phoneme itself].

And it will be stated further on: "The entire multitude of properties, such as shortness, length, and nasality, resides within the essence of the word and is dependent upon its manifesters. This has been explained in detail in the *Brahmakāṇḍa* itself: "Because sound (*nāda*) arises in a temporal sequence, it is neither prior nor posterior; though itself devoid of sequence, it appears as if possessed of differentiation through the form of sequence," and so forth. Therefore, in this context, this temporal distinction—which is like the difference between slow and rapid cognition—is not inherent in the nature of the word itself, such that one could argue that because it sublates the real non-difference, there would be no distinction in the effect.

Rather, because listeners do not distinguish between the manifested (vyaṅgya) and the manifestor (vyañjaka)—namely, the word-sound (śabda) and the resonance (nāda)—and because they determine them to be non-different, the temporal distinction inherent in the internal resonance (dhvani) serves as a basis for linguistic usage even in the absence of the manifestor. This is the meaning. For resonances do not relate to the word in the same way that an object relates to a cognition; for while the form of the object—consisting of hundreds and so forth—is perceived as distinct from the form of the cognition, there is no such distinction between the word and its resonances.

In the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), however, the appearance of difference was suspected through the "blindfolded gaze of an elephant" (*gajanimīlita*) without regard for its own essential nature; and thus, the impossibility of the distinction between effects was urged. 65.

He states that the reality of sound is not only undivided in cases such as short and long vowels, but is so throughout the entire domain of words and sentences: "Thus, whether it be a division of a quarter-mora or of a ten-syllable verse, no distinction exists within the essence of sound due to variations in measurement. (66)

There is no difference in the nature of the collection of the *Daśatayas*—the groups consisting of ten parts whose essence is the *Ṛgveda*, which are manifested by a more condensed sound and comprise sixty-four [hymns] as a mass of Vedic scripture—compared to the fourth part of a *mātrā*, which is manifested by a more attenuated sound; for both sounds are equal in their eternity, and thus the difference pertains solely to the duration of the manifesting factor.

Just as in the cognition of an elephant and a mosquito, although they are identical in their essential nature (*svarūpa*), they are experienced as if distinct due to the distortion of their forms (*ākāra-upaplava*); so too, the essence of sound, whose nature is the *sphoṭa*, is everywhere undifferentiated across the objects of words and sentences, yet it appears as if differentiated due to the diversity of its manifestors. 66.

If, then, the distinction between short [vowels] and so forth arises from the difference in phonetic sounds (dhvani), how could there also be a difference in the linguistic functions (vṛtti) that denote different effects? Consequently, one might suspect that when the *tapara* rule is applied to a fast tempo (*druta*), an additional enumeration would be required for the medium (*madhyama*) and slow (*vilambita*) tempos. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Those words which, by way of being co-produced, exist as if in the interval, serve as means for the perceivers to achieve comprehension. (67)

When the reality of sound (*śabdatattva*) has been manifested by the primary articulations (*prākṛtadhvani*), there subsequently arise secondary sounds (*dhvanis*) in the form of reverberations (*anuraṇana*). These exist as a continuous stream, as if situated within the space between the ears; because they proceed in a rapid succession, they reach the location of the ear and, by virtue of the quality of the auditory organ, become the cause for the perception of the accumulation of sound. Thus, they produce the distinctions of tempo (*druta*) and other rhythmic modes (*vṛtti*). Consequently, being external to the reality of sound, they do not divide it.

As it has been said: "The modified sounds (dhvanis), through their various modes of manifestation, bring about a differentiation in the function of the word-sound (śabda) as it is manifested; however, the essence of the sphoṭa is not divided by them. This is also stated in the Vārttika: "It is established that the phonemes (varṇas) remain constant, but their functions are distinguished by the speaker’s utterance being either slow or rapid. Thus, having raised the objection that for eternal words—which are not delimited by time like things subject to birth—such [differentiation] would be impossible, it has been resolved by attributing it to the manifesting agents (vyañjakas). 67.

Now, he demonstrates the conventional usage of time's differentiation, which is based on external conditions: "Taking up various specific limits as its conditions, Time—though one—is conceived by those who possess the power of calculation as possessing the distinctions of moments, months, and seasons. (68)

Time, which delimits entities that possess parts, are composed of portions, and are impermanent, attains its arrangement into divisions such as *lava*s and *muhūrta*s by means of grasping limits for the arising of determined objects. (68) Nevertheless, he states that this arrangement is not ultimately real: "Because it exists within the nature of conventional usage through the distinctions of mental apprehension, time is exactly as much as a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), or even as much as an age (*yuga*) or an intermediate period (*manvantara*). (69)

Whatever extent of a momentary continuum is grasped by the synthesizing cognition as a unity, that much time—consisting of months and so forth—is established as a single unit. However, the moment (*kṣaṇa*) is the limit of diminution, while the period of a Manu (*manvantara*) and so forth is the limit of accumulation. Thus, although time is a single substance in its essential nature, this conceptualization of it is mental (*bauddhī*). But according to the view that time is the synthesis of cognitions, this [conceptualization] is primary (*mukhyā*). 69.

One might object: "Since the conventional usage of time—such as moments, days, nights, and so forth—is established by the flow through a tube, let that [flow] itself be time; what is the use of postulating another [entity]? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The flowing of water situated within the cavity of a tube, which occurs through obstruction and permission, is the very activity of Time. (70)

When water contained within a jar flows out through a hole, the fact that one portion emerges first while another has not yet emerged at that same time is due to the power of Time’s capacity to obstruct and permit. Otherwise, because of its weight, the whole body of water would flow out simultaneously, pervading all its parts. Since it flows out sequentially, Time is here an active agent distinct [from the water]; thus, the flow of water itself is not Time, but rather that which delimits it.

For that [time] is delimited by the action of winking, the flow of breath, or the succession of moments of cognition, and is thus capable of delimiting other subsequent times. Even the winking of an eye and so forth is itself delimited by subtle time in the form of a sequence, and is thus capable of delimiting other subsequent times. Since even the winking of an eye and so forth is delimited by subtle time in the form of a sequence, the power of time known as "sequence" is subtly interwoven within all entities; for it is experienced as being impossible to deny.

For all consciousness is indeed permeated by the form of succession; thus, the supreme reality, which is beyond succession and whose nature is that of Agni and Soma, extends the activity of the cosmic egg for the sake of the benefit or injury of living beings, revolving incessantly by assuming the various states of manifestation in the forms of the moon, the sun, and so forth. This has been determined by us in detail in the *Vākyapadīya*. 80.

Anticipating the objection that since time is of a single nature, how can its distinction be determined by the flow of water through a small or large aperture due to the decrease or increase of the opening, he says: "Whether the aperture be small or large, the activity of time does not differ when connected to it; its own essence also follows that very [aperture]. (81)

When water comes into contact with the aperture of a small hole, the operation of time—characterized by obstruction and permission—is not different from when it comes into contact with a large aperture. Even so, the nature of time, though undifferentiated, conforms precisely to that connection with the aperture. And because of this conformity, this same [time] is determined as a long duration when there is an abundance of obstructions and permissions in the case of a small aperture. This is the meaning.

Even though time is indivisible here, a distinction is perceived as being conditioned by its connection with specific apertures. For this very reason, water enclosed within a water-clock (*ghaṭikā*) does not flow out, whereas when the aperture is opened, it flows; thus, one should not ask what purpose time serves. This is because the fundamental operation of time cannot be denied. Those very same [functions] of restriction and permission performed by time are themselves followed by the parts of the water-clock and the aperture.

Just as the seed’s two functions—the obstruction of the production of a sprout and the permission thereof—are nurtured by time and place through the granary and the field respectively; for this very reason, it has been said that the self also follows that very [sequence]. For, since the visible cause and the power of time are mutually compatible and coexist, it is not logical to reject one on the basis of relying solely on the other. || 81 ||

What need is there for more? He says that although the nature of time is non-different [from all things], it manifests differentiation in all entities due to the variety of its own powers: "That which is seen through its own powers as if it were the playground of Time appears manifoldly differentiated among entities because of its many forms. (82)

Because he gazes upon the faces of time, this Lord, sporting with these playful diversions, brings about the rising and falling of those [entities] like the play of a swing; thus, by his own power, he displays the differentiation of the Self as it is presided over by its own capacity through the variety of forms such as the present and so forth. || 82 ||
For instance: whether it be the growth of a bamboo stalk or the growth of a blade of grass, the reality of time is conceptualized through its association with that growth. (83)

To that same extent—that is, with that very same measure—the principle of time (*kālatattva*), which is undivided from the causes of mere obstruction and permission, brings about the growth and accumulation of the bamboo (*vaṃśa*) until the sequential production of its fruit; yet, it produces a greater growth for the palmyra palm (*tāla*). Thus, through this differentiation in connection with growth—which serves as a playground for all entities—time is differentiated. Consequently, the time reaching the limit of the bamboo's growth is short, whereas for the palmyra palm, it remains much longer.

In the same way, the division of time should be illustrated elsewhere as well, in relation to other entities, through the connection with the distinctions between the states of birth, duration, and destruction. || 83 ||

If, then, there is a difference in time due to a difference in states, one might suspect that its permanence would not exist even upon the destruction of those states; anticipating this, he says: "Even when the constituent parts (mātrās) undergo change, there is no change in that [time]. There is no difference in the path whatsoever caused by the difference between the traveler and the act of traveling. (84)

Because time is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of all entities, even when those entities and their states have ceased, there is no departure of the substratum. Just as the path or road does not disappear even when travelers and their acts of going have come to rest; for it is only upon the cessation of activity that the cessation of time, such as spring and so forth, is conventionally designated. In reality, however, time does not depart, because it is eternal. 84.

For instance: "By means of the rising and setting of the luminaries as established in the world, even though time itself does not undergo transmigration, it acquires, as it were, the properties of those luminaries. (85)

The essence of time (*kālātman*) is that which possesses divisions brought about by the movement of the sun and other celestial bodies; therefore, even though it does not actually depart when those divisions cease, it is perceived as if it has passed away, such that one thinks, "the day has gone," "the night has dawned," or "the cold season has ended. (85)

Since the conventional distinction of various time-units is based on the movement of luminaries, some of limited vision consider that very movement itself to be time; thus he says: "Others, who know time, understand time—which is differentiated by the distinct movements [of the sun]—as the revolution of the sun, the planets, and the lunar mansions. (86)

The day is the movement of the sun beginning with sunrise and ending with sunset; the night is the period of time beginning with sunset and ending with sunrise. Fifteen such cycles constitute a *pakṣa* (fortnight); thirty times that makes a month. Alternatively, a month may be conceived as the time taken by the moon to pass through all the lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*). A year is the passage of Jupiter through one zodiacal sign (*rāśi*).

In this manner, the divisions of time—such as the *yuga*, *manvantara*, *kalpa*, and *mahākalpa*—of other planets and lunar mansions are to be understood according to the distinctions in their movements and courses well-known in the science of astronomy (*jyotiṣaśāstra*). || 86 ||

Thus, since this action is well-known as time, it measures other actions that are themselves well-known; so he says: "That action which, being engaged in delimiting another action, has its own measure already determined, is designated as 'time' (kāla). (77)

The movement and motion of the sun and other celestial bodies, denoted by words such as "day" and so forth, as well as specific actions like milking a cow, receive the designation "time" because they possess a determinate measure and serve as the means for delimiting other specific actions whose measures are otherwise unknown. [Examples include: "He studies for a day," "He studies for a night," or "He sits while the cows are being milked. The phrase "engaged in delimiting another action" already covers this; however, the repetition of the term "with respect to an action" is intended to demonstrate that time is not invariably restricted to being an action, depending on the particular perspective.

And likewise, even a water-jar (godohana) or similar object, whose own dimension is established through other means, becomes time itself by delimiting actions such as the drinking from the mouth performed by Devadatta and others. || 77 ||

How does one who is turned inward, situated within a chamber, and not perceiving the movement of the sun and so forth or the dripping from a water-clock, understand the divisions of time? To this he says: "The transfer of form into cognition and its subsequent withdrawal by cognition itself—therefore, in the absence of any other action, that very activity is held to be time. (78)

Even when turned inward, [the self] cognizes some specific activity—such as the flow of the vital breath—which has been transferred to the intellect (*buddhi*) in the form of its mental image. Furthermore, by means of subsequent moments of cognition, it synthesizes those moments of activity residing in the intellect. Thus, even in the absence of external action, this activity residing in the intellect is called "time" (*kāla*), because it delimits other external actions.

For instance, when a greater number of cognitions arise, one perceives a long duration regarding external objects, whereas when fewer arise, one perceives a short duration; thus, yogis indeed determine objects by means of the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), as is well known even for others through the counting of the moments of the breath. To illustrate this: by calculating the flow of the breath according to the measure of a *nāḍikā*—which consists of three hundred and sixty breath-movements—they state that there are twenty-one thousand six hundred breaths in the calculation of a day and night. (78)

If, then, time does not exist apart from action, one might object: "Since there can be no connection between the action called 'existence' (sattā) and another existence that has become an action, how can it be said that 'existence has passed'? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "This notion that 'the jar has passed' is simply the state of having passed belonging to existence itself. When it is said that 'existence has passed,' the existence of existence is designated as 'having passed. (79)

In the expression "the jar is past" (*bhūto ghaṭaḥ*), to what does "pastness" belong? It cannot belong to the jar itself, because as a substance (*dravya*), it is not in contact with time; for actions, whose very nature is to be accomplished, are related to time which serves as their locus. However, the action called "existence" (*sattā*), which is denoted by the verbal root, is indicated as "past" by the past-participial suffix (*niṣṭhā-pratyaya*).

That existence, being inherent in the jar (*ghaṭa-samavāyinī*), is connected to the jar through a mediated sequence, but not directly between the substance and time. Even when a distinct time is perceived, there is no direct connection; rather, that connection is mediated through the action.

The meaning is as follows: even in the case of the expression "beings are thus," there is a verbal existence denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*) which is of the nature of action (*kriyā*), and another existence denoted by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) which functions as a substance (*dravyāyamāṇā*). When there is a connection with this other existence, the cognition that the existence functioning as a substance has become [past] occurs precisely through the fact that the existence denoted by the verbal root has become past; thus, there is no inconsistency whatsoever. Even for an eternal existence, when a distinction arises through the conditioning of its own substratum, its connection with the three times via that medium is not contradictory. This point is established. || 79 ||

Now that the true nature of time has been determined, the linguistic usage based upon it as found in the treatises is being examined. Regarding the rule "The *laṭ* [present tense suffix] is used for the present," it was stated: "And [it is used] for eternally occurring things because there is no division of time. Since there is an absence of temporal division in eternal objects, the designation "present" would otherwise be untenable; therefore, this rule must be taught. But surely, being "present" consists in being current, and is the counter-correlative of the past and the future?

Furthermore, since there is no distinction between past and future in the case of eternal things that proceed without interruption, the occurrence of such designations is even more untenable. To this it is replied: Here, these designations based on time, which possess mutually distinct forms, are appropriate only for entities that receive assistance from time; and these [entities] are subject to birth. For in that case, this [designation] is possible through the acceptance of a birth with a fixed limit. Thus, when the means [of production] are present, those things whose arising is imminent are "future."

Those who have obtained birth through [karmic] accomplishment and remain until their final state are "present" (*vartamāna*), whereas those whose bodies have passed away are "past" (*bhūta*). Therefore, this designation "present" exists within the interval between the past and the future; it is simply not possible where both the past and the future are absent. As it is stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "The present is the opposite of the past and the future... The meaning is that wherever the past and the future exist, there the present exists as their counterpart.

Furthermore, since past and future do not exist in eternal things, [action] is absent there. And it was stated that "the suffix *śatṛ* occurs" with reference to the context [of non-eternal things]. However, all temporal suffixes (*kāla-pratyaya*) are indeed taught [in this sense]. For this very reason, he says: "Because of the non-differentiation of time... and so forth. And this being the case, because there is an absence of temporal limitation here, action—which consists of the limiting adjuncts of time—does not exist at all. For that [action], as a limiting adjunct of time, possesses succession and has the nature of being something to be accomplished (*sādhyamāna*).

And since that [distinction] is absent here, it follows that every systematic arrangement must be stated as being based on the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) of action and its factors (*kāraka*). To this, the following solution has been stated: "And there are divisions of time," such as "the mountains will stand," "they stand," and "they stood. Again, it was asked: "Are these words capable of being employed? If so, then there are divisions of time. This is the intended meaning.

If it is objected that the usage of these words [denoting time] is unestablished precisely because of the divisions of time, how can this very [usage] be said to be the determiner? To this it is said: "Not necessarily from the usage of the word alone. Since a sequence of prior and posterior is understood from the verb (*ākhyāta*), and for those who hold the word to be the authority (*śabdapramāṇaka*), the determination of the object arises from that very source, the usage of the word might indeed be the means of knowing the division of time; however, even disregarding that, it is the object itself that is here presented as the division of time—this is the meaning.

Regarding this, he says: "The actions of kings belonging to the past, future, and present are the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of the verb 'to stand' (*tiṣṭhati*). He explains this commentary as follows: "Everything else is differentiated by another, but the Self is not subject to conceptual differentiation (*vikalpate*). Therefore, the stability of mountains and the like is differentiated by means of other forms. (80)

Even for eternal entities such as mountains and rivers, a distinction in time is established through a differentiation of existence (*sattā*) based on their reliance upon the existence residing in other objects that accompany them. For indeed, the entire collection of existent things is differentiated by virtue of contact with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), but not by its own essential nature; thus it has already been stated: "The notion that they are 'different' is due to external adjuncts. For the actions of kings are conventionally designated as the "locus" of the stability of mountains and so forth, precisely because those actions serve as the differentiators of that stability.

For just as the activities of a king possess a threefold temporal relation, a sequential order, and a state of being accomplished, so too do mountains and other things associated with them; thus, by superimposing those [qualities] upon them, figurative usage regarding the three times is appropriate here, and the logical arguments are thereby established. || 80 ||

Alternatively, the state (*sthiti*) existing in association with royal activity experiences assistance from its respective substratum at every stage and is itself differentiated in the case of mountains and so forth. However, because its true nature is not apprehended due to its similarity [to other states], its differentiation is made known through the differentiation of the associated activities; thus he says: "Activities whose constituent parts are dissimilar are well-known as distinct; those whose constituent parts are similar are differentiated by virtue of their association. (81)

Those operations whose constituent actions possess dissimilar natures—such as the forms of the actions of cooking (*pacati*) and splitting (*bhinatti*)—are well-known to be distinct, occurring at different times, and characterized by difference. For indeed, the constituent parts of cooking, such as placing [the pot] on the fire and so forth, are distinct; likewise, the constituent parts of splitting, such as lifting [the object] and so forth, are distinct.

However, those activities of the constituent parts of mountains and the like which consist of the state of maintenance characterized by self-supporting, have their distinctions difficult to discern due to their similarity; they are made known as distinct through temporal differences by means of royal activities that are dissimilar in their continuum, whose divisions are clearly determined, and which accompany them. Therefore, because these royal activities serve as the delimiting factors for the stability of the mountain and so forth, they are conventionally designated as "time."

Furthermore, the various states of stationary objects such as mountains, which are characterized by the specific movements of the sun and other celestial bodies, are [considered] actions because they serve as indicators of royal activities; for royal activities are indeed described as the most well-known [examples] in the Bhāṣya. Since a state of stability arises at every moment through its dependence on a substratum, it possesses a sequence of successive stages, and thus its nature as an action is not contradictory. For it has been stated: "Stability is simply birth (origination) itself, assuming a similar form."

Moreover, even for eternal entities, the state of being sustained at every moment by their substratum receives the designation "birth" precisely when their prior and posterior states are not conceptually differentiated. And in verbal usage, since the word-meaning is designated as "artha" (the object), the meaning perceived as having a sequence necessarily conforms to the definition of action (*kriyā*). || 81 ||

This has been stated in the *Vārttika*: "When an action that has begun is not yet finished, [the suffixes] become 'present' because of its non-pastness. When there is no cessation for one engaged in an action due to the non-attainment of the primary result, and yet, because of the commencement of another action, that commenced action has already passed away, then the designation of the present tense must be applied. For example: "We dwell here," and "We are sacrificing for Puṣyamitra."

One engaged in another action, even while officiating as a priest (*yājayat*), employs [the present tense] in this way because the primary fruit, such as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), has not been obtained and the intention to officiate has not ceased. Regarding this, the solution has been stated: "But it is logical [to use the present tense] because there is no cessation from the undertaking. Since the primary fruit has not yet been accomplished and the action extends until its completion, the action remains uncompleted even when interrupted by another action; thus, it is logical that the present-tense suffix occurs.

Now, if it is intended here that [the action] is not present because it is interrupted by other intermediate actions, then what was stated—“and there is an interruption in the case of ‘one who is free from doubt’”—is illustrated. For even in cases such as “he eats,” there is undoubtedly an interruption by intermediate actions while the action is ongoing. As it is said in the Bhāṣya: “Even he, while eating, necessarily laughs, talks, or drinks water. He explains this very point: “The collection of actions, such as eating and so forth, approaches as if interrupted; it appears as if ceased, due to the activities occurring in the intervals. (82)
And even though it appears in a fragmented form, that [action] does not cease because there is no interruption; for every action whatsoever is perceived as being intermingled with another. (83)

A collection of actions such as eating, which consists of a synthesis of successive parts, appears to be interrupted by intervening actions such as laughing or conversing, which possess the characteristics of the past and the future. Furthermore, because satisfaction is the fruit of the act of eating, the single continuum of that action remains established; thus, the word "as it were" (*iva*) is used. For there is no interruption of the aggregate itself, but rather of the individual moments. Moreover, the nature of an action does not consist merely of those [intervening] moments.

Intending the absence of future parts and through the conceptualization of past parts, that collection of actions appears as if it has ceased. Even so, because it continues until the attainment of the result by means of intermediate actions through its constituent parts, its nature is not interrupted; rather, it remains established in its present nature as something uninterrupted. Not only [actions] such as eating, but even [actions] such as laughing or conversing are likewise separated by other intervening actions.

There is an interruption even by the blink of an eye, and ultimately by the occurrence of exhalation and inhalation as well; because the undertaking of action occurs after repeated pauses, it is as if mixed, yet not entirely mixed, since there is no cessation until the attainment of the fruit. This is because intermediate actions, which are necessarily present, cannot function as auxiliary causes. Action is a collection of moments extending up to the final result, such as the act of seeing.

And in that case, even when physical activity has ceased, there is no cessation of mental activity—such as seeing or praying—for as long as the attainment of the fruit continues. Thus, because activities such as eating also persist, their status as "present" is established. || 82, 83 ||

Thus, it has been established that a collection culminating in a result constitutes "action" (*kriyā*), even by accepting the intervention of other actions caused by other results. Alternatively, he states that the other action occurring in the interval is not of a different genus: "Or rather, every constituent action perceived in the interval is grasped as a subordinate part of that [primary action], because of its similarity despite the difference. (84)

Those specific actions such as laughing that occur within the action of eating and so forth are indeed parts (*avayava*) of that eating; they consist of subordinate operations (*guṇavyāpāra*) because they provide assistance, like the ritual rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*). Consequently, due to their similarity to the rinsing of the mouth and other such acts, even when laughter and the like are occasionally absent, they are grasped as parts of the eating because of the completion of the act of eating—just as by means of well-known auxiliary elements such as the addition of curd—as in the case of a load carried by two men, where a third person joining them [is considered part of the carrying].

The word *tu* has the sense of *api* (also). For two friends whose minds are at ease engage in eating while performing mutual laughter, conversation, and so forth. Thus, in this case, with respect to each individual limb [of the action], the completion of the action (*kriyāsamāpti*) occurs at the beginning [of the act] in the sense of an incipient action (*ādikarman*); the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) proceeds with the intention of supporting the use of the past participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*) by the principle stated as "But it is logical because of the completion at the beginning" (*nyāyyā tvādyapavargāt*). However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is based on the collection of actions culminating in the fruit; thus it is settled. || 84 ||

Now, he raises the objection that the existence of action at all times is untenable: "An entity must be either existent or non-existent; there is no third possibility whatsoever. Therefore, apart from the past and the future, no middle [present] exists. (85)

Action is said to be the state of being in the process of accomplishment (*sādhyamānāvasthā*). In that regard, the moment (*kṣaṇa*) which has passed is existent and possesses an established nature; thus, action is "past" therein. And that which is non-existent is yet to be accomplished; it is the future moment, and thus action is characterized by the attribute of "future-ness" therein. Furthermore, there is no other moment whatsoever that possesses both existent and non-existent natures, because a single entity cannot possess contradictory natures. Consequently, presentness as a qualifier of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is not tenable.

This has been stated in the Bhāṣya: "When [the world] has not yet fallen, this entire world falls; even the Himavat moves. [Objection: Since the action is beyond the senses and its pastness is inferred from its result, how can it be expressed by a present tense suffix? [Response: The meaning is: why would the Himavat—which possesses as its effect the action of conjunction and disjunction observed in its vicinity—not be designated by a present tense suffix as "it does not fall"? 85.
