If it is argued that the very state of being in the process of accomplishment (*sādhyamānāvasthā*) is the action’s existence in its own form, which is its "presentness," [the author] replies: "The nature of completion (*nirvṛtti*) is not possible for a single entity because there is no differentiation [within it]. Therefore, how could that which is one be of a sequential nature, whether it be existent or non-existent? (86)

Since there is no division within the nature of a single entity, the characteristic of action—which consists in a sequential form as the process of production—does not exist. To explain: an object must be either existent or non-existent. Among these, that which is existent, by virtue of its very existence, cannot be produced and thus does not depend on a sequential form. That which is non-existent, likewise, by virtue of its non-existence, lacks the form of a completed production in that state; how then could it be sequential? For there is no sequence whatsoever for a non-existent thing that is devoid of all properties. Furthermore, since there is no third category, there is no sequential form of action being produced; how then could such a thing be present? || 86 ||

Now it might be argued: "A plurality of moments, arranged in a temporal sequence, constitutes an action; thus, prior to the production of the fruit, it attains the status of being present. That too is not correct, because since many [moments] do not persist simultaneously, only one is perceived. Furthermore, recollection occurs there in accordance with that very perception. || 87 ||

The parts arise sequentially and possess a nature that is dispersed; they do not exist simultaneously. Consequently, only a single present moment is perceived, and since that moment lacks internal differentiation, there is an absence of sequence. Now, if it is argued that many sequential [parts] are remembered simultaneously, that too is not the case. For memory is preceded by experience, and since no sequential experience of a single [object] has occurred, how could memory itself indicate a sequence therein? (87)

Furthermore, it is not logical for many things to have the nature of a single action; thus he says: "If one were to conceive of everything as a unity, then that which is of the nature of both existent and non-existent would be one. Or else, [that unity] would be a universal (*sāmānya*) consisting of the form of cessation, because of its cessation. (88)

If one accepts that moments—whether past, future, or existing in the forms of being and non-being—possess a single nature of activity, it would follow that every entity possesses a contradictory unity consisting of both being and non-being. This is not tenable, because the experience of contradictory attributes subverts unity. Alternatively, since there is a contradiction in many distinct things having a single nature, one must postulate some persisting (anvayī) essence as the one.

And thus, for an action (*kriyā*) that is being accomplished—that is, one whose nature is beginningless—there would have to be a generality (*sāmānya*) consisting of the capacity for accomplishment in the form of completion, which exists in each individual moment and takes the form of having a single action as its essence. And in that case, a single action could not be established; this is the intended meaning. For you have accepted some recurring nature (*svabhāva*) common to many things as being the essence of action, but you do not accept that many [moments] constitute a single action; therefore, there is simply an absence of any manifestation of action.

For it is only among distinct moments that there is a continuity in the form of their production, but it is not established that each of them possesses the nature of a specific individual action. Consequently, how could actions be present? (88)

Regarding this, he states the [correct] position: "Or rather, that [entity], being capable of producing an effect by its own nature, would be perceived as such in its true essence; and that [perception] constitutes its existence in the present. (89)

In this context, unity is conceptually attributed to an action that consists of a collection of moments (*kṣaṇa*). For instance, moments occurring in a fixed sequence and proceeding toward a single result are called "action"; because the result is non-different, that action is one. Likewise, action is differentiated according to the difference in its respective results. Furthermore, even though the moments may be existent or non-existent, their status as "present" is indeed possible; for existence is not the defining characteristic of the present, but rather the state of having begun but not yet being completed.

And that [volition] indeed exists as a non-differentiated determination of the entire collection of moments, from its inception until the attainment of the result; and it alone is capable of producing the effect. Furthermore, it precedes the mental activity and culminates in the bodily activity, being inferable from the exertion of the means and the resulting fruit.

And in that case, when that which consists of an aggregate and is endowed with its own sequential nature (*krama*) is perceived as having an essential reality (*ātmatattva*), that is, by means of its own existing intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then the existence of such a thing is its "presentness" (*vartamānatā*). The word "or" (*vā*) indicates an alternative in view of what is to be stated later. This is the meaning: an aggregate characterized by a fixed sequence of priority and posteriority is, first of all, sequential (*kramika*).

And although that [action] consists of both existent and non-existent forms, even as it possesses a mutually superimposed sequence culminating in a result, each individual moment, being present at its own time, experiences the state of being "present. And although this [moment] is not a single sequential entity and thus not an action in itself, nevertheless, the sequence residing in the subsequent moments is indeed determined therein through the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of experience; thus, there is no fault whatsoever. As it has been stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "That which is the cause for the commencement of action, and for the sake of which the exertion is performed..."

"Then, having observed [the result], one should employ [the means] without hesitation, thinking 'it goes. Thus, the desire for the fruit is a mental activity (*mānasa-vyāpāra*) that serves as the cause for engaging in physical action (*bhautika-kriyā*). The exertion of the means (*sādhanānāṃ saṃrambhaḥ*) is the movement directed toward the action. And their being for the sake of that [action] occurs through the relationship of general and particular (*sāmānya-viśeṣa-bhāva*). In this way, it has been clearly stated that the bodily activity preceded by mental activity—which culminates in the fruit, is determined as non-different [from the mental activity], and possesses the nature of a present action—is what is expressed by its own denotative word. (89)

He states another alternative indicated by the word "or" (vā): "That which consists of the continuity of action, when internally restrained and its reflection concentrated in one place—that they call 'presentness'. (90)

Previously, the unity of the collection of moments was established on the basis of their being directed toward a single result. Now, however, the actual unity of that [collection] as it ascends into the conceptual synthesis (*saṅkalanābuddhi*)—by virtue of its taking the form of a mental image—is being stated. For instance, when a series of actions with dispersed parts, whose forms have been transferred into the nature of cognition, is apprehended within a single [act of] consciousness, then, due to its non-difference from that single cognition, it is determined to be present and one, just like that cognition itself.

Furthermore, even for things experienced sequentially, a synthesis indeed occurs because of the proximity of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of those experiences; otherwise, there would be an absence of cognitions such as those of a collection. For while it is certain that recollection is preceded by experience, it is not the case that what was perceived sequentially cannot be recollected simultaneously, since that would entail the impossibility of cognitions such as "one hundred" and so forth. And because the form of the cognition is determined (*adhyavasāya*) as being an external object, an external, unitary, present thing in the form of an action is conventionally treated as such.

And since that [present time] is established, the establishment of the past and future occurs in dependence upon it, and not otherwise; thus it is proven that action is qualified by the three times. This [point] is concluded. 90.

In this context, when the conditional (*lṛṅ*) is prescribed for the non-occurrence of an action (*kriyātipatti*), both the past and the future are taken as the temporal referents. An objection is raised regarding the impossibility of these two: "The non-occurrence of an action is characterized by the absolute non-arising of that action; and what is past has not arisen, nor is the future of such a nature [as having already arisen]. (91)

"If Kamalaka had called [the ox], the cart would not have overturned"—this refers to the non-occurrence (*atipatti*) of the action characterized by Kamalaka’s calling and the cart’s not overturning; it is a certain non-arising due to a deficiency in the causal capacity (*sādhana-śakti*). Furthermore, the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of an action that has not arisen cannot be established as either past or future. For only that which has arisen can be designated as "past" when its existence has passed away, and that which is capable of arising upon the presence of efficient causes can be designated as "future."

And here, because of the absence of a means of accomplishment, even that which was previously considered possible does not arise; for this very reason, non-arising is specified by the term "absolute" (atyanta). || 91 ||

Here, he establishes the conventional usage of "past" and "future": "Before the production of a contradictory action, or when a contradictory operation has already ceased, the object is differentiated therein by means of a distinction in its temporal limit. (92)

If he had summoned Kamalaka, the cart would not have overturned; thus, imagining that the summoning of a capable agent would have been the cause of non-defeat, he speaks in this manner. And so, because of the difference in the time required—which is to be expected—due to the distinction between the departure for another region (which is contrary to the summoning) and the loading of the heavy burden onto the cart (which is contrary to the non-defeat), the conditional mood (*kriyātipatti*) is also divided according to its future scope.

The accomplishment of the action consisting of the overturning of the cart would not occur due to the absence of the summoning of Kamalaka; and since that summoning will not be realized because of his departure to another region, there is a non-realization of that future [action]. Consequently, even for the non-occurrence of the action—which is characterized by its absolute non-arising—there is futurity. For if the summoning of the capable means were to take place, then the action would be accomplished; thus, while that [action] has futurity, its absolute non-existence also possesses futurity.

Likewise, if he had been seen by that seeker of alms, or even if he had eaten—or perhaps he would have eaten—but since he did not eat, because the action of non-eating, which is the opposite of eating, has passed away, there is a designation as "past" (bhūta) due to the fact that the *kriyātipatti* (the conditional mood expressing the non-occurrence of an action) also pertains to the past, owing to the difference in its temporal limit. This point is concluded. 92.

Now, in connection with the discussion of time, he examines the rule *dhātusaṃbandhe pratyayāḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.1), for the purpose of prescribing suffixes that do not conform to the [standard] time periods. "When the cause [of an action] deviates [from its expected time], grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) cannot be established. By the rule *bhāvyāsīt*, it is taught that [the suffix] applies elsewhere at that same time. (Verse 93)

Since conditions are prescribed for each [word] at its own specific time, if there were a deviation from that specific time, those words would not be grammatically correct (*sādhutva*) at another time. For example, in such cases as *bhāvī āsīt* ("he was one who will be") or *agniṣṭomayājyasya putro janitā* ("the son of one who has performed the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice will be born"), the suffix in *bhāvī* is prescribed for the future time; it could not then enter into a connection with the past time expressed by *āsīt*.

Likewise, the rule is commenced so that a suffix denoting the past, as in "he has sacrificed with the Agniṣṭoma," would not be incompatible with its connection to a future time, as in "he will cause [the sacrifice] to be born. Since verbal roots have no inherent relationship [between themselves], it is stated here that "root" (dhātu) refers to their meaning. Furthermore, because a relationship is based on distinction, there is an inclusion of multiple numbers within the compound (vṛtti). And by means of the instruments of action (sādhana), there is a relationship characterized by the qualifier-qualified (viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya) relation extending to the end of the root-meaning.

Furthermore, since the inclusion of suffixes is already established by the governing context of "suffix" (*pratyaya*), the purpose of the repeated mention of "suffix" in the *Bhāṣya*—namely, "one was a possessor of cows" (*gomān āsīt*) and "one will be a possessor of cows" (*gomān bhavitā*)—is stated so that even a suffix such as *matup*, which is prescribed under the governing context of "non-root" (*adhātu*), may be considered grammatically correct when it denotes a relationship with a verbal root at another time, provided that its qualification as "existence in the present time" is set aside.

This very sūtra has been rejected in the Vārttika with the statement: "It is established because the suffixes are prescribed according to their respective times when there is a connection between verbal roots. The meaning is that, since suffixes are prescribed for their own respective times within the view that the formation of words (*pada-saṃskāra*) occurs [simultaneously], the desired result is established even without this sūtra. || 93 ||

To this it is replied: If [the word] were correct only at its own time, how could there be an application when the time has changed? In that case, the distinction [of the word] from meanings other than its own would not be established. (94)

If the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of words such as *bhāvya* is admitted to occur at their own [primary] time, then how can there be a cognition of another time in connection with the usage of "it was" (*āsīt*)? Regarding this, it is stated in the *Vārttika*: "But the difference in time belongs to the adjunct (*upapada*). This means that because the adjunct—that is, the qualifier—is connected to the qualified, its belonging to that [past] time is understood from the sentence; thus, this sentence-meaning, being absent at the time of the word-refinement, is not a factor (*aṅga*). He explains this as follows:

If there are words whose meaning is not subject to the contemplation of the sentence-meaning—that is, if they possess meanings other than that, or meanings incompatible with the sentence-meaning—then, because the sentence-meaning is not delimited by them, it does not attain its specific character (*viśiṣṭatva*). Thus, since the word *bhāvī* (future) does not include the past tense, there would be no connection with the word *āsīt* (was), and consequently the sentence-meaning would not remain as a qualified whole.

Therefore, since the qualification of the temporal attribute is established through the force of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) by the persistence of the time of the qualificand, the purpose of the sūtra is not required. This is the meaning. || 94 ||

On the contrary, he states that at the commencement of the Sūtra, the intended meaning would not be understood: "If a constituent part [of the future] were to signify the state of having already come into being, then absolute futurity alone would be impossible therein. (95)

If, in a sentence such as "the action was to be," the word *bhāvī* (future) and so forth—which function as qualifiers—are established as denoting a time that is the object of the primary verbal form (*ākhyāta*), then that intended expression of the future action's pastness would not be understood. For although pastness is already conveyed by the word *āsīt* (was), the word *bhāvī*, being equivalent to a mere repetition, would instead be perceived as a restrictive emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*).

And thus, the meaning of the sentence would be established as "this object, which is of the nature of an action to be performed (*kṛtya*), was indeed [in the past] and was indeed existent (*bhūta*). Yet this is not what is intended to be expressed. Therefore, because the verbal derivation (*anvākhyāna*) occurs at its own time, the understanding of the future action as being "past" is established through a reflection on the sentence-meaning. Although the state of this action to be performed is intended to be future, it is now present and has come into being. For it has been previously demonstrated that linguistic entities (*padārtha*) belong to the three times.

And thus, it is logical that the future time-path enters into the past time-path, as stated by the venerable sage Vyāsa: "Destruction, being inevitable, is brought about by its very nature; for this very time of yours, which was previously the future, has now arrived. (95)

[Objection: But in this way, even if a word whose time is prescribed at its own time brings about a different time within the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of abandoning the time that was originally assigned to it. [Reply: There is no such consequence; as he says: "Even though the specific time [of the verb] was previously [assigned], nevertheless, because that [time] belongs to the qualifier, it will be correct there due to its being *antaraṅga* (internal) by virtue of its substratum. (96)

Because the word "future" (*bhāvin*) and so forth is taught to possess its own specific time even before its connection with another word, it possesses grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*). And when that [word] is connected with another word, even while qualifying [the other], it likewise retains its specific temporal character; for, without relinquishing its own connection to time, it follows the time of the qualified object (*viśeṣya*). For the future indeed possesses the nature of the past.

Therefore, since that which is dependent on its own time (*svakāla*)—namely, the *saṃskāra* (grammatical operation)—is adopted first as the cause, it possesses internal status (*antaraṅgatva*). Consequently, the correct word, such as *bhāvī* and so forth, remains valid even when joined with another word; there is no abandonment of its own time, because its distinction from the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is understood precisely through its being contained therein. Thus, in the case of "the son of one who has performed the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice is born," the future state of what is actually past is derived from the sentence-meaning. However, if the Sūtra were to be composed, an absolute futurity would be understood; thus, the Sūtra is rejected. || 96 ||

Some, however, justify [the position] according to the intention of the Vārttika. How so? He says: "That category of object under discussion is indeed mixed; for a solitary thing, being mixed with something else is not possible in the case of an eternal entity. (97)

Since words are explained here either for the sake of grammatical derivation (*anvākhyāna*) or for the purpose of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), it is the sentence itself that must be explained as their constituent basis. Thus, because the instruction of words is preceded by the extraction (*apoddhāra*) of word-meanings capable of being connected with the meanings of other words, in this grammatical analysis which has the sentence as its limit, every word-meaning is initially grasped precisely as it is—distinct and yet intermingled—just as it is determined from the actual use of the sentence.

However, if the instruction of words were independent of the connection with other word-meanings, then when a word established previously in its isolated state later enters into a connection with other words to form a qualified meaning, the eternal relationship between word and meaning would be contradicted. [For] the general meaning, having vanished, does not persist in the particular; how can there be the abandonment of what has been grasped? Where could that which has ceased exist? Such are the objections stated here. (97)

Having thus stated this in general terms, he now applies it to the present subject: "In the case of a pure [speech], it has been explained that [correctness] is not established when there is a mixture; therefore, correctness when occurring at the wrong time is taught by the Sūtra. (98)

The statement that "bhāvī" (future) means "it will be" is correctly explained as a suffix applied when [the action] is not mixed with what has already occurred (*bhūta*). However, that [suffix] does not apply when it is mixed with what has already occurred, since the expectation [of the future] is fulfilled by the first [tense] alone. Therefore, the prescription of the suffix for a time that is blended [with past and present] is established by the Sūtra. || 98 ||

[Objection: "In that case, since there is no distinction [between the past and the future], why is it not correct to say 'it was' or 'it will be' when [the action] is mixed with the future time? [The author] replies: "In the meaning expressed by a verbal form (ākhyāta-pada), there is primacy because it is that which is to be accomplished (nirvartya). Since the qualifiers are implied by that [primary element], they are restricted to its own time. (99)

"It is taught that what has come into being [the accomplished] is for the sake of what is yet to be [the process]. Thus, the action expressed by the verb (ākhyāta), which is by nature something being accomplished (*sādhyamāna-svabhāva*), is everywhere the primary element as the meaning of the sentence. However, the factor of action (*kāraka*) expressed by a noun-word (*nāman-pada*), which is by nature already established (*siddha-svabhāva*), is subordinate. And subordinates follow the principal; the principal does not follow the subordinate. Therefore, the meaning expressed by the noun-word, being drawn in for its own benefit by the meaning expressed by the verb, follows it as a subordinate at that time.

And thus, by this very logic—namely, the impossibility of the syntactic connection (*samanvaya*) otherwise established—the subordinate elements (*guṇa*), when in proximity to a principal element (*pradhāna*) within a single sentence, follow the principal; therefore, for the sake of assisting the principal, even that which has its own time follows [the principal] without abandoning its own time. Since the usage such as *bhāvya āsīt* is thereby established, there is no purpose for the rule in the Sūtra. This is what is meant: for whenever there is a connection between word-meanings, their mutual intermingling (*āmiśratva*) is indeed always present in a qualified manner, according to their respective application.

It is simply that, without the employment of another word, that [meaning] is not ascertained; it is on this basis alone that a word is said to function in a general sense, whereas a sentence is said to function in a specific sense. However, there is no such thing as "relinquishing" or "taking up" [the meaning]. 99.

In such a case, even when the meaning is mixed due to the grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the words, the refinement itself is established precisely according to the initial context (*prakrama*). For there is no negation of a cognition within its own time that has been intermingled with another time. Therefore, he says that there is no need for effort here: "Either it is an imitation of the cognition, or it is simply the operation of the word; it is superimposed upon a contradictory object, yet it is not contradicted by that [contradiction]. (100)

In this case, since words do not transcend their inherent nature (*svābhāva*), comprehension does not arise from a mere instruction regarding correctness at a later time; therefore, the Sūtra is ineffective. As for the connection (*saṅgati*), however, it has been shown that because the relationship through the status of subordinate and principal is possible, there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) by virtue of conforming to the time of the principal element. Alternatively, these cognitions [of meaning] occur even with respect to the relation itself, just as they do at their respective times; the connection, however, is established through superimposition (*adhyāropa*).

Likewise, by the expression "one who has performed the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice" (*agniṣṭomayājī*), an object qualified by the past tense alone is conveyed. However, when this term is connected with the word "born" (*janita*), that form of cognition delimited by the past time becomes untenable; consequently, it is superimposed upon—that is, projected onto—the contradictory future time. This present past time is adopted by relying on the completion of the Agniṣṭoma-performing sacrifice at a time subsequent to birth, which belongs to the future of the one who is to be born. Therefore, the meaning is as follows:

"He shall be his son who will sacrifice with the Agniṣṭoma"—this is the meaning. Alternatively, the operation (*vyāpāra*) of the word "Agniṣṭomayājī," which consists in denoting its own primary meaning, is superimposed upon the future time; for since it is impossible for this [word] to convey a meaning that is yet to arise, its operation is future. The sense is: "He shall be his son who, once born and grown up, having sacrificed with the Agniṣṭoma, will receive this designation. This very point has been stated in the Bhāṣya: "And when will he be designated in this way?"

When this is intended, then, by means of the operation of a word that superimposes [an object] in accordance with the resulting cognition, that object which is considered contradictory is not contradicted; the meaning is that there is no contradiction here with the principle of systematic harmony (samanvaya). || 100 ||

He explains this very point by means of an illustration: "The past and the future—these two temporal relations, without abandoning their state of being present, attain a nature that has a contradictory substratum. (101)

The meaning is this: when these two notions—“that object was past” and “it will be future”—arise within cognition, although they themselves exist in the present time, they bear the forms of their respective objects which belong to the past and the future, times that are contrary to the cognition’s own time; thus, it is logical here that there is a superimposition of another time without abandoning one’s own time.

For two cognitions, which possess the forms of past and future [objects] that are included within the object to be established (*sādhya*) through positive concomitance (*anvaya*), determine their own forms as being past and future, yet they do not abandon their own nature as present self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). In the same way, even the cognition "one who has performed the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice" follows the likeness of a present conviction; it assumes the form of a contradictory future object—which is being superimposed—without abandoning its own time. For the thing being superimposed does not abandon its own essential nature, just as "cowness" does not abandon it when [superimposed] upon a *vāhīka*. (101)

Now, in connection with the discussion of time, he examines the similarity between the present and other times: "That which is the remainder of the present time-path and that which is its commencement—these are shown as distinct types of 'proximity to the present' in the technical treatises. (102)

It has been stated that the "present" time is the uninterrupted continuity of an action from its beginning until the completion of its result. Of that [continuity], the remainder—characterized by the persistence of residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) even after the action is finished—is the presentness pertaining to the past. And the mental inception, the volition (*saṅkalpa*), which is the commencement of the present [action], is the second type of presentness pertaining to the future.

In that case, because no bodily activity is perceived, when there is a determination of the present state, the present verbal suffixes are extended to [expressions] whose nature is past or future. Because of the word "or" (*vā*), which indicates that in some instances past and future suffixes are prescribed, this [present state] is not taken as being exclusively present by way of distinction. Here too, as before, the linguistic refinement (*saṃskāra*) of words such as "I am going" occurs precisely at its own time; therefore, there is indeed the cognition of the present. However, when another word is employed, there is a superimposition (*adhyāropa*) upon that time.

Because of the mention of the word "or" (vā), the suffixes denoting past and future time occur by resorting to a form superimposed upon the object optionally; therefore, there is no need for further effort.

Since *āśaṃsā* (expectation) has the nature of a prayer and is a specific kind of cognition, how can it—which is present and currently manifest—be said in the *Bhāṣya* to belong to the future tense? To this he says: "Though *āśaṃsā* is present, by virtue of its future object, it is designated as 'future tense' in the *Bhāṣya* for the sake of the grammatical operation (*kārya*). (103)

Because its nature is that of cognition, even though it belongs to the present time, it is designated by the property of the object—which is yet to come—as having the expectation of a future time. Thus, it is appropriate to extend (atideṣṭum) the grammatical operation characterized by the past participle suffix (*kta*) to the future object. || 103 ||

If there is designation even by means of the property of the object, then since that which is desired is future, the desire itself would also belong to the future time; thus, one might suspect that in that case, verbal suffixes indicating the present time, such as in *cikīrṣati* ("he wishes to do"), should also be extended [to the future]. Anticipating this, he says: "In the case of *icchā cikīrṣati*, the desire conforms to its own time; in the future sense of the root-meaning, it does not conform to that time. (104)

In the expression *cikīrṣati*, this desire (*icchā*) expressed by the verbal root ending in the desiderative suffix (*san*) is the primary element; the action of "doing" (*karoti-kriyā*), being subordinate to it, is its object. Even though that subordinate element has a future time, since the rule states that "the root and the suffix express the meaning of the suffix together," and because the desire expressed by the desiderative verbal root is present, that same [present] time is carried over; thus, the present tense suffix is established.
For it is not the case that the principal [action] conforms to its subordinate elements; thus, here there is no persistence of the time of the subordinate action of *karoti*. 104.

He explains how it is that even in the case of *āśaṃsā* (expectation), the persistence of its own time does not occur: "In the case of *āśaṃsā*, there is a reversal because it is dependent on that which is expected; the property of the speaker is attached by the words themselves to the meaning of the word. (105)

Just as *icchā* (desire) is primary because it is the meaning expressed by the suffix, so it is not with *āśaṃsā* (expectation). For that [expectation] is not what is denoted by the suffix; rather, it is the object of that [suffix], which is being expected, that is the denotation of the suffix. Indeed, expectation is a property of the speaker, not the meaning of the word. Thus, for example, in the case of "If the teacher has come, grammar has surely been studied," both the teacher’s arrival and the study of grammar—which are being expected—are denoted by the suffix as the governing primary elements (*tantra*); therefore, it is logical that the temporal application follows that [of the primary element].

Since this statement was uttered by one who harbors such an expectation (*āśaṃsā*), it is understood that the expectation is present [in the mind of the speaker]. How then can an expectation, which is a property of the speaker, be the cause for the grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the word? For it is logical that only the meaning of the word—not something else—should be the cause for the refinement of the word. Anticipating this doubt, it is said: "The property of the speaker is superimposed upon the meaning of the word by the words themselves. That is to say, the property of the speaker is superimposed by the word itself onto the denoted object (*abhidheya*) of the word being employed.

For when that [suffix] is employed, it is understood that "that property (dharma) resides in the agent"; thus, because it is being understood, it is logical for this [suffix] to be the cause of the grammatical refinement (*śabdasaṃskāra*) of the word, just like [the suffixes expressing] negation (*bādhā*) and so forth. Indeed, it has been discussed in the *Vākyapadīya* that the scripture (*śāstra*) is also concerned with the properties of persons (*puruṣadharma*). This point is settled. || 105 ||

In this regard, the author of the Vārttika recited: "The word denoting completion is used for that which is not yet completed, because of its state of being incomplete. The meaning is that past participles (*bhūtapratyaya*) should be employed even when an action has not yet been finalized. For example: "If it rains, the rice will be harvested" (*devaśced vṛṣṭo niṣpannāḥ śālayaḥ*). Here, by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), the term "incomplete" refers to a sense similar to completion; thus, it denotes a potential completion occurring upon the presence of suitable causes. Consequently, past participles are not used for that which is merely future.

When it is said "unaccomplished" (*aniṣpanna*), the phrase "because of its unaccomplished state" (*aniṣpannatvāt*) is shown as the reason. The meaning is that this grammatical usage (*prayoga*) is not to be understood as being figurative (*upacāreṇa*). The sense is that the effect is perceived here precisely in its future form, which is not a non-figurative past state; thus, the suffix denoting the past (*bhūta-pratyaya*) must be supplied. For this very reason, the *Bhāṣya* states, "In that case, it must come to be: 'The rice will be produced,'" thereby asserting the propriety of the future suffix alone.

The rebuttal to this is: "But [the past tense] is established because of the prohibition regarding the future. When someone says, "If it rains, the rice will grow," another replies, "Do not say that; say instead, 'the rice has grown. Thus, in common usage, one observes the prohibition of words expressing the future, whereas there is permission for words expressing what has already occurred; such is the meaning of the Vārttika.

He explains the intention of the Vārttika regarding how this occurs: "When the production [of rice] exists upon the conjunction of water and the rice seed, there is a negation of what is yet to come, because [the production] resides in the constituent parts. (106)

In this context, "completion" (*niṣpatti*) is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), primarily signifying the arising of the result when all the means of accomplishment are fully assembled. When that [completion] is superimposed upon merely a part—namely, the mere connection of water and rice—then, because such a mere portion is accomplished by the mere falling of rain, the verbal root's meaning is considered "past," and thus past participial suffixes (*bhūtapratyaya*) are established. This is not at all the domain of future participial suffixes (*bhaviṣyatpratyaya*), as the completion of the conjunction of water and rice has not yet occurred; therefore, the negation of the future is appropriate. || 106 ||

But when the primary sense of "accomplishment" (niṣpatti) is intended, how then can there be a past tense here? To this he says: "However, in the case of accomplishment consisting in the production of a fruit, there is a past tense; with respect to other properties, that form [of accomplishment] is superimposed and thus conceptualized. (107)

When the verbal root *niṣ-pad* occurs in reference to the meaning of a root (*dhātvartha*)—characterized by completion and culminating in the production of a result—which is to be accomplished through the presence of all necessary means, then that form of the completion of the effect is superimposed upon the preceding factors conducive to the accomplishment of the effect and upon the subsequent properties residing in the causes, such as the excellence produced by the contact of seed and water. Since these [preceding factors] have passed away, the production of the fruit is also conceived as having passed; thus, the past participial suffixes (*bhūtapratyaya*) are established. 107.

He states another way of figurative usage (upacāra): "When the operation of the causes has been employed for the sake of accomplishing the result, that form which was superimposed there [upon them] is perceived at that time. (108)

Since an effect is accomplished by a causal complex (*sāmagrī*), many causes are required as its cooperative producers. Because their activity—the assistance (*upakāra*)—is utilized in the production of the fruit, the nature of the fruit, though yet to be realized (*bhāvya*), is superimposed upon that very form of the cause’s assistance. Since that causal activity has passed away, being of the past time, the fruit—which has attained non-difference from it—is likewise determined to belong to that same past time.

Previously, there was the superimposition of the properties of the cause upon the effect; here, however, the distinction is that the properties of the cause are [superimposed] upon the effect. The purpose of this figurative usage (*upacāra*) is to demonstrate the superior efficacy of the causes in this context. By this, the second *Vārttika* on the refutation—"or because it is observed at the time when it has become the cause"—is explained. The past time of the rain, which is the instrumental cause (*nimitta*), is superimposed upon the effect; the meaning is that it is so perceived in order to demonstrate the absence of dependence on any other cause.

Having raised the objection—"If they are already accomplished (*niṣpanna*), why do rice grains not perform their accomplished functions at that very moment?"—it was said: "Something else is being stated now. If the accomplishment of rice grains were simply the performance of causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*), then even those stored in a granary would not be accomplished, because the causal efficacy characterized by eating requires threshing and other such processes. (108)

Now, if accomplishment depends solely on the completion of the causal assistance, then the conventional usage of "accomplishment" is established as occurring at the point when the application of causes has reached its respective fulfillment; thus he says: "In the case of accomplishment, there is a certain limit, or rather, a specific point intended for each [case]. Because it depends upon the arising of the cause, it is called 'the arising of the fruit. (109)

In this regard, some consider the production of rice to depend solely on the conjunction of the seed and water, while others consider it to depend on a succession of benefits produced by the conjunction with sunlight and other factors occurring at a later time; thus, the cause of production is unsettled. For such a statement is made precisely to demonstrate a specific benefit conferred by the cause. In that case, if one assumes a greater degree of benefit residing in the very first cause, then by precluding the operation of any further intervening causes, the conventional designation of "the birth of the fruit" is attributed to that much alone as the cause.

Or [the term "produced" may refer to] that which is born from a cause characterized by contact with heat and so forth; since that [cause] has passed away, the effect is also fit for the conventional designation of "having passed away. And this conventional usage, which relies solely on metaphorical application (*upacāra*), occurs through the consideration of the time when it was a cause; thus, it does not exist without superimposition (*adhyāsa*). However, the former resolution relies on the mere contact of water and seed as the meaning of the word "produced" (*niṣpatti*); here, the meaning of "produced" is figurative. But in the latter resolution, the meaning of "produced" is primary. Since there is a superimposition of non-difference between cause and effect, the alternative [interpretation] is established. (109)

Since an effect is accomplished by a causal complex (*sāmagrī*), how could its accomplishment occur through the mere attainment of a single means? To investigate this objection, he says: "Where the intended accomplishment is not dependent on external means, it is taught as 'accomplished' because of the absence of other means. (110)

When a certain internal means (*antaraṅga-sādhana*) is present, there arises in worldly usage the well-established convention that another external means (*bahirbhūta-sādhana*) is disregarded, such that the intended object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is regarded as if it were already real (*satkalpa*) and indeed accomplished (*siddha*). It is precisely in accordance with this that the systematic arrangement (*vyavasthā*) in the technical treatises (*śāstra*) is justified; for the treatise follows the linguistic usage of words and meanings as they are commonly established in the world. Thus, in this context, usage is established according to intention through the connection with the three times. || 110 ||

He concludes: "Therefore, by means of the distinction of limits (avadhi), the primary state of being (bhūtatā) is established; future-ness (anāgatatva) and existence (astitva) depend upon the observation of causal properties. (111)

In the case of accomplishment (*niṣpatti*), the limit which is the cause [of that accomplishment] is primary as "past" because the effect is superimposed upon it according to its differentiation; for there is a metaphorical designation of the effect in the cause, but not of past time itself. However, when the operation of another cause toward the production of a future effect is expected, then the effect's status as "future" or "to-be" exists in its primary sense.

However, when the operation (*vyāpāra*) of another cause—consisting of a series of operations that extends from its beginning to its culmination in the production of the effect—is intended to be expressed, then, because that series of operations is treated as a single unit delimited by the result, it possesses existence even while comprising prior and subsequent parts; thus, the three usages are established: "the rice has been produced," "it will be produced," and "it is being produced. This point is concluded. 111.

Furthermore, the author of the Vārttika recited: "For verbs meaning 'to exist,' all case-endings (vibhakti) are applicable because the agent is present. This means that when the sense of the *laṅ* suffix—that is, the present time—is intended, verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) expressing past and future meanings should be prescribed; for if it were only the present time, only the *laṭ* suffix would occur.

In this context, even though it has been stated that "the things exist there," the formulation of the reason—"because the agent exists"—is intended to demonstrate that the existence [of the agent] as apprehended by the speaker is based on linguistic convention (*śabdanibandhana*) and not something ontologically real (*vāstavika*). The meaning is that whether one uses the forms *kūpa āsīt*, *abhavat*, *babhūva*, or *bhaviṣyati*, at the time of usage, the agent—the well—is perceived precisely as being undestroyed.

And thus this explanatory commentary (*vyākhyānabhāṣya*)—“‘The well was not perceived by him at any time, nor does he see its disappearance’—explains that ‘existence’ (*vidyamānatva*) is simply the state of being perceived at the present moment. Here is the refutation (*pratyākhyāna*): “But it is established (*siddham*) through utterance at their respective times (*yathāsvakālam*). The meaning is that this usage of the *tiṅ*-inflections occurs according to their appropriate respective times, and not exclusively at the present; therefore, there is no need for an additional rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*).

To establish this very point, it was stated: "because of being non-existent" (*asattvāt*). Because these usages are free from conceptual construction (*avikalpatvāt*), their utterance occurs only at their own [proper] time. For if their grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) were to be attributed to the present tense, then all verbal case-endings (*sarvāstiṅ-vibhaktayaḥ*) would be seen there in alternation. Yet they are not so seen; thus it was said: "and there is a reversal of what is unestablished" (*asiddhaviparyāsaśca*). The meaning is that the reversal is unestablished. Indeed, when one intends to use the expression "there was a well," one does not use the expression "there will be a well."

Therefore, from that non-conceptual application and from its application without confusion, the utterance of the *tiṅ* case-endings at their respective times is established. He explains the intention of the Vārttika as to how this is logically possible: "Because of the connection with the sense organs, that very existence (*sattā*) is distinguished; for practical usage through differentiation is based on other entities. (112)

It has already been stated that all linguistic usage regarding objects here occurs through the permeation by another property belonging to a related entity. Therefore, in this case, this existence (*sattā*) of the well, once apprehended, becomes the cause for the employment of words; for if it were not apprehended, it would be as if non-existent. Thus, the condition of apprehension enters into linguistic usage. And since apprehension is caused by the contact of the sense organ with the object, where there will be contact between the sense organ and the well on the path, the future existence is what is expressed in linguistic usage.

Where, however, that [action] has come into being (*bhūta*), there it is the past (*bhūta*); where it is present (*sampratitana*), there it is the present (*vartamāna*). Thus, linguistic usages pertaining to the three times are established, even though they consist of both general and particular aspects. For when the connection with the sense organs is remote and the action is past, the *laṅ* and other suffixes denote a particularity of the past; and when it is remote and future, the *luṅ* and other suffixes denote a particularity of the future. (112)

Now, one might object: "Just as the grammatical tenses of the past and the future do not encompass the present object, so too that [cognition] would not encompass its objects; thus, the usage 'the well exists' would not apply when there is a connection with the senses in the past or the future. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Existence belongs to the thing-in-itself, but it is grasped by the intellect; however, the distinction arising from its acquisition is not intended to be expressed therein. (113)

The meaning is that when one does not intend to express the distinction characterized by past and future states—which is caused by the connection or non-connection with the sense organs—the usage "the well exists" (asti) is appropriate here in a general sense, having intended the mere existent (sanmātra) by means of the mind; however, specific particulars, being mutually contradictory, do not intermingle. || 113 ||

Or rather, what is the use here of a distinction in existence based on adventitious conditions? He states that the distinction in existence itself is established as real: "Whether through conjunction with femininity or masculinity, nothing remains [as such] in its own self; therein, another thing is spoken of as past or future. (114)

"No one remains even for a moment established in their own self; rather, they either increase as much as they are to increase, or they are joined with decline. This is the commentary on the *Strīsūtra*. In that regard, he will state in the *Liṅgasamuddeśa*: "Increase is masculinity (*puṃstva*), and decrease is femininity (*strītva*); for others, birth is considered production (*prasava*) and destruction is considered contraction (*saṃstyāna*)."

Thus, because all entities are connected with the constant activity of diminution and augmentation through femininity and masculinity, the connection with the three times—occurring as a distinction of states within the nature of a continuum that is at every moment similar to its preceding form—is indeed established as real. Consequently, the past form, which has transcended connection with the senses, is one thing; the future form, which will have connection with the senses, is another; and the present form, which possesses connection with the senses, is yet another.
However, by examining through non-differentiated cognition that a commonality of form exists, it is established that there is a denotation for the present tense. || 114 ||

Thus ends the ninth chapter, the *Kālasamuddeśa*, in the *Prakīrṇakaprakāśa* composed by Helārāja, son of Bhūtirāja. The *Puruṣasamuddeśa* (Chapter 3.11) and the *Saṅkhyāsamuddeśa* (Chapter 3.12): Now he investigates number (*saṅkhyā*). "Every entity that possesses number and exists as a substantive (*sattvabhūta*) is denoted [by words]. For in the world, the distinction between difference and non-difference is based upon number. (1)

Number, characterized by the abstraction of distinctions (*bheda-apoddhāra*), begins with one and culminates in the highest unit (*parārdha*). "Distinction" (*bheda*) refers to that which resides in an object capable of being referred to by pronouns such as "this" or "that. Consequently, every substance (*dravya*) as an entity is designated in worldly discourse as being distinct and associated with numbers such as "one," "two," or "many. Numbers beginning with duality cause the distinction and the unity-number to be applied to their substratum in practical usage. Thus, through this effect, number is determined within the substance.

For it is due to the distinctness (*pṛthaktva*) of substances that linguistic usage proceeds by way of their distinctness; however, the usage of "one" and so forth is accepted by the proponents of inherence (*saṃsargavādin*) as being dependent on number (*saṃkhyā*). Furthermore, even in a compound (*vṛtti*), the subordinate member (*upasarjana*)—being an existent entity—is determined to possess number, distinguished from indeclinables (*avyaya*) which lack number. And this very number, namely the number of non-different unity (*abhedaikatvasaṃkhyā*), will be explained later. Moreover, because there is no basis for the cognition of specific distinctions, a difference in number is not determined [in such cases].

However, where there is a basis for it—as in the case of *śaurpika* and so forth—there indeed occurs a determination of a specific [number], as will be explained later. Thus, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established: every entity that has become a real thing (*sattvabhūta*) is denoted as possessing number. Even in cases such as the indication of the meaning of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), where number is not a constituent part (*anaṅga*), the real thing that is necessarily concomitant (*nāntarīyaka*) still takes on a number; therefore, the pervasion exists. Consequently, in this way, the distinction between the unity and plurality of a real thing is based upon number. || 1 ||

For the Vaiśeṣikas, number is a quality (guṇa) residing in substance (dravya). It should not be argued that there is no separate quality characterized as number distinct from substance, because [they claim] that a category (padārtha) itself is "oneness" when without a companion, while being "twoness" and so forth according to circumstances when with a companion, since the absence of a companion and its presence are not distinct properties (dharmāntara) from the substance. This is incorrect, because of the difference in cognition (pratyayabheda). For the cognition of "having a companion" is one thing, and the cognition of "two," "three," and so forth, is another.

Furthermore, since there exists a cognition of oneness even in the case of things accompanied by others, numerical oneness is not merely the absence of that [plurality]. For it is logical that entities, whose existence is established by distinct cognitions that are not sublated, should possess distinct natures according to their respective characteristics. Moreover, numbers such as "a hundred" and so forth—which reside in multiple substances—are indeed determined to have a distributive occurrence (*vyāsajyavṛtti*), being brought forth by a relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), just like conjunction, disjunction, and the like. For it is not the case that multiple substances do not exist, nor is it the case that this cognition does not occur with respect to them.

The [number] "hundred" and so forth differs from the universal (*sāmānya*) even though it has multiple substrata. One should follow the arguments stated by the Vaiśeṣikas, such as: "Because the universal of number is fully present in each individual substratum, whereas number [as a quality] depends upon another entity [the substratum]. However, those who maintain that qualities are non-distinct [from their substrata] consider number to be non-distinct from its substratum. This view is held because the distinction is obscured by inherence (*samavāya*) and because the difference is not perceived. In this case as well, the arguments shown by them should be stated.
For they consider that since a cognition qualified by that [difference] does not arise if there were absolute difference, difference is therefore merely conceptual. || 1 ||

For us, however, who take scripture as our authority, since we do not concern ourselves with the investigations of other schools regarding the nature of categories (*padārtha*), the various non-Buddhist outsiders have devised their own conceptualizations of categories according to their respective views. Relying upon those [conceptions], he states that the categories, which are the limbs of the definition, must be established: "Whether that property (*dharma*) is distinct from them or is their very essence, it is designated as 'number' (*saṅkhyā*) by relying on its being the cause of differentiation. (Verse 2)

Let this property characterized as number (saṅkhyā) belonging to those entities that are sentient beings—whether it be non-different from the countable objects themselves, or distinct from them—be what it may. What is the use of this useless deliberation for us, since our undertaking here is the investigation of the meaning of words? From the word itself, some property is determined to be the cause for the conventional usage of distinctions such as "one," "two," "three," and so forth; for conventional usage is not possible based on the mere object alone without a qualifying attribute.
And because it enumerates, that property is designated by the etymologically meaningful name "number" (saṅkhyā). || 2 ||

If number resides in substances, how can there be a linguistic usage based on it for qualities and so forth? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Residing in that which is to be delimited, it exists elsewhere; thus, number brings about the distinction of number among entities as well as within itself. (3)

Number, which is the cause of differentiation when a substance is to be delimited, is inherent (*samaveta*) in that very substance because it is a quality (*guṇa*). However, when it delimits qualities and so forth, it resides in a substance other than them; because it is inherent in that [substance] alone, and because those [qualities], though themselves devoid of qualities, are inherent in a single object (*ekārthasamavāya*), it brings about the conventional usage based on its own cause. Furthermore, number belonging to the self (*ātman*) also resides in a substance and brings about the convention of differentiation, as for example: "a hundred," "in a hundred," or "hundreds," and so forth.

For unity, duality, and plurality do not inhere in the number "one hundred" due to contradiction, as it is not a substance and is devoid of qualities. Thus, the number residing in a substance is superimposed upon color and the other qualities; hence the conventional usage, "there are twenty-four qualities. Similarly, one speaks of "five classes of motion," "two types of generality," and so forth. Likewise, regarding the expression "four kinds of non-existence" and the like, since non-existence—which is indefinable—cannot possess the attributes of a real entity, this distinction is merely a conventional usage based on limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

And thus, since the application of linguistic usage is established through the distinction between the secondary and the primary, and since only that much is required here, the number characterized merely by the enumeration of divisions is described everywhere without distinction, disregarding the systems imagined by the non-Buddhist outsiders. || 3 ||

He provides an example for the fact that number serves as the cause for the linguistic usage of distinction even among qualities and so forth, despite their inherence in a substance: "Just as the verbal expression is the same for priority, posteriority, and difference, so too is the denotation by the word 'number' [the same] for a quality which is the cause of distinction. (4)

In this world, due to connection with space, two qualities characterized as priority (*paratva*) and posteriority (*aparatva*), which are produced by relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), arise as inherent in a substance. Consequently, the substance is designated as "prior" or "posterior" by virtue of those two qualities. In the same manner, qualities and other categories are also expressed by the terms "prior" and "posterior."

Furthermore, just as in this context regarding the distinction between qualities, those very two—the substance and the quality—are active [in the cognition], such that the non-distinct designations "prior" and "posterior" apply; likewise, even in the case of qualities and so forth, the linguistic usage of words such as "one" and so on occurs precisely through number which is inherent in the substance as the cause of distinction. The meaning is that there exists no separate unity or other number residing in the quality itself.

Since spatial relation belongs directly to the substance alone, it is certain that the inherence of priority and posteriority—which are caused by that [spatial relation]—occurs in the substance alone; thus the illustration is established. || 4 ||

What more need be said? He states that all conventional usage regarding things dependent [on others] is seen to be by means of the properties of their own substratum: "Just as independence, which is the property of another, [is attributed] to a quality when it is not independent; so too, the state of being divisible, which is the property of a substance, [is attributed] to a quality when it is indivisible. (5)

Just as the independence (*svātantrya*) of a substance is designated in the case of a quality—which resides in a substance and is eternally dependent—by such expressions as "the color of the cloth," so too, although it is not possible to delimit [a quality] by means of number, the state of being delimited by it will be appropriate as a property of the substance that is inseparable from independence, as in "one, two, or three colors of the cloth. This is the intended meaning here.

In this context, when a quality such as "white" is expressed as being subordinate to a substance—as in "a white cloth"—it indeed undergoes coordination with that substance through its shared grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). However, when the quality is abstracted from the substance, as in the expression "the whiteness of the cloth," its own inherent independence and its nature as a substance would be impossible; therefore, its dependence upon its substrate must be established. And that very dependence follows from the expressive power of the word itself. (5)

For in this way, having extracted that [meaning] by means of his own intellect, even the world, relying on tradition, explains it through another property for the sake of comprehension, rather than its own inherent property.

Not only does the Vaiśeṣika maintain that the linguistic usage of a quality (*guṇa*) proceeds by way of the properties of a substance (*dravya*), but he also holds that a quality is something distinct from the substance and inheres within it. Following the Vaiśeṣika tradition, the world at large likewise—having determined through an analytical cognition (*apoddhārabuddhi*) that the quality is separate and independent from that substance—demonstrates to another that it possesses properties such as number, which are distinct from the properties of a quality, by conforming to the power of words.

For example, this is one variegated color of a cloth. However, in the case where that [unitary variegation] is absent, there would be multiple distinct colors for each individual part; thus, there would be many colors in the whole. (6)

Alternatively, he states that when a thing is denoted by a word as being colored by its associated properties, then substance, quality, and so forth are common to it: "A word that denotes all things independently of their true nature as auxiliaries to others is removed from its own inherent property. (7)

Those entities whose true nature (*tattva*) or essential form (*svarūpa*) is being affected or delimited by another distinct factor (*para*) are called "objects qualified by external adjuncts" (*paropahitopakāra*); thus, in linguistic usage, the unconditioned essential form of all things—such as substances, qualities, and so forth—is not touched by words. For objects do not enter into linguistic discourse in their own pure, real form, divested of associated attributes (*saṃsargidharma*).

And likewise, just like a substance, even a quality—when expressed independently as "the color of the cloth"—is expressed precisely as something assisted by its relation to number and other properties of the related entity. For a word does not denote qualities alone; rather, it distances itself from its own primary function [of denoting the ultimate object] because it denotes substances as well when they are characterized by secondary attributes. This is because it is impossible to establish the relationship of a word with that which is unassociated with universals (sāmānya) and the like. Thus, in all cases, a word has only an object presented through another [mediating factor]. || 7 ||

He provides an illustration for the point that even an object possesses its specific character only through the benefit conferred upon others: "Just as knowledge that has no object does not manifest anything at all, so too an entity that is unconnected [to another] is not perceived as anything whatsoever. (8)

Knowledge (*jñāna*), whose nature is mere awareness, is necessarily fit for linguistic usage; however, due to its dependence on an object, it cannot be practically dealt with when separated from the coloring (*uparāga*) produced by that object. Just so, the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) as well—when devoid of the coloring of associated attributes and existing merely as a thing-in-itself—does not attain the status of being knowable or nameable. In this regard, the matter depends entirely upon the assistance of another. 8.

If this is so, one might object: "In this way, the universal (sāmānya) is the cause for the designation and cognition of non-difference among distinct things, while the particular (viśeṣa) is the cause for the cognition of exclusion; thus, how can there be a linguistic usage regarding universals and the like that is distinct from their connection with substances, since such [a usage] would lack any further limiting adjunct (upādhi)? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "But the fact that even common worldly usage follows a specific designation is described as a linguistic practice similar to that of the scriptures, based on tradition. (9)

Since there arise cognitions of non-difference and difference regarding substances by means of both the universal and the particular, it is indeed appropriate—on the basis of analytical abstraction (*apoddhāra*)—to present limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), which possess an abstracted nature and are eternally dependent, as if they were distinct and independent; for even common people follow that [presentation] through the influence of the treatises (*śāstra*). Thus, worldly usage is extended by ordinary people in accordance with the tradition of the Vaiśeṣikas. || 9 ||

And thus, because it is well-established, he says that even here the conceptualization of a property belonging to the related [object] is logical: "When these [objects] are present in the cognition, such superimposition is not difficult to obtain; for in this case, the existence or non-existence of the property of another is not the determining factor. (10)

When universals and the like are thus designated as distinct from the substance by means of the very cognition of abstraction (*apoddhāra-buddhi*), it is not difficult to superimpose upon them the property of another—namely, "possessing an adjunct" (*upādhimattva*)—which is not their own independent domain; for since they are rendered capable of being referred to by pronouns through the intellect, it is logical that the conjunction with an adjunct occurs within their state of possessing an adjunct.

Furthermore, in the case of superimposition (*adhyāropa*), neither actual existence nor non-existence is the determining factor; for if the substrate (*upādhibhūta*)—whether a universal (*sāmānya*) or a particular (*viśeṣa*)—exists as a real entity, it lacks independence, and thus one might object: "How can a non-existent connection with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) be imagined? However, even when an external object is absolutely non-existent, its mental imposition is observed, just as in the case of [imagining] "the ocean" in a small water-pot (*kuṇḍikā*). Therefore, the superimposition of mere attributes (*dharmamātra*) upon something that has some kind of external existence is not contradictory. For this very reason, non-existence (*asattva*) is likewise of no use so long as there is no superimposition.

Even though [the son] exists, because of the superimposition of non-existence, it is said that non-existence is also not the cause [of the designation], for the purpose of making known the excellence [of the statement] "this is sonless. || 10 ||

And because superimposition occurs independently [of external reality], therefore—universality is projected upon universals, particularity upon particulars, number upon numbers, and gender upon genders; in this manner, it is conceptualized. (11)

When the various universals such as "cowness" (gotva) have been determined by the intellect, there is no contradiction in their connection with another universal through the conceptual construction of a common form, because they are determined by the intellect as if they were substances (*dravyāyamāṇa*). Likewise, when the particulars (*viśeṣas*) are similarly determined by the intellect as if they were substances, it is logical that there exists a universal which is the cause of the non-differentiated designation and cognition "particular, particular," and that there exists a particularity which is the cause of mutually exclusive cognitions.

Because it is determined as possessing an adjunct (*upādhi*) just like a substance (*dravya*), when a number such as "hundred" is expressed by a nominal stem—as in "a hundred," "in a hundred," or "hundreds"—where that number itself acts as a substance, another number is superposed upon it as a property of a substance.

And likewise, when gender-marks such as femininity (*strītvam*) and so forth—which are themselves substances (*dravya*)—are denoted by words, there occurs a connection with another gender-mark that is a property of the substance, such as "man" (*pumān*), "masculine" (*pauṃsnam*), or "masculinity" (*puṃstā*). Similarly, in the case of "Gārgyāyaṇī" and "Kārīṣagandhyā," although femininity is already present, there is a second feminine suffix based upon that very femininity. And thus the author of the Bhāṣya says: "A state (*bhāva*) is also joined with a state; femininity with femininity. (11)

Having thus concluded this incidental discussion, he summarizes the subject at hand: "Therefore, those who maintain the doctrine of inherence (saṃsargavādinaḥ) declare that number resides in substances, effecting both difference and non-difference in things that are themselves beyond [the categories of] difference and non-difference. (12)

Since, by the principle already stated, the linguistic usage regarding qualities and so forth is established through number as residing in the substance itself, therefore the followers of Kaṇāda (Kāṇādas), who maintain that the properties [of number, etc. reside in a single substance through conjunction, assert that number inheres in the substance alone. This refers to the cause of the cognition of non-difference and difference in substances and qualities which are devoid of limiting adjuncts and which transcend [the categories of] difference and non-difference.
The meaning is: the number one is the cause of the cognition of non-difference, while duality and so forth are the causes of the cognition of difference. || 12 ||

If, then, the entities themselves are beyond both difference and non-difference, how can number—which is distinct from them—cause them to be treated in such a way? To this, he says: "Because of its association with things that do not possess its own form, it appears as if it were of that same nature to other selves; this is its conformity with the cause. (13)

In this world, categories such as substance and the rest are perceived by means of valid cognition according to their respective definitions as mutually distinct entities. Among them, due to the relation called inherence (*samavāya*), other substances and qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth—though not of that nature—are perceived as if they were of that nature, as if their essence were the form of the quality and so on, because inherence conceals their difference. That [perception] is merely an appearance; the similarity of the cause, such as the quality and so forth, is the sole basis for it.

The state of having that as its nature (*tatsvabhāvatā*) means that its very form is its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); however, this is not its being of that nature in an ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), because they are perceived as distinct according to their respective valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). Thus, the meaning is that even when functioning through the influence of another, entities do not become confounded. || 13 ||

Anticipating the objection—“How is it that they do not become confounded, given that their substratum is always exactly the same?”—he states their distinction based on the difference in their effects: "Just as causal efficiency (arthakriyā) is perceived [distinctly] even when the indivisible elements are combined, so too is it perceived in all the constituent factors (mātrā) such as *sattva* and the rest. (14)

Just as the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) characterized by support, cohesion, digestion, disintegration, and providing space is distinct for each of the elements such as earth when they have attained conjunction in a non-separate state, so too is the causal efficiency characterized by illumination, activity, and restraint distinct among the qualities (*guṇa*)—sattva, rajas, and tamas—even though they are inseparable and pervade all entities; likewise, it is so among the constituent factors (*mātrā*) characterized as substance, quality, action, generality, and particularity, even though they are inseparable through their mutual association.

When the various constituent parts (*vastubhāga*) remain established in their own respective forms, their causal efficiencies (*arthakriyā*) are indeed distinct. For instance, a substance (*dravya*) performs its causal efficiency by serving as the substratum for qualities (*guṇa*), whereas qualities are useful in their respective ways by imparting their own specific natures (*svarūpa*) to the substance. The same should be stated, as appropriate, for the remaining categories as well. Thus, even though there is a convergence of essential natures (*svarūpasambheda*), the distinction between cause and effect is established through the difference in their causal efficiencies. Now, number (*saṃkhyā*) is examined in its own nature.

In this regard, as for numbers such as duality and so forth, are they different from unity or not different? If they were different, then the production of duality and the rest would not depend upon unity. However, if they were not different, then their distinction would be without foundation. Therefore, he says: "Unity is the source of duality and the rest, since differences are preceded by that; without it, there is no possibility of other numbers. (15)

Since the possibility—that is, the production—of other numbers such as duality and so forth does not exist without that unity (*ekatva*), therefore unity is the source or cause of duality and the rest; the production of duality and so forth depends upon that [unity], and the numbers such as duality are not non-different from it. As for the reasoning as to why they cannot possibly exist without it: "differences are preceded by that. Differences are preceded by non-difference; thus, the innate unity of entities is primary. However, it is observed that duality and the rest, being preceded by that [unity], arise only when there is the proximity of another object. (15)

When the two singularities are accompanied by cognition, they serve as the cause for the production of duality; or rather, it is perceived as having been produced precisely from those two singularities. (16)

First, when two substances in contact with the sense organ possess unity inherent [in them], the universal residing therein is perceived through the sense-object contact known as *saṃyuktasamavetasamavāya* (inherence in that which is inherent in the conjoined). Consequently, there arises the cognition of the two qualities of unity as delimited by those qualifiers; dependent upon that [cognition], those two unities produce duality, which inheres in the two substrates of those unities.

For two substances are the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of duality; the two qualities of unity (*ekatva*) are the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), by virtue of the proximate relation characterized as "inherence in the same object as the effect. Apprehension (*apekṣābuddhi*) is the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*); for indeed, one who does not perceive the unities does not have the cognition of duality—thus, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*), the causality of cognition is established.

Inherence belongs to substance alone; and because of the absence of proximity, even non-inherence does not belong to it. Therefore, cognition is established as the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*). For a cause distinct from both the inherent (*samavāyin*) and the non-inherent (*asamavāyin*) is called "efficient" by way of a general designation. Thus, according to the system of Kaṇāda, when duality is produced from this triad of causes, first there is the cognition of its generality (*sāmānya*), then the cognition of that quality (*guṇa*), and then the cognition of the two substances qualified by that [duality], namely, "two substances. This is the doctrine of the followers of Kaṇāda.

"The cognition of the qualified cannot exist without the apprehension of the qualifier"—this is their traditional teaching (*āmnāya*). Others, however, maintain that since the function [of number] in determining duality is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) as residing solely in the two cognitions of unity, duality is produced by the two unities themselves, independent of any further cognition. Thus, they believe that once duality has been produced, it is subsequently apprehended preceded by the cognitions of the two unities. The differences in these procedural analyses are not demonstrated here for fear of making the book too voluminous; they have already been discussed in the First Book (*Prathamakāṇḍa*). || 16 ||

He states that there is also a difference of opinion regarding the nature of duality: "Either it is a collection of unities, or it is [a property] residing separately in each of the two correlates; thus, 'duality' would be the dual number applied to those two. (17)

Duality is not produced as something new from two unities; rather, duality is their aggregate, which—like a forest or a herd—is non-different from its parts. Thus, it is logically consistent that there arises a cognition based on the parts that appears with distinct forms, while there also arises a cognition based on the aggregate that appears with a single form. Just as an aggregate of trees is expressed by the distinct term "forest," so too is the aggregate of unities called "duality. In this way, the aggregate is primary.

But when there is an intention to emphasize the parts (*avayava-prādhānya-vivakṣā*), then "duality" is designated as two onenesses that are mutually dependent; there is no other quality whatsoever [apart from these]. This is the first view regarding the position of non-distinction (*avyatireka-pakṣa*). And in this view, there would be a dual number (*dvivacana*) for those two onenesses because of the emphasis on the parts. However, since duality is observed to be preceded by the appearance of a single form, and thus appears as a singular number (*ekavacana*), this position is not logical. For it is said: "In the case of two or one... (*dvay-ekayoḥ...*) [Pāṇini 1.4.22].

Thus, the dual number (*dvivacana*), being prescribed for duality, would apply only to two unities because duality is not distinct from those two unities. And so, since the phrase "of two or one" (*dvayekayoḥ*) would have three unities as its object within a copulative compound (*dvandva*), the plural number would be required; this is the intended meaning.
