Therefore, it is logical that duality is something entirely other than the two unities, produced by them and being the object of a cognition appearing in a single form. In the same way, numbers beginning with three and ending with ten should be understood. However, an investigation regarding numbers such as twenty will follow later. || 17 ||

[Objection: But if, in this way, the distinction between the numbers two and many is [ultimately] one, how can there be the linguistic usage that "the dual number is used for two" and "the plural number is used for many"? To this, he says: "Even a single entity may, through the distinction of its qualities, bring about a conceptualization of plurality; for the distinction between substratum and superstratum is dependent upon those [qualities]. (18)

The duality [of the Samkhya position] consists in this: is the Saṅgha, characterized by duality, plurality, and so forth, something that has arisen as a distinct entity, or is it merely imagined? Regarding these two views, in the case of the theory of origination (*utpatti-pakṣa*), the qualities (*guṇas*) are the producers because they are dependent on what is produced; however, in the case of the theory of imagination (*kalpita-pakṣa*), the parts are the qualities because they are subordinate to the whole. Through their differentiation, there is a differentiation of duality, plurality, and so forth, even though [the Saṅgha] is one in its own nature. And thus, the linguistic usage of "in two" and "in many" is established.

For the distinction between the locus (*ādhāra*) and the located (*ādheya*), as well as the conventional usage of their difference, arises by means of the relation that serves as its basis. Thus, when there is a distinction in some respect regarding the locus through the distinction of the located, it is conventionally treated as distinct. For example, due to a distinction in acuity, even though the essence of the object is one and the same, one says: "Last year you were not clever, but this year you have become quite another person, being much more clever"; thus, it is treated as distinct.

The meaning is as follows: here, since unity is relied upon as the producer [of duality and so forth], when there is a difference among the substrata (āśraya), that which is based upon them and produced by them—namely plurality and the rest—is designated according to its difference. However, in the expression "dvayekayoḥ" (in the case of two or one), duality is indicated by its own internal non-difference. || 18 ||

Thus, the number ending with the count of ten has been examined. Now, the distinctions of numbers beginning with twenty and so forth are being examined. In that regard, their production occurs through unities accompanied by relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), which is the same as the previous case. However, the word denoting them is seen to express both the number and the numbered object, as in "twenty of cows" (*gavāṃ viṃśatiḥ*) or "twenty cows" (*viṃśatir gāvaḥ*), and so on.

In that regard, if it is described as a derivation in its own sense—namely, that "twenty" (*viṃśati*) is the form resulting from two tens (*daśatau*)—without depending on the explanation of the meaning under discussion, then compounds such as *viṃśatigavam* ("a herd of twenty cows") and *triṃśatpūlī* ("a bundle of thirty") would not be possible.

For two groups of ten make twenty, and three groups of ten make thirty; thus, there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the numerable objects, nor would the singular number be possible—neither for "twenty" nor for "three groups of ten make thirty"—because it would follow that the distinction in number must correspond to the specific division of the groups.

This has been stated in the Vārttika: "If words such as *viṃśati* were used in the sense of 'ten,' the formation of a compound would be impossible. It is intended that the suffix *śati* be applied to the word *dvi* (meaning 'two') when it denotes two groups of ten (*daśadvaya*), and that *dvi* undergoes the change to *vin*. However, [if this were the case], neither the desired compound nor its usage would be possible. Yet, the compound *goviṃśati* ("twenty cows") does indeed occur. Furthermore, due to the indicative evidence (*jñāpaka*) found in expressions such as "a hundred *krośas*" and "a hundred *yojanas*," the prohibition "not with a quality-word" (*guṇena na*) does not apply here.

Alternatively, because numbers such as twenty and so forth reside within the qualities (guṇa), they are designated by the qualities situated therein; this is a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) to the prohibition of a compound with a quality-word (*guṇa*), namely "not [with a word ending in] a quality. Now, since the term "group" (*saṅgha*) is understood from the previous rule, when the suffix is applied to the group as the possessor of the measure (*parimāṇin*) based on the limiting condition of the measure (*parimāṇa-upādhika*), as in "a group whose measure is two tens is twenty," then the singular number is established because the group is a single entity. However, the impossibility of forming a compound remains in that same state.

Furthermore, it would be undesirable for there to be the expression "a herd of cows is twenty" (*viṃśatir gosaṅghaḥ*); rather, "a herd of cows consisting of twenty" (*viṃśako gosaṅghaḥ*) is what is intended. And so says the Vārttika: "If [the suffix] is applied to that which possesses a measure (*parimāṇin*), then the suffix is prescribed again in its own sense (*svārthe*). Thus, a herd of cows whose measure is two tens is designated as "twenty."

In this context, since there is no possibility of another sangha possessing the measure "twenty," the sense is that the suffix *ḍvun*—as prescribed by the rule *viṃśatitriṃśadbhyāṃ ḍvunasaṃjñāyām*—must be stated as being applied in its own sense (*svārthe*) in order to establish the form *viṃśakaḥ saṅghaḥ*. Likewise, it has been stated: "And there is the rule for the genitive case."

In this case, regarding a collective (*parimāṇin*) such as a group of twenty or more, the use of the bare words "twenty" and so forth is not desired. However, when the production of a suffix is based on individual objects (*dravya*) that constitute the measure, since the word "twenty" denotes those objects, there is no distinction [between the measure and the measured]; consequently, the genitive case in the expression "twenty of cows" (*viṃśatir gavām*) would not occur. Furthermore, because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the objects, there would be the undesirable consequence of using the plural number.

Thus, having stated the objections against the position that [words] are derived through etymological analysis (*vyutpatti*), one should reject the undertaking [of the treatise] by resorting to the faultless position that they are not so derived (*avyutpatti*), according to the principle: "Or rather, there is no undertaking because of the recognition of nominal stems (*prātipadika*), as in the case of 'thousand' (*sahasra*) and other such words. Here, the word *vā* (or) has the sense of *tarhi* (then/in that case); thus, like 'thousand' and others, 'twenty' (*viṃśati*) and the rest are indeed non-etymological (*avyutpanna*). This is based on the rule: "That which is meaningful and is not a verbal root... (*arthavad adhātuḥ...* Pāṇini 1.2.45).

Thus, having acquired the designation of *prātipadika* (nominal stem) and possessing the grammatical correctness authorized by the rule *arthavat*, these words—functioning by their very nature through a variety of applications toward both number (*saṅkhyā*) and the numbered object (*saṅkhyeya*), like the word *akṣa* and others due to their possession of multiple meanings, and because they are conventional terms (*rūḍhaśabda*)—possess permanent gender and number, as in the examples *āpaḥ* (waters) and *dārāḥ* (wife/wives). When the author of the Vārttika had thus established this position, the author of the Bhāṣya supports the view of etymological derivation (*vyutpattipakṣa*), stating that the suffix is applied by irregular derivation (*nipātana*) when [the base] denotes a collection (*saṃgha*) which is the measure (*parimāṇin*).

In this context, "saṅgha" (collection) is understood in its general sense, and not merely as a collection of living beings. Therefore, the expression "twenty of trees" is also valid. Regarding this, the *Bhāṣya* provides a solution for the application of the suffix in its own sense (*svārthe*): "That which functioned in the sense of a composite whole (*saṃhanana*) will now function in the sense of a composite whole. This he explains: The collection that enumerates a group of things to be counted is called a "number" (*saṅkhyā*). In words such as "twenty" and so forth, it is the differentiator of another substance-collection (*dravya-saṅgha*). (Verse 19)

This is the meaning: a single collection (*saṅgha*) of countable things such as cows and so forth is called a "substantial collection" (*dravyasaṅgha*). A collection of two such substantial collections, each consisting of ten, is designated by the word *viṃśati* ("twenty"). That is called a "collection of enumeration" (*saṅkhyānasaṅgha*), being the aggregate of two groups of ten which are themselves enumerations. And that [aggregate] is what is expressed by the word *viṃśati*. That number expressed by the word *viṃśati* is the differentiator of another substantial collection of things such as cows; it is a qualifier characterized by its magnitude (*parimāṇopādhi*).

Therefore, from the word *viṃśati*, which expresses a number and a collection, the suffix *ḍvun* occurs when it denotes a collection such as cows that serves as a measure (*parimāṇin*), as in "a group of twenty cows" (*viṃśako gosaṅghaḥ*) and so forth. Thus, the meaning of the Bhāṣya is this: since the word *viṃśati* functions to denote a collection—a conjunction of ten units—it will function to denote a collection of substances such as cows as its measure; and because "functioning" (*vṛtti*) is defined as the expression of another's meaning (*parārthābhidhāna*), it will thereby produce the suffix.

There is no ultimate difference between individual substances and a collection of substances, nor between ten and a collection of ten; this distinction is merely constructed by the intellect (*buddhi*). Furthermore, words, which are based on objects established by the intellect, produce a mental image of the object and thus convey a sense of difference even when no real difference exists. By virtue of their conventional application (*nipātana*), these words refer to a specific collection of ten. As it has been said by the Teachers:

"From *dvi* [meaning] two, when followed by *vin*, from a word denoting measure (*parimāṇa*), and after the sense of 'ten' (*daśan*), [the suffix] *śati* is applied by the teachers; however, in the case of a collective compound (*saṃghāta*) meaning 'a hundred,' it is *dāśata* due to irregular derivation (*nipātana*). This is the meaning [of the verse]. "From *dvi*" means from the word *dvi*. "From *vin*" means from the word *vin* which possesses the *vin* suffix; for there is an intention to express non-difference between the original base (*sthānin*) and its substitute (*ādeśa*), so the word *dvi* itself is stated as the word *vin*. "Denoting measure" means having the attribute of measure (*parimāṇa*).

For a numeral word denotes that which is to be numbered (*saṅkhyeya*), not the measure itself (*parimāṇa*); however, it does indeed become qualified by the measure. As for the sentence "two tens are its measure," the phrase "from the meaning of *daśat*" means "from that which functions as a number consisting of groups of ten. Thus, the suffix *śati* occurs after a word in the first case in grammatical agreement (*prathamāsamartha*) when the denotable object is a collection (*saṅghāta*) possessing a measure.

Since there is no distinction between the group of cows and the group of ten in terms of being the recipient of the dedication (*pariṇāmitva*), the referent (*pratyaya*) applies specifically to the group of ten by virtue of the force of the grammatical restriction (*nipātana-sāmarthya*), and not to the group of cows, nor to the individual cows. Likewise, words denoting mere properties (*dharma-mātra-vacana*), such as "white" and so on, are sometimes employed in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*) through the metaphorical treatment of non-difference (*abhedopacāra*), as in the expressions "twenty cows," "pots," or "Brāhmaṇas."

Because it possesses its own inherent gender and number, there is no contradiction in its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) even when the object to be numbered (*saṅkhyeya*) has a different gender and number; thus, the formation of a compound is also justified. For this very reason, we have such expressions as *viṃśatigavam* (a group of twenty cows) and *triṃśatpūlī* (a bundle of thirty). Indeed, the number "twenty" inheres in the aggregate of substances and does not terminate in each individual one—as is the case with qualities like "white"—and therefore it does not follow the gender and number residing in the substance. However, words such as "five" and so on always denote the numbered objects themselves, and it is therefore logical that they conform to the gender and number residing in those objects.

But when there is a conventional usage based on the distinction between the quality (*guṇa*) and the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*), then the genitive case is established, as in "twenty of cows" (*gavāṃ viṃśatiḥ*). Now, an objection is raised: the group of ten is what is denoted by the word "twenty," and its countable possessor of the quality is not the cow and so forth; rather, its possessors of the quality are the two groups of ten. So how can it be qualified by "cows"? It is said in reply: because there is no ultimate difference between the cows and the two groups of ten, the cows themselves are also the possessors of the quality.

In that context, because there is no deviation [in the number] from ten, twenty is not qualified by ten—that is, one does not say "twenty of ten. For it is not said "the blackness of the black," but rather "the blackness of the crow. Likewise, due to the possibility of deviation, the number twenty is qualified by "cows" to exclude horses and so forth, as in "twenty of cows. And since twenty consists of a collection of ten units, cows are indeed related to it through a traditional succession.

Because the bringing of the action (bhāva) follows from the bringing of the substance (dravya), when it is said, "Bring twenty cows," the cows are brought. Thus, the theory of etymological derivation (vyutpattipakṣa) has been established. As for words such as *sahasra* and others, their correctness is permitted by virtue of belonging to the class beginning with *pṛṣodara*; or rather, they too may be derived in this very same manner. || 19 ||

By way of illustration, words such as "twenty-one" and "thirty-one" are also indeed number-words. For in these cases, neither the components nor the aggregate denote a number; rather, it is because—regarding the number twenty-one—the conceptualization of two parts occurs within a single cognition without repetition, just as if they were two distinct numbers of a similar form. (20)

Having raised the objection, "If [the compound] 'ekādīnāṃ daśādibhiḥ' were a dvandva, there would be the undesirable consequence of plural number in cases such as 'viṃśati'," the Vārttika states: "But it is established that a number ending in 'adhika' [is used] in the section on grammatical coreferentiality (samānādhikaraṇa), and there is the elision of 'adhika'; thus, 'twenty plus one' is 'ekaviṃśati'. Having rejected this analysis of the tatpuruṣa compound due to a fault regarding the accent, the Bhāṣya accepts the derivation as "one and twenty," i.e., *ekaśca viṃśatiśca* = *ekaviṃśatiḥ*.

Thus, it is stated [in this way] to avoid the undesirable consequence that the number would belong to the parts and not to the whole. This is merely an etymological derivation based on the conceptualization of the meaning of the parts; however, in reality, there is no "one" or "twenty" as a number residing in the parts. For, like the figure of Narasiṃha, this number is indeed something distinct, devoid of any division into parts, and is apprehended by a cognition that grasps it as a single unity. Indeed, the cognition does not recur with respect to each individual part here, because the number is determined as a single, undifferentiated whole.

The conceptualization of the means [of expression], however, is diverse. Some indeed, having combined nine and twelve, understands it to be twenty-one; another [combines] ten and eleven, and so forth; yet another [combines] one and twenty. For the sake of grammatical exposition, this conceptualization occurs within this single number—which is ultimately one—just as in the case of two parts [of a word]. It is like the extraction of parts such as "man" or "lion" for the purpose of conveying a specific genus (*jāti*).
For in this case, the cognition does not recur toward the two parts, because [the number] is indivisible. || 20 ||

Let it be granted that this number is composed of two numbers; however, one might object: "What is the use of another number whose constituent parts have been discarded? Anticipating this doubt, the author states the following to refute it by showing that it would lead to the impossibility of the functions prescribed by the treatises (śāstra): "Because it is a collection of non-numbers, the function of a number is established. But if it were merely a collection [of parts], that function would not exist, just as in the case of a collection of one's own limbs and so forth. (21)

Since this number is entirely distinct—being devoid of any division into constituent parts, being the object of Vedic usage as an indivisible whole with identical components, and existing like the "ten" (daśan) and so forth—the grammatical operation prescribed for a number applies here. For example: "one hundred and twenty-one" (*ekaviṃśaṃ śatam*) means "twenty-one is in excess of this hundred," and likewise "one hundred and thirty-one. The suffix *ḍa* is applied according to the rule: "after [stems ending in] *śat* and after *viṃśati*."

For in that context, having stated, "When there is the mention of a suffix (*pratyaya*), the mention of 'end' (*anta*) is for the purpose of including that which begins with what [the suffix] follows," and then stating "and the mention of 'number' (*saṅkhyā*)" in order to prevent over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), it follows that words ending in *śat* and *viṃśati* are understood as denoting numbers, but not such forms as *go-ṣaṣṭiḥ* or *go-viṃśatiḥ*. Furthermore, in the form *ekaviṃśatitayam*, the suffix *tayap* expresses the number-property in the sense of a whole (*avayavin*). And in the forms *ekaviṃśatitamam* and *ekaviṃśam*, the suffix *ḍaṭ* expresses the ordinal sense of completion (*pūraṇa*).

And in that context, the suffix *tamaṭ* is applied according to the rule: “*viṃśatyādibhyastamaḍanyatarasyām*” [Pāṇini 5.2.56]. In the expression *ekaviṃśatikṛtvaḥ*, the suffix *kṛtvasuc* is applied according to the rule: “*saṃkhyāyāḥ kriyābhyāvṛttigaṇane kṛtvasuc*” [Pāṇini 5.4.17]. In the expression *ekaviṃśatimayam udaśvadyavānām*, the suffix *mayaṭ* is applied to a numeral word denoting the standard of measurement (*nimāna*) according to the rule: “*saṃkhyāyā guṇasya nimāne...*” [Pāṇini 5.2.47], since it refers to the thing measured (*nimeya*). In the expression *ekaviṃśatikaḥ*, the suffix *kan* is applied to a numeral ending other than *ati* or *śad* according to the rule: “*saṃkhyāyā atiśadantāyāḥ*” [Pāṇini 5.1.22], as it denotes the possessor of the measure (*parimāṇin*).

In this context, there is no absolute negation, because the word *ti* is understood there as having a meaningful referent. Furthermore, in the case of the expression *adikaikaviṃśāḥ*, although it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound according to the rule *saṃkhyayāvyayāsanna...* (Pāṇini 2.2.25), it nevertheless exhibits the grammatical function (*saṃkhyākārya*) of a number. However, if this were merely a collection consisting of two constituent numbers, the grammatical function of a number would not apply to this collective number *ekaviṃśati*.

For example, since a collection of one's own limbs (*svāṅga-samudāya*) does not initiate another limb that performs a distinct function, the collection of limbs is not itself a "limb. Consequently, in the expression *kalyāṇapāṇipādā* ("one with beautiful hands and feet"), the suffix *ṅīṣ*—which applies by the rule "after a word denoting a limb... (*svāṅgāt...*)—does not occur. Similarly, because a collection of districts (*janapada-samudāya*) does not initiate another district, the collection is not included under the term "district" (*janapada*). Therefore, the suffix *vuñ*, which is prescribed for [words denoting] districts, does not apply here; instead, in the sense of "belonging to" (*bhava*), only the suffix *cha* applies by the rule "after a word containing a *vṛddhi* vowel, *cha*" (*vṛddhācchaḥ*), resulting in *kāśikosalīya*.

Thus, since in this case one number does not originate another number that is designated differently and characterized by distinctness, there would be an absence of the effects of number if it were merely a collection of those [units]; therefore, it is a different number. Furthermore, the number twenty-one could be explained in some way through the conceptualization of its constituent parts; thus, there is no occasion for the application of the dual number. || 21 ||

In this regard, how is there a compound by way of number in cases such as *dvidaśāḥ* (twelve) and *tridaśāḥ* (thirteen)? For what does the number "ten," when connected with numbers such as "two" and so forth, denote? To this he says: "That number which operates within other numbers that are dependent on the objects to be numbered (*saṃkhyeya*), and which consists of repetitions and groups of those objects to be numbered—that kind of number they know [to be the meaning]. (22)

In the compound *dvirdaśa dvidaśāḥ*, this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound according to the rule beginning with *saṃkhyā-avyaya-āsanna...*. In that context, "those numbers" refers to the numbers ten and so forth in which the number to be counted (*saṃkhyeya*) is the primary element—that is, those numbers where the object to be delimited (*paricchedya*), the "other number to be counted" distinct from the scope of the numbers two and so on, is the principal (*tantra/pradhāna*). Regarding such numbers ten and so forth, in which the number to be counted is primary, whatever number such as duality (*dvitva*) and so on occurs—that is, enters into a relationship—is the occurrence of that [number] within the numbers ten and so forth, which constitutes the meaning of the compound.

Repetition (*pravṛtti*) occurs again and again; or, a "group" (*varga*)—defined by numbers such as ten—is a collection of ten parts, which is countable (*saṃkhyeya*) and delimited. Grammarians indeed know—that is, they understand—that such a number, beginning with duality (*dvitva*), has that repetition, group, and countable object as its primary constituents. This [number] does not have a number as its delimited object; for since it is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) among the ten countable objects, it does not enter into a connection with duality.

For this very reason, the cause for the lack of connection is stated by the phrase "dependent on another number" (*saṃkhyeyāntaratantrāsu*). Because it would contradict even the number ten that is to be numbered, duality (*dvitva*) cannot be connected [to it]. For it is not logical to say "ten are two. Therefore, the repetition of the number ten is what is delimited by duality; for this number ten occurs twice, as in "two tens" (*dvirdaśa*). For this same reason, the *suc* suffix has repetition as its object in the sentence. There is a coherent connection [in the sense] that a group consisting of ten parts is to be delimited as "two tens."

Anticipating the objection—“Once the number ten has been heard, or the ten objects numbered by it have been perceived, how is it that they are not delimited by the number two?”—the author sets forth the very reasoning already explained: “It is impossible for ‘two’ and ‘ten’ to coexist in the number, nor in the object numbered; because there is no distinction [between them] in the case of the number, and because of contradiction in the case of its substratum. (23)

It has already been stated that the number ten, being subordinate to the objects to be numbered (*saṃkhyeya*), cannot enter into a relationship with the number two. Even if it were subordinate, a connection with the principal object to be numbered would occur through reflection by the intellect, provided that the subordinate element were capable of such a relation. However, since the number ten is a singular unit, it cannot be connected with the number two; consequently, the ten objects to be numbered are also not delimited by the number two due to this contradiction. For it has indeed been said that "ten do not become two."
For a subsequent number subverts the designation established by a preceding number. || 23 ||
Therefore, the two groups of ten are counted as "twenty" by way of number; or rather, when the objects to be counted possess that form, the repetition is reckoned.

A single group delimited by the number ten is designated as "two" in order to express another such [group]. By this, the duality of two groups of ten is indicated here. Thus, "dvidaśāḥ" means two tens. Since the relationship [of the compound] would otherwise be untenable, the word "daśa" (ten) here functions, within the scope of its derivative application (*vṛtti*), to denote a group of ten. Furthermore, since the group is intended to be conceived as distinct from its members, the plural number is employed based on the distinctions residing in the parts.

In this context, the suffix *ḍati* denotes a group (*varga*); for this very reason, the form *daśad* is not employed, because the members of the group (*vargin*) are predominant. When the number ten itself is the object to be numbered (*saṃkhyeya*), the repetition or recurrence of the number ten is counted as being twofold. Thus, "twice" means two times; "ten twice" is *dvidaśāḥ*. Here, the word *daśa* denotes only the object to be numbered. However, by way of the subordinate number, the objects to be numbered—namely, ten—are joined with the quality of being twofold.

The number ten, however, experiences a connection with the number two by means of its repetition as a subordinate quality (*guṇabhūta*). For when "tenness" recurs among the ten things to be numbered, it is delimited by duality. And thus, through the connection of related entities, duality persists even across all ten things to be numbered; consequently, the plural number occurs because it has those [dualities] as its substratum. Furthermore, since the meaning of the suffix *suC* (the plural marker) regarding the counting of repetitions is already expressed by the compound, it will not be employed. This has been stated in the Vārttika: "The absence of *suC* in a compound is due to its purpose having been already expressed. This point is settled. || 24 ||

Regarding the rule *saṃkhyāyā avayave tayap*, when the question was raised in the Bhāṣya, "Why does [the suffix] not apply here in the case of: 'she whose parts are many' (*bahavo'vayavā asyāḥ saṃkhyātāḥ*)?", it was stated: "The suffix is prescribed for that number which belongs to a part (*avayava*). However, there is no such thing as a 'number' belonging to a whole (*avayavin*) of which the word *bahu* could be a part. This is the meaning: it has been stated that "when a whole is to be designated, the suffix applies to the whole."

Furthermore, there exists no distinct composite entity denoted by the word "number" (*saṃkhyā*). But how can it be said that it does not exist, when the sentence "there are many parts to this number" is indeed employed? To this, the *Bhāṣya* replies: "Is it not the case that 'this very thing is number'? The answer to this is: "This is not a number. What then? It is a name (*saṃjñā*). This term "number" is a general designation or appellation for specific numbers such as unity and so forth; it does not, however, denote any composite entity whatsoever.

Consequently, this name, which resides in the generality of number, persists through each particular instance. Furthermore, there is no relationship of part and whole between the universal and the particular. Even if the whole is conceptualized, the difference in function, the difference in form, and the difference in designation remain distinct. For example, the function of a forest as a collective is different from the function of individual trees taken separately; for this very reason, there is a difference in form. And the designation is also distinct: "trees" and "forest" are different names.

In this case, however, there is no effect characterized by delimitation (pariccheda) belonging to number that is distinct from unity and so forth. Nor is any form whatsoever perceived as distinct from one and so on, just as a color is not perceived as distinct from white and the like. As for the designation, it is not different simply because of the absence of an object; rather, this name "number" refers to a generality whose scope is a particular object.

Furthermore, since plurality (*bahutva*) is likewise a generality (*sāmānya*) of three and so forth, the relation of part and whole (*avayavāvayavibhāva*) does not exist between "many parts" and this "twenty" or "thirty. Rather, it exists only as a relation of generality and particularity (*sāmānyaviśeṣabhāva*). And thus, just as there is no such thing as "color-ness" apart from white and the other colors because there is no whole (*avayavin*) called "color" distinct from them, similarly, there is no such thing as "twenty-ness" or "thirty-ness" apart from the individual units.

For it is not possible that a number such as twenty, which has a delimited form, could have "multiplicity" (bahutva)—which is a general form whose specific details are undetermined—as its qualifier. This very point, introduced in the Bhāṣya, is restated here: "Just as it is said that what is called 'number' does not exist as a [real] number, but is merely a designation; so too, what is called 'form' is not a [real] form, for it is a designation applied to white and other [colors]. (25)

Just as there is no such thing as a distinct color called "form" (rūpa) that possesses a unique causal nature apart from white, yellow, blue, and so forth—where the designation "form" is merely a conventional name for the commonality of those colors—likewise, apart from the distinctions of numbers such as unity and so on, there exists no other composite entity called "number. The meaning stated here is that this [number] is merely a common designation for all of them. 25.

He establishes that this is indeed a case of a general designation: "But because of its connection with the universal *saṃkhyāna*, it is called 'number' (*saṃkhyā*); and because of its connection with the universal *rūpatva*, it is traditionally known as 'color' (*rūpa*) in the case of color. (26)

This designation, though it takes two forms, is recorded by the author of the Bhāṣya as being based on the genus (jāti) and not dependent on a distinct object; therefore, there is no usage such as *bahutayī saṃkhyā* (a number consisting of many) or *bahutayaṃ rūpam* (a form consisting of many). [Objection: In that case, would the expression *bahutayaṃ citrarūpam* (a variegated form consisting of many) not occur? [Reply: It does occur, because the whole (*avayavin*) which is the variegated form is a single entity, and thus its connection with parts such as blue and so forth is logically possible.

Regarding the notions "one," "variegated," and "even more variegated," we have already examined in the *Advayasiddhi* that categories such as the whole (*avayavin*) and the universal (*sāmānya*), whose true nature is made known by the cognition of their distinctions, are simply impossible to deny. For fear of excessive length, we do not elaborate on this here; it should be understood from that very work. Furthermore, in the case of what is called "variegated," which is a color inherent in a single whole, it necessarily undergoes delimitation by virtue of the multiplicity of its parts.

Indeed, one variegated [color] is composed of two parts, beginning with yellow and blue; another, however, is composed of many kinds of parts, such as white, red, yellow, and so forth. Thus, the qualification [of the variegated color] is not fruitless. The distinction has been explained. (26)

Another matter concerning number is now considered. Here, by the rule "the plural is used for many" (*bahuṣu bahuvacanam*) and so forth, number is prescribed as the meaning expressed by the case-endings (*vibhakti*). In that context, since this [number] is already denoted by its own word (*svaśabda*), the nominative case would be obtained from the mention of "singular and so forth" (*ekādibhyaḥ*) in the term *vacana*. But how [would the endings] apply to duality and the rest?

For it has been stated that even in the case of [grammatical] relations such as the object (*karman*), singularity and so forth must necessarily be accepted as the causes [of the application of suffixes]. Therefore, since one resorts to the view that "in the case of the object" means "in an object delimited by singularity and so forth," the case-endings apply to singularity and so forth when they reside in an unexpressed object and the like; however, in the case of what is already expressed, those [endings] are absent. Anticipating the objection—"How then [are forms] such as *ekam*, *dvau*, and *bahūni* [accounted for]?"—he says: "In the expression 'the cause is one,' singularity is not denoted by the case-ending; rather, the case-ending resides in the singularity belonging to that [possessor of the property]. (27)

This is the primary and unique rebuttal: for instance, when the nominative case (*prathamā*) is prescribed—whether it refers to a number inherent in the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), or to the meaning of the nominal stem itself as that which is related to the number, or by resorting to another alternative—the oneness (*ekatva*) and so forth, which constitute the grounds for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of words such as "one" (*eka*), are not denoted by that [nominative case]; because that [oneness] is denoted by the nominal stem itself, just as it is by the word "one" and the like.

When there is another [quality] such as singularity (ekatva) to be expressed—distinct from the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) which is delimited by singularity and so forth that serves as the ground for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*)—the first case ending (*vibhakti*) is prescribed to denote that [other quality], either as the primary element or as a qualifier of the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*). Thus, even though the nominal stem itself expresses the singularity and so forth that serve as its own grounds for application, it still proceeds to express another singularity and so forth, as in "one," "two," or "many. Since the word "one" is intended merely as an illustration, he states: "but the singularity belonging to that [possessor]."

For even duality and so forth are apprehended as the objects of words such as "two" and so on. Likewise, because the mention of case-endings (*vibhakti*)—which is common to the second case and the others—is employed, it follows that the second case and so forth express duality and so forth not already expressed by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), as in examples such as "he sees one," "he sees two," or "he sees many. For in these cases, the nominal stem does not touch upon the singularity and so forth residing in the object (*karman*) and other factors; therefore, the second and subsequent case-endings have those [numbers] as their domain. || 27 ||

But is it not the case that two distinct numbers are not perceived here as being expressed by the base and the suffix? To this he says: "The accumulation of one [unit] is observed, and likewise the collection of two; since this occurs even without a difference in the cause, number must therefore be something distinct [from the object]. (28)

In this context, accumulation (*pracaya*) is observed when one thing is conjoined with another. For instance, when such accumulation exists alongside the coexistence of other factors, numbers such as duality (*dvitva*) and so forth arise. Furthermore, a collection (*samūha*) or aggregate (*samudāya*) is observed to be non-different from its constituents; for example, in expressions such as *dviputra* ("having two sons"), even though the dual suffix has been elided, that [aggregate] is understood as being inherent (*antaraṅga*) within the formation.

Therefore, because we observe a collection or an aggregate (*pracayasamūha*), there exists a number such as unity and so forth—which is the cause of the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) and falls within the scope of words like "one" and so on—that is distinct from and other than that [meaning of the stem]; this is the number expressed by the case-ending (*vibhakti*). One should apply the reasoning that even an aggregate of many is observed, as in examples such as "one who has many sons" (*bahuputra*). Thus, this number, which differentiates and delimits the meaning of the nominal stem by establishing its specific state, is indeed determined here as being expressed by the case-ending.

For instance, from the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), unity is understood as common to both the accumulated (*pracita*) and the non-accumulated (*apacita*). From the case-ending (*vibhakti*), however, there is a determination of the specific [number], because the meaning is fully completed; thus, "one" refers to this non-accumulated unity. In the same way, "two" and "many" consist of a non-aggregate form. If this were so, the case-ending would not apply to unity in the case of accumulation, such as in the expression "one and one. This is not correct. It is said that while unity is expressed by the nominal stem in its general sense, the case-ending illuminates the specific [number].

And thus, in this case, the singular number—unaccompanied by accumulation—is conveyed by the case-ending (*vibhakti*) itself, as it does not serve as a cause for the production of duality or other numbers. However, once the meaning of the word has been established, the particle *ca* indicates accumulation, but this pertains to what follows after the meaning of the word (*padārtha*), not to the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*). For if one intends to express an accumulation of the meanings of the nominal stems, the single word is not employed in the domain of simultaneous expression. || 28 ||

Regarding the rejection of the *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one word) by means of the argument beginning with "because the meaning of the other word [in the compound] is not the referent of the number," the use of words such as *dvi* and so forth—which have the same meaning as those [retained words]—will result in case-endings (*vibhakti*) through convention (*samaya*) in the domain of the accumulation of the meanings of nominal stems (*prātipadika-artha*), because duality and so forth are produced therein. If it is asked why other [case-endings] do not necessarily occur even by convention, another response stated in the *Bhāṣya* is that it is because [the specific grammatical relations] such as the object (*karman*) and so forth are absent.

For instance, because of the rule "A base alone should not be employed" and the rule "And [an affix] follows," when a case-ending is prescribed for the sake of maintaining this convention, a confusion of number would result since no specific meaning is being relied upon; therefore, case-endings are accepted in accordance with their respective meanings. Likewise, even when the meaning of number is already expressed, it is admitted that from words such as *eka* ("one") and so forth, case-endings follow the sense of the base in accordance with that very [number].

Since the denotation of meaning is inherent [to the base], the rule that the stem denotes its own meaning together with the case-ending has been established by the statement of the opponent. This very point he explains: "And although that singularity is one, it is not expressed by that word without the hearing of a case-ending; rather, it is expressed together with the case-ending. (29)

The co-expression [of the base and the suffix] is natural and is established everywhere according to the respective application of case-endings (*vibhakti*). However, in a compound (*vṛtti*), expression by means of elision (*luk*) alone is indicated. For a specific capacity (*śaktiviśeṣa*) arises in words within a compound; thus, expression by the base alone is not contradictory. In the same way, even when the vocative ending (*saṃbuddhi*) is elided, its usage as a bare base is natural. (29)

Another solution to this problem has also been stated in the Bhāṣya: "This number is subordinate to something else; by it, the thing numbered (saṃkhyeya) is to be qualified. And if the nominative case-ending were not used here, the thing numbered would remain unqualified. This [verse] explains that: "If there were positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), there would be another verbal form; and in its absence, the meaning of the base (prakṛti-artha) is not postulated. (30)

In examples such as *vṛkṣaḥ*, *vṛkṣau*, and *vṛkṣāḥ*, there exist positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) between the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*). Thus it has been said: "For even when there is no [real] difference, a difference is observed provided that there is positive concomitance," and so forth. Consequently, in that case, whatever meaning follows a particular word belongs to that word; thus, the conceptual abstraction (*apoddhāra*) through differentiation is logical.

In this case, however, from the word *eka* there is only the singular number, from the word *dvi* only the dual, and from the word *bahu* only the plural; there is no other number. Since there is no negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), positive concomitance (*anvaya*) cannot be ascertained, and thus the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) cannot be determined through distinction. For when another number is absent, both positive and negative concomitance do not exist; therefore, in this context, the denotation of the base—characterized by words such as *eka* and so on—is not possible apart from the meaning of the suffix, by which the base alone could delimit the object to be numbered.

And so, since the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of the singular number and other suffixes has been determined with respect to [words] such as *vṛkṣa*, this meaning—which is expressed by the combination of base and suffix—is present here in the absence of those suffixes; it is that by which the thing to be numbered (*saṃkhyeya*) is qualified through the characteristic of number. And thus, it exists precisely because its meaning has not yet been explicitly stated. However, in a compound (*vṛtti*), the meaning of the subordinate element (such as "one king" and so on) is understood from the single base alone, having entered into a fusion with the primary meaning; consequently, the case-ending (*vibhakti*) ceases to function, as its purpose has already been fulfilled.

For just as in a compound (vṛtti), even without an abstract suffix (bhāvapratyaya), the understanding of that meaning remains unconfused—as in "he spoke wisely" (sadhīram uvāca) and so forth—so too here, even in the absence of a case-ending, the subordinate meanings such as singularity and so on, which are observed to be present through proximity, are indeed understood. Thus, in the previous resolution, it was intended that [the words] are merely reiterative of the meaning of the stem (prakṛtyartha); for even when the stem-meaning is already present, the words are said to function as reiteratives of that meaning according to their respective roles.

However, in this case, what is intended is that [the number] has a common referent (*sādhāraṇārthatva*), because the specific object to be numbered is expressed by the meaning denoted by the combination of the base and the suffix; such is the distinction between the two solutions stated by the author of the Bhāṣya. || 30 ||

Another solution to this objection has been stated here in the Bhāṣya: "These words denote both; they express both substance and quality. Since that quality [denoted by the base] has not had its number expressed, the nominative case ending will occur [to express it]. This he explains: in the expression "oneness is one," oneness is a qualifier of the pure substance; however, the meaning of the nominal stem (prakṛti), when accompanied by a quality, is differentiated by the meaning of the case ending (vibhakti). || 31 ||

When a pure substance has first been determined by the intellect through its qualifiers, the state of being a qualifier—namely "oneness"—is expressed by the nominal stem as "one. For the word "one" denotes a substance qualified by oneness, and not mere enumeration like "twenty" and so forth. Therefore, it is intended in the Bhāṣya that these words denote both [the substance and the quality], meaning they denote a qualified entity; however, it is not possible for them to denote a mere quality, as is the case with words such as "white."

Alternatively, because of the grammatical rule "of two or one" (*dvyekayoḥ*), it is clear that [the word *eka*] denotes not merely the number, but also the thing qualified by it. Thus, when this substance—which is denoted by the word *eka* and qualified by oneness—is further qualified by the oneness expressed by the case-ending (*vibhakti*), the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*), being now possessed of a quality, becomes differentiated by the meaning of the case-ending and comes to reside in a specific instance.

This single object is qualified by oneness (ekatva) and not by any other quality; thus, that which is denoted by the base (*prakṛti*) is internal (*antaraṅga*), whereas that which is denoted by the case-ending (*vibhakti*) is external (*bahiraṅga*). He will state that in cases such as "two sons" (*dviputra*), the external distinction denoted by the case-ending is set aside for the duals and so forth.

Others, however, considering *śuddham* and *dravyaviśeṣaṇam* as a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*), explain that the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) expresses oneness (*ekatvam*)—which consists of the common form of both number and the numbered object—as having enumeration alone as its primary meaning and the numbered object as its subordinate element. They further explain that the meaning of the nominal stem, which exists together with the quality of enumeration, is differentiated, delimited, and manifested by what is expressed by the case-ending; thus, the numbered object denoted by the word ending in a case-suffix is the predominant element.

The meaning of the Bhāṣya here is as follows: "In whatever substance a quality resides, its enumeration—namely, oneness and so forth—is not mentioned" means that they are not mentioned because they serve to delimit the substance. || 31 ||

[Objection: Since that which is to be numbered (*saṃkhyeya*) is expressed by means of [words] ending in case-terminations, and since these [words] are never used in isolation, how can it be determined that words such as "one" (*eka*) and so forth denote merely a quality (*guṇamātra*)? To this, he says: "Because of the rule *dvayekayoḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.2), they are possible even in the sense of mere number (*saṃkhyāmātra*). However, it is stated that the well-known meaning of 'one' and so forth is that which is to be numbered (*saṃkhyeyārthatva*). (32)

Because of the use of the dual number in the expression "of two and one," duality and singularity are established as being themselves dual and so forth. This is logical when referring to duality and singularity as extracted from the numerable objects; otherwise, if the numerable objects were always predominant, there would be a plural form such as "two and one are three."

Relying on the common worldly convention that "numbers up to ten function as numerals," the Bhāṣya states, "This might be so where a number necessarily functions as a numeral," thereby expressing their status as designators of the numbered object (*saṃkhyeya*). This is the meaning here: in ordinary usage, these [words] do not function as mere acts of numbering (*saṃkhyāna*); for in that context, it is the *pada* (word) that is employed, and a *pada* is that which ends in a case-ending.

And since a case-ending expresses a number inherent in the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the determination of the thing to be numbered (*saṃkhyeya*) therein is fixed. However, in the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*), by means of the analytical cognition (*apoddhārabuddhi*), it is possible—provided that the case-suffix is not actually functioning—that the number resides solely in the act of counting itself. || 32 ||

Thus ends the eleventh section, the *Saṃkhyāsamuddeśa*, in the *Prakīrṇakaprakāśa* composed by Helārāja, son of Bhūtirāja. The *Upagrahasamuddeśa*: Now, in order to examine *upagraha* (voice) as a meaning of the verb (*ākhyāta*), he demonstrates its nature, as it is not [ordinarily] perceived in common worldly usage: "That distinction which is sometimes understood from the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), and which is also [understood] from other substitutes of the verbal suffixes (*lādeśa*)—that they consider to be *upagraha*. (1)

The distinction of an action or its instrument—consisting of the agent's intention, the opposite thereof, and so forth—which is manifested by the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) or the active voice (*parasmaipada*), has been accepted by the ancient masters as *upagraha* (voice/mode). This meaning, well-known among the ancient masters and denoted by the term *upagraha*, is employed here in this treatise. (1)

He analyzes what was stated in general terms—namely, "of which object is this the distinction?"—as follows: "In some cases it is the means itself; in some cases it is its qualifier. In that context, the 'means' refers to the object (*karman*) and so forth, while for words with explicit denotation, it is the qualifier. (2)

The *sādhana* (means of accomplishment) is the object (*karman*) and the recipient (*upagraha*), which is manifested by the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), as in "it is cooked" (*pacyate*) or "he goes" (*gamyate*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the agent (*kartṛ*) and the state (*bhāva*) are also included. Among these, the agent is manifested by both types of *l*-suffixes, as in "he prospers" (*edhate*) or "he goes" (*yāti*). The state, however, is manifested exclusively by the middle voice, as in "it is sat" (*āsyate*) or "it is slept" (*śayyate*). And that external state, denoted by the *lakāra* suffix, becomes the *sādhana* by making known the internal state—which consists of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*)—as the action’s abiding within itself, because [the former] does not enter into the *sādhana*s denoted by the same word [as the latter].

Those whose speech is manifest (*vyakta-vācaḥ*), or those in whom speech is manifest, are "those with manifest speech. Even while qualifying the meaning of the verbal root—which consists of the act of utterance—they become, by implication, qualifiers of the agent who is the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), and thus they come to be designated by the term *upagraha* (voice/mood). For example: "The Brahmins converse together" (*saṃpravadante brāhmaṇāḥ*). || 2 ||

In some cases, he states that the "upagraha" (voice) is a qualifier of the action (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*). An action differs in livelihoods and the like according to the distinction of its objects; that differentiation of action is also regulated within sentences by means of the substitutes for *l* (the verbal suffixes). (3)

Action is differentiated by its dependence on specific objects; and that differentiation of it is manifested by the substitutes for *l* characterized as *parasmaipada* (active voice) and *ātmanepada* (middle voice), as in *pacanti* ("they cook") and *yajanti* ("they sacrifice"). For here, the primary fruit of the action does not go to the agent, since the servants' fruit consists merely in their wages. An action set in motion by a sacrificer (*yajamāna*) or similar person with the aim of the primary fruit is understood from the *ātmanepada*, as in *yajate* ("he sacrifices") and *pacate* ("he cooks").

In some cases, however, that very same distinction of action is determined by its own word even when sentences are present; thus it is understood through the sentence. For example: *svaṃ yajñaṃ yajate* (he sacrifices his own sacrifice), *svaṃ yajñaṃ yajati* (he sacrifices his own sacrifice). Because of the grammatical rule, "The substitution of *l* [for *tiP*] is optional when the meaning is already conveyed by a co-occurring word (*upapada*)," the fact that the primary fruit of the action goes to the agent—which is to be ascertained from a sentence constructed through the connection with another word, namely *svam*—is understood. 3.

He states that in some cases, even without a difference in the object (*viṣaya*), a specific direct action (*sākṣāt kriyā*) is what constitutes the "auxiliary" (*upagraha*): "The meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) and its specific qualification (*viśeṣa*) are also said to be the 'auxiliary' (*upagraha*) in certain instances. The meaning of the root may be [actions such as] threatening (*gandhana*) and so forth; the qualification is reciprocity (*vyatihāra*). (Verse 4)

Specific actions such as "scenting" (*gandhana*) and "throwing down" (*avakṣepaṇa*), although they are denoted by verbal roots (*dhātu*), remain unmanifest without the middle voice (*ātmanepada*). Therefore, because they are manifested by the middle voice, they are designated by the term *upagraha* (grammatical mood/voice). For example: *utkurute*, *avakurute*, and so forth. Furthermore, reciprocity (*vyatihāra*) is a specific action manifested by the middle voice and is thus an *upagraha*, as in *vyatipunate*. 4.

To the question, "How can it be specified that 'the fruit of the action accrues to the agent' (*kartrabhiprāye kriyāphale*), given that every fruit of an action necessarily accrues to the agent who initiated it? he says: "Regarding the engagement in an action, some declare its being for one's own sake or for the sake of another; whether such [distinction] exists or not, it is based solely on the speaker’s intention. (Verse 5)

"All these beings strive for their own welfare. Since everyone acts for their own sake, self-interest (*svārthatā*) is ultimate; whereas interest in others (*parārthatā*) is simply non-existent. To say that it exists is merely a conventional expression. For instance, the intention to speak (*vivakṣā*) is the basis and cause of this [notion of] interest in others; however, since self-interest is primary, it cannot have the intention to speak as its basis.

Thus, so that the ātmanepada suffix does not occur when there is an intention to express benefit for another (*pārārthya*), the term "fruit" (*phala*) is specified as being "the fruit of the action intended for the agent" (*kartrabhiprāye*). However, others—on account of the statement by some [grammarians]—propose an alternative view (*matāntara*) that the distinction between benefit for oneself and benefit for another exists in reality (*vastutaḥ*) with respect to the intention toward the principal fruit. For instance: one who seeks the primary fruits such as heaven or cooked rice employs others in that regard and undertakes the provision [of rewards] through wages.

Consequently, for that officiant who seeks the primary fruit, the undertaking is for his own benefit; therefore, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used in such cases, as with the sacrificer and others. However, one who is employed by him and whose fruit consists merely of a fee considers his purpose accomplished simply by following the master’s will; thus, since his undertaking is for the sake of another, the middle voice does not apply there. || 5 ||

And thus, since the application of the *ātmanepada* ending and the *ṇic* suffix occurs in that very same context, he states that the scope of these two is identical: "For some, the *ātmanepada* ending is optional with the *ṇic* when the result accrues to the agent; for others, the base form itself has that [resulting] meaning. (6)

Some consider the meaning of the *ṇic* suffix to be mere "arrangement" (*saṃvidhāna*). Thinking that "all these beings strive for their own sake," the instigator (*prayojaka*) of one who acts for his own benefit is called an "arranger" (*saṃvidhātṛ*) because he performs actions conducive to that end. For activity does not arise merely from the command of one who is not to be obeyed, nor from one who cannot accomplish his own purpose; thus, the *ṇic* suffix does not have the sense of a command (*praiṣa*).

Rather, it is merely an arrangement (*saṃvidhāna*); since the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) also applies in that very same case, these two have the same scope and are therefore used alternatively—as in *yajate/yājayati* ("he sacrifices/sacrifices for another") and *pacate/pācayati* ("he cooks/cooks for another"). For the agent expressed by the middle voice requires an arrangement; thus, the middle voice has the same scope as the causative suffix (*ṇic*) and is optionally used alongside it. Just as the base verbal root (*prakṛti*), whose meaning is that of the [causative] sense, is optionally used together with the *ṇic* when its purpose is production.

Those others who consider that the term *hetumat* (having a cause) functions as a qualifier of the root-meaning (*dhātvartha*) maintain that the suffix *ṇic* is an indicator (*dyotaka*) of an operation (*vyāpāra*) residing in the one who possesses the cause. Since, by the force of some semantic implication (*arthasāmarthya*), there is an understanding of the operation of the one possessing the cause as being qualified by a specific arrangement—just as in cases such as *krīṇīṣva* ("buy") and so forth—they believe that the pure base form (*prakṛti*) is indeed fit for usage even when accompanied by *ṇic*.

However, those who maintain that because the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is not understood without a further *ṇic*, the term "having a cause" (*hetumat*) must be the meaning of the suffix, for them it follows that just as the base of the *ṇic* does not optionally alternate with the *ṇic* itself, so too the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) would not. By saying "of some," he indicates an alternative view. For instance, the agent's exertion (*saṃvidhāna*) within the scope of the middle voice would be a property residing in the action, expressible by the verbal root (*dhātu*).

For, by the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), which indicates that the fruit of the action accrues to the agent, it is by implication stated that the agent is connected with the fruit of the giving; however, the command (*praiṣa*) is not touched upon. Indeed, in the case of verbal roots ending in the middle voice, unlike those ending in the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the operation of the one being prompted and the prompter is not perceived. For this very reason, the verbal cognition differs: "he sacrifices" (*yajate*) means that one who desires the fruit, being independent, brings about the sacrifice.

In that context, because it is appropriate for one who is independent and not prompted by another to perform the *bhāvanā*, the operation (*vyāpāra*) understood is the act of arranging [the means]; however, there is no comprehension from this verbal operation that "one prompts another" beyond that. In the case of *yājayati* ("he causes to sacrifice"), the verbal comprehension is precisely that "he prompts another regarding the sacrifice. From the perspective of the intended meaning (*tātparya*), however, there would be a similarity of subject matter (*viṣaya-sāmya*) based on the locus of the actual operation. Therefore, since the subject matters are distinct, there is no optionality (*vikalpa*) here; this is the accepted final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

Otherwise, because they would share a single object (*ekaviṣayatva*), the *ātmanepada* prescribed for specific roots by the rule "svarita-jitaḥ... would supersede the *ṇic* suffix prescribed for the general class of roots, and thus there would be no option. If it is argued that since the rule "laḥ parasmaipadam... prescribes [the endings] such as *ti*, *tas*, and *jhi*, the rule "svarita-jitaḥ... and so forth is not a prescription [but rather a restriction], then it must be a restrictive rule (*niyama*). And that, being part of a single syntactical unit, is indeed a supplement to the prescription. Otherwise, how could the *ātmanepada* even supersede the *parasmaipada*?

Thus, in this way, the *ṇic* affix and the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) have distinct domains: the middle voice occurs in the sense of "arranging" (*saṃvidhāna*), whereas the *ṇic* affix occurs in its specific sub-sense of "commanding" (*praiṣa*). However, where the fact that the meaning of the verbal root is for the sake of another is understood from some other source, the middle voice does not occur there. For example, in the cases "he acts when told" (*uktaḥ karoti*) and "he acts when commanded" (*preṣitaḥ karoti*), since the agent's being for the sake of another is understood through the command (*praiṣa*), there is no perception of it being for his own sake; therefore, the middle voice is absent here.

Thus, in the expression "he causes the rice to be cooked" (*odanaṃ pacati*), even though there is an instigation toward other factors of action such as the instrument, the *ātmanepada* ending does not occur because the instigating agent (*prayojyakartṛ*) lacks the status of being for the sake of the primary fruit. Likewise, in the case of "he leads the goat to the village" (*ajāṃ nayati grāmam*), if one intends to express merely the instigation regarding the meaning of the verbal root, the *ātmanepada* occurs with respect to the agent within his own self, as in: "he leads himself [the goat] to the village" (*ajāṃ nayate grāmam*). || 6 ||

Now, he demonstrates the seed of the error regarding the perception of a common scope for those who maintain that the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is optional with the causative suffix (*ṇic*): "Buy! You weave! You place! You gather! And you also collect!"—these are seen in the usage of authoritative masters (*āpta*), wherein the meaning of the causative is expressed. (Verse 7)

When Vinatā was addressed with "Buy yourself," she said to her sons, "Buy me"; this is an instance of the usage by the learned (*śiṣṭa*). Here, in the usage ending in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), "krīṇīṣva," the meaning of the causative (*ṇyartha*) is understood as an instigation (*praiṣa*).

For Vinatā had indeed fallen into servitude; she was directed toward the act of purchasing herself from slavery by Kadrū with the words, "Buy yourself and free yourself from slavery. Some consider this *ātmanepada* ending to express the sense of the causative (*ṇyartha*), based on the understanding that there is a state of being impelled by another (*paraprayojyatā*). However, they regard this as a source of confusion because the scope of the causative suffix and the *ātmanepada* ending are identical. For instance, in this case, the sense of the causative is understood through contextual implication (*sāmarthya*), not from the *ātmanepada* ending itself. Indeed, it is Vinatā who is directed toward the act of purchasing.

In this context, the fruit of the act of buying—characterized by the removal of the state of servitude—accrues to the self of the agent, the buyer; thus, the *ātmanepada* ending is prescribed because the fruit of the action goes to the agent (*kartrabhiprāya*). When the meaning of the word is exhausted at this point, the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) of "causing to buy" (*krāpayati*) is subsequently determined through the force of the context. For instance: how does that Vinatā buy herself—that is, how does she liberate herself from slavery? [She does so] if she performs a service for the sons of Kadrū.

And since she herself was not able to repay the favor, she said to her sons, "Buy me. Thus, by considering the force of the context, the meaning of the word *krīṇīṣva* (buy) is obtained as "save yourself from slavery through your sons" or "ransom yourself"; therefore, the *ātmanepada* ending here does not share the same scope as the causative (*ṇic*). Similarly, the usage *keśaśmaśru vapata* (shave your hair and beard) is seen to be a source of confusion.

For instance, they maintain that when there is the same scope for the causative (*ṇic*) and the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), the meaning is "he causes another to shave his head," as in the expression *vapate paranaṃ muṇḍanam*. In this case, since the fruit of the action is understood from the verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*) to accrue to the agent (*kartṛdāmi*), the middle voice is employed; however, by implication (*sāmarthyāt*), it is understood that one who is himself unable to perform the act employs another. Similarly, the usage of the learned is seen in the phrase *tṛptā patnī reto dhatte* ("the satisfied wife deposits the seed"), where the sense of "she causes [him] to deposit the seed" (*reto dhāpayati*) is understood through implication.

For it is not possible for a woman to possess that which belongs to a man—that is, the capacity to retain semen—since such retention occurs through the male organ, and the woman lacks the male organ capable of retaining semen. Thus, the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) here is obtained through implication and is not directly expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), such that the causative would share the same scope as the middle voice (*ātmanepada*). Indeed, from the middle voice, one understands merely the autonomy of the act of retaining.

And that [agency], due to its connection with the wife and through reflection on the meaning of the sentence, is understood to refer solely to the instigating agent (*prayojaka-kartṛ*). For a word, independent of other words, conveys only its own primary meaning; however, the comprehension of a qualified meaning arises from the power of the sentence. Even in the passage, "This indeed is the prosperity of the sacrifice: he who piles the fire, he who causes it to be piled, and that which is being piled," the term *cinute* (he piles) is understood, in its usage by the learned, as referring to the one who arranges the piling.

However, by the force of the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), the act of instigation (*preṣaṇa*), though not directly denoted by the word, is understood as the domain of the causative suffix (*ṇic*). For one who performs the piling (*cayana*) himself while being prompted by another is understood from the very form *cinoti*; thus, the third [agent], the prompter, is understood from the sense of the verb *cinute*.

Therefore, although the meaning of the causative suffix is established in these usages through the force of the context and so forth, some—mistakenly thinking that the meaning of the causative suffix is the literal meaning of the word ending in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*)—have maintained everywhere that the domains of the causative suffix and the middle voice are identical, and have thus proposed an option (*vikalpa*). This matter is concluded. (7)

It has been stated here that the *ātmanepada* [middle voice] occurs when there is "preparation" (*saṃvidhāna*). However, since roots such as *pac* (to cook) express primarily the action of softening (*viklitti*) and so forth, how can "preparation" be included [as their meaning], such that the *ātmanepada* would occur for those verbal roots because they express an action qualified by that preparation? Anticipating this objection, he says: "In some cases, 'preparation' is understood as the meaning of roots like *pac*; likewise, other actions such as placing [the pot on the fire] are also caused by it. (Verse 8)

"What is the primary meaning of the root *pac*? It is that softening (*viklitti*) of the rice grains. Now, would it not be appropriate for the act of commanding or requesting to also be the meaning of *pac*, such that everything [involved] would be the meaning of the root? "Certainly it would be appropriate. Thus, in the *Bhāṣya*, the operation of the instigator (*prayojaka-vyāpāra*) is also presented as being the meaning of the verbal root.

Thus, even one who is indifferent may be an instigator (*prayojaka*); by nourishing the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), he is a facilitator (*saṃvidhātṛ*) and an agent (*kāraka*). Therefore, his activity is denotable by the verbal root (*dhātu*). In the case of *pacati* ("he cooks"), because the meaning is the softening (*viklitti*) [of the rice], the activity of the instigated agent (*prayojyakartṛ*)—such as placing [the pot] on the fire, pouring water, and so forth—is expressed. Thus, *devadattaḥ pacati* has the sense of "Devadatta places [it] on the fire, pours water [into it]," and so on. *Devadattaḥ pacate* has the sense of "Devadatta provides the necessary materials."

However, when the instigation of the person to be employed is intended to be expressed, the causative suffix *ṇic* occurs, as in *pācayati*. For instigation (*praiṣa*) is not merely the act of providing the means (*saṃvidhāna*), but rather the impelling that precedes it, by performing which one is called an employer (*prayojaka*). Indeed, even while providing the means, one is not called an employer so long as one does not exercise instigation. 8.

He explains how the *ātmanepada* ending, which is prescribed when the result is intended for the agent (*kartrabhiprāya*), implies that the verbal root has the sense of "arranging" (*saṃvidhāna*): "In the sūtra, 'intended for the agent' is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of a distinction in the action (*kriyābheda*). For it is by means of such an action that its agent becomes a partaker of the fruit. (Verse 9)

By the inclusion of the phrase "the fruit of the action intended for the agent," an action characterized by a specific arrangement (*saṃvidhāna*) is indicated; because when an action is of such a nature—that is, distinguished [by that arrangement]—its agent is joined with the fruit. For a priest or similar officiant does not enjoy the fruit of the action, such as heaven, without performing the arrangement. Therefore, it is stated that the *ātmanepada* occurs there because the action, which is the cause, is indicated by its connection to the fruit, which is the effect. || 9 ||

He provides an illustration regarding secondary indication (upalakṣaṇa): "Just as time is indicated by the non-appearance of stars and so forth, so too is the distinction between actions demonstrated by means of specific results. (10)

Just as the injunction "one should release speech upon seeing a star" uses the sight of a star to indicate a specific time characterized by the passing of twilight—so that even when stars are absent in a sky thick with clouds, the release of speech still occurs once the time is determined by means of a water-clock (nālikā) or similar device—likewise, because the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) serves to indicate the arrangement of the connection with the primary fruit, it occurs even when disregarding the manifestation of a specific fruit, and applies to the mere arrangement itself. || 10 ||

Since the inclusion of the terms *svarita* and *ñit* has been rejected in the Bhāṣya, one might ask why the Ātmanepada does not occur even after roots such as *yāti*. To this he says: "The capacity [of the root] to express a specific action is obstructed. However, some other roots have been made *svarita-ita* and likewise *ñit*. (11)

The expressive power (*śakti*) of verbal roots such as *yāti* and others is obstructed when the specific action characterized by "arrangement" (*saṃvidhāna*), which is marked by the fruit of the action intended for the agent, is to be conveyed. For the power of words is indeed restricted. Those [roots], however, which are capable of denoting "arrangement"—namely those marked with the svarita accent and those marked with the letter *ṇ*—are listed in the *dhātupāṭha* in order to manifest their capacity to express an action qualified by arrangement; this is the meaning.

For the inherent power of verbal roots has a restricted scope and is difficult to ascertain; therefore, grammarians have introduced indicatory letters (*anubandhas*) such as *ñ* in order to understand it. (11)

If this is so, how can the mention of the *svarita* accent and the *ṅit* marker be rejected? For if that were absent, how could the *anubandhas* (indicatory letters) be recited? For they constitute their function; in their absence, that function would not exist. And if that were the case, how could one understand that verbal roots possess the power to denote actions qualified by specific arrangements [of phonemes]? To this he says: "And the *anubandha* is attached for the sake of a traditional rule (*smṛti*) regarding an established meaning. Even among those things that have the same meaning, it is not necessarily the case that all possess the same property. (Verse 12)

In this context, although verbal roots have a common denotation insofar as they all signify mere action (*kriyāmātra*), not all of them possess the nature of signifying mere action; rather, due to the diversity of the expressive power of words (*śabdaśaktivaicitrya*), each signifies a specific action according to its own nature. For instance, although the semantic definitions are identical in the cases of *yā* "in the sense of going" and *ṇīñ* "in the sense of leading," it is understood that for *yāti*, the meaning is "attainment" (*prāpti*) or "causing to reach" (*prāpaṇa*), whereas for *nayati*, the meaning is understood as "the act of arranging" (*saṃvidhāna*) or "leading" (*prāpaṇā*).

In this way, it should be understood that the inherent purpose of other [suffixes] is also for the sake of providing a specific application (*saṃvidhāna*). To indicate that very purpose, an indicatory letter (*anubandha*) such as *ñ* is inserted for the sake of recollection (*smaraṇa*). For one who is unable to ascertain the specific nature [of a suffix] from its usage alone, the attachment of an indicatory letter serves the purpose of recollection; however, for one who knows the usage, it serves no purpose. Thus, it has been rejected in the Bhāṣya that the mention of *svarita* and *ñit* need not be made for one who observes the usage.

However, this [rule] is indeed applied with respect to one who follows the explicit statement (*vacanānusārin*). Thus says the Bhāṣya: "For the teacher, knowing the *vṛtta*, attaches suffixes that are capable of it. In this context, *vṛtta* refers to that in which operations (*kārya*) occur; it means usage (*prayoga*), occurrence (*vartana*), or the operation of words (*śabdavyāpāra*). The meaning is that the author of the Sūtras, knowing that [the *vṛtta*], attaches the letter *ñ* for one who follows the explicit statement but does not know the *vṛtta*. || 12 ||

Regarding the point that even when the referents are identical, there is not a single uniform nature [of the roots], he provides an illustration: "Even though the referents of *dṛśi* (to see) and *īkṣya* (to look at) are similar, there is no identity between them when preceded by *pra*; therefore, those roots which include the sense of the causative (*ṇyartha*) do not have the same meaning as *pac* and other such roots. (13)

Even when the roots *iṣ* (in the form *īkṣ*) and *paś* are recited together in the *gaṇa*-lists as being identical, there is no identity nor synonymy between these two roots when preceded by the prefix *prati*; rather, the meaning of *pratīkṣate* is entirely different, namely "to wait for" (*pratipālana*). However, the meaning of *pratipaśyati* is "to look back" (*pratīpadarśana*). Furthermore, the mention of *dṛś* and *īkṣ* is illustrative; it includes *rakṣ* and *pāl* as well, for the meanings of *pratirakṣati* and *pratipālayati* are likewise distinct. In the same way, examples such as *saṃharati* and *saṃnayati*—from the roots *hṛ* and *nī* when preceded by the prefix *sam*—should also be cited.

Thus, those who accept even the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇyartha*) as being [merely] a relationship do not share the same denotation with roots such as *pac* and others which denote "arrangement" (*saṃvidhāna*). For it is not the case that all verbal roots are identical in their denotation simply because they connect with the meaning of the causative suffix; this is due to the difference in their capacities (*śakti*). Indeed, the meaning of the causative suffix is "commanding" (*praiṣa*), whereas "arrangement" is something other than that, though it has been stated that it is the cause of it. Therefore, it is precisely "arrangement" that is not intended here as the meaning of the causative suffix.

For in this way, there would be no difference in meaning between those [terms] that denote them and [the roots] *pac* and so forth; since *pac* and the others also denote the arrangement [of action], and because it has been stated generally as "by *pac* and the others," it follows that there is no difference in meaning between those ending in *parasmaipada* and those ending in *ātmanepada*. || 13 ||

He states that by this arrangement, it is not the case that those [roots] other than *svarita* and *ṇit* are entirely incapable of expressing the causative meaning; rather, even when they do express it, they lack the specific power to denote that [causative] sense. "For the root *kṛ*, which possesses distinct properties when functioning in its own primary sense, there is a fixed capacity to take on the causative (*ṇi*) meaning; therefore, the powers of words are restricted. (Verse 14)

In the case of *udumbhāñcakāra*, the root *kṛ* is employed after a verbal base whose meaning is not clearly manifest (*anabhivyakta-padārthaka*) for the purpose of making that meaning manifest. Since *kṛ* denotes action in general, it functions here in the sense of the root *umbh*. Consequently, when a specific action occurs, it is observed that—just as in the case of the causative suffix *ṇic*—there is an application (*saṃvidhāna*) of the meaning of *ṇic* toward that which possesses distinct properties and diverse natures; that is, it expresses that [specific action]. And thus this [root] is taught with the suffix *ṇic*. Because this is so, the capacities (*śaktayaḥ*) of words are restricted.

For even with respect to a single object, the root *unbh* lacks the capacity to denote "arrangement" (*saṃvidhāna*), whereas the root *kṛ* possesses it. Thus, there is a connection between *unbh* and arrangement, by virtue of which the root *kṛ*, when employed for that purpose, has the power to denote it.
