Even though that [connection] exists, this [root *unbh*] lacks the capacity to denote it. Furthermore, if in reality there were no connection between *unbh* and arrangement, then the meaning of *kṛ* would likewise not be qualified by arrangement. (14)

How is it determined that the meaning of the root *kṛ* here is qualified by "arrangement" (*saṃvidhāna*)? Anticipating the objection that this is because no middle voice ending (*ātmanepada*), which would convey that meaning, is observed, he states the agreement of the author of the *Bhāṣya* regarding this point as a corroborative authority: "For thus, when the middle voice ending follows the auxiliary verb *kṛ*, the mention of 'as before' (*pūrvavat*)—which would otherwise apply—is superseded by the occurrence of the *svarita* accent. (15)

In this context, the prescription of the *ātmanepada* ending for the auxiliary verb *kṛ* (in the rule *ām-pratyayavat-kṛño 'nuprayogasya*) is rendered meaningful when the result of the action does not benefit the agent (*akartrabhiprāya*). However, when the result benefits the agent (*kartrabhiprāya*), since the *ātmanepada* would already be applicable to the auxiliary *kṛ* by the rule *svaritañitaḥ kartrabhiprāye kriyāphale*, the author of the Bhāṣya maintains that the term *pūrvavat*—which carries the implication of the *svarita* accent—is understood as being carried over from the preceding rule *pūrvavat sanaḥ*.

And likewise, because the mention of "as before" (*pūrvavat*) is for the purpose of restriction—namely, that when the *ātmanepada* affix follows the verbal root preceding the suffix *ām* of the auxiliary verb *kṛ*, it occurs only when the action benefits the agent and not otherwise—there is an absence of *ātmanepada* here [in the case of *cikīrṣitum icchati*]. And how is this justified? Only if the auxiliary verb *kṛ* possesses the capacity to express "arrangement" (*saṃvidhāna*). Otherwise, since the *ātmanepada* would not even be applicable, what would be the use of the mention of "as before"? || 15 ||

Even though they denote meanings appropriate to their respective functions, it is not to be inferred that all verbal roots possess the capacity to convey grammatical arrangement (saṃvidhāna); this he establishes by presenting the following illustration: "Even though the action denoted by a verb is a single entity, it is differentiated by the number residing in the substratum of the means (sādhana); however, the distinction known as gender is not differentiated there, for it does not reside in that [action]. (16)

Since action (*kriyā*) has the nature of what is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), it possesses no inherent distinction. However, in the case of verbal forms ending in *tiṅ*-suffixes, distinctions such as "they two cook" (*pacataḥ*) or "they cook" (*pacanti*), and "they two are cooked" (*pacyete*) or "they are cooked" (*pacyante*), arise from the duality or plurality residing in the substances that serve as the substrates for the factors of accomplishment (*sādhana*)—namely, the agent and the object—as conveyed by a single word. For in these instances, it is accepted that the action is to be accomplished by two or many factors of accomplishment.

Just as there is a connection with the number of the substances that serve as the means (*sādhana*), why should there not also be a connection with the specific gender residing in them? It cannot be said [that this does not occur], because no specific gender is perceived from the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*). When a single word is employed, there is only the comprehension of duality and so forth belonging to the substratum of the means; it is not understood from the verbal suffix that "this action inheres in an object qualified by femininity or masculinity. For the communication of meaning by words is inherent to them, not something arrived at through logical reasoning.

Although it would have been sufficient to say simply "by means of number," the author indicates by the inclusion of the term "substratum" (*āśraya*) that what is denoted by the verb is a substance (*dravya*) itself, engaged in activity and endowed with number, rather than mere power (*śakti*). Thus, in the expression "Devadatta cooks," grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is observed between the verb and the substance. For this very reason, those who maintain the reality of substance (*dravyavādin*) accept that even the meaning of the verb is a substance. (16)

Therefore, this illustrative example is applied to the point to be proven: "Consequently, even when an object exists, the power of a word is restricted to something; that [restriction], however, is described in the treatise as a rule (vidhi). (17)

Since the designation [of the action] depends on the specific power of the word in this way even elsewhere, it has been stated that although there is a connection through arrangement (*saṃvidhāna*), the capacity of certain verbal roots such as *yāti* (to go) to convey that [arrangement] is obstructed. Thus, while the root *karoti* has the same meaning as *unneti* and so forth, it possesses the capacity to denote arrangement, whereas *unneti* does not. This method, which serves to restrict the power of words, is made known and revealed in the grammatical treatise by the mention of the term "svarita" and "ṇit. This point is now concluded. || 17 ||

Having cited here as examples of cases where the fruit of the action is not intended for the agent—namely, "the priests sacrifice" and "the cooks cook"—and having raised the objection that the priests intend the fee (*dakṣiṇā*) as their fruit and the laborers intend wages (*bhṛti*), [the author] replies: "In every case, the fruit of the action is intended for the agent; however, the degree of excellence is understood there, insofar as [the agent] intends the fruit of the action more effectively."

Furthermore, he explains what is established in the *Bhāṣya*: "Moreover, that for whose sake an action is undertaken is more significant. [The verse says: "That purpose for the accomplishment of which actions such as cooking (*pac*) and others are undertaken is their primary fruit; acquisition and the like are not the motive. (18)

In this context, since the fruit of an action performed with reference to the agent (*kartṛbhiprāya*) serves as the indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), it is stated that the *ātmanepada* suffix occurs after a verbal root (*dhātu*) that expresses the act of preparation (*saṃvidhāna*). And in such preparation, it is logical that only that which is the fruit itself should serve as the indicator.

Furthermore, that for the sake of which the undertaking of an arrangement is made—that toward which the arranger first initiates the arrangement, the acquisition of means, and the commencement of activity according to suitability—must be understood as the primary fruit, such as heaven and so forth. Since the causal factors (*kārakas*) employed by the arranger proceed by his will, their reward or wages are secondary fruits; for it is impossible for activity to have commenced previously for the sake of those [secondary fruits].

Furthermore, the agent (saṃvidhātṛ), although remaining indifferent for the sake of the primary action, exerts himself in many ways; thus, through the intention toward the principal fruit, he alone sets in motion actions such as cooking and the like. Therefore, this excellence of the fruit has already been explained by its being for the sake of that [primary action], even prior to the commencement of the primary action. || 18 ||

Regarding the rule *saṃvidhāne ātmanepadam* (Pāṇini 1.3.32), it is raised as an objection in the final position (*siddhānta*) in the Bhāṣya: "In this case, how should it be? [For example: *svāmidāsau pacataḥ* ('the master and the servant cook')? This he explains: "When both the master and the servant undertake an action together, the verbal root (*dhātu*) does not apply there simultaneously according to their different properties. (Verse 19)

When the master and the servant are expressed together through a copulative compound (*dvandva*), the verbal root cannot attain the status of denoting [the action] simultaneously at one and the same time, because of the difference between the activity undertaken and the operation to be accomplished by it. To explain: the arrangement consisting of the preparation of materials is to be accomplished by the master, whereas the form of the primary action is to be accomplished by the servant; thus, due to this dissimilarity in the nature of the operations, their expression by a single verbal root is not tenable.

And thus, the doubt does not cease as to whether the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) should be employed with reference to the creator, or whether the active voice (*parasmaipada*) should be used with reference to the servant. || 19 ||

Moreover, even if by some means the root, despite its two distinct actions being of different characteristics, were to express them both due to its polysemous nature, nevertheless, where the root *pac* has the sense of "counteracting" (*pratividhāna*), there the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs; elsewhere, when it expresses "preparing" (*saṃskāra*) and so forth, the active voice (*parasmaipada*) occurs. (20)

The *pratividhāna* (counter-action) and *saṃvidhāna* (preparation) are taught as being expressed by the *ātmanepada* ending of the root *pac* because they denote the refinement (*saṃskāra*) characterized by the employment of means culminating in the softening (*viklitti*) inherent in the sentence; however, the *parasmaipada* ending is used for [other] denotations. Thus, even though two distinct meanings are present within the form of a single root, it is impossible for two contradictory verbal suffixes (*ādeśa*) to occur in a single usage. || 20 ||

In this case, the property [of being a servant] is attributed to the slave through the proximity of the agent who ordains it, just as the state of being a *plakṣa* tree is attributed to a *nyagrodha* tree through the proximity of the word "plakṣa. (21)

This is the meaning: if it is accepted that two things of unequal status are denoted by a single word, then, because the formation of a *dvandva* compound is prescribed when there is simultaneous expression of multiple substrates (*yugapadadhikaraṇavacanatā*), both the master and the slave indicated by the *dvandva* are intended together within a single verbal sense (such as "cooking"). In that case, due to the mutual superimposition of their respective attributes, there is "association" (*sāhacarya*); thus, through association with the master, the application [of the term] to the slave occurs, and his activity is superimposed [upon him].

And likewise, because of the statement regarding the arrangement when two masters act as agents—namely, that "a servant is equal to his master"—the *ātmanepada* ending is applied to the verbal root in such cases as "the master and the servant cook" (*svāmidāsau pacete*). Just as in the case of "the *plakṣa* and the *nyagrodha*," where there is a desire to express them together, the form of the *plakṣa* is superimposed upon the *nyagrodha*, since the *nyagrodha* is also a *plakṣa* by virtue of its oozing sap; so too, because a collection whose internal distinctions are subsumed is denoted, the dual number arises from the *dvandva* compound due to mutual dependence.
We shall determine this further in the discussion on *dvandva* compounds [below]. || 21 ||

He explains by means of an example how there can be the superimposition of one form upon something that does not possess that form, merely through proximity: "Just as the designation 'sacrificial cake' (puroḍāśa) applies to parched grains and the like by way of their being situated [therein], and just as the status of being denoted by the word 'umbrella-bearer' (chattrin) belongs [to others] due to their connection with one who holds an umbrella. (22)

At the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), it is stated: "They proceed with the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*). Since it is impossible for a single sacrificial cake to possess the number of plurality, this usage occurs when there exist sacrifices to which the term "sacrificial cake" is metaphorically attributed (*adhyāropita*) because they are associated with it. In that context, five types of sacrificial cakes are mentioned: the *puroḍāśa*, the parched grains (*dhānā*), the flour-mash (*karambha*), the fried grains (*parivāpa*), and the curd-mixture (*payasyā*).

Similarly, in the expression "those with umbrellas are going" (*chatriṇo yānti*), even those who do not possess an umbrella are designated by that word due to their association (*sāhacarya*) with those who do, because the plural number would otherwise be inexplicable. Likewise, in the case of a servant as well, there is an attribution of the master's properties due to association with the master; thus, because the dual-number designation (*dvandva-nirdeśa*) would otherwise be inexplicable, the *ātmanepada* suffix occurs. For here, the difference between the activities accomplished by the master and the servant is not intended to be expressed; rather, there is the occurrence of a property residing in the primary substratum, which consists of the action denoted by the non-different verbal root. || 22 ||

Alternatively, he states another opinion on this matter: "The mutual subservience understood from the sense [of the words] is not intended to be expressed; this is the scope of the *śeṣa* (subsidiary) as described here by some. (23)

The way in which the master and the servant contribute to the action differs: one does so with the intention of obtaining the primary fruit [of the action], while the other does so without such intention. However, disregarding this distinction and intending only the general agency in the action—just as one says "the mother and father produce a son"—the rule *śeṣāt kartari parasmaipadam* ("after the remaining [roots], the *parasmaipada* endings occur when the agent is expressed") applies.

For it is precisely from the proximity of the master's term (*svāmin*) that the arrangement [of the action] is understood, and from the capacity of the meaning of the servant's term (*dāsa*) that the fruit of the action goes to another; thus, since the purpose of the verb (*ākhyāta*) has been fulfilled, it has no further operation here. Because the verbal root (*dhātu*), which expresses the general nature of the action, is not applicable for the prescription of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), the active voice (*parasmaipada*) applies by the rule "the rest" (*śeṣāt*), as in: "The master and the servant cook. || 23 ||

The author of the Bhāṣya has introduced the example "he ploughs with five ploughs" (*pañcabhir halaiḥ kṛṣati*) in order to demonstrate the possibility of the application of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) for the master who acts as the one being assisted. Regarding this, an objection is raised: "Now, as for the assistant who ploughs with the five ploughs—why was he not cited in the Bhāṣya? For in that case, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) would be required. (24)

The pulling with five ploughs simultaneously belongs to the owner, not to the cultivator; thus, why has the commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*), despite the rule that the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs after the root *prati-vi-dhā* when it signifies "counteracting" (*pratividhāna*), failed to apply the grammatical characteristic [of the middle voice] as required? || 24 ||

Anticipating an objection here, he refutes it: "If its status as a subordinate element (śeṣatva) were to be assumed because its meaning is already well-known, then that [rule] which allows for an option when [the condition] has already been reached would not exist, as it would be superseded by the svarita accent. (25)

Since it is impossible for a servant to plow with five plows simultaneously, the master himself must do so; and since this meaning is already established, the provision [of the rule] is of no use for the prescription of the ātmanepada. If, therefore, the status of being a "remainder" (śeṣatva)—which is the cause for the parasmaipada—is posited here, then a contradiction with other passages results.

For instance, in the rule *na veti vibhāṣā*, the option (*vibhāṣā*) is counted as an "option based on what is obtained" (*prāptavibhāṣā*). This is because, in cases where the fruit of the action accrues to the agent (*kartrabhiprāya*), the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is obligatory for roots marked with the svarita accent by the rule *svaritetaḥ kartrabhiprāye kriyāphale*; the present rule serves to allow its non-occurrence in one alternative. Now, if the middle voice were not to occur when the meaning is indicated by an accompanying word (*upapada*), then it would not occur even in examples such as *svaṃ yajñaṃ yajati* ("he performs his own sacrifice"), since [in that case] the condition for the middle voice would not be met; therefore, the rule *vibhāṣopapadena...* [is necessary].

Thus, there would be a contradiction even with respect to the operation [of the rule] by way of a positive injunction (*vidhimukhena*) because it is an *aprāpta-vibhāṣā* (an option regarding what has not been established). Therefore, since it is understood from the statement of the *prāpta-vibhāṣā* that the application [of the suffix] is indicated by both—the upapada and the ātmanepada—itself, how could the ātmanepada not occur here? || 25 ||

On this point, some say: "If agriculture were intended here merely as a preparatory act (saṃvidhāna), then it would be accepted by some that the sacrifice possesses its properties; consequently, the middle-voice ending (ātmanepada) would not occur there. (26)

Those who maintain that the causative suffix (*ṇic*) and the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) share the same domain hold this view: since the root *kṛṣ* functions in the sense of mere preparation (*saṃvidhāna*), the middle voice does not occur as it would with the causative suffix. For it has been stated in order to exclude the causative suffix: "There is no application [of the suffix] to *kṛṣ* and others, because various actions constitute the meaning of 'plowing' (*kṛṣi*). Plowing does not necessarily occur only in the sense of scraping or furrowing; rather, it also occurs in the sense of preparation (*pratividhāna*).

Thus, when the meaning of "arranging" (*saṃvidhāna*) is pure and uninterrupted by "plowing," agriculture (*kṛṣi*) is said to be occurring; since the operation of the prompted agent (*prayojya-vyāpāra*), which is "plowing," is impossible [in that context], the suffix *ṇic* does not arise, and likewise the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) does not occur either, because there is no other verbal root-meaning (*dhātvartha*) qualified by "arranging. For the middle voice occurs from a verbal root that expresses an object qualified by "arranging," but not from one that merely denotes "arranging" in its pure form.

And although in this case the verbal root-meaning (*dhātvartha*) is merely "scratching" (*vilekhana*), nevertheless, due to the inherent nature of the word's expressive power (*śabdaśaktisvābhāvyāt*), the word *kṛṣi* denotes a specific counteraction directed toward that [scratching]. For example: when the elision (*luk*) [of the suffix] was rejected on the grounds that "the statement regarding elision is purposeless because it is a different base form," even though it is a conventional term (*rūḍhiśabda*), due to the inherent nature of the word's expressive power, a specific fruit produced by a particular species of tree—such as the *āmalaka*—is denoted. This [conventional usage] he now precludes.

For if it were stated in this way here, then since the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) would also have that [preparation] as its property just as *kṛṣ* (to plow) does, it would be "possessing that property" (*taddharmā*), namely, possessing the property of plowing; consequently, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) would not occur even in that case. For just as the act of plowing occurs in the sense of preparation, so too the act of sacrificing would occur [in that sense]. And thus, the function of the root *yaj* in the sense of preparation has been stated in the Bhāṣya. For this objection is raised there: "In this context, it is desired that 'the priests cause the sacrifice to be performed' (*yājakā yājayanti*)."

"If *yaj* were used solely to denote the act of throwing the oblation (*havis-prakṣepa*), then since the officiating priests throw the oblation, the statement that 'the sacrificer, employing them, causes them to sacrifice' (*yājayati*) would be a contradictory expression. To this, the following solution is stated: "There is no contradiction in the case of *yaj* and other such terms, because various actions constitute the meaning of *yaj*. It is not necessarily the case that *yaj* refers only to the throwing of the oblation; rather, it also refers to renunciation (*tyāga*). The sacrificer performs that [renunciation], while the officiating priests cause it to be performed."

And thus, if the meaning of *yaji* (to sacrifice) were merely the relinquishment of a substance (*dravyatyāga*), then the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) would not occur there either, as it does not in the case of *kṛṣ* (to plow). Now, if it is argued that the meaning of *yaji* is the performance (*pratividhāna*) qualified by relinquishment, then the middle voice occurs; likewise, since the meaning of *kṛṣ* is also the performance qualified by scratching (*vilekhana*), the occurrence of the middle voice would follow as a necessary consequence. However, the causative suffix (*ṇic*) does not apply because the instigation (*praiṣa*) is not understood [in this context]. For it has already been determined previously that the performance itself is not the meaning of the causative suffix. || 26 ||

How then is it that the ātmanepada does not occur? He states the established conclusion: "In this case, however, this distinction of meaning is understood through the accompanying word (upapada). Since an option (vibhāṣā) is applied to what is already established, therefore there is no ātmanepada. (27)

By the word "with five ploughs" (pañcabhir halaiḥ) being heard in proximity, this specific meaning characterized by a particular arrangement is understood; therefore, since the optionality (*vibhāṣā*) is prescribed here for the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) which would otherwise have been mandatory by the rule "vibhāṣopapadena pratīyamāne," it does not occur in one alternative case. Thus, the correct usage *kṛṣati* as established in the Bhāṣya is proven as desired. || 27 ||

Thus ends the twelfth section, the *Upagraha-samuddeśa*, in the *Prakīrṇaka-prakāśa* composed by Helārāja, son of Bhūtirāja. Having examined the meanings pertaining to uncompounded words (*asamasta-pada*), the investigation of words according to the five types of grammatical derivation (*vṛtti*) is now introduced in order to examine those pertaining to compounded words (*samasta-pada*). Among these, first is the investigation of the compound and secondary derivative (*taddhita*) derivations based on coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). To illustrate: in the sense of "contemptible" (*kutsita*) and so forth, the application of gender and number [to the suffix] would otherwise be untenable.

If it is argued that [the suffix is applied] after a word standing in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with "contemptible" (*kutsita*) and so forth, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), as in the case of the feminine suffixes *ṭāp* and others. Having thus demonstrated the defects in both the view that the meaning of the suffix is primary and the view of grammatical apposition, the position that the base-meaning (*prakṛtyartha*) is the qualifier was established by the statement: "But it is established because the suffix is prescribed in its own sense (*svārthe*) after a word joined with that which expresses contempt and so forth."

The meaning of the Vārttika is as follows: from a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that denotes an object associated with a quality (*dharma*) such as contempt (*kutsā*) by which that contempt and so forth are conveyed, the suffixes *kan* and others should be prescribed in their own sense (*svārthe*) to indicate that very contempt, since that contempt has already been expressed [by the base]. In this way, the meaning of the primary element (*prakṛti*) is qualified, and the meaning of the suffix is not merely the property of contempt and so forth; thus, the occurrence of gender and number is logically justified.

And because of the word *ca* ("and"), the suffix occurs only after [a nominal stem] that already possesses expressed contempt (*kutsā*) and so forth; therefore, there is an absence of that suffix after [stems] such as *idam*, which stand in grammatical apposition with it but do not themselves possess expressed contempt and so on. This being the case, it was stated by what property contempt and so forth are characterized: "Having denoted its own meaning, the word [becomes] independent... and so on. The view that the base-meaning is the qualifier (*prakṛtyarthaviśeṣaṇapakṣa*) is as follows: suffixes such as *kan* are applied to a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that denotes its own meaning and the other four [categories], in order to express the contempt and so forth directed toward those very bases—namely, the contempt caused by the basis's own meaning and so forth.

Furthermore, the statement "this [suffix] recurs when [words] such as *kutsana* (contempt) follow [a word ending in] *priya*" does not intend to prescribe a suffix after a *subanta* (a word ending in a case-suffix); rather, because contempt and so forth serve as the cause for the fivefold meanings (*pañcakārtha*), when the suffix merely indicates contempt and so on—as in *devadattakaḥ*—the specific cause thereof, such as gender and so forth, is determined from context or other means.

And since that [suffix] is expressed by a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), it is said that the word ending in a case-suffix functions in order to convey a specific meaning such as contempt (*kutsā*) and so forth. This is explained as follows: "But a word whose meaning is already complete is joined with contempt, praise, or intensity; for all [factors] beginning with its own primary meaning (*svārtha*) are causes of contempt and the rest. (Verse 1)

A word whose denotable meaning is complete with respect to an object characterized by its own referent, substance, gender, number, object [of action], and so forth, is understood as being joined with a specific sense such as contempt, which has its own referent and other factors as its cause. Since the own referent and the rest have been explained elsewhere, they are not elaborated upon here. Therefore, because contempt and the like are caused by the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the suffix is introduced from that very nominal stem which denotes the meaning qualified by those [factors].

It is stated that when a suffix follows a case-ending, there is the manifestation of a specific quality due to causes such as contempt (*kutsā*), and thus it is said to be connected with that [base] for the sake of completing the meaning. In this regard, an example of contempt based on the object's own meaning (*svārtha*) is: *paṭukaḥ*, *paṇḍitakaḥ*, *mṛdukaḥ*. The object is deprecated because its proficiency and so forth are incomplete or defective. Similarly, examples for praise and excellence based on the object's own meaning should be cited, such as *paṭurūpaḥ* (one who is quite proficient) and *paṭutaraḥ* (one who is more proficient).

Since the substance (*dravya*) is primary as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), the contempt or other [emotions] caused by it must be understood solely through the medium of another attribute (*dharmāntara*). An example of contempt based on gender (*liṅga*) is as follows: to demonstrate a man’s lack of virility, there is contempt expressed by superimposing femininity upon him, as in "this man is a woman" (*strī*); or, to proclaim his shamelessness, there is contempt expressed by superimposing masculinity upon a woman, as in "this woman is a man" (*puruṣa*). Since contempt is already understood from the very use of the word for the sake of another [meaning], this is not the domain of the suffix *ka*.

Thus, because it is difficult to sustain when concentrated in one place, there arises a contempt based on the attribution of multiplicity—such as "this very [thing] is my thousand"—due to the cause of number. In this case, as before, there is no suffix (*pratyaya*). In the same way, this should be demonstrated as appropriate for cases of praise and so forth as well. || 1 ||

In this regard, one might ask: why do [the suffixes] *kutsitakaḥ* and *anukampitakaḥ* not apply? [The answer is: because the meaning is already expressed by its own word (*svaśabda*). To state the objection raised in the Bhāṣya and to provide its resolution, he says: "The word *kutsita* (‘despised’) applies to the contempt directed at Devadatta and others. But what [suffix] is prescribed for the purpose of that contempt which resides in the despised person himself? (Verse 2)

The word *kutsita* (contemptible) applies to Devadatta by relying on contempt (*kutsā*) as its basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*). Since it denotes a substance (*dravya*) characterized by a connection with contempt and qualified by gender, number, object, and so forth, it does not rest upon its own primary meaning alone. Because it has an intentionality (*tātparya*) toward other factors such as gender, and because it lacks the capacity to convey external contempt itself, the suffix arises in that [context].

For the contempt expressed by Devadatta and others is denoted by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) as its own meaning (*svārtha*); however, that which is distinct from it—external, and caused by [the speaker's] own meaning and so forth—is denoted by the suffix (*pratyaya*). Just as, for example, the suffix *ka* following the word "Devadatta"—which denotes a meaning common to both "beloved" and "contemptible"—manifests a connection with contempt, so too the suffix *ka* following the word "kutsita" (contemptible)—which denotes contempt as the cause for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*) toward another object—manifests an external contempt residing within its own meaning.
This is the sense. || 2 ||

In this way, even when excellence (*atiśāyana*) is already expressed by its own word, the objection that the suffix [of excellence] would not apply arises; since the logic is the same, it is raised. To provide a solution for the matter at hand, he replies: "The word *prakṛṣṭa* expresses the excellence of 'white' and so forth; however, the suffixes *tarap* and so on are prescribed for the excellence of that which is already excellent. (Verse 3)

That which is white to a superior degree is "whiter" (*śuklatara*); it is called "excellent white" (*prakṛṣṭa-śukla*). For, in relation to that which is unsurpassed (*niratiśaya*), the surpassable white is expressed either by the word *śukla* with the suffix *-tara*, or simply by the word *prakṛṣṭa*. Thus, since the word *prakṛṣṭa* denotes the excellence inherent in "white" and so forth, the suffix *-tara* is not applied to that very same [excellence].

However, as for that further excellence (*prakarṣa*) which belongs to what is already excellent, since it has not been expressed, the suffix *tarap* is employed to express it, as in *prakṛṣyataraḥ*. Just as in *jyeṣṭhatamāya*, there is another suffix denoting excellence (*atiśāyana*). Because of the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), one should cite other suffixes based on the attribute of praise (*praśaṃsā*), such as *praśastarūpaḥ*. Likewise, in *kutsitakaḥ*, the suffix *ka* occurs when there is a further degree of contempt (*kutsā*) regarding what is already contemptible. 3.

But what is the point of a further denigration of that which is already denigrated? To this he says: "Whether it is contemptible by virtue of being contemptible, or not even properly contemptible—when the meaning is already expressed by its own word, by what could it be qualified? (4)

When a meaning is expressed by a general term such as "kutsita" (despised) using its own word, the specific nature of that meaning is not determined: is his state of being despised due solely to his being unworthy of censure because he fails to perform his duty, or is he censured because, even while performing his duty, he is falsely attributed with wickedness by an enemy? However, once the suffix has been produced, the specific nature is determined.

For instance: from the word *kutsita* (despised), it is understood through the suffix that "its state of being despised is itself despised; this is not a proper state of being despised, but rather one superimposed by an enemy through hatred. For that [suffix] is applied precisely to something already despised in order to express its contemptibility; or else, it is a specific kind of contempt because even contempt itself is more blameworthy.

Thus, there is a distinction: contempt based on unspecified particularities of a property (*dharma*) is the occasioning cause for the application of the word "contemptible" (*kutsita*), whereas that based on specific instances such as the killing of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*) is the cause for the suffix *kap*. In this way, the [use of the suffix] has been established by relying on a second contempt inherent in the object of contempt. (4)

Alternatively, there is no secondary contempt here at all. Rather, the suffix occurs only in that case where contempt has already been expressed by the prefix *pra-*; thus he says: "And contemporary contempt is not perceived because of the absence of distinction [between the two]; for what is honored is censured as being contemptible, and what is contemptible is praised as being excellent. (Verse 5)

Because a substance characterized by "kutsā" (contempt) is denoted by the word *kutsita*—which is common to both the expression of affection and contempt—the connection with a present contempt is not determined from this [word]. For instance, that substance characterized by contempt may at some time be honored or praised as being "of a contemptible form," such as "one who has the form of a vṛṣala" or "one who has the form of a dasyu. Similarly, a substance characterized by praise may be censured as "praśastaka" (the praised one), meaning either that its praise is incomplete or that its praise is merely superimposed.

For in some cases, praise is not completed because it is interrupted by a partial [defect]; in others, praise does not exist at all because it has been superimposed by an enemy; and in yet others, even that which has been praised by an enemy is superimposed with the quality of being unpraiseworthy. Thus, since the possibility of deviation from censure exists, the suffix *kap* is appropriate for indicating, from a word denoting something censurable, a connection with present censure that has not yet been perceived.

In this way, by this very same principle, the suffix *ka* in the word *anukampitaka* should be justified as expressing compassion; thus, a brief consideration has been made regarding the formation of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). || 5 ||

Just as a word is connected with another to complete its meaning by means of [suffixes] such as *kutsā* (contempt), so too is it connected through the relation of the delimited (*avacchedya*) and the delimiting (*avacchedaka*). Thus, in order to examine the grammatical operation (*sub-vṛtti*) of coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*), he says: "The state of being the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*) arises between two words; and in that very case, the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) is thus distinguished. (Verse 6)

In this context, in the expression "the brave man" (*vīraḥ puruṣaḥ*), words such as "brave" (*vīra*) denote their own respective meanings alone, without requiring a mutual relationship with other words. Thus, even when another word is in proximity, the denotation of that [word] is determined to be only that much. Since a relationship of subordinate and principal (*guṇapradhānabhāva*) necessarily exists therein, the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*)—namely, the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*)—arises as something additional between the two words once they are combined, not between the meanings of the nominal stems (*prātipadika*) themselves.

Just as in the case of *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* ("the king's man"), where the referent of the nominal stem *rājan* alone functions as the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) regarding the domain of words with different grammatical bases (*vyadhikaraṇa*), the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is applied to that [qualifier] and not to the qualified (*viśeṣya*), because the latter is self-contained (*svaniṣṭha*) by virtue of being the beneficiary (*upakārya*). And thus it is stated in the rule *ṣaṣṭhī śeṣe*: "The nature of the meaning is such that..."—meaning that the form characterized as the qualified is non-distinct from its own referent and is self-contained.

And when, in the case of coreferential (*samānādhikaraṇa*) relations, the status of being a sentence-meaning (*vākyārthatā*) belongs to the relation between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) by virtue of following upon the word-meanings, then the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) therein is not set apart nor transformed into another form; thus, the nominative case (*prathamā*) need not be added as a supplement. And so it has been said: "Or rather, it is not so, because it is like the sentence-meaning; whatever surplus there is here, that is the sentence-meaning."

Regarding the case of different substrata (*vyadhikaraṇa*), however, having concluded that the qualifier undergoes a change of form and failing to perceive the distinction [between them], it was objected: "When the first case ending is prescribed for the mere meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*), an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made for cases where there is coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between words, because [the meaning] is additional. Furthermore, the lack of restriction regarding the relationship of delimiting and delimited (*avacchedyāvacchedakabhāva*) was raised: "Since both the qualifier and the qualified possess the nature of being qualifiers and the nature of being the qualified, there is no established status of being a subordinate element (*upasarjana*)."

Since that which is intended as the qualificand (viśeṣya) also restricts that which is intended as the qualifier (viśeṣaṇa) within its own self, the latter also functions as a qualifier with respect to the former; thus, both would possess the status of a qualifier. Consequently, according to the rule for compound formation (*samāsa*), because both are designated by the nominative case, they would both receive the technical designation of *upasarjana* (subordinate member), and their placement at the beginning of the compound would occur alternatively. Regarding this, the solution has been stated: "Or rather, there is no [such ambiguity], because one of the two is the primary element (*pradhāna*), and the other is established as a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) due to its being a qualifier of that primary. (6)

In this regard, he explains what determines the relationship of subordinate and principal (*guṇapradhānabhāva*) by necessity: "The qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is that which is not yet known, while the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is that whose meaning is already known. Subordination (*śeṣatva*) consists in being for the sake of another; this applies to all things that provide assistance. (7)

In this context, the definition of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*) has been made known by their very names according to their literal meaning: that which is to be distinguished is the qualified, and that which distinguishes is the qualifier. This [definition], however, is for the purpose of making known the status of subordinate and primary. To this it is replied: the relationship of subordinate and primary is established because a connection would otherwise be impossible, since a connection between two equals is untenable; so how could there be any confusion? [The distinction] is established through what is well-known and what is not.

To explain: when a qualificand (*viśeṣya*) has been introduced as being connected to an action by way of its universal nature (*sāmānyātmanā*), even though it is known, it remains undetermined because of its own inherent qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*). Therefore, for the sake of determining that [qualificand], a quality (*guṇa*) or other factor—which is already determined—functions as the qualifier precisely because it acts as a signifier (*jñāpaka*). Consequently, that which is to be made known (*jñāpya*) is the primary qualificand; whereas that which makes known (*jñāpaka*), being employed for the benefit of another, is subordinate (*śeṣabhūta*), non-primary, and thus the qualifier. Furthermore, since substance (*dravya*) is directly connected to the action, it alone is the primary element in that context.

A quality (*guṇa*), however, while experiencing a connection with the action through that [substance], serves as a delimiting factor for the substance and is thus subordinate. In all cases, it is a substance endowed with qualities that is enjoined as being connected to the action. Alternatively, the connection of qualities with the action is mediated by their substrate (the substance). It is not the case that, having referred back to the substance, the quality is enjoined separately in relation to the action; such is the established relationship between the subordinate and the principal.

Therefore, in cases such as "he spreads a black antelope skin beneath the mortar," "he initiates [the sacrificer] with a black antelope skin," and "he scratches himself with a black antelope horn," since in every instance a substance qualified by a quality is being enjoined, that substance alone possesses primacy and thus functions as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), while the black quality functions as the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). Thus, for the sake of establishing the status of the subordinate element, a rule regarding the primacy and subordination of the two is established. And this [rule] applies in both coordinate compounds (*sāmānādhikaraṇa-samāsa*) and genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*).

For instance: "The distinction of case-endings necessarily belongs to words denoting a quality and its possessor; the well-known grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) pertains to two words denoting substances. (8)

In the expression "the cloth is white" (*paṭasya śuklaḥ*), where words denoting a substance and a quality are employed, there is a verbal relationship of subordinate and predominant. For in this case, the subordinate term denotes its own meaning as it has been transformed into a state that assists the predominant; thus, it takes the genitive case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*), which is the case-ending of a subordinate element. The predominant term, however, remains established in its own nature and does not assist another; thus, it is joined with the nominative case-ending (*prathamā*). Therefore, a fixed distinction of case-endings exists in the domain of grammatical disagreement (*vyadhikaraṇa*).

In cases such as "the brave man" (*vīraḥ puruṣaḥ*), however, where there is co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), both words denoting substances express their own meanings as residing in themselves. Consequently, only the nominative case applies there. Nevertheless, the relationship of subordinate and predominant (*guṇapradhānabhāva*) based on semantic capacity has been explained by the rule beginning with "the qualificand is that which is not yet known" (*viśeṣyaṃ syādanirjñātam*). Thus, even though this relationship of subordinate and predominant exists, there is a distinction between co-referentiality and non-co-referentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) caused by whether a word denotes a substance or a quality; this constitutes the difference between a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) and a co-referential compound (*sāmānādhikaraṇasamāsa*). || 8 ||

If, then, in a case of grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*), both words denoting substances (*dravya-śabda*) express their primary meanings without mutual assistance, and [the relation] consists of the qualifier-qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*) relationship, then how is there a mutual connection between these two? To this he says: "When the substance is not yet known as belonging to a particular class (*jāti*), the word 'black' (*kṛṣṇa*) is employed; and when the quality (*guṇa*) is not yet known, the word 'sesame' (*tila*) is applied. (9)

The word *kṛṣṇa* (black) applies to a substance either through metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) or by the force of the possessive suffix *matup*. Since it is based on a quality, there is no certainty therein regarding its belonging to a specific genus; however, due to invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), the genus alone is indeed determined. Similarly, the word *tila* (sesamum) also applies to a substance whose connection with a specific quality is not ascertained, being based on a genus. Thus, both words stand in need of a further specification. 9.

Even so, he explains how there can be a mutual relationship: "Because universals have no connection, those two [particulars] are established as distinct; due to the non-difference of their form, they are unable to manifest that particularity. (10)

In this context, the substances denoted by the terms "black" (*kṛṣṇa*) and "sesamum" (*tila*), which possess indeterminate and non-fixed genera and qualities, are intended as universals (*sāmānya*). Since these, when established in their own natures, lack mutual assistance, no relation between them would otherwise exist; therefore, by virtue of the requirement for a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) and because a relation other than that [of qualifier and qualified] is untenable, the two words "black" and "sesamum" are established here from the very beginning as referring to particulars (*viśeṣa*). For here, by the word "black," it is precisely a member of the genus sesamum that is intended to be expressed, and by the word "sesamum," a substance possessing the quality of blackness.

And that specific distinction cannot be determined by the cognizers prior to their mutual association; for the word *kṛṣṇa* (black) applies even to things of a different class, and the word *tila* (sesame) applies even to things possessing other qualities. Thus, with respect to the cognizer, it is said that such [words] are the cause for manifesting a qualified object. However, from the perspective of the speaker’s intention (*tad-abhiprāya*), the very object intended as qualified is the "relation" (*sambandha*). || 10 ||

He says that this very [meaning] is manifested by virtue of the unity of the sentence: "When those two are thus brought together in their presentation as distinct, they remove doubt by creating, as it were, a delimitation. (11)

Thus, because there is no difference in their form, the words "black" (*kṛṣṇa*) and "sesame" (*tila*), being unable to convey the intended specific [quality] to the cognizer, function by removing the doubt residing in the cognizer regarding whether the substance is a sesame or a non-sesame, or black or non-black; having established the exclusion from other classes in the word "black" and the exclusion from other qualities in the word "sesame," they bring about the cognition of the substance as characterized by those specificities.

For the word *kṛṣṇa* (black) denotes an object belonging to the class of sesame seeds (*tilajātīya*) alone when in proximity to the word *tila*; thus, there is an exclusion of that [word] from what does not belong to that class. Likewise, the word *tila* denotes only the quality of blackness; thus, there is a delimitation (*avaccheda*) of this [quality] from other qualities. And since that [delimitation] has already been accepted here, the particle *iva* is used. For the cognizer, when a relationship exists, arrives at precisely such a delimitation. As it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "The word *kṛṣṇa*, being connected with the word *tila*, becomes a term denoting a specific [object]."

"In the same way, the word 'sesame' (tila), when connected with the word 'black' (kṛṣṇa), becomes specific in its denotation. This means that at that time, there is the manifestation of its specific denotative character. || 11 ||

Thus, the relation has been established. And here, that [relation] is of the nature of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Coreferentiality is the occurrence of two words—employed on account of different grounds—in a single referent. If it is defined as having a common denotation, then the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) between those two [words] would not be possible by way of the object, because that [relation] depends upon difference; for that [qualifier-qualified relation] is absent when there is identity of the object.

Now, if grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) consists in two meanings having a common substratum (*samānāśrayatva*), then how can it be established here, given that there is no distinct substratum for a quality and a substance? However, the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) could exist between a substance and a quality. But if one relies on the single substratum of a quality and a substance-class (*dravyajāti*), then the relation of qualifier and qualified would not be possible.

Anticipating the objection that "since the two [the substance and its qualities] function by delimiting one another's substances, they cannot be related to each other," he says the following to provide a justification: "The nature of a substance is apprehended as distinct through the differentiation caused by its association with qualities; and through the differentiation caused by its connection with universals (jāti), it is perceived as if it were a second [entity]. (12)

In this context, the substantial self (*dravyātmā*), which is a partless entity appearing as various distinct forms due to its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and thus fit for conventional usage, is perceived as if it were something else—distinctly qualified by the inherence (*samavāya*) of the quality blackness—when designated by the term "black sesame. Because words are restricted to denoting the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of each individual [from others], that which is denoted by them is necessarily perceived as having a fragmented, partial form. Consequently, by the word "sesame," a second substance, characterized by the universal (*jāti*) and the inherence, is communicated as if it were a separate entity.

Because it conveys a single entity as delimited by both genus and quality, the word is called *viśeṣa* (the particularizer), since it produces a cognition that appears as if distinct with respect to the individual functions of each word. || 12 ||

To support this very point, he says: "Due to its connection with limiting adjuncts (nimitta), that which possesses a form similar to those adjuncts—by means of that, even a single [entity] is conceived as manifold, despite the non-difference of its essential nature. (13)

When a suffix that has the same form as its cause arises with respect to a substance—the object possessing the cause—such as a quality (guṇa) or a genus (jāti), it presents its own suffix as indeed distinct [from the cause]. || 13 ||

And thus, two distinct substances are the substrata due to their coloring by genus (*jāti*) and quality (*guṇa*). However, at the time of their connection, a third substance, which serves as their locus, is mentally distinguished; so he says: "But there is a third state of substance in which the two are conjoined. Due to the distinction between those two states, [the third] is appointed as the substratum for them. (14)

That third substance, which serves as the substratum and the delimited locus where the two bodies—distinguished by their association with the limiting conditions (upādhi) of genus and quality—are joined together and attain integration, is conceived and assigned as the support for those two, being distinct from them both as the delimiting factors. || 14 ||

How can there be a conceptual differentiation of distinctions within a single entity that is substantially one? To this he says: By means of the intellect, the one is differentiated, and the differentiated attains unity. By the intellect, states are divided, for it is the intellect that establishes the object. (15)

In this context, words denoting objects established through cognition (pratyaya) carry out linguistic usage through both difference and non-difference according to that cognition. And cognition, as if externally projecting the forms of objects by conforming to its own causes, manifests them. Thus, prior to the compound, there is the denotation of two distinct substances colored by the difference of their limiting adjuncts (upādhi). But in the compound, however, the difference is concealed; that object being internalized, a single word consisting of a collection of words denotes the object "black sesame" without distinction.
And thus, in the case of "nīlamañjarī, mattamadhukarī," the masculine form (puṃvadbhāva) characterized by grammatical coreferentiality (samānādhikaraṇa) is established. || 15 ||

He states that even the teacher Kātyāyana accepts the conventional usage of difference and non-difference as constructed by the intellect: "In a single entity, there is a conceptualization of multiple objects through the intellect, as if it were something possessing distinct designations; by means of that [intellection], the nature of the object, though its differences are mentally constructed, is designated. (16)

In this regard, the author of the *Vārttika*, by rejecting the statement "the mention of 'like that which possesses a designation' (*vyapadeśivat*)—namely, 'for the sake of the first [rule] concerning single-vowel stems (*ekācaḥ dve')"—on the grounds that "it is established through common worldly understanding even without such a statement," accepts that the meaning of a word is a mental appearance (*buddhipratibhāsin*). For it is thus established that operations such as reduplication (*dvirvacana*), which apply to what is primary, are accomplished even for a single entity by relying on a distinction superimposed by the intellect.

Furthermore, because of the use of the same word, there is no distinction between the secondary (gauṇa) and primary (mukhya) senses; rather, the reverse is stated as a distinction. For in the case of the statement "consciousness is the very nature of the person," although [the two] are non-different, the demonstration of a distinction results in a similarity of cognition, just like [the cognition arising from] the phrase "the king's man. || 16 ||

The example "the body of a stone-son" (*śilāputraka*) is cited as an illustration of how distinction is attributed even where there is no actual difference, by means of the principle of "designation as if distinct" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*). He explains this [verse]: "Of stones and other such things that are perceived through various actions, one perception is designated again and again by another perception. (17)

The cognition of objects such as a "stone statue" (*śilāputraka*), which possess distinctions determined by various actions like being sent and so forth, is delimited by its connection to a single intended action through a cognition that relates to multiple actions. [This is expressed as: "Of this stone statue, which is connected to various actions, this is the specific body connected to this one particular action. (17)

In this way, even regarding roots such as *iṇ* and others that have multiple forms, the status of having a single vowel (*ekāctva*) is established through the conceptualization of difference: "Having conceived the manifold nature of roots due to the difference in usage, the status of having a single vowel is stated in some cases by resorting to both difference and non-difference. (18)

Regarding the term *ekāj* ("having one vowel"), when this is understood as a *bahuvrīhi* compound—meaning "that which has a single vowel"—there arises no possibility of reduplication because, among single-vowel [elements], there is no external referent (*anyapadārtha*) distinct from the meaning of the constituent member (*vartipadārtha*). It has been stated that even in the case of single vowels, the designation is applied as if they were distinct entities (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*). Consequently, by relying on the various forms found in diverse usages such as *eti*, *ayanam*, *itaḥ*, *etā*, *etavyam*, and *āyan*, and by postulating an external referent based on the diversity of those applications while postulating the constituent member based on the non-difference found in fixed applications, the establishment of reduplication in forms such as *iyāya* has been explained. (18)

Alternatively, that which is endowed with meaning through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) is postulated as a single [phoneme]; it is metaphorically designated as a "letter" (varṇa) due to its departure from the meaning of the verbal root (dhātu). || 19 ||

In cases such as "of the root *iṇ*," even though the word-forms differ according to their suffixes, there is a persistence [of a commonality]; therefore, that persisting meaning is what is denoted. In other instances, when that same suffix is used with a different root, that [meaning] is not perceived; thus, while this [suffix] possesses meaning, this form consisting of letters is devoid of meaning. By means of the conceptualization that "this is a single vowel (*aj*"), it is so designated. For the word *dhātu* is a technical term for that which expresses action, and thus it is said to possess meaning; however, the term *aj* denotes a form consisting of specific letters whose connection to a meaning is disregarded.

And thus the designation is logically consistent: that which has only one vowel (*aj*) is called "ekāj. Furthermore, its being "first" is a superimposition, since there is no actual "first" thing to be depended upon because it is unprecedented; this is as established in the statement, "killed by her first pregnancy. || 19 ||

Thus, just as the justification for designation here is based on a distinction constructed by the intellect (*buddhi*), so too is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) based on a conceptual distinction; he concludes the subject at hand: "Therefore, the three substances are established as distinct in the intellect; this is the traditional teaching (*āgama*) from the predecessors regarding the relationship between substratum and superstratum. (20)

Two substances are to be superimposed, colored by genus and quality; however, the third, which serves as their substrate, is distinct due to the difference in cognition qualified by quality and genus. Thus, the distinct apprehension of the self (*ātman*) everywhere denotes an impartite entity. This indicates that even when there is cognition through the distinction of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), the ultimate rest is in the impartite entity, just as grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is established even in a sentence. And thus, the application of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) is justified therein.

And this tradition of the elders (*vṛddha*) is to be respected, not something fabricated by one's own imagination. Thus, regarding the objection raised against the view that the substance (*dravya*) is the word-meaning—namely, "An addition [to the rule] is required for words in apposition because of their lack of syntactic capacity (*asamarthatva*); since, according to the view that the substance is the word-meaning, both the words *dvāra* and *puruṣa* express a single substance, there is an absence of distinct denotata, and consequently, due to the absence of a relation (*saṃsarga*) which is the locus of distinction, there can be no compound"—this [objection] applies even when the substance is the word-meaning.

Based on the distinction of substance (dravya) produced by the difference in qualities such as heroism (vīratva) which are being perceived, [the co-referentiality] is established. For even in the case of a category (jāti) as a word-meaning, one must resort to a common substratum (sāmānādhikaraṇya) based on a single perceived substance, as in the case of "heroism" and "manhood," because otherwise it would be logically untenable. Thus, the co-referentiality of the two meanings is established through the differentiation of their respective substrata. For this very reason, the relationship of qualifier and qualified (viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva) is also proven.
For it is observed that whatever adheres to another through non-difference necessarily colors it with its own nature. || 20 ||

Having thus established the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the two meanings, he speaks in order to establish it for the two words as well: "And grammatical coreferentiality between two words is asserted by some [to consist] either in the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyatva*), or precisely in the relation of name and named (*saṃjñāsaṃjñitva*). (21)

When the two words *kṛṣṇa* (black) and *tila* (sesame), which are applied on the basis of different causes, function with reference to a single substance qualified by a genus and a quality, their state of having a common denotation is called *sāmānādhikaraṇya* (grammatical co-referentiality). Likewise, the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) also belongs to those two alone; for the word *kṛṣṇa* establishes the referent of the word *tila* as qualified by its own meaning. And the word *tila*, being withdrawn from other specific [referents] because it conveys its own particularity, is that which is to be delimited (*avacchedya*). Furthermore, the relation of name and named (*saṃjñāsaṃjñibhāva*) also belongs to those two when they are mutually restricted.

To explain: the word *vṛddhi* situated in its own location, having been made known by the word *vṛddhi* occurring in the rule that establishes the relationship between the name and the named (*saṃjñā-saṃjñi-vākya*), conveys the named object through the imposition of its own form—that is, as qualified by the form of the words *āt*, *aiC*, and *auC*. And because it conveys [the object] through the imposition of its own form, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and the use of a single case-ending for the qualifier and the qualified, namely the name and the named, as described in the rule defining *vṛddhi*.
This has been pointed out here by including it within the illustration. 21.

He states another way in which two meanings may possess grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya): "The application [of this] is held by some to occur when a genus and a quality are both inherent in a single object, as in the case of 'black sesame seeds' (kṛṣṇatileṣu), where the word denotes a substance. (22)

When *kṛṣṇa* (black) and *tila* (sesame) are to be expressed [in a compound], the function (*vṛtti*) known as "integration into a single meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*) is desired. For instance, that function occurs when there is a relationship between qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and qualified (*viśeṣya*). And such a relationship exists here, because the genus (*jāti*) and the quality (*guṇa*) reside in a single substratum (*āśraya*). That very substance which is established in the genus and is understood through the word *tila* as being expectant of further specification (*sākāṅkṣa*), is precisely what is delimited by the word *kṛṣṇa*. Therefore, the quality denoted by it is the qualifier.

For the word *kṛṣṇa* (black) has quality as its cause and denotes a substance (*dravya*); thus, its intended meaning is the quality, since the substance is also implied by the word *tila* (sesame). He states that the word [denotes] a substance within the word [complex] in order to establish grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*): for if the word *kṛṣṇa* denoted only the quality, there would be grammatical non-coreferentiality (*vaiyādhikaraṇya*) in the expression "the black sesame" (*tilasya kṛṣṇaḥ*). And in that case, no compound formation (*vṛtti*) would be possible, because of the prohibition against forming a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) with a word expressing a quality.

Thus, since the word "sesamum" (tila) denotes the genus alone, even in this position, it denotes a substance qualified by that genus. Let there be a difference between the two positions based on the status of the quality as subordinate or primary. Accordingly, in the view where the substance is the primary meaning, because in reality there is no other locus for the substance being denoted as primary, it was previously established by relying on a conceptual distinction. This, however, is stated in the view where the genus is the primary meaning.

Furthermore, genus (*jāti*) and quality (*guṇa*) cannot here be conveyed by the words "sesame" (*tila*) and "black" (*kṛṣṇa*) without a substratum, such that their co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—the state of having a single substratum—would not occur. Nor can these two be primary qualificands (*viśeṣya*) in themselves, because they function to delimit a substance and thus lack mutual connection with one another. Therefore, it is intended here that the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyabhāva*) occurs solely by means of a substance.
Since the word "sesame" denotes a substance residing in a genus, it is logical that the word "black" is a qualifier therein by way of its own ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*). || 22 ||

However, where there is no denotation of a substance (*dravya*) and only the denotation of qualities (*guṇa*), even though a substance is necessarily implied, there is no co-referential compound (*samānādhikaraṇa-samāsa*) because the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*) does not exist. Thus he says: "But since the substratum of color, taste, and so forth is not denoted, they—lacking the denotation of a substance—result in a copulative compound (*dvandva*). (23)

Words such as *rūpa* (form) and *rasa* (taste), by their very nature, express their own referents as forms abstracted from substance (*dravya*). However, since a quality cannot exist without a substratum, the substance is here implied by the force of the context. Thus, because the substance is not made the object [of the expression] through the medium of denotation, and because form and taste have no mutual connection, there is an absence of the relationship between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*); therefore, a coordinate compound (*samānādhikaraṇasamāsa*) does not occur here. Rather, they result in or attain a copulative compound (*dvandva*), or it is said that a copulative compound is what accrues to them.

The terms denoted by a copulative compound (dvandva) are form, taste, and so forth; or rather, those words such as "form" and "taste" themselves participate in the copulative compound. Thus, both grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) and the relationship between qualifier and qualified have been examined. || 23 ||

However, this must be addressed: since both the compounds *kṛṣṇatila* and *śabda* are substance-words (*dravyaśabda*), they apply to a substance by taking as their basis qualities (*guṇa*) and universals (*jāti*). Because the concealment of difference through inherence (*samavāya*) is the same in both cases, and because the connection with action is equally mediated by the substance, there would be no fixed rule regarding which is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and which is the qualified (*viśeṣya*). Thus, when the objection was raised that the status of the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) would not be established, the Bhāṣya resolved it by stating that the substance is the primary element (*pradhāna*).

How is it that only that which is based on genus (*jāti*) possesses primacy as a substance-word (*dravyaśabda*), and not that which is based on a quality (*guṇa*)? To this he says: "A word denoting a substance, such as 'black' (*kṛṣṇa*), proceeds while possessing expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*); because it follows its cause [of application], that [expectancy] does not exist in the case of sesame seeds (*tila*) and the like. (24)

In this context, due to the metaphorical treatment of the non-difference between quality (*guṇa*) and the possessor of quality (*guṇin*), the word "black" (*kṛṣṇa*), being a substance-word (*dravyaśabda*), denotes the substance itself. A quality does not enter into a direct relationship with an action, but rather through the medium of the substance, since it is the substance alone that serves as the locus of capacity (*śakti*). Thus, a quality proceeds toward an action while requiring a substance. Furthermore, because it lacks even a constant connection with the substance, the quality is distinct from it and is itself incapable of entering into a relationship. For instance, a quality is sometimes expressed even when abstracted from the substance.

For appearance and disappearance belong to the quality with respect to the substance; for this very reason, the possessive suffix *matup* and the genitive case occur [in expressions such as *guṇavān* and *guṇasya*]. It has been stated: "If it is argued that [the relationship] is established because there is no distinction [between the two], we reply that distinction is indeed observed. A universal (*jāti*), however, possesses an inseparable connection with the substance from its production until its destruction, because it lacks form.

Therefore, the universal (*jāti*), having acquired its relation at the very moment of the word's production, persists throughout the time of usage without its distinction being perceived; this is the case for words such as *tila* (sesame) which denote the object itself. In that context, there is no occurrence of expectancy toward anything else. For instance, while a quality (*guṇa*), being dependent on a substance (*dravya*), attains its connection with an action through the mediation of that substance, the universal does not function in this way, because a substance devoid of a universal cannot exist. Since the universal is essentially identical to it, the substance possessing the universal (*jātimat*) is directly connected to the action.

Therefore, the substance possessing a genus (jāti) is said to be the qualified (viśeṣya) and the primary, while the quality (guṇa) is the qualifier (viśeṣaṇa); thus, even though two words denoting these two are mutually delimiting one another, there exists a fixed relationship of qualifier and qualified. This is the meaning. || 24 ||

This is what he says: "Thus, when a substance possessing a genus is proximate to an action, the substance, permeated by its qualities and characterized by the properties of those qualities, serves to differentiate [it from others]. (25)

"Thus" means as follows: because it conforms to the aforementioned cause, the word *tila* denotes a substance permeated by a genus (*jāti*), and therefore that [substance] alone has a direct connection with the action. However, the word *kṛṣṇa* denotes a substance permeated by a quality (*guṇa*), not as if it were permeated by a genus; rather, it is said to be "subordinate" (*guṇabhūta*) because its very nature is that of the quality itself, and thus it has an indirect connection with the action. Therefore, the meaning here is that this [word *kṛṣṇa*] is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) because it delimits the qualified (*viśeṣya*).

"One sees a blue lotus," "one tastes a sweet fruit," "one smells a fragrant flower"—in these cases, it is understood that the action is connected to the substance as a whole, which is qualified by its attributes and whose status as an object is indicated by the sense of hearing (the auditory organ). Even in expressions such as "one sees the color of the lotus," the connection with the action belongs to the quality (color) only through the medium of the substance, because of the relation of inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyukta-samavāya*).

However, by means of its audible form—such as color and so forth—it is precisely the substance (*dravya*), which is fit for the application of pronouns like "this" or "that," that is being communicated. Likewise, in cases such as "the color of the cloth arises," even though the audible form is [expressed], it is the substance itself that is connected with the action; thus, there is no deviation from the rule regarding the connection of a quality (*guṇa*) with an action through the mediation of the substance. In this way, it has been established that even though words like "black" denote a substance, they function as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*). || 25 ||

Now, in order to demonstrate that [the word] expresses that even in its absence, he says: "Some maintain that in verbal derivatives (vṛtti), there is the expression of the mere quality (guṇa-mātra), because of the connection with things such as horses and so forth, just as conventional meanings (rūḍhi) are connected with conventional words. (26)

In a sentence, the word *kṛṣṇa* denotes a substance qualified by a quality; however, in a compound (*vṛtti*), since the substance is already denoted by the word *tikta* itself, it is logical that [the word *kaṭuka*] expresses only the quality as a qualifier. Because the substance qualified by the quality is perceived, the quality is established as the differentiator. This is just as, in the expression "the king’s man" (*rājapuruṣaḥ*), the meaning of "king" is understood even in the absence of the genitive case.

It is also observed that even a word denoting a substance (*dravyaśabda*) expresses only a quality (*guṇamātra*) when it occurs in a compound; for example, in the expression "Devadatta is a goat-horse" (*ajāśvo Devadattaḥ*), since the words *aja* (goat) and *aśva* (horse) denote specific substances by way of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), there would be no connection [between them] due to contradiction. Therefore, the word *aja* functions as a designation of a mere attribute characterized by the absence of birth—namely, "one whose horses are unborn"—and thus the formation of the compound is logically established.

Likewise here as well, since there is no connection between two distinct substances, such as black sesame seeds, and since the substance is already denoted by the genus-word itself, there would be no purpose in denoting it again. Therefore, the word *kṛṣṇa* (black), which denotes a quality alone, is restricted to that [quality] within the compound (*vṛtti*) by virtue of its semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*). And this distinction in the compound is produced by the state of having a single referent (*ekārthībhāva*); thus he says, "in compounds" (*vṛttiṣu*).

And thus, even in the absence of a case-ending expressing distinction (*vyatireka-vibhakti*), a quality that is not distinct from its substrate qualifies the substance, just as in the expression "the king’s man" (*rājapuruṣaḥ*), the referent "king"—having attained a state of oneness with the referent "man"—qualifies the man. As for the Mīmāṃsakas, they say that in the compound, the word "king" denotes the referent "man" through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*); but that is incorrect, because when the primary referent "king" itself can appropriately serve as the qualifier through the process of unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), there is no need for secondary indication.

For when the primary sense is possible, that [primary sense] must indeed be accepted. Furthermore, if there were figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), then in the sentence "He waits upon the king’s man" (*rājānaṃ puruṣam upāste*), the word "king" would also indicate the man; moreover, the relationship of master and servant would not necessarily be understood. Since figurative indication can have proximity and other factors as its grounds, and since the purpose of the man is already conveyed by the word "man" itself, there is no need for figurative indication.

And since the literal meaning of the Vedic text—"he draws the black upper garment"—is possible, how can there be figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*)? Nor can it be said that this [compound] is not a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), because the determination of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) on the first member leads to the conclusion that it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. || 26 ||

He states a rule regarding the qualification of words expressing qualities, such as "black" (*kṛṣṇa*), by means of another perspective: "Or, when 'sesame' (*tila*) is mentioned first, the possessive suffix *matup* is intended for that very [word]. And since that quality is subordinate within compounds, it is therefore a qualifier. (27)

When the substratum (*viśeṣya*), delimited by the genus *tila* (sesame), has first been apprehended and determined through its universal nature, the word *kṛṣṇa* (black) functions with respect to that very same entity for the purpose of determining it as possessing a specific quality; thus, it is a word denoting a quality (*guṇavacana*). This occurs through the elision (*lopa*) of the possessive suffix *matup*. For here, [the analysis] "it has blackness" (*kṛṣṇo 'syāsti*) implies that the suffix *matup* is applied to the substance *tila* itself as the related possessor, because it is derived from a word denoting a quality. The elision of this suffix, governed by the rule "there is elision after words denoting qualities" (*guṇavacanebhyo luk*), is obtained through the force of the context and is not explicitly stated.

And that property called "relation" (sambandha), being understood as the meaning of the suffix -mat due to its proximity to the usage of that suffix, is included within the compound. Since that expressed meaning, having been included, becomes the meaning of the nominal stem (prātipadika), it follows that for this reason—namely, on account of the property called "relation" which is the object of the compound—the gender alone is the delimiter, because it provides the essential form (svarūpa) to the substance (dravya) within the relation.

However, a genus (*jāti*) does not delimit a substance previously denoted by a word expressing a quality (*guṇaśabda*), because the genus is more closely related to the quality; it is therefore appropriate that the substance be first defined by its very nature as [possessing] that quality. This point has been explained. || 27 ||

Having thus examined the function of apposition (*samānādhikaraṇavṛtti*), he speaks in order to examine the function of the copulative (*dvandva*) and the remainder (*ekaśeṣa*): "When a single appearance arises as if permeated by two distinct [entities], that is what they call the co-intention (*sahavivakṣā*) in the cases of the copulative and the remainder compounds. (28)

In this context, meanings (arthas) being examined by the intellect for the purpose of establishing action and quality enter into a state of aggregation through the medium of action and quality, in mutual dependence upon one another.
