Intended to be expressed as co-existent, they become denotable by compound words characterized as *dvandva* (copulative) or *ekaśeṣa* (single-remainder). Furthermore, the aggregate here is not something distinct from its constituents; rather, those very constituents are joined together. Thus, in this case, there is a constant cognition permeated by the appearance of the distinction between the constituents.

And because the members [of the compound] appear as distinct, the dual and plural number endings are not contradicted. For it is not the case that, as in other types of compounds, there is only one primary referent delimited by others; rather, here, since all the word-meanings are of equal status, the collection—whose distinction of parts is manifested through the force of a single unified appearance following from the difference of its parts—is what is denoted by the compound term. And since that collection is not separate from its parts, it is designated by the very words for the parts themselves, as in "dhava, khadira, and palāśa."

That which is distinct from the parts is expressed by another word, such as "forest" (*vana*) or "herd" (*yūtha*), and so forth. Furthermore, because a single cognition would otherwise be impossible, this aggregate is expressed by each word individually through mutual dependence. In that case, because the form of difference is concealed by the aggregate being apprehended, there is the appearance of oneness.

Furthermore, even though a *dvandva* compound denotes a single collective entity (*ekasamudāya*), the rule for masculine substitution (*puṃvadbhāva*) characterized by grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—as in the case of *paṭavīmṛdvī*—does not apply. This is because such a rule is based on the coreferentiality found in the corresponding analytical sentence (*vākya*), where deviation is possible; however, in the compound (*vṛtti*), there is no such deviation due to the state of semantic unification (*ekārthībhāva*). In the sentence *paṭvī ca mṛdvī ca*, the predominance lies in the perception of distinction. For this very reason, since it is connected with a conjunction (*samuccaya*) that has difference as its basis, there is an absence of a single denoted referent (*samānābhidheyatva*).

Since there is no difference in the simultaneous desire to express the penetration of distinction [between the two types of compounds], one might ask: what is the distinction between a collective (samāhāra) and a copulative (itaretara) compound? To this he says: "But the copulative (itaretarayoga) belongs to those words that denote a collection of distinct things; and this collection, though belonging to each individual member, is fully realized in the members themselves. (29)

When there is the intention to express [the members] together (*sahavivakṣā*)—in which case there is a single appearance (*ekaprakhyā*) permeated by many [members]—there is duality and the predominance of the parts (*avayavaprādhānya*). Among these, the predominance of the parts is the domain of mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*). For instance, regarding those who denote a collection or aggregate (*saṅgha/samūha*) whose distinctness is manifest, this [collection] is the denotation of the *dvandva* words; for that aggregate culminates in each individual part. Consequently, it is the denotation of each single member as well. Indeed, a whole (*samudāya*) that is fully present in every part is perceived even when only one part is seen.

In this way, even by means of a word denoting only a single member [of a compound], the object is expressed; and just as it is clearly apprehended when many members are perceived, so too there is a clear cognition from a collective whole that expresses a distinct meaning. Thus, even though there is comprehension of each individual member, other words are not rendered useless. However, when the aggregate is predominant, it is implied by the sense that it is a "samāhāra" (collective compound). Although the state of having parts interwoven is common to both, this specific distinction—characterized by the predominance of the members—is what is indicated by the word [the suffix -ka]. And this very point constitutes the domain of *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one), which is an exception to the *dvandva* (copulative) compound. || 29 ||

Regarding the statement that a collection (*samudāya*) whose constituent parts are manifested is said to be fully present in each individual part, he provides a similar illustration: "Just as the operation of a collective [action]—such as placing [the pot on the fire] and so forth—occurs in each individual instance like a genus (*jāti*), so too does it occur in the case of words forming a *dvandva* compound. (30)

Just as a single visible constituent of an action, such as "he cooks" (*pacati*), which is part of a sequential series of actions like placing [the pot on the fire] and so forth, is established as being denoted by a word ending in a suffix expressing the present time—because it occurs through superimposition upon the state (*bhāva*) consisting of those operations (such as placing on the fire) belonging to that specific action, just as [one speaks of] a universal (*jāti*)—so too the aggregate denoted by a *dvandva* compound occurs in each individual member; thus, it results in every single word becoming the expresser of its own meaning.

In the case of dual compounds (*dvandva*), the cognition of each member as being dependent upon the other is completed upon hearing the final member. This very process constitutes the cognition of the aggregate as permeated by its parts. A universal (*jāti*) also, because it is fully realized in each individual instance (*vyakti*), is conveyed even by words such as "cow" which denote a single individual. Upon seeing the first individual, the universal appears clearly; upon perceiving another individual, it becomes even more manifest. In the same way, the cognition of "cooking" (*pacati*) becomes clear through the actions of placing the pot on the fire and so forth, which are mutually dependent. || 30 ||

It might be argued as follows: since they are for that purpose (*tādarthya*), it is correct to designate even the acts of placing [the pot] on the fire and so forth as "cooking" (*pacati*); in that case, there is a denotation by means of a genus-term even when the genus is present. However, in this case, how could words such as *dhava* and *khadira*, which are known in sentences to have distinct meanings, denote a single meaning in a compound? Anticipating this doubt, he explains it by means of an example: "The examples here are *śauṇḍa*, *ardharca*, *puroḍāśa*, and *cchattrin*; and the expression 'those Viṣṇumitras' with respect to various associated individuals. (31)

In the rules "saptamī śauṇḍaiḥ" and "ardharcāḥ puṃsi ca," the plural number is employed based on the distinction between the words *dhūrta* and others listed in the *gaṇa* (group) [of *śauṇḍādi*]. This is justified only if *dhūrta* and the others are also denotable by the term *śauṇḍādi*. And how could they be so? Only if, through association (*sāhacarya*), the state of being *śauṇḍa* and so forth is superimposed upon them. Thus, because the plural form *puroḍāśāḥ* would otherwise be inexplicable, the *karambha*, *parivāpa*, *dhānā*, and *āpayasyā*—though associated with it—are also denoted by that term.

Likewise, in such cases as "the umbrella-bearers are going," "the banner-bearers are going," or "those are the Viṣṇumitras," it is observed that through association (*sāhacarya*), things are designated by those words even when they have had a different form superimposed upon them. In this way, in the case of *dvandva* and *ekaśeṣa* compounds, the fact that each individual word has multiple referents is established because the dual and plural number endings would otherwise be inexplicable; for, through association, they acquire the mutual forms of one another by virtue of being the objects of a single action or quality. || 31 ||

Regarding this, it is said: "The state of denoting a different meaning [belongs] to those words that reside in different meanings; and by means of those two [functions], one word has multiple meanings, while by those same two [functions], the other word [is established]. (32)

Just as in cases such as *śauṇḍa* and others, there is the denotation of another meaning through association (*sāhacarya*), so too has this been applied here to the case under discussion (*dārṣṭāntika*). For when two things that are associated are denoted through the superimposition of each other's form, there is no denotation of anything else that is not associated; thus, in the expression "the *dhava* and *khadira* trees," the multiplicity of meanings is to be understood from the very words employed. And so, the intention is that there is an absence of the plural number.

And here, action (*kriyā*) is stated to be the cause for superimposing one meaning upon another; if [the term] *plakṣaḥ* means "that which exudes sap," this applies equally to the *nyagrodha* tree as well. Thus, the simultaneous occurrence in a single substratum (*yugapadadhikaraṇatā*) has been explained according to the statement of the Vārttikakāra. For he, having raised the objection that "if the term *dvandva* were used in the sense of *ca*, there would be the undesirable consequence [of it applying] even where there is no compound because the sense of *ca* is understood," recited an alternative formulation (*nyāsāntara*): "But it is established by the rule stating that *dvandva* occurs when there is simultaneous occurrence in a single substratum."

The meaning is that when a single substratum—the referent expressed by the compound—is denoted by a single word simultaneously, in the form of a collective whole whose individual meanings are mutually superimposed, then a *dvandva* (copulative compound) should be stated. Thus, it is said that a *dvandva* occurs when there is a desire to express [the members] together (*sahavivakṣā*), because it is precisely in that case that simultaneous expression of the substrata (*yugapadadhikaraṇavacanatā*) is established.

Now, one might object: since the sequence of the denotata must necessarily follow the sequence of the designations, how can there be simultaneous expression of multiple substrates (*yugapadadhikaraṇavacanatā*)? This is not so. In cases such as *plakṣanyagrodhau* (the *plakṣa* and the *nyagrodha*) or *dhavakhadirapalāśāḥ* (the *dhava*, *khadira*, and *palāśa*), if at the time of the cognition of the meaning of *nyagrodha* the meaning of *plakṣa* were not apprehended, and if at the time of the cognition of the meaning of *palāśa* the meaning of *dhava* and the others were not apprehended, then because the words *nyagrodha* and *palāśa* would each have only a single referent, only the singular number would occur, and not the dual or the plural. Therefore...

Since the dual and plural numbers would otherwise be untenable, it is determined through inference that each individual word here denotes multiple meanings; thus, simultaneous denotation is established. As it has been said: "If it is argued that the sequence of meanings follows from the sequence of words, then the dual and plural numbers would be impossible. Therefore, since the aggregate possesses manifested internal distinctions, the singular number based on the aggregate is not to be questioned.

Co-occurrence (*sāhacarya*) is stated as the reason for denoting a different object because, according to worldly convention, they are distinct objects. However, since the act of "flowing" (*prakṣaraṇa*)—meaning existing extensively—is also present in the *nyagrodha* tree, that [co-occurrence] belongs to its own primary meaning (*svārtha*) alone. As it has been said: "If it is argued that the application of the word is restricted to the substance due to the instrument [of the action], it is established because the cause is the same. Nor does this lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), such as the undesirable consequence that the word *nyagrodha* would also convey the meaning of a *plakṣa* tree in a sentence; for it has been stated: "And because it has that as its scope."

The meaning is that, within the scope of their function, words denote other meanings due to the diversity of their expressive power (*śakti*), but this does not occur everywhere. For this very reason, it is stated that in those cases, because of association (*sāhacarya*), when one [word] is used, the other is not employed, and thus its absence is indicated. If it is argued that the employment of the second is untenable because the first has already expressed the meaning, [the reply is: since it has not been expressed by the *plakṣa*, there is the employment of the word *nyagrodha*.

Thus, it has been stated that because words manifest their mutual powers in proximity to one another—like the sun and its rising—the mutual denotation of words is restricted to specific objects; furthermore, this denotation is inherent (*svābhāvika*). In this way, the simultaneous expression of multiple substrates (*yugapadadhikaraṇavacanatā*) has been established. However, the author of the Bhāṣya, having remarked that "this [theory] is difficult and hard to justify," instead supported the arrangement of Pāṇini’s own sūtras.
This [theory] does not ascend to common experience (*pratīti*), and thus it is difficult; moreover, it is hard to justify due to a lack of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). (32)

He explains that: "And because it belongs to a different aggregate, such a meaning is not worldly; moreover, even as a scriptural meaning, it is not observed through positive and negative concomitance. (33)

In this world, the determination of word-meanings is based on worldly usage. Here, no single meaning denoted by each individual word—which possesses a fixed definition and is useful for worldly transaction—is ascertained. Indeed, in common worldly practice, it is not observed that one word denotes the meaning of another word. Furthermore, because the worldly meaning is conventional (*rūḍha*), a *nyagrodha* tree is not called a *plakṣa* merely because of its similarity [in shape]. For a person is not called a "cow" simply because he moves, even though he is moving; [only a cow is so called].

Therefore, this collection, which is denoted by the aggregate characterized as a *dvandva* (copulative compound) and which is expressed as something distinct from the meaning of the individual members, should be understood as a non-worldly (*alaukika*) aggregate. Alternatively, this meaning of each member denoted by the *dvandva* word might be considered a technical (*śāstrīya*) abstraction, obtainable through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), similar to the meanings of stems and suffixes. That too is not correct.

Because, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the specific meaning of each word itself is established here; however, it is not possible to establish a capacity for denoting a different meaning. For when the word *plakṣa* is in proximity, it is said that the *nyagrodha* tree is also the meaning of *plakṣa*, because of the cognition [that arises]. And since that cognition is established by the word's own primary term alone, there is no [genuine] positive or negative concomitance.

Granted that when only one [member] remains, because another word is not employed, the capacity of a single [word] to convey multiple meanings is established by this principle—based on the maxim of the rising sun (*bhārodyantṛnyāya*)—due to the mutual manifestation of their capacities; however, since a *dvandva* compound cannot occur for a word whose own expressive power is unimpaired, why would the capacity of another word be postulated there, given that it is not perceived? But as for a collective (*samudāya*) in which the distinction between its parts has emerged, because it is denotable by a compound, the use of the dual and plural numbers is justified.

For it is from a compound (*samāsa*) that the dual and plural numbers arise, and not from the final member alone—which would necessitate an effort to establish the connection of its own meaning with duality and so forth. Furthermore, when multiple objects are made the object of a single cognition through their association with a single action or quality, they cannot be denoted by a single word; thus, they are expressed by a compound, which is termed a "collection of words" (*padasamūha*). And although that compound-word is indivisible, it is explained through the conceptualization of parts for the sake of grammatical derivation (*anvākhyeya*).

And since those parts are similar to other distinct words, it is their respective meanings alone that are understood. Thus, when there is instruction through division, even a word that possesses expectancy (sākāṅkṣa) culminates in its own specific meaning. Furthermore, this aggregate, which is brought about by mere mutual expectancy, constitutes the very essence of the sequential meanings; how then could it appear when only the meaning of a single word is perceived, such that the sentence could be said to be realized only upon the perception of the meaning of the subsequent word? This is because the aggregate is the object of a synthetic cognition (saṅkalanā-pratyaya), and it is apprehended at the time of determining the majority of its constituent parts.

Nor should it be suspected that the members of a *dvandva* compound do not coalesce because of the impossibility of a qualifier-qualified relationship (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*). For every nominal word-meaning is connected only with an action; however, the distinction among other types of compounds is merely this: for one [member] there is a direct connection with the action, while for another there is a connection by way of being its qualifier. In a *dvandva*, however, because the connection of the collective meaning with the action is indicated by the case-ending of the whole, the meanings of the individual parts attain the nature of the whole as they seek the action.

And this is also the opinion of the opponent. Otherwise, how could even a single [word] have two meanings? For it is only when two meanings are mutually expectant that there is a "collection" (samudāya). Precisely for this reason, since the meanings are understood from the collection itself through mutual expectancy, and because its purpose is fulfilled, the word *ca* ("and") is omitted. In a sentence (*vākya*), however, because the meanings appear as distinct, the word *ca* is required to indicate conjunction.

Therefore, since the dual and plural numbers are possible based on the collection itself—which is characterized by duality and so forth produced by mutual expectancy—there is no disagreement whatsoever. || 33 ||
Since it is thus—both painful and difficult to accomplish—it has been cited even in the Bhāṣya; however, that simultaneous pronunciation is resorted to for the sake of conventional usage.

It is called *duḥkhā* because "it causes pain and does not satisfy the mind," since it fails to ascend to the level of established understanding and its purpose is otherwise accomplished; for this very reason, due to the absence of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it cannot be communicated to another through pleasure, and thus it is difficult to establish. Furthermore, objects that are the domain of synthesis (*saṅkalana*) attain the state of a collective whole even within a compound (*samāsa*), and thus there is a desire to express them together.

Objects belonging to the same class are denoted by a single word; this is what is expressed by the term *ekaśeṣa*. When the author of the Bhāṣya speaks of "simultaneous expression of multiple substrates" (*yugapadadhikaraṇavacanatā*) in the context of simultaneous intention (*sahavivakṣā*), he has implicitly accepted this [theory], even though it was formulated as a difficult solution to establish his point. Therefore, this very principle is indeed admitted. || 34 ||

He states the seed for the possibility of that [interpretation]: "Having begun with the aggregate, a word is applied to it; when explained through its divisions, it is then said to have two meanings. (35)

In this context, a worldly aggregate such as "the *plakṣa* and *nyagrodha* trees" or "the *dhava*, *khadira*, and *palāśa* trees" is a word that is to be analyzed (*anvākyeya*), and it is explained through the conceptualization of its constituent parts. In that process, whatever meaning belongs to the whole is established within each individual part being analyzed. For in this domain, a constituent word such as "*plakṣa*" does not rest in its own primary meaning alone; rather, it expresses the complete meaning [of the entire aggregate].

And thus, when a collection [of words] is introduced, because they are mutually related according to the method of *anvitābhidhāna* (denotation of the related), each individual word denotes an object that is already connected with the objects denoted by the other words; therefore, [the word] indeed possesses multiple meanings. When there is a simultaneous intention to express [all meanings], the word is employed by referring to the collection as the denotable object. In the same way, within the analytical process (*prakriyā*), the sentence for extraction (*apoddhāra-vākya*)—namely, "both *plakṣa*s and both *nyagrodha*s"—expresses only two meanings. It should be understood that the same applies to cases such as "dhava, khadira, and palāśa," where many meanings are expressed.

For the meaning of words is that which has ascended to the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*). Here, the intention is "these two. However, in ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), the compound is indeed non-different and denotes the collective meaning of the whole; thus, there is no multiplicity of meanings in a worldly sentence. But in the analytical sentence (*prakriyāvākya*), because the whole is denoted through the properties of its parts—due to its being composed of *plakṣa* parts, this whole is called "two *plakṣas*" with the distinction of its parts manifested, and due to its being composed of *nyagrodha* parts, it is called "two *nyagrodhas*."

For example, because the parts are equal, it is called "equal powder" (*sama-cūrṇa*). In the case of a compound (*vṛtti*), however, because there is a unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) and the distinction [between the members] dissolves, and because the word *ca*—which indicates a collection based on that [distinction]—is not employed, the term for a member (*avayava-śabda*) functions with equal predominance (*samaprādhānyena*) toward the whole (*samudāya*).

Otherwise, because the members of a *dvandva* compound possess equal prominence (*samaprādhānya*), it would be impossible for their referents to be directly connected with the action; consequently, in the absence of mutual integration (*itaretaropaśleṣa*), they would denote distinct meanings just as in a sentence, and thus the use of dual and plural endings would be untenable. For in other types of compounds, the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) is joined with the action through the medium of the principal member and thereby becomes integrated with it; but this is not the case in a *dvandva*, since all its members are equally predominant.

Therefore, in that case, it must necessarily be admitted that the meaning of the whole is denoted by each individual word, so that, while the mutual connection of their meanings is established, the dual and plural number are justified through the denotation of a whole whose internal distinctions have become manifest. For it will be demonstrated later that gender and number are determined here by way of the substratum.

Since the diversity of word-powers (*śabdaśakti*) between grammatical function (*vṛtti*) and sentence (*vākya*) is well-established, it is logical that a word which possesses the power to denote a different object observed in a worldly sentence should, in its grammatical function, denote that same [combined] object. For this very reason it was said: "And that is its object. Thus, it is established that both *dvandva* (copulative compound) and *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) possess simultaneous reference to multiple substrata (*yugapadadhikaraṇavacanatā*). 35.

He explains the distinction between the derivative form (*vṛtti*) and the sentence (*vākya*), which arises solely from the variety of the expressive power of words: "In a sentence as well as in a derivative form, certain properties are fixed; likewise, in both cases, those [properties] are described as being identical, pertaining only to the potentiality [of meaning]. (36)

Although there is a distinction in that certain differences in meaning are restricted to syntactic expectancy (*vyapekṣā*) in a sentence, some to the state of unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) in a compound, and others common to both the compound and the sentence, nevertheless, this [distinction] has not been pointed out in the treatise by its specific nature according to the difference in their objects; rather, under the rule "A grammatical operation concerning words requires semantic competency" (*samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ*), these various properties have been described solely with respect to the generality of competency (*sāmarthya*). Once competency has been indicated without regard for its specific details, they are distinguished accordingly. The meaning is that this mere competency has been stated in its restricted form. || 36 ||

Having thus stated it in general terms, he speaks in order to determine it specifically: "Because they function as qualifiers in a compound, words such as *śyāma* (dark) are cited as examples of expressing a universal (*sāmānya*) when [the compound] denotes a particular (*bheda*), as in the case of the *upamāna-samāsa* (simile-compound) and others. (37)

Regarding the rule *upamānāni sāmānyavacanaiḥ*, the example *śastrī śyāmā* ("the knife is dark") is cited. Therein, an objection is raised: since the word *śyāmā* (dark) refers to a specific object—the knife which serves as the standard of comparison—or to Devadattā who is compared to it, it functions as a particular term (*viśeṣavṛtti*); how then can it be called a general term (*sāmānyavacana*)? This objection is resolved in the Bhāṣya by the statement: "That which is a general term prior to the connection [with the specific object]."

Where objects are connected through direct confrontation (*ābhimukhyena*) and the non-distinction of their own natures (*svabhāva-saṃbhedena*), that compound is here expressed by the term "connection" (*abhisaṃbandha*). Therefore, prior to this [compound], in the sentence, because they have separate meanings, words such as "dark" (*śyāma*) express generalities. For in the case of "dark like a knife-stand" (*śastrī iva śyāmā*), the word "dark" functions by relying on the generality of darkness residing in both the object of comparison and the subject of comparison. In the compound, however, due to the state of "becoming one meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*), there is an exclusion of these particularities.
This should be understood similarly in other cases, such as the "comparison compound" (*upamita-samāsa*) and so forth. || 37 ||

He states another example: "The occurrence [of a compound] in the sense of another word is impossible in sentences; and there is no occurrence of dvandva words in the sense of 'ca' (and) when there is a distinction. (38)

In the sentence "His sprouts are glossy," there is no *vṛtti* (compounded expression) regarding the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) of the words—as there is in the *vṛtti* "the tree has glossy sprouts"—because the external referent "his" is already conveyed in the sentence by its own word. In a *vṛtti*, however, because the possessive relation (*matvartha*) is included within the compound, the words, having attained a unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), convey the related object.

Likewise, since there is no occurrence of the sense of *samāhāra* (aggregation) or *itaretarayoga* (mutual conjunction) when there is a separation of the members of a *dvandva* compound within a sentence, the word *ca* is employed there as a signifier. However, in a compound (*vṛtti*), because the words denote a collective meaning by virtue of a single action, the *ca* is not employed there when the aggregated [elements] are primary. || 37 ||

He says something else as well: "If there were a difference [between the individual and the universal], it would be impossible for words such as 'nir' (prefixes) to have meanings such as 'transcending' (*krānta*); nor could there be denotation of a genus (*jāti*) based on prior occurrence, as in the case of words like 'gaurakhara' (a white donkey). (39)

A "sentence" (*vākya*) is so called because meanings are differentiated within it; in such a sentence, prefixes like *nis-* do not possess the capacity to denote meanings such as "departed," as seen in examples like *niṣkrāntaḥ kauśāmbyāḥ* ("departed from Kauśāmbī"), and thus the root *kram-* and its derivatives are employed there directly. However, in a compound (*vṛtti*), as in *niṣkauśāmbiḥ*, there is indeed the expression of meanings such as "departed. For in a sentence, it is impossible for prefixes like *nis-*, which denote non-substantial entities (*asattvavācin*), to function with respect to a substance (*dravya*) such as "having departed" that is connected to an action.

In a compound (*samāsa*), however, because the meaning of the prior member (*pūrvapadārtha*) is predominant, that referent—which has become a substance (*dravyabhūta*)—is denoted as being connected with multiple actions. This is the distinction produced by "unification of meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*). Thus, in examples such as *gaurakharaḥ*, *kṛṣṇasarpaḥ*, and *lohitaśāliḥ*, the capacity to convey a specific genus (*jāti*) does not exist in the sentence prior to the derivative word (*vṛttipada*).

For in expressions such as "the white donkey," "the black snake," or "the red rice," there is no cognition of a specific genus (jāti), because the genus is not denoted by the collection of words; rather, what is cognized is an object delimited by a specific color. Indeed, regarding a specific genus, no regard is paid to a specific color. However, due to their having a single referent and because the compound functions as a single word, a qualified genus is expressed by the compound.

And likewise, when a connection with a genus (*jāti*) is intended, a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) is applied to a *karmadhāraya* compound, as in "a forest full of white donkeys" (*gaurakhara-vad araṇyam*), "an anthill containing black snakes" (*kṛṣṇasarpa-vān valmīkaḥ*), or "a village of red rice" (*lohitaśālinām grāmaḥ*). Therefore, in this case, because the *bahuvrīhi* is more concise than the *karmadhāraya* and the possessive suffix, the principle [of parsimony] does not apply here. When one says "a village of red rice" (*lohitaśālir grāmaḥ*), the intended connection with a specific type of rice is not understood. This should be applied similarly to other examples as well.
And so says the Bhāṣya: "There is a distinction here; in this case, the connection is made by means of the genus (jāti). || 39 ||

Regarding that natural distinction between occurrence (*vṛtti*) and sentence (*vākya*), he states the teacher’s corroborating opinion: "In the case of play and livelihood, because there is no expression by means of a sentence, the inclusion of the term 'nitya' (constant) is not appropriate, just as in the rule for the *yaṅ* affix [which applies] to the sense of crookedness. (40)

The author of the Vārttika recited: "Since no specific distinction is understood from the analysis of the latter two [sūtras], the mention of 'nityam' (always) is redundant. Regarding the two rules "nityaṃ kauṭilye gatau" and "lupasada-", the mention of "nityam" need not be made for the purpose of precluding the formation of a periphrastic compound (*vākya*), because the crookedness of movement and the censure of the action are already expressed by the periphrastic construction itself. For instance, in the expression "kuṭilaṃ krāmati" (he moves crookedly), there is also the perception of improper conduct through the sense of crookedness.

However, in the case of *caṅkramyate*, a specific action characterized by going back and forth (*gatapratyāgata*) is understood. Likewise, in *garhitaṃ lumpati*, the censure of the root meaning (*dhātvartha*) is not necessarily understood, because the censure of the instrument (*sādhana*) is also perceived. In the *vṛtti* [on Pāṇini 1.4.36], however, in the form *lolupyate*, there is the perception of the censure of the state (*bhāva*). By this very logic, the mention of the word "always" (*nityam*) in the rule *nityaṃ krīḍājīvikayoḥ* should be rejected; thus, that too has been cited under the guise of an illustration.

Alternatively, just as in the case of the rule *nityaṃ kauṭilye* ("always [used] in the sense of crookedness"), the explicit mention of *nityam* was rejected in the Vārttika, so too should it be for the rule *nityaṃ krīḍājīvikayoḥ* ("always [used] in the sense of play and livelihood"). This is presented as something yet to be proven (*sādhya*). The other [example] serves as an illustration, because only that which is already established (*siddha*) can serve as an illustration. Thus, the Master’s (Patañjali’s) view is consistent with this corroborating evidence. From the sentence "a breaker of *uddāla* flowers" and "a carver of teeth," there is no comprehension of [the senses of] play or livelihood.

Because even wealth, which is not an auxiliary to pleasure (*krīḍānaṅga*) and is merely a means of livelihood, is understood [from these roots], and likewise because the repetition of action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*) is not perceived from forms such as *caṅkramyate* or *lolupyate*, the suffix *yaṅ* does not occur after them. Thus it has been said: "In the case of the repetition of action, [the suffix *yaṅ*] does not occur after these. For this purpose, some explain the inclusion of the word *nit* [in the rule] as follows: "The suffix *nit* is always used for crooked motion (*kuṭilā gati*), and always for the censure of an internal state (*bhāvagarhā*), but not for the repetition of action."

Just as the inclusion of the term "nitya" (constant/permanent) was rejected because the intended meaning cannot be understood from the sentence [alone], so too, since the sense of "repetition of action" (*kriyāsamabhihāra*) is not understood therein, there is an absence of the suffix; for this reason as well, the inclusion of "nitya" is not necessary. However, for those who follow the explicit statement of the rule, it ought to exist even for the purpose of excluding the [simple] sentence.

Just as these specificities regarding the function and the object have been stated, so too have the specificities regarding number, the qualification of a subordinate term (*upasarjana*), grammatical connection (*yoga*), and the denotation of the individual (*vyakti*) been declared as being restricted to the sentence alone. However, because of the relationship between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*), both [the word and the sentence] must be followed as the basis for these. || 40 ||

Thus, since there is a difference between the function [of a compound] and that of a sentence—because in cases such as selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) and so forth, only syntactic expectancy (*vyapekṣā*) persists—therefore, there is no purpose for prohibitions regarding compounds.

The capacity [of words] characterized by mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*) is established as restricted to the domain of syntactic unity (*vākya*), definite determination (*ekaniyata-nirdhāraṇa*), and fixed by its very nature—as in the example "among cows, the black one has the most milk" (*gavāṃ kṛṣṇā sampannakṣīratamā*). Consequently, the prohibition of compounding (*samāsa-pratiṣedha*) by the rule *na nirdhāraṇe* need not be undertaken. For here, when the compound is formed through the state of semantic unification (*ekārthībhāva*), the act of definite determination (*nirdhāraṇa*) is not perceived as "the black cow among cows has the most milk. The intended meaning is that because there exists an external factor to be expected as the cause of determination, there is a lack of semantic capacity (*asāmarthya*), and thus no compounding occurs in this case.
In this same way, it should be understood that the prohibition beginning with "pūraṇa-" and so forth is also not to be prescribed. || 41 ||

Since the treatise is merely indicative, the undertaking of the science is intended to follow the inherent diversity of the powers of words, which is established by their very nature; thus he says: "By means of injunctions and prohibitions, the demonstration of difference and non-difference is effected, as in the case of a dual compound functioning as a singular, or like the instruction on collective function. (42)

By the rule of composition (*samāsa*), non-difference, connection, and the state of becoming a single meaning (*ekārthībhāva*)—which are established by their very nature—are made known; whereas by means of prohibition, difference, non-connection, and the characteristic of mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*) are indicated for those of dull intellect. For example: the operation of a *dvandva* compound denoting living beings, musical instruments, or parts of an army occurs naturally in a collective sense where the difference between the members is obscured in the aggregate. By the rule "of the parts of living beings, musical instruments, and armies," there is a prescription that it must be a singular aggregate (*samāhāra*) alone.

In the case of curd, milk, and the like, however, their application in a collective sense (*itaretarayoga*) occurs naturally when there is a distinction between the constituent parts; this is [established] by means of prohibition. Regarding trees, wild animals, and so forth, the rule concerning the optionality (*vibhāṣā*) applies in both cases; thus, the grammatical treatise is merely reiterative. For the expressive power (*śakti*) of words cannot be created even by a hundred declarations if it does not already exist. Since the status of being established is already secured by the explicit statement in the *Vārttika*, "Or rather, not [so], because the aggregate is a single entity," which serves as a direct refutation of the treatment as a singular (*ekavadbhāva*), its presentation here is by way of illustration.
The underlying logic (*nyāya*), however, is the same. || 42 ||

Thus, regarding the general capacity (*sāmarthya*) specified in the rule "A grammatical operation concerning words applies when they are semantically connected" (*samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ*), those who follow the power of the word have distinguished it according to the difference between mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*) and unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*). To this effect, he says: "Although capacity is stated without distinction, it is divided by those competent in usage—namely, the cognizers—according to worldly convention, into [the states of] composition (*vṛtti*) and non-composition (*avṛtti*). (43)

It has been stated that the state of having a unified meaning (*saṅgatārthatva*) between a word expressing a general sense and a semantically capable word is indistinguishable whether it occurs in a compound (*vṛtti*) or in a sentence (*vākya*). However, those who know the technical definitions (*lakṣya-jña*), following the intention of the author of the *Sūtras*—since the traditional rule (*smṛti*) is based on the actual usage (*lakṣya*)—have made this distinction: that in a compound there is "integration of meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*), whereas in a sentence there is "mutual expectancy" (*vyapekṣā*). Consequently, even in the case of rules for the substitution of *ṣatva* and so forth, since mutual expectancy as semantic capability (*sāmarthya*) is possible under the view of the *paribhāṣā*, it is precisely this [expectancy] that functions there.

And because the distinction in capacity has a restricted scope, it was stated: "Or else, the use of the suffix *vā* is purposeless, since [the meaning] is established by its own nature. Furthermore, in the case of a compound (*vṛtti*), specific features such as the cognition of the sense of "gone beyond" (*krānta*) and so forth—which arise from the state of unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*)—have been explained; whereas in a sentence (*vākya*), specific features such as particular numbers and so forth are produced by the absence of unified meaning. (43)

Anticipating the objection—"How is this distinction possible when no specific difference has been stated? Why might the opposite not also be conceivable here?"—he says: "Because the meaning has ceased [to be expressed as separate], the elision (*luk*) and so forth are not contradictory; therefore, the designation 'compound' (*samāsa*) is prescribed only for that state where there is a single unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*). (44)

In this context, there are two types of function (*vṛtti*): *jahatsvārthā* (abandoning its own meaning) and *ajahatsvārthā* (not abandoning its own meaning). That function in which subordinate words abandon their own meanings is *jahatsvārthā*; the opposite of that is *ajahatsvārthā*. This distinction is based on different philosophical views. Among these, in the case of *jahatsvārthā*, the meaning of the subordinate term is simply non-existent.

Even in the case of a compound that does not abandon its own meaning (*ajahatsvārtha*), since it results in a merging with the principal member, the basis for distinction—the relation—is removed by the expression "not existing separately" (*pṛthagasan*). Furthermore, because the specific number is obscured, the non-appearance of the case-ending (*vibhakti*)—which is due to the absence of its own inherent meaning—is justified as being what is described by the grammatical rule. Thus, a compound is appropriate when there is "unification of meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*). However, in the case of mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*), since both distinction and specific numbers are possible, a sentence remains present when a case-ending is heard.

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "luka etc.," the statement regarding the singular treatment (*ekavadbhāva*) in the absence of elision (*aluk*) in the example *stokānmukta* ("slightly released") is understood. For, because distinctions are concealed in a compound, there arises a non-differentiated unity of number; thus, the expression of a single referent (*ekārthābhidhāna*) is recognized as being inherent. And so it has been said: "The mention of the singular treatment is redundant, [since] there is no compound in the dual or plural. Thus, it has been stated that the grammatical description of elision (*luk*) and so forth serves as an indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the rule prescribing compounds when a single referent is present.

And thus, since both the sentence and the compound have fixed domains of application, it is impossible for them to obstruct each other's scope; therefore, the teaching of an option between them is untenable. || 44 ||

Some, however, maintain that the restriction of the scope [of grammatical rules] is purely based on explicit scriptural statement (vācanika). He demonstrates this: "And some maintain that the optional rule (vyavasthita-vibhāṣā) applies to the general case; likewise, a sentence is taught for the state of mutual expectancy (vyapekṣā), while a compound (samāsa) is taught for other cases. (45)

That which is common to both *vyapekṣā* (mutual expectancy) and *ekārthībhāva* (integration into a single meaning)—namely, mere relationship (*sambandhamātra*)—is stated without distinction as "capacity" (*sāmarthya*). In that regard, both the sentence (*vākya*) and the compound (*samāsa*) are permitted by way of an option (*vibhāṣā*). Furthermore, because this is understood as a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), it is stated by those who follow the intention of the author of the Sūtras that there is a restriction of scope based on the power of words: in the case of *vyapekṣā*, where capacity is differentiated, only the sentence occurs; whereas in the case of *ekārthībhāva*, only the derivative formation (*vṛtti*) occurs.

The author of the Vārttika rejected the mention of the word "vā" (or), and thus, according to the principle stated previously, he establishes the rule. However, for the author of the Sūtras, the option remains established as a general *vyavasthita-vibhāṣā* (restricted option). 45.

And so, even though there is the same verbal form due to their reliance on a common meaning, he states that this is another distinction caused by the unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*): "Even when the identity [of the words] is accepted because they have the same phonetic form (*tulyaśrutitva*), the expectation for qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇākāṅkṣā*) ceases in the case of a compound (*vṛtti*) because [the compound] is not expressive [of its parts]. (46)

Even though the identity of the *vṛtti* and the sentence is accepted on the basis of the similarity of form—namely, that the very same words such as "king" (*rājan*) which appear in the sentence also appear in the *vṛtti*—nevertheless, just as in the sentence "the man of the wealthy king" (*ṛddhasya rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), in the *vṛtti* "the king's man" (*rājapuruṣaḥ*) as well, the subordinate meaning (*upasarjanārtha*) cannot be connected with the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), because there is a lack of signifying power (*agamakatva*). For it is impossible for "wealthy" (*ṛddha*) and so forth to be connected with a "king" who, being conjoined with the principal member (*pradhāna*), is no longer independent.

For when a relation is included within a compound due to the unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), how could there be a connection with a qualifier that possesses a distinct [external] separation? Thus, one must state: "There is no formation of a compound for words accompanied by qualifiers, nor is there a qualifier for a word already compounded. For once a compound is formed, the connection with a qualifier is not perceived because the meaning of the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) lacks intelligibility—that is, it lacks the capacity to convey [the intended sense]. Consequently, there is no expectancy for a qualifier in that case. However, such expectancy exists in a sentence, because [in a sentence] the meaning is intelligible.

Therefore, due to the difference in the expressive power (*śakti*) of words, there is an absolute difference between the *vṛtti* (compound) and the sentence when there is a difference in meaning. The perception of non-difference, which is caused by their similarity of form, is an error. Even by that person who puts forward the argument here that "because of the unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) in a *vṛtti*, there is no connection with qualifiers since the subordinate element lacks distinctness," it is stated that the very difference between the *vṛtti* and the sentence—arising from the distinction produced by unification of meaning—is caused by the expressive power of words; nothing new has been said. (46)

And so, where there is the capacity to convey meaning (*gamakatva*), there the connection with a qualifier occurs even when there is a unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*); thus he says: "Every relative term (*saṃbandhiśabda*) is always employed as dependent [on another]. That dependence, like its own primary meaning, is not lost even in the state of *vṛtti* (compound formation). (47)

In this context, certain words are called "relational" (*saṃbandhiśabda*) because they express their own meaning as necessarily dependent upon another. For example: teacher and pupil, father and son, mother and brother, and so forth. Consequently, even when these words form a compound (*vṛtti*), they convey their own meaning precisely as it is connected with another object; thus, because they possess the capacity to indicate [the relationship], a compound may occur even for those words that have qualifiers (*saviśeṣaṇa*). Therefore, in the rule stating "there is no compounding of words with qualifiers" (*saviśeṣaṇānāṃ vṛttir na*), one need not specify "except for *aguruputra* and the like."

"Devadatta’s teacher’s family," "Devadatta’s teacher’s son," and so forth. For in these cases, the qualification required by the nominal stem alone is not manifested through a distinct external relation (*vyatireka*); thus, because of the state of unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), even though the external relation is included within [the compound], it is connected with the subordinate member (*upasarjana*). Indeed, since the expressed meaning of "teacher" and the like requires a correlate such as "pupil," that expectancy does not cease even in the state of unified meaning, because there is no cessation of the word's own primary referent. (47)

Right here, he states another perspective: "Those things which have a connection with a whole, such as a teacher’s family and so forth, come into contact with their parts and are thus joined with that which possesses them. (48)

The teacher’s family (*gurukula*) is well known to be like a maidservant’s house; it is the principal member that is qualified by Devadatta, and not here is there a dependence on the subordinate object—the teacher—with respect to Devadatta. Even in this justification, when the doubt arises as to whether "the teacher’s family is near Devadatta" or otherwise, it must necessarily be stated: "the family of him who is Devadatta’s teacher. Thus, having accepted the members such as the teacher and so forth through their relationship, those [members] such as Devadatta are connected with the whole (*samudāya*) which possesses them as its parts.

Thus, the connection with the whole occurs precisely through its parts, as in the case of expressions such as "the curd is made of two [parts] of barley. And so, the very same meaning that exists when Devadatta is directly in contact with the teacher is what is produced here; there is no difference in the manner [of the relationship]. This is the intended meaning. || 48 ||

Anticipating the objection that there might be no absolute difference [between a sentence and a compound] because they are both explained through grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*) by means of the dissolution of the sentence (*vākyopamarda*), he says: "The means for the comprehension of those who are ignorant are diverse; therefore, due to their being different words, there is an absolute difference between a sentence and a compound. (49)

In this world, compounds such as *rājapuruṣa* (king’s man) and the like, which function to denote specific meanings, are in reality partless; yet they are analyzed by imagining a division into prior and subsequent members. Thus, those of dull intellect, due to the similarity in sound between the means and the end, conclude that the two are identical. However, in actual fact, just as when a real gavaya is understood through a line-drawn gavaya, the line-drawn gavaya is one thing and the real gavaya is another, so too the analytical sentence (*prakriyāvākya*) contained within the scattering of dust [during grammatical analysis] is entirely distinct from the compound (*samāsa*).

Indeed, by this means, the sentence—which is inherent in the process of formation—is demonstrated. And that [sentence] is strictly limited to mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*) and is entirely distinct from the compound (*samāsa*), which is the domain of unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*). This is because words differ according to their difference in meaning; and the difference in meaning has been shown to include specific number and so forth. Furthermore, in some cases, there is also a difference in form due to the occurrence of compound-final suffixes (*samāsānta*) and the like. Because the primary meaning, characterized by either distinction (*bheda*) or connection (*saṃsarga*), is non-different, the derivative form (*vṛtti*) is explained as being far removed from the nature of the sentence.

Likewise, in some cases, the expression of a word is used for the sake of the sentence-meaning; thus, there are various means of instruction within the grammatical system (*prakriyā*). And therein, because the case-endings (*vibhakti*) are seen in the sentence, the elision (*luk*) is prescribed for compounds (*samāsa*) in order to accomplish operations characterized by suffixes, such as the elision of *n* (*nalopa*), and so forth. (49)

If this is so, why is there no mention of elision (*lopākhyāna*) for words such as *yukta* when they are observed in sentences regarding the application of terms like *goratha*? To this, he says: "Because [words] such as *yukta* are not seen in both non-compounds and compounds in cases such as *goratha*, their removal or inclusion has not been effected by the grammatical treatise. (50)

Since case-endings (*vibhakti*) are observed to be employed in sentences (*vākya*) that are not compounds (*asamāsa*), their occurrence would logically follow in the grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*) during the instruction on word-formation (*vṛttyanuśāsana*). Thus, it is appropriate that the Teacher, seeking a basis for the characteristic of suffixes (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) by requesting their natural cessation due to the absence of meaning, should have prescribed their elision (*luk*). However, in cases such as *gorathaḥ* ("ox-cart") and *dadhighaṭaḥ* ("curd-pot"), the suffixes *yuk* and others, which belong to the derivative sentence of the derivation, are not seen; nor is there any grammatical operation (*kārya*) to be perceived based upon them. Therefore, there is no prescription of elision (*lug-anvākhyāna*) for those [suffixes].

And so, when it is argued that there can be no compound because substances lack the capacity [to relate] without an action—as in *dadhnā odanaḥ* ("rice with curd") or *gavāṃ rathaḥ* ("a chariot for cows")—it is stated: "It is established, however, that under the heading of *samānādhikaraṇa* (co-referential) compounds, there is the elision of the suffix *-kta* and of the third-case word as the prior member and the subsequent member; and there is also a genitive compound ending in *yukta* or *pūrṇa*. Thus, *dadhnā upasiktaḥ* becomes *dadhyupasiktaḥ*; *dadhyupasikta odanaḥ* becomes *dadhyodanaḥ*; *dadhnaḥ pūrṇaḥ* becomes *dadhipūrṇaḥ*; and *dadhipūrṇo ghaṭaḥ* becomes *dadhighaṭaḥ*.

Regarding the statement that there is elision of the final member in a compound such as *gavāṃ yukto goyuktaḥ* ("yoked with oxen") or *goyukto ratho gorathaḥ* ("an ox-yoked chariot"), this rule of elision was rejected by the following arguments: "Or rather, [there is no elision], because it is not observed in non-compounds," "because the capacity [for the compound] exists through the comprehension of the meaning 'yoked'," and "because the determination of that meaning arises from the comprehension [of the parts]. Thus, the rule concerning elision has been refuted.

In expressions such as *dadhyodanaḥ* (curd-rice) and *guḍadhānāḥ* (molasses-grains), because the relationship between food and condiment is understood through the capacity of the action of mixing—which is the cause of that [relationship]—the sentence is actually constructed as *tena dadhnā odanaḥ* (rice with that curd), and so forth. There is no word such as "mixed" (*upasikta*) present here at all. Similarly, the sentences are simply *gavāṃ rathaḥ* (a chariot of cows) and *dadhno ghaṭaḥ* (a jar of curd). However, the understanding of meanings such as "yoked" (*yukta*) arises through the power of the related terms.

For instance: the relationship between the oxen and the chariot as draught-animals and the vehicle conveys the sense of "yoked"; likewise, the relationship between the curd and the jar as container and contained conveys the sense of "full. This should be understood accordingly, as the case may require. || 50 ||

But surely, in sentences such as "the chariot joined with a cow," "rice mixed with curd," or "a jar full of curd," words like *yukta* (joined) and so forth are indeed seen; likewise, in expressions such as *pragataparṇaḥ* ("one from whom leaves have departed") or *prapatitaparṇaḥ* ("one from whom leaves have fallen"), where they function as compounds (*vṛtti*), the word *gata* (departed) and others are heard in the sentence. Therefore, the elision (*lopa*) must certainly be explained. To this, he says: "Because they are distinct words, *yukta* and the like are employed in certain sentences; and in compounds such as *praparṇa* and *prapalāśa*, the word *gata* is used in the derivational formations (*vṛtti*). (51)

In this context, there are two kinds of sentences: the worldly sentence, which is eternally integrated into linguistic usage (*prayogasamavāyi*), and the analytical sentence (*prakriyāvākya*), which is non-eternal and non-worldly (*alaukika*), standing in the place of a "line-drawing gavaya" (*rekhāgavaya*) that serves as the basis for grammatical derivation (*samāsaprakṛti*). In that [analytical sentence], elements such as *yukta* (in *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ yuktaḥ*) are not observed; they are observed only in the worldly sentence. Furthermore, that [worldly sentence] is entirely distinct from the compound (*samāsa*) itself, being merely a synonym (*paryāya*) for it—just as *goratha* is distinct from the compound *rājapuruṣa*. Consequently, it is not tenable to justify the deletion (*lopa*) of words in synonyms such as *gaja*, *mataṅgaja*, *vṛṣa*, and *vṛṣabha* by taking into account their relative weight (*gurulāghava*).

In cases such as *praparṇa* and the like, when there exists a state of unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) within compounds, the word *gata* is sometimes employed in ordinary usage—as in *pragataparṇa*—as a distinct word; this is the logical connection (*samanvaya*). || 51 ||

And he says that even though there is a difference in the intermediate meanings, the function of a worldly sentence employed in practice is one with respect to its primary meaning: "The relationship of qualifier and qualified, as well as a single substratum, is accepted by some as the identity of function between the word and the sentence regarding the means to seeing reality. (52)

Since it is impossible to provide a grammatical derivation (*anvākhyāti*) for a compound that is partless, a procedural sentence (*prakriyāvākya*) resembling an ordinary worldly sentence is postulated as a means. In this [procedural sentence], the extraction of meanings for the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) is achieved through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). However, the ignorant, mistaking the means and the goal to be one and the same, perceive no difference in meaning here [between the compound and its analysis].

To explain: the very same relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) that exists in the sentence "the blue lotus" (*nīlam utpalam*), as well as the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) based on non-difference, remains entirely unchanged in the compound "blue-lotus" (*nīlotpala*). Likewise, even in the case of different substrates (*vyadhikaraṇa*), such as "the king's man," the relation of qualifier and qualified—which consists of a connection (*saṃsarga*)—is identical to that in the compound "king-man" (*rājapuruṣa*); thus, the compound and the sentence are non-distinct. Accordingly, there is the view of some scholars that "capacity" (*sāmarthya*) is "mutual expectancy" (*parasparavyapekṣā*).

Even in this compound, semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) consists precisely in mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*); for in the view that holds that words denote their own meanings (*kārya-śabda-darśana*), since the compound arises by subsuming the sentence, there is no application of a different meaning. Furthermore, because the meaning of the case-ending is expressed by the nominal stem itself—based on the view that [the stem] possesses the fivefold meaning—the elision of that ending is merely described grammatically, not because the meaning is absent. Thus, in cases such as *tāvakīna*, when the cognition of the qualifier is present, the specific number is indeed determined. In every respect, however, it would be understood here as being due to the absence of "single-meaningness" (*ekārthībhāva*).

The prohibition of qualifying adjuncts for subordinate members, namely the rule "there is no compound formation (*vṛtti*) for those that possess qualifiers," is based on scriptural injunction (*vacana*). Furthermore, the non-employment of the word *ca* ("and") in a copulative compound (*dvandva*) serves that same purpose; this follows from the grammatical instruction (*anuśāsana*), not from the disappearance of distinction, because there is an absence of conjunction residing in those [members]. Thus, the proponents of the theory of words as products (*kāryaśabdavādin*) mistakenly conclude, due to delusion and the like, that there is absolute identity between the sentence and the compound—both being synonyms—on the grounds that their primary meanings are non-different.

There is no such thing as "integration of meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*) that produces some specific distinction; rather, it is simply mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*), since this is possible even in cases such as the substitution of *ṣatva* (the change to *ṣ*). Thus, they maintain that in all instances, there is semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*). And in this way, because a single object is conveyed by two words having different causes [of application], grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and the relation of qualifier and qualified (*avacchedyāvacchedakabhāva*), which depend on difference, are also appropriate within a compound formation (*vṛtti*); therefore, that [result] is not something to be achieved through deliberate effort. Furthermore, in their view, the option (*vikalpa*) is made by the rule itself regarding distinct domains; thus, that [rule] is not purposeless. (52)

To refute this illustration, he says: "Just as a word such as 'tree' is established in a specific object, so too even [a compound] like 'blue lotus' functions without [the need for] two distinct parts. (53)

Since the meaninglessness of individual phonemes (*varṇa*) has been established in the case of words such as *vṛkṣa*, the word—as a *sphoṭa* by nature—is partless and conveys an indivisible meaning; it possesses a fixed meaning through its own power. In this same way, a compound such as *nīlotpalam* is explained through the conceptualization of similar parts, like a base and a suffix, by means of a sentence that is not far removed [from the compound]. Just as in the case of *vṛkṣa* and other words, the division between the meanings of a base and a suffix—though non-existent—is imagined for the sake of grammatical exposition (*anvākhyāna*), so too is there a distinction of constituent meanings even within a compound (*vṛtti*).

For in a sentence (*vākya*), there is a distinction of meaning; hence, the case-ending expressing relation (*sambandha-vibhakti*) is employed. But in a compound (*vṛtti*), because the meaning undergoes non-distinction—becoming unified like dust and water—the relation dissolves due to this loss of differentiation, and thus the case-ending naturally ceases. Furthermore, there is no specific number [expressed], because when the five meanings of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-artha*) are present, they are not perceived due to the absence of any indicator (*dyotaka*). In the expression *payo jaraṇam payaḥ* ("milk is the digestion of milk"), the power (*śakti*) is understood through the fact that the connection with the action would otherwise be inexplicable.

Furthermore, the number one as non-difference (*abhedaikatvasaṅkhyā*) is the universal common to all specific numbers; it exists in the subordinate element (*upasarjana*) because a substance cannot be devoid of number. Thus, when there is a word that indicates a distinction, its comprehension occurs according to the circumstances, and this is not contradictory. Moreover, because the meaning of the subordinate element is merged with the primary meaning, it is not deprived of its own qualification. However, since it is impossible for words to impart their expressive power (*śakti*) through grammatical number alone, the distinction between their respective scopes is difficult to determine.

Even in a *dvandva* compound, there is an absence of word-repetition because of the predominance of the combined elements, and not because of an injunction regarding the sense of "and" (*ca*). For here, meanings are not indicated within words as things to be enjoined, since that would be impossible due to their infinite variety. As it has been said: "Because meanings are not taught [in grammar], and that [absence of repetition] is for the sake of brevity. Furthermore, in all cases, there is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) of worldly meanings already established. However, the view of some is that "capacity" (*sāmarthya*) consists in mutual expectancy (*parasparavyapekṣā*).

Because it is established as a settled doctrine that the aphorism [Pāṇini 2.1.1] becomes more concise by defining *sāmarthya* (semantic competency) as *ekārthībhāvaḥ* (the state of having a single unified meaning) and as a *paribhāṣā* (technical rule), there is thus an absolute difference between a derivative form (*vṛtti*) and a sentence (*vākya*), due to the observation of distinctions produced by this state of having a single unified meaning. Any determination of similarity based on some partial aspect, however, is an error. || 53 ||

Furthermore, there is no universal conformity between the application [of a term] and its sentence-meaning; thus he says: "In the world, the cognition of terms such as *śrotriya* and *kṣatriya* does not occur through differentiation [based on a common property], because they lack a connection with an identical form, unlike the case of *Vāsiṣṭha* and *Gārgya*. (54)

Just as in the case of *taddhita* derivatives such as *vāsiṣṭha* and *gārgya*, there is an understanding based on the division into base (*prakṛti*) and suffix (*pratyaya*) for the sake of grammatical analysis (*anvākhyāna*), it is not so with words such as *śrotriya*, *kṣetriya*, and *pāraśava*. For here, no correspondence to the form of a base is observed, because the words *chandas*, *kṣetra*, and *strī* do not correspond [to the bases]. Thus, the word in a derivative formation (*vṛtti-pada*) is indeed something other than the sentence (*vākya*). This should be understood everywhere in this manner.

For this very thing—the "inference from general observation" (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*)—is the corroborating mark (*liṅga*) here, since the establishment [of the meaning] occurs precisely through the cognition of the object. || 54 ||

He states that even when there is a difference in words between a compound (vṛtti) and its analytical sentence (vākya), sometimes there is no correspondence in meaning: "In some cases, as with the word *saptaparṇa* and others, no difference exists in the compound; yet the distinction between conventional (*rūḍhi*) and non-conventional (*arūḍhi*) usage is made for the sake of comprehension. (55)

The word *saptaparṇa* is etymologically derived as "that which has seven leaves on every joint (*parvaṇi parvaṇi*). Yet, not every tree of this description is so called; rather, only a specific species—even if its leaves are withered—is designated by that term. If this is so, why are words such as *saptaparṇa* well-known as conventional (*rūḍhi*) terms, whereas words like *rājapuruṣa* (king’s man) are not? To this he replies: "conventional and non-conventional. This distinction is made for the sake of clear understanding, in order to stabilize the recognition of the identity of a meaning established through logical derivation.

The means of demonstration [is as follows]: because it conforms to the primary meaning, terms such as *rājapuruṣa* (king’s man) possess a derivative (*yaugika*) nature; however, because there is a deviation from conformity with the meaning residing in the constituent words, terms such as *saptaparṇa* (seven-leaved) possess a conventional (*rūḍhi*) nature. Thus, usage proceeds through this distinction. For a listener is led to understanding step by step. Moreover, conventional status does not arise merely from conformity with the meaning, since even in the case of *saptaparṇa* and similar terms—which are objects of convention—such conformity may occasionally occur.

For instance, even in the case of conventional (ruḍhi) words such as *saptaparṇa* and others, there is sometimes a correspondence with the meaning of their parts; yet this does not constitute etymological (yaugika) derivation, as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Thus, compounds such as *nīlotpala* and the like, which do not actually incorporate the meanings of their constituent parts, are explained by artificially postulating a division of those parts; consequently, they are in reality distinct from sentences. Therefore, the absolute difference between the compound form (*vṛtti*) and the sentence (*vākya*) is established. || 55 ||

If the difference between a compound (vṛtti) and a sentence (vākya) is caused by the state of having a single unified meaning (ekārthībhāva), then, since multiple words can occur in an external operation (bahirvīhi), why does another compound not arise when those words mutually connect within the sense of "another’s word" (anyapadārtha)—a connection that would otherwise be impossible without such unification? To this he says: "That designation which rests upon a general [category] and that which has a specific [instance] as its object—due to the mention of the term *bahula*, there is no application of either of these two. (56)

If the compound were to apply to parts such as *susūkṣma-jaṭa-keśa* (having very fine matted hair), then the accent of the member [of the compound] would be the sublater, because it is internal (*antaraṅga*) to the other rules. 57.

He whose matted locks (*jaṭā*) and hair (*keśa*) are exceedingly fine is *susūkṣmajaṭakeśaḥ*. Here, if there were a connection between the words *sūkṣma* and *jaṭā*, then in a *viśeṣaṇa-samāsa* (descriptive compound), the final member of the compound would be accented (*antodātta*). For the accentuation of the final member in a three-word compound belonging to a *bahuvrīhi* would indeed set aside [the *antodātta* rule] because they share the same domain. However, since the two constituent parts [of *sūkṣmajaṭa*] do not form a *bahuvrīhi*, the *antodātta* accentuation of the final member would remain unprevented.

Nor can it be argued that, because it is a *paranimitta* (dependent on a subsequent element), the accent of the *bahuvrīhi* compound takes precedence over the accent of the constituent member—which is *antaraṅga* (internally conditioned)—just as in the case of *pūrvaśālāpriya*. Therefore, it must be stated that here, for the purpose of setting aside the accent of the constituent member, neither the designation of *karmadhāraya* compound (*viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa*) nor the general designation of *samāsa* derived from the rule *sup supā* by means of a separation of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*), applies due to the inclusion of the term *bahulam* ("in various ways"). 56, 57.

Now, one might object: "Since the two types of compound designation (*samāsa-saṃjñā*) do not apply to the two parts [of a compound] by the very nature of the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, why is it not stated that their absence [of designation] results from the mention of 'variously' (*bahulam*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And when the whole (*samudāya*) undergoes grammatical operation (*vṛtti*), a single part is not subject to optionality (*vibhāṣyate*); for optionality has as its fixed domain only the case of differentiation (*bheda*). (Verse 58)

Because the *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (restricted option) is understood, there is no option (*vikalpa*) in the process of forming a single unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*). Since that [process] is strictly determined by mutual dependence (*vyapekṣā*), for those parts which undergo the operation of the compound in the sense of another word (*anyapadārtha*), the formation of a single unified meaning is indeed logical due to the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) between their mutual association; thus, the designation "compound" (*samāsa*) would have applied, but it is precluded by the mention of the term *bahulam* ("in various ways"). For when there is an operation (*vṛtti*) [of the whole], there is necessarily an operation of its constituent parts.

For example, in the case of "pañcagavadhanaḥ" (one whose wealth consists of five cows) and "vāk‌tvacapriyaḥ" (one who loves speech and skin), the *tatpuruṣa* and *dvandva* compounds operate in between; thus, the application of the compound-ending suffixes (*samāsānta*) based on those [compounds] is established. This very point was stated in the Bhāṣya—namely, as a resolution for the statement of the Vārttikakāra, "The rule regarding obligatory composition applies to the final member in *dvandva* and *tatpuruṣa* compounds"—with the words: "When there is a formation (*vṛtti*), then the operation applies to all [the constituent parts]. || 58 ||

[Objection: But surely, in a single application (*prayoga*), let it be established by this option (*vibhāṣā*) that the designation *bahuvrīhi* exists [for the whole] while the designation *tatpuruṣa* is absent in its constituent parts; for this alone is its primary domain, and if it were not operative here, it would be rendered purposeless. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Since that which is its non-domain does not exist for it, there is no lack of purposeful efficacy; for in the context of non-difference (*abhedaprakrama*), all distinctions are completely set aside. (59)

Since there is an absence of separate meanings within the domain of *ekārthībhāva* (the state of having a single unified meaning), there is no occurrence of *vibhāṣā*—which consists of various modes of expression and is restricted by *vyapekṣā* (mutual expectancy)—because it does not apply where it has no scope. How, then, could this [term *vibhāṣā*] be considered "not having its purpose fulfilled"? [The word] *atyantam* [is used]. Not only is there no distinction pertaining to the whole (*samudāya*), but even that pertaining to the parts (*avayava*) is absent. This is because the meanings of the individual parts, being subordinate to the primary meaning of the whole, lose their distinctness, like sand mixed with water.

Thus, in this case, the application of a compound that would otherwise result is prevented by the inclusion of the term *bahulam* (in various cases), for the sake of achieving the desired accentuation of the individual members. For in examples such as *susūkṣmajaṭakeśaḥ* ("one with very fine matted hair") and *sunatājinavāsāḥ* ("one clothed in a beautiful antelope skin"), only the accentuation of a *bahuvrīhi* compound is desired.

In some cases, however, the accent of the whole does not differ from the accent of its constituent parts; thus, a compound of the two parts certainly occurs there. To this he says: "In the case of *mahā-kaṣṭa-śrita*, there would be no such difference in the three words, because the substitution of *āt* for the final vowel of the member in composition is not prohibited. (60)

Thus it is said: If one accepts that when a whole (samudāya) undergoes a compound formation (*vṛtti*), its constituent parts (*avayava*) also possess the state of having a single unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), then a great difficulty arises. In the case of the three-word compound *mahatkaṣṭaṃ śritaḥ*, once the compound of the two constituents is established by the rule *sanmahatparamottamotkṛṣṭāḥ pūjāyām* (Pāṇini 2.1.61), the acute accent (*āttva*) prescribed for the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) would apply. However, in this three-word compound, that acute accent would not occur because, according to common worldly understanding, the status of being an "subsequent member" (*uttarapadatva*) applies only to the very last word; since it is absent in the middle word, the compound must be understood as occurring between the constituents. Regarding the accent, however, there is no difference here.

In a *dvigu* compound, the accent of the suffix added at the end of the compound (*samāsāntodāttatva*) is superseded by the accent beginning with *sthā* (i.e., the *thāthādi-svara*). That [accent] in turn is superseded by the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛti-svara*) according to the rule "in an *ahīna* compound, the second case [member retains its accent]. That very same [accent] is the final acute of the constituent compound (*avayava-samāsāntodātta*). || 60 ||

But he says that in some cases there is a difference regarding the accent: "When the *mahāraṇya* [section] has passed, however, the accent differs from the three-word [rule]; because therein, due to its being internal (*antaraṅga*), the accent of the constituent part is the sublater. (61)

In the three-word *dvitīyā-tatpuruṣa* compound *mahad-araṇyam-atītaḥ*, the accentuation of the final member of the compound (*samāsāntodāttatva*) would be superseded by the *thāthādi*-accent, which is internal (*antaraṅga*) as it depends on a constituent part. However, in this case, the accent differs between the three-word and the two-word *tatpuruṣa* compound; specifically, the *thāthādi*-accent would override the *samāsāntodātta* in the three-word form. || 61 ||

For instance: because that which is more specifically prescribed is stronger, the accent of the *thā-thādi* group [the *udātta*] alone applies; therefore, in a two-word compound, the triad [of rules] is not applied simultaneously. (62)

Regarding the expression *mahadaraṇyaṃ mahāraṇyam*: first, when the compound *sanmahat-* (Pāṇini 2.1.61) is applied as *mahad-araṇyam*, and subsequently the word *mahāraṇya* is compounded with the word *atīta* in an accusative (*dvitīyā*) compound, the accent resulting from the rule *thāthādi-* (Pāṇini 6.2.144) becomes the final acute (*antodātta*), because that accent is stronger due to its being "left over" (*tiśiṣṭa*). This is because, since the original member-accent (*avayavāntodātta*) remains as a residual element, it possesses superior force through its attainment of a different level (*kakṣyāntaraprāpti*) and thus acts as a sublater. Thus, there is this distinction: in a three-word compound here, the accent falls on the middle syllable (*madhyodātta*), whereas in a two-word compound, it falls on the final syllable (*antodātta*).

And thus, according to the rule *sup supā*, when the number [of words] is intended to be significant, a compound of three words does not occur. However, in the case of *mahā-kaṣṭa-śrite*, since there is no difference in accent even when it is a compound of three words, there is no fault whatsoever. || 62 ||

But surely, since there is a grammatical coordination (*samanvaya*) based on the sense of "resorting to" (*śrita*), how can there be a compound of the words *mahat* and *kaṣṭa* when there is no mutual connection between them? Furthermore, in that case, the substitution of *āt* prescribed for the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) would not occur. To this, he says: "For those things whose status as objects of worship is absent, even the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyatva*)—for the sake of following the meaning of another—is not possible. (63)
