For those who claim that because there is no great connection (*sambandha*) when following the meaning of the constituent parts (*aṅga*) for the sake of a difficult-to-understand meaning, the state of being honored (*pūjyamānatva*) does not exist, there would likewise be no relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) between the members [of a compound], due to the lack of connection. Consequently, in cases such as *pañcagavadhana* ("one whose wealth consists of five cows"), since there would be no compound (*samāsa*) between the two members, the udātta accent on the final syllable of the compound (*samāsāntodāttatva*) would not occur. Yet, this [accentuation] has been established as a settled doctrine: "It is not [an accent] belonging to a member-tatpuruṣa; its being udātta on the final syllable is due to a conflict of rules (*vipratiṣedha*)."

In the expression “*khādiretaraśamyaḥ*,” the masculine gender substitution (*puṃvadbhāva*) is based on a compound of parts (*avayavasamāsa*). Furthermore, for the sake of favoring the principal element, the parts indeed become mutually connected; for it is a substance (*dravya*) together with its qualities (*saguṇa*) that is linked to the action. Even when the connection is Vedic (*śrauta*), because [the quality] rests upon the substance, the quality is joined to the action only by means of its specific qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*).

Therefore, even when proceeding with a collective compound (*samudāya-samāsa*), there is indeed a mutual connection between the two members; thus, because there is no difference in accent (*svara*) or form (*rūpa*) in what relies on great difficulty, a three-word compound was stated even by way of concession. However, since the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) holds that "a case-inflected word with another case-inflected word" (*sup-supā*) implies a specific number, there is no three-word *dvitīyā*-compound. Consequently, in the example "gone beyond the great forest" (*mahāraṇyātītaḥ*), the desired accent is achieved through a two-word compound.

In the case of *bahuvrīhi* and *dvandva* compounds, because of the inclusion of the term "multiple" (*aneka*), it is established as a general rule that the compound is formed without distinction. In those cases, only when preceded by a direction or a number does the *tatpuruṣa* function as a constituent member; this is prescribed for the final member (*uttarapada*) by the rule *taddhitārthottarapada-*. Consequently, in that very instance, the internal accent (*antaraṅga-svara*) based upon that [compound] applies. However, in examples such as *susūkṣmajaṭakeśa*, due to the inclusion of the term "diversely" (*bahula*), there is an absence of the descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) for the two constituent parts.

Furthermore, since the parts of a whole lack the capacity to produce their own effects independently when they exist in dependence upon that whole, the status of being a single word is established by the very formation of the aggregate compound (*samāsa*). For example, when there is reduplication of the whole—as in *papāca*—there is no reduplication of the individual parts. However, in cases such as *pūrvaśālāpriyaḥ*, the term "dvigu" is explicitly stated in the rule for the sake of establishing the accent and the final suffix of the compound within the subsequent member (*uttarapada*).

In the case of "khādiretaraśamyaḥ," first the compound *itara-śamyā* is formed as a descriptive determinative (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) meaning "the other peg. Then, in the two-word possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*) "that which has a khadira-peg as its other peg" (*khādirī itaraśamyā yasya*), the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) for the final member is established; thus, all desired results are achieved. || 63 ||

He demonstrates the very distinction between the sentence (*vākya*) and the compound (*vṛtti*) that was under discussion, for the sake of another investigation: "Even if a qualifier (*viśeṣa*) is heard [as part of the meaning], it exists either in the primary elements (*pradhāna*) or in the subordinate elements (*guṇa*). However, because of the difference in the words themselves, such a qualifier never exists in a compound (*vṛtti*) as it does in a sentence (*vākya*). (64)

In the sentence "the king's man who is prosperous" (*ṛddhasya rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), a qualification of the king characterized by prosperity is heard; however, in the compound *rājapuruṣaḥ*, there is no such qualification of "prosperous" for the king, because that which is merged with the principal meaning cannot be connected with its own qualifier. And this is possible only if the compound and the sentence are distinct words. But when the compound is derived from the sentence, the properties belonging to the sentence persist in the compound.

In the case of "the cows of Devadatta are variegated" (*citragavo yasya devadattasya*), although the specific individual such as Devadatta—the primary referent of the external compound—is heard in the sentence and is intended [to be conveyed], he is not included within the compound *citragu*. Thus, when the objection is raised that the subsequent application of the verb (*anuprayoga*) is untenable because the meaning of the word has already been expressed, it is resolved by the statement: "Or rather, it is not so, because [the specific] has not been expressed" (*na vā anabhihitatvāt*). For it is the general sense of the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) that is included in the compound, but not its specific particulars. || 64 ||

Now, one might object: since in a compound (vṛtti) a quality cannot be connected with its own qualifier, in the case of *kṛtapūrvi kaṭam* ("one who has previously made a mat"), there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between "made" (*kṛta*) and "mat" (*kaṭa*). Thus, in the absence of a connection to an action, the status of being an object (*karmatā*) would not obtain. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Even when the connection with a specific object has been exhausted by words such as 'made' (*kṛta*), another word 'made' (*kṛta*) functions independently of that specific [object]. (65)

In sentences such as "The mat was previously made by him" (*kṛtaḥ pūrvaṃ kaṭo'nena*) or "Rice was previously eaten by him" (*bhuktaḥ pūrvamodano'nena*), the mat and so forth are connected with a qualified object (*viśiṣṭa-karman*). Because that qualified object has been expressed (*nirbhukta*) and denoted (*abhihita*) by the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*), the accusative case does not occur. However, in the compound *kṛtapūrvī kaṭam*, since the meaning of the root *kṛ* (the act of making) follows the primary meaning [of the suffix], there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with its own object, the mat and so forth, because it lacks independence. || 65 ||

Therefore, he says that this word *kṛta* in the compound (*vṛtti*) is indeed different from the transitive word *kṛta* found in the sentence; thus, while being intransitive, it connects with an external object such as a mat (*kaṭa*). He states: "When [the root] is intransitive, the form ending in *-kta* expresses the abstract state (*bhāva*); therefore, there occurs a connection between that [state] and objects through an agent who possesses the action. (66)

Because there is an absolute difference between a derivative form (*vṛtti*) and a sentence (*vākya*), even though the word *kṛta* is capable of being construed with a qualified object in a sentence, in a derivative form it is understood as having only a general object, since the expression of a specific [object] is not possible therein. And because that [specific object] is invariably concomitant (*nāntarīyaka*) and thus unintended to be expressed, this word *kṛta* becomes intransitive (*akarmaka*), signifying the abstract action (*bhāva*). For it is well known that the general object is invariably concomitant.

Just as it is well known that "one who has been initiated does not give," implying an action devoid of an object, so too is this [the case here]; thus, the state (*bhāva*) is said to be the culminating point (*niṣṭhā*) in this context. And accordingly, the agent denoted by the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is delimited by the action, as in "Devadatta who previously made" (*kṛtapūrvī devadattaḥ*). Furthermore, his connection with an external object such as a mat is observed, as in "the mat."

Furthermore, since the relation between factors of action (*kāraka*) and their activity is inseparable, and because no other activity is present here, it is logical that the connection is made precisely with the activity that serves as the qualifier for the meaning of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*). Therefore, the status of being an object (*karman*) for the mat (*kaṭa*) and so forth is dependent on that very activity, as in *kṛtapūrvī kaṭam* ("one who has previously made a mat") and *bhuktapūrvī odanam* ("one who has previously eaten rice"). Since the past passive participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*) here denotes the abstract state (*bhāva*), the activity itself is what is expressed by the word ending in that suffix. This very point was stated in the Bhāṣya: "That relationship between 'the one who has made' (*kṛta*) and 'the mat' (*kaṭa*) ceases once the suffix has been produced."

"And since there is a semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) between the verb *karoti* and the mat (*kaṭa*), the accusative case will indeed occur. [Response: The connection of that which is produced by a specific object such as a mat, which exists at the level of the sentence (*vākya*), ceases once the nominal derivation (*taddhita*) has occurred in the compound (*vṛtti*). Due to the inherent nature of linguistic power (*śabdaśakti-svābhāvyāt*), there is no expression of the specific [object] in the compound, because the relationship is understood through the general object alone. Thus, according to established usage, this action is "without an object" (*akarmikā*) because it expresses a state (*bhāva*); therefore, the suffix *kta* denotes the state. Consequently, the mat and so forth, being pervaded by the action expressed therein, becomes the "object" (*karman*); this is the meaning of the logical consistency (*samanvaya-upapatti*). || 66 ||

Now, one might object: "In the formation of a secondary derivative (taddhita), the action, being subordinate to the agent, is understood in its undifferentiated state within the compound; it is not perceived as distinct from the agent with its own primary nature. Therefore, how can there be a connection between that action and an object such as a mat? Anticipating this doubt, he explains this point by means of an illustration: "Just as an action residing in [verbs] such as 'gone' (gata), though itself without a physical form, is connected with objects such as a village, so too is the action situated in formations such as *kṛtapūrvi* (one who has previously done) connected [with its object]. (67)

In expressions such as "Devadatta has gone to the village" (*grāmaṃ gato devadattaḥ*) or "he goes to the village" (*grāmaṃ gacchati*), because the agent of the action of going is denoted by the word *gata* (gone) and so forth, there is no separate apprehension of the action of going from that agent; therefore, it is *avigrahā* (without a distinct analytical separation).

For in all cases, the meaning of the base (prakṛti) is subordinate to the meaning of the suffix (pratyaya), because the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) as engaged in an operation is understood from the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*); thus, action (*kriyā*) attains primacy only through the medium of the factors of action (*kāraka*), and not by itself, since in every instance the meaning of the base is subordinate. Consequently, action is never perceived as distinct from the factor of action. For action, being of the nature of a specific activity of the factors of action, must properly be expressed by the base that follows the suffix denoting those [factors], as it is inherent in them.

Furthermore, there is no usage of a verbal root that expresses action alone; rather, it is conveyed as something already accomplished by means of suffixes such as *ik*, *ktin*, and so forth, and not in its essential form as a state being brought into existence. Therefore, since every action is necessarily conjoined with a factor of action (*kāraka*), it is connected with the object (*karman*); thus, even in cases such as *kṛtapūrvī* ("one who has previously done"), the logical connection is established precisely through such [an action]. || 67 ||

If the word *kṛta* were unable to include the specific object within the verbal complex (*vṛtti*), then in cases such as *muṇḍaṃ karoti* (he makes [him] bald), *muṇḍayati*, *sūtrayati*, *miśrayati*, and so forth, there would likewise be no manifestation of the specific [object], such as the boy (*māṇavaka*). Furthermore, since words like *muṇḍi* do not denote the action in the same way that *kṛta* does, how could there be a connection with an external object like the boy, given that [the action] is already included within the specific action? To this, he says: "Verbal roots (*dhātu*) such as *muṇḍi* and *sūtri* are, as it were, followed by unreal parts;
they are divided and possess imagined natures, like *kuṭṭi* and *carci*. (68)

The statement "he makes [the head] shaven" (*muṇḍaṃ karoti*) and so forth is merely a means of grammatical derivation through the conceptualization of bases (*prakṛti*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*); thus, there appears here a following of parts due to the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of difference residing therein. In reality, however, these verbal roots (*dhātu*), which express a qualified action and from which the distinction between subject and object has been eliminated, are derived in this manner; for the cognition of the whole sublates the cognition of the parts. Consequently, their connection with their respective objects is not contradicted.

For the division is postulated for the sake of grammatical exposition: that which is expressed by the verbal root (*prakṛti*)—such as *muṇḍa* and the like—is the quality (*guṇa*), while that which is expressed by the suffix (*pratyaya*) is the meaning of the action (*karoti*). For the verb *muṇḍayati* denotes the cutting of hair; thus, the student (*māṇavaka*) is its direct object. Similarly, in cases such as *sūtrayati*, the grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) and so forth are the objects. Alternatively, words like *muṇḍa* are inherently dependent on a quality (*guṇa*) and are therefore connected with an external possessor of that quality (*guṇin*), such as a student. Or else, the cutting of hair, being a specific form of action, is the object of the root *kṛ*.

But the boy and so forth are the object (*karman*) of that which is qualified by it. As in the case of *kuṭṭi* and *carci*, it is logical that these two serve as examples because their partlessness is well-established due to their being recited directly among the verbal roots (*dhātu*). || 68 ||

Thus, he states that even elsewhere the distinction between base and suffix is merely a means of grammatical exposition: "In the form *putrīyati*, there is no actual son; rather, there is such a specific desire which, without following an existing son, is fixed upon [the mere concept of] a son. (69)
In this context, the word "putra" (son) is an unreal, imagined constituent part; thus, the desire qualified by a son is expressed by the term "putrīyati. (69)

If, then, [the desire] resides in the son, one might suspect that this desire would be connected with external particularities of the son; anticipating this doubt, he says: "Just as the body, while living, performs the functions of the vital breaths even without them, so too here there is neither the body nor the vital breaths; rather, 'living' is simply another action. (70)

The meaning of "he lives" (jīvati) is "he sustains the vital breaths" (prāṇān dhārayati). Yet, in this [expression], the word "breath" (prāṇa) does not appear, nor is there the verbal root "to sustain" (dhārayati). Nevertheless, such an action is perceived as having a specific object; thus, because the object is internalized, it receives the designation of being "objectless," just as in the following example: || 70 ||

Likewise, in the *Putrīyā* [section], there is another ritual procedure performed by the two sons of the Subduer (the Buddha). These various distinctions are explained for the sake of further elucidation, as they serve as similar means of instruction. (71)

The "pursuit of sons" (*putrānugama*) is merely a figurative means; however, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārthataḥ*), in the word *putrīyā*, another distinct action is understood. Or rather, the expression "another action within the action of desiring a son" is a designation emphasizing the abstract state (*bhāvapradhāna*). Thus, the meaning is that it is a different action. And so, just as the root *jīv* (to live) lacks connection with an external object, likewise, in the case of *putrīyati*, this is an intransitive action.

And thus says the Bhāṣya: "Now, what are the factors of action (*sādhana*) for that which ends in *kyac*? They are the state of being (*bhāva*) and the agent (*kartṛ*). Now, what about the object (*karman*)? There is no object. However, the rule "after a word ending in a case-suffix, *kyac* is added when there is a desire for the object" is merely a means of exposition; it is an analytical description (*anvākhyāna*) by way of distinction. Here, due to the similarity with words such as "son" used in their separate forms, there arises the delusion of a division [where none exists]. (71)

One might object: "Why does the application [of the suffix *kyac*] not occur in 'putrīyati māṇavakam' (he desires a son for the boy), even though there is a different action due to an external object, just as in 'maṇḍayati māṇavakam' (he adorns the boy)? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And because of the implication by the usage of [the verb] residing in a different domain, even though the object of the desiderative suffix *kyac* exists, it is employed only in the sentence. (72)

The specific object "son" (putra), as in the action expressed by *māṇavaka* and so forth, although present in the desire for a son (*putreṣaṇā*), is not employed [as a separate object] because, in the verbal form, it is understood as a distinct meaning within the context of conduct (*vṛtti*). For when one says, "he treats the boy as a son" (*putrīyati māṇavakam*), another domain—namely, conduct—is indicated; since the suffix *kyac*, which expresses that [conduct], is employed, the sphere of desire is subsumed by *kyac*, because the meaning of conduct is what is perceived. Therefore, the employment of the specific object occurs only in the sentence itself: "he desires a son, [namely] the boy" (*putram icchati māṇavakam*). || 72 ||

By this same principle, he establishes another similar point by way of a further application: "A verbal root that expresses censure of an action is formed with the suffix *kṛt*; because its form remains identical even when repeated, it is not employed with the suffix *yaṅ*. (73)

In forms such as *lolupyate*, *caṅkramyate*, and *jaṅgamyate*, once the intensive suffix (*yaṅ*) has been applied, because both the repetition of the action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*) and the censure of the state (*bhāvagarhā*) are perceived, this [intensive] form is not used even when it is similar [to the base], because the repetition of the action is not perceived from the intensive form. Since the phrase "denoting the censure of the state" is intended as an illustration, it should also be understood as "denoting crookedness" (*kauṭilya*). Thus it has been said: "And these [intensive forms] are not used in the sense of the repetition of an action. Some explain the inclusion of the word "always" (*nitya*) for this very purpose.

Repetition (*abhyāsa*) is frequency, the intensification of an action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*). And thus, in this context, the intensification of an action is expressed solely by the sentence itself; for example, "he strides intensely" or "he strides again and again," and so forth. (73)

Thus, this conceptualization of the division of parts is merely a means for grammatical exposition (*anvākhyāna*). However, because the cognition of the meanings of the parts is sublated by the cognition of the meaning of the whole, the parts are unreal. For it is said: "Just as words are analyzed through imagined parts, so too are they to be explained by the science [of grammar]; yet the reality remains far removed from that. (74)

The word *yathā* (as) emphasizes repetition (*vīpsā*). Just as [words] are analyzed into parts as if they were conceptual constructs—since in reality they are partless and thus must be explained accordingly—so too the means of explanation consists in the conceptualization of parts; this is what is meant. However, in the ultimate sense, the treatise (*śāstra*), which consists of the conceptualization of the division of members, stands at a great distance from the eternal, partless essence of speech (*śabdatattva*) that is to be explained. For the grammatical explanation resides in the words used for the purpose of instruction.

And by means of that [analogy], which stands in the place of a "line-drawn gavaya," there occurs the comprehension of the word as it truly exists, like a real gavaya. For this very reason, there is a difference in the procedures of the various methods (*upāya*). Some indeed derive the word *bhavati* from the root *bhū* with the suffix *ti*, others from the root *bhū* with the suffix *ati*, and still others with an intermediate verbal augment (*vikaraṇa*) in between. Similarly, some derive *jñāgārika* from the word *ekaśabda*, while others derive it from the word *ekāgāra*.

The suffix *gha* is prescribed for the sense of "one who hears" (*śrotr-bhāva*) from the word *chandas*, as in the expression "one who studies that" (*tad-adhīte*). Thus, various derivational processes (*prakriyā-bheda*) have been stated, such as "the meaning of the sentence" (*vākya-artha*) and "the word" (*pada-vacana*). In the same way, one should infer the various derivational processes for words such as *putrīya*. The derivation may be from *putra* with the suffix *rīyaṇ*, or with *postrīya*, or with *ḍīya* after *putra*. And thus, even in its derivation, the word *putrīya* denotes a specific action; therefore, it is intransitive (*akarmaka*). Furthermore, when there is no fixed rule regarding derivation, some words belonging to the *uṇādi* class are also derived within the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*. || 74 ||

Thus, he concludes that the unreality of parts is universal: "Having perceived some semblance of meaning as merely imagined—whether it be a word within a sentence, a verbal root within a word, or a stem-part within a root—it is like [the fragments of] a shaven head. (75)

The sentence-meaning alone possesses the established definition [of meaning], because the indivisible sentence itself is the signifier. Accordingly, by means of the analytical cognition (*apoddhāra-buddhi*), the word—which is merely a name—is extracted and separately explained from the specific sentence-meaning, having abstracted the general form of the object that persists within it; for it is impossible to explain an indivisible sentence that possesses multiple forms. Indeed, since a word maintains an identical form across all sentences, it can be etymologically derived as denoting a general object.

And that [word-meaning], having been derived accordingly and occurring within various sentences, becomes the means for accomplishing the usage of specific meanings by virtue of accepting the particularities inherent in each respective sentence. It is not the case that it first exists as a general meaning and is then capable of accepting a particularity; for such faults as these would arise: "A general meaning that has vanished does not persist in the particular; how can there be the abandonment of what has already been grasped? Once ceased, where could it remain? Therefore, it is said that the form of the meaning is postulated as being of a general nature.

For just as that [word] is of an imagined nature because there is no linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) by means of its individual parts, so too is its meaning. Furthermore, since the word is itself analyzed through the conceptual construction (*parikalpanā*) of stem and suffix, even there, by relying on grammatical abstraction (*apoddhāra*), the respective meanings of the stem and the suffix are distinguished according to the power of imagined positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). The term "root" (*dhātu*) is an illustration for the form of the stem; the suffix (*pratyaya*) is also included.

And even there, the base form (*prakṛti*) is explained through the analysis of its constituent parts—such as *muṇḍi*, *sūtri*, and *putrī*—by means of the conceptualization of base and suffix (*prakṛti-pratyaya*). Likewise, some maintain that the letter *s* belongs to the root *as* (to be), while the letter *a* is an augment (*āgama*) here; or similarly, that *ati* is a suffix (*pratyaya*), *ti* is a suffix, and [the *a*] is an infix (*vikaraṇa*). In this way, in forms such as *syati*, *syataḥ*, and *syanti*, [the *sy-*] are suffixes, or the *syo* is an infix; other cases should be inferred in the same manner.

And if one imagines such divisions, the result is that [the word] must reside in the phonemes themselves, because those parts—such as the fourth part and so on—are not subject to conventional usage. Alternatively, if one imagines divisions down to the level of atoms, there would be no word at all; therefore, the proponent of difference must necessarily admit non-difference among the phonemes, since they are perceived as non-different.

And thus, why is it not stated that difference is unreal because it is sublated by the non-dual consciousness inherent in the sentence from the very beginning? Even in worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), the sentence alone is what is first perceived; therefore, let that very [sentence] which is conveyed by the cognition of non-duality be the truth. And this is to be ascertained from the *Vākyakāṇḍa*. (75)

Thus, even though there are differences in the methods of analysis—grammar is the means for correctness, while etymological derivation is unstable—one should not consider these various means of understanding to be ultimately real.

Regarding the subject of correctness (*sādhutva*), there is no manifold application—that is, no diverse mode of presentation—because the word, whose definition is fixed, remains of a single form despite the diversity of the means (*upāya*) by which it is reached. For the means, being constituent parts of the presentation, vanish once the goal to be reached has been attained; thus, one should not harbor the conceit that they possess ultimate reality. Furthermore, due to the variety of both the object to be communicated and the communicator, linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*) differs solely according to their respective inclinations in engaging with the material. And this same sequence applies everywhere.

For ignorance itself is the means to knowledge. Since there is no other way at the time of realization, and because it is possible to lead one [to the goal] by any means whatsoever, the attainment of the goal is seen to occur through that very ignorance. As it has been said: "In the scriptures, it is ignorance alone that is described through various systematic elaborations; but when free from traditional constructs, knowledge manifests of its own accord. (76)

Furthermore, since all means (upāyas) are unreal, even a word based on a cause (naimittika-śabda)—like an arbitrary word (yadṛcchā-śabda)—is devoid of any real division of parts; thus, there is no real distinction between words. He says: "Just as the root *ḍī* [is used] in the word *ḍittha*, and the root *pac* in the word *pācaka*, so too are both *ḍī* and *pac* themselves non-worldly (alaukika). (77)

"‘Just as... This is its clarification: both of these are *alaukika* (extraordinary), being unestablished in worldly usage. Since the division into *prakṛti* (base) and so forth is not recognized in the world, and since a partless aggregate such as ‘ḍittha’ or ‘pacati’ is what is employed in the world, the comprehension of the meaning is identical in both cases, because they are aggregates of non-different meanings. However, through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), the verbal root *ḍayi*, which has an impossible meaning, is extracted for the purpose of grammatical derivation (*anvākhyāna*) of the word ‘ḍittha’."

The only difference is that for the word *pacati*, the meaning is "possibility" (*sambhava*). And thus, when the correctness (*sādhutva*) [of words] is real, the fourfold application of words is proclaimed. || 77 ||

Therefore, he says that from that which is non-different, various divisions preceded by non-difference have been conceptually constructed by the learned for the sake of instruction regarding ignorant people: "The base and the suffix are to be inferred from the word; likewise, the word [is inferred] from those two. The treatise was not composed by the learned for the sake of those [ignorant ones], based on [the distinctions of] phonetic markers (anubandha), accents, and so forth. (78)

The learned (śiṣṭas) are the authority regarding words. For they, being in accordance with the true nature of things, accept as correct whatever serves as an auxiliary to Dharma; having inferred suitable roots and suffixes, they first analyze the worldly word extracted from the sentence. Likewise, they understand the word to be conveyed by those two [roots and suffixes] as having been inferred. Since words such as "Dittha" are taught as if they were perceived directly, this constitutes the reason for inferring suitable roots and suffixes.

However, in the case of forms such as *pacati* and the like, since they involve the inference of roots and suffixes through instruction, the entire complex (saṅghāta) is inferred within the science of grammar (*śabdānuśāsana*). For the instruction undertaken by the learned is of two kinds: either by the direct mention of the goal, as in the case of irregular forms (*nipātana*), or by following the mention of the means, as in the case of a rule (*vidhi*).

In that regard, the assignment of *anubandhas* (indicatory letters) for the *prakṛtis* (bases) is established as fixed by observing the non-perception of forms such as the letter *ñ*; however, for the *pratyayas* (suffixes), the assignment of *anubandhas* is likewise determined by observing [phenomena] such as vowel-quality (*svara*) and vowel-increment (*vṛddhi*). As for the remaining [words], because they consist of unobscured manifestation (*nirāvaraṇakhyāti*), they are already fully unfolded within the nature of intuitive awareness (*pratibhā*); since they manifest correctly as pervading all entities, there is no need for instruction at present, as they are established through the study of the beginningless scripture alone.

And thus, since in some cases there is even no dependence on a means [for their application], they are indeed unreal. For this very reason it is proclaimed: "The *Aṣṭādhyāyī* is for the sake of the thorough knowledge of the learned (*śiṣṭa*). (78)

But he who, disregarding the tradition of the learned, takes refuge in the scripture alone—[regarding him it is said]: "The vision of the scripture is not certain even when the scripture is merely obtained; for those who do not see the scripture as their eye, [acting] is joined with transgression. (79)

Since the general rule "bahulam anyatarasyām ekeṣām" and others merely establish the possibility of an application without determining the specific scope of a particular injunction, one who employs words according to his own whim—without following the usage of the learned—is connected with demerit due to the use of incorrect words. For merit and demerit are rooted in usage; therefore, the grammatical definition must be established by determining its specific scope in accordance with the usage of the learned.

If this is so, let it be simply the usage of the learned (*śiṣṭa*); what is the use of a purposeless treatise? To this he says: For those who do not perceive the usage of the learned—that is, for those who do not directly observe it—the treatise itself is the eye, as it were, because it is a compendium that reveals the true nature of words (*śabdatattva*). And thus, having learned the words characterized by the treatise, they infer the learned who employ correct forms independently of the grammatical rules. Furthermore, by removing their error regarding the general characteristics [of correct speech] from them, the treatise also becomes fruitful.
And thus it has been said: "Grammar consists of the defined and the definition"; and also: "This *Aṣṭādhyāyī* is for the purpose of identifying the learned. (79)

If, then, the treatise is the eye, why is it sometimes rejected with the statement, "or because an undesirable [consequence] is not seen"? Anticipating this objection, he says: "And because it expresses a different meaning, the sequence [of words] does not differ—in cases such as *rājadanta* (king’s tooth), *āhitāgni* (one who has established the sacred fires), and *rājāśva* (king’s horse), and so forth, in every respect. (80)

Regarding the fixed worldly sequence found in terms such as *rājadanta* ("king-tooth" or "teeth-king"), it is not altered and never occurs otherwise; thus, because no deviation is observed, the formal rule (*śāstra*) in this case is set aside. Where both usage and non-usage are seen with respect to a single meaning, there the commencement of a formal rule is fruitful by way of preventing non-usage.

In this case, however, when there is a reversal of usage—as in *dantārājaḥ* (king of teeth) or *aśvarājaḥ* (king of horses)—a meaning contrary to what was intended is understood; but this is not the case in expressions such as *rājadantaḥ* (king-tooth). When the meaning is the same, that which is in accordance with the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*) excludes that which is not so in accordance. As for compounds like *āhitāgni*, although there is no fixed rule regarding the order of usage, no difference in meaning is observed; therefore, a total rejection [of the rule] is indeed more appropriate. In some places, however, the reading is: "The meaning is that there is no priority or posteriority in terms of being presented [as the primary element]. || 80 ||

If, then, the grammatical rule (*śāstra*) regarding this [suffix] is rejected because its non-occurrence is not observed, one might ask: "In cases such as *gargāḥ*, what function would the rule for elision (*luk*) serve? To this, he says: "Those words such as *garga* and others, which denote distinct meanings even without suffixes when used in a compound (*vṛtti*), their correctness is established by means of elision (*luk*). (81)

Regarding the view that the denotation of meaning by words is inherent (*svābhāvika*), [the author] states in the *Vṛtti* that in cases of *ekārthībhāva*, such as *gargāḥ* and *vatsāḥ*, the suffixes express the meaning of the offspring—which is distinct from the meaning of the base—even without the application of a secondary suffix (*apatyapratyaya*). Furthermore, forms such as *gārgyaḥ* are observed to denote that meaning when accompanied by a suffix. Since it is established by the rule *paraśca* that "a base alone should not be employed," it follows that according to the formal procedure of the grammar (*śāstraprakriyā*), the base in its isolated form would be considered ungrammatical (*asādhutva*). Therefore, the prescription of elision (*lug-anvākhyāna*) becomes logically justified. || 81 ||

Even so, the application of *garga* and other such terms to a descendant is not established merely by the relation "this is that" (*so 'yam*). For instance, in expressions such as "Bhṛgu moves" or "Aṅgiras moves," the term is used for the descendant even when the possessor of the descendant (the ancestor) is present; therefore, what is the purpose of explaining the elision (*luk*)? To this, he says: "If terms such as *babhru* were to be employed for a descendant without a suffix, due to the relation 'this is that,' then there would be a restriction [only] regarding the descendant. (82)

This [term] "Gargas" is applied to the descendant by means of a metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) as "this very person," based on a prior relationship between the offspring and the offspring-like [ancestor]. Thus, the relationship of non-difference (*abheda-sambandha*) is expressed. For, due to the impossibility of the plural number [otherwise], the descendants of Garga are what are denoted; since the primary source [the ancestor] is a single entity, the plural number would otherwise be untenable.

In that case, since a relationship of difference (*bheda-sambandha*) is not intended when there is a relationship of non-difference (*abheda-sambandha*), it can be argued that the patronymic suffix (*apatya-pratyaya*) does not exist and thus its elision (*luk*) need not be mentioned; however, because a metaphorical relationship of non-difference cannot exist without being preceded by a fixed relationship of difference, it can also be argued that even the students (*antevāsinaḥ*) of Garga—who have the form "Garga" superimposed upon them—are conveyed by the plural number. Therefore, it is not understood as a rule that [the term] denotes only offspring and the like.

Therefore, in the case of offspring (*apatya*), the elision (*luk*) of the secondary suffix (*pratyaya*) is stated for the purpose of restriction. However, by its very nature, the base (*prakṛti*) itself expresses that meaning even when devoid of a suffix. Elsewhere, elision serves the purpose of applying the grammatical operations conditioned by a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*); here, however, it serves the purpose of restricting the meaning. 82.

If it is argued that the elision (*luk*) of the suffix must be initiated for the sake of this understanding of the meaning "she is to be led as a wife," otherwise one might suspect that the wife would not be understood by necessity, [the author] says: "In the case of the connection 'this is he,' without the indication of gender and secondary marks, the wife alone is not necessarily understood in the case of words such as *praṣṭhī*. (83)

It is true that even in this case, there would be no restriction [to denote the wife] through non-difference without an effort; for here too there is an effort, since the feminine suffix is a marker of gender according to the rule *puṃyogādākhyāyām*.

For by the mention of the word *ākhyā* (name/designation), it is explained that the feminine suffix is applied only to a word that has been observed in usage in such a form when referring to a male; thus, because a word ending in a *taddhita* suffix lacks the nature of being a *ākhyā*, its non-arising is inferred, and consequently, despite the existence of a relationship of non-difference, the understanding of the wife arises from words such as *praṣṭhā* only with the assistance of the feminine suffix.

[Objection: But why is there no such understanding [of the word "man"] even in the case of *Ṛbhu’s sister* and others? [Response: Not so; for since the agency of setting out belongs to the male, the masculine term is applied even to a woman when she performs the arrangements for the departure. And the role of being the one who makes the arrangements belongs only to the wife, not to anyone else. || 83 ||

Anticipating the objection that, in cases such as "a *prastha* of rice" (*prastho vrīhiḥ*), the elision of the suffix must be formally prescribed (*anvākhyeya*) in order to convey the restrictive sense that "it is measured by a *prastha*," he says: "When a specific relationship between the measure and the thing measured is accepted, then, in that case, words such as *prastha* would be grammatically incorrect (*asādhutva*) without the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*). (84)

The derivative [suffix] may optionally form either a compound or a sentence according to the distinction of usage; furthermore, in that case, when there is an excess of measure, the nominative case is prescribed again.

In this case as well, the connection between the means of knowledge (*māna*) and the object of knowledge (*meyayoga*) is not invariably perceived through the relation of non-difference by means of superimposition (*adhyāropa*), since relations such as proximity (*samīpya*) are also possible; therefore, the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) would apply by the rule "that is its measure" (*tadasya parimāṇam*) through a separation of the grammatical rule (*yogavibhāga*). Alternatively, the full sentence may be formed by the "great option" (*mahāvibhāṣā*): "A *prastha* is indeed the measure of the rice. A separate effort has been undertaken to formulate the definition of the nominative case (*prathamā*) when the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) exceeds [the mere measure] by including the measure itself.

When there is the denotation of a secondary term such as *vrīhi* (rice) measured by a *prastha*, the nominative case is established simply by the inclusion of the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself, through the relation "this is that" (*so 'yam*). [Thus one says] *prastho vrīhayaḥ* ("A *prastha* [measure] of rice"), meaning "the measure (*parimāṇa*) of these rice-grains is a *prastha*. When the object of cognition (*prameya*) exceeds the measure, it is taught by again employing the word for the measure; therefore, from a word for a measure ending in the nominative, the object of cognition is understood in its primary sense alone. Furthermore, even a *taddhita* suffix is not barred by the force of the explicit statement, as in *prāsthikaḥ* ("measured by a *prastha*"), which is optionally prescribed (*vibhāṣita*). A full sentence (*vākya*) also occurs. || 84, 85 ||

But how can a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) denoting a measure (*parimāṇa*) function in reference to that which is measured (*parimeya*)? To this he says: "If [the suffix] is correct when distinct [from the stem], that itself is the illustration; it is joined with all case-endings (*vibhakti*) once the addition [of the suffix] has been accepted. (86)

Therefore, the re-enactment of the nominative case (*prathamā*) by means of measurement (*parimāṇa*) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the expression of an object distinct from that which is conditioned by the relationship between the measure and the measurable. For it is made known that the denotation of the object by measures such as a *prastha* is inherent. And thus, just as by a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*), a distinct object of cognition (*prameya*) is expressed, so too is it expressed by the nominative case.

In that context, when the internal relationship between the means of knowledge (*māna*) and the object of knowledge (*meyasaṃbandha*) has fulfilled its purpose, the nominative case (*prathamā*) is superseded by other case-endings, such as the accusative (*dvitīyā*), when an external distinction—such as the object (*karman*) manifested through action—is required for the sake of further specification. Therefore, a word denoting the object of measurement (*parimeya*) is joined with, or connected to, all the case-endings from the second onwards, according to the specific increase in meaning characterized by the various powers (*śakti*) of the object and so forth manifested through external action, which it has accepted and embraced.

"‘He cooks a *prastha* [of rice],' ‘purchased for a *prastha*,' and so forth. Even though the expression occurs through such metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*), the effort to formulate rules such as elision (*luk*) is undertaken for the sake of restriction. || 86 ||

Since the connection between a quality and that which possesses the quality is fixed by their very nature, for what purpose is the elision of the *matup* suffix prescribed after words expressing qualities? To this he says: "The elision of *matup* after words such as *śukla* (white) is because a distinction [between the quality and the qualified] is observed. They are prescribed for the sake of preventing ungrammaticality, just like [the suffixes] *bidādi*. (87)

The distinction [of the quality from the substance] is observed in the expression "the whiteness of the cloth" (*paṭasya śuklaḥ*). Likewise, in the case of "the white cloth" (*śuklaḥ paṭaḥ*), where there is no such distinction, the suffix *matup* would be required; thus, there might arise the suspicion that the base word alone is ungrammatical. Therefore, it is appropriate to prescribe the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *matup* which has been produced based on that distinction. For, having stated that [the form] is established because there is no distinction, the elision itself is subsequently justified by the remark, "no distinction is perceived."

Furthermore, by way of explaining the suffix *lug*, it is stated that the application [of the term] to the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*) occurs through a relationship, just as in the case of words such as "the Bidas" (*bidāḥ*) or "the Gargas" (*gargāḥ*). For just as words like "the Bidas" are fit for usage because they denote the meaning of offspring qualified by its own [original] meaning, so too are words like "white" (*śukla*); the point is that it is not solely due to a relationship expressed as "this is that" (*so 'yam*) [that they apply]. || 87 ||

Thus, having concluded the discussion that arose incidentally—preceded by the establishment of the relationship between qualifier and qualified (viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva) through the introduction of co-referential application (samānādhikaraṇa-vṛtti)—he speaks as follows to first explain the very subject at hand, the relationship between qualifier and qualified, which appears untenable given the perception of non-difference (*abheda*) in the compound, according to the opinion of certain [grammarians]: "When there is an intensification of the identity [of the qualifier] with the object qualified, and when there is a subsequent withdrawal [of that intensification], some declare this to be the function [of the compound]. (88)

In this case, if two things—the qualifier and the qualified—were grasped by a single cognition, there would be no apprehension of their mutual assistance; what kind of relationship of qualifier and qualified could there then be? For in reality, there is nothing such as a "qualifier" that is restricted to a specific genus. Furthermore, a single verbal cognition is not appropriate here; for due to the sequence of denotation, it is logical that the cognition of the denoted objects occurs only sequentially.

Consequently, according to the principle that "there is no cognition of the qualified without the apprehension of the qualifier," there is first the apprehension of the qualifier. Then, when the state of being the qualifier—which consists of the form of the qualifier—is superadded (abhyuccaya) to the qualified object as its delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) because it has been apprehended as such, and when this superaddition of the state of being the qualifier is subsequently withdrawn due to non-proximity (*asannidhi*), the resulting operation of disregarding that very superaddition is *ekārthībhāva* (the unification into a single meaning).

For a qualifier, having fulfilled its purpose by imparting excellence to the qualificand, does not further augment the specific nature of the object in its own form, lest there be a futile conclusion. And thus, the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) in the application (*vṛtti*) is appropriately understood as pertaining only to the qualified entity. || 88 ||

He refutes this view as follows: "The prior cognition [of the cause] has not reached the causal object; nor does the intellect possess the same form as the causal object when it perceives that which possesses the cause. (89)

There is no connection [of the object] with cognition even when accompanied by mental impressions (saṃskāra), nor even with memory; for if it were through their operation, an object of such a kind would not be graspable.

This is the refutation against the theory that the substratum (ālambana) of cognition is distinct from its cause (nimitta). In this view, the first cognition regarding the qualifier—which is intended to be the limiting factor (avacchedaka) of the cause—is not attained by the qualificand (viśeṣya), which is intended to be the substrate of that cause. For in this position, there is no apprehension of the qualificand at the time of the apprehension of the qualifier, because the former has already ceased to exist by then. Furthermore, in the cognition or knowledge regarding the object intended as the qualificand—that is, the substrate possessing the cause—the cause, being the qualifier, does not appear; therefore, the object is not "colored" (ācchurita) by it.

And thus, how could cognition, which consists merely in the apprehension of the essential nature of an object, grasp therein the state of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatā*) and the state of being a qualificand (*viśeṣyatā*)? For the state of being a qualifier is dependent upon the qualificand, and the state of being a qualificand is dependent upon the qualifier; therefore, since the respective natures of each do not appear within the other's cognition, the relative relationship of qualifier and qualificand would not be grasped.

Now, if it is argued that because a subsequent cognition depends upon the latent impression (*vāsanā*) deposited by a prior cognition, therefore—even though both are experienced sequentially—a protracted memory arises later through the sequence of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), which then makes known the relationship of the delimitum and the delimiter (*avacchedyāvacchedakabhāva*); that too is not correct. For since memory arises in accordance with the experience, how could it conceive of an addition to the form of the object grasped in that experience—namely, a conjunction, a mutual linking, or a synthesis in the form of the relationship between the delimited and the delimiter?

For in this way, its status as having an object that has already been experienced would be undermined, and thus it would be invalid (*apramāṇa*). Now, just as memory is said to have that [external] object as its domain because of its connection with an external object, so too, since the external object does not exist at that time, the various powers (*śakti*) belonging to the internal cognizing subject (*pramātṛ*) who connects [the experience] are also the cause of that [memory]. When the utility of those causes in relation to the relationship between the delimiting factor and the delimited (*avacchedyāvacchedakabhāva*) is being stated here, the external thing graspable by experience—

It would not possess the form of qualifier and qualified; for since objects are joined together by the power of the cognizer alone, even when no actual conjunction exists, a real relationship of qualifier and qualified is not established. (89, 90)

If it is argued that [the object] must be real (bhāvika), he says: "And when it is a modification of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇavṛtti), the postulation of an external object is useless. Therefore, either it does not assist [the cognition], or the object of apprehension does not exist in that manner. (91)

The internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is the activity; he who possesses it is called the synthesizing cognizer (*anusandhātṛ*), that is, the knower (*pramātṛ*). Alternatively, the internal organ is the mind (*manas*) which grasps all objects. When its function—its operation—is admitted here with respect to the relationship between qualifier and qualified and so forth, in every case it is the internal organ itself whose reflection is superimposed as an external form upon the object. Since the course of worldly life is accomplished by that alone, what is the use of postulating an external object that is logically untenable? [Thus addresses] the proponent of external objects (*bāhyārthavādin*).

This is now explained: for that [conceptual construction], the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) and so forth is intended to be inherent in the real entity (*vastusamavāyin*). Thus, since conceptual constructions are rooted in experience, this conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*) of qualifier and qualified arises from the experience of that [entity]. And in that case, because the cognition exhausts itself within its own respective object, there is no assistance—characterized by delimiting the qualified—rendered to the object standing apart [from the cognition].

However, if a mental conceptual construction is admitted on the basis of a synthesizing subject (*anusandhātṛ*), then it has been stated that the apprehended object is devoid of that [subject’s] form; this is the conclusion regarding the matter at hand. || 91 ||

Having thus demonstrated the inconsistency in the opponent's view regarding the position that cognition has distinct objects as its support, he speaks—according to his own view, by means of the doctrine that cognition has a single object as its support—in order to establish the real relationship between qualifier and qualified: "Cognition proceeds toward an object as if it were permeated by its connection [with other qualities]; however, commentators then describe it by dividing it into its distinct parts. (92)
And while that [object] is undivided within the self, those who rely on another cognition imagine, as it were, a distinction between the qualifier and the qualified. (93)

In this world, cognitions arise in accordance with the object. An object, though qualified by adjuncts such as genus (*jāti*) and quality (*guṇa*), is non-differentiated; thus, the cognition is indeed non-differentiated. For genus and the other factors, whose differences are concealed by inherence (*samavāya*), are the appropriate causes for objects. In that regard, when the whiteness of the inherent cause is perceived, there arises a cognition of the white [object]. These two are said to stand in a relation of cause and effect based on the dependence upon a difference between ultimately real categories; however, this is stated because [otherwise] it would be inappropriate [to speak of a sequence].

However, at the moment of appearance, there is no sequence, because a specific object arises instantaneously as a single manifestation. For this very reason, some deny that universals (*jāti*) and other such factors are related [to the object]. Thus, since there is an absence of a relation preceded by a perception of difference, this cognition is said to be "as if permeated" by the related factors such as universals. In reality, however, because objects lack a relation preceded by difference, it is spoken of in this way according to the actual state of things.

Thus, in the case of a blue lotus and the like, where quality and substance appear in a non-differentiated cognition, there is an absence of the relationship between the delimited and the delimiting (*avacchedyāvacchedakabhāva*) which is preceded by difference; rather, because a partless entity can be communicated to others, at the time of communication, the speakers—by means of an analytical cognition (*apoddhārabuddhi*)—separate those objects such as universals (*jāti*) and so forth, which are actually conjoined, and [distinguish them] through the differentiation of another cognition according to the previously explained method: "this is the quality or universal, the qualifier," and "this is the substance, the qualified."

They provide instruction, and those who practice do so in exactly that manner. Thus, because the instruction follows the seed of the actual entity (*vastu*), the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyatva*) exists externally as a real state of being. For it is precisely that external reality, when conjoined, which is analyzed for the sake of explanation. In that context, there exists a quality (*guṇa*) and so forth as a qualifier that colors the substance (*dravya*), since a substance devoid of genus (*jāti*) and the like is impossible; and the relation is inherence (*samavāya*). Therefore, everything is real.

And thus, by means of the conceptualization of division (*vibhāga-kalpanā*), that very object, which is in essence indivisible, becomes presented [to consciousness]. And it is precisely through that cognition of division, assuming the form of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya*), that speakers engage in linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*). Although the state of division belongs to the stage of the sentence (*vākya-daśā*), nevertheless, due to the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the knowledge present at the stage of the sentence, there indeed exists in the word-meaning (*vṛtti*) the cognition of the qualified and the qualifier as distinct. However, in ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the object in the word-meaning is indeed partless; therefore, it is established that the expressive word-meaning is also partless.
Thus, by means of the distinction between their respective properties, the absolute difference between the *vṛtti* and the sentence has been established. || 92-93 ||

Another view is also proposed in the Bhāṣya: "Now, as for those who maintain the *vṛtti*, what do they say? They say that *vṛtti* is the imparting of meaning for the sake of another. This he explains: "Those who, for the sake of the ignorant, maintain the *vṛtti* as something contrived, declare that in the expression of meaning for another, it possesses the nature of both relinquishment (*tyāga*) and addition (*abhyuccaya*). (94)

Unwise practitioners, being unable to comprehend the indivisible nature of the *vṛtti* as the meaning of words, are those who grasp only what they have heard; for they consider the word as it is uttered to be merely literal. Consequently, for their sake, when the *vṛtti* is explained within the grammatical system (*prakriyā*) by means of analyzing the sentence, that *vṛtti* remains fundamentally based upon the sentence. And since the sentence is eternal with respect to its own object and thus cannot be destroyed, the *vṛtti*—which is superimposed and imagined as having the sentence as its source—is thereby brought about.

In that regard, it is observed that an effect possesses a function exceeding that of its cause, as in the case of a cloth and the like. Likewise here too, since it is logical that the effect characterized by the *vṛtti* should possess an excellence over the meanings of the words contained within the sentence, the definition of *vṛtti*—which consists in the expression of a meaning for the sake of another—is now commenced.

Regarding the meaning of another principal word (*pradhāna-pada*), its communication by means of a subordinate word (*upasarjana-pada*): in that context, according to the view of certain investigators who state, "Some say that a single word has multiple meanings," the expression of the other's meaning in a compound (*vṛtti*) is said to occur in consideration of the obstruction of the subordinate word’s capacity to denote the other’s meaning during the state of being a sentence (*vākya-avasthā*). For, due to its capacity to communicate multiple meanings, that very own-meaning of the word becomes the "other's meaning" (*parārtha*) in that instance.

When the principle that "it is improper for a word to have multiple meanings" is applied, then in a *vṛtti* (compound), the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) takes on a different meaning altogether. Thus, when it expresses the meaning of another, duality arises. Having abandoned the meaning present in the state of the sentence, the subordinate member denotes the meaning of another in the compound. This is just as when the curd situated in a jar is removed and milk is placed there; it cannot be placed while the curd remains. This is the *jahatsvārthā* (abandoning its own meaning) type of *vṛtti*.

If it is asked, "How can there be an abandonment [of the primary meaning] when the relationship between word and meaning is non-human (apauruṣeya)?"—we say no; for here, "abandonment" is a figurative expression for "non-adoption. Just as contact with fire ceases among atoms after having produced particular qualities born of cooking (*pākaja*), so too the subordinate meaning, having imparted a distinction to the principal meaning, ceases because its purpose has been fulfilled by that much alone. An illustration for this has been stated in the Bhāṣya: "In that case, just as a carpenter engaged in the king's work abandons his own work."

A carpenter engaged in royal service, such as the collection and storage of treasury funds, abandons his own activity—such as the cutting and squaring of wood—because it is impossible to carry out the king’s work without relinquishing his own. By this illustration, it is shown that in a compound (*vṛtti*), it is logical for subordinate members to adopt the meaning of another word while not adopting their own primary meaning.

Others, however, hold this view: even when the original meaning remains fixed, there is an addition of another meaning; this is the "excess of meaning" (*arthādhikya*) belonging to subordinate words. For instance, water placed in a jar of sand remains [within it]; likewise, the intense redness produced by lac and other causes persists even in the finished product of the threads. In the same way, the own-meaning of a subordinate word persists even when another meaning is assumed. And this is logical, because it is impossible for words to abandon a perceived object in the same manner as they abandon their own essential form.

Regarding this, an illustration is stated in the Bhāṣya: "A beggar, having obtained a second alms-offering, does not abandon the first; he strives only for accumulation. Thus, this is a *vṛtti* (compound operation) that does not abandon its own meaning (*ajahatsvārthā*). And in this way, because the meaning of the man is qualified by the meaning of the king, there arises the cognition of a qualified object. If this were so, since the meaning of the king would also be [separately] present, the dual number would result in the compound *rājapuruṣaḥ*, just as in the case of *dhavakhadirau*.

This is not the case; for in a *dvandva* compound, because the members possess equal prominence (*samaprādhānya*) and because the distinction between the two parts has emerged within the aggregate, the dual number is appropriate. Here, however, a distinct meaning (*arthāntara*), delimited by the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*), which is not directly denotable by the parts, is conveyed by the aggregate. This is as in a *bahuvrīhi*, such as "one whose garment is red" (*lohitavasana*) or "one who possesses variegated cows" (*citragu*).

Furthermore, because the external object (*parārtha*), whose internal distinctions are not expressed by its individual parts, is denoted by the whole, the case-ending attached to it takes on a number that resides in the meaning of that whole. Thus, regarding the meaningfulness of the whole, the resolution of the plural form has been stated: "Because the aggregate has a single meaning, there is no production of a *su*-suffix based on the number of the parts. Therefore, they say that this state—namely, the nature or essence of this *vṛtti* consisting of the properties of exclusion (*tyāga*) and inclusion (*abhyuccaya*)—is characterized by the expression of the external object. || 94 ||

Regarding that, it has been objected to the *jahatsvārthā* (abandoning its own meaning) theory of composition (*vṛtti*) as follows: "When it is said, 'Bring the king’s man' (*rājapuruṣam ānaya*), it would follow that any man whatsoever is brought; and when it is said, 'Bring the son of Upagu' (*aupagavam ānaya*), it would follow that any offspring whatsoever is brought. Now, one might ask: why is it not objected that there is no purpose for the usage of subordinate words (*upasarjana*) if they abandon their own meanings? This is not a valid objection, because the usage of the term "king’s man" (*rājapuruṣaḥ*) is justified as a synonym (*paryāya*), just as "barley" (*yāvaḥ*) and "barley-gruel" (*yāvakah*) are synonyms.

Likewise, so that the designation "compound" (*samāsa*) may also apply—being based on the capacity (*sāmarthya*) characterized by the unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*)—the resolution has been stated without distinction: "Even though it [the word] abandons its own primary meaning, it does not abandon it entirely; or else, it will become a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) through syntactic connection (*anvaya*). He explains this as follows: "That meaning is understood through syntactic connection, or the contradictory meaning is set aside; whether it possesses two meanings or even another meaning, they call that a subordinate member (*upasarjana*). (95)

It has been stated that the specific qualities produced in atoms by contact with fire persist even after that contact with fire has ceased. In this way, when a subordinate term ceases its function of qualifying the principal object, the person is perceived as qualified by the persistence of the specific qualities it imparted, and not merely as a person in general. Regarding this, the *Bhāṣya* provides the example of a jasmine-bag (*mallikāpuṭa*). Because the specific fragrance imparted by contact with the flower persists, the bag is still designated by that name even after the flower has been removed.

If this is so, how can it be said that "one does not abandon the object entirely" when there is a relinquishing of the object? Anticipating the objection that "the object is withdrawn in one part while it remains in another part," he states an alternative view: "or the contradictory [part] is withdrawn. That is to say, the nature which is the opposite of the delimitation of the primary object departs from the subordinate object.

And who is its counter-correlative (*pratidvandvī*), which would be the primary element? For, if these two were both primary, there would be no mutual relationship between them; consequently, the specific, delimited primary meaning could not be cognized, and thus the primary status of the subordinate element (*upasarjanārtha*) would be lost. For this very reason, it is not connected with its own qualifiers such as "prosperous" (*samṛddha*) and so forth. However, that form consisting of qualification which exists for the sake of assisting the primary element does not depart, because there is no contradiction; hence the statement that "it does not abandon [the primary] entirely."

For in every respect, if its own meaning were abandoned, the subordinate term (*upasarjana*) would lose its very nature, because there would be no benefit to the principal (*pradhāna*) by means of its own referent; indeed, the status of being a subordinate is defined by its service to another. And if there were no service to another, the usage would be purposeless, since the meaning of the principal would already be understood from the subsequent term alone. Furthermore, since that which is meaningless cannot have a connection with anything else, the designation of "compound" (*samāsa*), which is based on semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*), would not apply; therefore, there is no abandonment of the entire meaning.

Even a carpenter does not abandon coughing, laughing, and so forth—which are invariably concomitant with being a living being and are compatible with royal duties—[merely because he is a carpenter]. In the case of *jahatsvārthā* (abandoning its own meaning) operation, one's own primary [meaning] is indeed lost. However, in the case of *ajahatsvārthā* (not abandoning its own meaning) operation, the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) retains its meaning in every respect; for in that case, the subordinate word denotes the primary meaning as qualified by its own qualifiers, and is thus said to have a dual meaning.

Furthermore, because there would be a loss of distinction—like that between dust and water—in the case of the primary element due to the absence of differentiation, the category of the subordinate (guṇa) cannot be logically joined with its own particularity. Moreover, since the variety of meanings of words arises from the difference in their objects, it is logical that subordinate terms denote two meanings—one subordinate and one primary—within a compound. However, as has already been stated previously, the dual number does not occur.

Some, however, maintain that in a *jahatsvārthā* (abandoning its own meaning) compound, the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) completely abandons its own meaning and functions solely for the sake of the principal meaning. For the subordinate member, like a mere phoneme, is devoid of meaning when it has become a constituent part of the compound word. Furthermore, the term "king’s man" (*rājapuruṣa*) is a synonym for the word "man. To this, the objection is raised that in such a case, there would be no cognition of a specific type of man. || 95 ||

If, then, as in a sentence, there is also in a compound (*vṛtti*) a cognition of a qualified meaning, and thus there is no absolute abandonment [of the individual word-meanings], then the state of "abandoning one's own meaning" (*jahatsvārthatva*) would be a mere matter of words. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Diversity is merely a means; that aggregate, however, is indeed one. Or rather, the conceptualization of difference and connection arises through alternative (*vikalpa*) or cumulative (*abhyuccaya*) [modes of expression]. (96)

In a sentence (*vākya*), there is the expression of meaning through division and commencement; however, in a compound (*vṛtti*), a distinct meaning is perceived as a unity. Thus, from the ultimate perspective (*paramārthataḥ*), the word in a compound is indeed partless. The analysis based on the distinction of word-meanings found within a sentence is merely a pedagogical means (*upāyamātra*). Because it abandons its primary [literal] sense, it is described as "having abandoned its own meaning" (*jahatsvārtha*). Therefore, the Bhāṣya immediately following this states: "Alternatively, in a compound, the rule regarding semantic competency (*samartha*) is applied; for 'competency' consists of either separation (*bheda*), conjunction (*saṃsarga*), or both separation and conjunction."

He explains this with the words beginning "vikalpa" (alternative). Those who consider the word in its *vṛtti* state to be the source of the sentence construct mental constructs (*kalpanā*) regarding difference (*bheda*) or relation (*saṃsarga*) pertaining to the sentence. To illustrate: there is an alternative (*vikalpa*) as to whether the meaning of the sentence is difference or relation; there is an accumulation (*abhyuccaya*) or conjunction (*samuccaya*) of both. In that regard, when the word "man" (*puruṣa*) denotes a servant, the word "king" (*rāja*), while the master is understood in a general sense, conveys the exclusion [of the man] from other specific masters; thus, difference is the meaning of the sentence.

And here, the relation (*saṃsarga*) is that which is being inferred. However, when the word *puruṣa* denotes a genus (*jāti*), then it is understood that the meaning of this [word] is connected with the meaning of the word *rājan* as qualified [by it]; thus, the sentence-meaning is the relation. And because the relation is qualified, its distinction from other meanings is what is being inferred. Thus, there is an option (*vikalpa*) based on the distinction between the subordinate and the principal. Or, since both are cognized from the word without distinction, both possess the capacity [to denote]. Therefore, in this way, the word is a "function-word" (*vṛttipada*) whose function consists in denoting a qualified object; hence, there is no fetching of the person alone, even though the individual component [meaning] may be devoid of purpose. 96.

For this very reason, because division is a means [to the goal], the diversity of opinions is not contradictory; for since means are unstable due to the variety of individual inclinations, he says: "For those who maintain this conduct for the sake of the understanding of the ignorant, the various means of instruction are not fixed among men. (97)

For those teachers who demonstrate [the relationship] through the principle of the modification of the base (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*) while viewing the *vṛtti* and the sentence as non-different, there exist various and distinct means of instruction for the persons who are the learners; these differ due to the diversity of their inclinations (*ruci*). For those who determine that the *vṛtti* and the sentence have the same meaning, it is said that they do not abandon their own sense (*ajahatsvārthatva*). However, for those who perceive an inherent difference in meaning between the two, it is said that they abandon their own sense (*jahatsvārthatva*). Thus, the distinction is established based on a reliance upon a connection with a difference that is unreal. (97)

Thus, since there is an absolute difference between the *vṛtti* (compound) and the sentence from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the specific features of the *vṛtti*, such as the concealment of numerical distinctions, have been explained. In this regard, when it is objected that "the concealment of numerical distinctions occurs precisely because of the absence of case-endings," it was stated: "The meaning should not be caused by the word, nor should the word be caused by the meaning; rather, let it be seen that this very thing is of such a nature that its form is essentially the meaning itself."

He explains this as follows: "Whether they are expressive or indicative, those case-endings (vibhakti) which belong to numbers—when [the word] functions with respect to a constituent part possessing that same form, the distinction of number ceases. (98)

In a *trika* (a group of three meanings), case-endings (*vibhakti*) express number (*saṅkhyā*) when they follow the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*); however, in a *pañcaka* (a group of five meanings), they merely indicate it. These endings are seen employed for their own specific meanings in sentences such as "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*) or "the man of the kings" (*rājñāṃ puruṣaḥ*). Even in a compound (*vṛtti*), such as "king’s man" (*rājapuruṣa*), the first member of the word is exactly like that in the sentence; consequently, even there, case-endings prompted by specific numbers would have to be heard.

For if that word were to denote its meaning [only] when it exists, then it would not be logical to prescribe the absence of meaning when the function [of the compound] is based on the word itself; rather, because of the absence of the numeral-word in the compound (*vṛtti*), it is inferred that there is no specific number. Thus, since the distinction of number ceases due to the lack of differentiation in the subordinate member's meaning caused by its merging with the principal meaning, the non-arising of case-endings is inherent to that absence; the elision (*luk*) is merely prescribed for the sake of the technical designation "suffix" (*pratyaya-lakṣaṇa*).

Thus, the intended meaning here is that there is only an apparent similarity between the compound (*vṛtti*) and the sentence (*vākya*), and not an identity in reality; for while number and distinction exist in the sentence, they are absent in the compound. || 98 ||

Thus, first of all, is the opinion of some: that the meaning of the subordinate [word] has its numerical distinctions ceased. Others, however, think: "Either a different unity of non-distinction arises there, or that which is called the undivided form of the numbers is their state of conjunction. (99)

In a compound, because the meanings of the subordinate members (*upasarjana*) have attained the status of being existent entities (*sattvabhūta*), their connection with number is necessary. For it is not appropriate for the meaning of a subordinate member to be devoid of number like an indeclinable (*avyaya*), since there would be no cognition of its mere existence (*sattvamātra*). Nor can a specific [number] be determined. Therefore, it is inferred that there exists a form of general number which encompasses all particular numbers by way of being their common substratum (*saṃsargirūpa*).

For unity is the opposite of duality and so forth; by excluding duality and the like, it is not capable of encompassing all the various distinctions of number. This non-dual unity, however, is all-pervasive. For within this, all the various distinctions of number exist in a state of conjunction and non-separation. And such being the case, when the cause is present, those [distinctions] are seen to manifest from it, just as specific qualities such as fragrance [manifest] from the pressing of [fragrant substances] like sandalwood.

And for this reason, it will be stated that there is a determination of the specific [object] in your case regarding things such as "the month-old Śaurpika" (or Pārpika). Something may be undivided because it possesses a single nature, but it is not [necessarily] mixed. Furthermore, even in the case of a mixture, there would be distinction; therefore, both are mentioned: the form of the mixture and the undivided. || 99 ||
He explains this very point through an illustration: "Just as all the juices of medicinal herbs, when placed within honey, exist without distinction; they know that state to be such a number. (100)

In honey produced by bees (*mākṣika*), the juices of many flowers have their own forms merged within it because they constitute its effects; thus, when the sweet taste is produced through the blending of juices from various species of medicinal herbs, those diverse tastes are not perceived individually. Nevertheless, in accordance with the juices of the medicinal herbs that served as the causes, the taste, potency, and post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*) of the honey are determined; and since their capacities are inferred from the observation of their respective effects, it is concluded that those [causal juices] remain present [within the honey].

In the same way, because the determination of distinctions among numbers occurs according to their specific signs (*nimitta*), and because all particular numbers abide without distinction within the subordinate category (*upasarjana-padārtha*), the number "one" (*abheda-ekatva-saṅkhyā*) should likewise be understood as being of that very nature. For it is called "number" (*saṅkhyā*) because the various distinctions of number are abstracted from it, and not because something is counted by it—as is the case with duality and so forth. Furthermore, since the form of the connection between number and its substrate cannot be determined through a distinction from the connected entity, this [number] consists of both the universal and the particulars of number.

He states another alternative right here: "Or, through the abandonment of particularities, that [universal] which consists of number exists in such a manner by means of the operation of the generic portion, through the exclusion of particularities. (101)

Excluding those very distinctions by setting aside all differentiation, this [number] also attains the designation of "number.
