Thus, this essence of number, which is of the nature of non-dual unity, exists by means of the form of a universal (*jāti*), through the concealment of the differences between individual instances (*vyakti*). For the form of a universal is the common element underlying all numbers, characterized by the exclusion of difference (*bhedāpoha*). In the preceding case, non-dual unity was described as consisting of all differences, being merely the conjunction of all those differences.

The distinction here, however, is that this [universal] has a form that follows all particular instances and consists of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*). For just as oneness excludes duality and so forth, and duality excludes triad and so forth, so too does this non-dual oneness exclude all [other numbers] such as oneness and the rest; thus it possesses the nature of number. And since duality, oneness, and so forth are perceived when there is a basis for them, its nature as a universal is accepted here. (101)

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that universals such as 'cowness' (gotva) are known through a cognition of non-difference? And in this regard, no function whatsoever is served by non-difference or unity; for it is only the particulars (bhedas) that are connected with the operations of the treatises. Therefore, what is the evidence for their existence? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Just as a possessor of form is perceived by means of a form whose specific qualities have not been grasped, yet its specific forms—such as white and so forth—are not grasped. (102)

When immersion into the form of differentiation occurs in such a way that it is not intended to be expressed, a certain portion is manifested and is grasped as a subordinate limb (aṅga) in the scripture. || 103 ||

Just as a substance, though its specific qualities such as blue are not perceived, is understood in a general sense as "possessing form" due to its inseparable connection with those qualities—as when it is seen from a distance—so too, when the specific inherence of a particular number is not intended to be expressed, the mere understanding that "it possesses a number" arises; and because this [quality] is subordinate since it is a property of an existing entity (*sattvabhūta*), that portion which is conjoined with it becomes manifest through a specific cause, namely the substitution of *tavaka* and so forth. That [portion] is then adopted in the grammatical treatise as the cause for the derivation of words such as *tāvakīna*.

And thus, in this case, the very cognition of numerical finitude (*saṃkhyāvattva*) constitutes the effect of the non-different unity of the subordinate object. (102, 103) If, then, this non-different unity—which consists in the connection with all numbers—is not distinct from the substance, why is it that the subordinate words do not convey it as having a specific nature? To this he says: "At that time, that aspect is perceived in the form of a general number; for while an object possesses manifold powers, words possess restricted powers. (104)

Thus, the "part" (*aṃśaḥ*)—which is a portion of the meaning of the prior member and constitutes the subordinate element (*upasarjana*)—is expressed by the subordinate word precisely as a non-differentiated whole, even though, being of the nature of a substance (*sattva*), it is capable of being associated with a combination of multiple numbers. However, it possesses no power to express its specific forms. For, just as in a sentence, even in a compound (*vṛtti*), an object that possesses multiple powers is not touched by words in their entirety; this is because the powers of words have restricted domains. || 104 ||

Now, one might object: "If there is non-difference of number within the meaning of the subordinate element (*upasarjana*), how can there be a perception of difference? Or, if there is difference, how can it have the nature of non-difference? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The property of indeclinables (*avyaya*) and the sequence of those possessing difference—between these two, there exists an intermediate state worthy of being designated as non-different. (105)

"Without gender, innumerable, and indeclinable"—this innumerability is the very nature of indeclinables. For such is the power of words that indeclinables express an object that transcends the nature of *sattva* (substantial existence), and therefore they denote an object that is beyond number.

Words possess distinctions and are delimited by specific case-endings; it is their inherent nature (*svabhāva*) to convey meanings delimited by specific numbers such as singularity and so forth. Thus, their referents are endowed with specific numbers. However, when these words transcend both these states [of being distinct and numbered], the meanings of subordinate words [in a compound] do not appear. Therefore, since in a *vṛtti* (compound) there is the comprehension of non-differentiation and the number one, while in a sentence there is distinction, there is an absolute difference [between the two]. || 105 ||

Regarding this, the author of the Vārttika states a corroborating point: "The absence of elision (aluk) and the formation of a singular compound (ekavadbhāva) do not apply when that [condition] exists; yet that property belongs to words such as *goṣucara* and others in another grammatical rule. (106)

In this context, even in sentences such as *stokābhyāṃ muktaḥ* ("released by two small [amounts]") or *stokebhyo muktaḥ* ("released by many small [amounts]"), the formation (*vṛtti*) is desired only as *stokānmuktaḥ*. Thus, when it was objected that "the treatment as a singular unit (*ekavadbhāva*) must be stated," the author of the Vārttika replied: "The expression 'as if singular' is unnecessary; there is no compound in the dual or plural. How is this justified? If, in the formation, the number one in the sense of non-differentiation arises, resulting in the absence of the perception of duality or plurality.

And thus, since there is an absence of the dual and plural numbers when that non-dual unity exists, there is an absence of compound formation; therefore, even when duality and so forth are intended, the compound consists only of words ending in the singular, so there is no purpose in the rule for "treatment as a single unit" (*ekavadbhāva*). It follows from the principle: "The singular number shall be used as the general rule. Alternatively, even in the case of non-dual unity, there is no contradiction, because the rule is prescribed based on unity in a general sense.

If it is asked, "How then can there be a compound of words ending in plural forms, as in *goṣucaraḥ*, *varṣābhūḥ*, and *apsuyoniḥ*? [the answer is: "It is because of that [property]," namely, the property called non-differentiated unity (*abhedaikatva*). This property exists here even in the plural number, which is other than the singular number. For in this case, the plural is not used to denote a plurality of individuals; rather, according to the rule, "The plural is used for one when referring to a genus (*jāti*)," it is so. Thus, even a single living being that moves among cows is designated as *goṣucara*, as is the term *indragopa*.

Even a single atom (*paramāṇu*) is denoted by the word *āpaḥ* (waters), which ends in the plural; and even a single rainy season (*varṣārātra*) is denoted by the word *varṣāḥ* (rainy seasons), which ends in the plural. This is due to the inherent nature of the power of words (*śabdaśaktisvābhāvyāt*). In this case, the number of non-difference and unity does not obstruct the difference in grammatical number (*vacanabheda*). Nevertheless, the meaning is that there is still the cognition of non-difference and unity itself. || 106 ||

However, the dual number has not been prescribed for the genus (*jāti*); therefore, he states that in all derivative formations (*vṛtti*), because the distinction of number is concealed in the genus, the dual does not occur: "Because the dual is absent in the genus, it does not exist in derivative formations; however, if the rule [Pāṇini 2.4.62] is rejected, then in the case of substances (*dravya*), there are forms such as *goṣucara*. (107)

That dual number does not exist in compound formations (vṛtti), because it is not taught for the genus (jāti) and because the distinctions residing in individuals are concealed therein; however, the plural number does exist [in compounds] because of the rule "jātyākhyāyām. Thus, although both singular and plural numbers occur in a compound, the absence of the dual number remains as the result of non-differentiation and unity.

However, when the *sūtra* "jātyākhyāyām" (Pāṇini 1.2.58) is rejected on the grounds that the use of the plural number is justified by the plurality residing in the substrata (*āśrayopādhika*) of the genus (*jāti*), then in the case of *goṣucaraḥ*, the plural ending in the compound is based precisely on the distinctions residing in the individual cows (*godravya*). For the word *goṣucaraḥ* refers to the individuals as a whole (*anavayavena*). Similarly, in the cases of *apsuyoniḥ* and *varṣāsujaḥ*, the plural is used despite the unity of the individual, either because of a plurality of parts (*avayavapracaya*) or because of a plurality of properties (*dharmabahutva*).

For, due to the inherent nature of the power of words (*śabdaśakti*), some plural expression denotes a multiplicity of parts (*avayava*), while others denote a multiplicity of substances (*dravya*) or qualities (*guṇa*). [Objection: This is untenable; to this he says: "Because of the substratum, there is a connection with all distinctions for that which possesses distinction; moreover, the position that [the word] denotes the substance does not exist when a genus (*jāti*) is being expressed. (108)
In this way, the transition of all substances occurs, yet the "remainder of one" (ekaśeṣa) is not stated; otherwise, if the sūtra were rejected, there would be a transition of distinct substances.

If, on the basis of a plurality of substances, the plural number were accepted in cases such as *goṣucara* (one who moves among cows), then in the compound (*vṛtti*), the connection with a specific number would clearly be admitted. And thus, since the state of possessing distinctions is relied upon, a connection with all numbers—singularity, duality, and plurality—would necessarily follow; so what then is this "number of non-dual unity"? Furthermore, the designation *goṣucara* applies even when [the agent] moves among one or two [cows].

And thus, this plural number is not dependent on a difference of individuals (*vyakti*), but rather occurs only when denoting a genus (*jāti*). Since, in that case, there is no possibility of the view that the word denotes a substance (*dravya*), how can this plural number be explained as being based on a difference of substances? The same should be said for expressions such as *apsuyoniḥ* ("born from water"). Therefore, it is logical that this plural number occurs only when denoting a genus. Furthermore, it is not appropriate to reject the grammatical derivation (*yoga*) by resorting to the intention to denote a substance.

For in this way, the rule for *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one) would have to be commenced [separately], on the grounds that since a word is applied to each individual object (*pratyartham*), a single word cannot denote multiple objects. However, when the universal (*jāti*) is denoted, the comprehension of all substances occurs through even a single word ending in the plural; thus, the *ekaśeṣa* sūtra is rejected by the statement: "Vājapyāyana holds that because the universal is denoted, there is a single [form] in the case of a case-ending (*vibhakti*)."

Thus, the rule *jātyākhyāyām* has been justified by the statement: "In the case of a designation by genus (*jātyākhyā*), there is a single referent because the genus is being denoted. Now, one might ask: what is the specific advantage in this designation by genus, such that its commencement is justified? To this he says: "It has been rejected," and so forth. If this rule *jātyākhyāyām* were not formulated, then when an injunction refers to a genus (*jāti*), since the plural number would not apply, in cases such as *goṣucaraḥ* ("one who moves among cows"), where there is a plurality of substances, the plural number would instead convey a plurality of individuals (*vyakti*).

And this is not accepted; for the meaning is that the designation "goṣucara" applies when [the animal] moves among two cows as well as one cow, and the term "goṣucara" is a conventional name (*rūḍhi*) for a specific type of bird called a *kukkuṭa*. Therefore, this is appropriate only when denoting a genus (*jāti*); thus, even though there is non-differentiation and unity, this plural number should be understood as being prescribed by rule (*vācanika*) in that very context. 108, 109.

Now, since the number of non-dual unity (*abhedaikatvasaṃkhyā*) consists of all specific numbers, he begins with an objection to explain how its own nature is manifested when it functions through differentiation: "In the application [of the rule], the status of being 'like that which possesses the suffix' (*yuktavadbhāva*) is taught for words such as *varaṇā* and so on; however, in the case of the number of non-dual unity, the form *godau* is not established therein. (110)

Regarding the rule *lupi yuktavad vyaktivacane*, two interpretations are possible. To explain: when "gender and number" (*liṅgasaṃkhye*) are understood as "manifestation and count" (*vyaktivacane*), then, since there is no cessation of the meaning even when the case-ending has disappeared in a secondary derivative (*taddhitavṛtti*) characterized by elision (*lubanta*), this is the position that there is an extension (*atideśa*) of those very manifestation and count belonging to the compound (*vṛtta*).

However, when the word *vyakti* means "individual" (*vyakti*) and the word *vacana* is intended to mean "number"—such as the singular number and so forth—by way of eliding one part [of the compound], then, because these two are not observed in the formation of a *vṛtti*, this extension (*atideśa*) applies to the meaning of the *lu*-suffix in the state prior to the *vṛtti*, namely the state of mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*). This is the second position. In that regard, according to the first position, the form *godaugrāmaḥ*—"a village not far from two cows"—is not established. For it has been stated that in the formation of a *vṛtti*, the subordinate element (*upasarjana*) manifests with the number of non-distinct unity (*abhedaikatvasaṃkhyā*).

Furthermore, since the extension (*atideśa*) applies only to that meaning which possesses the characteristic of number, the dual number would not occur here because there is no extension of duality. However, the plural number in cases such as *pañcālāḥ* is established on the basis of the genus (*jāti*). || 110 ||

Now, as for the second position, he says regarding that: "In the case of a compound (yuktavadbhāva) following a prior occurrence, the genitive case would be based on a distinction; however, in the compound, because specific numbers are abandoned, the distinction ceases. (111)

In the sentence "The village is not far from the Godāvarī," the genitive case is observed to be based on distinction (*vyatireka*); therefore, it would also occur in the compound (*vṛtti*), because of the extension of application (*atideśa*). Even though there is non-difference and unity in the distinction [between the two rivers], it is stated in the *Bhāṣya* regarding the form "Godau" that "the genitive is indeed a statement. Here, the solution is stated by resorting to another position: "Those gender and number which belong to the compound are extended [to the constituent members]. He explains this with the words beginning "In the compound, number... and so forth.

The meaning is this: when a compound is formed, the distinction between numbers—due to the abandonment of the various numbers belonging to the subordinate base-meaning which is connected with the sense of the suffix—is absent; therefore, only an operation based on the number of non-distinct unity is extended [to the compound], and not the genitive case, which is dependent upon differentiation. Immediately following this, there is a passage in the Bhāṣya: "Even prior to the formation of the compound, those gender and number [of the base] are extended [to the compound]; the genitive does not occur because, when there is an extension of a general property, there is no extension of its specific particulars."

In this context, that which is connected to the meaning of the base—namely, the singular number and so forth, which is a general term following the commonality—is extended [by *atideśa*] to the meaning of the elision (*lub-artha*), where it would otherwise not apply because of its connection with a different number. And although that [general term] functions only by way of its particulars, nevertheless, the particulars such as the singular number and so forth, being non-deviant, are obtained through the extension; but the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is not. Because that [genitive] is based on distinction (*vyatireka*), it does not occur when that [distinction] is absent, and thus it is deviant with respect to the general category of number.
Just as, for example, Vasiṣṭha and others [are used] for the word "Brāhmaṇa. (111)

And thus, under this view that "the gender and number belonging to the constituent members [of a compound] are extended [to the compound]," the objection remains that the forms *godau* (in the dual) would not be established when there is the number of non-differentiated unity (*abhedaikatvasaṅkhyā*). To resolve this, he first restates the previously mentioned definition of the number of non-differentiated unity: "Some recognize another number among existing numbers, called 'non-differentiation,' which is inclusive; and that arises in a compound. (112)

"Some" refers to those who consider non-dual unity (*abhedaikatva*) to be the nature of the synthesis of all numbers. For in this view, non-dual unity incorporates all the distinctions of number within its own self. However, he indicates that in the opinion of those for whom non-dual unity is defined as the exclusion of difference—according to the principle that "the distinction of numbers ceases in the operation upon the part that possesses that form"—the acceptance of distinct numbers is not tenable. || 112 ||

And since the number "one" (ekatva-saṅkhyā) manifests in its operation when other numbers are already present, the form *godau* is established; thus he says: "In some cases, it enters into activity through its own constituent parts called 'differences' (bhedākhya); in other cases, its own self, independent of differences, becomes the instrumental cause. (113)

Thus, that non-dual unity which includes differentiation is sometimes employed by way of an internalized duality and so forth, where there exists a cause for the manifestation of distinctions. But in other cases, it is employed in its undifferentiated essential nature, free from distinctions, where no cause for distinction exists. (113) Regarding this very point, he provides an example: "The husband of a slave-girl" and "the cow of a god" are observed; thus, the differentiation of function belonging to that number is established in this manner. (114)

In the phrase *dāsī sambandhitayopāttā* ("the female slave is mentioned as being related [to the husband]"), for the purpose of expressing the husband's reproach, only that much is intended; thus, there is no regard for duality or plurality. Therefore, it is certain that the number "one" (ekatva) in its aspect of non-differentiation (*abheda*) functions here by its very nature. However, in the case of *godau*, the proximity of two cows is intended; since the village is one, the expression *godo grāmaḥ* ("the village has two cows") is not perceived. Thus, it is certain that the number "one" in its aspect of non-differentiation functions here by relying on the internal duality.

And thus, even when there is an extension (*atideśa*) of gender and number belonging to the state of the derivative base (*vṛtti*), the number two and so forth, being possible, can appropriately be extended to the meaning of the elided suffix (*lub-artha*). This property of number is observed elsewhere as well. For example: although the number twenty is composed of two groups of ten, it does not function through duality, but rather through its own property of non-differentiation, as in "twenty cows" (*viṃśatir gāvaḥ*). However, the form *viṃśatī* occurs when one intends to express a collection of twenties; in that case, it is a residual formation (*ekaśeṣa*).

The numbers "two" and "three," however, are designated by taking into account the difference in their substrata (*saṅkhyeya*), even though there is no difference in their own essential nature (*svarūpa*). Likewise, what contradiction is there in the case of the number "one" (non-duality), which is non-distinct, if one adopts distinction and non-distinction based on the difference of its objects? Nor should it be argued that because there is no further number within numbers, another number is impossible even for the number "one" (non-duality); for we observe that numbers are included within other numbers even in the absence of a connection with a distinct number.

For example: "How many sons do you have? In this case, because the preceding number is included within the subsequent answer, the question applies without distinction to oneness, twoness, and so forth. And thus an answer is seen: "One, two, or many. In this way, even within the number of non-differentiated unity (*abhedaikatva*), other numbers are contained; and they emerge by virtue of specific causes? Otherwise, if they were absolutely non-existent, how could they emerge?

And this very number, which constitutes the commonality of all numbers, is inherent in expressions such as "the king’s man" (*rājapuruṣaḥ*) precisely because of the employment of the subordinate term (*upasarjana*); for by their very nature, subordinate terms express their own meaning as a generality (*sāmānya*). 114.

If this is so, how is duality understood in the case of *dviputra* (two sons), since [duality] belongs to the meaning of the subordinate element (*upasarjana*)? To this he says: "In compounds such as *dviputra*, the external distinction of two and so forth, which is expressed by the case-ending (*vibhakti*), ceases because it is merely its own referent; however, the causal basis [of that number] remains. (115)

In the analytical sentence (*vibhaktivākya*) "two sons" (*dvayoḥ putra*), duality—which is distinct from the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*)—is first established; that very [duality] ceases upon the emergence of non-differentiated unity in the compound (*vṛtti*). However, that which constitutes the meaning of the nominal stem does not disappear. Otherwise, if [the stem-meaning] were devoid of meaning, the employment of the word "two" would not even occur. And it has been stated that even in a compound where the own-meaning is abandoned (*jahatsvārthā vṛtti*), there is still the meaning of the subordinate element (*upasarjana*). The same should be understood for cases such as "three sons" (*triputra*). || 115 ||

If, then, duality as its own meaning does not cease [in the compound], and thus the number one—which implies non-differentiation—is absent here, then he says, anticipating this objection: "The word *dvi* (two) occurs there in reference to a collective group (*saṅgha*) where duality is subordinate; because of the connection [expressed by] 'this is that' (*so'yam*), it is not so in the case of the word *ubha*. (116)

In a sentence (*vākya*), because the individual members are predominant, two distinct entities are expressed as having manifest difference. However, in a compound (*vṛtti*), due to the superimposition of non-difference between the whole and its parts, the whole—qualified by the quality of duality—is considered one; thus, even here, the difference of the subordinate meaning (*upasarjana*) is excluded, since non-difference and unity have not yet emerged. This state of being a collective function (*samudāyavṛttitva*) regarding the word *ubha* cannot occur in that manner—namely, with duality as a subordinate attribute—and therefore the compound *ubhaputra* never occurs.

For it will be stated immediately thereafter: "In a compound (*vṛtti*), both [forms] are always employed with the same meaning. However, an expression such as *ubhābāhuḥ* is correct because it belongs to the class beginning with *dvidaṇḍi*. If it is asked: "How is it that the word *ubha*, although a synonym for 'two,' does not denote a collection (*saṅgha*) in a compound in the same way [as other numerals]? We reply: "Because of the inherent nature of the word's expressive power (*śabdaśaktisvābhāvya*). And thus says the Vārttika: "The absence of others [i.e., the absence of the dual number and the feminine suffix *ṭāp*] is because [the word *ubha*] is restricted to the domain of the dual number; *ubhaya* occurs elsewhere. (116)
Regarding this, he says: "In its application, both [the word *nitya*] have the same meaning; the inclusion of the term 'always' (*nitya*) in the Sūtra is stated for that very purpose. (117)

In expressions such as *ubhayaputraḥ*, *ubhayathā*, and *ubhayataḥ*, the word *ubhaya*—which has the same meaning as the word *ubha*—is employed in the compound (*vṛtti*). For that [word *ubhaya*] is capable of denoting a collection in which duality is subordinate, whereas the word *ubha* is not. Thus, their identity of meaning is based on the non-difference of the object, and not on the function of denotation; for while "both" (*ubhau*) conveys the sense in a form characterized by distinction, "both" (*ubhaya*) conveys it in the form of a whole.

In the sūtra *ubhādudātto nityam*, the inclusion of the word *nityam* (always) is for this purpose: namely, to indicate that the word *ubha* lacks the capacity to denote a collective aggregate (*samudāya*) where duality is a subordinate element (*upasarjana*). For the word *ubha* does not express a number; thus, under the view that the suffix *ayaC* is applied [by P. 5.2.43], since the suffix *tayap* would not otherwise apply, the inclusion of *nityam* would not be necessary to preclude its optional application alongside it.

The word *ubha* denotes a number, and its substitute is *tayap*, which here becomes *ayaj*. Even in this view, since the option is already excluded by the fact that [the suffix] is not *svarita*-marked, the inclusion of the term *nityam* (always) serves the stated purpose: namely, to indicate that in the context of a compound (*vṛtti*), the form with *ayaj* alone is obligatory. Furthermore, the inclusion of *nityam* in the sūtra is a restatement of the logical principle that the word *ubha* denotes a collection consisting of two parts, whereas the word *ubhaya* denotes the same thing; thus, if they were synonymous, an option between them would arise. However, due to the inherent nature of linguistic capacity (*śabdaśakti*), the word *ubhaya* indeed denotes the aggregate as a whole. Therefore, the mention of *nityam* in the sūtra is merely a formal restatement of this established rule. || 117 ||

However, since the denotative power [of the word] exists, the word *ubha* is indeed employed in the domain of the dual suffix *ṭāp*; thus he says: "Even when the suffix *āp* is present, because it does not have another as its referent, no non-difference arises. Therefore, the word *ubhe* is employed in its own primary sense (*svārthe*) with a distributive function (*bhedavṛtti*). (118)

From the nominal stem *strīvṛtti*, the suffix *ṭāp* is added in its own sense (*svārthe*); likewise, the suffix *ka* is added in its own sense to indicate contempt and so forth. Since in those cases the meaning of the suffix does not attain the status of a subordinate quality (*guṇabhāva*), and since no distinction has arisen [between the base and the derivative], this word *ubha*—being independent and functioning within its own sense despite the presence of a distinction—is fit for usage as *ubhe* or *ubhaka*. However, when the suffix is not in its own sense (*asvārthika*) or when it occurs as a subsequent member of a compound (*uttarapada*), because it is dependent on another and because its unity of meaning with the principal sense is obscured, its distinctness becomes manifest (*udbhūtabhedatā*). Consequently, its own sense is lost, and thus its usage in such instances is improper. || 118 ||

Now, one might raise the objection: "If, in the rule *striyām*, the view is adopted that the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*) is the primary qualificand (*viśeṣya*), then since [the word] is employed there as a qualifier for a meaning distinct from the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*), it would not be used in its own sense (*svārtha*); how then can both words [the base and the suffix] be applied there? Anticipating this, he says: "Even in the view that femininity (*strītva*) is what is denoted, there is a reversal of the subordinate status (*guṇabhāva*). Because [the base] is not for the sake of another by its very nature, the distinction [between them] is not lost there. (119)

In words such as *gārgya*, the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is subordinate, while the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) is understood as the primary element. However, in the case of words ending in feminine suffixes, even when the meaning of the suffix is the primary factor, a substance qualified by femininity is what is expressed here, due to the inherent nature of the word’s expressive power. Indeed, it is not possible to dictate the meanings of words; for although there may be differences in the grammatical procedures (*śāstraprakriyā*) of the treatises, the worldly meaning, which possesses a fixed character, remains unchanged. Therefore, in the expression “both” (*ubhe*), the distinction is not set aside, because [the gender] does not exist for the sake of another.

Since this is so: therefore, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is seen after both [the word ending in] the dual number in other instances, except when the suffix *tayap* follows; furthermore, it does not occur again when there is a subsequent member of a compound (*uttarapada*). (120)

The word *ubha* has been stated to apply specifically to the dual number (*dvivacana*) and to the feminine suffix *ṭāp*; it does not occur elsewhere than in these two cases. Consequently, in any other suffix or as an *uttarapada*, the word *ubha* does not exist; rather, there is the word *ubhaya*, which has the same meaning. Nevertheless, by virtue of the inclusion of *ubha-* as a base form in the rule *ubhād* [Pāṇini 5.2.44], the word *ubha* is employed even in those instances of unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*). Examples such as *ubhā-hasti* and so forth are like *dvi-daṇḍi* and so forth.
And in that case, due to the very nature of the expressive power of words (*śabdaśaktisvābhāvyāt*), the word *ubha* denotes the meaning in its collective form, just like the word *dvi*.

Thus, having arrived at this topic by way of the discussion on the number one in terms of non-difference (*abhedaikatva*), a certain point has been determined. However, the following objection is raised here: regarding the rule *īdūded dvivacanaṃ pragṛhyam*, it is stated in the Vārttika: "If [the definition] is 'that which ends in *ī*, *ū*, or *e* and is a dual ending,' then there is a prohibition in the case of elision (*luk*). An objection is raised that in the example *kumāryagāram* (the house of two girls), since it ends in *ī* by its phonetic form (*śruti*) and is a dual ending by the characteristic of being a suffix (*pratyaya-lakṣaṇa*), the designation *pragṛhya* would undesirably apply.

That is not tenable; for if one accepts that the number "one" (ekatva) and non-difference (abheda) reside in the *vṛtti* (the compound), then a compound ending in a dual suffix would be impossible. Thus he says: "There would be no attainment of the designation *pragṛhya* by virtue of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule; for in the case of 'kumāryagāre', there is no compound when another number [is involved]. (121)
The meaning of these verses has been explained. || 121 ||

He states another objection as well: "If there were an option (*vibhāṣā*) for *luṅ* after [the suffixes] *yañ* and the rest when applied to two [words], then forms such as *yauṣmākasta-* and *tāvaka-* would not be established due to the absence of distinction. (122)

The author of the *Vārttika* has stated that, according to the view that "there is an addition [of the rule] for the sixth case [genitive] when one or two members beginning with *yañ* occur in a *tatpuruṣa* compound," elision (*luk*) takes place. This is for the sake of establishing such usages as *gārgyakulam* or *gargakulam* (meaning "the family of Gārgya"), and likewise *gārgyakulam* or *gargakulam* (meaning "the family of the two Gārgyas"). However, this contradicts the position that accepts non-difference and unity; for if non-difference and unity are accepted, there can be no compound of words ending in dual suffixes, and since even the singular number would lack a counterpart to "two or more," [the rule regarding elision] becomes untenable.

Likewise, even according to the view of the author of the Sūtras, non-dual unity is contradicted. For instance, in the rule "tavakamamakāvekvacane," he prescribes the substitutes *tavaka* and *mamaka* as replacements for *yuṣmāka* and *asmāka* in the singular. Consequently, in the compound *yauṣmāka*, duality and so forth are intended; whereas in *tāvaka*, singularity is intended as the opposite of duality and so forth. Thus, how could there be non-dual unity? (122)
Furthermore, a distinction is observed between "Gārgyatarā" and "Gargatarā"; likewise, the two designations "your father" and "my father" are established as distinct. (123)

In many instances, because the elision (*luk*) is prescribed by the rule *yañañośca*, when the suffix is heard—as in *gārgyatara*—duality and singularity are invariably perceived; and in *gargatarāḥ*, plurality is perceived. How, then, can there be the manifestation of non-differentiation and unity in a compound (*vṛtti*)? Likewise, according to the rule *tvamāvekavacane* regarding suffixes and subsequent members of a compound, unity is perceived in *tvatpitā* and *matpitā*; whereas in *yuṣmatpitā* and *asmatpitā*, duality and plurality are understood.
All of this would be contradicted if one were to accept non-differentiation and unity in a compound. (123)

To this, the following reply is given: The number that resides inherent in primordial matter (prakṛti) as its limiting adjunct (upādhi) is manifested either by verbal suffixes (ādeśa), by technical names (saṃjñā), or even by case-endings (vibhakti). (124)

It has been stated that when specific numbers are present, a non-dual unity (*abhedekatvasaṅkhyā*) consisting of their conjunction manifests. Thus, wherever there is a basis for a particular number, that very number is indeed perceived. Consequently, in the case of a subordinate word (*upasarjanapada*), regarding the nominal stem (*prakṛti-prātipadika*), the distinct number (*bhedasaṅkhyā*) inherent as a delimiting factor of its meaning is indeed perceived through the application of the *pragṛhya* designation, as in the example "kumāryagāram" (the girl's house).

For if the designation *pragṛhya* were to apply here, then, given the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*), the meaning of the subordinate element (*upasarjana*) would be understood as being in the dual; this is because the *pragṛhya* designation is prescribed for forms ending in the dual. Similarly, in cases such as *tāvakaḥ* and *tvatpitā*, a specific distinction is understood from the substitution (*ādeśa*), since that substitution is prescribed for the singular. For even though a subordinate nominal stem (*prātipadika*) has the capacity to accept the number one, it lacks the capacity to manifest that specific distinction; thus, in that case, it requires the assistance of the case-ending (*vibhakti*). The same applies to the substitution and so forth.

For this very reason, some explain that just as *prakṛti* is the nature of a specific number, so too is the number "one" (abhedaikatvasaṅkhyā) its nature; since it arises from that [number], it remains there in a state of identity with it. Though not manifested due to the obstruction of its power by the word containing the subordinate element (*upasarjana*), it is manifested by the case-endings (*vibhakti*) themselves through their substitutes (*ādeśa*). And in cases such as *gargakula*, where there is the elision (*luk*) of even one or two [case endings], the determination of the specific [number] will occur through the context (*prakaraṇa*).

If, however, the elision (*luk*) were not prescribed for the plural, then because the rule for *luk* applies only to the plural, there would be no perception of duality or singularity in the case of "the family of the Gargas" (*gargakulam*). But since the elision of the patronymic suffix must necessarily be introduced as a restrictive rule for the plural, [the meaning is secured]. Likewise, in cases such as "your father" (*yuṣmatpitā*), the determination of the restriction to duality or plurality is made through context, as it is in the case of "the family of the Gargas" (*gārgyakulam*). And this being the case, the statement that "there is no compound of words ending in dual or plural suffixes" is impossible, because a compound occurs only when a specific [singular] understanding has been reached.

In cases such as *rājapuruṣa* (king’s man), however, because there is no basis for apprehending a specific [number], and because a corresponding sentence is postulated during the analytical process (*prakriyā*) so that the compound word may be explained, it is appropriate that only those [words] ending in the singular number be joined [in the analysis]. Thus, this is merely a restatement of a meaning established by logic. But where the manifestation of duality and so forth is possible—as in the analytical sentences for compounds such as *kumāryor agāram* (the house of two maidens)—there the dual number and so on are indeed employed in the analytical sentence which is the source of the compound; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever. || 124 ||

By this very logic, the following is also established, as he says: "In the case of a *śaurpika* and a *māsaja*, the measure exists by its own nature; it functions through differentiation by relying upon a number that serves as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). (125)

One who has been purchased for a *śūrpa* (a measure) or one whose birth is measured by a month is called *śaurpika* or *māsajāta*. In this context, if the number "one" (*ekatva*) were to function as a non-distinctive unity that does not include specific internal numbers, then, because the qualifier would have an indefinite number, there would be no determination of the fixed price for what was purchased or born, nor would there be a comprehension of the specific age. Furthermore, words such as *śaurpika* and others are employed for the purpose of delimitation.

And in that case, since it would be improper to subvert the fundamental [meaning], the word *parimāṇa* (measure) undergoes its function by taking up a number-difference as a delimiting factor of the meaning of the nominal stem—a unity that is the very nature of things due to the essence of their usage, which is primary and conceptualized. || 125 ||
He says this very thing: "Even in the case of what has been purchased, O youthful one, no delimitation is perceived; since [the object] is desired without distinction, size is useless there. (126)

The intended and desired determination [of the measure] cannot be understood for the purchased and the produced types without the distinction characterized by the number one; therefore, if unity were not employed therein, the use of the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) and the *āsya* would be fruitless. Now, it might be argued that the use here is fruitful for the purpose of excluding what is not a winnowing basket and for the purpose of distinguishing it from the seven-night sacrifice and others. This is not so. If the measure were of indefinite number, the specific nature of the thing measured (*parimeya*) could not be ascertained.

And it is precisely for the sake of determining those specific qualities that words denoting measure (*parimāṇa*) are employed. By their very nature, they denote objects whose forms are delimited. Consequently, due to the authority of such usage, there is here an understanding of the subordinate element as qualified by singularity, because words denoting measure express an object characterized by a specific measure. || 126 ||

For this very reason: "The rule for the suffix *śas* after words such as *prastha* is established because it expresses non-difference despite difference; however, it is not seen after words such as *ghaṭa*, because [the individual] is non-different from its properties. (127)

When the suffix *śas* is prescribed after a singular number (*ekavacana*) denoting a count (*saṅkhyā*) to express distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), the word "singular" (*ekavacana*) is used in its etymological sense (*anvarthatva*); thus, *śas* occurs after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that expresses a meaning delimited by the number one, but not after that which ends in a singular case-ending. Consequently, in the *vṛtti*, there is non-difference (*abheda*) of distinct substances (*dravya*), but not of the genus (*jāti*); since it expresses that oneness which is non-difference, the suffix *śas* occurs after words of measure (*parimāṇaśabda*) such as *prastha* and the like.

For these [words] denote their own referents as delimited by the number one, due to the inherent nature of the power of words; because that [number] is their property, and because they express a referent of the aforementioned measure, the suffix *śas* is produced even when non-differentiation and unity manifest in a compound (vṛtti), so that one understands the singular: "he gives prastha-wise" (*prasthaśo dadāti*) or "he gives khārī-wise" (*khāriśo dadāti*). However, the suffix *śas* does not occur after words such as *ghaṭa*, for those are genus-words (*jātiśabda*).

And thus, because there is no difference in the genus (*jāti*), there is a connection with the number "one" due to non-difference; however, these [words] do not express the non-difference of a distinct substance, but rather of the genus. And since that [genus] persists even when the individuals differ, if words such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*) denote a genus that rests upon an indefinite number [of individuals], they lack the capacity to necessarily include the singularity of the individual within their operation. Therefore, the cognition [of oneness] is not caused by the expression of a single object. Furthermore, the inclusion of the word "seen" (*dṛśi*) here is for the purpose of avoiding [the application of this rule to] actual usage.

The usage "he gives a jar" (*ghaṭaṃ dadāti*) is not observed. However, where even genus-words (*jātiśabda*) are employed with the intent of conveying a specific individual (*vyaktiviśeṣa*), the suffix *śas* indeed occurs because the cognition of singularity and so forth is seen there; for example: "He who bestows this speech syllable by syllable, word by word, or even letter by letter, he becomes one who possesses the priestly office (*ārtvijīna*)."

For here, since a word consists of a collection of phonemes (*varṇa-samudāya-rūpatvāt*), the intention to denote a single individual entity is determined by the force of its distinct designation from those phonemes. Thus, the contradiction that was raised regarding the acceptance of non-differentiated unity (*abheda-ekatva-saṅkhyā*) has been refuted; for it is logically established that when that [unity] is devoid of any inherent nature of association with distinctions between all numbers, the manifestation of specific features occurs according to the basis [of usage]. Following this principle, the statements of the Sūtras and Vārtikas are to be understood. || 127 ||

Now, regarding those who maintain that when a word functions with respect to a constituent part (*avayava*) of that same nature, the distinction of number ceases—meaning they hold that there is a number of non-dual unity characterized by the exclusion of difference—he begins [his argument] to resolve the contradiction even in their view: "Where a verbal suffix (*vacana*) is heard, there the entity is qualified; where the verbal suffix ceases, the existence of that [entity] is not found. (128)

In a sentence where the singular number and so forth are heard, the property characterized as number is distinguished; it is determined as being distinguished by its exclusion from others. As for that which ceases or departs in a compound (vṛtti)—namely, the singular number and so forth—the corresponding property characterized as number, which would be the signified object, does not exist there. Indeed, it is precisely because of the absence of that [number] that the expression for it ceases in that case. || 128 ||

But that very same [non-existence] is described as *luk* (elision) for the sake of establishing the characteristics of suffixes; thus he says: "The effect is dependent on existence; according to the treatise, there is no operation [of a rule] where there is non-perception. That which is seen in a sentence to be absolutely non-existent is [treated as such] in the *vṛttis*. (129)

In this context, because the meanings of the case-endings (*vibhakti*) are absent, their non-application—that is, their non-arising—is simply prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), which is what is meant by "non-appearance. Relying upon that [non-appearance], the *luk* rule is initiated in order to apply, on the basis of the existence of the suffix, the grammatical operation derived from the rule "when a suffix is elided, the operations conditioned by it still take place" (*pratyayalope pratyayalakṣaṇam*). Substitutes such as *tavak* and so forth, as well as the designation of *pragṛhya*, are taught only when a suffix is present; since these would not occur in a compound (*vṛtti*) due to the absence of a specific number [of suffixes] when the suffix is absent, the suffix is produced during the process of derivation (*prakriyā*).

The non-appearance (*adarśana*) of that [suffix] which has become attached is termed *luṅ* (elision); its establishment is by means of the technical definition of a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). If it is asked, "How can there be non-occurrence? Is non-appearance not simply prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*)?"—the answer is: because of the non-appearance in the *vṛtti* of that which was seen in the sentence (*vākya*), due to the statement [of the rule]. For since there is an absolute difference between the *vṛtti* and the sentence as they are distinct words, the non-occurrence of the word in the *vṛtti* is due solely to the absence of the referent (*arthābhāva*), and not due to a state of destruction (*pradhvaṃsabhāva*); such is the meaning. || 129 ||

If this is so, since suffixes are not produced, how can rules based on specific verbal forms (*vacanaviśeṣa*) also be obtained through the definition of suffixes? To this he says: "For the sake of distinguishing the scope of technical names (*saṃjñā*), non-observation of what is expected is prescribed; however, a specific verbal form is perceived as being heard. (130)

In order to prevent the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) that all a condition (*pratyaya*) is never seen except in its own domain, and for the purpose of restricting the scope of the technical term *lopa* (elision), it is stated: "But [the result] is established because that which is not seen when it has become applicable is designated as *lopa*. Although here, due to the absence of meaning, there is no application even according to the technical rules of grammar (*śāstra*), nevertheless, the natural non-usage itself is made known by means of *luk*. For a word whose meaning is possible cannot be set aside by a formal statement.

Indeed, sublation (*bādhā*) consists precisely in the inference of non-attainment (*aprāpti*). And thus, since the application [of case endings] is here explained by the very rules for elision (*luk*), the case endings (*sup*) produced during the formal derivation (*prakriyā*) are set aside. For it is in the sentence as it occurs in actual usage (*prayoga-samavāyin*) that the case endings are invariably heard; and that [sentence] is indeed different from the compound (*vṛtti*). However, a derivative sentence similar to that is postulated as the source (*prakṛti*) of the compound.

And in that case, the case endings (*sup*) are postulated solely in accordance with the sentence that constitutes the actual application; thus, in that procedural sentence (*prakriyāvākya*), a qualified number alone is heard. For whatever number is perceived there is understood to be qualified precisely because of its being a hundred.

Furthermore, because the effect conforms to its cause, even when there is elision (*luk*)—which is indicated [by the rule]—it is precisely a specific number that prompts its own grammatical operation by means of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the presence of the suffix). Thus, in cases such as *rājapuruṣa*, since there is no operation based on a specific number, operations such as the elision of the final *n* (*nalopa*) proceed by relying on number in general. Consequently, in that case, a previous distinction in number is not perceived, and thus there is an absence of cognition regarding a specific number.

The substitutes such as *tavaka* and so forth, as well as the designation *pragṛhya*, involve operations characterized by affixes (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) that are bound to specific numbers; thus, because a difference in number from a previous state is understood therein, the determination of a specific number arises based on that. As it is said: "Where a grammatical form (*vacana*) is heard, there the state [of the object] is specified. For indeed, the comprehension of a distinction in number is based on a distinction in grammatical form.

The meaning is: since its proximity is inferred here by means of the *ādeśa* (substitute) and so forth, how could it not convey its own denotation? Thus, it has been established that previously, through the *ādeśa* itself—which is included within the number of non-dual unity (*abhedaikatva*)—there is an understanding of a specific number. Here, however, even though there is no inclusion of a specific number, when the base (*prakṛti*) is inferred as qualified by the *ādeśa* and so forth through the number of non-dual unity, the comprehension of the distinction of numbers occurs precisely through its own designator; this is the difference. || 130 ||

Regarding this view, he states the fault: "In a case where either an absence (*abhāva*) or a *luk*-elision is prescribed, or where a form possessing a specific shape (*rūpavān*) is prescribed, because the cause (*nimitta*) is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*), an ungrammatical form (*asādhu*) results there. (131)

In a derivative sentence (*prakriyāvākya*), whatever specific expression [is used], exactly that is said to undergo elision (*luk*) when it occurs in a compound (*vṛtti*). Consequently, in cases where there is no elision—such as in the rule *pañcamyāḥ stokādibhyaḥ*—there would result forms like *stokābhyāṃ muktaḥ* or *stokebhyo muktaḥ* when expressing duality or plurality. However, what is desired is only *stokānmuktaḥ*; thus, one would necessarily have to state that there is a singular collective form (*ekavadbhāva*) even when there is no elision. And since it has been stated that this [singular collective form] does not apply to the benedictive (*āśīḥ*), there is a contradiction.

For unity (*ekatva*) is understood in a compound (*vṛtti*). In cases such as "released by two small [amounts]" (*stokābhyāṃ muktaḥ*), because the cause of the compound—the notion of unity—is abandoned when another number is heard, this would result in the word *stokānmuktaḥ* being ungrammatical (*apaśabda*) with respect to duality and so on. Likewise, the substitution of *rūpavat*, *bhāvātman*, *stavaka*, and so forth is also prescribed when there is a single referent (*ekārthatva*). For in that context, the term "singular" (*ekavacana*) is indeed etymological (*anvartha*).

In that case, if in the compound (*vṛtti*) a non-dual unity-number characterized by the exclusion of difference (*bhedāpoha*) is admitted, then—since the basis for the designation of "oneness," which is the opposite of duality and so forth, has been abandoned in the compound—the forms *tvakā* and others would be ungrammatical there and thus unfit for usage. || 131 ||

Therefore, he states that in both these systems this is the conclusion regarding the ultimate reality: "The distinction, the number, or the specific qualification explained for the *vṛtti* and the *vākya* may everywhere differ; however, such [a difference] is not necessarily of that kind. (132)

What is the use of this acceptance of an identity that lacks practical efficacy? For the denotative powers of words are diverse; they cannot be followed in their specific details, but are made known by relying upon some general characteristic.

And thus, by the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*), while demonstrating the distinction of a compound (*vṛtti*) from a sentence (*vākya*) based on the formation of a single integrated meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), that specific distinction characterized by the comprehension of a difference in number—which was explained as existing in the compound and as a "particular number" (*saṃkhyāviśeṣa*) in the sentence—is to be understood as being non-distinct [from the sentence], by taking the words of the compound without relying on their individual particular differences. For instance, it is not the case that a particular number is never perceived in the words of a compound; for a particular [number] is perceived in examples such as *śaurpika* ("a measure of a *śūrpa*"), *māsajāta* ("born after a month"), and *tāvakīna* ("your own").

However, since there is no difference [in meaning] between "rājapuruṣa" (king’s man) and similar compounds, it is precisely by this much that the distinct function (*vṛtti*) of the compound is indicated from the sentence. For example, when it is stated that "substance (*dravya*) is that which possesses action, possesses qualities, and is an inherent cause," the distinction of substance from qualities and so forth is established even though ether and other such things lack possession of action; for while those [qualities, etc. never possess action at any time, some substance may at some time be characterized as such.

Thus, since a distinction in number is perceived everywhere in a sentence, it is indeed indicated that in some cases there is a function (vṛtti) of a different nature from that [of the individual word]. For every grammatical rule (lakṣaṇa) operates by way of generality, because it is impossible to formulate such a rule for each individual instance.

Because the *mātrās* vary according to differences in place, time, and inherent nature—and particularly because it is impossible to establish a fixed rule for the denotative power (*abhidhāna-śakti*) of words—your objection does not succeed in demonstrating a deviation from the definition, provided that a restrictive basis (*nibandhana*) exists; for the definition applies to the general case, and its purpose is fulfilled even by a single application. This is the meaning. || 132 ||

Just as a specific number is not perceived in certain instances within a compound, so too is a specific gender. Consequently, the application of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) to words such as *kukkuṭī* (hen) before words like *aṇḍa* (egg) was rejected by the rule: "Or rather, it does not apply, because the preceding word is not feminine when its own meaning is intended. This he explains: "And because genus (*jāti*) is the cause of distinction, [the object] is not qualified by gender; this is the case for the primary element in examples such as 'deer-milk' (*mṛgadugdha*), but that same principle does not apply in the case of 'Gārgī's son' (*gārgīputra*). (133)

In expressions such as "deer-milk," "hen's egg," and "goat-meat," the preceding member (pūrvapada), such as "deer," is employed as a qualifier to delimit the subsequent member (uttarapada), which is the primary referent, such as "milk. Thus, when an injunction refers to a genus (*jāti*), there is no intention to express a specific gender (*liṅga*); therefore, the analytical resolution (*vigraha*) is simply "the milk of a deer" and so forth.

When an injunction is directed toward the exclusion of other species, words such as *mṛga* (deer) and others—denoting a restricted genus and devoid of gender distinctions—are capable of delimiting the primary object through the intended meaning. This is expressed as follows: "It is not feminine, because the preceding word is intended [to denote the genus]."

For if the first member of the compound has the meaning of "female," what else could there be intended by the expression of the genus (*jāti*)? In that case, since eggs and so forth are common to both female and male, qualifiers such as "of a cock" (*kukkuṭasyāṇḍam*) or "of a goat" (*chāgasya māṃsam*) would be purposeless, because they do not differentiate [the object]. However, when the exclusion of other genera is precisely what is intended by the qualifier, then it remains a sentence and not a compound; for in that case, the specific [gender] is not determined.

For when the feminine suffix has ceased—that is, when femininity is no longer manifested—it is precisely that same intention to express the general [gender] that is indicated by the rule for the masculine form (*puṃvat*). However, in some cases, there is an association with a specific gender in every respect for the meaning of the subordinate member (*upasarjana*). This is as in the case of *gārgīputra*, *chāgalīmūtra*, *mahiṣīmūtra*, and so forth. For in these instances, because the purpose is to convey either censure or praise regarding the son, and because the specific type of urine produces a distinct practical effect (*arthakriyā*), it is appropriate that the feminine alone serves as the qualifier.

And likewise, in such cases as these, that sequence which exists in the case of [the words] *kukkuṭī* and so forth (i.e., *kukkuṭāṇḍī* and so forth) does not apply here. For in those instances, the meaning of the first member of the compound is endowed with a common gender (*liṅgasāmānya*). Therefore, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), only those types of feminine forms such as *kukkuṭī* that refer to a genus (*jāti*) are intended. However, in cases like *gārgīputra*, where there is a purposeful intention to express an individual (*vyaktivivakṣā*), even those such as *gārgī* and others are included; thus, these serve as counter-examples here. And having established this, one should understand that, just as with number (*saṃkhyā*), the intention or non-intention to express gender (*liṅga*) is determined by the restriction of its scope. 133.

And because the distinction of gender and number is obscured when the primary meaning is the genus (*jāti*), for that very reason—since [the application of] gender and number would otherwise result in the expression "the white cloth" (*śuklaṃ paṭāḥ*) due to their connection with non-difference—the treatise has been commenced for the sake of establishing [the rules for] gender and number. (134)

In this system of grammatical derivation where the word is the ultimate unit, when a word is being processed independently of other words, because the specific details contained within the sentence cannot be determined, the word remains in its general form—merely its own meaning—due to its association with the neuter gender as a universal (sarvanāman) for gender, and its association with the number "one" as a universal for number. Thus, the word *śuklam* (white) remains established; even when the connection with another word such as *paṭāḥ* (cloths) arises, the internal processing that has already been accomplished does not cease. Consequently, because the meaning [of *śuklam*] would otherwise remain unconnected, it is treated as having a non-co-referential status (*asamānādhikaraṇa*).

When the general application [of gender and number] has been established by the rule *viśeṣaṇānāṃ cājāteḥ* ("and for qualifiers, except when denoting a genus"), this new rule is commenced in order to ensure that the specific gender and number [of the qualified object] are realized. For, since the qualifiers of a form ending in *lub* (elision) stand in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with the meaning of that which is elided, the gender and number residing in the elided meaning would already be established by the rule *lupi yuktavad* ("when *lub* occurs, the word behaves like that which is joined with it"). Therefore, the *Bhāṣya* establishes this sūtra for the purpose expressed in the maxim: *guṇavacanānām āśrayato liṅgavacanāni* ("for words expressing qualities, the gender and number depend on the substratum"). The meaning of the sūtra is that for qualifiers, the expression of the individual instance (*vyakti*) and the number (*vacana*) is the same as it would be for the thing they qualify. || 134 ||

Regarding this, he explains how a quality (*guṇa*) alone is denoted by a word that expresses a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), which denotes a universal: "That which, in its various functions, assumes a subordinate state for the sake of another, is designated as a 'qualifier' (*viśeṣaṇa*) in the Sūtra. (135)

Although it is well known that a "qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇa*) is that which differentiates, nevertheless, here only that which is dependent (*paratantra*) is intended. To explain: because of the recurrence of the term *yuktavat* (as in the rule *yuktavad vyaktivacane*), when there is a connection with the meaning of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), and within the application of a secondary derivative where there is a unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), whatever state (*bhāva*) is heard [in the word]—which assists another meaning of the secondary derivative by means of its own presence—that is called a "quality" (*guṇa*) and a "qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇa*) in this context.

For that [quality], having been introduced as a general substance either through the elision of the possessive suffix (*matup*) or by means of the suffix *-a* expressing possession (*matvarthīya*), becomes a qualifier because it is entirely dependent on that [substance] due to its being supported by it. However, that which is in a different grammatical case, such as "the white of the cloth" (*paṭasya śuklaḥ*), is established solely in the quality; since it is being qualified by the substance, it does not function as a qualifier at all. Furthermore, regarding a masculine gendered quality, because it has already acquired its grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) at the very outset in that single instance, there is no requirement for a distinction of gender or number.

However, in the case of that which is co-referential with a substance (*dravya-samānādhikaraṇa*)—which resides in the generality of substance (*dravya-sāmānya*) characterized by neuter gender and singular number, and which requires attributes (*dharma*) that serve as the basis for defining a particular substance—it is appropriate to understand it as conveying the gender and number of that specific substance. Therefore, in this sūtra, "quality-expressive" (*guṇavacana*) refers to words such as *śukla* (white) and so forth, which denote a quality; they are called qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*). Even though, when their suffixes are elided, these words function as denoters of the substantive (*viśeṣya-vacana*), nevertheless, because they reside in the generality of the substantive and require a specific [substantive] to complete their sense, they indeed function as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇatva*) with respect to that substantive. || 135 ||

If, however, grammatical analysis (*anvākhyāna*) is restricted to the sentence, then in a construction such as "this cloth has the quality white" (*śuklo guṇo 'sya paṭasyāsti*), where the specific gender and number are established by dependence on other words, one might ask: what is the purpose of the rule? Anticipating this objection, he says: "Although specific qualities are heard in sentences because they consist of different words, the compound formation (*vṛtti*) does not apply to them, because the form [of the compound] is non-different [from that of the sentence]. (136)

Regarding the specific sentence "This cloth has the quality white," it has already been established that the function [of the compound]—whether by the elision of the *matup* suffix or by having a form ending in the abstract suffix *ākara* denoting possession—is indeed of a different nature [from the sentence]. Consequently, the particulars contained in the sentence are not included within the compound.

Since the function (*vṛtti*) is indeed uniform across specific instances such as cloth and the like, there is no manifestation of specific distinctions within that [function] belonging to a fixed sentence; thus, the grammatical instruction regarding the term *vṛtti* is in every respect dependent solely upon the universal (*sāmānya*). Therefore, this sūtra must certainly be commenced for the sake of establishing the specific gender and number. || 136 ||

But even so, since it is only a universal (*sāmānya*) residing in a specific [gender or number] that is to be conveyed, will not an unspecified particular nonetheless serve as the basis for grammatical derivation (*anvākhyāna*)? Or, because the connection [of the universal with its substratum] would otherwise be inexplicable, will not the gender and number of the substratum be awaited, even though they are extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*)? Otherwise, how could that be established even if there were an explicit rule? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Since the refinement of a word (*śabda-saṃskāra*) has as its object the universal by virtue of its form (*rūpa*), therefore gender and number are necessarily attached to that substratum. (137)
Then, that word which denotes a substance is connected with both the gender and the number; in that case, there would be a distinct hearing for those two. (138)

In this context, that meaning alone which is understood from the word serves as the cause for grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*). From this word-form of the stem (*vṛtti-pada*), which is undifferentiated, common to all particular instances, and by nature a general auditory perception (*śruti-sāmānya*), the general meaning (*artha-sāmānya*) is understood, but not the particular. Thus, since even the intended particular remains unperceived and is therefore equivalent to non-existence, it is proper that the grammatical analysis (*anvākhyāna*) be based solely on the general meaning; consequently, the application of gender and number is obtained based on that general meaning. (Verses 137, 138)

When those two internal [operations] have been performed, even though a specific [word] is present, because there is no abandonment [of the original form] and because of the lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vyadhikaraṇatva*), a connection would not occur for one who follows the literal statement. In response to this, it is said: "By the rule, the gender and number of the future external [operation], which belong to its substratum, are established for the qualities. (139)

Because there is no simultaneity in the employment of words within a sentence, the mention of the "future" (bhāvin) is intended to demonstrate a lack of contemporaneity; for even when [the gender and number] of the substratum have been previously established, it is not required for the grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) of another word that depends upon it. For this very reason, there is "externality" (*bahiraṅgatva*) because the substratum is not required for the refinement of that which rests upon it. Nevertheless, by the force of the explicit statement [of the rule], even an external factor is taken into account, whereby the establishment of the specific gender and number is achieved, as evidenced by the commencement of the sūtra "viśeṣaṇānām" (Pāṇini 1.2.52). || 139 ||

If, then, it is intended from the very outset that the substantive (viśeṣya) is to be expressed as denotable by a secondary derivative (taddhita), what is the purpose of the explicit statement? To this he says: "Moreover, because there is no difference in form even when [the word] functions as a particular (viśeṣa), that particular remains unmarked; therefore, in this case, the function of differentiation is not assumed. (140)

Even when a specific meaning is intended to be expressed, because the word *vṛtti* is common to multiple senses, there is an uncertainty [regarding its precise referent]; thus, it has already been stated that this specific meaning—which is not the literal sense of the word *tataḥ*—cannot be the cause for the grammatical derivation (*anvākhyāna*). || 140 ||

Now, one might object: since the universal is established in the particulars, an effect based upon it must necessarily follow even when the universal is mentioned first, because there exists no universal devoid of particulars. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The universal is indeed the particular, since it is distinguished from the particular; for non-difference, being dependent on the particulars, is what brings about their exclusion. (141)

In this context, exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is the defining characteristic of a particular (*viśeṣa*). For it is those things which exclude one another that are called particulars. Likewise, even a universal (*sāmānya*), when apprehended as non-differentiated, becomes a particular because it excludes other particulars. Indeed, when there is an intention to express a universal, specific particulars are excluded. In that regard, just as a fixed particular, being relied upon, excludes other particulars, so too does the universal exclude particulars; therefore, that [universal] is also a particular.

As it has been said: "Just as the universal is also [a qualifier] like the particular, so too is that which possesses it. And thus, since the grammatical instruction (anuśāsana) is independent of other words, the non-difference (abheda) based on the universal serves to exclude the particulars; how then could there be the acquisition of gender and number residing in the particular? || 141 ||

Now, one might object: "If non-difference were to exclude difference, then that [non-difference] would not be established at a later time by them; nor would it produce in them a cognition corresponding to itself. Therefore, it could not exist. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Whatever is relied upon as a basis, that very thing excludes its opposite. However, the distinction between difference and non-difference is not determined within the universal. (142)

Since the employment of a word has as its result the exclusion of other [possibilities], even a universal—like a particular—functions by relying on the exclusion of specific instances; thus, through the use of the distributive suffix (*vīpsā*), the capacity for exclusion, which is the defining characteristic of a particular, is attributed to the universal as well. Nevertheless, a universal is not called a "particular," because it persists among its own substrata by excluding other universals.

Nor can non-difference (*abheda*) be established, because specific qualifiers (*viśeṣa*) and other universals (*sāmānya*) serve as differentiators. Thus, just as the word "cow" (*go*), when explained in its primary sense, denotes a *vāhīka* through the superimposition (*samāropa*) of cowness due to the otherwise inexplicability of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), so too words such as "white" (*śukla*), being refined in their primary sense as universals, would have to be joined with specific qualifiers presented by other words; consequently, there would be a distinct auditory form (*śruti*) for each. Therefore, it remains settled that this *sūtra* exists for the sake of establishing the gender and number residing in the external substratum. || 142 ||

Now, one might object: "In the case of the meanings expressed by words, unlike physical objects, no persisting form is observed; so what is their commonality (sāmānya)? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And the abstraction (apoddhāra) is the commonality," [he says] for one who explains that [commonality]. Therefore, it is grasped through its own property as being merely the state of the cause. (143)

Although only the sentence—having as its object a specific meaning characterized by a stable [sentence-level] form—is the expressive unit (*vācaka*), nevertheless, from that [sentence] which consists of a relational synthesis (*saṃsarga*), when words are extracted (*apoddhriyamāṇānām*), there remains a certain trace of meaning characterized as a universal (*sāmānya*) that is conducive to extraction; because it is extracted in accordance with the sentence-meaning, it is established as being helpful to that [sentence]. "Extraction" (*apoddhāra*) means that it is extracted, i.e., separated, from the relational synthesis; thus, it is called a "universal" (*sāmānya*).

The meaning is as follows: by being thus abstracted, that universal (*sāmānya*) is the benefactor which serves as the means for the comprehension of the particular (*viśeṣa*) that constitutes the sentence-meaning. For from a word abstracted in its isolation, there arises an intuition (*pratibhā*) whose object is the general meaning; therefore, its object is the universal, not the particular. To explain: that which remains in a state of expectancy toward a cause (*nimitta*)—and not in the nature of a particular—is determined by its own inherent essence, and not by way of differentiation, because the latter is subject to instability and confusion.

And for this reason, the word-meaning is not connected with [grammatical] gender, case-ending, or number. Now, one might object: "Since words occur within a fixed sentence, even when they are extracted [for analysis], the things denoted by the words are indeed particulars; what else could a universal be? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Because their specific properties have not yet been determined, the particulars themselves, being conceptualized, are designated by various causes (nimitta) as being qualified by the name 'universal'. (144)

Because words lack the capacity to denote specific particulars, those very differences whose specific forms are not individually apprehended are understood from them and established by the conceptual designation "universal," rather than by the name "particular. And since they are designated in such forms as "cow," "white," or "goes"—being delimited by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) characterized by genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*kriyā*)—it is therefore determined that these are indeed nothing but particular differences (*bheda*).

For although an object whose nature is differentiated is not directly denoted by words, nevertheless, because the object is denoted through the exclusion of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), it is precisely the differences that are denoted; for that which is without limiting adjuncts—being undifferentiated from everything—is incapable of being used in linguistic practice. Even from a distance, an individual is not determined by its mere form alone. Therefore, since every cognition of exclusion is grounded in difference, it is established that while the cognition of the universal arises merely from the non-apprehension of the particularity of word-meanings—which is to be understood through other words—the [particular] differences themselves are what are denoted.

From the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvadṛṣṭi*), however, because no specific distinction is found in the employment of those words and because there is a lack of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), the cognition of word-meanings is indeed unreal due to its distorted nature. It has already been determined that this [cognition] is merely a means toward the comprehension of the sentence-meaning. || 144 ||

Thus, the introduction of the rule "of the qualifiers" (*viśeṣaṇānām*) has been justified. Its rejection in the Bhāṣya on the grounds that "this is inherent" (*svābhāvikam etat*) has also been stated. To demonstrate this, he says: "But when gender and number are designated by their own nature, then correctness (*sādhutva*) is undertaken only with respect to the usage within the sentence. (145)

When the grammatical description (anvākhyāna) of words situated within a sentence—delimited by that sentence—is undertaken precisely while the various word-uses (*prayoga*) themselves are being employed, then at the very outset, due to the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a specific substratum, it is stated that the connection of "this is that" results in white and other qualities being associated with specific gender and number; this is their inherent nature. For in this view, because there is no difference in form, the distinction [between the quality and the qualified] is unperceived.

Nor is there any distinction between the "internal" (*antaraṅga*) and the "external" (*bahiraṅga*), because at the very outset, a specific substratum (*āśraya-viśeṣa*) is required. Thus, the grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) culminates in the internal general meaning. Therefore, in the previous analysis where the process begins with a disjunction, having relied upon the distinction between quality (*guṇa*) and the possessor of quality (*guṇin*), it was stated that when a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is employed, the application of gender, number, and pronoun—which occurs in the general substratum—is "internal."

Now, however, by relying on the non-difference [of the word] based on the relation "this is that" (*so'yam*), it was stated from the very beginning that the function [of the suffix] resides in a specific [meaning] as presented by the fixed sentence. Thus, because there is no relation of difference here, neither the elision (*luk*) nor the substitution of *a* for the possessive suffix *matup* is prescribed; therefore, the function does not possess an undifferentiated form, since those [grammatical operations] are prescribed only when there is an intention to express a relation of difference. || 145 ||

Now, one might object: "In this case, it is logical to intend non-difference; otherwise, just as the elision of the suffix *matup* is prescribed after words denoting qualities when there is a relation of difference, why is it not likewise prescribed after words denoting universals (*jāti*) when their connection is intended? Anticipating this doubt—and noting that although universals and qualities are alike in being inherent in substances—[the author] speaks in order to explain a further distinction between them: "In that regard, the application of qualities with their substrata is unrestricted; whereas that which is a universal is strictly inherent in that very [substratum]. (146)
