Qualities such as whiteness and the like inhere, without fixed necessity, in a substance that has already come into being due to the influence of various causes; furthermore, they do not persist for the entire duration of that substrate. Thus, there is an indefinite usage, both in terms of distinction and non-distinction, as in "the whiteness of the cloth" (*paṭasya śukla*) and "the white cloth" (*śuklaḥ paṭa*).

The genus (*jāti*), however, possesses a relationship with the substance that is constant from its very production until its destruction; therefore, through non-difference from it, it is always designated by the relation "this is that" (*so 'yam*), and never by way of difference, as in the case of "the cloth is white" (*paṭasya śuklaḥ*). Thus, the meaning is that only quality-words (*guṇaśabda*) necessitate the elision of the possessive suffix *matup* when there is an intention to express a relationship of difference. In this way, the commencement of the Sūtra at the point of interruption is justified. || 146 ||
He clarifies this very point: "The cowness of a *śābaleya* (spotted cow) is not designated as 'cow'; the whiteness of a *bāhuleya* (black cow) is not designated as 'white'. (147)

Without a suffix denoting an abstract state (*bhāvapratyaya*), the universal (*sāmānya*) extracted from the individual (*vyakti*) is not denoted; even when one says "the word-meaning resides in the genus" (*jāti*), it is always denoted as having attained the form of the individual through non-difference. For, due to the relationship expressed as "this is that," the universal, having attained the form of the individual, is fit to be designated in that very way. However, when the form extracted from the individual is intended to be expressed, then it is denoted by means of a suffix denoting an abstract state, as in "the cowness of the brindled cow" (*śābaleyasya gotvam*).

For even when the referent is a genus (*jāti*), because the genus is denoted as having attained non-difference from the substance (*dravya*), the cognition "the cow-ness of the cow" (*goḥ gotvam*) is distinct [from the cognition of the mere genus]. It has already been stated that qualities (*guṇa*), however, are expressed even with difference. Consequently, the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *matup* is prescribed after them. 147.

Otherwise, if there were indeed a distinction [between the substance and its qualities], the suffix -matup would be heard [in the word *rasavat*]. Therefore, the elision (*luk*) is prescribed; thus, that suffix does not exist after words such as *rasa*. (148)

In the case of "the cloth is white" (*paṭasya śuklaḥ*), since there is a distinction [between the substrate and the quality], that [quality] would be expressed by a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya-pratyaya*) when functioning as a relation; therefore, so that the form remains simply "white" (*śukla*) even there, the elision (*luk*) of the possessive suffix *matup* is prescribed. If it is argued that "it is established because there is no distinction," [we reply] that the elision is justified precisely where there is a distinction and a relation, as stated in the rule: "The elision is seen where there is a distinction. However, in the case of a genus (*jāti*), there is no relation of distinction; therefore, the possessive suffix *matup* is not produced after a word denoting a genus.

And this very distinction of domains is explained by means of elision (*luk*), being the cause for the restriction of expressive power (*abhidhānaśakti*). Consequently, it is stated that just as when a suffix (*pratyaya*) is heard, the meaning of the suffix is expressed as delimited by the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), so too is it [expressed] even when [the suffix] is elided in cases such as *śukla*. Furthermore, that elision does not occur after words such as *rasa*. (148)

For indeed, those [words] devoid of a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) are not able to denote their own substratum; thus he says: "Because it exists through a relationship of 'this is that' (*yat-so'yam*), it functions as non-different from its form, like 'white' and so forth; therefore, the elision [of the suffix] does not occur in the case of its taste and other qualities. (149)

By the force of the mention of the word *vacana* ("number"), the suffix *matup* is prescribed to be elided after those [words] which, having expressed a quality (*guṇa*), apply to the substance (*dravya*) possessing that quality through the relation "this is that" (*so'yam*) in exactly the same manner as they applied to the quality alone; this is done because their application to the quality alone is observed, in order to declare their application to the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*).

In that case, when there is an intention to express non-difference through the superimposition of the form of the cause (*nimitta*), and given the view that words such as "white" (*śukla*) denote the substance itself, the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*)—which is the cause for expressing difference—is not applicable; so what is the use of elision (*luk*)? Nor can it be argued that elision of the possessive suffix is desired in a case like "there exists a white cloth belonging to whom," where an external distinction (*vyatireka*) is intended; for since the literal meaning (*śrauta-artha*) is untenable here, a figurative meaning (*lākṣaṇika-artha*) is resorted to.

Those words denoting substances which are caused by qualities have been observed to be undifferentiated in form through the relation "this is that" (*so 'yam*). Now, lest there be the hearing of the suffix *matup*—which would express the desire to indicate difference and relation—from those words that currently function solely as denotations of the quality, the elision (*luk*) is prescribed. And in this way, [qualities] such as taste (*rasa*) are excluded, because words like *rasa* do not apply to the possessor of the quality (*tadvat*) by way of non-difference from its own form. For they always denote their own substratum only when ending in a possessive suffix, as in *rasavān* ("possessing taste") or *gandhavān* ("possessing smell").

Accordingly, the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) is introduced with the rule *rasādibhyaśca*. Since the suffixes *-in* and *-thañ* are not seen following these words, the possessive suffix (*matup*) alone is prescribed. Thus, the Vārttika states: "The repetition [of the mention] of *rasa* and so forth is for the purpose of excluding others. This means it is for the purpose of excluding other suffixes that might otherwise be applicable. In the expression *rūpiṇyapsarāḥ*, however, what is understood is a connection with beauty, not the inherence of the quality of color (*rūpa*) perceivable by the eye.

In cases such as *rasiko rājā* ("the king who possesses aesthetic relish"), however, the connection with the *rasa* (aesthetic flavor) such as *śṛṅgāra* is intended, and not a connection with a quality (*guṇa*) perceivable by the gustatory organ; thus, because the word *guṇa* is specified in the list [of the rule], the suffixes *ini* and *ṭhan* are excluded from words for *rasa* and the like, and they occur from other [words]. However, the claim that the suffix *luk* is mentioned in the Vārttika by the word "other" (*anya*)—on the grounds that *luk* would otherwise not apply according to the stated principle—is a misinterpretation. || 149 ||

Thus, at the very outset, when there is an intention to express a qualified substance, it is established that this [application] is natural; once the relation of non-difference (*so 'yam*) between the qualities and their substratum is established, gender and number [are attributed to the word]. Even in this view, he begins to demonstrate the utility of the Sūtra: "In some cases, there is an 'entering' (*āveśa*) by gender and number, as in the case of [the word for] 'platforms' (*mañca*); however, such [entering] does not exist in the case of a leader (*praṣṭha*) and the like, because of the relation of identity (*so 'yam*). (150)

In this context, regarding the relation of non-difference expressed as "this is that," when one object is superimposed upon another, two things are observed: duality, and the presence or absence of gender and number inherent in the original. In the example, "Look at the young women on the platforms" (*mañcān yuvatīḥ paśya*) or "the garments on the platforms" (*vasāṃsi vā*), the word *mañca* (platform), being superimposed by virtue of their location (*tātsthya*), functions with respect to its own substratum while retaining its own gender and number.

Similarly, in cases such as "the rivers Giriprabhā and Vāsū," it is observed that the word *giri* (mountain), through its proximity, applies by entering into the form of the mountains [of those names] while not abandoning its own gender and number, as in the expression: "Behold the flowing rivers, the mountains. However, words such as *praṣṭhapracara* (one who goes ahead) and others, which apply due to their connection with actions like setting out (*prasthāna*), are seen to abandon their own gender and number and instead adopt the gender and number of the objects they enter.

And likewise, the *praṣṭhī* (the leading cow) is designated by the feminine gender itself as "female. Thus, in this case, both gender and number are abandoned by the word *praṣṭha* and others when they apply to the substratum (*nimittin*). However, some words such as *mañca* (bed), applying to a substratum through metaphorical transfer (*upacāra*), adopt their own inherent gender, as in "the women are beds" (*mañcā yoṣitaḥ*) or "the myrobalans are fruits" (*harītakyaḥ phalāni*). Others, however, follow their own inherent number, as in "the forest is a thicket" (*khalatikaṃ vanam*).

Furthermore, some maintain that a word functions by taking as its basis the gender and number inherent in the indicator (liṅga) itself, while applying to the possessor of that indicator (nimittin). For example: "twenty Brāhmaṇas" and so forth. And this restriction is established through the division of domains due to the inherent nature of the word's expressive power. || 150 ||

He states that there is also an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for this very point in the technical treatise (*śāstra*): "In the rule concerning the abandonment of gender, there is the teaching of a suffix; because of the connection 'this is that,' the feminine word [is applied] to a masculine term. (151)

The rule *puṃyogād ākhyāyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.48), which prescribes feminine suffixes after words such as *praṣṭha*, is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the following principle: that these words function in the feminine gender through a relation of identity (*so 'yam*)—having abandoned their own original gender and number. For it is by virtue of the mention of *ākhyā* ("designation") that those masculine words which denote the female through a relation of non-difference (*abheda-sambandha*) are included; however, those ending in secondary suffixes (*taddhita*), such as *praṣṭhasya iyam* ("this belongs to the leader"), are not included, because they involve a relation of difference (*bheda-sambandha*).

And thus the Bhāṣya says: "For that which ends in a taddhita suffix does not become a designation [of gender]. The meaning is that when a taddhita suffix is present, there is no application [of the word] to the feminine for those designations of males whose forms remain unchanged. || 151 ||

Thus, because of the inherent nature of the power of words and because of indicative marks (*liṅga*), only words such as *praṣṭha* (leader) function with respect to another object by abandoning their own gender and number, and not others. Consequently, since there would be the undesirable consequence that even words like *śukla* (white) would apply to a substance—just like the word *mañca* (bed)—with its own gender and number through the connection "this is that" (*so 'yam*), the author states that the rule *viśeṣaṇānām* is commenced for the purpose of establishing the gender and number residing in the substrate (*āśraya*). "The substrate is designated by means of the gender and number of that which is supported [by it], according to the established grammatical principle: 'And [the gender and number] of qualifiers [apply] except in the case of a genus (*ajāti*). (Pāṇini 1.2.52–53)" (Verse 152).

Since the assumption of the gender and number of the substratum is established by the very nature of the word’s expressive power—just as in the case of words such as *praṣṭhī*—the rule "of qualifiers" (*viśeṣaṇānām*) is merely a restatement (*anuvādaka*), similar to the rule "in the case of a name derived from connection with a male" (*puṃyogādākhyāyām*). Consequently, it is established that the form of the quality, such as "white," which is the dependent (*āśrita*), is denoted by its own gender and number, which belong to the substratum; for otherwise, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) would be inexplicable. || 152 ||

For instance: "Because they follow upon their causes, those properties which exist in the grounds of differentiation are understood to exist in the substratum as well; thus, the notion [of their being distinct] is set aside. (153)

The meaning is as follows: since a suffix similar in form to the cause (*nimitta*) arises in the sense of that which possesses the cause (*nimittavat*), the substratum (*dravya*)—which is the possessor of the cause—is expressed by means of the quality (*guṇa*) such as "white" while its own specific form remains concealed. Thus, whatever properties belong to those causes (*nimitta*) which serve as the grounds for differentiation, all of them would apply to their substratum, the possessor of the cause (*nimittin*). Therefore, just as words such as "white" apply there, so too would the gender and number belonging to that [cause] apply; it is for this reason that the present *sūtra* is commenced.

And likewise, the apprehension of gender and number residing in qualities such as "white" is precluded by the treatise; for even when a substance is denoted by a word expressing a quality, it is designated only by its own gender and number. Indeed, the application of the gender and number belonging to the cause (the quality) is observed in the case of the effect (the substance). For example, in the expression *pañcālāḥ* ("the Pañcālas"), plurality belongs to the residence as it is denoted by way of delimiting it through the Kṣatriyas. Similarly, in *godau grāmaḥ* ("the village of Godau"), duality belongs to the village as it is denoted by way of its proximity to the Godu [river]. || 153 ||

Now, one might object that in cases such as *pañcālāḥ*, the application of the gender and number belonging to the cause [the individuals] follows from the rule: "When the elision of a suffix occurs (*lup*), the word is like that which possesses the suffix, both in its form and its number. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And it is declared by the treatise that in words such as *godā* (referring to the river Godāvarī), the application of gender and number—which is established in common usage by their very nature—is equal to that of the cause. (154)

In expressions such as "the village of the two Gods" (*godau grāmaḥ*) or "the country of the Pañcālas" (*pañcālā janapadaḥ*), it is established in common worldly usage that the application of a word to its referent follows the cause [of application] due to the inherent nature of the word's power; this is merely made manifest by the grammatical rule (*vacana*), but the rule itself is not capable of bestowing the word's power. Thus, this [rule] has been rejected by the statement: "That [gender and number] need not be taught, because the conventional name is the authority" (*tadaśiṣyaṃ saṃjñāpramāṇatvāt*). For a "name" (*saṃjñā*) is indeed a cognition (*saṃjñāna*); it is a conventional understanding rooted in worldly usage.

It is said that some words denote the possessor of a quality by means of that quality as the cause (nimitta), such as the word "mañca" (bed-platform) and so forth. When a similar doubt arises regarding words like "white" and the like, the denotation of the object by means of the property that serves as the cause—just as in the case of the word "praṣṭha" (leader)—is clarified by the rule stating "of qualifiers" (*viśeṣaṇānām*). || 154 ||

Since the power of the word itself is followed by its verbal expression, the distinction of their respective domains is established here; thus he says: "In the case of *harītakī* and so forth, the individual [is denoted]; in the case of *khalatika* and so forth, the number [is denoted]. For the specific types of humans and *lup*-derived forms, both [the individual and the number] depend upon the thing to be expressed. (155)

This has been stated in the Vārttika: "In the case of [words like] *harītakī* and so on, it is the individual (*vyakti*); in the case of [words like] *khalatika* and so on, it is the number (*vacana*); and there is a prohibition regarding the elision of the suffix *manuṣya*. In that regard, since this is based on explicit scriptural statement (*vācanikatva*), this distribution of domains concerning gender and number is not subject to any underlying restrictive rule.

For by this statement, it is indicated that the meaning is established by its own inherent nature (*svabhāva-siddha*), because a word lacks the capacity to bring about the manifestation of its meaning; thus, in cases such as *harītakyaḥ*, *phalāni*, *nakharajanyaḥ*, *kāśāḥ*, and *drākṣāḥ*, the gender alone is the uniform cause [of the word-form], whereas the number belongs solely to the cause residing in the denoted object (*abhidheya-nimittigata*). Consequently, because there is a plurality of fruits (*phala*), the plural number alone occurs.

For when there is a superimposition of another form (*pararūpasamāropa*), the own-form (*svarūpa*) of that which is the object [of the superimposition] is not entirely concealed; thus, because the nature of the result is not obscured, plurality (*bahutva*) is based upon it. However, this word has no expressive power (*śakti*) regarding the adoption of the number belonging to the cause (*nimitta*). Likewise, in cases such as *khalatikasya parvatasyādūrabhavāni* ("those situated near the mountain Khalatika") or *vindhyasyādūrabhavāni* ("those situated near the Vindhya"), the word’s expressive power lies in adopting the number residing in the cause; whereas the gender (*liṅga*) belongs only to the thing caused (*nimittin*). Consequently, because the forest (*vana*) is neuter, [the forms] *napuṃsakaṃ khalatikaṃ* (the neuter Khalatika) and *vanāni* (forests) and so forth are used.

And likewise, in the case of *cañcaiva manuṣyaḥ* (a man like a *cañcā*) and *cañcā manuṣyaḥ* (a *cañcā*-like man), when the suffix *kan*—prescribed by the rules *lum manuṣye* and *ive pratikṛtau*—is elided (*lup*), those qualifiers that are employed, such as *abhirūpaḥ*, *svākṛtiḥ*, *darśanīyaḥ*, and so forth, take on the gender and number of their cause (*nimitta*), just as in the expression *pañcālā bahvannāḥ*. Thus, since this point is established by reasoning (*nyāyasiddha*), even the rule *ajāteḥ* has been rejected in this context.

Because the genus (*jāti*) possesses the gender of that which is entered [by it], in the case of "the Pañcāla country" (*pañcālā janapadaḥ*), the country will not follow the gender, number, and so forth of its cause. || 155 ||

Regarding that which was explained as "in the absence of the use of a genus" (*ajāteḥ*), namely that qualifiers [of a substance] follow the gender and number inherent in the word ending in *luP* (the nominative singular suffix) provided they are not used with a genus, whereas qualifiers of a genus do not do so—the author explains this: "When a qualifier enters into a relationship with a genus through the employment of a genus, it then acquires from that genus its properties. (156)

When a qualification is employed with the intention of [denoting] a genus (*jāti*) through a delimitation based on free usage (*kāmacārāt*), then the gender and number inherent in that [genus] are established; for example: "The Varaṇā city has beautiful groves, clear water, and fragrant flowers. (156)

But when a qualifier is employed with the intention of referring to that which has undergone elision (*lup*), then: "When another qualifier than *jāti* (genus) is applied to that which has undergone elision, it is designated by the properties of that [elided] suffix, because the suffix that has undergone elision is the primary element. (157)

Since gender and number are inherent in the genus (*jāti*), it is established that any other qualifier standing in grammatical apposition with a word ending in a *lu*-suffix must possess the same gender and number. For example: "The Pañcālas are hospitable guests, clearly named, well-dressed, and abundant in food" (referring to the *janapada*); or "The two *godau* trees have fine thorns. Having established this, there is no need for a rule to this effect; rather, the rule has been applied here to the meaning: "The gender and number of qualifiers (*guṇavacana*) follow from the substrate (*āśraya*)."

In this case as well, when the form of that which is supported (the quality) is projected onto its support (the substance), then because the form of that which is supported is predominant, the support would come to possess not only the word-form [of the supported] but also its gender and number; therefore, the sūtra was composed. However, when the form of the support is projected onto that which is supported, it is logical that only the properties of the support are understood; thus, the sūtra was rejected on the grounds that this [usage] is natural (*svābhāvika*).

For when there is a superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the nature of the substrate (*āśraya-dharma*) upon the substratum (*āśrita*), the word "cloth" denotes the quality of whiteness; thus, its connection with gender and number is primary (*mukhya*). Nor does this preclude the expression of the quality by its own word; therefore, it must necessarily possess the same gender and number as the co-referential term "white. Alternatively, another view has been stated here by the learned regarding the rejection of the initial position (*ārambha-pratyākhyāna*).

For instance: since a quality cannot exist without a substratum, it must reside in whatever serves as its substratum. In that case, when there is the possibility of applying gender, number, and pronouns belonging to the substance (*dravya*) and the universal (*sāmānya*), the rule (*sūtra*) is formulated. However, when the intention is to express a specific substance from the very outset, such that the quality resides in a determined substance, then this [application of gender and number] is considered natural, and the rule is thus rejected.

For it is precisely at the commencement [of the application] that grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) is introduced in the actual usage of sentences; thus, the word possesses the capacity to convey a specific distinction. Here, there is also a third difference of view regarding the optional nature of the relationship between the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśe�ṣya*). When the quality (*guṇa*) is the qualified, then—since it would naturally be connected with its own inherent gender and number due to its predominance—the present *sūtra* is commenced to establish the gender and number belonging to the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*).

Although it is stated in the Sūtra that "of the qualifiers" (*viśeṣaṇānām*), nevertheless, here a quality (*guṇa*), even while being the qualified (*viśeṣya*), is indeed called a "qualifier" because it is adopted primarily [as the subject] and because it is dependent upon its own substratum. Even in this state of being primary, the word "qualifier" is intended here to mean merely that which is dependent, not necessarily that which differentiates; and since a quality possesses dependence even when it is primary by way of being the qualified, there is no fault whatsoever.

But when a quality (*guṇa*) is a qualifier (*viśeṇa*), then because it conforms to the principal (*pradhāna*), the understanding of the properties of its substratum (*āśraya*) is established by logic; thus, the word "rejection" (*pratyākhyāna*) refers to this as being inherent. Consequently, this aphorism (*sūtra*), which demonstrates a meaning established by logic, pervades the entire treatise. || 157 ||

He examines, in due order, those applications of the *bhāṣya* and *vārttika* in which this [work] is useful: "The various distinctions regarding gender and number that occur in negative compounds (*nañ-samāsa*), bahuvrīhis, dvandvas, and expressions of excellence (*atiśaya*) must be stated in accordance with the *bhāṣya*. (158)

In these sections of the Bhāṣya, the specific genders and numbers based on the substratum (*āśraya*) are discussed. Here, we follow the exposition in the Bhāṣya regarding the particular genders and numbers based on the substratum—which set aside those [genders and numbers] that would otherwise apply by following the cause (*nimitta*)—and which were introduced as "distinctions" (*bhedāḥ*). || 158 ||

In this regard, because it is easier to explain in reverse order, he first explains the Vārttika and Bhāṣya on the *atiśāyana* sūtra: "If the suffixes such as *tarap* were applied to a base ending in the genitive or accusative case that is inferior, they would be denoters of the inferior; [consequently], there would be a discrepancy in gender with respect to the original base (*prakṛti*) when it is superior. (159)

Regarding the rule *atiśāyane tamabiṣṭhanau*, there are several interpretations as to whether the word *atiśāyana* is derived with the agent (*kartṛ*) as the primary sense, the instrument (*karaṇa*), or the abstract action (*bhāva*). *Atiśete* (he surpasses) is *atiśāyana*. By virtue of the rule allowing for various meanings (*bahulavacanāt*), the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied in the sense of the agent; the lengthening of the vowel is due to irregular derivation (*nipātanāt*). Thus, *atiśāyana* refers to a quality (*dharma*) characterized by excellence in virtue or action, which resides in a substance (*dravya*).

For since a substance lacks excellence (*prakarṣa*) by itself, that [excellence] is established through the medium of a quality (*dharma*) which it possesses. In that context, when the substratum of the quality (*dharmī*) is intended as the agent of the act of surpassing, then it "surpasses" (*atiśete*); thus, the agent is the meaning of the suffix. But when here the operation belongs to the quality alone, then the instrument is the quality alone, which is the meaning of the suffix. For a cloth surpasses others by means of the quality of whiteness; therefore, that very quality is the primary factor of excellence (*atiśāyana*).

Therefore, since it is the instigator (*prayojaka*) of that [action], the designation is logical when the sense of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is established as "it causes to excel" (*atiśāyayati*). Even when the formation is based on the abstract state (*bhāva-sādhana*), "excelling" (*atiśayana*) means "excellence" (*atiśaya*), which is "intensity" (*prakarṣa*); and since that is caused by a quality residing [in the object], that very quality remains the meaning of the suffixes *tamap* and so forth, or else it is a property characterized by action. When these meanings are prescribed for the suffix, by virtue of the inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*), it becomes superior to its correlate (*pratiyogin*), which is inferior.

And since no specific base (*prakṛti*) is mentioned there, the general category of *ṅy-āp-prātipadika* stands as the base denoting that which is inferior. It has been stated that the case-ending expressing capacity (*samarthavibhakti*) is not mentioned in the rule; thus, the question arises: "From what ending should the suffix be produced? To this, it is said: "From a word ending in the second case (*dvitīyānta*), [denoting] that which is being surpassed. Although the root *śī* is intransitive, by virtue of a prefix it functions transitively in the sense of "overpowering" (*abhibhava*); therefore, the agent who overpowers (*abhibhavitr*) is the meaning of the suffix.

Since its connection with the meaning of the base [the word *nyūna*] is with that which is to be surpassed by something inferior, suffixes expressing inferiority [are applied]. Furthermore, in the Sūtras, the meaning may be indicated by any word whatsoever. When the sentence consists of a finite verb (*tiṅanta*), then the accusative case is logical for the inferior object; thus he says "from that ending in the second case. When the sentence consists of a nominal stem ending in a primary suffix (*kṛdanta*), then the genitive case is used for the object when a *kṛt* suffix is employed; thus the possibility from a form ending in the sixth case is also explained here.

Alternatively, the genitive case as a governing inflection (*samarthavibhakti*) indeed continues from the rule "ṣaṣṭhyā rūpya ca. Furthermore, there is no difference in meaning here, as the governing inflection is the same in both instances; this is the intended sense. However, in the Bhāṣya, it is stated that because the genitive used in connection with a *kṛt*-suffix might refer to the agent as well, there would be ambiguity regarding the state (*bhāva*); thus, to avoid this, it is understood that the suffix applies only after a word ending in the second case (*dvitīyā*), since the object (*karman*) is clearly indicated by that case alone. Consequently, in this view where the meaning of the suffix does not qualify the meaning of the base, a discrepancy arises between the meanings of the base and the suffix, such that the gender of the suffixal meaning would necessarily be the opposite of the gender of the base. || 159 ||

He further clarifies that very difference in gender through an illustration: "From *kālāt*, ending in the second case, [the suffix] *tarap* occurs after *kālyāḥ*; likewise, after *gārgye*, which denotes a contemptible agent, the suffix occurs after *gargebhyaḥ*. (160)

[Kālī] surpasses Kāla; [if one were to apply the suffix] *atiśāyini* (expressing that which surpasses) to the word *kālī* ending in the second case (*dvitīyānta*) or the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*), then from the base being surpassed, the form *kālatarā kālī* would result. However, *kālatirā* is what is intended. Likewise, Kāla surpasses Kālī; in this case, [if one were to apply the suffix] to the word *kāla* expressing the surpasser of *kālī*, the form *kālitaraḥ* would result. However, *kālataraḥ* is what is intended. Furthermore, in this context, "difference in gender" (*viliṅgatā*) is merely an illustration; "difference in number" (*vibhinnasaṅkhyatā*) also follows as a consequence. For example: [Kāla] surpasses the Gargas, [resulting in] *gārgyaḥ*.

In that regard, when expressing inferiority (*nyakkartṛ*), one would expect *gargatara*, whereas *gārgyatara* is desired as correct. This is because [the suffix] expresses "the Gargas excel" (*gārgyam atiśerate*). When expressing excellence (*atiśāyika*) among those [Gargas], if the rule were applied to *gārgya*, one would expect *gārgyatarāḥ*; however, *gargatarāḥ* is desired. Furthermore, it has already been established that in this context, the comprehension of a specific number occurs precisely through the presence or absence of the elision (*luk*) of the suffix, and thus the comparative suffix *tarap* applies even after words ending in the singular or plural.

Thus, the position that the suffix serves as a qualifier of the meaning of the *pratyaya* (suffix) has been declared defective in the Bhāṣya. Immediately thereafter, the position that it is a qualifier of the meaning of the *prakṛti* (base) is accepted with the words: "In that case, it will be a *svārthika* [suffix] added after a word ending in the first case. For instance, in the word *atiśāyana* (exceeding), derived from the root *śī* with the prefix *ati* according to the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*, the word *atiśāyana* denotes the agent (*kartṛ*) itself. Since there is no external cause for a distinction expressed by the suffix, the first case ending is applied internally based solely on the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*); the rule is then applied after that [stem] which ends in the first case.

And because they do not denote a different meaning, suffixes such as *itarā* and *tara* [retain] their own original meaning (*svārtha*). A suffix that occurs after a word expressing excellence (*atiśāyana*) is applied in its own sense. For example: *kālī atiśete* (she who is dark excels) becomes *kālitarā*; *kālaḥ atiśete* (he who is dark excels) becomes *kālataraḥ*. Thus, there is no change in gender; likewise, *gārgyaḥ atiśete* (one who is a descendant of Garga excels) becomes *gārgyatarah*. And in *gargāḥ atiśerate* (those who are descendants of Garga excel), there is no change in number either. || 160 ||

However, this undesirable consequence has been stated here: if [the suffix] were *svārthika* (denoting its own meaning) after a word ending in the nominative case, as in *kumāritarā*, then because age (*vayaḥ*) is not distinct [from the girl], the suffix *ṅīp* would apply by the rule "in the first age" (*vayasi prathame*). He explains this as follows: "And among the Gargas who are disparagers, [the suffix] would arise from *gārgya*; and that is not desired. If it were *svārthika* for a girl (*kumārī*), the suffix *ṅīp* would apply, for the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) would not be additional. (161)

In the cases "she excels among maidens" (*kumāry atiśete*) and "she excels among young girls" (*kiśory atiśete*), the forms *kumāritarā* and *kiśoritarā* would require the suffix *ṅīp* by the rule *vayasi prathame* (Pāṇini 4.1.20), because the comparative suffix *tarap* is used in its own primary sense (*svārthika*); for there is no excess over the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), which is characterized as a female in her first stage of life. Indeed, the femininity of that excellence, which is manifested by the first *ṅīp*, has already been indicated. But surely, since the excellence of the very meaning of "maiden" is revealed by the suffix *tarap*, the femininity of that preeminent object is understood precisely through it.

And thus says the Bhāṣya: "Because that meaning has already been expressed, it will not occur. The meaning is that since it is precisely the feminine gender that is being intensified, the feminine gender is already indicated by the suffix *tara* itself; therefore, the *ṅīp* suffix will not occur. Here an objection is raised: "In that case, even the *ṭāp* suffix would not apply. The meaning is that the fact that the meaning is already expressed is equally a cause for the non-arising of all feminine suffixes.

The solution to this objection has been stated: "For even when [the feminine gender] is already expressed, these suffixes such as *ṭāp* and others occur in their own sense (*svārthika*). This is the meaning: the suffixes *ṭāp* and so on are prescribed after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that denotes a female. Thus, just as the feminine gender—though already included by the nominal stem—is not necessarily perceived because the meaning of the nominal stem is common to all genders, and therefore it is manifested by the first feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*), so too would it be in the case of *kumāritarā* if the suffix *ṭāp* were absent.

The objection that there would be the undesirable consequence of understanding a contrary meaning does indeed arise; however, it is not the case that [the suffix] must always be *svārthika* (denotative of its own base meaning), because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) regarding what has already been stated. If this is so, then the objection raised in the Bhāṣya—that the suffix *ṅīp* would also apply as an exception to *ṭāp*—stands as a valid challenge. Now, one might argue: since the first *ṅīp* itself has already expressed the delimitation of the first stage of life, it is more logical that *ṭāp* alone should be used for the purpose of manifesting mere femininity (*strītva*). This is not correct; rather, on account of the suitability of the meaning, the use of *ṅīp* alone is more logical.

For example, regarding the statement "one, two, many," although the meaning has already been expressed, it is said that the nominative case (*prathamā*) will arise by convention (*samaya*). To this, an objection is raised: "If it is conventional, why do other cases not necessarily occur as well? In response, the solution is stated: "The determination is based on the meaning. The sense is this: although there is no requirement for the meaning in the case of an inflection when one observes the rule of usage—that the bare stem (*prakṛti*) alone must not be employed—nevertheless, because it conforms to the meaning, the nominative alone is logical.

In this view, even in cases such as *tatra* and *yatra*, the locative case alone is appropriate. Likewise, here too, for the sake of consistency with the initial grammatical context (*prakrama*), it is correct to say that only the suffix *ṅīp* is appropriate; thus it was rightly stated that "the suffix *ṅīp* would also follow. Furthermore, even without suffixes such as *-tarap*, the base word itself conveys excellence by virtue of context and other factors. In the absence of context and the like, the suffixes *-tarap* and others, which indicate excellence, certainly exist as *svārthika* (denoting their own meaning), but they are not denoters (*vācaka*) [of that excellence].

For instance, words that convey a meaning independently, without depending on another, are called "denoters" (*vācaka*). However, those that depend on such [a primary word] and illuminate the meaning residing therein are "svārthika" (suffixes expressing their own meaning). In the case of illumination, it is precisely through these [suffixes] that positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) become operative. Furthermore, because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in expressions such as "Devadatta is very clever," "clever-like" (*paṭukalpa*), or "of a clever form" (*paṭurūpa*), it is determined that these suffixes, such as *-tarap* and others, are *svārthika*, since they merely restate the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*).

Regarding the expressive words such as *yañ* and others—for instance, in the case of "the descendant of Garga is Gārgya"—there is a difference in grammatical coreference (*vyadhikaraṇatva*). However, from the Bhāṣya statement, "as much as Kālī is, so much is Kālitara," one cannot conclude that [the suffix] functions as an expressive word (*vācaka*). For Kālī is one whose excellence is unmanifest; when she herself is being intensified, she becomes Kālitara. Thus, the Bhāṣya proceeds by relying on a distinction characterized by the presence or absence of the expression of excellence.

Therefore, it is only the worldly object that is fixed and established, which is followed in the treatise through the distinction between the denoter and the indicated; however, these conceptual constructs belonging to the grammatical analysis do not possess a distinct objective reality of their own. || 161 ||

Having thus pointed out the defect even in the case of the suffix being used in its own primary sense (*svārthika*), it was stated immediately thereafter: "In that case, either a quality (*guṇa*) is denoted, or else an action (*kriyā*) is denoted. To explain this *Bhāṣya*, [the author] says: "Therefore, when something additional follows a word ending in the genitive case, the suffix is prescribed either for a quality residing in its own substratum, or for an action inherent in a superior [entity]. (162)

By means of the instrumental derivation (*karaṇasādhana*), the word *atiśāyana* denotes a quality that overpowers; or, by means of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) followed by the agentive suffix *lyuṭ*, it is called *atiśāyana* because it causes its own substratum to excel—that is, to overpower—by excelling itself. For it is through a quality being intensified that a substance attains excellence relative to other substances possessing similar qualities, since there is no excellence inherent in the substance itself.

And because that quality, which inheres in its own substrate, gives rise to a distinction from its own substrate, the base word *prakṛti*—which denotes the substrate of the quality—becomes the object of the genitive case, while the quality itself is the meaning of the suffix. For example, "the quality that is more excellent than that of the white" is *śuklataraḥ*. By stating that [the quality] resides in its own substrate, he implies that the suffix does not apply when it resides in a different substrate; thus, he says that the previously mentioned fault regarding the discrepancy of gender (*viliṅgatā*) and so forth does not arise.

However, when the suffix *lyuṭ* (ana) has a nominalizing function (*bhāvasādhana*)—such that "excellence" (*atiśāyana*) means "the act of excelling"—then the suffix occurs when this [excellence] is expressed as an action known as "intensity. And when a distinction (*vyatireka*) is produced by the action, the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used for the base (*prakṛti*), as in "the excellence of the white" (*śuklasyātiśāyanam*), resulting in *śuklatara*. Furthermore, since the meaning of the suffix here is a distinct quality characterized by action, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* does not apply after a word ending in that suffix, because a young girl (*kumārī*) is subordinate (*aprādhānya*) as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) to a woman (*vayasvinī*). || 162 ||

Regarding this position—that the meaning characterized by quality (*guṇa*) and action (*kriyā*), which is denoted by the suffix, is the primary element—[the author] asks: why was the lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇyābhāva*) with words like *paṭa* (cloth), which denote substances (*dravya*), not raised as an objection in the Bhāṣya? He replies: "The substance, which is the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), is indeed taken up as the substratum for those two [quality and action]. Through the connection 'this is that' (*so'yam*), it is perceived as non-different [from them]. (163)

Whatever substance (dravya) is denoted by the base (prakṛti) or the nominal stem (prātipadika) and is present here, that very same [substance] is perceived as the locus of these two—the quality and the action denoted by the suffix—through the relation of identity expressed as "this is that" (so 'yam). Thus, grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) occurs. Since a word ending in a suffix of excellence (prakarṣa) is never observed to function with reference to a mere quality or action, the sense of distinction (vyatireka) is accepted for words such as *karabha* and others solely within the context of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*) in order to justify the application of the feminine suffix *ṅīp*.

However, these [suffixes] are indeed *svārthika* (meaning "belonging to its own meaning"), because they serve to illuminate an excellence (*atiśaya*). For this very reason, the gender and number [of the word] are determined by the basis for employing a substance qualified by excellence through a suffix denoting excellence. || 163 ||

But surely, by the word "white" (*śukla*), a substance qualified by a quality is expressed here; and by the form ending in *-tara*, that very same [substance] is expressed as distinguished by excellence. Thus, since nothing at all is denoted apart from what is dependent [on a substrate], one might ask: "Of which dependent [quality] would the gender and number belong, as they do to its substrate? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And because there is no difference in form, that substance is perceived as possessing expectancy; it is then connected with the particular qualities—which have distinct forms—as if they were its own substrates. (164)

Here, by the word "white" (*śukla*), mere substance (*dravyamātra*) with qualities as its subordinate elements is denoted. That very same [substance], when distinguished by excellence, is expressed by the suffix *-tara*. Therefore, there is no cognition [of it] in specific instances such as cloth, because the mere substance is common to all specific instances. And thus, that [substance] is perceived as not depending on specific instances such as cloth; those specific instances which are depended upon are distinct, external, and—because they are connected subsequently—are designated as the "substrata" (*āśraya*). And that [substance] exists by virtue of being dependent upon them. || 164 ||
And therefore: "That mark which is established in particulars of diverse forms, as well as number—by means of these two, the substance-soul is designated as non-different from them. (165)

That essence of the object, being devoid of distinction, is expressed by a word denoting a collection; thus, the extension (*atideśa*) of the gender and number belonging to the particular [object] with which it is connected is established by the Sūtra. Therefore, it is presented as characterized by those two—the gender and number of its substratum (*āśraya*). Thus, according to the view that [the universal] is a quality (*guṇa*), because it resides in its own substratum, the expression belonging to that [substratum] is logically justified.

Regarding the view that [the root] *śī* belongs to the class of action (*kriyāpakṣa*), the Bhāṣya raises the objection: "In that case, both the one who surpasses and the one who is surpassed would be the substrata (*āśraya*); thus, even so, the dual number would result. To this, the following answer is stated: "The root *śī* is intransitive (*akarmaka*). (165)

Here follows the objection: "Even roots that are intransitive become transitive when accompanied by prepositions. The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin), however, reveals the intention with which he stated that [the root] is intransitive: "The rules prescribed for the object apply to those whose state (bhāva) resides in the object and whose action (kriyā) resides in the object; but the root *śī* has its state residing in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvaka*). Indeed, because it lacks an object as its inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), it is thus designated as intransitive.

He explains this as follows: "The substratum is the inherent cause (samavāyin) of the gender and number; therefore, the root *śī* (to lie down), which has its state of being located in the agent (kartṛsthabhāvaka), is cited in the Bhāṣya. (166)

That in which an action inheres is its substratum (*āśraya*). And since that [substratum] is singular, the singular number is used. For here, the sense of "overpowering" (*abhibhavana*) inheres in the agent (*kartṛ*), not in the object (*karman*) to be overcome. Whatever object is mentioned as a cause (*nimitta*) is designated as an "object" (*karma*); thus, even the dual number is stated in the *Bhāṣya* as being "designated as an object" (*karmāpadiṣṭa*). || 266 ||

For if the oneness of the action were expected [to determine the agent's number], then duality would arise here for the agent. He says this [in response] to the objection that the action might be grasped as an inherent cause (*asamavāyin*): "If the means (*sādhana*) were grasped as the substratum (*āśrayatva*), then the application of gender and number would occur there [in the action] as prescribed by the object (*karman*). (167)

Regarding the rule "the gender and number of words expressing qualities (guṇavacana) follow those of their substratum (āśraya)," if by the word *āśraya* one were to mean merely the cause (*nimitta*), then—since two things are required for an action to acquire its own existence, namely the agent and the object, which here constitute the means (*sādhana*)—the gender belonging to the object would also apply [to the quality]. Furthermore, because the production of duality depends upon that [object], the dual number would also occur; for indeed, the act of overcoming requires that which is to be overcome.

In this regard, since the action is well-known to reside in both the agent and the object, the objection regarding the contingency of a plural number based on the instruments and other factors has not been raised. Thus, the *Atiśāyana* commentary has been explained by way of the incidental discussion concerning the extension (*atideśa*) of gender and number. || 167 ||

Now, by that same reverse order, he says the following in order to explain the Vārttika on the *strī-sūtra* (Pāṇini 4.1.3) and its Bhāṣya, in connection with the investigation into the extension (*atideśa*) of gender and number: "In the grammatical treatise, the feminine meaning is extracted from the aggregate [of the base and suffix] as something lacking a specific cause; its connection with that [base] occurs optionally, either with the stem (*prakṛti*) or with the suffix (*pratyaya*). (168)

The worldly object, characterized by its established nature, which consists of a substance qualified by femininity and so forth, is cognized from an indivisible word (*niraṃśa-pada*). However, when that word is explained through the conceptual construction of base (*prakṛti*) and suffix (*pratyaya*), that very object—though indivisible—is divided into the meaning of the base and the meaning of the suffix, as those two (base and suffix) serve as the constituent parts of the grammatical instruction.

In this regard, in cases such as *samit* and *dṛṣad*, the expression of femininity is observed even by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) alone; whereas in cases such as *gaurī* and *kiśorī*, it is expressed by the stem together with the suffix. Since there is no fixed rule governing these positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the analysis of the meaning of the stem and the suffix is carried out according to the speaker’s intention, which follows the actual usage. || 168 ||

For instance: because it is a word denoting a quality (*guṇaśabda*), the word "woman" (*strī*) shares the same properties as "white" and other such terms; it is employed either to denote the quality itself or to denote a substratum possessing the quality of contraction (*saṃstyāna*). (169)

The quality (*guṇa*) is the coagulation or integration of color and other such properties; the word *strī* (feminine) applies either to that [quality] itself or to the possessor of that quality (*guṇin*). Thus, it is equivalent to words such as *śukla* (white) and others. For these too are observed in usage both for the quality alone and for the possessor of the quality, as in expressions such as *paṭasya śuklaḥ* (the white of the cloth) and *śuklaḥ paṭaḥ* (a white cloth). And so, in the rule *striyām* (in the feminine), when the word *strī* functions solely to denote the quality, then—according to the view that the base-meaning (*prakṛtyartha*) is the qualifier—the suffix is introduced after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that denotes the quality of femininity.

The view that the suffixes *ṭāp* and so forth denote the feminine gender (*strītva*) as the meaning of the suffix arises when [the word] refers to the denoted object (*abhidheya*). However, when the application [of the suffix] is to that which possesses [the quality] (*tadvati*), then the view that the base-meaning (*prakṛtyartha*) is the referent arises: namely, that *ṭāp* and so forth occur in their own sense after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that denotes a substance (*dravya*) possessing contraction (*saṃstyāna*, i.e., femininity). In this latter view, however, there is no nominal stem whatsoever whose application to a substance has femininity as its cause, in the same way that [stems] such as *śukla* ("white") apply to that which possesses the quality by taking the quality as their cause. For it is only the word *strī* itself that functions in such a manner.

For that very reason, in the rule [Pāṇini 4.1.3], the mention of "in the feminine" (*striyām*) would be meaningless if it were intended as applying universally to all base forms (*prakṛti*). Therefore, the word "feminine" (*strī*) indicates the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*), in the sense that "that nominal stem which occurs when the meaning signified by the word 'feminine' is present. || 169 ||

And thus, the suffix *ī* arises after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that exists in a meaning coreferential (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with the word "woman" (*strī*), according to the rule [Pāṇini 4.1.3]. However, it has been stated that this is undesirable: "If it is argued that [the suffix applies] when coreferential with 'woman,' there would be over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to words such as *bhūta*; furthermore, there must be a prohibition for those stems designated as *ṣat*. This he explains as follows: "If that which is the meaning of 'woman' is a substance (*dravya*) characterized by contraction (*saṃstyāna*), and if this [contraction] is the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), then, in that case, contraction would merely serve to indicate the substance. (Verse 170)

"Endowed with condensation" means that which is delimited by condensation acting as its cause. The intention is this: if there were such a thing—that is, if the object which is the cause of condensation were designated by the word *strī*—then condensation would merely be an incidental characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the substance denoted by another word; for no [word] whatsoever would apply to that object which is the cause [of the property]. || 170 ||

If this were so, what would be the fault? He says: "A substance is observed in some cases through contraction (saṃstyāna), which is characterized by it; there would arise a cognition [of that substance] from its occurrence in that [contraction], even though contraction has not been admitted [as a cause]. (171)

If [the feminine suffix] were applied to a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that functions by denoting an object brought to mind by the word "strī" (woman), where femininity (*strītva*)—meaning the state of being female—is either not accepted or not taken as the expressed meaning (*vācyatva*), then a suffix would result [inappropriately]. This is because, in the grammatical derivation (*anvākhyāna*), only an external factor—the meaning indicated by another word—is required as the cause [for the application of the suffix]. || 171 ||

Regarding this, he states an illustration: "When the six [suffixes] beginning with *bhūta* and those called *ākhya* occur after words such as *brāhmaṇī*, which are characterized by the quality of diminution (*saṃstyāna*), then suffixes are applied from them. (172)

Just as the word *kumāra* (boy) is applied to an object denoted by the word *strī* (woman)—as in "a girl"—and thus, in this view, it acquires a feminine suffix; so too, in cases such as *bhūtam iyam*, *kāraṇam iyam*, or *āvapanam iyam brāhmaṇī*, the suffix *ṭāp* would have to be applied because the word *brāhmaṇī* occurs in a sense of femininity that is already indicated by words such as *bhūta*.

Likewise, in the case of *pañca-brāhmaṇī*, *ṣaṭ-brāhmaṇī*, *sapta-brāhmaṇī*, *nava-brāhmaṇī*, and *daśa-brāhmaṇī*, where there would otherwise be the undesirable application of feminine suffixes after words beginning with *pañca*, a prohibition must be stated: "not after [words] ending in -ṣaṣ, nor after *svasṛ* and so on. Under the view that the base meaning (*prakṛtyartha*) is qualified [by femininity], since the suffixes such as *-tāp* (ṬāP) are introduced by the expression "femininity" (*strītva-vacana*), they do not apply because [the word] is not accepted as denoting "contraction" (*saṃstyāna*). Thus, this fault applies only to the view that [the word] is in grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with a feminine term. || 172 ||

For instance: "Since those possessing [the quality] are primary, they are the motivators of the suffixes; therefore, even when there is grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), the occurrence of feminine suffixes such as -tāp and so forth is possible. (173)

In this view, the expression of "concretion" (*saṃstyāna*) is not relied upon by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) when the suffix is produced; rather, the meanings characterized as feminine—which possess concretion—are the primary factors that trigger the suffixes. Consequently, because concretion is subordinate (*upasarjana*), even though there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with another word external [to the base], the suffixes *iṣṭhā* and so forth would indeed occur for such a concretion once it has been perceived.

For it is not possible to say here: "How can a meaning understood through another word be the cause for the grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) of a word?"—because one resorts to exactly such [a meaning] by means of verbal expression. || 173 ||

Thus, having refuted the position that [the feminine suffixes] are coreferential with the female gender (*strī*), the position that they qualify the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*)—namely, "But it is established that the feminine suffixes such as *ṭāp* occur in their own sense (*svārthe*), because the word 'female' (*strī*) qualifies the nominal stem (*prātipadika*)"—is stated. He states the seed for the emergence of this [position]: "When the word 'female' (*strī*) is described as denoting only a quality (*guṇa*), and when the meaning of the base is 'concretion' (*saṃstyāna*), then the suffixes are *svārthika* (occurring in their own sense). (174)

When "mere contraction" (*saṃstyānamātram*) is what is denoted by the word *strī* (feminine), and that [contraction] serves as a qualifier for the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), then—since no other referent for them has been specified—the meaning is that the suffixes *ṭāp* and so on occur after a nominal stem existing in the state of femininity; thus, they are considered "self-referential" (*svārthika*). However, when the meaning is "when femininity is to be expressed," then the position arises that they are qualifiers of the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārthaviśeṣaṇapakṣaḥ*). || 174 ||

Now, one might object: since it is impossible for any nominal stem (*prātipadika*) to function with respect to "femininity" alone, how can it be said that [the suffixes] depend on a specific meaning of the base? To this he says: "The application of bases is not found in mere contraction (*saṃstyāna*); therefore, they are understood as residing in a substance (*dravya*) permeated by that [contraction]. (175)

When a worldly object characterized by its established nature is employed as a factor in grammatical derivation, it is understood according to its possibility; thus, even when "in the feminine" (striyām) is stated, since no occurrence of the nominal stem's application is observed in mere femininity alone, the rule is understood by implication to apply to a nominal stem that denotes an object qualified by that [femininity]. 175.

And thus, since the suffixes produce a cognition while residing in a substance that is entered into and permeated by that femininity, the aforementioned fault does not arise; so he says: "In those words for which the *saṃstyāna* (concretion) is required as a contributing factor, the suffixes *ṭāp* and so on [are applied]; however, that [concretion] is not intended to be expressed in cases such as *bhūtā*. (176)

The meaning is that among those words in which [the quality of] being denotable (*vācyatva*) is applicable, the suffixes *aṣṭan* and so forth are used; however, this is merely an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*), and the point is that there is an absence of suffixes after words such as *bhūta* when [the quality of] "concretion" (*saṃstyāna*) is intended. As it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "This Brāhmaṇī woman is *bhūta*" (*bhūtamiyaṃ brāhmaṇī*). "In this case, femininity (*strītva*) is not intended to be expressed; rather, it is the state of having lived (*pautanya*). When femininity is indeed intended to be expressed, the suffix certainly occurs, as in "*bhūtā brāhmaṇī*," which means "one who speaks the truth" or "one who has passed away," and not the state of having lived.

Likewise, in the expression "this Brāhmaṇī woman is the cause," prominence (*prādhānya*) is intended; in "this basket is the receptacle" (*āvapana*), containment (*sambhavana*) is intended; and in the case of the measure of the container not exceeding the measure of the thing contained, non-excess (*anatireka*) is intended. Furthermore, for words such as *pañca* ("five") and so on, the denotable meaning is a number consisting of the counting of distinct entities, not femininity; thus, since the application of feminine suffixes would not follow from them, the prohibition [of such suffixes] was rejected. In this way, the position that the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) serves as a qualifier has been established as faultless. (176)

The third alternative was also stated: "Or rather, let it be that when 'femininity' (strītva) is the meaning [of the suffix], the suffix denotes that. Having presented the grounds for this possibility, he explains the defect [in this view]: "When the meaning of the suffix is taken as pure *saṃstyāna* (contraction), then the occurrence of dual endings and multiple suffixes is not established. (177)

When *saṃstyāna* (concretion), which is pure, absolute, and has not yet attained the status of a qualifier of a substance (*dravyaviśeṣaṇabhāva*), is accepted as the meaning of the suffix by virtue of its being indicated [in the rule] as "femininity" (*striyām*), then because that [concretion] is a single entity, the dual and plural forms—such as *kumāryau* and *kumāryaḥ*—would not occur. Furthermore, since there is only one concretion to be conveyed, the feminine suffix would have to be only one; consequently, multiple feminine suffixes—as in *gārgyāyaṇī*, *kārīṣagandhyā*, and *kālitara*—would not be possible.

This has been stated in the Vārttika: "If it is argued that [the rule] 'in the feminine' means 'denoting the meaning of a feminine,' then the occurrence of dual and plural suffixes, as well as multiple suffixes, would be untenable. || 177 ||

Now, regarding the view that "these three genders alone are established everywhere," one might suspect that the gender of femininity (*strītva-jāti*) is indicated here as the meaning of the suffix. And since its variation according to the difference in individuals would be appropriate—just as in the cases of *gāvau* (two cows) and *gāvaḥ* (cows)—the author says, anticipating this objection: "If it is a genus, then this [genus] is simply femininity; the distinction [of other genders] is not intended elsewhere, because even by means of different substances, that single [genus] is qualified. (178)

Since the term "in the feminine" (*striyām*) refers to a genus (*jāti*) as the meaning of the suffix, and because—according to the principle that "the base and the suffix express the meaning of the suffix together"—that [genus] alone is intended to be expressed as the primary element, the distinction or particularity known as duality and plurality, which occurs elsewhere in the individual (*vyakti*), is not intended here as the object of expression.

Since that single femininity (*strītva*) is delimited by many distinct substances (*dravya*)—which serve as its substrata and are denoted by the base (*prakṛti*)—and which possess various numbers, it is logical that there should be only the singular number, which rests upon the unity of the femininity that is not denoted by the predominant suffix (*pratyaya*). However, in cases such as *gāvau* (two cows) and *gāvaḥ* (many cows), a difference in number is appropriate because the individuals are denoted through the influence of the genus (*jāti*). ||178||

Now, regarding the view that "the state of the qualities (guṇāvasthā) is the mark" (liṅga), it might be argued that because the states are distinct, there will be a difference in their verbal expression; therefore, he says: "For when the constituent elements (mātrās) are concealed, no measurement exists. Thus, [the term] 'maidens' (kumāryaḥ) would apply, since a distinction is possible within a single maiden. (179)

When the concealment, dissolution, or diminution of the *mātrās*—which consist of the qualities (*guṇas*) such as *sattva* and so forth, and whose forms are color, taste, and the like—is intended to be expressed as "femininity" (*strītva*) characterized by contraction (*saṃstyāna*), and when a difference in grammatical number is stated based on a difference in states (*avasthābheda*), the usage would necessarily always be in the plural, as in "the maidens" (*kumāryaḥ*). This is because, even in a single instance, the limit of those different states cannot be determined, and thus their underlying meaning—contraction—possesses plurality.

For it is said that "the functioning of the qualities (*guṇa*) is mobile"; thus, because transformation (*pariṇāma*) is momentary, there is a constant difference in states (*avasthābheda*). If femininity were considered a single entity based on the persistence of the cognition [of "female"] while disregarding these differences in state, then this would not differ from the position of a universal (*jāti*); consequently, by necessity, the singular number would have to be used. For this very reason, since a universal must also be sought here, the author—considering that the two positions effectively converge in their result—uses the particle *hi* to illuminate the reason for establishing the previously stated point, rather than using the particle *ca* in the sense of conjunction.

Just as in this view there is the fault that dual and plural suffixes and multiple affixes would not arise, so too there is the absence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a substance. Consequently, it would follow that the form *kumārī* (young girl) would apply to this [state of] contraction alone. Furthermore, since contraction is merely a property (*dharma*), its connection with an action is not tenable; thus, one could not say "the young girl is adorned" (*alaṅkriyāyāṃ kumārī*). || 179 ||

Regarding this, the author of the *Vārttika* has stated the resolution: "And because a quality [assumes] the gender and number of its substratum. He begins to explain this as follows: "Just as actions proceed toward a substance that is accompanied by a genus, a number, or a collective aggregate—even though that substance is expected to be of a single nature—[so too does it happen here]. (180)

Because the non-difference of the properties of the forms from the forms themselves is thus observed, grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) and connection with action are both possible. (181)

In such cases as "Let the cow be milked," "Let a hundred Brahmins be fed," or "Let a five-bread bundle be brought," because the words denote universals (*jāti*), numbers, and aggregates (*samāhāra*) which serve as instruments, and since these cannot exist in themselves, the actions are performed upon the substance (*dravya*) which is invariably concomitant with them. This occurs when, due to the inherence (*samavāya*) of the universal and its possessor, their difference is concealed and non-difference is established; likewise, because the distinction between attribute (*dharma*) and substratum (*dharmin*) is not apprehended, even though there is a real difference, they are determined by the intellect as having a single nature. Thus, from the [limited] forms...

Because the non-difference—that is, the non-separation from the substance—of those properties such as contraction (*saṃstyāna*) and so forth from their objects appears, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is established, as is the connection of the substance with the suffixes. For, by its very nature, femininity is not conveyed by the suffix as something distinct from the substance. However, in the formal grammatical analysis (*prakriyā*), there is an extraction of the meaning of the suffix as a separate element.

Furthermore, since the word *mūrti* in the Bhāṣya—where it states, "And all *mūrtis* have this nature: they possess the qualities of contraction (*saṃstyāna*) and production (*prasava*)"—denotes any entity whatsoever, here too the word *mūrti* indicates any entity whatsoever; for even formless things such as the directions (*diś*) can possess the property known as femininity (*strītva*). (Verses 180, 181)

Some say: "Words such as *kumārī* (maiden), which have lost their possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*), stand in grammatical apposition with words denoting substances. He refutes that view: "But if apposition is required through the elision of the possessive suffix (*matup*), then [the rule] *luk taddhitaluki* would apply; moreover, in that case, [the word *taddhita*] is also an elliptical indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). (182)

If it is accepted that a word ending in a feminine suffix expresses only a property (*dharma*) characterized by contraction (*saṃstyāna*), and because it is a quality-word (*guṇavacana*), the *matup* suffix is elided—just as in the case of *śukla*—so as to allow grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a substance, then the rule "there is elision [of the feminine suffix] when a *taddhita* suffix is elided" (*luk taddhitaluki*) would entail the elision of the feminine suffix itself. Alternatively, if it is argued that the feminine suffix will not be elided because words ending in feminine suffixes always denote a substance, and not merely the *matup* suffix, then indeed the elision of the feminine suffix would never occur.

Therefore, even without the suffix *matup*, the gender of a substance is conveyed by its very nature (*svabhāva*) without distinction. Thus, even in cases such as *śukla* where the elision (*luk*) of *matup* has been prescribed, that elision is merely an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) intended to make known that the expressive power of the base itself is restricted to its own meaning. But if the meaning were not expressed in that way, what would be the purpose of the elision?

Thus, in the view that the meaning of the suffix is the primary referent (*pratyayārtha*), its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the substratum and its difference in number have been established through the metaphorical attribution of non-difference (*abhedopacāra*) based on its being a word expressing a quality (*guṇavacana*). Furthermore, there is more than one suffix because femininity—which has substance as its subordinate element—is by its very nature expressed by multiple suffixes in certain instances. To support the view that the meaning of the suffix is the primary referent (*pratyayārtha*) alone, he states another way in which coreferentiality and so forth are justified: "For some [grammarians], [the feminine suffix] is prescribed for substances themselves in which the distinction [between quality and substance] has been abandoned."

In the case of substances characterized by contraction [of qualities], suffixes such as *ṭāp* and others are applied because they are connected non-differently [to the substance]. Regarding substances characterized by contraction, the suffixes *ṭāp* and so forth are prescribed even under the view that the meaning of the suffix is the primary referent (*pratyayārtha*), by relying on the fact that the word *strī* ("female") functions to denote that which possesses [the quality] when [the rule] says "in the feminine" (*striyām*). For, since a substance is invariably understood from a word ending in a feminine suffix, it is logical to assume that very [substance] is what is expressed by the suffix.

If this were the case, then with respect to one [element], the substance would be the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), while with respect to the other, it would be the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*); thus, there would be the undesirable consequence of the cognition of two separate substances. Furthermore, two substances are not perceived as distinct, and there would be the consequence that the meanings of the base and the suffix would have no mutual connection. Anticipating this objection, it was stated: "in the case of indivisible [meanings]."

Because there is no contradiction with the meaning due to the non-distinction between ignorance (*avidyā*) and mind (*manas*), there occurs a connection with the specific [meaning] denoted by the base (*prakṛti*) through non-differentiation; for everywhere, there is a comprehension based on a universal (*sāmānya*) characterized by the form "it is feminine" (*strī*). Therefore, through the distinction between substance (*dravya*) based on the conceptualization of the universal and the particular as being denoted by the base and the suffix respectively—the base denotes the qualified substance, while the suffix denotes the substance-universal—and that very [universal] attains the particular state as delimited by the meaning of the base.

For instance: since a non-differentiation such as "femininity" (strī) is perceived as following through the specific substances denoted by the base (*prakṛti*), this distinction between the base and the suffix (*pratyaya*) is merely conceptual; it is not that two separate substantial entities exist in mutual isolation. (183) For instance: the substance (*dravya*), which is of the nature of a universal (*sāmānya*), is grasped as a delimited whole; it is joined with actions and exists as distinct parts. (184)

Due to the delimitation by the specific substance denoted by the base (prakṛti), the substance-nature denoted by the suffix (pratyaya)—which is mentally constructed—is like a universal (sāmānya), but it is not actually a universal. For, because of the coloring [of the cognition] by the particularity associated with a single word, the substance does not abide here in the nature of a universal; rather, it is a delimited apprehension. And this being the case, its connection with action is not contradictory.

And because those particularities expressed by the *prakṛti* follow through everywhere that [referent] which consists of a collection, it is established as having that form through a delimitation (*avaccheda*) similar to the parts of a universal; thus, even grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is logical. This is the intended meaning here: since a qualified substance is cognized from the combination of *prakṛti* and suffix, one posits the status of being the meaning of the *prakṛti* and the suffix by resorting to a distinction between universal and particular through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) during the analytical process (*apoddhāra*).

That very substance, when determined as distinct from other objects by virtue of its *prakṛti* (base), and when followed by a nature that conforms to the meaning of the feminine suffix and so forth, is called a "universal" (*sāmānya*). However, in common usage, the understanding culminates in the particular; thus, everything is logically consistent. (184) Thus, under the view that the meaning of the suffix is the primary referent, it has been demonstrated in two ways that the expression [of gender] pertains to its own substratum. This [view] is challenged: "In the case of words like 'white' (*śukla*), the substrate-substance is denoted primarily."

Since femininity (*strītva*), however, is the meaning of the suffix and thus falls within the domain of what is expressed (*abhidheya*), it is logical that words such as *śukla* (white), which denote a substance with a quality as its subordinate element, follow the gender and number residing in their substratum, because the substratum is predominant. But since femininity is primarily denoted by the suffixes *ṭāp* and others, while the substance—the meaning of the base—is here subordinate, how could the primary [element] here adopt the properties of the subordinate quality?

By the rule "of qualifiers" (*viśeṣaṇānām*), both number and gender are extended to the qualifiers just as they are to the qualified (*viśeṣya*), but not to the qualified as they are to the qualifiers. Regarding the phrase "within the scope of denotation": even though the substance is primary in reality, words do not conform to that; rather, their expression follows their own inherent capacity—this is the meaning. (185) He refutes this [objection]: "Through the connection 'this is that,' one apprehends the substratum."

Femaleness is either established by its own nature, or it is a reversal of the status of a quality. (186) Although, in grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*), it is established that femaleness is the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), nevertheless, due to the inherent power of the word, a reversal—that is, a contrary state—is observed here regarding the status of the quality: namely, that femaleness is subordinate while the substance (*dravya*) is predominant. For the meaning of the suffix is not predominant in every instance.

For example: when the verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) are prescribed for the expression of the *sādhana* (the factor of action), they do not denote the *sādhana* as the primary meaning; rather, they denote it as subordinate to the action (*kriyā*). Furthermore, when case-endings (*vibhakti*) are prescribed for the expression of number (*saṃkhyā*), they denote that number as subordinate to the thing numbered (*saṃkhyeya*). And when suffixes such as *ṭhak* are prescribed in the sense of "playing" (*dīvya*) and so forth, they denote the possessor of the action (*kriyāvant*) as the primary meaning. Thus, in all cases, one must follow the very power of the word (*śabdaśakti*). And since the substratum (*āśraya*) itself is the primary element, its number is what is expressed here.

Alternatively, even though its denoted meaning is merely *saṃstyāna* (concretion), nevertheless, the suffix denotes the individual instances which are the referents of the base (*prakṛti*), as they are metaphorically identified with that [concretion]; thus, the statement is established. In this way, there are three modes regarding grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*): the communication of femininity as non-distinct from the substance, as stated in "of the properties of form from forms"; the metaphorical identification of non-difference; or the predominance of the substance—these are what has been explained here. ||186||

Now, even under the view that [the suffix] denotes a commonality (*sāmānya*)—just as it does for *saṃstyāna* (solidity)—since the commonality which constitutes the meaning of the suffix can also possess real quality-status (*guṇatva*), [the author] states the following in order to apply the extension of gender and number from the substratum (*āśraya*) on the basis of its being a "word denoting a quality" (*guṇavacana*): "Or rather, the commonality is taught as a quality because it is dependent [on a substance]; this is an inherent property (*ātmadharma*) of individuals, the basis for their being perceived as one. (187)

That which was described as a substance (*dravya*), consisting of a generality (*sāmānya*) denoted by a suffix (*pratyaya*) through non-differentiation and characterized by a state of aggregation (*saṃstyāna*), is expressed in the Sūtra by the word "qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇa*), which is a synonym for "quality" (*guṇa*).
