For although the substance-generality is primary as the meaning of the suffix, it is fit to be designated by the word "quality" because it depends upon the specific substances contained within the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*); this is because an object that requires a substance is conventionally known as a quality. Furthermore, it is not distinct from the specific individuals (*viśeṣa*).

For this [universal] has attained the nature of a quality (*guṇasvabhāvatā*) with respect to individuals, which are specific substances (*dravyaviśeṣa*). Indeed, the nature of individuals, which is the basis for their being perceived as one, is called the "universal" (*sāmānya*). Even when there is a perception of difference, because its own form is obscured through inherence (*samavāya*), it simply attains the state of being a nature [of those individuals]. ||187||

[Objection: But surely, because it requires a complement, let the status of being a quality belong to the generality of substance (*dravyasāmānya*) as imagined by the intellect; however, in reality, since the substance characterized by its contraction (*saṃstyāna*) is a single entity, how can there be a relationship of locus and located? To this he says: "And such is that state when the apprehension of distinct parts has been performed by the intellect alone, and the status of being a locus for those differences has been conceived. Then, even when the differences have been extracted, the gender and number are attained through the reflection upon the gender, based on the individual form as the locus. (188–189)

The construction [of the sentence] is as follows: that variegated state (*śabalāvasthā*), which consists of both the universal and the particular, conveys gender and number when based on an individual (*vyakti*), and it conveys them when based on a substance (*dravya*) qualified by something else. To explain: when the division into base (*prakṛti*) and suffix (*pratyaya*) is performed through the analytical cognition (*apoddhārabuddhi*), by that very same process the meaning expressed by the whole is divided between the base and the suffix; thus, one part—the nominal stem (*prātipadika*)—is conceived as having a distinct form, while the other part, expressed by the suffix, is conceived as being permeated by the notion of "concretion" (*saṃstyāna*) and appearing as a mere aspect (*aṃśa*).

And when a distinction is conceptually constructed, and the status of being the substratum for qualifiers denotable by their own *prakṛti* is superimposed, then even though those qualifiers are considered separately and independently, when they are examined as specific instances (*viśeṣa*), they acquire the gender and number belonging to their substratum—just like "femininity"—because they are dependent upon it through the reflective awareness of gender (*liṅga-pratyavamarśa*) such as "it is feminine."

In other cases, because gender and number are observed to occur together, the term "gender" (*liṅga*) is used here; however, the extension (*atideśa*) of another, opposing gender characterized by femininity is not possible in this instance. Thus, the impossibility of the dual number has been refuted. But the impossibility of multiple suffixes (*anekapratyaya*) has not yet been refuted here. Since this is being stated in the context of an investigation into gender and number, the impossibility of multiple suffixes is irrelevant to the topic; furthermore, this [objection] is easily refuted.

In some cases, it is said that because femininity—which is subordinate to the substance—can be manifested by multiple suffixes due to its inherent nature (*svabhāva*), there is no fixed restriction regarding the manifestors (*vyañjaka*). It is precisely to follow this power of the word (*śabdaśakti*) that the *ṣit* designation for *ṣpha* was established for the sake of [triggering] *ṅīṣ*; likewise, the *ṅit* designation for *ṣyaṅ* is for the purpose of including it generally in the rule *yaṅaścāp*. However, in the *Bhāṣya*, a different resolution is stated: the *Vārttika* says, "And because *bhava* is connected with the state of being (*bhāva*)."

The meaning is that because femininity is of the nature of a transformation of a quality (*guṇapariṇāma*), its connection with "femininity" is logically established. A detailed explanation of this is found in the *Vārttikonmeṣa*. Furthermore, this was stated by relying on the primacy of the process (*prakriyā*) regarding the state of contraction (*saṃstyāna*) under the view that the suffix denotes the meaning (*pratyayārthapakṣa*), without following the actual power of the word. However, since the primacy of the substance (*dravyaprādhānya*) is intended here in accordance with the power of the word, the position already established—that the manifestation of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyapratīti*) is observed even through multiple manifestors (*vyañjaka*)—is superior.

For in this way, due to the difference in designation, the connection of femininity with femininity is expressed: since the substance-aspect is denoted by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) and the attribute-aspect is denoted by the suffix (*pratyaya*), the occurrence of two suffixes is justified. Just as that very same object is made known as having the form of a capacity (*śakti*) through case-endings such as the accusative, it is made known as a real entity (*vastubhūta*) by the nominal stem. For this distinction in cognition based on a difference in words regarding a single meaning is thus established. (vv. 188, 189)

In the sequence of topics, the utility of the extension of gender and number to a *dvandva* compound is now examined. In that context, since the rule for forming a *dvandva* applies when there is a sense of conjunction (*cārtha*), the objection that it would consequently lack gender and number was raised; the rebuttal stated that this is due to their "inherent nature" (*svābhāvikatvāt*). How is that justified? For, since the sense of conjunction is subsumed by the *dvandva*, its [the compound's] own usage therein should not be precluded.

Raising the objection that, since the meaning of the *dvandva* compound is also expressed by the word "and" (*ca*), why should it not likewise lack gender and number, he says the following in order to demonstrate this point step by step: "Even without the use of the word 'and,' the fact that the members of a *dvandva* function with an undifferentiated meaning is perceived due to the non-difference of their form. (190)

Words such as *dhava* and *khadira* either bring about or attain a copulative compound (*dvandva*), or they are those for whom a copulative compound is to be formed; in these cases, it is understood that they function with an undifferentiated meaning even without the employment of the word *ca*. Since they do not depend on the specific relation called "conjunction" (*samuccaya*), words like *dhava* and so forth are denoters of objects belonging to the class of *dhava* etc. in an undifferentiated form—that is, in a form not qualified by the word *ca*. Thus, for the purpose of indicating conjunction, they require the word *ca* within the sentence. || 190 ||

For it is said: "Whether the function [of the particles] involves conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) or whether they denote a combined object to be excluded, their power—which was previously unknown—is regulated by the indicator (*dyotaka*). (191)

Furthermore, if the initial word (*ādi-pada*) were not employed, the expressive power of the words forming a *dvandva* compound—or of the constituent parts of a sentence—would not be established with respect to a meaning qualified by conjunction (*samuccaya*) and so forth. For there would indeed be doubt regarding alternatives (*vikalpa*) and the like. Consequently, just as the expressive power of the words is made known by the word "or" (*vā*) when an alternative is being considered, and by the negative particle (*nañ*) when that which is to be excluded is being negated, so too is it made known by the word "and" (*ca*) when a conjunction is being expressed.

By the word "dyotakena" (by the indicator), he makes known the definition of an indicator, because a word whose primary function resides in another word lacks expressive power (*vācakatva*). It has been established in the *Vākyakāṇḍa* that an indicator is a word that is not used in isolation. || 191 ||

Thus, the use of the word "ca" (and) has been justified in the case of a sentence; however, he states that in a compound, specifically in a *dvandva*, there is no such use: "And because it assumes a distinct form in a compound (*vṛtti*), the word 'ca' is excluded. Even though there is a difference in meaning, [the compound] is designated by that [meaning] due to its similarity [to the constituent parts]. (192)

Because of the difference between a compound (*vṛtti*) and a sentence (*vākya*) produced by the unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), the words in a compound denote their meaning through a distinction from the properties found in a sentence; thus, even without the word *ca*, the denotation of a specific meaning based on the condition of conjunction (*samuccaya*) is inherent (*svābhāvika*) in a *dvandva* compound, and not merely because of the rule stating "a *dvandva* occurs in the sense of *ca*. For meanings are not directly enjoined [by the word *ca*].

For when there is the intention to express [the items] together (*sahavivakṣā*), in the formation of a compound (*vṛtti*), the collection is denoted by each word as mutually dependent, with their individual differences woven together; thus, because difference has dissolved therein, the conjunction (*samuccaya*) based upon that difference is not indicated. In a sentence (*vākya*), however, because difference is predominant, the conjunction based upon difference is indicated by the particle *ca*. Therefore, even though there is an absolute difference in meaning, the meaning of a copulative compound (*dvandva*) is pointed out by the sense of *ca*, merely because of the similarity in the mutual dependence of the actions.

For the purpose of grammatical exposition, an object already established in common worldly usage—which by its very nature is distinct from everything else—is somehow indicated through words by following a slight trace of similarity. Since it would be impossible to indicate each individual meaning for every word—because such meanings are infinite and distinct from all else—and because it would result in excessive complexity (*prakriyā-gaurava*), it is logical to indicate the meaning with brevity (*lāghava*). || 192 ||

And in that case, just as in the instruction on the meaning of secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), because the etymological meaning (*nairdeśika*) is not primary, one follows the specific meaning established by its very nature. However, if the meanings were exactly according to their etymological derivation, then— "If the non-substantial meaning of the word *ca* were accepted [as the primary sense], then the property of being a dual compound (*dvandva*) would apply; for in the case of *ca* and so forth, that [duality] is indeed determined by the meaning. (193)

Regarding the statement "it is without gender, without number, and indeclinable," since the designation "indeclinable" (avyaya-saṃjñā) is applied based on its meaning, and because a copulative compound (dvandva) is prescribed for that same meaning, the property of being devoid of gender and number—which belongs to that very meaning—would also attach to the dvandva. Anticipating the objection that the designation "indeclinable" would not apply to a dvandva because it is not listed among the words beginning with *ca* (the *cādi* group), it is said: "For that [designation] is based on the meaning within the *cādi* group."

Furthermore, the status of *cādi* particles as indeclinables (*avyaya*), which is established by their very nature as being devoid of gender and number, is merely restated (*anūdyate*) by their inclusion in the list; it is not the list itself that is prescriptive (*vidhāyaka*), since its purpose is illustrative (*udāharaṇārthatva*). Consequently, even in a copulative compound (*dvandva*) where the same meaning applies, the status of being an indeclinable would certainly follow. Alternatively, even if the technical designation "indeclinable" were not fixed by the list, who could prevent the quality of being devoid of gender and number—which depends on the meaning itself? Indeed, the designation "indeclinable" would also apply [to such compounds] because it is based on the actual meaning (*anvarthatvāt*). || 193 ||

Therefore, the meaning of words does not conform strictly to their literal expression; thus, he illustrates the variety of meanings arising from the variety of expressions: "In some cases, the meaning exists in a certain way due to a distinction in power; particles such as *ca* are its indicators, while a copulative compound (*dvandva*) is the speaker of those [meanings]. (194)

Just as the word *samuccaya* (conjunction) denotes an object associated with gender and number due to a specific power of the word (*śabdaśaktibheda*), so too the term *dvandva* (copulative compound) denotes an object characterized by conjunction. However, particles such as *ca* are indicators (*dyotaka*) that reside in the meaning provided by other words. This distinction between denotation (*vācakatva*) and indication (*dyotakatva*) is precisely what constitutes the difference between non-connection and connection in the case of individual words and compounds. || 194 ||

For instance: "If the object denoted by the conceptual construction and so forth were the referent of another word, then because [the particle] functions as an indicator (*dyotaka*), it would not be possible; therefore, it is observed to exist. (195)

If the meaning expressed by words such as "option" (*vikalpa*), "conjunction" (*samuccaya*), or "negation" (*pratiṣedha*) were to be conveyed by another form—namely, by being associated with gender and number—it would not be possible for the particle *vā* and others to function as indicators (*dyotaka*) of meanings such as option and so forth, since there would be no difference between the meaning [of the particle] and the meaning [of the word].

However, because an object associated with gender and number is expressed by words such as *vikalpa* (option), there is the status of being the "meaning of another word" (*anyapadārthatā*). Thus, according to the view that "the meaning of a word is the [external] object," this distinction of objects is indeed natural, insofar as a single reality is manifested in various forms due to the diversity of the powers of words. Consequently, the entity (*sat*)—which is a positive existent (*sattvabhūta*)—is indicated by the word *ca* (and), which functions as the subject matter of a copulative compound (*dvandva*), on account of some commonality.

The meaning is that this [neuter gender] is not denoted in reality by the dual number, just as it is not by the word *ca*. This very point has been stated in the Bhāṣya: "This lack of gender and lack of number is not based on a formal rule (*vācanika*); rather, it is inherent (*svābhāvika*). (195)
He says this very thing: "In that regard, when the property of a word is expected as the natural indicator (liṅga), a certain word conveys that very meaning in some way. (196)

The meaning is that this has been stated in the Bhāṣya with reference to the properties of words (*śabdadharmāḥ*) and the intrinsic nature of words (*śabdasvabhāva*). For instance—even when the object (*vastu*) is one, there is a diversity of meanings due to the difference in words. For example: *kārśyam*, *kraśimā*, and *kṛśatā*. Although there is no difference in the form of the base (*prakṛti*) between the base and the suffix-meanings, the distinction between "stasis" (*sthiti*), "production" (*prasava*), and "dissolution" (*saṃstyāna*) is based on the difference in the sound of the suffix (*pratyaya-śruti*). Furthermore, in the cases of *jalam*, *āpaḥ*, *dārāḥ*, and *bhāryā*, the difference in gender and number arises from the difference in the expressive power of the words (*śabdaśakti-bheda*).

Likewise, in the case of *dvaidham*, which is without gender (*aliṅga*) and number (*asaṃkhya*), that very same [word] is thus established as having both gender and number (*saliṅgasaṃkhya*) in the form *atidvaidhāni*. For here, according to the rule "the suffix *ḍa* is seen after words ending in *dhamuñ* in the sense of the base itself," there is a difference in word-form due to the addition of a different suffix. In this way, even a *dvandva* compound denotes an object possessing both gender and number. || 196 ||

It might be argued that the determination of meanings arises from the speaker’s intention and not from the nature of the word itself; anticipating this doubt, he says: "Meanings are conveyed through words, and they are the establishers of distinctions. There exists no means of inference for the speaker’s intention other than the word. (197)

The singular number is used for the genus (*jātāvekavacanam*), as in the phrase "from words" (*śabdāt*). Since a speaker utters appropriate words to convey a meaning as intended, it is from those words—through the inference of the speaker’s intention—that words alone are capable of establishing the object in linguistic usage. Even in the case of things such as the winking of an eye, they function as inferential indicators only through words, because they have been conventionally associated with them. For instance, although real objects possess a single nature, they undergo expansion when expressed by words, because various forms are manifested through them.

And so, the word *dāra* denotes a woman as qualified by masculinity; the word *bhāryā* denotes her as qualified by femininity; and the word *ap* expresses that same referent consisting of parts, delimited by plurality. However, the word *udaka* [denotes] it as a single aggregate; such is the nature of words to be understood. Therefore, the word *sa-* (the pronoun "that"), by virtue of its own power, is the ordainer and creator of the distinctions that qualify its denoted object. The meaning is that, although there is no actual division of parts within the entity, a multiplicity produced by the word is superimposed upon the object through its very nature. || 197 ||

Thus, the application of gender and number based on the inherent nature [of the members] has been established for a *dvandva* compound. Now, in order to examine another alternative mentioned in the *Bhāṣya* as a scriptural statement—namely, "Alternatively, the gender and number will be according to the substratum"—he says: "The meaning of a *dvandva* may be a collection in which the collection is subordinate; or the collection itself may be that in which the collection is subordinate. (198)

There are two alternatives: either the objects conjoined, which have conjunction as their limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), are expressed by a copulative compound (*dvandva*), or it is the conjunction itself that has the conjoined objects as its subordinate element (*upasarjana*). || 198 ||

In that regard, when the collection is primary, gender and number [of the verb] follow their own inherent nature; when the collection itself is primary, the grammatical rule would be the means of expression. (199)

It has been stated that when a collection (*samuccaya*)—which is a subordinate element consisting of entities—is expressed by a *dvandva* compound, its gender and number are inherent. However, when the collection is expressed as the primary meaning of the *dvandva* through the explicit statement of the referents, then the gender and number are prescribed according to their substratum by the very rule stating "of qualifiers" (*viśeṣaṇānām*). Since the collection is of the nature of a property (*dharma*), the grammatical treatise serves as the prescriptive authority for the gender and number that would otherwise not be obtained, even though they are desired.
In that case, even though the conjunction (samuccaya) is predominant, the extension [of the rule] is appropriate because that which is merely dependent is denoted by the qualifying word. || 199 ||

Even when the collective [meaning] is primary, he states the utility of the treatise according to the opinion of others: "Others know that even when the meaning consisting of a collection is primary, there is no establishment of gender and number because [the word] conforms to its cause. (200)

When the possessor of a characteristic (*nimittin*) is apprehended through its characteristic (*nimitta*), the form [of the latter] is obscured due to its absorption [into the former]; likewise here, because the compounded [word]—which is delimited by the cause known as "conjunction" (*samuccaya*)—is unfit for the realization of its own grammatical properties, the gender and number belonging to it do not apply, and thus there is an extension (*atideśa*). Therefore, the grammatical rule (*śāstra*) is useful in both of these two positions. || 200 ||

He says that this is incorrect: "If conjunction were the cause, there would be a following of that cause; furthermore, by means of positive and negative concomitance, the meaning is based on the copulative compound. (201)

The meaning "collection" (*samuccaya*) is not what is directly expressed by the *dvandva* compound, such that it would have to conform to its cause [the word]. Rather, that meaning which is determined to be the denotation of the *dvandva* through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is restated as "that meaning" (*sa cārthaḥ*) for the sake of grammatical derivation (*anvākhyāna*) of the *dvandva*. And that [meaning] is a collection of objects of equal status with respect to the action, in which the power of the case-role (*kāraka-śakti*) has emerged.
Because it is observed that this [collection] is sometimes designated by the word "collection" (*samuccita*), the "collection" is erroneously superimposed as its cause. || 201 ||

He states that this is the ultimate truth in this matter: "Even when the cause has been combined or when the object has disappeared, the gender and number of the dual compound remain fixed as established by its own nature. (202)

When *ca* is combined as the basis for a *dvandva* compound, then, because it follows the properties of the principal element, its gender and number are determined by the rules of logic (*nyāya*). Alternatively, due to their absolute dissimilarity, there is no semantic conjunction (*cārtha*) of meanings at all, such that one could consider a relationship of subordinate and principal (*guṇapradhānabhāva*) between it and the substance (*dravya*). However, in the grammatical instruction (*śabdānuśāsana*), the meaning is indicated in some way or another merely through a trace of similarity; thus, it is designated as "the meaning of *ca*" (*cārtha*) by virtue of being the cause for the *dvandva* compound.

However, since the meaning of a copulative compound (*dvandva*) is inherently a plurality of entities, there can be no status as a causal factor (*nimittabhāva*) for a conjunction (*samuccaya*), precisely because such a thing does not exist. || 202 ||

The meanings of the words contained within a *dvandva* compound are expressed by the *dvandva* itself through mutual dependence, and that very [expression] is *samuccaya* (aggregation). Anticipating the objection, "In that case, why is it said that the meaning of *ca* disappears?", he recalls the previously stated distinction between their meanings: "Because it serves as an indicator (*dyotaka*) of the meaning residing in another word, it is not appropriate [for *ca* to express it]; however, the particle [in a *dvandva*] expresses the meaning [of its members] without regard for gender or number. (203)

The meaning is that although the substantial object (*vastvartha*) remains non-different, the referent (*śabdārtha*) is differentiated due to the difference in the operation of denotation (*abhidhāvyāpāra*). Thus, because a substance-like object is denoted in a *dvandva* compound, the disappearance of the object seen as non-substantial in the sentence is described. Furthermore, this is the play of the expressive (*vācaka*) and indicative (*dyotaka*) powers, as has already been stated previously. || 203 ||

Furthermore, he criticizes the view that [the self] conforms to the marks: "And because, in the case of conforming to the marks, there is no regard for the properties of a substance, the connection with action through the relation of primary and subordinate cannot be established. (204)

If [the word] conforms to the cause (nimitta), then because it denotes the substance (dravya) which is the possessor of the cause (nimittin) as permeated by the form of that cause, its capacity (śakti)—which is its property (dharma)—cannot be determined by the intellect. Consequently, there would be no connection for this [substance] with actions, whether as a primary factor or as a subordinate quality. For a substance is the means of accomplishment (sādhana); and how could that which has not had its own capacity determined be connected with actions? Furthermore, the cause itself cannot be connected with an action, because it is not an entity (asattvabhūtatvāt).

In that regard, there is a connection with actions through its status as a subordinate factor (guṇabhāva) in the form of an instrument (karaṇa) and so forth; and through its status as a primary factor (pradhānabhāva) in the form of an object (karman), it is connected with those actions because it is the locus of their production (utpatti), refinement (saṃskāra), and attainment (pratipatti). || 204 ||
If it is argued that there should be no *kriyāyoga*, he says: "For one who has no *kriyāyoga*, independence does not exist; in that case, the mention of the compound would be meaningless. (205)

"A word-meaning is not cognized without connection to an action. Thus, there is no such thing as a word-meaning that is independent, self-contained, or unconnected with actions. Consequently, since there is an absence of connection with an action when that meaning is colored by its causes (nimitta), the adoption of the *dvandva* compound as its denoter would be purposeless; therefore, it would not be subject to grammatical derivation (*anvākhyeya*) and would be non-functional. For this reason, it is understood from the very process of derivation that there is no conformity to the causes in this case. (205)

Nor does it follow that [a word] always conforms to its cause; thus he says: "The designator of an object possessing a collection [of qualities] does not conform [to those qualities]; moreover, its meaning (the object) is then joined with its own properties. (206)

Even those words such as *samuccita* (collected) and others, which are well known for denoting objects qualified by the attribute of collection (*samuccaya*), do not conform to that cause [of cognition]. This is all the more true of the *dvandva* compound, where there is an illusion of the attribute of collection being present; for conformity to a cause occurs only where there is a cognition of the substratum (*nimittin*) whose own form is concealed by the form of the cause, as in the case of "white" and so forth. Here, however, there is no such thing, because the object is designated as delimited by a distinct cause.

For this very reason, the suffix *matup* is employed in the expression "possessing a collection" (*samuccayavataḥ*). By means of the suffix *matup*, he demonstrates that there is a designation here of something delimited by a distinct cause. However, where there is a denotation in the form of the cause itself—as in the case of "white" (*śukla*) and so on—the suffix *matup* does not arise. Therefore, because it does not conform to the cause, the word "collection" (*samuccita*) here denotes its own primary meaning as endowed with its own gender and number; since a *dvandva* compound is likewise [denotative], there is no fault whatsoever.

Thus, regarding the position that "the meaning of a *dvandva* compound would be a collection (*samuccita*)," it is precisely this [view]—that gender and number belong to the [constituent members] by their very nature—that is logical. However, if the emphasis were on the collection (*samuccaya*) itself, then the prescription of gender and number according to the rule "of qualifiers" (*viśeṣaṇānām*) would have to be stated in that very context. || 206 ||

Anticipating the objection—"What is the substratum (āśraya) denoted by the co-referential (samānādhikaraṇa) term for a *dvandva* compound that expresses items of equal status, such that one might understand [the number] in terms of its individual instances?"—he says: "In a *dvandva*, there is no external substratum; for in that case, two particulars are what are heard. Their conjunction (*samuccaya*) is the substratum, and it is designated by their properties. (207)

Just as in the expression "white cloths" (*śuklāḥ paṭāḥ*), there exists a substratum for the quality-denoting word provided by the word "cloths" (*paṭa*), such a substratum provided by another word does not exist in a *dvandva* compound. This is because the two distinct particulars are apprehended directly through the two *dvandva* words themselves; they are internal [to the compound]. In the case of "the *dhava* and the *khadira* trees," those very two particulars, being conjoined, constitute the substratum or locus of the conjunction. Therefore, the gender and number belonging to that [conjunction] belong to the *dvandva* which expresses the conjunction.

In that case, since it is impossible to designate [the compound] simultaneously with two contradictory genders residing in the preceding and following members, when an option (paryāya) would otherwise result, the gender of the final member is prescribed. As for number, it belongs to the *dvandva* based on the substrates of its parts, having the nature of duality or plurality which consists of the aggregate of the singularities residing in the individual parts. || 207 ||

Thus, in this view, it has been established that the meaning of a *dvandva* compound is simply the meanings of its constituent parts in mutual dependence. Now, he says the following to establish the impossibility of the meaning [of a *dvandva*] being expressed as a simultaneous reference to multiple substrata (*yugapadadhikaraṇavacanatā*): "Or rather, a single aggregate which is associated with two distinct parts—as if they were themselves distinct—partakes of the properties belonging to those two portions. (208)

A collection (*samudāya*) that follows from the distinction of its parts is expressed by a *dvandva* compound when there is a desire to express them together; however, the actual denotation is natural (*svābhāvika*). According to the view that "the other word [of the compound] has the same two [parts] as that which expresses a single manifold meaning," the meaning is denoted by each individual word. In this perspective, when there is a mention of individuals based on the parts, it is clear that the collection is what is obtained. And because the collection, whose internal distinctions are interwoven, is presented by the *dvandva*, he says "as if by two things possessing distinction."

The meaning is that [the compound] does not [refer] to two things that are absolutely distinct. Furthermore, because of the persistence of non-difference (*abhedānugama*) between those two parts which constitute the substratum, the aggregate (*samudāya*) conforms to the gender and number [of the members]. Otherwise, if there were a denotation like that of a forest (*vana*) or a herd (*yūtha*), wherein difference is eliminated, then since the two parts serving as the substrata would not be expressed, the question arises: "To what would the *dvandva* compound belong in terms of gender and number, given that the two constituent words do not themselves possess them? This is the intended sense. || 208 ||

[Objection: "But even so, since no collection is perceived apart from its constituent parts, where does the relationship of locus and located (āśrayāśrayibhāva) reside? To this he says: "This single object consists of two natures, being endowed with both difference and non-difference. It attains the gender and number residing in those two differences upon which it depends. (209)

The aggregate, being apprehended as consisting of its constituent parts, is distinct; yet, by virtue of being based on a single cognition, it is non-distinct in itself—thus it possesses two forms. Consequently, while the substratum is conveyed by each individual word as having the nature of a distinction, it is [conveyed] as a collective whole as resting upon the meaning; thus it is established that gender and number depend upon those qualities inherent in the word-meanings residing within that substratum. || 209 ||

Now, in order to explain step by step the utility of extending the denotation of the individual [meaning] to a bahuvrīhi compound, he says: "Just as the word 'Caitra' is not employed when the referent Caitra has already been expressed by its own name, so too there would be non-employment of the word [in the compound] within the bahuvrīhi. (210)

In this context, a *bahuvrīhi* compound is explained as having a meaning external to its constituent members (*anyapadārtha*). Consequently, since that external referent has already been expressed by the compound itself, the use of words such as "Caitra"—which denote that very referent—would not occur, just as in the case of a *dvandva* compound where the word "and" (*ca*) is not used. For example, once the meaning of the word "Caitra" has been expressed, the word "Caitra" is not used again; for there is no employment of words whose meaning has already been stated. As it is said in the *Vārttika*: "When the meaning of the word has already been expressed, further usage is untenable because it has already been denoted."

The refutation stated here is: "Or rather, it is not so, because [the meaning] is not unexpressed; for when there is the expression of a general property, there is indeed no expression of its specific particulars. || 210 ||
He explains this as follows: "Just as there is no denotation of 'white' and so forth by the word 'cow', so too, first of all, that which has a connection with cows is what is perceived. (211)

Since a *bahuvrīhi* compound denotes the general relation [of possession], the cognition of its specific instance does not arise from it alone. For example, the word "cow" (*go*), which expresses the universal, is incapable of denoting a particular; therefore, a further word is employed to bring about the cognition of that particular, such as "the cow is white" or "the cow is black. Similarly, the usage "Citragu is Caitra or Maitra" is logically required for the cognition of a specific individual, because the expression "one whose cows are brindled" (*citragavo yasya*) conveys only the owner in general. (211)

However, where a specific distinction is accepted through a *bahuvrīhi* compound alone due to the inherent nature of the word's power (*śabdaśakti*), a term denoting that [distinction] is not employed there. Thus he says: "A fixed, conventional relationship of the *citras* (the variegated ones) does not exist, as is the case with cows; nor is there one established for them as there is for the Vajrapāṇi or the Three-eyed One. (212)

One who has a vajra in his hand and one who has three eyes—thus, Śakra and Śiva are understood through their well-known, fixed, and invariable conventional meanings (*rūḍha*) even without the employment of specific qualifying words within the sentence. Therefore, in that case, the *bahuvrīhi* compound occurs when the specific relationship constitutes the external referent (*anyapadārtha*). In the example "citragu" (one who has brindled cows), no specific [owner] is determined, because it is possible for the mere owner to be connected with the brindled cows without distinction; thus, the employment of the substantive (*viśeṣya*) here is not contradictory.

"But when the specific meaning is understood from the context and so forth, there is no application of that [compound] here either. (212) Thus, once the author of the Vārttika has established that the subsequent employment [of the verb] is possible for the sake of expressing a specific meaning, it is objected in the Bhāṣya: "It would be established when the function [of the compound] pertains to the general; but when the function pertains to the specific, it is not established—as in: 'These variegated cows belong to Devadatta. To this, the resolution is: "These two do not occur simultaneously: the sentence and the compound."

When there is a sentence (*vākya*), there is no compound (*samāsa*); when there is a compound, there is a derivative operation (*vṛtti*) in respect to the general sense. In that case, one who desires a specific detail must necessarily employ a word expressing that specific detail, as in "Who is the 'possessor of brindled cows'?"—[the answer being] "Devadatta. This he explains: "Even though specific details are heard in sentences because they are different words, this word of the compound (*vṛtti-śabda*) is indeed something else, denoting the general sense. (213) It has already been established that there is a difference between the word of the compound and the sentence by way of a difference in their meaning and form, such that they are distinct words.

Even though the sentence proceeds with a specific [meaning], it is indeed appropriate to employ the word *vṛtti* (verbal root) in subsequent usage, for its expressive power is not obstructed by the denotation of the specific. For the sentence itself, because it is immediately subsumed within the *vṛtti*, does not express that [specific] as a mere generality. Rather, the meaning of the *vṛtti* is indicated by the sentence through a lack of great distance [from it]. However, the denotative power of the word *vṛtti* does not extend to the sentence-meaning as a whole when it is completely delimited [by particulars], because particulars such as specific number and so forth are not perceived from it. ||213||

Anticipating the objection—"If this is so, what is the purpose of employing this Bahuvrīhi compound, which expresses only a general meaning, is expectancy-laden, and fails to convey a specific distinction?"—he says: "Because of the difference in form, [the word 'citragu'] excludes the non-cow and the cow that does not possess variegated cows; likewise, because there is no difference in form among the specific [variegated cows], it denotes them. (214) By the word *citragu*, an object is denoted that is excluded from the state of having no connection with cows (*agauḥ*) due to the absence of such a relation. Furthermore, by the qualification of "variegatedness," there is an exclusion of the cow that does not possess variegated cows (*acitragoḥ*).

And thus, this word is not a general term (*sāmānyaśabda*) in every respect; rather, it is capable of being employed because it denotes a particular (*viśeṣa*) that is distinguished by the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*). Having set aside this much intention (*vivakṣā*), when the connection with variegated cows is to be conveyed, this word indeed possesses a distinct form. However, since it is incapable of conveying another particular residing in that [connection] due to the sameness of its form, it is called a denoter of the general.

"For there would be no distinction [in meaning] between 'Caitra is the owner of brindled cows' and 'Maitra is the owner of brindled cows. (214) When the employment of specific terms (*viśeṣaśabda*) as subsequent members has thus been established, it is again objected: "In that case, the employment of a general term (*sāmānya*) alone would not be possible, as in: 'That is the owner of brindled cows,' 'What is the owner of brindled cows? or 'Is everything the owner of brindled cows? The resolution here is: "Just as a general term can function as a specific one, so too, when 'the owner of brindled cows' is said, a doubt may arise as to whether it refers to 'everything' or 'the universe'; therefore, a specific term must necessarily be employed as the subsequent member."

Regarding this, he explains how there can be a similarity between a universal and a particular: "Just as when the term 'citragu' (owner of brindled cows) is employed, [the word 'cow'] is not employed; so too, if the universal were present, there would be no separate mention of it. (215) When the owner of brindled cows is designated by the term 'citragu', a word whose meaning is already expressed by that [compound] ought not to be used again, as its meaning would not be required.

If such a general term as "all" and so forth were not intended to be sought after, then, because it would denote the exclusion of others, this would be merely a particular term; thus he says: "But 'all' and the rest are particulars that exclude specific locations, just as specific locations set aside other general locations. (216)

Here, the defining characteristic of a particular (*viśeṣa*) is its differentiating nature. Just as when "Caitra" is uttered, the exclusion of other particulars such as Maitra is understood, and the cessation of the universal (*sāmānya*) occurs, so too, even when a general term such as "the entire universe" is employed, there is an understanding of the cessation of particulars. Thus, the meaning is that this universal, being a delimiter of others, becomes a particular by virtue of relative dependence. (216) In this way, the objection regarding the impossibility of subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) under the view that words denote individual objects (*padārtha*) has been resolved.

But when the *bahuvrīhi* compound "one whose cows are variegated" (*citrā gāvo yasya*) is formed in the sense of another word (*anyapadārtha*)—namely, the relation denoted by the case-ending—then the sixth case-ending, which expresses that relation, should not be employed [in the subsequent verb]. However, since the substance (*dravya*) is not expressed [by the compound], the employment of a subsequent verb (*anuprayoga*) for the purpose of expressing that substance is indeed appropriate. As it is stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "Alternatively, the meaning of the case-ending is expressed. And this is appropriate here; for in this case, the final word occurs last of all."

Just as in the expression "Citrā gāvo Devadattasya" (Devadatta’s brindled cows), this word ending in the genitive case, through its denotative function (*abhidhā-vyāpāra*), expresses the meaning of the case-ending as primary, with the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-artha*) as subordinate; likewise, it is logical that the relation—of which the related term is subordinate—should be the meaning of the external referent (*anyapadārthatā*). Thus, at the very end of the process, the word indicates, by means of its denotative function, the occurrence (*vṛtti*) of the word ending in the genitive case in that sense of the case-ending, characterized as a relation (*sambandha-lakṣaṇa*) involving distinction (*vyatireka*).

According to the maxim, "A cognition of the qualified [object] does not arise without the qualifier having been apprehended," there is first an application (*vṛtti*) to the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-artha*), which is the relatum and the delimiting factor; subsequently, there is the relation to the particular as qualified by that [delimiting factor]. Therefore, it is logical that this very [delimiting factor], being the predominant element, constitutes the meaning of the other word (*anyapadārtha*). This is what he says: "Or, because the meaning of the case-ending is already expressed, the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is not employed; however, because the substance (*dravya*) is not expressed, that word [the nominal stem] is employed [again]. (217) The meaning of this verse is self-evident. (217)

Regarding this position, it is objected: "If the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*) is denoted, the metaphorical application (*upacāra*) of gender and number to the substance (*dravya*) would be untenable. This means that because the meaning of the case-ending is of a non-substantial nature (*asattvabhūta*), the metaphorical application—that is, the linguistic usage—of the gender and number belonging to the substantial entity (*sattva*) would not occur here in the case of a compound word (*samāsavācya*). The resolution stated for this is: "But it is established as in the case of adjectives (*guṇavacana*). In that regard, the gender and number of adjectives follow from their substratum (*āśrayataḥ*).

In cases such as "white" (*śukla*) and so forth, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) because of the elision of the possessive suffix *matup* with its respective substrata. However, in this case, since the *bahuvrīhi* compound expresses a mere relation, coreferentiality with words expressing the relata is not tenable through the elision of *matup*. Thus he says: "If coreferentiality is established through the elision of *matup*, then since *matup* itself would have that same meaning, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would result. (218)

Since even the *matup* suffix, like the *bahuvrīhi* compound, expresses only the relation (*sambandha*), if the relatum (*sambandhin*) is not denoted, another *matup* would have to be prescribed; if that too does not convey the relatum, yet another would be required—thus an undesirable infinite regress (*anavasthā*) of *matup* suffixes would result here. However, if the *matup* suffix denotes the relatum, then because the *bahuvrīhi* is prescribed in the sense of possessing that [relatum] (*matvartha*), and if that [compound] likewise denotes the meaning in that same way, the position that the case-suffix (*vibhakti*) denotes the meaning would not hold. 218.

Not only is there an infinite regress, but furthermore: another relation would necessarily follow as the relation of that relation; moreover, when the meaning of the case-ending is primary, connection with a verb is not possible. (219)

The relation expressed by the *bahuvrīhi* compound is the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*). By that [base], another relation expressed by the possessive suffix (*matup*) is delimited. Furthermore, because the meaning of the suffix is colored by the meaning of the base, the meaning of the suffix—being delimited by the relation that constitutes the meaning of the base—would become a relatum of the meaning of the base. And thus, the status of the meaning of the base as being itself a relation is lost. The intended sense is that its status as a relatum is attained because it possesses an adjunct (*upādhi*).

Furthermore, in a *bahuvrīhi* compound where the meaning of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyartha*) is predominant, there would be no connection with an action, such as in the phrase "Let the one who has variegated cows be brought," because a relationship, being a non-substantial entity (*asattvabhūta*), cannot give rise to the capacity for a grammatical factor (*kāraka*). (219) Now, if it is argued that even in cases where the meaning of a case-ending is predominant—such as in "Look there" or "Look from there"—a connection with an action is observed, [the author] says "no": Because they are predominant in the sense of a case-ending, the words "there" (*tatra*) and "from there" (*tataḥ*) do not admit an action such as "seeing" (*dṛśya*) and so forth, since they serve merely as the basis for [grammatical roles] such as object (*karman*) or agent (*kartṛ*). (220)

In the case of the two [words] *tataḥ* and *tatra*, which primarily denote the powers of the ablative (*apādāna*) and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), an action such as "seeing" or "standing" does not manifest the powers of agent (*kartṛ*) or object (*karman*), because that would contradict the meaning of other case-endings. Rather, what is perceived here is the connection of the action with the limit (*avadhimat*) and the thing contained (*ādheya*). Therefore: "Look from there," and "He stands there. || 220 ||

Thus, there is a fault in the position that the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhakti*) is denoted [by the compound]. Furthermore, if the meaning of the case-ending were denoted, would there not be a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in the expression *citragur devadattasya* ("the owner of brindled cows belongs to Devadatta")? It will not occur, because "that meaning, having been denoted, is included within [the base] and becomes the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Anticipating the objection that for this very reason there will be a connection with the verb [in the sentence], he says: "And how could the relation be included when it has been denoted as the primary [meaning]? And how could that [relation] become the meaning of the nominal stem in such a state? (221)

Just as in the case of "Caitrasya" (of Caitra), the relationship is expressed primarily and in its manifest form by means of the genitive case, how could that [relationship] be included here by means of a *bahuvrīhi* compound? For a relationship that is expressed as subordinate to the related term (*sambandhin*) is included within the compound;

for example, in "rājapuruṣaḥ" (the king's man), because the referent "man" qualified by the "king" is primary, the relationship is subordinate, and thus it may be considered the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*). But in this case, since [the relationship] is expressed with a sense of distinction (*vyatireka*), how could it be the meaning of the nominal stem? || 221 ||

Now he first establishes the nature of *kriyāyoga*: "But because [a direct] connection is impossible, there occurs a [figurative] connection with that which accompanies the actual connection, just as there is the occurrence of the grammatical operations concerning genus, number, and collective aggregation. (222)

Just as when words denoting universals and the like are enjoined—such as "One should sacrifice a cow," "Bring a hundred Brahmins," or "Let a bundle of five be tied"—the action is performed upon the substance that accompanies them and is inseparable from them because the application of the action to the universal alone is impossible; likewise, in the case of "Let the owner of brindled cows be brought," since the action is impossible with respect to the mere relation, the action is applied to the related entity (the possessor) which is inseparable from that relation. || 222 ||

It might be argued as follows: In the case of genus-words (*jātiśabda*), it is logical that they denote their own form as permeated by the genus and as co-occurring with it [the individual] non-differently; thus, there the connection with action is possible. But here, since the relation is primary, how can this be? Anticipating this doubt, he says—in order to establish grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) even in this case: "Because of the connection 'this is that,' for words denoting a qualified substratum, gender and number will occur just as in the case of 'white' and so forth, due to the commencement of the grammatical treatise. (223)

Let it not be that there is coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) here through the elision of the possessive suffix *-matup*; rather, based on the relation of "this is that" (*so 'yam*), the relatum—possessing a superimposed non-difference through a relation like "white" and so forth—is denoted by the word *vṛtti*. Even when the application [of gender and number] is prescribed for the relation alone, because of the inherent nature of the word's expressive power (*śabdaśaktisvābhāvyāt*), the rule "of the qualifiers" (*viśeṣaṇānām*) establishes the gender and number residing in the relatum, in order to avoid following the [gender and number of the] occasioning cause (*nimitta*), as is the case with [the word] *mañca* ("bed-platform").

However, because the relation [of the word] is observed to conform to the individual forms (*nimitta*), the dual number would [otherwise] result. But because of the commencement of the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*), the expression of the individual (*vyakti*) and the number (*vacana*) are established as being based on the primary meaning (*apradhāna-apadārtha*). || 223 ||

If this is so, how is it that the following was stated in the Bhāṣya: "If, then, the meaning of the case-ending is expressed, how does the entire word-meaning become expressed—possessing substance, gender, and number? Anticipating the objection that gender and number are established through the relation of "this is that," the author explains the intention of the Bhāṣyakāra: "But when there is a desire to express [the meaning] as distinct, or when the general sense is intended to be expressed, there would be no comprehension of the word-meaning as possessing gender and number."

When it is intended that the relation be expressed by means of a *bahuvrīhi* compound through the exclusion of the related entities, then, because of its lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*asāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the substance, there is no connection with its gender and number; thus, it is said that the complete meaning of the word is not apprehended.

It has been stated that if one intends to express a relation as "this is that," or if the denotation is intended solely to exclude what is not the owner of the variegated [cow]—as in the case of a quality-less universal where one says "this is the owner of the variegated [cow]"—then, because there would be no substratum (āśraya) other than what is understood from external words such as "Caitra," there would follow the application of gender, number, pronouns, the neuter gender, and the singular number; thus, how could the entire meaning of the word be expressed?

Therefore, even in this case where there is the relation expressed as "this is that" (*so 'yam*), because there is no denotation of the entire meaning of the word, the position that the case-ending expresses the meaning must be abandoned; rather, one must resort solely to the position that the substance (*dravya*) is what is denoted. || 224 ||

He explains how this is established: "Correctness (sādhutva) is not seen to reside merely in the meaning of the case-ending; correctness belongs to that which functions with the entire meaning—thus the term 'meaning' (artha) was included. (225)

Since the usage of a *bahuvrīhi* compound—which functions through *ekārthībhāva* (the unification of meaning)—is not observed when it occurs merely in the sense of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyartha*) devoid of a substance (*dravya*) or other qualifiers, because from such a compound one perceives only the referent of another word (*anyapadārtha*) as primarily consisting of a substance; therefore, the inclusion of the term "meaning" (*artha*) was made in order to indicate the usage of that which expresses every kind of meaning.

This has been stated in the Bhāṣya: "Since the rule would have been established by the mere mention of 'another word' (*anyapade*), the fact that he includes the term 'meaning' (*artha*) has this purpose: so that the meaning of the word may be understood as a complete entity, namely as possessing substance (*sadravya*), gender (*saliṅga*), and number (*sasaṃkhya*). Even with such a designation as *sadravya*, it is the substance alone that is intended as primary; qualities and the rest are not considered equal to it, because from the perspective of the speaker's intent, it is the substance itself that is perceived as being colored by qualities and so forth.

In this context, when "pada" (word) is mentioned, the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*) is understood by implication as being proximate, because a word cannot function [as a synonym] for another word. However, if the term "artha" (meaning) were used instead, the "meaning" qualified by "pada" would be understood as extending to the meanings of all words.

For just as the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*) is excluded here due to its excessiveness, so too the mere meaning of the case-ending would be excluded due to its deficiency; thus, the substance (*dravya*) which constitutes the word-meaning—possessing gender and number—is itself the "meaning of the other word" (*anyapadārtha*). Therefore, the position that the word itself denotes the meaning (*padārthābhidhānapakṣa*) is superior. Consequently, the subsequent application of the verb (*anuprayoga*) is justified. || 225 ||

And since, in this view, there is no utility for the extension of the singular number, he states that it does have a purpose in another view: "When this [word], through its connection as 'this is that' (*so'yam*), functions as a substance (*dravyavṛtti*), then its correctness (*sādhutva*) is said to belong to that which possesses gender and number. (226)

In the view that the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*) is primary, although the relationship with the general substance (*dravyasāmānya*)—which is characterized by a metaphorical non-difference—is denoted, the author of the *Vārttika* stated the utility of extending the designation of the individual (*vyaktivacana*) "as in the case of adjectives" (*yathā guṇavacaneṣu*), for the sake of establishing the gender and number residing in the particular. This, however, is not the case in the view where the meaning (*artha*) is primary. The sense is that because the entire substance is denoted by virtue of the inclusion of the word "meaning" (*arthagrahaṇāt*), gender and number are inherent here [in the primary view]. || 226 ||

In this regard, the following objection is stated in the Bhāṣya: "If, then, the entire category of meaning (padārtha) is denoted, the objects [of inference] for the followers of the Nyāya and the Sāṃkhya would not be established. He explains that very point: "Just as the genitive case is not heard when its meaning is already included within [the nominal stem], so too the non-occurrence (aśruti) of those [suffixes] denoting gender and number would follow. (227)

Because of the inclusion of "meaning" (*artha*), when a substance (*dravya*)—possessing gender and number—is denoted as the primary object, the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*), namely the relation (*sambandha*), is included as a subordinate quality (*tadguṇabhūta*) within the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*). Just as the sixth case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhīvibhakti*) does not occur [in such cases], so too there would follow the non-hearing, that is, the non-usage, of those suffixes: the *laiṅga* suffixes such as *ṭāp* and others which occur in gender (*liṅga*, specifically femininity), and the *sāṅkhya* suffixes such as *sva* and others which occur in number (*saṃkhyā*, such as singularity and so forth). This consequence would result. || 227 ||

Anticipating the objection—“In the absence of an object to be tasted (svādya), how can *prakṛti* alone be fit for usage?”—he says: “When that is the case, there would be grammatical agreement (*sādharmya*) with an indeclinable (*avyaya*) in the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, because of the removal of the grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) caused by gender and number. (228)

Since there is an absence of grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*)—characterized by the production of feminine suffixes such as *ṭāp* and so forth, or case endings such as *svādi*—which would otherwise be necessitated by gender and number, there would be a single "yoga-kṣema" (shared grammatical status) for the members of a *bahuvrīhi* compound with respect to the absence of gender and number. The meaning is that just as an indeclinable (*avyaya*), being devoid of feminine suffixes and case endings, is used in its isolated form because it is an exception to the rules governing usage, so too would it be for a *bahuvrīhi*. || 228 ||

If it is asked how there can be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with another word such as "Caitra" which expresses existence, he says: "And through its connection with that which is employed, the hearing of 'Caitra' and so forth occurs; for a connection exists even without a case-ending, while [the expression of] the case-ending exists without [that connection]. (229)

When a *bahuvrīhi* compound, such as *citragu* ("possessing brindled cows"), which denotes a substance in general, is uttered without a case-ending, it would follow that words like *Caitra*, which denote specific individuals, should likewise be used without case-endings, because they share the same denotation (*samānābhidheyatva*) as that compound. It is logical that a word devoid of a case-ending should be connected only with another word devoid of a case-ending, and not with one possessing a case-ending, due to their absolute dissimilarity (*atyantavaidharmya*).
Consequently, if there were no connection, there could be no expression of a specific substance residing within the general substance. (229)

Thus, in this context, the objection (*codyabhāṣya*) has been explained according to the view that words denote their referents (*padārthābhidhānapakṣa*). Regarding this very point, the response (*parihārabhāṣya*) states: "In the case of derivative words (*laiṅga*), it has been said: 'But [the feminine suffixes] *ṭāp* and so forth are established for the female because they qualify the nominal stem (*prātipadika*); therefore, they [denote] their own meaning. The meaning is that just as *ṭāp* and so forth function as indicators (*dyotaka*) elsewhere, so too will they function for the *bahuvrīhi* compound. It is also stated in the *Sāṅkhya* texts: "'Since [factors such as] object and so forth have not been mentioned, the numbers such as singularity and so on [will be expressed],' whereby the accusative and other cases will arise," and so on.

He explains this as follows: "Even when number is denoted, its status as a number does not cease; however, when the meaning of the genitive case is denoted, it becomes the meaning of the nominal stem. (230)

Even when expressed by means of *bahuvrīhi* compounds, number indeed brings about its own function, characterized by [the application of] case endings and so forth; as for example in "one," "two," or "many. For even though it has been expressed, number does not abandon its own nature. Consequently, second and subsequent case endings arise in order to express the number that serves as a qualifier for the object (*karman*) and other factors. Even the nominative case ending will arise in order to maintain the linguistic convention that "a base alone should not be employed."

However, this restriction on usage is set aside by the explicit rule regarding the elision (*luk*) after indeclinables (*avyaya*). Furthermore, elision has not been prescribed for words that are *bahuvrīhi* compounds. If it is asked, "Since the preservation of the conventional meaning is the same [in both cases], why do the accusative and other case endings not occur?"—the answer is no, because of the absence of the required meaning. For the accusative and other case endings occur when there is an object (*karman*) and so forth; in the absence of such [grammatical relations], how could they occur? Therefore, just as in the case of words like *eka* and others, the nominative singular and other case endings will occur after these [indeclinables] in the sense of the mere meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*), in accordance with the sense.

As it has been said: "The determination is based on the meaning. Alternatively, because of the inclusion of the word *vacana* ("number"), the nominative case will apply even though its meaning has already been expressed. However, when the relation of the genitive sense—which is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*)—is denoted as part of the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), that meaning is already expressed and thus internalized; consequently, the genitive case does not occur. For the domain of the genitive is where the relation is predominant and manifest.

Thus, in order to resolve the objection regarding the impossibility of subsequent application (anuprayoga) when denoting the meaning of a word (*padārtha*), the position that the meaning of the case-endings (*vibhaktyartha*) is what is denoted has been adopted. In that view, both grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and connection with the action (*kriyāyoga*) have been established. Furthermore, by the inclusion of the term "meaning" (*artha*), it is established—on the basis of the authority of usage—that correctness (*sādhutva*) belongs to that which functions toward the entire meaning. || 230 ||

Furthermore, he states that some express a different opinion: "Some declare that the postulation of a case-meaning is not for the sake of accomplishing the application [of a suffix], but rather that a distinct entity (vastvantara) has been introduced. (231)

In order to provide a rebuttal to the objection that "the subsequent employment [of a verb] would be untenable in the denotation of the word-meaning because it has already been denoted," the position that the case-endings denote the meaning was not adopted; for the subsequent employment has been established by the principle: "Or rather, it is not so, because [the meaning] has not been denoted; for when the general is denoted, the particular remains undenoted. However, according to the opinion of others, this is merely another philosophical system presented here as a subject for deliberation regarding what is logical and what is not.

For even here, it is maintained that the substance is denoted through the connection expressed as "this is that" (*so 'yam*); and thus, since the subsequent application of the verb would be untenable, the same defect remains. In that case, the remedy must be applied in the very same way as before: "Or rather, it is not so, because [the substance] has not been denoted. How then can this be considered a different solution? By the use of the word "some" (*kocit*), he indicates a lack of approval for this view. For indeed, in the *Bhāṣya*, the introduction of this point with the words "or rather" (*athavā*) is precisely as an alternative resolution.

"And this is logical here, for in this case the word stands at the very end"; thus the superiority of this position has been stated. Even though, under this view as well, there is a denotation of the substance (*dravya*) due to the connection [expressed by] "this is that" (*so 'yam*), nevertheless, in the grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*), the predominance of the meaning of the case-ending alone is intended for the sake of establishing the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*). However, because of the authority of the subsequent application, the established doctrine (*siddhānta*)—that there is a denotation of the whole [meaning] due to the inclusion of the sense—is indeed superior, as has been stated previously.
And in that case, the gender and number are inherent; however, according to another view, they are determined by the grammatical treatise. || 231 ||

Observing the presentation of another entity, he states the synthesis of the two positions: "Either relations qualified by their relata would be the cause, or the possessors of those [relata] qualified by the relations would be the cause. (232)

In the case where the meaning of a case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*) is denoted [by the compound], relations delimited by the members (*vartipada*) that serve as relata (*sambandhin*) function as the cause for the application of a *bahuvrīhi* compound. The plural number here is also to be understood as before. 232.

He explains this very point through the observation of the suffix denoting "possessing" (*atvarthīya*), which shares the same acquisition and security (*ekayogakṣema*): "Some say that from a staff, which is related by conjunction (*saṃyoga*), and from horns, which are related by inherence (*samavāya*), there arise cognitions of that which possesses them; and they likewise [apply this] to a *bahuvrīhi* compound. (233)

They explain that in cases such as *daṇḍī* ("staff-bearer") and *viṣāṇī* ("horned"), the possessive suffixes characterized by *ini*, *thañ*, and *matup* arise from the cognition of the possessor, based on the staff—which is distinguished by the relation called "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*)—and the horn, which is assisted by the relation called "inherence" (*samavāya*), both serving as the grounds for the application [of the suffix] toward their respective relata. Specifically, they arise from the cognition of that which possesses the staff related by conjunction and that which possesses the horn related by inherence.

In exactly that same manner, those who rely on the view that the compound denotes a substance (*dravyābhidhānapakṣa*) declare that in a *bahuvrīhi*, the cause for the application [of the compound] is a related entity (*sambandhin*) assisted by a relation (*sambandha*). Just as, for example, two related entities assisted by their connection with a staff or a horn are the very cause for the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*), so too, in its respective case, a related entity characterized by the meaning of the constituent members (*vartipada*), assisted by its own relation, is the cause for the operation of the *bahuvrīhi* compound.

The meaning is that, according to the view that words denote [their own] word-meanings (*padārthābhidhānapakṣa*), the relatum (*sambandhī*)—which is characterized by another word-meaning—is what is expressed. In the case of "a staff made of *pālāśa* wood," the relatum assisted by conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is the cause [of the cognition]. In the case of "sharp-horned," the relatum assisted by inherence (*samavāya*) is the cause. || 233 ||

He states another alternative: "Others know that the relation is distinct according to the difference in the relata; the cause [of the relation], which is the meaning of the case-ending, is expressed by means of a compound. (234)

In this context, the basis for the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) is either the relation itself—assisted by the specific relata and the meaning of the stem—or the relation as it is appropriately differentiated. To illustrate: when one says "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*) or "horned" (*viṣāṇin*), since both the relatum and the relation are present, they are determined to be the cause [of the word's application] without distinction; for both produce a corresponding mental impression (*anurāga*) upon cognition. Any difference in grammatical derivation (*prakriyābheda*), however, is merely constructed by conceptual imagination (*kalpanā*).

Thus, it has already been stated that even in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, that case-meaning—namely, the relation qualified by its specific relata—is conveyed. Since there is no finality here in the mere relation itself, there is denotation of "that which possesses it" (*tadvat*) through the relation expressed as "this is that" (*so 'yam*) in both cases. || 234 ||

Thus, when in a *bahuvrīhi* compound the referent of the "other word" (*anyapadārtha*) is the relation (*sambandha*), and that relation functions merely as the cause (*nimitta*) [of the cognition], while the relatum (*sambandhin*) delimited by it is the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*)—this being understood through the force of the mention of "meaning"—then there is the first position (*pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ*). But when the relation itself is primary as the referent of the other word, and it is the denoted expressed meaning delimited by its own subordinate attributes (*guṇabhūta*) which serve as its adjuncts (*upādhi*), then there is the second position. To conclude this, he says: "The primary [element], being distinct from others for the sake of another, is delimited by its own subordinate adjuncts; whether it be the cause or the expressed meaning, it is expected last of all. (235)

This concludes the first position: that the primary meaning of the compound is the relation itself, which—being delimited by the subordinate meanings of the constituent members (*varti-pada*)—serves as the basis for the *bahuvrīhi* when it applies to the related entity (*sambandhin*). Alternatively, that very relation is what is to be expressed. Thus, he corroborates the position that the relation is denoted by the statement in the *Bhāṣya*: "It is expected last of all. For it is stated there in the *Bhāṣya*: "In this case, the word occurs at the very end."

By means of the function of denotation (*abhidhāna*), because a word ending in the genitive case has as its primary meaning a relation delimited by its relata, the superiority of this position has been established. || 235 ||

Now, one might object: in the expression "one whose cows are variegated" (*citragavaḥ*), since the owner—who is distinct from the cows—is subordinate, it is the cows themselves, which constitute the word-meaning, that are qualified and thus the primary element. How then could either the related party as qualified by the relation, or the relation as qualified by the related party, be the denotation of a *bahuvrīhi* compound? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Even if a distinction [of the owner] from [the cows] is observed in the sentence, his primacy is intended only when a *bahuvrīhi* is meant to be expressed. (236)

Since there is an absolute difference between a derivative formation (*vṛtti*) and a sentence (*vākya*), a difference in meaning is invariably concomitant; thus, although the referent of another word (*anyapadārtha*) is subordinate in a sentence, its predominance is intended in a derivative formation. || 236 ||

And thus, he says that this statement is not appropriate: "When [a word] functions as qualified by cows—as in 'one who possesses them' (tadvān)—then the bahuvrīhi compound does not exist for that meaning, such as in 'these are his' (asyaitāḥ). (237)

When, upon the desire to know to whom these variegated cows belong, the sentence "he whose cows are variegated" (*citrā gāvo'sya*) is employed, then, since the owner of the cows—who possesses those cows—is understood from this sentence as being subordinate (*upasarjana*), the meaning of the grammatical function (*vṛtti*) would not be fully demonstrated. 237.

He says the following statement is appropriate: "When there is a reflective awareness [of ownership] such that 'he is the master of those cows,' then the connection with the cows serves as the causal basis [for the application of the term]. (238)

When there arises the desire to know who the owner of these "variegated cows" is, and the variegated cows are resorted to as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the sake of identifying a specific owner, then the connection of the referent of the other member (*anyapadārtha*) with the referents of the constituent members (*vartipadārtha*), namely the cows, becomes the cause for the formation of the *bahuvrīhi* compound. Consequently, the meaning is that when the referent of the other member is predominant, the sentence "he whose cows are variegated is this [person]—he is Citragu" is appropriate here. || 238 ||

When, however, the related entity (*sambandhin*)—on account of its relation (*sambandha*) as the cause—is not directly denoted by the compound, one might ask whether there is still any utility for the transfer (*atideśa*) of gender and number. To this he says: "Requiring a relation in order to avoid being [treated as] a conventional term (*rūḍhi*), it follows that [the compound] would possess the properties of that [relation], because it conforms to its cause. (239)

The relatum (*sambandhin*) is denoted as delimited by a relation (*sambandha*); thus, the "conformity" (*anuvidhāna*) of the cause—the relation—is its "occurrence" (*anupravṛtti*). Consequently, it follows that the object denoted by the *bahuvrīhi* would possess the property of being devoid of gender and number, which belong to that very relation. For the relation is the cause; and since it is non-substantial (*asattvabhūta*), it cannot be said that it does not conform here because it is the cause, for if it did not conform to the cause, the *bahuvrīhi* would be a conventional term (*rūḍhiśabda*).

Because in established conventional meanings (rūḍhi) there is no pursuit of the meaning of the individual parts; however, in cases such as "citraguḥ" (one who has brindled cows), the meaning of the individual parts is indeed followed.

He confirms this very point by means of an illustration: "Just as [the word] 'nānācitras' follows its grammatical cause, so too, although it occurs in a plural state, 'bahuvrīhi' would likewise come to be. (240)

The indeclinable *nānā* denotes merely the state of non-coexistence (*asahabhāva*). It always refers, by taking that non-coexistence as its cause, to that which possesses it—that is, to an entity (*sattva*)—and even then, because it conforms to its cause, it remains essentially non-substantial (*asattvabhūta*). The same would apply to the *bahuvrīhi* compound. Since a suffix similar in form to the cause arises for the object possessing the cause, the pure nature of the possessor of the cause does not manifest; thus, in the absence of its own function, it is logical that only the function of the cause should prevail—this is the reasoning implied here, for the establishment of a meaning does not arise from a mere example alone. || 240 ||

Thus, when it follows that the cause (nimitta) must conform [to the gender of the base], the extension of the expression of the individual (vyaktivacana-atideśa) becomes fruitful. However, when the relata (sambandhin)—which constitute the meaning of the suffix—are the cause for the gender of the substance (dravya) as the meaning of the other word (the base), then there is no need for such an extension. Thus he says: "But when the relatum is the cause, the property of the substance is not lost; for the absence of gender exists by way of being contrary to gender. (241)

Whether the ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is the related object itself or the relation, in either case the related object is capable of being connected with gender and number; thus, on this view, gender and number are inherent, and there is no need for their extension (*atideśa*). For even when the ground for application follows [the properties of the primary], there is no loss of the substance's property of being endowed with gender and number, since the ground for application itself is also endowed with gender and number.

Although the gender and number of the related members—such as the variegated cows—are different [from those of the whole], and the denoted meaning of the *anyapadārtha* (the external referent), Devadatta, likewise possesses a different gender and number, nevertheless, the related members, which constitute the constituent meanings (*avayavārtha*), do not obscure the form of the whole (*nimittirūpa*) that serves as the ground for the application of the term (*pravṛttinimitta*). This is because they function as causes for the application of the term through their distinctness. Thus, the *anyapadārtha*, being perceived as a related member whose own nature is not suppressed, remains capable of being joined with its own gender and number; therefore, there is no contradiction.

If the relation (*sambandha*) were the ground for the application of the word, then that [relation], being expressed by its own term, would convey the related entity (*sambandhin*) without contradicting its own form. And thus, by means of that ground—which lacks gender and number—the related entity, its own form being obscured, does not undergo the grammatical operations pertaining to its own gender and number.
