The absence of gender is what contradicts gender; it is not the possession of another gender. (241)

For instance: "In the case of number, the gendered object has non-different properties by virtue of its cause; because it is proximate to substantiality (*dravyatva*), it is not contradicted by those [substantial] properties. (242)

When the related member (*sambandhin*) is the cause (*nimitta*), and that very same [cause] possesses the gender and number as the meaning of the other word (*anyapadārtha*), then it has non-different properties (*abhinnadharma*), that is, identical properties (*tulyadharma*). To the question "In what respect does it have non-different properties?", he says: "by way of the cause" (*nimittataḥ*). This is the ablative case with elision of the suffix *-lyap*; the meaning is "with reference to the cause. That is to say, it has identical properties by virtue of the cause, because both related members consist of the nature of existence (*sattva*).

And thus, because the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) shares the same properties as the cause (*nimitta*), it is proximate—that is, near and not too distant—just as in the view where the relation itself is the cause. Consequently, the external referent is not contradicted by the distinctions of gender and number belonging to the properties of the cause. For when it is expressed with its own unobscured nature, it will be joined with its own gender and number; this is the meaning. However, in some cases, when a contradiction does arise, there is indeed a persistence of the properties of the cause. For example: *harītakyaḥ phalāni* ("the fruits are myrobalans") and *khalatikaṃ vanāni* ("the forests are a thicket").

Thus, there are two possible courses for a cause that is perceived through distinction: either it conforms to the properties of that [cause], as in the case of *harītakī* and other such things; or its absence [is indicated], as in the case of the *bahuvrīhi* compound. However, when a cause is perceived as non-different through the entry of its own form [into the effect], the property of the cause is indeed followed by the caused. This has been explained. (242)

However, this must be addressed: even in the view that the meaning of the case-ending is primary, since [the word] refers to a relatum through the relation "this is that," what is the difference from the view that the word denotes the object itself? To this, he says: "Substance exists in two ways: as qualified by the meaning of the case-ending and as pure. That which is a property of the pure [substance] could not belong to one possessing a different property. (243)

The distinction between the two positions arises from the two ways in which substance (dravya) is presented: in the view that the case-ending expresses the meaning of the suffix, the substance is expressed as having its non-difference brought about by a relation denoted by the sixth case-ending (the genitive); whereas in the view that the word itself expresses the meaning of the referent, it is expressed as pure and unconditioned by anything else. Thus, there is a difference of position based on these two modes of operation regarding substance.

In that regard, when a pure [substance] is denoted by its own form, whatever properties it possesses—namely gender and number—those do not belong to it when it is expressed as being entered into a relation, because of its coloring by the form of another; thus, the extension (*atideśa*) of gender and number here is purposeful. However, in the view that [the compound] denotes the meaning of the whole word (*padārtha-abhidhāna-pakṣa*), since the pure substance or the meaning of the other word is denoted as qualified by the meanings of the constituent members (*varti*), the relations characterized by the meanings of those constituents serve as the ground for the application (*pravṛtti-nimitta*); therefore, the loss of the properties of the substance has been stated. || 243 ||

This very [point] regarding the two modes of existence of the denotable object distinguishes between the two positions: "In the indication of the mere substance, this distinction is not intended; however, in the former part of the treatise, the distinction is presented in the second [position]. (244)

The specific distinction characterized by the penetration of the meaning of case-endings—which was previously raised as an objection regarding the impossibility of subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) in the exposition of a pure substance alone, unconditioned by relations, in the passage beginning with "or rather, because it is not already expressed" (*na vā'nabhihitatvāt*) and which was resolved in the Bhāṣya—is not intended to be denoted under the view that the individual word-meaning (*padārtha*) is what is expressed.

However, this specific point was stated directly in the second section of the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "Or rather, the meaning of the case-ending is expressed. Here too, it is the substance (*dravya*) itself as qualified by the meaning of the case-ending that is denoted; otherwise, if the substance were not denoted, how could the expression "denoting an existing individual" (*sadvivacana*) be obtained even through extended application (*atideśa*)? For it is the relation (*sambandha*), which is the primary factor here, that is intended to be expressed. (244)

If this is so, then since the substance (dravya) has its own nature concealed [by gender and number], there would be no designation of it; how then can it be said that "it possesses substance, gender, and number"? To this he replies: "And here, the apprehension of the substance is qualified by gender and number. For those two [gender and number] are dependent upon the substance; therefore, they are not established for anything else. (245)

Although substance (*dravya*) is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) of gender (*liṅga*) and number (*saṅkhyā*), nevertheless, the mention of "substance" here should be understood as a qualifier for those two. This is intended to demonstrate that neither gender nor number can be associated with anything other than substance, such as a quality (*guṇa*). Furthermore, even when the relation (*sambandha*) is expressed, the phrase "possessing substance" (*sad-dravya*) is stated for the sake of establishing gender and number; for the relation, which is the manifest form denoted by the genitive case, is here expressed as non-different from the substance, and thus becomes designated as "possessing substance."

However, it is not because the substance (dravya) is a subordinate factor here that it is not denoted; for in its actual nature, the substance alone possesses primacy. Nevertheless, the verbal primacy of the relation has been assumed for the sake of distinguishing the alternative views.
For instance: "The compound operates upon a substance-universal that follows after a qualified object, being delimited by a relation distinct from its relata. (246)

In the view that the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*) is denoted [by the compound], the *bahuvrīhi* functions as the expressive word with respect to a substance-universal (*dravyasāmānya*)—which is delimited by a relation qualified by the relata that constitute the members of the compound (*vartipadārtha*), and which is thus determined through the non-confusion of its own form (*svarūpasambheda*). He states this even in the view where there is merely the justification for the subsequent employment (*anuprayoga*) of the specific referents (*padārthaviśeṣa*) of the compound when they have not been expressed, just as in the other alternative. || 246 ||

And therefore, because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with particulars, he states the result regarding its conformity to them: "Not transcending the properties of substance, yet abiding in the properties of particularity (due to its own power), it assumes gender and number in relation to its future substratum. (247)

Because it resides in the generality of substances (*dravyasāmānya*) by virtue of mere fitness (*yogyatāmātra*), the compound does not transcend the gender and number that characterize the properties of a substance; yet, because its form is undifferentiated, it is incapable of conveying the gender and number pertaining to a specific substance. Therefore, by the force of the grammatical rule "of qualifiers" (*viśeṣaṇānām*), the compound adopts the respective gender and number residing in the specific substance determined by the employment of another word. Thus concludes the investigation of the *bahuvrīhi*. 247.

In order to examine the extension of gender and number in the negative compound (*nañsamāsa*) which follows in sequence, he establishes the three questions introduced in the *Bhāṣya*: "Even though there is a difference in the application of the grammatical rule, the worldly meaning does not differ; for it is in the case of the negative compound that these three positions have been examined. (248)

Since the status of being primary or secondary cannot coexist in one and the same thing, how can the three possible positions (pakṣatraya) be established? For it has been argued that because the external referent (*anyapadārtha*)—such as a Kṣatriya—is specifically determined in expressions like "non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇa*), it is logical that this [external referent] alone should be primary. To this objection, the following is provided in support: by stating, "And that is for the sake of brevity," it is shown that the meaning is defined by its established nature; thus, even though there are differences in grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*), the worldly meaning remains unerring.

To explain: when the meaning of the other word (*anyapadārtha*) is predominant, then the subsequent member of the compound denotes an individual (*vyakti*); thus, [in *abrāhmaṇa*] it means "this Kṣatriya or the Kṣatriya class in which no Brāhmaṇa individual exists as a substratum. However, when the meaning of the first member—the negation (*nañ*) consisting of exclusion—is predominant, then because that non-existent thing cannot be connected with an action, and because a negation must presuppose a prior application [of the term], one perceives precisely that which resembles the meaning of the subsequent member.

Thus, even when the meaning of the subsequent member is predominant, it is understood that a Kṣatriya or other [caste] is determined by the status of being a Brāhmaṇa; therefore, there is no difference in the established meaning of the referent. However, the isolated word-meaning (*apoddhāra-padārtha*) is a mere auxiliary for grammatical derivation (*anvākhyāna*); thus, it is differentiated within the process of analysis (*prakriyā*).

And likewise, having presented the three positions—namely, "Of what is this compound the primary referent? Is it the primary referent of the final member, the primary referent of the initial member, or the primary referent of another word?"—the discussion in the Bhāṣya is not contradictory, as it aims to establish that position in which the grammatical system of the treatise is not subverted. 248.

Although the referent of the term *nañ* (negation) is not resident in the expressive word itself, nevertheless—investigation proceeds by relying on the oneness [of the referent] even when another word is present; for the employment of *nañ* is not found in cases such as "non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇa*) and the like. (249)

The grammatical instruction (*anuśāsana*) regarding words—which are established as momentary entities—is formulated for the sake of brevity by means of a conceptual analysis of the meanings of preceding and following word-components, based on words that express an analytically constructed division of parts such as "he is not a Brahmin" (*na brāhmaṇaḥ*, *abrāhmaṇaḥ*). For just as even in the process of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*), although there is a difference between the sentence and the derived form (*vṛtti*), an investigation is conducted by assuming non-difference from the sentence.

Likewise, although the particle *nañ* is not visibly present in compounds such as *abrāhmaṇa*, it is nevertheless derived [as being present] because it is observed in the corresponding analytical sentence (*vākya*), by virtue of its non-difference from that sentence. For in every compound whose meaning is a synthesis of parts, the distinction between qualifiers, qualificands, and so forth, belongs to the meanings [of the words] based on their non-difference from the sentence-meaning, since the sentence-meaning is understood within the compound. Consequently, because the meaning of *nañ*—characterized as exclusion—is understood in terms such as *abrāhmaṇa*, it is determined that this form beginning with the letter *a* is connected to *nañ*.

In cases such as *adhika-apanaya* (excess removal) and the like, however, only the form of the word itself persists, not the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*). In ultimate reality, moreover, a non-Brahmin (*abrāhmaṇa*) and so forth is devoid of any division of constituent parts, just like a shaven-headed person or one wearing a sacred thread; this has indeed been determined by such statements as, "Just as there is no 'Brahmin-meaning' whatsoever in a Brahmin's blanket. || 249 ||

Having thus explained the logical justification for the investigation of the three positions, he states how the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is perceived in a sentence, and how there is a consistent application when its function is analyzed as being non-different from that [meaning]: "Prior to compounding, the negation of word-meanings is indicated by the negative particle (*nañ*). Because those meanings are naturally excluded, this negation remains unperceived due to the non-difference of their form. (250)

When the negative particle (*nañ*) is employed in a sentence, a cessation [of something] is understood. And since that cessation is not independent—because an absence devoid of qualifications is never perceived—it resides within the word-meaning itself. In this regard, a positive word-meaning cannot cease to exist merely through the employment of the negative particle. Furthermore, when other words are employed, it is illogical for there to be either a deficiency or an excess in what is expressed by those words. Therefore, the negative particle is merely an indicator (*dyotaka*) of the cessation of things that have already ceased by their very nature.

If it is asked how things that have ceased can then be expressed by a word, [the answer is: the meaning of a word is not the actual entity (*vastu*). Rather, that which is common to both existence and non-existence, which relies upon metaphorical existence (*upacārasattā*), and which appears in cognition, is the denotation of a word. Thus, it has been established that "in the designation of things, there is another, metaphorical existence. Accordingly, because it is common to both existence and non-existence, the unmanifest cessation is also indicated by the negative particle (*nañ*); since it does not convey an object residing in another word-meaning, it is called "indicative" (*dyotaka*). || 250 ||

If this is so, there is no independent word-meaning for the negative particle (*nañ*) that could serve as the primary element. Or, even if such a thing existed, how could the meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), being qualified by that [negative] which consists of non-existence, attain primacy while having fallen away from its own nature due to being non-existent? Furthermore, if there were a connection between the meanings of the two constituent members, even the expression of a different word-meaning delimited by them would not be possible; thus, how can the three positions be established?

Now, if the action residing in the meaning of the subsequent member is negated, then there is no compound at all; thus he says: "When there is a connection with an action—expressed by a verbal form—that resides in [words] such as 'brāhmaṇa' within sentences, for that [word], a *vṛtti* (compound formation) does not exist. (251)

An action being negated must either be expressed by the introduction of another word or be denoted by a member of a compound. In the first case, as in "the Brāhmaṇa does not eat" (*brāhmaṇo na bhuṅkte*) or "the Brāhmaṇa does not study" (*brāhmaṇo nādhīte*), since the negative particle (*nañ*) is connected with the action conveyed by the finite verb (*tiṅanta*) and residing in the Brāhmaṇa and so forth, there is no compound because of the lack of semantic connection (*asāmarthya*) between that [negative] and the subsequent word. For here the connection of the negative particle is with the action, not with the subsequent words such as "Brāhmaṇa."

Consequently, since there is no compound at all in this case, the alternative regarding the status of subordinate (*guṇa*) and principal (*pradhāna*) among the meanings of the constituent members (*varti-pada*) is without foundation. However, when the negative particle (*nañ*) is joined with the verb "to be" (*asti*), which constitutes the very essence of the word-meaning, a compound does indeed occur; for at that time, the capacity (*sāmarthya*) resides solely in the meaning of the subsequent member, as in "there is no Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇo nāsti*).

For existence (*sattā*) is invariably concomitant with a word-meaning; thus, even when a verbal form (*kriyāpada*) is not employed, it is understood. Since its negation—which is obtained through this inherent capacity—is to be expressed by subsequent words that have ceased [to denote] their own primary meanings, the compound will be established by the employment of the negative particle (*nañ*) as that which illuminates the meaning. || 251 ||

[Objection: "Surely, by this same principle, let there be a compound even when the negative particle (*nañ*) has a connection with some other action (*kriyā*) that is understood from the second member of the compound. To this, he says: "If the action residing in a word such as *pācaka* (cook) is not connected with the negative particle, then because existence (*sattā*) is not being predicated there, the threefold alternative (*tripakṣī*) is untenable. (252)

If the action of cooking and so forth, which is presented as subordinate by the subsequent member such as *pācaka* (cook) and the like, were to be connected with the negative particle (*nañ*) as a signifier—as it is in a sentence—then, because existence (*sattā*) would be grasped by the *nañ* as the expressed meaning delimited by its own referent, the three positions [of the opponent] would not be tenable. For, due to the connection with the very subsequent member that signifies the meaning, there would be only one [position]: the predominance of the meaning of the subsequent member.

Indeed, the negative particle *nañ* does not possess any independent meaning that could be defined as either primary (*pradhāna*) or secondary (*guṇa*), because it is merely indicative (*dyotaka*) and thus dependent upon the meaning it indicates. Consequently, a compound is not formed where there is a connection with an indicated meaning characterized by an action, as in examples such as *apācakaḥ* ("non-cooker"). For in these cases, the action is denoted by the secondary final member (*uttarapada*), and thus it is that action which is connected with the negative particle as the object of negation.

However, in the case of words such as *brāhmaṇa*, the action—even though it is subordinate—is not the expressed meaning (*vācya*). Consequently, because there is no connection with the negative particle (*nañ*), the three previously mentioned positions are untenable. Therefore, since the status of the negative particle as a mere indicator (*dyotaka*) is untenable due to the resulting impossibility of the distinct positions, its denotative function (*vācakatva*) must be accepted within the scope of the compound formation (*vṛtti*). And thus, because the negative particle denotes non-existence, it can connect with subsequent words such as *brāhmaṇa* whose referents have been negated; in this way, the three positions become logically consistent.

For the negative particle (*nañ*), which expresses non-existence in general, when it enters into connection with words expressing particular instances of that [non-existence], undergoes its various functions according to the speaker's intention, by relying on the predominance of the preceding word, the subsequent word, another word, or the mutual relation [of the two]. || 252 ||
If this is so—if a connection with existence itself is postulated everywhere—then in this compound "asat" (non-existent), another existence must be postulated. (253)

Since the connection with existence (*sattā*) is invariable for all categories of entities, if it is postulated that the negative particle (*nañ*) is connected only with existence—which constitutes the very essence of an entity—and not with some other variable action, then even in the case of the negative compound *asat*, another related existence based on the subsequent member of the compound would not need to be postulated as what is conveyed by the *nañ*. Furthermore, no distinction between existences would be perceived in this way, because only a single existence is understood here as being negated. (253)

Right here, he states another fault: "In a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*), the relationship of qualifier and qualified is not observed between that which ends in a *ktvā* suffix and that which ends in a *tumun* suffix, [nor] with words denoting existence (*sattā*) when used with the negative particle (*nañ*). (254)

In the expression *akṛtvā* (having not done), because the meaning [of the root] is presented as the primary element—being fit for connection with suffixes such as *kṛtvasuc* precisely through the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) itself as "that which is to be accomplished" (*sādhya*)—the connection between the root *kṛ-* and the negative particle *nañ*, whose meaning is "immediate proximity," in the sense of a relationship between the delimited and the delimiter (*avacchedyāvacchedakabhāva*), is not tenable. For a connection of the root *kṛ-* with the negative particle *nañ*, which negates existence (*sattā*), is not appropriate; since it must relate only to that which is to be negated (*pratiṣedhya*), how could there be such a connection?

Therefore, if the negative particle (*nañ*) were to denote non-existence, neither of these two cases would be tenable; thus, here the *nañ* expresses a mere negation. Consequently, in the case of "non-existent" (*asann*), it negates existence (*sattā*), which constitutes the referent of the subsequent member of the compound; thus, the logical connection is established. However, there is an inconsistency in cases such as "non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇa*), because it is impossible to negate an existing entity that is the meaning of the word "Brahmin."

Even here, how can the meaning of the root *kṛ* (to do), which ends in a present participle suffix (*sannanta*) and is of the nature of an action (*bhāvātmaka*), be negated? If that is so, then the negative particle (*nañ*) is employed in a compound (*vṛtti*) to indicate an object that has ceased by its own nature, just as it is used in a sentence (*vākya*). In this case as well, there are two possible ways: since a mere word-meaning cannot be established without connection to an action, either the essence of the object, which is the substratum of a specific action, must be indicated as having ceased by its own nature, or [the object] which is the substratum of action in general must be indicated.

In the first case, there is no occurrence [of the negative particle] because of a lack of capacity; or, even if capacity were present, it was stated that the three possible positions (pakṣas) would be untenable. In the second position, if the general action characterized by existence—which is manifested by the negative particle—is connected with the subsequent word that expresses the general category, then "infinite regress" (anavasthā) has been stated. However, since there is no connection with a word expressing a particular instance, its function as a "manifestor" (dyotaka) is not tenable here.

For if it were merely indicative (*dyotaka*), then because it would be dependent on the meaning to be indicated, even though a relationship exists, there would be only the predominance of the meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapadārtha-prādhānya*). Therefore, its status as a denoter (*vācaka*) must be accepted. And thus, since the negative particle (*nañ*) has an independent meaning, once its subordinate or predominant status is established as appropriate, the investigation of the three positions follows. || 254 ||

In this regard, he demonstrates how the negative particle (*nañ*) expresses non-existence, such that a second existence does not follow, and how its connection is logically consistent in cases like *akṛtvā* and so forth: "The negative particle is established in the general substratum of the means of action; from there, it is connected with specific substrata such as 'Brāhmaṇa' and the like. (255)

Even though the negative particle (*nañ*) expresses a general sense, because it denotes non-existence, the action (*kriyā*) intended here by the context is characterized as existence (*sattā*). For the meaning of the negative particle consists of non-being, which takes the form of the negation of existence—that is, of being. Since that [negation] is an accomplishment (*sādhana*), and because it is intransitive, its agent-power (*kartṛ-śakti*) is [the agent]. Since it is impossible for a means of accomplishment to exist without a substratum, the substratum—which is obtained through implication—is indicated here as a support that is not restricted to any particular [instance], but is a generality (*sāmānya*) in the form "it exists. In this regard, the negative particle is established and functions as the signifier.

Is the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) something that exists in the form "the object is not"? We say: no. How then is it said that "the negative particle is established in the general sense of the locus of the means of action (*sādhana*) for the verb (*kriyā*)"? It is said thus because it introduces its own meaning, which consists of non-existence (*abhāva*), into that [general locus]. Consequently, in the scope of its function (*vṛtti*), the negative particle signifies the general locus of the means of action for the verbal action as qualified by non-existence; thus, the meaning of the negative particle is precisely of the form "it is not."

In that regard, the specific expectation of "what is not there? is fulfilled by the subsequent words. Thus, because of that general state [of non-existence], the negative particle (*nañ*) is connected with words such as "Brāhmaṇa," which denote specific bases for establishing particular forms of existence that are distinct from it. Consequently, the relationship of qualifier and qualified is established between their respective meanings through the relation of generality and particularity. For a non-existent general form is indeed joined with particular non-existent things, just as "cowness" is joined with the Śābaleya cow and others.

In that regard, concerning the expression "non-existence of a Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇatva*), when there is a desire to express a distinction between the qualifier and the qualified through the freedom of usage, then the meaning of the first member of the compound is predominant. When it functions by referring to another meaning—such as "his Brahminhood is non-existent"—the predominance of the meaning of the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) over the meanings of the constituent members is established. Likewise, since a general property is never found apart from its particular instances, in cases such as "cook" (*pācaka*), the distinction of the locus for the general action consisting of existence—which is followed by specific actions like cooking—is established.

Thus, because the universal does not deviate from the particular, there is the establishment of distinct substrates for the general action consisting of existence (*sattā*), which follows through the specific actions such as cooking in the case of "the cook" and so forth. In this way, [the agent] is connected by the word *karoti* (he does) precisely with existence as its essence, and not with a specific form; therefore, in expressions such as "not to do" (*akartum*), the negative particle (*nañ*)—having rendered the universal of non-existence suitable for negation by means of existence itself as the inherent property (*samavāyinī*) within the particular—assails that [existence].

In the case of the term "non-existent" (*asat*) here as well, by virtue of the context, it is precisely that existence which is restricted to a particular [category] that is negated by the general concept of non-existence (*asattva-sāmānya*), which serves as its basis. This is because non-existence whose object is unrestricted cannot be established, as it would serve no purpose. For it is only a specific existent, such as a Brāhmaṇa, who is brought forward for the sake of negation, not "existence that is a Brāhmaṇa. However, since the specific [category] is determined through the context, there is no need to employ words such as "Brāhmaṇa."

And thus, since the meaning here is simply "the Brāhmaṇa and so forth," this relationship of qualifier and qualified pertains only to the general and the particular. For there is no employment of two generalities, as that would result in a lack of mutual expectancy; therefore, the fault of postulating a further existence does not arise. Furthermore, in all such cases, there is a cognition of something similar to the meaning of the subsequent word. Indeed, elsewhere, the negation of what has been superimposed—which has ceased by its own nature—is easily expressed. Thus, by accepting that [words] possess denotative power, everything is logically consistent. (255)

If it is asked, "In that case, how is it possible for the negative particle (*nañ*), which is merely indicative, to possess denotative power within a compound? he says: "Just as in a compound [such as *nirgata*], words beginning with *nis-* are joined with the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) or the substratum (*ādhāra*) by taking on the meaning of 'gone' (*gata*) and so forth; such is the procedure even in a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*). (256)

In derivative compounds such as *niṣkauśāmbiḥ*, *atikhaṭvaḥ*, and *praparṇaḥ*, the initial members—*nis*, *ati*, *pra*, and so forth—are observed to denote entities possessing substantiality (*sattvabhūta*) within the sentence, even though they do not denote substantiality when functioning as members of a compound. For instance, words expressing actions accompanied by instruments, such as "gone" (*gata*) or "transcended" (*krānta*), are connected with substances such as Kauśāmbī, which serve as the substrates for instrumental capacities like the ablative (*apādāna*).

If they were words denoting only non-existence, then there would be no connection with those words denoting existence; therefore, since this [connection] is otherwise inexplicable, it is inferred that these [words] function with respect to a substance (*dravya*) which is the substratum of the capacity for accomplishment (*sādhana-śakti*) and is subordinate to actions such as "going out" (*niṣkramaṇa*). Furthermore, because the restriction of the expressive power (*abhidhāna-śakti*) occurs only where the function is observed within a sentence, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). As the author of the *Vākya-kāṇḍa* said: "Or, because the meaning of that [substance] is understood."

The meaning is as follows: by means of an object such as Kauśāmbī, the capacity (*sāmarthya*) of a term like *nir-* arises; because that [capacity] cannot be otherwise established, it is through that very [object] that the meaning is cognized. Thus, just as in this compound (*vṛtti*), the preceding member incorporates a specific distinction—seen in the sentence (*vākya*)—by virtue of its meaning being merged with another word, so too is it the case in *abrāhmaṇa* and similar forms; this is the point of similarity. For here too, since the connection with the meaning of the subsequent member cannot otherwise be accounted for, the negative particle (*nañ*) is postulated to denote a general absence (*asat-sāmānya*); thus, that same sequence (*anupūrvī*) is the means for its denotative function. || 256 ||

Even if it is thus the case that [the word "non-Brahmin"] denotes a non-existent universal, how can the three positions be established? For those three positions would only be possible if there were no fixed rule regarding the subordinate or primary status of the meanings of the preceding and following words. To the question of how there can be such a lack of restriction here, he says: "In that case, because the negative particle functions where something is absent, the relationship of qualifier and qualified is postulated between [the negation] and [terms such as] 'Brahmin' or 'Kshatriya,' like [the relationship between] a hunchback and a lame man. (257)

In the *Bhāṣya*, it is stated that because both the words *khañja* (“lame”) and *kubja* (“humpbacked”) are based on qualities (*guṇanimitta*), there is no fixed rule regarding their status as qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and qualified (*viśeṣya*); thus we have both *khañjakubjaḥ* and *kubjakhañjaḥ*. Likewise, since the negative particle *nañ* functions as the denoter of the general category of non-existence (*asatsāmānya*), its relationship as qualifier and qualified with specific terms such as “Brāhmaṇa” and so forth occurs according to one’s preference, with the quality and the primary substance alternating in their roles. (257)

Thus, regarding what is established in cases such as "a non-Brahmin" (abrāhmaṇa) or "a non-Kṣatriya" (akṣatriya), he says: "When there is freedom of usage [in negation], in this way the non-existent would have primacy, while the others would have the status of a subordinate quality; or else, those [others] themselves might have primacy. (258)

"However, [the formation] is established because the qualifier and the qualified may be used as desired. Thus, in cases where there is no fixed rule—as in the case of "lame-and-humpbacked" (khañjakubja) and so forth—when the non-existent universal (*asatsāmānya*) is intended as the primary meaning, functioning as the qualified (*viśeṣya*), then the compound has the prior member as its predominant sense (*pūrvapadārthapradhāna*), provided that the other members, such as "Brāhmaṇa" and so on, are intended as subordinate (*guṇa*). But when the predominance of those latter members is intended, then the *nañ* compound has the latter member as its predominant sense (*uttarapadārthapradhāna*).

For this very reason, when the connection between the preceding and following words is intended to refer to a different object, the predominance of the *anyapadārtha* (the meaning of the whole compound) is also stated. However, in a sentence (*vākya*), since the negation is not understood as being restricted solely to the thing to be negated, the negative particle (*nañ*) is not an independent word-meaning; thus, because it does not denote [an independent meaning], it functions as an indicator (*dyotaka*). Consequently, since there is no fixed rule regarding the intention to express the subordinate or predominant status [of the elements involved], the three alternative positions do not arise in that case. For this same reason, the quality of having no gender or number—which is a property of indeclinables (*avyaya*)—belongs to the meaning of the negative particle in a sentence, but not in a compound (*vṛtti*), because in the latter it denotes a meaning that has become a positive entity (*sattvabhūta*). || 258 ||

Thus, having established the validity of the three positions, the predominance of the subsequent member (*uttarapadārthaprādhānya*), which was first introduced in the *Bhāṣya*, must now be examined. To this end, he says: "Because of contradiction, how could the Brāhmaṇa and others be qualified by that which is non-existent? Therefore, those whose functions are general according to the Veda were previously adopted as predominant; however, the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and so forth, are directed toward the specific [meaning]. (259)

Since it is impossible to negate existence itself, words such as "brāhmaṇa" are capable of denoting a qualified object only when it is characterized by exclusion; thus, they function here solely through the process of affirmation (pravṛtti). However, when their form as a word is heard even in the sense of a positive entity, then that exclusion which constitutes its own meaning is manifested by the negative particle (nañ). For when the word *nañ* is employed, that specific distinction is revealed; thus, in the absence of contradiction, the relationship between qualifier and qualified is established. || 259 ||

The phrase "relying primarily" adopts the position that the meaning of the final member of the compound is predominant. He explains this very point by means of an illustration: "Just as their distinction is established by [the qualifiers] 'white' and so forth, so too is their identity—which, though non-existent and unmanifest, is manifested. (260)

Just as in expressions such as "the fair Brahmin" or "the white Brahmin," where the general category of "Brahmins" and so forth is delimited by qualifiers like "fair" and so on, likewise, words denoting non-existent particulars—which, due to their similarity to Vedic [terms], have their specific meanings uncomprehended—are delimited by the negative particle (*nañ*). || 260 ||

Now, it may be argued that words such as *gaura* (white) are rightly qualifiers because they impart a specific quality to an existing object. But how can there be a relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyabhāva*) with the negative particle *nañ*, which uproots the meaning of the subsequent word? For when *nañ* is employed, it is determined that the meaning of the subsequent word is non-existent; and thus, due to the non-existence of the subsequent word’s referent, the very use of words such as *brāhmaṇa* would become impossible. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Just as a positive entity is postulated for the sake of denoting existence, so too is an indefinable [non-entity] postulated for the sake of denoting existence. (261)

In this context, from the utterance of a word, an object that is common to both existence and non-existence is conveyed. Yet such an object is not external, because the external object is restricted solely to existence. If that [external object] alone were denoted by words, then, since its existence would never deviate [from it], a requirement for it [as a predicate] would be impossible; consequently, a qualifier-qualified relationship (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*) such as "a Brahmin who exists" (*san brāhmaṇaḥ*) would not be tenable. And yet, it is indeed tenable.

Therefore, an object that has ascended to the level of metaphorical existence (*upacārasattā*) is postulated as the denotation of a word by virtue of its general connection with both existence and non-existence. Consequently, even in the case of "a non-Brahmin" (*asan brāhmaṇaḥ*), the employment of the negative particle (*nañ*) is not contradictory, as it is based on a conceptualized object. For it has already been determined that the intellect, determining the form of an object without regard for its external existence or non-existence, renders that object a referent of a word (*padārtha*) capable of being associated with various qualifying attributes, whether contradictory or non-contradictory.

In this regard, just as an object is determined by the cognition "blue lotus" through the conceptual construction of parts and is then connected with the qualifier "blue" by way of its universal nature, so too is it logical that "exclusion" (*nivṛtti*) serves as a qualifier for that which is grasped by a cognition common to both existence and non-existence. For there is no such thing in the world called a "universal" named "lotus" that could serve as a substrate for a particularity through its connection with "blue. Indeed, even that [lotus] is a single, partless entity; the attribution of distinct parts occurs only through the cognition "blue lotus."

Likewise here as well, since a negation that lacks an object cannot function—as in the case of "non-Brahmin"—existence (*sattā*) is figuratively treated as the object of negation. And because existence, which resides in the intellect, is superimposed as being external, the negation remains directed toward external existence.

Therefore, this is not to be questioned; for once it has been established that the word *brāhmaṇa* is used even for the appearance in the intellect [of a non-Brahmin], he says the following in order to demonstrate that in a negative compound (*nañsamāsa*), there is an understanding of a substratum similar to that [Brahmin]: "Having taken its place upon the Kṣatriya and others, the cognition—which rests upon another form of existence—thereby removes the existence that was implied as distinct from the [Brahmin] universal. (262)

When the cognition whose object is the existence of a Brāhmaṇa arises with respect to a Kṣatriya due to some cause of error, then the word "Brāhmaṇa" is applied to him. This false determination, when it ceases through the knowledge of reality, is the occasion for the employment of the negative particle (*nañ*); this is the scope of the negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*). The understanding of that [negation] occurs through its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "Kṣatriya," as in: "This is a non-Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya."

And thus, the correct cognition arising from the employment of the negative particle (*nañ*) excludes and removes from the Kṣatriya that existence which, through the application of the word "Brāhmaṇa," was erroneously superimposed upon him as being co-inherent with the single object "Brāhmaṇahood. One concludes: "This is not a Brāhmaṇa; he is false; he is a non-Brāhmaṇa because he resembles one. In this way, the meaning of the compound is established as being the Kṣatriya or similar [caste] who is the actual referent, and not a clod of earth or the like, because of the absence of similarity and other such qualities that would serve as the basis for superimposition. As it has been said: "When joined with *nañ*, it refers to something else that is similar, for such is the understanding of the meaning. (Pāṇini-vārttika 2.2.6) || 262 ||

In this case, how can there be a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) in the word "non-existence" (*abhāva*)? For here there is no comprehension of a meaning similar to that of the second member (*uttarapada*), but rather a negation of the object denoted by the second member, which is an existent thing, is perceived. And how can that which is non-existent fall within the scope of a word denoting an existent? To this he says: "When the negation of an existent is intended, as in the term 'non-existence,' the negation cannot be established without relying on its having a positive designation (*sopākhyatva*). (263)

In this case as well, because the word "existent" (*bhāva*) is employed by relying on a form determined by the intellect for the purpose of establishing the object of negation, its status as having a non-existent object is not understood due to its similarity in sound [to the word "existent"]. Therefore, the employment of the negative particle (*nañ*) is justified in order to bring about that understanding. For the meaning is that the negative particle is used when, through delusion, there is a superimposition of the nature of an existent upon that which is indefinable (*nirupākhya*), and thus there is a determination of it as being [an existent] reality. And this is so.

Alternatively, the view that "all these words denote a collection of qualities" is introduced here in this Bhāṣya. Relying on that, he says: "Words that express a collection and denote multiple properties, by their very nature, function with identical forms when applied to individual parts. (264)

He expresses this by means of the word *dharma*, intending that here the word *guṇa* refers to a property (*dharma*) characterized by genus, quality, and action. Since the collection [of these properties] is understood from the word, it is logical that that very collection is the meaning of the word. And this has been stated: "Austerity, sacred learning, and birth—these constitute the cause of being a Brahmin. He whose properties, such as genus and so forth, as well as sacred learning and so forth, are complete is the primary (*mukhya*) Brahmin. The word *brāhmaṇa* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) as denoting him. A word with the same phonetic form as that [primary term] applies to a constituent part [of that collection].

For words that function with respect to a whole (samudāya) also function with respect to its parts (avayava). For example, it is said: "oil has been consumed," or "ghee has been consumed. Although, due to a difference in meaning, a word denoting a collection and a word denoting a single part are by their very nature absolutely distinct, nevertheless, because of the similarity in sound, those of limited vision do not perceive the difference; thus, assuming non-distinction, it is stated that [the word] functions both with respect to the whole and its parts.

Likewise, when the term "brāhmaṇa" is applied to a kṣatriya who lacks the brāhmaṇa caste but possesses certain characteristics such as learning and discipline, its application to only one part [of the full meaning] is not initially understood due to the similarity of sound; however, it is determined through the use of the negative particle (*nañ*). Or, one who is devoid of austerity and learning is called a "pseudo-brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇaka*), being a brāhmaṇa by birth alone but lacking in qualities.

And thus, in this case, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the preceding and following words is established because they both have a collection of qualities as their object. For here, by the negative particle (*nañ*), only that quality whose inherent cessation is indicated is expressed; consequently, the existence of the remaining qualities is understood by implication. In that regard, it was previously stated on the basis of metaphorical existence (*upacārasattā*).

Now, however, it is explained that even when some ultimately real entity (*pāramārthika*) is negated by a negative particle (*nañ*), the application of a word is not without an object (*nirviṣaya*), because it functions through the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the whole upon the remaining collection of parts. Furthermore, since both of those two parts are superimposed as having the nature of the whole, it is precisely that [whole] which is negated, and it is precisely therein that the word functions. || 264 ||

This is not a valid objection, because the negation applies only to the portion that does not take up the meaning of the subsequent member; thus, how could there be a connection with the subsequent member? For instance: "Just as something is called 'done' because one part of it has been done, yet it is also called 'not done'—that same process applies to the compound [abrāhmaṇa] in relation to the non-Brahmin. (265)

Just as a composite whole is designated as "partly done and partly not done" because one part has been accomplished while another part remains unaccomplished, so too—since a collection is composed of its constituent parts—the metaphorical attribution of the properties of the parts to the whole is not contradictory. In this same way, the application of the terms *brāhmaṇa* and *abrāhmaṇa* to a collection of qualities occurs through the engagement with or the cessation from [certain] parts thereof. 265.

Regarding this, he states the fault: "From that [notion of] presentation, it follows that a Brahmin would be a non-Brahmin; or, because of the attachment to what is already accomplished even when it is not yet accomplished, the unaccomplished would be indistinguishable from the accomplished. (266)

Having determined one part [of a person] to be of the nature of a composite whole, one says, "This is a Brāhmaṇa. Since the other parts are non-existent, it follows that he is again a non-Brāhmaṇa; thus, a contradiction arises.

Alternatively, just as the word *kṛta* (done) is employed even when the aggregate has not been completed at all—due to the possibility of its accomplishment based on the proximity of effective means—so too, when the word *brāhmaṇa* is applied to a Kṣatriya or similar person because one perceives qualities common to a Brāhmaṇa, and this application indicates a figurative meaning by the negation (*nañ*) of its primary sense through the possibility of *brāhmaṇa*-hood regarding that mere collection of factors denoted by the word *brāhmaṇa*, then this *nañ* in the compound is equivalent to the word *akṛta* (not done). Thus, the objection is refuted by the second half of the verse. || 266 ||

Furthermore, since the word "brāhmaṇa" is used in a secondary sense in one particular instance, there may arise a misconception that it is primary due to its similarity [to other instances]. To dispel this, he states that the negative particle (*nañ*) employed as a qualifier serves to exclude that [misconception]: "When a secondary meaning is possible, the negative particle is employed as a specifier at the time of explaining the grammatical rule in order to exclude the primary meaning. (Verse 267)

The meaning is this: since the word *brāhmaṇa* is employed in a non-primary sense (*amukhya-artha*) as a mere expedient (*upakrama*), yet without the intended primary meaning being destroyed, the use of the negative particle *nañ* is justified for the purpose of deriving the uncompounded worldly term *abrāhmaṇa*, so that the intended meaning may be established through such an analysis (*vibhāga*). || 267 ||

Regarding this, it is raised in the Bhāṣya that when the meaning of the final member is predominant, [the objection is]: "When it is said, 'Bring a non-Brahmin' (*abrāhmaṇam ānaya*), the bringing of any Brahmin whatsoever would follow. How is that so? For one might object that, as in the case of *rājapuruṣa* ("king's man") and similar compounds, there is a cognition of the meaning of the final member as qualified by the meaning of the prior member. Anticipating this, he explains the intention of the author of the Bhāṣya: "And a qualifier is seen without subverting the meaning of the word; thus, some property of the object possessing the genus is excluded. (268)

In cases such as *rājapuruṣa* (the king’s man), the meaning of the first member, "king," qualifies the meaning of the second member, "man," by adding a specific attribute without negating it; thus, its status as a qualifier is appropriate. But here, how could the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) be a qualifier when it negates the meaning of the subsequent member? In this case, the *nañ* would be entirely meaningless. And so, the intention of the author of the Bhāṣya is that only the Brāhmaṇas would be brought [if the compound were taken as a simple negation]. Now, one might argue: "It is not that the meaning of the subsequent member is negated here in every respect; rather—" [this is the sense of the remaining portion of the objection].

Because the universal (jāti) serves as the cause for the application [of a word] when a collection of qualities has arisen, the negative particle (nañ) indicates the exclusion of only a portion of that possessing collection; however, since the remaining portion persists, there occurs a determination of a specific distinction. || 268 ||

If this is so—then necessarily, no particular dharma whatsoever exists in the Brāhmaṇa; since no specific [dharma] is mentioned there, the hearing of the negative particle (nañ) would be purposeless. (269)

For not every Brāhmaṇa is found to possess complete qualities; thus, the word "Brāhmaṇa" applies only partially to everyone, since it functions even when only the genus (jāti) is present, regardless of whether the qualities are complete. And so, even when the negative particle (nañ) is employed, it is redundant.

Furthermore, in this view: "The synonym for that which is unqualified becomes qualified by the negative particle; for it is from grammatical derivation (*anvākhyāna*) that correctness (*sādhutva*) is understood in such a case. (270)

Whatever meaning belongs to the word *brāhmaṇa* when one part of it is negated, that same meaning belongs to the word *abrāhmaṇa*. Thus, by the rule of the negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*), the word *abrāhmaṇa*, whose correctness has been established, would result in being a synonym for the word *brāhmaṇa*. [Objection: This is answered as follows: "Even though there is no negation of the referent (padārtha) here, the negative particle (*nañ*) illuminates a particular state of the referent as it exists through metaphorical usage. (271)

The meaning is as follows: even if there is a single defect here, the term is applied to him by way of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), based on the cognition that he belongs to the Brāhmaṇa caste; thus, his state characterized by metaphorical indication (*sopacarita-lakṣaṇā*) is revealed by the negative particle (*nañ*). Consequently, this qualification is also appropriate without any impairment to the primary meaning of the word. || 271 ||
For instance: "In whatever manner a thing exists as established among its substrata, in that very manner its existence is apprehended through the causes of differentiation. (272)

Just as in cases such as *rājapuruṣa* (the king’s man) or *nīlotpala* (the blue lotus), the meaning of the object qualified (*viśeṣya*) is understood according to its specific nature through the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), which serve as the grounds for differentiation; so too here, it is rightly considered a qualifier that the meaning of the word *brāhmaṇa* is understood from the employment of the negative particle (*nañ*) as having a form superimposed by the intellect (*buddhyupacaritarūpa*). As it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "Now, when it is said here, 'Bring the king’s man,' why does one not bring just any man? There is a distinction in this case."

"In this case, the word *rājan* (king) is employed as a qualifier; by that, the bringing of one qualified by a king occurs. So too here, the negative particle (*nañ*) is employed as a qualifier; therefore, there will be the bringing of that which is qualified by the negative particle. To this, it is objected: "But what is this [thing]? To that, it was said: "That whose referent has ceased. This [objection] challenges that point: "How can a word apply to a constituent part when its referent has ceased? For the application of a word is not possible without a cause. (273)

Even when a word functions with a form grasped by the intellect (*buddhi*), it nonetheless relies upon an external seed (*bīja*). Thus, because of the determination of identity between the perceived and the conceptualized, people consider the external object itself to be the meaning of the word. Therefore, in cases such as "Kṣatriya" and so forth, since [the term] "Brāhmaṇa" and the like denote a part [of that class], how could a partial word (*avayava-śabda*) function in the absence of a cause? It is for this reason that it is said that this state is indicated by the negative particle (*nañ*). || 273 ||

Now, if it is argued that the word "brāhmaṇa" applies to a kṣatriya as well because its application is natural (svābhāvikī nivṛttiḥ), then: "If a word can naturally apply to two contradictory meanings—just like the word 'ārāt'—then the explicit mention of the negative particle (nañ) would be purposeless. (274)

Just as the word *ārāt* functions to denote both distance and proximity, so too the word *brāhmaṇa* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) by its own nature to denote both a Brahmin and a Kṣatriya. If this is accepted, then even without the employment of the negative particle (*nañ*), the understanding of a Kṣatriya will arise from the word *brāhmaṇa* through the force of context and other factors; what, then, would be the purpose of the *nañ*, such that a *nañ*-compound is prescribed? For it is not necessarily observed that words with multiple meanings must have their specific sense manifested only through the employment of another word. As it is said in the Bhāṣya: "If the exclusion is inherent, what does the employed *nañ* do? (274)

Immediately following this, it was stated: "Alternatively, it is based on verbal testimony (*vācanikī*). That must be explained: when the negative particle (*nañ*) is employed, it excludes the meaning of the word. This [verse] explains that: "Alternatively, the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) deserves to be explained through verbal testimony; however, because that [nature] is not well-established as something to be expressed, the meaning of the negative particle is excluded. (275)

If the nature [of the negative particle] is made known by the word *nañ* because it is difficult to ascertain, then this too must be explained by the statement that "when *nañ* is employed, the well-known meaning of the words is set aside. Alternatively, if this nature is to be determined through traditional usage (*prayogapāramparya*), then since no operation whatsoever would depend on other words, the negative particle *nañ* would not need to be expected even when the subsequent word expresses the exclusion (*nivṛtti*). This is the meaning. || 275 ||

Immediately following this, [the opponent] objects: "The cessation [of the meaning] is based on explicit scriptural statement (*vācanikī nivṛttiḥ*), like a stake and its counter-stake. If such were the power of the negative particle (*nañ*), then kings would never maintain elephants and horses. Having thus refuted [the first view], the inherent cessation (*svābhāvikī nivṛttiḥ*) is established as the final position (*siddhānta*). And in that case, the perception is caused by the negative particle (*nañ*). As it has been said: "In the darkness, the perception of objects is caused by a lamp. This [verse] explains it: "Even though it occurs in both [the primary and the secondary senses], the primary sense is what is perceived.
When the [negative particle] is pure, the departure [from the primary sense] is understood; even when it is in the sense of 'not standing' (*atiṣṭhat*), [it functions in the same way]. (276)

The meaning is as follows: just as the verb *tiṣṭhati* ("stands"), which is well known to signify the cessation of motion, is incapable of conveying the sense of "setting out" (*prasthāna*) without the prefix *pra*, even so the word *brāhmaṇa*, though denoting a Kṣatriya [in a specific context], does not produce a determination of that meaning without the negative particle *nañ*. For the prefix *pra* does not have "setting out" as its primary meaning, because that would result in the root *sthā* being rendered meaningless; rather, *sthā* is the primary meaning, while the prefix *pra* is merely indicative (*dyotaka*).
This should be understood to apply here as well. || 276 ||

"But surely, if the primary meaning of 'Brāhmaṇa' does not apply to a Kṣatriya, then for what purpose is the word 'Brāhmaṇa' accepted there as denoting a doubtful object? And its secondary meaning is determined by the use of the negative particle (nañ). To this, the Bhāṣya says: "But if this [negative] were one whose referent has ceased [to exist], why would the word 'Brāhmaṇa' be employed? To that he replies: "Why, when such [a primary application] exists and the primary meaning is possible, is the occurrence of the word 'Brāhmaṇa' accepted in a different sense? (277)
The meaning of this verse has already been explained. || 277 ||

Regarding this, there is an explanatory passage for the rebuttal: "It is so that it may be understood that the referent of this term has ceased [to apply]. For if one were simply to say 'no,' doubt would arise—[the question being] 'of what referent has the application ceased? To eliminate such doubt, the word 'Brāhmaṇa' is employed. This he explains: "This referent does not exist in this [person], such as a Kṣatriya and the like; thus, the word denoting that [referent] is employed for the sake of cognition. (278)

The meaning is as follows: Suppose that due to ignorance or a faulty instruction, someone has attributed the referent of "Brāhmaṇa" to a Kṣatriya. He is then informed: "This is not a Brāhmaṇa; this is a non-Brāhmaṇa. However, if one were simply to say "Kṣatriya," the negation of the referent of "Brāhmaṇa" would not have been effected there, and thus the intended meaning would not be understood. Therefore, it is logical that by means of the intellect, having first assumed the referent of "Brāhmaṇa" in that [Kṣatriya], the negation of that referent is expressed through the determination of the scope (*viṣaya*) of the negative particle (*nañ*). || 278 ||

And since the meaning of a word is indeed always applicable as a superimposed form upon the cognizer, he says: "When an object has attained the status of being an object of cognition through a word, activity or cessation is understood; for it is through the word that the object is connected [to action]. (279)

In this context, it was previously established by the statement "meanings are understood from words" and so forth, that the meaning understood from a word is a factor in linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) regardless of whether it exists externally or not. Thus, since the object of its own denotation is manifested by words that are common to both existence and non-existence, even when a specific referent is not fixed in each respective case, an appropriate qualifier—whether of the nature of an existent or a non-existent—is indeed applicable. (279)

In that regard, concerning a *nañ*-compound where the meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is predominant, it has been stated: "That which is joined with *nañ* [denotes] something other than that, or what is similar to it, for such is the comprehension of the meaning. Therefore, because the word *brāhmaṇa* is used through error only in a specific instance, the negation of its meaning applies only to that specific locus and not everywhere; thus, to avoid the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), the *Bhāṣya* states: "The word *brāhmaṇa* functions due to doubt and due to faulty instruction," and so forth.

He explains that: "The application of words occurs either due to incorrect instruction or due to doubt; however, there is no such [application] in the case of clods of earth and the like, nor is there any perversion. (280)

The application of the term "brāhmaṇa" to a *kṣatriya* arises from a false instruction (*durupadeśa*). This occurs when someone, having been instructed by a person with a limp, disheveled hair, or similar traits, determines the subject matter based on that instruction. Here, the word "doubt" (*saṃdeha*) refers to the quality (*guṇa*) that serves as the cause of doubt.

For instance: since the application of the word [‘non-Brahmin’] occurs there based on similarity—which is the cause of doubt—the word ‘Brahmin’ does not apply to lumps of earth and the like, which are utterly dissimilar. Therefore, from the word *abrāhmaṇa* (non-Brahmin), it is understood that the Kṣatriya alone is similar to the referent of the latter member [of the compound], and not a lump of earth or the like. Indeed, the use of the negative particle (*nañ*) is for the purpose of warding off error; and since error cannot exist without a basis when a cause is present, its object is necessarily restricted to that which is similar.

For this very reason, when the primary meaning of "Brāhmaṇa" is excluded by the negative particle *nañ* in reference to a Kṣatriya, it is understood that the Kṣatriya remains present as the substratum; thus, in expressions such as "bring the non-Brāhmaṇa," he functions as the instrument (*sādhana*) in the action. If the compound consisting of the negative particle were exhausted merely by negation, then the meaning of the compound here would be a non-instrument, and its function would not consist of the mere negation of a superimposed form.

Furthermore, because the perception of those who engage in superimposition (*samāropa*) is distorted, there is no fixed rule; thus, even in the absence of actual similarity, when a negative compound (*nañsamāsa*) is established everywhere due to some cause of error, one must understand that superimposition is occurring.

For a negative compound is understood to have the meaning of the second member as its primary sense by negating the meaning of that second member, as seen in usages such as *aprāṇinām*, *astrīviṣayāt*, and *ayopadhādacittavat-kartṛkā*. Therefore, by following the basis for the superimposition, the cognition of something similar to the meaning of the second member should be recognized. || 280 ||

"Furthermore, this is also included under the predominance of the meaning of the final member [of the compound]. What is it? 'Many' (aneka)," so says the Bhāṣya. He explains that: "When there is predominance [of the meaning of the final member], the form *asa* is established from 'many'. Thus, dependence is appropriate for the principal elements alone in the application of the suffixes -tva and -tal. (281)

In this case, since the meaning of the word *eka* is the primary element, the singular number is applied based on that [meaning] because it possesses the number one; furthermore, because it is not a subordinate member (*anupasarjana*), it undergoes the grammatical operations associated with the designation of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), such as the substitution of *smāy* and so forth. However, if the meaning of the preceding member or the meaning of the compound as a whole were the primary element, then the meaning of the word *eka* would be a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), and by the rule "the designation of a pronoun is prohibited for a subordinate member," the designation of a pronoun would not apply.

Likewise, in the case of *asaḥ*, the internal class-based operation (*antargaṇakārya*)—such as "the substitution of *a* for [stems] beginning with *tyad*" and so forth—is established when its referent is primary. For it has been stated that the recitation of the list (*gaṇapāṭha*) is qualified by its universal application and its primacy: "The exclusion [of others] is based on the recitation; the assignment of technical names (*saṃjñā*) to those items recited is for the sake of operations occurring immediately after *sarva* and the rest."

Likewise, regarding the statement in the Bhāṣya—“The *nañ* compound with [stems ending in] *tva* and *tal* was previously prohibited for the sake of establishing the accent of *tva* and *tal*”—which was stated as a rebuttal, that [prohibition] is appropriate when the meaning of the final member (*uttarapada*) is predominant. Why? Because of a lack of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*). This is logical when the meaning of the subsequent member is primary.

For instance: when a division is made for the purpose of explaining the conventional word *abrāhmaṇatvam*—which has its internal divisions already discarded—the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) as a negation and the abstract state (*bhāva*) extracted from it are analyzed as "the state of that which is other than a Brāhmaṇa. When there is a desire to express both simultaneously, then, because they are subsequent [rules], the suffixes *-tva* and *-tal* would apply. Once those two have been applied, by the principle of "re-occurrence" (*prasaṅgavijñāna*), the compound accent (*samāsasvara*) would apply to the negative compound (*nañsamāsa*).

Since the word *śiṣṭa* exists [as a remainder], it would follow that the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the indeclinable preceding member (*avyayapūrvapada*) applies, whereas the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*) is also desired; thus, when this contradiction regarding the *nañ*-compound is raised, the following solution is stated in the Bhāṣya beginning with "Not here" (*nātra*), etc. Because the meaning of "being other than a Brāhmaṇa" requires a negation (*pratiṣedha*), the sense of "Brāhmaṇa" must first enter into a state of semantic unification (*ekārthībhāva*) with the taddhita suffix as its prior constituent. Therefore, the *nañ*-compound is formed first in this case.

But surely, even though it depends on the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*), the meaning of "Brāhmaṇa" remains dependent [on other factors], and thus the *nañ*-compound would not be possible either. This is not so; for a compound occurs when that which is the primary element (*pradhāna*) is dependent. However, in the case of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), it is the subordinate element (*upasarjana*), namely the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*), that is dependent. How, then, is this consistent if the *nañ*-compound has the meaning of the subsequent member as its primary element? For if the primary elements were the meaning of the prior member or the meaning of another word, the *nañ*-compound would share the same grammatical status as the negative particle (*abhāva*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*).

In both cases, because the quality (*guṇa*) is dependent, the explanatory commentary (*bhāṣya*) stating the resolution would not be tenable; thus, there is an elevation of the status of the final member of the compound as the predominant element. Now, even in the view that words are eternal (*nityaśabda*), according to the method of analytical derivation (*vibhajyānvākhyāna*), by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the rule *vāha ūṭh*, even when [the two operations] occur simultaneously, it is established that among internal operations (*antaraṅga*), the more internal is stronger; therefore, based solely on its connection with the negative particle (*nañ*), the negative compound (*nañsamāsa*) itself occurs first. This is true.

However, considering the meaning of the positive element (*bhāvārtha*), it is more logical that the Brahmin, whose distinction has emerged, is connected with the negative particle (*nañ*); thus, it is here the principal member that is dependent. The statement regarding the "prior prohibition" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) is stated as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) to the effect that: "Therefore, another abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) occurs before the *nañ*-compound. And so, in that case, there is the vowel-lengthening (*vṛddhi*) of the final member and the accent (*svara*) of the *nañ*. || 281 ||

Immediately following this, the commentary asks: "What is included here? Singular number. He explains that: "Because the singular is primary, when it is in proximity to its qualifiers, repetition—which is a property of the primary—occurs; therefore, there is no other grammatical number. (282)

Because a single referent is primary, by means of its negation in the expression "not one," even when many things are to be expressed, the singular number alone occurs in accordance with the primary meaning, and not the plural; such is the meaning. || 282 ||

But surely, since "two" and so forth are expressed here by the word "one" with superimposed unity, when that single referent is negated by the negative particle (*nañ*), there is a cognition of "two" and so forth which are based upon it; therefore, it might be argued that the number residing in those [duals] alone is logical. Anticipating this objection, he says: "In this case, because it is the object to be differentiated, the primary referent is the single entity modified by the negative particle. Having abandoned their own properties, 'two' and the rest also come to assume unity. (283)

In the expression "aneka" (many) qualified by the negative particle (*nañ*), the single referent (*ekārtha*) is the primary element because it is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). Consequently, the duals and other numbers—which have acquired a form similar to that of the cause [the singular] by being permeated by it and having abandoned their own inherent properties—are perceived as singular due to following the nature of the cause; therefore, the singular number alone is logical. || 283 ||

If it is asked how unity can be associated with dualities and so forth which are contradictory, he says: "Just as Kṣatriyas and others, when joined with the negative particle *nañ*, come to possess the status of being 'non-Brāhmaṇas,' so too is unity figuratively attributed to dualities and the like through the application of *nañ*. (284)

Just as the word *brāhmaṇa* in the application of the negative particle (*nañ*), as in *abrāhmaṇa*, is understood to function with reference to a Kṣatriya, so too in the case of *aneka*, the word *eka* functions with reference to two or more. For an object similar to the meaning of the subsequent term is indeed perceived; and in that regard, the meaning of the subsequent term is superimposed due to causes such as faulty instruction—this is the same in all cases. (284)

For instance: "Having applied the connection with oneness, that property is negated; the word for them functions in reference to two or more [individuals], just as in the case of 'Brāhmaṇa' and so forth. (285)

Through delusion, oneness is superimposed upon two or more things, and this is what is negated by the negative particle (*nañ*), not the word "one" itself. For if the intended removal of delusion were not perceived, then the word "one" would be as inappropriate to use here as the word "Brāhmaṇa" is in reference to a Kṣatriya or others. Indeed, if the word "one" did not exist, there would be no superimposition of oneness upon two or more things; so what would the negative particle have to negate? || 285 ||

Therefore, since the word *eka* is employed for the purpose of defining the scope of the negative particle (*nañ*), it follows its own grammatical properties as the primary referent; thus he says that there is no distinction between the compound (*vṛtti*) and the analytical sentence (*vākya*): "In a sentence, this [negative particle] is used with a number attached, such as 'two' and so forth; in the compound, because it is the primary element, that number does not cease. (286)

Just as in a sentence one uses the word "one" (*eka*) even when there is another number—such as "if one [of two] is not *ṅit* or *kit*, not one [of two or more]"—without abandoning its own inherent number, so too in a compound, because that meaning is predominant, there is no abandonment of its own inherent number in the word "many" (*aneka*). || 286 ||

But he says that if those [words] were omitted, the intended meaning would not be understood: "The object to be negated is connected exactly as it exists; for when joined with another statement, that very object is not negated. (287)

The subsequent member of the compound is employed even with an unreal meaning for the purpose of establishing the object of negation; thus, whatever form the superimposed object of negation takes, the subsequent member is adopted to denote that very form. Since it is singularity that is to be negated in the case of "two" and so forth, this intended negation is understood only when the subsequent member is in the singular number. However, if the dual or other numbers were employed, the singularity being negated would not be perceived.
Therefore, because it serves the intended meaning, the singular number alone is logical. (287)

"But how can there be a cognition of two or many when there is the negation of one?"—this objection from the *Bhāṣya* proceeds with the intention that the negation is of the form of a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) consisting merely in the cessation of oneness; [the author] supports this by resorting to the view of exclusion (*paryudāsa*): "Just as in the case of 'non-white,' an object such as black is understood as the actual referent, so too in the expression 'many,' another number is denoted. (288)

Just as in the case of a relative negation (paryudāsa), blue and other colors are understood without distinction from the word "non-white" through the exclusion of white, so too are numbers such as two and so forth understood from the word "many" through the exclusion of the number one, without any distinction. || 288 ||

To support this very point, the Bhāṣya states: "Having first engaged in an action or a quality, one subsequently effects its cessation; for example: 'Feed him, let him eat, let him lie down—[but] not alone. This is explained as follows: "Because of the engagement in an action, when all [actions] have been accepted and even one has been prohibited, another that was previously applicable is still perceived. (289)

A verbal action, by the force of its meaning, implies the means of accomplishment (sādhana) without distinction. Thus, when "he sits" (āste) is said, the general category of object (karman) is understood. Since cessation is preceded by an injunction, there arises the contingency of various numbers of objects being implied by the power of the action; therefore, because one [object] is prohibited, it is understood that only those means which possess other numbers—being themselves unprohibited—serve as the instruments of accomplishment. || 289 ||

To the question, "In which sense is this stated? he says: "Action and scriptural injunction apply to what has been commenced by way of a prohibitive negation (prasajya-pratiṣedha). But in the case of an exclusionary negation (paryudāsa), another specific number is invariably expressed. (290)

In the case of a non-presuppositional negation (prasajya-pratiṣedha), because the function of the word is exhausted by the negation itself, the employment of a means of proof occurs with the exclusion of that which is negated, due to the capacity of the action. However, in the case of an exclusionary negation (paryudāsa), it has already been stated that from the word "not one" (aneka) itself, there is the employment of a specific means of proof that is similar to the meaning of the subsequent term.

He explains the intention of the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra) regarding the mention of contradictory actions through the inclusion of the commands of the instigator and the instigated—namely, "sit," "make sit," and "feed"—as follows: "The meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha), having as its object the action, is designated by its own instruments; consequently, all [subsidiary] actions remain implied beforehand. (291)

When the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*)—which possesses an object (*sakarmaka*), is distinguished by various states such as sitting and so forth, and was previously specified as being delimited by its own instruments (*sādhana*) such as the prompted (*prayojya*) and the prompter (*prayojaka*), and thus having a nature consisting of contradictory actions—at that time, because it is impossible for that [meaning] possessing multiple contradictory natures to be accomplished by a single instrument, multiple instruments were already employed. Therefore, by the negation of one [instrument], there is the comprehension of that very [meaning]. || 291 ||

The subsequent commentary states: "Even though this may be said in cases where action and quality are involved, how can there be a plurality [of things] remaining in a case where they are not so involved?
