The response to this is: "In such cases as well, when one is negated, there is still the cognition of many. Here, the meaning of the objection in the commentary is that in a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation), since it is exhausted merely by the negation itself, there would be no apprehension of "two" and so forth.

The intention of the rebuttal is that, in the case of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), the cognition is established because a different number of the same class serves as the basis for the superimposition of unity. He explains this [as follows]: "Where a verb is employed with a substrate whose means [of accomplishment] are already known, the word 'many' (*aneka*) subsequently follows [and is understood], and the word 'stands' (*tiṣṭhati*) is supplied. (292)

Because it is that which is to be accomplished, action is characterized there by a substance already established; since the substance has already been accepted [as the substratum], it is therefore distinguished from the former [action]. || 293 ||

Where, for some reason, the substance (*dravya*)—which serves as the locus of the power of the means of accomplishment—is determined to be a unity within the verb (*ākhyāta*), yet because of the subsequent determination that the action denoted by it is not as it appears, [the verb] is employed after first negating its multiplicity and then remaining as the verbal element (*kriyāpada*).

In that case, because the substance possessing power—which was previously determined—is being employed for the sake of another, it implies an action that conforms to its own nature; it is not the case that the substance is implied by the capacity of the action. This is the distinction between this [type of implication] and the previous one. Furthermore, here too, because the object of the established means of accomplishment presents itself, the means of accomplishment is understood through the avoidance of what has been prohibited, following the negation of a single [possibility].

Thus, even when a verbal root (kriyāpada) is not heard previously, the sentence does not terminate in a mere single negation, because of the expectancy for an action; therefore, even in that case of a single negation, the status of another number as a means [of accomplishment] is understood. || 292, 293 ||

Thus, even in cases where there is no intended meaning in the verbal expression [itself], another number is nevertheless understood; this is illustrated in the Bhāṣya by the example: "not not one beloved, not not one happiness. He explains that: "The number itself, through negation, requires another number; therefore, even in the sentence, it is not mere oneness alone that is set aside. (294)

The sentence is: "na na ekaṃ priyaṃ, na na ekaṃ sukham" (not not one dear thing, not not one happiness). In the rule "ābādhe ca" (and in the case of affliction), there is reduplication; here, there is affliction for the speaker caused by the enemy's happiness and what is dear to him. And since no verbal action is heard here, even though the function of the sentence consists merely in the negation of happiness and what is dear, happinesses and dear things qualified by another number are understood: "the enemy does not have one happiness, but many," and likewise, "many dear things."

This is indeed the meaning of the sentence here: because a specific prohibition has as its scope the permission of the remainder. If there were a prohibition of all happiness and all that is dear, the employment of the single word [“all”] would be purposeless. And since this capacity exists even in a sentence, what doubt can there be regarding the comprehension of an exclusion (paryudāsa) of a meaning similar to the meaning of the subsequent member in a compound (vṛtti)? For in that case, a single word expresses two or many; thus, the cessation does not apply to oneness alone, but rather the comprehension of "two" and so forth, characterized by that cessation, is established. || 294 ||

[Objection: But how is it that only "two" and so forth are understood by necessity? One might suspect that when one [number] is negated, something else—the remaining form—should be understood. Anticipating this, he says: "When oil is obtained for the meal, because of the exclusion of other fats and because of its suitability, no other condiment is used. (295)

Just as when it is enjoined that "food should be prepared without oil," by the force of the prohibition of oil, the exclusion of other fats such as ghee is understood as a qualification of the food—due to its proximity and belonging to the same class—and not [the exclusion] of curds or milk; so too here, when one number is prohibited, another number which performs the same function and belongs to the same genus of number is understood, rather than some other thing indistinctly. Thus it is established that, in the case of the predominance of the meaning of the subsequent member (uttarapada), [this is the result].

This is the justification for the rule *nañ-samāsasyānekaṃ* [Pāṇini 2.4.63]. How then is the usage of the venerable Patañjali—"the mind is the cause of the differentiation of functions for both the one and the many"—to be explained? We say it is by resorting to *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one from among identicals). For even when there is a negation of "one," since one may intend to imply a specific individual due to some particular cause, the application of *ekaśeṣa* is logical here. However, the author of the Bhāṣya has justified the singular number, but he did not prohibit the plural number. || 295 ||

Now, for the sake of examining the position in which another word-meaning is predominant, he says: "When an external different class, such as a Kṣatriya and so forth, is designated by two words—'non-existent' (asat) and 'Brāhmaṇa'—which reside in a single referent," (296)

Therefore, it should be understood from the context that the *nañ*-compound is one in which the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*) is predominant. Here, in the case of *nañ*-compounds such as "non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇa*) and so forth, we observe the communication of a thing that is the opposite of the meaning of the final member (*uttarapada*). And in that regard, when the method of grammatical derivation (*anvākhyānaprakriyā*) follows the principle that the members of the compound—such as Kṣatriyas and others—are those who have had the status of Brahmins and so forth superimposed upon them by virtue of being designated by the final member, then the predominance of the meaning of the final member has been established by the statement beginning with "previously resorted to as predominant" (*prādhānyenāśritāḥ pūrvam*).

But when this negative particle (*nañ*), although its function is to denote the absence of a general property (*asat-sāmānya*), enters into a relationship of coreferentiality with the word "Brāhmaṇa" by way of a specific relation to a particular existent (*sad-viśeṣa*)—that is, through a general-particular relationship—and then follows upon an external term introduced by another word, such as "Kṣatriya," which possesses a superior meaning obtained through that connection and does not rest merely there, then it is a *nañ*-compound in which the meaning of the other member is predominant (*anyapadārtha-pradhāna*).

For instance, when there is no Brāhmaṇa—that is, when the individual Brāhmaṇa who serves as the substratum for a certain Kṣatriya or Kṣatriya caste is absent—the exclusion (*avaccheda*) of that external object (the referent of the compound) by the two word-meanings (the absence and the Brāhmaṇa) results in a distinct, external class [of non-Brāhmaṇas]. || 296 ||

But when the meaning of the final member (*uttarapadārtha*) is predominant, because the Brahmin caste superimposed upon the Kṣatriya and others is negated, another similar caste such as the Kṣatriya—which is indeed denoted by the final member—is what results, rather than something external. With the intention that, unlike in a *bahuvrīhi* where there is no explicit mention of the "meaning of another word" (*anyapadārtha*), the application of the term is more appropriate to its own constituent meaning (*svapadārtha*) as an internal factor, he explains this by citing other examples of similar *tatpuruṣa* compounds: "Just as a dark woman is designated as 'a knife' or a girl [is called] 'dark,' so too, through the two expressions 'non-Brahmin' and 'not a Brahmin,' the Kṣatriya and others are designated as something else. (297)

In the example "The girl is sword-dark" (*śastrīśyāmā kanyā*), it is stated that in the compound, the object of comparison (*upameya*)—the girl—is expressed by the compound even though she is not explicitly denoted by the two constituent words (*vṛttipada*). This is because the compound attains grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "girl. Similarly, in the case of *asat* (with the negative particle *nañ* meaning "non-existent") and *brāhmaṇa*, although the Kṣatriya is not explicitly denoted by the negative particle in its sense of non-existence, nor by the specific term "Brāhmaṇa," he is nevertheless denoted by the compound.

And just as the *upamāna-samāsa*, being specifically prescribed, is not superseded by the *bahuvrīhi* which is prescribed in a general sense, so too is the *nañ-samāsa*; this is the meaning of the statement that "this [compound] is a *tatpuruṣa* even when the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) is the object. || 297 ||

On this very point, he states another illustration: "Just as a gavaya is designated by the phrase 'a hornless cow,' it is not the absence of a dewlap in a cow that is perceived, but rather a different species. (298)

The word "cow" is necessarily connected with a dewlap; therefore, when it is said "this is not a cow," if nothing more than its dewlap is absent, there arises the cognition of a *gavaya*—which resembles a cow in the arrangement of its remaining parts—but not of a cow itself, since the cow is excluded by the absence of the dewlap. Thus, from this sentence, there is a cognition [of similarity] through co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the *gavaya*. Similarly, when it is said "this is not a Brāhmaṇa," another caste, the Kṣatriya, is understood; for when the Brāhmaṇa caste alone is negated, there arises the cognition of similarity to his remaining attributes. (298)

Likewise: "Just as one recognizes a *khadira* tree—which appears identical [to other trees]—from its thorns (*kaṅkaṭa*) that serve as the cause for differentiation, by means of a distinction in species from a *kharjūra* (or *barbura*) tree. (299)

Having first understood *khadira* and *kharjūra* (or *khadira* and *barbura*) as non-different—since they both have white trunks and small leaves—and subsequently learning that "the *khadira* has thorns" (*kaṇṭakavān*), one then perceives the distinction of the *khadira* from those [other trees] through those very reasons for differentiation, since thorns are absent in the *kharjūra* (or absent in the *barbura*).

And likewise, just as a *khadira* tree is indeed different from a *kharjūra* (or *barbara*) tree, yet one does not perceive it as having any additional connection to things like thorns (*kaṇṭara* or *kaṅkaṭa*), so too, having determined a similarity with the qualities of a Brāhmaṇa, when the word "Brāhmaṇa" is about to be applied to a Kṣatriya based on the conclusion that he is a Brāhmaṇa, it is said: "This is not a Brāhmaṇa. This indicates merely a difference in caste; everything else is similar, and thus he is understood to be of another caste. ||299||

He states the illustrative example (dārṣṭāntika): "Just as a Brāhmaṇa might be [defined] by one for whom no actual Brāhmaṇī exists, so too is another object expressed by means of an accepted analogy. (300)

Just as in the expression "the girl is like a sword," where the word *kanyā* (girl), though not explicitly mentioned by either of the constituent words (*śastrī* or *śyāmā*), conveys the relationship between the object of comparison and the standard of comparison; and just as in the expression "a hornless cow" (*asāsno gauḥ*), the similarity of parts—excluding the dewlap—is the basis for denoting the distinct entity [the gavaya] through its similarity to a cow, and the similarity of the *gaura* and *akāṇḍa* etc., excluding the armor (*kaṅkaṭa*), is likewise intended; thus, in all these cases, there is the denotation of another meaning based on a standard of comparison (*upamāna*). The same applies here in the case of "non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇa*).

And thus, because of its similarity with other properties—excluding the property of being of the Brāhmaṇa caste—the meaning denoted is something else, namely a Kṣatriya or the like. For instance: "This non-Brāhmaṇa is like a Vaiśya or a Kṣatriya, as is a Brāhmaṇa. In that case, since there is no similarity whatsoever between absolute difference and absolute identity—as in the case of a cow and a gavaya—one must resort to a certain degree of both difference and non-difference. For just as a Brāhmaṇa has had the universal of Brāhmaṇahood removed from him due to some cause, so too is this person of a similar kind; such is the meaning.

For if even the status of being a Brāhmaṇa were merely a relation [of exclusion], then how could the designation "non-Brāhmaṇa" not also apply to a Kṣatriya and so forth? This statement is made with such an exaggeration (*atiśayokti*) in mind. Thus, by accepting the relationship between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), the negative compound (*nañsamāsa*) attains its purpose through the inclusion of specific castes such as the Kṣatriya. Furthermore, the inclusion of similarity within a negative compound is observed; for example, in the expression "the non-rainy season (*avarṣā*) winter. For here, in this negative compound, winter is denoted as being similar to the rainy season. 300.

To the question "How is there similarity here?", he says: Just as rainless years are covered by mist and clouds, because it possesses that same nature, that winter is perceived as non-different [from them]. (301)

"Not *varṣā* (the rainy season), but [something] like *varṣā*" is the meaning; that is, the activity of raining is non-existent. Just as the rainy season consists of masses of mist being spread abroad, with the quarters of the sky covered by hanging dark clouds, so too this winter has its light obscured by a continuous stream of darkness. Because of such a resemblance to the rainy season, it is designated as "*varṣā*. For this *tatpuruṣa* compound, though derived in its own primary sense (*svapadārtha*) through identity (*tādrūpyeṇa*), functions in the sense of another word (*anyapadārtha*) by internalizing the comparison (*upamā*).

However, non-existent rains are not taught as the referent of another word (*anyapadārtha*) in the initial derivation [of *avarṣā*] in the sense that "this has the nature of non-rain," because that would entail the shortening of the subordinate member (*upasarjana*). Thus, according to the view of some, negative compounds (*nañ-samāsa*) containing an implicit comparison (*garbhīkṛtopamā*) pertain to cases where the referent of another word is predominant during their formal derivation (*prakriyā*). || 301 ||

Others maintain that for all words denoting castes, such as *brāhmaṇa* and so forth, when a substance is the external referent (*anyapadārtha*), there is a connection with the negative particle *nañ*. (302)

In the view that the word denotes the universal (*jāti*), words such as "brāhmaṇa" primarily express the universal itself as distinct from its substratum; thus, because the substance (*dravya*) is not conveyed by the constituent member (*varti-pada*), a compound expressing that [substance] has the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) as its predominant meaning. In the case of *asan brāhmaṇaḥ* ("one who is not a Brāhmaṇa"), this refers to one for whom the Brāhmaṇa-ness (*brāhmaṇya*) does not exist—that is, in the sense of a Kṣatriya substance—and thus it forms a *tatpuruṣa* compound with the word *brāhmaṇa*, which denotes the universal.

In this regard, a prohibition is appropriate only where the co-inherence of the Brahmin caste is possible within another substratum, and not with that which is absolutely heterogeneous; thus, it is stated that the referent of the other word is specifically the substance of a Kṣatriya or the like. || 302 ||

In this view, even the distinction between the respective domains of the *bahuvrīhi* and the negative (*nañ*) compound is established; thus he says: "And no such *bahuvrīhi* is conceived as having such a domain [as that of the negative compound], for there is no pervasion (logical entailment) such as 'non-heavy horse' which is not [already] covered by the negative compound. (303)

A *bahuvrīhi* compound whose scope is such that it denotes a substance (*dravya*) belonging to another word-class (*anyapadārtha*) delimited by a genus (*jāti*), is not possible in the same way as a *nañ*-compound; for the rule for *bahuvrīhi* is prescribed in the sense of possession (*matvartha*) when [the first member] signifies abundance (*bhūman*) and so forth. The meaning is stated implicitly: this *bahuvrīhi*—such as "one for whom cows do not exist" (*avidyamānā gāvo yasya*)—or "this horse is not a cow" (*agur ayam aśvaḥ*)—is possible only when its domain has not been occupied by this *nañ*-compound. For the understanding of a *nañ*-compound is indeed as follows: "that which does not exist is the cow or cowness (*gotva*) of this horse; thus, this horse is 'non-cow' (*agaura*)."

Because the negative compound (*nañsamāsa*) denotes by its very nature that which is of a different class from the meaning of the final member, whereas the possessive *bahuvrīhi*—as in "one for whom cows do not exist"—denotes a possessive sense (*matvartha*), the distinction between the scopes of these two is established.

However, when the *bahuvrīhi* compound based on *nañ* is prescribed by the specific rule (*pratipadavihita*)—"*naño'styarthānāṃ bahuvrīhir vā cottarapadalopaś ca*"—it is explained as follows: no *bahuvrīhi* can be formed whose scope (*viṣaya*) is such that it does not find its application (*vyāpti*) or occasion (*avakāśa*) through a *nañ*-compound. Therefore, since both [the *nañ*-compound and the *bahuvrīhi*] would apply to the same domain, one must understand from the force of the context (*sāmarthya*) that the natural distinction between their domains is exactly as previously described. Thus, even though the meaning is consistent, a fault has been stated here regarding the procedure (*prakriyā*) under the view that the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) is predominant. || 303 ||

"If [the compound] were predominant in the meaning of the other member (anyapadārthapradhāna), then in the case of *avarṣā hemantaḥ* ('the non-rainy season, i.e., winter'), whatever gender and number belong to 'winter' (*hemanta*) would apply to the compound"—so it is stated in the Bhāṣya. He explains this [verse]: "Since the rule that the gender and number of a Dvandva or an Ekadeśin follow those of the final member has already been stated, there is consequently a failure [to establish] the desired gender and number in the case of *avarṣāḥ*. (304)

If, in the case of *avarṣā hemantaḥ*, the meaning of the other member (*anyapadārtha*) were predominant, there would be the consequence of the gender and number belonging to *hemanta* (masculine singular); thus, the intended plurality and femininity would not occur. Nor does the rule “the gender of a *dvandva* and a *tatpuruṣa* is that of the final member” apply here. The application of the gender of the final member is restricted specifically to the *ekadeśisamāsa* type of *tatpuruṣa*; for if the gender of the final member applied to all *tatpuruṣas* indiscriminately, there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of such a gender in cases like *prāptajīvikaḥ*.

And thus the *Vārttika* states: "It is established by the mention of the 'part-possessor' (*ekadeśin*) in [the rule concerning] *prāpta* and so forth. [One might object: "In this case, the shortening of the *upasarjana* would also apply," as in *avarṣāḥ* and *agauḥ*, because there is no difference in their being dominated by the meaning of the other member (*anyapadārtha*), just like a *bahuvrīhi*. Nor can this be avoided by the rule "the gender is that of the final member" (*paravalliṅgam*), since that refers to the word and its meaning [rather than the compound itself]. Because this statement applies specifically to the *tatpuruṣa*, the position that the other member’s meaning is dominant is flawed. (304)

Now, with reference to the predominance of the prior member of the compound: when a qualifier such as "brāhmaṇa" and so forth is distinct from its object because it is not connected to the action, then its non-existence is perceived. (305)

When the meaning of non-existence (*asadartha*), introduced by the word *nañ*, is presented as being connected with an action, then that very [non-existence], being delimited by the meaning of the subsequent member, *brāhmaṇa*, is perceived as qualified. Since the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*)—namely non-existence—is perceived as primary when it is differentiated and delimited by the qualifier *brāhmaṇa*, the position arises that the meaning of the prior member is predominant (*pūrvapadārthapradhānatā*). || 305 ||

Now, raising the objection, "How can that which is non-existent have a connection with action?", he says: "Because it is non-existent by virtue of being a Brahmin, it is called 'non-existent' in one sense; yet even the term 'non-existent' negates the existence of that which is existent by means of its own existence. (306)

An object that exists in the form of a *kṣatriya* and so forth is apprehended by the negative particle (*nañ*) as being non-existent in its capacity as a *brāhmaṇa*; thus, the negation refers to a qualified object and does not signify absolute non-existence. Consequently, there is no contradiction regarding its connection with verbal action. For this very reason, it is established that there is no lack of comprehension of the intended meaning. Furthermore, in the compound *asad* (non-existent), the phrase "by way of existence" (*sattvena*) is understood; here too, the word "otherwise" (*anyathā*) is to be supplied.

Since an absence that is not qualified by a specific positive state (bhāva-viśeṣa) cannot be the object of linguistic usage, what is being negated here is the existence of a subsequent referent (uttara-padārtha) which is characterized as a real entity (vastu) in another manner. Thus, this [negation] indeed possesses a connection with a specific action that conforms to a positive form (bhāva-rūpa). || 306 ||

Regarding this position in which the meaning of the first member of the compound is predominant, it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "The designation *avyaya* (indeclinable) would apply; for its first member is indeed an *avyaya*. This he explains: "Because they reside in a general substance (*sāmānyadravya*), [words] conform to their causes (*nimitta*). There would be a non-connection with gender and number, or else there would be the status of being a general property (*sāmānyadharmatā*). (307)

Since the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) qualified by the meaning of the subsequent member is expressed as the primary sense, it would follow that the compound meaning is devoid of gender and number. This is because, in this context, the substratum such as a *kṣatriya*—which is of the nature of a general substance—is the cause for the application of the word; and since that [substratum] lacks gender and number, the possessor of that cause (the compound) cannot be designated by its own [gender and number] in accordance with the cause. Consequently, even though it possesses the nature of a real entity (*sattva*), it would incur the designation of an indeclinable (*avyaya*) based on the definition of "that which has only a meaning" (*arthamātra*). Thus, the compound meaning would be without gender and number.

For in a sentence, the meaning of the negative particle *nañ* is observed to be the general absence (*abhāvasāmānya*), which is non-substantial (*asattvabhūta*). That very same [absence], when it occurs here in a compound (*vṛtti*), is denoted primarily as qualified by the meaning of the subsequent member; thus, how could gender and number belong to it? Now, if it is argued that because the compound is not included among the indeclinables (*avyaya*), it lacks the designation of "indeclinable," and therefore the case-ending (*vibhakti*) does not occur—nevertheless, even though the designation has ceased, the actual object does not cease to exist; thus, the properties of an indeclinable would indeed apply.

And thus the Bhāṣya states: "When the designation *avyaya* (indeclinable) is established by the rule of recitation (*pāṭha*), the gender and number [of the word] follow those of the thing denoted. And: "Whatever meaning is expressed here, that has no connection with gender or number. Alternatively, even if the cause [for gender and number] were not followed, the universal gender (*liṅgasarvanāma*) would apply, as would the singular number, resulting in the usage *abrāhmaṇam* alone; however, forms such as *abrāhmaṇau* and *abrāhmaṇāḥ* would not occur.

For the distinction between gender and number is based on a specific individual (vyakti). In this case, however, a specific individual is not the expressed meaning; because the denotative function (abhidhā-vyāpāra) of the negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) operates upon mere existence (*sattva*) that is capable of engaging in action, no particularity is perceived. || 307 ||

Regarding this, the solution is stated in the Bhāṣya: "This [status of being] without gender or number is not based on an explicit rule; rather, it is inherent," and so forth. To that, one might ask: "What can we say about this, other than that prior to compounding there is no connection with gender or number, whereas in the compound there is? This he explains: "Prior to [compounding], it expresses non-existence; in the compound, it denotes a substance. And conformity to external causes does not occur everywhere by its very nature. (308)

In this context, the non-human (apauruṣeyī) power of words to convey meaning—designated as "fitness" (yogyatā) and restricted to specific objects—is established in its true nature through the authority of usage. In that regard, since the word in its derivative form (*vṛtti*) and the sentence (*vākya*) are distinct, they possess distinct powers; thus, although the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) in a sentence is non-existent (*asattvabhūta*), it is expressed by the derivative form as something existent (*sattvabhūta*). Consequently, its connection with an action is observed.

To explain: in a sentence (*vākya*), since the negative particle (*nañ*) expresses the negation as distinct from the object to be negated, the meaning of the indeclinable is expressed as primary; thus, there is no connection with gender or number. In a compound (*vṛtti*), however, because the object to be negated—subordinate to the negation—is the meaning of the negative particle, its connection with gender and number is appropriate due to the predominance of that which is to be negated. Furthermore, it is not necessary that [the gender and number] must conform to the cause [the object negated] in all other cases as well, since we observe a fixed application of gender and number in words such as *harītakī* and others.

And therefore, since the connection with gender and number is observed in a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*), the meaning is that there is no conformity to the cause [of the meaning] as there is in the case of words like "white" (*śukla*). || 308 ||
For instance: "If [the effect] conforms to its cause, then the connection with action is not possible; likewise, because it would be indefinable, the material cause would be useless. (309)

If the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*), which is of the nature of non-existence, were to follow its own grammatical cause (its lack of gender and number), then the referent of the compound would not be connected with gender and number, and consequently, it could not function as the means for actions such as "bring the *abrāhmaṇa*" or "see the *abrāhmaṇa*. Thus, the mention of a nominal word-meaning that is not a factor in an action would be fruitless, and the negative compound (*nañsamāsa*) would be ungrammatical. However, since its status as a factor in an action is observed, it is appropriate that the negative compound denotes a substantive entity (*sattvabhūta-artha*) through the authority of usage, even though it does not follow the [non-existent] cause of gender and number. || 309 ||

By this much, there would be a mere connection with gender and number through the assertion of their inherent nature; however, since specific genders and numbers are intended according to their respective applications following actual usage, another alternative view is presented here in the Bhāṣya for the sake of establishing that: "Or rather, the gender and number of words denoting qualities (guṇavacana) are derived from their substratum (āśraya). He explains this: "Or, [the word] whose function is in the universal (sāmānya), being differentiated by its substrata—such as Kṣatriyas and others—which are employed as particulars, assumes the gender and number of those [substrata]. (310)

The meaning of the compound is a non-existent universal (*asat-sāmānya*) qualified by the meaning of the final member, which is not yet determined in its specific particulars. When there is a desire to know that particularity, and specific terms are employed, that meaning of the compound becomes qualified by those specific bases and thus fit for usage; therefore, it is logical that it should possess the gender and number of those [bases]. Since meanings do not deviate from mutual exclusion—such that the cessation of "Brāhmaṇa" and so forth implies only "Kṣatriya" and so forth—it is appropriate that the gender and number belong precisely to what resides in those [bases].

Since all forms possess all genders, when the gender of a word's power is restricted, just as the same referent "kṣatriya" and "kṣatra" are expressed by two words of different genders, so too in the expression "an-Brāhmaṇa kṣatra," the referent qualified by masculinity is conveyed by the word "an-Brāhmaṇa. This is because, through the figurative application of non-difference with a term denoting exclusion (nivṛtti), it is that very possessor [of the quality] which is being referred to.

Just as other genus-words (*jātiśabda*) are inherently associated with gender and number, so too is the negative compound (*nañsamāsa*). Therefore, its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with words such as *kṣatra*, even though they possess different genders, is established. In this way, expressions such as "non-water" (*anāpaḥ*) and "non-earth" (*apṛthivī*) are justified. For this very reason, here too, the inherent nature (*svābhāvikatva*) alone is the cause for the determination of gender and number. However, in the previous solution, the fact that [the word] denotes a substance (*dravyavacanatva*) was the basis for its inherent nature; this is the distinction. || 310 ||

[Objection: Since there is no universal devoid of particularity, the particular is already included by the very word "universal"; so how can there be the employment of a term that denotes that [particular]? To this he says: "For the substratum, which was previously internalized within the primary [universal], is seen as if divided again by a subsequent reflective awareness. (311)

Although, when an absence is expressed by a compound, its own locus—the particular—is already implicitly included from the very outset, nevertheless, because there is no definitive determination of the particular from the hearing of the general term alone, that particular is indeed referred back again by means of a word denoting the particular. Thus, as if the distinction of the particular from the general were based on the word itself, the connection with the number residing in the locus is stated upon the cognition of the relationship between the locus and the located. || 311 ||

For it is thus: that by which the own-meaning (svārtha) is heard in a compound is its substratum; however, the substance (dravya), along with gender and number, is internalized as something non-existent [within the word]. (312)

In the *vṛtti* (the analytical commentary), because the negative particle (*nañ*) has as its primary meaning the existence [of the negation], there is a general substance (*dravyasāmānya*) associated with gender and number that is colored by absence (*abhāva*). Thus, it is concluded that the meaning of the previous resolution—which demonstrated the inherent nature [of the negation]—is that this [substance] is internalized and expressed by the word "non-existent" (*asan*), which is a term for the non-existent. However, in the second resolution, according to the view that [the negative particle] expresses a quality (*guṇavacana*), the meaning expressed by itself is understood within the compound (*samāsa*). That which possesses the general non-existence (*asatsāmānya*)—such as a Kṣatriya and so forth—is determined to be qualified by exclusion (*nivṛtti-viśiṣṭa*), and it is the substratum (*ādhāra*) of that [exclusion]. || 312 ||

It has been stated that when a signifier conforms to its signified, it takes on gender and number like an adjective; but how is it that the referent—whether its own word-meaning or the meaning of another word such as "Kṣatriya"—is established, so that both positions may be tenable? To this he says: "Two words whose objects are identical [refer] to that [same thing], even while functioning with different meanings. Thus, there is a comprehensive inclusion of all distinctions, though they are non-existent. (313)

Prior to the compound, in the sentence, the negative particle (*nañ*) indicates exclusion (*nivṛtti*), and the word "Brāhmaṇa" denotes an object qualified by that exclusion. Thus, these two words function with distinct meanings. However, in that compound, the meaning of the negative particle—delimited by the meaning of the subsequent member—is conveyed as a single entity; for those two [words] then have a single referent, since it is only the single meaning of the negative particle, as merged with the subordinate member, that constitutes the expressed sense.

However, because all these distinctions—such as the Kṣatriya and so forth—are accepted through the sense of negation due to their non-existence, the function of the final member [of the compound] consists merely in indicating that; therefore, there is predominance of the meaning of the prior member. || 313 ||

But when the other member of the compound is predominant, he says: "They [the meanings] are to be expressed by the words 'kṣatriya' and so forth, or they are to be expressed by pronouns; for, due to the non-conceptualization of the form of the negative particle (nañ), they seem to attain the status of being the meaning of the other member. (314)

Words such as "kṣatriya" and "vaiśya," when employed, clearly convey the specific distinctions contained within the term "non-Brahmin" through their mutual differentiation; however, in the absence of those specific terms, the pronominal word expresses that meaning only in a general form.

And having established this, even though this meaning is grasped by the two constituent words (*varti-pada*), it cannot be definitively determined without the employment of another word (*padāntara*). Thus, failing to discern the power of the word itself, those who perceive the Kṣatriya and others as the "meaning of the other word" (*anyapadārtha*) assert that the negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) has the "meaning of the other word" as its primary referent. For they are deluded, thinking that while the word *nañ* expresses negation, the word *brāhmaṇa* denotes its own class [of Brahmins], and therefore the Kṣatriya is the "meaning of the other word."

For those who follow the primary power of words (*śabda-śakti*), however, the word *iva* here signifies that the very meaning of its own term is the object characterized by similarity. To explain: there is a misconception among those for whom the form of the negative particle (*nañ*) is not conceptualized or specifically understood in this way—namely, that the meaning of *nañ* is a non-existent universal (*asat-sāmānya*) qualified by the existence of the subsequent word's referent, and which possesses distinctions imagined through the differences in substrata such as "Kṣatriya" and so forth. [In contrast,] when the prior member of the compound is predominant, there is utility in the extension of gender and number. (314)

In this regard, he points out a fault in this position: "But if the specific [gender] is not employed, then gender and number are not established; furthermore, there is a fault in cases such as *avarṣā* and so on, because *hemanta* would then have a different substratum. (315)

If the non-existent universal (*asatsāmānya*), assisted by the meaning of the subsequent member, is what is expressed by the compound, then when specific instances such as *kṣatriya* and so forth are employed, let there be the establishment of specific gender and number based on those employed instances. However, when they are not employed, since gender and number would not be established based on a particular individual, they must instead reside in the universal itself, characterized by the neuter gender and the singular number.

In cases such as *avarṣā hemantaḥ* (the winter season is not-rainy), *anāpaḥ pṛthivī* (the earth is waterless), *apañcālā janapadaḥ* (the country is non-Pañcāla), *agodau grāmaḥ* (the village is without cattle), *atejaḥ sikatāḥ* (the sands are without brilliance), *anartho gṛhāḥ* (the houses are useless), and *anidāgho varṣāḥ* (the rainy season is without heat), the establishment of gender and number would not occur. This is because, in the case of *avarṣā hemantaḥ*, the referent of the compound's meaning is "winter" (*hemanta*), which is distinct from "rainy seasons" (*varṣā*); thus, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the gender and number belonging to "winter. The same logic should be applied to the other examples.

Because the mention of "hemanta" (winter) is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*), and because the meaning of the first member of the compound would be subordinate (*upasarjana*) due to the predominance of the meaning of the preceding member, the occurrence of a short vowel would follow; thus, the view that the meaning of the first member is predominant is also flawed. Rather, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) here is precisely the predominance of the meaning of the subsequent member. Consequently, the gender and number belonging to the meaning of the subsequent member are established accordingly. However, this is not the scope for the rule of extension (*atideśa*).

For those words which vary according to the differences in their connection with external objects are adjectives (*guṇavacana*), and they convey the gender and number of their own substratum (*svāśraya*). Such are words like "white" (*śukla*) and compounds such as the *bahuvrīhi*. However, the negative compound (*nañsamāsa*) follows its original [referent] absolutely, without abandoning the specific gender and number already acquired; thus, as in the case of genus-words (*jātiśabda*) whose gender is fixed, there is no following of the gender of the substratum here.

For instance, in expressions such as *abrāhmaṇaḥ kṣatram* (a non-Brahmin Kṣatriya) or *abrāhmaṇaḥ kṣatriyaḥ* (a non-Brahmin Kṣatriya), the gender (*liṅga*) observed is precisely that which inheres in the meaning of the subsequent member [of the compound]. Therefore, it has been stated that this is inherent (*svābhāvikam*). Number (*saṅkhyā*) also, in cases such as *avarṣāḥ* (non-rainy years) and the like, inheres only in the meaning of the subsequent member; thus, that too is inherent. However, in instances such as *abrāhmaṇau* (two non-Brahmins), number sometimes depends upon an external object.

If this is so, then because the power of words is restricted in this way, even when the specific [negative particle] is not employed, the gender and number of the qualified [compound] are indeed established; thus, the position that the meaning of the prior member is predominant (*pūrvapadārthapradhāna*) should not be abandoned. For this very reason, this [position] has been supported in the *Bhāṣya* through the resolution of an objection. Furthermore, the functions of a pronoun (*sarvanāma-kārya*) do indeed occur in forms such as *asaḥ* and *asarvasmāt*, because the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) does not effect exclusion and because it stands in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*).

For in cases such as *atisarvāya*, the meaning of the word beginning with *sarva-* is subordinate only when it functions as a non-co-referential (*vyadhikaraṇa*) qualifier, but not when it is co-referential (*samānādhikaraṇa*), as in a negative compound (*nañsamāsa*). Indeed, just as in a sentence, in a negative compound the words beginning with *sarva-* function as qualifiers of the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) without abandoning their own inherent meaning; thus, the grammatical operations pertaining to pronouns (*sarvanāma*) still apply. For this very reason—due to its coreferentiality with the principal member, its possession of various case-endings, and its not being designated by the nominative case—the status of being a subordinate element (*upasarjana*) does not arise, and consequently, even the rule for shortening (*hrasvatva*) does not apply.

Furthermore, when a technical definition (*pāribhāṣika*) for the functions of a subordinate element (*upasarjana*) is available, a worldly subordinate element should not be adopted. Therefore, the observation regarding the predominance of the meaning of the prior member is established. Thus, in the case of negative compounds (*nañ-samāsa*) and others, the extension (*atideśa*) of gender and number has been followed according to the Bhāṣya. || 315 ||

Just as in the case of negative compounds (*nañ-samāsa*) and the like, so too, when the *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one) is rejected on the basis of the theory that the word-referent is the universal (*jāti*), as stated in the rule: "Vājapyāyana [holds] that there is only one [word] denoting the form (*ākṛti*) when a case-ending follows," it is said: "The establishment of gender and number [occurs] because the quality (*guṇa*) is non-eternal. Here, "quality" refers to duality, femininity, and so forth. And this quality, through its co-inherence (*sāmavāya*) with a single object, serves to delimit the universal. Since the universal is conveyed by words for universals whose gender and number are fixed, its "non-eternality" is stated with respect to the inherent nature of the word's expressive power (*śabda-śakti*).

It is said that one universal (*jāti*) is conveyed by a word associated with femininity, another by one associated with masculinity, and so forth; likewise, some are associated with singularity and so on—thus there is variability. For this very reason, the reading in the *Bhāṣya* is "because the desire to express qualities (*guṇavivakṣā*) is not constant. In this very context, an alternative view is stated: "or like words denoting qualities (*guṇavacanavat*)," meaning that the establishment of gender and number [is achieved] in this manner. He begins to explain this: "When the form (*ākṛti*) is perceived as the denotable object of all words, it is logical that there be a single word for it because of its unity, and this is described in relation to that [form]. (316)

"Because there is no difference in the cognition [of the object], and because that [cognition] arises from the injunctions regarding the existence of the form (ākṛti), and it is known to be taught as one—it is thus determined that the form alone is the meaning of the word. Thus, since the unity of the word is established based on that [form], the *ekaśeṣa* (the rule for retaining only one of several identical words) is rejected. Because the form is a single entity, the apprehension of its relationship [with the word] is possible; therefore, that [form] alone is what is denoted by the word. Furthermore, since a specific individual (*viśeṣa*) restricted to each instance is not cognized from the word, there is only the expression of the universal (*sāmānya*).

Furthermore, even when there is the disappearance or appearance of the substrata (āśraya), it is logical that the word remains one and the same, because the universal (jāti)—which is the basis for the cognition of oneness—is devoid of disappearance or appearance. For the difference among words is based on the difference of their objects; and since the object is primarily the universal, which is one, the word itself must be one. || 316 ||

Having thus introduced the subject, the gender (*liṅga*) is now examined. To explain: this form (*ākṛti*), when denoted by words, is said to be "possessing an inherent gender" (*āviṣṭaliṅgā*). That which has a gender inherent (*āviṣṭa*) within it is "possessing an inherent gender," meaning its gender is fixed. Although all genders are present everywhere [in the universal], a particular gender is conveyed by a specific word; thus, its "possession of an inherent gender" is stated with reference to that specific word. This is what he says: "Its possession of an inherent gender would be like a herd of domestic animals;
and because there is unity despite the difference in individual substances, the singular number is used therein. (317)

In the rule [Pāṇini 1.2.73], "A feminine [word] denotes a herd of domestic animals that are not young," once the category of the word-meaning as a *jāti* (universal) has been rejected, the assumption of specific gender distinctions occurs by virtue of the word's inherent nature (*svabhāva*). For instance—in those cases which constitute the primary examples of the rule—there is only femininity, as in "these cows" (*gāva imāḥ*). However, in the cases of the counter-examples, there is only masculinity, as in "among the young ones" (*taruṇeṣu*). Thus, the fixed gender of genus-words (*jātiśabda*) arises from their inherent nature.

For if one rejects the Sūtra on the grounds that gender is based on the perception of the individual object (*jātipadārtha*), then the restriction of gender would instead have to rely on a difference in the expressive power (*śakti*) of the word. Consequently, even in cases such as *brāhmaṇaḥ* (masculine) and *brāhmaṇī* (feminine), when the genus (*jāti*) is being denoted, the expression of both genders would be caused solely by the expressive power of the word. However, in cases such as *vṛkṣaḥ*, the masculine gender alone is fixed, because it is the genus itself that is being denoted.

Even though there is a plurality of substances being inferred, since that plurality is not conveyed by the word, the singular number alone would apply based on the genus (jāti) being expressed; therefore, the rule "the plural is used for a single thing when denoting a genus" is initiated. As for the phrase *yad yadā* in the previous verse, it should be construed here as *tadā* due to its connection; thus, the logical consistency (*samanvaya*) is established. || 317 ||

If, then, the connection [of the genus] is by means of the gender of the individual, how is it that the genus possesses an inherent gender? To this he says: "For it is connected only with the fixed genders of its substrata; thus, the prohibition regarding the treatment as having the same gender [as the substrate] would be meaningless. (318)

Through inherence in a single object (*ekārthasamavāya*), the universal (*jāti*) adopts the gender residing in its substratum (*āśrayagataliṅga*), having accepted a restriction according to the expressive power of the word (*śabdaśakti*). For instance: in the case of *vṛkṣaḥ*, *pādapaḥ*, and *taruḥ*, the universal of "tree-ness" (*vṛkṣatvajāti*) adopts only the masculine gender residing in its substratum; here, feminine or neuter genders are never observed. Words such as *śiṃśapā* adopt only the feminine gender. Words such as *panasa* adopt only the neuter gender. Words such as *iṣu* (arrow) and *aśani* (thunderbolt) possess two genders, as do words such as *padma* (lotus) and *śaṅkha* (conch).

Words such as *taṭa-* (bank) possess all three genders (*triliṅga*); *brāhmaṇa-* and *brāhmaṇī* possess two genders (*dviliṅga*). For here, no confusion of gender is ever observed; thus, this restriction of gender depends on the specific power (*śakti*) of the word. This intended state of having an inherent gender (*āviṣṭaliṅgatā*) belongs to the genus (*jāti*). For this very reason, the prohibition regarding genus in the rule "and [the singular number] of qualifiers, except for genus" (*viśeṣaṇānāṃ cājāteḥ*) would be rendered fruitless. Indeed, words denoting a genus take on gender according to their own capacity, and they conform to the gender of the [substantive] they qualify. || 318 ||

[Objection: But in this way, if the gender residing in the substratum is adopted just as with words denoting qualities (*guṇavacana*), then a genus (*jāti*) would have no inherent connection with gender at all, since gender is a property of substance (*dravyadharma*). [Reply: This is true. However, because this usage is so prevalent, gender here is merely for the sake of grammatical refinement (*śabdasaṃskāra*). Alternatively, the word *pādapa* (tree), having its own gender fixed (*āviṣṭaliṅga*), enters into grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a different gender, just as in the case: "This Brāhmaṇa is neuter."

For all things that possess activity are inseparable from the three types of activity and are thus followed by words according to their respective [genders]. For this very reason, he states that this "inherence of gender" (*āviṣṭaliṅgatva*) in a genus (*jāti*) is not tenable if one were to adopt worldly gender-indicators such as breasts and hair: "In the case of adopting worldly gender-indicators, the inherence of gender would apply everywhere; however, because of contradiction, that which is based on the world is not accepted. (319)

If one relies upon gender as established by worldly convention, then because the manifestors—such as breasts and so forth—are restricted [to specific individuals], there would arise a contradiction regarding the co-inherence in a single object of the femininity and other qualities manifested by them; consequently, these words would necessarily possess a fixed gender with respect to every object. For instance, a woman whose femininity is manifested by her connection with breasts and hair would be designated only by a word of the feminine gender, and not by the words *dāraka* (husband) or *kalatra* (wife), which are masculine and neuter respectively.

Furthermore, tastes (*rasa*) and the like would not be expressed by the neuter word *vāhana* (vehicle). Therefore, one's own established doctrine (*siddhānta*) regarding the meaning of words must be accepted in such a way that it accounts for the occurrence of multiple genders. Since all things are designated through the words *artha*, *vyakti*, and *vastu*, the convention (*paribhāṣā*) should be formulated so that their possession of three genders is achieved. Thus says the Bhāṣya: "Therefore, it is not possible for grammarians to rely upon worldly gender;
some established doctrine of one's own must necessarily be adopted. (319)

For instance: "The universal (sāmānya), the form (ākṛti), the entity (bhāva), and the genus (jāti)—these are the worldly [meanings]; gender is not possible [in this context], therefore another [meaning] is accepted. (320)

Words such as *sāmānya* (universal) and others denote a single category (*padārtha*) while possessing different genders; yet that category has no gender recognized in common worldly usage. Consequently, if these words were to rely upon that [category], they would result in being "genderless" (*aliṅga*). Therefore, another, all-pervasive gender belonging to the technical system (*śāstrīya*) is resorted to. || 320 ||

"What is that? it is asked; and it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "The marks [of gender] are contraction and expansion. To explain this, he says: "Activity is stated to be its general definition; it is then divided into manifestation, disappearance, and persistence. (321)

The general definition of the characteristic mark (*liṅga*) is simply "evolution" (*pariṇāma*), which is the activity of the qualities (*guṇa*) that possess inexhaustible measure, regardless of their specific modifications. For instance, having raised the objection, "Of what, then, is contraction (*saṃstyāna*) female, or is expansion (*pravṛtti*) male?", the *Bhāṣya* states: "Of the qualities, beginning with form (*rūpa*). The femininity of certain attributes consists in the contraction, the gathering together, and the dissolution of the qualities such as form—which are the configurations of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—into their primordial nature (*prakṛti*) by remaining in a state of distinctness. This is their cessation.

For others, "procreation" (prasava) means arising or manifestation, which is the state of masculinity. It is the appearance of *rajas*, whose nature is activity (*pravṛtti*), when it attains predominance. And because the *guṇas* are absolutely concomitant with one another, there is "disappearance" (*tirobhāva*) of *tamas* when it has arisen, in accordance with the activity of *rajas* which has become subordinate.

Even for that which has the nature of a substratum (*dharmin*), there is persistence during the state when its specific attributes (*dharma*) are concealed. Just as darkness persists through its coloring by the attribute of *sattva*, the neuter gender is understood as the state of concealment (*sthiti*), characterized precisely by the negation of both female and male; it is not perceived as distinct from them. For this very reason, because it pervades the states of both withdrawal (*saṃstyāna*) and manifestation (*prasava*), the neuter is the universal term (*sarvanāman*) for gender. Since concealment and the state of being concealed involve the activity of the attribute of *rajas*—which, while persisting even within other qualities, permeates them—it constitutes the commonality of all genders. (321)

It has been stated in the Bhāṣya that "all categories (padārthas) are pervaded by this indicative mark (*liṅga*)," namely: "Indeed, activity (*pravṛtti*) is eternal; for no one remains even for a moment within their own self," and so forth. He explains this as follows: "All objects possess activity and are never devoid of the three types of activity; moreover, it is here [in these objects] that speech arises. (322)

"There is a constant non-separation from specific activities characterized by manifestation and so forth, for those entities undergoing transformation when the causes of benefit or injury are present—such that they increase as much as they are to increase, or else they encounter decay. For instance, transformation is inferred because the determination of successive states at every moment would otherwise be impossible. As it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "Furthermore, all material forms possess this nature: they have the qualities of contraction and expansion."

And such categories of objects are followed by words; for the pure, transforming reality of a thing is not the object of verbal expression, because it is denotable by words only through the assumption of a form (ākāra). Thus, the restriction of gender for all words is consistent with their respective inherent capacities. || 322 ||

In this regard, since *prakṛti*—which consists of the three *guṇas*—possesses by its very nature a state of constant activity through the quality of *rajas*, as do its transformations which are of the nature of objects of enjoyment (*bhogya*), one might raise the following doubt: "How can the conscious *puruṣa*, the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), who is of an entirely different nature from the class of objects of enjoyment, being devoid of *guṇas* and not experiencing activity himself, come to be the object of specific designations such as 'self,' 'consciousness,' or 'cognition'? Anticipating this, he says: "And that which, having the nature of non-activity, is grasped in the form of consciousness, seems to follow the activities of others which have various substrates. (323)

Because experience is accomplished through the transfer of the reflection of consciousness (cicchāyā) onto the mirror of the intellect (buddhi), consciousness is perceived in worldly transaction as being variegated by the state of being an object of enjoyment. And that very [consciousness] is the range of words, for it is impossible to designate that which is absolutely unknown. Thus, although consciousness is without appearance (nirābhāsa), there is a metaphorical attribution of distinctions among the "appearances" (ābhāsa)—namely, the specific modifications (pariṇāmaviśeṣa) and activities that follow the nature of other, distinct, and immeasurable objects of enjoyment—to that [consciousness]. 323.
For instance: "By that [means], its nature as consciousness and the time of consciousness are differentiated; however, no differentiation whatsoever exists in its own essential nature. (324)

By means of that multitude of objects of experience reflected upon the mirror of the intellect (*buddhi*), the cognitive activity (*citikriyā*) of this experiencer is differentiated; it is apprehended with discrimination for each respective object. For knowledge is divided according to the form of the objects, as if taking on their nature. Therefore, although this cognitive activity is undivided, it is determined as having distinct durations through the metaphorical attribution of temporal differences residing in the objects of cognition. In ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), however, for the experiencer whose nature is pure consciousness alone, there is no differentiation whatsoever, whether by essence, space, or time.

The activity of consciousness (*citikriyā*) is also not different from that [Self], because its nature is purely non-manifesting consciousness (*nirābhāsasaṃvinmātra*). The distinction expressed as "the consciousness of the Puruṣa," however, is a form constructed by conceptualization (*vikalpa*), like the expression "the head of Rāhu. Those of limited vision, for whom discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) has not yet arisen, operate by conflating the essential natures of the *guṇas* and the Puruṣa. (324)

And having established this, he says that there is an absence of empirical transaction (vyavahāra) from the perspective of ultimate reality in its form as pure consciousness: "Consciousness, as it were, appears to have been transferred into insentient things; that which occurs by way of the property of reflection is the basis for the use of words. (325)

When the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest—which are insentient—reside within the forms of the intellect (*buddhi*), there occurs an "imprint" of consciousness (*caitanyoparāga*) due to the excellence of the purity inherent in the nature of *sattva*. In that [intellect], which resembles the surface of a mirror, the reflected image is the empirical consciousness that becomes the object of verbal designation. Thus, by conforming to the activities of others, it experiences the application of logical marks (*liṅgayoga*).

However, that which is the leaf (the Self), being self-luminous, free from the knots of transformation, and non-evolving, does not descend into empirical transaction. As it has been said: "The power of consciousness (*citiśakti*) is non-evolving," and so forth. || 325 ||

Thus, in common usage, even though consciousness is [the subject], because of its connection with a logical mark (liṅga)—there is no such state that is not joined with a logical mark. However, in some cases, there is a grammatical refinement of the word when the logical mark has no substratum.

Since it has been established that the accompaniment of gender (*liṅga*) by the experiencer (*bhoktṛ*) and the experienced (*bhogya*) exists, and since there is no other category of entity apart from these, this state of being an entity does not exist wherein there is no connection with gender. Thus, this definition of gender is all-pervasive and applies even to the universal (*jāti*), because the three states are inseparable from all entities, and even for an eternal universal, those states do not depart. Furthermore, although this gender is possible [in every case], it is sometimes set aside due to a lack of intention to express it. As the author of the Bhāṣya says: "And both of these [gender and number] apply everywhere."

If both [sexes] exist everywhere, how is the distinction established? It is by intention (*vivakṣā*). When there is the intention to express "stasis," it is feminine; when there is the intention to express "procreation," it is masculine; and when neither is intended, it is neuter. Thus, it is merely a grammatical refinement (*śabda-saṃskāra*) based on the rule that "the base form (*prakṛti*) alone should not be used," whereby a gender suffix (*liṅga-pratyaya*) is applied there. As it is said: "When the meaning of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is not specified, the mention of gender is not authoritative, because it is not intended to be expressed. (326)

As it has been said: "There is no such state that is not connected with a gender. He clarifies that very point: "The gender of entities denoted by primary derivatives (kṛt) and secondary derivatives (taddhita) is not contradicted; likewise, the gender is held to be a state of quality (guṇāvasthā) as well as a form (ākṛti). (327)

The action expressed by a *kṛt* suffix—such as *pākaḥ*, *paktiḥ*, or *pacanam*—being differentiated according to its various stages, undergoes a change in gender that follows those stages and is thus made the object of words with fixed genders. Similarly, [words] such as *garimā*, *gurutā*, and *gurutvam* denote the same thing through *taddhita* suffixes. For even a single entity, as long as it exists, necessarily undergoes a succession of different states; indeed, nothing remains in its own nature for even a moment. This is why: [the verse follows].

And thus, a single state derived from the verbal root—such as *saṃstyānam*, *saṃstyāyaḥ*, or *saṃstyi*—is conveyed by words based on differences in gender. In this way, the definition of gender (*liṅga*) as a characteristic state of qualities (*guṇāvasthā-lakṣaṇa*), as formulated in the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*), is not contradicted, even though the entities denoted by primary (*kṛt*) and secondary (*taddhita*) suffixes are distinct. Otherwise, because an entity is unitary, only a single gender would be appropriate for it.

Thus, having established the pervasiveness (*vyāpitva*) of this definition of the mark (*liṅga-lakṣaṇa*), he concludes: "And thus, the form is accepted. This is the conclusion: such being the case, the genus of the mark (*liṅga-jāti*), which consists in the commonality of activity (*pravṛtti-sāmānya-rūpa*) and comprises the states of manifestation and so forth of the qualities (*guṇa*)—namely, color and the rest—which are themselves transformations of the *sattva* and other *guṇas*, is admitted. || 327 ||

And thus, since the pervasion of gender by genus-words is established, that objection which was raised—that there would be a failure to establish gender in the case where "substance" (dravya) is the referent—is resolved. He says: "In the view that substance [is the referent], there is no difference whatsoever regarding gender. Therefore, those seven alternatives are themselves what constitutes 'having an inherent gender' (aviṣṭaliṅgatā) here. (328)

Even in the view that the substance (*dravya*) is the word-meaning, gender (*liṅga*) is a state of qualities (*guṇāvasthā*). Even in the theory where the form (*ākṛti*) is the word-meaning, those very same [qualities]—the individuals from which distinctions have been set aside—are the genus (*jāti*); thus, because states of qualities are possible, in both philosophical systems there is no difference regarding gender, as words convey either the genus or the substance with a fixed gender according to their respective capacities and in accordance with their own power.

One might object: "How can there be no difference [between the two], given that a genus (*jāti*) possesses fixed gender (*āviṣṭaliṅga*), whereas a substance (*dravya*) has indeterminate gender? Anticipating this, he concludes with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). By stating, "And seven varieties of gender-assignment have been shown through the options of taking up [the gender] as two, three, or one," he explains that when a genus is grasped by means of genus-words, its possession of fixed gender is asserted because the gender is taken up in a non-confused manner according to those very [fixed] rules. It is not, however, the case that it is restricted to the adoption of only a single gender; thus, the two positions are equal. For the Grammarians do not accept gender as an inherent property of the object (*vastudharma*).

Rather, the connection with gender belongs to the meaning of the word. And from words, the universal (jāti) is perceived as accompanied by its associated gender; therefore, the gender of the universal is its own. Consequently, one does not insist upon [the universal] possessing a gender through the gender of its substratum. For this very reason, it is justified that "the desire to express a quality is not fixed," since even in the case of a universal, the desire to express qualities such as femininity and so forth is established despite the deviation [of the universal] from the substance. || 328 ||

Thus, the proponent of the *jāti* (universal) as the referent of words has established the parity of his own position with the position that holds the substance (*dravya*) to be the referent, with respect to the logical mark (*liṅga*). Now, in order to establish [the parity] with respect to the word (*vacana*), he says: "Regarding the word, a restriction is accepted for the substance on the basis of scripture; because the scripture is otherwise justified with respect to the universal form (*ākṛti*). (329)

Even under the view that the substance (*dravya*) is the word-meaning, the restriction of number is established by the force of grammatical rules such as "the plural is used for many," and not because the substance itself possesses number; for the rule must necessarily be formulated to avoid confusion. If, therefore, the systematic arrangement relies upon the scripture, then even when the universal (*jāti*) is the word-meaning, that same scripture is explained in a different manner.

To the question "How so?", he says: When a meaning that occurs in many [words] is intended to be expressed in its specific differentiation, and is pointed out by its own bases (the words), its verbal expression is said to be "stated in the treatise" (*śāstre vacanam*). (330)

When a genus-character (*jātilakṣaṇa*) resides in many [individuals], and when its inherence in distinct substrata (*bhinnādhārasamavāya*) is intended to be expressed, the plural number is prescribed in the technical treatise (*śāstra*) for that which is designated as "in many" by means of its own substrates. In the same way, it should be stated that the dual number applies to that which is designated as "in two," and so forth.

The meaning of this is as follows: a genus (*jāti*) residing in specific individuals delimited by the number two is conveyed by a word ending in the dual suffix; one inhering in a substratum delimited by the number many is conveyed by a word ending in the plural suffix; and one delimited by a substratum possessing the number one is conveyed by a word ending in the singular suffix. This very point has been stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "Now, for one for whom the individual substance (*dravya*) is the word-meaning, how can there be singular, dual, and plural suffixes?"

Thus he will say: "The singular number is used for one thing, the dual for two, and the plural for many. If, then, even for him these are merely conventional designations (*vācanika*) and not inherent (*svābhāvika*), I too shall say: "The singular number is used for one, the dual for two, and the plural for many"—meaning that the genus (*jāti*) which resides in one [entity], and so forth.

Some, by eliding the vowel *a* [in the compound], read "of that" (*tasya*) in the sense of non-difference; they explain that this is intended to convey through the word "single" (*eka*) the state of being one (*ekatva*) as innate to it. In this way, even when the universal (*jāti*) has not yet acquired distinction, its verbal designation based on its substrata is justified. (330)
But when a difference is perceived solely through the difference of its substrata, then no difference exists for the generic form (ākṛti) from the standpoint of the substance (dravya). || 331 ||

When the distinction of the genus (*jāti*) follows from the distinction of its substratum (*āśraya*), the variation in grammatical number is inherent to the genus itself; likewise, the multiplicity of words is also inherent. Thus, since the "retention of one" (*ekaśeṣa*) must indeed be commenced, there is no difference between the view that the individual substance (*dravya*) is the meaning of a word and the view that the genus (*jāti*) is the meaning of a word, because in both cases a word is applied to each respective object. Furthermore, this view has been stated in the *Bhāṣya* as something to be rejected.

"If sometimes the form (*ākṛti*) is intended to be expressed as one, sometimes as two, and sometimes as many, then the thesis that 'the form is one' is abandoned. Furthermore, the purpose stated for adopting this position—that the *ekaśeṣa* (single-remainder) rule need not be taught—must now be addressed. || 331 ||

Therefore, he concludes that what was stated previously is indeed correct: "But since there is a single word for non-difference and because of the scripture, when the expression exists, a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) need not be mentioned; for such expressions are possible [without it]. (332)

Even in the absence of a distinction based on individual instances (*vyakti*), when a genus (*jāti*)—by means of the rule "the plural number is used for many," etc., and according to the aforementioned logic—undergoes a distinction in its mode of expression (*vacanabheda*) based on the distinction of its own substrata (*svāśrayabheda*), then, since the word is established as being singular because its motivating referent (*prayojaka-artha*) is one, the sūtra defining *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one) is rejected. || 332 ||

On this point, an objection is raised: "But surely, if substance is inexpressible, then this benefit which belongs to the configuration (ākṛti) by depending upon that [substance] cannot be established due to the absence of substance. (333)

If the meaning of a word is the form (ākṛti), then since the substance (dravya) is not being denoted, how can there be the establishment of gender and number, which reside in that [substance]? For the grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) of a word is caused by the word's meaning; and for that which is not being denoted, even if it exists in reality, it is as good as non-existent with respect to grammatical refinement. (333)
To avoid this [objection], he says: "In the treatise, no designation is adopted based on a denotable object; nor is that category of entity called 'substance' (dravya) being refuted. (334)

In the grammatical rule beginning with "the plural number is used for many things," the various numbers are said to be based on a distinction in the substratum (*āśraya*); however, no such [external] number exists. Rather, this is stated by way of a general principle. And thus, a universal (*jāti*) residing in distinct substrata indeed undergoes a variation in number. Furthermore, in the view that the universal is the word-meaning (*padārtha*), there is no such thing as a "substance" (*dravya*) as a separate word-meaning.

And so says the Bhāṣya: "For one for whom the generic form (ākṛti) is the word-meaning, it is not the case that the substance (dravya) is not the word-meaning; nor, for one for whom the substance is the word-meaning, is it the case that the generic form is not the word-meaning. For the proponent of the view that the generic form is the word-meaning, that which is called substance is not non-existent as a word-meaning; rather, it truly exists. Thus, there is no contradiction in the difference of number found in the substratum of a universal (jāti) when it is connected with distinct substances. || 334 ||

Immediately following this is the commentary: "But for some [word], something is primary (pradhāna), while something else is subordinate (guṇa)," and so forth. He explains that: "The state of being a quality (guṇabhāva) with respect to the denotable object (abhidheya) does not depend upon the substance (dravya). A quality is that which is beneficial (upakārī); it is a subordinate element (śeṣa), according to the conceptualization of categories. (335)

In this context, it is not intended that for a word whose referent is a genus (*jāti*), the genus is the primary meaning denoted by the word, while the substance (*dravya*) is denoted as a subordinate quality (*guṇa*). Rather, even though the substance is not explicitly expressed, it is called a "quality" with respect to the genus because it serves as its auxiliary. For instance, in common worldly usage, whatever is an auxiliary to something else is conceived of as being for the sake of that thing—a subordinate factor or a quality. Thus, it is stated that "the substance [subsists] in the genus," and through that connection, the comprehension of the various grammatical distinctions (such as number) residing in the substance is achieved. || 335 ||

Since the subordinate status of substance (*dravya*) with respect to the state of being the denotable object of a word is clear in this *Bhāṣya* and is not explicitly explained, he says: "There is no subordinate status for a substance [in a word] without its being the denoter of a substance; nor is there primacy in the form (*ākṛti*). For this very reason, it is thus established. (336)

"Without denoting a substance. Here, since there is no denotation of a substance, and because a quality cannot exist as a subordinate element within a substance, nor can a genus possess primacy [therein], the Bhāṣya is thus explained: "The state of being a quality (guṇatva) consists in being an auxiliary to the substance, not in being denoted. For if it were being denoted, the form (ākṛti) would be the delimiter of the substance, and thus that very form, being denoted, would be the primary element. However, the form, which serves as the means of delimitation, is itself merely a quality and not the primary element.

And so, just as in the case of "the king's man" (*rājapuruṣa*), the meaning of "king" does not depend upon a numerical distinction residing in the principal [element], so too the genus (*jāti*) would not depend on one. However, even though it possesses the status of a subordinate quality (*guṇatva*), if it were to persist [as a distinct entity], the resulting difference in number would render the rejection of *ekaśeṣa* (the grammatical rule for retaining only one of identical words) untenable. But when the substance (*dravya*) is not denoted, then that which is not being denoted serves as a differentiator of the denoted genus—just as molasses (*guḍa*) is of sweetness and so forth—and because it thus assists by providing its own gender and number as substrates, it is appropriate to call it a "quality. || 336 ||

Some maintain that even when both genus (*jāti*) and substance (*dravya*) are being denoted, there exists a relationship of primary and subordinate; thus he says: "Some maintain that there is a relationship of primary and subordinate [between them], just as between a noun (*nāman*) and a verb (*ākhyāta*); however, the state of being subordinate for that which exists for the sake of another is not described as being like [the case of] a compound (*vṛtti*). (337)

Just as in the expression "the cook cooks" (*pācakaḥ pacati*), there exists a relationship of primary and secondary status between the action and the factor of action (*kriyā-kāraka*) that are being denoted, so it is here as well. To explain: by means of a nominal word (*nāmapada*), that which is the substratum of the means (*sādhana*)—subordinate to the connection between the action and the factors of action—is denoted primarily; for in this case, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) serves as a qualifier for the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*). And since that [substratum] is qualified here by both what has already come into being (*bhūta*) and what is yet to be (*bhāvin*), the action is not the primary element, because its status as such occurs only in its future state.

For this very reason, the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is used here for the relation (*sambandha*), because that alone serves as the ground for the application of the word. Action (*kriyā*), however, although subordinate here, is apprehended as distinct [from the relation]. But by means of the verbal suffix (*ākhyātapada*), action—having received support from a specific efficient cause (*sādhana*)—is expressed as the primary element. For in this context, action in its state of being brought about (*bhāvyamānāvasthā*) is qualified by the efficient cause that is actively engaged, even though that cause is itself the meaning of the suffix.

For *bhāvanā*, which consists in the activity of the agent, is grounded in the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), which is its object to be brought about (*bhāvya*). Thus, through the penetration of this primary activity, whatever cognition arises regarding the agent is itself the cause for the cognition of the primacy of even that which exists for the sake of another [the root-meaning]. In this way, although the means (*sādhana*) here is subordinate, it is apprehended as distinct. And so it is joined with qualifiers, as in "Devadatta cooks. For this very reason, it benefits the action by its own number, as in "they two cook" (*pacataḥ*) or "they cook" (*pacanti*).

Thus, for those who hold that the category of universal (*jāti*) is the word-meaning, the universal is expressed by the word as the primary element; for those who hold that the category of substance (*dravya*) is the word-meaning, the universal is expressed by the word as a subordinate element. However, for those who hold that substance is the word-meaning, it is the substance [that is primary], for the status of being subordinate or primary is determined by the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*). Just as in compounds such as *rājapuruṣa* (the king’s man), in the derived form (*vṛtti-pada*), the meaning of the subordinate member—the object of another—is subordinate and lacks primacy, it is not so stated regarding the relationship of the goal-to-be-accomplished (*sādhya*) and the means-of-accomplishment (*sādhana*) between the noun and the verb.
