For instance: in a *vṛtti* (compound), because the subordinate meaning merges with the principal meaning, their distinction cannot be grasped; therefore, it is not possible for [the compound] to be caused by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by its own constituent words. For its state of being a subordinate element (*guṇabhāva*) is purely verbal. Consequently, qualifiers such as "prosperous" (*ṛddha*) and so forth are not applicable. However, in the case of "the cook cooks" (*pācakaḥ pacati*), both elements—being of the nature of action and agent—are indeed perceived through the delimitation of the relationship between the goal (*sādhya*) and the means (*sādhana*). Only through the force of implication (*sāmarthya*) is the relationship of subordinate and principal understood according to the circumstances.

For instance, that which is already accomplished (*pariniṣṭhita*)—such as "the past" for the sake of "the future"—is a means (*sādhana*) for the sake of another, because it is employed precisely for the benefit of something else due to its being already accomplished. That with reference to which its activity occurs is the goal (*sādhya*), the primary element expressed by the verbal form (*ākhyātapada*). In a nominal word (*nāmapada*), however, the causal capacity (*kārakaśakti*) is the cause of its application; therefore, its substratum (*ādhāra*) is denoted primarily.

Thus, even though there is a difference in perspective here, when both [the individual and the form] are treated as the meaning of the word, the substance is taken up for the purpose of producing an excellence conceived as the substratum of the form; in that case, the form is primary because it is introduced as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). But when the introduction of the form is intended solely to delimit a particular individual, then the reverse is the case. || 337 ||

If this is so, then even in the view that the universal (ākṛti) is denoted, since the substance is also being denoted, there would follow a difference in words corresponding to the difference in number belonging to that [substance]; thus, one might suspect that "single-remainder" (ekaśeṣa) must be applied here as well. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Because the quality [of the universal] is manifold, the universal itself possesses a single word; and the difference in number is established through its connection with the differences in the substances. (338)

For those who hold that the universal form (*ākṛti*) is the word-meaning, the substance is subordinate and distinct; thus, the multiplicity of words does not depend on a distinction between subordinate word-meanings. Rather, it is logical that there is unity of the word solely based on the non-distinction of the primary word-meaning. Therefore, the purpose of the *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one) is not required here. Furthermore, a difference in number is all the more established in that case, because of its connection with the denoted substance, which is distinct. This is the intended meaning: since distinction and non-distinction, when functioning as subordinate and primary respectively, are contradictory, unity of the word is indeed appropriate in the case of the primary.

Indeed, it is not proper to enjoin a subordinate element while disregarding the primary act. However, let the subordinate element—characterized by a distinct verbal expression—bring about its own purificatory rite for the sake of assisting the primary act, provided that it does not obstruct the primary act; what contradiction is there in this? || 338 ||

For instance: "Just as a means of accomplishment (sādhana) differentiates an action by virtue of being a subordinate factor (guṇabhāva), so too in verbal forms (ākhyāta), substance (dravya) is said to differentiate the universal (jāti) which is denoted by a single word. (339)

Just as even when action is predominant in a verb, there is a difference in number based on the substratum of the means (the agent or object) which has become subordinate—as in *pacataḥ* (they two cook) or *pacanti* (they cook)—so too, when a substance is denoted by that very same word through a genus (*jāti*) which is its primary signified meaning, this quality (*guṇa*), being present and expressed, imposes a distinction of number upon its own substratum. For a quality necessarily presents itself for the sake of assisting the primary element with whatever characteristic of a quality does not result in an obstruction to that primary element.

Otherwise, its very status as a quality (*guṇatva*) would be lost, because that status is produced by the benefit [it confers]. Thus, the example "like a noun and a verb" is stated as being well-suited, and not "like a compound. For in the case of "the king’s man" (*rājapuruṣa*), there is no grammatical modification such as a change in number caused by the meaning of the king; this is because the subordinate meaning has attained absolute non-difference from the principal meaning. And in this case, the means (*sādhana*) does not contribute a distinct number to the action.

However, even though no actual difference exists [in the action itself], it is said that [the action] is expressed by a finite verb (tiṅanta) such as *pacataḥ* or *pacanti*, depending on the difference in number belonging to the substratum of the action (*kriyāśraya*) itself. And thus, since the difference is already determined solely by the difference in the subordinate factors (*sādhana*), finite verbs do not necessitate the formulation of the rule for *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one); this is what is stated in the Bhāṣya. || 339 ||

Thus, although a substance qualified by a genus is denoted, because the genus is accepted as the primary meaning, the establishment of gender and number has been demonstrated; for gender and number are not established [by the substance alone] because the quality is non-eternal. Here, "quality" (guṇa) is intended to mean "substance" (dravya). But when there is the denotation of the genus alone, he says the following to explain how gender and number follow from the substrate, just as in the case of words denoting qualities: "When the expression of the possessor of that [genus] occurs through a cause [in the form of a word] whose form is identical despite the unity [of the genus], then there is a specific apprehension of the object. (340)
Through the connection expressed as "this is that," when the form (ākṛti) functions together with its substrates by means of distinct words, gender and number are established.

When there is non-difference between the substrata and the universal (jāti), and when communication is carried out by means of words, those words which denote a substance qualified by the universal and those words which denote the universal alone are determined to be non-distinct because they possess an identical form.

For instance, in the communication of its own meaning, a genus-word (*jātiśabda*)—relying on the genus-characteristic as a cause superimposed upon the substance (*dravya*) that possesses it—conveys the substance qualified by the genus through non-difference. Thus, when the genus attains non-difference from those substances that serve as its substrata via the cognition "this is that," the denotation of the possessor of the cause (the substance) follows the cause (the genus), and consequently, the assumption of the gender and number belonging to that [substance] is not contradictory, even though the application [of the word] occurs through distinct [entities], just as in the case of the word "white" (*śukla*).

For when both the universal (*jāti*) and its possessor (*tadvat*) are denoted by a single word, the application of that single word has already been explained. Here, however, since only the universal is conveyed by the word, there is the application of a distinct word. Furthermore, in this case as well, because a cognition similar to the cause [of the universal] arises, and because the word denotes [the object] according to that cognition, the application of the word occurs precisely through the transference of the cause.

For in this case, since a distinction such as "this is a cow" is not perceived, the establishment of the gender and number of the substratum occurs through metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*). Thus, in effect, there is no difference between the two positions. However, the distinction is this much: in the former case, both are denoted by way of a relationship of subordinate and principal (*guṇapradhānabhāva*), whereas here it is through metaphorical identification. || 340, 341 ||

Alternatively, even though substance (*dravya*) was not explicitly mentioned previously, it was intended as a contributing factor. Thus it was objected: "But surely there is the state of being unexpressed," and so forth. Furthermore, without conforming to a cause characterized by a genus (*jāti*), individuals do not enter into their respective specific linguistic usages; therefore, he says: "Prior to the connection with a genus, things are denotable by pronouns; words such as *tat* (that) are employed toward an entity as qualifiers (*upalakṣaṇa*) of its existence. (342)

As long as the form of the universal (*jāti*) is not projected onto its substratum (*ādhāra*), so long, because the forms of individual instances (*vyakti*) cannot be determined, the qualifier remains undetermined. For it is the formless universal, by determining its substratum, that enables linguistic usage through its respective particular terms. However, in the absence of the determination of the universal's form as qualified by particular terms, the referent of words becomes beyond the scope of particular terms; thus, pronouns such as *tyad* and others—which are indicators of mere existence, substance, established nature, or the thing-in-itself—are employed.

For those [words] cause one to understand an object merely as a generality by means of the form "some thing" (*vastu kiñcit*). Therefore, in order to convey specific distinctions, objects—which have attained the status of being causes [of cognition] through the superimposition of the form of a universal (*jāti*)—are denoted by class-words (*jātiśabda*) such as "cow" and so forth, according to their respective [particulars]. Thus, because of the metaphorical treatment of non-difference (*abheda-upacāra*), the denotation of substance (*dravya*) by class-words is not figurative (*gauṇa*), but rather primary (*mukhya*) itself; in this way, the establishment of the gender and number [of the word] based on its substratum has been explained. || 342 ||

Right here he states another opinion: "Just as some maintain that the word *pāka* (cooking) refers to the substrate itself, so too this property [of being a cooking] is accepted by those who denote qualities as being without a material cause (*anupādāna*). (343)

The word *pāka* (cooking), which denotes the property of the action (*kriyā-dharma*), does not [directly] denote its substratum (*tad-āśraya*). Nevertheless, even without being denoted, the substratum of the action here serves as a differentiator. For instance, the dual and plural number endings occur; since these reside in the object (*karman*) of the act of cooking, when that [object] is differentiated, there is here the expression of a differentiation in the cooking itself.

Thus, it is accepted by some that for words expressing qualities (*guṇavācin*), even when there is no explicit mention of the substratum (*āśraya*) based on the relation "this is that" (*so'yam*), that unmentioned substratum serves as the differentiator; consequently, because genus-words (*jātiśabda*) express qualities, a difference in number will be established even for those where the substance is not explicitly mentioned. However, this is not correct. In cases such as *pākau* (two cookings) or *pākāḥ* (many cookings), we do not observe the mention of a substratum through the relation "this is that. It is logical that, since the cooking differs according to the difference in its substratum, there is a difference in number inherent in the very expression when the objects denoted by the distinct words are differentiated.

For this [quality] does not reside within the substratum (*āśraya*). Since the supported (*āśrita*) is differentiated by the difference of the substratum, a distinction in the supported is indeed logical. Thus, in expressions such as "the cooking of jaggery, sesame, rice, and barley," because the difference in the substratum is understood, the difference in the supported is also perceived; hence, the plural number is not used. In the case of words such as "white" (*śukla*), however, the substratum is observed to be taken up through the relation "this is that" (*so 'yam*). And these very examples are presented in the *Bhāṣya* as illustrations for genus-words (*jātiśabda*), in the phrase "like words denoting qualities" (*guṇavacanavat*).

For instance—even genus-words (*jātiśabda*) indeed take up their substratum through the metaphorical attribution of non-difference (*abhedopacāra*). Since it is intended that a quality (*guṇa*) is merely that which is dependent [on a substratum], the genus (*jāti*) is likewise established as a real entity. Thus, words such as *śukla* ("white") function as the standard of comparison by virtue of being expressive of qualities. Furthermore, there is no difference in the genus despite a difference in the substrata, as is the case with "cooking" (*pāka*) and so forth. Therefore, when the use of a single word for multiple instances has been rejected, the establishment of gender and number here is intended to occur through the application of that [word] to its instances via the metaphor of non-difference within the operation of the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one), and not by means of not taking up the substrata. || 343 ||
For instance: "If the universal were to obtain only the properties of its substratum when that substratum is not taken up [as a cause], this was examined previously. (344)

Since the universal (*sāmānya*) denoted by a genus-word (*jātiśabda*) is indeed pure (*śuddha*), having an unappropriated substratum (*anupāttādhāra*), it acquires the properties (*dharma*)—namely gender (*liṅga*), number (*saṃkhyā*), and so forth—belonging to its substratum; therefore, this [explanation] is not suitable as an interpretation for the rebuttal that "this is not like a quality-word (*guṇavacana*). For this very point was explained as an alternative view (*pakṣāntara*) in the previous rebuttal: "The establishment of gender and number occurs because the quality is non-eternal" (*liṅgavacanasiddhirguṇasyānityatvāt*).

For instance: having raised an objection there with the words "But surely, if [the universal] were not denotable," and so forth, the response was given that "no designation based on a denoted object is resorted to in the science [of grammar]. Furthermore, the second alternative is explained here by the passage beginning "by some, the relation of subordinate and principal," characterized by the fact that both are being denoted through a relationship of subordinate and principal. However, in this solution, let the universal alone be denoted; yet, through metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*), when its substratum is brought forward, the properties of that [substratum] are established. (344)

Regarding this, it is stated in the Bhāṣya how there is a metaphorical treatment of non-difference: "From that which functions in the universal, a function arises [in the individual]. To explain this, he says: "For words denoting universals that have previously been applied to a universal, the individual also comes to be expressed through a relationship with that which is not directly denoted by the word. (345)

The operation of those who rely on signs is preceded by a sign; thus, the application of a word occurs first with respect to the genus (*jāti*), which serves as the sign. Since that genus cannot exist without a substratum, even though it is not directly made an object [of cognition] by the expressive word, the individual (*vyakti*)—which possesses that genus—enters the path of cognition through the force of its relationship, characterized by concomitance (*sāhacarya*). And so it has been said: "The apprehension of the substratum [occurs] through concomitance. (345)

Since words function according to their respective conditions (*pratyaya*), the sequence [of cognition] is also logically established here; thus he says: "Through the connection expressed as 'this is that,' the properties of the universal (*jāti*) are metaphorically attributed [to the individual]; the substance is its substratum, and the particularity (*bheda*) is admitted as belonging to the universal. (346)

Due to the superimposition of non-difference, just as in the case of a genus (*jāti*), a substance is expressed by a word denoting a genus through the [expression] "this has the property [of the genus]. This is because it attains the nature of the genus. Since the object is understood as permeated by the form of the cause [the genus], the application of the designation occurs in that very manner. Thus, having superimposed the cause characterized as the genus onto the individual (*vyakti*), the word functions therein through identity with it.

And thus, even in the case of a substance that is colored by a causal factor (*nimitta*), its designation by a word based on that causal factor arises by implication (*arthataḥ*). Consequently, the distinction of number, which resides in [the substance], is also asserted with respect to the causal factor. For a substance is not denoted by a genus-word (*jātiśabda*) in its own form; rather, because the causal factor is present therein, the word—while denoting the causal factor—implies the substrate of that factor by its own capacity (*sāmarthyāt*), since there is no abstracted causal factor apart from the possessor of the causal factor (*nimittin*).

However, the acquisition of the meaning (*dharmapratilambha*) occurs once the sign has been grasped. Furthermore, because it is impossible for a word to cease its operation [once uttered], this sequence does not apply to the denotative function (*abhidhā*). Rather, it is the cognizers who divide that single, integrated meaning according to their own conceptual constructions; it is with reference to this intention that the sequence is stated in the *Bhāṣya* as "because [the word] functions in respect of the universal" (*sāmānye vṛtteḥ*). || 346 ||

He establishes this very point by means of an illustration: "Just as the word 'bed' refers to the object placed upon it while being established in reference to the beds themselves, so too does a genus-word (jāti-śabda) denote substances in their true nature. (347)

In the expression "The beds cry out" (*mañcāḥ krośanti*), since the connection with the action is possible only for the living beings situated upon the beds—the substrata—it is determined that the word *mañca* (bed), although denoting the substratum, denotes the objects contained therein through its non-difference from the form of the substratum. Similarly, in the case of "Let the cows be brought," since the connection with the action is not possible for the genus (*jāti*), it is understood that the individuals, which have attained non-difference from that [genus], are what are capable of being connected with the action; these are what are denoted by the word based on the genus. || 347 ||

If this is so, how is it that the universal (*jāti*) alone is the word-meaning? To this he says: "In that regard, the status of the universal as the word-meaning is accepted in exactly that way; however, the universal, together with its number, inheres in the substance (*dravya*). (348)

Just as the word "platform" (mañca), even when denoting that which is placed upon it, is said to express its substratum, so too, although the substance that serves as the locus is included, the genus-word is established as having the genus alone as its meaning. For it does not denote the substance in its own form, but rather through the superimposition of the form of the genus; thus, the expression of the substance is metaphorical due to the penetration of the form of the genus, like the expression of the Vāhīka. However, the primary function is indeed the expression of the genus. And because this usage is conventional (nirūḍha), there is no perception of it as a mere metaphor.

If this were so, the denotation of the cause (nimitta) would be exactly like that of [the word] "beds" (*mañca*) and so forth. And in that case, all individuals (*vyakti*), being permeated by a single genus (*jāti*), would be denoted as a unity, and thus there would be no difference in the grammatical number of the words. Anticipating this objection, it is said: "The genus has its number relinquished," and so on. Since the genus is inherently devoid of number, it is merely superimposed upon the substance in a form where its own number has been discarded; therefore, no number residing in that [genus] itself is obtained here. Nor is there gender, because the genus is without gender; thus, it is only logical that it should adopt the gender and number belonging to its substratum. || 348 ||

Thus, the connection of genus-words with gender and number is established in this way, like words such as "white" (*śukla*). In that regard, words such as "white" apply to the possessor of the quality (the substrate) either through the elision of the *matup* suffix or through metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*). However, for genus-words, since their distinction [from the individual] is never observed, there is no need for the elision of the *matup* suffix; rather, they apply to the possessor of the genus solely through metaphorical identification. Since their distinction is never observed, there is no need for the elision of the *matup* suffix; rather, for genus-words, application to the possessor occurs precisely through metaphorical identification.

Nevertheless, by relying on the commonality of mere verbal expression in that same manner, the suitability of white and other qualities as examples is established here, regardless of the difference in means; thus he says: "Wherever the Vedic usage occurs either as 'this belongs to that' or as 'this is that,' it functions through the attribute of another, and thus that [other] is denoted. (349)

Let a word apply to another object either by virtue of a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) or through metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*). However, the designation of the substratum (*nimittin*) by means of the superimposition of the form of the cause (*nimitta*) is the same [in both cases]. The point here is that this much alone serves as the purpose. And thus, just as words such as "white" (*śukla*) are said to be quality-words (*guṇaśabda*) even when they denote a substance, so too there is no loss whatsoever in the fact that words such as "cow" (*go*) are genus-words (*jātiśabda*). 349.

For instance: That which is primary has no intrinsic nature of its own because it cannot be defined; and a substance is characterized by the quality through its very existence as that [quality]. (350)

The pure form of an object—which is devoid of limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhi*), consists of substance (*dravyātman*), and is capable of connection with action—does not exist in empirical usage, whether linguistic or conceptual. For empirical usage is preceded by a process of determination (*nirūpaṇa*), and that determination occurs only through the object's being permeated by the form of its limiting adjuncts. Consequently, in empirical usage, a substance is perceived as having assumed, according to the case, the nature of a quality such as "whiteness" (*śukla-jāti*) and so forth; it appears as if it has attained the state of being that quality itself. The meaning is that the substrate (*nimittin*) has come to possess a form identical to that of the cause (*nimitta*). || 350 ||

And thus, even in this case, the primacy of the genus is not violated; so he says: "But at the time of distinguishing a quality, its own primacy arises; for the scriptural expression of conjunction does not apply directly to the objects themselves. (351)

When a substance is intended to be expressed as the primary object, it is denoted as being conditioned by its genus (*jāti*). When, however, there is a primary expression of a quality as distinct from others, then that [quality] is communicated through the penetration of its own universal (*sāmānya*), having attained non-difference [from it]. But when the genus itself is intended as the primary object, then it is denoted through the superimposition of the word's own form (*śabdasvarūpa*) upon it.

For instance—words are capable of denoting an object as qualified by its association with other attributes (dharma), but not in its pure state. For this very reason, verbal cognition (śruti) is called "word" (śabda) because it is based on association; and that [cognition] enters into objects by way of another attribute, not by means of a qualification, because that which is without qualifications cannot be directly determined, and words function only with respect to what has been previously determined. || 351 ||

Thus, since there is the consequence that [the word] would have "birth" (*jāti*) as its referent, he explains how it can also have "substance" (*dravya*) as its referent: "If, through the connection 'this is that,' the word denotes a substance, and yet the category of 'birth' remains the referent, then how is it that substance is the referent? To this he says: "When a word, having first applied to a genus (*jāti*), applies again to a substance, at that time the status of being the referent is not accepted for the genus alone. (352)

When, after denoting the universal (jāti), the word also denotes the substance qualified by that [universal], and the expressive power of the word does not cease with the universal alone, then the universal by itself is not the meaning of the word. Furthermore, because of the metaphorical treatment of non-difference through the relation "this is that," it is maintained that there is no acceptance of the substance as the primary referent; rather, this is the sense in which it was stated in the previous refutation that the word refers to the possessor of that [quality or universal]. || 352 ||

But surely, since simultaneous multiple operations are untenable, how can the very same word, having operated upon the genus (*jāti*), operate upon the substance (*dravya*)? For according to different philosophical views, words are indeed distinct—some denoting the genus alone and others denoting that [substance]. To this he says: "Furthermore, the recurrence of words already in operation is described as being through oneness; in the means of comprehension, the ultimate reality is not followed. (353)

Due to similarity, there is a determination of non-difference; thus, linguistic usage as a unity is merely a means of exposition. For the expression of a combined meaning, though it is actually without sequence, is presented as having a sequence through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). Furthermore, it is not logical for the means of communicating to others to conform to ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), because they are to be abandoned. And so, according to the theory of denotation (*abhidhāna-naya*), both [meanings] are denoted without sequence.

And here too, when both are denoted, the status of the universal as the word-meaning and the substance as the word-meaning arise according to the distinction between different philosophical views, depending on whether prominence or non-prominence is intended; thus he says: "When a universal is resorted to for that which is expressed by a word not distinct [from the individual], while there is contact with the substance, then the universal is the word-meaning. (354)

Even though the word *eka* (one) is used in the sense of a material substratum (*dravya*), when the universal (*jāti*)—which, although its distinctions are conceptually constructed based on differences among substrata—is primarily resorted to for the performance of an action, as in "Brahmins are to be served," "This cow that drinks water must not be touched with the foot," or "A cow is to be sacrificed," then even though there is contact with a material substratum through the word, it belongs exclusively to the position where the universal is the word-meaning; for in such cases, the substratum is merely incidental to the primary purpose of conveying the distinction of the universal. || 354 ||

When a substance is perceived through contact and is then resorted to as a substance, it must be expressed by that very word; thus, at that time, the substance constitutes the referent of the word. (355)

Even when a substance is denoted by a word that primarily denotes a genus (*jāti*), if there is a connection or contact with that [genus] solely as its expressed meaning (*abhidheyatā*), and the substance is relied upon as the primary factor in relation to the action—while the genus is exhausted merely as a qualifier—as in "Feed this Brāhmaṇa" and similar injunctions where the command is directed toward the substance, then that is the position in which the substance is the word-meaning (*dravyapadārthapakṣa*). This is what was stated: "For some, however, something is primary. (355)

He states that even when the injunction (*codanā*) is directed toward the genus (*jāti*), since only a substance (*dravya*) is capable of being connected with action, the substance alone remains the word-meaning from the perspective of the intended purport (*tātparya*): "Even though it is not denoted by a separate word, the genus functions [as the meaning] solely insofar as it possesses distinction; when it is associated with a relation [to action], that genus also attains the status of the substance-word-meaning. (356)

Since both [the universal and the individual] are derived from the word, and because the individual is capable of being understood as the effect [of the word], the followers of Vyāḍi and others maintain that the substance alone is the word-meaning, disregarding the universal. As they say: "And because it is that which is commenced in the injunctions. The universal, however, functions merely to differentiate its own substratum from others; even when expressed by a word, it operates only within the scope of such differentiation.

For example, in the case of "the king’s man" (*rājapuruṣa*), although the relationship is expressed by the compound, it serves merely to delimit the nature of the related entities; thus, the compound has the meaning of the final member as its primary sense, not the relationship as its primary sense. Similarly, words such as "cow" (*go*), though denoting a genus (*jāti*), have that [genus] as their primary sense in the same way. And just as words like "king’s man" denote an object qualified by a relationship only once [in its entirety], so too, according to different philosophical perspectives, the two types of word-meanings are distinguished. || 356 ||

However, regarding the view that the category of the universal (*jāti*) alone is the denotation of a word, there is the position of the universal as the word-meaning; and regarding the view that the pure substance (*dravya*) is the denotation of a word, there is the position of the substance as the word-meaning. Thus, he states this other pair of positions: "But when it is maintained that the two—denoting the universal and denoting the substance—are absolutely distinct, and that [the word] serves as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaka*) of that which is not directly denoted, then both serve as its meaning. (357)

The word denoting a genus (*jāti*) alone is one thing, and the word denoting a genus and two [other categories] together is another. In both cases, the genus or the substance—which is not itself being denoted—assists [the denotation] by establishing a distinction of substratum as appropriate, and by establishing properties such as gender and number inherent in itself; this is the view of the venerable teacher Pāṇini, which was set forth last of all. Accordingly, due to the difference in scope, the status of the genus as the meaning of a word is sometimes resorted to for the sake of establishing forms such as *madrahrada*.

In some cases, the status of a substance as a category (*dravyapadārthatā*) is resorted to for the sake of establishing [grammatical operations] such as *dadhy-ukā* and so forth; it is for this very reason that the Teacher (Pāṇini) commenced the pair of rules beginning with *jātyākhyāyām* and *sarūpāṇām*. 357.

Thus, by way of this digression, the various views have been introduced. He now concludes the subject at hand: "But for one who accepts the difference produced by the substratum when [the universal] is dependent [upon it], the fact that a single word applies to the class-term is further described. (358)

When a genus (*jāti*) residing in specific individuals is denoted by a word, the author of the *Bhāṣya*, in this former position (*pakṣa*) which maintains that the distinction of gender and number is based on the proximity of the substratum and serves as the cause for the phonological refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the word, has described—and thus stated—that there is a single word-form (*ekaśabdatva*) because the efficient word-meaning (*prayojaka-śabdārtha*) is non-different. He expressed this while saying: "If even for that [genus] the numbers were not based on usage (*na āvacanikāni*), I too would say: 'Where the referent resides in many, there the plural number occurs.'"

And thus, the *ekaśeṣa* (the grammatical operation of retaining only one of identical words) is rejected. Since it is established that the genus (*jāti*) is primarily denoted by the word, a single word denoting that [genus] remains even when there is a difference among individuals (*vyakti*). However, those who hold that the related individuals [denote] the genus bring about, through their differences, a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the single word.

In the second alternative as well, by the principle that "like words denoting qualities, [the gender and number] follow from the substrate," it is established that even though the substance is being expressed as subordinate (*guṇabhūta*), it does not serve as a cause for a difference in the word-form; thus, that very unity of the word is demonstrated. For it has been explained that the intent of these two solutions is that the related genus (*jāti*) is either brought near by implication or is grasped as permeated by the form of the occasioning factor (*nimitta*). || 358 ||

Thus, having concluded the investigation into the establishment of gender and number based on the substratum for words expressing qualities (*guṇavacana*)—in accordance with the relevant passages of the Bhāṣya and as the occasion for the discussion of grammatical function (*vṛtti*) required—he now begins the investigation into compounds involving comparison (*upamāna*). In this regard, first of all, there is the Bhāṣya pertinent to the definition of comparison: "For that which is called a means of measurement (*māna*) is employed for the purpose of knowing what is not yet known; [it is used] with the thought, 'I shall know the object not yet known.'"

He explains this as follows: "That by which the unknown is known is called a means of knowledge (pramāṇa). By means of it—such as a measuring vessel (prastha) and the like—the object of measurement is determined in its entirety. (359)

That by which something is measured—that is, delimited—is called *māna* (measurement). It refers to that which, having established a general object through ascertainment, serves as the basis for determining its specific form, and which delimits it in its entirety; examples include the *prastha*, the *khārī*, and the *āḍhaka*. This is the general definition of measurement (*māna*). By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "the *prastha* etc.," other types such as *pramāṇa* (linear measure) and *unmāna* (weight) are also included. For measurement is qualified by the prefixes *ut*, *pra*, and *pari*. Among these, the *prastha* and so forth are *parimāṇa* (capacity measure), the *diṣṭi* and so forth are *pramāṇa* (linear measure), and the *pala* and so forth are *unmāna* (weight). || 359 ||

He speaks in order to explain comparison (*upamāna*), which is proximate to mental cognition (*mānasa*): "That by which an unknown object is understood through its properties via a well-known [object], because of the lack of complete knowledge [of the former], is called comparison (*upamāna*). (360)

Comparison (*upamāna*) is the means of establishing what is to be established through well-known similarity. For instance, an unknown and unperceived object such as a *gavaya* is determined by its similarity to a well-known cow—meaning it possesses the same properties as that [cow]—according to the principle "it is like that. This determination is not based on mere similarity alone, nor on height and girth, nor in its entirety, but rather through its specific characteristics.

For this very reason, similarity (*sādṛśya*) is clearly ascertained here by perception; thus, since comparison (*upamāna*) depends upon that [perception], it is not an independent means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Rather, it is "near" to that [perception], because it determines [the object] in a certain manner. For this same reason, they indeed dispute the validity of comparison as a means of knowledge. They maintain that only a statement whose meaning is already established is the means of valid cognition, whereas the description of similarity is merely a means (*upāya*). Furthermore, based on the derivation from the instrumental case (*karaṇa-vyutpatti*), comparison is the cognition of similarity—that by which something is compared—because through it, the object of comparison (*upameya*) is directly determined.

For some, the result is the comprehension of the relationship between the name and the named; for others, the result is the cognition, "My cow is similar to this one. However, the cow and so forth are designated by the term 'means of knowledge' (upamāna) because of their indirect utility, just as the eye and other sense organs are designated by the term 'means of knowledge' (pramāṇa). || 360 ||

When the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) has been thus explained, by implication the object of comparison (*upameya*) is also explained, because the act of comparison has the object of comparison as its domain. Consequently, he explains the meaning of the aphorism, beginning with the explanation of the common attribute (*sāmānyadharma*): "That attribute which is common to the two—the standard of comparison and the object of comparison—is [expressed] in compounds by words denoting the standards of comparison. (361)

The property (*dharma*) that necessarily exists here as the ground for the relationship of standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and object of comparison (*upameya*) between two things is called similarity (*sādṛśya*) or commonality (*sāmānya*). Because it occurs in two instances, those words which express a commonality are called "expressive of commonality" (*sāmānyavacana*). The meaning of the grammatical rule (*sūtra*) is that there is a compound (*samāsa*) of these words with words expressive of the standard of comparison. Examples: *śastrīśyāmā* (dark like a knife) and *śarakāṇḍagauraḥ* (fair like a reed-stalk). || 361 ||

Now, one might object: "Since qualities such as blackness are distinct because they are inherent in their respective substrates, how can they be a universal? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The distinction in blackness that arises from the difference of its substrates is not intended [to be emphasized]. This quality, while residing in a single entity, is perceived as having distinct substrates. (362)

The distinction in the quality of blackness resulting from the difference in its substrata is not intended to be expressed here by those who speak of "general terms. Although the quality inheres in specific substrata, that unity which is required [for the application of the term] is understood precisely through the power of the general term itself. For even when the substrata are distinct, the quality certainly possesses an underlying form by virtue of which the possibility of a non-different designation and cognition—such as "it is black"—arises. Yet, it is not absolute non-difference that is intended here. (362)

Furthermore: there is a fixed distinction between two qualities, yet likewise unity between their generic classes; for neither in absolute unity nor in absolute difference is the existence of comparison possible. (363)

In the case of absolute identity, there is no relationship of standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and object of comparison (*upameya*), because similarity—which is the substratum of difference—is absent; for it is not the case that "a cow is like a cow. Nor does the comparison "a clod of earth is like the Himalayas" exist when there is absolute difference, as there is no common form (*anvayirūpa*) [to connect them]. Therefore, in the case of comparison, by reflecting upon both difference and non-difference, one relies on difference due to the distinction between the substrata and on non-difference through the power of the common form according to its own specific characteristic (*svālakṣaṇya*). It is precisely such an objective essence (*arthātmā*) that is denotable by words.

For words do not convey the difference among objects by way of their specific individuality (*svalakṣaṇya*), because the apprehension of the relationship [between word and object] occurs only with respect to the universal (*sāmānya*).

One might object: "Let there be no simile in the case of absolute difference; but why should it not exist in the case of non-difference? For a single quality indeed establishes the relationship of the standard and the object of comparison between two things. Anticipating this, he says: "When there is dependence on mere genus (jāti), there is no purpose for a simile at all. For blackness as a single quality resides in both of these [qualities]. (364)

When there is an intention to express mere blackness, devoid of any distinction between the substratum and that which rests upon it, the verbal formulation is simply this: "The blackness is a single universal (*sāmānya*) inherent in both the sword-blade and Devadatta as their common quality of blackness. And thus, there is an absence of determination by way of similarity. || 364 ||
For instance: "By the very same cause through which the dark woman is perceived as a 'knife-wielder' there, that cause does not differ in the cognition of Devadattā. (365)

By that very same quality of blackness (*śyāma-guṇa*), which is inherent and follows an undivided universal, the sword is apprehended as "black"; and by that same quality, which serves as the substratum for an undivided universal, Devadatta also enters into the cognition "he too is black. Thus, the cognition arises that the blackness of both is one and the same; there is no further purpose for comparison here. || 365 ||
Therefore, through both the distinction of the quality from its substratum and the non-distinction of the universal, the substance-nature is perceived as being endowed with activity. (366)

The nature of a substance (*dravyasvabhāva*), known as comparison (*upamāna*), is determined to be operative in the process of defining the object of comparison (*upameya*) by means of two causal factors belonging to the category of qualities (*guṇa*): distinction (*bheda*), which is caused by a difference in substrata, and non-distinction (*aviveka*), which is caused by a pervasive form. Consequently, when the relationship between the standard of comparison and the object of comparison is established, their connection—characterized as that of the *upamāna* and the *upameya*—is maintained. || 366 ||

Anticipating the objection that difference and non-difference are contradictory and how they could both function in one place, he says: "This very worldly transaction, which relies upon both unity and multiplicity, proceeds through a synthesis of the reflective awareness of difference and non-difference. (367)

He says that this [usage] cannot be denied because it is established by experience as "this is that. What difference is there in the fact that this conventional usage of similarity, relying upon both difference and non-difference, persists through a cause consisting of a mixture of unity and plurality and thus ascends into the intellect? For indeed, when there is absolute non-difference, the cognition arises: "This is that very same thing"; whereas when there is absolute difference, the cognition is: "This is something else entirely. However, the cognition "it is similar" arises as a blend of both forms—difference and non-difference.

And thus it has been stated in the *Jātisamuddeśa*: "When there is a single occurrence [of a cognition], unity is attained; when there is a repeated occurrence, the nature of similarity is attained by individual entities that possess distinct natures, through the exclusion of difference. (367)

He establishes this very point by way of negative concomitance (vyatireka): "When only the genus is intended to be expressed, one says simply 'dark' (śyāmā); in that case, there is no purpose for the inclusion of [qualifiers] such as 'knife-wielder' (śastrī). (368)

If it is intended to express that the mere quality, as accompanied by the universal of "darkness," serves as a qualifier of the substratum, then one should simply say, "This Devadatta is dark" (*śyāmeyam devadattaḥ*), since the relation with such a specific type of thing is conveyed by this much alone. In that case, for what purpose is it said, "like a sword" (*śastrīva*)? Since the connection with the unqualified quality is already understood from the word for the quality itself, words of comparison do not convey any additional excellence; therefore, their employment is purposeless. (368)

[Objection: But in this way, by considering both difference and non-difference, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding the relationship between the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the subject of comparison (*upameya*). To explain: the quality of "darkness" (*śyāma*), though residing in all its substrates, is distinct due to the difference of its loci, yet it is one due to the unity of its genus (*jāti*). How then can the sword alone be the object of comparison? Anticipating this objection, he first states the distinction between the two qualities that serve as the objects of comparison, according to their specific characteristics (*svālakṣaṇya*): "That difference which is not denotable by words and does not reside in mere darkness [in general], but whose occurrence is restricted to certain dark things—that is what is intended here. (369)

The uncommon [quality] is the substratum of subtle distinctions for each respective substrate; it is a term not recognized as such because its own designator is impossible. It is a specific quality of darkness (*śyāma-guṇa-viśeṣa*) which, despite the absence of a designating word, exists because the thing designated does not depart [from it]. Being non-connexive with respect to everything, yet occurring only in certain instances, it is required in this relationship between the object of comparison and the standard of comparison—it is resorted to by virtue of its functional operation. For instance, from the very compound word *śastrīśyāmā* ("dark like a knife"), a distinct quality of darkness belonging to both the standard and the object of comparison is perceived.

Since this [quality] cannot exist elsewhere, there is no over-extension [of the definition]. Thus, due to the difference in their substrata, even though another [quality] has its distinction not yet determined through some mode of apprehending its own nature, it is said that the quality itself establishes a comparison by means of both difference and non-difference with the universal. || 369 ||

He states that not every quality or genus has an operation here [in this case]: "In some dark things, a certain [quality] exists; in all [dark things], a certain [genus] exists; a certain universal [of darkness] resides in one dark thing; and a particular difference is established in another. (370)

A certain lower-order generality (*aparasāmānya*) resides in some dark qualities and is active in providing the basis for a simile. However, that which resides everywhere—the great generality (*mahāsāmānya*)—does not serve as the cause for a simile because it lacks differentiation. Yet, a certain specific difference (*viśeṣa*) or particularity resides in a restricted dark quality; this too certainly becomes the cause for a simile in order to manifest excellence. For example, a specific excellence of luster in the moon serves as the cause for a simile with the face of a maiden, through the superimposition of an extraordinary degree of beauty.

For praise arises from the superimposition of excellence through the comparison of one possessing inferior qualities with one possessing superior qualities; however, it was previously stated that an absolute distinction is not a constituent element of simile. || 370 ||

Anticipating the objection that no other universal (jāti) is perceived here apart from the commonality of qualities, he says the following in order to establish its existence: "For while there is a difference in fragrance among various types of blue lotuses (*utpala*) and the like, a similarity is nevertheless observed among those fragrances when their differences are taken into account. (371)

Apart from the great universal (mahāsāmānya) of "fragrance" (*gandhatva*) belonging to the scents of the *jāti*-lotus and so forth, when there exists another universal characterized as "exquisite fragrance" (*śobhanāmodatva*) within their sweetness (*saurabhya*), a distinction is determined. From those things which lack such sweetness, a differentiation is perceived. For instance, having smelled the scent of a lotus, one recognizes it even in total darkness, thinking, "This is a lotus. The same applies to the scent of jasmine and other such fragrances.

Furthermore, there exists another universal, namely "fragrance" (*surabhitva*), which is restricted to specific substrates; it is because of its connection with this that substances are determined as "fragrant" or "sweet-smelling. And even though such fragrance exists, there is still a degree of similarity among certain odors despite their particular differences.

For instance—by means of fragrant substances such as *nakha* and *śaileya*, which are composed of various fragrant materials, another distinct substance is produced that possesses a fragrance similar to the scent of a lotus or other flowers, due to some inherent affinity (*svabhāvapratyāsatti*), such as "having the scent of a lotus," "having the scent of filaments," or "having the scent of jasmine.

In this same way, it is logical that there are sub-species within the category of color (*rūpa*) which possesses fragrance; thus, that which exists in certain dark-colored things is established as a further commonality (*aparasāmānya*) characterized by the occurrence of specific qualities. || 371 ||

He asks: "What causes the specific determination of the qualities (guṇas)? and replies: "The distinction among the qualities is understood either from their substratum, or by itself, or through an indefinable particularity, or through their commingling with other qualities. (372)

A certain distinction among qualities arises from a substratum characterized as a substance (*dravya*) that has acquired differentiation through its own causes. For example, the blackness residing in a garland of blue lotuses and the like. And thus, based on this similarity of essential nature (*svabhāva*), a simile (*upamā*) is employed: "The sky is dark like a bee, a venomous serpent, or a *tamāla* tree; [the warriors] in battle have their hands occupied with swords as stainless as the sky."

Even when there is a co-inherence in a substrate of a single class, a certain distinction will indeed be perceived among the qualities—such as their greyishness and so forth—because they arise as specific [qualities] due to the inconceivable nature of their own essence (*svarūpa*). On the other hand, there is another kind of distinction among the qualities which is not a term of common cognition; it does not arise from the mere cause [of production] but is caused by the lapse of time (*kālaparivāsa*). For example, through the attainment of a specific transformation, there arises a variety of taste and smell in liquors and the like.

For in that case, since the effect is not produced in fragments by the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), it is impossible to point out that "this excellence" belongs to a specific cause within that complex. Nor can there be a distinction among qualities (*guṇa*) due to their being mixed with the qualities of another substance, as for example, the difference between liquor perfumed with the scent of *sahakāra* flowers and oil perfumed with *mālatī* blossoms.

Thus, when certain qualities that possess distinct individualities are present through some proximity, and there exists a further commonality (*aparasāmānya*) among them, the formation of a compound is established by expressing the general term [for the whole] while omitting the specific terms [for the parts]. (372)

Furthermore, it is not an absolute rule that the equality of qualities alone is the cause of comparison; rather, the object of comparison (*upamāna*) may possess superior qualities. Thus he says: "The object of comparison (*upamāna*) excels in every respect because of its well-known status; its role as the object of comparison (*upameyatva*) does not cease even when there is superiority [of the subject] or when there is equality. (373)

In this context, "distinction" (*vyatireka*) is intended to mean "superiority"; thus, the meaning is that the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) possesses superior qualities. Whether that superiority exists in an actual, objective sense or not is irrelevant; however, because it is well-known and recognized, it is logical that what is resorted to as a signifier (*jñāpaka*) toward the object of comparison (*upameya*) must indeed be well-known. Therefore, the excellence of its qualities consists precisely in its renown. Consequently, even a face with inferior qualities is designated as the standard of comparison for the lunar orb by women who are intent on intensifying the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*).

For among those possessed of desire, the face of the beloved is renowned for its superior qualities. As it is said: "O beautiful one! Having attained a likeness to your face—which has come to possess a turbidity due to the power of jealousy from afar—the moon, its entire body now filled with an abundance of joy in its heart, cannot contain itself even within its own limbs today. In this way, since that which possesses inferior qualities is compared to that which possesses complete qualities, the state of possessing complete qualities should be explained according to common renown. Therefore, he says: "in all cases."

It is not only the case that, in reality, that which possesses superior qualities serves as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*); even that which possesses inferior qualities may serve as the standard of comparison by virtue of its own renown, and it is established as such through the excellence [of the subject]. However, the status of being the object of comparison (*upameya*) does not cease, nor does it depart, whether the quality is in reality superior, excessive, equal, or equivalent. The meaning is that the standard of comparison must necessarily be intended to possess superior qualities, whereas there is no such restriction regarding the object of comparison. || 373 ||

Now, in order to define comparison by way of another method, he explains the Bhāṣya on the definition of *māna* differently: "Others, however, describe *māna* as genus (*jāti*) and so forth, which belong to the object to be divided; for an object of knowledge whose nature is not yet ascertained is measured by that. (374)

Because a substance that is divisible and capable of being delimited is not apprehended when it is abstracted from its limiting adjuncts (upādhi), the universals (jāti), qualities (guṇa), and actions (kriyā) are perceived as they depend upon it, thereby attaining the designation of "measure" (māna). || 374 ||
But that which is established by its own measure as a substratum of qualities functions, by means of its own property, for the measurement of another substratum. (375)
The contact of things possessing different forms with another form, by means of which there is a comparison for those things to be compared through that distinct [form], is called *upamāna*. (376)

When that which is well-known—that is, recognized—as the substratum of specific qualities, being delimited by its own inherent attributes such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth, exerts itself through a quality inherent in itself alone for the purpose of making known another unperceived quality, then, by means of that distinct form, it is called *upamāna* (analogy), which serves as the delimiting factor for things to be delimited—distinct entities possessing other forms.

In this context, since contact—that is, a relation—between absolutely distinct things is not possible, there is by implication an attraction toward a common property (*anvayidharma*). Consequently, through the consideration of both difference and non-difference, even this [comparison] is a form of analogy (*upamāna*). Furthermore, because it determines an object merely through similarity, the definition of analogy is established as "that which is not an absolute means of valid cognition" (*māna*). In that regard, in the expression "the sword-blade is dark like Devadatta," the quality of darkness belonging to both the sword-blade and Devadatta is the basis for the relationship between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*). (375, 376)

But when it is said, "This [face] is similar to that [lotus] because of its dark color," then: The common attribute, such as darkness, belonging to both the object of comparison and the standard of comparison, is differentiated by another attribute which is intended to be predominant. (377)

When a property such as "darkness" (śyāma), which establishes the relationship between the standard of comparison and the object of comparison, is taken primarily as the object of comparison—by excluding its function as an auxiliary and being distinct from its substratum—then, because it acts as a substance (adravyāyamāṇatvāt), it must be qualified by another property residing within itself; thus, in this case, a different property serves as the basis for the relationship between the standard and the object of comparison. || 377 ||
He illustrates this very point: "When it is asserted that 'the sword and the youth are alike in being dark,' the ground for the designation 'by means of this' resides in the two qualities. (378)

By means of this property (*dharma*) such as brilliance (*dīpti*), which belongs to the quality of darkness (*śyāma-guṇa*) and serves as the instrument [of comparison], it must be determined that "this quality of darkness is similar [to that]. Furthermore, in that case as well, one must seek another property within the primary property—such as the property called brilliance—which is common to both qualities of darkness; thus, there is indeed an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) here, as explained in the *Brahmakāṇḍa*: "Whatever generality (*sāmānya*) is resorted to in the case of the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object compared (*upameya*), for each of those, yet another property is distinguished within the comparisons. (378)

As long as there is an intention to speak here, the intention regarding phenomena is inexhaustible; however, upon cessation, there is a stopping. And when this [similarity] is intended to be expressed as distinct from the object of comparison (the *upameya*), then the relationship of standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and object of comparison (*upameya*) is verbal. Thus he says: "When those possessing the causes [of similarity] proceed as if they were that very essence through those causes, then that description of the standard and object of comparison is based on their difference. (379)

When the two—the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*)—attain, as it were, a state of identity through the quality (*guṇa*) such as "darkness" which serves as the cause for their relationship of comparison, by means of the metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) of the quality and the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*), then the designation based on their difference is maintained through their distinction. Consequently, in that case, a word such as "as if" (*iva*), which indicates the relation characterized by the status of standard and object of comparison, is employed; thus, this is a complete simile (*paripūrṇopamā*). For example: "Devadatta’s knife is dark, just like [the color of her complexion]"; or "The *gavaya* is like a cow."

"Like mountains, the clouds. Here, because the relationship between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) is based on a quality (*guṇa*), that quality is designated as non-different from its possessor (*tadvat*); thus, since the relation is expressed, the nominative case is used.

According to the maxim, "That meaning which is included [within the word] becomes the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*)," there is no case-ending to express that [quality]. Therefore, the nominative endings of the two [terms] would not be syntactically connected; hence, particles such as *iva* are employed to indicate this connection for the sake of syntactic cohesion. Thus, there is completeness due to the employment of the words expressing the standard of comparison, the object of comparison, the relation between them, and the word denoting the common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*). || 379 ||

But when the superimposition of non-difference is caused by similarity, then the relationship of the standard of comparison and the object of comparison is implicitly contained; thus he says: "When difference ceases in those cases where there is a desire to express non-attachment to reality, they call them 'elliptical similes' (luptopamā), because they rely upon that common attribute. (380)

When the superimposition of non-difference (*abhedādhyāropa*)—the merging of the identity of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*)—is intended to be expressed, then, because difference has ceased, the relationship of standard and object of comparison dependent upon it also disappears. For example: "The Bāhīka is a cow," or "The boy is a lion. Since the employment of words for the sake of another [to convey a meaning] would otherwise be inexplicable, teachers such as Yāska and others, through the inference of the cause from the effect by including a common attribute (*samānadharmāntarbhāvana*), declare these to be instances where the standard of comparison is elided (*luptopamāna*).

"Those in whom the simile is lost because it is not directly perceived" means: by virtue of sharing that common attribute (*taddharmeṇa*), that is, through the inclusion of that identical attribute which is implicitly contained within the word for the standard of comparison (*upamāna-śabda*), there is an apprehension of the object of comparison (*upameya*). This is the meaning. || 380 ||

And thus, it has been stated that an effect is preceded by a specific cause. Now, he explains with his intended meaning (*tātparya*) the *Bhāṣya* passage: "But others [say] that the means of knowledge is genus (*jāti*) and so forth; that which does not measure [its object] absolutely is analogy (*upamāna*). [The verse says: "The dark color well-known in the *śāstra* is the measure (*māna*); it is measured by that [analogy]. But another dark thing, being of a different nature from that [known one], is not measured by it absolutely. (381)

A means of knowledge (*māna*) is that which delimits [an object] in its entirety. And this [means] is the blackness residing in the knife; for that is well-known as the delimiter in that context. But another woman, Devadattā, though she too is black, is not so well-known; therefore, she is delimited by that blackness acting as the instrument. Even when delimited in this way, she is not measured in every respect. For it is not possible to determine an object in its totality merely through the conformity of a common property (*dharma-sāmānya*). || 381 ||

Thus, when Devadatta is not fully determined by the blackness residing in the knife, then the knife becomes the means of cognition (*māna*) for comparison (*upamāna*) in its ultimate sense; so he says: "Therefore, they declare that the comparison (*upamāna*) is the knife, which, while measuring [Devadatta] through its own quality, is itself a substratum whose quality is not yet fully established. (382)

They call the knife the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) because it delimits the other substratum—characterized by Devadatta—by means of its own completed quality of blackness (*śyāmaguṇa*), which is a quality not yet completed [in the subject]. This is because of "establishment" (*siddheḥ*); that is to say, because of the state of having fully perfected qualities. || 382 ||

Having thus explained the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) through two modes, the status of the word as a general term (*sāmānyavacana*) is now examined. For, since the word denotes the possessor of the attribute (*nimittin*) as having attained identity with the attribute (*nimitta*), that attribute is expressed either as residing in the standard of comparison—having attained identity with it—or as residing in the object of comparison; however, it cannot be expressed simultaneously as residing in both. Thus, one might suspect that because of this non-repetition (*ananvaya*), how can there be the status of being a general term? Anticipating this, he says: "The attribute (*dharma*) residing in the object of comparison is heard [directly] and inferred in the other; or else, the attribute residing in the standard of comparison is heard and inferred in the object of comparison. (383)

In this context, the relationship between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) is prompted by a common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*). Since it is impossible to express that common attribute as residing in both simultaneously, when it is said, "Devadattā is dark like a knife-blade" (*śastrīśyāmā devadattā*), because the connection is established through the very word heard—namely, "darkness"—it is illogical to postulate an unexpressed [attribute]. Thus, even though the word has ceased its function with respect to one [of the two], the determination of the connection to the quality occurs through inference regarding the other meaning; therefore, even when only one of the two is expressed, the status of being a term denoting a general property (*sāmānyavacanatva*) is justified for that common attribute. || 383 ||

Regarding that, he states an illustration based on the hearing of the word in the object of comparison: "The Kṣatriyas are seen studying like Brāhmaṇas. Because the object of comparison is distinct [from the standard of comparison], the verbal ending (vacana) is based on the Kṣatriyas. (384)

Because the objects of comparison (*upameya*), the Kṣatriyas, are numerous, the plural number heard here indicates that the common attribute (*dharma*) of study resides in the object of comparison. However, by implication (*sāmarthya*), its connection with the objects of comparison—the Brāhmaṇas—is understood. Since the object of comparison serves as the basis for the comparison, the attribute heard in relation to it must necessarily be understood as residing in the object of comparison; therefore, it was not explicitly cited in that instance [in the previous example]. || 384 ||

And thus, even though it is not expressed as residing in both, its status as a term denoting a universal (sāmānyavacana) is justified; so he says: "By expressing a property that is common [to many] yet established in only some [particular instances], a word is designated as 'denoting a universal' in the Sūtra. (385)

Even when a property (*dharma*) is denoted by a word as residing in either one [of two things], it is a universal (*sāmānya*) because, in its real form, there is no consideration of distinction; thus, a word expressing that [property] becomes a "universal-denoting" (*sāmānyavacana*) word. It is not the case that a property becomes common simply because the word expresses it as residing in both; for even though a specific [individual] such as a Brahmin is denoted by a word through a universal [form], it lacks commonality.

Therefore, in its actual form, the universal of "darkness" (*śyāmatva-sāmānya*), even when designated as residing in a single instance, is expressed as being common [to others] through inference; thus it remains common. || 385 ||

Thus, a word denoting a universal (sāmānyavacana) is applied to a genus of qualities (*guṇajāti*). Even when it refers to a specific quality such as "dark" (*śyāma*), a word like "dark" remains a term denoting a universal; so he says: "A quality residing in two [entities] is not denoted either through non-difference or through difference. Of two distinct properties, one is heard [directly], while the other is understood [by implication]. (386)

The quality characterized by blackness, which resides in both the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object compared (*upameya*), is not denoted by the word through non-difference—that is, by entering into a form that is common to both. This is because it is delimited either by the object of comparison or by the object compared. Thus, being qualified as residing in only one [of the two], there is no denotation through non-difference; nor is it denoted by its own distinct, individual nature. For words do not touch upon difference in its specific character (*svālakṣaṇya*), since they denote universals (*sāmānya*). Nor is there any utility for the distinct individual nature in the context of a simile.

Therefore, by the word "dark" (śyāma), a quality is first expressed without distinction; even though it is delimited by its connection with one [of two objects], it is determined through the force of the context to reside in the other as well; thus, that word is a general term. || 386 ||

Having thus explained the commentary according to its intended meaning (*tātparya*), he now explains it directly following the literal text: "That which, being established in a universal (*sāmānya*), does not measure [the object] absolutely, causes the object of comparison (*upameya*) to be mentally constructed in proximity by means of similarity. (387)

That which delimits the body of the object of measurement (*meyasarīra*) to its ultimate extent is a measure (*māna*), such as a *prastha* or a genus (*jāti*) and so forth; this has been explained. That which is in proximity to that is the standard of comparison (*upamāna*). And here, by the word "that" (*tat*), the primary object of comparison—the subject under discussion as something to be made known—is referred to. That which is in proximity to that object of comparison is the standard of comparison. Furthermore, this proximity is produced by the close connection of their attributes (*dharma*).

And thus, because it determines [the object] by means of similarity, comparison (*upamāna*)—which is established upon a common property (*sāmānya*), a shared characteristic that serves as the cause for the connection—is dependent on that [similarity] and does not determine [the object] to the full extent. For the determination of the object of comparison (*upameya*) here is effected by the comparison through that much alone, namely, the common property, and not by any other property. Indeed, Devadatta is delimited by the quality of being dark through the sword, but not by such forms as "thick" and so forth; therefore, this means of knowledge (*māna*) is incomplete when it remains in proximity to the object of comparison. (387)

He states another interpretation of the commentary on the phrase "in proximity to that" (tatsamīpe): "Or, [the object] is perceived as being near the means of knowledge (māna) by virtue of its similarity; for here, the similarity between the means of knowledge and the object of comparison arises from their shared capacity for delimitation. (388)

In this context, when a subordinate factor (*guṇa*) is employed for the sake of favoring the primary factor (*pradhāna*), there should be no reference to it because of its subordination. However, here, although the means of knowledge (*māna*) is useful for the determination of the object of knowledge (*meyam*), it is the primary factor when its own nature is being characterized; therefore, that alone is referred to by the word "that" (*tat*). Thus, that which is in proximity to the means of knowledge is the analogy (*upamāna*). And proximity arises from the connection with a common property. Here, there exists a similarity between the means of knowledge and the analogy, namely, the quality of being a cause of determination. The distinction is that one is a completely definitive determiner, while the other is not completely definitive. || 388 ||

Thus, the commentary on the definition of comparison (*upamāna*)—"For that which is called *māna* (measurement) is employed for the purpose of knowing what is not yet known—that is, with the thought 'I shall know the unknown object'—that which measures [the object] in its vicinity, but not absolutely, is *upamāna*"—has been explained. Therefore, the introductory question (*praśnabhāṣya*) regarding the reason for introducing the definition of comparison comes first: "Is that which is the object of comparison (*upameya*) the same as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), or is the standard of comparison one thing and the object of comparison another? He explains this: "In dependence upon the perspective of belonging to the same genus (*ekajāti*), it is determined that they are the same;
in dependence upon the perspective of difference (*bheda*), it is understood that they are indeed different. (389)

In this world, objects attain a state of being conventionally designated according to their respective conditions. In that regard, when the common feature (*anvayirūpa*) of the object of comparison and the object compared is intended as non-different—concealing the distinction between individual instances and consisting of a single quality or genus—then, through the superimposition of that single form, their non-difference is determined; thus, it is said, "it is that very thing" (*tadeva*). But when the inherent difference—the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*)—is intended by defining the nature of the individual instances, then, because of the ascertainment of a well-known distinctness from other things, the expression "it is something else" (*anyadeva*) is used.
The intention is to ask whether absolute non-difference is required for the status of being a point of comparison, or rather, absolute difference. || 389 ||

But surely, the designations "standard of comparison" (*upamāna*) and "object of comparison" (*upameya*), which follow the distinction between the means [of cognition] and [the object], demonstrate the difference between these two. For since the suffixes functioning as the object (*karman*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*) have different meanings, how can there be a suspicion of non-difference? To this, he concedes: "Since the state of being an object and the state of being an instrument are resorted to as distinct, there would be no doubt here regarding their absolute identity. (390)

Since both the state of being an object (*karmatva*) and the state of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) are apprehended through their distinct conditions (*pratyaya*), therefore, in this case, that real unity—which is devoid of all basis for differentiation—is not tenable as the subject or object of doubt. Thus, it is not contradictory that the object of doubt is the unity superimposed upon two distinct things by means of a common property (*sāmānyadharma*). || 390 ||

And he says that such linguistic usage is indeed observed through an imagined non-difference, even among things that are distinct: "Because they possess an identical form despite their difference, one observes [the expression] 'those rice grains'; because there is no difference in genus, a distinct object is designated as 'this is that very same thing. (391)

Even though rice grains have distinct individual identities, they are designated as "those very same [grains] being eaten" because they are apprehended non-differently by cognitions that suppress their differences through the commonality of form (*rūpasāmānya*). Similarly, one says, "those very same clothes are being worn. This commonality of form, which is synonymous with similarity (*sādṛśya*) and serves as the basis for non-difference, has been stated in the treatise in the *Ākara-vārttika*: "or because of the commonality of form. To demonstrate this very point, the example is given: "we are eating those very same rice grains that were seen in Madhurā."

Moreover, the determination of non-difference is not based solely on the cause of mere similarity; it is also grounded in the non-difference of the genus (*jāti*). For instance, individual instances (*vyakti*) that are superposed by a single universal are designated as non-different, as in the case of "Four Brahmins should bring water-jars," and so forth. Here, although there is a difference between Māṭhara and the others, their non-difference is apprehended through their commonality as Brahmins.

Similarly, in this context as well, because of the proximity caused by the common attribute of similarity between the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object compared (*upameya*), or because of the merging of a single quality belonging to them, the state of being an object of doubt regarding their non-difference is appropriate. (391)
He says that even the distinction is logical: "For how could a part belong to another, and yet be called 'other'? Where there is absolute difference, there is plurality, and no reality exists. (392)

Regarding the rule *halantāt* (Pāṇini 1.2.10), when the word *anta* is taken to mean "part" (*avayava*), the rule is explained as: "from that which has an *ik* vowel at its end (*ante*) [i.e., a part]. To this, the following objection is raised: "How indeed can an *ik* vowel be 'at the end' (*anta*) of something else? One thing cannot be another. In this context, the validity of the argument rests precisely on the difference between the part and the whole; thus, an absolute distinction (*atyantabheda*) is intended here. For it is only where there is an extreme difference between two things that identity (*tattva*) or non-difference (*abheda*) is not possible in any way whatsoever.
