This was stated with the intention of referring to that absolute diversity which exists when [the two] are present, namely, "one is different from the other. By means of both words "different" (*anya*), he indicates an absolute difference. However, a part (*avayava*) is in some sense non-different from the whole (*avayavin*), because its distinction is obscured by inherence (*samavāya*). A phoneme (*varṇa*), on the other hand, is entirely distinct from another phoneme because it does not originate another; thus, it is not logically possible for it to be a part.

Thus, in this case, although there is some kind of non-difference (*ananya*) [between the parts], the impossibility [of the doubt] has been stated with the intention that the parts are absolutely distinct (*atyantabheda*). Likewise here as well, although there is some kind of non-difference between the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the subject of comparison (*upameya*) due to the non-difference of their genus (*jāti*) or their common form (*rūpasāmānya*), by disregarding that [non-difference] and relying instead on absolute distinction, it is stated that they are "something else entirely" (*anyad eva*), thereby becoming the object of doubt. || 392 ||

In this regard, he states that while non-difference is possible between parts and the whole even when they are distinct, it is not so for two phonemes that do not stand in a relationship of producer and produced: "When there is an intention to express non-difference, there is oneness between the collection and the possessor of the collection; however, there is no such non-difference between two possessors of collections. Thus, their distinctness has been illustrated. (393)

The Saṅgha is the whole (avayavin), and the members are the parts (avayava). When there is a desire to express those [members] as being devoid of difference through their collection, then non-difference alone is intended. A "saṅgha" or a "collection" refers to a forest and the like; those possessing it—the members—refer to trees and so forth. When one wishes to express their non-distinction from the collection, that is, their lack of separation, then in such cases as "the forest is the trees" or "the Brāhmaṇas are the assembly," there is oneness and non-difference. For instance, words such as "forest" denote those members by way of the collective nature of the group.

Trees and the like, however, through their association with specific class-distinctions (*jāti-bheda*), are those very [individuals]; thus, there is the occurrence of two words applied by different causes in a single locus, which is co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). But when there is here a desire to express distinction, then words such as "forest" (*vana*) and so forth denote merely the property characterized as a collection; thus, there is the denotation of the members of the collection as distinct from that [collection]—as in "the forest of trees" (*vṛkṣāṇāṃ vanam*) or "the assembly of Brahmins" (*brāhmaṇānāṃ saṅghaḥ*). In this way, there is both difference and non-difference between the collection and its members.

Regarding two collections (*saṅghin*): there can never be non-difference between two things that constitute a collection, because they lack a relationship [of identity]. For instance, there is no cognition of non-difference between a *śiṃśapā* tree and a *palāśa* tree, nor between Mādhara and Kauṇḍinya. Likewise, since phonemes (*varṇa*) do not originate from one another, they are absolutely distinct as constituents of a collection; thus, they are incapable of being cognized as non-different from one another, and it is precisely their difference that has been stated.

And thus, since difference and non-difference can both exist as mutually interpenetrated and also in their pure forms, here—having set aside the pure forms—the other two are intended; therefore, a question based on difference regarding the diversity of cognitions and a question based on non-difference regarding unity is indeed appropriate. Alternatively, this is a restatement of the well-known difference in the world—that which is recognized as the "standard of comparison" (upamāna) and the "object of comparison" (upameya)—taken as the subject of inquiry as to whether that is one or many. || 393 ||

Immediately following this, beginning with the words "Furthermore, O friend," the commentary states: "If that which is the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) were the very same as the object of comparison (*upameya*), what would be the purpose of the comparison here, as in 'a cow is like a cow'? Or, if the standard of comparison is one thing and the object of comparison is another, what would be the purpose of the comparison here, as in 'a cow is like a horse'? He explains this in sequence: "In that case, when there is no distinction [between the two], the purpose of comparison does not exist. For that which is the cause for the cognition 'it is a cow' exists in another cow as well. (394)

In this context, that by which one thing is well-known serves to make known what is not so known; thus, it functions as a simile (*aupamya*). However, we perceive no purpose whatsoever in requiring a commonality (*sāmānya*) that is non-distinct [from the objects themselves] to serve as the cause of comparison. For instance, in the case of "a cow is like a cow," the very same generic form (*jātirūpa*) that is the basis for determining the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is also present in that which is intended to be the object of comparison (*upameya*). Consequently, because there is no making known of an unknown object of comparison, the relationship of standard and object of comparison does not exist.
Thus, it is stated that even in the case of a cow and a gavaya, if one relies merely on a recurring property (*anvayidharma*), there is no purpose for a simile. (394)

He explains that even in the case of absolute difference, there is no purpose for a simile: "But when the operation of distinct particulars is intended to be expressed, there is no assistance rendered by one cognition to another cognition. (395)

Even if one considers distinct entities that are not followed by a common property and are entirely excluded from it, there is no assistance whatsoever for the cognition of the object of comparison (*upameya*) through the cognition of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), because—just as in the case of a cow and a horse—there is an absence of concomitance (*samanvaya*) without a common property (*dharmasāmānya*). (395)

For here is the explanatory commentary (*parihārabhāṣya*): "In that case, wherever there is some commonality and some distinction, there exists the relationship of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*). He explains this as follows: "If there is some commonality present, and if there are also certain differences—cowness (*gotva*) is the commonality in cows, while the brindled cow and others are the differences. (396)

In this context, the remainder [of the sentence] is "the relationship of the standard of comparison (upamāna) and the object of comparison (upameya). And so, it has already been explained previously. Having established this, he states that for both cows, there indeed exists a relationship of the standard and object of comparison based on the expectation of the general and the particular: "And therefore, just as a *śābaleya* [cow] is like a *bāhuleya* [cow]. The meaning is that even though they are distinct by their subordinate species such as *śābaleya*-ness and so forth, because they perform the same function and so on, they possess a commonality; thus, through this proximity, the relationship of the standard and object of comparison certainly exists. || 396 ||

Alternatively, this is an objection to the commentary on [the verse beginning] "whatever commonality" (*yatra kiñcit sāmānyam*): namely, that because all things consist of both general and particular aspects, there would be over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of comparison; thus, even "a mustard seed is like Mount Meru" or "a cow is like a cow" would be possible. This is the meaning of the half-verse. For this very reason, the following passage, which is about to be stated as a resolution to this objection, is logically consistent.

For instance: a "universal" (sāmānya) in its highest sense is not intended here; rather, it is simply [the quality] such as blackness and so forth, for that is common to both. It is this very thing that is designated as "difference" by virtue of being established in one case and unestablished in the other. || 397 ||

In the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the phrase "wherever there is some commonality" (*yatra kiñcit sāmānyam*), the word "commonality" (*sāmānya*) does not intend to denote a universal (*jāti*), but rather something other than that, such as "darkness" (*śyāmatva*) and the like. And because that [quality] is shared and persists through both the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object compared (*upameya*), it is called "commonality. For thus there is a later commentary: "It is not necessarily only that which expresses the commonality of many things; even that which expresses the commonality of two is 'expressive of a commonality' (*sāmānyavacana*). And in this way, it is understood that here "commonality" refers to a quality such as darkness that resides in two things.

And that very same thing is called both a "universal" (*sāmānya*) because of its existence [as a commonality], and a "particular" (*viśeṣa*) because of its exclusion [from others]; this is stated in the *Bhāṣya* regarding the phrase "and some particular. For instance, there is a distinction in that it is not exactly as it is well-known in the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), because of its deficiency in the object of comparison (*upameya*).

Thus, similarity other than genus (*jāti*), which is interwoven with both difference and non-difference, is here expressed by the term "universal" (*sāmānya*) as a synonym for "commonality. It is thereby stated that the relationship of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) belongs to those two things whose common property consists in the perception of what is well-known and what is not well-known; this is its basis. And having established this, even in the case of two members of the same class, such as Śābaleya and Bāhuleya, the relationship of standard and object of comparison—produced by the similarity of properties such as shape—is not based on a single genus alone, as in the case of "cow like cow."

Right here, he states another opinion: "For others, blackness alone is established as the universal (sāmānya) common to both; because it is complete, it is understood to be the particular (viśeṣa) in relation to anything else. (398)

Previously, the distinction was stated in terms of being well-known (*prasiddha*) or not well-known (*aprasiddha*); now, however, the distinction is in terms of being complete (*sampūrṇa*) or incomplete (*asampūrṇa*). To explain: a quality characterized by blackness, though existing in two instances and thus distinct due to the difference in its substrata, is called a "universal" (*sāmānya*) because its differentiation is unperceived due to subtlety. That very same quality, because it is fully present in its entirety in the object of comparison (*upamāna*), whereas it is deficient in some respect in the object compared (*upameya*), is called a "particular" (*viśeṣa*) when it is qualified by the difference [of substrata], even if that difference based on the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of the distinct substrata is not explicitly grasped.
And thus, similarity is simply a quality determined through both difference and non-difference; it is not a separate entity from that [quality]. || 398 ||

Alternatively, let it be that even the universal (jāti) is active within the simile; however, it is not apprehended solely through non-difference, but rather also through difference. Thus he says: "Or else, in the case of a configuration (ākṛti) or a universal (sāmānya), qualities such as 'dark-complexioned' and so forth are apprehended as being established in only certain [individuals]; these particularities (viśeṣa) are what are relied upon here. (399)

When those subtle particularities (*viśeṣa*) which are inherent in the same object as the universal (*jāti*), and which reside only in specific substrata of that universal, are relied upon as the causes of differentiation for the universal, then the universal—qualified by them—is active and becomes inherent only in a specific instance within the relationship characterized by the nature of the standard of comparison and the object of comparison.

For instance: the genus of the quality "darkness" residing in both the sword and Devadatta, being experienced through specific attributes such as brilliance located in their respective substrates, gives rise to a cognition of similarity due to the interpenetration of difference. However, in the case of "a cow is like a cow," since the existing distinction that differentiates the genus is not apprehended from the word, no simile occurs. But in cases such as "Devadatta is dark as a sword" or "Bāhuleya is like Śābaleya," the distinction is indeed apprehended precisely because of the difference between the substrates of the qualities.

Having thus explained the passage from the Bhāṣya, he states the summarized meaning: "Whether there is non-difference or difference of the universal (jāti), they declare that to be similarity (sādṛśya). Sometimes some [entity] whose nature is the object [of cognition] is designated as being such [a thing]. (400)

This is a restatement of the point just mentioned: that even when there is no difference in genus (*jāti*) and thus no otherness, a distinction is produced by the non-distinction residing in the same object. Or, as for the phrase "or in the case of difference," this is a restatement of the previously mentioned point: "the universal [is] just like blackness, etc. Thus, they say that what has been called a "universal" is similarity (*sādṛśya*). And by means of that similarity, only a certain thing—not every thing—is an object of cognition; such a thing is called "similar" and is so determined, because naming is preceded by determination.

And thus, being an entity, being an object of knowledge, and so forth, are not similarity; for there is no cognition of similarity [arising] from them. Therefore, since comparison occurs only through the connection with a common property (*sāmānyadharma*), there is no over-extension of the definition. || 400 ||

Now, in order to establish the object of a homogeneous cognition, he cites another type of cognition that serves as its contrast: "In whatever object there is no differentiation of cognitions at any time, it is understood to be 'one' because its differentiation is non-existent. (401)

That entity (*vastu*) whose form is never subject to alternation with a conceptual cognition of difference—because it always arises in a non-differentiated form—is the nature of the substratum (*dharmirūpa*). Even though there is no multiplicity in its basis, because the difference produced by that [multiplicity] is not perceived, and because that which appears in worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is as good as real, it is the object of a single cognition as something "without difference. (401)

He provides an example of the cognition of recognition: "That very object which was perceived as having various parts is designated as being the same; even in that case, they acknowledge the operation of the universal-part. (402)

They say that even in the case of an object whose difference is well-known, when it is recognized as being "that very same thing," the operation belongs to the aspect of the universal (*jāti*). The expression regarding "parts" [of the universal] occurs because the universal attains identity with the individuals. Thus, the operation of the universal alone pertains to the cognition of recognition, not to the cognition of similarity. Wherever recognition arises from the superimposition of identity based on similarity, that is an error—just as in the case of hair that has been shaved off and grown back—and it is produced by the universal.
However, for distinct entities, recognition is based solely on their actual identity. (402)

For how can there be a contact with difference and non-difference regarding an object through cognition? To this he says: "In that case, the manifestation based on the aspect of the universal proceeds as non-different; the cognition based on the aspect of the individual arises there with distinction. (403)

Through the operation of the universal aspect, that which is of a single class is apprehended as non-different, [in the form] "this is indeed a cow. However, in that case, the cognition based on the individual form arises as characterized by difference. || 403 ||

Now he defines the cognition of similarity (sadṛśapratyaya): "An existent cause, which resides in one place and is endowed with both difference and non-difference, is nevertheless perceived in another place as if it were manifold. (404)
Having placed its foot upon the substrata, it then approaches that which is based upon them; this is designated by others as the "object of similarity" (sādṛśyasya viṣaya). || 405 ||

The "sign" (*nimitta*)—namely, the quality called "darkness" residing in another substrate, such as a knife—which is the cause of a similar cognition due to its inherent nature, exists primarily in that [other] substrate; yet, when it subsequently occurs in another locus, such as the quality of Devadatta, it is perceived as if through multiplicity or distinction, because it is delimited by that other substrate. However, the word [denotes it] non-differently (*abheda*) by virtue of its pervasive connection (*samanvaya*). Therefore, the meaning is that it is endowed with both difference and non-difference, being connected in the form of both universal and particular.

Thus, having placed its foot upon the qualities that serve as the substrata—that is, its own loci—and having produced a cognition of similarity based on them, [the universal] reaches the substance which is the substratum of that quality; through inherence-in-the-inherent (samavetasamavāya), it generates a cognition of similarity therein. Consequently, that substance which is the locus of the quality is the object of the similarity. The meaning is that the relationship of the standard of comparison and the object of comparison (upamānopameyabhāva) exists there, with similarity as its cause.

In this way, this similarity—arising from the coexistence of difference and non-difference—is distinct from the universal (*jāti*), which is of the nature of non-difference. Furthermore, the universal is not perceived elsewhere as a plurality, but rather precisely as a unity. And by means of this passage, the *Bhāṣya* statement, "Where there is some generality and some particularity," has been explained otherwise according to the opinion of certain [teachers].

For instance—the intended meaning is this: previously, it was held that the relationship of *upamāna* (the standard of comparison) and *upameya* (the object of comparison) occurs where there is some commonality (*sāmānya*) and some particularity (*viśeṣa*) in a substrate (*ādhāra*), because the state of being [commonality and particularity] is indicated by the two entities that possess it; thus, the relationship of *upamāna* and *upameya* exists therein. But here, when a causal condition (*nimitta*) characterized by both difference and non-difference exists, and a cognition appearing as commonality and particularity arises with respect to a substance (*dravya*), then, given that causal condition, the two substances become the *upamāna* and the *upameya*.

The meaning is that the similarity, which has that [object] as its cause, inheres there [in the cognition] through a mediated succession (*pāramparyeṇa*). Regarding this, there is another commentary: "Is this something that needs to be stated? No. How will it be understood if it is not stated? For [comparison] is indeed a means of valid cognition (*māna*)," and so forth. That has already been explained previously as having the nature of the definition of comparison (*upamāna*), because it is useful for the purpose of the sūtra. (404, 405)

Immediately following this is the commentary: "In that case, by this very same reason, for one who has definitely cognized a *gavaya* but has not yet cognized a cow, it would follow that he ought to perform [the act of comparison] thinking, 'The cow is like the *gavaya*. [To this the opponent replies: 'Certainly, it ought to be performed. By this, the lack of fixed status between the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object compared (*upameya*) is admitted. To explain this through an illustration, he says: "Just as the designation 'cause' (*kāraṇa*) applies to an entity that is dependent upon another, so too they declare that comparison (*upamāna*) is dependent upon the cognition of something else. (406)

The status of being a cause is dependent upon the effect; thus, although there is a dependence on another, there is no confusion regarding the relationship between cause and effect. For that which is an effect in relation to one thing is not itself the cause in relation to that same thing. Likewise, although the object of comparison (upameya) is unestablished and the standard of comparison (upamāna) is established, and they are designated in relation to one another, nevertheless, because there is no confusion between what is established and what is unestablished, there is no reversal of the relationship between the standard of comparison and the object of comparison. This is the meaning. || 406 ||
Right here is another illustration: just as the activities of teacher and disciple, father and son, time and so forth, are conventional transactions, so too is comparison based upon relativity.

A teacher is not a teacher in relation to another teacher; a student is not a student in relation to his own student; a father is not a father in relation to another father; and a son is not a son with respect to his own son. An action is to be accomplished in relation to its own specific means, for it is not [accomplished] in relation to another action. Likewise, a means is not [a means] merely in relation to its own means. As it has been said: "In that regard, an action is 'to be accomplished' (sādhya) in relation to that [agent] for whom it is unestablished (asiddha); but it is established (siddha) in relation to that [agent] for whom it is no longer 'to be accomplished.'"

Thus: An action of well-known duration is "time" (kāla) with respect to another action to be delimited, because it is the delimiting factor; however, it is not itself that which is to be delimited. By the inclusion of the word "etc. (ādi), there is a collection of relative relations such as the qualifier-qualified relationship (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyabhāva*). Similarly, for one to whom the *gavaya* is well known, that [animal] is the means of comparison (*upamāna*) for a forest-dweller, while the cow (*go*), being unknown, is the object of comparison (*upameya*); for the city-dweller, however, the reverse is the case.

For this very reason, it has been stated that because those possessed by desire are intent upon nourishing the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*), the face of a woman—being renowned for its preeminent qualities—serves as a point of comparison for the orb of the moon. || 407 ||

Following this, the commentary states: "What, then, is the example here? 'Śastrīśyāmā' (dark as a sword). But where does this word *śyāmā* (dark) apply? He says: 'To the sword. By what means, then, is Devadatta denoted? 'By the compound,' he says. This [verse] explains it: "If the quality of darkness (*śyāmatva*) resides in the object of comparison (*upamāna*), yet is employed in the compound (*vṛtti*), then the object of comparison (*upameya*), being external to that [compound], is denoted by the compound. (408)

Since another alternative will also be stated later, the word "if" (*ced*) indicates the acceptance of this particular position. If it is accepted that the quality of dark-blue (*śyāmatva*) resides in the *upamāna*—the sword—within the *vṛtti*, that is, the compound (*samāsa*), then, because the two constituent words (*varti-pada*) function as the *upamāna*, it follows that the *upameya* (the object of comparison), which is external to them and not grasped by them, is what is expressed by the compound. Consequently, even though this is a *tatpuruṣa* compound, it would have the meaning of the other member (*anyapadārtha*) as its predominant sense.

For there is no rule that the meaning of the final member (*uttarapada*) must be predominant [in all cases], as that would lead to the impossibility of analyzing the *nañ*-compound according to the three alternative positions (*pakṣatraya*). Nor does the indication of meaning follow the literal wording, since it merely restates a meaning already established in common usage. Thus, here, in accordance with the requirement for a coordinate compound (*samānādhikaraṇasamāsa*), even when the word *śyāmā* is used in coordination with the word *śastrī* within the compound, the understanding of the object of comparison (*upameya*) occurs; therefore, the determination is made on the basis of the predominance of the external referent (*anyapadārtha*).

If this is so, then since the predominance of the meaning of the other member (*anyapadārtha*) is established in a *bahuvrīhi* by this very same logic, what is the purpose of explicitly mentioning "the meaning of the other member"? True; however, not everything can be rejected, as one must follow actual usage. Therefore, it is appropriate to include the mention of "the meaning of the other member" in order to dispel the suspicion that the compound might be understood as referring to its own constituent member (*svapadārtha*), which is an internal factor (*antaraṅga*). Furthermore, because the *bahuvrīhi* is prescribed under the heading of "the remainder" (*śeṣa*), it is not sublated by that [other rule].

Otherwise, if it were designated as a *bahuvrīhi*, the word *śyāmā*—which denotes a quality (*guṇavacana*)—would have to be placed first because it functions as a qualifier. This difficulty is avoided by understanding that the established rule regarding the optionality (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*) applies here. As for the accent, it remains unchanged; even in this case of a *tatpuruṣa*, the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*) occurs precisely because it is based on a comparison (*upamāna*). Now, one might object: "In a *bahuvrīhi*, when the connection is 'one whose knife is dark' (*śastrī śyāmā yasya*), there would be no perception of comparison. This is not so.

In the expression *śastrī śyāmā yasyā devadattāyāḥ* ("Devadattā, whose knife is dark"), the *bahuvrīhi* compound is used in the sense of a general relationship. And a general [relationship] must reside in a specific instance. What, then, is the specific relationship here? Only the relation of "standard of comparison" (*upamāna*) and "object of comparison" (*upameya*) would be understood, as no other [relationship] is possible. Therefore, this is not the domain of the *bahuvrīhi* according to the rule concerning the "remainder" (*śeṣa*). Now, when the mention of the "remainder" is rejected on the grounds that "there is a fault in compounds with numerals, coreferential terms, and the negative particle (*nañ*"), how [is the case to be explained]?

Even then, according to the view that "after *kaḍāra*, [the compound] is posterior (*para*)," this *tatpuruṣa* occurs by virtue of the force of the specific rule; since this [compound] has no other scope, the restriction "only after" would be untenable. Even when the view is that "before *kaḍāra*, there is only one designation," even then, by means of this specific injunction, [the word]—relying on a particular [quality] such as similarity—denotes the object of comparison (*upameya*) by including similarity within itself, because the definition of the object of comparison would otherwise be inexplicable. For example, in the expression "Devadatta is like a sword-woman (*śastrī*) in her dark complexion," she is called "sword-woman-dark" (*śastrīśyāmā*).

In the sentence "Devadatta is like a sword-blade" (*śastrīva śyāmā devadattā*), because the word *śyāmā* (dark-complexioned) is capable of being connected with both [the object of comparison and the subject], when one is set aside, the other becomes the meaning of the sentence. However, in a compound (*samāsa*), since the context concerns terms in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*), the general term (*sāmānyavacana*) occurs only once and refers specifically to the object of comparison; thus, the object of comparison is described as the meaning of the compound. Therefore, he says: "in its specific application" (*viśiṣyavṛttau*). || 408 ||

Immediately following this, the commentary states: "If this is so, why is the suffix *ṭāp* not heard in the expression 'Devadatta is as dark as a sword' (*śastrīśyāmo devadattaḥ*)? He explains this as follows: "The word *śyāmā*, when ending in *ṭāp*, would indeed apply in such cases as [the name] Caitra; however, because there is no nominative case (*prathamā*) in the rule, *śyāmā* and the like cannot function as a subordinate member (*upasarjana*). (Verse 409)

When the word *śyāmā* (dark-complexioned) occurs in the feminine gender (*śastryām*), because words expressing qualities take the gender and number of their substratum, it functions as a feminine noun ending in *tāp*. Consequently, if this were to be expressed through a compound, the result would be *śastrīśyāmā caitraḥ*, where *caitra*—the object of comparison—is the subject. Furthermore, because the rule "with words expressing a common quality" (*sāmānyavacanaiḥ*) employs the third case ending, the requirement for being "first-named" (*prathamānirdiṣṭam*) is absent; thus, the technical designation of "subordinate member" (*upasarjana*) does not apply here, and the shortening of the vowel does not occur. However, when it functions as a term denoting the object of comparison, its [proper] gender is established.

Immediately following this, the Bhāṣya states: "The shortening of the *upasarjana* will occur here. In that context, in the absence of a nominative case indication, the status of being an *upasarjana* would apply by virtue of the rule "having a single case-ending" (*ekavibhakti*), or because it is non-primary (*apradhāna*) due to its etymological meaning. Accordingly, the subsequent objection in the Bhāṣya says: "If, then, such items are indeed *upasarjanas*, then in the cases of *tittirikalmāṣī* and *kumbhakapālalohinī*, the long vowel *ī*—which is the characteristic of a non-*upasarjana*—would not be obtained."

He explains this as follows: "Alternatively, because it has a single case-ending or because it is a subordinate element (*guṇa*), the feminine suffix would not be desired after *tittirikalmāṣī*. (410)

Even when the counter-correlative word (*pratiyogin*) is joined with various case-endings (*vibhakti*), that which possesses a non-different case-ending is called a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), as in the case of *Kauśāmbī* and similar examples. Here too, when a compound is to be formed, the analytical sentence (*prakriyāvākya*) serves as the locus; in that sentence, the word denoting the primary meaning of the other member (*anyapadārtha*) possesses multiple case-endings due to its involvement in various actions, whereas in relation to it, the word expressing the quality (*guṇavacana*) indeed possesses only a single case-ending. For even when the primary element is involved in various actions, the subordinate element does not deviate from its own essential nature.

And so, in the case of the *bahuvrīhi*, the statement that "the plural number [is used] for the sake of the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) because it does not have a single case-ending" has been rejected. In that context, it was based on the fact that the principal member—the word whose meaning is the referent of another word (*anyapadārtha*)—has various case-endings, whereas the word functioning as the subordinate member has a single case-ending. Likewise here too, there will be subordination (*upasarjanatva*) due to having a single case-ending. However, in other instances, such as in a coordinate compound (*samānādhikaraṇa-samāsa*), there is no undesirable consequence; for since the meaning of the final member is predominant, the meaning of the final member is the primary element (*guṇa*).

Nor is the application of technical designations (saṃjñā) fruitless when such worldly meanings are relied upon, because even a principal member may be made the object of a designation for the sake of its prior placement (pūrvanipāta). For example: *puruṣavyāghraḥ* (a tiger-like man), *pācakavṛndārikā* (a woman who is a cook), *pūrvakāyaḥ* (the front part of the body), and *ardhapippalī* (half a long pepper). In these cases, since the meaning of the first member (*pūrvapada*) is the principal element according to the rules of compounding (*samāsaśāstra*), the designation of "subordinate" (*upasarjana*)—due to its being indicated by the nominative case—is indeed fruitful.

Furthermore, because the treatise (*śāstra*) adopts both the artificial (*kṛtrima*) and the non-artificial (*akṛtrima*) based on the distinction of their respective domains (*viṣaya*), the worldly (*laukika*) subordinate element (*upasarjana*) is not adopted here. Consequently, there is no lack of fixed order regarding prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*). For instance, in the compound *rājño goḥ kṣīram* ("the milk of the king's cow"), since both [members] are in the genitive case according to the rules for compounds (*samāsaśāstra*), the designation of one as the subordinate element is established solely on the basis of its being etymologically meaningful (*anvarthatva*) due to that initial mention in the nominative.

And thus, although the status of *kauśāmbī* and so forth as *upasarjana* (subordinate element) is already established in a compound simply because they serve the purpose of another (*parārthatva*), the designation of *upasarjana* is nevertheless appropriate for the sake of establishing the artificiality (*kṛtrimatā*) of the "single case-ending" (*ekavibhakti*) rule and for the sake of ensuring their prior placement (*apūrvanipāta*). Even when there is both an artificial and a non-artificial [definition] of *upasarjana*, in the matter of prior placement, one must resort to the artificial one alone. When both are artificial, the determination is made by virtue of the term's etymological meaning (*anvarthatva*). However, in the rule prescribing the short vowel (*hrasva*), both are resorted to on the principle of pervasion (*vyāpti*).

By the rule "luk taddhitaluki," even though there is no mention of the feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) in the nominative case because it serves as the final member of a compound (*uttarapada*), it nonetheless possesses the status of a subordinate element (*upasarjana*) by virtue of qualifying the meaning of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*). Thus, in this context, the subordinate status of *śyāmā* and the like is established, and consequently, the short vowel is achieved.

Even though the referent of the other word—the object of comparison (upameya)—possesses various case-endings, its having a single case-ending is dependent upon that [object]; and since the standard of comparison (upamāna) exists for the sake of the object of comparison, it occupies a subordinate position (guṇabhāva). Thus, the alternative—that the quality of being subordinate (guṇatva) belongs here to "dark-complexioned" (śyāmā) and so forth in relation to the standard of comparison—must be justified. Otherwise, if subordination were dependent solely on the object of comparison, the alternative that there is a single case-ending by virtue of that [subordination] would not be tenable.

In this manner, even when the formation is short, the feminine suffix *ṅīp*—as prescribed by the rule "anyato ṅīp"—would not be intended in the case of *tittirikalmāṣī*. For if the feminine suffix were applied first, there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the word *kalmāṣī* and the masculine term *tittiri* used as a standard of comparison; therefore, without applying the feminine suffix beforehand, the compound is formed from the two constituent words based on their coreferentiality while they function as the standard of comparison.

Furthermore, since the object of comparison (*upameya*) in the compound is feminine, the suffix *ṅīṣ* would not apply because of the rule governing non-qualifiers (*anupasarjana*). This is because, in the compound *kalmāṣopamā*, the word *kalmāṣa* functions as a quality (*guṇa*) in relation to the object of comparison. Consequently, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* would result here instead. Similarly, in the case of *kumbhakapālalohinī*, the suffix *ṅīp*—prescribed by the rule "after a low-pitched [final vowel] denoting a color" (*varṇādanudāttāt*)—would not apply. This statement was made while provisionally accepting this undesirable consequence on the assumption that the word is a qualifier (*upasarjana*). However, in this context, its status as a qualifier is not logically tenable.

For when a rule concerning "short" [vowels] is possible for both the technical (kṛtrima) and the non-technical (laukika), it is proper to understand that very [technical term] is intended. In the rule *luk taddhitaluki*, because the technical [term] under discussion is impossible [there], one resorts to the non-technical, etymological sense by the force of its recurrence (*anuvṛtti*). Therefore, elsewhere, it is proper to rely solely on the non-technical. And here, there is no technical status. For the expression *ekavibhakti* is explained thus: the word *samāse* is a locative of support (*ādhāra-saptamī*), not a locative of domain (*viṣaya-saptamī*).

Therefore, [the definition of] an *upasarjana* applies only where there is a common substratum (*samānādhāra*) and a single case-ending (*ekavibhakti*), while the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) possesses various case-endings. In this context, since the word that serves as the counter-correlate within the compound lacks connection with a different case-ending—given that this is indeed a *samānādhikaraṇa-samāsa* (co-referential compound)—how could there be a connection with a different case-ending? For this very reason, the author of the *Bhāṣya* indicated his dissatisfaction with this [definition], stating: "But if, on the other hand, such items were truly *upasarjanas*..."

The meaning is that the designation of *upasarjana* (secondary member) is not applicable to such cases. Therefore, since there is an absence of *upasarjana*-status, the shortening [of the vowel] would not occur here; this remains established: "In words such as *caitra*, the word *śyāmā* would remain [unchanged] precisely because it ends in *ṭāp*. As for what was raised by some—namely, that even if the shortening of the *upasarjana* were to apply, the long vowel *ā* would recur due to the transfer of gender (*liṅga*) from the subsequent word according to the rule *paravalliṅgam*—that is untenable.

In the rule *dattā yavati*, since this is an extension of the term [ti], there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of a second occurrence of the word *ti*; that [objection] has been refuted, so how could there be a further consequence of the vowel *ā*? || 410 ||

Having accepted the status of being a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), the fault regarding the feminine suffix was stated. Having raised an objection there, he refutes it by showing the consequence of another fault: "Even if the *ṅīṣ* suffix were present due to the strength of the rule 'sati-śiṣṭa-balīyastva' (the later taught is stronger), the accent of the comparative would not occur; therefore, that which ends in a feminine suffix is compounded. (411)

Once the compound has been formed, because that [term] which denotes the object of comparison (*upameya*) is not a subordinate member (*anupasarjana*), the feminine suffix will arise from that compound as something external (*bahubhūta*). For words such as *tittiri*, *kalmāṣa*, *kumbhakapāla*, and *lohita* are conventional (*rūḍha*) designations for specific colors as integrated wholes. However, since the rule regarding the application of suffixes after a final element (*tadantavidhi*) is prohibited when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is accompanied by a governing term (such as *varṇa*), it is stated here—even while accepting that the feminine suffix arises from the whole—that it applies specifically to *kalmāṣa* and the others when they denote color.

For this very reason, he says: "even when *ṅīṣ* is present. Alternatively, the rule "from a non-derivative (*anupasarjana*)" has been explained as intended to apply the *tadanta*-vidhi (the rule that a suffix applies to a word ending in such a base) by means of the principal member. And here, according to the intention of the Bhāṣya, since there are no such items as derivatives (*upasarjana*), the feminine suffix arises from the compound through the *tadanta*-vidhi applied to the principal member denoting a color. Even so, the desired *prakṛtisvara* (original accentuation) of the first member, which begins with a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), would not occur here. For instance, once the compound is formed, the *prakṛtisvara* of the first member would apply only to that much [of the compound].

It has been stated that the inclusion of the word *pada* is for the purpose of defining a specific measure (of syllables), not for the purpose of including both *subanta* (nominal) and *tiṅanta* (verbal) forms. In that regard, if a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) were used, the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), being the "last remaining" (*satiśiṣṭa*), would override the original accent of the first member (*upamānapūrvapadaprakṛtisvara*). This same fault applies in the case of the suffix *ṅīṣ*; for in that case, since there is no udātta accent belonging to the suffix itself, the accent of the first member (the standard of comparison) alone remains. Therefore, it was specified as *ṅīṣi* (in the case of the suffix *ṅīṣ*).

Since there is thus a fault regarding the accent (*svaradoṣa*), therefore, when the compound has not yet been formed, one should first form the feminine suffix and then form the compound of that word ending in the suffix—which is now a general term—with the standard of comparison (*upamāna*). This being so, because it is "taught later" (*atiśiṣṭatva*), the desired accent of the standard of comparison itself is established. However, this is not obtained when the general term occurs in composition with the standard of comparison; for, due to its coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a masculine *tittiri* or a neuter *kumbhakapāla*, the feminine suffix would not arise. Thus, this is the fault when the general term occurs in composition with the standard of comparison. (411)

Furthermore: "Nor can dependence be postulated when the standard of comparison resides in a subordinate quality; likewise, there would be no observation of gender [variation] in cases such as 'vyāghra' (tiger-man) if it were merely a subordinate element. (412)

In the compound *puruṣavyāghra* ("tiger-like man"), meaning "this man is as brave as a tiger," the rule *upamitam vyāghrādibhiḥ sāmānyāprayoge* (Pāṇini 2.1.56) applies. According to this rule, when a word expressing a common quality—such as "brave"—is not used, a comparison may be compounded with words like "tiger. However, if the word expressing the common quality were actually employed, the compound would not occur because of a lack of syntactic capacity (*asāmarthya*), since the primary term would then be dependent upon that quality-word. Therefore, what purpose is served by the phrase "when the common quality is not used"? It serves to indicate that a compound can indeed occur even when the principal member is dependent; this is established as an observation of a linguistic indicator (*liṅgadarśana*).

Furthermore, if this [term] referred to a quality (*guṇa*)—a general property such as courage residing in the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) like a tiger—then the principal entity (*pradhāna*), such as a man, would not be dependent upon it; for it is the subsequent subordinate element (*upasarjana*) that is dependent on the former. Thus, the intended meaning could not be conveyed. Indeed, this indicator is appropriate when the quality resides in the object of comparison (*upameya*), not when it resides in the standard of comparison (*upamāna*). Therefore, even by considering other passages, it is not logical for a word expressing a quality to reside in the standard of comparison. (412)

He states the following to conclude that this position—namely, that the justification for the short vowel [of *prātipadika*] on the grounds of its being a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) is untenable—is to be rejected: "Therefore, even though it possesses the status of a subordinate member (*guṇatva*), it maintains primacy (*prādhānya*) in another grammatical analysis (*vigraha*). A subordinate member (*upasarjana*) of such a nature does not exist within the technical rules of the science (*śāstra*). (413)

Because that which resides in the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) serves as an adjective for the object of comparison (*upameya*), although it lacks primacy [in the compound], qualities such as "dark" (*śyāma*) possess primacy in other analytical sentences (*vigraha*). When the quality resides in the object of comparison, then the sentence is as follows: for instance, in the sentence "Devadatta is dark like a female sword-bearer" (*śastrīva devadattā śyāmā*), the quality "dark" residing in the object of comparison possesses primacy. Furthermore, even though it resides in the standard of comparison, because the object of comparison is expressed by the compound, the quality is in fact primary; its status as a subordinate element (*guṇatva*) is merely relative to the analytical sentence (*prakriyāvākya*).

And thus, in reality, such a thing as the *pradhāna* cannot logically be a subordinate (*upasarjana*) even in the technical treatise (*śāstra*). For even when there is a difference in grammatical operation (*prakriyā*), the worldly meaning must be followed by the treatise. And in the world, this [thing] is indeed the principal; therefore, even though it is expressed at the end [of a compound], it possesses no subordination in the treatise, which merely restates meanings already established in the world. It is for this very reason that it was stated that the disapproval [of the view] was indicated in the *Bhāṣya* by the remark: "Even those of this kind are subordinate. (413)

Having thus stated that it is untenable for a word denoting a quality (*guṇavacana*) to function as a term of comparison (*upamānavṛttitva*), the Bhāṣya immediately thereafter declares: "In that case, the word *śastrī* (knife) applies only to the knife, while the word *śyāma* (dark) applies to Devadatta; thus, its application to the object of comparison (*upameyavṛttitva*) is explained. However, an objection is raised here: "Even so, the quality remains unspecified. Furthermore, there are many qualities in the knife, such as being sharp and very soft."

Since the word expressing the common attribute (sāmānyavacana) applies to the object of comparison (upameya), it is established that it assumes its gender accordingly; thus, the predominance of the meaning of the final member (uttarapadārthaprādhānya) is maintained as the primary principle.

However, in the expression *śastrīva śyāmā devadattā* ("Devadattā is dark like a knife"), because the object of comparison (*upameya*) is indicated as being characterized by the quality of darkness (*śyāma*), and because that specific quality residing in the standard of comparison (*upamāna*)—which is restricted [to the knife]—is not touched upon by the word *strī* (which denotes a meaning qualified by gender), there would be no communication of the specific property that serves as the cause for the simile; such is the meaning of the *Bhāṣya*. Regarding this, the *Bhāṣya* provides the following resolution: "Even when a quality is not explicitly mentioned, it is understood in common usage."

He explains this as follows: "That which exists in the subject of comparison (upameya), such as the dark [complexion], is explicitly denoted; that which is not specified among the objects of comparison (upamāna) is understood through the force of implication. (414)

Although the common attribute, such as "darkness" (*śyāma*), residing in the object of comparison (*upameya*), is expressed by its own word, and because of the single act of denotation (*sakṛd-abhidhā-vyāpāra*) of the word, that [attribute] is already exhausted; nevertheless, since another common attribute is not heard in the comparison (*ūmāna*), and because of proximity and the presence of an expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*), a connection is postulated with the very one that is heard. For it is logical that a connection with what is heard takes precedence over the postulation of what is unheard. || 414 ||

Right here is the illustrative commentary: "For example—'Devadatta has a moon-like face. And there are many qualities in the moon; that which is its pleasant appearance is what is understood. This he explains: "Even when only the substance is indicated, as in 'moon-faced,' what is understood is a specific quality residing in the moon, and not [qualities such as] eclipses and the like. (415)

In the expression "moon-faced" (*candramukhī*), even though only the substance serving as the standard of comparison is mentioned without an explicit common property, the shared attribute—which is the cause for the cognition of the comparison—is understood to be [the face's] being a source of delight and so forth; however, other lunar attributes such as *upaplava* and the like are not [intended]. *Upaplava* refers to the stain called the hare (*śaśa*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the conjunction with waxing and waning is included. Others, however, explain that *upaplava* refers to the conjunction with waxing and waning or its state of constant motion, while by the word "and so forth," they include [attributes] such as having the mark of a hare (*śaśalāñchana*).

And thus, where a quality not explicitly mentioned is understood as a distinguished ground for comparison based on common renown, how could that which is heard in one instance not be understood in the other through the force of implication? Therefore, the element of excellence (*atiśaya*) is implicitly contained within the *nidarśana*. || 415 ||

Thus, this is the position that the word expressing the common property resides in the object of comparison (*upameya*). And it is in this context of grammatical analysis (*prakriyā*) that this diversity is elaborated. But in ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), the worldly word such as *śastrīśyāmā* ("dark like a female sword-bearer") is an indivisible (*akhaṇḍa*) expression denoting a qualified object of comparison; thus he says: "And by means of the conceptualization of difference (*bhedabhāvanayā*), even in a compound this [word] is described [as follows]: another word is employed to denote an object distinguished by its specific qualities. (416)

When the general term functions as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), there is one sentence; when it functions as the object of comparison (*upameya*), however, there is a second. Through the latent impression (*vāsanā*)—the mental trace deposited by the experience that such a distinction or multiplicity constitutes the meaning of the standard of comparison and the meaning of the object of comparison—one determines that the function [of the word] has the same meaning as the sentence. Consequently, even in that case, it is stated that the general term expresses the meanings of both the standard of comparison and the object of comparison.

However, when the object of comparison (upameya) is qualified by qualities such as "dark" which possess a distinction imposed by the standard of comparison (upamāna), a compound word that is indivisible (*niraṃśa*) is uttered as something entirely distinct from the sentence. The conceptualization of the means for its grammatical analysis (*anvākhyāna*) must be performed in accordance with the rules of derivation (*prakriyā*), so that no other collection of faults arises; thus, it is established that the general term functions as a modifier of the object of comparison. For in this way, the form *śastrīśyāmo devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta is dark like a sword") is successfully derived, and the desired feminine suffix in *tittirikalmāṣī* ("speckled like a partridge") is obtained. || 416 ||

Regarding this position as well, an objection is stated in the Bhāṣya: "Even so, since the term 'by way of grammatical coreferentiality' (sāmānādhikaraṇena) continues to apply, a compound of non-coreferential terms would not be obtained. The meaning is that if the word *śyāmā* functions as the substratum of the object of comparison (*upameya*), it lacks coreferentiality with the word *śastrī*, and thus the section on coreferential compounds would not be applicable. To this, the resolution is stated: "For what reason would it not occur by virtue of a specific rule? (vacanāt).

The intention of the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra) is that, elsewhere, because its purpose has been fulfilled, the context (*prakaraṇa*)—being weaker due to its lack of fulfillment—is sublated by the direct statement (*śruti*). Now, one might object: "If [the word] functions as a comparison, there is scope for the general statement; thus, the context is also favored. This is not so. When explaining a word that functions with a specific meaning, one must not resort to an isolated (*apoddhāra*) word-meaning if it leads to the collapse of the grammatical system (*śāstraprakriyā*).

Furthermore, when the object of comparison (*upamānaviṣaya*) is expressed by a general term (*sāmānyavacana*), since both words are subordinate with respect to the object of comparison (*upameya*), there would be no formation of the compound due to a lack of semantic capacity (*asāmarthya*) arising from mutual dependence. However, when the term refers to the object of comparison, the relationship, having both as its locus in close proximity, exists without expectancy. Thus, because there is semantic capacity, the rule prescribes the formation of the compound even for terms in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇa*), as they possess the power of indication (*gamakatva*). Therefore, the subsequent Bhāṣya states: "Even though [the compound] might occur by virtue of the explicit statement (*vacana*)."

"But here, indeed, [the word] *mṛgacapalā* means 'fickle like a doe'; since it is characterized by having a common substratum (*samānādhikaraṇa*), the masculine substitution (*puṃvadbhāva*) does not apply. He explains that very point: "If [the compound] were understood according to the statement as having different substrata (*bhinnādhikaraṇa*), then in the case of 'fickle like a doe' (*mṛgīva capalā*), the masculine substitution would not be established. (417)

If, by the force of the statement, this compound were to be prescribed even for two words in different grammatical cases (*vyadhikaraṇa*), disregarding the topical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), then in the case of *mṛgacapalā*, the masculine-like substitution (*puṃvadbhāva*)—which relies on a *karmadhāraya* compound and finds its application elsewhere in the case of coreferential words—would not occur.

Regarding this, he anticipates a solution—though not stated in the Bhāṣya because it has been mentioned in another section—by saying: "But the masculine form (puṃvadbhāva) will occur because the preceding word is not feminine; likewise in cases such as *mṛgadugdha* and so on, provided that the feminine meaning is not intended to be expressed. (418)

In the case of an injunction (*codanā*) intended to exclude other species, the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) applies to terms such as *mṛgakṣīra* ("deer-milk"), and its result—the use of the word *pum-artha* ("masculine meaning")—is established; thus, the application of the masculine form was rejected by the rule: "Or rather not, because the preceding non-feminine term is intended [to denote the genus]. Likewise here, in cases such as *mṛgacapalā*, since the fickleness belonging to the deer-species is intended, the analysis is simply "fickle like a deer" (*mṛga iva capalā*); thus, when femininity is not intended, the desired result is established.

For instance—even if the masculine substitution (*puṃvadbhāva*) were applied, since femininity is not conveyed by the word, it must be concluded that it was simply not intended to be expressed. For that alone is the intended meaning which is conveyed by the word. However, when there is an intention to express femininity because the comparison with a woman is appropriate for a specific kind of feminine fickleness, then the masculine substitution must indeed be applied here. And once that has been applied, it must be stated that femininity is included within the compound (*vṛtti*).

For this very reason, it was suspected that this rebuttal is merely optional, on the grounds that the meaning of "female" (*strī*) is not intended to be expressed; and with this same intention, it was not set forth in the Bhāṣya.

For this very reason, immediately following this, the commentary (*bhāṣya*) relies on the faultless position: "If that is so, then both [qualities] reside in that very [single entity]. This it explains: "Just as in the expression 'the dark woman with a sword,' Devadatta alone is being described; therefore, in the analysis of the compound (*śāstravigraha*), it is said that both [qualities] reside in that very [entity]. (419)

In this case, regarding the occurrence of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), it has been stated that when there is a word expressing a common property (*sāmānyavacana*), the object of comparison (*upameya*) must be explicitly expressed. Thus, in this sentence, let the occurrence of both words [the standard and the common property] reside in the object of comparison itself. For instance, by metaphorical transfer (*upacāra*), Devadattā is called "śastrī" (knife-like), as if she were a knife. Therefore, since both the word for the standard of comparison and the word for the common property reside in that very object of comparison, Devadattā, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is established, and the rule for masculine substitution (*puṃvadbhāva*) is thereby accomplished. Furthermore, the context remains uncontradicted.

And by internalizing the relationship with the object of comparison, the word *śastrī* (knife) is applied to Devadattā; this is understood through the superimposition of identity (*abheda-adhyāsa*). The employment of a word for the sake of another is appropriate only when its meaning is implicitly included, and not otherwise—as in such cases as "The boy is a lion" and so forth. Furthermore, we observe linguistic usage with metaphorical words, such as "Teach the lion," where the term is used figuratively. In the same way, here too, Devadattā herself is designated by the word *śastrī*.

And this [distinction] is stated in a sentence occurring within the analytical exposition (*vigraha*) of the treatise or within the formal derivation (*prakriyā*) of the treatise, as both [aspects] reside in that very [sentence]. For it is in the state of the sentence that this is asserted for the sake of establishing grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). And therein, in the formal derivation of the treatise, there is the apprehension of various distinct meanings through the method of abstraction (*apoddhāra*). However, in the case of a worldly word (*laukika-pada*), which expresses a qualified meaning and is partless, there is no division; therefore, there is no occasion for this presentation.

For in that case, since the division into words is as unreal as the phonemes themselves, there is neither any word "teacher" nor any referent for it; thus, the intention is that one could not describe anything as having a figurative meaning. || 419 ||

This very position is established as the final doctrine (*siddhānta*) in the Bhāṣya. For immediately thereafter, the Bhāṣya states: "And this is logical here: that both [the masculine form and the feminine suffix] reside in that very [feminine base]. Otherwise, there would be a great deal to depend upon. He explains this [verse]: "For the sake of establishing the masculine-like form (*puṃvadbhāva*) and [the retention of] the feminine suffix in certain cases, there must be a great deal to depend upon; therefore, both are taught in that [base]. (420)

When the position is taken that the word *śyāmā* occurs in the sense of the object of comparison (*upameya*), then in this view, because there is a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), one must rely on a restrictive rule regarding the non-feminine nature of the prior member in order to establish the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) even within the compound—this being necessitated by the force of the specific statement [in the rule]. One must follow the principle that, as in the case of *mṛgakṣīra* ("deer-milk") and similar examples, here in *mṛgacapalā* and so forth, it is the general property alone that is intended to be expressed, not the specific individual. Since this restrictive rule of intention (*vivakṣāniyama*) is not explicitly stated in the words [of the rule] and must be inferred here, it causes cognitive complexity; thus, there is a great deal of dependence [on unstated factors] in this case.

However, when the position is taken that *śyāmā* is the object of comparison (*upamāna*) in the compound *śastrī-śyāmā*, then—since the shortening of the *upasarjana* would already be established by the rule for *śastrī-śyāmo devadattaḥ*—it must be stated that in cases such as *tittiri-kalmāṣī*, the desired feminine suffix is achieved because these [words] denote a specific color as a whole and are not *upasarjana*s; thus, by the principle of "extension to what ends with [the word]" (*tadanta-vidhi*) based on the principal member, the suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs outside the compound.

And thus, the fault regarding the accent (*svara*) is something that must be considered extensively here; since much needs to be considered regarding these two positions, the meaning is that the *Bhāṣya* accepts precisely that [view] which expresses both the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*). || 420 ||

Since the feminine suffix desired for words such as *kalmāṣī* (speckled) is established even before compounding—because it functions as the object of comparison—and since the gender residing in the object of comparison is established accordingly, [the author] explains here that this [type of simile] requires much more by means of another method: "Just as one says, 'The woman is dark like a knife,' or 'She is like a dark knife,' in those cases the word 'dark' (*śyāmā*) is required for both the object of comparison and the other [the standard of comparison]. (421)

In the phrase *śyāmā śastrī yathā* ("like a dark-complexioned girl"), the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) for the word *śyāmā* is shown when it functions as the object of comparison (*upameyavṛtti*). In the phrase *śyāmā śastrīkalpā* ("a girl resembling a dark-complexioned one"), the analytical sentence for the word *śyāmā* is [shown] when it functions as the standard of comparison (*upamānavṛtti*). In this regard, some say that when a quality residing in one [entity] is expressed, its existence in the other is conceived through implication (*sāmarthyāt*), because the similarity of attributes necessitates the proximity of the standard and the object of comparison; thus, although the common attribute is heard in only one place, it is inferred in the other, which constitutes a state of "dependence on much" (*bahvapekṣatva*).

This has been stated in the Bhāṣya: "If the analysis [of the compound] is made thus—'Devadatta is dark like a knife' (śastrīva śyāmā devadattā)—then 'darkness in the knife' would be what is required [as the object of comparison]. Or, if the analysis is made thus—'Just as a knife is dark, so is this Devadatta'—even then, 'darkness in Devadatta' would be what is required. (421)

[Objection: Surely, since the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) must be shown to conform to the worldly meaning, the word *śyāmā* should be employed in the sentence in both cases. However, in the compound (*vṛtti*), because the second occurrence of the word *śyāmā* is included within it, it is not used; so how can it be said that much [of the meaning] is expected? To this, he says: "Now, when it is used as 'the dark one is like a knife' (*śyāmeva śastrīva śyāmā*), only this much is understood: 'this [woman] is dark just like a knife. (422)

Just as in the case of "The knife is dark" and "This Devadattā is dark," when two instances of the word *śyāmā* (dark) are employed—one residing in the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the other in the object of comparison itself (*upameya*)—as in "As this [knife] is dark, so is she," when the word *śyāmā* is used only once, the object is understood to possess exactly that same magnitude. || 422 ||

For instance: "If the scriptural mention of this quality were intended merely as an indicator, then even though it is heard separately from the two [the substance and the action], it would not express the desired meaning. (423)

If the word "quality" (*guṇa*) were employed merely to indicate the substance itself, then even when used repeatedly, it would not convey the intended simile. For there is the cognition that "the knife, which is characterized by the quality of blackness, serves as the differentiator of Devadattā who is likewise [black] through another property (*dharmāntara*). Thus, the basis for the simile would not necessarily be understood from the word as heard, even if it were used repeatedly. (423)

Now, regarding the presence of activity in the simile, if it is here that the heard [word] possesses such activity—namely, when the qualities possess activity in the communication of that which is the expressed object of comparison (upameya)—then there is the statement of everything upon a single hearing. (424)

When the qualities (*guṇa*) are employed for the purpose of making known the specific form of that which is to be compared—the *upameya*—which is the primary object to be expressed or denoted through the relation of comparison (*upamāna*), then even if only one quality is used, the communication of all the qualities of the *upamāna* occurs by implication; thus, a twofold mention is not required. For the quality is introduced in order to restrict the relation by means of delimiting the similarity (*sādṛśya*), so that there may be comprehension of the intended meaning exactly as it was meant to be conveyed.

Thus, whether the word expressing the common property functions with respect to the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) or the object of comparison (*upameya*), because it requires the other [term] to be understood through implication, there is much that must be expected. Therefore, the author of the *Bhāṣya* has established this very position as the final conclusion: "In that [compound], both [the standard and the object of comparison] reside. (424)

After this, the author of the Vākyapadīya recited: "In a compound involving comparison (*upamāna-samāsa*), because the word expressing the quality (*guṇavacana*) possesses a specific [quality], there is no established usage of a word expressing the general. He explains this as follows: "Established in a particular through the distinction between the mode (*prakāra*) and the substratum (*ādhāra*), how could a word be expressive of the general when it is connected with another word? (425)

Although it was previously established through the statement "stating a common property" (*sādhāraṇaṃ bruvan dharmaṃ*) and so forth that [the word] possesses a general denotation (*sāmānyavacanatva*), this objection is nonetheless justified: since the quality (*guṇa*) is here stated as residing either in the object of comparison (*upameya*) or in the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), how can there be commonality when one of the two is excluded? For indeed, if the mere quality were expressed by abstracting from its substratum, there would be a general denotation due to the delimitation by an unrestricted substratum.

At that time, this quality (*guṇa*), being denoted in its own primary capacity within the simile (*upamā*), is possessed of function; however, it is connected with another property (*dharma*) which serves as the ground for the comparison. As it has been said: "The common property (*dharma*) is 'dark-complexioned' (*śyāma*) and so forth," and so on. Even when there is a superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of identity based on the ground of a common quality, there is no employment of a word expressing generality (*sāmānya-vacana*) at all. But when, through metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) or by the elision of the possessive suffix (*matub-lopa*), the word expressing the quality functions in grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with the substance (*dravya*), then this is a *samānādhikaraṇa* compound.

A "universal" (*sāmānya*) is a common property (*dharma*), a quality (*guṇa*); having stated that, it is said that a word which applies to that which possesses such a quality is a "denoter of a universal. In that case, because of its connection with a specific substratum, the quality is indeed qualified by that particularity, either through the distinction of the substratum itself or through the distinction from other related properties and so forth. As it has been said: "The distinction of qualities [from one another] arises from their substrata, not inherently," and so on.

Although it has been stated that what is heard in one place may be understood in another through implication (*sāmarthya*), nevertheless, because of the mention of "utterance" (*vacana*), what is intended here is commonality by way of the function of denotation (*abhidhā-vyāpāra*), and not by way of direct statement (*śruti*) or meaning (*artha*). Furthermore, even when the word *śyāmā* conveys merely a quality, its application is restricted to a specific [meaning]—namely, a woman—either through connection with another word expressing a standard of comparison (*upamāna*) or through its fixed usage. Now, one might object: "But this sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) does not obstruct the grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the individual words. This is not so.

Since the word "functioning" (*vṛtti*), whose internal distinctions have been discarded, is that which is to be explained [grammatically], when the division into a preceding member and a succeeding member is made, the meaning of the extracted words (*apoddhāra-pada*) must be divided precisely according to the meaning of that [whole]. In that case, it is logical that the word *śyāma* itself, which denotes a qualified object, should be divided; how, then, could it be said to denote a universal? (425)

To this, the rebuttal is as follows: Some maintain that the universal (*sāmānya*) is merely similarity residing in two [objects]; or rather, it is intended as a quality (*guṇa*) that, despite the difference [between the objects], functions in both by way of non-difference. (426)

Either the operation of the generic portion or that of the two substances is intended to be expressed; or, it has been stated previously that the word denotes the universal by virtue of its form even before the application [of the name]. (427)

In this context, by the term "universal" (*sāmānya*), what is intended is merely a similarity residing in both [the object of comparison and the standard of comparison]. And similarity occurs only through the relation of difference-cum-identity (*bhedābheda*). Thus, even when it is expressed as residing in one [of the two], because it depends upon the other, its status as residing in both is understood from the very operation of the denotation itself; therefore, its character as a "universal" is logically established. Here, the quality (*guṇa*) alone—though qualified by its mode and substrate—is intended, without distinction, as residing in both the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), being set apart [from other qualities] within the simile.

The meaning of the term "denoting a universal" (*sāmānyavacana*) is that which is intended to be made known [by the word]. Thus, similarity is simply a quality (*guṇa*) expressed through a form that possesses positive concomitance (*anvayin*); it is not a separate entity from that [quality]. This very point has been stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "It is not necessarily only that which expresses the universal of many things that is 'denoting a universal'; even that which expresses the universal of two things is also 'denoting a universal'."

As for what was stated by the author of the *Vākya*—namely, "Or rather, because blackness exists in both [places] and because the word denotes that [quality], there is the established usage of the term as a general expression"—he explains that with the words beginning, "The function of the class-part... and so forth. What is intended by the term "general expression" (*sāmānyavacana*) is the communication of the relationship of similarity between two substances characterized as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), by means of the function of the class of qualities (*guṇajāti*) which effects the cognition of non-difference between those qualities.

Although it has been stated that a quality-universal (*guṇajāti*), because it inheres in its own specific substratum and is non-different from it, is not useful for comparison (*upamā*), nevertheless, through the coloring of subtle particularities residing in its own substrate, it attains the nature of a subordinate universal (*avāntarasāmānya*) and becomes useful for comparison as denoted by the word "likeness" (*sādṛśya*). Thus, the word expressing the commonality (*sāmānyavacanaśabda*) denotes the quality of blackness—which has had its difference removed by the universal and which inheres in both the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*). As it is said: "The status of being a denoter of a commonality [arises] from form."

The meaning is that the status of being a word denoting a universal (*sāmānyavacanatā*) is established for a word such as *śyāma* when it conveys a quality residing in both the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), which—due to the entry of a common form (*rūpasāmānyāveśa*)—is perceived as non-different. Furthermore, because of the metaphorical treatment of non-difference (*abhedopacāra*), the word here functions with respect to the two substances; thus he says "of the two substances. This alternative resolution is clearly stated in the Bhāṣya: "Or rather, it is said 'by words denoting universals'."

"Every word, when connected with another word, becomes expressive of a specific [meaning]; therefore, we shall understand that it is 'expressive of the general' prior to such connection. He states this very point: "Or rather, it was exemplified prior to its application. By the term *abhisambandha* (connection), a compound (*samāsa*) is intended, in which meanings are connected through mutual orientation and intermingling of their respective forms; for in that state, the meanings are indivisible.

Just as the linguistic usage of rules such as *viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa*, *dvitīyā śritādibhiḥ samānādhikaraṇena*, and *ardhaṃ napuṃsakam* is resorted to by virtue of the conceptualization of difference existing within the sentence, so too is the usage of generality [resorted to]. For instance, although there is a difference between a compound (*vṛtti*) and a sentence (*vākya*) due to their having respectively combined and uncombined meanings, the designation of non-difference is possible because of the similarity of form; thus, the grammatical derivation (*anvākhyāna*) of the compound by means of the properties belonging to the sentence is indeed justified through the conceptualization of word-meanings derived via analytical abstraction (*apoddhāra*).

Furthermore, although in a compound the general term (*sāmānya*) is already restricted to the object of comparison (*upameya*), its status as a general term remains possible because, prior to that, when it is employed in a sentence where words convey distinct meanings, there is no restriction to a specific [object]. Alternatively, the designation "general-term" (*sāmānyavacana*) is understood as one that has expressed a generality; thus, the status of being a general term observed during the state of the sentence is relied upon by way of its prior existence (*bhūtapūrvagati*). Just as the word *śastrī*, although it refers to the object of comparison in a compound, is considered to denote the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) by virtue of its prior usage, so too is all that is desired established.

Now, the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *upamitaṃ vyāghrādibhiḥ* is examined. For instance, in that context, it is stated that the general term must not be employed so that a compound such as *puruṣo 'yaṃ vyāghra iva śūraḥ* ("this man is a tiger-like hero")—where the word *śūra* (hero) would otherwise be used—does not occur. However, in this case, because the meanings of the preceding and following members are respectively the object of comparison (*upameya*) and the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), they are distinct; thus, due to their lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), the formation of the compound does not take place anyway.

If this is so, then how is there grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) even in the primary example "puruṣavyāghra" (man-tiger)? To this he says: "When the word 'tiger' stands for the meaning of 'man' by virtue of [the man's] heroism, then, because of the non-difference of the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*), the formation of the compound is possible. (428)

When words such as *vyāghra* (tiger), which denote a standard of comparison, come to function as attributes of the object of comparison (*upameya*) through the superimposition of identity—by virtue of being included within other qualities such as bravery that are common to both—then, because they possess a common referent, the formation of a compound governed by the rules for co-ordinate (*samānādhikaraṇa*) compounds is justified, as in *puruṣavyāghra* (tiger among men) and *puruṣasiṃha* (lion among men). And in these cases, because the common property is already included [within the meaning of the compound], it is not explicitly stated. || 428 ||

But when that [word] is employed—namely, when the word "hero" (śūra) is used—the word "tiger" (vyāghra) resides in the animal; since they function with different substrates, there is no possibility of their co-occurrence there. (429)
