When the common attribute residing in the object of comparison (*upameya*) is denoted by its own word, the word *vyāghra* (tiger) functions as a denoter (*vācaka*) in its own primary sense (*svārtha*) as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), and not in the sense of the object of comparison, the man; for since the relation of difference is manifested by words such as *iva*, it cannot be joined with [the object] through non-difference (*abheda*). And thus, because they would have different substrata (*bhinnādhikaraṇatva*), the compound belonging to the context (*prākaraṇika*) would not be applicable; what, then, is the purpose of the prohibition? This is the meaning. || 429 ||

He supports this point: "Even though there is grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), because a distinction of qualities is possible, the application of the word 'hero' (śūra) persists even in a compound. (430)

Even when the word "tiger" (*vyāghra*) is applied to a man by including [his qualities] within those of equal quality, the word "hero" (*śūra*) would still be employed in order to specify the particular common attribute. Otherwise, because grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) would otherwise be inexplicable, the quality that serves as the cause for superimposition is understood to be restricted. For instance, while there is a possibility of a difference in qualities in a tiger—such as the qualities of heroism, ferocity, and strength—it is determined that these qualities are included [in the man] due to their possibility [of being present].
And thus, even when the word *śūra* is used for the sake of restriction (*niyama*), the compound would still occur; therefore, this prohibition is purposeful. || 430 ||

One might object: "Is it not proclaimed that 'lion' and 'tiger' are used for praise, while 'dog' and 'crow' are used for censure? Thus, in expressions such as *puruṣavyāghra* (tiger among men) or *puruṣasiṃha* (lion among men), valor itself is the quality included for the sake of praise; so how can there be no fixed rule? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And that which is seen as a condition for praise, and those which are conditions for censure—because their causes are distinct, the repeated mention [of the word] is for the purpose of restriction. (431)

Because they are intent on the presentation of worship, those qualities that assist the object of comparison (*upameya*) are included by means of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*). These are numerous—such as "tiger" and so forth—and are found in various specific contexts. Consequently, since they are not necessarily understood from this general term alone, the word "hero" (*śūra*) and others must indeed be employed again for the purpose of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). Thus, there is a repetition of the word.

For example, in the case of *abhimanāyate*, *sumanāyate*, and *durmanāyate*, although the meanings of the prefixes *su*, *duḥ*, and *abhi* are already conveyed when they qualify the meaning of the suffix, their use with the suffix is justified for that purpose because the form *manāyate* is common to all of them; thus, even though the specific distinctions are not explicitly manifested, the usage occurs as a general form ending in that suffix. It is the same here.

Thus, even when used with the intent of conveying censure—as in the expression "puruṣavāka" (a man who speaks like a crow)—there are many grounds for censure, such as the crow's consumption of impure things and its instability; therefore, the repeated mention [of the word] serves as a restriction. Consequently, when a compound would otherwise be applicable according to the general rule, the prohibition is appropriate. In cases such as "candramukha" (moon-faced), it has been stated that a specific attribute is understood by virtue of conventional usage (*prasiddhi*). Here too, although a specific meaning may be understood through the force of context and so forth, when such context and the like are absent, the prohibition of compounding for a word used in its general sense is indeed justified. || 431 ||

Or what is the use here of supporting the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)? For instance: even when a general term is employed, because it lacks the capacity [to form a compound] due to being dependent on another, a compound would not otherwise apply; therefore, this was stated for the sake of providing an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that "a compound occurs even for a principal member when it is dependent. And thus, even though a compound would not apply through grammatical non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), this very indicator remains valid; so he says: "Or rather, even in the absence of a compound formation, this may serve as an indicative mark (*liṅga*); just as the rule 'not after *aci*' (Pāṇini 6.1.159) serves as an indicative mark for the inclusion of words like *bhṛśa* even in the absence of a suffix. (Verse 432)

Since there is no possibility of composition due to lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), and since composition is not otherwise applicable, this statement—"the non-employment of the general term"—would serve as an even stronger indicator (*liṅgadarśana*) [of the rule's existence]. It is not only because of a lack of semantic capacity (*asāmarthya*) due to mutual expectancy that composition is precluded, but also because of lack of coreferentiality. Furthermore, it is established by logic that a principal entity, being independent, can properly be connected with multiple qualifiers; for a subordinate element (*guṇa*), once controlled by one [principal], cannot be connected with another.

For in that case, it would indeed abandon its status as a subordinate quality (*guṇatva*). The connection of a principal element with many simultaneous benefactors is itself an ornament, because it nourishes its primacy; this is a scriptural indication (*liṅga*) regarding a matter established by logic. Furthermore, a scriptural indication is observed to be employed even when [the literal sense] is impossible, provided it is taken merely as a possibility.

For example: regarding the rule "bhṛśādibhyo bhuvyacveḥ" (Pāṇini 3.1.12), when the suffix *kyaṅ* is prescribed in the sense of "becoming" (*bhavati*), the suffix *cvī* is also applied in that very same sense of "becoming. Once *cvī* has been produced, since the meaning of "becoming" is already expressed by that [suffix], it would follow that *kyaṅ* should not be produced after words like *bhṛśa* ending in *cvī*. Nevertheless, the prohibition "except for *cvī*" (*acveḥ*) is formulated, anticipating such a possibility; this serves as an indicator (*liṅga*) that *kyaṅ* applies only in that specific sense where *cvī* applies. Thus, *kyaṅ* is established in the sense of "the becoming of what was not previously so" (*abhūtatadbhāva*). For instance, in the case of *abhṛśo...* [bhṛśo bhavati].

"It becomes intense" (*bhṛśo bhavati*) means "it becomes very much so" (*bhṛśāyate*). Similarly here as well, although a compound would not otherwise apply due to the difference in grammatical case (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), the prohibition [of the general term] by the phrase "the non-employment of the general term" (*sāmānyāprayoga*)—based on the possibility that it might otherwise apply—serves as an indicator (*liṅga*) for the principle that "a compound occurs even when the principal member is dependent. By this, forms such as *rājapuruṣaḥ śobhanaḥ* ("a beautiful king's man") are established. Furthermore, it has already been determined that in this context, the general term refers to the subordinate element (*aprādhānya*) when it resides in the object of comparison (*upameya*), and not otherwise. || 432 ||

Now, in connection with the topic of comparison (*upamāna*), he says that this other matter is being considered: "When a comparison is perceived within a sentence whose constituent parts end in the suffix *vati*, this grammatical rule regarding the application of that suffix is now examined. (433)

In such sentences as "he studies like a Brāhmaṇa," "he fights like a Kṣatriya," or "he acquires wealth like a Vaiśya"—which consist of a portion of a word ending in the suffix *vat*—the relationship characterized by the nature of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) is determined. For in these cases, a common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*), characterized by actions such as studying and so forth, is heard as residing in the object of comparison; its existence in the standard of comparison is understood by implication. Thus, there arises the comprehension of the similarity.

Regarding this comparison, the suffix *vati* is that which expresses it; the specific formulation of its rule, namely the statement "When there is equality with that [in respect] to an action, the suffix *vati* is used," is now examined. To explain: here, is the action indicated as the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), or is it indicated as the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*)?

Although [the suffix] is to be understood as expressing the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), there is no difference in the result because the relationship of standard of comparison and object compared (*upamānopameyabhāva*) is conditioned by the commonality of the property (*dharma*). Nevertheless, there is a purpose for this investigation: to determine which relative is logically appropriate in the action, and how the established status of the indicated meaning (*lakṣya*) is not rendered inconsistent. || 433 ||

Regarding this, the Bhāṣya states: "This is incorrect. What here is incorrect? That [the word] *kriyā* (action) should be that which is capable of being construed with the third case. What is the intention of the author of the Bhāṣya in this regard, such that he objects by accepting the position that the qualification belongs to the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*)—namely, that "the action is that which is capable of being construed with the third case"? To this, he says: "Although 'action' (*kriyā*) is an adventitious attribute (*upādhi*) because it is the primary [meaning] of the base-meaning, a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) cannot there be expressive of an action. (434)

The word *tena* is a case ending expressing capacity (*samarthavibhakti*), which is based on a specific semantic relation. For instance, in relation to the object of comparison (*upameya*), the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*)—characterized as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*)—is subordinate for the sake of assisting it; having thus adopted a distinction (*vyatireka*), it becomes fit for syntactic connection (*samanvaya*) with the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*) by means of this case ending expressing distinction (*vyatirekavibhakti*). Therefore, this is called a "case ending expressing capacity. Furthermore, since the capacity belongs to the meaning of the base in relation to the meaning of the suffix, this case ending belongs to the base (*prakṛti*).

The meaning of the suffix is "equal" (*tulya*), because that [quality] is determined as something not previously understood when the suffix is present. In this context, the qualifier "action" (*kriyā*), being mentioned, must be connected either with the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) or with the meaning of the suffix, due to its proximity. Furthermore, regarding the application of subordinate elements (*guṇa-viniyoga*) among word-meanings through direct statement, indicative mark, syntactical connection, context, position, and name, here the determination is based on position (*sthāna*).

For instance: in the case of [the rule] *tena* occurring in the first position, since there is no purpose for its transposition, it is logical that *kriyā* (action) serves as its qualifier. For example: in *sāsya devatā*, *set* (that) has *devatā* (deity) as its qualifier; and in *tena raktaṃ rāgāt*, *tena* (by that) has *rāgāt* (from dyeing) as its qualifier. Here, the status of being a qualifier of the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) arises from the very mention of these five [categories], not by virtue of their positional strength.

Thus, although no one has stated here at the outset that "the third case-competent element is *kriyā* (action)," nevertheless, by the force of logic (*nyāyabala*), it is correct that the qualifier (*upādhi*) "action" belongs to the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) because of its primacy. This is expressed in the *Bhāṣya*: "When it is said 'that which is competent for the third case, provided it is an action,' [it means this]. Since this meaning arrived through logic must necessarily be accepted, it is designated in the *Bhāṣya* as being "stated" (*ucyate*) because of its suitability (*kalpatvāt*). In that context, the third case is prescribed after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) denoting an existent entity (*sattvavācin*).

And that [word *kriyā*] does not denote an action (*kriyā*), because an action, whose nature is being brought about (*sādhyamāna-rūpā*), is the exclusive domain of verbal suffixes (*tiṅanta*). Therefore, how can it serve as a qualifier for "the action" (*kriyā*) when it follows a word ending in the third case, since such a connection is impossible? This is the objection. || 434 ||

If it is argued that, by virtue of the power of its qualification, [the word] expresses an action and will therefore be in grammatical agreement with the third case, he says: "Whether it be a residual relation (*śeṣa*) for that which exists as a substance (*sattvavṛtta*), or even an instrument (*sādhana*), both of these do not apply here; because verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) do not denote substances. (435)

*Sat-tvam* (substance) is said to be that which is capable of being designated as "this" or "that," wherein genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*kriyā*) reside. In that context, there is a connection with the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that has occurred [in the sentence]. For instance—that referent of the nominal stem, because it is capable of receiving assistance from another, relies upon a case-ending that expresses it through a distinction produced by that assistance. And that distinction is a certain residual relation (*śeṣasambandha*) caused by the connection between action and its factors (*kāraka*). An example is: *adhyayanena vasati* ("He dwells for the sake of study").

"Stupid by reason of curds," "emaciated by reason of asceticism," and "a lineage by reason of wealth"—this is a causal relationship (*hetu-hetumadbhāva*), which is a type of residual relation (*śeṣasaṃbandha*). However, some maintain that the distinction (*vyatireka*) itself is simply a relationship between an action and its factor (*kriyākārakasaṃbandha*); in that case as well, the instrumental case occurs, as in "he cuts with a sickle" or "he chops with an axe," and so forth. Both of these uses of the instrumental are impossible for finite verbs (*tiṅ*) that express an action, because a verb is the expression of an action.

Furthermore, action (*kriyā*)—whose nature consists in the operation of the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), which is extended through its constituent parts, and which is yet to be accomplished (*sādhyā*) and thus distinct from substances whose nature is already established—is not the locus of the potencies that contribute to its accomplishment. Moreover, when established entities of an accomplished nature assist one another, their remaining relationship is brought about by the power of the means of accomplishment; it does not belong to action, which is of the nature of something yet to be accomplished. Therefore, the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) does not occur after a verb (*ākhyāta*) that expresses action.

The fact that a *tiṅ*-ending word is not a nominal stem (*aprātipadikatva*) has been left unstated here because the intention is to demonstrate the contradiction in its being capable of being construed with a third-case ending when it expresses an action; for the impossibility of a third case [occurring] with it is already established simply by the contradiction in meaning. And although, since the suffix *vat* is prescribed in the sense of "equality," a third case governed by that [suffix] would be expected here only in the domain of the "remainder" (*śeṣa*), nevertheless, in order to declare the total impossibility [of such a construction], the third case is introduced even in the context of an instrument (*sādhana*).

But is it not the case that, according to the rule *karaṇe ca stokālpakṛcchrakatipayasyāsattvavacanasya*, the status of being an instrument (*karaṇabhāva*) is stated even for words denoting things that are non-substantial (*asattvabhūta*)? Since the status of being an instrument would be untenable if [the word] were entirely non-substantial—because it could not function as a means toward an action—an expression denoting a mere property (*dharmamātra*) is intended here. For a mere property, when acting as a substance (*dravyāyamāṇa*), possesses the possibility of being an instrument because it is established in its own nature;
whereas an action, having its own essence unobtained due to its being something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), is in no way capable of assisting anything else. || 435 ||

In that case, one might argue that verbal derivatives such as *pāka* (cooking) will function as words denoting action when used with the third case-ending; to this he says: "Words such as *pāka* are not designated as 'action' when they end in the third case, because they possess the nature of a substance (*sattva*). This is just like [words] formed with suffixes having the sense of 'having done' (*kṛtvo'rtha*). (436)

Since suffixes such as *ghañ* are prescribed when the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) has reached the state of being accomplished (*siddhatā*), these [nominal stems] ending in such suffixes do not denote action; rather, because they are connected with the property of accomplishment—which is a property of a substance (*dravyadharma*)—they are not designated as verbs. Precisely for this reason, since they do not express action, their connection with gender and number is possible; thus it is said: "An action expressed by a *kṛt* suffix is like a substance" (*kṛdabhihito bhāvo dravyavat*). Furthermore, since the state of accomplishment is a property of action and does not itself become a substance, the term "like a substance" (*dravyavat*) is indicated by means of the suffix *-vat*.

Because the operation of the means (*sādhana*) has been withdrawn, the state of accomplishment (*siddhāvasthā*) is not an action (*kriyā*), since it lacks the quality of being something to be accomplished (*sādhyatva*); rather, it is designated as "having that [action] as its property" by virtue of the action that previously occurred. However, the state of being accomplished does not itself possess the state of being something to be accomplished, because of their contradiction and the impossibility of their coexistence. And this being the case, when suffixes such as *ghañ* are employed, those suffixes which are used to express the exclusion of action or the counting of actions do not occur; for example, *pañcakṛtvaḥ pākaḥ* ("cooking five times") and *dviḥ pākaḥ* ("cooking twice").

Therefore, the inclusion of the term "repetition" (*abhyāvṛtti*) is for the purpose of excluding such cases as "five cookings" (*pañca pākāḥ*). Otherwise, because of the apprehension of non-difference between the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*), there would be the possibility of counting the actions here [in the case of "five cookings"]. However, the connection [of the suffix] is with the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) by way of its repeated occurrence, which consists in its non-cessation (*avyāvṛtti*). And if that which is to be accomplished were denoted by the *ghañ* suffix and others, it too would be connected with suffixes whose objects are non-cessation; yet it is not so connected.

Therefore, in this context, regarding the scope of suffixes expressing frequency (kṛtvas-artha), just as it is determined that words such as *pāka* do not denote action precisely because those suffixes do not arise [after them], so too, in all cases, the absence of denoting action for these [words] is established by logic (*nyāyasiddha*). This is the meaning. || 436 ||

If that is so, then since the suffix *tumun* is prescribed in its own sense (*svārtha*), a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in it must denote an action. Consequently, in the expression "five times to go" (*pañcakṛtvo gantum*), the adverbial suffix expressing frequency (*kṛtvasuc*) would be attached to that which ends in *tumun*. Furthermore, suffixes such as *ktvā* and others, which are prescribed in the sense of *tumun*, also denote an object yet to be accomplished (*sādhya-artha*) and are thus fit to be joined with adverbial suffixes of frequency, as in "having eaten twice" (*dvirbhuktvā*). Anticipating this objection, he says: "And those certain indeclinable derivatives (*avyayakṛt*) which are endowed with the properties of action—their denotation of non-substance (*asattvābhidhāyitva*) is not distinguished from that of words ending in verbal suffixes (*tiṅantair na viśiṣyate*)."

The meaning of these indeclinables ending in *kṛt* suffixes is that which is in the state of being brought about (*bhāvyamāna-rūpa*); thus, they are equivalent to verbal roots (*ākhyāta*) and, for that very reason, are not joined with the third case. However, the nominative case is not contradictory here when used in the sense of the mere nominal stem (*prātipadika-artha-mātra*). || 437 ||

One might argue that it is logical for an action denoted by a *kṛtya* suffix to serve as the means (*sādhana*) for another action while existing in its own form, and thus be expressed by the instrumental case; to this he says: "Even in cases such as *śayitavya*, where there is an action that serves as the domain of the suffix *kṛtvasuc*, the relationship of standard of comparison and object of comparison (*upamāna-upameyatva*) is ultimately impossible even there. (438)

Regarding the statement "one must lie down five times," although words such as *śayitavya* express actions whose nature is yet to be accomplished (*sādhya-svabhāva-kriyā*)—as seen from the presence of the suffix denoting frequency (*kṛtvasuc*)—nevertheless, in this context, because the relationship of standard of comparison and object of comparison (*upamānopameya-bhāva*) is impossible, these words expressing action with the third case ending are not intended here as bases (*prakṛti*). Now, one might object: since the action to be accomplished is already conveyed by the verbal root (*dhātu*) itself, what other distinct action could be the meaning of the suffix in cases like *śayitavya*? Furthermore, these suffixes are not merely pleonastic (*svārthika*).

This is because [the suffixes] *kṛt*, *kt*, and those having the sense of *khala* are prescribed for the states of being (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*) by the rule "tayoreva kṛtyaktakhalarthāḥ. Herein it is explained: in this context, the verbal root denotes an action that delimits its means (*sādhana*) within the domain of *kṛt*-suffixes, characterized as a state yet to be realized (*bhāvyatva*) as perceived in a future condition, and not as characterized by a present state of being realized. Consequently, the state of being realized (*bhāvyatā*) of the present action is manifested through its connection with the means, which possesses its own operation as conveyed by the suffix.

For example, in the expression "Devadatta cooks" (*pacati devadatta*), the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) attains the status of being that which is to be brought about (*bhāvyatā*) due to its connection with the agent denoted by the *l*-suffix (*lakāra*). This is likewise the case in forms such as "cook" (*pācaka*). Similarly, in the expression "Devadatta is seated" (*āsyate devadattena*), the meaning of the verbal root experiences the status of being that which is to be brought about due to its connection with the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) denoted by the *l*-suffix; thus, there is a distinct "being" (*bhāva*) denoted by the *l*-suffix, and it is this very same [denotable] entity that persists in the case of gerunds (*kṛtya*) and the like. Even in instances such as "having done, one should lie down" (*kṛtvā śayitavyam*), since the suffix is prescribed in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāve*), this external "being" is what is denoted by the suffix. (438)

How is it that here there is an absolute impossibility of the relationship between the object of comparison and the standard of comparison? He says: "Neither a substance nor a quality alone, nor even that which possesses them, is compared; because in cases such as 'one who is to lie down' (śayitavya) and so forth, there is no sense of comparison whatsoever among them. (439)

There are various positions regarding what may be compared by means of an action expressed as "to be slept" (*śayitavya*) and so forth: either a substance (*dravya*), or a pure quality (*guṇa*), or that which possesses it—namely, a substance-possessor (*dravyavat*) or a quality-possessor (*guṇin*). Among these, a substance cannot be the object of comparison because it is established in its own nature; for there is no common property (*dharma*) serving as the basis for similarity that could connect an action and a substance such that one might say, "Devadatta is equal to the act of sleeping. Nor is there any purpose for comparison regarding a substance-possessor, such as "Devadatta's property is equal to the act of sleeping."

Nor is there a comparison between the quality of "thickness" and the object to which it belongs, such that one might say "the thickness is equal to the thing to be slept upon. For a comparison between a quality and its possessor does not exist, because there is no common attribute serving as a basis for similarity with an action. Indeed, the relationship of subject and object of comparison (upamāna-upameya) is observed in cases such as "moon-face," where it is based on well-known qualities or actions; however, no such established usage exists here. || 439 ||

In this regard, it might be argued: "Even though a common property (*samāna-dharma*) exists among action, substance, quality, and so forth, it is not employed here; therefore, because a word denoting another similar property is not used, the relationship of *upamāna* (standard of comparison) and *upameya* (object of comparison) is not apprehended. This is not correct, as he says: "In the case of the status of *upamāna* and *upameya*, when the substratum (*dharmin*) is not explicitly stated, actions and qualities—whether based on conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) or etymological derivation (*yoga*)—are understood as the grounds [for the comparison]. (440)

Even when not explicitly stated, qualities and actions that possess established relations [with the object] are perceived as if they were inseparable from it—having become a part of the word-meaning—as the cause for the relationship of *upamāna* (standard of comparison) and *upameya* (object of comparison), by virtue of conventional usage (*prasiddhi*), even regarding a similar property (*sadṛśa-dharma*) that is unexpressed. Thus, they do not invariably depend upon verbal expression. For instance, it has already been stated that when it is said, "Her face is like the moon," qualities such as being pleasant to behold and being radiant are understood even though they are not explicitly heard.
Likewise here, when it is said, "He is equal to one who ought to sleep," some property would be understood provided that a comparison is appropriate.

If that is so, then one who possesses an action (kriyāvān) is compared [to another] because of their proximity to the action; therefore, he says: "In the case of 'the sacrificer is like one who has sacrificed,' no such meaning exists here either. Because of the contradiction with the action, therefore one who possesses an action is not compared [with another who possesses an action]. (441)

The agent (*śāyaka*) is equal to the act of lying down (*śayitavya*), and the sacrificer (*hotṛ*) is equal to the act of sacrificing (*hotavya*); thus, by means of a verbal noun ending in a *kṛtya* suffix—which denotes an action—the substratum itself, as the possessor of the action, cannot logically serve as the object of comparison. For an action, being of the nature of something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), is incompatible with that which is of an already established nature (*siddha-svabhāva*) and therefore incapable of forming a relationship [of identity] with it. Furthermore, how could an action, whose own form is not yet attained due to its state of being something to be accomplished, inform another? Moreover, a comparison arises from the connection with common qualities, whereas there is an absolute difference between an action and a substance; thus, in this case as well, there is no purpose for the simile. (441)

Anticipating the objection that, since they are thus similar, the relationship of standard of comparison and object of comparison should belong directly to the two actions themselves, he says: "An action is not compared to another action of the same genus, because of their being that [genus]. Even when there is a difference in genus, cooking-actions and the like are distinct from one another by virtue of the specific act of cooking. (442)

Would the action serving as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) for another action be of the same class (*tulyajātīya*) or of a different class (*bhinnajātīya*)? In the former case, because of their identity due to that very nature, the actions cannot be objects of comparison. To illustrate: "that which is to be slept is equal to that which is to be slept," or "that which is to be studied is equal to that which is to be studied"—since there is absolute non-difference, there is no sense of comparison at all, just as in the expression "an ox is like an ox. And thus says the author of the Bhāṣya: "If that which is the standard of comparison is the very same as the object of comparison, what purpose is served by the comparison here, [as in] 'an ox is like an ox'?"

The intention is that even distinct objects, when apprehended through the imposition of a single genus (*ekajāti*), do not constitute a simile, because a simile must depend upon difference. In the second alternative, however, there is no purpose for a simile due to extreme difference; for it does not occur that "that which is to be spoken of is equal to that which is to be recited. Indeed, once the difference is already known from the very distinction of genus, the repetition of the word "distinct" (*bhinnā*) is intended to indicate the impossibility of a common attribute (*samānadharmā*), which is the cause of a simile. For where things belong to different genera, there is an absence of a common attribute, and thus no purpose for a simile.

And so says the Commentary: "Now, the object of comparison is one thing and the object compared is another; what sense of comparison is there here in 'a cow is like a horse'? Thus, it is stated that since there is no similarity here by any means whatsoever, the relation of object compared and object of comparison is absolutely impossible. By the use of the word "absolutely" (*atyanta*), he indicates that even a similarity consisting of a mere trace of a quality (*guṇaleśa*) is not possible here.

Nor should it be argued that even when things belong to different classes, a comparison may be established by relying on a similarity between substances, qualities, and so forth, through properties such as existence (*sattva*) or knowability (*jñeyatva*). This is because, as explained in the *Pūrvapakṣa-bhāṣya*, since properties like existence are common to all objects, they cannot serve as the basis for comparison in this particular cognition. || 442 ||

Now, in order to establish the distinction that serves as the basis for the relationship between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) among actions of the same class situated in [different] loci such as "lying down," he says: "The possibility of a standard of comparison arises when [the action] is differentiated by a difference of locus; the study of the Vaiśyas is equal to the study of the Brāhmaṇas, which is to be studied. (443)

Since there is equality based on the difference between the substances that serve as the substrata for actions of the same class, and because of the persistence of a specific universal (viśeṣajāti), the possibility of being an object of comparison—characterized by both difference and non-difference—is present. For instance, we observe such usage as: "The study of these [kṣatriyas and others] is similar to the study of brāhmaṇas," and "Devadatta’s act of lying down is equal to the king’s act of lying down. (443)

Now, one might raise this objection: "In this case, a word denoting an action, requiring a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) for the sake of conveying its distinction, becomes incapable due to its dependence; thus, it cannot undergo the formation of a secondary derivative (*taddhita-vṛtti*). Anticipating this, he says: "Where [the required element] is understood either from the sense (*artha*) or from the context (*prakaraṇa*), the formation of a derivative occurs for that [word] which, by virtue of its own capacity (*sāmarthya*), is independent. (444)

When, in a given context, the required substratum is ascertained either through implication or from some introductory discussion, then—since the specific delimitation of the locus of the word (such as that which is to be studied) is understood from that very [word] itself—one may experience that [function] based on semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) without dependence on the employment of a word expressing it.

In the case of "the study to be undertaken by a Kṣatriya is equal to the study to be undertaken by a Brāhmaṇa" and "Devadatta’s lying down is equal to the king’s lying down," once the compound is formed, there is no distinction; since there is a unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), there is an absence of the presence of a qualifier (*sopakṣatva*). Likewise, "going is equal to standing because of slowness," and "going is equal to dancing because of many transformations"—thus, even for actions of different classes, the relationship of standard of comparison and object of comparison (*upamānopameyabhāva*) certainly exists.

Furthermore, when an action is expressed by a *kṛt*-suffix, it does not only behave like a substance (*dravya*); its behavior as an action (*kriyā*) is also observed. For instance, one sees the suffixes *tumun* and *ṇvul* prescribed when an action functions as a subordinate element (*upapada*), as in "cooking to eat" (*bhoktuṃ pākaḥ*), "reading to understand" (*boddhuṃ pāṭhaḥ*), and "the movement of the agent" (*kārakasya gatiḥ*). Since these suffixes are seen even when subordinate elements ending in *ghañ* and other such suffixes are present, it is certain that they possess the properties of an action. || 444 ||

[Objection: But surely, in this case, the suffixes *tumun* and *ṇvul* will apply by taking as their basis the action expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu-bhāga*). [Reply: This is not so; for it is precisely the accomplishment (*nirvṛtti*) inherent in the action, which is expressed by the suffix, that serves even more directly as the purpose of eating and so forth. [Objection: If that is so, when the subordinate word (*upapada*) is designated by the term "action" (*kriyā*), how can it possess a completed form? [Reply: Its property (*dharma*) is also grasped as being the subordinate word. Since one may rely on the non-difference between a property and its possessor (*dharmadharmiṇor abhedāśrayaṇa*), there is no fault in the fact that the property is also conveyed by the word "action. Thus, there is no defect.

If that is so, why do suffixes expressing frequency (*kṛtvas-artha*) not also occur in the case of words ending in *ghañ* and other such nominal suffixes? It is said in reply: because of the requirement of repetition (*abhyāvṛtti*), it is in that context that the action (*kriyā*) is employed in its own form as something to be performed (*kartavyatā-ātmaka*), and not as something already accomplished (*siddhatayā*). This is because that which has already been brought into existence cannot be brought into existence again, and thus further activity is impossible. Consequently, since the necessity of performing the action is not understood there without the use of a verb (*ākhyāta*), repetition is absent, and therefore those suffixes do not occur.

However, when there is the employment of a verb (*ākhyāta*), the sentence is complete; since the verb denotes an action whose nature is to be accomplished (*sādhya-svabhāva-kriyā*), the suffix expressing frequency (*kṛtvas-arthapratyaya*) takes that [action] as its basis, as in "cooking occurs five times" (*pañcakṛtvaḥ pāko vartate*). Now, one might object: on the basis of the non-difference between the attribute (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*), let the suffix [denoting frequency] arise due to the presence of the action "cooking" as a subordinate element (*upapada*) for the purpose of eating—since the accomplishment [of cooking] results in the purpose of eating—and thus there would be a syntactic connection (*samanvaya*) of the words.

But how can there be a connection with the object (*karman*) in cases such as *odanasya pākaḥ* ("the cooking of rice")? For it is impossible for that which is the primary meaning of the suffix—namely, the state of being already accomplished (*siddhatā*)—to be connected with a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), since it is only that which is yet to be accomplished (*sādhya*) that is joined with the factors of action (*kāraka*). True; however, the connection with the object occurs by way of the verbal root-meaning (*dhātvartha*), which serves as a subordinate element. If this is so, then let the connection also occur through repetition (*abhyāvṛtti*) by way of the verbal root-meaning, which is subordinate and has the nature of being yet to be accomplished. It does not, because of contradiction.

For thus, the connection of the primary element (*pradhāna*) with other objects does not occur through the property of a subordinate factor (*guṇadharma*), because that would contradict its own nature. Repetition (*abhyāvṛtti*), indeed, is incompatible with the state of being already accomplished, since that which has ceased cannot engage in activity again; therefore, even that which is expressed by the word—namely, the action ending in the third case—is possible here as the basis of comparison, serving as the meaning of the suffix. Thus he says: "When it is intended to express that the cooking of ghee is equal to the cooking of oil, the suffix may occur even though [the action] is like an action, because such a result is observed among effects. (445)

It has been demonstrated that not only are the grammatical operations—characterized by gender and number—associated with an action expressed by a *kṛt* suffix seen to occur as they do with a substance, but this applies even to suffixes such as *-tumun*. Consequently, in the expression "the cooking of ghee is equal to the cooking of oil," the suffix *-vat* would arise from a word denoting an action standing in the third case (instrumental). Furthermore, there is no state of dependence (*sāpekṣatva*) here, because the substratum is conveyed within a single word.

Regarding the fact that when a word ending in *ghañ* or similar suffixes functions as an *upapada*, the *tumun* and *ṇvul* suffixes—which denote action—apply to both the action and its result, he states the view of the author of the Vārttika as a corroborating authority: "But the mention of *atiṅ* (non-verbal) thus serves to exclude [the application of] *samāsa* (compound formation). In the case of 'gamanaṃ kārakasya' with the suffix *ṇvul*, it would not be possible otherwise. (446)

Regarding the rule *upapadam atiṅ* (Pāṇini 2.2.19), since the governing context is *sup supā* (2.1.4), there is no possibility of compounding at all for an *upapada* ending in a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), as in examples such as *kārako vrajati*. When this objection was raised—asking what purpose the prohibition *atiṅ* serves—the author of the *Vākyapadīya* stated: "*upapadam atiṅ*: this is a prohibition based on its meaning (*tadartha*). The word *tat* refers back to *tiṅ*. The sense is that this [prohibition] applies to that nominal stem (*subanta*) which possesses the meaning of that [verbal suffix]. By implication, this is a compound containing a comparison (*upamānagarbha*), similar to the expression *uṣṭramukha* ("camel-faced").

The meaning of "of that which has [another] as its object" is stated to be "of that which has an action as its object. The term *atiṅ* is an indication where the meaning is primary; this is the sense. For this very reason, he says that this should be clearly recited as: "*kriyāpratiṣedho vā*" ("or there is a prohibition of [compounding with] an action"). The meaning is that a clear formulation of the rule should be made as "*upapadam akriyā*" (an *upapada* that is not an action), which conveys the intended meaning. And thus, when a nominal stem (*subanta*) whose primary element is an action is an *upapada*, this prohibition applies upon the potential occurrence of a compound.

For example, it is stated: "the going of the agent," "the movement of the agent," and "the departure of the agent. And how would this be possible if the suffixes *tumun* and *ṇvul* were applied when words such as "going" (*gati*) are used as upapadas?

Otherwise, since it would merely state what is already established, how could this serve as the purpose for the prohibition of compounding in its absence? Furthermore, this prohibition of compounding for a word denoting an action ending in *ṇvul*—which is prescribed by the general rule "ṇvultṛcau" (*Pāṇini 3.1.133*) when another [word] is present—is not tenable, because in that case there is no *upapada* (governing word). For if the possibility of compounding for a word denoting an action already exists, a prohibition would be meaningless.

Thus, in cases such as *kāraka-gati*, since the elements beginning with *gati* are *sub*-ending words (*sup-anta*), there arises the possibility of a compound formed with an *upapada*. Consequently, the prohibition that applies when an *upapada* is present indicates that the grammatical operations of a verbal action—such as the suffixes *tumun* and *ṇvul*—apply to words ending in *ghañ* and other such suffixes; however, it does not lead one to understand that this established form of meaning possesses the nature of a "verbal action" (*kriyā*) simply because its essence consists of meanings such as *gati*. This is because it is impossible to demonstrate a contradiction in the actual nature of things (*vastu-svabhāva*). || 446 ||

Thus, although words such as *śayita* ("lying down") and *pāka* ("cooking"), which denote actions, are logically capable of being construed with the third case (*tṛtīyā-samartha*), with what intention [the author] begins by saying, "This is not a fault; all these are quality-words (*guṇa-śabda*) that function in reference to wholes," and concludes by stating, "Words that function in reference to wholes also function in reference to parts," based on the premise that words such as *brāhmaṇa* function solely in reference to actions characterized by study and so forth, [he states]: "If it is an action, then it may be that which is capable of being construed with the third case."

Anticipating the objection that the view of the base-meaning as a qualifier (*prakṛtyarthaviśeṣaṇapakṣa*) has been supported by the author of the Bhāṣya, he says: "In order to avoid [the aforementioned] objections for all cases, the status of being a collective whole (*samudāyatva*) is resorted to; otherwise, because a pure action is impossible in the case of Brahmins and so forth, [the rule would fail]. (447)

Even though words denoting an action, such as *hotavya* (to be offered), are capable of being construed with a third-case ending, the Bhāṣyakāra has accepted as his final position (*siddhānta*) that the meaning of these words is a "collection" (*samudāya*), stating: "All these words refer to a collection of qualities. In this regard, the following intention is crushed [by the opponent]: so that there may be a universal solution applicable to all cases.

Otherwise, since a pure, isolated action—expressed by words such as *śayita* (having lain down) and so forth—could exist as a verbal root (*prakṛti*) for an affix and thus be capable of being construed with a third-case ending, the suffix *vati* would not occur in instances such as "the Kṣatriya studies like a Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇavad adhīte kṣatriyaḥ*). This is because the word *brāhmaṇa* and others denote an action only figuratively through a partial application (*ekadeśavṛtti*). However, words such as *hotavya* (to be offered) or *pāka* (cooking) denote action in its primary sense; and when a primary referent exists, how could there be an adoption of a figurative one?

[Objection: "But surely, if the expression of action can be established even by imagining that [the word] denotes a part of a composite whole, then how can one not raise the objection: 'Since a primary sense is possible, why is a figurative sense adopted? [Response: There is no fault, because the entire [composite] is accepted on the basis of the principle of pervasion (*vyāpti*). Alternatively, the intention is this: having accepted that it is untenable for an action to be construed with the third case-ending, the author of the *Cūrṇi* offers a different solution; thus, there is simply no possibility of a word denoting a pure action being construed with the third case-ending. 447.

For instance: "When there is an intention to express a comparison, the speaker's own attribute is excluded; for the comparison is completed by the action, not by what is heard [as a verbal suffix]. (448)

When there is a requirement for an action—such as that denoted by the word "cooking"—to serve as a point of comparison, its own property, characterized by being an inherent nature or a state of existence, is excluded; for the reality of the object of comparison is not fully established merely by hearing it. || 448 ||

If it is argued that, in view of the common property (*anvayidharma*), one should rather attend to that common property itself, [the author replies]: "Does the common property of the object of comparison thereby depart? To this he says: 'Even a third property, being dependent and shared by both, possesses activity; yet a complete similarity of the whole with the whole does not exist. (449)

The third [factor], required for the establishment of the essential nature through the comparison of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), is that specific quality which is excluded from others and common to both of them; yet even this is not expected to be indifferent, such that—because it would be ineffective—it would fail to produce its own effects due to a lack of activity. Rather, it possesses activity, because it inheres in both.

And thus, because the status of being a point of comparison (upamānatva) depends upon an action, it is "engaged" or occupied with its accomplishment; consequently, since the action is dispersed by virtue of being the locus of common attributes (samānadharmā), it departs from its nature as something yet to be accomplished (sādhya). For when [the object] exists as a substance (dravyāyamāṇa) in its own right, it manifests itself as established (siddha) by virtue of the attributes residing within it, having become an auxiliary factor for the determination of the object of comparison (upameya).

Indeed, it is not logical for the very nature (*svabhāva*) of an action residing in a form to serve as the cause for designating [the action] with respect to the object of comparison, because that which is unestablished cannot function as a subordinate factor (*aṅga*) for another. And thus, when the cooking of oil and so forth is reflected upon as "this is that," it attains the status of being a substratum of common properties; therefore, this is a substance (*dravya*). Since the act of offering (*hotavya*) and so forth, even as a locus of common properties such as excellence, is likewise [a substance], this word ending in the third case does not denote an action in this state.

In this context, a category such as action (*kriyā*) or substance (*dravya*) is not described according to its real nature; rather, it is expressed by words in the form of that which is already established (*siddha*) or that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), and so forth. For instance, even a single sound (*dhvani*) is denoted as having the nature of an action, a quality, or a substance. When one intends to express a continuous stream of sound (*śabdasantāna*)—which arises sequentially through its constituent parts, is characterized by a temporal sequence of prior and posterior, and whose production is dependent upon causal factors—as "the bell sounds" (*ghaṇṭā dhvanati*), then this action, with its parts spread out in time, is denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) as "it sounds" (*dhvanati*).

When, however, for the purpose of excluding other causes, it is qualified by its related bell—expressed as "the sound of the bell"—then this quality, having attained a completed form, is denoted by a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*). But in the expression "sound-ness" (*dhvanitvam*), the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*), which has become a substance and is subordinate to the universal (*jāti*), is expressed by a word ending in an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*). And in the phrase "the sound sounds," that very same referent is denoted as being endowed with a causal capacity (*kārakaśakti*).

Furthermore, in this context, the status of being the agent belongs to that which possesses manifest phonemes (*vyaktavarṇa*), while the status of being the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) belongs to that which is unmanifest (*avyakta*); thus, the categories of meaning in grammar are unstable. Therefore, even from a verb (*kriyāpada*), the action is not perceived here as having the nature of something to be accomplished (*sādhya-svabhāva*), but rather as having the nature of an established entity (*siddha-svabhāva*). Consequently, this is merely a substance (*dravya*), and since it ends in a nominal suffix (*subanta*), it does not denote an action. The same applies to the finite verb (*ākhyāta*) itself. And because it is not a nominal stem (*aprātipadika*), there is no third case ending.

For this very reason, the word has been stated briefly as being twofold, through the distinction between nouns (*nāman*) and verbs (*ākhyāta*), based on the difference between the accomplished (*siddha*) and the to-be-accomplished (*sādhya*) objects. In this regard, it might be asked: "Why is the common property (*dharma*) active? To this it is said: "Not of the whole," and so forth. If there were equality of all properties between the entire object and the whole [of the other], then because there would be no distinction, an equality or similarity that establishes the relationship of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) could not exist; for it has already been stated that such a relationship is established only through both difference and non-difference. || 449 ||

One might object: "Let the common property (sādhāraṇadharma) here function through both difference and non-difference; it is required by the substance (*dravya*) in its established form, not by the action (*kriyā*), which is of the nature of something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and serves as the basis of comparison. Anticipating this, he says: "Whether in the case of a substance or an action, that [commonality] is conceptualized on account of a causal factor (*nimitta*). If [the commonality were restricted to] actions alone, there would be no application [of the comparison] in the case of cows and the like, because [their] actions are not present [at all times]. (450)

The word "tat" (that) refers back to the similarity previously introduced. Whether it be a substance (*dravya*) or an action (*kriyā*), by means of the cognition of another object, it constitutes a simile; in every case, since the similarity of objects is based on resemblance, one must seek a common property (*sādhāraṇo dharma*) which is its cause or ground. For instance, a pure substance existing in its own state cannot serve as the determiner of another object—the object of comparison—and therefore it requires a common quality for that purpose.

For it is from that cause (*nimitta*) that a delimitation through similarity becomes possible. Likewise, an action (*kriyā*) that does not depend on a common property is incapable of assisting another object to be made known; therefore, this [action] must also necessarily depend on a cause. And thus, acting as a substance (*dravyāyamāṇā*), this [action] abandons its status as an action (*kriyātva*). For an action becomes such when it is being brought into existence and is presented as primary for the sake of apprehending the state of the operation of the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*).

But when the state of the operation of the means is not intended to be described, nor is the action itself taken up as possessing primary importance, but rather another property (*dharma*) which serves as its substratum is taken up independently of the operation of the means—then, because it is independent of operations and serves as the substratum for other properties, that which is designated as "this is that" is called *dravya* (substance) alone, and not action.

If, however, it were logical for actions to possess the status of a standard of comparison (*upamāna*) by their very nature alone, without depending on an external cause, then since such pure actions existing as standards of comparison would be possible, why would the suffix *vat* be applied to words like "cow" (*go*), which denote figurative actions? For when a primary object is available, it is improper to resort to a figurative one; thus, the usage "like a cow" (*govat*) or "like a Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇavat*) would not occur. || 450 ||

But when a comparison is based on common properties (*sādhāraṇadharma*), then—since even actions require other properties and thus, according to the stated principle, would lose their own essential nature and become impossible in the primary sense—it is appropriate to resort to a secondary meaning (*gauṇa*). Thus he says: "However, because of the absence of that [comparison] in its absolute form, the meaning of 'that' (the monkey) is understood; since the primary sense is impossible, the hearing of the word for 'action' is rightly taken as having a figurative purpose (*lakṣaṇārtha*). (451)

Since there is no purpose for deviating from the natural order of sequence, when the word *tena* (by that), heard first [in the compound], is connected with the action as a limiting adjunct (*kriyopādhi*), then—even under the view that it qualifies the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha*)—the pure action cannot possibly exist according to the aforementioned principle. Thus, upon abandoning the literal (*śrauta*) meaning, a figurative (*lākṣaṇika*) meaning is resorted to. Furthermore, because an action is eternally inseparable from its own substratum, that very substratum is indicated by way of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvitā*). Therefore, what is taken as the referent of the third case-ending (*tṛtīyāsamartha*) is a word denoting a substance qualified by the action.

And consequently, by virtue of occurring in only one part [of their referent], terms such as "brāhmaṇa" are designators of actions and are the base; the same applies to words such as "śayitavya" (that which must be slept).

For even in the case of these [examples] being used as analogies here, they share a complete similarity with the Brahmins and others; thus he says: "Just as the Brahmins and others are taken for the sake of assistance in relation to other actions, so too action-words are dependent upon other actions regarding other properties of action. (452)

In the case of another action—such as the action characterized by a Kṣatriya’s duty to study and so forth—for the sake of assistance or for delimitation through similarity, verbal expressions denoting actions, such as "to be studied by Brāhmaṇas" and the like, which function as terms of comparison, are employed expectantly toward other actions that serve as the grounds for comparison, such as proficiency and the rest.

Therefore, just as words such as "brāhmaṇa" are employed for the purpose of distinguishing [others] like the kṣatriya and so forth, depending on actions characterized by similarity to the study of the Vedas and the like, so too do these [words "ete"] function in every respect as similes for action-words through their denotation of substances; thus, both types of words undergo the same mode of operation—this is the meaning. || 452 ||

In this regard, one might object: "If even the action (*kriyā*), when being employed as a standard of comparison, were to depend upon another property (*dharmāntara*), then there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Anticipating this doubt, he says the following in order to accept that [dependence] by means of an illustration: "Just as excellence (*prakarṣa*) everywhere has another cause as its basis, so too, in the case of a word denoting a quality (*guṇaśabda*), it depends upon a basis, just like a substance (*dravya*). (453)

"Indeed, excellence (*prakarpa*) and deficiency (*apakarṣa*) do not exist in a substance by its own nature," because there is no excellence in that which lacks limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhi*). Therefore, its excellence has been established as being caused by another property belonging to a related entity (*saṃsargi*). For instance, in the expression "the whiter cloth" (*śuklataraḥ paṭaḥ*), the excellence is caused by the quality of whiteness inherent (*samavāyin*) in it. Likewise, when that very quality of whiteness is intended to be expressed as possessing excellence, then—functioning as a substance and denoted by its own word—it is spoken of in that way with reference to its own internal cause, such as brilliance, as in "its color is whiter."

On this very point, he states another illustration: "Whatever word is uttered is based upon its own form; likewise, in the case of comparisons, the requirement [of a common property] does not cease. (454)

In this context, it has been established in the Brahmakāṇḍa that the expressive word is that which is situated in the arrangement of its constituent parts (*karaṇa*) and assumes a sequence, as in the injunction: "Recite the word *agni* with the acute accent on the final syllable. And since the capacity to express belongs to the word in its unconditioned state, it takes its own form and sequence as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). Thus, the Vedic utterances (*śruti*), being grounded in that [form], enter into the object to be conveyed. Furthermore, it has already been determined that when that very form has its sequence withdrawn, it is the denotatum; and even in this case, the word expresses the meaning as permeated by its own form.

In that regard, when that which is situated in the instruments [of articulation] and permeated by its own form (*svarūpa*) functions as the signifier, the form of the signified (*vācya*) present in actual usage is [the object]. Furthermore, when even that [signified] ascends onto the instruments, then yet another signified—the form whose sequence has been withdrawn—becomes its denoted meaning; it has already been established that in this case, the word expresses even this meaning as being permeated by its own form. Among these, when that which is situated in the instruments and permeated by its own form functions as the signifier, the form of the signified present in actual usage is [the object].

Even that [denotable object], when it is situated within the instrument (karaṇa), must likewise be conceived as having another denotable object whose sequence has been withdrawn; thus, in every case, a triad is inherent: the cause (nimitta), the possessor of that cause (tadvān), and the denotable object (abhidheya). He demonstrates this very point through repetition as being universal with the words "whichever... whichever.

For even that which is the intrinsic nature (svarūpa) serving as the ground for application (pravṛttinimitta), when it becomes established in the instrument, then another ground for application must necessarily be required, because there is no denotation of that which is devoid of limiting conditions (upādhi); this has already been determined in another section, and since it was previously mentioned here as well, it is not elaborated upon again here.

Thus, just as in the case of excellence (*prakarṣa*), where there is a conceptualization (*parikalpanā*) of another property (*dharmāntara*) to the extent that words can reach—both in respect to its own nature and in respect to another nature—so too in the case of comparison (*aupamya*), because of the conceptualization of its cause, there is the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), the object of comparison (*upameya*), and their common property (*sādhāraṇo dharma*); thus, this triad is unavoidable in every instance. And for this reason, in the statement "the Kṣatriya has studied like the Brāhmaṇa," study (*adhyayana*) is the common property.

If that [kṣatriya’s study] were also to serve as a standard of comparison, then another common property such as fluency and so forth would have to be postulated, on the grounds that the kṣatriya’s study is similar to the brāhmaṇa’s study. If that too were to serve as a standard of comparison, yet another property would be required; however, because the operation of the word ceases at this point, there is no infinite regress that would undermine the foundation, since a finality is possible. || 454 ||

Thus, the objection in the *pūrvapakṣa* commentary—that a pure action (*kriyā*) standing in the third case-relation (*tṛtīyāsamartha*) is impossible—is established. Now, regarding the commentary which states, "In this very context, the following is improper," that is understood by way of restating the established *pūrvapakṣa*: "Since this [usage] is inconsistent with a word ending in the third case expressing an action. In the commentary, the root *yuj* is cited as an example of a well-known rule for the formation of an instrument (*karaṇa*). (Verse 455)

To the objection—"This is improper; why has the instrument (*karaṇa*) of the action denoted by the root *yuj* not been mentioned?"—it is said that the author of the Bhāṣya did not mention it by way of explicit statement because the instrument is well-known. For instance, according to the reasoning already stated, the impossibility of a word ending in the third case expressing an action has been demonstrated; thus, the instrument, being defined by that very reasoning, is not directly specified here due to its conventional familiarity. Therefore, the meaning is "improper" (*ayuktam*) by virtue of that reasoning.

Indeed, when the means (*sādhana*) is understood through a consideration of the capacity inherent in the very nature of the action (*kriyā*), its explicit mention by its own word is disregarded. For example, in the case of "the Arhat," since a specific object such as honor and so forth is already implied, it is not mentioned by its own word. Furthermore, in the expression "it rains" (*varṣati*), because the object is well-known, this action is stated as being "without an object" (*akarmikā*); likewise, since the agent here is also well-known, it is not necessarily expressed by its own word, such as "the god. (Verse 455)

However, as for the one who thinks that since the instrument (*karaṇa*) defined by logic is already included within the very nature of the action (*kriyāsvarūpa*), it does not require a formal application (*prayoga*), he refutes that view: "But if the instrument were already included, its formal application would not occur again; [this would be] illogical according to the system, just as [the term 'life'] is not applied to the vital activity while life itself is present. (456)

Just as one says "he lives" (*jīvati*) because he sustains the vital breaths (*prāṇān*), or "the self exists" (*asty ātmā*) because it maintains itself—since the action characterized by the vital breaths and so forth is included within the very nature of the act itself, the expressions "he lives the vital breaths" (*jīvati prāṇān*) or "the self exists [as] the self" (*asty ātmānam*) do not occur—likewise, since the instrument characterized by reasoning (*nyāya*) is included within the act of "joining" (*yukti*), expressions such as "it is joined by reasoning" (*nyāyena yuktam*) or "it is joined by logic" (*upapattyā yuktam*) would never occur. For an instrument that is external to an action deserves a separate usage from that action, but one that is internal does not.

Therefore, in this case, common usage alone must be followed when the instrumental case is not employed. This is stated for the sake of maintaining the conventions of grammatical derivation (*anvākhyāna*): in the derivation of the word *yuktam*, the meaning of the verbal root *yuj-* is the sense of "joining," while the instrumental case signifies "method" (*nyāya*). || 456 ||

From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), however, this word is devoid of any division of parts; thus, no action whatsoever is applicable here of which one could speak as its "instrument" (*karaṇa*). This action is merely postulated for the sake of etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*). Thus he says: "This distinction is described as 'inappropriate' for the study of the treatise (*śāstra*); the conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) is established as being 'unattractive' and 'incoherent. (457)

In the grammatical exposition (*anvākhyāna*), because the root *yuj* is employed here with its etymological sense of "joining" (*anuguṇā yujikriyā*), it is impossible for it to be without an instrument (*akaraṇikā*). Therefore, we explain this as the intention of the author of the Bhāṣya: that the well-known principle is that the instrument is not directly mentioned. However, in common usage (*laukika prayoga*), the word *ayukta* conveys something that lacks the analysis of its constituent parts, is unseemly, disconnected, improper, incoherent, and unfitting; it is with this very intent that the author of the Bhāṣya did not specify an instrument here. (457)

Thus, since there is no third-case ending expressing an action, the objection regarding the specific qualification of the base-meaning (*prakṛtyartha*) is raised. To demonstrate that this position is indeed impossible, he says: "How could a different case-ending be an attribute (*upādhi*) with respect to the base-meaning? And if one were to assume a transformation of the case-ending, another object-domain would have to be postulated. (458)

In the phrase "tena" (by that), the base form (*prakṛti*) standing in the third case is the primary element here because it is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). How can this adjunct (*upādhi*), defined as "an action directed toward the object of that [base]," be logically consistent when it appears in a different case-ending as a nominative (*prathamānta*), given the absence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)? For it has been stated that "an adjunct is a specific meaning expressed by the same word ending in that [base]. Thus, an adjunct is characterized as a coreferential meaning, as for example: *dṛtihariḥ paśuḥ* ("a beast with a mane") or *daṇḍaḥ praharaṇam asyām dāṇḍā* ("that in which a staff is the weapon").

"His deity is this," thus [it is] "pertaining to Prajāpati" (prājāpatya), and so forth. A qualifier, however, is characterized merely as that which delimits; even when separated by a case-ending, it functions as such. For example, in the expression "he praises by means of being a Gārgya" (gārgikayā ślāghate), it is the praising itself [that is meant]. In this regard, one might argue that a change in case-ending is to be inferred because the relationship would otherwise be untenable.

And that is not so; since the nominative case-ending of what is heard in the text constitutes its very originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), it has no other purpose elsewhere—how, then, could there be a modification? For a modification would require the postulation of another context in which it might find its purpose; otherwise, the nominative hearing in the text would be rendered fruitless. Indeed, modification follows the logic of *ūha*; and in this case, it is logical that what is heard in the archetype (*prakṛti*) should be altered in the ectype (*vikṛti*). [458]

He establishes this very point: "For when something is connected with one case-ending in relation to a particular object, its connection with another case-ending is inferred through the force of the context. (459)

However, due to similarity, it is figuratively designated as "this is that very same thing"; yet in the grammatical treatise, when joined with another word and a case-ending, that [identity] is not heard.

When a word whose case-ending has been heard [in a certain context] attains syntactic connection with some benefit in a particular domain, yet in another application—where the related term is not explicitly mentioned—it must depend on the indicator of the *svarita* accent due to its being the subject under discussion; then, since it cannot be connected through that very heard case-ending, one infers a connection with another case-ending suitable for that coordination, because such a connection would otherwise be impossible.

And in that regard, because the relationship between word and meaning is eternal, it is not possible for an already employed word or its meaning to undergo alteration; therefore, another word itself—endowed with a different grammatical inflection—is mentally projected, even though it is not directly uttered. However, when, due to similarity with the preceding form, there is a determination of non-difference regarding the stem portion, one speaks of "transformation" (*pariṇāma*), in the sense that the very same word undergoes transformation by means of a different inflection. For example: "that very milk has become curd"—this is transformation.

For here too, even though there is a difference between milk and curd as observed when some things possessing the nature of milk undergo transformation, there is still the conventional usage of "transformation" and the recognition that "this is that very same thing. Likewise, in this case as well, despite the difference in the cognitive aspect (*pratyayabhāga*), there is the determination of non-difference due to the persistence of the primordial material aspect (*prakṛtibhāga*).

And thus, since modification (*ūha*) consists in the alteration of case-endings and the conceptualization of something else in place of the original, how could it be appropriate for that which is heard in the very originative injunction (*utpattivākya*)? For modification is logically applicable only to that which has been employed in the archetype (*prakṛti*) [and is then applied to the ectype]. To illustrate: in the rule "roots beginning with *bhū* are called *dhātu*," once the connection with the technical name is established and the nominative form *dhātavaḥ* has fulfilled its purpose, another word ending in the ablative—namely *dhātoḥ*—is inferred in rules such as "from a root marked with an indicatory *ṅ* or *ṭ* [the suffix *a* is added]," because the application of those rules would otherwise be inexplicable.

Therefore, a case-ending being uttered must be shown to have utility in some meaning of the sentence; hence, a modification of the case-ending is postulated. Otherwise, if the meaning intended by the sentence were not dependent on the meaning of the case-ending of the word-part that was uttered, then the utterance of that specific case-ending would be entirely purposeless. Indeed, no merit is perceived in a speaker who utters one thing when another ought to be uttered.

Indeed, there would otherwise be the fault of stating something entirely irrelevant. However, in some cases, because the reference is made with the intention of including [the term] within a single case-ending, its application is indeed appropriate according to the context. For example, in the expression *analvidhau*, it is a compound ending in all case-endings (*sarvavibhaktyanta*). For the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) is intended here to include the meanings of various case-endings even when expressed in a single mention.

Thus, in the *Arthatantra*, regarding that specific explanation, it was established that the case-ending heard there is inseparable [from the meaning], and it was described that the intended meaning is obtained even without an injunctive word (*vidhiśabda*). However, in this case, because the meaning of the case-ending is fixed as "action" (*kriyā*), it is not appropriate to describe it in that way, since its connection is desired solely through the sense of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyārtha*). || 459, 460 ||

Furthermore, because the word *prakṛti* (nature) is understood as being in the nominative case from the word *tena* (by that), the word *kriyayā* (by action) must also be indicated as being in the instrumental case in accordance with it. Otherwise, if it were indicated in the nominative, how could there be a syntactic connection (*samanvaya*), since there would be no modification of the principal term which ends in the instrumental? Thus he says: "If *prakṛti* is understood from the word *tena* as ending in the instrumental case, how can *kriyā* [be understood] as ending in the nominative? (461)
Since the impossibility of transformation has already been established, it has been stated how there could be a relationship [between them] given their distinct grammatical case-endings. || 461 ||

Or, even if one were to change the case-ending, there would still be no syntactic connection between "tena" (by that) and "kriyayā" (by the action); thus he says: "And as for the instrumental case in 'kriyayā', with what could it be construed? For no connection exists between 'tena' and [the word] situated in the sūtra. (462)

By the phrase "by that which was heard in the Sūtra," there is no connection with the word *kriyā* (action) due to a difference in gender; therefore, for what [word] being employed could the instrumental suffix (*tṛtīyā*) be postulated as a qualifier (*upādhi*) for *kriyayā*? The meaning is: for none at all, because a coreferential (*samānaliṅga*) relative term to be employed is impossible. If, however, there were a coordination with the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*) such that "[equal to the action]," then this would not be a qualifier of the base (*prakṛti*). || 462 ||

Having thus raised the question regarding the connection, he says in order to establish it: "In the case of aphorisms that require supplementary words (*sopaskāra*), the ellipsis is supplied within the sentence. Therefore, when there is that word ending in the third case, it is understood as 'if it is an action' (*kriyā*). (463)

In this case, because no finite verb (*kriyāpada*) is heard in the words of the Sūtra, it is determined that a word must be supplied (*sādhyāhāratva*). Since a definition is formulated in accordance with the object to be defined (*lakṣya*), the finite verb must be supplied according to the specific differences among those objects as appropriate. Consequently, since the word *cet* here indicates a particular relationship, the ellipsis of the sentence is established as "that which is capable of being construed with the third case—*if* it is an action, then it becomes [the object]," and thus the connection is justified. This is the intended meaning here: let there be no modification (*vipariṇāma*) of the Sūtra itself.

However, regarding that statement of concordance (*samanvaya-vākya*) which is of the nature of an explanatory commentary (*vyākhyāna*), there is the logical possibility of transformation (*pariṇāma*). If it is argued that the use of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) in the word "by that" (*tena*) has fulfilled its purpose merely in making known the instrumental status of the material cause (*prakṛti*), we reply: it is indeed appropriate for that [cause], which has been rendered independent by the experience of its connection with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), to undergo transformation through those very adjuncts, as indicated by the word "again" (*punar*) in the text. This is just as the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "guṇa and vṛddhi replace *ik*" serves to assist the entire scope of the primary grammatical rules.
But where one says "guṇa and vṛddhi," there it should be understood that the word "eka" is present; this is established by supplying the missing words from the sentence. || 463 ||

Thus, in this context, the connection between the "action" (kriyā), which is the attribute (upādhi), and the "agent" (tena), which is the possessor of the attribute (upādhimat), occurs through the syntactic ellipsis (*vākya-adhyāhāra*) of the word "by him" (*tena*). Furthermore, it is not necessary that the attribute must be expressed by the same word [as the possessor], since it can occur otherwise; therefore, in order to demonstrate the various types of attributes, he says: "In a sentence, the employment of some attribute is observed, which is never employed [separately] when its property is already implied. (464)

The statement “*tadasyāṃ praharaṇam*” (that is the weapon in this [game]) is not itself the direct rule for the formation of the suffix, because the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is not heard therein. Rather, it is a general imitation of various distinct sentences such as “*daṇḍaḥ praharaṇam asyāṃ krīḍāyām*” (the staff is the weapon in this game) and “*muṣṭiḥ praharaṇam asyāṃ krīḍāyām*” (the fist is the weapon in this game). Furthermore, since in the actual usage-sentences the status of being a weapon (*praharatva*) of the staff and so forth—which is subject to deviation—is presented through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the sūtra likewise imitates that very form.

Thus, this adjunct (*upādhi*) is one whose word is identical [to the term it qualifies] and which is employed in common worldly usage regarding non-difference because of its deviation [from that state]. Another adjunct, however, is not even heard in actual usage because its nature is to be understood through implication (*sāmarthya*). Consequently, since it is not heard in usage, there is no such imitation of it in the Sūtra either. It must simply be introduced into the Sūtra in some way or another; and so, in this case, this adjunct is characterized by the action (*kriyā*).

In the expression "the Kṣatriya studies equally with the Brāhmaṇa," the action is not directly employed as residing in the Brāhmaṇa; rather, it is understood through implication (sāmarthya).
