Therefore, there is no objection whatsoever to the mention of this limiting adjunct (upādhi) in the Sūtra even when it is in the nominative case, since its syntactic connection is established by supplying the necessary words from the sentence. || 464 ||

Regarding that, he provides an example of the implied adjunct (*pratīyamānopādhi*): "In the expression 'a blue lotus,' no word denoting a property of either the substantive or the qualifier is employed within the sentence. (465)

In the sentence "A blue lotus" (*nīlotpalam*), because the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyatva*)—which is a property of those two—is already understood through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) itself, the words "the qualifier is 'blue' and the qualified is 'lotus'" are not employed. Their use occurs only in the Sūtra itself, namely in the phrase "the qualifier [is compounded] with the qualified" (*viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa*), for the purpose of delimitation. || 465 ||
And therefore, because [the meaning] follows through absolutely, there is no need for any modification of case-endings either in the sūtra or in the analytical explanation (vigraha). // 466 //

Because the relationship of the delimited (avacchedya) and the delimiter (avacchedaka) is entirely subsumed [within the compound], in the sentence "it is blue and it is a lotus," there is no result of transformation for the word denoting the substantive (viśeṣya) when it appears as the third-case ending in the rule; for the status of being the substantive is already understood from the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) itself.

And thus, since there is no usage of such words as the "qualified" (*viśeṣya*) in a sentence, what word in the Sūtra could this [term *viśeṣyeṇa*] be an imitation of, on account of which the third-case form *viśeṣyeṇa* would have to be transformed into a nominative? In matters of this kind, the non-application of the transformation of case-endings is stated for the purpose of establishing the subject at hand; however, a transformation of case-endings in the word *viśeṣyeṇa* is not conceivable for the sake of syntactic connection (*samanvaya*), because the connection is established by the word as it is heard. || 466 ||

Therefore, taking this very point as an illustration, he says [the following] in order to apply it to the present subject: "The term 'action' (kriyā) ending in the third case is not employed in a *vigraha* [analytic compound], as is seen in the example: 'a staff is the instrument for playing. (467)

In the expression "the Kṣatriya studies equal to the Brāhmaṇa," there is no usage of the word *kriyayā* (by means of action) ending in the third case. This is because the word *kriyā* (action) is heard [only] in relation to the object of comparison (*upameya*), and by virtue of that, it is understood [by implication] in relation to the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) as well; otherwise, the relationship between the standard and the object of comparison would not exist at all. Thus, there is no fault in this adjunct (*upādhi*) even if it is introduced in some manner or other. However, in the sentence "this game has a staff as its weapon" (*daṇḍaḥ praharaṇam asyāṃ krīḍāyām*), the usage of the adjunct "weapon" (*praharaṇa*) is actually observed.

For the fact that the staff is the most effective instrument for the action of striking is not understood merely from the use of the word "staff" (*daṇḍa*), since that word conveys only its own primary meaning; rather, its status as such is communicated by the word "striking" (*praharaṇa*) itself. And thus, it is represented exactly in that way in the Sūtra. (467)

In this regard, one might object: "Since usage such as 'the blue is the qualifier' and 'the lotus is the qualified' is also observed, how can this be an illustration of an adjunct (*upādhi*) whose property is internally included? Anticipating this doubt, he provides another undisputed example: "In the rule *ghavidhau ghaś ca saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 3.3.118), the mention [of the letter *gha*] in its actual application is not found at all. (468)

Regarding the rule "the suffix *gha* is generally used in the masculine when a name (*saṃjñā*) is to be expressed," the condition (*upādhi*) "when a name" employed in that prescription of the suffix *gha* is not uttered at all in actual usage; because the entire aggregate of base and suffix constitutes the name itself, this condition—which is a term identical [in meaning] to what is already established—is not explicitly mentioned, as its purpose has already been served. The same applies to the expression "by means of an action" (*kriyayā*). 468.

In this regard, one might think: "Since the qualities (guṇas) conform to the primary element (pradhāna), when there is a connection with that [primary], the word 'kriyayā' (by means of the action) must necessarily be modified. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Those [factors] by which a grammatical refinement (saṃskāra) is perceived in the primary elements, even though the case-endings (vibhaktis) differ, are designated as limiting adjuncts (upādhis). (469)

Since this adjunct—that action occurs even without an application—is capable of serving to enhance the primary element, what is the use of following the case-ending of that primary? For instance, if the assistance to the primary were thwarted even when there is a difference in case-endings, then the case-ending of the primary would have to be adopted. However, since the assistance of the primary is obtained through the adjunct—even with a different case-ending—because the adjunct has as its sole result the mere exclusion [of others], there is no regard here for the case-ending of that [adjunct].

For instance—even when the instrumental case is employed in the word "by action" (kriyayā)—because it possesses a different grammatical gender, the lack of coreferentiality (asāmānādhikaraṇya) remains as it was. Thus, it is established that even if the qualities are introduced in any manner whatsoever, there is a connection [between them] because the intention of their employment is to accomplish the assistance of the primary element (pradhāna), which serves as the substrate (upādāna). || 469 ||

Thus, since it is impossible for that which expresses an action to be in the instrumental case under the view that [the instrumental] qualifies the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*), he now explains the *Bhāṣya* passage—"all these words refer to collections of qualities"—which was intended to justify the instrumental status of words expressing action: "Words refer to collections of concomitant entities when there is no intention to express their individual reality, [occurring] in cases of conjunction (*samuccaya*) and option (*vikalpa*). (470)

The words "brāhmaṇa" and so forth function as denoters for that collection of coexistent properties—such as fairness of complexion, purity of conduct, and tawny hair—which are invariably associated with a specific caste. Although these properties may occasionally deviate and thus do not necessarily coexist, nevertheless, those properties which are concomitant with a particular caste are expressed by a word based on that caste; thus, the intended meaning is the non-deviation consisting in coexistence with the caste of *brāhmaṇatva* (brahminhood) and the like.

For this very reason, there is no confusion between the word and its meaning. Even though all [words] are dependent upon a collection of phonemes (*mātrākalāpa*), the meanings of words remain strictly determined, being characterized by their association with specific universals (*jāti*). Furthermore, when neither conjunction (*samuccaya*) nor option (*vikalpa*) is intended, words are said to denote a collective whole (*samudāyavacanatva*). This refers to the intention to express a collective whose nature is such that an option—consisting of the form "either this or that"—is absent, and a conjunction—consisting of the form "both this and that"—is likewise absent. (470)

One might object: "Granted that there may be no conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) here because it contradicts the meaning of a collective whole; however, how does conjunction (*samuccaya*), which consists of multiple objects occurring simultaneously, not contradict the status of being a collective? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "But conjunction is effected in those cases where [the words] apply to each individual object; for them, there occurs a connection with number by means of a substratum of distinction. (471)

Alternatively, if the expressive word functions toward each individual object, then the aggregate would have to be expressed in its collective form. For instance, when the parts contained within an aggregate are denoted with equal status, all of them are expressed as primarily combined. And thus, because the distinction [between the parts] is manifest, the plural number would be employed due to the primary object; just as in the case of "trees" (*vṛkṣāḥ*), which, being denoted with the predominance of distinction, possess plurality.

But when the collection is denoted as a single unity—just as in the case of the word *vana* (forest)—then, because there is oneness of referent, the singular number alone is logical. And in that case, there is an absence of conjunction (*samuccaya*), which is based upon plurality. Thus, since the meaning here consists of a collective whole, it is impossible for [the suffixes] to function with respect to each individual referent; consequently, there is an absence of conjunction. || 471 ||

If, then, the collection of phonemes is not denoted as being of equal status [to the universal], what is the difference between this position and the view that the word denotes a substance qualified by a universal? To this he says: "By all those co-occurring objects, the universals are qualified; cognitions of these are produced for the perceivers. Therefore, they know those [universals] to be the meanings of words. (472)

Since objects are distinguished for cognizers by means of genus, quality, action, and co-existent entities, there arise cognitions colored by these [factors] which grasp objects as delimited by genus; therefore, because a word is employed with respect to an object determined according to such cognitions, and because the object is understood in that very same way from the word, it is established that the meaning of a word is precisely the collection of qualities as it is perceived.

Because a substance (*dravya*) is connected with causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), it alone is primary; thus, when conjoined with properties such as genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*kriyā*), it is the object of verbal expression. This means that because the referent is one, the singular number is used here as well. However, under the view that the substance is denoted, it is the substance itself as permeated by the genus that is expressed. The distinction of this position from other positions is that actions and qualities—which are impossible for a substance that is [otherwise] devoid of action and devoid of qualities—are understood through implication (*sāmarthya*). In this [position], everything is within the range of verbal expression. (472)
This is what he says: "All objects, when combined within cognitions, are mutually contributory; therefore, all of them possess denotability by words through their form as cognition. (473)

An external object is distinct by its very nature because it is partless; there is no conventional usage of conjunction preceded by division in that regard. Nevertheless, as it appears to cognitions affected by the delusion of beginningless latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), it is determined through an imagined division of parts, even though it is not an object for those cognitions in their entirety. And having been so determined, it is subsequently synthesized by separate cognitions.

And thus, since objects—characterized as genus, quality, action, and substance—undergo association preceded by differentiation only within the conceptual cognitions (*pratyaya*), the expression "aggregate" (*samudāya*) is used with that intention. For instance, words denoting forms mounted upon conceptual cognition enter into the Absolute (*brāhma*), due to the determination of non-difference; thus, all words are established as denoters of an object consisting of a collection of elements (*mātrākalāpa*) by conforming to the form revolving in the intellect (*buddhi*).

Moreover, even in the case of a *buddhi* (cognition), because objects appear according to their external state through the relationship of quality and qualified, there is a single referent (*ekārthya*) since it is the substance itself—conjoined with genus, quality, and action—that is denoted primarily. || 473 ||

Anticipating the objection that "if this is so, let there be the denotation of the substance alone; what is the point of the theory of a collection of qualities?", he says: "But the form of isolated entities is not apprehended; and toward those whose forms are not determined, a word does not apply. (474)

Since verbal designation is preceded by conceptual determination (*nirūpaṇa*), and since the mere substance (*dravya*) devoid of its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is not an object for such determination, a substance whose adjuncts are conjoined is what is denoted by a word when there is a perception of a collection of qualities. In that regard, words functioning with respect to a whole also function with respect to its parts. For example, it has been said: "The eastern Pañcālas.

Since the well-known word *pañcāla*, which denotes a country, is a singular entity, and since it is impossible for that country to be qualified by the word "eastern," the word denoting the whole functions with respect to its part. [474]

Then, fearing that a word—having fallen away from the whole (samudāya) and operating upon a constituent part (avayava)—might imply a non-eternal connection with its meaning, he says the following to provide a justification: "And because of the prior usage of the word, it does not cease from the whole; nor, even when it operates upon a constituent part, does it ever abandon what was previously employed. (475)

Because the relationship between word and meaning is eternal, the word *pañcāla* does not deviate here from its denoted collective sense. Furthermore, due to the usage of the preceding term, it does not acquire a novel expressive power in respect to a single constituent part. For neither the abandonment of an established [meaning] nor the adoption of a new one is ever desired for words in any given context. (475)

If, then, there is no relinquishing of the appropriated aggregate, how can there be a connection [of the self]? Therefore, suspecting that this word for the aggregate must also denote a part because the connection with the aggregate would otherwise be inexplicable, he says: "And if that which denotes the aggregate were to qualify the distinction, then there would be a lack of grammatical coordination (atulyavibhaktitva), as in the case of 'the front part of the body' (pūrvakāya) and so forth. (476)

Since the country (*janapada*) is a single entity, there is no prior distinction [within it] by means of the word "eastern" (*pūrva*). Therefore, the word *pañcāla*, which denotes a whole, would have to denote a specific part—that is, a division—only by conforming to its connection with the word "eastern. In that case, because a distinction (*vyatireka*) would be produced by way of a constituent part, the whole would require the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), and thus grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānavibhaktikatva*) would not obtain. For example, one says "the eastern or western part of the body" (*kāyasya pūrvaḥ paraḥ vā bhāgaḥ*). Similarly, one would have to say "the eastern [part] of the Pañcālas" (*pañcālānāṃ pūrvaḥ*). And in that case, coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) would be contradicted.

Furthermore, even when grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is not contradicted, it is not proper to abandon the primary meaning and adopt the meaning of the constituent parts (*avayavārtha*), because the relationship [between word and meaning] is eternal. Therefore, the primary meaning must indeed be maintained; however, the adoption of the constituent meanings would occur here through grammatical non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), and not through coreferentiality—this is the meaning. || 476 ||

Now he establishes the application [of the term] to a part: "The word 'five' is seen to apply both to a collection and to a location; likewise, the qualification 'all' is thus rendered appropriate. (477)

These words such as *pañcāla* and others would either be derived by following their status as the locus of residence (*nivāsādhikaraṇabhāva*), or, if such derivation is rejected, they would be accepted as having a natural connection with a specific meaning. In the former case, just as the entire collection of inhabitants denoted by the term "country" (*janapada*) experiences the state of being the substratum for particular owners, so too does a single part thereof; for this [collection] is not like a physical body (*kāya*) or the like, but rather stands in the place of a forest (*vana*).

And thus, because the entire collection of parts is not perceived [as a single unit] and because [the name] is completed in each individual part, the substratum-hood is attained only part by part. Consequently, this word, denoting the possessor of the cause (nimittin) in accordance with the form of the cause (nimitta), functions identically toward both the whole and its parts; for in both cases, the state of being the locus of residence for the form of the cause is the same. Indeed, even the whole is employed in various operations solely through the medium of its parts.

For example: "He has entered the Pañcālas," "The Pañcālas were seen," or "It was done among the Pañcālas. Even when the word denotes its own inherent meaning, it is entirely logical for it to apply to both a collection (*samūha*) and a part of that collection (*ekadeśa*), because words have multiple meanings. Therefore, there is no need here for the purpose of exclusion (*tyāga*) or inclusion (*upādāna*). Consequently, since the word *pañcāla* is observed to apply in both ways, and thus the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) exists, the word "all" (*sarva*) is stated as a qualifier when one intends to express the entire collection, such as: "All the Pañcālas were obtained," "taken," or "seized."

Otherwise, because the collection is a single unit, the qualification "in its entirety" would not be applicable. Thus, it has been stated that even for a well-known collective term, its application to a constituent part is indeed primary. || 477 ||

Right here, he states the opinion of the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra) as corroborative: "Likewise, in the case of *ardhapippalī*, for the purpose of excluding other classes [of objects], the word is employed in its divided form as 'half' (*ardham*) and 'pepper' (*pippalī*). (478)

By accepting the formation of *sāmānādhikaraṇa* (appositional) compounds, the *ekadeśin* compound has been rejected in the *Bhāṣya*. Accordingly, how could the appositionality in the expression "half-and-pippalī" (*ardhapippalī*) be justified if the word *pippalī* were not accepted here as denoting a part (*avayava*) within the sense of a portion (*khaṇḍa*)? And this is logical: because this generic term (*jātiśabda*) functions here with respect to the individual (*vyakti*) independently of increase or decrease.

For instance, even in a *ekadeśisamāsa* (partitive compound), such as *ardhaṃ pippalyāḥ*, the term "half" (*ardham*) is delimited by the word "pepper" (*pippalyāḥ*) for the purpose of excluding other types [of substances]. Likewise, in a *sāmānādhikaraṇasamāsa* (co-referential compound) as well, the word "pepper" qualifies the word "half" precisely for the purpose of precluding other types; thus, in terms of their result, there is no difference between the two cognitions. However, due to the difference in their formal derivation (*prakriyā*), the *ekadeśisamāsa* is characterized by the predominance of the meaning of the first member (*pūrvapadārthapradhānatā*). It is for this reason that the rule regarding the gender of the compound following that of the final member (*paravalliṅgatā*) is initiated, since it is intended to apply specifically to that *tatpuruṣa* which is a *ekadeśisamāsa*.
As for the argument that in a *samānādhikaraṇa* compound, that [result] is established simply because the meaning of the final member is predominant, that has been rejected. || 478 ||

Just as here the word *pippalī*, although denoting a whole capable of manifesting a genus, is used for one of its parts when there is an injunction intended to exclude other genera, so too is the word *pañcāla* used here. Thus he says: "Even a region of the Pañcālas is distinct from other countries; yet, when a word is used for the purpose of excluding another [part], no distinction is perceived therein. (479)

Just as the entire country of Pañcāla is distinct from other countries such as Magadha and so forth, so too are its constituent parts, such as villages and the like; thus, when the word "Pañcāla" is employed in an injunction intended to exclude other countries, because the distinction between the whole and its parts is not intended to be expressed, that specific difference characterized by the whole and its parts is not apprehended. Therefore, disregarding that [distinction], the meaning is that the word functions here primarily with respect to the proximate object itself.

And thus, because there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a part, there is no difference in case-ending here; for when there is the intention to exclude other classes [of things], the usage of the whole and its parts is indistinguishable. || 479 ||

If this is so, and since the denotable meaning of those two is equal, why is it said that "words function with respect to wholes"? To this he says: "But they are well-known specifically as established in the whole; their appearance in a particular part [is determined] by means of context, purpose, and so forth. (480)

Just as words such as "Pañcāla" are well-known to denote a collection (*samūha*) and not so [well-known] to denote a part (*avayava*), because their application to a part is determined by the force of context (*sāmarthya-prakaraṇa*) and other factors, it is said that these have primacy (*mukhyatva*) in denoting collections; the meaning is that this is because they are more commonly established (*prasiddhatara*) in that sense. || 480 ||

Thus, he states that for words such as "brāhmaṇa" and others, just as there is a primary application (mukhyā vṛttiḥ) to the whole, so too is there a primary application to the individual parts: "That which is a secondary mark (upavyañjana) of a genus, or that which is concomitant with its activities, or that in which a conventional relationship is established, or that which is generally characterized [by it]. (481)
When that [substratum] is not relied upon as being either a whole or a part, the terms "Brāhmaṇa" and so forth apply without distinction to the object itself.

The substance that manifests the genus (*jāti*), augmented by specific sacraments such as initiation (*upanayana*) and assisted by instruction, is that which is invariably concomitant with the performance of rituals such as sacrificing and officiating at sacrifices; namely, purity, faith, learning, and so forth. In that context, the word—functioning by relying upon that [substance] whose connection to the genus is established through conventional usage and whose application is well-known, and which is frequently inferred from qualities such as gentleness of mind, truthfulness, and freedom from enmity—is determined to be denotative of the whole (*samudāyābhidhāyī*).

Because of its established usage. Furthermore, since this word—whose application is based on a genus—is used in an injunction intended to exclude other genera by not relying on a distinction between the whole and its parts, its application to a part is not contradictory. However, because the determination [of its specific meaning] occurs through the force of context, purpose, and so forth, it remains strictly non-primary (amukhya). || 481, 482 ||

If that is so, then the meaning of the whole (*samudāya*) is indeed one thing, and the meaning of the parts (*avayava*) is another; since a distinction between words and their meanings is established through this difference, how can there be the designation—based on non-difference—that "words functioning in wholes function in parts"? To this, he says: "And that which is observed to have an identical phonetic form when situated in a whole, by means of that [form], a metaphorical unity is perceived even in the part. (483)

It has been stated that because the phonemes are identical and the forms are similar, one determines their oneness; thus, a word established as denotative with respect to a whole (samudāya) also functions with respect to its parts (avayava). For it has already been said that there is no application of that very same word to a part after being withdrawn from the whole, as that would entail the consequence of the non-eternality of the relationship [between word and meaning]. || 483 ||

Thus, because of similarity and through the metaphorical application (*upacāra*) of a term denoting a whole to its part, the first example—"the eastern Pañcālas"—has been explained. Another example is also given: "oil has been consumed; ghee has been consumed. He explains this: "Because of refinement (*saṃskāra*) or because of damage (*upaghāta*), a generic term (*jātiśabda*) is applied here to oil and the like, even when the specific measure [of the substance] has not been stated; this is understood by implication (*sāmarthyāt*). (Verse 484)

The fact that genus-words (*jātiśabda*) fall under the category of collective expressions (*samudāyānupātitva*) has not been observed [in the case of words like *taila*]. For it is these [words] that denote the genus, while the individual (*vyakti*) is the substratum of the genus. This is the response to the objection: "If words such as *taila* (oil) have the genus as their cause [of application], how is it possible for them to serve as examples here for being expressive of a collective? To explain: when clarified butter (*ghṛta*) or oil (*taila*), having been prepared with specific medicinal ingredients to pacify a particular disease, is taken in a measured quantity, it is that which is intended here as the denotation of the word *taila* and so forth.

And because that [measure] has a limited dimension—being sixteen, thirty-two, and so forth, in *pala*s—it constitutes a collective whole (*samudāya*). Alternatively, [substances] such as ghee or oil, which have been defiled by dogs, crows, and the like, are to be discarded; however, in this context, it is precisely a fixed measure of ghee, oil, and so forth that is intended, due to the force of the context. Otherwise, if the words "oil" and so forth were based on the universal (*jāti*), then since there would be no distinction regarding the inherence of the universal, it would be untenable to claim that the term applies either to the collective whole or to the individual part.

However, in the case of a pot of fixed measure, even when only a portion of that ghee or oil is consumed day by day, the application [of the name] to the part is justified through the superimposition of non-difference upon the whole, thinking, "This very same thing has been eaten. Likewise, even when it is defiled by contact with a dog or other such things, the application [of the name] to the part occurs through the superimposition of the whole, thinking, "This is that same dog-ghee or dog-oil. || 484 ||

If it is asked how this intention of the commentator is to be determined, he says: "In the case of words denoting genus (*jāti*) or quality (*guṇa*), a difference in physical form (*mūrti*) is not intended [to be expressed]. Those [words] are based solely on the difference in the relation to the genus or the quality. (Verse 485)

Words based on genus (*jāti*) and quality (*guṇa*) function with respect to the mere possessor of those [genus and quality], without depending upon a distinction of form or a specific dimension of a non-pervasive substance. For their application proceeds to determine the connection with a particular genus and quality, regardless of increase or decrease. That is to say: since the very relation between the genus and the quality is what distinguishes it from others, "distinction" (*bheda*) means "particularity" (*viśeṣa*); this alone, independent of a distinction of form, is the basis (*nibandhana*) or cause (*nimitta*) for these [words].

However, those words denoting measure, such as *droṇa* and the like, express an object whose measure has already been determined; thus, they do not apply when a portion has been removed. Consequently, if the application [of these terms] were based on a genus (*jāti*), there would be no distinction between the whole and its parts in the case of words like *taila* (oil). Therefore, it is inferred that in this context, the author of the Bhāṣya intends the word *taila* and others to refer to an object characterized by the destruction of its processed state (*saṃskāra*). For in another passage, the Cūrṇikāra establishes the distinction between words for measure and words for genus or quality, stating: "A *droṇa*, a *prastha*, a hundred. (485)

Now, in order to explain another example—namely, "white," "blue," and "black"—right here, he says: "And the designations 'black' and so forth are due to qualities (guṇas) that reside in all the parts; yet those [qualities], though situated in only one part, serve as the differentiators of the cloth and other such objects. (486)

It has just been stated that words denoting qualities do not depend on a distinction of physical form (*mūrti*). Nevertheless, in common usage, when a quality pervades all the constituent parts (*avayava*), the designation of that quality is established—as in "the cloth is black" or "the cloth is white. Thus, these are called collective terms (*samudāya-śabda*) in their primary sense (*mukhya-vṛtti*). However, even where one part is white and another is black, the application of terms such as "white" occurs through the superimposition (*āropa*) of the whole upon the parts.

For when even a single part of a cloth is not white, yet an injunction is directed toward the exclusion of that [non-white], the application of words such as "white" occurs through the superimposition of the whole upon the parts. Indeed, when even a single part of a cloth is not white, this usage occurs in an injunction intended to exclude it, provided there is an intention to express the non-difference between the whole and its parts. For instance, when the soiled state of a part of a cloth that has just been washed is observed, speakers full of indignation say, "The cloth has been made black. (486)

Regarding that very point, he states another perspective: "But when cloth and the like exist there as subsisting in the parts of the cloth, then, like [the word] 'oil' and so forth, they are said to be class-words (jātiśabda). (487)

When a cloth that is black in only one part is designated as "the cloth is black," there are two possible explanations. First, the word "black" is applied to the part through the superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of the blackness belonging to the whole, as was explained previously. Second, when the word "cloth" is applied here to a single part, then the black part situated there is denoted by the word "black" in its primary sense (*mukhyatayā*), based on the quality of blackness that pervades all parts of the whole. In this case, the word "cloth," which denotes a collection, is applied to a single part; this is the example cited here.

And in that case, it should be understood that the word [denotes] the genus (*jāti*), just like the word "oil" (*taila*) and others. For just as even genus-words such as "oil," having acquired the status of collective terms (*samudāyaśabda*) with respect to a substance that has attained excellence through processing or refinement, convey their meaning by superimposing that form upon a part when the expression is intended to exclude other things; so too do these words, such as "cloth" (*paṭa*), function even with respect to a part. And by this very same principle, the word "ghee" (*ghṛta*) and others have their primary meaning.

However, the word *bhukta* (eaten) should be understood as being applied to the aggregate through the superimposition of the form of its individual parts, provided that it is possible to follow the established usage of the action-word *bhukta* even when the object (*karman*) has a limited measure.

To explain: when it is doubtful whether oil or the like has been consumed, spoiled, or refined, then, in order to exclude the possibility that it has not been consumed, when it is stated "the oil has been consumed" (*tailaṃ bhuktam*), it is logical that the constituent part is denoted by the word for the whole, since there is no intention to express a distinction between the whole and its parts. This is the ultimate truth here: when the cloth (*paṭa*) is intended as the primary object, then the word "white" (*śukla*) refers to a constituent part.

But when the white part is intended to be expressed as predominant, then the word "cloth" (*paṭa*) applies to that part. The same should be understood in the case of the expression "oil has been consumed" (*tailaṃ bhuktam*). Just as the word "Pañcāla" is primary even when applied to a part [of the country] when the injunction aims at the exclusion of other regions, and just as the word "pippalī" is primary even for a single part when there is an intention to exclude others, so too the word "oil" and others are denotations when they aim at the exclusion of other things. || 487 ||

To provide a conclusion, he says: "For those for whom scripture has the purpose of negation, distinction among them is not required; in either a particular instance or a collection, a quality [mentioned] elsewhere serves as the negator. (488)

When a word—whether it functions with respect to a part or to a whole—is employed in an expression intended primarily for the exclusion of others, it denotes qualities and so forth while disregarding the distinction between the whole and its parts; thus, a word such as "black" indeed effects the exclusion of other things, and this operation of the word is primary. || 488 ||

Having thus established the illustrations, he speaks the following verse in order to explain the corresponding commentary (*dārṣṭāntika-bhāṣya*): "In this way, this word 'Brāhmaṇa,' which is applied to the whole, also applies to a part": "The term 'Brāhmaṇa' is used there [in the case of a Kṣatriya] because of his study of the Brāhmaṇas; for a similarity is indeed observed there with respect to the study of the Kṣatriyas and so forth. (489)

Some, however, say: in the expression "the Kṣatriya studies like a Brāhmaṇa," since the study is heard [expressly] in the object of comparison (*upameya*), the similarity here is perceived as being caused by that very [study]. Thus, the word *brāhmaṇa* refers to the constituent part, namely study alone; for the word *brāhmaṇa* is well-known in its primary sense as referring to the whole—as in "austerity, sacred learning, and study" (*tapas-śruta-adhyayana*)—and is therefore used figuratively (*samupacarita*) for the single part, study alone.
Consequently, according to this one view, the suffix *vat* is applied after a word denoting the action of studying, provided it is in the third case (*tṛtīyā-samartha*). (489)

To show that this is untenable, he says: "If the activity [of the teacher] were based on the Vedic study of a Brāhmaṇa because of the Vedic revelation concerning Brāhmaṇas, then it must be stated by what property there is equality between the two actions. (490)

If the word *brāhmaṇa* were to denote merely the act of studying, then the relationship of standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and object of comparison (*upameya*) would be understood as existing only between two acts of studying, not between two teachers based on that [act]. Furthermore, the property serving as the basis for the comparison—such as excellence (*sauṣṭhava*)—would have to be predicated of the two acts of studying themselves. Consequently, since that act of studying, having become the locus [of the comparison], would be designated as "this is that," it would lose its status as an action; thus, the intention is that the capacity of a word denoting an action to function with a third-case ending would not be established. || 490 ||

Therefore, he presents his own established conclusion (siddhānta), stating that this is what is logical here: "When the application of the Vedic term 'Brāhmaṇa' is said to reside in the student, it then functions as a causal indicator (nimitta); for the action itself resides in the student. (591)

Since it is impossible for a word denoting pure action to end in the third case, a word denoting a substance qualified by action is understood. In that context, although the word "brāhmaṇa" denotes a collective whole, its application is assumed to refer to a substance in which study is predominant, specifically to a member of that group.

Thus, from the word *brāhmaṇa*, which primarily denotes the activity of the act of studying and ends in the instrumental case, when the suffix *vati* is applied—as in "the Kṣatriya studies like a Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇena tulyam adhīte kṣatriyaḥ*)—the relationship of standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and object of comparison (*upameya*) between the Brāhmaṇa and the Kṣatriya is understood as being caused by the study explicitly expressed by the words; thus, the desired conclusion is established. || 491 ||

Regarding the view of certain [opponents], he states another defect: "If there were a connection with the word 'lion' denoting mere valor, then the genitive case would follow after Caitra, just as it does when [the word 'lion'] is used in conjunction with [qualities] such as valor. (492)

If someone were to claim that in the expression "like a Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇavat*), the word *brāhmaṇa* denotes merely the act of Vedic study, then—by analogy with the connection of Caitra with the word *siṃha*, which denotes merely valor—the genitive case based on distinction would result in the expression "Caitra’s lion" (*caitrasya siṃhaḥ*), just as one says "Caitra’s valor. However, in our view, since the word *siṃha* applies to that which possesses [the quality of] it, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the standard of comparison and the object of comparison is established through their identity.

He states another point of view regarding the perception [of objects]: "In cases such as 'it should be given to a Brāhmaṇa' or 'to a Vaiśya,' the connection with the recipient and so forth is not possible in the case of a mere action. (493)

If the word *brāhmaṇa* were denoted solely in reference to the act of studying, then in cases such as "one should give to a Vaiśya as to a Brāhmaṇa," "one should study from a Vaiśya as from a Brāhmaṇa," or "one should behave toward a Vaiśya as toward a Brāhmaṇa," there could be no connection with the recipient (*sampradāna*), the source (*apādāna*), the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), and so forth; for such relationships are impossible in the case of a mere action alone. Indeed, it is not possible to study from the "studying" of a Brāhmaṇa. However, in our view, where the word denotes the possessor of that quality (the person), all of this is logically consistent. (Verse 493)

Furthermore, he states that even the contradiction with the Bhāṣya belongs to the opinion of some: "Because *vṛt* does not denote mere action, its inclusion among the indeclinables (*avyaya*) need not be performed at all; for both positions are equal. (494)

Regarding the view that the suffix is a qualifier of the meaning of the affix (*pratyayārthaviśeṣaṇapakṣa*), the author of the Bhāṣya states precisely this: "Moreover, it would not be necessary to include *vat* among the indeclinables (*avyaya*); for when it occurs as a verbal action (*kriyā*), it will not be connected with gender and number."

Furthermore, if even in the view where the base-meaning (*prakṛtyartha*) is qualified [by the suffix], words denoting the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) express only action, then since the meaning of the suffix must logically be an action equal to that [standard] action, and because that [action] is non-substantial (*asattvabhūta*), its status as being devoid of gender and number is already established; consequently, its inclusion among the *avyaya*s (indeclinables) for the sake of the technical designation would not need to be listed among the "substantial" (*sattvavacana*) items such as the *svarādi* group. Thus, how is it that the listing occurs in that very place in order to favor the view where the suffix-meaning (*pratyayārtha*) is qualified?

The author of the Bhāṣya states that [the suffix] must be understood as denoting something to be performed (*kartavya*). For if words such as *brāhmaṇa* and so forth denote action alone, then both positions—namely, that the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) qualifies the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), or vice versa—are equivalent, since in both cases the action is the meaning of the suffix.

However, when in our view the word *brāhmaṇa* denotes one who possesses action (*kriyāvat*), then it is logical that the object of comparison (*upameya*) must likewise possess action to be similar to it. Consequently, since it would be an existent entity (*sattvabhūta*), gender and number would apply to it; therefore, the inclusion of the suffix *-vat* among the indeclinables (*avyaya*) would have to be made specifically for this view. Thus, it is appropriate to state that the superiority of the view which takes the meaning of the suffix as the qualifier is demonstrated by that very inclusion. 494.

Having thus exposed the faulty nature of the opinion of the other school, he states his own view as being faultless by way of conclusion: "It [the word] abandons either the genus (*jāti*) or the substance (*dravya*); therefore, it does not reside in a constituent part. For since there is a scriptural injunction regarding action, it resides in the object possessing that [action]. (495)

Since there is a fault in denoting mere action in this way, therefore the word *brāhmaṇa*, even when applied to a single part [of the whole], does not abandon either the genus (*jāti*) or the substance (*dravya*). It should be understood that the genus is employed here as a point of comparison: just as a word, even when applied to a collection of qualities in order to avoid confusion, does not relinquish its basis in the genus, so too a word, even when applied to a single constituent part, does not lose the substance as its denotable object.

And since in the Sūtra the action is heard as a qualifying attribute (upādhi) of the meaning of the verbal root, therefore the word "Brāhmaṇa" and so forth is understood here as referring to a substance (dravya) possessing that [action], while other concomitant properties are abandoned; thus, its application by way of a part (avayava-vṛtti) is also justified. || 495 ||

If, then, that which possesses action is the denoted meaning, how is it that action has the capacity to be construed with the third case? To this he says: "Since the mention of 'action' here is for the purpose of excluding non-actions, therefore the word 'action' is understood as referring to that which is characterized by action. (496)

Since it is impossible for a primary word denoting mere action to end in the third case, the term "action" (kriyā-śabda) mentioned here—intended to exclude substances, qualities, and their possessors from that which is not action—indicates by implication (upalakṣayati) that which possesses action; for when the primary meaning is possible, figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) is observed in cases such as the word "Ganges. || 496 ||

How is this so? For [one might argue that] words such as *hotavya* (that which is to be offered) denote merely an action. To this he says: "Since in words such as *hotavya*, another action must be expected—just as in the case of [words like] *brāhmaṇa* and so on—with respect to a pure meaning, therefore there is no application [of the suffix] for anything [else]. (497)

When it is said "like a Brāhmaṇa," just as the act of studying must be required as a common property (sādhāraṇadharma) for the purpose of the comparison, so too in the case of the statement "the Kṣatriya's sacrifice is equal to the Brāhmaṇa's sacrifice," another action would have to be required as the common property; otherwise, the syntactical connection (samanvaya) would be untenable. And thus, the acts of sacrificing and so forth would be equivalent to the words "Brāhmaṇa" and so on, which denote the quality of being a sentient being (sattva).

In that case as well, an action (*kriyā*), while undergoing the state of being a substratum for other properties, departs from its own essential nature because it attains the state of existence (*sattva*). Thus, since there is no expression of "pure action" (*kevalakriyā*) and the primary meaning is impossible, it is indeed logical that the word "action" serves as a figurative indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for that [substratum] which possesses it. || 497 ||

In this regard, one might argue: "If, because an action is heard in the object of comparison (*upameya*), that very same [action] is also attributed to the object of comparison (*upamāna*) as the common property (*sādhāraṇo dharmaḥ*), then what is the point of the laborious effort of postulating a partial function (*avayavavṛtti*)? Let the whole (*samudāya*) alone be the expressed meaning; even so, we shall simply depend upon the action residing therein as the contributing factor. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Whether the whole or a single part is resorted to in any instance, they call that which possesses a specific function 'the whole' (*sarva*) when established in its differentiation. (498)

Whatever word expresses a whole and whatever word expresses a part, they declare all such words to function specifically (*viśeṣavṛtti*) as denoters of a qualified object (*viśiṣṭārtha*), because every word is established in its application to a particular distinction (*bheda*). For instance: when there is usage with respect to a part, then the form of the whole is not required; thus, by the exclusion of that [whole], the meaning of the word is the specific [part] alone. Likewise, when there is usage with respect to the whole, then a single constituent part is not required; thus, by the exclusion of that [part], the meaning of the word is the specific [whole] alone.

Even when the term is applied to a collection (*samudāya*), a single part is not required [for its application]; thus, by the exclusion of that [part], the word denotes only the particular (*viśeṣa*). For just as a location (*pradeśa*) is called a "particular" because it delimits another location, so too a collection is a "particular" because it excludes a constituent member; therefore, even though the word applies to both [the whole and the part], its object remains the particular.

Furthermore, since an object permeated by all its attributes cannot be determined [in isolation], when it is denoted by a word in that very manner, and it is thus established that words have as their domain a collection of qualities (*guṇasamudāya*), then, when the word "Brāhmaṇa" denotes that collection, how can the individual part be perceived—given that it has been excluded by the delimitation [of the whole]—such that, even though the word refers to the collection, the relationship of standard and subject of comparison (*upamānopameyabhāva*) could be understood on the basis of that part? For, in the case of denoting a collection, its very predominance has been stated by the exclusion of both option (*vikalpa*) and conjunction (*samuccaya*).

For it is a composite whole (*samudāya*) in its integrated form that is denoted; however, the parts (*avayava*) here are not described as possessing distinctness (*bheda*). For if there were an intention to express distinction—either through alternation (*vikalpa*) or conjunction (*samuccaya*)—then there would indeed be either alternation or conjunction. But when the parts are denoted as having attained non-distinction (*abheda*) in their combined state, then there is neither alternation nor conjunction. Precisely for this reason, because the roots and other parts are not denoted separately by the word "tree" (*vṛkṣa*), the plural number does not occur.

Therefore, since a part is denoted by means of the denotation of the whole, it receives no benefit from that [part] which is not being denoted in its extracted form; thus, the meaning of the word *brāhmaṇa* to be expressed here is the part extracted from the whole, characterized as a substance whose function is fully integrated. Since the fault of taking the action alone as the denotable object has been stated, the substance directed toward the action must be the denotable object; in this way, its equality [with other castes] is established by way of the action. (Verse 498)

If the word, when applied to both the parts and the whole, possesses the quality of denoting the particular, then what would now be the general term? To this he says: "Whether as a conjunction (*samuccaya*), or as an option (*vikalpa*), or all the modes (*prakāra*) together—all these are described as 'particulars' (*viśeṣa*); or else, the unqualified [whole] is the 'general' (*sāmānya*). (Verse 499)

If all the distinct particulars (*bheda*) are denoted by a word either as a collection (*samuccita*) or as alternatives (*vikalpita*), in every case words possess the nature of expressing specific distinctions (*viśeṣavacanatva*). For instance, when multiple objects—consisting of universals (*jāti*), qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*kriyā*), and so forth—which are of different forms, are denoted with equal status, they are said to be expressed as a collection. In that context, since there is the exclusion of only one part [of the collection] and of the alternatives, this is indeed a specific distinction (*viśeṣa*). Likewise, when those very same objects are denoted by turns (*paryāyeṇa*), they become the subject of alternatives.

And even there, because conjunction (*samuccaya*) is excluded, they possess the nature of being specific modes (*viśeṣarūpa*). Although it has been stated that a collection (*samudāya*) or a non-optional conjunction (*avikalpasamuccaya*) is what is to be expressed, nevertheless, option (*vikalpa*) and conjunction (*samuccaya*) are introduced here in connection with the enumeration of the types of manifoldness of meaning. Furthermore, because they are introduced as distinct from conjunction, they are called "modes" (*prakāra*). Thus, the "modes" are properties (*dharma*) specified as subordinate to the substance (*dravya*).

And thus, this is the third position: that the properties (*dharma*) intended here are those attained through a general penetration (*sāmānyāveśa*), expressed by way of the relationship between the subordinate and the principal (*guṇapradhānabhāva*). These possible modes—equal predominance (*samaprādhānya*), synonymy (*paryāya*), and the relationship between the subordinate and the principal—have been set forth in sequence. All these modes, when expressed, are to be understood as "particulars" (*viśeṣa*) alone, because they serve as the cause for the exclusion of specific differences (*pratiniyatabhedāpoha*).

Even a universal, when denoted primarily as something undifferentiated, functions as a particular itself, because it excludes other specific particulars. For instance, many particulars being expressed simultaneously through the coloring of a universal form necessarily exclude one another’s specificities, since all are connected to the action by way of being permeated by that same non-differentiated universal. Therefore, the Bhāṣya states: "The universal is just like a particular. (499)

Thus, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of words in their capacity as denoters of particulars has been demonstrated. Likewise, its establishment [is shown] even in their capacity as denoters of a collective whole (*samudāya*). However, this must be explained: since in a comparison (*upamāna*) there is assistance only through action and quality, what kind of collective denotation of words is there with respect to that object? To this he says: "For in the case of the word 'Brāhmaṇa,' no distinction whatsoever is resorted to, nor is any excluded; therefore, this [word] is established as denoting a collective whole. (500)

If one were to establish a specific distinction [of the word *brāhmaṇa*], then because everything else would be excluded, it could not have the status of denoting a collective (*samudāyavacanatva*). Nor is it logical here that some specific [individual] is accepted while another is excluded; thus, the status of denoting a collective is appropriate. For the word *brāhmaṇa*, independent of context and the like, denotes the group itself. And since, in this way, when it denotes a collective, both the action and the quality constitute the meaning of the word, its utility lies in being the basis for a comparison within the domain of simile (*upamāna*). || 500 ||

For indeed, it is through effort that the subsistence in parts occurs therein; thus he says: "But that difference in which action is resorted to is determined; likewise, whether otherwise or in every way, it does not exist in the absence of application. (501)

In whatever object of comparison (*upamāna*) an action is relied upon—that is, expected as a common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*)—there that property called "action" is determined to belong to the word functioning as a whole (*samudāyavṛtti*). For in the expression "he studies like a Brāhmaṇa," since there is a reliance on study as the common property, the application of the term "Brāhmaṇa" is justified by the proximity of another word (*śabdāntarasannidhāna*) to refer specifically to that constituent part.

Since that intended specific mode [of expression] is restricted when another word is not employed, and no other [mode], whether individual or collective, is possible; and since a word that does not depend on the employment of another word expresses its own well-known meaning in its collective form immediately—therefore, in the domain of simile (*upamā*), it means that through effort, the function of a collective word occurs in its constituent part (*avayava*). || 501 ||

He states that very effort: "In the case of a comparison, the mention of the action in the object of comparison causes the recurrence of the action [in the subject]; making this understood, it renders the difference as if it were a distinct category of meaning. (502)

In the expression "the Kṣatriya studies like a Brāhmaṇa," the action heard in relation to the object of comparison (upameya), the Kṣatriya, indicates that the word *brāhmaṇa*—which is the object of comparison (upamāna)—also has the sense of an action. For the relationship between the object of comparison and the object of comparison (upamānopameyabhāva) is necessitated by a common attribute; thus, there is a shared commonality of action in both cases. Consequently, it is determined here that the word for the object of comparison denotes a specific instance of the action. The hearing of the action in the object of comparison does not directly denote the action residing in the object of comparison, but rather, from that [hearing], it is inferred that the word for the object of comparison signifies an action; such is the function of the particle *iva*. 502.

Since it is not possible for a verbal suffix to denote a pure action, even when the relationship of standard of comparison and object of comparison is intended between two actions, the suffix *vat* is prescribed from a word denoting a substance that is entered by an operation (vyāpāra), provided that the third case-ending is applicable; thus he says: "When similarity is intended through the operation alone, and the operation itself is what is meant to be expressed, the suffix is taught to follow a word that denotes [the substance] as having an action (*kriyāvat*). (503)

In the case of "the study of a Kṣatriya is equal to the study of a Brāhmaṇa," even though there is equality between two actions, the action—which is being presented as the substratum for other properties such as excellence (*sauṣṭhava*) and so forth—is treated as a substance (*dravyāyamāṇa*) and constitutes the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*). Here too, as before, since the mention of the action serves as a mere indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), the suffix *vat* is applied after a word denoting a substance qualified by an action that is in the third case; thus, this is the same as the previous rule. || 503 ||

If it is accepted that a suffix may occur even after a word denoting a substance when that substance is primarily characterized by an action it has undertaken, then—since action is of a non-substantial nature and thus established as lacking gender and number—one might ask: for what purpose is the inclusion of *vati* among the *svarādi* (the list beginning with *svara*) being urged? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Even when there is a desire to express similarity between two things possessing action, the suffix does not cease to apply when [the standard of comparison] is something possessing action, as in: 'He studies like a Brāhmaṇa. (504)

Even in the case of two substances possessing action that serve as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), if one were to rely on a similarity mediated by the expressed action, forms such as *brāhmaṇa ivāyaṃ kṣatriyo 'dhyetā* ("this Kṣatriya is a student like a Brāhmaṇa"), *brāhmaṇena tulyo 'dhyetā* ("a student equal to a Brāhmaṇa"), or *brāhmaṇavat* ("like a Brāhmaṇa") would result in the undesirable suffix *-vati*. Consequently, it has been stated that because it possesses substance (*sattvavattva*), the suffix *-vati* must be included in the list of indeclinables (*avyaya*). For if substance were predominant, the form ending in *-vati* would possess gender and number. Therefore, its status as an indeclinable is established by its inclusion in the list beginning with *svar*.

But surely, even for those possessing an action, the relationship of standard of comparison and object of comparison is mediated by the action itself; and since the suffix *vat* is indeed desired there, why was it said that the cognition [of its application] does not cease because it is undesired? To this he says: "In 'he studies similarly' (*adhīte tulyam*), the qualifier is in the masculine gender; but when the word *tulya* refers to the action in relation to the possessor of the action, it is neuter. (505)

When the suffix *vat* is prescribed to express similarity between two things possessing action (*kriyāvat*), because those two things are of the nature of a substance (*sattva-rūpa*), the word "equal" (*tulya*) employed for them is used in that same gender—as in: "The Kṣatriya studies equal to the Brāhmaṇa. Consequently, equality based on action is not necessarily understood; since one can also understand "he studies equal [to him] by some other quality," and because there is no cognition of equality specifically through action, the formation of the suffix is not desired here.

However, when similarity is based on action (*kriyā*), the suffix [is applied]; thus, the word *tulya* (equal), falling [into that category], because it is not a substantive (*asattvabhūta*), adopts the universal neuter gender (*napuṃsaka*) for the sake of the grammatical refinement of that [word]. And so, since similarity based on action—such as "he studied equally with a Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇena tulyam adhītam*)—is necessarily understood, the suffix *vati* is desired only in that case.

And in this view, even though the adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*) is a substantive, because it follows the properties of its qualificand (*viśeṣya*) and is therefore incompatible with specific genders, there should be no inclusion of the suffix *vati* among the indeclinables (*avyaya*).

Now, in this very context regarding the position that the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is qualified, [it is argued]: "If, then, the word capable of being in the third case is qualified, the meaning of the suffix remains unqualified. What is the fault in that? Even when there is equality of quality, the suffix would apply from a word denoting an action that is capable of being in the third case."

Regarding the objection raised in the Bhāṣya—"He is as fat as his son," "He is as tawny as his son"—how can such a suffix be justified even when the similarity pertains to a quality? For one might object that the word *putra* (son) does not denote an action. Anticipating this, the author provides the following justification to support the Bhāṣya: "Even though the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is qualified, because the meaning of the suffix is not qualified [by it], the application of the rule would result in the sentence 'He is tawny like his son' (where the comparison is between qualities). (Verse 506)

The objection in the Bhāṣya has been explained as follows: since the verbal action denoted by the word is a single entity, when the qualification of the base-meaning (*prakṛtyartha*) is set aside, the meaning of the suffix—namely, similarity—is not specifically qualified; therefore, even by means of the quality of "tawny" (*kapila*), the suffix *vati* should be applicable after the word *putra* when it is in the third case-ending, provided it denotes something similar. || 506 ||

In order to justify that the word *putra* denotes an action, he says: "Those actions which, having a conventional relationship with the son, are intended to be expressed in the world—by means of those [actions], the suffix *vat* occurs after the word *putra*, which possesses the action, when [the son] is equal [to another] in terms of qualities. (507)

He who abides by his father’s command, studies, and continues the lineage is called a son because he maintains virtuous conduct (*sadācāra*). However, one who does not carry out his duties, does not study, and lacks virtuous conduct is designated as "one who is no son. Thus, the word *putra*—whose etymological application (*nirūḍhayoga*) is established through actions such as abiding by commands and so forth—includes within its meaning those very qualities, just as the term *brāhmaṇa* and others include the religious duties (*dharma*) of study and the like.

In the same way, since this [suffix] also expresses a collective, when the intention is to express equality even by means of a quality—based on a word denoting a part, such as "son," which possesses action through the actions mentioned therein—the suffix *vati* occurs after a word ending in the third case. (507)

In this regard, one might object: "Since he protects [the father] from the hell named *put* (sonless), he is therefore called a *putra* (son). Thus, disregarding the primary etymological cause (*pravṛttinimitta*) consisting of the act of purifying (*pavana*) and so forth, why is there such regard for external activities—such as residing in a command or other functions—which merely accompany the meaning of "son"? To this, he says: "Even though the etymological cause is internal in the case of conventional words (*rūḍhiśabda*), the accompanying actions are nevertheless established as part of the word's meaning, just like the referent itself. (508)

In these conventional (ruḍhi) words, there is no following of the etymological meaning; thus, disregarding even the internal action that serves as the ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), one relies upon well-known actions such as "standing at the place of instruction" (*nideśasthāna*) and so forth, which—due to their constant association—are perceived as being equivalent to the substance denoted by the word. For it is the action serving as the ground for application that is primarily relied upon as the basis for the word's derivation (*vyutpatti*); it has no function regarding actual causal operations (*arthakriyā*).

Thus, since it is impossible for both [qualifications] to be expressed by a single qualification, when the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) has been qualified by the inclusion of "action" (*kriyā*), the mention of "action" serves merely as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for that which possesses action. Consequently, even though the application of the suffix after words such as *brāhmaṇa*—which denote those possessing action—is established, because the meaning of the suffix itself remains unqualified, there would still be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of applying the suffix even to things that possess qualities similar [to action]. || 508 ||

"Let it then be a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix," [the author] says, introducing another alternative presented in the Bhāṣya—"namely, that which is common, if it is an action"—in order to explain it: "But if, setting aside the sequence, it stands as a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix, because it favors the principal [meaning], because of similarity, and because of the case-ending. (509)

The sequence has been stated based on position (*sthāna*). Since it is the first [to appear], the word *tena* (by that) is qualified by the action-word (*kriyāśabda*); thus, its [application] is set aside there. Because of its shared case-ending and because it is the primary element, it is reasoned that it is proper for *tulyam* (equal) to be qualified by *kriyā* (action), as it is the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*). For when a qualification is applied to the primary meaning of the suffix, it is untenable for it to apply to the subordinate meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*).

And since a connection is possible through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), it is not logical to connect the word "by that" (*tena*) with "action" (*kriyā*) by supplying an ellipsis; for while the case-ending is identical [to the verb], the sequence [of words] is non-verbal. (509)

Thus, having set aside the position that [the suffix] qualifies the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*), if one instead postulates the position that it qualifies the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*), then here too the previous fault remains equal; so he says: "Because the base is not qualified, it would follow [that the suffix applies] to things equal to the action (i.e., substances), even in the case of words for qualities such as 'son' and the like, through the reversal of what was stated previously. (510)

Because two [qualifiers] cannot be connected with a single qualifier, the base (*prakṛti*) would here remain unspecified by the mention of "action" (*kriyā*). Consequently, from words denoting qualities such as *sthūla* ("large") and so on, the previously mentioned rule (*pūrvoktanideśa*) would result in the suffix *vat* being applied when a son is to be expressed as equal [to the father] by means of an action beginning with "being large" (*sthānādi*). For instance, that which was cited as an example when the meaning of the base is qualified—namely, "a son equal to the large one"—should be cited here in reverse: "a son equal to the large [father]" (*sthūlena tulyaḥ putraḥ*). Thus it is said in the Bhāṣya: "Even so, the third-case form (*tṛtīyāsamartha*) remains unspecified."

In that case, what is the fault? [The fault is that] a suffix would also result after a word in the third case-relationship that does not denote an action, even when there is equality with an action. || 510 ||

Some, however, because it is not explicitly cited here in the Bhāṣya, cite "sthūlena tulyo yāti" (he goes like a stout man) as an example. They consider this alone to be correct, thinking that from a verbal suffix (ākhyāta), there is the cognition of the object of comparison (upameya) as qualified by action. But that is not so; for: In the case of "sthūlena tulyo yāti," the hearing of the action (kriyā) is extrinsic (bahiraṅga). [Therefore] the suffix *vati* is not the cause [of the upamāna]; rather, in the case of "tulyaṃ yāti" (he goes similarly), *vati* is desired [as the cause]. (511)

Because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the masculine noun "goes" (*yāti*), it is not necessarily understood that the similarity pertains to the action. For even when Devadatta is similar to someone else in some other quality, such as stoutness, the cognition "he goes" still occurs. Thus, once Devadatta has been determined to be similar by means of another established quality, the subsequently occurring hearing of the word for action (*kriyāśruti*) does not serve as the cause or the basis for the production of the suffix *vat*.

For a verbal action would serve as the basis for the relationship between the standard of comparison and the object of comparison; yet here, at the time of the connection between the two words "sthūlena" (by the fat one) and "tulyaḥ" (equal), there is no proximate action present that could serve as the cause for the production of that [comparative] cognition. This is because the word *sthūla* denotes a quality (*guṇavacana*), and the word *tulya*, being masculine in gender, lacks the capacity to have an action as its object.

But once the relationship that serves as the cause for the arising of the suffix has been established, an action perceived subsequently from another word is "external" (bahiraṅga) and cannot be the cause for the connection with the comparison. And thus, there is no difference between this case and the expression "the son is equal to the coarse one."

But when there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the word *yāti* with the neuter noun *tulyam*, as in "it goes as [something] equal to a large object," then the primacy of the action is necessarily understood; for since the action is not a substance (*asattvabhūta*), its qualifier must also be neuter, which is logically consistent. And thus, the suffix *-vat* is desired here: "He goes like a large man, with slow placement of steps and his belly-jar swaying."

For here, at the very moment of the syntactic connection of the two words expressing the meanings of the base and the suffix, the action denoted by the word itself becomes possible as the basis for the relationship between the standard of comparison and the object of comparison—just as in the case of "he studies like a Brāhmaṇa"—and thus there is no cognition [of the comparison] based on something external. || 511 ||

Thus, regarding the fault that has been leveled against both positions, the *Bhāṣya* states the following resolution: "This is not a fault. When it is said that 'that which is equal is an action,' the word 'equal' (*tulya*) means that which is measured by a scale (*tulā*). And if the third-case correlate is an action, and the meaning of the suffix is also an action, then they become equal. He explains this very point according to its intended meaning (*tātparya*): "By that [word], two things are qualified when there is a single qualifier;
for the word 'equal' depends upon that property residing in both. (Verse 512)

The mention of "action" (*kriyā*) heard in one place serves as a qualifier; by that mention of action, two things—namely, the meanings of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*)—are qualified and delimited. [Objection: How can there be a qualification of both by a single term? For in that case, there would be a difference in its application (*pravṛttibheda*). To this, he says: "For the word 'equal' (*tulyaśabda*)," and so forth. Since similarity has both as its locus, the word "equal" accepts that property called "action" as residing in both; therefore, it stands as a qualifier of both by implication (*sāmarthyāt*), even though by direct statement (*śruti*) it resides in only one. || 512 ||

For this reason, he says that the meaning of the word "tulya" (equal) is thus established: "If there is a single common property between the object of comparison and the subject of comparison, then it is logically consistent to say that what is measured by a scale is 'tulya'. (513)

It is stated in the Bhāṣya: "That which is measured by a scale is 'tulya' (equal). Although the word *tulya* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the sense of "similar," the intention is that its etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) follows the action [of measuring]. Thus, just as something is delimited by a scale, so too is there a delimitation by a common property; therefore, the state of being "measured" (*saṃmitatva*) is identical.

And thus, even when [the property] is heard in only one instance, it is understood through implication (*sāmarthya*) as a common attribute (*anvayī samāno dharmaḥ*) in the other; this is the intended meaning behind the statement that [the object] is "measured by a balance" (*tulayā saṃmitatvam*). Therefore, even though it qualifies the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*), the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*) is the action (*kriyā*). For there is no other thing equal to action, other than action itself. || 513 ||

Thus, even when the meaning of the suffix is qualified, there is no fault occurring in either of the two positions, because the action denoted by the base (prakṛti) is implied through the power of the identical word. Furthermore, the common property (*sāmānyadharma*) here is not just any property whatsoever; rather, it is that which is present in the injunction (*codanā*). Thus he says: "That [property] is heard in the Sūtra and exists in both [the base and the suffix]; it is understood without distinction. And because it is a general term, the action is not understood as something unheard. (514)

In the Sūtra, this property [of comparison] is heard under the name "action" (*kriyā*) in the words "if [the standard of comparison] is action" (*kriyā cet*). Although the word [“action”] indicates that [the quality] resides in one [of the two], when it is enjoined, by virtue of its equal capacity, it is determined to reside in both. And thus, in cases such as “the son is as fat as [he is]” (*putreṇa tulyaḥ sthūlaḥ*) or “the son is as similar to [him] as fatness is” (*sthūlena tulyaḥ putraḥ*), the [comparative] suffix does not occur. For where action is explicitly heard, there let it be expected to reside in both; but this is not the case here, since the word for action is not heard. Nor is the word “son” itself expressive of action, because it is a general term.

For the word "son" (putra) functions as a signifier without distinction between one who possesses activity and one who is inactive. Consequently, there is no understanding that similarity exists necessarily through action alone; for when similarity can be established by other properties as well, there is no evidence that a collective term must apply to a part possessing action. Indeed, it has been stated that the application of a word to a specific instance is something to be understood through effort. || 514 ||

But surely, since qualities such as "abiding by instructions" have an established connection [with the word *putra*], and these actions are prescribed for the sake of a son, why is there no cognition of them from the word *putra*? To this, he says: "And even though not heard [explicitly], qualities such as abiding by instructions are understood; however, those properties which are fixed [in that specific context] do not exist in the case of sons and the like. (515)

Since verbal testimony (*śruti*) is the cause of cognition, it was asked how things not mentioned in such testimony can be cognized; the answer given was that they are "restricted" (*niyata*). This is the meaning: due to the absence of direct verbal testimony, there is no cognition [of a specific rule] that "this alone is the duty. However, when there is a general cognition, there exists a basis for it called "restriction. For instance, because of established usage (*nirūḍha-yoga*), even without the employment of the word that directly denotes them, a general cognition arises from the word "son" regarding actions that constitute a part of the referent of that word, by virtue of its well-known conventional sense.

Even so, because those many properties are firmly established [in the objects compared] and there is no fixed expressive word [to denote them], one cannot necessarily understand that the action alone serves as the cause of comparison. Therefore, since those common properties do not function as a relation (*sambandha*) with respect to the objects denoted—such as "sons"—there is no application of the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita-vṛtti*). In the case of "this boy is like a son" (*putravān ayaṃ māṇavakaḥ*), an action must be supplied by implication through the force of the meaning of the suffix *-vat*, such as "this boy is to be looked upon like a son" (*putravān ayaṃ māṇavako draṣṭavyaḥ*). And so forth.

Likewise, in the rule *sthānivad ādeśaḥ*, the meaning is that "the substitute functions like the original. In this way, the usage *sthūlavad yāti* ("he goes like a stout man") is explained as "he goes in a manner similar to a stout man. However, when the verb is not required, there is no such comprehension. || 515 ||

He concludes this very point: "Therefore, one who does not depend on action is not equal to one who possesses action; for when action is heard [of], that state of possessing action is also perceived. (516)

Since a common action is not necessarily understood when a verbal form is not employed, there is no *vṛtti* [of the compound] because, in the case of "son" and so forth, the relationship of standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and object of comparison (*upameya*)—which is based on an action—is not necessarily perceived. Therefore, one who does not require a specific action does not exist as being similar to another who possesses an action.

In examples such as "the Kṣatriya studies like a Brāhmaṇa," where the action is heard directly as residing in the object of comparison (upameya) in a case of *mala* [fault], it is understood that the action serves as the basis for the connection with the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) as well; thus, the rebuttal of the fault is equal in both positions. || 516 ||

Even so, the position that the qualifier belongs to the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārthaviśeṣaṇapakṣa*) alone has been established as the final doctrine (*siddhānta*). For thus says the Bhāṣya: "What, then, is superior here? The position that the qualifier belongs to the meaning of the suffix alone is superior. Why is this? Because it is for this reason that the Teacher has recited the sūtra in this way; he has made it coreferential (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *vat*. Furthermore, the reading of *vati* among the indeclinables (*avyaya*) need not be performed, since this [suffix], being used in the sense of an action (*kriyā*), will not be connected with gender and number."
