He explains this as follows: "And because it provides a counter-argument to two [positions], its superiority is declared; for, since it expresses eternal non-existence, it serves as a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix. (517)

Since both positions are commendable due to their successful rebuttal of objections, the position that takes the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) as the qualifier is considered superior. Indeed, its status as more excellent is declared because it possesses brevity (*lāghava*) in comparison to the other effort. For instance, since the suffix *vat* invariably and necessarily conveys an action (*kriyā*) which is non-substantial (*asattvabhūta*), it is established as an indeclinable (*avyaya*) by virtue of lacking gender and number; thus, there is no need to include it in the list of "etcetera" (*svarādi*) words. || 517 ||

Now, one might object: even in this view, since the suffix *vat* expresses something possessing action—that is, an entity (*sattvabhūta*)—the *vat* must indeed be included among the "svarādi" (words beginning with *svara*) [in the list of indeclinables]. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Since the activity (*vyāpāra*) exists in the suffix solely as a non-entity (*asattvabhūta*), there is no purpose for it to serve as a grammatical indicator (*lakṣaṇārthatva*) when the word is heard as an action (*kriyāśruti*). (518)

Since, when the suffix (*pratyaya*) is the object [of denotation], there exists a purely non-substantial operation characterized as "action" (*kriyā*) which is devoid of substance, for that reason, in this view, the verbal expression of action (*kriyāśruti*)—that is, the word denoting action—does not possess the quality of being an indicator (*upalakṣaṇatva*) of that which possesses action (*kriyāvat*), just as was previously stated regarding the view where the base-meaning (*prakṛtyartha*) is the qualifier, because a pure action qualified by an instrumental case is impossible. Indeed, when a primary meaning (*mukhya-artha*) is possible through direct denotation (*śrauta*), the resort to indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is untenable.
And thus, since the suffix denotes mere action (kriyāmātra), its status as an indeclinable (avyaya) is established; therefore, it need not be included in that [list]. || 518 ||

In this regard, one might object: "Just as in the view where the base-meaning (*prakṛtyartha*) is the qualifier, the employment [of the suffix] is due to the impossibility of a pure action, so too in this view, since the action expressed by the suffix is equal to [another] action, there is no pure action; thus, the suffix follows from the very expression of an action. What, then, is the distinction between the two views? To this, he says: "But because of the inclusion of that which possesses action (*kriyāvat*), when there is equality with an action alone in the case where the base-meaning is the qualifier, the status of denoting a non-substance (*asattva*) is established. (519)

In the view where the meaning of the base (prakṛti) is qualified, since that which possesses the action is taken as the meaning of the base, the state of being an indeclinable for the form ending in *vat* is established because it has the nature of denoting a non-substantial entity (*asattvabhūta*), according to the position that the action itself is the object of comparison by virtue of the force of similarity. || 519 ||

But when the position is that the meaning of the suffix is the action, he says: "When, however, there is a similarity based on the action between two things possessing action, then, because it is the possessor of action that is denoted, there is no denotation of a substance. (520)

Because it is qualified by the neuter term "tulyam" (equal), it is understood that the action itself is what is similar. And when that action is compared to another action through a common property such as excellence (*sauṣṭhava*), then we have the position where the meaning of the suffix is a qualifier [of the action]. But when the possessor of the action (*kriyāvat*) is compared, then there is a duality: either the predominance belongs to the agent as permeated by the operation, or to the agent as characterized by the operation. In the former case, because it has not yet attained the status of a substance (*asattvabhūta*), its indeclinability (*avyayatva*) is established.

Since the object of comparison (upameya) is expressed by the verb, the verb possesses the status of an indeclinable (avyaya) because its primary meaning consists of that which is not a substantial entity (asattvabhūta). || 520 ||

However, when the substance characterized by action is predominant, both the base (prakṛti) and the meaning of the suffix are possessed of action due to their equality; thus, because the suffix *vat* expresses a substantive (sattvabhūta) meaning, its status as an indeclinable (*avyaya*) is stated by its inclusion in the list [of indeclinables]. He says: "The suffix *vat* should be included among the indeclinables there, like *svar* and so forth; and in the case of 'one who studies equally with a Brāhmaṇa,' the suffix would occur. (521)

Words beginning with *svar* denote substances (*sattva*), as seen in examples such as *svaḥ* (heaven), *rohāvaḥ* (we two ascend), and *svaryāti* (he goes to heaven), where the status of being an object (*karman*) and so forth is invariably connected with a substance. For this very reason, they were not included among the particles (*cādayaḥ*) which do not denote substances. By listing them separately, their designation as indeclinables (*avyaya*) is established. Likewise, since a word ending in the suffix *-vat* denotes a substance, its designation as an indeclinable should be effected by including it in that [separate] list. Indeed, by the force of such inclusion, the designation of indeclinability applies even when the word denotes a substance.

In the former view, however, the status of being an indeclinable (*avyaya*) is established through its etymological meaning (*anvarthatva*). For according to the opinion of the author of the *Bhāṣya*, the definition is simply "that which does not pass away (*na vyeti*) is an indeclinable. The recitation [of the list] is for the sake of elaboration (*prapañca*). Even in the opinion of the author of the *Sūtra*, since some [items] are not included in the recitation, it is logical that the etymological designation itself is the definition, while the recitation is for the sake of elaboration. According to the opinion of the author of the *Vārttika*, however, the definition of an indeclinable is precisely this: "that which is without gender (*aliṅga*) and number (*asaṃkhya*) is an indeclinable."

Even according to the views of the three sages (Pāṇini, Kātyāyana, and Patañjali), in the view where the suffix-meaning is qualified, the designation of *avyaya* (indeclinable) is established even without a specific recitation [of the word *vat*]; thus, this position—that the suffix ending in *vati* is an indeclinable—is superior. Furthermore, by the subsequent rule (*tadarham*), the suffix *vati* is prescribed for an action, just as the suffix *vat* prescribed by that rule expresses a non-substantial (abstract) meaning like the word *iva*; therefore, there is no need for its recitation [in the list of indeclinables] for that purpose either.

And in the view that the meaning of the base [the verbal root] is qualified [by the suffix], by way of the injunction for their inclusion in the list of indeclinables (*avyaya*), the Commentator clearly states through implication that while there is a "non-substantiality" (*asattvarūpatā*) when the suffix denotes action alone, there is a "substantiality" (*sattvarūpatā*) when it denotes that which possesses such action; thus, in that very case where it denotes the possessor [of the action], the formation of a derivative suffix would be undesired. || 521 ||

Now, in order to explain the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the suffix *-vat* in this context, he says: "And coreferentiality is indicated by the meaning of the suffix *-vat*; otherwise, an unstated remainder of the sentence would have to be imagined as 'equal' (*tulyam*). (522)

In the Bhāṣya, by the word *vat*, the meaning of the suffix *vat*—namely, the word *tulya* ("equal")—is expressed. For instance: because it is that which is being prescribed (*vidhīyamāna*), the suffix *vat* in its unestablished state cannot be qualified. Indeed, the employment of a qualifier is purposeful only for the sake of distinguishing something already established. Furthermore, when there is a requirement for a qualifier in order to ascertain grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*), the suffix *vat* does not possess the capacity to function simultaneously [with that qualifier].

Furthermore, this [word *tulya*] possesses neither the nature of an action (*kriyārūpatā*) nor the nature of a non-action (*akriyārūpatā*), such that the qualification "action" (*kriyā*) would have to be employed for the purpose of excluding non-action. Therefore, what is intended in the Bhāṣya is the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the word "action" with the word "equal" (*tulya*), which is characterized by the suffix *-vat* and expresses the meaning of *-vat*. For it is appropriate that the word "equal" has both actions and non-actions as its referents; thus, when that which is equal is an action, it becomes one—this is indeed a coreferential relationship based on direct hearing (*śrauta*).

In the view that [the word *kriyā*] qualifies the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*), however, because *tena* (by that) would not be in grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇya*) with *kriyā* (action), one would have to assume a syntactic connection by supplying an ellipsis (*vākyaśeṣādhyāhāra*) such as: "that which is the third-case-competent [word], if it is an action, becomes [the object]. But when a direct (*śrauta*) syntactic connection is possible, its justification through ellipsis is more cumbersome.

Furthermore, in this view, an undesirable suffix would not apply to the one who studies; thus he says: "When there is similarity between two agents of action, and that similarity serves as a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix, the rule for the suffix *vat* does not apply in a case such as 'one who studies is similar to a student. (523)

In this view, because the action alone is qualified by similarity through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the suffix here denotes the agent as permeated by that action, and not the substance which is the primary referent. And thus, the verbal expression "one studies like a Brāhmaṇa" indicates the action as the predominant element.

In the former position, since the action (*kriyā*) is subordinate (*guṇatva*), there would result an undesirable suffix (*pratyaya*) when the substance (*dravya*) is predominant, because the similarity of the very same suffix-meaning (i.e., the base-meaning) with the suffix-meaning possessing the action is taken as the cause for the simile. Nor is a suffix desired by the subsequent rule, *tatra tasyeva*, in cases such as *putreṇa tulyaḥ sthūlaḥ* ("as thick as a son").

The term *bāhyena* (by an external factor) refers to that which is produced by a related word (*sambandhin*). Because it arises from the exclusion of the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the suffix is desired after a word ending in the sixth (*ṣaṣṭhī*) or seventh (*saptamī*) case. Therefore, in the expression *putravat sthūlaḥ* ("as fat as a son"), the suffix should not arise at all. However, when it is said *putravat sthūlo vartate* ("he exists as fat as a son"), the relationship between the standard of comparison and the object of comparison (*upamānopameyabhāva*) is produced by action (*kriyā*) and not by a quality (*guṇa*); thus, the suffix occurs. In every case, if action is not relied upon, that [suffix] is absent.

Thus, since the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) found in the Vedic scripture is thereby established, and because there is no occasion for [the word] to be listed among the indeclinables (*avyaya*), and furthermore because there is no occasion for an undesirable cognition regarding the student when [the two terms] are equal, the position that the meaning of the suffix is the qualifier has been established as the superior conclusion (*siddhānta*). || 523 ||

Now, this suffix *vati* in the rule "tatra tasyaiva" (Pāṇini 5.1.116), which has the sense of "like that" (*iva-artha*), is examined. Regarding this, the Bhāṣya states: "For what purpose is this stated? Is it not already established by the rule 'na tena tulyaṃ kriyā ced vatiḥ' (Pāṇini 5.1.115)?"

He explains the intention of the *pūrvapakṣa* (the prima facie argument) in the Bhāṣya—asking how the rule could be established by the preceding one, given that although the words *tulya* and *sadṛśa* have the same meaning, the former prescribes [the suffix] after a word ending in the third case (*tṛtīyā*), while this [latter rule] prescribes it after a word ending in the seventh (*saptamī*) and the sixth (*ṣaṣṭhī*)—due to the difference in the governing case-endings (*samartha-vibhakti*). [Verse 524: "In the rule *tulyārthaiḥ*, the meaning of that third case does not differ from the meaning [of the word] even when there is a difference in all the other case-endings."

Regarding the rule "With words having the sense of *tulya* (equal), when used with *atula* or *upama*, the third case is optionally employed": the meaning conveyed by that third case prescribed in connection with words having the sense of *tulya* is not different from the meaning expressed by all the other case-endings (*vibhakti*) being employed as instruments (*karaṇa*) in connection with the word *iva*. The phrase "even though there is a difference" means that, by implication, although the case-endings are distinct; or rather, even though there is a difference in the operation of expression (*abhidhā-vyāpāra*), there is no difference in the actual object (*vastu*).

For in this case, since the case-ending has disappeared in the compound (*vṛtti*), it is impossible for there to be a delimitation (*avaccheda*) produced by a difference in its meaning, because the cognition of a similar meaning remains the same. Only the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) itself differs here. Therefore, due to the non-difference of the underlying reality (*vastu*), the establishment [of the meaning] is said to be accomplished by the former [word] alone. || 524 ||
He illustrates that very non-difference of meaning: "It is eaten by a twice-born man just as it was eaten by a Brāhmaṇa; he sees [it] with a Vipra just as he sees a Brāhmaṇa. (525)
It was understood by the Brahmin as equal, and known as such by the twice-born; let it be given to the Brahmin as an equal gift, let it be given by the Vipra as an equal gift.
"Study much from a Vaiśya as well as from a Brāhmaṇa"—in such statements as these, there is no distinction whatsoever regarding the third case. (527)

When used in connection with the sense of "equality" (*tulyārtha*), the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is the remaining case-ending (*śeṣavibhakti*); when used in connection with the sense of "like" (*ivārtha*), the various case-endings are employed as means of action (*kriyāsādhana*). Since the remaining relation (*śeṣasambandha*) is preceded by a relation between an action and its factors (*kriyākārakasambandha*), there is no difference in the actual meaning here, because the entire relation between action and factor—which serves as the cause—is implied by the third case. By the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), [examples such as]: "Learn much study from a Vaiśya, equal to a Brāhmaṇa," and "This wealth has come to the Vaiśya just as it did to the Brāhmaṇa."

"This wealth has come to the Vaiśya equal to that of a Brāhmaṇa; these many qualities found in a Kṣatriya stand here like those of a Brāhmaṇa. "Many qualities equal to those of a Brāhmaṇa exist in a Kṣatriya"—thus it should be cited. (525–527)

On this point, an objection is raised: "I study with the same intensity as Madhurā, and I remember her with the same intensity as my own mother; how can there be a conceptualization of similarity between Madhurā and my mother? (528)

In such cases as "I study in Pāṭaliputra as [if] in Mathurā" (*madhurāyām iva pāṭaliputre 'dhīye*) and "I remember Devadattā’s mother" (*mātuḥ iva devadattāyāḥ smarāmi*), the suffix *vati* is desired by the rule "tatra tasyeva" (Pāṇini 5.1.116), resulting in "I study like Mathurā" (*madhurāvad adhīye*) and "I remember like my mother" (*mātṛvat smarāmi*). However, since this is already established by the preceding rule (Pāṇini 5.1.115), the following formulation would be applicable here: "I study similarly to Mathurā" (*madhurayā tulyam adhīye*) and "I remember similarly to my mother" (*mātrā tulyam smarāmi*). Thus, there is a similarity between the act of studying and Mathurā, and between the act of remembering and the mother.

In that case, with respect to the mother who is being remembered and the city of Mathurā which serves as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), no such action is observed that would be equivalent to the acts of studying and remembering; therefore, the function of the words "mother" and "Mathurā" is postulated [in this sense]. Only if there were another instance of studying distinct from the first study, and another instance of remembering distinct from the first remembering—being similar yet differentiated by a difference in substratum (*āśrayabheda*)—and if that [action] were inherent in the agent (*kartṛsamaveta*), then this [function] would be impossible in the case of the mother and Mathurā, who are respectively the object (*karman*) and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). || 528 ||

Therefore, how can there be a cognition here by means of the former? To this he says: "The recitation whose object is Madhurā, and the memory whose object is the mother, are denoted non-differently by the two words 'Madhurā' and 'mother'. (529)

In the expression "studying like Madhurā," although the action of studying is explicitly heard only in relation to the object of comparison (*upameya*), it is understood to apply to the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) as well, because a comparison is necessarily based on a common attribute. Thus, this usage occurs when one intends to express the non-difference between the locus and that which is contained within it, such that the study whose locus is Madhurā is itself called "Madhurā. Similarly, the remembrance directed toward one's mother is expressed by the word "mother" through the intentional identification of the object and the subject; hence, the usage "I remember like my mother" (*mātrā tulyaṃ smarāmi*).

The usage is: "I remember [it] as being equal to the study [conducted] with Madhurā as its locus. This means that the study in Pāṭaliputra is equal to the study with Madhurā as its locus, and the remembrance of Devadatta is equal to the remembrance regarding one's mother. Although the mother is here a *śeṣa* (a residual relation), nevertheless, with reference to her actual status as an object (*karman*), it is stated that "the remembrance has the mother as its object. For in this case, the residual relation is indeed conditioned by the status of being an object.

And thus, it has already been determined that in the rule "adhīgarthadayeśāṃ karmaṇi," this genitive case is prescribed when one intends to express the object as a residual relation (śeṣatva), and its purpose is to prevent the formation of a compound. 529.

Just as it was previously demonstrated that words denoting a whole can function with respect to a part, so too is it the case here; thus he says, preceded by an illustration: "Just as the word 'camel' applies to faces resembling the parts of a camel, so the word 'Madhurā' applies to a palace resembling a house. (430)

The word *uṣṭramukha* is derived as "one whose face is a camel" (*uṣṭraḥ mukham asya*). In this regard, the elision of the final member of the compound (the *uttarapadalopa*)—where the first member is a standard of comparison (*upamāna*)—is rejected in the *Bhāṣya*. For, since grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) would otherwise be impossible, the word *uṣṭra* here refers to the face, which is a part of a camel. Furthermore, since the face of one living being cannot belong to another living being, the relationship here is established through the internalization of the sense "as it were" (*iva*), by virtue of the semantic necessity (*sāmarthya*).

And thus, just as a word denoting a whole (*samudāya*) is used here for a part (*avayava*), so too the word *madhurā*, although denoting a whole, is used here for a single part—a house. Therefore, the meaning of "the houses in Pāṭaliputra are like those of Madhurā" is that "the houses in Pāṭaliputra are equal to the houses of Madhurā. Here, the word *ca* (and) has the sense of the word *tathā* (so). Alternatively, by including another illustration, the application of the rule is justified through the conjunction of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the thing illustrated (*dārṣṭāntika*). In this way, by means of this [sūtra], the suffix *vati*—which pertains to the sense of "like" (*iva*) in the expression "the houses of Pāṭaliputra are like those of Madhurā"—is subsumed. || 430 ||

Alternatively, lest there be a figurative application of a term denoting a substance to an action here, [the author] says—in order to demonstrate by way of an illustration that the similarity between two substances is mediated by the action—that the similarity between two students is predicated on their studies; likewise, the properties residing in the means of accomplishment (sādhana) are expressed through the properties belonging to the action. (431)

In the expression "the Kṣatriya studies like a Brāhmaṇa," the equality or similarity between the two acts of studying is expressed here through their respective agents, who are the means of that action. For in this way, the relationship of standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and object of comparison (*upameya*) is established by means of the act of studying between the two who are engaged in study. Similarly, in "he studies like Madhurā" and "he remembers like his mother," Madhurā and the others—who serve as the substrata for the case-roles (*kāraka-śakti*)—are described by means of properties characterized by similarity, which are based on the actions known as studying and remembering.

For, by way of the study and the recollection, the relationship characterized as that between the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the subject of comparison (*upameya*) is established between that action and its locus. Indeed, it is not only the agent who experiences a connection through the medium of the action; for the action is invariably concomitant with the instrument (*sādhana*) in general. Thus, in cases such as "he studies like Madhura" (*madhurayā tulyam adhīte*) or "he remembers like his mother" (*mātrā tulyaṃ smarati*), the suffix *vati* is likewise established by the preceding rule [Pāṇini 5.1.115].

In this regard, one might object: "The previous rule applies when similarity is conditioned by action (*kriyopādhi*); and since the action is already included by the suffix *-vat*, there is no need for the use of a word expressing that [action]. Here, however, the rule is prescribed for similarity in general; thus, there is a distinction. Anticipating this, he says: "The expression used in the sense of *iva* and the rule established in the previous sūtra—no difference whatsoever exists between these two when a word denoting action is heard. (432)

If a verb is employed, the scope of this rule (*tatra tasyaiva*) is already covered by the preceding sūtra, "When there is equality with that [standard], provided it refers to an action, the suffix *vati* is used"; therefore, this [present rule] need not be commenced. || 432 ||

Nor is it the case that there is no use of a verb in the prescriptive portion of the preceding [text], for it is said: "Even though a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is not employed elsewhere because it is already established, here the action is heard again, though its specific nature is not yet fully determined, because its form is undifferentiated. (533)

In rules such as *haraterdṛtināthayoḥ paśau* ("after the root *hṛ*, when *dṛti* or *nātha* follow, provided they refer to an animal") and *sāsya devatā* ("that which is its deity"), this limiting adjunct (*upādhi*)—such as "animal" and so forth—is a qualifier; therefore, in usages like *dṛtiharir* ("one who carries a skin-bag"), it is not expressed by its own word because it is already conveyed by the suffix itself. For a suffix prescribed for a specific meaning does not give rise to doubt regarding any other meaning.

In this case, however, since the suffix -vatī denotes "having an action as its limiting adjunct" (kriyopādhika) in a general sense, a specific action is necessarily understood by rule; therefore, the employment of a word expressing that specific action is inevitable. For a derivative term (*vṛttipada*) is incapable of conveying an action in its unqualified form, yet it lacks the power to indicate a restricted action. || 533 ||

He establishes this very point by means of an illustration: "Just as *sudarā* and others, when formed with the suffix *kyaṅ* after the verbal root *vyutpṛ*, are cited as examples because there is no difference [in meaning], even though the meaning of the suffix is present. (534)

The rule for the suffix *ṇaṅ* has been stated in connection with the meanings of "throwing up" (*udāsana*), "throwing away" (*vyasana*), and "shaking off" (*paryasana*). Accordingly, when the root *puccha* is used with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), since there is no distinction between these meanings such as "throwing up" and so forth, they are understood in a general sense. To manifest the specific meaning, the use of prefixes beginning with *ud-* is accepted even though the suffix itself already implies actions such as "throwing away" (*vyudāsana*) and the like. Thus we have: *utpucchayate*, *vipucchayate*, and *paripucchayate*.

Likewise, in cases such as *abhimanāyate* (he becomes well-disposed) from the roots *bhṛśādi* and *abhimanas*, when the position that prefixes (*upasarga*) qualify the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) was established because of the fault [of over-extension] regarding *aṅ* and other suffixes, the alternative position—that they qualify the meaning of the suffix characterized by the sense of "becoming" (*bhavati*)—was accepted. Even though the meaning is already grasped by the suffix itself, since there is no difference in form, the use of the suffix-final form is admitted for the sake of manifesting a specific distinction, as in: *abhimanāyate*, *sumanāyate*, and *durmanāyate*.

Thus, since the suffix *vati* is prescribed only for the mere action (*kriyāmātra*), when a specific action is not manifested by that form ending in *vati*, it is logical to employ a verbal root (*kriyāpada*) to manifest that specific action. And so, since there is no distinction [in meaning] once the word denoting the action is heard, it is established that the desired result is accomplished by the preceding rule alone. || 534 ||

He concludes this very point: "And this being so, the rule for the suffix *vati* established by the preceding [sūtra] applies here as well; whether it denotes a restriction (*niyama*) or a designation (*abhidhāna*), the verbal expression of the action (*kriyā-śruti*) does not differ. (535)

In this context, when the suffix *vati* is applied by the preceding rule (*pūrvasūtra*), since that [rule] expresses action in general, there is a restriction that a verbal form must be employed to manifest a specific [action], because it excludes other specific [actions]. However, the *vati* applied by this present rule (*yoga*) conveys mere similarity; thus, because it is not itself a verb, the communication of an action by means of a verbal expression following a word ending in *vati* remains an unprecedented phenomenon. Such is the distinction here.

The intention of the *pūrvapakṣa* (the prima facie argument) in the Bhāṣya has been explained as follows: "The employment of the word denoting action (*kriyāśabda*) does not differ at all nor is it distinguished [from the previous case]; therefore, the rule for the suffix *-vat* is useless because there is no distinction in the object of application (*lakṣya*). || 535 ||

He explains that the purpose of this [sūtra] is stated to be the commencement for the sake of non-repetition: "The cognition whose objects are substance and so forth is stated again; however, in the previous sūtra, it was prescribed only for the similarity of actions. (536)

By the expression "equal to that" (*tena tulyam*), because equality is qualified by action, the suffix *vati* is stated when similarity is based on action. Thus, in the case of "the *gavaya* is equal to a cow," the suffix *vati* does not occur when the similarity pertains to action. However, there is a distinction: by this [rule], the suffix *vati* is extensively prescribed in the sense of "like" (*iva*) even when the similarity is based on substance or quality. || 536 ||

For an example of this is as follows: "Like houses in Madhurā, like the white [houses] of a Brāhmaṇa. In this case, the suffix *vat* would not occur after the first [word] when referring to a substance (*dravya*) or a quality (*guṇa*). (537)

In the examples "the houses in Pāṭaliputra [are like] those in Madhurā" and "the houses have accumulated new jewels," there is a similarity based on the commonality of the houses' substance (*dravya*). In the example "the teeth of the Kṣatriya are white like those of the Brāhmaṇa," there is a similarity caused by the quality (*guṇa*) of whiteness. In these cases, the suffix *vat* does not occur according to the preceding rule, because that rule is restricted to similarities based on action (*kriyā*); therefore, it is stated here again. || 537 ||

He raises this objection: "If the undertaking has no purpose other than action, there is no purpose for yoga; for apart from action, [the goal] is accomplished through the prior yoga by means of grasping. (538)

If the application of the rule *tatra tasyeva* is accepted for the purpose of expressing similarity between substances and qualities (*dravyaguṇatulyatva*) when used as an instrument (*karaṇe*), then this [subsequent rule] need not have been commenced, since the mention of "action" (*kriyā*) was not made in the preceding rule. For instance, the purpose of mentioning "action" was so that [the suffix *vat*] might not apply to similarity based on substances or qualities. Furthermore, even in that case, its mention would be useless under this present rule, because there is nothing to be excluded; therefore, let it simply be "like that" (*tena tulyam*). The meaning here is that the prescription of *vat* applies to all cases of similarity. || 538 ||

Now, one might object: "It is not the case that 'houses are like Madhurā,' nor that 'teeth are like Devadatta'; rather, others are similar to houses which are the locus of Madhurā, and other teeth are similar to the teeth belonging to Devadatta. Therefore, since the previous [rule] is not established, it is indeed appropriate to prescribe the suffix *vat* after words in the genitive or locative case. Anticipating this objection, he says: "The occurrence [of the word] 'Madhurā' as referring to a part [of Madhurā] has been explained by the fact that the word 'Madhurā' is heard [in the compound]. The word 'Brāhmaṇa' will likewise denote the teeth, which are parts of a Brāhmaṇa, because the word 'Brāhmaṇa' is heard [in the compound]. (539)

This objection is not a new one, for this matter has already been settled. For instance, just as the word *aṣṭrā* (a goad) applies to the mouth as a part [of the elephant], so too the word *madhurā* (sweet) will apply to the house as a part [of the city]; thus, the analysis of the compound in *madhurayā tulyāḥ* (equal to the sweet [city]) is justified. Furthermore, the specific selection of parts here is determined by the fact that the teeth and other such features are employed as the objects of comparison (*upameya*). || 539 ||

Now, demonstrating what is excluded by the mention of "action" (*kriyā*) in the preceding rule, and in order to justify the introduction of the suffix *vati* when its object is a meaning (*artha*), he says: "But in the case of connection with *iva*, no genitive is prescribed without an external related word; in that case, the suffix [should be] by the preceding rule. (540)

If the mention of "action" (kriyā) were not made in the preceding rule, then the suffix *vati* would also occur in such an instance as *gauriva gavayaḥ* ("the gavaya is like a cow"). For when joined with the word *iva*, no ablative case (*vyatireka-vibhakti*)—that is, the genitive—is ever taught in reference to the mere sense of *iva* itself, without depending on an external related term. Indeed, the meaning of *iva* connects only through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), and it does not produce a relation of distinction (*vyatireka*). Consequently, when joined with it, only the nominative case occurs. || 540 ||

Now, one might ask: "In the previous rule, 'vat is [added] after that which is in the third case-relationship' (*tṛtīyāsamarthād vat*), how could there be an application [of the suffix] from that which is in the first case-relationship? To this, he says: "An excess arises through connection with the word *tulya* (equal). In that context, the genitive and the third case endings occur, for the word *tulya* is indeed expressive [of that relation]. (541)

The word *tulya* (equal) denotes an independent meaning; therefore, when it is used in conjunction with a term expressing an existent entity (*sattvabhūta*), the exclusion (*vyatireka*) of its correlate arises. Thus, according to the rule "with words having the same meaning," the sixth and third case endings—the case endings of exclusion—occur optionally. || 541 ||

However, when the word *eva* is employed as having the same meaning as the word *tulya* (equal), then—when the word *iva* is used, there is no excess in the object of comparison even without an external correlate; [in that case] it is employed as a mere indicator (*dyotaka*). (542)

Because it is employed as being dependent upon another object, the word *iva* reveals a specific quality residing therein; since it cannot be connected with an independent meaning, the word *iva* does not bring about a sense of distinction (*vyatireka*). Consequently, when similarity is indicated by the word *iva*, which has the same meaning as the word *tulya*, then—in the absence of a case-ending expressing distinction (*vyatireka-vibhakti*)—the suffix *vat* would occur according to the preceding rule even if the mention of "action" (*kriyā*) were absent. Therefore, this mention of "action" must necessarily be made for the purpose of excluding such cases.

Thus, the meaning is that this undertaking is appropriate as one whose purpose is not [merely] to state a fact (*akriyārtha*). Nor does this result in the undesirable consequence of [applying the suffix] after a word in the nominative case—as in *gaur iva gavayaḥ* ("a gavaya is like a cow")—because of the restriction on the case-ending for the governing relation (*samarthavibhakti*) in the rule *tatra tasyeva*. Therefore, there is nothing undesirable. || 542 ||

One might object: "In the previous rule, similarity ought to have been indicated by the word *tulya* itself, as the cause for the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) is the *vyatireka-hetu* (the sense of distinction). Since there is no syntactic connection (*samanvaya*) of the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) with the meaning of the particle *iva* without depending on an external correlative, it is impossible to indicate similarity by means of *iva*. Therefore, how can there be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of applying that rule to the example 'the *gavaya* is like a cow'? Anticipating this objection, [the author] demonstrates the difference between the two types of *vyatireka*—namely, those caused by *iva* and those caused by *tulya*—stating that if the mention of "action" (*kriyā*) were not made, then according to the preceding rule, the term *tulya* would apply to a *vyatireka* based on similarity.

Since the suffix *vati* being prescribed would lead to over-extension even when similarity is indicated by the word *tulya*, he says: "The distinction (*vyatireka*) that exists here [in the case of *iva*] is caused by [factors such as] sweetness and so forth; in the case of *tulya*, a superiority arises in relation to its object. (543)

In such cases as "the palaces in Pāṭaliputra [are like] those in Madhurā" or "Yajñadatta’s teeth [are like] Devadatta’s," this distinction (*vyatireka*) observed through the use of the word *iva*—which is caused by the genitive and locative case endings—is not based on the meaning of the particle *iva*. Rather, even without regard for the connection with the sense of *iva*, this [distinction] is caused by the teeth, the palaces, and so forth.

Furthermore, since a *vyatireka* (distinction) caused by the meaning of the suffix [in the sense of "like"] is impossible here, the suffix *vati* is established by implication after a word ending in the sixth or seventh case whose external relation serves as the cause. However, in the case of the suffix *vati* used in the sense of "equal" (*tulyārtha*) according to the preceding rule, the suffix *vati* occurs after a word ending in the third case, based solely on the meaning of "equality" itself without depending on an external relation; thus, these two [rules] have different domains. 543.

And thus, since the term "action" (*kriyā*) was not previously mentioned, he provides an example of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of a negative comparison (*vyatireka*) based on a common property: "The ox is similar to the *gavaya*"; in that case, there would be a derivative usage (*vṛtti*). But in the expression "it is like a cow," there is no such basis for a negative comparison. (544)

If the mention of "action" (*kriyā*) were disregarded on the grounds that it is identical [to the general cause] even when action is the basis for comparison, then the suffix *vati* would also apply in the case of "the ox is similar to the *gavaya*," since the similarity would then be directly between two substances. Therefore, the mention of "action" in the preceding rule must necessarily be maintained; thus, since that [first rule] does not account for similarity between substances or qualities, the commencement of the second rule is appropriate for cases of similarity between substance and quality.

Furthermore, the second application [of the suffix] does not occur in the case of "the ox is like a gavaya," because a distinction based on the meaning of *iva* (like) is not possible; since that [suffix] depends upon an external correlate, the suffix *vat* does not occur by way of the second application. Moreover, there is no pursuit of an external correlate here; for this very reason, there is an absence of similarity.

Furthermore, even in the case of "gaur iva" (like a cow), a derivative suffix would not be obtained through connection with a second [word], because there is no absence (*vyatireka*) based on the meaning of "iva," as there is no recourse to an external related entity. Thus, since there is an absence of the genitive case here, only the nominative occurs. Nor has a suffix been prescribed by connection with a second word when the first word is its semantic support. However, when an external related entity is expected—as in "gaur iva gavayasya saṃsthānam" (the shape of the gavaya is like that of a cow)—then the suffix *vat* indeed occurs, as in "govat. || 544 ||

Thus, having established the commencement of the two *yogas* by supporting the inclusion of the term "action" (*kriyā*), he states the distinction between the scopes of the preceding and succeeding *yogas*: "But prior to the connection with the object of comparison (*upameya*), however, the existence of the suffix *vati* occurs when the cause is a palace or the like; it does not, however, occur when the cause is something equal or similar. (545)

Prior to the connection with the object of comparison (*upameya*), when a distinction (*vyatireka*) has arisen by virtue of causes such as excellence or inferiority, and once the sixth or seventh case-endings have been produced, the suffix *vati* subsequently joins with the sense of "like" (*iva*) and connects with the object of comparison. When the external relation has given rise to the distinction, and the internal [distinction] has fully emerged, the third case-ending is capable of expressing that causal distinction.

For in that case, since the exclusion (*vyatireka*) arises solely from a cause that is identical in meaning [to the standard of comparison], the dependence on an external related entity would be without proof. However, if the mention of "action" (*kriyā*) were not made, the suffix *vat* would apply even to a similarity based on other properties—as in "the Kṣatriya is equal to the Brāhmaṇa"—even though the two rules have distinct scopes; therefore, the mention of "action" must indeed be made. Thus, the purpose of excluding non-action has been established by the commencement of the rule "tatra tasyeva" (Pāṇini 5.1.116). || 545 ||

In this regard, one might ask: "Why is the case-ending currently under discussion abandoned and a word ending in a case-ending denoting capacity (*samartha*) is adopted instead? To this, the *Bhāṣya* states: "No instrumental case is prescribed when used in conjunction with the word *iva*. He explains that: "In connection with the word *iva*, the instrumental case is not prescribed; therefore, having abandoned the case-ending under discussion, another case-ending has been resorted to. (546)

When the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*) is indicated by the word *iva*, a connection with that very case-ending under discussion (*prakṛtā vibhaktiḥ*) would have to be assumed; for if, in connection with the word *iva* regarding the remaining scope (*śeṣaviṣaya*), the third case were prescribed by the rule "with words having the sense of 'equal' (*tulyārthaiḥ*)," then [this would not apply here] because the third case is not prescribed in connection with the word *iva*, since *iva* is a mere indicator (*dyotaka*) and thus lacks the sense of "equality. Thus, in the first place, there is no third case in connection with *iva* when an internal relation (*antaraṅga-sambandha*) exists; nor is it intended to be taught that the third case applies in its connection within the remaining scope, as is the case with the seventh case.

However, when there is a dependence on an external relation, the case-ending of the "remainder" (*śeṣa*) does not apply in the case of a connection with meaning; rather, the case-ending of the *kāraka* (participant in action) occurs according to its respective connection with the action. Nor is every sense of a case-ending pervaded by that instrumental *kāraka*-case-ending—as was previously demonstrated—such that it would apply like the instrumental in a connection with a synonymous term. Therefore, setting aside the instrumental which is impossible in the present context, the genitive and locative are specified as being caused by the distinction (*vyatireka*) produced by the connection with an external object.

Furthermore, since the application of the term *tulya* (equal) to those two [the *tulyaśabda* and the *sādṛśyaśabda*] is untenable, the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) is also indicated here by the word *iva* as if it were something else. Thus, there is a clear distinction: the former rule [Pāṇini 2.3.72] applies when the relation is internal, whereas this [present rule] applies when there is dependence on an external correlate. Therefore, the subsequent Bhāṣya states: "But surely even the locative case (*saptamī*) is not prescribed [here]. If that is so, then since [the locative] is already established, the fact that the scripture teaches the locative in connection with the word *iva* indicates that the Teacher intends the locative to occur in connection with the word *iva*."

What is the purpose of making this known? [It is so that] this usage—“as among the gods,” “as among the Brahmins”—becomes justified. Just as there is no third case (*tṛtīyā*) in the domain of the remainder (*śeṣa*), so too there is no seventh case (*saptamī*); therefore, by this very indicator (*jñāpaka*), just as the seventh case occurs, so too will the third case occur.

Since the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) would already be established by the suffix *vatu* following the word ending in the third case—by virtue of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the very same indicator (*jñāpaka*) regarding the use of the word *iva*—the mention of the seventh case (*saptamī*) in the rule *tatra* indicates that when the word *iva* is used in the sense of a "remainder" (*śeṣa*), the seventh case is employed. The meaning of the *Bhāṣya* is that the third case is not desired [in this context], and therefore it is not indicated [by the rule]. || 546 ||

He explains this: "Even the seventh [case-ending] does not exist there; it was employed merely for the sake of making it known. It is accepted in the domain of the 'remainder' (śeṣa) among the restricted case-endings. (547)

Since the external relation of the cause (*nimitta*)—namely, its absence (*vyatireka*)—is already subsumed by the genitive case itself, the locative case (*saptamī-vibhakti*) does not exist here, just as it does not exist for the instrumental (*tṛtīyā*). Consequently, this [locative] also need not be employed. But surely, when a rule is prescribed based on a word ending in the genitive, the meaning of the locative is not included, such that one would employ a locative-ending term as the object of comparison (*upameya*), as in: "The walls in Pāṭaliputra are like those in Mathurā"? For the meaning of the genitive is the residual relation (*śeṣa*), whereas the meaning of the locative is the locus (*ādhāra*), which is a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*).

Furthermore, it is not logical to intend both the remaining [elements] and the means of proof simultaneously, because of their contradiction; for it has been stated that the non-intention of the means of proof constitutes the "remainder" (*śeṣa*). Here it is demonstrated: even when the suffix *vatu* follows a word in the genitive case, since no specific case-ending is heard in the formation of the compound, only the relationship between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) is understood. Since all particular relations are included within the general category of "relation" (*sambandha-sāmānya*), it is appropriate for the object of comparison to be expressed in the locative case.

For instance: by the suffix *vat*, only the general similarity (*aupamya*) is conveyed, because in common usage it lacks the power to manifest specific distinctions; this is followed accordingly in the grammatical treatises (*śāstra*), where the suffix *vat* is taught as being derived from a word ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) when it signifies a general relation (*sambandha-sāmānya*). And since all specific relations are included within the general relation, when the object of comparison (*upameya*) is employed in the locative case, then—by the intention to express its status as a locus (*adhikaraṇatva*) there—it is understood that the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) likewise has the locus as its domain.

For here, the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is subordinate; it is the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), whereas the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*)—the sense of *vat*—is the subject of comparison (*upameya*). Thus, there is a determination of its distinction from the object of comparison. Accordingly, it is proclaimed: "The doubt that exists regarding the standard of comparison is excluded by the object of comparison. Now, one might object: "By this same logic, the suffix *matup* should also be prescribed as being derived from a word in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhīsamartha*), since it likewise conveys the sense of the locative (*saptamyartha*); so what is the purpose of specifying the locative case with 'in this' (*asmin*) in that [rule]? This is not the same.

For the meaning of the genitive and locative cases alone is to be expressed as the primary sense of the suffix *matup*. Thus, in examples such as "the mountain possesses trees" (*vṛkṣavān parvataḥ*), the state of being a locus (*ādhārabhāva*) is understood through direct expression; therefore, it is proper to indicate this by means of the genitive case with the distinction "in this" (*asmin*). For in grammatical analysis (*anvākhyāna*), a meaning that is already perceived in common usage is taken up as a subordinate element (*aṅga*). And in this case, there is indeed a specific perception [of the locus].

Furthermore, since the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) is subordinate (*upasarjanabhūta*) to the suffix *vat*, the cognition of mere similarity arises from that which ends in it, while the primary meaning is that of the suffix. Therefore, that very [suffix] must be joined with the genitive case as the governing inflection (*samarthavibhakti*) and with the base-meaning as its subordinate element. Since the locative sense is already encompassed by that [genitive], the locative case should not have been employed; however, being employed for the sake of indication (*jñāpana*), it is understood [as serving that purpose].

For instance—since it is logically impossible for case-endings (*vibhakti*), which abide in fixed domains according to their respective applications, to penetrate one another's domains, it is here made known that the locative (*saptamī*) occurs in the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) when there is a "remainder" (*śeṣe*). The meaning is that just as the genitive occurs in connection with the particle *iva* due to an external relational cause, so too does the locative. || 547 ||

But the other case-endings, as if restricted to their own respective domains, do not become confused even when used in connection with this [particle *iva*]; thus he says: "If, however, the case-endings were to function in this domain by way of exclusion (*vyatireka*), then only the third case-ending would demonstrate deviation (*vyabhicāra*). (548)

If it were intended here that all case-endings (*vibhakti*) should apply without distinction—even those not within their own proper domain—by transgressing their respective spheres and through mutual confusion regarding the object of the "remainder" (*śeṣa*), then the third case (*tṛtīyā*) currently under discussion alone would be capable of conveying this meaning; thus, having abandoned it, one should not resort to other case-endings. However, since the adoption of another case-ending implies that only the seventh case (*saptamī*) applies here in the domain of the remainder and no other case-endings do, it is determined that a specific restriction is intended.
Consequently, usages such as *devair iva nāmnā* are incorrect. (548)

To conclude this very point, the Bhāṣya states "In that case, it is established," which he summarizes as follows: "When deviation is thus established even without the mention of the locative case, then every [case-ending] is said to be the locative itself; there are no other case-endings. (549)

By the phrase "so it is" (*tathā*), the third [rule] is carried over; thus, once the confusion [of cases] is determined, the fact that the seventh case is mentioned even without the explicit inclusion of the word "seventh" (*saptamī*) demonstrates that the indicator [of the rule] has a restricted scope. || 549 ||

In that case, let the locative case alone be employed here. For in this way, the purpose of making known [the rule] is also accomplished. Whatever meaning is obtained from the suffix *vatu* when it follows a word ending in the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*), that same meaning is also obtained from a word ending in the locative (*saptamī*). Indeed, the meaning of the locative—characterized as the state of being the object (*viṣaya*)—is capable of encompassing the meaning of the genitive as well. And so says the Bhāṣya: "Anticipating the objection that 'that which is to be grasped is always dependent upon the grasper,' he says: By the locative case, used for the purpose of making known the absolute [rule], The genitive case, though set aside, is withdrawn; it is therefore taken up again. (Verse 550)

In this view, since the locative case (*saptamī*)—which cannot occur when it has the sense of "like" (*ivārtha*)—is prescribed [in such contexts], it invariably indicates the non-existence of its own [referent] therein; thus, the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would not occur at all. Therefore, the inclusion of the genitive here in this view is for the purpose of indicating its existence. Now, one might object: if the genitive were not employed and there were only the prescription of the locative, then since the locative would be applicable only to the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) when an external related factor (*bāhyasambandhinimitta*) is present, how could the existence [of the relation] be indicated in the domain of the "remainder" (*śeṣa*)?

For it is only when the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) exists that this [term] "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is determined, since the genitive occurs precisely there. Therefore, the locative (*saptamī*), being mentioned in association with that [genitive], would indicate its own domain as being the same as that of the genitive. Consequently, if the genitive were not mentioned, the locative's status as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) would not even be possible; how much less could the genitive be sublated by it? This is true; however, because the other case-ending alone establishes the pervasion of the respective domains, through the employment of both, one becomes intended for the purpose of indication.

And in that regard, since the genitive case is undesired in the domain of the locative, the locative itself is stated in the Bhāṣya for the sake of providing this indication (*jñāpana*). Furthermore, because the suffix *vat* is desired even after a word ending in the genitive, the genitive does not withdraw from its own domain here; thus, this very [locative] is called its "non-obstruction" (*abādha*). Now, if it is said that this locative pertains to the "remainder" (*śeṣa*) precisely because of this indication, then the suffix *vat* would not occur after a locative expressing the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), as in: "walls in Pāṭaliputra, just as in Mathurā."

For in this context, since this locative case is one pertaining to the "remainder" (*śeṣa*), the locative case in *pāṭaliputre* would not occur in the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) unless there were an intention to express the relationship between the locus and the located (*ādhārādheya*). Indeed, it is taught that the locative case pertaining to the "remainder" occurs in connection with the word *iva*. However, the word *iva* does not exist in the subsequent application. Therefore, [the construction] would only be established as *madhurāyām iva pāṭaliputrasya prākārāḥ* ("The walls of Pāṭaliputra are like those in Mathurā"). This is true.

In this context, the word *tatra* recurs; or rather, it is presented by way of *tantra* (a single mention serving multiple purposes). The teachers explain that the intention of the Bhāṣyakāra is that the locative case ending (*saptamī*) is indicated for the remaining scope [of the rule] by means of an ablative construction (*vati*). Others, however, say: "The meaning of the locative—the relation of locus and located (*ādhārādheyabhāva*)—can indeed be subsumed under the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*), which is prescribed for general relations. Therefore, even when the suffix is applied after a locative form, the affix occurs only after a genitive form."

For here, when there is an intention to express the relationship between locus and located (*ādhārādheyabhāva*), the suffix *-vat* is not prohibited in the sense of the locative case; rather, it is merely made known that the locative occurs when the word *iva* is employed with the intention of expressing a residual relation (*śeṣa*). This point has been explained. || 550 ||

Now, in the order of succession, the suffix *vat* prescribed in the sense of "deserving that" (*tadarham*) is examined. To illustrate: there is an objection in the commentary: "Why is this stated? Is it not already established by the rule 'when [the comparison] is with that, if there is an action, the suffix *vat* is used'? He explains this as follows: "By means of the two preceding rules themselves, through the construction of a different analytical compound (*vigraha*), the suffix *vat* is established even in the sense of 'deserving'; however, that is demonstrated by a single example. (551)

In this context, "one who deserves the conduct of a king" (*rājānamarhati vṛttam*) is cited as an example of *rājavad vṛttam*. Here, because the term "action" (*kriyā*) is understood from the previous rule, the suffix *vati* occurs after the word *tad* (the second case-ending form) when it denotes the agent of the verb *arhati* (to deserve), provided that the action serves as the defining characteristic. Thus, the suffix is applied to that action characterized by conduct and so forth, which is the agent of the verb *arhati*. This meaning is also understood even when the analytical sentence is formulated as: "he conducts himself in a manner equal to a king" (*rājñā tulyaṃ vartate vṛttim*).

Consequently, in this case, the suffix *vati* is established by the rule "tena tulyam" (Pāṇini 5.1.115) following a word ending in the third case. Even when there are examples such as "rājānam arhati dhairyam" (patience is worthy of a king), resulting in *rājavad dhairyam* or *veṣaḥ* (king-like patience or dress), or "brāhmaṇam arhaty upaśamaḥ," resulting in *brāhmaṇavad upaśamaḥ* (tranquility worthy of a Brahmin), the suffix is still established by the rule "tatra tasyeva" (Pāṇini 5.1.116). Because there is an absence of equality of action (*kriyā*), it is not established here by the rule "tena tulyam."

That which is indeed the lack of fortitude in kings can be described as "the fortitude of a king," though this is merely a formal syntactical construction for another [term] that is worthy [of such usage]; in reality, there is no difference. However, in the Bhāṣya, where the accomplishment is stated by a single rule—"it is established simply by [the rule] *tena tulyam*"—that should be understood as not being for the purpose of defining a technical term (*alakṣaṇārthā*). For that is merely an illustration. Thus, the suffix *vat* is pointed out or indicated by means of a single [rule];
the intended meaning is simply that the establishment [of the form] occurs by the preceding [rule] alone. || 551 ||

Regarding that, he explains how the proof is established by the phrase "equal to that": "When 'equal to that' is employed, the action serves as the limiting adjunct (upādhi). In the expression 'he behaves like a king,' the difference [between the two] is intended. (552)

The suffix *vati* is established as having an adjunct (*upādhi*)—that is, a qualifier—by way of delimiting the meaning of the cognition (*pratyaya*) characterized by an action that has an equivalent object (*tulyārtha*). The meaning is that [the application of *vati*] occurs here either by the rule "tena tulyam" itself, or by this present rule. The sense is "he behaves like a king"; how so? For instance, the very meaning "his conduct deserves a king" is identical to "his conduct is equal to that of a king."

But surely, [the comparison] would be established when the intention is to say "the Brahmin behaves like a king"; however, when one says "like a king," a comparison with himself is not possible. To this he replies: "In this case, difference is intended. Since difference is intended here, the comparison exists. || 552 ||

He explains how there can be a division of what is one: "Those kings, beginning with Pṛthu and ending with Yudhiṣṭhira, who are renowned for their sovereignty, serve as the standard of comparison for other rulers. (553)

In this world, there were kings beginning with Pṛthu, Bharata, Yayāti, and Dilīpa, whose conduct was irreproachable and who fulfilled the duties of royalty, down to Yudhiṣṭhira. These kings of the primordial age are employed as a standard of comparison for the sake of praising the present king, whose conduct does not fully meet the requirements of royalty; [the intention being] that his conduct is equal to that of a renowned king, or that "this king behaves like a king."

For since it is possible that one whose royal conduct is incomplete might even behave contrary to what is befitting a king, it is said in praise, "his conduct is like that of a king. Thus, there exists a relationship of standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and object of comparison (*upameya*) only when there is a distinction. Furthermore, the determination of such a distinction here arises from the very force of the usage, because the suffix *vati* would be untenable in the absence of a distinction. || 553 ||

But surely, since the status of being a king exists even for the object of comparison (the upameya) by virtue of protecting subjects, why is he compared to something else as "this is indeed a king"? If, on the other hand, he does not possess the royal duties such as protection, then how could there be a comparison with a well-known king due to a lack of similarity? To this, he says: "The distinction between the standard of comparison (upamāna) and the object of comparison (upameya) is based on success and failure; for in every case, that which is unestablished is compared to that which is well-established. (554)

The relationship of analogy between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*)—characterized by the qualities of being complete or incomplete and governed by established or unestablished usage—exists everywhere and not only here; there is no doubt about this, since it has already been explained that such a relationship is untenable whether there is total difference or total identity. For instance, in the expression "the Kṣatriya studies like a Brāhmaṇa," the study of the Brāhmaṇa is the well-known standard of comparison for the less well-known study of the Kṣatriya, due to the excellence of the means employed.

Thus, in this context, he whose kingship is complete through the protection of the earth bounded by the girdle of the four oceans is designated as a "king," such as Bharata and others; however, for him [the mere ruler], there is no designation as one who "deserves the conduct of a king. But he who is a lord of only a single region, who is destitute of the means of treasury, army, and so forth, who has not secured his own protection, and whose conduct is unrestrained, is praised as one for whom "the conduct is like that of a king."

Thus, by means of a well-known Brahmin such as Vasiṣṭha, another person who behaves like a Brahmin is compared [to him] with the expression "this is a Brahmin. In this way, the establishment [of the comparison] here occurs through the rule "tena tulyam" (Pāṇini 5.1.115). || 554 ||

By the phrase "tatra tasyeva" (in that case, as if belonging to that), he states where the establishment [of the comparison] occurs: when the king himself is intended [as the object of comparison] in the sense "its form is like a king's," it will be established by means of the second [type of] connection, which does not have action as its purpose. (555)

It has been established that this undertaking [of the present rule] is for the sake of non-action (akriyārtha). And thus, by this [present rule], the suffix *vati* is established even in cases where [the quality] is equal to qualities such as form (*rūpa*), as in: "His form is like that of King Bharata," or "His fortitude and tranquility are like those of a king. Furthermore, even if the [previous rule] *tadarham* were undertaken, since the suffix is desired only after the verb *arh* when it denotes the agent (*kartṛ*) in relation to an action (*kriyā*), it would not be established; therefore, it must necessarily be accomplished by the preceding [rule]. Thus, the establishment [of the desired forms] by means of the preceding [rule] has been demonstrated. 555.

Immediately following that, the commentary (*bhāṣya*) is provided for the purpose of supporting the initial objection: "It is not established. When another person performs an action that ought to be performed by someone else, then the suffix arises [from the word] standing in the third case. But here, however, the suffix arises from [the word] standing in the second case, with respect to an action appropriate to oneself, when the agent is capable of performing it and has attained a certain degree of strength. This he explains: "When the comparison is not intended to be expressed, this [rule] is stated for the sake of restriction.
Dharma is the agent of the action 'to be worthy of' (*arhati*); therefore, there is a further statement for its sake. (556)

In this context, when the word *rājan* (king) is employed in its general sense, since only the genus (*jāti*) is being taken up and no specific distinction is intended, the relationship of standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and object of comparison (*upameya*) based upon that [distinction] does not exist. For in that case, there is an intention to express a restriction: "this conduct is worthy of the king alone, and not of another. Even though the conduct is already restricted by its connection with the king, what is intended here is the strengthening and stabilization of it by excluding any connection with others, as in the expression: "this conduct proceeds like that of a king" (*rājavad idaṃ vṛttaṃ vartate*). || 556 ||

Furthermore, when someone is said of those very well-known kings, "He behaves like a king," there is no relationship of standard of comparison and object compared. Thus it is said: "The expression 'like a skilled hand' (kṛtahastavat) is seen only among those who are already well-known; and even the expression 'like a king' applies only to a king who is already established as such. (557)

One who has made his hand steady through practice—that is, one who has gained mastery—is known as "kṛtahasta," such as Arjuna and others. It is precisely such a person who is described by the phrase, "he cut like one with a steady hand" (*kṛtahastavat*). Here, the intention is not to express a similarity to some other person named Kṛtahasta; rather, the intended meaning is that he performed that very severance—the rending of the body—which is appropriate for one with a firm grip.

Likewise, because there is no relationship of standard of comparison and object of comparison [in that case], the phrase "like one skilled with the hand" (kṛtahastavat) is heard again for the sake of restriction, even though it has already been understood that he alone deserves the title "skilled with the hand" and no other. Similarly, although a king is already well-known as such and his kingship is established—as in the case of Pāṇḍu: "O Vidura, perform all the funeral rites for Pāṇḍu like a king; [he was] a lion among kings"—this expression is employed. And here, no comparison of Pāṇḍu with any other king is possible, because his qualities are complete.
Therefore, this is the meaning here: "Perform those duties which are worthy of the king alone, to be accomplished for the deceased who has reached the other world. || 557 ||

And so, he states that this is the essential subject matter of this yoga: "Those properties whose absolute impossibility is observed in one who is not a king are regulated by the king; those that deviate from this are abandoned. (558)

When it is intended to provide strength and produce stability for those qualities (*dharma*) which are observed only in a king and are already determined therein, then the usage serves as a restriction (*niyama*). Since a restriction entails the exclusion of others, the restriction is established in both directions: "this conduct (*vṛtta*) is fit for the king alone" and "this [conduct] does not belong to others. As it has been said: "the deviant [cases] are abandoned. This conduct is fit for the king alone; it is not common to others, nor is its occurrence possible among non-kings.

This is the meaning of the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the rule: "In the case of an action worthy of oneself, when the agent is determined to possess strength. The meaning is as follows: the "agent of the action worthy of oneself" refers to the conduct (*vṛtta*), that is, the activity (*vyāpāra*) or action (*kriyā*). When the distinction of that agent's activity from other agents is intended to be expressed, then by this sūtra the suffix *vat* is applied. Furthermore, that action is "worthy of oneself" (*ātmārhā*); it is worthy of the referent denoted by the word ending in the second case (the object), and not worthy of anything else.

In cases such as *rājavad rūpam* ("a form like that of a king") or *rājavad dhairyam* ("fortitude like that of a king"), the suffix *vati* is applied by the rule *tatra tasyeva* [Pāṇini 5.1.116] alone. This is because the suffix *vati* prescribed by the rule *tadarham* [Pāṇini 5.1.117] is not applicable here, since that rule prescribes *vati* for an action (*kriyā*) when it is the agent (*kartṛ*) of the action denoted by the root *arh*. Thus, the intended meaning here is this: when difference (*bheda*) is intended to be expressed, the suffix *vati* is established by the former rule; however, when non-difference (*abheda*) is intended to be expressed, there is an absence of the relationship between standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and object of comparison (*upameya*), and thus the suffix *vati* is applied by this [latter] rule, which serves as a restrictive provision (*niyamaphala*). || 558 ||

But surely, why does this suffix *vat* not occur in such cases as "this garment is worthy of the king" (*rājānamarhatyetadvāsaḥ*) or "this water-pot is worthy of the Brahmin" (*brāhmaṇamarhatyeṣa kamaṇḍaluḥ*)? Because there is no such usage (*anabhidhānāt*). Thus, he explains that because the term "action" (*kriyā*) is understood here from the previous rule, this suffix occurs only when the action itself is the agent of the verb *arhati*: "And the suffix *vat* is desired after the root *arh*, provided that the action which is the agent is [the object of comparison]; but it is not so in cases such as 'the umbrella is worthy of the king' (*rājānamarhatichatram*). (559)

Although there is a general rule stating that the suffix occurs when the agent (*kartṛ*) is capable (*arhati*), it is intended that the suffix applies only to an action such as "wearing" (*vṛtta*), and not to a substance such as an umbrella when the agent is capable. || 559 ||

To the question "Why is this so?", he says: "For there is a systematic following of correct words through the treatise; however, regarding the statement concerning the sense of 'umbrella' (chatra) and so forth, a rejection [of the grammatical derivation] would not be possible. (560)

It has already been established that since the relationship between word and meaning is eternal (*siddha*), words are not produced by the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*); rather, the treatise merely follows the correctness (*sādhutva*) of those words already existing and employed in the continuous usage of the learned (*śiṣṭa*). Consequently, regarding the expression "the umbrella is like a king" (*rājavac chatram*) or "the water-pot is like a Brahmin" (*brāhmaṇavat kamaṇḍaluḥ*), if one does not accept the relationship of standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and object of comparison (*upameya*), then the intended meaning of "worthiness" (*arhatva*) would not be conveyed. Thus, its grammatical analysis (*anvākhyāna*) as an incorrect form (*asādhutva*) would be untenable.

Furthermore, since this rule is already established by the very expression "equal to that" (*tena tulyam*), the rejection (*pratyākhyāna*) that is made of this *yoga* would not be valid if that were the case. To explain: in examples such as *rājavac chatram* ("the umbrella [is] like the king's"), there would be no establishment [of the suffix] by the rule "equal to that," because that rule prescribes [the suffix] when similarity is conditioned by action (*kriyopādhi*); since [similarity] is not established in cases where the umbrella and so forth are the agents (*kartṛ*), this *sūtra* would be necessary for that purpose—so how can it be rejected? Moreover, even if one accepts that rejection, when the matter is explained otherwise, [in the case of] *rājavad*...

The intention is that by using expressions such as "vṛttam" (it has occurred), the Bhāṣyakāra clearly states the absence of an affix when the agent is [implied] in cases such as "chatra" (the umbrella-bearer). Consequently, even if [the sūtra] were formally commenced, the action alone would be its denoted meaning; thus, the formal commencement and the rejection of the commencement yield the same result. || 560 ||

Thus, its commencement has been justified in the Bhāṣya. But as for the rejection [of it], since that is not found there, how is it certain? To this he says: "The rule *tadarham* was not commenced in another grammar; even by way of analogy, the assumption of a distinction is possible. (561)

The followers of Āpiśali and Kāśakṛtsna do not study this sūtra; therefore, it is understood that it has been rejected. For instance, the author of the Bhāṣya has indicated with his own words a matter already established from another system (*tantrāntara*). The reasoning in that regard is: "The opinion of another is accepted if it is not refuted. In this context, what was the intention of those teachers who do not study this sūtra? It is said:

since the relationship between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) is possible even when the meaning is not distinct, by means of a conceptual differentiation (*bhedaparikalpanā*), the suffix *vat* is already established by the preceding rule; thus, there is no need for the commencement of this [present] rule. (561)

How is the conceptualization of difference [established]? He says: "When a single thing has been established through the full cognition of its causal function, a distinction is conceptually constructed by the intellect when one intends to express that it possesses the properties of other objects. (562)

When the fact that even a single object, whose function is already known in one context, possesses that same nature—that is, the capacity to perform that same function—in another context is intended to be expressed, then multiplicity is superimposed by the intellect through a conceptualization based on the performance of those respective functions. Thus, because multiplicity is established while intrinsic non-difference remains, the relationship of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), which rests upon both difference and non-difference, is logically justified.

For instance: just as you previously cut [something] in another battle with manual dexterity due to the force of prior practice, so too do you cut [something] at other times in a manner equal to that. Thus, although there is a distinction between the actions based on their occurrence in earlier and later times, and a conceptualization of difference based on what is well-known and what is not, the relationship of standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and object of comparison (*upameya*) is established even in a single instance through the expression "like one skilled in hand" (*kṛtahastavat*). Consequently, the suffix *vati* is established by the very rule concerning the preceding [word].

Likewise, even when the word "king" (rājan) is used in a general sense, there is a comparison of that which is not well-known with that which is well-known through a property observed in another context where its specific application is already established. Or rather, the meaning is: "Perform for Pāṇḍu those funeral rites (pretakārya) which were performed for kings of former times, treating him as equal to them. || 562 ||

And this must necessarily be understood in this way. Otherwise, let there be the suffix *vati* at the beginning of the Sūtra; however, because there is no distinction [between the two], the word *iva* would not be used here. Thus he says: "Because of this commencement of the Sūtra, the use of the word *iva* does not exist; rather, its application is found in the same domain as that of *vati*. (563)

When the sūtra is being formulated, the suffix is obtained by virtue of the explicit statement; however, the employment of the word "iva" (like/as) would not be possible without the conceptualization of a distinction from what is well-known—thus, a distinction is necessary here. || 563 ||

Furthermore, the particle *iva* is observed even in other cases where a conceptual distinction is intended; thus he says: "The phrase 'Indra like a bandit' is employed in a mantra addressed to Indra [when the intended meaning is] that Indra is one whose actions are seen elsewhere, as in this case. (564)

"For you are praised like Indra; be a slayer of Dasyus like Indra; release the fields"—in this mantra dedicated to the deity Indra, the word *iva* (like) seen here indicates the relationship of comparison (*upamānopameyabhāva*) through the superimposition of difference (*nānātvādhyāropeṇa*). To explain: in the expression "Indra himself is like Indra," he is compared to himself. And this "difference" occurs here when there is a desire to express that a property already known to belong to one object is likewise a property of another object.

And thus the meaning is this: "Just as you were Indra elsewhere, engaged in the activity of striking down thieves, so may you be here as well"—this is called *indra* (Indra-like) because of the conceptualization of a distinction based on the difference between visible and invisible effects produced by what is well-known and what is not well-known. || 564 ||
Right here he provides even a worldly illustration: "When a state is designated by relying upon a prior state, it is expressed in that very way, as in: 'You are like yourself. (565)

The cognition of similarity is observed by relying on a difference in entities based on a difference in states. For example, another state, namely old age, is compared by relying on the well-known state of youth which possesses an excellence of beauty, as in: "You are similar to yourself. Indeed, when there is a difference in states, one relies on the difference of the possessor of those states; thus, by the statement "you are equal to you," the very same person is compared to himself. || 565 ||
Thus, the summary here is as follows: Where there exists no other well-known object of comparison, the nature of the subject of comparison is there distinguished by one's own intellect. (566)

In the absence of actual difference, the relationship between one and the same thing as both the object of comparison (upameya) and the standard of comparison (upamāna) is well-known through the figure of speech *ananvaya* (non-correspondence), intended to express an excellence of praise.
