For example: "The battle between Rāma and Rāvaṇa was like that between Rāma and Rāvaṇa. In this way, the meaning is praised by the impossibility of any other standard of comparison, stating: "No one else exists who is your equal; if there were another, you yourself would be his equal. In that case, a distinction must be resorted to through conceptual construction (*buddhiparikalpanā*).

Thus, since this conceptual distinction has already been established by the previous argument—on the grounds that it would otherwise be impossible to employ the word "as if" (*iva*) in expressions such as "you are the king, as if [he were]"—its refutation is thereby proven. || 566 ||

In this regard, it might be argued: "This subject matter is secondary; since there exists a primary, real domain of difference in the preceding sūtra, how can there be an application here? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Even that difference which is innate is based upon cognition. Therefore, in this domain, neither the distinct nor the non-distinct exists. (567)

Even that distinction which resides in the actual object (*vastu*) functions as a linguistic convention of difference only when it has ascended into the intellect (*buddhi*). Thus, because the intellect alone possesses sovereignty here in this linguistic usage, neither multiplicity nor unity exists in reality; for linguistic usage proceeds by means of the superimposition of difference upon what is non-different, and the superimposition of non-difference upon what is different—as in the expression, "We eat those very same rice-grains. Furthermore, it has already been established previously that in the case of comparison (*upamā*), the cause is precisely this distinction conceptualized by the intellect. || 567 ||

Right here, he cites the commentary author’s corroboration: "By pointing out the reasons for difference—such as 'he has armlets' and 'he has earrings'—one says of Caitra, 'He is like this,' because of the apprehension of states of the intellect. (568)

Regarding the rule *upadeśe 'janunāsikaḥ*, the definition of *uddeśa* (designation) is "the bringing about [of an object] by means of its qualities. This is illustrated in the Bhāṣya with the example: "Aṅgadī, Kuṇḍalī, Vyūḍhoraska, Tāmrāyatākṣa, Vṛttabāhu—such is Devadatta. In this case, by characterizing Devadatta alone through defining qualities such as being adorned with armlets (*aṅgaditva*) and so forth, the speaker declares, "Such a one is equal to him. Here, it is not intended that he be equal to anyone else.

What then? It is intended that [the object] is similar to that which, characterized by properties such as having arms and so forth, flashes forth at that time within the intellect. And thus, because the external object is described as having a similarity with the reflection in the intellect, the relationship of standard of comparison and object of comparison—with its distinction superimposed by the intellect—is clearly stated. || 568 ||

He asks: what is the purpose of expressing it in this way? He replies: "By these words, the cognition arises exactly as it is; and by conforming to that cognition, the object also becomes established. (569)

By means of words such as "armed with armlets" (*aṅgadī*), a specific cognition arises in which an object appears; through its similarity to that form, the external object is cognized. This is because users of language determine (*adhyavasāya*) the very form of the cognition itself to be the external object. This is the intended meaning here: when an object appears externally to you, it arises in the intellect as a form colored by attributes such as "having armlets. You should then designate that [object] as "Devadatta. Thus, the success of linguistic usage is achieved through the determination of non-difference between the perceived and the conceptualized. || 569 ||

Therefore, he states the pervasion that conceptual distinction alone is useful in all cases: "Through the differentiation of mental states, the function of distinction is perceived; as if produced by the speaker's intention, all meanings of words [appear] to arise. (570)

Whatever function of differentiation is prescribed in the grammatical treatise, each of those is based on a distinction created by the intellect. For instance, it has been stated that the linguistic usage of "factors of action" (kāraka) is dependent upon mental states; likewise, one should consider such rules as "the treatment of what is designated as something else" (vyapadeśivadbhāva), and "the doubling of a monosyllabic root. This is logical, because words—forming syntactic units based on objects brought into proximity solely by the speaker's intention—do not depend at all on the external existence or non-existence [of those objects].

And thus, the manifestation of the meaning of words is established according to the intention of the speaker; for even in the case of those long-past such as Kaṃsa and others, whose forms are brought before the mind through cognition, there occurs the usage of expressions such as "he causes Kaṃsa to be killed" (kaṃsaṃ ghātayati) and "he causes Bali to be bound" (baliṃ bandhayati), based on the determination of the relationship between the instigator and the instigated. || 570 ||

Therefore, he says that the referent of a word is not the actual object: "Even when an external object exists in such a state, cognitions differ regarding it; in that case, no similarity, even if it were present, is conveyed. (571)

Even regarding objects that possess similarity to other individuals, as long as cognitions based on common characteristics have not arisen, no perceiver—disregarding the similarity even though it exists—conceives of a resemblance, because [the object] is delimited by a cognition whose form is entirely distinct [from others]. For indeed, when the configuration of a gavaya is not perceived, there is no cognition of similarity to it in the cow. (571)

And since cognition is based on an identity superimposed by the intellect upon things that are absolutely distinct, he says: "As long as the manifestation does not differ with respect to objects that are utterly distinct, so long does recognition not cease for anyone. (572)

Even though the individual manifestation is absolutely distinct, because a separate cognition does not arise, there occurs through the permeation of a recurring property (*anvayidharma*) a firm, unwavering reflective awareness in a single form—“this is that very same thing”—based on the determination of non-difference. For instance, in a place of dim light or from a distance, when an object is apprehended merely by its form and its specific distinctions are not determined, there arises a determination of non-difference through the recollection of the form perceived previously.

Even when an object is nearby and clearly visible, at the very first contact of the sense organ, there arises an immediate recognition that "this is that very same thing" due to the awakening of prior latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Likewise, without having ascertained the difference between Devadatta and Yajñadatta, there occurs the apprehension of their identity.

Thus, since an investigation into the external existence or non-existence of difference is of no assistance for the linguistic usage of difference, the relationship of *upamāna* (standard of comparison) and *upameya* (object of comparison) is possible for a single entity by means of a differentiated form appearing in cognition. Since this is already established by the previous rule (*rājavad vṛttam*, etc.), the author states that the rule "tadarham" was introduced for the purpose of informing the ignorant: "But this very distinction has been shown by the Sūtra through a distinction [of its own]. Even that which is well-known is understood by the ignorant only when it is difficult to grasp. (573)

This very basis of the states of cognition is explained through the undertaking of the *Yoga* [system] by means of the conventional usage of "distinction" (*bheda*). Although this distinction is already distinct from the "real" distinction, it is made manifest as a separate entity through the commencement of the *Sūtra*. For not everyone is capable of discerning such a matter on their own. Furthermore, since the operation of a treatise is intended for the benefit of all persons, it is appropriate to commence the treatise even when a matter is already understood, in order to provide instruction for those of dull intellect.

Another analysis is also seen: "one who is worthy of a king" (rājānam arhati), which serves as a cause for those of dull intellect to conclude that [the suffix] is not established by the former [analysis]. || 573 ||

In this regard, one might argue that the difficulty of comprehension arises because a single entity cannot simultaneously function as both the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*). However, that is not tenable; for the relationship of *upamāna* and *upameya* is indeed observed even in the case of a single entity. Thus, he says that this [treatise] need not be undertaken even for the sake of enlightening the ignorant: "A grammarian does not always speak like a grammarian; therefore, he is also addressed with the words, 'Speak like a grammarian. (574)

For someone who knows grammar, yet has overstepped the status of a grammarian by employing vulgar and unfortunate expressions and by using words devoid of refinement, is compared by grammarians skilled in the use of correct words as follows: "Speak like a grammarian; speak equally with others; abandon the unintelligible speech of barbarians. || 574 ||
Likewise: "Some men speak like women, and women speak like men; even one's own duty (svadharma) is taught by them as being subject to transgression. (575)

"Deviation" refers to one's own characteristic. And thus, objects possessing their own possible characteristics are compared only with those of the same class. "Let it be spoken like a man. Let it be told by you in a manner equal to others who do not overstep the speech appropriate for men; why is your self being led to ridicule in the assembly by means of unconfident utterances, as if you were suspected of being a woman? Likewise, a certain woman who speaks very boldly is addressed: "Let it be spoken like a woman."

Let it be said that she is equal to other women who are modest; do not make her a laughingstock by using excessively bold speech, for she is the very limit of womanly decorum. Similarly, when someone behaves with effeminacy, one says to him: "Fight like a man! The meaning is: "Fight in such a way as those who have not overstepped their manhood would fight. Thus, because we observe the abandonment of one's own appropriate conduct, it is seen that even one's own behavior is employed as a standard of comparison (*upamā*) due to its lack of renown [in that specific context]. And so, the relationship of subject and object of comparison (*upamāna-upameya-bhāva*) between a single entity is not difficult to discern.

Regarding what was stated previously—that based on one's own prior state, one's own subsequent state is compared to it as "you are like yourself"—he explains the intended meaning of that statement: "When it is said in the world, 'You are like yourself,' any other possible object of comparison is thereby excluded. (576)

"This statement—'You have transcended all comparable phenomena'—is explained as being primarily a praise through the exclusion of other points of comparison, by way of the shadow of the *ananvaya* (non-comparison) ornament. Thus, since the relationship between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) is established everywhere by conceptualizing a distinction [where none exists], this rule was not undertaken in other grammatical systems. Here too, its non-undertaking when there is an intention to express a standard of comparison is indeed accepted. || 576 ||

But since this [suffix] is necessary when there is a different intention to express, he says: "In the illustration of the meaning 'fitting' or 'suitable for a king,' the form *tadarham* is prescribed when there is no intention to express a simile. (577)

"This is proper, this is fitting, this is the conduct of a king, and this is a means for the maintenance of the kingdom"—thinking "this belongs to the king alone and not to another," there is no intention to express a relationship of comparison (upamānopameyabhāva) when the strength [of the king] is being made known. Therefore, since the suffix *vati* prescribed in connection with that [relationship] has its scope restricted to noble matters (*ārya*), a separate rule is recited here for the purpose of prescribing the suffix; thus the commencement of this [rule] is justified. This is the underlying intention: the formation would be established if there were an intention to express a standard of comparison (*upamāna*).

And thus, in another grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), this [treatise] was not commenced. Likewise here too, it was not commenced, because the opinion of others, being non-contradictory, is not prohibited. However, since its commencement is fruitful when there is a desire to explain the state of Arhatship, the charge of "non-pervasion" (*avyāpti*) in the other grammar has been raised. For this very reason, the author of the commentary (*bhāṣyakāra*) desisted from establishing the purpose alone and did not reject [the treatise] on the basis of the lack of a point of comparison.

And thus, it is established that even in cases such as "speak like a grammarian" (*vaiyākaraṇavat brūhi*), when the comparison is not intended to be expressed and only mere fitness (*yogyatā*) is sought to be conveyed, the suffix *vat* occurs by this very rule. || 577 ||

Now he states the subject matter of what is about to be discussed: "The remaining portion concerning the suffix -vat, which follows as a secondary consequence of the primary topic, is now being explained. This suffix -vat is cited here because of its connection with the standard of comparison (upamāna). (578)

In this work, the investigation of the word *vṛtti* is primarily undertaken. Within that context, as a consequence of the investigation into compounds involving comparison (*upamāna-samāsa*), the introduction of the suffix *vat*—which is prescribed in connection with a standard of comparison—is presented here for the sake of analysis; thus, the suffix *upamānavati* follows as a relevant topic. Following that, the suffix *anupamānavati*, which arrives in its proper sequence, is also examined for the purpose of analysis by means of this incidental discussion, based on the rule "upasargāc chandasi dhātvarthe. This is the connection between the sections. || 578 ||

In that regard, for what purpose is the inclusion of the word *artha* (meaning)? [The answer is: No; it was objected in the Bhāṣya that one should simply say "after a prefix, before a verbal root in the Vedic language" (*upasargāc chandasi dhātau*). He explains the intention behind [including] *artha* there: "In the absence of the assumption of a primary [meaning], because the word 'guṇa' (secondary/attribute) is observed, the assumption of the meaning of the verbal root is established after the prefix *vati*. (Verse 579)

The meaning is as follows: since the word *dhātu* primarily denotes verbal roots such as *bhū* and others, when it is said "in a root" (*dhātau*), that word [itself] cannot be the object denoted by the suffix; therefore, even without the explicit mention of "meaning" (*artha*), the meaning associated with the root is obtained through the superimposition of the form of the root and the attribution of its properties by virtue of contextual capacity (*sāmarthya*). Thus, what is the purpose of explicitly mentioning "meaning"? For this very reason, the Bhāṣya states: "Since an operation is impossible upon the word itself, the operation shall be understood to apply to the meaning. (579)

In that case, how can there be a necessary comprehension of the meaning through association (*sāhacarya*)? [One might argue: "Because another property of the word (*śabdadharma*) related to the verbal root is also associated with the root. To this, he says: "In this rule *svaṃ rūpam* (Pāṇini 1.1.68), the meaning is also included. Therefore, since it is taught as being like a form (*rūpa*), the non-existent meaning will be understood [as the referent]. (Verse 580)

Since the word *sva* (one’s own) refers to that which is internal (*antaraṅga*), non-removable (*adeya*), and unique (*asādhāraṇa*), its meaning is already established as being qualified by "one's own" when it is used; thus, the inclusion of the term *rūpa* (form) in the rule *svaṃ rūpam* is for the purpose of making it known that the referent is accepted as having the status of a form. Consequently, the related object (*sambandhin*)—which is of the same order as the form, more closely proximate, and well-known as the denoted meaning (*vācyārtha*)—will be understood. The sense is this: since the meaning of the sentence is fully accounted for by that much alone, how could the related object be taken as a property of the word (*śabdadharmā*) out of mere compliance [with the literal expression]? || 580 ||

To this, the Bhāṣya provides the following answer: "In that case, the purpose [of the definition] is so that the elision of the latter member may be understood. 'Dhātvartha' means the meaning produced by the verbal root (dhātu). But what is the meaning produced by the verbal root? It is the *sādhana* (the means of accomplishment). This he explains: "The *sādhana* is that which is brought about as a means of accomplishment by the meaning of the verbal root; it is understood in this sūtra as being 'produced by the verbal root' (*dhātunā kṛtam*). (581)

Since the word *dhātu* here indicates its own meaning by implication, the "meaning produced by the root" (*dhātukṛta*)—that is, the meaning manifested through action—is what is indicated here; and that [meaning] is the means (*sādhana*), the factor of action (*kāraka*).

For instance: although a factor (*kāraka*) whose nature is already established is employed as a means (*sādhana*) toward an action, nevertheless, it is not made a means or produced by the action in its own essential form; rather, it is [made so] as a means. This is because the state of being a means depends upon that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), and because it is the action itself that sets the means in motion—both in their general form and in their specific forms such as the object (*karman*) and so forth. For activity first proceeds without depending on anything at all; it then draws forth the powers (*śakti*) residing in a single substratum, like a flowing stream.
This has already been determined previously by such statements as these. || 581 ||

Regarding what was stated—that there is an elision of the latter member (uttarapadalopa)—one might ask: "What is this so-called 'elision of the latter member' that has not been formally explained by the author of the Sūtras? To this, he says: "When a word, having already fulfilled its purpose, is no longer used at all because it is not observed in its [expected] domain, the elision of that [word] is designated therein. (582)

In this case, when a word is employed for its intended meaning and that meaning is present, its usage cannot be prevented even by a hundred utterances; for it has already fulfilled its purpose and accomplished its function. Thus, the non-appearance of what was expected is designated as "elision" (lopa), just like the non-appearance of an affix, and this is applied everywhere in linguistic practice.

Furthermore, since the word *dhātu* denotes action (*kriyā*), the object produced by that [action] is metaphorically designated as being that very [action]; thus, "the meaning of the root" (*dhātvartha*) refers to the meaning of the root itself. When this occurs in a figurative grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the compound is formed according to the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* group as "the object produced by the root. This resulting entity is what was demonstrated by the author of the Bhāṣya. Alternatively, this is analyzed as a *bahuvrīhi*: "that whose purpose (*artha*)—meaning its objective—is the root and its meaning, namely the action (*kriyā*). Thus, the compound is constructed.

And action (kriyā) becomes the purpose (prayojana) precisely because it is that which is to be accomplished by the means (sādhana). From the prefix (upasarga) occurring in relation to that means, the suffix -vatī is applied in its own sense (svārthe). || 582 ||

Thus, the purpose for obtaining the *sādhana* (the means) through the power of grasping the meaning has been stated: "In this *sādhana*, it will be joined with gender and number. To the question—since the *sādhana* is, like the action (*kriyā*), of the nature of a potency and thus non-substantial (*asattvabhūta*), how can it be joined with gender and number?—he says: "Those [prefixes] such as *pra* and others which are established in relation to the action, the *sādhana*, and the substance (*dravya*)—from those which denote a substantial entity (*sattva*), the suffix *vati* is prescribed in its own sense (*svārthe*). (483)

In this context, the word *sādhana* (means of accomplishment) is intended to signify the substance (*dravya*) which is the substratum of the power of accomplishment, because there is no difference between the power and that which possesses the power (*śaktimat*). When that substance is implied by the means of accomplishing an action, the prefixes (*upasarga*) such as *pra* and others function as denoters [of it]. From these, which denote both the means of accomplishment and the action, this suffix *vati* is prescribed in the sense of the thing itself (*svārthe*). Thus, because they express a meaning that has become a substantial entity (*sattvabhūta*), their connection with gender and number is logically established. || 583 ||

In this regard, it might be argued: "It has been determined that particles such as *pra* and others indicate specific actions; their capacity to denote a substance has not been established. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Without a suffix, a particle such as *pra* is employed there with its own meaning; however, when it is designated by a distinct name [as a noun], a division is conceptually constructed. (584)

Certain properties are restricted to sentences, while others belong to the *vṛtti* (compound). Although, due to the specific restriction of word-potency (*śabdaśakti*), prefixes such as *pra-* and others employed in a sentence lack the power to denote a substance (*dravya*), nevertheless, this potency is understood to exist within the domain of the *vṛtti*.

The words *udgatāni* (risen) and *udvataḥ* (elevated), as well as *nigatāni* (descended) and *nivataḥ* (depressed), are indivisible units that, when analyzed through the division of stem (*prakṛti*) and suffix (*pratyaya*), are explained such that the stem portion denotes a substance subordinate to an action-denoting factor, while the suffix portion is understood as being merely expressive of its own meaning (*svārthika*). Thus, in this context of grammatical formation (*vṛtti*), the inherent nature of the prefixes (*upasarga*) is followed by the inclusion of their meanings; for they are employed as constituent parts of the grammatical derivation solely for the sake of expressing worldly meaning.

Furthermore, if there were no apprehension of the object (*artha*), since the effect [of the word] would be impossible with respect to the sound alone, the action (*kriyā*)—being perceived through its inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*)—would merely indicate the capacity of the means (*sādhana-śakti*). However, because of the apprehension of the object, the substance (*dravya*) is perceived as having attained non-difference from that [action]. Otherwise, the apprehension of the object would be fruitless. || 584 ||

And if by the word "means" (sādhana) mere capacity were intended, then: "But if a means were apprehended as lacking established existence, there would be no connection with case-endings, just as in the case of [suffixes] such as -tasi. (585)

If only the instrument (*sādhana*) were grasped as residing in an unappropriated substratum (*anupāttādhāra*), then—just as in the case of [the rule] *tataḥ* and *tan na*—because a capacity characterized by absolute predominance cannot be joined with another capacity, all case-endings (*vibhakti*) would not occur as they ought. By conventional agreement (*samaya*), there would be only the singular number. Consequently, since it would lack all case-endings, the designation of an indeclinable (*avyaya*) would follow, and thus its connection with gender and number would be contradicted.

However, because of the capacity to grasp the meaning (*arthagrahaṇasāmarthyāt*), it follows that the substance (*dravya*)—which is the means for accomplishing the action that has been made subordinate (*guṇīkṛtakriyāsādhana*)—is understood here as the primary denotation of prefixes (*upasarga*). Thus, when a word ending in *vat* denotes a substance (*sattvavacanatā*), if it is connected with an action as appropriate, it can take all case-endings; consequently, there is no lack of the designation "indeclinable" (*avyaya*), and the usage of plural forms such as *udvataḥ* and *nivataḥ* is established. Furthermore, the connection with different genders is not contradicted by the principle: "A difference in gender is observed due to a difference in words even when the referent is one and the same. (585)

Now, even so, since *vati* is included among the *svarādi* (indeclinables), its status as an indeclinable would follow; to this he says: "For those by whom the absence of case-endings (*avibhaktitva*) is inferred for words ending in *vati* on the basis of their inclusion in the list [of *svarādi*], for them the presence of case-endings must be stated in the case of *udvati*. (586)

The state of being devoid of case-endings (*avibhaktitvam*)—that is, the non-appearance of case-endings—is stated to be the basis for the designation "indeclinable" (*avyaya*). Thus, according to the view of those who accept that a word is an indeclinable by virtue of its inclusion in the list beginning with *svar* (Pāṇini 1.1.37), where the state of being an indeclinable results from the non-appearance of case-endings due to the force of that rule, [the following must be addressed]: in the case of the word *udvataḥ*, since it would be an indeclinable, the elision [of the case-ending] would apply; therefore, its state of possessing a case-ending (*savibhaktitā*) must be explicitly stated or established. For, by the force of the inclusion of the term "meaning" (*artha*) in the definition, it does not become an indeclinable.

For that [term] remains a designation based on its literal meaning (anvarthasaṃjñā) precisely when it lacks gender and number. And here, because the means (sādhana) is understood as substance (dravya), it denotes an existent entity (sattvavacana); therefore, the meaning is that [gender and number] are absent in that case. || 586 ||

Thus, the suffix *vat* has been examined. In connection with that, another point therein is also investigated—the author of the *Vārttika* recited: "The addition of *vat* after the words *strī* and *pums*. By specifying the limit in the rule "after *strī* and *pums*, the suffixes *nañ* and *snañ* [are applied] before *bhavana*," the suffixes *nañ* and *snañ* are taught as being applicable to this specific base prior to *bhavana*. For the sake of establishing these suffixes in meanings such as "offspring" (*apatya*) and so forth, the suffix *vat* must be added here as a supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*).

In this context, "therein" (*tatra*) is an indication of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of the meaning associated with the suffix *vati*. Alternatively, the meaning is that when *vati* is prescribed, this [suffix] is also to be prescribed after the words *strī* and *puṃs*. This locative case is used in the sense of characterizing a state (*bhāva-lakṣaṇe*). Regarding this Vārttika, a refutation is stated in the Bhāṣya: "The activity of the Teacher indicates that the suffixes *nañ* and *snañ* do not occur in the sense of *vati*; for he provides the formal instruction 'striyāḥ puṃvat'."

He explains this as follows: "Because of the observation of the form *puṃvat*, [the suffixes] *vat* and *yartha* do not apply; that specific nipātana (irregular formation) sublates the exception consisting of *nañ* and *snañ*. (587)

From the enunciation of the rule *striyāḥ puṃvat* ("as in the masculine for a feminine"), it is understood that the suffixes *nañ* and *snañ* take precedence over the sense of the suffix *vati*. For if these two were to encompass the sense of *vati*, then the suffix *vati*—having been set aside by this exception (*apavāda*)—would not be heard. But since it is indeed heard, it indicates that these two [suffixes] transcend that meaning, because the general rule (*utsarga*) is heard to apply in their domain. Now, one might object: "Since there is the mention of *puṃvat*, let *vati* also exist; and since *nañ* and *snañ* occur as they naturally do, they too would be brought into proximity by the governing rule (*adhikāra*) within the scope of the sense of *vati*. Anticipating this, it is said: "That [mention of *puṃvat*] is an exceptional enunciation (*nipātana*) which sets aside [the application of *vati*]. (587)

He clarifies precisely how this constitutes a sublation: "When one thus departs, the suffixes *vat* and *nañ-snañ* certainly apply; when those two are in operation, the general rule does not hold because of the sublation. (588)

The operation of a general rule (*utsarga*) within the domain of an exception (*apavāda*), being otherwise inexplicable, sets aside that exception; therefore, there is a certainty regarding its sublation (*bādhakatva*), for the inference of non-attainment is indeed what constitutes sublation. Otherwise, while the enemy—the exception—is present, how could this wretched general rule operate therein? Thus, the determination of its status as a sublater is established.

In this regard, just as a negative particle (*apavāda*), even when accompanied by an emphatic particle (*saṃrambha*) in the establishment of its own form, indicates the non-application of a general rule (*sāmānyavidhi*) within its own scope, so too a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*), though occupied with the acquisition of its own specific form, results in the sublation of what would otherwise apply. Since the *nipātana* in the *sarvādi-vārttika* is of this same nature, such *nipātanas* have been established as sublaters. Consequently, the usage *pauṃsnam* and others in the sense of the suffix *-vat* (as in *puṃvat*) are incorrect. || 588 ||

Having raised the objection, "Even so, [the rule] 'like a woman' (strīvat) is not established," the Bhāṣya states: "The indicator depends upon a grammatical rule (yoga). He explains that: "The rule by which the suffixes *nañ* and *snañ* are prescribed does not apply here; for it is the suffix *-vat* itself that is supported as the indicative mark. (589)

This indicative mark (*liṅga*) is an inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭam*), serving as a means of cognition. To explain: the rule "the suffixes *nañ* and *snañ* [are applied] after the root *bhū*, when preceded by words denoting a female or a male" (*strīpuṃsābhyāṃ nañsnañau bhavanāt*) does not extend its scope to the meaning of the suffix *vat*; thus, this indicative mark is established as having such a function. This refers to the section concerning *vati*. The meaning is that even though the suffix *vat* is prescribed by the three rules—"that which is equal to that" (*tena tulyam*), "as in that, so in this" (*tatra tasyeva*), and "worthy of that" (*tadarham*)—the suffixes *nañ* and *snañ* do not overstep their application to those meanings.

And thus, because it depends on these yogas, the sūtra that indicates them is "yogāpekṣam. Consequently, since there is no absence of the suffixes *nañ* and *snañ* in the sense of the suffix *vati*, the form *strīvat* is also established, because gender is indicative [of the meaning] independently of any specific qualifier; this is proven. || 589 ||

Thus, the suffix *vat*, which arose in the context of the discussion on analogy (*upamāna*), has been examined. Now, in this investigation of analogy, the following must be scrutinized: when a single object of comparison (*upamāna*) is employed for many objects of comparison (*upameya*), does it follow the distinctions of those objects of comparison, or is it capable of serving its purpose as a non-distinct entity? Regarding this doubt, he says: "Through the non-difference of the object of comparison, there occurs the application to distinct objects; likewise, the mental modification (*ūha*) associated with the name 'analogy' is not perceived, just as in the case of a limb. (590)

In this regard, there is a logical principle that when subordinate elements (guṇas) are employed for the sake of favoring the principal element (pradhāna), they conform to the nature of the self [the principal] in such a way that the principal is favored. However, since a single simile, endowed with its own inherent property, is capable of assisting multiple objects of comparison (upameyas), why should it resort to differentiation out of mere compliance? For this very reason, even when there is a plurality of upameyas in the modified form (vikṛti), the singular verbal form belonging to the original form (prakṛti) indicates the non-differentiation of the meaning; thus, in the case of a simile, no difference in number is observed corresponding to the number of upameyas. This is the rule of modification (ūha).

For example, among the names of the subordinate parts (*aṅga*), there is an absence of modification (*ūha*) precisely because of the difference in the principal part (*aṅgin*), since their distinction is already well-known, and because the transformation into another number has already been accomplished; thus, in this case, there is simply no sublation of the connection. And so says the traditional teaching (*āmnāya*) of those who know modification: "The names of the classes (*jāti*), the subordinate parts, the similes, and the sense organs—these do not undergo modification; for that [modification] would be improper in the *adhṛigu* formula. In that context, the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the thing illustrated (*dārṣṭāntika*) are cited as being already included within the modification itself.

The non-modification (*anūha*) of a subordinate member (*aṅga*) is as follows: regarding the mantra, "Whatever lowing the animal has made, or whatever it has struck with its feet, may Agni release me from that sin," the word *uraḥ* (chest) is a subordinate member in the singular number in the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti-yāga*) involving a single animal. Even when there are two animals in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti-yāga*), because there is no modification (*ūha*) of this term, one says *paśū* (animals) [in the dual] and *āhaṃsātām* (may they not strike), which is merely a transformation of this very same word; however, it is not transformed into *urasi* (on the chests). The principle here is that the distinction in the number of subordinate members is determined precisely by the distinction in the principal members (*aṅgin*).

Similarly, even in a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti-yāga*) involving many animals, it is inferred that "the animals cry out" (*paśava āhaṃsate*), but not "the waters" (*norāṃsi*). Likewise, there is no modification (*anūha*) of the words for the objects of comparison (*upamāna*); for example: *kaśyape vāsām acchidre śroṇī kavaṣorūsrekaparṇe*, etc. Because the words for the objects of comparison—such as *kaśyapa*, *kavaṣa*, and *streka*—which denote the tortoise, fish, and *karavīra* plant respectively, have the capacity to signify [their referents] without distinction [from the object of comparison], they do not undergo transformation according to the gender or number of the object being compared (*upameya*). || 590 ||

Thus, the absence of *ūha* (modification) is well-known among those who know the *nyāya*; here, it is stated that comparison (*upamāna*) is a corroborative means [of knowledge] by way of non-difference. He states another corroborative means as well: "In the case of the *gāvedhuka* porridge, the eyes of the ox-cutter and the hair-shaver are seen; for these two are like Rudra with respect to the animals," thus there is the scriptural hearing (*śruti*) of the singular number. (591)

"It is heard in the Veda: 'Like Rudra, these two, the govikarta and the akṣavāpa, take pleasure in [slaughtering] animals. For instance, when a sacrificial pap (caru) prepared with *gavedhu*—a specific kind of grass—is the subject at hand, there is this simile regarding the two slaughterers, the govikarta and the akṣavāpa: 'Like Rudra, these two are slaughterers. One who cuts up cows (*gāḥ*) is a *govicarta*; one who sows dice (*akṣān*) is an *akṣavāpa*. These are the names of the two slaughterers of animals."

Moreover, those two objects of comparison (upameya) are seen here through the word *rudra*, the standard of comparison (upamāna), which is in the singular number. Thus, because this singular form "Rudra" is observed in this sacred tradition (āmnāya), it is determined from that very tradition that the standard of comparison "refines" the object of comparison—even if it is multiple—by means of the single number it has assumed. || 591 ||

If, however, the standard of comparison were to differ according to the differences among the objects of comparison, then— "Due to the difference in the standards of comparison, the suffix *añ* would be prescribed for many [objects]; there would be elision [of the suffix] as in the case of 'Kaśyapas,' and likewise even in the case of images. (592)

Regarding the rule *yañañośca*, the elision (*luk*) is prescribed when there is a plurality [of referents]. An objection is raised here: in the case of *baidasya* or *baidayoḥ patnyo bahavo māṇavakā bidāḥ* ("many students who are the wives of a descendant of Bida, or of two descendants of Bida, are Bidas"), if the suffix *añ* is explained as being applied in the sense of plurality, then the elision would not apply to the plural. This is because the suffix *añ* arises after a single instance or two instances—namely, *baidasya* or *baidayoḥ*. To this, it is said: "Let it not be so. It will be understood as 'that which ends in *añ* when there is plurality'. To that, it is replied: "It cannot be so. For in that case, it would also apply here: *kāśyapapratikṛtayaḥ kāśyapāḥ* ('images of Kāśyapa are Kāśyapas')."

*Kāśyapa* is the offspring (*apatya*) of Kaśyara, formed with the suffix *yañ* according to the rule for the *bidādi* group. Regarding the form *kāśyapāḥ* (in the plural) as images (*pratikṛti*) of Kāśyapa—where the suffix *kan* is introduced by the rule "ive pratikṛtau" (Pāṇini 5.3.96)—the elision (*lup*) occurs by the rule "jīvakārthe cāpaṇye" (Pāṇini 5.3.99). Since the suffix ending in *añ* remains when there is a plurality of images, the rule "añ-antam bahuṣu" (Pāṇini 2.4.64) would require the elision (*luk*) of that suffix. Consequently, the form *kaśyapāḥ* would be correct for images, but this is not desired. Since the form *kāśyapāḥ* alone is desired, it is established that the suffix *yañ* [is applied] in the plural.

In the case of *bidāḥ* (the descendants of Baida), however, there is no fault, because it has been stated that "when [a patronymic] ending in the singular or dual is applied to many [descendants], there is elision of the suffix before a *yuvan* [derivative]. Furthermore, if the difference in the upamāna (standard of comparison) were to follow from the difference in the upameya (object of comparison) here, then—since the *pratimās* (images/replicas) which are the upameyas are many—the upamāna, Kāśyapa, would also have to be differentiated; consequently, this suffix *añ* would apply only to the plural. And thus, by the rule *añyo bahuṣu*, elision (*luk*) would undesirably follow here as well, which would contradict the Bhāṣya.

Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of [applying] the term "Kāśyapas" to mere images; therefore, even when the object of comparison differs, the standard of comparison does not differ. (592)

[Objection: "In that case, just as in the example *kāśyapa iva pratikṛtayaḥ*, when there is elision (*lup*) of the suffix prescribed by [Pāṇini 4.3.100], the singular number alone would result due to the treatment as the base form (*yuktavadbhāva*). To this he says: "But in this way, due to the treatment as the base form (*yuktavadbhāva*), the singular number would indeed occur here. However, it was stated thus regarding the elision of the suffix after a non-human (*lummanuṣye*) for the sake of establishing a single gender. (593)

If it were so—that is, if the singular number of the *upamāna* (the standard of comparison) were to apply even when the *upameya* (the object of comparison) is divided [into many], then despite the plurality of the counterparts (*pratikṛti*), the use of the singular would result as an undesirable consequence due to the extended application (*atideśa*). Regarding this, he states a proposed solution: "From the inclusion of the word 'gender' (*liṅga*) in the Vārttika ‘*lummanuṣye*’ for the sake of establishing gender, it is determined that in this context, the [application of] number does not occur through extended application from the bare [base]. Otherwise, the statement would have been simply "for the sake of establishing gender and number."

Just as one says "a wooden doll is a man," "two wooden dolls are men," or "wooden dolls are men," the number (saṃkhyā) remains that of "man" alone; however, the gender (liṅga) belongs to the wooden doll itself. Likewise, in the case of "the Kāśyapas," although the masculine gender is extended [from the original], the number remains that which pertains to the representation itself. || 593 ||

Now, since it has been stated without qualification that "when *lup* occurs, [the base] is like that which is joined [to it], including both gender (*vyakti*) and number (*vacana*"), how is it that in this case the number (*vacana*) is excluded based on the mention of only the gender (*liṅga*) in the Vārttika? Furthermore, let it be that even what is obtained through extended application (*atideśa*) applies only when *lup* occurs after a non-human [name], in accordance with the authority of the Vārttika.

Regarding this, one might object: "Since the rule states that 'in those cases [such as *harītakī* and others], the individual instance (*vyakti*) is what is established,' how could the word *kāśyapāḥ* not be subject to the treatment of the associated form (*yuktavadbhāva*)? Anticipating this doubt, he states another solution: "When the objects of comparison are distinct, some single [quality] persists; in that case, when a suffix is prescribed, the treatment of the associated form is always desired. (594)

Regarding various distinct objects to be compared, which exist in the form of representations, there are two possible positions: either a single, undivided simile functions as the cause of production for all of them, or it is divided according to each respective object of comparison (*pratyupameya*). In that case, if an undivided [simile] functions, then when there is a plurality of representations, the rule "the elided [suffix] behaves like the word with which it was joined" (*lupi yuktavad*) necessarily applies. And since this is exactly what is intended, there is no undesirable consequence whatsoever. || 594 ||

But when the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) applies to the object of comparison (*upameya*) through differentiation, then the form "Kāśyapāḥ" is established; thus he says: "But when [the standard] is situated as one with each respective object of comparison, then, due to the distinction of external objects, that which ends in a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) is accumulated. (595)

When the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) operates individually with respect to each object of comparison (*upameya*) for the sake of distinction, then there is no difference in the primary sense of the term. Thus, "an image of Kāśyapa" is *kāśyapa*; likewise, a second [image] is also *kāśyapa*, and a third is also *kāśyapa*. Because of this individual connection, there is no plurality here. It is merely that this word-form, ending in a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) and involving the notion of an image, is accumulated; it attains accumulation, which is to say, multiplicity.

For instance, by means of the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) among identical forms, "Kāśyapa and Kāśyapa and Kāśyapa" becomes connected with plurality as "the Kāśyapas. Now, the operation of the extended rule (*atideśa-śāstra*), namely "in the case of *lup*, it is like that which is joined," does not apply here, because that operation has already been completed. However, when the cognition arises at the very outset that "this collection of images is like a Kāśyapa," then its operation [does apply]. For in that case, there exists a distinction of number for that which is joined, and that serves as the basis [for the application of the rule].
But now, since there is a collection of representations, this other distinction of number based on the differentiation of external objects does not exist. || 595 ||

Now, one might object: "Even so, since this [collection] is being accumulated (*pracīyamāna*), why does the treatment as a word ending in *yuk* not apply? Anticipating this doubt, he explains by means of an illustration: "Just as in the accumulation of a collection (*samūha-pracaya*) there is a difference in number for *dvigu* compounds—as in the case of *pañcapūlī* and the like—so too it should be in the accumulation of words ending in case-suffixes (*subanta-pracaya*). (596)

When five bundles are collected, the term *pañcapūlī* is formed by applying the rule *dvigurekavacanam*, which effects a singular form; then, through the process of *ekaśeṣa*—where one says *pañcapūlī ca pañcapūlī ca pañcapūlī ca*—the plural form *pañcapūlyaḥ* arises. To the objection, "Why does the singular form not apply again despite this plurality? the answer is given: "It is not so; rather, this plurality belongs to another word that is a *ekaśeṣa* [compound], because there is multiplicity of other [individuals]. For this *dvigu* compound does not denote multiple objects; rather, this plurality belongs to another word that is a *ekaśeṣa*.

For the formation of a singular compound (*ekavadbhāva*) has been prescribed for the meaning of a *dvigu* compound. And since the single-remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) has not yet been performed, the singular formation applies to that very meaning which belongs to the *dvigu* itself when it does not depend on any other meaning; for that indeed is the logical meaning of a *dvigu*. However, once the single-remainder has been performed, the collective mass of the *dvigu*'s meanings—which has accumulated—is distinct from the original meaning of the *dvigu*. Consequently, because the singular formation has already fulfilled its purpose regarding the internal, primary meaning of the *dvigu*, it cannot apply again.

Thus, in this case, the meaning of *lup* is that which is understood from the word ending in *lup* itself, independently of anything else; consequently, once the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) has been performed, because it is a different word, the application of *yuktavadbhāva* (the treatment as if joined), which finds its scope in the internal (*antaraṅga*) operation, does not apply here to the external (*bahiraṅga*) plurality of accumulation. || 596 ||

Regarding this, he says that this example is inappropriate: "But when an accumulation is divided, the number is divided among the heaps; however, no difference in meaning whatsoever is observed in the case of words ending in the suffix *luP*. (597)

The meaning understood from a *dvigu* compound such as *pañcapūlī*—namely, "five bundles brought together"—is not the same as that expressed by *pañcapūlyaḥ* when the intention is to indicate a collection (*pracaya*) and the *ekaśeṣa* (single-remainder) formation is applied. For in the former case, the referent is delimited by the number five; however, when *ekaśeṣa* is performed, it is delimited by the number fifteen. If, moreover, *ekaśeṣa* were applied to two [sets], as in *pañcapūlyau*, it would be delimited by the number ten. Therefore, when the collection of duality, plurality, and so forth differs, a number distinct from the number of the *dvigu* referent arises.

And thus, it cannot be said that this [compound] does not have the meaning of a *dvigu*. Since it denotes the object being collected as delimited by the number five, it is correct here to apply the solution to the term *dvigu*: "Or rather, no, because another [number] is manifold. However, in this case regarding the scope of the elision (*lub*), there is no difference whatsoever in the meaning.

For indeed, the very same meaning that arises when *ekaśeṣa* is applied after expressing a collective sense (*pracaya*) through the individual connection of each item with the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), is identical to the meaning when a single standard of comparison is connected to many objects of comparison (*upameya*), provided that the plural number is employed from the very outset. Thus, since there is no difference in meaning here, it can be said that even the meaning of the collective (*pracaya*) is included within the meaning of the elision (*lub-artha*); consequently, the transfer of the number (*vacanātideśa*) would certainly apply in that case. But surely, there is indeed a difference in meaning here?

To explain: when each individual image (*pratikṛti*) is connected with the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), and the plural form is used by means of *ekaśeṣa*, then for each single image, Kāśyapa is perceived as the standard of comparison. However, even though there is a distinction among many objects of comparison (*upameya*) regarding a single, non-different standard of comparison, there is indeed a difference. This is true; such is the distinction. Nevertheless, because the meaning is not lost in the case of a word ending in the elision (*lubanta*), the accumulated meaning—by virtue of its connection through that elision—is certainly capable of being delimited.

For indeed, that very meaning which is expressed by a nominal stem (*lubanta*)—namely, the form of the "counterpart" (*pratikṛti*)—it is this alone that attains plurality in the sense of accumulation (*pracaya*), and no other. Furthermore, in an expression such as *kāśyapa iva kāśyapaḥ*, the extended application (*atideśa*) does not operate due to the absence of a purpose, because both the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) denote the same referent. Thus, the function of the treatment as a plural (*yuktavadbhāva*) is appropriate only when there is an intention to express accumulation.

In the case of *kāśyapa iva pratikṛtya*, since the plurality of the *pratikṛtis* (the objects of comparison) is understood precisely through the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one), the application of the rule for *yuktavadbhāva* would indeed proceed only when the external referent [plurality] is possible. Therefore, the derivation of *kāśyapāḥ* here must be explained by another means; it cannot be established even by means of *ekaśeṣa*. || 597 ||

He states another variety of that [simile]: "In cases where no other word denoting the object of comparison (upameya) is employed, a distinction in number between it and the standard of comparison (upamāna) by others is desired. (598)

In those cases where, when [the suffix] *lup* is elided, no word other than that ending in *lup* is uttered to denote the object of comparison (*upameya*)—that is, the object to be delimited—the distinction of number for the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), such as Kāśyapa, is desired; the meaning is that the standard of comparison operates here with a different number. For indeed, if the word denoting the object of comparison were employed, then because plurality would be understood from that very word, the standard of comparison would be unable to assist the object of comparison unless it itself were distinct [in number].

For example, in such cases as "These are the likenesses of Kāśyapa, Devadatta, Yajñadatta, and Viṣṇumitra," when the word denoting the object of comparison (*upameya*) is not employed, a doubt arises upon hearing the word "Kāśyapa": is this a likeness of one [person], or of many? For if it were a likeness of many, the singular ending of the word *kāśyapa* would be justified by the rule of *yuktavadbhāva* (the treatment of a compound as its prior member).

Therefore, in this context, for the purpose of defining the distinctions among the objects of comparison (*upameya*), at the very outset Kāśyapa assumes the role of a standard of comparison (*upamāna*); thus it is established that "the Kāśyapas are the images. Furthermore, the mention of "by others" here is because another opinion will be stated subsequently. (598)

Regarding this very point, he provides an illustration: "Just as molasses, sesame seeds, and so forth, through their application [in a single process], attain the status of a single number; yet when cooking and other such processes are not applied, they are designated by different numbers. (599) In instances such as "the cooking of molasses, sesame, and rice," or "the redness that arose in the copper and the *palāśa* leaves," although the cooking and other actions are determined to be manifold due to the plurality of the objects to be cooked (*pākya*) and so on, the cooking and the rest are nevertheless indicated as being one.

However, when there is no employment of another word (śabdāntara) based on the determination of a distinction between things to be cooked, nor based on the determination of a distinction in its own substratum, then, upon the statement "cooking" (pākaḥ) or "coloring" (rāgaḥ), a doubt arises as to whether this cooking belongs to a single substance to be cooked or has multiple substrates. To ensure a certain understanding, the meaning is indicated as being endowed with multiple numbers, such as "two cookings" (pākau) or "many colorings" (rāgāḥ). || 599 ||

Applying this principle here as well to the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*), he says: "The distinction residing in the correlate (*saṃbandhin*) is perceived in the actual usage; therefore, the distinction [between the two] correlates is not apprehended in the object of comparison (*upameya*). (600)

That entity which is not distinct in itself, but rather assumes distinction based on the difference of its correlates (*saṃbandhin*), attains the cognition of distinction when there is the employment of a word denoting that correlate. For example: [the change of state such as] cooking in the case of the employment of words like "molasses" (*guḍa*).

However, when a word denoting a related entity (*saṃbandhivacana*) is not employed, just as a specific distinction such as "cooking" and so forth cannot be determined, so too, when a word denoting a representation (*pratikṛtivacana*) is not employed, the difference—the specific distinction—of that which possesses it cannot be determined in the object of comparison (*upameya*), which is to be delimited. Therefore, the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) functions precisely by having its own difference already established. And thus, the meaning is that the difference of the object of comparison is communicated by means of a distinct standard of comparison. || 600 ||

He concludes this very point: "Therefore, in order to avoid the consequence of [the word] being a general term, a distinction residing in the object of comparison is observed in the standards of comparison. (601)

When "Kāśyapa" is uttered, one understands the offspring or the lineage, but not necessarily a likeness. Even if there is a comprehension of a connection with a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), because the object of comparison (*upameya*) is understood as being common to both the singular and the plural, it is called a general term (*sāmānya-śabda*). Consequently, in order to exclude that [general sense] and to convey the distinction based on the specific substratum of the object of comparison, the standard of comparison relies upon its own distinction, since qualities follow the nature of their primary subject. || 601 ||

Now, one might object that when the word expressing the object of comparison (*upameya*) is employed at the very outset, then because its meaning is already conveyed, the plural marker should not be used. Anticipating this objection, the author begins to state another view—which was indicated here by the phrase "by others" (*anyaiḥ*)—regarding the matter: "In some cases, a single common attribute (*upamāna*) is heard as applying to all [the objects of comparison] collectively; or, when the objects of comparison are distinct, each one is compared individually. (602)

In this regard, there is a twofold distinction: sometimes a single simile applies to multiple objects of comparison taken together, while at other times the application of similes occurs individually for each distinct object. || 602 ||

Regarding the previous position, he states an illustration: "Just as 'like Garuḍa' is employed with reference to a multitude, where there is a similarity between elephants and Vainateya [Garuḍa] by means of a single [attribute]. (603)

A particular arrangement of elephants is compared to Garuḍa, as in "these elephants are like Garuḍa"; likewise, a particular formation of horses is compared to a sea-monster (*makara*), as in "these steeds are like sea-monsters"; and similarly, "these bricks are like hawks. Thus, this specific arrangement or variety of formation of soldiers and so forth—such as the *Garuḍavyūha* and others—is capable of being compared to Vainateya and the rest, provided that the word "Garuḍa" is employed in its primary sense alone.

For instance: when it is said, "elephants are perceived as having the form of Garuḍas," the specific configuration (saṃsthānaviśeṣa) becomes delimited by the Garuḍa; thus, because the relata are identical, no difference [between the elephant and the Garuḍa] arises here. Indeed, elephants are not the immeasurable relata of the Garuḍa, but rather that particular formation (vyūha). However, when there is the use of the plural number, such as "these elephants are like Garuḍas" or "these horses are like Makaras," then each individual elephant and horse is understood to possess the status of being the object of comparison (upameya).

And thus, through such similarities as rapidity of movement and so forth, its status as a point of comparison would be understood; however, the array itself could not be determined as having a measurable extent. || 603 ||

In the same way here as well: even for a single person, a distinct reflection is perceived simultaneously [in others]. Because it belongs to Kāśyapa, this [reflection] remains individual for each. (604)

If, as in the case of "like Kāśyapa, these images [are] Kāśyapa," the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is employed in the singular, then they are equal to the array of elephants belonging to Garuḍa; in that case, the manifold image of Kāśyapa is understood to be equal to [the array] by virtue of some common property such as its configuration. However, the comparison would not be understood as applying to each individual [image]. The word *saha* has the meaning of "equal" (*tulya*). In connection with that, the genitive case is used in "of Kāśyapa."

Therefore, in order to convey the status of each [object] as a separate object of comparison (*upameya*), the word *kāśyapa* here remains distinct for every individual object of comparison. In the previous view, it was stated that when the word denoting the object of comparison is not employed, the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) assumes its own distinctness for the sake of another, so that the distinction among the objects of comparison may be understood.

Here, however, since the standard of comparison is seen to be distinct even when the word denoting the object of comparison is employed, the standard of comparison is taken up at the very outset in its distinct form for the purpose of conveying that there is one standard of comparison for each respective object of comparison; such is the difference between the two views. (604)

Now, he states another more well-known illustration for the comparison of things combined as a single unit: "When it is said, 'The clouds are like a mountain,' the similarity of the [clouds] taken as a whole with the mountain is understood; therefore, it differs from the case where [the similarity] applies to each [individual cloud]. (605)

"These clouds are like mountains, being of great magnitude and possessing many peaks variegated with various colors and diverse shapes"—when the clouds are compared to a single mountain in this way, their similarity to a mountain is determined in their collective state, not individually. For no single cloud is like a mountain, as each individual cloud lacks the common attributes of a mountain, such as being variegated with various colors and having many peaks of diverse shapes; for it is only when they are gathered together that they possess such characteristics.

Since the simile thus ends in the singular, its meaning is not determined; therefore, for the sake of perceiving the connection of the simile with each individual [member], this *kāśyapa*-type simile undergoes a division of itself at the very outset. This is the sense. Thus, for the sake of conveying the intended meaning, the use of the plural form "kāśyapāḥ" has been established. Now, if this is so, since the distinction is understood at the very outset, the suffix *añ* would arise in the plural, and consequently, by the rule "the elision of *añ* when [the base] is plural," elision (*luk*) would occur here.

This is not a fault. For it is precisely when there is non-unity of meaning that [the singular] arises; and thus, since the singular number would have been required by the rule of *yuktavadbhāva* (the treatment of a compound as its constituent member), the plural number is justified through the principle of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one). Furthermore, even there, having raised the doubt regarding the non-application of *yuktavadbhāva*, this plural number is justified for the sake of conveying the distinction between the objects of comparison (*upameya*). Thus, in accordance with the communication of the intended meaning, the grammatical number resulting from *yuktavadbhāva* is here set aside.

Incorporating this very principle, it was stated [in the *Mahābhāṣya*] that "the individual form (*vyakti*) [is denoted] in the case of *harītakyādi*s"; this too should be understood in that same context. Furthermore, even if one were to adopt the view that "that which ends in *añ* denotes many," the objection raised in the *Bhāṣya* regarding the non-occurrence of elision (*luk*) remains valid. For instance, in the rule "yañañośca" (Pāṇini 2.4.64), because the term "gotra" is carried over from the preceding rule "yaskādibhyo gotre" (Pāṇini 2.4.63), and because "gotra" there refers to the worldly definition of offspring, one must rely on the interpretation: "that which ends in *añ* is a gotra when it denotes many. Since plurality in the sense of a physical representation does not constitute plurality of a *gotra*, this [case of *harītakyādi*s] falls outside the scope for the elision of the suffix.

And having established this, since the plural form *bidāḥ*—meaning the many descendants of one *baida* or two *baidas*—is already accounted for by this very rule (*luk*) because the suffix ending in *añ* denotes a plurality of lineages (*gotra*), the Bhāṣya establishes the final conclusion that the rule *yūni* need not have been commenced; for even a youth (*yuvan*) is considered a lineage (*gotra*) because the term *gotra* is understood in its worldly sense in the rule *yañaśca*. This point is concluded. || 605 ||

Now, in connection with the discussion on comparison (*upamāna*), this rule for the suffix *cha*—namely, *samāsācca tadviṣayāt*—which has the sense of "like" (*iva*) as its object, is being examined. Regarding this, the *Bhāṣya* asks: "What is referred back by the word *tat*? It is appropriate that a pronoun refers back to the principal element. However, in this context, the compound (*samāsa*) is not the principal element because it functions as a subordinate member (*guṇabhāva*) to the derivative suffix; likewise, the sense of "like" (*ivārtha*) is also subordinate in the rule for the suffix *cha*. Since no other candidate remains, the question arises: what is it that is being referred back?

Regarding the statement "the suffix *cha* is what is heard here": the intention is that this very suffix, because it is the element to be prescribed (*vidheya*), is the primary factor and thus fit for connection with a pronoun. Immediately after, it was asked: "How could a compound be the domain (*viṣaya*) of the suffix *cha*? While there might be a reference to the suffix *cha* due to its predominance, there is nevertheless an inconsistency in the meaning. For, in that case, the resulting sense would be: "from that compound which has the suffix *cha* as its domain (*viṣaya*), the suffix *cha* occurs."

How could a compound (*samāsa*) be the domain (*viṣaya*) of the suffix *cha*? For a word cannot be the domain of another word; rather, it is logical that only the meaning (*artha*) is the denoted domain of a word. A word, however, could be the domain of an imitation (*anukaraṇa*), as that which is to be conveyed by it. But there is no imitation of a compound, for only the suffix *cha* itself would be such [an imitation]. Now, the intended meaning here might be this: the sense of "domain" is "occurrence nowhere else. Thus, a compound is the domain of *cha* if that compound does not occur elsewhere than before the suffix *cha*.

He says that this too is incorrect: "The dependence [of the word] upon that [object], and its having that as its referent, is not understood from its being something to be enjoined; for in the expression 'kākatālīya' (accidental), it is well known that [the suffix] functions as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). (606)

Since a compound does not occur except where the suffix *cha* is present, it is impossible for the compound to have that [suffix] as its domain by depending on the suffix *cha*, such that one could say "from that, *cha* occurs. This is demonstrated in the case of *kākatālīyam*, because only that which is already known can logically serve as the cause for the cognition of something else.

Since it is not established that this suffix *cha* must be prescribed for the very first time by this [rule] alone, how can the compound—which serves as the base (*prakṛti*)—be delimited as having this [suffix] as its object by relying on this [suffix], which is itself unestablished? For if the suffix *cha* were to have its own form established through another rule, then it would be appropriate to employ it for the purpose of prescribing the suffix, having determined the fixed nature of the compound as the base; however, *cha* has not been prescribed by any other rule.

For this alone is the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*) for it. And thus, prior to the prescription of the suffix *cha*, the fact that the compound is the domain of *cha* is unestablished; how then can it be stated? If, on the other hand, the status of being the domain of *cha* is justified by recourse to its future state, then what is the point of saying this? For if it is understood in this sense—that "since the suffix *cha* will be prescribed after the compound, and if that [compound] is the domain of *cha*, then the suffix *cha* occurs"—no benefit whatsoever is expressed regarding the base (*prakṛti*).
Because a compound whose base consists of [only] two elements never deviates from being the domain of *ch* [as a suffix], there is no other established entity that could be excluded. || 606 ||

But surely there is a purpose for the qualification based on the state that is yet to be produced (*bhāvyavasthā*). For instance, one might object: "Since the compound is qualified by its status as having *cha* as its domain, and because the meaning of the domain consists in its not existing elsewhere, it is thereby made known that this compound is not employed other than with the suffix *cha*. Anticipating this, he says: "The domain [of the suffix] may be *rājāśva* and so forth, or it may be something else; thus it is uncertain. Therefore, prior to the prescription of *cha*, no designation [of it as such] exists. (607)

By the expression "tadviṣayāt" (from that which has that as its object), it is not determined that every compound having *cha* as its object—being taken up without being specified as a qualifier—whether it be the well-known compounds such as *rājāśva* and so forth, or any other compound having *cha* as its object that might be conceived through some other means, would be included; for [if it were so], the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of the compound would be indicated by way of the well-known status of having *cha* as its object.

For, since it is impossible for the suffix *cha* to have [the compound] as its object in any other way, the compound must be its object precisely because it serves as the base (*prakṛti*) for the suffix *cha*. And thus, since it is possible for every compound to serve as such a base, what would be excluded by this qualification? Nor does it mean that every compound is ungrammatical (*asādhutva*) except when followed by the suffix *cha*, for that is not desired. Furthermore, it is not logical to assume the formulation of a grammatical rule (*śāstra*) for an unintended purpose. Therefore, let some other thing be postulated as the referent of the word "that" (*tad*).

Therefore, since a fixed compound (*samāsa*) with a well-established scope does not exist prior to that rule concerning *ś* (the substitution of *ś* for *s*), the qualification "from the scope of *ś*" (*ś-viṣayāt*) is not appropriate. For a qualification of the base form (*prakṛti-rūpa*) is observed only when a suffix (*pratyaya*) has already been established, as in the rule: "by a genitive case ending or by a suffix having the sense of 'from' (*atas-artha*). However, it is not logical for something that has not itself attained its own existence to qualify its own cause; for that which makes another known becomes an indicator (*jñāpaka*) only when the object [to be indicated] is already established.

Thus, since a direct reference (*pratyavamarśa*) to the primary element [the *upamāna*] is impossible, the meaning of the suffix—which serves as the cause for the application of the rule regarding the word-form ending in *cha*—is referred to by the pronoun, even though it is subordinate; this refers to the sense of "as if" (*iva*). For it has been stated that "this [sense of *iva*] is also present here because it is the subject under discussion," as expressed in the words: "In that case, the sense of 'as if' is being specifically pointed out."

Since the meaning of "as if" (ivārtha) is expressed here by the suffix (*pratyaya*), how could the compound, which constitutes the base (*prakṛti*), be its domain? Therefore, by the force of referring back [to that] via the pronoun (*sarvanāma*), two functions of the meaning of "as if" are accomplished here: by one function, the meaning of "as if" serves as the delimiter of the compound; by the other, it becomes expressed by the suffix. The meaning is: from the compound, which has the meaning of "as if" as its domain, the suffix *cha* occurs in the sense of "as if."

Without understanding this intended meaning, it was objected: "Since the meaning has already been expressed by the compound (*samāsa*), the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) would not apply. The point is that because there is no distinction in the operation of a single referent, if it were a qualifier of the compound, the suffix *śa* would not occur, as it would already be denoted by the compound itself. For a meaning cannot enter into the scope of a compound without being explicitly designated; such is the sense.

Now, if a suffix were to apply even when the meaning is already expressed by a word—as in the case where, due to the rule "the *dvigu* compound [expresses] the meaning of a *taddhita* suffix," the meaning of the *dvigu* and the *taddhita* suffix are common—then a suffix such as *cha* would also have to be applied to words like *śastrīśyāmā* (dark as a sword-blade), because they express a meaning that is already conveyed by the compound itself. To this, the following solution has been stated: "The two meanings are distinct. The intention behind this—that there is indeed a difference in the operation regarding the meaning, necessitated by the fact that otherwise the reference by a pronoun would be inexplicable—has already been determined previously. || 607 ||

He states what these two meanings are: "In this case, the causality of two meanings is perceived; by one, the suffix is joined with a member [of the compound], and by the other, it is joined [with the whole]. (608)

In the expressions *kākatālīyam* and *ajākṛpāṇīyam*, two meanings are understood. Of these, by one meaning—the sense of "as if"—the preceding member and the following member of the compound are connected; thus, the compound, by conveying that "as if" meaning, becomes one whose domain is the sense of "as if. Alternatively, with respect to the word ending in a secondary suffix (*taddhita*), the compound itself, as the base form (*prakṛti*), is the constituent part here. And even that [base] is connected with the meaning only through its own parts, not directly. The suffix *cha* is connected with the other meaning, which is the expressed sense (*vācya*).

Furthermore, in the case of "dark as a sword" (*śastrīśyāmā*), just as Devadatta is compared to a sword that possesses the well-known quality of darkness, so too is another [person]. Since the object of comparison (*upamāna*) is also embellished by the object of comparison (*upameya*) named Devadatta, there is only a single sense of the particle *iva*. || 608 ||

In that regard, he states the specific meaning by which the constituent parts are connected: "Caitra’s arrival there is like the arrival of a crow; the attack of the bandit, however, is like the falling of a palm fruit. (609)

In the expression *kākatālīyam*, the crow’s arrival is the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), and Caitra’s arrival is the object of comparison (*upameya*). Likewise, the falling of the palm fruit is the standard of comparison, while the encounter with the bandits is the object of comparison. The common property (*sāmānyadharma*) in both cases is the quality of occurring unexpectedly. This, therefore, is the meaning expressed by the compound. He also states that which is expressed by the suffix (*pratyaya*): "Whatever action arises there in the conjunction of those two, such as killing and so forth, in the sense of the object of comparison, a derivative formation (*taddhita-vṛtti*) is desired [to express it]. (610)

When there is a meeting between a crow and a palmyra tree (*kākatālayoḥ samāgame*), another action arises caused by that encounter—such as killing, breaking a limb, or bursting—and when that [action] is the object of comparison (*upameya*) and the thing to be defined (*paricchedya*), such as the killing of Caitra and so forth, the suffix *ch* is prescribed by the rule for the second sense of the word *iva*, which connects the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) with the object of comparison (*upameya*). || 610 ||

But surely, the arrival of Caitra is compared to the departure of a crow, and thus the latter stands in a subordinate (guṇa) relation to the former; and the encounter with bandits is compared to the falling of a palm fruit, and thus the latter stands in a subordinate relation to the former. Consequently, since there is no mutual relationship between the crow and the palm fruit, how can there be a compound (*samāsa*) when there is a lack of semantic capacity (*asāmarthya*)? If you argue that the compound is established here by this very rule as an *jñāpaka* (indicative proof) in the Bhāṣya, even so, the Bhāṣya has shown that the operation belongs specifically to the rule "a nominal stem ending in a case-suffix is compounded with another nominal stem" (*sup supā*). Therefore, how could that rule apply in the absence of semantic capacity? Or, let us grant that the compound does indeed occur.

However, raising the objection that since the meaning of the whole is not produced from the meanings of the parts taken separately, by what meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) could the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) be qualified, he says: "When [the action] is inherent [in the object], the word for the substance remains [fixed]; likewise, the words *kāka* and *tāla* remain fixed in their respective meanings of 'falling' and 'coming'. (611)

Just as in expressions such as "curd-rice" (*dadhyodana*) or "jaggery-grains" (*guḍadhānā*), where substances possessing an established nature lack mutual connection, the words for the substances—such as "curd"—are applied to the act of sprinkling and so forth which depends upon them because that [connection] would otherwise be inexplicable; likewise, here the two words "crow" (*kāka*) and "palmyra" (*tāla*) apply to the actions that have come together. Consequently, the arrival of the crow is denoted by the word "crow," and the falling of the palmyra is denoted by the word "palmyra"; thus, there is no mutual connection [between the two terms].

Furthermore, it has been established—in such instances as *brāhmaṇavad adhīte* ("he studies like a Brāhmaṇa")—that even a word denoting a substance (*dravya-śabda*) may function with respect to an action when occurring outside its primary referent. Consequently, the meaning here is as follows: since the connection between the meanings of the preceding and following words is possible through mutual comparison—namely, "this arrival of the crow is like the unexpected arrival of the palm fruit," and "this falling of the palm fruit is like the unexpected arrival of the crow"—the status of being a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix is logically established.

For when the concomitance between the crow’s arrival and the palm fruit’s falling is established, since Devadatta’s arrival and the bandit’s attack are the objects of comparison (upameya) by means of those two, the compound is justified when the sense of "like" (iva) is to be expressed; consequently, upon the destruction of that [comparison], the suffix *cha* occurs in the object of comparison, namely, the destruction of Devadatta. || 611 ||

But surely, why is the killing of Devadatta by the bandits not compared to the killing of a crow by a falling palm fruit—an event that arose unexpectedly at the very outset?
