For instance, since it is not appropriate to assume here a figurative application (*gauṇī vṛtti*) of the words *kāka* (crow) and *tāla* (palm tree) to the movements of the crow and the falling of the palm fruit respectively, what is the point of comparing the crow’s movement with the palm’s fall? To this, he says: "That which is the explanatory sentence (*anvākhyāyaka-vākya*) is thus conceptualized;
but that which is the actual sentence used in common practice (*prayoga-vākya*) in the world is not used in such a way. (612)

In this system, the derivation (*anvākhyāna*) proceeds by means of the division between base (*prakṛti*) and suffix (*pratyaya*); thus, through this method, a sentence of grammatical derivation (*prakriyāvākya*) is produced, wherein the words have their meanings fully integrated. For, like "the crow’s flight is like the palm’s fall" and "the palm’s fall is like the crow’s flight," this sentence serves as a means for derivation through mutual comparison; however, it is not employed in common worldly usage.

Otherwise, the crow would be connected only with the act of striking (*vadha*) performed by the palm-fruit, and not with the palm-fruit itself, were it not for this fabricated derivative sentence. However, the worldly *prayoga-vākya* (usage sentence) which conveys the meaning according to its established definition is not like this; for in common usage, the word *kākatāla*, being of the nature of a compound, is never employed without the suffix *-cha*. This [derivation] is merely a contrived means for providing a grammatical analysis (*anvākhyāna*) of the worldly term *kākatālīya*. Indeed, since such a contrivance follows the actual usage, this method is more appropriate. 612.
Regarding this, he says: "When the unexpected meeting of two things is observed, like that of a crow and a palmyra fruit, a compound formation is accepted for the basis of those two. (613)

Just as there is a relationship between the crow and the palm fruit—occurring unexpectedly and resulting in death or the like—so too is such a relationship observed between two individuals, such as a bandit and Devadatta. When that relationship serves as a limiting condition (*upādhi*), it is accepted that the function of the suffix occurs from the base (*prakṛti*) characterized by the compound, even though the actual meeting of those two is not explicitly expressed. Thus, the meaning of the base, conditioned by the relationship between the crow and the palm fruit, is analyzed.

However, the suffix *cha* occurs in the sense of the object of comparison (*upameya*), such as in the case of "killing" (*vadha*) and so forth; and since this verbal root is restricted exclusively to that domain, it lacks grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) elsewhere. This very point has been demonstrated at length in the *Bhāṣya*. || 613 ||

To the question, "In what sense is the occurrence [of the suffix] admitted? he says: "Just as the killing of a crow by a palm fruit [is used figuratively], when another [subject] is made the object of wonder, the suffix *cha* is desired [to denote] that which is the subject of comparison (*upameya*). (614)

The meaning of the compound as a whole, which is like the meeting of the crow and the palm fruit—the encounter between the bandit and Devadatta—has already been shown. Now, however, another meaning is demonstrated here, which is not directly expressed by the suffixes: namely, "if [something] is here" or "in another [place]."

Just as the killing of a crow occurred by chance when a palm fruit fell upon it unexpectedly, so too did the killing of Devadatta occur by a bandit who arrived unexpectedly and without prior intent; thus, the suffix *cha* is applied to an object of comparison that has attained such a marvelous nature. The meaning is that the rule for *cha* applies to another specific action that is compared to a specific action produced by the coincidence of the "crow-and-palm" (*kākatāla*) event.
The meaning is this: just as a crow was killed by a palm fruit by chance, so too that which occurs unexpectedly and is wonderful is called *kākatālīya*. This point has been explained. || 614 ||

In the context of comparison (*upamāna*), as the topic of meaning arises, something else is also examined here according to the rule for suffixes. For instance, regarding the rule "the suffix *kan* is added to *sthūla* and others in the sense of 'kind' (*prakāra*)," similarity (*sādṛśya*) is the meaning of "kind. In that regard, it is stated: "An addition [to the list] is made for *cañcat* and *bṛhat*. Thus, one similar to *cañcat* is *cañcatka*, and one similar to *bṛhat* is *bṛhatka*. To the question "Of what does this denote? he says: "Others say that *cañcatka* is one of the *cañcat* kind, and *bṛhatka* is one of the *bṛhat* kind; they declare these to be similar to a gem, a frog, and a firefly, respectively. (Verse 615)

In this context, "manner" (prakāra) means similarity; thus, the teachers (ācāryāḥ) consider that *cañcatprakāra* and *bṛhatprakāra* are designations for any one among [the gems] such as the *cañcatka* and *bṛhatka*. The phrase "others" (*apare*) is a reference to those teachers whose views are not different [from his own]. || 615 ||

To explain what kind of similarity exists here with the gem and other objects, he says: "In that regard, by means of its opening and closing [of the eyes], it is compared to a firefly; by means of the flow of breaths, to a frog; and by means of its throbbing radiance, to a gem. (616)

Even though it is motionless, a firefly, being suffused by its own light, is perceived as if moving and is thus designated by the term *cañcatka*. For instance, due to the distinction between the opening and closing of its own light, it appears as if quivering. Similarly, a frog, because its body is swollen by the force of incessant inhalations, is perceived as if its body were moving and thus becomes the object of the designation *cañcatka*.
Likewise, a gem whose form appears to move due to the circle of rays shining forth in an unbroken stream is called *cañcatka*.

Regarding the word *bṛhatka*, he asks what the meaning of the suffix *-ka* is, and says: "Even that which is small is perceived as great when its radiance expands; it is precisely in such a case that the word *bṛhatka* is applied to a gem. (617)

Even a gem that is thin is perceived as having a much thicker form due to the power of its spreading mass of luster from all sides; thus, it is designated as "bṛhatsadṛśa" (resembling something large) or "bṛhatka" (large). || 617 ||

In this context, he examines the nature of the "mode" (*prakāra*) through various philosophical perspectives: "Some maintain that similarity alone is the mode everywhere; however, others accept the designation 'mode' even in the case of difference. (618)

In all instances throughout the grammatical treatise—such as "the suffix *thāl* is used in the sense of manner" (*prakāravacane thāl*), "of a word denoting a quality, [the suffix *thāl* is used] in the sense of manner" (*prakāre guṇavacanasya*), and "the suffix *kan* is used after words like *sthūla* in the sense of manner" (*sthūlādibhyaḥ prakāravacane kan*)—the meaning of the word "manner" (*prakāra*) is simply similarity (*sādṛśya*). To illustrate: in expressions such as "in this way" (*yathā tathā*), it is precisely equality that is indicated. In the term "of a sharp kind" (*paṭujātīyaḥ*), however, the suffix *jātīyar* primarily denotes one who is similar. In the reduplicated form "sharp-sharp" (*paṭupaṭuḥ*), it is similarity itself that is indicated as a subordinate attribute residing in the possessor of that quality. The same applies to "a thick manner" (*sthūlaprakāraḥ*) or "thickish" (*sthūlakaḥ*).

However, by some, even where there is difference (*bheda*), that which is called "manner" (*prakāra*) is desired. Here too, in the phrase "in all cases," whether it be "as such" (*yathā*) or "so" (*tathā*), it is precisely difference that must be expressed. That very [difference] is common and the cause of similarity; thus, that too is understood by implication. This is also the case in expressions such as *paṭupaṭuḥ* (very clever) and *sthūlakaḥ* (very thick). And so, since both difference and similarity are perceived everywhere, one view distinguishes "manner" by holding that one is denoted by the word (*abhidheya*) while the other is understood through the power of meaning (*sāmarthya-gamya*).

In the expression "Devadatta is a type of animal" (*paśuprakāro devadattaḥ*), since a relationship of general and particular (*sāmānyaviśeṣabhāva*) is impossible, the general category itself is the "type. Even in the case of "The animal is Devadatta," because this expresses non-difference (*abhedābhidhāna*) through the inclusion of that [general category], what is understood from the effect is merely a similarity to its cause; however, in neither of these two usages is a difference (*bheda*) determined here. But regarding the statement "The Māṭharas and others are types of Brāhmaṇas" (*brāhmaṇaprakārā māṭharādayaḥ*), since the general category is connected to the particular and no difference is perceived, and thus similarity being impossible, they say that difference itself is the "type. (Verse 618)

Let there be similarity, difference, or a mode (*prakāra*). However, this is now investigated: "Is the suffix *thāl*, which is prescribed after many pronouns in the sense of a mode (*prakāra*), an annulor (*bādhaka*) of the suffix *jātīyar*—which is prescribed after nominal stems (*prātipadika*) in general? And if so, how could forms such as *kiñjātīyaḥ* not be established? Furthermore, if the mode is expressed by *thāl* alone, how can the usage *tathājātīyaḥ* occur? To this, he says: "A certain [suffix] expressing a mode is situated within that which possesses the mode (*prakāravat*); another, having operated upon the mere mode (*prakāramātra*), transcends it. (619)

The word *kaścit* consists of the suffix *jātīyar*, the suffix *kañ*, and reduplication. For in this suffix, by its very nature, there is the expression of the "manner" (*prakāra*) which is subordinate; thus, it is the possessor of the manner (*prakāravat*) itself that is expressed as the primary element. Therefore, since this suffix occurs after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) when that which expresses a manner is spoken of—as in the phrase "that in which such a manner is expressed"—it applies to the possessor of the manner. The suffix *thāl*, however, applies to the manner alone, and not to the possessor of the manner.

However, it should be understood by implication that, having occurred in the form, it exists in the possessor of that form accompanied by its class-character (*jāti*), and not because its occurrence in the possessor of that form is seen here as being with the suffix *-tva*, as is the case with words like *śuklatva*. And thus, because their objects are different, there is no relationship of sublation (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*). Furthermore, the usage "of such a kind" (*tathājātīya*) occurs.

In the expression "as Devadatta, so Yajñadatta," the suffix *thāl* does not denote the possessor of the mode (*prakārin*) alone; rather, since this sentence is completed by a verb such as "is" or "is seen," which is required [for the sense], it is understood that the mode itself has attained the status of an instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to that action. The meaning is: in whatever manner Devadatta exists, in that same manner Yajñadatta also exists.

Therefore, in this context, the mode (*prakāra*)—being connected with the action as an instrument (*karaṇa*)—does not bring about a sense of separation (*vyatireka*) in the possessor of the mode (*prakāravat*), which would be the cause for the use of the genitive case. Nor, however, can the expression of that [possessor] be inferred from the absence of the genitive, because the absence of the genitive is established by other means. || 619 ||

If, then, the suffix *thāl* expresses similarity (*sādṛśya*) as its meaning, one might ask: "Since the formation of an *avyayībhāva* compound has already been prescribed for the sense of 'as' (*yathā*), why is it restated here specifically for the sense of 'similarity'? To this he says: "The mention of *sādṛśya* (similarity) in the rule is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of *sadṛśa* (that which is similar). In the case of an *avyayībhāva* compound expressing equality, the word *saha* is the expressive term. (620)

The function of the word *yathā* when it denotes repetition (*vīpsā*) or similarity (*sādṛśya*) is that which expresses its meaning; this distinction regarding the indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva*) has thus been shown by way of differentiation.

In the sūtra beginning with “*avyayaṃ vibhakti*,” by the inclusion of the term *sādṛśya* (similarity), the substratum (*dharmī*) possessing similarity is indicated. For a property (*dharma*), being non-deviant, is indeed sufficient to indicate its own locus. Thus, in the case of the *avyayībhāva* compound *sasakhī* [meaning] “one who has a companion similar [to himself],” the word *saha* denotes that which possesses similarity, rather than mere similarity itself; therefore, by implication, in this sūtra, the property of the substratum serves as the indicator of that which possesses similarity.

For the earlier commentators have stated that this is the illustrative example here; based on that, the word *saha* is said to be denotative—that is, expressive—of the substratum (*dharmin*) called "the similar. And thus, when an indeclinable is expressive of the sense of similarity, its compound formation with the term "similarity" (*sādṛśya*) is declared. Furthermore, even though it denotes a substantive meaning, its status as an indeclinable is established by the rule "and [the compound] is an *avyayībhāva*," just like the words beginning with *svar*.

Furthermore, regarding that indeclinable which expresses the actual meaning and is designated as participating in a compound, its occurrence is in the sense of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) and similarity (*sādṛśya*), and it applies to the property (*dharma*) alone, not to the substratum (*dharmī*). For example: *pratyartham* (with respect to each object) and *anurūpam* (in accordance with). Because of the prohibition "the word *yathā* is not compounded when not expressing similarity," the word *yathā* denoting similarity is not compounded. However, the particle *yathā*, which is a substitute for a form ending in the suffix *thāl* and denotes distributive repetition, is indeed compounded. And distributive repetition is a specific instance of the meaning of *yathā*.

For instance, in the expression *pratyartham*, the suffix *prati* manifests a specific quality of the pervasion (*vyāpyamānatā*) of the action with respect to the generality of objects (*arthasāmānya*). Thus, the complete connection of all things with the action constitutes the specific distinction (*viśeṣa*) of the general distributive sense (*vīpsāsāmānya*), which serves as its mode (*prakāra*) according to the object (*yathārtha*).

Consequently, since an *avyayībhāva* compound would occur even for mere similarity (*sādṛśyamātra*) in the sense of "according to" (*yathārthe*), this rule is enjoined again by including "possessing that" (*tadvati*) when grasping similarity; this distinction between the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmī*) is intended here precisely because of their separate formulation. || 620 ||
He states another variety right here: "Some do not accept that similarity is fitness; rather, that which is a commonality residing in the form [of the object] is designated by the term 'sāha'. (622)

In the domain of the word *anu*, whatever fitness (*yogyatā*) is to be illuminated by that word *anu*, that very similarity (*sādṛśya*) is what constitutes the sense of "as" (*yathā*) in this compound. Thus, in the example *anurūpaṃ surūpo vahati* ("The handsome man wears [it] appropriately"), the meaning is that he, being handsome, wears a necklace, bracelet, or some other ornament—or perhaps another [quality]—which, because it is a cause of excellence in beauty, is equal to his own form (*rūpa*). In this way, the *avyayībhāva* compound is formed here with the sense of "as" (*yathā*) in the similarity of the quality of form. For the sense of "as" (*yathārtha*), characterized by fitness, has as its object only the quality of similarity.

However, that similarity which resides in a physical form, is grounded in the object itself, and consists of the arrangement of parts and so forth—having substance (*dravya*) as its domain—is expressed by the word *saha* in the compound *sasakhī*. For instance, the similarity is "with a friend" (*sakhyā saha*), and thus it is *sasakhi*, not *sadṛśa*. Thus, the similarity distinct as residing in substance is what is taken up by the word *sādṛśya* in the rule; whereas by the word *yathā*, that which is called "fitness" (*yogyatā*) residing in quality (*guṇa*) is intended. Therefore, the two compounds have entirely different domains.

But when "yathā" is specified as having distinct meanings—namely fitness (*yogyatā*), repetition (*vīpsā*), and similarity (*sādṛśya*)—then in the expression "he carries what is suitable" (*anurūpaṃ vahati*), the meaning of the word "fitness" must be something other than similarity; for "suitable" refers to that which is appropriate for a form by virtue of its producing beauty. In that case, the very same distinction between property and substratum (*dharmadharmibheda*) must be stated as the reason for their separate mention. || 622 ||

As for what was stated—that similarity alone is the "mode" (prakāra) in all cases—that is underinclusive. To demonstrate this, consider the example: "The student is distinguished by his water-pot. Here, the distinction is that the general category of "humanity" has the specific instance of "student" as its mode; in this case, the mode is a difference, not a similarity, because no other distinct entity is required. To support this point, he says: "Even in the case of 'being thus' (itthambhāva), similarity is based on the state of the intellect. When there is a grasping of mere difference, something else is designated therein. (623)

By means of [the description] beginning with "wearing armlets and earrings," one previously formed the cognition that Devadatta was "of such a kind" (*itthambhūta*); thus, here too, when there is a grasping of this state of being, it is merely the difference [between the object and the cognition] that is expressed in the suffix. Because of the coloring (*uparāga*) of the external object, there is a mere trace of difference, but not a difference in reality. Consequently, since the conformity to the cognition is what establishes the external object, "manner" (*prakāra*) is [defined as] similarity; thus, similarity is also appropriately termed a "manner" in this context.

In expressions such as *pañcadhā bhuṅkte* ("he eats fivefold") and *tredhādhīte* ("he studies threefold"), the meaning of "manner" (*prakāra*) must be established through similarity, since the appearance of the suffix *-dhā*—governed by the rule *saṃkhyāyā vidhārthe dhā*—"replicates" an external [division]. For what is accomplished here is the performance of a specific action that resembles the divisions as they have been mentally conceived. || 623 ||

This very point, when reinforced by scripture, appears beautiful; thus, demonstrating that one who delights in scripture has served the elders, [the author] states the opinion of the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) as a corroborative authority regarding the fact that the word "prakāra" everywhere signifies similarity: "In the case of the two-fold application [of the term], 'The Vāhīka is a cow,' similarity is cited as the counter-example. When [qualities] such as whiteness have been established [in the Vāhīka], the Vāhīka is not expressed twice. (624)

Thus [it is said]. Regarding the rule for reduplication, *prakāre guṇavacanasya* ("in the sense of 'manner,' after a word denoting a quality"), the *Bhāṣya* provides the counter-examples: *agnirmāṇavakaḥ* ("the boy is fire") and *gaurvāhīkaḥ* ("the Vāhīka is a cow"). This is appropriate if "manner" (*prakāra*) means similarity; for it is because of his similarity to a cow that the Vāhīka is called a "cow," and because of his similarity to fire that the boy is called "fire. However, this is not a particular instance or a distinction of the universal (*sāmānya*) such as "cowness" (*gotva*) or "fireness" (*agnitva*).

By this, it is indicated that the method for the rule of reduplication applies elsewhere as well, namely, similarity (*sādṛśya*), since that very [method] is demonstrated even in the absence of reduplication. Now, one might object: "Since words such as *go* (cow) are applied to a *vāhīka* and so forth precisely through the determination of non-difference based on a quality (*guṇa*), how can it be said to be a 'word expressing a quality' (*guṇavacana*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "When the white [quality] and so forth have been established, the *vāhīka* is not expressed twice."

The meaning is that when a word such as *śukla* (white), which is well-established as expressing a quality (*guṇa*) whose form is fully completed, is already in use, the word *go* (cow)—which denotes a Vāhīka—is not employed twice [in the same sense]. The term *iti* marks the end of the treatise. For a word such as *śukla*, while denoting a quality, or its possessor (*tadvat*), or one with whom the quality has been superimposed, remains indeed a "quality-expressing" (*guṇavacana*) word. The word *go*, however, is so [a quality-expressing word] only in reference to the Vāhīka, not in reference to the universal (*jāti*). Precisely for this reason, it is called "quality-expressing" because it has expressed a quality.

However, the word *go* when applied to a *vāhīka* has not expressed a quality (*guṇa*), because it was previously applied to the genus (*jāti*). Having established this, it was stated: "It is established because it is a qualifier of the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*). Because it is the cause for the doubling (*dvirvacana*), the base is here called the substitute (*sthānin*) for the dual suffix. Its meaning is qualified by the rule *guṇavacanasya*, but not its sense as a mode (*prakāra*). Thus he says: "Since all words would be 'expressive of qualities' (*guṇavacana*) in the sense of a mode, there would be an over-extension (*sarvaprasaṅga*)."

Since even words denoting substances, such as *go* ("cow") and others, are applied to [people like] the Vāhīkas by virtue of a similarity based on a quality, what would be excluded by the qualification "quality-word" (*guṇavacana*)? Therefore, by the force of the inclusion of the term "quality-word," the rule means that when a word is known to be a "quality-word," its reduplication occurs to indicate the mode [of application], namely similarity; thus there is no over-extension. Consequently, reduplication applies only to words like *śukla* which denote a substance with a quality as a subordinate element, as well as to those denoting a quality alone; thus the desired forms—*śuklaśuklaḥ paṭaḥ* ("a very white cloth"), *śuklaśuklaṃ rūpam* ("very white color"), and *paṭupaṭuḥ* ("very clever")"—are established.

Thus, the word-meaning in its state of syntactic combination has been examined by extracting it from the sentence-meaning through the prior analysis of words; thus concludes the investigation of words by way of their meanings. May there be auspiciousness! (624) Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, the *Vṛttisamuddeśa*, in the *Prakīrṇakaprakāśa* composed by Helārāja, son of Bhūtirāja. And this *Padakāṇḍa* is completed.
